units.la: POstquam ante aliquot annos tractatum de ERUDITIONE pollicitus sum, idem mihi fere accidit ac Cartesio, qui librum ejusdem argumenti aggressus, eum non perfecit, forte nec inceperat. Et ille quidem ob principiorum suorum insufficientiam (ut sic dicam) ab opere ejusmodi non poterat non abstinere. Ego vero ob rationes à Lectorum parte desumendas, & alicubi dicendas, laborem inceptum interrumpere & premere decreveram, nisi crebris amicorum instantiis, quando post partem primam libri primi per triennium & ultra ab opere cessaveram, illud ut resumerem absolveremque impulsus fuissem novissime. Inde ergo nunc
units.tr: After I had promised some years ago a treatise on ERUDITION, the same thing happened to me as to Descartes, who took up a book on the same subject, did not finish it, and perhaps had not even begun it. Indeed he, on account of the insufficiency of his principles (so to speak), could not but refrain from such a work. For my part, I had decided to interrupt and suppress the undertaken labour, on account of reasons which must be drawn from the side of the readers and which must be stated in places, had I not at last been driven, by the frequent urging of friends, to take up again and complete the work, after I had left it alone for three years and more, once the first part of the first book was finished. Hence now...

units.la: Ad Lectorem.

units.la: nunc prodeunt qualescunque vides, Lector, de Eruditione solida, superficiaria & falsa Libri Tres, in quibus deprehendes rem cognitionum & scientiarum non declamatorio modo tractari, sed philosophico & per principia deduci. Præmisi Tractatum de Vera Methodo inveniendi verum, qui cum omnium ultimo compositus sit, & surperpondii loco possit haberi, non miraberis si in libris sequentibus de quibusdam sic agitur, ac si de iis nil dictum fuisset prius, de quibus tamen actum est in hoc tractatu, cujus rationem dicet ipsiusmet Exordium. Libri Primi contenta si sublimiora aut abstractiora videantur, solida tamen esse, eademque, si ad ea penetraveris, omnium quam maxime radicalia & fæcunda principia complecti, deprehendes vividius: post quæ in Secundo detegere poteris (absit dicto jactantia!) penitius quam quidem hactenus sit factum, humanarum cogni-
units.tr: Here, reader, are the three books, as you see them, On Erudition, solid, superficial and false. In them you will find that the subject of knowledge and the sciences is treated not in a declamatory way but philosophically, and deduced from principles. I have prefixed a treatise On the True Method of finding the truth. Since it was composed last of all and may be regarded as a make-weight, you will not be surprised that in the following books some matters are handled as if nothing had been said about them earlier, although they were treated in that treatise. The reason for this the Preface itself will state. If the contents of the First Book seem rather lofty or abstract, they are nevertheless solid, and if you penetrate them you will see more clearly that they embrace the most radical and fruitful principles of all. After these, in the Second Book, you will be able to uncover (let me not seem boastful!) more thoroughly than has been done hitherto the human cogni-

units.la: Ad Lectorem.
units.tr: To the Reader.

units.la: cognitionum & scientiarum fundamenta, valorem & defectus; in Tertio autem earundem errores: & hæc quidem non tantum generaliori modo ibi tractantur; sed & plura ex præcipuis in specie commemorantur, inter quæ, omissis infinitis variorum philosophantium nugamentis, ne quidem recensione dignis, id honoris Cartesiani‐ smo delatum est, ut ejus opiniones propius considerare & examinare duxerim operæ esse pretium. De Apologeticis, præmonui initio eorum, cur adjecta sint; & ex sequentium Indicum exhibitione, opera data est ut omnium quæ toto opere tractantur argumentorum conspectus & series brevibus exponi posset, in quibus nisi tanta tamque multiplex materiarum præstantissimarum & exquisitarum, quæ illic contineri & explicari indicantur; varietas curiositatem tuam, Lector, sciendique desiderium vel delectent, vel alliciant, haud sane is fueris qui magno sciendi ardore percitus haberi possis.
units.tr: the foundations, worth and defects of human cognitions and sciences; in the Third its errors. These are treated there not only in a more general way, but several of the principal ones are also mentioned individually. Among them, leaving aside the endless trifles of various philosophers, which are not even worth recounting, the honour has been given to Cartesianism that I thought it worth while to consider and examine its opinions more closely. Concerning the Apologetics, I stated at the beginning why they were added. From the display of the following Index, care has been taken that a survey and sequence of all the arguments treated throughout the whole work can be set out briefly. Unless the so great and so manifold variety of the most excellent and exquisite subjects, which are indicated there as contained and explained, pleases or attracts your curiosity and desire to know, Reader, you would certainly not be the sort of person who could be regarded as driven by a great ardour for learning.

units.la: Caeterum opus esse arbitror, ut unam atque alteram nonnullis conquerendi ansam hic tollam, inter quas eam, quae stylum concernere posset, minime numerabo; siquidem quid de fucandis verbis sentiam, suo loco videbitur. Sed causabitur quis forte, primum quidem multa, quae non paucis aestimabilia censentur, vilius ac par est a me contemni. Ad quod respondeo, nil eorum quae scientias concernunt, a me ita contemni, quin si quaedam horum in me sint, ea prius in me (quod utique mihi licet) despiciam; quae ipsa etiam solidiorum aeternorumque respectu ita contemptibilia sunt, ut conceptis Dei verbis in Scriptura S. dicantur merae vanitates, idola, stultitiae, imo & stercora. Cur ergo non liceret ea parvi facere, abusum eorum si consideremus, quando nempe aut sola curantur, neglectis caeteris; aut solidioribus vixdum obiter curatis, ipsa solent præponi?
units.tr: Furthermore, I think it necessary to remove here one or two grounds of complaint, among which I will not count the one that might concern style; for what I think about the adornment of words will become clear in its proper place. But someone will perhaps allege, first, that I despise many things that are considered by not a few to be worth esteem, more cheaply than is right. To this I reply that nothing of those things which concern the sciences is so despised by me that, if some of these things are in me, I do not first despise them in myself (which is certainly permitted to me). Indeed, these things are so contemptible even in comparison with the more solid and eternal things that, in God's words in Holy Scripture, they are called mere vanities, idols, follies, even dung. Why, then, would it not be permitted to hold them of little account, if we consider their abuse, when namely they are either cared for alone, with the rest neglected, or when they are usually preferred while the more solid things are scarcely attended to in passing?

units.la: At magis forte displicebit quibusdam, opiniones aliorum, quæ interdum examinantur, in partem quæ sequior apparet, sumi, vel absurdis malisve consequentiis nimium aggravari, aut non laudatis appellari titulis. Optarent nonnulli, plus æquo indulgentiores, omnia in benignam partem trahi & boni consuli; quibus ego libens concedam modum illum agendi, quem improbant, a malignitate posse produci: at quin idem a charitate atque a necessitate provenire queat, ipsi, attente si rem considerent, fateri utique cogentur; & eum adeo juxta legem suam, in bonam partem potius quam in malam interpretari debebunt. Dantur enim interdum, ac sæpius quidem quam optandum esset, errores ita perniciosi, & quorum sequelæ adeo sunt noxiæ, ut quotquot se iis patiuntur persuaderi, ad privationem æternam omnis luminis & boni paulatim modoque insensibili abducantur, qualis v. g. error ille est, quo interna Dei in animis operationegatur, & quo uni rationis corruptæ activitati superstruuntur omnia. Qui tamen errores, omnium malorum sontes, ob tenebras & corruptionem rationis, non agnoscuntur quales sunt, cum noxiis consequentiis suis, ab eis qui illos producunt vel tuentur, neque a plurimis qui eos ex auctoribus suis legunt & amplectuntur: auctores siquidem ipsi eos potius nituntur tanquam probabiles aut veros multis argumentis proponere, nec non istiusmodi artibus & ornamentis induere, quibus tanquam veritates quam maxime gratæ & delectabiles a lectoribus admittantur, tametsi æternæ veritatis lumen, amorem, suique fanandorum curam, ipsamque adeo beatitudinem inde sint amissuri, nisi hinc dum tempus est revocentur: quo quidem eos illinc revocandi officio, evidens est nil charitatati magis esse congruum; prout e contra nil esset crudelius, quam in periculoso ejusmodi statu homines vel silentio, vel dulcibus & benignis commentariolis confirmare. Itaque si quis hoc in casu prodat, ornamenta verborum, quibus opiniones noxiae incrustantur; fucos esse; tum argumenta quibus nituntur, sophismata; ex erroneis opinionibus consequi ea quae saluti animae Deique cognitioni & amori adversentur; siquae haec omnia, ut ficus ficus, sic proprio nomine a mala arboris & fructuum natura appellentur, quo homines, his cognitis, ab aeterni exitii periculo liberari aut praemuniri possint; nescio sane an in omni genere officiorum detur quicquam praestantius atque utilius. Qui haec mecum non fatebuntur, eos ad res aeternas obduruisse & sensu divino carere oportet. Equidem nil, quoad me, novi melius, quam ab ejusmodi erroribus, dum tempus est, revocari: quapropter si accidat me hic ejus-
units.tr: But perhaps it will displease some more that the opinions of others, which are sometimes examined, are taken in the less favourable sense, or are overloaded with absurd or evil consequences, or are called by titles they do not deserve. Some, more indulgent than is right, would wish everything to be taken in good part and kindly received. To these I will gladly concede that the manner of proceeding they disapprove may arise from malice; but that the same may arise from charity and necessity, they will surely be compelled to admit if they consider the matter attentively. And so, according to their own law, they ought to interpret it in a good part rather than a bad. For there are sometimes errors so pernicious, and whose consequences are so harmful, that all who allow themselves to be persuaded by them are gradually and imperceptibly led away into the eternal privation of all light and good. Such is, for example, that error by which God's internal operation in souls is denied, and by which everything is built upon the sole activity of corrupt reason. Yet these errors, the sources of all evils, on account of the darkness and corruption of reason, are not recognised for what they are, together with their harmful consequences, either by those who produce or defend them, or by most who read them in their authors and embrace them. The authors themselves strive rather to propose them as probable or true with many arguments, and to clothe them with such arts and ornaments that readers admit them as truths most welcome and delightful, although by embracing them they will lose the light of eternal truth, love, the care of their own healing, and indeed blessedness itself, unless they are recalled from there while there is time. Clearly nothing is more fitting to charity than the duty of recalling them from there; on the contrary, nothing would be more cruel than to confirm people in such a dangerous state, either by silence or by sweet and kindly little commentaries. Therefore, if anyone in this case exposes the ornaments of words with which harmful opinions are encrusted as mere disguises (fucos), and the arguments on which they rest as sophisms, and shows that from erroneous opinions there follow things hostile to the salvation of the soul and to the knowledge and love of God, and if all these things are named by their proper name, as a fig is called a fig, from the evil nature of the tree and its fruits, so that men, having learned them, may be freed or forearmed against the danger of eternal ruin, I do not know whether anything more excellent and useful can be found in any kind of duty. Those who will not admit these things with me must have grown hardened toward eternal things and lack divine sense. For my part, I know nothing better than to be recalled from errors of this kind while there is time. Wherefore, if it should happen that I here ...

units.la: Ad Lectorem.
units.tr: Ad Lectorem.

units.la: ejusmodi nonnullorum errores detegere, quia id ex charitate velim fieri & amore, quo errantes inde liberari opto, sperem eorum in me animum potius gratum fore quam offensum. Neque propterea eos præ me minoris æstimo quod in erroribus ipsos esse judicem, me (eo respectu) in veritate. Est veritas, in quocunque sit, gratuitum Patris luminum donum, ob quod nemo magis gloriari possit quam corpus opacum de affuso sibi lumine: & accidit sæpe, eos, qui prius aliis veritatem recepêre, eandem etiam prius aliis violare agnitam: quo pacto deteriores iis fiunt qui eam, quippe nondum agnitam, nondum etiam tam indigno & contumeliose modo potuerunt offendere. Idcirco si qui se errorum argui per me putent, velim credant, se mihi a me in animo meo præponi, & meliores exis-timari; meque optare, ea mens mihi ut semper remaneat.
units.tr: I hope that those who find themselves in such errors will take it in good part, rather than as an offence, when I expose some of these errors; for I do so out of charity and love, desiring that those who err may be freed from them. Nor on that account do I esteem them any less than myself, though I judge them to be in error and I, in that respect, to be in the truth. Truth, wherever it is found, is a free gift of the Father of lights, and for it no one can boast more than a dark body that has had light poured upon it. It often happens that those who were earlier to receive the truth and teach it to others are also earlier to violate it once they have recognised it; and so they become worse than those who, not yet having recognised it, could not yet offend against it in so unworthy and insolent a manner. Therefore, if anyone thinks that by my hand he is being charged with error, let him believe that I place him before myself in my own mind and count him the better man; and I pray that this same disposition may always remain in me.

units.tr: As for my not naming the persons by their own names, ...

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: nonnulli sint in ejusmodi elenchis designati, ideo factum est, quod errores momentosi non pauci cum sæpe recipiantur, aut ut probabiles opiniones considerentur, ob nomen celebris alicujus Auctoris vel libri, cui etiam multi implicite credere volunt antequam ejus mentem sciant explicite; necesse sit, hoc fulcrum ut corruat, ejusmodi errores non generalius tantum, sed & addito nomine auctoris sui confutari; non ut hic infametur; sed ne sub nominis auctoritate errori, animabus noxio, serpendi detur locus, utque sciatur librorum, qui multis nocuerunt, errores alicubi esse deletos. Quod præprimis non potest non esse æquissimum quando res agitur cum iis veritatis aggressoribus aut irrisoribus, qui nominatim eos, quorum ope vera publicata sunt, ideo sunt aggressi, quod suis, quos tecte insinuare volebant, erroribus adversentur: tunc enim eos & refelli posse, & nominari, & causas veras insensi animi (errores ipsorum amatos) declarari, quis prohibeat? Charitas quidem non permittit ut proximi desectus recenseantur cum gaudio & irrisione, aut eo fine & modo unde odiosus aliis reddatur: at quemadmodum quando conducit aliquem de morbo corporeo convinci, non idcirco exponi censetur odio hominum; sed potius eorum commiserationi & precibus; ita etiam est de erroribus noxiis, qui sunt morbi animarum: compassio & sanitatis vota erga ejusmodi ægros sic possunt in animis aliorum excitari, quibus ad sanitatem adjuvari queant: ad quam cum aliquando redeunt, eo major est lætitiæ atque dilectionis erga eos dilatatio, quo major erat ipsorum morbus, qui statim atque serio agnitus est, protinus nullus est, nec amplius ad eos pertinet: sunt namque errores talis naturæ, ut statim atque eos ex animo improbat qui eis infectus est, ejus esse desinant; quapropter etiam non amplius possunt
units.tr: That some are named in such lists is because not a few serious errors are often accepted, or regarded as probable opinions, on account of the name of some famous author or book, which many people also want to believe implicitly before they know his meaning explicitly. So that this prop may fall, such errors must be refuted not only in general but with the name of their author added. This is not done to defame him here, but so that error harmful to souls is not given room to creep in under the authority of a name, and so that it may be known that the errors of books which have harmed many have been removed somewhere. This is especially just when the matter concerns those assailants or mockers of truth who attacked by name the very people through whose help true things were published, because they oppose their own errors, which they wanted to insinuate covertly. For then who would forbid that they be refuted, that they be named, and that the true causes of their ill-will (their beloved errors) be declared? Charity indeed does not permit a neighbour's faults to be recounted with joy and mockery, or with the aim and manner of making him odious to others. But just as, when it is useful to convince someone of a bodily disease, he is not thought to be exposed to the hatred of men, but rather to their pity and prayers, so it is also with harmful errors, which are diseases of the soul. Compassion and wishes for health can thus be stirred up in the minds of others toward such sick persons, so that they may be helped to health. When they return to health at some time, the joy and the love that spread toward them are all the greater the greater their disease was. As soon as it has been seriously recognised, it is at once no longer present and no longer belongs to them, for errors are of such a nature that as soon as the one infected with them rejects them from the heart, they cease to be his. For this reason also they can no longer

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: ei exprobrari ut ipsius ; sed habendus is est tanquam qui eos nunquam habuisset. Quâ de causa lætabor, si per ejusmodi errorum, qui hic (in fine præsertim operis) indicantur, renunciationem, (si speranda sit) possim quæcunque de his dicta sunt, aliquando pro indictis habere & haberi velle ; atque deinceps veritatem in charitate cum quibusvis colere. Quodsi tamen nonnullis videar durius interdum egisse alicubi ; id, si ita placeat, mex imputent infirmitati, quæ non potuit adversantium irrisorum ideam sine alicujus interdum indignationis motu diutius (quod in scribendo fieri debet) præ oculis habere : pro quo meo defectu, veluti animæ meæ morbo, nec non ob alios meos infinitos, optent mihi & Deum propitiabilem, & ab eodem vim omnia mala, dum tempus est, emendandi, quod etiam omnibus opto ex animo, ut quamdiu hic vivitur, hoc est, quamdiu in statu fumus nos
units.tr: not to be reproached for them as his own, but to be regarded as one who had never held them. For this reason I shall rejoice, if (should such a thing be hoped for) through the renunciation of such errors as are pointed out here, especially at the end of the work, I may someday wish whatever has been said about them to be regarded as unsaid, and thereafter cultivate truth in charity with everyone. But if I seem to some to have dealt somewhat too harshly at times in places, let them, if they please, put it down to my weakness, which could not always keep before its eyes the idea of mocking opponents without some movement of indignation for a while (which ought not to happen in writing). For this defect of mine, like a sickness of my soul, and for my countless other faults, may they pray that God be merciful to me and grant me the power to amend all my evils while there is time, which I also wish from my heart for everyone: that, as long as we live here, that is, as long as we are in a state in which we can change and remake ourselves

units.la: in formas malo oppositas immutandi & refingendi, nec coctorum vasorum instar adhuc fumus inflexiles, ei operæ gnaviter benedicente Deo incumbamus.
units.tr: into forms opposed to evil, and, not yet hardened like fired vessels but still pliable, may we diligently apply ourselves to this work, with God blessing it.

units.la: Udum & molle lutum es: nunc, nunc properandus, & acri Fingendus fine fine rota.
units.tr: You are damp and soft clay: now, now you must hurry, and be shaped on the sharp wheel without end.

units.la: Superest Lectores rogem, ut fphalmata, quæ frequentius ac optaffem, commissa sunt, dum liber in loco unde aberam imprimebatur ex apographo, cui ultimam non potui adhibere manum, neque ejus impressionis specimina videre, æquo mecum tolerent animo, nec dedignentur antequam ad lectionem fe accingant, eis corrigendis femihorulam impendere, ne dictorum sensus vel nullus vel absurdus appareat. Minutula, quæ nulla difficultate agnosci possunt, ex fe quidem facile animadvertent: quæ momentosiora sunt, ex apposito Erratorum Indice emendabunt, fi placet, ac præterea ver-ba
units.tr: It remains for me to ask the readers that they bear with an equal mind the slips which, more often than I would have wished, were committed while the book was being printed in a place away from me, from a copy to which I could not give the final hand, nor see the specimen sheets of the printing; and that they not disdain to spend half an hour correcting them before they set themselves to reading, lest the sense of what is said appear either nonexistent or absurd. Very small errors, which can be recognised without any difficulty, they will easily notice for themselves; those which are more significant they will correct, if they please, from the appended Errata index, and moreover the words

units.tr: You who wish to enter the path of erudition, go on securely. Seeing here the index and guiding plate of the ways you seek, attend to what the silent page says:

units.la: Caverna multis quam tenebris obsitam Tantâ celebrem conspicis frequentiâ, Hæc ERUDITIONIS est FALSÆ domus, Præjudiciorum tecta densis nebulis, Queis fascinati, qui videntur, hospites Omnes ad unum turgidas vento levi Conflare bullas vel docentur vel docent. Cave librorum ne strues fucum tibi Titulis superbis faciat, aut te schematum Contagiosa fascinent præstigia. Nil hic latet quam quæstionum putidæ Spina, & chimæræ somniorum, quæ fere Minus juvant aranearum stamine, Ovisque vel serpentis haud minus nocent. Abrupta quæ sequuntur montis ardui Sterilisque, vix uni vel alteri gradu Tentata dubio, (namque & in præceps ruunt, Abyssus ingens & ruentes excipit) Provinciam scias SUPERFICIARIÆ Esse ERUDITIONIS, in viam nimis,
units.tr: The cave you see, shrouded in so many shadows and crowded with such a throng, is the house of FALSE ERUDITION, roofed over with dense clouds of prejudice. The guests who are bewitched by these, all of them, are either taught or teach to blow empty bubbles with a light wind. Beware lest the pile of books make a sham for you with proud titles, or the bewitching tricks of figures infect you. Nothing lies hidden here but the stinking thorns of questions and the chimeras of dreams, which help hardly more than a spider's thread and harm no less than an egg or a serpent. The steep, barren paths of a lofty mountain that follow, scarcely tried by one or two cautious steps (for they also rush headlong, and a huge abyss receives those who fall), you should know to be the province of SUPERFICIAL ERUDITION, a path too narrow, and trodden by very few books.

units.la: Paucissimusque vix celebratam libris. Hic picta tantum Veritas acquiritur, Quam radiolis a Sole per nubeculasAdspersa Ratio adumbrat ideis suis. Hinc Solis umbram vivido sine lumineTantum gerit, nec frena vel virgam tenetImbellis, animos nec coercens, nec regens.
units.tr: Here only a painted Truth is acquired, which Reason, its rays from the Sun scattered through small clouds, shadows forth with its own ideas. Hence it bears only the shadow of the Sun, with a feeble light, and the weak one holds neither reins nor rod, neither restraining nor ruling the minds.

units.la: Hac vero quanto dignior nubes proculTransvecta, cuboque insidens immobilisIn monte lato apparet ERUDITIOSOLIDA, rudes quae sola mentes perpolitPertinne cujus possidens Solis jubarAngusta nil sinit latere dextera, Longaque noctis dira solvit vincula: Sinistra vero frena virgamque afferensAnimosa corda temperat feliciter, Pedesque dirigit Salutis in viam.
units.tr: How much more worthy is the one carried far off on a cloud, sitting immovable on a cube, which appears on the broad mountain: SOLID ERUDITION, which alone polishes rough minds. Holding in its right hand the Sun's radiance, which allows nothing to lie hidden, it loosens the dire, long chains of night. In its left hand it bears reins and a rod, and skilfully tempers spirited hearts and directs their feet into the path of salvation.

units.la: Ad hanc, procul post se relictis omnibus, Juvenis Viator, nudus a praejudiciis, Solus licet, nec obrutus libris, graduVotisque seriis anhelat, impiger. Nec fallet illum spes: profanos nam quidemA monte murus arcet; at fideliterPulsantibus tandem patebit janua; Qui sic refecti fructibus montis sacriLaeta deinceps verticem ascendant via, Ferantque digna pro labore pramia.
units.tr: To this, leaving all far behind, the young traveller, naked of prejudices, alone though not overwhelmed by books, pants with serious vows and eagerly presses on. Hope will not deceive him: a wall keeps the profane off from the mountain, but the door will at last open to those who knock faithfully. Those thus refreshed with the fruits of the sacred mountain may then climb the summit by a joyful way, and carry away worthy rewards for their labour.

units.la: Viro Eruditissimo PETRO POIRET
units.tr: To the most learned man, PETER POIRET

units.la: S. P. D.
units.tr: Sends greetings.

units.la: Iterumque, ut subsequentem Oden, in Veritatis animique grati testimonium, suis de Eruditione libris adjungere dignetur, ipsum rogat.
units.tr: He asks him again to deign to add the following Ode to his books on Erudition, as a testimony of the truth and of a grateful mind.

units.la: G. V. E.
units.tr: G. V. E.

units.la: VElles ergo, Vir integerrime, ita mea me concepisse verba, nequis ex illis sensus elici posset vel tibi minime gratus, vel a mente mea quam longissime forte alienus. Et ego profecto idem tecum desiderarem, nisi ex innumeris sibi ipsis, aliisque contradicentium Theologastrorum colloquiis scriptisque perquam manifestum foret, ipsa Dei Verba, & quae Sapientissimus ejus Spiritus humano generi gratificatus est scripta, omnium quidem maximè huic malo expósita esse: utpote quae ab omnibus fere, tam publicè quam privatim, pessime soleant detorqueri. Attamen ut pro humanissimo tuo desiderio, quantum potis sum, impediam ne quis, Veritatem nondum ut decet assecutus, eive malevolè etiam inimicus, è non satis commoda moda interpretatione versiculi, (quo Virum te dixi omnibus nunquam nimis laudandum Eruditis;) præ invidia vel ignorantia, crucem sibi malumve quærat, aut inveniat; palam profiteor atque protestor me profundiffimam quidem hactenus in scriptis tuis animadvertisse Eruditionem; puriorisque Metaphysices, Ethices, Politices, ut & Physices, omniumque scientiarum principia solidissima simul & fertilissima: imo in illis, præsertim in Oeconomia tua Divina, non tantum reperisse me claram distinctamque veræ Religionis ideam; sed & exactissimas atque plenissimas decisiones intricatissimarum quarumvis controversiarum; quibus dirimendis vel maximorum Theologorum ingenuissimus quisque sese longe imparem sponte semper fallus est. (a) Quibus addo, innumeris memet ipsum & quotidianis admodum experimentis compertum habere, adeo perspicua adeoque fœcunda esse Oeconomia illa tuæ principia, ut nullus queam dubitare quin quivis, bona mente non nimium destitutus, illorum auxilio admodum facile sibi solvere, penitusque tollere possit omnes omnino quæstio.
units.tr: Would that you, most upright man, had understood my words in the way I meant them, so that no sense could be drawn from them that would be either unwelcome to you or perhaps far removed from my mind. I would indeed wish the same with you, were it not perfectly clear from the countless conversations and writings of contradictors, and of theologasters, that the very Words of God, and the writings which his most wise Spirit has granted to the human race, are above all exposed to this evil, since almost everyone, both publicly and privately, is accustomed to twist them in the worst way. Nevertheless, in keeping with your most humane wish, I will do what I can to prevent anyone who has not yet attained the truth as he should, or who is maliciously hostile, from seeking or finding for himself a cross or harm, out of envy or ignorance, from an interpretation of a little verse that is not very fitting (in which I called you a man whom learned men can never praise enough). I openly profess and declare that I have so far observed in your writings a most profound erudition, and the most solid and at the same time most fruitful principles of purer Metaphysics, Ethics, Politics and Physics, and of all the sciences. Indeed, in them, especially in your Divine Economy, I have found not only a clear and distinct idea of true religion, but also the most exact and complete decisions of the most intricate controversies of every kind, in settling which even the most gifted of the greatest theologians always, of their own accord, prove themselves far unequal. To this I add that I have learned, from countless and almost daily experience, that the principles of your Economy are so clear and so fruitful that no one can doubt that anyone who is not too lacking in good sense could, with their help, very easily resolve for himself and entirely remove every question whatever.

units.la: (a) Quales sunt quæstiones illæ de S. S. Trinitate, de Providentia Dei, de Peccato, de Libero arbitrio, de Prædestinatione, &c. stiones difficultatesque, quæ vel unquam de rebus Theologicis, Fideive, inter homines motæ fuere, vel etiamnum forte moveri possent. Quamvis igitur non sine causa videri posset Virum te appellasse, qui non tantum dignissimus sit qui a doctissimo quoque commendetur; verum etiam, cujus prædicandis pro merito laudibus ne omnes quidem Eruditi pares unquam futuri sint; (Hæc enim forsitan in foro Soli, ubi humana fere semper prædominatur Veritas, locum sibi vendicaret interpretatio;) Palam tamen, inquam, profector alium longe verborum meorum esse sensum; atque etiam talem, cujus ipsissima (nisi fallor,) verborum conceptio non superficiarium lectorem manifeste satis admonere apta sit; nimirum, Te Virum non esse, quem Eruditorum quispiam (etiamsi omnes doctrina antecelleres,) multum unquam debeat laudare. Siquis autem interpretationem hanc minus congruam, minusque metro dignam exististimet; ejusmodi tamen non ideo minus Christianum decere, talesque fortassis solas in foro Poli (ubi Divina tantum Veritas imperium obtinet) admittendas esse, à temet ipso, Vir Humanissime, jam dudum edoctum me sciat:
units.tr: (a) Such are those questions concerning the Holy Trinity, the Providence of God, Sin, Free will, Predestination, etc., and all the questions and difficulties which have ever been raised among men concerning theological matters or faith, or which might perhaps still be raised. Although, therefore, it might seem not without reason that I called you a man who is not only most worthy to be commended by every learned person, but whose deserved praises not even all learned men will ever be equal to proclaiming (for perhaps this interpretation would claim its place in the forum of the Sun, where human truth almost always prevails), nevertheless, I say, I openly declare that my words have quite a different sense, and even such a sense that their very wording (unless I am mistaken) is apt to warn a superficial reader plainly enough: namely, that you are not the man whom any learned person, even if you surpass all in learning, ought to praise much. If anyone thinks this interpretation less fitting and less worthy of measure, let him know that I have long since been taught by yourself, most humane man, that such interpretations are nonetheless not unbecoming to a Christian, and that perhaps only such are to be admitted in the forum of Heaven (where Divine Truth alone holds sway).

units.la: Nempe, creaturis, nosti, quantum ipse CREATOR(a) Praestet; & hoc coram quantula res homo sit.
units.tr: Indeed, you know, as creatures, how far the CREATOR himself excels, and how small a thing man is in his presence.

units.la: Scis bene, quam recte moneant, divinior unquam Spiritus haud vane queis sapere alta dedit:
units.tr: You know well how rightly they advise, to whom the more divine Spirit has given lofty things to be wise in, not in vain:

units.la: OMNE, sicum Nihilo dedit omne; hinc & Nihil, OMNI Omne etiam nihilum debet, & omne, suum. (b)
units.tr: ALL, since from nothing he gave all; hence also nothing owes all to ALL, and each thing owes its own.

units.la: Sic illi dixere: horum tamen optima doctos Cernimus haud raro sensa latere viros.
units.tr: So they spoke; yet we often see that the best of their meanings lie hidden from learned men.

units.la: Scilicet hinc discant, verborum quisque suorum Optimus interpres quam fit, & haud alius:
units.tr: Let each one learn from this how good an interpreter of his own words he is, and that no one else is better:

units.la: Atque adeo Sacri si quis velit intima nosse Codicis, a solo haec saepe petenda Deo. (c)
units.tr: And so, if anyone wishes to know the inmost things of the Sacred Code, these are often to be sought from God alone.

units.la: Negligit haec quisquis proprio, ridetque, superbit (d) Ingenio, & populum pessima quaeque docet.
units.tr: Whoever neglects this, and scorns, and is proud of his own wit, teaches the people all manner of evil.

units.la: Hinc illae lites, quas per tot saecula mundus Sustinet: hinc Verum (prob dolor!) exul agit.
units.tr: Hence those quarrels which the world has endured through so many ages; hence Truth, alas, wanders in exile.

units.la: Tollere ut has pergis, Falsum fugit: in sua Verum Et, postliminio jura redire facis.
units.tr: As you go on to remove these, Falsehood flees; you make Truth return to its own rights by the law of return.

units.la: Ergo dicans tibi me Veroque, remuneret ut te Ille, cui soli (e) gloria danda, precor.
units.tr: Therefore, saying this to you and for Truth, I pray that He, to whom alone glory is to be given, may reward you.

units.la: Hagae-Comitis Kal. Octob. clo. Ioc. xcI. Æternum tibi divinissimus G. V. EWYCK. J. U. D.
units.tr: At The Hague, Count's Kalends of October 1691. Yours for ever, most divine G. V. EWYCK, J. U. D.

units.la: (a) OEcon. Creat. c. II.
units.tr: (a) Oecon. Creat. ch. II.

units.la: (b) Deus a se ipso, & in se ipso perfectissimum Totum est, omnisque boni (in creaturis causa. 1. Cor. XV. 28. & XII. 6. Jacob. I, 17. Rom. XI, 36.
units.tr: (b) God is, of himself and in himself, the most perfect whole, and the cause of every good in creatures. 1 Cor. 15.28; 12.6. James 1.17. Rom. 11.36.

units.la: Homo a se Nihil est, nulliusque (in se, aliisve creaturis) boni causa. Gal. VI, 3. 2 Cor. XII, 11. 1 Cor. XV, 10. & III, 7. 2 Cor. III, 5. Videfis Oecon. Creat. c. IV. Cogit. Rat. I. 3, c. 13. §. 28 & 29.
units.tr: Man is nothing of himself, and the cause of no good (in himself or in other creatures). Gal. 6.3. 2 Cor. 12.11. 1 Cor. 15.10; 3.7. 2 Cor. 3.5. See Oecon. Creat. ch. IV; Cogit. Rat. I. 3, ch. 13, §§ 28 and 29.

units.la: (d) Prov. III, 5.
units.tr: (d) Prov. 3.5.

units.la: (e) Oecon. Creat. cap. VIII, §. 3 & 4. Cogit. Ratiop. I. 4. c. 5. §. 12 & 13.
units.tr: (e) Oecon. Creat. ch. VIII, §§ 3 and 4. Cogit. Ratiocin. I. 4, ch. 5, §§ 12 and 13.

units.la: Ad CLARISSIMUM VIRUM PETRUM POIRET; Cum in publicum daret suos De Eruditione Solida, Superficiaria, & Falsa, Libros Non omnibus forte placituros:
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, PETER POIRET, when he was publishing his books On Solid, Superficial, and False Erudition, which perhaps will not please everyone:

units.la: Ille namque hodie longe plurimus vivit, sibi suisque plaudens, Qui, nisi quod ipse facit, cogitat, approbat, Nihil rectum, verum, bonum, putat.
units.tr: For he today who lives by far the most, pleasing himself and his own, thinks, approves, and deems nothing right, true, or good except what he himself does.

units.la: ODE.
units.tr: ODE.

units.la: Quærenda Virî principia optima Justiquæ quondam, omnisque scientiæ Desiderandæ, in Cogitatis Cartesii Hobbesiique duxi.
units.tr: I have sought the best principles of justice and of all knowledge worth desiring in the thoughts of Descartes and Hobbes.

units.la: Verùm, Eruditis Vir nimis omnibus Laudande nunquam, dum tua sedulus Evolvo scripta, errasse & ipsum Cartesium Hobbesiumque vidi.
units.tr: But, O man never to be praised enough by all the learned, while I diligently unroll your writings, I saw that Descartes and Hobbes too had erred.

units.la: Hic, tollit: Ille, ignorat amabile Vitæ beatæ principium unicum, Feliciores nos statim omnes, Mens nisi læva foret, daturum.
units.tr: The one raises up, the other ignores the one lovable principle of the blessed life, which would at once make us all happier, were the mind not left-handed.

units.la: Eò colendam quisque scientiam Plùs clamitat, nos quò indubiè & facit Beatiores & tuetur Utile dum sibi dulce jungit.
units.tr: The more each one cries out that science should be cultivated by him, which undoubtedly makes us happier and protects us, so long as he joins the useful to the sweet for himself.

units.la: At quæ (stupendum!) hæc ars, studiumque sit Præcæteris quod præstet id optimè, Indoctus omnis atque doctus Æquè hodiè dubium fatetur. Hinc turba tot diversa sequentium Timens & optans, innumerabilis; Contenta nunquam, & pœnitendis Mox aliis agitanda votis. Sic quisque manes jam patimur suos. Sed nos docendo, Candide, vindicas Quis eruditus, quis beatus Veridico queat ore dici? O ter beatum! Justitiam Bonus (a) Veraxque servans qui didicit pia, Fortunâ in omni, mente amare; Magnanimum ut decet & fidelem. Qui vitam, Amico ut prosit, & omnia Edustus audax spernere, prævio Confidit Illi, his sempiterna Omnipotens bona qui reservat. Præcepta Amoris fac, Deus, impleam! Sit mentis hæc una ambitio meæ; Hinc usque Amici effata Summi Da meditér, imiterque facta. Sic eruditus, pectore candido Omnes amabo, Te super omnia O Veritas! ô Puri Amoris Justitiæque imitanda Virtus!
units.tr: But what this art and study is (how amazing!) that excels all others in doing it best, every unlearned and learned person alike today admits is doubtful. Hence the crowd of so many diverse followers, fearing and hoping, innumerable; never content, and soon to be driven by other wishes that must be repented of. Thus each of us suffers his own ghosts. But you, Candidus, by teaching us, claim: who is learned, who is blessed, can be said with a truthful mouth? O thrice blessed the one who, good and truthful, keeping justice, has learned piously to love in every fortune with the mind, as becomes a magnanimous and faithful man; who, to benefit a friend, and having tasted all things, bold, scorns them, trusting in the one who leads, to whom the Almighty reserves eternal goods. Make me, O God, fulfil the precepts of love! May this be the one ambition of my mind. Hence grant that I may meditate on the sayings of the highest Friend and imitate his deeds. Thus learned, with a candid heart I will love all things, above all you, O Truth! O virtue to be imitated of pure love and justice!

units.la: Dabam Hagæ Comitis Anno, A mundi Salvatore benedicta Virgine nato, 1691. | Amor & Divina Voluntas Quo nos cunque trahunt retrahuntque, sequamur. *.* Ad
units.tr: Given at The Hague in the year 1691, after the Virgin blessed had borne the Saviour of the world. Love and the Divine Will, wherever they draw us or pull us back, let us follow.

units.la: (a) Videfis Cogit. Ration. secundæ editionis pag. 254. & seqq. ubi de S. S. Trinitate.
units.tr: (a) See the Cogitationes Rationales, second edition, p. 254 and following, where it treats of the Most Holy Trinity.

units.la: Dn. PETRUM POIRET,
units.tr: To Dn. Petrus Poiret,

units.la: De Eruditione solidè ac erudite scribentem.
units.tr: On the one who writes solidly and learnedly about erudition.

units.la: UNa brevisque via est, Doctrinam ex Fonte petendi,
units.tr: There is one way, and a short one, to seek learning at its source;

units.la: Una brevisque licet sit via, nota parum est.
units.tr: though the way is one and short, it is little known.

units.la: Nota parum, sed trita minus, satis esse putatur Ad rivos variis ire redire viis.
units.tr: Little known, but less trodden, it is thought enough to go to the streams and come back by various paths.

units.la: Nec mirum infelix si passim exuberet Error: Quid Verum invito quaerere Fonte juvat?
units.tr: No wonder, unhappy one, that Error grows rank everywhere. What use is it to seek the Truth from a reluctant Fountain?

units.la: Rectius ista doces qui dedoceantur, Amice, Lectorique unum hoc & breve pandis iter.
units.tr: You teach these things more rightly, friend, having first been untaught yourself, and you show the reader this one short road.

units.la: Pandis idemque præis, præeuntem ut rite sequantur Ad meliora quibus fertur anhela sitis.
units.tr: You point it out and go before, so that those who follow the leader may rightly press on to better things, toward which their panting thirst is carried.

units.la: Queis degustatis dabitur discernere, quanto Purius ex ipso Fonte bibantur aqua.
units.tr: Having tasted these, they will be able to judge how much purer the water is when drunk from the very Fountain.

units.la: Amstelodami. JUSTUS SCHRADER. d. 4. Dec. Med. D. clɔ IƆc xcI.
units.tr: Amsterdam. Justus Schrader, Doctor of Medicine. 4 December 1691.

units.la: In Clarissimi Domini POIRETI
units.tr: On the most distinguished Lord POIRET

units.la: Libros de Eruditione, Methodumque inveniendi Verum.
units.tr: On his Books concerning Erudition and the Method of Finding Truth

units.la: ERgone tandem quid sit Eruditio, Quidve valeant Scientiæ, videbimus, Viæque, quæ sint Veritatis: qua sine Nunquam quiescet mentis ardor anxius? At at nimis plerique ab ipso limine Erramus, à Ratione quærentes malis Nostris medelam, quæ gravantur sic magis. Namque illa, quicquid se valere somniet, Morbo gravi correpta languet, impotens Sanare semet & nihil certi ferens, Nugas tot inter, queis onustum dat caput, Præter figuras atque numeros. Hæc tamen Idola mente culta devotâ & mihi Fuêre, cùm lubuit Mathesin abditam Adire, Speciosamque sacro nomine (Cujus, ferunt, arcana virtus mentibus Erroris excutit tenebras) Algebram. Sed quicquid hisce temporis diu datum, Næ perditum fuisse dicerem; nisi Vel hac mihi constaret experientiâ, Feliciori quod patet compendio Ex hisce paginis, Amice, quàm viâ Aliâ solidior sit petenda Veritas: A qua profecto tortuosis tot nodis Ambagibusque mens aberrat longius. Vos ergo nunc valete bullæ splendidæ, Numeri quadrati, cubici, multanguli: Rectaque, curvarúmque classes cum suis
units.tr: Shall we at last learn what erudition is, what the sciences are worth, and which are the ways to truth, without which the anxious ardour of the mind will never rest? Yet very many of us go wrong from the very threshold, seeking a remedy for our ills from Reason, which only makes them weigh more heavily. For she, however much she dreams of her own power, lies languishing, seized by a grave disease, unable to heal herself, and bearing nothing certain amid the many trifles with which she burdens her head, except figures and numbers. Yet these idols, cultivated with a devoted mind, were once mine too, when it pleased me to approach the hidden mathematics and its Speciosa, called by the sacred name (whose hidden power, they say, drives the darkness of error from minds) Algebra. But whatever time I gave to these things for so long, I would say it was utterly lost, had I not learned by this very experience, from these pages, friend, how much more solid a truth must be sought by a shorter and happier road than the other. From the other road the mind, caught in so many tangled knots and windings, wanders far astray. Farewell, then, to you shining bubbles, square, cubic and polygonal numbers, and the straight and curved classes with their

units.la: Locis, cerebrosæque tot mysteria Subtilitatis, cujus inter plurima, Vir Docte, quæ brevi libro complecteris Laboriosæ quò valerent næniæ, Non passus es latere Lectorem tuum. Faxit Deus, ne solidiora quæ doces Tantùm otiosis imbibantur auribus Oculisve, sed recocta ritè cordibus In intimis Æternitatis omnibus Fiant beatæ fructuosa germina!
units.tr: places, and the many mysteries of brain-racking subtlety. Among the many things you, learned sir, have embraced in your short book, showing what those laborious trifles were good for, you have not allowed your reader to remain ignorant. May God grant that the more solid things you teach are not merely drunk in by idle ears or eyes, but are properly warmed in the inmost hearts and become fruitful seeds of blessedness in eternity!

units.la: P. J. H. J. B. P.
units.tr: P. J. H. J. B. P.

units.la: Ad Reverendum Clarissimumque Virum Dn. PETRUM POIRET, Cum Libror de Eruditione Methodumque inveniendi Verum ederet.
units.tr: To the Reverend and Most Illustrious Man, Mr. Peter Poiret, on the Publication of His Books on Erudition and the Method of Finding Truth.

units.la: Scripta quæ nobis dedisti, Docte Vir, quidni colam, Æstimemque quovis auri cariora pondere? Scripta quorum occasione coeperam cognoscere, Quid lupinis æra distent, quid Superficiariâ Litteraturâ Solidior præstet Eruditio, Aut Polymathias inanis apparatu splendido. Hæc sacrum mentita nomen Veritatis nos quidem Glandibus diu repavit, quotquot ad Scientias Litterasque humanitatis aut Sophorum tradita Impotens curiositatis æstus ablegaverat. Quin & abstractæ (minoribus relictis) jussierat Initiarier Mathesseos & interioribus Algebræ quondam sacris, qua propitiante plurimos Improbo videas labore cuncta (si Diis placet)
units.tr: Learned sir, why should I not cherish the writings you have given us, and prize them above gold by any weight? It was through them that I first came to understand how far bronze differs from lupins, and how much more solid erudition excels a superficial literature or an empty polymathy with its splendid show. These, pretending to the sacred name of Truth, had long fed us on acorns, along with everyone whom the impotent heat of curiosity had sent off to the sciences, to humane letters, or to the traditional teachings of the wise. Indeed, it had even ordered us to be initiated into abstract mathematics (leaving the lesser studies aside) and into the inner sacred mysteries of algebra, under whose favour you may see most people labouring wickedly over everything (if it pleases the gods).

units.la: Et sacrata cum profanis velle subjici sibi, Præferentibus facem quos vulgus ipsi VindicesEt Statores Veritati cœlitus datos putant. Ast ad hanc quid conferant quæ non nisi superbiæAc amori proprio carnisve desideriisSeruiunt, tumidaque mentem vanitate distrahunt?Quàm pol istis digniora & tuta, quæ mihi DeusIn tuis deinde scriptis obtulit: queis intimaGratiæ principia Naturæque vera seminaSic recludis, utriusque sicque leges & viasPandis, ut sincera mens perculsa vivo lumineVeritatis Solidioris, non queat non uniceIntimis ad hanc sequendam pertrahi præcordiis. Inde quantum Vanitatis, quæ ferat periculaNosse cœpi, Æternitati quicquid haud impenditur, Nec rudes cœlestibus consortiis animos parat. Hincque nil moras juvabat nectere, aut erroribusQuos amaveram tenendis usque causas quærere, Nec licebat vel voluisti memet intus fallere, Conscientiâ palam clamante, me esse conditumAd superna, non ad alta seculi subselliaAut honores comparandos, cæca vel suffragiaPlebis, aut caduca quævis aucupanda commoda. O mihi si serio licuisset his tunc obsequiVocibus, vel nunc liceret, quando eas in intimisRursus innovat meis hæc, Erudite Vir, tuaEruditione Commentatio de triplici!Fructuosam quam benignus fazit in multis DeusQui creaturis suis non velle non potest bene, Quas suæ similes imagini creavit, singulasTotius Divinitatis ut bearet gaudiis: Quiquefe calamitatis perditis socium dedit,( Mira vis Amoris! Ipse carne tectus fragiliA periculis ut exitialibus reduceretNolsque aberrantes Supernæ Veritati redderet.
units.tr: And they wish sacred things to be subjected to profane ones, holding the torch before those whom the common crowd thinks are the avengers and guardians of Truth sent from heaven. But what can those contribute to it who serve only pride, self-love, or the desires of the flesh, and distract the mind with a swelling vanity? How much more worthy and safe are the things that God has offered me in your writings. In them you unlock the inner principles of grace, sow the true seeds of nature, and so disclose the laws and ways of both, so that a sincere mind, struck by the living light of a more solid truth, cannot fail to be drawn, wholly and from its innermost heart, to follow it. Hence I began to know how much vanity there is and what dangers it brings, and how it prepares no unrefined minds for heavenly fellowship, nor anything for eternity. Hence it did not help me to delay, nor to seek reasons for clinging to the errors I had loved, nor was I allowed to deceive myself inwardly, since my conscience cried out openly that I had been made for things above, not for the high seats of this age, nor for honours to be won, nor for the blind votes of the common people, nor for any fleeting advantages to be sought after. Oh, if it had been permitted me then to obey these voices seriously, or if it were permitted now, since your learned commentary on the threefold (erudition) renews them again in my innermost heart! It is the fruitful work which the kindly God bestows on many, for he cannot will anything but good for his creatures, whom he created like his own image, so that each might be blessed with the joys of the whole Divinity. He also gave a companion to those lost in calamity (wonderful power of love!), himself clothed in fragile flesh, so that he might lead back those wandering into deadly dangers, and would not let those who had strayed fail to return to supernal Truth.

units.la: VERA METHODUS INVENIENDI VERUM.
units.tr: THE TRUE METHOD OF FINDING TRUTH.

units.la: O{nstitueram} ea quæ tribus de Eruditione libris complexus sum, sine ulla alia animorum præparatione emittere, contentus sola exhibitione eorum quæ illic continentur, quippe quæ si rectè animadvertantur, sufficere posse videntur ad hoc, ut qui ea observare voluerint, non eligant falsa pro veris, non amplexentur umbratilia pro realibus, verum ad solidam pertingere possint Eruditionem. Sed cum dein animo mecum volverem, quantis quamque adeo multis præjudiciis & impedimentis & pravis dispositionibus, iisque non satis penitatis, ne dicam parum admodum aut minime detectis, omnium ferè undique obsessæ essent mentes, coepi postmodum, divina fretus ope, (quæ spes mea est) de Dissertatione aliqua præliminari concinnanda cogitare, qua comprehenderem nonnullas veluti observationes aut leges, quibus præcipua ex istis obstaculis possent removeri, animique disponi ad faciliorem Librorum sequentium captum, praxin & usum. Quod dum exsequi contendo, Tractatus integer sub manu nascitur de vera Methodo inveniendi verum observatis primis cognitis primisque erratis
units.tr: I had intended to send out what I have comprised in the three books on Erudition without any other preparation of the mind, being content with the mere presentation of what is contained there; for if those things are rightly observed, they seem sufficient to enable those who wish to observe them not to choose falsehoods for truths, not to embrace shadowy things for real ones, and to be able to attain to solid Erudition. But when I afterwards turned over in my mind what great and how many prejudices, obstacles and bad dispositions, and these not sufficiently examined, not to say very little or not at all detected, almost all minds are beset on every side, I began after that, relying on divine help (which is my hope), to think of composing some preliminary Dissertation, in which I would set down certain observations or rules, as it were, by which the chief of these obstacles could be removed and the minds disposed for an easier grasp, practice and use of the following Books. While I am striving to carry this out, a whole Treatise is taking shape under my hand, on the true Method of finding truth, observing first the first-known things and first errors of the Philosophers.

units.la: Philosophorum. Hunc tractatum praeparationis necessariæ vice libris meis de Eruditione præmittendum, & ante eos legendum credidi, à quo ut exordium facere velint candidioris notæ Lectores, amicè praemoneo. Et ne ipse remoram injiciam, negotii totius dispositionem tribus verbis indi-gito.
units.tr: I have believed that this Treatise, serving as the necessary preparation, should be placed before my books on Erudition and read before them; and I kindly forewarn the more candid readers to begin from it. And so that I myself may not cause a delay, I shall point out the arrangement of the whole matter in three words.

units.la: Scilicet in tres partes eundem disperscui.
units.tr: Namely, I have divided it into three parts.

units.la: Prima continebit annotata sex insignia, vel axiomata, quæ pro totidem Methodi ad veritatem legibus haberi poterunt, & inter cognita prima recenseri; eorum vero neglectio aut violatio inter errata prima numerari. Quibus interserentur quam plurima tum de veritatis lumine & criteriis, tum de mentis ejusque facultatum dispositionibus, indispositionibus, harumque remediis, quæ absolutè cuivis serio veritatem indaganti scitu & observatu sunt ita necessaria, ut obea non animadversa, necesse fuerit Philosophos in præcipitia ruere.
units.tr: The first will contain six notable observations, or axioms, which may be regarded as so many laws of the Method to truth, and be reckoned among the first-known things; their neglect or violation, however, is to be counted among the first errors. Among these will be interspersed very many things, both concerning the light and criteria of truth, and concerning the dispositions and indispositions of the mind and its faculties, and their remedies, which are so necessary for anyone who seriously seeks truth to know and observe that, without these being noticed, philosophers must necessarily rush headlong into precipices.

units.la: Altera pars tum specialius explicabit nonnulla quæ in regula Sexta de mente ab indispositionibus suis sananda obiter indicata erant; tum varietate quæstionum ac responsionum de istiusmodi satis raro argumento, inserviet exercitii loco mentibus similli materiæ excellentiori parum assuetis, ut inde ad hæc magis reddantur idoneæ.
units.tr: The second part will explain more specifically some matters that were touched on in passing in the Sixth rule, concerning the mind's cure from its indispositions; and through the variety of questions and answers on such a rarely treated subject, it will serve as an exercise for minds little accustomed to this more excellent matter, so that they may thereby become more fit for it.

units.la: Tertia verò exhibebit in magnis Philosophis, in Cartesio v. g. ejusque Methodo & Meditationibus, nonnullisque aliis ejusdem afflectis exempla errorum in quos inciderunt propter non obiervatas eas regulas, quas tanquam veras Methodi verum inquirendi & inveniendi leges, serio commendamus.
units.tr: The third, however, will set out, in great philosophers, for instance Descartes and his Method and Meditations, and in some others of the same kind, examples of the errors into which they fell on account of not observing those rules which we seriously commend as the true laws of the Method of seeking and finding truth.

units.la: PARS PRIMA,
units.tr: PART ONE,

units.la: Sex Methodi ad Veritatem Leges, observatus multis expositas continens.
units.tr: Six Rules for Seeking the Truth, containing the observations expounded in many ways.

units.la: I. Nter primas ad veritatis semitam inveniendam leges, Cognitaque generalia & prima nemo negabit, opinor, recensendum esse illud: Ea quae fiunt, cognitum ut recte fiant, ordine fieri debere. Constant omnia solida suo quaeque ordine, hoc est, debita rerum, facultatum, objectorum, veritatum, affectuum, & rei uniuscujusque ad alias applicationes, pro proportione & mensura naturae, dignitatis, locique debiti. Ordinem si solvas vel non observes, quamvis optimum sit subjectum, meraeque adeo veritates in quibus versaris, omnia fient obscura, tenebrosa, confusa, perdita. Cer-te qui membrorum sani corporis ordinem transponere aut disjungere vellet, mortem ei conciliaret; qui a tecto aedificii constructionem ordiri tentaret is & materias bonas perderet, & operam luderet omnino: qui mathematicae demonstrationis partes ordine inverso aut turbato consideraret, quamvis unaquaeque seorsim sit vera, nil aliud tamen inde efficeret præter mentis confusionem, haud secus acsi Euclidem a propositione ultima libri XV. retrogrado vellet aggredi ordine.
units.tr: I. Among the first rules for finding the path to truth, I think no one will deny that the following general and basic principle must be recalled: What is done in order to be done rightly must be done in order. Everything stands firm in its own order, that is, in the due arrangement of things, faculties, objects, truths, affections, and the application of each thing to others, according to the proportion and measure of its nature, dignity and proper place. If you dissolve this order or fail to observe it, then however excellent the subject and however true the very truths you are dealing with, everything will become obscure, murky, confused and lost. Certainly, one who tried to rearrange or separate the members of a healthy body would bring death upon himself; one who tried to begin building from the roof would waste good materials and labour altogether; and one who considered the parts of a mathematical demonstration in an inverted or disordered sequence, although each part taken by itself is true, would achieve nothing but confusion of mind, no differently than if he tried to work through Euclid backwards, beginning from the last proposition of Book XV.

units.la: II. Qualis autem ordo in rebus tractandis sit observandus, non ita omnibus liquidum est. Cartesius vult a simplicioribus & cognitu facillimis incipiendum esse, eaque ratione continuandum. At vero si illa simplicissima & facillima de futilibus fuerint & nugacibus, hominisque dignitate indignis, multumne hoc ordinis genere adjuvabimur? Rectius igitur ordo primùm inter materias assumendas & tractandas instituendus est, ut illæ videlicet primo assumantur & omnes cæteras præcedant, quæ primo exsiitunt, quæ digniores sunt, quæ solidæ sunt nec evanidæ, quæ necessariæ, sanæ, persectæ: in quarum unaquaque specialius deinceps inspicienda, a simplicissimis & cognitu facillimis poterit duci exordium, & eodem tenore ulterius porro res penetrari. Ita bene demum & ordinatim progressus fieri poterit.
units.tr: II. What order is to be observed in handling things is not clear to everyone. Descartes wants us to begin with the simplest and easiest things to know, and to proceed in that way. But if those simplest and easiest things are trifling and frivolous, and unworthy of human dignity, will we be much helped by this kind of order? It is better, therefore, that order be set first among the matters to be taken up and treated, so that those which come first, which are more worthy, solid and not fleeting, necessary, sound and perfect, are taken up first and precede all the others. Within each of these, to be examined more closely afterwards, one can begin from the simplest and easiest things to know, and carry the matter further in the same manner. Only in this way can progress be made well and in order.

units.la: III. At si accidat homines, quamvis Philosophos, primum assumere & præponere accessoria necessariis, corrupta sanis, activa pallivis, umbratilia realibus, inferiora superioribus, imperfecta & naturalia perfectis & gratiis, arbitraria sufficientibus, (quæ omnia aliter ordinanda esse inter prima Cognita numerari potest, maximè ubi pluribus eas res reddiderimus clariores,) hæc inquam ordinis & tractationis inverfio si fiat, ecce erratum omnium primum, perniciosissimum & cunctorum calamitorum fons eo ipso committitur; quo admisso, non potest non evenire quin inde in omnis generis tenebras, confusiones, errores-que continuos incidant mentes perpetuo, maneantque ibidem, rerum ordinem quamdiu non restituerint. Ex quo articulo suspicor jam non paucos fore qui vereantur, ne vel inde inferendum sit rarissimos dari qui veritatem possideant, aut qui veri dici possint Philosophi. Sed reprimamus nunc minus gratam conclusionem.
units.tr: III. But if it happens that people, even philosophers, take up first and place before the necessary the accessory; before the sound the corrupt; before the real the superficial; before the substantial the shadowy; before the superior the inferior; before the perfect and the gracious the imperfect and natural; before the sufficient the arbitrary (all of which may be reckoned among the first things known to be ordered otherwise, especially when we have made these matters clearer in many ways), and if this inversion of order and of treatment is made, then, behold, the first and most pernicious error of all, and the source of all calamities, is thereby committed. Once this is admitted, it cannot but happen that minds fall thence continually into darkness, confusions and errors of every kind, and remain there perpetually for as long as they have not restored the order of things. From this point I suspect that there will now be not a few who fear that it may be inferred from this that very few exist who possess the truth, or who can rightly be called philosophers. But let us now restrain this less welcome conclusion.

units.la: IV. (2) Primorum Cognitorum, quorum assumtione ad ulteriores leges in Methodo quaerendi veri recte instituenda opus est, alterum, & quidem pro lege altera recenseo: Eum qui veritatem vult detegere, rademque erui, sinceritatem mentis praeditum esse debere. Neque id tantum velim dictum de vulgari quadam sinceritate, qua animi sensa sibi intus quisque fateatur; aut de externa, qua eadem aliis non dissimulet; verum etiam de penitiori, qua sui ipsius scienS impostor aut deceptor non sit. Quod uti per se clarum est, ita inutiliter & incassum a me dici putarent multi, (adeo impossibile aut contradictorium videtur, hominem posse se scientem decipere, aut decipere velle) nisi id aliquantulum clarius ob oculos ponerem.
units.tr: IV. (2) Of the first things known, the assumption of which is needed in order to set up rightly the further rules of the method of seeking truth, I count a second, and indeed as a second rule: He who wishes to uncover the truth, and to draw it out, ought to be endowed with sincerity of mind. And I would not want this said only of a certain common sincerity, by which each person confesses to himself the feelings within him, or of external sincerity, by which he does not conceal the same from others; but also of the deeper sincerity, by which the mind is not an impostor or deceiver of its own knowing self. As this is clear in itself, many would think I say it uselessly and in vain (so impossible or contradictory does it seem that a person can knowingly deceive himself, or wish to deceive), unless I set it a little more clearly before their eyes.

units.la: V. Potest unusquisque in se animadvertere, animum suum, inter alia, tribus vel-luti dam menluti facultatum generibus præditum esse: conscit enim primo se multis desideriorum motibus, qui & sensibiles valde sunt plerumque, & affectibus multis juncti, commoveri: deinde se facultatem percipiendi contemplandique, sive considerandi objecta moventia & cupita, habere: ac tertiò, se quoque gaudere potentia, qua desiderium suum faciat quiescere in objecto plus minusve percepto, tanquam in re desiderium explere apta: quæ facultas acquiescentiæ & affirmationis est. Ex quo autem homo corruptione tenebrisque intectus & inter plurima objecta inordinata, ipsius desiderium moventia, positus est, accidit ordinarie, ut primis multisque vitæ suæ annis desideriorum motibus pravis quidem, sed sensibilitati crassiori, commoditati, fastui, amori proprio gratissimis afficiatur, sive ii motus à propria internaque mentis corruptione nascantur, seu etiam ab aliis, quibus sua mens ipseque vinculo aliquo adstringuntur, sint excitati: & secundum hos motus quidem, de rerum actionumque veritate & bonitate homo ita corruptus sic judicat & judicare consuevit, ut inde impellatur ad interpretandum omnia audita, visa, cognita, imo & ipsa Scripturarum oracula, (expresse ad motus istos compescendos & delendos data,) eo modo, qui quam maxime corruptioni suæ faveat. At que hinc suas quisque cudit veritates, bonitates, æquitates, virtutes, doctrinas, ob quas sæpe & sibi & aliis ex mera carne meroque sanguine {ut Scripturæ verbis utar} rerum divinarum & humanarum peritus habetur animalis homo. Porro quando O. rigo illa bona & luminosa, unde profluxit Mens & quo remeare debet, Deus nempe O. M. alios ei sive immediate, sive intercedentibus etiam organis aut mediis quibusdam, incutit motus, eosque revera bonos; quando & idem luminibus nonnullis intellectum ferit, e quibus Mens incipiat percipere, etsi obscurius, sua quidem illa priora, ut ut sensui grata, haud tamen ita ac putavit se recte habere; posteriora vero hæc, & quæ inde consequentur, meliora esse & veriora, licet initio & amariora, & eis quæ prius placebant, incommoda atque adversa; ecce, tunc stat anima in puncto unde deceptioni propriæ aut sinceritati veræ sese ex libertate tradat, vel tradere vere peroptet. Namque si eligat motibus illis primis corruptis, simulque naturæ corruptæ gratissimis adhærere, nec non iis magis magisque sic attendere, ut diviniores motus, attentione mentis alio se conferente, fiant ipsi insensibiliores, ipsamque minus afficiant, unde illa minus eis affecta eosdem præterea contemnat veluti res pauci vel nullius momenti, quarum illa neglectu nil adeo veri & boni perdat, ut potius iis rejectis ac fugatis, supersedeat a labore immenso acquiescentiam suam ab assuetis gratioribus retrahendi, eamque ad contraria & adversantia applicandi; hoc inquam modo, ea Mens se ipsam sciens volensque decipit, fibique ipsi imponit admodum dolose : non quod directe ipsa velit falli, & videat evidenter errores & tenebras quo prolabetur : sed vult tamen ea unde fluunt error & tenebrae, quæ sensui, consuetudini & commoditati magis sunt amica. Et vidit quidem generalius ex iis errores & mala consequi, oppositosque motus & radios lucis revera præstare; sed quia hi videntur ei amari, ideo avertit inde attentionem suam; unde iis non amplius affecta, reddi tota & affici possit primis jucundioribus, quibus proinde (verioribus motibus deletis) tota vacare ut prius concupiscit. Hæc est dolosa, fallaxque impostura, qua qui detinentur (quotnam vero non detinentur!) omnes veritatis admittendæ fiunt incapaces, etsi omnes ejus capaces reputari velint, profiteanturque se veritati, tametsi concupiscentiis suis adversanti, favere velle: id nempe ore amant dicere, intus autem amant aliud facere: quod est cor illud duplex adeo veritati invisum, erratum alterum capitale veritati viam præcludens.
units.tr: V. Each person can notice in himself that his mind is endowed, among other things, with three kinds of faculties, as it were. For he is aware, first, that he is moved by many motions of desire, which are for the most part very sensible and joined with many affections; second, that he has the faculty of perceiving and contemplating, that is, of considering objects that move and are desired; and third, that he also enjoys a power by which he makes his desire rest in an object more or less perceived, as in a thing fit to satisfy the desire. This is the faculty of acquiescence and affirmation. But because man, enveloped in corruption and darkness and placed among many disordered objects that stir his desire, ordinarily happens, in the first and many years of his life, to be affected by motions of desire that are indeed bad, but most pleasing to a grosser sensibility, to convenience, to pride and to self-love, whether those motions arise from the corruption of the mind itself within, or are excited by others to whom his mind and he himself are bound by some tie; and according to these motions the man so corrupted judges, and is accustomed to judge, the truth and goodness of things and actions in such a way that he is driven to interpret everything heard, seen and known, and even the very oracles of Scripture (given expressly to restrain and destroy those motions), in the way that most favours his corruption. And from this each person forges his own truths, goodnesses, equities, virtues and doctrines, on account of which, often to himself and to others, the animal man, made of mere flesh and mere blood {to use the words of Scripture}, is held to be skilled in divine and human things. Further, when God, the Best and Greatest, from whom the mind has flowed and to whom it ought to return, strikes it with those good and luminous motions, either immediately or through intervening organs or certain means, and these are truly good; and when he also strikes the understanding with certain lights, from which the mind begins to perceive, though more obscurely, that its former motions, however pleasing to the senses, were not as right as it had thought; but that these later ones, and what follows from them, are better and truer, although at first bitter and inconvenient and adverse to those which were earlier pleasing: behold, then the soul stands at the point from which, by its freedom, it may surrender itself either to its own deception or to true sincerity, or truly wish to. For if it chooses to cling to those first corrupt motions, and at the same time to what is most pleasing to corrupt nature, and to attend to them more and more, so that the more divine motions, as the attention of the mind turns elsewhere, become more insensible and affect it less, then the mind, thus less affected by them, further despises them as things of little or no moment, by neglecting which it loses nothing so true or good. Rather, having rejected and banished them, it refrains from the immense labour of withdrawing its acquiescence from the accustomed and more pleasant things and applying it to the contrary and opposing ones. In this manner, I say, the mind, knowing and willing, deceives itself and imposes upon itself most craftily. Not that it directly wishes to be deceived, and it clearly sees the errors and darkness into which it slips; but it nevertheless wishes those things from which error and darkness flow, which are more friendly to sense, habit and convenience. And it does indeed see in general that errors and evils follow from them, and that the opposing motions and rays of light truly offer something; but because these seem bitter to it, it therefore turns its attention away from them; and so, no longer affected by them, it can be wholly given over to and affected by the first, more agreeable things, to which, therefore (the truer motions having been destroyed), it desires to devote itself entirely as before. This is the crafty and deceitful imposture by which those who are held captive (and how many are not held!) all become incapable of admitting truth, although they wish all to think them capable of it, and they profess that they want to favour truth, even though it opposes their desires. They love to say this with their mouth, but within they love to do something else. This is that double heart so hateful to truth, the second capital error, which blocks the way to truth.

units.la: VI. Sinceritas autem huic fraudi oppositæ animæque ad veritatem aptæ dispositio primaria, hæc est: ut quam primum diviniores lucidiorésque motus & veri radios perspentiscit anima, etsi suis dudum assumtis, gratis & affuetis oppositos, ipsa tota statim eis attentionem, in quantum ei regendæ ex libertate præest, dedere parata sit, eos consideret, desideretque & optet illos augere, quo evidentius percipiens ens se per hæc ad diviniora, superiora, saniora, perfectiora, solidiora magis magisque deduci, acquiescentiam suam a prioribus motibus desideriisque gratis retrahat totam, eamque in hæc refundat; quin & priores istos corruptos motus, consuetudines, perfuasiones, judicata, utut grata & commoda, impugnet viribus totis, quamvis priorum omnium, propriorumque inde scaturientium emolumentorum jacturam facere debeat in amplexatione & praxi veriorum & solidiorum, quæ ipsi magis magisque poterunt detegi. Hæc est animi illa sinceritas infucata & fraudis expers, cujus amplexu potiri gaudet solida Veritas, & cujus encomium inter multa declarat sacer sermo exclamans: (a) O beatus vir in cujus spiritu non est dolus! Unde quia pauci nunc sane inter homines sunt beati, licet conjicere, paucos admodum esse quorum sincerus & infucatus sit spiritus; paucosque admodum qui veritatis admittendæ sint proximè capaces. Nam extra hæc, Mens veritatibus iis solidis adversa quæ ejus priores voluptates, commoda, imaginationes de se deque sua eruditione & doctrina inolita, nec non & virtutibus acquisitis (scilicet!) turgidas impugnant, non poterit eisdem veritatibus affici, neque eas proinde plenius perspicere, nosse, possidere: sed potius ab eis aversa, fiet insensibilis; nisi etiam earum aliquatenus odiosè memor, easdem omnibus animi sui affectibus insectabitur.
units.tr: VI. Sincerity, the opposite of this deceit and the primary disposition of a soul fit for truth, is this: as soon as the soul perceives the more divine and clearer movements and rays of truth, it should be ready at once to give its whole attention to them, so far as its freedom allows it to govern itself. It should consider them, desire them, and wish to increase them, so that, perceiving ever more clearly that through these it is led on to what is more divine, higher, sounder, more perfect and more solid, it withdraws its whole assent from its earlier motions and desires, which it had taken up long ago and which were pleasing and familiar, and pours it into these new ones. It should even attack with all its strength those earlier corrupt motions, habits, persuasions and judgements, however pleasing and convenient they are, although it must give up all its former advantages and the gains that flowed from them, in embracing and practising what is truer and more solid, which will be revealed to it more and more. This is that unfeigned sincerity of mind, free from deceit, in whose embrace solid Truth delights, and whose praise the holy word declares among many others, crying out: (a) O blessed is the man in whose spirit there is no guile! Hence, since there are indeed few blessed people among men today, we may conclude that there are very few whose spirit is sincere and unfeigned, and very few who are close to being fit to receive the truth. For apart from this, a mind opposed to those solid truths, puffed up with its former pleasures, conveniences and fancies about itself and its own learning and doctrine, and also with its acquired virtues (as it supposes!), cannot be affected by those same truths, nor therefore see, know or possess them more fully. Rather, turned away from them, it will become insensible; unless, remembering them with some hatred, it attacks them with all the feelings of its mind.

units.la: VII. (3) Tertia Methodi ad veritatem
units.tr: VII. (3) The Third Method for Reaching Truth

units.la: (§) Ter. lex, quæ & censeri potest cognitum genetia verx ralius, unde ad specialiora deveniemus; illud esto : In inquisitione verì quemlibet debere initium facere a se ipso, et in se ipso. Et hoc per se satis patet, siquidem nil abfurdius esset, quam alteri velle veritatem inquirere antequam eam ipse possideas. Neque hoc tantum, sed & ubi veritas ab alio inventa est, eamque ipsus possidet, quamvis eandem omnibus fieri communem optare possit & debeat, ipsamque, ubi ad id sese obligatum vere conscit, verbis etiam aut scriptis, quantum appositè fieri potest, proponere; non tamen pro scopo sibi proponat, hominum mentem ad eam veluti flectere, & vi quadam sic ei conformare, ut nisi is effectus accidat, quietus non sit, & se scopo excidere judicet. Istud inquietis ardelionibus ac sectariis est relinquendum, quo nihil equidem stultius, nihilque magis Philosopho vel Philosophaturo indignum. Quis enim libertate aut potentia sua aliorum desiderium ad meliora flectere & veriora, quis intellectus eorum impedimenta & ineptitudines removere; quis alieno desiderio acquiescentiam in objectis certis largiri potis est? De se unusquisque tollici, tus sit id ut faciat sincerius modo.
units.tr: The third rule, which may also be called the first general principle of knowing the truth, from which we shall proceed to more specific ones, is this: in the search for truth, everyone ought to make a beginning with himself and in himself. This is sufficiently plain in itself, since nothing would be more absurd than to want to inquire into the truth before one possesses it oneself. Nor is this all: even when someone has found the truth from another and possesses it, although he may and should wish it to be made common to all, and, when he truly knows himself bound to do so, should put it forward in words or writing as fittingly as he can, he should not nevertheless set for himself the aim of bending people's minds towards it and forcing them into conformity with it, so that he is not at rest unless that result follows, and judges himself to have failed in his aim. That is to be left to restless busybodies and sectaries, and nothing is more foolish, or more unworthy of a philosopher or one aspiring to be one. For who can, by his own liberty or power, bend the desire of others towards better and truer things? Who can remove the obstacles and incapacities of their understanding? Who can grant, by another's desire, rest in fixed objects? Let each one attend to himself, and let him see to it that he does so more sincerely.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: VIII. Atque adeo indignum Philosopho homine esse reor, vel saltem ei non necesarium, & forte damnosum, nec ab errato, aut errandi periculo immune (quod mox offendam,) ut sibi proponat alios, eosque
units.tr: VIII. Indeed, I think it unworthy of a man who is a philosopher, or at least not necessary for him, and perhaps harmful, and not free from error or the danger of error (as I shall soon show), to set himself the task of convincing others of the truth, especially those who are obstinate and less sincere, such as the Sceptics were.

units.la: vel pertinaces & minus sinceros, quales erant Sceptici, de veritate convincere. Si enim ejurata omni conscientia & finceritate delirare velint, nosque etiam reputare pro delirantibus; quid hoc ad animum philofophi, veritate in fe intus possessa contentum?
