An propter ejusmodi sponte infanientes ipse mentis suæ vires alio distrahet, & inutilibus, quæ, veluti pondera, mentis vires lassant & minuunt, sese onerabit & occupabit? Certè qui veritatem nulla sinceritate cupit, ei per nos quantum quidem ipse volet, delirare & insanire permittatur.
units.tr: For if they want to rave, having renounced all conscience and sincerity, and want us too to count as madmen, what is that to the mind of the philosopher, who is content with the truth possessed within himself? Shall he, on account of such people who go mad of their own accord, distract the powers of his own mind elsewhere, and burden and occupy himself with useless things which, like weights, wear down and diminish the powers of the mind? Surely, let one who desires truth without any sincerity be allowed, by us, to rave and rage as far as he himself wishes.

units.la: IX. Ex quo principio approbare nequeo, Cartefium Scepticorum næniis audiendis & retundendis adeo dedifle locum in Philofophiæ suæ initio: Siquidem absque recensitis istis dubitationibus hyperbolicis & insanis, vigilemne an somniem, corpusne habeam, an non habeam, poterant dari & stabiliri solida Philosophiæ fundamenta, ex cogitatis intimis & consciis desumpta, iisque non pauca fuperexftrui egregia, quibus deinde fi isti graculi suas venifient obiectatum murmuratiunculas somniorum, obiter ad summum responderi potuisset, datis morbo huic particulari veluti potiunculis quibusdam specialibus, quarum contra id genus phrenefeos validitatem lectores cæteri tunc quidem animi gratia perspicere potuissent, non autem credere feque initiò gerere acsi ipsi etiam istis opus haberent pharmacis, putareque ea in omnem debere influere certitudi- Male Cartefium duxisse in principio Philosophiæ opus esse concinere Scepticos. tudinem : quo ipso multi se spectantes ac si quoque isto stultitiæ dubitatricis genere laborarent, ex ea imaginatione ad hunc morbum de facto sic dispositi sunt, ut ex eodem postea liberari vix potuerint.
units.tr: IX. I cannot approve, on this principle, that Descartes gave so much place, at the beginning of his philosophy, to listening to and refuting the nonsense of the Sceptics. For without reciting those hyperbolic and mad doubts, whether I am awake or dreaming, whether I have a body or do not, solid foundations of philosophy could have been laid and established, drawn from inner and self-conscious thoughts, and not a few excellent things could have been built upon them. Then, if these jackdaws raised their little murmurs of objection about dreams, one could have answered them in passing, as a summary, giving this particular disease some special remedies, so that the other readers could then have seen, for the sake of their minds, the strength of those remedies against that kind of madness; but not that they should believe, or act at the outset as if they too needed these medicines, and think that these must flow into every kind of certainty. Descartes was wrong to suppose that at the beginning of philosophy it was necessary to make terms with the Sceptics. By this very thing, many who looked upon themselves as if they too suffered from this kind of doubting folly were, from that imagining, so disposed to this disease in fact that they could scarcely be freed from it afterwards.

units.la: X. Id quod in Philosophia Cartesiana pessimum habuit effectum, non solum quod ex hoc argumento multorum vexationibus ea mire fuerit exagitata: sed etiam quod multi Cartesiani, iique vel omnium consensu subtilissimi, inde devenerint in ejusmodi Scepticismum ex quo postea per Philosophicum apparatum omnem exsolvi nequiverunt. Exemplum præbet in se vel primarius inter eos Malebranchius, qui hac via eousque in Scepticismum protapsus est, ut nisi ad eum relevandum revelationis machina admoveatur, concedat incertum esse dari corpora, contendatque omnia præter apparentias posse nil aliud esse. Nempe accidit interdum ut qui volunt simulare se ægros esse, aut sibi id imaginari, & ægros agere nituntur, ægri revera fiant non modo; sed &, quod plus est, inde quandoque moriantur. Accidit etiam interdum ut qui medicamen, quo ipsi opus non habent, volunt tamen adsumere, acsi eo haberent opus, morbum inde contrahant. Quid opus est ut homo sanæ mentis, qui dubitare nequit de rebus de quibus nemo sanus unquam dubitavit, ad sanæ Philosophiæ fundamenta stabilienda necessarium esse putet ferio sibi proponere insanias meditatione perpendendas, quasi fine earum solutione ipse nec bene certus esset, nec sane & solide fundatus? Quis non videt eo modo ipsum disponi (praesertim si minus cautae sit prudentiae) ut suam priorem firmitudinem, quam nemo sanus in dubium revocavit unquam, tanquam minus certam sibi repraesentet, eamque talem postmodum sibi persuadeat; tum eam perdat; & deinceps in ratiocinationibus nullum certitudinis, priori quidem aequalis, fundamentum reperiens, realia dimissae deprehendatur, evanida ut sefaretur? Simili methodo nonnulli, prius in intimis suis certo certius supraque omnem ratiocinationem de Deo existente certi, cum certitudinem illam solidam seponere vellent, ut alii ex ratiocinationibus metaphysicis petendae inhiarent tenacius, & priorem amiserunt, & posteriore etiam non gaudentes ad lubitum, athei miserae facti sunt. Nempe quoniam non potest respondere istis insanis dubitationibus per ratiocinationes tantam certitudinem habentes & ingenerantes, quanta erat realitas soliditasque, qua de rebus istis ante dubitationem certiores fiebant; hinc postquam solido remoto & postposito, solidius quid quaerebant in eo quod revera & infirmius erat & umbratile, utrumque amiserunt, similes cani isti aesopico, qui non contentus vera carne quam tenebat, umbrae etiam ejus in aqua inhians, dum seponeret realem ut umbratilem arriperet; utraque privabatur.
units.tr: X. This had the worst effect in the Cartesian philosophy, not only because from this argument the philosophy was wonderfully troubled by the harassments of many, but also because many Cartesians, the most subtle of all by common consent, came thereby to such a Scepticism that afterwards they could not free themselves from it by any philosophical apparatus. The foremost of them, Malebranche, provides an example: by this route he slid so far into Scepticism that, unless the machinery of revelation is brought to bear to relieve him, he concedes that it is uncertain whether bodies exist, and contends that all things apart from appearances can be nothing else. Indeed it sometimes happens that those who want to pretend they are sick, or to imagine it, and strive to act as if they were sick, become truly sick, and not only that, but, what is worse, sometimes die of it. It also sometimes happens that those who want to take a medicine they do not need, as if they needed it, catch the disease from it. Why should a man of sound mind, who cannot doubt things about which no sane person has ever doubted, think it necessary, for establishing the sound foundations of philosophy, to set before himself madnesses to be weighed in meditation, as if without their solution he were not himself well certain nor soundly grounded? Does anyone not see that in this way he is disposed (especially if he is less careful in prudence) to regard his former firmness, which no sane person ever called into question, as less certain, and to persuade himself of this afterwards; then to lose it; and thereafter, finding in his reasoning no foundation of certainty equal to the former one, to be found wandering, his realities gone, vanishing into nothing? By a similar method some, who had earlier been certain beyond certainty within themselves, and certain of the existence of God above all reasoning, wished to set aside that solid certainty so that they might cling more eagerly to what was to be sought from metaphysical reasonings; and having lost the former, and not being content with the latter at will, they became miserable atheists. For since these mad doubts cannot be answered by reasonings that have and produce as much certainty as the reality and solidity which made them more certain of those things before the doubt, therefore, after the solid thing was set aside and put behind, they sought something more solid in what was in truth weaker and shadowy, and lost both. They are like that dog in Aesop, who, not content with the real flesh he held, gaped at its shadow in the water, and while he let go of the real one to snatch at the shadowy one, was deprived of both.

units.la: Sufficere igitur debet cuique non insano & & sincere Philosophaturo , veritatemquequæsituro , eam ejusque certa fundamenta in fe ipso stabilire line respectu ad talia dubitantium scepticorum deliramenta , quæ postea vel calcis ictu proterere licebit. Atque id fieri posse , in Libris sequentibus
units.tr: It should therefore be enough for anyone who is not insane and who sincerely sets out to philosophize and to seek the truth, to establish truth and its certain foundations in himself, without regard to the delusions of the doubting Skeptics, which may afterwards be trampled underfoot with a kick of the heel. And that this can be done, in the following Books

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: XI. Ex illo cognito , quemque debere in fe quærere veritatem, hoc quoque colligitur vel intelligitur , debere eam quæri, præfentem quidem in modis quibus conscii fumus nos affici & tangi; futuram autem & possibilem in modis quibus affici & tangi poterimus. Et hac quidem occasione antequam ad ulteriores Methodi inceptæ leges pergam , libet hic nonnullas à me & in me veritates proximas, primarias & capitaliores inquirere & exponere , tum etiam de notis five caracteribus aut criteriis quibus veritas insignitur & agnoscitur, quædam exactius dissere : quæ ipsa nos a filo orationis & methodi continuandæ non sunt avocatura.
units.tr: XI. From this known point, that each person must seek truth in himself, it is also gathered, or understood, that truth is to be sought as present in the ways in which we are conscious of being affected and touched, but as future and possible in the ways in which we shall be able to be affected and touched. And on this occasion, before I proceed to the further laws of the Method I have begun, I think it fitting here to inquire into and set out some truths proximate, primary and of greater importance, which I find from and in myself; and also to discuss somewhat more exactly the marks or characteristics or criteria by which truth is distinguished and recognized. These matters will not draw us away from the thread of the discourse and of the method we are continuing.

units.la: XII. Conscius sum omnium primo, me
units.tr: XII. I am first of all conscious that I

units.la: tangi & vivide affici mei conscientia & sensu; me desiderare ut intelligam vera & bona, quo desideratis, perceptis atque intellectis, desideria mea meque quantum fieri potest, jungens, iis, si pote, fruendo desideriaque exsatiando, acquiescam; & in veris quidem, acquiescentia affirmationis; in bonis autem, amoris; in utrisque, lætitiæ. Vivida etiam tangor & minime dubia conscientia de corpore mihi præsente & ad me pertinente, deque multis aliis mihi per illud præsentibus, quæ in corpus meum, & hoc in meam animam, immotæ certitu- dinis vividitatem consciam imprimant & excitant. Nec minus indubia experior conscientia, me facultates desiderandi, attendendi seu percipiendi, assentiendi, & plures alias, posse pro lubitu, modo ad hæc, modo ad illa obiecta, idque plus minusve applicare & determinare. Ita ut quicquid stridula futilitate auribus meis occinant Sceptici nasutuli (quos insanos aliis hinc secuturis fundamentis & ratiocinationibus, eorum nænias evententibus, confutandos relinquo) nullatenus apud me serio dubitare possim, me esse, conscium & cogitantem esse, optandi, intelligendi, acquiscendi, amandi, lætandi actibus & potentiis gaudere; & corpore proprio multis aliis circumcinćto esse præditum; ac præterea pollere libertate, sive potentia determinandi cogitationes motionesque plurimas ex principio mihi intimo, nec a me diverso, nec ab alio quam a me determinato.
units.tr: am touched and vividly affected, by my consciousness and sense; that I desire to understand true and good things, and that, once the things desired are perceived and understood, I join my desires and myself, as far as I can, to them, enjoying them and satisfying my desires, and so find rest; in true things, the rest of affirmation; in good things, of love; in both, of joy. I am also touched by a vivid and by no means doubtful consciousness of the body present to me and belonging to me, and of many other things present to me through it, which impress and stir in my body, and in my soul through the body, a consciousness of the vividness of unshaken certainty. Nor do I experience with less indubitable consciousness that I am able, at my pleasure, to apply and direct the faculties of desiring, attending or perceiving, assenting, and many others, now to these objects and now to those, and to do so more or less. So that whatever the shrill and trifling chatter of the little nosed Skeptics may sing in my ears (whom I leave to be refuted by the foundations and reasonings that follow hence, which will overturn their dirges), I can in no way seriously doubt that I exist, that I am conscious and thinking, rejoicing in the acts and powers of wishing, understanding, resting, loving, and rejoicing; that I am endowed with my own body surrounded by many other things; and moreover that I possess liberty, that is, the power of determining very many thoughts and movements from an inner principle, which is neither separate from me nor determined by anyone other than me.

units.la: XIII. Insuper quamprimum per ætatem licuit generalius cogitare de rerum causis, deque objecto aliquo quod sit causa mei & rerum omnium potens, bona, vera, justa, immortalis, infinita, sapientissima, liberrimaque, & perfectissima, modus intimus quo objectum illud cogitata mea tangebat, desiderium inimitabiliter inescabat, intellectum veluti objectum illo dignum implebat & absorbebat, acquiescentiam sedabat,
units.tr: XIII. Moreover, as soon as my age allowed me to think more generally about the causes of things, and about some object which is the cause of me and of all things, powerful, good, true, just, immortal, infinite, most wise, most free and most perfect, the inner mode by which that object touched my thoughts, inescapably enticed my desire, filled and absorbed my intellect as if it were an object worthy of it, calmed my rest,

units.la: xiii. Deinde eundem ex sensu intimo ante omnem aliam demonstrationem, convinci de Dei existentia. bat, amorem percellebat, lætitiam alliciebat, conscientiam justi & injusti, bóni & mali immutabilibus i&ibus feriebat, meque totum penetrabat & afficiebat, modus inquam ille erat talis, ut fine ulla alia demonstratione & ratione præter sensus immediatos, quos de hoc objecto habebam ubi primum ejus eram ita conscius, nequaquam permiserit me magis de illo exsistente, hoc est, de Dei exsistentia, dubitare, quam de exi-stentia mei ipsius meique corporis, vel Solis vivide aspecti, uti & aliorum corporum, de quibus etiam nemo sanus unquam dubitavit; & de quibus ante & super omnem ratiocinationem & demonstrationem ego cum aliis indubitate convincor.
units.tr: xiii. Then, from inner sense, before any other demonstration, I was convinced of the existence of God. It struck my love, drew in my joy, struck my consciousness of just and unjust, good and evil with immutable blows, and penetrated and affected me wholly. That mode, I say, was such that, without any other demonstration or reasoning besides the immediate senses which I had of this object as soon as I first became conscious of it, it in no way allowed me to doubt that it exists more than I doubt my own existence and that of my body, or the vivid sight of the Sun, and of other bodies, about which no sane man has ever doubted either; and about which, before and above all reasoning and demonstration, I am convinced without doubt along with others.

units.la: XIV. Et quamvis dentur qui de hoc objecto exsistente, Deo scilicet, dubitent, hoc me nunc (qui solus a me, in me & pro me initio philosophari debeo) non magis movet aut dubium reddit, quam moveor inde quod dentur etiam insani qui dubitent an corporibus sint præditi, an Sol quem respiciunt exsistat, an ipsi inter corporea versentur. Fortallis istiusmodi de Deo dubitatores de industria sese excœcarunt, intimis suis non satis nec debite attenderunt, illa corruperunt, ad alia se converterunt, facultates suas sine ordine direxerunt, aut alia commiserunt errata illis similia quæ mox recensebimus; unde non mirum si objectum, cujus exsistentiam alii vel mediocriter dispositi indubitatam agnoscunt, ipsi non percipiant male dispositi: haud secus ac si quis vel oculos sibi eruisset, vel in obscurum barathrum se præcipitasset, Solem corporaque circa se exsistentia non posset amplius percipere, quorum tamen existentiam citra omnem dubitationem, demonstrationem, ratiocinationemque alii certissimæ agnoscunt. Atque ex quo animadverto, mentis meæ functiones circa intellectualia per corporea, quibus implicatus sum, impediri multum; plane persuadeor id ni esset, intellectualia, maxime vero ea quæ Deum concernunt, mihi non modo indubitata fore; sed & omnium prima occursura, meque sua penetrantissima affectione perplene tranquillatura.
units.tr: XIV. And although there are some who doubt the existence of this object, namely God, this does not move me or make me doubtful now (I who alone must begin to philosophize from myself, in myself and for myself), any more than I am moved by the fact that there are also madmen who doubt whether they have bodies, whether the Sun they look at exists, or whether they themselves live among corporeal things. Perhaps such doubters about God have blinded themselves on purpose, have not attended sufficiently or properly to their inner selves, have corrupted those things, have turned to other matters, have directed their faculties without order, or have committed other errors similar to those we shall presently list. Hence it is no wonder if those who are ill-disposed do not perceive an object whose existence others, though only moderately disposed, acknowledge as beyond doubt: just as if someone had torn out his own eyes, or had thrown himself into a dark pit, he would no longer be able to perceive the Sun and the bodies existing around him, whose existence others acknowledge as most certain, without any doubt, demonstration or reasoning. And from this I notice that the functions of my mind concerning intellectual things are greatly hindered by the corporeal things in which I am entangled; I am fully persuaded that if this were not so, intellectual things, and above all those which concern God, would not only be indubitable to me, but would also be the first to present themselves and would fill me completely with their most penetrating affection.

units.la: XV. Ut autem & ejusmodi dubitatores, si forte quidam ex infirmitate nec irrisorio & malo animo eo delapsi sint, at sed suo que ad frugem possint redire, ) de veritate exsistentiæ Dei convincantur via eis accommodata; id, quia non potest commodè fieri antequam de erratis videamus quæ hactenus commissa sunt ab iis, qui se professi sunt veritati quærendæ incumbere quatenus ea ex intima mentis conscientia erui potest; id inquam paululum differemus, prolaturi forsitan (a) suo loco demonstrationes, præ quibus ipsæ Cartefianæ, etsi verae, umbræ tamen fuerint tenues. Nunc autem, ne ordinem pervertamus, tempus nondum est de aliis convincendis cogitare: saltem unusquisque adhuc, a se, & in se philosophari incipiens, sibimet intus bene attendat, quodsi faciat, certum est eum de se constante ex mente & corpore, facultatibusque intellectuali- (a) vid. infr. in parte tertia num. IX. &c. ctualibus & corporeis, nec non de Deo potente, vero, bono, justo, libero, persectissimoque exsistente, fore cum acquiescentia certa securissimum.
units.tr: XV. But so that such doubters too, if perhaps some of them have fallen into this through weakness, and not with a mocking and evil mind, may be able to return to their senses, and be convinced of the truth of the existence of God by a way suited to them: this, because it cannot conveniently be done before we see the errors which have so far been committed by those who have professed to devote themselves to seeking truth, insofar as it can be drawn from the inner consciousness of the mind, I shall postpone for a little while, perhaps setting out demonstrations in their proper place (a), by comparison with which those of Descartes, though true, will be but thin shadows. Now, however, lest we pervert the order, it is not yet time to think about convincing others. At least let each one, beginning to philosophize from himself and in himself, attend well to himself within; if he does so, it is certain that he will be most securely at rest with a certain acquiescence concerning himself, consisting of mind and body, and of intellectual and corporeal faculties, and also concerning God, who exists as powerful, true, good, just, free and most perfect. (a) See below in part three, number IX, etc.

units.la: XVI. Vixdum Philosophi, maxime vero Cartesius cum suis, partem horum de mente & Deo stabiliverant suo more, cum protinus hinc aberrarunt, seseque inde recipere cogitarunt ad specialiores rerum facultates, quales sunt voluntatis, intellectus, libertatis, aliarumque rerum cogitantium explicandas, & praesertim ad rerum corporearum naturam veritatesque inquirendas, quibus praemittunt aliqualem inquisitionem de criterio veri. Verum enimvero non satis animadverterunt, ingentem hic adesse hiatum, qui implendus ante & pervadendus erat, quam de istiusmodi & de quam plurimis aliis veritatibus cogitaretur: sine quo, dum pes ulterius protenditur, in praecipitia falsorum innumerorum si se conjiciant omnes, haud adeo mirandum fuerit.
units.tr: XVI. Scarcely had the philosophers, and Descartes above all with his followers, established part of these matters about the mind and God in their own way, when they straightway went astray from here, and planned to withdraw from there to the more specific faculties of things, such as the explanation of the will, the intellect, liberty, and other thinking things, and especially to inquire into the nature of corporeal things and their truths, for which they set out some preliminary inquiry into the criterion of truth. But truly they did not sufficiently notice that there was here a great gap, which had to be filled and crossed before such matters and very many other truths were considered: without which, while the foot is stretched further, it is hardly to be wondered at if they all cast themselves into the precipices of countless falsehoods.

units.la: XVII. Si quis mensurandarum rerum quarumlibet ignarus, eas tamen discere velet mensurare; atque ideo mensuram primo forte obviam, v. g. ulnam aut decempedam, pro mensurationis criterio arriperet; deinde vero nullius ductoris auxilio adjutus, quin & tenebris obsitus, & membris atque animo haud bene sanus rem inceptaret, quid aliud quam ineptiret, & in mille absurditates atque errores incideret, in rebus etiam aliunde facillimis? Criterium enim istud ut aptum quibusdam rebus mensurandis est, ita ad
units.tr: XVII. If someone ignorant of whatever things are to be measured wished nevertheless to learn to measure them, and therefore by chance seized first on the measure that came to hand, for example an ell or a ten-foot rod, as the criterion of measurement; and then, without the help of any guide, and even beset by darkness, and with his limbs and mind not very sound, began the task, what would he do but blunder, and fall into a thousand absurdities and errors, even in things otherwise very easy? For that criterion, while it is suitable for certain things to be measured, is so for others, which are measured by scales or hollow vessels, and it is most unsuitable for remote and inaccessible things; moreover, it lacks the necessary aid of...

units.la: XVII. Cartesii & suorum in inquisitione veri triplex incogitantia, plurium erratorum causa. 1. Primum quodvis criterium arripiunt. ad alias, quæ bilance aut vasis cavis mensurantur, tum & ad remotiora & inaccessa est ineptissimum : præterea & de auxilio necessario & de sanitate facultatum recuperanda prius fuerat cogitandum. Simile quid est in veritate rerum perquirenda. Errari statim atque omnino ineptiri potest, 1. si quis primum quodvis criterium arripiens, applicet id rebus aut veritatibus quæ ex alio criterio perpendendæ sunt : 2. si causam omnis luminis, omnisque boni & veri, Deum, nec satis noscat, nec in mente habeat : 3. si denique ipse facultates proprias earumve statum, firmus-ne an debilis & corruptus sit, nesciat. Quæ omnia præcedere debere, ipse rerum ordo, nemini sine tenebris & erroribus inde proventuris violandus, evidenter indicat. Et hujus quidem rei ordinisque omissionem inter prima errata Philosophorum modò enumeravimus, eamque cæterorum esse fontem universalem annotavimus, quam proinde evitare satagemus confiderando de veritatum variis generibus, de Deo, deque mentis nostræ facultatibus, ea quæ ad hoc facere videbuntur, ut deinceps in veritatis via & fruitione sine erroris periculo possimus pedetentim proficere.
units.tr: XVII. The threefold thoughtlessness of Descartes and his followers in the inquiry after truth, a cause of many errors. 1. First, they seize on whatever criterion comes to hand. Just as that criterion is most unsuitable for things weighed on scales or measured in hollow vessels, and equally for things remote and out of reach, so too one should first have thought about the necessary help and about the health of one's faculties to be restored. Something similar holds in the search for the truth of things. One can err, and utterly play the fool, at once: (1) if someone, seizing at first on whatever criterion, applies it to things or truths that must be weighed by another criterion; (2) if he neither knows well enough nor keeps in mind God, the cause of all light and of all good and truth; (3) if finally he does not know his own faculties, or their state, whether they are firm or weak and corrupted. That these things must come first, the very order of things indicates plainly, and no one should violate it without the darkness and errors that will arise from doing so. We have just listed the omission of this matter and order among the first errors of the philosophers, and we have noted that it is the universal source of the rest. We shall therefore take care to avoid it, by considering the various kinds of truths, God, and the faculties of our mind, and whatever seems to contribute to this, so that afterwards we may advance step by step on the way of truth and its enjoyment without danger of error.

units.la: XVIII. Observandum primo (quod nec multos latet, tametsi nec penitus satis inspectum) Veritatem recte initio distingui in veritatem materialem sive facti ; & in veritatem mentis, sive conceptus aut conscientiæ, tem primo sive, ut sic loquar, afficientiæ. Veritas materialis consistit in hoc, quod res sint prout revera sunt, sive corporeæ sint, sive cogitantes : ita, in his, quando cogito solem, circulum, chimæram, veritas est nie hæc cogitare : & quando sum in tenebris aut error, veritas est me errare & esse in tenebris. Hæ veritates materiales tanti æstimandæ sunt, quanti materiæ ipsæ, quæ si sint magnæ, mediocres, parvæ, futiles, malæ; veritates hæ fuerint etiam magnæ & momentosæ; mediocres, parvæ, futiles, pessimæ, & quas optandum esset non dari. Ita, Deum non amari, hominem peccare aut damnari, veritates sunt pessimæ, quæ utinam nunquam fuissent, nec forent in posterum : pulviculos tot numero totque motibus agitatos dari inter hoc illudve spatium, & sexcenta ejusmodi, veritates sunt nullius momenti; quales & infinitæ dantur aliæ. Quæ ideo annotanda, ut quando quis vacare volet mentalibus sive conceptuum veritatibus, quæ potissimum in conformitate conceptus cum rebus aut materiis ipsis consistunt, non patiatur sibi splendido veritatis nomine imponi, quasi omnia quæ glorioso hoc encomio insignirentur, digna essent occupatione & existimatione nostra: sed vel hinc sciat, res si fuerint vanæ, inutiles, aut malæ, vanas inde, futiles atque noxias veritates se adepturum. nisi animo id faciat ipsa vana aut mala impugnandi & averruncandi. A dignitate veritatis rei, dignitas veritatis mentalis & affectionis pendet & exsurgit potissimum.
units.tr: XVIII. It must be observed first (which does not escape many, although it has not been examined thoroughly enough) that truth is rightly distinguished at the outset into material truth, or truth of fact, and truth of the mind, or of concept or consciousness, that is, the primary affection, as I may so call it. Material truth consists in this, that things are as they really are, whether they are bodily or thinking. Thus, when I think of the sun, a circle, or a chimera, it is true that I think these things; and when I am in darkness or in error, it is true that I err and am in darkness. These material truths are to be valued as much as the matters themselves: if those matters are great, moderate, small, trifling, or bad, then these truths too will be great and momentous, or moderate, small, trifling, or very bad, and such as it would be better not to exist. Thus, that God is not loved, that man sins or is damned, are most evil truths, which would that they had never been and never were in future. That tiny particles, so many in number and moved by so many motions, exist between this or that space, and six hundred such things, are truths of no importance; and there are infinitely many other such truths. This must be noted, so that when someone wishes to occupy himself with the mental truths of concepts, which consist chiefly in the conformity of a concept with things or with the matters themselves, he should not allow himself to be deceived by the splendid name of truth, as if everything marked with this glorious praise were worthy of our occupation and esteem. Rather, let him know from this that if the things are vain, useless, or bad, he will obtain from them vain, trifling, or harmful truths, unless he does so in order to attack and avert those vain or bad things. The dignity of the mental truth and of the affection depends chiefly on, and arises from, the dignity of the truth of the thing.

units.la: XIX. Hæc autem consistit in eo, ut mens, ejusve facultates percipiendi, sive intellectuales sive sensibiles & quae corporea respiciunt, ita evidenter & luminose assiciantur suis objectis, ut in hujusmodi assectionibus characteres sint cum objectis ipsis aut cum objectorum habitudine ad nos conformes. Veritas itaque haec in conformitate aut in correspondentia consistit, quando perceptio mea afficitur eo modo cui respondeat in Dei natura aut ideis, aut in rerum constitutione, principiis, statu aut connexione, aliquid simile vel conforme, quo sine, veritas ejusmodi in me nulla est, chimaerica est, & tantum de genere veritatis materialis modo dictae, nempe, verum tunc erit, res quidem extra me esse id quod sunt; me vero intus chimaeras & somnia inania concipere.
units.tr: XIX. This mental truth, however, consists in this: that the mind, and its faculties of perceiving, whether intellectual or sensible and concerned with bodily things, are affected by their objects so evidently and luminously that in such affections there are marks that conform to the objects themselves, or to the relation of the objects to us. Therefore this truth consists in conformity or correspondence, when my perception is affected in such a way that there corresponds to it something similar or conformable in the nature or ideas of God, or in the constitution, principles, state, or connection of things. Without this, such a truth is not in me at all; it is chimerical, and it is only of the kind of material truth just described. That is, it will be true that things outside me are what they are, but that within me I conceive chimeras and empty dreams.

units.la: XX. Has autem correspondentiae aut conformitatis veritates ex conscientia eorum quae in me expertus sum, in duas vel tres species aut classes divido, quarum unaquaeque proprium suum habet criterium. Nempe quae hactenus me affecerunt, ea fuerunt vel res ipsae; vel rerum veluti umbrae, picturae atque icones, non vividae, quales sunt res; sed steriles, frigidae, mortuaeque. Nam quando perceptiones de me meisque cogitandi facultatibus intimioribus habui, tunc me ipsum, rem scilicet ipsam cogitantem & spiritualem realiter percepi: idemque de Deo quoque, re spirituali, potentissima, optima, justissima dicere non dubito: perceptiones enim illae vividae de eo, quas modo recensui, non potuisse ab alio quam ab illo, mihi sic in intimis meis præsentissimo & me movente, proficisci, indubitate ipse ego quoad me (quod jam mihi sufficit) certus sum. Similiter quando oculos aperui, & Solem atque alia cum meo, corpora percepi, tunc me ipsas res corporeas percepisse vividis sensationibus, nisi sponte insanire velim, in dubium quoque nequeo revocare. At quando vivida Dei affectione absente, aut clausis Soli oculis, volui nisu quodam & contentione activa in me revocare & veluti præsentes sistere menti reseas (Deum, Solem,) alioqui absentes, aut mihi repræsentare præterea alias quasdam earum proprietates & affectiones; tunc bene sensi, ideas istas Dei, proprietatum ejus a mea ratione inquisitarum, ideam Solis luminisve ejus absentis, & si quæ illius proprietates, jam non res ipsas ; sed rerum pictoras steriles & veluti mortuas esse, quæ nec me vivide afficiunt, illuminant, calefaciunt, nec rebus me faciunt potiri. Unde distinguo veritates in veritates reales, hasque in spirituales, quibus ipsis rebus spiritualibus afficimur ; & corporeas, quibus tangimur ipsis rebus corporeis; & in veritates pictas sive umbratiles, quibus rerum ideis seu picturis tantum gaudemus, sive picturæ sint de rebus spiritualibus, sive de corporeis, hisque vel imaginatione, vel ratione pura seu intellectione depictis. Has maximi necessariique momenti distinctiones an cæteri capiant, rescio; nescio; mihi quidem sincere mecum agenti omnium sunt indubitatissimæ, easque in omnire animadvertere queo vel palpabilissimis omnium modis. Dei, rerum, affectionumque divinarum ideas dæmones & pessimi quique habere possint, ipsas res & assectiones nequaquam: divitiarum ideas habet mendicus, ciborum famelicus, res affectionesque earum reales nequaquam.
units.tr: XX. From the consciousness of what I have experienced in myself, I divide these truths of correspondence or conformity into two or three species or classes, each of which has its own criterion. Namely, whatever has affected me so far was either the things themselves, or shadows, pictures, and images of things, which are not lively as things are, but barren, cold, and dead. For when I have had perceptions of myself and of my more inward powers of thinking, then I have really perceived myself, the thinking and spiritual thing itself. I do not hesitate to say the same of God too, a spiritual thing, most powerful, best and most just: for those lively perceptions of him, which I have just recounted, could not have come from anyone other than him, who is so present to me in my innermost parts and moves me. I am certain of this, as far as I am concerned (and this is already enough for me), beyond doubt. Likewise, when I opened my eyes and perceived the sun and other bodies with my own eyes, then I cannot, unless I wish to rave of my own accord, call into doubt that I perceived the bodily things themselves by lively sensations. But when, in the absence of the lively affection of God, or with my eyes of the sun closed, I wished by a certain effort and active exertion to recall in myself, and as it were set before my mind as present, those things (God, the sun) which are otherwise absent, or to represent to myself certain of their other properties and affections, then I clearly felt that those ideas of God, of the properties of him inquired into by my reason, and the idea of the sun or of its light when absent, and whatever of its properties, are not the things themselves, but barren and as it were dead pictures of things, which neither affect me vividly, nor illuminate or warm me, nor make me master of the things. Hence I distinguish truths into real truths, and these into spiritual ones, by which we are affected by spiritual things themselves, and bodily ones, by which we are touched by bodily things themselves; and into painted or shadowy truths, by which we rejoice only in the ideas or pictures of things, whether the pictures are of spiritual or of bodily things, and whether they are depicted by imagination or by pure reason or intellection. I do not know whether others grasp these very important and necessary distinctions. For my own part, dealing sincerely with myself, they are most certain of all, and I can notice them in every case by the most palpable of all modes. Demons and all the wicked may have ideas of God, of things, and of divine affections, but by no means the things and affections themselves. The beggar has the ideas of riches, the starving man of food, but by no means the real things and their affections.

units.la: XXI. Tribus hisce veritatum speciebus destinatæ sunt in omni mente suæ facultates, nempe realibus spiritualibus, intellectus quem passivum appellabimus; realibus corporeis, facultates sensuum corporeorum tam externorum quam internorum; pictis vero & umbratilibus, facultas intellectus quem activum dicemus, qui idem est cum facultate humanæ rationis. Atque sic cavendum est, ne quis unius generis veritatem per facultatem alteri generi propriam capere contendat: perinde enim erraret, ac is qui lumen auribus, aut sonos oculis, aut cogitata manibus percipere vellet. Si quis ergo res spirituales atque vividas, lumenque ipsum Dei, per rationis suæ activitatem percipere & intelligere vellet, is omnium erraret turpissime; haud secus ac si corporum existentiam & posituras ex intellectus supremi facultate, aut ex rationis suæ umbratilibus ideis percipere tentaret. Hoc male observatum, inter prima veritatem quærentium seu philosophantium errata omnino est annotandum.
units.tr: XXI. Each mind has its faculties appointed for these three species of truths: namely, for real spiritual truths, the intellect, which we shall call passive; for real bodily truths, the faculties of the bodily senses, both external and internal; and for painted and shadowy truths, the faculty of the intellect which we shall call active, which is the same as the faculty of human reason. And so one must take care not to strive to grasp a truth of one kind through a faculty proper to another kind. For he would err just as one who wished to perceive light with the ears, sounds with the eyes, or thoughts with the hands. If therefore someone wished to perceive and understand spiritual and lively things, and the very light of God, through the activity of his reason, he would err most shamefully of all; no differently than if he tried to perceive the existence and positions of bodies through the faculty of the supreme intellect, or through the shadowy ideas of his own reason. This badly observed matter must certainly be noted among the first errors of those who seek truth, or philosophise.

units.la: XXII. Respondent autem terris hisce
units.tr: XXII. Now these classes of faculties correspond to these three kinds of truth,

units.la: facultatum classibus, insuntque tribus istis veritatum speciebus, tria luminum genera, Divinum, naturale externum, & umbratile rationis, five (fi mihi sic loqui fine repugnantiæ specie liceat) naturale metaphyficum, vel philosophicum. Quorum unumquodque quando facultates sibi deftinatas & aliquatenus bene dispositas ferit, evidentiam talem in iisdem, atque adeo in anima, parit, ut quamvis ista claritas forte millies evidentior fieri queat, & crescere (uti revera in multis potest) in infinitum, acquiescat tamen anima veritati de objecto, saltem quoad existentiam, fruitionem, affectionesque generaliores spectato, aut (fi res fit de facultate rationis) de ejus natura generaliore.
units.tr: and in these three kinds of truth there are three kinds of light: the divine light, the external natural light, and the shadowy light of reason, or (if I may speak thus without appearing to contradict myself) the natural metaphysical or philosophical light. When each of these strikes the faculties assigned to it and is suitably disposed to some degree, it produces in them, and so in the soul, such evidence that, although this clarity may perhaps become a thousand times clearer and grow (as in fact it can in many cases) without limit, the soul nevertheless rests in the truth about its object, at least as regards its existence, enjoyment, and more general affections, or, if the matter concerns the faculty of reason, as regards its more general nature.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: XXIII. Quæ ut diftinctius percipiantur nonnulla insuper sunt prænotanda. 1. Veritatum istarum species debere præterea distingui in generales quæ concernunt generaliora & maxime necessaria naturæ exiftentiæque rerum, mentis, corporis, eorumque modos, actus, partes, nec non & numeros, motus & quæ sunt hujus generis communiora, fine quibus de naturæ rerumque existentia nil constaret; & in speciales ac particulares, quæ concernunt fpecialiora, quæ in rerum statum individuum & singularem, ex principiis generalibus singula per singulariora principia, singularioreisque vias, in suum quæque statum & locum discreta devenere. 2. Quamvis sæpe una eademque res diversis evidentiæ gradibus in infinitum crescentibus percipi potest, minorisque gradus defectus ad majorem paratus pro gradu obscuritatem involvente non possit haberi; non tamen ideo perceptionem minoris gradus fieri vel incertam vel dubitationi obnoxiam: tum quia ista obscuritas non est positiva (ut sic dicam,) hoc est, ex confusione aut inordinatione aliqua oriunda; tum quia percipiens, eo in statu, nec est nec esse potest gradus absentis conscius; tum maxime quia Deus quemcunque gradum evidentiæ illius sic constituit, ut indubitato conscium faceret mentem de objecti exsistentia & generalioribus ejus actibus atque effectis. 3. Tertio non confundenda est evidentia perceptionis objecti in me indubitatè agentis neque afficientis, cum evidentia cognitionis formæ, naturæ, proprietatum & effectorum ejusdem objecti in me agentis. 4. Quarto notandum est aliud esse, seu alium esse mentis actum, quo possidetur evidenter id ipsum per quod noscitur, sentitur & acquiescenter possidetur veritas; alium vero actum, quo scitur reflexivo modo, quid sit hoc ipsum, quod criterium vocatur veritatis. Prius ad veritatis possessionem est necessarium & essentiale, posterius non est. Rusticus qui videt solem in meridie, non minus vere videt, scitque indubitate se videre, etsi nesciat tam bene quo criterio hæc sua visio distinguatur a somno nocturno ubi sibi visus est eundem Solem videre; quam Philosophus qui illhæc ex arte & ideis suis deduceret. Ita simplicion non minus vere, Deum exsistentem & in ipsis operantem sciunt indubii, quam Philosophi exsistentiam hanc ex rationis ideis demonstrantes: imo hi forte eum minus norunt, quando plus roboris putant ineße pictis vel umbratilibus idearum suarum argumentis, quam vividis objecti ipsius actibus & praesentiae efficaci in simpliciorum mente.
units.tr: XXIII. So that these matters may be perceived more distinctly, several points must be noted beforehand. 1. These kinds of truth must further be distinguished into general truths, which concern the more general and most necessary features of the existence of things, of mind and body, and their modes, acts, parts, as well as numbers, motions, and other more common matters of this sort, without which nothing would be established about the nature and existence of things; and into special and particular truths, which concern the more specific matters, which, from general principles, through more specific principles and more specific ways, have arrived each at its own individual state and place. 2. Although one and the same thing can often be perceived with degrees of evidence increasing without limit, and a lesser degree of defect, compared with a greater one, cannot be regarded as involving obscurity in proportion to its degree, the perception of the lesser degree does not for that reason become either uncertain or open to doubt. This is so, first, because that obscurity is not positive (so to speak), that is, does not arise from some confusion or disorder; second, because the perceiving mind, in that state, neither is nor can be aware of a degree that is absent; and third, above all because God has so constituted whatever degree of that evidence there is that it makes the mind undoubtedly aware of the object's existence and of its more general acts and effects. 3. Third, the evidence of the perception of an object that acts upon me undoubtedly and affects me must not be confused with the evidence of knowledge of the form, nature, properties, and effects of that same object acting on me. 4. Fourth, it must be noted that there is one act of the mind, or another kind of act, by which the very thing through which truth is known and felt is evidently possessed, and truth is possessed with assent; and there is another act by which it is known in a reflexive way what that very thing is which is called the criterion of truth. The former is necessary and essential for the possession of truth; the latter is not. A countryman who sees the sun at midday sees it no less truly, and knows undoubtedly that he sees it, even if he does not know as well by what criterion his seeing is distinguished from the nocturnal sleep in which he seemed to see the same sun, than a philosopher who would deduce this from art and his own ideas. So simple people no less truly know, beyond doubt, that God exists and works in them, than philosophers who demonstrate this existence from the ideas of reason; indeed these philosophers perhaps know Him less, when they think more strength lies in the painted or shadowy arguments of their ideas than in the living acts of the object itself and its effective presence in the minds of simple people.

units.la: XXIV. His positis vel ab unoquoque in se penitatis & observatis, concludo sequentia de diversis criteriorum veri speciebus.
units.tr: XXIV. With these points established, or each person having examined and observed them within himself, I conclude the following about the different kinds of criteria of truth.

units.la: Primo. Veritas realis rerum spiritualium, maxime vero divinarum, quoad generalior ra, puta, exsistentiam operationesque in mente communiores, constat charactere & criterio non evidentiae sive claritatis cognitionis penitioris objecti, ejusve naturae proprietatumque intimarum & reconditiorum; sed charactere & criterio evidentiae perceptionis divinae, sive affectionis meae qua vivide afficior ab objecto in me vires suas exercente eis modis, quibus superius (a) dixi me de ejus exsistentia convinci. Et notandum est, hanc certitudinem veram atque realissimam interdum a claritate cognitionis objecti operationumque ejus sic dissolvi, ut in meris tenebris sibi aliquis esse videatur; imo & vividitatem affectionis aliquando, (quo craßior sensus amorque proprius deponantur & elevetur animus,) sic disparere posse, ut sola fere imperceptibilis remaneat in reconditioribus mentis supra omnem sensum acquiescentia in Deo occulta: quae immota & ineffabiliter sublimis acquiescentia summum & purissimum animae fidelis & perfectioris signum & probatio est, ut alibi dudum (a) demonstravi. Sed ad priora faciliora, & quae incipientium sunt, ut revertar, non dubito quin unusquisque, qui ordine & cum sinceritate in sese ea, quae modo diximus, perpendere volet, eorum sentiat mecum realem veritatem. Si qui autem dicant, id se non ita experiri, quid nostra refert? Erratis, imputent suis quod eousque insensibiles facti sint.
units.tr: First. The real truth of spiritual things, and especially of divine things, as far as the more general matters are concerned, namely their existence and the operations more common in the mind, consists in the mark and criterion not of the evidence or clarity of a deeper knowledge of the object, or of its nature and innermost and more hidden properties, but in the mark and criterion of the evidence of the divine perception, or of my affection by which I am vividly affected by the object exercising its powers in me, in those ways by which I said above (a) that I am convinced of its existence. And it must be noted that this true and most real certainty is sometimes so dissolved by the clarity of the knowledge of the object and its operations that a person may seem to himself to be in mere darkness. Indeed, the vividness of the affection can sometimes disappear (when the grosser sense and self-love are laid aside and the mind is raised up) so that there remains almost only an imperceptible, hidden acquiescence in God, lying in the deeper parts of the mind above all sense; this unmoving and ineffably sublime acquiescence is the highest and purest sign and proof of a faithful and more perfect soul, as I long ago demonstrated elsewhere (a). But to return to the easier matters that come first, and that belong to beginners, I do not doubt that everyone who wishes to weigh in himself, in order and with sincerity, the things I have just said will feel with me the real truth of them. If some say that they do not experience it so, what does that matter to us? You are mistaken; let them impute to themselves that they have become so insensible.

units.la: XXV. Secundo, Veritas realis rerum divinarum & spiritualium specialior, puta rerum quoad naturam suam, suas proprietates, actus, effecta individua quaedam vel plura penitius cognoscendarum, constat intus charactere & criterio evidentiae sive claritatis objecti cogniti, intus (quatenus cognitum est) lucentis & se manifestantis ejusmodi lumine, ad quod si omne aliud lumen cogitabile comparetur, mera obscuritas esse videatur. Haec qui experti sunt, de iis magis sunt certi, quam de propria sua, ut sic dicam, exsistentia; namque revera se & minus sentiunt & minus vident, quam lumen illud ineffabile quo se repletos & absorptos experiuntur. Sed pauci sunt ob plerorumque dispositiones malas (de quibus postea) quibus ista experiri liceat. Rem tamen sic esse debere, patet ex eo, quod ipse Deus, qui & omnipotens est & infinitus, hocce sit ipsemet lumen, idemque
units.tr: XXV. Second, the real truth of divine and spiritual things, of a more special kind, namely of certain individual or several things to be known more deeply, as regards their nature, their properties, their acts, and their individual effects, consists within in the mark and criterion of the evidence or clarity of the object known, which, so far as it is known, shines within and manifests itself by such a light that, if every other conceivable light were compared with it, it would seem mere obscurity. Those who have experienced this are more certain of these things than of their own existence, so to speak; for indeed they feel and see themselves less than that ineffable light by which they experience themselves filled and absorbed. But because of the bad dispositions of most people (of which more later) there are few to whom it is permitted to experience these things. Yet that the matter must be so is clear from the fact that God Himself, who is both omnipotent and infinite, is this very light,

units.la: b j que adeo omnipotenter & infinita virtute luceat, ubi se suasve perfectiones videndas vult exhibere. De quibus adhuc alibi agemus.
units.tr: and so shines with omnipotent and infinite power, whenever He wills to exhibit Himself or His perfections to be seen. Of these things we shall speak further elsewhere.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: XXVI. Veritas realis rerum corporearum quod sive naturalium, quoad generaliora, communiora & maxime necessaria, constat charactere & criterio evidentiae tum objectorum quatenus nos vivide afficiunt & ad nos spectant; tum affectionis ipsius vividae, praesentiam & actionem objecti involventis; non autem evidentiae objecti quoad naturam intimam suam suarumque proprietatum afsectionumque cogniti. Sic constat veritas realis exsistentiae corporis nostri, corporumque extra nos aliorum, diverse figuratorum, motorum, quiescentium, nosque multifariam afficientium, v. g. Solis, ex lumine suo vivido; aliorumque corporum, ex aliis quibus nos afficiunt modis, certis illis utique & indubiis, quamvis de natura & constitutione penitiori illorum corporum nondum hactenus constet.
units.tr: XXVI. The real truth of corporeal things, whether natural or artificial, as to their more general, common and most necessary features, rests on the mark and criterion of evidence of objects insofar as they vividly affect us and bear upon us. It also rests on the vivid feeling itself, which involves the presence and action of the object. It does not rest on the evidence of the object as to its inner nature and its properties and affections as known. Thus the real truth of the existence of our own body, and of other bodies outside us, variously shaped, moving or at rest, and affecting us in many ways, is established. For example, the Sun is known from its vivid light. Other bodies are known from the other modes by which they affect us. These are certain and undoubted, although the deeper nature and constitution of those bodies is not yet established.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: XXVII. Quartò, Veritas realis rerum naturalium quoad specialiorem suam constitutionem, suarumque proprietatum & effectuum naturam, statum, vires, ordinationes individuas, constat charactere & criterio evidentiae objectorum intus radiantium & afficientium iis modis vividis, quibus a Deo ad representationem realem ejus virtutum excogitata fuerunt objecta, constitutaque & donata dotibus suis prodierunt, ac inter se collocata sunt, suaque sibi communicant. His modis nemo res naturales veritate novit reali, nisi is cui Auctor naturæ detexit per vividas atque lucidas affectiones, earum rerum exemplares quæ in ipso sunt causas & vires donatas, atque inter sese ordinatissime & admirabilissime vivideque compositas. Hoc uno oculi nictu, ubi vult, exhibere potest; sed quam rarum id nunc fit, dictu opus non est.
units.tr: XXVII. Fourthly, the real truth of natural things as to their more specific constitution, and the nature, state, powers and individual arrangements of their properties and effects, rests on the mark and criterion of evidence of objects shining within and affecting us in those vivid modes by which the objects were devised by God for a real representation of his powers. They came forth constituted and endowed with their qualities, were placed among one another, and communicate their own to one another. In these ways no one knows natural things in real truth, except one to whom the Author of nature has disclosed, through vivid and clear affections, the exemplars of those things, which in him are the causes and bestowed powers, and which are composed most orderly, admirably and vividly among one another. He can display this, when he wills, in a blink of an eye. But how rarely this now happens, there is no need to say.

units.la: XXVIII. Quinto, Veritas umbratilis & picta rerum tum spiritualium tum corporalium, quoad generaliora sua, nec non & ea quæ in eis earumque proprietatibus & actibus maxime sunt obvia, communia & necessaria, constat characterē & criterio evidentiæ & claritatis idearum quarundam sola attentione opus habentium, ut certo sciatur eas non esse imagines rerum & proprietatum fictarum & chimæricarum; sed rerum saltem possibilium, & ideali modo veratum. Ita in cogitantibus, idea desiderii cujus objectum sit bonum; idea facultatis percipiendi, cujus objectum sit verum: idea determinationis libertatis, cujus norma sit rectum aut justum & similia: in corporeis vero considerandis, extensio, motus, figurarum proprietates simpliciores, numerique minus compositi, ideali hoc certitudinis modo per evidentiam, sola attentione convincentem, cognoscuntur.
units.tr: XXVIII. Fifthly, the shadowy and painted truth of things, both spiritual and corporeal, as to their more general features, and also as to those features in them and in their properties and acts that are most obvious, common and necessary, rests on the mark and criterion of evidence and clarity of certain ideas that need only attention. Thus it is known for certain that these ideas are not images of fictitious and chimerical things and properties, but at least of possible things, and true in an ideal manner. Thus, among thinking beings, there is the idea of desire whose object is good; the idea of the faculty of perceiving whose object is truth; the idea of the determination of liberty whose norm is what is right or just; and similar ideas. Among corporeal things to be considered, extension, motion, the simpler properties of figures, and numbers that are less compound are known in this ideal mode of certainty, through evidence that convinces by attention alone.

units.la: XXIX. Sexto, Veritas umbratilis & picta earundem rerum quoad specialiora, pænitioraque sua essentialia, vires, proprietates
units.tr: XXIX. Sixthly, the shadowy and painted truth of the same things as to their more specific and deeper essentials, powers, properties,

units.la: veri, de tates, effectus, combinationes, cognoscendarum & deducendarum, ita ut vel totius universitatis vel cujusvis in ea particularis systematis compages idealis complete habeatur, constet oportet characterc & criterio evidentiæ & claritatis non tantum in ideis generalioribus, penitius & attentius quam præcedente articulo perspiciendis; sed & in partitione, deductione, combinatione & consequentiis illarum: in quibus seorsim deducendis & percipiendis sua adefse debet evidentia, ut & (quantum fieri potest & optandum effet) in omnibus simul resumtis & coagmentatis evidentia totius systematis & ejus combinationum. Quod sane & arduum est, & admodum paucorum: etsi dentur plures qui hinc inde unam forte atque alteram rei alicujus particularis veritatem idealem evidenter & inconfuse aliquatenus percipiant. Aliud est ubi Deus, qui in anima agere valet, rerum vel universarum, vel quarum ipsi lubebit, particularium ideas & icones in ratione volet excitare. Tunc veritas hæc idealis sua claritate & partium distinctione sese tanquam indubitato prodet criterio. Verum id non accidit frequentius.
units.tr: truths, effects and combinations, to be known and deduced, so that a complete ideal grasp of either the whole universe or any particular system within it is had, must rest on the mark and criterion of evidence and clarity. This must be found not only in the more general ideas, which are to be perceived more deeply and attentively than in the preceding article, but also in their division, deduction, combination and consequences. When these are deduced and perceived separately, evidence must be present in them. And, as far as can be done and as would be desirable, there must also be evidence of the whole system and its combinations when all are taken up and joined together. This is indeed both difficult and open to very few, although there are several who here and there perceive, in some measure, clearly and without confusion, perhaps one or another ideal truth of some particular thing. It is otherwise when God, who is able to act in the soul, wills to excite in the mind the ideas and images of things, either all things or whichever particular things he pleases. Then this ideal truth reveals itself by its clarity and the distinctness of its parts, as by an undoubted criterion. But this does not happen very often.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: XXX. Non est tamen quod quis adeo sit sollicitus, si forte has criteriorum & evidentiæ sex species non possit primo nisu adeo facile concipere, aut conceptas, diu animo præsentes retinere: siquidem earum sit natura, ut experientia sua sit suum cuique criterium aut sui criterii præsentia, atque adeo, quemadmodum dictum est, ubi adsunt, ignorari non possint : & vero recte quærenti verum, se ipsas ex se offerant, & per se animos certos faciant. Unde earum reflexa cognitio, hoc est, cognitio quod in his consistant criteria & characteres diversarum veri specierum non tam ad inveniendum aut agnoscendum verum necessaria est vel utilis, quam ad hoc, ut a falsitate sive a persuasione falsa possit veri abstineatur, utque ab ea recedat quisquis in eam incidit.
units.tr: XXX. Yet there is no reason for anyone to be so anxious if perhaps at first effort he cannot easily grasp these six kinds of criteria and evidence, or, having grasped them, cannot keep them long present to his mind. For it is their nature that their experience is each person's criterion, or the presence of their criterion. And so, as has been said, where they are present they cannot be ignored. Indeed, they offer themselves to one who rightly seeks truth, and make minds certain through themselves. Hence their reflexive knowledge, that is, the knowledge that the criteria and marks of the various kinds of truth consist in these, is not so necessary or useful for finding or recognizing truth. Rather, it is useful for this: that one may abstain from falsity or from a false persuasion, and that whoever has fallen into it may withdraw from it.

units.la: Interim, ut brevius ista omnia animo teneantur, huc redeunt cuncta. In nobis dari tres facultatum species, divinas, naturales, umbratiles : unamquamque sua habere obiecta, adeoque & dari trium generum obiecta : & præterea pro facultatum & obiectorum numero, tria luminum genera, divinum, naturale, & rationale; & denique tres affectionum seu sensationum (voce late sumpta) species, emergentes unaquæque ex conjunctione facultatis cum obiecto & lumine ejus; atque hic latet veritas, (eaque triplex) & criterium ejus, quando nempe facultas debita, jungitur apte cum obiecto proprio in suo lumine. Et quoniam unaquæque ex tribus facultatibus, item & obiectis, & luminibus, & affectionibus, vel generaliter agunt. spectantur, lucent & afficiunt, vel specialius; ideo quod trinum ex se est, in senariam abit divisionem vel considerationem prout modo explicui.
units.tr: Meanwhile, so that all these things may be held more briefly in mind, everything comes back to this. In us there are three kinds of faculties: divine, natural and shadowy. Each has its own objects, and so there are objects of three kinds. Besides, in proportion to the number of faculties and objects, there are three kinds of lights: divine, natural and rational. Finally, there are three species of affections or sensations (the word taken broadly), each emerging from the conjunction of a faculty with its object and its light. Here lies truth, and that truth is threefold, and its criterion is here too: namely, when the due faculty is aptly joined with its proper object in its own light. And since each of the three faculties, likewise the objects, lights and affections, either act, are regarded, shine and affect in general, or else more specifically, therefore what is threefold in itself passes into a sixfold division or consideration, as I have just explained.

units.la: Præcipuus autem harum distinctionum fructus in hoc est, quod nemo, qui omnes veri species nondum expertus est, debeat unam speciem examinare aut sibi persuadere se eam possidere, multo minus ad ejus adeptionem adspirare, per facultatem, aut lumen, aut affectionem criteriumve vel characterem alterius speciei, quemadmodum contingeret si quis reales vividasque veritates divinas, generaliores aut specialiores, examinaret per facultatem, aut per lumen aut per criteria veritatum umbratilium & idealium, quae de rationis genere sunt; aut etiam per facultates, vel per lumen, aut per criteria veritatum realium physicarum quae ad facultates sensuum corporeorum pertinent: veluti si oculis animam ad lumen solis tentaret perspicere: aut denique si quis veritates ideales specialiores de natura peniori aut facultatibus rerum cogitantium vel corporearum, earumve aliquot systematum, probare vellet a se possideri, ex comparatione vel allegatione veritatum generaliorum & maxime obviarum atque communium, quales sunt veritates ideales maxime obviae de numeris, figuris aut motibus simpliciori bus, ex quarum comparatione caetera sua conaretur afferere & comprobare. Quod ut committant, facile inducuntur ii Philosophi, qui rebus Mathematicis sunt assueti, veluti sunt utplurimum Cartesiani: evidentia namque qua percipiuntur Mathematica sua principia communiora, haud ratio comprobare volunt, se & rerum ipsarum naturas, sive ideas atque proprietates, eadem evidentia perspectas habere: qua in re cum
units.tr: The chief fruit of these distinctions, however, is this: no one who has not yet experienced all the kinds of truth ought to examine one kind, or persuade himself that he possesses it, much less aspire to attain it, through the faculty, light, affection, criterion or mark of another kind. This would happen if someone were to examine real and vivid divine truths, whether more general or more specific, through the faculty, or through the light, or through the criteria of shadowy and ideal truths, which belong to the kind of reason. It would also happen if he examined them through the faculties, or light, or criteria of real physical truths, which pertain to the faculties of the bodily senses. It is as if one were to try to see the soul with the eyes by the light of the sun. Or finally, if someone wished to prove that he possesses more specific ideal truths about the deeper nature or the faculties of thinking or corporeal things, or of some systems of them, by comparison with or appeal to the more general and most obvious and common truths, such as the most obvious ideal truths about numbers, figures or simpler motions, from whose comparison he would try to assert and confirm his other claims. Philosophers accustomed to mathematical things, such as for the most part the Cartesians, are easily led into doing this. For because the evidence by which their more common mathematical principles are perceived is not, in their view, a reason for proof, they believe that they have the natures, or ideas and properties, of things themselves perceived with the same evidence. In this matter,

units.la: Mathematicos & Cartesianos quando- que hic peccare. cum magnum subsit erratum, penitius ea est inspicienda.
units.tr: the mathematicians and Cartesians sometimes go wrong here; since a great error lies beneath, it must be examined more deeply.

units.la: XXXI. Hic supponamus, si placet, (id quod postmodum probatum dabo,) facultates mentis nostrae, praesertim rationis sive intellectus activi, corruptas esse, torpidas, haut recte se moventes, lumineque vel caecas prorsus, vel admodum deminutas.
units.tr: XXXI. Here let us suppose, if you please (which I will afterwards prove), that the faculties of our mind, especially reason or the active intellect, are corrupted, sluggish, not moving rightly, and either wholly blind to light or greatly diminished.

units.la: In hac suppositione, sive (quia illam ut talem assumo) in hac veritate, patet omnes de rerum universalium specialiumque naturis ideas exactiores & penitiores, harumque formandarum aut noscendarum facultates, in mente violatas aut obscuratas vel omnino deletas esse debere, mentemque ipsam eo in statu ineptam & inidoneam quae eas rectas restituat. Attamen, quoniam mens non supponitur annihilata prorsus, sed superstes adhuc ac sui suorumque actuum, praeterea & corporis sui aliorumque conscia; eo ipso sequitur non posse ex corruptione hac mentis inferri talem obscurationem aut deletionem veritatum generaliorum matheseos, aut facultatum quibus illae noscuntur & tractantur; quemadmodum ex eadem necessario infertur obscuratio & deletio idearum de naturis quarumcunque rerum & systematum, aegritudoque facultatum eas respicientium.
units.tr: In this supposition, or (since I assume it as such) in this truth, it is plain that all the more exact and deeper ideas of the natures of universal and particular things, and the faculties of forming or knowing them, must be violated, obscured or wholly destroyed in the mind. The mind itself, in that state, is unfit and unsuited to restore them rightly. Yet since the mind is not supposed to be wholly annihilated, but still surviving and aware of its own acts, and of its body and of others besides, it follows from this very fact that from this corruption of the mind one cannot infer such an obscuring or destruction of the general truths of mathematics, or of the faculties by which those truths are known and handled. Yet from the same corruption there is necessarily inferred the obscuring and destruction of the ideas of the natures of whatever things and systems there are, and the sickness of the faculties that regard them.

units.la: Namque mens utut corrupta, modo supponatur sui suarumque actionum conscia, nec non & inter corporea vivens, seque ibidem cum corpore suo sustentans, impossibile est quin debeat scire, aut debeat posse scire, se unam aliquam cogitationem semel habere, bis aut ter iterare, suum corpus duabus esse præditum manibus, digitisque in unaquaque quinquies repetitis, qui cum totidem simul additi faciant decem : caput esse alius figuræ atque brachium aut crus ; & hæc alius quam lapis cui impingit : omnes partes corporis sui simul sumptas æquari corpori toti ; id totum esse majus qualibet sua parte, & similia, quæ si deberet ignorare, tunc nec esset sui compos, & vero sese regere atque vivere inepta foret. Itaque hæ veritates cum annexis suis, sunt menti sui conscientiæ & inter corporea viventi veluti naturales : at non ita de veritatibus ideisque exactis & philosophicis rerum naturæ, quippe quæ dos gratuita & ornamentum ejus arbitrarium magis videntur, quæque utique experientia teste, ab homine, salvo ejus naturali regimine, ignorari possunt, & ex corruptionis accessu ignorantur. Ergo probare atque illustrare velle, se hasce ultimas adhuc habere ex allegatione aut comparatione priorum, perinde est, ac si cæcus ex figuris aut numeris vel ex palpandi facultate, vellet ostendere se veras lucis & colorum ideas habere, easque per priora illa explicare aliis cæcis tentaret. Nolim equidem affirmare omnes sic præcise ab unis harum veritatum ad alias progredi aut argumentari ; at subest tamen quædam de possessione clararum idearum circa rerum naturas præsumptio, quando ejusmodi comparationibus agunt ; & verò postea sibi fa-
units.tr: For the mind, however corrupted, provided it is supposed to be conscious of itself and its own actions, and living among bodily things and sustaining itself there together with its body, it is impossible that it should not know, or should not be able to know, that it has one thought once and repeats it twice or three times; that its body has two hands, and that the fingers, counted five times on each hand, make ten when added together; that the head is of a different shape from the arm or the leg, and that this is different from the stone that strikes it; that all the parts of its body taken together equal the whole body; that the whole is greater than any of its parts; and similar things. If it were obliged to be ignorant of these, it would not be master of itself and would be unfit to govern itself and to live. Therefore these truths, with their attached consequences, are, as it were, natural to the mind living among bodily things and known to its consciousness. But it is not so with the exact and philosophical truths and ideas about the natures of things, which seem rather a gratuitous dowry and an arbitrary ornament of the mind. Experience bears witness that a man can be ignorant of these while his natural governance remains intact, and through the onset of corruption they are in fact unknown. Therefore to wish to prove and illustrate that one has these last truths by appeal or comparison to the former is just as if a blind man, from shapes or numbers or from the faculty of touch, wished to show that he has true ideas of light and colours, and tried to explain them to other blind men through those earlier things. I would not indeed assert that everyone progresses or reasons in this precise way from some of these truths to others. Yet there is nevertheless a certain presumption of possessing clear ideas about the natures of things when people argue by such comparisons; and afterwards they most easily persuade themselves

units.la: ciilicillime persuadent fe rerum ipsarum ideas eadem evidentia nolle, qua effata sua Mathematica per comparationem allata; quod sane longe a veritate abest, gratis affumitur, multis contrariatur causis, ipsique, ut videbitur suo loco, experientiæ.
units.tr: that they do not have ideas of the things themselves with the same evidence as the mathematical statements they bring forward by comparison. This is certainly far from the truth; it is assumed without warrant, it is contrary to many causes, and it is contrary to experience itself, as will be seen in its place.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Interim animadverti velim istam veritatum Mathematicarum allegationem complecti ipsissimam ignorantiæ rerum naturæ allegationem. Etenim numeri & figuræ, ut quid reale sint & exsistens, resnumeratæ & figuratæ esse debent; puta res cogitans vel extensa, a quibus numeri & figuræ non differunt nisi modaliter, non autem realiter: siquidem in natura non exsistant sine iis rebus unum, duo, tria, triangulus, similiaque abstracta; sed tantum res cogitantes vel extensæ, una, duæ, tres; triangulata, idealiter ut cogitatio; aut formaliter ut extensio: a quibus rebus cum numeratio & figuratio abstrahitur & seorsim consideratur, sit tantum consideratio unius atque alterius cujusdam crassioris & communioris affectionis rerum earum; quarum naturas cæterasque proprietates sibi nihilominus incognitas esse, fateantur necesse est Mathematici, ipsi si sint ere rem fateri volent. Aut vero interroga sodes, an vel naturam tantilli alicujus subjecti, aut pauculorum aliorum, quibus illud suum, unum, duo, tria, sex, triangularis figura, applicant, vere cognoscant, illamque ut explicent pete: & tunc eos, ni desipere velint, quovis pisce magis mutos videbis. Ut jam non provocem ad innumeras rerum cogitantium corporearumque species, proprietates, facultates, naturas, systemataque infinita particularia, e quibus ne unius quidem capilli, aut pedis muscae vel pulicis naturam intimam norunt. Ergo numeri & figurae quando ad subiecta & rerum naturam referuntur, nec otiose in solo cerebro circumvolitant, designant & inculcant nobis res, quarum immensa nos tenet ignorantia. Adeoque ea, quae ex isthac ad veritates mathematicas provocatione glisci t in animo fastuosu nimis de vero praesumtio, magnae in iisdem subiectis ignorantiae agnitione temperanda est; nec vero ob unius atque alterius crassioris, communioris indelebilisque proprietatis cognitionem jactitare se debet animus, quasi per hoc ipsum divitiarum suarum in caeteris notionibus possidendis daret specimen & argumentum: ne forte per suum illud bis duo sunt quatuor, & trianguli tres anguli duobus rectis aequantur, & similia ties decantata, pueruios illos imitari videatur, qui ut se mulices peritos ostendant, miseram unam cantiunculam ad eandem chordam semper stridunt. Non usum, sed abusum hic carpi, eumque obiter, & unum quidem, nemo non videt; taceo namque nunc perabsurde a Cartesio tentatum esse, ut ex Mathesi Physices desumeret principia, quibus hanc potius totam perdidit. Sed ista alinde constare poterunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile I would have it noted that this appeal to mathematical truths embraces precisely the appeal to ignorance of the nature of things. For numbers and figures, as to what is real and existing, must be numbered and shaped things: for example, a thinking or extended thing, from which numbers and figures differ only modally, not really. Indeed, one, two, three, triangle, and similar abstract things do not exist in nature without those things; there are only thinking or extended things, one, two, three, triangular, ideally as thought, or formally as extension. When numbering and figuring are abstracted from these things and considered apart, there is only a consideration of one or another cruder and more common affection of those things. The mathematicians must confess, if they are willing to speak the truth, that the natures of those things and their other properties remain unknown to them. Or, I beg you, ask whether they truly know the nature of some tiny subject, or of a few others, to which they apply that "one, two, three, six" or triangular figure, and bid them explain it; then, unless they wish to play the fool, you will see them more mute than any fish. Not to appeal now to the countless species, properties, faculties, natures, and infinite particular systems of thinking and bodily things, of which they do not know the inner nature of even a single hair, or of the foot of a fly or a flea. Therefore numbers and figures, when they are referred to subjects and the nature of things, do not merely flit idly about in the brain, but designate and impress upon us the things of which we are held in immense ignorance. Accordingly, the presumption of truth that rises in an overly proud mind from this appeal to mathematical truths must be tempered by the acknowledgement of great ignorance about those same subjects. Nor should the mind boast of its knowledge of one or another cruder, more common, and indelible property, as if by this it gave a sample and proof of its riches in acquiring the other notions; lest perhaps by its "twice two is four" and "the three angles of a triangle equal two right angles," and similar things repeated a hundred times, it seem to imitate those boys who, to show themselves skilled musicians, always screech one wretched little tune on the same string. Here it is not the use but the abuse that is criticised, and that in passing, and indeed one abuse, as everyone sees; for I say nothing of how absurdly Descartes attempted to derive the principles of physics from mathematics, by which he rather ruined the whole of physics. But these things may be established elsewhere.

units.la: XXXIII. Jam ad orbitam ut redeatur, patet quid respondendum sit quaerentibus.
units.tr: XXXIII. Now let us return to our track: it is clear what must be answered to those who ask.

units.la: Quis sciat sein recensitis veritatum speciebus per-
units.tr: Who can know, with the kinds of truths reviewed, through

units.la: XXXIII. Quaestio capitalis: perquirendis, & admittendis, claritate & evidentia ad unamquamque requisita potiri? Respondetur; illum id scire qui revera has veritates & evidentias experitur. At, multi putant se eas experiri, & tamen falluntur; Verisimum. Quomodo igitur hanc fallaciam, & detegent ipsi, & evitabunt, si eam ex parte veritatis & evidentiae quam quaerunt, & ad quam respiciunt, nequeant evitare? Id procul dubio ab iis fieri poterit, si quod (a) supra dixi, non tantum ad criterium verigeneralius animum advertant; sed & ad omnis boni & luminis fontem Deum bene recurrant &attendant, infspiciantque praeterea, num suae forte (a) supr. facultates, mensque tota in malo quodam corruptoque statu languide & inordinate versentur. Hoc si fuerit, tunc sciant perinde secum esse, ac cum homine; qui tergasoli obvertens, omni interim conamine abumbra sese expedire, puroque solis lumine frui eniteretur: aut ei qui versus lucem, radios sibi communicantem respiciens, oculis praeve dispositis, non posset non videre omnia perperam, quacunque etiam praesentis fulgoris abundantia collucтraretur.
