units.tr: XXXIII. The chief question: how, with the truths and evidences to be sought and admitted, can one attain the clarity and evidence required for each? The answer is that only one who actually experiences these truths and this evidence knows them. But many think they experience them and are nevertheless mistaken, very likely. How, then, will they themselves detect this error and avoid it, if they cannot avoid it from the side of the truth and evidence they seek and look to? Undoubtedly they will be able to do so if, as I said above (a), they give attention not only to the more general criterion of truth but also turn back to God, the fount of all good and light, and attend to him. Moreover, they should examine whether their faculties and their whole mind are perhaps languidly and disorderly engaged in some evil and corrupt state. If so, let them know that they are in the same position as a man who, with his back to the sun, strives by every effort to free himself from his shadow and enjoy the pure light of the sun; or as one who, turned toward the light and looking at the rays shining on him, but with his eyes ill-disposed, cannot help seeing everything amiss, however much he is bathed in the abundant brightness of the present splendour.

units.la: XXXIV. Atque hic certe, si velimus in veritate proficere, neque vero falli, aut incertitudine fluctuare, ubi veritate nos potituros sperabamus, examinanda sunt ista duo, quorum discussio necessaria admodum est, ut quis veri admittendi criterioque ejus utendi, sit & capax & certus.
units.tr: XXXIV. Here, certainly, if we wish to make progress in truth, not to be deceived, and not to waver in uncertainty where we hoped to attain the truth, these two things must be examined. Their discussion is very necessary, so that one may be both capable of admitting the truth and certain of using its criterion.

units.la: 1. Et primum quidem, quisquis se ipsum intus (juxta tertium cognitum legemque reqqirequisitam) intuebitur, & sine dolo (juxta fecundam) examinabit, plus satis deprehenquantum Deo, immensi luminis omnisque boni fonti, sit obversus: non tantum ex eo, quod illo, immensæque ejus liberalitatis, potentiæ, luminisque omnia penetrantis, tum bonitatis nunquam deficientis, felicitatisque abundantissimis fluentis, atque virtutum & bonorum omnium copia optata non utatur, nec liceat istorum ad arbitrium fieri participem, quemadmodum deceret utique inter Ens optimum suique omnium maxime communicativum, & inter ens indigens quod abeo aversum non esset: aut inter patrem & filios, amicumve cum amico: sed & hinc maxime, quod ne quidem ista ut decet, curet quisquam, multo minus desideret optetque cogitatione & affectu, aut quærat opere, prope Deum ut semper sit, eumque respiciat perpetuo. Verum isthæc pertinere videntur ad alterum membrum, corruptionem videlicet, de qua mox agendum, & ex qua abalienatio hominis a fonte veri amplius patebit. Itaque, ex primo hoc defectu, sive aversione a Deo, fonte veri, mirandum non est, hominem veritate quæsita frui non posse, quamvis etiam haberet in genere criterium veri; veluti non esset unde miraremur si quis luciterga obvertens ejusque haud particeps, nec nosse, neque mensurare objecta posset, utut norma & mensuris aptis esset aliunde instructissimus.
units.tr: 1. First, whoever looks into himself (according to the third thing known and the law required) and examines himself without guile (according to the second), will discover quite plainly how far he has turned away from God, the fount of immense light and of all good. This is so not only because he does not make use of the abundant riches of God's immense liberality, power, all-penetrating light, never-failing goodness, and the most abundant flowing felicity, and the wished-for store of virtues and all goods, nor is it permitted for him to become a partaker of these at will, as would surely befit the best Being, who is most communicative of himself, and a needy being, which would not be averse from him; or as between a father and his children, or a friend with a friend. But above all it is so because no one takes care, as he ought, even to think of these things, much less to desire and wish for them in thought and feeling, or to seek them by deed, so that he may always be near God and look upon him continually. But these matters seem to belong to the second member, namely corruption, which must be treated shortly, and from which the alienation of man from the fount of truth will become clearer still. Therefore, from this first defect, that is, aversion from God, the fount of truth, it is no wonder that man cannot enjoy the truth he seeks, even though he had in general a criterion of truth. It would be no wonder if someone who turned his back to the light and had no share in it could neither know nor measure objects, however well equipped he might be elsewhere with a rule and suitable measures.

units.la: 2. Sed & illud ipsum multo magis est impossibile ex defectu altero, corruptione videlicet nostra , omniumque facultatum & totius hominis, atque adeo & facultatis ratio-nis : cujus rationis partes maxime hic sunt considerandæ, quando etiam generalius loquemur de universis cæteris.
units.tr: 2. But this too is far more impossible because of the other defect, namely our corruption, and the corruption of all our faculties and of the whole man, and so also of the faculty of reason. The parts of this reason must be considered here especially, since we shall speak more generally also of all the others.

units.la: XXXV. Corruptio autem ista nostra, seposita revelatione , ex principiis cuique innatis facile patet , modo juxta legem requisitam alteram tertiamque, utisupponimus, unusquisque in se & secum sincere ac sine dolo , nec sibi ipsi blandiens , rem attente considerare velit.
units.tr: XXXV. This corruption of ours, setting aside revelation, is easily made plain from the principles innate in each person, provided that, according to the second and third law required, as we assume, each one in himself and with himself wishes to consider the matter attentively, sincerely and without guile, and without flattering himself.

units.la: 1. Et primo quidem experientia & factis constat, corruptam esse mentem , ejusque facultates, intellectum præsertim seu rationem: quæ experientia sese nimio plus prodit intus & extus effectis mancis, ex quibus omnino colligendum est , causam depravatam & corruptam esse. Scilicet, constat naturale & legitimum intellectûs elementum, ut sic
units.tr: 1. And first, it is established by experience and by facts that the mind, and its faculties, above all the understanding or reason, is corrupted. This experience shows itself too plainly within and without, in defective effects, from which it must necessarily be concluded that the cause is depraved and corrupted. Namely, it is established that the natural and lawful element of the understanding is, so to speak, light; and yet in fact all men swim in immense darkness on every side. It is also established that the goal and aim of the understanding is truth; and nevertheless all, in fact, for one or another meagre and sterile little scrap of truth, if they have one, become entangled in infinite and fruitful errors about themselves and about everything else.

units.la: dicam, esse lumen, & tamen de facto omnes immensis undiquaque tenebris innatant: constat & finem scopumque intellectûs esse veritatem; & nihilominus omnes de facto, pro una atque altera macra & sterili veritatis uncula, si quam habent, infinitis & foecundis circa se ipsos caeteraque omnia erroribus implicantur. Constat & illud, humanorum intellectuum naturam esse eandem, veritates etiam in se unas easdemque esse: & nihilominus experimentis patet dissentire omnes inter se de rebus iisdem; ut vere sint quot capita tot sensus. Tandem constat rationis incorruptae & sanae actum debere esse sanum, atque adeo approximare homines veritati; tametsi videamus accidere, eosdem, quo plus intellectus activitate utuntur, eo magis in dissensiones infinitas dissipari. Ergo constat, 1. intellectum revera esse extra suum elementum; 2. eum a suo scopo fineque aberrare; 3. eundem in diversas & oppositas perpetim ruere confusiones; & 4. activitatem ejus, qua se ad scopum restituere, inque elementum suum vult referre, ita inepte constitutam esse, ut non tantum id non efficiat, sed & se potius magis ab eo abducat atque removeat. Hoc est, ni fallor, constat, intellectum esse nunc de facto non modo simpliciter corruptum; sed & multo maxime & horribilem in modum corruptissimum: nisi incolumitatis rei statusque incorrupti proprietate & signa dicenda sint, esse extra bonum statum naturalem, extra finem & scopum suum, extra concordantiam, & extra activitatem bene agentem: id quod nemo, opinor, cogitaturus est.
units.tr: It is also established that the nature of human understandings is the same, and that the truths themselves are one and the same; and yet experience shows that all disagree among themselves about the same things, so that there are truly as many opinions as heads. Finally, it is established that the act of a sound and uncorrupted reason ought to be sound, and so bring men near to the truth; although we see that the same people, the more they use the activity of the intellect, the more they are scattered into endless disagreements. Therefore it is established that: (1) the understanding is really outside its own element; (2) it strays from its aim and end; (3) it continually falls into diverse and opposing confusions; and (4) its activity, by which it wishes to restore itself to its aim and bring itself back into its element, is so ineptly constituted that it not only does not accomplish this, but rather draws itself further away and removes itself from it. This, unless I am mistaken, is what is established: that the understanding now, in fact, is not merely corrupted in a simple way, but also corrupted in a very great and dreadful manner. Unless the properties and signs of a thing's soundness and uncorrupted condition are to be called being outside a good natural state, outside its end and aim, outside agreement, and outside a well-working activity; which, I suppose, no one will be inclined to think.

units.la: 2. Secundo eadem, & universaliter adhuc totius omnino hominis corruptio, demonstrative patet ex eo, quod infinitae corruptionis causa efficiens, (aut, si mavis, deficiens) saepissime in ipso fuerit in actum deducta: unde necessario sequitur, effectum seu corruptionem ipsam in eodem esse producta.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, the same thing, and the corruption of the whole man in general, is clearly demonstrated from the fact that the efficient cause of an infinite corruption (or, if you prefer, its deficient cause) has very often been brought into act in the man himself. From this it necessarily follows that the effect, or corruption itself, has been produced in the same man.

units.la: Ex secunda & tertia lege requisita & cognita, descendat quisque in se, & sibi in sincerITATE nullo dolo adspersa attendat: hinc discet utique non dubitante conscientia, 1, nos. Ens summum, omnipotens, luminosum, optimum, nostri & omnium causam munificentissimam, laudibus & gratiis continuis ac debitis non agnovisse & affecisse.
units.tr: From the second and third law required and known, let each one descend into himself and attend to himself in sincerity, with no guile mixed in. From this he will surely learn, with a conscience that does not doubt: (1) that we have not acknowledged and loved the supreme, almighty, luminous, best Being, the most bountiful cause of ourselves and of all things, with the continual and due praises and thanks.

units.la: 2. Ad idem, bonorum uti fontem ita & scopum, nos nec retulisse nos ipsos, neque etiam cætera; sed omnia potius ad nos, ac si omnium scopus essemus ipsi, inclinavisse.
units.tr: (2) Likewise, that while he is the fount and also the goal of good things, we have not referred ourselves or other things to him, but have rather inclined everything toward ourselves, as though we ourselves were the goal of all.

units.la: 3. Neque nos rebus, facultatibus nostris nobisque ipsis totis legitime & juxta ordinem Dei esse usos; sed pro inordinatissima cupiditate omnia turbasse; rebus, objectis & facultatibus æternis caduca præposuisse, corporea spiritualibus, superficiaria internis, necessariis accessoria, superioribus infima, umbratilia realibus, & perdita nostra placita propria sanctissimis Dei beneplacitis:
units.tr: (3) Nor have we used things, our faculties, and ourselves wholly, lawfully and according to the order of God; but, through most disordered desire, we have thrown everything into confusion. We have preferred perishable things to eternal objects and faculties, bodily things to spiritual, surface things to inner, accessory things to necessary, lowest things to highest, shadowy things to real, and our own perverse pleasures to God's most holy good pleasure.

units.la: 4. & denique nos non curavisse auxilium lumenque Dei continuo nobis ut adessent; sed quasi ipsis non haberemus opus, essemusque & fortes & luminosi per nos satis, omnia exlubitu & propria industria voluisse agere & regere; atque 5. quod pejus est, nos nec adhuc dum inverso & confirmato esse animo ut ista emendemus. Quae omnia quid aliud loquuntur quam (ut idem aliis verbis exprimamus) nos esse actibus & habitudine ingratos, philautia plenos, inordinatos, superbos & impœnitentes? Atqui hæc peccata causa sunt & in actum deducta & continuo agens corruptionis: eaque causa est in intimis animæ nostræ penetralibus: ejus igitur effectus, hoc est, corruptio, intimis nostris inest facultatibus, desideriis, intellectui, rationi, cæterisque etiam infimis, quæ sane incolumes & incorruptæ esse nequeunt: quem admodum si cor sit ægrum, cætera membra etiam externa & minus nobilia, male quoque que se habere necesse est.
units.tr: (4) And finally, that we have not cared for the help and light of God to be continually present with us; but, as though we had no need of them, and were strong and luminous enough of ourselves, we have wished to act and rule everything by our own will and our own industry. And (5), what is worse, we have not yet turned our minds and set them firm so as to amend these things. What do all these things say, other than (to express the same thing in other words) that we are ungrateful in our acts and disposition, full of self-love, disordered, proud and unrepentant? Yet these sins are the cause, both brought into act and continually acting, of corruption; and this cause lies in the innermost recesses of our soul. Therefore its effect, that is corruption, dwells in our innermost faculties, our desires, our understanding, our reason, and also in the lowest parts, which certainly cannot remain sound and uncorrupted. It is as when the heart is sick: the other limbs, even the external and less noble ones, must also necessarily fare ill.

units.la: XXXVI. Præterea cum Deus se suam que justitiam negare non posset; justum autem sit, aversis a Deo, ingratis, philautia captis, inordinatis, superbis, & quos istorum criminum nondum pœnituit, quinecdum ea ejuravere, non subministrari ea quibus sunt indigni, & quibus dudum quidem abusi sunt, mox vero adhuc sunt abusuri, sequitur ex justitia Dei, eis subtrahi debere, vel potius, non continuari lumen,
units.tr: XXXVI. Moreover, since God cannot deny himself or his justice, and since it is just that those who are turned away from God, ungrateful, captivated by self-love, disordered, and proud, and who have not yet repented of these crimes or renounced them, should not be given the things they are unworthy of, and which they have indeed abused in the past and will abuse again, it follows from God's justice that these things should be withdrawn from them, or rather, that the light,

units.la: auxilium, vires, rectitudinem, quibus utique intellectus eorum, ratio, activitas aliaeque facultates corruptissimae, vellent omnis generis rerum veritates, naturas, vanissimaque etiam & futilia perreptare, ad delectationem commoditatemve amori suo proprio & superbo quaerendam & exhibendam. Haec illis si praestaret Deus, approbaret sui ipsius, quae ab illis fit, praetermissionem, & a se ipso justo dissentiret.
units.tr: help, powers and uprightness should not be continued to them. By these their intellect, reason, activity and other most corrupt faculties would wander through every kind of truth and nature, and even through the most vain and frivolous things, seeking and offering them for the delight and advantage of their proud self-love. If God were to grant these things to them, he would approve the neglect of himself that they practise, and would be at odds with his own justice.

units.la: XXXVII. Hic igitur Veritatis cognitioni ulteriori ejusque fruitioni acquirendae, ab aversione & defectione hominis, ab ejus depravatione, a Deo justo, clausa est janua, firmissimusque objectus obex. Eum autem quis removebit? januam quis aperiet? Hic nos inter, & amabile veritatis pomerium, ingens abyssus interjacet & hiatus maximus, de quo prius implendo non cogitant Philosophi: unde eos gressus suos veritatem ver- sus continuari putantes, in tenebras & falsa præcipites ruere, necesse est. Hunc autem hiatum vel ex cæcitate Mentis corruptæ non perspiciunt; aut ex dolo animi minus sinceri, ea quæ superbiæ suæ amara sorent & ingrata refugientis dissimulant. Sunt enim, hiatus ille hominum, præcipue vero Philosophorum, pudenda ERRATA sex, inter PRIMA & præcipua annumeranda, nempe 1. desertio Entis summi: 2. ingratitudo erga illud: 3. amor proprius & adhærentia cujusque sui: 4. inordinatio & ἀπαξία-sui, facultatum, regiminis, studiorum, rerum: 5, superbia animi propriaque in se confidentia: & 6, impœnitentia. Quæ errata nisi prius ante omnia corrigantur, ad veritatem ulterius progredi non dabitur; ita ut revera oleum & operam perdant atque nugentur Philosophi, quotquot de minusculis nescio qualibus erratiunculis circa sutilia quædam objectula evitandis sunt folliciti, dum interim principes hosce errorum fontes, omnes mentis capacitates & facultates venenatis fluentis suis inundantes, obstruere prætermittunt. Æger ubi de se non cogitans festucis quibusdam & pulvisculis colligendis incumbit, est profecto deploi ati status. Medicus qui ægri capillis curandis & tuendis sese daret, dum interim nobiliores partes exitiali morbo impugnatas negligeret, alium utique quam Medici titulum mereretur. Et tamen ita se gerunt omnes in mentis suæ ægritudine propria homines; in alio-rum rum ægrirudine faranda , Philosophi.
units.tr: XXXVII. Here, then, the door is closed against further knowledge of the truth and the attainment of its enjoyment, by the aversion and defection of man, by his depravity, and by the just God; and a very firm bar stands in the way. But who will remove it? Who will open the door? Between us and the lovely boundary of truth lies a vast abyss and a great gap, which the philosophers do not think of filling first. Hence, supposing their steps are continuing toward truth, they must plunge headlong into darkness and falsehood. They do not see this gap clearly, either because of the blindness of their corrupted mind, or from the insincerity of their hearts, which hide those things that are bitter to their pride and that they shun as unwelcome. For that gap of men, and especially of the philosophers, is made up of six shameful ERRORS, to be counted among the FIRST and chief ones, namely: (1) desertion of the Supreme Being; (2) ingratitude toward him; (3) self-love and attachment to one's own self; (4) disorder and [ἀναξία] unworthiness of self, of faculties, of government, of studies, and of things; (5) pride of mind and self-confidence; and (6) impenitence. Unless these errors are corrected first of all, one will not be permitted to advance further toward truth. So the philosophers truly waste their oil and labour and trifle, all those who are anxious to avoid some petty little errors about certain subtle trifles, while meanwhile they neglect to block up these chief sources of error, which flood all the capacities and faculties of the mind with their poisonous streams. When a sick man, not thinking of himself, busies himself with gathering straws and specks of dust, his condition is truly deplorable. A physician who devoted himself to caring for and tending the hair of a patient, while neglecting the nobler parts attacked by a deadly disease, would deserve some title other than physician. And yet all men behave this way in the sickness of their own minds, and philosophers do so in curing the sickness of others.

units.la: XXXVIII. Debebant potius inter COGNITA sua prima hoc, quod quartum est ordine , numerare , atque nobiscum quartam legem veræ methodi statuere hanc; AGNOSCENDUM ESSE CUIQUE SE ESSE CORRUPTUM, ATQUE IN EO STATU VERITATIS ACQUIRENDÆ INCAPACEM. Unde necesse eos, si pergant, in omne falsum & malum, ipsumque tandem Atheismum & Libertinifmum prolabi.
units.tr: XXXVIII. They ought rather to have counted among their first KNOWN things this one, which is fourth in order, and to have laid down with us this fourth law of the true method: EACH MAN MUST ACKNOWLEDGE THAT HE IS CORRUPT, AND THAT IN THIS STATE HE IS INCAPABLE OF ACQUIRING TRUTH. Whence it is necessary that they, if they persist, slip into every falsehood and evil, and finally into Atheism and Libertinism itself.

units.la: XXXIX. Id quod olim Paulus observavit gentilibus Philosophis ea de causa accidisse in loco nunquam satis memorando ad Romanos. Illi cum cognovissent Deum [post agnitionem sive demonstrationem exsistentiæ Dei] non sicut Deum glorificarunt [ei non adhæserunt tanquam fonti omnis veri & boni,] neque gratias egerunt [fuerunt ingra-ti;] sed evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis, [vano amore proprio tibi suisque cogitatis & speculationibus naturalibus, minutisque & evanidis adhæserunt] & obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum [facultates internæ omnes in tenebras, adeoque in confusionem & ἀναξίαν ruerunt,] & dicentes se esse Sapientes, stulti facti sunt: [& per superbiam suam & confidentiam in se, profitentes se sapientiam, veritatem, philosophiam esse adeptos, non modo longe a veritate in falsitatem, sed & in insaniam inciderunt.] Et mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum, & quadrupedum, & serpentum: [in hoc praeitium jam inciderunt qui ex Cartesianissese in Spinozianismum dedere præcipi-, quibus Deus nil jam aliud est quam ldus corruptus ipse cum universis creatu-, ita ut omnes & singulæ nil aliud apud s sint quam Deus vel substantia Dei diverode modificata ac disposita.] Propter d tradidit illos Deus in desideria cordis eo-r, [hæc est ejuratio omnis conscientiæ, ncipiorum internorum justi & æqui, veque & internus Libertinismus, quem nc apud multos latere, nec nisi per humos respectus præpediri quo minus erumt, timendi locus est: addit Paulus eos & ditos esse] in immunditiam aliaque externa lera abominanda, quæ ipsissimus sunt Litinismus externus; fructus scilicet omnium npletus & maturus, post quem nil exctandum superest, præterquam ejus mes& collectio, hoc est, excifio & projeo in abyssum illam, quo omnia mala tanm a Deo sunt præcipitanda.
units.tr: XXXIX. This is what Paul once observed was the cause of this happening to the Gentile philosophers, in a passage in Romans that can never be remembered enough: When they knew God [after the acknowledgement or demonstration of the existence of God] they did not glorify him as God [they did not cling to him as the fountain of all truth and goodness], nor did they give thanks [they were ungrateful]; but they became vain in their imaginations [they clung to their empty self-love, to their own thoughts and natural speculations, and to petty and fleeting things], and their foolish heart was darkened [all their inner faculties fell into darkness, and so into confusion and [ἀναξίαν] unworthiness], and professing themselves to be wise, they became fools [and through their pride and self-confidence, claiming to have attained wisdom, truth and philosophy, they fell not only far from truth into falsehood but also into madness]. And they changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things [in this error have already fallen those who from Cartesianism have passed over into Spinozism, for whom God is now nothing other than the corrupted intellect itself together with all created things, so that all and each are nothing other with them than God, or the substance of God variously modified and arranged]. Wherefore God also gave them up to the lusts of their hearts [this is the renunciation of all conscience, of the inner principles of the just and the right, and this is an inner Libertinism, which, as it is to be feared, lies hidden in many, and is hindered from breaking out only by certain human considerations. Paul adds that they were given up] to uncleanness and other external vices to be abhorred, which are the very external Libertinism itself; that is, the fruit of all of these fully ripe and mature, after which nothing remains to be harvested except its gathering and collection, that is, its cutting down and throwing into that abyss into which all evils must be cast by God.

units.la: XL. Verum ista omnia de corruptione
units.tr: XL. But all these things about corruption

units.la: ixerit forte nunc aliquis) Theologiam stant, & non Philosophiam, neque adeo s Philosophos. Audi sis, amice Obječta-, si dolosa mente (contra Leges & cognisuperiora) tecum ipse vis agere, ista utie & omnia sequentia, te non spectant: inque modo illa & perge in viis tuis. Agiis cum sinceris, qui si ordine, si in seidide rem aggrediantur, ea utique sic se bere observaturi sunt, quocunque postea nonomine ea indigitari debere contendas. Hæc de nomine cavillatio, hominis est dolosa mente se emendare tergiversantis. Paulum illa quæ diximus nævis Philosophorum accensere, causisque suorum errorum, modo vidimus; & ipli proxime ante tenebrarum hanc & errorum esse originem, ostendimus. Quæ nunc quidem sufiecerint: alibi de nomenclatura forsan disceptabitur. Nunc de rebus agimus quas in nobis interna detegimus meditatione.
units.tr: Perhaps someone will now say that these things belong to Theology and not to Philosophy, nor even to the Philosophers. Hear me, friend Objector: if with a deceitful mind (against the laws and knowledge of higher things) you wish to argue with yourself, then these things and all that follows do not concern you. Go on your way. Let us deal with sincere people, who, if they approach the matter in an orderly way and with an open mind, will certainly observe these things to be so, whatever name you later insist they must be given. This quibbling about names is the mark of a man who, with a deceitful mind, dodges correction. We have just seen that the things we have said are to be counted among the errors of the Philosophers, and that they themselves are the origin of this darkness and error. What has been said may suffice for now; the question of nomenclature will perhaps be debated elsewhere. Now we deal with the things we discover within ourselves through inner meditation.

units.la: Non est unusquisque in hominem duplicem, Theologum puta & Philosophum divisus, sed unum idemque est subjectum, unas easdemque habet facultates, quæ si ægræ sint & morbo corruptæ omnes, velitque tamen iis recte uti, sanentur illæ prius a morbo necesse est. Fateor dari in homine facultates, quarum aliæ Theologica, divina & æterna spectant, aliæ naturalia & caduca, externa, aliæ ideas rerum & philosophica. Sed quia a superioribus & divinis facultatibus pendent inferiores, inter quas & ratio (philosophiæ instrumentum,) illæ si obtenebratæ & corruptæ fuerint, corruptio hæc ad inferiores quoque devolvitur, quæ, quemadmodum eâ inficiuntur & debilitantur, sic nisi illâ sublatâ & sanatâ, in integrum restitui non possunt. Terra illuminatur a Sole & a Luna: sed si Sol obscuratus esset, profecto & lumine Lunæ careret terra, & a legitima Solis restitutione penderet luminis lunaris in integrum restitutio.
units.tr: Man is not divided into two beings, a theologian and a philosopher; he is one and the same subject, with one and the same faculties. If these are all sick and corrupted by disease, and yet one wishes to use them rightly, they must first be healed of the disease. I grant that there are in man faculties of which some relate to divine and eternal things, others to natural and perishable and external things, and others to the ideas of things and to philosophy. But since the lower faculties depend on the higher and divine ones, and reason (the instrument of philosophy) is among the lower, if the higher faculties are darkened and corrupted, this corruption also spreads to the lower ones; and just as these are infected and weakened by it, so they cannot be restored to their full condition unless it is removed and healed. The earth is illuminated by the Sun and by the Moon; but if the Sun were darkened, the earth would certainly lack moonlight too, and the full restoration of the lunar light would depend on the lawful restoration of the sun's light.

units.la: Pictor v. g. gaudet facultatibus sano modo se movendi, beneque videndi, deinde & penicillum icillum sua arte ducendi: at quia haec na facultas caeteris subordinatur, hinc imae sint aegrae, veluti si oculi laesi, exiue tamen a pictore uti recte icones deat, hoc impossibile ei fuerit, recteque rit, facultates priores motus debiti & atem oculorum prius esse incolumes a avatione restituendas: ad quae si objes, hoc medicinam spectare non artem oriam, illumque hac in causa duas illas s confundere inter se; deridendum omnite exhibere: nemo enim nescit utut dica ars cum pictoria non fit confundenpraerequiri tamen necessario ejus opeatque effectum in subjecto aegro, antem artem quamcunque aliam infimam rcere possit. Eodem modo se habet res r animae facultates superiores atque infees: objecta quidem atque artes diversas s utraeque habent, at inferiores suis ut tionibus debite utantur, superiorum srequirunt & efflagitant statum bonum in bonum statum restitutionem. Quid d ea argumenta, quibus modo corrunem Mentis evicimus, non minus tant rationis facultatem, quam quaevis asuperiores, ut cuilibet attente ea confinti evidens fieri poterit? Idem certe enter designat Paulus, quando affirmat, ui Deum glorificatione & laudibus deprosecuti non sunt, factos esse stultos, ratque postea habitus eorum adeo proiosos ac brutos, & ipsi naturae ac ratioleo adversos, ut horribilior rationis corio cogitari non possit.
units.tr: A painter, for example, has the faculties of moving his body in a healthy way, of seeing well, and then of guiding his brush by his art. But since these lower faculties are subordinate to the others, if the eyes are injured, as they would be if the sight were impaired, it would be impossible for him to use his art rightly and to paint correct images. In that case the earlier faculties must first be restored to their proper movement and health, and the eyes must be made whole. If anyone objects that this concerns medicine and not the art of painting, and that I therefore confuse the two, he deserves only ridicule. No one doubts that the medical art is not the same as the painting art; yet the former is necessarily required for the latter to produce its effect in a sick subject, and no other art, however lowly, can accomplish this without it. The same holds for the soul's faculties, higher and lower. Both have different objects and arts; but the lower ones, in order to be used properly for their own functions, require and demand the restoration of the higher ones from bad condition to good. What of those arguments by which we have shown that the faculty of reason in the mind is corrupted no less than any of the higher ones? It will become clear to anyone who considers them carefully. Paul certainly indicates the same thing when he affirms that those who did not glorify God or give thanks to him became fools, and that their later state was so foolish and brutish, and so opposed to nature and reason itself, that nothing more horrible could be imagined in a rational creature.

units.la: XLI. Dicent forte nonnulli, corruptionem esse in abusu libertatis, facultatibus male utentis: ipsas autem facultates non ideo esse corruptas, sed semper integras; abusum tantum earum ex libertate esse tollendum: veluti si quis igne, vino, pecunia, ferro, instrumentis male utens, multa perperam committat, non inde sequitur, res ipsas quibus utitur, ideo esse corruptas, sed mentem tantum abutentis. Infinita undique absurda, & in ipsos pugnans! Nam primo, abutens rebus externis, ipsas utique corrumpit, in quantum illae corruptionis admittendae sunt capaces: ignis negletus extinguitur; vinum indebite potatum perditur & perdit; & sic de caeteris. Secundo, idem magis atque etiam necessario accidit, quando res quarum fit abusus, substantialiter unitae sunt, sive unum componunt systema, cum re abutente, veluti facultates cum libertate unitae sunt. Meretrix ex libertate abutitur suo corpore: an propterea soli libertati corruptio inest, affectibus autem castitas, & corpori integritas? Αυτοχειρ ferrum sibi ipsi ex libertatis non recto usu in jugulum adigit, an propterea sola libertas depravationem patitur, neque corrumpentur cum facultatibus corporeis vita, ipsumque corpus? Quanto magis in rebus moralibus & spiritualibus valet regula, abusus facultatum facultates ipsas corrumpit eaque reddit habitualiter vitiosas & aegras. Denique, utinam qui in libertatis determinationem rejiciunt omne vitium, id faceerent ex animo ; ita ut postea ipsi a liberis suæ regimine abstinentes, eam totam nis boni regiminis auctori, ut sanarentur endam, traderent atque committerent! que enim quicquam est, ultra hoc, quod plenam in integrum restitutionem ab illis gi posset; sed ipsi sane ex hoc exercitio ruptionem suam sibi ipsis non extenuare, ulenter & plenissime condiscerent.
units.tr: XLI. Some will perhaps say that corruption lies in the abuse of liberty, which misuses the faculties, while the faculties themselves are not therefore corrupted but remain always sound; only their abuse arising from liberty must be removed. For example, if someone misuses fire, wine, money, iron or tools and commits many wrongs, it does not follow that the things he uses are therefore corrupted, but only the mind of the one who misuses them. What absurdities on every side, and self-contradictory! For first, one who abuses external things certainly corrupts them, insofar as they are capable of corruption: neglected fire goes out; wine drunk immoderately is wasted and wastes the drinker; and so on with the rest. Second, the same happens even more, and indeed necessarily, when the things that are abused are substantially united, or form one system, with the abusing thing, as the faculties are united with liberty. A prostitute abuses her body through her freedom: is corruption therefore present in freedom alone, while chastity belongs to the affections and integrity to the body? The self-murderer [αὐτόχειρ] drives iron into his own throat through a wrong use of his liberty: does liberty alone then suffer depravity, and does life not fall with the bodily faculties, and the body itself? All the more does the rule hold in moral and spiritual matters: the abuse of faculties corrupts the faculties themselves and makes them habitually vicious and diseased. Finally, I wish that those who throw all vice onto the determination of liberty would do so sincerely; then, abstaining from freedom's own government, they would hand over and commit the whole of it to the author of good government, so that they might be healed. For what is there beyond this which could bring about full restoration? Rather, from such an exercise they would learn, not diminish, their own corruption, and would learn it most fully and truly.

units.la: XLII. Quod si quis scire desideret, qua re consistat illa facultatum corruptio, ei & otem quatenus ad verum speculat, ei & oi sani & divinum lumen ad hoc perspicilum dari deberent, iis enim solis quæque inordinata sunt, detegi possunt. In im tamen crassiore & palpabiliore modo quod postulatur nominare licebit, intellectus tenebras, contractionem, arctitatem, inolentiam & stupiditatem, incrassation & ad pinguia & spissa conformation, indeque dispositionem ad ideisandum : mihi loquendum est) incomposita, chieras, & mille absurda, nullatenus cum is Dei rerumque naturis conformia. sed ut rem ipsam aliquatenus percipienn possem exhibere, quia ardua est & icilis, altius equidem resumenda esset, ctiusque pertractanda ac digerenda, m nostrum hic ferat institutum. Conabor lominus, adjuvante Deo, hic saltem subintre de sublimi ista materia quaedam quam vissime velut per aphorismos dispositta.
units.tr: XLII. If anyone wishes to know in what this corruption of the faculties consists, then, as far as it can be seen by the truth, the healthy eyes of the mind and the divine light would need to be given for this inspection, since only by these can things that are disordered be detected. Yet, in a cruder and more tangible manner, which is what is asked, we may name the darkness of the intellect, contraction, narrowness, sluggishness and stupidity, a thickening and conformity to what is fat and dense, and from that a disposition to think (I must speak as I can) in a disordered way, with confusion and a thousand absurdities, in no way conformed to the natures of God and of things. But so that I might present the matter itself in some measure to be understood, since it is difficult and obscure, it would indeed have to be taken up from higher ground and handled and arranged at greater length than our present purpose allows. Nevertheless, with God's help, I will try here at least to set down briefly, almost as aphorisms, some points about this sublime matter.

units.la: XLIII. 1. Fecit nos Deus res vividas & itantes, ut donaret nos, vel potius nos vestiret & induéret, formis tum sui ipsius, tum rerum omnium.
units.tr: XLIII. 1. God made us living and moving beings, so that he might endow us, or rather clothe and invest us, with the forms both of himself and of all things.

units.la: 2. Modi quibus voluit Deus nos rerum formis indui, sunt duplices: primus modus est realis, vividus, efficax: alter umbratilis, pictURARIUS, superficiarius. Utroque modo formà Dei & formis rerum possumus investiri & superindui.
units.tr: 2. There are two ways in which God willed us to be clothed with the forms of things: the first is real, living and effective; the other is shadowy, pictorial and superficial. In either way we can be invested and overlaid with the form of God and the forms of things.

units.la: 3. Id quod in nobis istas formas recipit, iisve induitur, aut in illas quasi vertitur, vocatur generaliter intellectus, qui, quoniam est cogitatio sui & eorum quæ actu in se siunt, conscia, quando formis rerum induitur, eo ipso ies scit & novit. Si cera efset suorum actuum conscia, & verteretur in figuram Alexandri, noslet tunc figuram Alexandri.
units.tr: 3. That which receives these forms within us, or is clothed with them, or is somehow turned into them, is generally called the intellect. Since it is a thought conscious of itself and of those things that are actually being done within it, when it is clothed with the forms of things it thereby knows and perceives them. If wax were conscious of its own actions, and were turned into the figure of Alexander, it would then know the figure of Alexander.

units.la: 4. Intellectus pro ratione diversitatis objectorum, seu formarum recipiendarum, est diversæ etiam capacitatis: & distingui potest in divinum, qui intelligentia dici potest, estque veluti capacitas quædam. Mentis intima & immensa, divinis formis recipiendis apta: in humanum vel ideale aut rationalem pro (a) ideis rerum; & ani-
units.tr: 4. The intellect, according to the diversity of its objects or of the forms to be received, also has a diverse capacity, and it can be distinguished into the divine, which may be called intelligence and is as it were a certain capacity of the innermost and immense mind, apt for receiving divine forms; and into the human, or ideal, or rational, relating to (a) the ideas of things; and the soul...

units.la: (a) Nota per ideas sæpius hic & in sequentibus specialius intelligi eas rerum formas quæ in intellectu actiwo sunt, & quas pictVRIS assimilamus, atque a divinis nec non & sensualibus & vividis perceptionibus distinguimus. Interdum tamen & his (quia alii id etiam fecerunt & cum illis nonnunquam loquendum) his inquam ultimis interdum nomen ideæ damus: quod ex ipso loco sine ambiguitate ut pateret, data est opera. nimalem sive sensualem, pro externis objectis: hi duo sunt menti velut superficiarii; ut unusquisque diversò se habeat modo, quibus (b) alio loco.
units.tr: (a) Note that by "ideas" here and in what follows, more often and more specifically, I mean those forms of things that exist in the active intellect and that we liken to pictures, and that we distinguish from divine perceptions and from sensual and vivid perceptions. Sometimes, however, because others have also done this and we must sometimes speak their language, I give the name "idea" to these last ones as well. I have taken care that this should be clear from the context and free of ambiguity. The animal or sensual intellect is for external objects. These two are, as it were, superficial to the mind, so that each one takes on a different mode, which (b) I discuss elsewhere.

units.la: 5. Unde patet, intellectum, quisquis sit, divinus, rationalis, animalis, esse primo omnium passivum sive recipiendarum se formarum capacem, ejusque naturæ, t admittere illas in se possit.
units.tr: 5. From this it is clear that the intellect, whatever kind it is, divine, rational or animal, is first of all passive, that is, capable of receiving forms and of admitting them into itself, and this is its nature.

units.la: 6. Sed quia intellectus est cogitatio viens, adeoque & actus habens, sive agens, inc & activus est omnis intellectus, divinus, rationalis, animalis. Et unusquisque ibi attendens, satis experiri potest, ubi quid percipere vult, quomodo sese intus gitet ac moveat ad se adaptandum conformandumque quarumvis rerum formis aut deis. Est intellectus tanquam Proteus illeabulæ, aut Vertumnus, qui in omnia vertitur. Est veluti agilis comœdus, qui omnes res, actiones, personas, regias pariter & viliores, ita imitari enititur, ut earum ormas omnes in se apparere faciat. Sed hic autela adhibenda est sedulo, ne concelus ille se revera etiam credat esse regem, ut se reipsa putet illa omnia esse atque habere ex sua activitate, ad quæ repræsentandam la adspirat.
units.tr: 6. But because the intellect is a thinking power, and so has an act, or is an agent, every intellect, divine, rational or animal, is also active. Anyone who attends to this can well experience how, when he wishes to perceive something, the intellect stirs and moves itself within, to adapt and conform itself to the forms or images of whatever things. The intellect is like Proteus of the fable, or Vertumnus, who turns himself into everything. It is like a nimble actor who strives to imitate all things, actions and persons, royal and humble alike, so that he makes their forms all appear in himself. But here great care must be taken, lest that conceited actor really believe that he is the king, and think that all those things truly are, and have, from his own activity, the things he aspires to represent.

units.la: XLIV. 7. Quando agitur de intellectu vide, realiter & efficaciter investiendo & inluendo rerum formis, earum maxime, quæ ipsius intellectus natura sunt sublimiores, tunc omnis intellectus activitas ad hoc est pror-sus sus inepta, nisi tantum hoc agat, ut se quiete & passive offerat formæ atque subjecto ipsum investituro & transformaturo. Atque hinc patet, intellectum nullum creatum posse se vivide transformare in formam Dei, ejusve attributorum aut proprietatum quarumvis, aut posse se ipsum, quacunque activitate se moveat & versét, ulla forma Dei reali & efficaci investire. Hoc si faceret, ipse esset aut Deus, aut factor Dei. Forma enim realis, vivida & efficax Dei, est ipse Deus. Adeoque ipse Deus solus est qui se intellectui creato insinuans & uniens, formam sui vividam, realem & efficacem ei imprimat, eumve illa investiat & superinduat, quantum quidem ab Omnipotente fieri potest in subjecto creato, Dei admittendi receptivo & capaci. Hinc Paulus, (a) Transformamur ad imaginem gloriæ Domini quemadmodum a Spiritu Domini: & (b) Qui adhæret Domino, Spiritus unus est cum illo, & plura alia. Atque in his mirabilia vitæ æternæ continentur. Ergo Intellectus noster divinus, sive ad divinas formas vivide & realiter recipiendas factus, excepto actu quo se offert Deo transformandum, mere passivus est.
units.tr: XLIV. 7. When we speak of the intellect seeing, that is, really and effectively being invested and imbued with the forms of things, and especially those forms that are more exalted in the nature of the intellect itself, then all activity of the intellect is entirely unfit for this, unless it only does this: that it offers itself quietly and passively to the form and the subject that is going to invest and transform it. And from this it is clear that no created intellect can vividly transform itself into the form of God, or into any of his attributes or properties, nor can it, by whatever activity it moves and turns itself, invest itself with any real and effective form of God. If it did this, it would itself be God, or the maker of God. For the real, vivid and effective form of God is God himself. Therefore God alone, insinuating and uniting himself to the created intellect, imprints on it his own vivid, real and effective form, and invests and clothes it with that form, as far as the Almighty can do this in a created subject that is receptive and capable of admitting God. Hence Paul: We are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord; and He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him; and many other passages. In these are contained the wonders of eternal life. Therefore our divine intellect, insofar as it is made to receive divine forms vividly and really, apart from the act by which it offers itself to be transformed by God, is purely passive.

units.la: XLV. 8. De transformatione reali intellectus animalis in
units.tr: XLV. 8. On the real transformation of the animal intellect into

units.la: X L V. 8. Quando agitur de intellectu vivide & efficaciter investiendo sive induendo formis rerum, intellectus natura & dignitate quamvis inferiorum; intellectus tamen sui sola activitate ad hoc ipsum etiam ineptus est; sed jungatur oportet ea moles. corporea cui unitus est, rerum objectis, eorum effluviis, quæ in illam agant: & unc per vim quâ Deus res uniri, certifin sese pollere potentiis voluit, immuar intellectus in formas rerum, quateillæ ad ipsum cum corporibus unitum ctant. Et hæc quidem non opus est hic luctius explanari: exempla vero eorum is proflant. Quisquis vult v. g. vivide recipere formam solis, luminis, plantam, animalium &c. Is non velit solum, c omni sua activitate tantum conetur in formas illas effingere; sed & corpus quole & oculos debite ad objecta appropiniet: atque tunc realiter, vivide & efficiter formis eorum, quatenus ad ipsum ectant investitur, sine ulteriore sui actitate. Hic intellectus est animalis, qui infusionis evitandæ causa non (nisi raro) omine intellectus venit indigitandus, sed receptio sensualis aptius dicitur. Estque huis hæc norma: Intellectus animalis, sive receptio sensualis, quatenus realiter, vivide efficaciter formis rerum investiendus est, accepto actu quo organa corporea objectis applicantur, mere passivus est.
units.tr: XLV. 8. When we speak of the intellect being vividly and effectively invested or clothed with the forms of things, the intellect, although inferior in nature and dignity, is nevertheless unfit for this by its own activity alone. Rather, the corporeal mass to which it is united must be joined to the objects of things and to their effluvia, which act upon it. And by the power by which God wished that things be united, and that they have a certain power in themselves, the intellect is changed into the forms of things, insofar as they are present to it while it is united with bodies. There is no need to explain this more fully here, but examples will make it clear. Whoever wishes, for instance, to receive vividly the form of the sun, of light, of a plant, of animals, and so on, must not only try, by all his activity, to fashion those forms in himself, but must also bring his body and eyes appropriately near the objects. Then he is really, vividly and effectively invested with their forms, insofar as they are present to him, without any further activity of his own. This is the animal intellect, which, to avoid confusion, is rarely called intellect at all, but is more fittingly called sensual reception. The rule for it is this: The animal intellect, or sensual reception, insofar as it is to be really, vividly and effectively invested with the forms of things, is purely passive, once the act has been accepted by which the bodily organs are applied to the objects.

units.la: XLVI. 9. Quando agitur de investiendo intellectu ideis seu formis rerum pictis, & umbratilibus, modoque non vivido & efficaci, sed sterili, mereque speculativo & umbratili icturæ instar, sive formæ illæ sint rerum divinarum intellecti sublimiorum, sive sint rationis humanæ in pictas rerum æqualium, sive infimarum; tunc intellectus activitate, potentia, industriaque c 4 & contentione sua potest sese vertere in illas formas ; non equidem reales & veras , sed pictas , ubi agat modo repraesentante, & vt luti fingente aut pingente ; quemadmodum homo aliquis sic sese potest vertere in alium, non quidem ut fiat alius ; sed ut eum exprimat & repraesentet voce , gestu,ingressu, modo agendi & ratiocinandi, & similibus. Hic intellectus activus est , & dicitur intellectus humanus , sive ratio humana. Atque hic est modus quo ratio ideas rerum in se ipsa excitat , conamine nempe suo sese itaque disponens , ut se vertat & transformet in formas rerum , sive eas sibi superinduat, aut, ut sic loquar , ad earum figuras & modos sese accommodet. Hic igitur est intellectus activus & active ad formas illas se habens.
units.tr: XLVI. 9. When we speak of the intellect being invested with ideas or forms of things that are painted and shadowy, and not in a vivid and effective mode but in a barren, purely speculative and shadowy manner, like a picture; whether these forms are of the more exalted things of God, or of the things of human reason, whether equal or lowest; then the intellect, by its activity, power, industry and effort, can turn itself into those forms. Not indeed real and true forms, but painted ones, where it acts in a representing mode and as if fashioning or painting. In the same way a man can turn himself into another man, not so that he becomes the other, but so that he expresses and represents him by voice, gesture, bearing, manner of acting and reasoning, and the like. This intellect is active, and is called the human intellect, or human reason. This is the way in which reason excites ideas of things within itself, namely by its own effort, disposing itself so that it turns and transforms itself into the forms of things, or superinduces them upon itself, or, to speak thus, adapts itself to their figures and modes. Therefore this intellect is active, and stands actively toward those forms.

units.la: XLVII. XLVII. ro. De illarum formarum seu idearum proprietatibus, & quomodo eae a realibus distinguantur, agetur (a) alibi. Sed hic observabimus, dari conditiones sine quibus ratio sese in rerum formas recte vertere non potest : quibus conditionibus igitur sese, dum agit, accommodet oportet, si bene velit agere. Ita conditiones praecipue sunt ut illa nec totum , nec praecipuum exercitii mentis tempus aut officium occurpet ; neve etiam se gerat ut solidum quid; sed ut temporis exercitiique partem aliquam lem eamque accessoriam & propter aliud quam se, peragat velut obiter. Hoc velimus permittat ratio Intellectum passivo-divinum, superioresque facultates saepius, praecipue, ue, ardentius, totasque uniri & exerceri m Deo, ejusque lumine, amore, deliciis, miratione, laudibus: ipsa vero interdum, veluti per lusum mentis, picturas Deo, quam arcus triumphales in se efformet & agat, imaginibus divinorum operum concoratas, ut ex omnibus illis iconibus & igiebus a se excitatis, recurrat ad Deum, iginale ipsum, cui congratuletur de opera suis, deque industria quam ab ipso habet ad ea in se depingenda, ad glorificandum Auctorem omnium.
units.tr: XLVII. 10. The properties of those forms or ideas, and how they are distinguished from real ones, will be treated elsewhere. But here we shall observe that there are conditions without which reason cannot rightly turn itself into the forms of things. Therefore, if it wishes to act well, it must accommodate itself to these conditions as it acts. The chief of these conditions is that this does not occupy the whole or the principal time or duty of the exercise of the mind, nor does it conduct itself as something solid, but carries on as a part of the time and exercise, and a small and subordinate part, and for the sake of something other than itself, as it were in passing. Reason should allow this, that the passive-divine intellect and the higher faculties are more often, chiefly, more ardently, and wholly united to and exercised in God, and in his light, love, delights, wonder and praises. But reason itself, sometimes, as if in a game of the mind, should form and work in itself pictures and triumphal arches, adorned with images of the divine works, so that from all those icons and shadows that it has excited, it may return to God, the original himself, and rejoice with him in the works, and in the diligence which it has from him for depicting these things within itself, for glorifying the Author of all.

units.la: XLVIII. II. Libertas, facultas, qua caeteræ facultates ab homine ad placitum exercentur, & objectis applicantur, regit intellectum in Mente divinum, humanum, imalem, ita ut quemlibet ex iis quando ad objecta seu exercitia admoveat, aut iis removeat. Hinc intellectus status cum de aut cum vituperio & culpa hominis mutari potest. Desiderium autem est stimulus intellectus omnis, quo veluti impetu llitur, enitítur, incenditur ad se convertendum & transformandum in formas rerum, ad se disponendum & offerendum cautransformationis sufficienti, ut per eam ma cupita investiatur. Hoc quando adicitur intellectus, tunc desiderium verti-
units.tr: XLVIII. 11. Liberty, the faculty by which the other faculties are exercised by a man at will and applied to objects, governs the intellect in the mind, whether divine, human or animal, so that whenever it brings any of them to objects or exercises, or removes them from them. Hence the state of the intellect can be changed, with praise or with blame and guilt on the part of the man. Desire, however, is the goad of every intellect, by which it is, as it were, driven with impulse, strives, and is kindled to turn itself and transform itself into the forms of things, to dispose itself and offer itself to a transformation sufficient for it, so that through it the desired thing may be invested. When this is added to the intellect, then desire turns

units.la: in acquiescentiam, quae est unitio ipsa n forma veritatis possessa, quaeque in iis consensu medullas ipsas, ut sic loquar, omnia penetrante sese insinuat & expandit foras autem se prodit per asseverationes, cisiones & judicia affirmativa. Tuncque talis
units.tr: into acquiescence, which is the very union with the possessed form of truth. It insinuates itself and spreads through those judgements, penetrating their very marrow, so to speak, and it shows itself outwardly through assertions, affirmations and affirmative judgements. And such a person

units.la: XLVIII. II. De habitudine libertatis, de fiderii & acquiescentiæ ad intellectum, ut bene se habeat. talis anima scit indubitato se non falli, quia est in unione, in communicatione cum Deo, cujus impressiones in se poslidet. Atque adeo, quemadmodum, quando Deus desideravit ideas rerum in intellectu suo arbitrario & activo excitare, illasque per omnipotentiam suam excitavit prout voluit, tunc desiderium ejus acquievit in adeptione illarum formarum; siquidem tunc habuit id quod voluit & quale voluit; ita etiam quando Mens acquisivit veras ideas sive formas rerum quas desideravit, quia illæ formæ seu ideæ, si quidem veræ sunt, ideis divinis sunt conformes; desiderium Mentis, ad Dei imaginem factum, ejusque impressiones retinens, non potest non fieri acquiescens: quandoquidem etiam ad hoc expresse a Deo conditum est; non ut semper maneat desiderium torquens & inquietum, sed ut veratur in acquiescentiam per adeptionem veritatis quaesitæ. Præterea quia videt hic in se facultatem eam, quam habet imitandi intellectum Dei arbitrarium ejusque ideas, eandemque cognoscit, hinc omnia ista (sui & Dei) inter se momento comparans, in eorum acquiescit assimilatione. Solummodo animadvertendum est, acquiescentiam debere a libertate concedi vel dirigi aut exerceri pro eo modo, cujusmodi est veritas, sive pro ut est idea & forma, qua mens tunc occupatur: quæsi sit summa, realis, viva, laxanda sunt fræna acquiescentiæ ultra omnes si fieri posset modos; si picta, umbratiliique; tunc accessoria tantum & veluti ludilibunda & transitoria acquiescentia adhiida est ; eodemque modo si de rerum mis aut impressionibus , vividis quidem realibus, sed transeuntibus tamen & correis quaestio fuerit. Alioqui acquiescentia oluta, totalis, vel etiam praecipua, hisultimis duabus , in praejudicium seu rimentum sublimiorum si concedatur ; ens ista foret ordinis perturbatio & mentlapsus.
units.tr: XLVIII. II. On the relation of freedom, of faith and acquiescence to the intellect, so that it is well ordered. Such a soul knows without doubt that it cannot be deceived, because it is in union and communion with God, whose impressions it possesses within itself. And so, just as when God wished to stir up ideas of things in his arbitrary and active intellect, and stirred them up by his omnipotence as he willed, his desire then rested in the attainment of those forms, since he then had what he willed and as he willed it; so too, when the Mind has acquired true ideas or forms of the things it desired, these forms or ideas, if they are true, are conformed to the divine ideas. The Mind's desire, made in the image of God and retaining his impressions, cannot but become acquiescent, since it has also been expressly designed by God for this end: not that it should always remain a tormenting and restless desire, but that it should turn into acquiescence through the attainment of the truth sought. Moreover, because it sees in itself that faculty by which it can imitate the arbitrary intellect of God and his ideas, and recognises that faculty, it compares all these things (of itself and of God) with one another at once, and rests in their likeness. It should only be noted that acquiescence must be granted, directed, or exercised by freedom in the manner that suits the kind of truth, that is, according to the idea and form with which the mind is then occupied. If the form is supreme, real, and living, the reins of acquiescence must be loosed beyond all measure, if that were possible; if it is painted and shadowy, then only an incidental, as it were playful and transitory, acquiescence should be given to it; and in the same way if the question concerns images or impressions of things, vivid indeed and real, but nonetheless fleeting and changeable. Otherwise, if an acquiescence that is excessive, total, or even principal is granted to these last two kinds, to the prejudice or hindrance of the higher things, that would be a disorder of the being and a fall of the mind.

units.la: XLIX. 12. Adeoque si quis intellectum ultatesque superiores minus ardenter nec ...
units.tr: XLIX. 12. Therefore, if anyone offers his intellect and higher wills less ardently nor...

units.la: de divinis offerat objectis, eaque tandem ligat ut intellectum activum totus exeat, spectaturus ludos & comoedias eius, missurusque, vel etiam ardenter jenixu-, ut actor ista suus formas, spectacula ideas omnis generis ipsi exhibeat feque omnia vertat ; ecce , lumen divinum lectum , ab illo subtrahitur ; & tunc acedus ille in petulantem & lascivum rionem aut cinaedum jam immutatus, tad instar Icari alas sibi quibus in coelum isferretur , machinatus effet , turpiter itur & procidit : atque ex lapsu & terosior evadit, & vero vulneratus, man, claudus, tortuosus , maculosus, coe, deformis , aeger ; praetereaque (ut illaccidit qui ex alto cadunt) stupidus & nsibilis, sic ut tot mala sua ne sentiat qui 1 miser ; sed nihil ea ducat , imo velit uc perpetuo histrionem agere & repraare rerum tam divinarum quam humaim admirabiles decorasque formas. Quae quidem in re eodem modo, imo & turpius: se gerit, ac si monstrosus aliquis Æsopus, crine rubê, niger ore, brevis pede, lumine luscus, lingua blæsus, pectore curvus, mente fatuus, repræsentare vellet atque induere formas hominum dotibus corporis, vultus, sermonis, gestuum majestate, mentisque præstantia excellentium: aut si forte reginæ alicujus formosæ, sapientis, admirabilisque in se personam, gestus, verba, habitum & regimen exhibere conaretur; ubi tamen revera præter monstrosos, deformes ac ridiculos motus ac gestus, cum repræsentandis similitudinem nullam habentes, nihil produceret: quandoquidem quomodocunque sese vertat, impossibile tamen ei sit, ullam vel minimam rem decori exemplaris imitari.
units.tr: to divine objects, and at last binds them so that the whole of his active intellect goes out, to watch its plays and comedies, and sends them forth, or even eagerly lends them, as an actor who presents to it those forms, spectacles, and ideas of every kind, and turns himself entirely into them; behold, the divine light is withdrawn from him; and then that man, now changed into a wanton and lascivious buffoon or catamite, having devised for himself wings like Icarus by which he might be carried to heaven, falls disgracefully and tumbles down. From the fall he emerges more wretched, truly wounded, maimed, lame, crooked, spotted, filthy, deformed, and sick; and moreover (as happens to those who fall from a height) stupid and insensible, so that the wretch does not feel his many evils; but he counts them as nothing, and indeed wishes to keep acting the actor forever and to represent the admirable and graceful forms of things, both divine and human. In this matter he behaves in the same way, or even more shamefully, as if some monstrous Aesop, red-haired, black-faced, short-footed, one-eyed, tongue-tied, hunch-chested, foolish in mind, wished to represent and put on the forms of men, with the bodily gifts, the countenance, speech, and dignity of gesture and the excellence of mind of the outstanding; or if perhaps he tried to exhibit the person, gestures, words, bearing, and rule of some beautiful, wise, and admirable queen; where in fact he would produce nothing but monstrous, deformed, and ridiculous movements and gestures, having no likeness to what he is representing; since, however he turns himself, it is impossible for him to imitate even the smallest part of the grace of the model.

units.la: Talis jam factus est noster & omnium hominum intellectus activus, ratio nostra, histrionalis ille ardelio, qui solus in anima nostra scenam obtinere voluit, nec vero pati in quiete & pausa, ut admiranda sapientia Dei sua in nobis ipsa exhiberet divina spectacula. Agyrtam similem jam quisque domi suæ, in proprio suo cerebro, in glandula, si vis, pineali habet, fovet, admiratur, audit, sequitur: & hoc est quod sapientiam vocant & reputant. Sed quoniam unusquisque ejusmodi gesticulator non valet omnia pro genio suo repræsentare, binc quivis sibi personam aut rem certam agendam assumit, in quam se totum vertat, & ubi exerceat; cæteris aliis prætermissis: unde (pro diversa quam uam quisque sibi assumsit forma) hominum lii sunt (vel Scriptura teste) bruta, lupi, serpentes; alii (ut dicebat Epictetus) venenes, intestina & partes pudendae; alii lineae, anguli & circuli, motus, figurae, numeri, a + bb—cc ꝏ dd; alii chimaerae metaphysicae & transcendentales aut critici cortices; lii tria elementa, vortices, machinae, alii alia similia. Ob quas quidem formas assumptas esse magnificiunt, sibique belle admodum videntur rerum divinarum atque naturalium naturas ideis suis debite exprimere, idque clare & distincte percipere: quando tamen coram Deo, luminosa veritate, tormisque & naturis rerum veris, monstrosae tantum & turpes chimaerae sunt, a vero & decoro rerum statu infinite abludentes, & non nisi cum genere illo stultitiae quo unusquisque est affectus, & forte cum nonnullis ex sordibus & deformitatibus statūs in quo cum caeteris jacet, conformes. Neque enim magis potest ulla in se recte repraesentare tenebrosus, depravatus & tortuosus intellectus; aut etiam vere scire an faciat erronea an vera, quam historio noster ridiculus & portentosus, qui in tenebris gesticulans, neque videre potest suam in omnibus deformitatem & turpitudinem, propudiosamque motuum inconcinnitatem & absurditatem, neque novit gestus suos formasque iis quae repraesentanda suscepit adversari magis quam congruere. Et tamen mirabilia sibi facere videtur, & vel angelicas posituras, res, actiones, formarum & gestuum quibus se induit elegantia superare: quod sine
units.tr: Such, now, has become our active intellect, and that of all men: our reason, that restless buffoon, who alone wished to hold the stage in our soul, and would not suffer, at rest and in pause, that the admirable wisdom of God should display in us its divine spectacles. Each of us has at home, in his own brain, in the pineal gland if you like, such a mountebank; he cherishes him, admires him, listens to him, and follows him; and this is what they call and reckon wisdom. But since not every such gesticulator can represent everything according to his own bent, each of them takes upon himself a certain person or thing to act, into which he turns himself entirely, and where he exercises himself, the rest being passed over. Hence (according to the different form each has taken upon himself) some men are (as Scripture bears witness) beasts, wolves, serpents; others (as Epictetus said) are gut-bellies, intestines, and shameful parts; others are lines, angles, and circles, motions, figures, numbers, a + bb—cc ꝏ dd; others are metaphysical and transcendental chimeras or critical husks; others are the three elements, vortices, machines, and others other similar things. On account of these forms they have assumed, they boast, and it seems to them very fine that they express the natures of divine and natural things duly through their ideas, and perceive this clearly and distinctly; when yet, before God, the luminous truth, and the true natures of things, they are only monstrous and shameful chimeras, infinitely at odds with the true and seemly state of things, and conformed only to that kind of folly by which each is affected, and perhaps to some of the filth and deformities of the condition in which he lies along with the others. For no darkened, depraved, and crooked intellect can represent anything correctly in itself, nor truly know whether it is making errors or truths, any more than our ridiculous and monstrous buffoon, who, gesticulating in darkness, cannot see his own deformity and foulness in everything, nor the shameful incongruity and absurdity of his movements, nor does he know that his gestures and forms are more opposed than fitting to the things he has undertaken to represent. And yet he seems to himself to be doing marvellous things, and even to surpass the angelic poses, things, actions, and the elegance of the forms and gestures with which he clothes himself; which without

units.la: — (no further notes) rum, quia, ut inquit, quidquid intelligs cum a Deo habeam ut intelligam, procul dubio recte intelligo, nec in eo potest fieri ut fallar: hæc quidem vera esse dent de intelligentia mentis primævæ, aut de ea quæ post rebellionem, pravitatem, ægritudinem admissam, inde sanata esset, & in primum statum restituta: at non ita de mente quæ revera ægra est & corrupta, nec tamen adhuc de se sananda meditata est, nedum inde fit restituta: hæc enim quicquid pro suo illo statu & captu intelligit, cum id non a Deo, sed a delirio morbi sui habeat ut taliter intelligat, procul dubio prave & defectuose intelligit, nec in eo fieri potest ne fallatur. Nam simulac desiderium corruptum amoris proprii, stimulat intellectum ægrum & monstrosum, ut ad delectationem ipsi pariat fœtus live ideas suas, & formarum quarumvis assumptione coram eo gesticuletur, is protinus pro morbosa sua indole meras & absurdas chimæras, ludosque ineptos coram illo non potest non fingere, qui non Dei & divinorum ejus operum, sed propriæ suæ stultitiæ & ægritudinis maxime sint repræsentativi, & quibus dum desiderium sese suaviter atque acquiescenter delectat, hoc ipso formam erroris constituit. Cujus erroris punctum saliens est cupiditas corrupta gesticulationum intellectus ægri, qui ex activitate monstrosa & vitiata materiam suppeditat chimæricam, quam admittens delectabiliter & acquiescenter desiderium, dicitur complete errorem admittere, atque adeo errare actualiter.
units.tr: — rum, because, as he says, whatever I understand, since I have it from God that I should understand it, I undoubtedly understand rightly, nor can it happen in this that I am deceived: these things are indeed true of the understanding of the primeval mind, or of that which, after the rebellion, depravity, and sickness had been incurred, was then healed and restored to its first state; but not so of the mind which is really sick and corrupt, and has not yet thought of healing itself, much less been restored: for whatever such a mind understands according to its own state and capacity, since it does not have from God, but from the delirium of its sickness, that it understands in this way, it undoubtedly understands wrongly and defectively, nor can it happen in this that it is not deceived. For as soon as the corrupt desire of self-love stirs the sick and monstrous intellect, so that it may bring forth offspring for its delight, that is, its ideas, and gesticulates before it by assuming whatever forms, it at once cannot but feign, in keeping with its morbid disposition, mere absurd chimeras and foolish plays before it, which represent not God and his divine works, but its own folly and sickness; and in which, while the desire pleasantly and acquiescently delights itself, it thereby constitutes the form of error. The salient point of this error is the corrupt appetite for the gesticulations of the sick intellect, which, out of its monstrous and vitiated activity, supplies a chimerical matter; and when the desire admits this with delight and acquiescence, it is said to admit error completely, and so to err in actuality.

units.la: Nota: text printed in full as above. er vel, si sic loquendum, etiam formalir. Ita ut, 6. Cartesius male statuit, id od formam erroris constituit, consistere ea privatione quae inest in liberi arbitrii on recto usu, quando nempe liberum artrium judicandi facultatem ad obscura vel gnota extendit: cum tamen in liberi arbiii non recto usu sola privatio illa inesse possit quae formam erroris moralis, sive culpa, ion autem erroris philosophici seu logici circa rerum ideas, constituit. Privatio multiplex in errore inest, & cum eo concurrit. Intellectus lumine primaevo privatus est, privatus item vi qua pollebat imitandi Deum in idearum activa excitatione. Desiderium ideifandi, privatum est scopo legitimo (glorificatione & delectatione in Deo) cui turpis cupiditas substituta est. Ipsae formae intellectus activitate & vertibilitate excitatae, privatae sunt decora & ordinata similitudine & conformitate cum ideis Dei & naturis rerum; & praeter figmenta nugacia ut plurimum, nihil sunt. Jam si mens hic subsisteret, nec istis largiretur acquiescentiam & complacentiam, (quae judicium internum atque affirmatio sunt,) sed displiceret ei intellectum suum istiusmodi chimaerarum tenebrosarum adeo esse vel invita illa feraeem, ut furentis histrionis instar vel invita mente gesticuletur; intus continuo garriat, fesequeque in omnes sine ordine formas vel relustante animo convertat adeo, ut nullus sui intellectus, omniumque actuum ejus, vel per diem unum Dominus sit & compos in fosolidum; tunc non dicenda effet Mens errare: quanquam enim tunc intus latet materia erroris,, illiusque materiæ forma deformis, formarum absurdarum inconcinnitas; attamen non adesset error approbative & complete, quippe qui demum adest quando in acquiescentia & delectatione interna admittitur. Et hæc est proprie & præcise forma actus erronei, quando videlicet acquiescentia nostra, quæ pro formis ideisque divinis & veris facta est, præsentiam & aspectum fictionum nostrarum, ludorumque ægri intellectus nostri activi, cum voluptate & placito sustinet & admittit. 7. Gratis etiam & male affumit loco dicto Cartefius, fe & quotquot in ejusmodi cum eo statu sunt, capaces esse claræ & distinctæ perceptionis, idearumque de rerum naturis clararum & diftinctarum, nec non agnoscendi quid fit aut quando adsit illa claritas, quod absolute falsum est, quamdiu facultates mentis non sunt fanatæ. Recurrent (opinor) instantiæ de ideis rerum mathematicarum, de quibus etsi aliquoties quædam monui, mox tamen ea addam quæ difficultatem & jactantiam funditus eliminent: nunc dicam tantum, illas non esse naturæ rerumve ideas; sed ideas solum corticum naturæ, quæ sub illis latens ipsis prorsus est incognita. 8. Tandem in dicta Cartefii Meditatione, quæ sæpe ibi occurrunt, libertas, intellectus, voluntas, judicandi vel affirmandi facultas & ejusmodi, quamvis clara per fe vulgo quidem putentur, revera tamen sunt naturæ abditæ & valde ignootæ atque obscuræ; unde qui his utuntur ulteriori explicatione, in multos inscii idunt errores, & multa garriunt de erroc vero, quæ tamen non assequuntur. Res ista nisi fallor & clarius percipientur ea quæ diximus de libertate facultates ad itrium objectis aut exercitio applicante: desiderio (quæ veluti prima voluntatis s quædam est) intellectum ad actum stilante; de acquiescentia, quæ est desiden completum voluntasque terminata, rmatioque & judicium internum: ut & intellectu sese activitate sua in formas ifvis vertente. Hæc enim in se quisque opria experientia fere palpare potest, madmodum & omnia quæ de corruptiohactenus diximus, modo (quod cogor essario repetere) quis juxta leges atque nita tria prima, cum ordine & sinceritanentis a se & in se rem aggrediatur. Cæis ut nil a nobis hic dicitur, ita quæ illi um occasione dicturi sunt, ad nos minime tare censemus.
units.tr: Note: the text is printed in full as above, or, if one may so speak, also formally. Thus, 6. Descartes wrongly holds that the form of error consists in that privation which is present in the non-right use of free will, namely when one extends the faculty of judging freely to obscure or unknown things. Yet in the non-right use of free will only that privation can be present which constitutes the form of moral error, that is fault, and not of philosophical or logical error concerning the ideas of things. Multiple privation is present in error and concurs with it. The intellect is deprived of its primal light, and likewise of the power by which it could imitate God in the active excitation of ideas. The desire to understand is deprived of its legitimate end (glorifying and delighting in God), and a base lust has been substituted in its place. The forms themselves, roused by the activity and mutability of the intellect, are deprived of the becoming and orderly likeness and conformity with the ideas of God and the natures of things; apart from trifling fictions for the most part, they are nothing. Now if the mind were to stop here, and did not grant these forms acquiescence and complacency (which are inner judgment and affirmation), but were displeased that its intellect is so driven by these dark chimeras, even against its will, that it gestures like a raving actor, chattering inwardly without end and turning its thoughts this way and that without order, with the mind resisting, so that not one part of its intellect, nor any of its acts, is master of itself in solidity for a single day, then the mind should not be said to err. For although the matter of error then lies hidden within, and that matter has its deformed form, the incongruity of absurd forms, yet error would not be present in approval and completely, since it is present only when it is admitted in inner acquiescence and delight. And this is properly and precisely the form of an erroneous act: namely, when our acquiescence, which has been given to forms and ideas taken to be divine and true, sustains and admits with pleasure and approval the presence and appearance of our fictions and the games of our sick active intellect. 7. Descartes also rashly and wrongly assumes, in the passage cited, that he and all who are in such a state as he is, are capable of clear and distinct perception, and of clear and distinct ideas of the natures of things, and can also recognise what that clarity is and when it is present. This is absolutely false, as long as the faculties of the mind are not sound. Objections will, I think, recur about the ideas of mathematical things. Although I have touched on these at times, I shall soon add what will entirely remove the difficulty and the boasting. For now I will say only that these are not ideas of the nature or of the things themselves, but only ideas of the outer shell of nature, which lies hidden beneath and is wholly unknown to us. 8. Finally, in the said Meditation of Descartes, where they often occur, liberty, intellect, will, the power of judging or of affirming, and the like, although commonly thought to be clear in themselves, are in truth hidden natures, very unknown and obscure. Hence those who use these terms without further explanation fall, unawares, into many errors, and chatter much about true error without attaining it. Unless I am mistaken, this matter will be perceived more clearly from what we have said about liberty: the faculties applied to objects or to exercise; desire (which is as it were the first movement of the will) urging the intellect to act; about acquiescence, which is complete desire and the terminated will, and affirmation and inner judgment; and likewise the intellect turning itself by its own activity into forms. Each person can almost feel these things in himself by his own experience, just as he can with everything we have said so far about corruption, provided that, as I am necessarily forced to repeat, he approaches the matter in himself and by himself according to the laws and the first three rules, with order and sincerity. But just as nothing is said here by us, so we judge that what they will say on that occasion does not pertain to us at all.

units.la: LI. Quæ hactenus dicta sunt, eo collint, ut cognitis vel cognoscendis primis & d annumeret sincera Mens, Se cum fatatibus suis corruptam esse; & ad veritais cognitionem & agnitionem eatenus otam: sciat autem hoc esse Philosophoerratum capitale, quod suam nolint devationem & ineptitudinem cognoscere.
units.tr: LI.
