The things said so far tend to this: that a sincere mind should know that it, together with its faculties, has been corrupted, and should know to what extent this bears on the knowledge and acknowledgment of truth. It should know, moreover, that this is the capital error of the philosophers: that they are unwilling to recognise their own deviation and ineptitude.

units.la: LII. Ex quo immediate sequitur, SA- TIONEM MEDIIS APTIS. ESSE NC ANTE OMNIA QUÆRENDAM, quod
units.tr: LII. From which it immediately follows that the healing of the mind by apt means must be sought before all else, namely that

units.la: (ȝ) Methodi versus quinta quod pro lege quinta & pro cognito quinto habemus, proque errato ei opposito, & a Philosophis admisso, quod hoc vel negligant prorsus, vel aliis suis occupationibus segniter postponant, agendi quadam ratione non minus absurda, nec minus contra ordinem, quam fi quis architectonicam discere & exercere vellet, & in ultimum locum rejiceret, aut prorsus negligeret, normamcinum, perpendiculum, cæteraque instrumenta habere recta; de quibus tamen ante omnia fuerat cogitandum.
units.tr: (ȝ) The fifth law of method, which we hold as a fifth known truth, and the error opposed to it, admitted by the philosophers, namely that they either neglect this altogether or lazily postpone it to their other occupations, is a way of acting no less absurd and no less contrary to order than if someone wished to learn and practise architecture but put last, or altogether neglected, the square, the plumb line, and the other instruments for keeping things straight, though these ought to have been thought of before all else.

units.la: LIII. Ad refitutionem fanctatum & intelligantur duo præcipua notanda.
units.tr: LIII. For the restoration of soundness, two principal points are to be noted.

units.la: LIII. Quomodo autem fiet illa insanum statum restitutio? Notandum in antecessum, primò, etsi omnes nævi nunc tolli non possint, ad minimum tamen præcipuos & capitaliores debere corrigi & deleri.
units.tr: LIII. But how will that restoration of the diseased mind come about? It must be noted in advance that, first, although all blemishes cannot now be removed, at least the principal and more serious ones must be corrected and blotted out.

units.la: Notandum fecundò, quamvis optetur forte ut tantum hic agatur de eis, quæ rationem, ideas & philosophandi actum spectant, non posse interim hæc inferioris subfellii fanari, nisi etiam superiora, quæ divinora, foedidiora, realia, maximeque radicalia concernunt, sanitati reddantur ipsa, unde fanus fiat in inferiora influxus. Alioqui (contra primam legem) turbabitur ordo: unde omnis generis confusiones, tenebræ, erroresque non poterunt non promanare.
units.tr: It must be noted, secondly, that although perhaps one would wish that only those things which concern reason, ideas, and the act of philosophizing were treated here, these lower matters cannot be healed unless the higher things also, which concern what is more divine, more foul, more real, and above all more radical, are themselves restored to health, so that from what is sound an influence may flow down to the lower things. Otherwise (contrary to the first law) the order will be thrown into confusion, and from this there cannot but arise every kind of confusion, darkness, and error.

units.la: LIV. Quomodo do ex vino præcripto intelligentes
units.tr: LIV. How the precept is to be understood

units.la: LIV. Jam fi homines & fimpliciores fent, & veritatum Euangelicarum æstimatores cupidi, dicerem simpliciter responsi loco, & conceptis Scripturæ verbis, quoniam origo mali est, quod (a) Deus quidem bainem creavit reStum. sed ipsi quasi vere ratiotiones multas, hoc est, histrionicum suum lectum activum, seu rationem humavoluerunt sic exercere, & in gesticulaibus ejus atque metamorphosi perpetua lelectari, ut desinerent facultates divi& superiores cum Deo exercere, unde en Dei amissum, & omnia mala introta: hinc jam e contrario capiendum esse rionem, ligandum, & (b) captivandum obedientia Christi, ita ut ad vocem Chrigesticulationes suas abnuget & relinquat; ratiocinationes deiciat armis justitiae, hoc, cruce & clavis Christi, ita ut ei imponacrux Christi, eumque sequatur in monte, dendo ad superiora, & ibi pedibus manfque (quoad totam sphaeram activitatis) sic cruci affigatur ut amplius gesticulari possit: sed moriatur quicquid in eo cortionis est, vitaeque & activitatis propriae. inc postea adorandus Spiritus Christi, qui a Dei sapientia est, super eum descenns, illum e morte in vitam novam cum risto suscitaret; & per divinam e supernis ram, mente ejus in mentem Spiritus Christi transformata, oreque ejus lingua flama donato, ex veteri histrione, stultis, oprii morbi impetibus prius agitato, faet mirabilem (impulsore Christo viyente eo) laudum operumque Dei admirabilium, in divinis quam in naturalibus quantum idem opus & necesse esset, praeconem & erpretem. Sed quae nostri Christianismi ne est calamitas, pudet fere omnes non tantum credere & fidere viæ & promissionibus Christi; sed & ejus verba vel ore profiteri vel auribus percipere. Non hæc sunt scilicet Philosophicis auriculis satis accommodata, neque artem & demonstrationes scientificas ad palatum histrionis nostri sapiunt. Aliis igitur & philosophicis utemur modis, si forte quis inde ad frugem revocari & persuaderi possit.
units.tr: LIV. Now if men were simpler, and eager lovers of the evangelical truths, I would simply answer in the words of Scripture, that the origin of evil is that (a) God indeed created man upright, but they themselves, as it were, have turned over many reasonings, that is, they have wished to exercise their own histrionic activity, or the reason, in this way, and to delight in its perpetual gesturing and metamorphosis, so that they ceased to exercise the higher faculties with God; whence the loss of God and all evils came in. Hence, on the contrary, one must now take captive the reason, bind it, and (b) bring it into captivity to the obedience of Christ, so that at the voice of Christ it may renounce and leave off its gesticulations; it must cast down reasonings with the weapons of righteousness, that is, with the cross and the nails of Christ, so that the cross of Christ may be laid upon it, and it may follow him up the mountain, rising to higher things, and there, with its feet and hands, be so fastened to the cross (as far as the whole sphere of its activity goes) that it can gesticulate no more; but whatever is of its own corruption, and of its own life and activity, must die. Then, after this, the Spirit of Christ, who is from the wisdom of God, is to be prayed for; descending upon it, he would raise it from death to a new life with Christ, and through the divine fire from above, his mind being transformed into the mind of the Spirit of Christ, and his mouth given a tongue of flame, he would be made, from the old histrion, once driven by foolish and morbid impulses, a wonderful herald and interpreter of the praises and admirable works of God, both in divine matters and in natural ones, as far as the same work and necessity require, with Christ driving him on. But what a calamity of our Christianity this is: almost everyone is ashamed not only to believe and trust in the way and promises of Christ, but also to profess his words with the mouth or to hear them with the ears. Of course, these things are not well suited to philosophical ears, nor do the art and scientific demonstrations taste right to the palate of our histrion. We will therefore use other, philosophical methods, if perhaps someone can thereby be recalled to sense and persuaded.

units.la: LV. Verum quam primum mentio fiet de fanando intellectu, jam protinus plurimi avolabunt, delirantes, aut se jam satis sapere, aut in incepta sapientia & dexteritate sua sibi pergendum esse. Alii, si quidem sibi auxilium optent, id suo modo comparatum esse volent, similes ægris Medicum instruere volentibus quid ipsis sit præscribendum. Ita enim depravatus, ita superbus, imo & propriæ cæcitati ita insensibilis stupidusque, & simul usque adeo audax asinus redditus est intellectus corruptus, sibi ut videatur quibusvis sapientior & prudentior. Optimi quique non sine tergiversatione, difficultatibus, quæstiunculis, instantiis, negotium suæ sanationis aggredientur: timent se circumveniri: semper ex se agere satagunt. Et cum primis quidem illis iterum nil agendum: hisce vero ultimis, quæstionibusque quæ ab illis moveri possent, satisfacere forsan conabimur. Sed vero prius indicanda pro sanationis medio proximo, proque Veræ Methodi regula sexta Axioma sequens, quod inter cognita prima meretur recenseri. Id autem hoc est.
units.tr: LV. But as soon as mention is made of healing the understanding, at once very many will fly off, raving that they are already wise enough, or that they must press on in the wisdom and cleverness they have already begun. Others, if indeed they desire help for themselves, will want it provided in their own way, like sick people who want to instruct the physician what is to be prescribed for them. For the corrupted understanding has become so depraved, so proud, and moreover so insensible and stupid to its own blindness, and at the same time such a bold ass, that it seems to itself wiser and more prudent than anyone. The best people will approach the business of their own healing not without evasion, difficulties, petty questions, and objections; they fear being circumvented and strive always to act of themselves. And while we shall perhaps attempt to satisfy them, with the first kind of people we must do nothing further, but with these last, and with the questions that they might raise. But first we must state, as the proximate means of healing, and as the sixth rule of the true method, the following axiom, which deserves to be counted among the first known truths. It is this.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: LVI. Mens ad incolumitatem cipiendam, agnita & deplorata gritudine impotentiaque, abneat ab actibus intellectus sui, iem offerat Deo passivum, solo :fiderio sanitatis a Deo impe-andæ agens, nec non firmiter :cernens se impofterum, si resti-ta fuerit, non recturam amplius .cultates suas ad placitum prorium; sed ad voluntatem Entis :mmi, juxta ordinem proporonemque quæ debet esse æterna ter & caduca, spiritualia & corprea, interna & superficiaria, ecessaria & accessoria, realia & mbratilia, divina Dei placita, & ssima proprii amoris se pro scoo statuentis cupita.
units.tr: LVI. When the mind, having recognised and lamented its sickness and powerlessness, is to receive healing, it must renounce the acts of its own understanding and offer itself to God as passive. It must act only in the hope of the health to be obtained from God. It must also firmly recognise that, if it is restored, it will no longer direct its faculties according to its own pleasure, but according to the will of the Supreme Being, in accordance with the order and proportion which ought to hold between the eternal and the perishable, the spiritual and the corporeal, the internal and the superficial, the necessary and the accessory, the real and the shadowy. It must desire the divine pleasures of God above the most base desires of its own self-love, which sets itself up as its goal.

units.la: Hoc qui non observaverint; sed in oppoim iverint, errato cætera præcedentia mpleatente cumulabunt omnia. Ast ubi æ hic præscripta sunt, vere in Mente int, explicabit se in illius intimis pro coide regularum & cognitorum ab ea debiadhibitorum, Operatio Dei eam fanans,
units.tr: Those who do not observe this, but go the opposite way, will by error pile up and fill everything that precedes. But when the things prescribed here are truly within the Mind, the Operation of God, healing it, will reveal itself in its innermost parts, in proportion to the abundance of rules and known truths that the mind has rightly applied.

units.la: (6) Sexta veræ Methodi lex, de medio fanatio-nis proximo: cum error ratio opposito. quidem in re eodem modo, imo & turpius: se gerit, ac si monstrosus aliquis Æsopus, crine ruber, niger ore, brevis pede, lumine luscus, lingua blæsus, pectore curvus, mente fatuus, repræsentare vellet atque induere formas hominum dotibus corporis, vultus, sermonis, gestuum majestate, mentisque præstantia excellentium: aut si forte reginæ alicujus formosæ, sapientis, admirabilisque in se personam, gestus, verba, habitum & regimen exhibere conaretur; ubi tamen revera præter monstrosos, deformes ac ridiculos motus ac gestus, cum repræsentandis similitudinem nullam habentes, nihil produceret: quandoquidem quomodocunque sese vertat; impossibile tamen ei sit, ullam vel minimam rem decori exemplaris imitari.
units.tr: (6) The sixth law of the true Method, on the proximate means of healing: error's reasoning is set against it. Error behaves in the same way, and even more shamefully, as if some monstrous Aesop, red-haired, black-faced, short-footed, one-eyed, lisping in tongue, hunchbacked in chest, foolish in mind, wished to represent and put on the forms of men excelling in bodily gifts, in the dignity of face, speech and gesture, and in the eminence of mind. Or, if he tried to display the person, gestures, words, bearing and rule of some beautiful, wise and admirable queen, he would produce nothing but monstrous, deformed and ridiculous movements and gestures, having no likeness to what he sought to represent. However he turns himself, he is quite unable to imitate even the smallest part of the grace of the model.

units.la: Talis jam factus est noster & omnium hominum intellectus activus, ratio nostra, histrionalis ille ardelio, qui solus in anima nostra scenam obtinere voluit, nec vero pati in quiete & pausa, ut admiranda sapientia Dei sua in nobis ipsa exhiberet divina spectacula. Agyrtam similem jam quisque domi suæ, in proprio suo cerebro, in glandula, si vis, pineali habet, fovet, admiratur, audit, sequitur: & hoc est quod sapientiam vocant & reputant. Sed quoniam unusquisque ejusmodi gesticulator non valet omnia pro genio suo repræsentare, hinc quivis sibi personam aut rem certam agendam assumit, in quam se totum vertat, & ubi exerceat; cæteris aliis prætermissis: unde (pro diversa quam quisque sibi assumsit forma) hominum alii sunt (vel Scriptura teste) bruta, lupi, serpentes; alii (ut dicebat Epictetus) ventres, intestina & partes pudendae; alii lineae, anguli & circuli, motus, figurae, numeri, aa + bb—cc ac dd; alii chimaerae metaphysicae & transcendentales aut critici cortices; alii tria elementa, vortices, machinae, alii alia similia. Ob quas quidem formas assumptas se magnificiant, sibique belle admodum videntur rerum divinarum atque naturalium naturas ideis suis debite exprimere, idque clare & distincte percipere: quando tamen coram Deo, luminosa veritate, tormisque & naturis rerum veris, monstrosae tantum & turpes chimaerae sunt, a vero & decoro rerum statu infinite abludentes, & non nisi cum genere illo stultitiae quo unusquisque est affectus, & forte cum nonnullis ex sordibus & deformitatibus statûs in quo cum caeteris jacet, conformes. Neque enim magis potest ulla in se recte repraesentare tenebrosus, depravatus & tortuosus intellectus; aut etiam vere scire an faciat erronea an vera, quam histrio noster ridiculus & portentosus, qui in tenebris gesticulans, neque videre potest suam in omnibus deformitatem & turpitudinem, propudiosamque motuum inconcinnitatem & absurditatem, neque novit gestus suos formasque iis quae repraesentanda suscepit adversari magis quam congruere. Et tamen mirabilia sibi facere videtur, & vel angelicas posituras, res, actiones, formarum & gestuum quibus se induit elegantia superare: quod fine risu videri non potest ab eis qui rei abfur­ditatem aperto utcunque oculo contemplan& shy;tur; nec fine lacrymis ab illis qui folicitius expendent, cum jactura temporis perdi & ludionis animam, si eo tempore relinquat mortalia, quo nugacibus hisce formis est in­vestitus, in quibus & perpetuo est remansu& shy;rus, & omnis generis mala, quibus dedo& shy;luerat, intra fe evigilare sentiet.
units.tr: Such already is our intellect, the active intellect of all men, our reason, that busy stage-player, who alone wished to hold the stage in our soul and would not suffer to rest in quiet and pause, so that the wonderful wisdom of God might display its divine spectacles within us. Each man already has such a charlatan at home, in his own brain, in the pineal gland if you like; he cherishes it, admires it, hears it and follows it, and this is what they call and consider wisdom. But since no such gesticulator can represent everything according to his own genius, each one takes up for himself some particular person or thing to play, into which he turns himself entirely and in which he exercises himself, leaving others aside. Hence, according to the different form each has assumed, some men are (as Scripture bears witness) beasts, wolves, serpents; some (as Epictetus said) are bellies, guts and private parts; some are lines, angles and circles, motions, figures, numbers, aa + bb—cc and dd; some are metaphysical and transcendental chimeras, or critical husks; some are the three elements, vortices, machines, and others other such things. Because of the forms they have assumed, they make great boasts and think themselves quite able to express the natures of divine and natural things properly through their ideas, and to perceive these clearly and distinctly. Yet before God, in the luminous truth and in the true natures of things, they are only monstrous and shameful chimeras, infinitely removed from the true and seemly state of things, and conformed only to that kind of folly by which each is affected, and perhaps to some of the filth and deformities of the condition in which he lies with the rest. Indeed, a darkened, depraved and crooked intellect can represent nothing rightly in itself, nor can it truly know whether what it produces is erroneous or true, any more than our ridiculous and monstrous player, who, gesturing in the dark, cannot see his own deformity and turpitude in everything, nor the shameful clumsiness and absurdity of his movements, nor know whether his gestures and forms are more opposed or more fitting to what he has undertaken to represent. And yet he seems to himself to do wonders, and even to surpass angelic postures, things, actions, forms and the elegance of the gestures with which he clothes himself. This cannot be seen without laughter by those who contemplate the absurdity of the thing with their eyes open in any way; nor without tears by those who weigh it more carefully, when, after losing time and the soul of a buffoon, he leaves mortal life at the very time when he is clothed in these trifling forms, in which he will remain forever, and when he will feel all kinds of evils, to which he had given himself, awakening within himself.

units.la: E paucculis hisce (vix enim quicquam tanti mali attigimus) animadvertat quæso lector attentus neque dolosus, quantâ nunc in ca& shy;ligine, quantisque in erroribus infeliciter tumultuetur humanum genus, utut inprimis sibi sapere videatur: dum revera ea est ejus corruptio, eæque tenebræ, ut crediderim hominem eum præ mentis admiratione exa­nimatum iri, cui divinum lumen humanæ depravationis absurditatem, deformitatem & immensitatem vivide aliquantum detegeret, quam ipse Dei Spiritus in Scripturis mi rari satis non potest, exclamando omnia va nissima esse & perdita, hominem jam bestiis non præstare, cogitationes etiam sapientiorum vanas atque stultas omnino esse, itidem cum omni sua sapientia: Confidunt in nihilo: loquuntur vanitates: conceperunt laborem & pepererunt iniquitatem. Ova alpidum erupe­runt, & telas araneæ texuerunt: qui comede& shy;rit de ovis eorum, morietur; & quod confotum est erumpet in basiliscum. Telæ eorum non erunt in vestimentum, neque operientur operibus suis: opera eorum inutilia.... cogitationes eorum, cō& shy;gitationes inutiles. Exspectavimus, lucem &c.
units.tr: From these few examples (for we have touched upon scarcely anything of so great an evil), I ask the attentive reader, who is not deceitful, to notice how great is the darkness now, and in how many errors the human race is unhappily stirred up, however wise it may seem to itself above all. For its corruption and darkness are so great that I believe a man would be so amazed by his own mind that he would be struck dumb, if the divine light vividly revealed to him something of the absurdity, deformity and immensity of human depravity. The Spirit of God himself in the Scriptures cannot sufficiently wonder at it, crying out that all things are most vain and lost, that man is no better than the beasts, and that the thoughts of even the wisest are altogether vain and foolish, and likewise all their wisdom: They trust in vanity and speak lies; they conceive mischief and bring forth iniquity. They hatch cockatrice' eggs and weave the spider's web: he that eateth of their eggs dieth, and that which is crushed breaketh out into a viper. Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works: their works are works of iniquity... their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity. We looked for light, and behold darkness, etc.

units.la: ecce splendorem, & in tenebris amlamus. Palpamus sicuti cæci parietem; & asi sine oculis attrectamus. impegimus meriquasi in tenebris: in caliginosis quasi mor& infinita hujusmodi.
units.tr: Behold darkness; for brightness, but we walk in darkness. We grope for the wall like the blind, and feel as if without eyes; we stumble at noon as in the dark, as dead men in dark places, and countless other things of this kind.

units.la: L. Animadvertat & hoc ex jam dictis tantam in transitu Lector sincerus, videlicet, tantis hinc inde scateat erratis Meditatio artefii quarta, quæ veluti pro clave introductionis ad veritatem & ad Sapientiam Philosophiamque veram interdum commendator & subministratur. In quâ præter errores libertatem (quam indifferentem esse egat ex natura) circa concursum, circa causam finalem, & alia quæ hujus loci non sunt, que alibi sunt annotata, occurrunt sequentes: 1. Culpam dissimulat Mentis qua se gessit tempore præterito. 2. Justitiam Dei ignorat, qua justum est ut intellectus rebellis, ingratus, & qui ex vana curiositate ad prorium amorem & dilectionem, suisque exi-mationem, inquirere vult in rerum ideas imbratiles, relictis necessariis & solidis ossiciis, ita tradatur tenebris, ut perpetuo a copo aberret & fallatur. 3. Ipsas facultates percipiendi, ratiocinandi, judicandi ægras tque corruptas esse, oblivisci tur, aut id ne cogitat quidem. 4. Supponit intellectum nulla re, sive idea debita, esse privatum; ed negative tantum destitutum. Contra, cum crearetur nulla quidem destituebatur: ut ubi se male gessit, omnibus sese privavit quæ naturas rerum luminose referebant. 5. Vim intelligendi non esse causam errorum, quia, ut inquit, quidquid intelligo cum a Deo habeam ut intelligam, procul dubio nõn intelligo, nec in eo potest fieri ut fallar: hæc quidem vera effent de intelligentia mentis primævæ, aut de ea quæ post rebellionem, pravitatem, ægritudinem admissam, inde sanata effet, & in primum statum restituta: at non ita de mente quæ revera ægra est & corrupta, nec tamen adhuc de se sananda meditata est, nedum inde fit restituta: hæc enim quicquid pro suo illo statu & captu intelligit, cum id non a Deo, sed a delirio morbi sui habeat ut taliter intelligat, procul dubio prave & defectuose intelligit, nec in eo fieri potest ne fallatur. Nam simulac desiderium corruptum amoris proprii, simulat intellectum ægrum & monstrosum, ut ad delectationem ipsi pariat fœtus live ideas suas, & formarum quarumvis assumptione coram eo gesticuletur, is protinus pro morbosa sua indole meras & absurdas chimæras, ludosque ineptos coram illo non potest non fingere, qui non Dei & divinorum ejus operum, sed propriæ suæ stultitiæ & ægritudinis maxime sint representativi, & quibus dum desiderium sese suaviter atque acquiescenter delectat, hoc ipso formam erroris constituit. Cujus erroris punctum saliens est cupiditas corrupta gesticulationum intellectus ægri, qui ex activitate monstrosa & vitiata materiam suppeditat chimæricam, quam admittens delectabiliter & acquiescenter desiderium, dicitur complete errorem admittere, atque adeo errare actualiter. r vel, si sic loquendum, etiam formali-. Ita ut, 6. Cartelius male statuit, id od formam erroris constituit, consistere ea privatione quae inest in liberi arbitrii 1 recto usu, quando nempe liberum armium judicandi facultatem ad obscura vel iota extendit: cum tamen in liberi arbinon recto usu sola privatio illa ineste poste quae formam erroris moralis, sive culpa, n autem erroris philosophici seu logici ca rerum ideas, constituit. Privatio mallex in errore inest, & cum eo concurrit. telle&tus lumine primaevo privatus est, ivatus item vi qua pollebat imitandi Deum idearum activa excitatione. Desiderium eisandi, privatum est scopo legitimo (gloricatione & delectatione in Deo) cui turpis pidicas substituta est. Ipsae formae inteltus activitate & vertibilitate excitatae, ivatae sunt decora & ordinata similitudine conformitate cum ideis Dei & naturis rem; & praeter figmenta nugacia ut plurium, nihil sunt. Jam si mens hic subsistet, nec iltis largiretur acquiescentiam & omplacentiam, (quae judicium internum que affirmatio sunt,) sed displiceret ei inlectum suum istiusmodi chimaerarum te-brosarum adeo esse vel invita illa feraim, ut furentis histrionis instar vel invita ente gesticuletur; intus continuo garriat, seque in omnes sine ordine formas vel restante animo convertat adeo, ut nullus ii intellectus, omniumque actuum ejus, el per diem unum Dominus sit & compos in fosolidum; tunc non dicenda esset Mens errare : quanquam enim tunc intus latet materia erroris, illiusque materiæ forma deformis, formarum absurdarum inconcinnitas ; attamen non adesset error approbative & complete, quippe qui demum adest quando in acquiescentia & delectatione interna admittitur. Et hæc est proprie & præcise forma actus erronei, quando videlicet acquiescentia nostra, quæ pro formis ideisque divinis & veris facta est, præsentiam & aspectum fictionum nostrarum, ludorumque ægri intellectus nostri activi, cum voluptate & placito sustinet & admittit. 7. Gratis etiam & male assumit loco dicto Cartesius, se & quotquot in ejusmodi cum eo statu sunt, capaces esse claræ & distinctæ perceptionis, idearumque de rerum naturis clararum & distinctarum, nec non agnoscendi quid sit aut quando adsit illa claritas, quod absolute falsum est, quamdiu facultates mentis non sunt sanatæ. Recurrent (opinor) instantiæ de ideis rerum mathematicarum, de quibus etsi aliquoties quædam monui, mox tamen ea addam quæ difficultatem & jactantiam funditus eliminent : nunc dicam tantum, illas non esse naturæ rerumve ideas; sed ideas solum corticum naturæ, quæ sub illis latens ipsis prorsus est incognita. 8. Tandem in dicta Cartesii Meditatione, quæ sæpe ibi occurrunt, libertas, intellectus, voluntas, judicandi vel affirmandi facultas & ejusmodi, quamvis clara per se vulgo quidem putentur, revera tamen sunt naturæ abditæ & valde ignootæ atque obscuræ; unde qui his utuntur ulteriori explicatione, in multos inscii dunt errores, & multa garriunt de errovero, quæ tamen non assequuntur. Res ista nisi fallor & clarius percipientur ea quæ diximus de libertate facultatesad trium objectis aut exercitio applicante: desiderio (quæ veluti prima voluntatis quædam est) intellectum ad actum stilante; de acquiescentia, quæ est desiden completum voluntasque terminata, confirmatioque & judicium internum: ut & intellectu sese activitate sua in formas ivis vertente. Hæc enim in se quisque opria experientia fere palpare potest, emadmodum & omnia quæ de corruptiohaktenus diximus, modo (quod cogor essario repetere) quis juxta leges atque nita tria prima, cum ordine & sinceritanentis a se & in se rem aggrediatur. Cæis ut nil a nobis hic dicitur, ita quæ illi rum occasione dicturi sunt, ad nos minime ctare censemus.
units.tr: Let the sincere reader also notice, from what has already been said, that this fourth Meditation of the Artist is in passing so full of errors on every side that it is commended and offered now and then as a kind of key to introduce us to truth and to true Wisdom and Philosophy. Apart from the errors about freedom (which he wrongly says is by nature indifferent), about concurrence, about final cause, and about other matters that do not belong here and have been noted elsewhere, the following occur: (1) He conceals the fault of the Mind, by which it conducted itself in past time. (2) He ignores the justice of God, by which it is right that a rebellious, ungrateful intellect, one that out of vain curiosity wants to seek its own love and delight and its own esteem in unreal ideas of things, leaving aside the necessary and solid duties, should be given over to darkness, so that it wanders and is deceived perpetually away from the truth. (3) He forgets, or does not even think about, the fact that the very faculties of perceiving, reasoning and judging are sick and corrupt. (4) He supposes that the intellect is deprived of no thing, no idea that is due to it, but is only negatively lacking. On the contrary, when it was created it was lacking nothing; but when it behaved badly, it deprived itself of all those things which used to reflect the natures of things in light. (5) He says that the power of understanding is not the cause of errors, because, as he puts it, whatever I understand, since I have it from God that I understand it, I undoubtedly do not misunderstand, and it cannot happen in this that I am deceived. These things would indeed be true of the understanding of the primeval mind, or of that understanding which, after rebellion, depravity and sickness had been incurred, would have been healed from there and restored to its first state. But this is not so for the mind that is really sick and corrupt, and has not yet even thought of healing itself, much less been restored. For whatever such a mind understands according to its own state and capacity, since it does not have from God, but from the delirium of its own disease, that it understands in this way, it undoubtedly understands wickedly and defectively, and it cannot happen in this that it is not deceived. For as soon as the corrupt desire of self-love, sick and monstrous, begets from the sick and monstrous intellect its own offspring, that is, its ideas, and, by the assumption of various forms, performs before it for its own delight, the mind immediately cannot help but feign, for its morbid disposition, mere absurd chimeras and foolish games before itself, which represent not God and His divine works, but chiefly its own folly and sickness. And while desire takes sweet and content pleasure in these, by this very act it constitutes the form of error. The salient point of this error is the corrupt pleasure in the gesticulations of the sick intellect, which, through its monstrous and vitiated activity, supplies chimerical matter. When desire admits this matter with delight and content, it is said to admit error completely, and thus to err actually, or, if we must speak so, even formally. So that, (6) Descartes wrongly lays down that what constitutes the form of error consists in that privation which is present in the right use of free choice, namely when the free will extends the power of judging to obscure or unknown things. Yet in the wrong use of free choice that privation alone cannot be what constitutes the form of moral error, that is, of fault, and not of philosophical or logical error about the ideas of things. The privation is indeed present in error, and concurs with it. The intellect is deprived of its primeval light, and likewise deprived of the power by which it was able to imitate God through the active excitation of ideas. The desire of the will is deprived of its legitimate end (glorying and delight in God), and a base and carnal end has been substituted for it. The forms themselves, roused by the activity and mutability of the intellect, are deprived of the becoming and orderly likeness and conformity to the ideas of God and to the natures of things, and, apart from trifling fictions such as many are, they are nothing. Now if the mind were to stop here, and did not grant to those forms its assent and approval (which are the inner judgment and affirmation), but were displeased that its intellect should be so full of such dark chimeras, even against its will, and that it should gesticulate like a raving actor, constantly chattering inside, and turning itself without order into all forms, and if the mind did not remain master and in control of the whole of its intellect and all its acts even for a single day, then the mind should not be said to err. For although error's matter then lies hidden within, and the form of that matter is deformed, with the incongruity of absurd forms, nevertheless error would not be present in the approving and complete sense, since it is present only when it is admitted in inner acquiescence and delight. And this is properly and precisely the form of the erroneous act, namely when our acquiescence, which has been given to what are taken to be divine and true forms and ideas, sustains and admits with pleasure and approval the presence and appearance of our fictions and the games of our sick, active intellect. (7) Descartes also takes it, without reason and wrongly, that he and all who are in that same state with him are capable of clear and distinct perception, and of clear and distinct ideas of the natures of things, and also of recognising what that clarity is and when it is present. This is absolutely false, as long as the faculties of the mind are not healed. I suppose the examples about ideas of mathematical things will come back, and although I have sometimes made some remarks about them, I will soon add what will remove the difficulty and the boasting altogether. For now I will say only that those are not ideas of the natures or of the things themselves, but only ideas of the outer husks of nature, which, lying hidden beneath them, is wholly unknown to them. (8) Finally, in the said Meditation of Descartes, where they often occur, liberty, intellect, will, the faculty of judging or of affirming and such things, although they are commonly thought to be clear in themselves, are in reality hidden and very unknown and obscure natures. Hence those who use these terms without further explanation fall, unaware, into many errors, and chatter much about the truth of errors, which nonetheless they do not grasp. Unless I am mistaken, this matter will be perceived more clearly from what we have said about liberty: the faculties applied to the objects of the three, or to their exercise: desire (which is in a way the first act of the will), stirring the intellect to act; of acquiescence, which is desire completed and the will brought to rest, and confirmation and inner judgment; and likewise the intellect turning itself by its own activity into various forms. For each person can almost feel these things in himself through his own experience, just as he can feel all that we have said so far about corruption, provided (as I am forced to repeat again and again) that he approaches the matter from himself and within himself, according to the laws and the three first rules, with order and sincerity. Since nothing is said here by us about those things, so we think that what they are going to say on the occasion of those things should by no means be attributed to us.

units.la: LI. Quæ hactenus dicta sunt, eo colli- nt, ut cognitis vel cognoscendis primis & id annumeret sincera Mens, Se cum fatatibus suis corruptam esse; & ad veritais cognitionem & agnitionem eatenus ptam: sciat autem hoc esse Philosophon erratum capitale, quod suam nolint derivationem & ineptitudinem cognoscere.
units.tr: LI. The things said so far lead to this: that the sincere mind should count among the first things to be known, or to be learned, that it itself, with its faculties, is corrupted; and that, to that extent, it is unfit for knowing and recognising the truth. And it should know that this is the chief error of the philosophers, that they are unwilling to recognise their own derivation and their incapacity.

units.la: LII. Ex quo immediate sequitur, SA- TIONEM MEDIIS APTIS ESSE INC ANTE OMNIA QVÆRENDAM, quod
units.tr: LII. From this it immediately follows that the means suited to healing (SANATIO) must be sought before all else, which

units.la: (ȳ) Methodi vera lex quinta. quod pro lege quinta & pro cognito quinto habemus, proque errato ei opposito, & a Philosophis admisso, quod hoc vel negligant prorsus, vel aliis suis occupationibus segniter postponant, agendi quadam ratione non minus absurda, nec minus contra ordinem, quam si quis architectonicam discere & exercere vellet, & in ultimum locum rejiceret, aut prorsus negligeret, normam, circinum, perpendiculum, cæteraque instrumenta habere recta; de quibus tamen ante omnia fuerat cogitandum.
units.tr: (ȳ) The fifth law of the true Method. We hold this as the fifth law and as the fifth known truth, and we hold the opposite error, admitted by the Philosophers, as an error: that they either neglect this altogether or sluggishly postpone it to their other occupations. This way of proceeding is no less absurd and no less contrary to order than if someone wanted to learn and practise architecture and placed last, or neglected altogether, the square, the compass, the plumb line and the other tools for keeping things straight, though these should have been considered before all else.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: LIII. Quomodo autem fiet illa in sanum statum restitutio? Notandum in antecessum, primò, etsi omnes nævi nunc tolli non possunt, ad minimum tamen præcipuos & capitaliores debere corrigi & deleri. Notandum secundò, quamvis optetur forte ut tantum hic agatur de eis, quæ rationem, ideas & philosophandi actum spectant, non posse interim hæc inferioris subsellii sanari, nisi etiam superiora, quæ divinitora, quotidiora, realia, maximeque radicalia concernunt, sanitati reddantur ipsa, unde sanus fiat in inferiora influxus. Alioqui (contra primam legem) turbabitur ordo: unde omnis generis confusiones, tenebræ, erroresque non poterunt non promanare.
units.tr: LIII. But how will this restoration to a sound state be brought about? First, it should be noted in advance that, although not all blemishes can be removed now, at least the principal and more serious ones must be corrected and destroyed. Second, it should be noted that, although it may perhaps be wished that only those matters be dealt with which concern reason, ideas and the act of philosophizing, these lower matters cannot be healed in the meantime unless the higher ones also are restored to health: those which concern the more divine, the more everyday, the real, and above all the most radical. From these the healthy influx into the lower matters must come. Otherwise (contrary to the first law) order will be thrown into confusion, and all kinds of confusion, darkness and errors cannot fail to spring forth from it.

units.la: LIV.
units.tr: LIV.

units.la: LIV. Jam si homines & simpliciores estent, & veritatum Euangelicarum æstimatores cupidi, dicerem simpliciter responsi loco, & conceptis Scripturæ verbis, quoniam origo mali est, quod (a) Deus quidem hahominem creavit reflum. sed ipsi quasi vere ratiocinationes multas, hoc est, hiftrionicum suum intellectum activum, seu rationem humanam voluerunt sic exercere, & in gesticulationibus ejus atque metamorphosi perpetua sic delectari, ut desinerent facultates divinas & superiores cum Deo exercere, unde lumen Dei amissum, & omnia mala introduꝯa: hinc jam e contrario capiendum esse histrionem, ligandum, & (b) captivandum sub obedientia Christi, ita ut ad vocem Christi gesticulationes suas abneget & relinquat; & ratiocinationes dejiciat armis justitia, hoc est, cruce & clavis Christi, ita ut ei imponatur crux Christi, eumque sequatur in monte, tendendo ad superiora, & ibi pedibus manibusque (quoad totam sphæram activitatis suæ) sic cruci affigatur ut amplius gesticulari non possit: sed moriatur quicquid in eo corruptionis est, vitæque & activitatis propriæ. Tunc postea adorandus Spiritus Christi, qui ipsa Dei sapientia est, super eum descendens, illum e morte in vitam novam cum Christo suscitaret; & per divinam e supernis auram, mente ejus in mentem Spiritus Christi transformatâ, oreque ejus lingua flammea donato, ex veteri histrione, stultis proprii morbi impetibus prius agitato, faceret mirabilem (impulsore Christo vivente in eo) laudum operumque Dei admirabilium, tam in divinis quam in naturalibus quantum quidem opus & necesse esset, præconem & interpretem. Sed quæ nostri Christianismi nunc est calamitas, pudet fere omnes non tantum credere & fidere viæ & promissionibus Christi; sed & ejus verba vel ore profiteri vel auribus percipere. Non hæc sunt scilicet Philosophicis auriculis satis accommodata, neque artem & demonstrationes scientificas ad palatum histrionis nostri sapiunt. Aliis igitur & philosophicis utemur modis, si forte quis inde ad frugem revocari & persuaderi possit.
units.tr: LIV. Now if men were simpler, and eager judges of the Gospel truths, I would simply answer with the words of Scripture as they stand, saying that the origin of evil is this: (a) God indeed created man upright, but they themselves, as it were, have wanted to conduct many reasonings, that is, to exercise their active histrionic intellect, or human reason, and to take such delight in its gestures and constant metamorphoses that they ceased to exercise the divine and higher faculties with God. Hence the light of God was lost and all evils were introduced. From this, conversely, the actor must be seized, bound, and (b) captivated under the obedience of Christ, so that at the voice of Christ he renounces and gives up his gestures; and he must cast down reasonings by the armour of righteousness, that is, by the cross and nails of Christ, so that the cross of Christ is laid upon him and he follows Christ up the mountain, striving toward higher things. There, with feet and hands (as far as the whole sphere of his activity extends), he is so fixed to the cross that he can no longer gesture, but whatever corruption is in him dies, along with his own life and activity. Then the Spirit of Christ, which is the very wisdom of God, is to be adored, descending upon him to raise him from death to a new life with Christ; and by a divine breath from above, his mind being transformed into the mind of the Spirit of Christ, and his mouth given a tongue of fire, he is made from the old actor, previously driven about by the foolish impulses of his own disease, into a wonderful herald and interpreter of the praises and admirable works of God, both divine and natural, as much as the work requires and is necessary, with Christ living in him as the driving force. But what is now the calamity of our Christianity is that almost everyone is ashamed not only to believe and trust in the way and promises of Christ, but even to profess his words with the mouth or to hear them with the ears. Surely these things are not well suited to philosophical ears, nor do they savour of the art and scientific demonstrations to the palate of our actor. We shall therefore use other and philosophical means, if perhaps someone can be called back to sense and persuaded by them.

units.la: LV. Verum quam primum mentio fiet de fanando intelleƨu, jam protinus plurimi avolabunt, delirantes, aut se jam satis sapere, aut in incepta sapientia & dexteritate sua sibi pergendum esse. Alii, si quidem sibi auxilium optent,id suo modo comparatum esse volent, similes ægris Medicum instruere volentibus quid ipsis sit præscribendum. Ita enim depravatus, ita superbus, imo & propriæ cœcitati ita insensibilis stupidusque, & simul usque adeo audax asinus redditus est intelleƨus corruptus, sibi ut videatur quibusvis sapientior & prudentior. Optimi quique non sine tergiversationibus, difficultatibus, quæstiunculis, instantiis, negotium suæ sanationis aggredientur: timent se circumveniri: semper ex se agere satagunt. Et cum primis quidem illis iterum nil agendum*: hisce vero ultimis, quæstionibusque quæ ab illis moveri possent, satisfacere forsan conabimur. Sed vero prius indicanda pro sanationis medio proximo, proque Veræ Methodi regula sexta Axioma sequens, quod inter cognita prima meretur recenseri. Id autem hoc est.
units.tr: LV. But as soon as mention is made of healing the intellect, very many will at once fly off, raving that they are already wise enough, or that they must press on with their begun wisdom and skill. Others, if indeed they wish for help, want it to be arranged in their own way, like the sick who wish to instruct the physician what he is to prescribe for them. For the corrupt intellect has become so depraved, so proud, indeed so insensible and stupid to its own blindness, and at the same time so audaciously asinine, that it seems to itself wiser and more prudent than anyone. The best of them will undertake the business of their own healing not without evasions, difficulties, little questions, and objections; they fear being circumvented, and they always strive to act on their own. And with the first sort we shall again do nothing; to the last sort, and to the questions which they may raise, we shall perhaps try to give satisfaction. But first the following axiom, which deserves to be counted among the first known truths, must be indicated as the next means of healing and as the sixth rule of the True Method. It is this.

units.la: LVI. Mens ad incolumitatem recipiendam, agnita & deplorata ægritudine impotentiaque, abstineat ab actibus intellectus sui, quem offerat Deo passivum, solo desiderio sanitatis a Deo impetrandæ agens, nec non firmiter decernens se impostesrum, si restituta fuerit, non recuram amplius facultates suas ad placitum proprium; sed ad voluntatem Entis summi, juxta ordinem proportionemque quæ debet esse æterna inter & caduca, spiritualia & corporea, interna & superficiaria, necessaria & accessoria, realia & umbratilia, divina Dei placita, & pessima proprii amoris se pro scopo statuentis cupita.
units.tr: LVI. The mind, in order to recover its soundness, having recognized and lamented its sickness and impotence, should abstain from the acts of its own intellect, offering it to God as passive, acting only from the desire to obtain health from God. It should also firmly resolve that, if it is restored, it will no longer govern its faculties according to its own pleasure, but according to the will of the highest Being, according to the order and proportion which must be eternal between the transitory and the eternal, the spiritual and the corporeal, the internal and the superficial, the necessary and the accessory, the real and the shadowy, the divine decrees of God and the most wicked desires of a self-love that sets itself up as its own goal.

units.la: Hoc qui non observaverint; sed in oppositum iverint, errato cætera præcedentia complectente cumulabunt omnia. Ast ubi quæ hic præscripta sunt, vere in Mente erunt, explicabit se in illius intimis pro coronide regularum & cognitorum ab ea debie adhibitorum, Operatio Dei eam fanans, atque ad lucem veritatefque quasvis recipiendas & agnoscendas supra modum & vim omnem actiνam & naturalem aptam reddens.
units.tr: Those who have not observed this, but have gone the opposite way, will heap everything up with an error that embraces all the preceding things. But when what is prescribed here is truly in the mind, the operation of God, healing it, will reveal itself in its inmost depths, as the crown of the rules and of the known truths to be applied by it, and will render it apt, beyond all measure and all natural power, to receive and acknowledge light and truths of every kind.

units.la: L V I I. Atque hæc est ultima regula ultimumque ex generalibus cognitis, quæ animadvertenda sunt antequam ad specialiores veritates cognoscendas descendatur. Ultra, nil requiri potest: sunt enim infra hæc generalia ipsæmet veritates speciales proxime constitutæ, quæ vel a Deo immediate dispensantur, vel a mente sanata ordine sibi in intimis attendente, detegi possunt: quæ quidem non sunt huius loci atque operis.
units.tr: LVII. This is the last rule, and the last of the general known truths which must be noted before one descends to the more particular truths to be known. Beyond this nothing more can be required, for below these general matters the particular truths themselves are immediately established, and these can be disclosed either by God immediately bestowing them, or by the healed mind attending to them in its inmost order. These, however, do not belong to this place or to this work.

units.la: Hic tantum superest ut ad ultimæ huius regulæ, cognitiquepleniorem dilucidationem, satisfaciam quibusdam difficultatibus, quæ à nonnullis forte moveri possent de materiis in eo contentis, nempe 1. de impotentia mentis seu intellectus, 2. de ejus quiete: 3. de statu passivo: 4. de actione seu operatione Dei in ea: 5. de divino lumine: 6. de statu mentis supernaturali: & 7. de desiderio ejus, ceu medio ad obtinendam restitutionem. Quibus de materiis, quia illæ, ut patet, ad rem præsentem spectant, utilissimæ atque necessariæ sunt, & nihilominus valde raræ & parum obviæ; quia denique circa hæc & similia, nonnullæ difficultates & quæstiones ex occasione eorum quæ de iis in Discursu præliminari Cogitationum de Deo, tetigeram, mihi motae sunt aliquando a Generoso quodam Veritatis solidioris Amatore; ea propter non pigebit nunc ex istiusmodi quaestionibus magis praecipuas hic subnectere enodatas, veritatesque momentosas, quas lectores vel ob minorem attentionem, vel ob habitus & praejudicia adversa, vel ob proclivitatem nostram ad partes oppositas, vel ob minorem in his exercitationem, facile, tametsi perceptas, oblivisci possent, vividius si potero, inculcare, nonnullasque pluribus modis, quo possint ipsis esse exemplorum vel exercitii loco, in quibus se aliquamdiu optem ut exerceant, donec haecce mentibus aeternis vere digna vereque prosicua materia, aliquantum ipsis fiat familiarior.
units.tr: Here it only remains that, for a fuller elucidation of this last rule and of what is known, I should satisfy certain difficulties which some may perhaps raise about the matters contained in it, namely: (1) on the impotence of the mind or intellect; (2) on its rest; (3) on its passive state; (4) on the action or operation of God in it; (5) on the divine light; (6) on the supernatural state of the mind; and (7) on its desire, as the means of obtaining restoration. Since these matters, as is plain, pertain to the present subject, they are most useful and necessary, and yet very rare and little encountered. Finally, since concerning these and similar things some difficulties and questions were at times raised with me by a certain noble lover of more solid truth, arising from what I had touched upon concerning them in my Preliminary Discourse on Thoughts concerning God, I shall not hesitate now to append here, from such questions, the more principal ones, resolved, and to inculcate more vividly, if I can, the weighty truths which readers, through lesser attention, or through adverse habits and prejudices, or through our inclination toward opposing parties, or through lesser practice in these matters, could easily forget even though they have perceived them. I shall also, in several ways, set out some examples or exercises in which I would wish them to exercise themselves for a while, until this material, truly worthy of eternal minds and truly profitable, becomes somewhat more familiar to them.

units.la: PARS ALTERA.
units.tr: PART TWO.

units.la: Ubi varia quaestiones & difficultates de intellectus impotentia, quiete, passivitate, de Dei in illo actione & lumine, deque ejus statu divinior & medio ad illum proximo, enodantur.
units.tr: Where various questions and difficulties concerning the impotence, rest and passivity of the intellect, concerning God's action and light within it, and concerning its more divine state and the intermediate means closest to it, are explained.

units.la: I. De impotentia Intellectus.
units.tr: I. On the Impotence of the Intellect.

units.la: QUaeritur primo, cur tanta praedicetur Intellectus impotentia, siquidem experientia constet eum plurimas veritates, tam circa divina quam circa naturalia, circa sui & erga Deum, erga se, erga alios regimen ossi-cia d
units.tr: The first question is why such great impotence is ascribed to the intellect, since experience shows that it discovers and recognizes in itself very many truths, both concerning divine things and natural things, concerning itself, concerning God, and concerning the rule of duties toward oneself and toward others.

units.la: d
units.tr: d

units.la: officiaque detegere & agnoscere in se ipso, unde hæ etiam veritates innatæ dicuntur; ut taceam nunc infinita naturalia, quæ in mentibus utut corruptissimis reperiuntur tamen ? Respondeo : Has veritates non exurgere mente qua ægra & sibi relicta , sed ex operatione & subministratione Dei, qui mentem ægram & mortaliter sopitam sanare volens, gratiam ipsi dat aliquatenus expergiscendi , lumina largiens quædam viresque nonnullas, quibus illa tum se agnoscat ægram, tum videre incipiat Medici auxilium & potentiam, quæ imploret. atque iis præterea sese in vita corporea , quæ (cum aliis degenda) sanationis tempus est, sustentare queat. Sed si anima præviis istis gratiis tam turpiter abutatur , eas ut sibi velut origini vendicet; seque inde potentem & auxilio opitulatoris non indigentem imaginetur, atque ad lubitum concessis, non ad emendationem, utatur; tunc profecto similis dicenda est ægro lethargo & peste laboranti, qui præparatorio medicamine a Medico accepto , a veterno evigilans, nonnullisque sese motitandi viribus præditum sentiens; id propriæ suæ potentiæ sufficientiæque, quæ alieno auxilio non indigeat, acceptum referret, neque Medicum & medicamenta curaret, sed valere juberet. Secundo, ipsæ illæ virium aut luminum primitiæ, ita sunt comparatæ, ut impossibile sit homini sibi de potentia sua fidenti, educere inde corpus aut systema aliquod completum veritatum divinarum aut naturalium, multo minus sese ex virtutis præscripto erga Deum, erga se aliosque regere: uti patet experientia mille systematum chimæricorum sibioppositorum, nec non diluvio universali tot vitiorum terras undique inundantium, non rusticorum modo, sed & literatorum. Quæ sane est convictio suæ in ipsis illis, quibus se jactant luminibus & viribus, impotentiæ, & quidem ideo culpandæ, quod eam, tametsi convicti, aut nolint agnoscere; aut ab ea agnita deficere, & ad paratum Opitulatorem Optimum omni nixu sibi submini-strato tendere recusent.
units.tr: These are called innate truths. To say nothing now of the countless natural truths that are found even in the most corrupt minds, what is the answer? I answer: these truths do not arise from a mind that is sick and left to itself, but from the working and provision of God. Wishing to heal the sick mind, which is mortally drowsy, God gives it the grace to wake up somewhat, granting certain lights and some strength, by which it may then recognize itself as sick, and begin to see the Physician's help and power, and implore it, and by which it may also sustain itself in bodily life, which (to be spent along with others) is the time for healing. But if the soul abuses these preceding graces so shamefully that it claims them as its own origin, imagines itself powerful and in no need of the help of its Helper, and uses what has been given at its own pleasure and not for its amendment, then it must surely be likened to a patient sick with lethargy and plague. Once he has taken a preparatory medicine from the Physician and wakes from his drowsiness, feeling himself endowed with some strength to move, he would credit this to his own power and sufficiency, which needs no outside help; he would neglect the Physician and the medicines and bid them farewell. Second, those very first beginnings of strength or light are so constituted that it is impossible for a man who trusts in his own power to draw from them any complete body or system of divine or natural truths, much less to govern himself by the rule of virtue in relation to God, to himself and to others. Experience shows this, in the thousand contradictory chimerical systems, and in the universal flood of so many vices pouring over the lands on every side, not only among rustics but also among the learned. This is certainly a conviction of impotence in those very lights and powers in which they boast. Yet it is to be blamed, because they either refuse to acknowledge it even when convinced, or, having acknowledged it, refuse to forsake it and to strive with all effort toward the Best Helper who stands ready for them.

units.la: 2. Quæritur Secundo: quænam sit proprie ratio fundamentalis, cur intellectus, in quo statu nunc est, rerum mathematicarum veritatibus indubie cognoscendis, scrutandis, detegendisque in infinitum aptus sit industria sua naturali; non autem ita se habeat ad veritates divinas, easque quæ rerum naturas concernunt? Ratio dubitandi: Si Deus, qui est liberalissimus, talem menti naturam dedit ut non possit perdere capacitatem veritates ejusmodi mathematicas agnoscendi & detegendi; quare non dedisset id quod liberalitati infinitæ congruum magis videtur, naturam nempe quæ non posset amittere capacitatem cognoscendi veritates animæ dignitati magis convenientes? Antequam responderetur, observandum primo, in omni quæstione mathematica, imo in omni linea, superficie, figura, particula & quanto, omnia maxima & minima, pluraque alia maxime radicalia & essentialia, esse incognita & menti inscrutabilia, ita ut fere exteriora tantum sint intellectui accessibilia, ut alibi (a) annotatum est. Observandum secundo, non negari, intellectum earum veritatum, quarum ex creatione & constitutione capax est, semper esse capacem: est equidem; at remote, non proxime: activitate item aliena, non sua: qua in re a capacitate veritatum mathematicarum differt sequentes ob causas altius repetendas.
units.tr: 2. The second question: what is the fundamental reason why the intellect, in the state it is now in, is undoubtedly fit, by its natural industry, to know, search out and discover without end the truths of mathematics; yet it is not so disposed toward divine truths, and toward those that concern the natures of things? The reason for doubt: if God, who is most generous, gave the mind such a nature that it cannot lose its capacity to recognize and discover mathematical truths of this kind, why did he not also give what seems more fitting to infinite generosity, namely a nature that could not lose its capacity to know truths more suited to the dignity of the soul? Before an answer is given, it must first be observed that in every mathematical question, indeed in every line, surface, figure, particle and quantity, all the greatest and smallest things, and many other most radical and essential things, are unknown and inscrutable to the mind, so that for the most part only the outer things are accessible to the intellect, as has been noted elsewhere (a). Second, it must be observed that it is not denied that the intellect is always capable of those truths for which it is capable by creation and constitution. It is indeed capable, but remotely, not proximately, and by an activity that is not its own but another's. In this respect it differs from its capacity for mathematical truths, for the following reasons, which must be traced back more deeply.

units.la: Veritates rerum duplicis sunt generis. Aliae concernunt rerum fundum naturalem & materialem; aliae rerum ornamenta, complementa, perfectionem, immeationem, combinationes, lumen, gloriam, beatitudinem. Hae, quia a Dei lumine, gloria, beatitudine, meraque gratia emanant in res, & non pertinent ad rerum naturales partes, adeoque amitti possunt, patet non posse eas capi & cognosci nisi a mente quae luminis divini adhuc sit particeps: & cujus corpus iisdem, quantum eorum capax est, non sit privatum: adeoque si quae Mens lumine Dei privata est, corpusque ejus gloria primaeva, consequitur eam non posse istius generis veritates de bono statu & connexione ordinata rerum cognoscere, quippe destituta tum cognitione causae earum efficientis, luminis scilicet & gloriae Dei; tum effectu sive experientia ejus in se ipsa, suoque corpore. Veritates autem quae concernunt ipsam rerum basin, ut sic dicam, & materiam naturalem, sine quibus res nullo modo esse possunt, sunt quoque duplices. Vel enim concernunt rerum ortum intimum, modumque quo illarum essentia, vires & facultates ex Deo natæ sunt, quid illæ sint, quid in Deo referant; & de his quoque patet, quod ea mens, quæ Dei lumen amisit, nec novit interiora Dei, non posset quoque nosse interiora rerum, quippe quæ ectypa sunt interiorum Dei: adeoque mens illam capacitatem non potest non amittere separando se a Dei lumine: Vel eæ veritates respiciunt rerum materialia externa, & veluti cutim atque terminos, qui cum maneant in rebus utut in statum omnium dejectissimum redactis, eorumque experientia cum in corporibus reperire sit miserrimis atque damnatis, tum in mentibus infelicibus; consequitur, corruptas hasce mentes & miseras, siquidem earum veritatum experientiam habeant, ideas quoque ratiocinatas earundem formare posse sine lumine & gloria Dei, cujus istiusmodi crassæ, externæ, supersiciariæque veritates neutiquam sunt emanationes gratiosæ. Quia vero mathematicæ veritates sunt ultimi hujus generis; veritates autem naturæ rerum spiritualium & corporearum, nec non & suorum statuum completorum, ad priores duas species pertinent; patet funditus ratio cur mens vel intellectus corruptus sive lumine Dei privatus, has non possit detegere & cognoscere; illas vero, utut miser sit & cœcus, extraque lumen Dei, assequi tamen possit.
units.tr: Truths about things are of two kinds. Some concern the natural and material ground of things; others concern the ornaments, completions, perfection, beauty, combinations, light, glory and blessedness of things. Since these flow into things from God's light, glory, blessedness and pure grace, and do not belong to the natural parts of things, and so can be lost, it is clear that they cannot be grasped and known except by a mind that still shares in the divine light, and whose body is not deprived of them, so far as it is capable of them. Hence if a mind is deprived of God's light, and its body has lost its original glory, it follows that it cannot know truths of this kind about the good state and orderly connection of things, since it lacks both knowledge of their efficient cause, namely God's light and glory, and the effect, or experience of it, in itself and in its own body. Truths, however, that concern the very base of things, so to speak, and their natural matter, without which things cannot exist in any way, are also of two kinds. For they either concern the innermost origin of things, and the manner in which their essence, powers and faculties have been born from God, what they are, and what they bear in relation to God. And here too it is clear that a mind which has lost God's light, and does not know the inner things of God, cannot know the inner things of things either, since these are copies of the inner things of God. So the mind cannot but lose that capacity by separating itself from God's light. Or else these truths regard the external material things, as it were the skin and boundaries. Since these remain in things, even though things have been brought to the most abject state, and since experience of them is found in bodies that are most wretched and damned, and in unhappy minds, it follows that these corrupt and miserable minds, if they have experience of these truths, can also form reasoned ideas of them without the light and glory of God. Such gross, external and superficial truths are by no means gracious emanations of God. But since mathematical truths belong to this last kind, while the truths about the nature of spiritual and corporeal things, and about their complete states, belong to the first two kinds, it is clear at the root why a corrupt intellect, or a mind deprived of God's light, cannot discover and know the latter, but can attain the former, however wretched and blind it may be and however far from the light of God.

units.la: 3. Quæritur Tertio: Unde constet, Rationem,
units.tr: 3. The third question: how do we know that Reason,

units.la: {3}nem sive Intellectum actīvum , nobis esse facultatem superficiariam & accessoriam , ac veluti accidentalem ; non vero præcipuam; & dari in nobis facultates magis intimas atque essentiales ? Respondeo : Dei potentia agendi in me ; non pendet a potentia, qua intellectus meus excitat in me ideas actīvitate sua. Ergo quamvis non esset in me potentia excitandi mihi ideas actīvitate mea, atque adeo quamvis omnibus rationis seu intellectus actīvi ideis carerem, posset tamen Deus, cujus , ut dictum , potentia a me non pendet , vividum in me sui ipsius lumen, suamque vividam ideam sine actu meo ponere & excitare. Et quia Deus est perfectissimum & beatissimum bonum, si hoc modo potirer solo Deo, soloque ejus lumine, tunc nullatenus externus essem , siquidem rerum externarum ideas nullas haberem, (hoc est essem intimus, ) & vero essem completē beatus atque perfectus, (perfecto quippe gaudens bono) sine facultate , ideis & actibus rationis humanæ. Ergo sequitur & me habere capacitates sive facultates magis intimas & essentiales quam sit Ratio; & vero Rationem esse respectu harum facultatum Dei capacium, accessoriam , superficiariam & veluti externam , sive, quod idem est, Rationem esse facultatem, quæ comparata cum capacitate qua Deus animæ jungi potest , sit veluti superficiaria, externa & accessoria.
units.tr: ...nem, that is the active Intellect, is for us a superficial and accessory faculty, and so to speak accidental, and not the principal one; and that there are in us faculties that are more inward and essential? I answer: the power of God to act in me does not depend on the power by which my intellect stirs up ideas in me by its own activity. Therefore, even if I had no power of stirring up ideas in myself by my own activity, and so even if I lacked all the ideas of reason or of the active intellect, God, whose power, as said, does not depend on me, could still set within me his own living light and his own living idea, and stir them up without my act. And since God is the most perfect and most blessed good, if I were to possess God alone in this way, and his light alone, then I would in no way be external, since I would have no ideas of external things (that is, I would be inward). Indeed I would be completely blessed and perfect, rejoicing in the most perfect good, without the faculty, ideas and acts of human reason. Therefore it follows that I also have capacities, or faculties, that are more inward and essential than Reason is. Reason, indeed, in relation to these faculties capable of God, is accessory, superficial and as it were external. Or, which comes to the same thing, Reason is a faculty which, compared with the capacity by which the soul can be joined to God, is as it were superficial, external and accessory.

units.la: Est etiam eadem superficiaria respectu fruitionis rerum : nam rebus ipsis non potest frui
units.tr: It is likewise superficial with respect to the enjoyment of things: for reason cannot enjoy the things themselves.

units.la: 3. Unde constat intellectum activum, nobis esse facultatem superficiariam accessoriam? frui Ratio, nec rerum interiora vivide penetrare, sic Ratio v. g. non potest percipere lumen Solis vivum uti oculus, vel intellectus sensualis oculo adjutus. Sensus animae tum interni, tum externi, multo plus foliditatis habent : & rerum interiora atque substantiam magis degustant ; quam intellectus activus , five Ratio quae tantum rerum quasi superficies & picturas veluti per vitrum lambit, succum non admittit. Plura de his in libro de Eruditione Superficiaria.
units.tr: 3. Hence it is clear that the active intellect is for us a superficial and accessory faculty. Reason cannot penetrate the inner nature of things vividly. Thus Reason, for example, cannot perceive the living light of the sun as the eye does, or as the sensory intellect does when aided by the eye. The senses of the soul, both internal and external, have much more solidity. They taste the inner nature and substance of things far more fully, whereas the active intellect, or Reason, which only licks the surfaces and pictures of things as if through glass, does not take in their juice. More on this is said in the book on Superficial Erudition.

units.la: II. De quiete Intellectus activi seu Rationis.
units.tr: II. On the quiet of the active intellect, or Reason.

units.la: 1. Quaeritur , quaenam fit illa quies requisita intellectus activi , five rationis , ut a morbo interim sanari & convalescere possit an debeat , & an possit ratio esse sine actu aliquo ? Responsio. Non requiritur ut ratio aut non agat prorsus, aut ideis omnino careat ; sed tantum postulatur ut ipsa studiose illas in se non excitet eas scientifice contemplandi & demonstrative connectendi gratia , atque etiam ut a lectione librorum qui hoc exercitium in illa supplent & fovent , non patiatur id in se fieri. Hanc abstinentiam a libris rationem scientifico modo nimis exercentibus, atque eam etiam perverse nimis commendantibus, non possim satis inculcare. De me ausim dicere, si ejusmodi libri, quales novitii quidam, qui rationem, ejus ideas, actusque, nobis commendant velut lumen ipsum Dei, velut Deum ipsum nobiscum se communicantem, exhibentem, colloquentem, in manus meas incidissent, antequam solidioris veritatis principiis eram instructus, æternum de me actum fuisset: quippe omnium perniciosissimo illo errore imbutus, rejectionem rationis scientificæ quasi rejectionem Dei ipsius consideraɾs, remedii admittendi fuissem incapax. Hæc ergo omnino seponantur.
units.tr: 1. It is asked what that quiet is which the active intellect, or Reason, needs in order to be healed of its sickness and recover in the meantime, whether it ought to be quiet, and whether Reason can exist without some act. Answer: it is not required that Reason either cease acting altogether or be wholly without ideas. It is only required that it not stir up those ideas in itself with zeal, for the sake of contemplating them scientifically and connecting them demonstratively, and that it not allow this to be done within itself by reading books which supply and foster this exercise. I cannot sufficiently urge this abstinence from books that exercise Reason too much in a scientific manner and commend that practice too perversely. I may venture to speak of myself: if books of this kind had fallen into my hands before I had been instructed in the principles of a more solid truth, books such as certain novices write, which commend to us Reason, its ideas and its acts, as the very light of God, as God himself communicating, presenting himself and conversing with us, it would have been the end of me for ever. Imbued with that most pernicious error of all, and regarding the rejection of scientific Reason as the rejection of God himself, I would have been incapable of accepting the remedy. These things, therefore, must be set aside altogether.

units.la: Atsi quas habet ratio in se ideas, si quas ex præparatoriis Dei gratiis ei assisis adipiscitur, eas contemplęur ipsa, licet, imo ex eis etiam ratiocinari possit, non demonstrationes scientificas curiositati suæ speculative exhibendi gratia; sed ut inde motus & affectus in se excitet laudum, amoris, admirationis Dei, sui contemtús & humiliationis, hortationis ad officia & diligentiam spiritualem. Atque id sane activitatis genus & salutare & perquam necessarium est, nedum ab hoc sit abstinendum: namque & gratiæ (quibus nos a Deo præveniri diximus ad quæst. 1.) ita impendi debent; & vero nisi hujus generis actívitas deberet intervenire, nidularetur profecto pigritia & amor proprius cum omnis generis nequitiis in mente simpliciter otiosa, aut veluti stupida: quæ pigritia, quantum quidem ad eos spectat de quibus agitur, alio modo quam hujusmodi actívitate dispelli non potest.
units.tr: But if reason has any ideas in itself, or obtains any from the preparatory graces of God that assist it, it may contemplate them, and indeed it may even reason from them, not to display scientific demonstrations for the sake of its speculative curiosity, but so that from them it may stir up in itself motions and affections of praise, love, and admiration of God, of self-contempt and humility, and of exhortation to duties and spiritual diligence. This kind of activity is indeed both wholesome and very necessary, far from being something to abstain from. For the graces (by which we said in question 1 that we are forestalled by God) ought to be spent in this way. And indeed, unless activity of this kind were to intervene, idleness and self-love would certainly nest, together with every kind of wickedness, in a mind that is simply idle or, as it were, stupefied. Such idleness, so far as concerns those of whom we are speaking, cannot be dispelled in any other way than by this kind of activity.

units.la: Cæterum quia in actívitate ipsa nostra, etiam in hac quam bonam esse diximus, in-est. est imperfectio, crassior captus & motus, a Dei ejusque actionum spiritualitate multum abludens; ac praeterea quoque in eadem occultatur adhaerentia quaedam nostri, studiumque nobis ipsis & nostris agendi modis complacendi; hinc suo tempore in iis, qui ad ulteriora bene sunt dispositi, efficit Deus, ut etiam hujusmodi cessare debeat activitas. Et tunc quidem ei pertinaciter non est obsistendum. Sed antea interim solet Deus, nec non & Sanctiores, media quaedam adhibere ad infringendam illam activitatem intellectus, in ipso bono nobis interdum nimis gratam, nimis placitam, & quae quandoque superbiae, pertinaciae, multorumque malorum suggerit occasiones; quam ille ideo eousque vult mortificare (ut lic dicam,) ut sibi fiat vel ut indifferens, mortua, quieta. Inter quae media unum ex maxime conspicuis illud est, ut intellectui proponatur, ne ipse de divinis meditandi materiam, quam quidem velit, ex se desumat; sed ut ea ipsi in sanctioribus quibusdam libris praescripta exhibeatur, quorum cogitatis debeat se continuè accommodare, & in quibus tamen invenit nullam artem, nullos nexus, materias ipsi minus gratas, & (quod gravius est) vel centies repetitas atque ubivis recurrentes de suis demeritis, corruptione, sui contemtu, odio, fuga, abnegatione, crucifixione, de amore rerum divinarum & aeternarum, virtutum acquisitione, & similibus; quae is se dudum scire sibi persuadet, quae tamen vel ad nauseam usque ei,
units.tr: Moreover, because even in this activity of ours, which we have said is good, there is imperfection, a cruder grasp and motion quite unlike God and the spirituality of his actions, and because a certain attachment to self and a desire to please ourselves and our own ways of acting lie hidden in it as well, God in his own time brings it about, in those who are well disposed for higher things, that this kind of activity too must cease. At that point one should not resist it stubbornly. But meanwhile, before that, God and the holier men are accustomed to apply certain means for breaking that activity of the intellect, which is sometimes too agreeable and pleasing to us even in the good itself, and which sometimes gives occasion for pride, obstinacy and many other evils. God wills to mortify it to such a degree (so to speak) that it becomes, as it were, indifferent, dead and quiet. Among these means, one of the most conspicuous is this: the intellect is set before itself, so that it does not draw from itself the matter of meditating on divine things as it might wish, but is shown these things as prescribed in certain holier books, to whose thoughts it must continually conform itself. In these books it finds no art and no connections, only matters less pleasing to it and, what is more grievous, things repeated a hundred times and recurring everywhere: about one's demerits, corruption, self-contempt, hatred, flight, self-denial, crucifixion, love of divine and eternal things, the acquisition of virtues, and the like. The intellect persuades itself that it has long known these things, yet they are thrust upon it and repeated until it is sickened by them,

units.la: d 5 ... acti ac si asinus esset stupidus, earum capiendarum inidoneus, ingeruntur & repetuntur, quaeque vel decies vel centies lecta, adhuc pluries legere debeat. Haec sane curiosum novorum intellectum ejusque pruritum ftrenuè coërcent, cujus & interna ab his aversatio patescit satis ex querelis de isto secum agendi modo; quibus ostendit se tum adhuc valde imperitum ac ignorantem esse in viis Dei, tum perquam adhuc opus habere similibus mediis activitatem suam reprimentibus; & hinc simul apparet nullis aptioribus remediis histrionis illius curiosam agilitatem ac desiderium quod habet mutabilitatem suam in omnia convertendi, deleri & rumpi posse; quo deinceps, ista praeparatione adhibita, omnes Dei impressiones sine propriorum motuum obstaculo recipere queat.
units.tr: ...as if it were a stupid donkey, unfit to grasp them, and having been read ten or a hundred times, they must still be read more times again. These things indeed vigorously restrain the curious eagerness and itch of the new intellect. Its inner aversion to them is plain enough from its complaints about being dealt with in this way, by which it shows both that it is still very inexperienced and ignorant in the ways of God, and that it still greatly needs such means to restrain its activity. From this it also becomes clear that by no more suitable remedies can that actor's restless agility and his desire to turn his changeableness into everything be destroyed and broken, so that afterwards, with this preparation applied, he may receive all of God's impressions without the obstacle of his own motions.

units.la: III. De passivitate hominis, ejusque facultatum:
units.tr: III. On the passivity of man and his faculties:

units.la: 1. Quid magis obtinet aut occurrit in homine ejusque facultatibus, activitas an passivitas? Haec de passivitate cum omnium sit momentosissima materia, aliquantum distinctius ad hanc & sequentes quaestiones de ea proferam, quae alta mente reponenda peroptem.
units.tr: 1. Which is more dominant or more evident in man and his faculties, activity or passivity? Since this matter of passivity is of the greatest importance, I will set out somewhat more clearly this and the following questions about it, which I wish to be deeply pondered.

units.la: In homine Activa sunt 1. ejus libertas, qua facultates regit & applicat: 2. ejus desiderium, quo motus in anima excitat, & forte etiam in corpore: 3. ejus ratio sive inintellectus activus, idearum faber & complicator.
units.tr: In man, the active things are: (1) his freedom, by which he governs and applies his faculties; (2) his desire, by which he stirs up motions in the soul, and perhaps also in the body; (3) his reason, or active intellect, the maker and combiner of ideas.

units.la: Et de his notandum: (1) Libertatem praeter determinationem vel regimen nil efficere aut operari, non facultates, non actus, objectave aut sensus facultatum. (2) Desiderii motus quoscunque per se solos esse tenebrosos & angentes, nisi aliunde accedat & lumen, & obiecti boni versus illos effusio atque operatio.
