(3.) rationis ideas itidem, praeterquam quod per se sint tantum picturae steriles & inefficaces atque mortuae, non posse insuper bene formari, ordinari, ac lumine suo condecorari, nisi id aliunde e superioribus ei affundatur.
units.tr: Concerning these it should be noted: (1) that freedom, apart from determining and governing, achieves or accomplishes nothing: not the faculties, not the acts, not the objects or the senses of the faculties. (2) That the movements of desire, of whatever kind, are in themselves only dark and distressing, unless light also comes from elsewhere, and the outpouring and working of a good object upon them. (3) That the ideas of reason likewise, apart from being in themselves only barren, ineffective and dead pictures, cannot be well formed, ordered, or adorned with their own light, unless this is poured into them from above.

units.la: Ita ut omnis & tota hominis activitas, in se sola considerata, sine ullo alio auxilio, passive aliunde recipiendo, in hoc consistat, ut suas facultates ad lubitum movere possit inter tenebras, anxietates & chimaeras. Et hic est infernus ille verus & proprius, portio aeterna omnium Dei desertorum, qui sibi ipsis, suis potentiis, suaeque activitati propriae voluerunt se dedere, adhaerere, iisque confidere & niti.
units.tr: So that all of man's activity, considered in itself alone, without any other help, passively receiving from elsewhere, consists in this: that he can move his faculties at will amid darkness, anxieties and chimeras. And this is that true and proper hell, the eternal portion of all God's deserters, who chose to surrender themselves to their own powers and their own activity, to cling to them, and to trust and rest in them.

units.la: In homine Passiva sunt,
units.tr: In man, the passive things are:

units.la: 1. Ipsissima illa, quae jam diximus, libertas, desiderium & ratio, idque duplici modo. Primo quidem ex origine: namque nos ea ipsa non effecimus nobis; sed accepimus, & passivo modo recepimus a Creatore: omne enim quod factum est, se fieri passum est, estque origine passivum. Deinde eadem etiam sunt, aut fieri possunt, sive popotentiâ sunt, passiva ex regimine, quando videlicet homo intuens se sola activitate libertatis, desiderii & rationis, nihil præter anxias tenebras efficere posse, sponte tradit & reddit Factori suo libertatem suam, desiderια & rationem, ut ille opus suum sua sapientia regat, lumine illustret, bonitate & liberalitate perficiat. Tunc enim Deus hominis libertatem assumit, regit, servat & perficit, isque tunc ut talis, vere potest cum Paulo dicere; equidem vivo; tamen non vivo ego; sed vivit in me Christus, & quod vivam in carne, (quod inter homines appaream vivere ut ipsi, me regere, disponere de meis actibus & facultatibus sicut ipsi) id vivo in fide Filii Dei, in commissione & traditione facultatum & regiminis mei Filio Dei, qui acceptas illas regit. Scio cui credidi, & cui commisi totum regimen meum cum omnibus meis facultatibus & actibus, & scio quod sit potens ad conservandum contra omnia pericula & mala quibus hac in vita sumus obnoxii, depositum meum, me facultatesque meas, usque ad diem illam, in qua praeteritis periculis, reddet omnia commissa extra periculum omne gloriosa & perfecta.
units.tr: 1. Those very things we have just mentioned, freedom, desire and reason, and this in a twofold way. First, indeed, as to their origin: for we did not make them ourselves; we received them, and received them passively from the Creator. For everything that has been made is itself passive in its becoming, and is passive in its origin. Then, these same things are, or can become, passive by way of governance, that is, when a man, seeing that by the activity of his freedom, desire and reason alone he can produce nothing but anxious darkness, freely surrenders and gives back to his Maker his freedom, his desires and his reason, so that He may govern this work of His by His wisdom, illuminate it with His light, and perfect it by His goodness and generosity. For then God takes up, governs, preserves and perfects a man's freedom, and then the man, as such, can truly say with Paul: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God (that is, I appear to live among men as they do, but He governs me, and disposes of my acts and faculties as He wills), by the faith of the Son of God, in the committing and surrender of my faculties and my governance to the Son of God, who governs those things entrusted to Him. I know whom I have believed, and to whom I have committed my whole government with all my faculties and acts; and I know that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day, against all the dangers and evils to which we are exposed in this life, and that He will return all that was committed to Him, myself and my faculties, glorious and perfect, free from every danger.

units.la: 2. Passiva sunt praeterea in homine, fundus ille vel recessus intimus mentis nobilissimus & immensus, Deo aeterno, qua tali, fruendo factus, quaque a sola ejus aeternitate affici & actuari potest: deinde Desiderium mentis, supremum, quatenus proxime ad fruendum Deo disponendum est: non enim desiderari potest modo ei proxime digno, nisi ipsemet desiderium actuet & inflammet atque investiat: Porro, intelligentia sive intellectus superior atque divinus mereque spiritualis, qui solo divino lumine potest afficiet & illustrari, & ad quem nulla activitas, nisi Dei solius, nullæque ideæ accedere possunt, inter mere passiva habetur: tum & acquiescentia & lætitia summa, quas nisi a solo summo ente & bono posse affici & impleri, manifestum est. Denique ipsa etiam via nostra, cum omnibus sensibus nostris, interais atque externis (hoc in statu saltem,) passiva sunt: neque activitate, sed passivitate & recipiendo, percipiuntur a nobis vitæ illæ sensationes sive imagines lucis & visibilium omnium; item soni, sapores, odores & alia hujusmodi quibus afficimur. De objectis jam nil dicam, quæ in nobis agentia, extra aut intra nos sunt; etenim per se patet illa a nobis non esse effecta; ac proinde nos ad illas sive ad illorum in nos effluxus esse etiam mere passivos.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, there are passive things in man: that inmost ground or recess of the mind, most noble and vast, made for enjoying the eternal God as such, and which can be affected and actuated by His eternity alone; then the supreme desire of the mind, insofar as it is disposed to enjoy God immediately: for it cannot desire Him who is immediately worthy of it unless He Himself actuates, inflames and clothes that desire. Further, the understanding, the higher, divine and purely spiritual intellect, which can be affected and illuminated by the divine light alone, and to which no activity but God's alone, and no ideas, can approach, is regarded as purely passive. Also acquiescence and supreme joy, which are plainly affected and filled only by the highest being and good. Finally, our very way, together with all our senses, internal and external (at least in this state), are passive: and those sensations or images of light and of all visible things, likewise sounds, tastes, odours and other such things by which we are affected, are perceived by us not by activity but by passivity and receiving. I will say nothing now of the objects which act upon us, whether outside or inside us; for it is clear in itself that we did not produce them; and therefore, with respect to them, or to their outflowing into us, we are purely passive as well.

units.la: Jam si ex collatione activorum & passivorum in nobis comparatio instituatur, evidens fiet, activitatis quidem nostræ ipsaram admodum parvam esse; passivitatis autem tantum non immensam.
units.tr: Now if a comparison is made from setting the active and passive things in us side by side, it will become evident that our activity is indeed very small, but our passivity almost immense.

units.la: i. Quæritur secundo: Quibusnam magis perficiamur vel possimus perfici, activis an passivis. Resp. Quamvis ex modo dictis paulo magis perficiatur, quid huic quæstioni possit responderi, dico tamen expressius: Passivis magis perficiuntur hominem quam activis. Nam perfectio seu beatitudo summa, a Deo actibusque ejus
units.tr: i. Second, it is asked: by which things are we, or can we be, more perfected, by active or by passive things? Answer. Although from what has been said we are perfected a little more, something can be answered to this question, but I say it more plainly: man is perfected more by passive things than by active. For supreme perfection or blessedness, proceeding from God and His acts,

units.la: 2. Quieiamur: utrum activis an passivis magis perficiamur. procedens, passivas facultates cum penetralibus intimis tanquam vasa sibi destinata, implet, agit, beat. Ipsa harum facultatum passivitas actualis sive passio Dei, sive τὸ pati Deum ejusque actus, est formalis animæ perfectio atque beatitudo. Equidem activitas ad hominis perfectionem etiam conducit; sed suo modo: hoc est, non efficienter, sed admissive: activitas admittit non efficit persectionem à Deo procedentem & animæ oblatam, veluti in mendico extensio manus admittit, non autem efficit, oblatas divitias. Et notandum est, hanc activitatem ejusque actus, non esse rationis neque etiam speciales desiderii actus; sed generalem, sincerum & constantem illum libertatis actum, quo se cum desiderio, ratione & omnibus tradit passivam Deo, ita ut is ipse actus perfectionis admissivus in passivitatem terminetur.
units.tr: 2. Let us consider: whether we are more perfected by active or by passive things. Proceeding, it fills, acts upon and blesses the passive faculties together with their innermost recesses, as vessels destined for itself. The very passivity of these faculties, actual passivity or the suffering of God and His acts [τὸ πάσχειν Θεοῦ], is the formal perfection and blessedness of the soul. Indeed, activity also contributes to the perfection of man, but in its own way: that is, not efficiently but admissively. Activity admits perfection that proceeds from God and is offered to the soul; it does not produce it, just as a beggar's outstretched hand admits, but does not produce, the riches offered to him. And it should be noted that this activity and its acts are not those of reason, nor even the special acts of desire, but that general, sincere and constant act of freedom by which it surrenders itself, with its desire, reason and everything, passive to God, so that this very act of admissive perfection ends in passivity.

units.la: Qui si se ipso sive sua activitate vellet terminari, vel potius continuari, regi, niti, hoc ipso redderet se perfectione oblata indignam, eamque repelleret, atque efficeret sui perditionem & miseriam æternam, quæ ubi per activarum facultatum culpam ita effecta est, in facultates quoque passivas redundat, a quibus percipitur quatenus & se privatas, summo bono sentiunt, tum etiam tenebris, inquietudine, chimærisque absurdis torquentur atque agitantur.
units.tr: If it wished to end, or rather to continue, to be governed, or to strive by itself, that is, by its own activity, it would by this very fact make itself unworthy of the perfection offered, and would repel it, and bring about its own perdition and eternal misery. When this has been brought about through the fault of the active faculties, it overflows into the passive faculties as well, which perceive themselves as deprived of the supreme good, and are tormented and driven by darkness, restlessness and absurd chimeras.

units.la: Ergo summa perfectio homini advenit & fit ab alio agente (Deo) per facultates passivas, in quibus habitat & consistit: admittitur autem tantum, at non fit, per actívas, quando hæ passivitati sese tradunt. Econtra, summa hominis miseria fit & admittitur per facultates activas, activitatis suæ vindices, & passionem divinam rejicientes. Et hæc est ratio quare Sanctissimi quique semper hic timeant quando se ut agentes respiciunt. Verebar omnia opera mea: inquit (a) Jobus, ipsique Ethnicorum saniores inter signa ejus, qui in vera eruditione proficit, posuerint, (b) se (b) ipsum velut inimicum & insidiatorem observare.
units.tr: Therefore the supreme perfection comes to man and is brought about by another agent (God) through the passive faculties, in which it dwells and consists; it is admitted only, not produced, by the active faculties, when these surrender themselves to passivity. On the contrary, the supreme misery of man is brought about and admitted through the active faculties, the champions of their own activity, which reject the divine passion. And this is the reason why the holiest men always fear here when they regard themselves as agents. I was afraid of all my works, says (a) Job; and the wiser of the heathen, those who make progress in true learning, have placed among the signs of this: (b) to observe himself as an enemy and a plotter against himself.

units.la: In perfectione accessoria, quæ externa & corporea respicit, similia queunt observari. Quamvis enim haberemus libertatem facultatesque activas movendi corpus, ejusque membra, os, oculosque aperiendi, desiderandi sensationes gratas, excitandi vel imaginandi in conceptu nostro ideas varias de objectis; si tamen præter actus istos non adesset aliunde objecta grata, luminosa, composita, nec ullæ eorum in nos essent actiones, quas passive reciperemus; quid aliud quam miseria, externæ tenebræ, anxietatesque foret totus homo cum suis omnibus actibus? Desiderium cibi, sine cibo, ipsum fame torqueret; desiderium luminis apertioque oculorum sine lumine, tenebras ejus neutiquam dispelleret; libertas active se movendi quo vellet, non impediret sane quo minus sese in præcipitia daret. Quod si objectorum bonorum luminisque absentiæ subveniri posse arbitraretur per actus & ideas rationis, atque adeo in se eniteretur excitare ideas ciborum & satietatis, ideas luminis, ideas viarum, urbium, regionum, corporum, plantarum, animalium, rerumque quibus ad regimen conservationemque sui opus haberet; quis non videt & meras eum chimæras effecturum, &, si se illis juvari posse crederet, deliraturum atque periturum? quamvis enim omni quâ potest industria vel per seculum integrum eniteretur unius radioli luminosi, aut simplicis cujusdam domunculæ rerumque quæ ibi continentur, ideas excitare, nihil tamen omni suo labore efficeret quod rectum sit, multoque minus quicquam sibi procuraret proficui. At si apertis ejus oculis, facultatibusque ex liberalitate Creatoris objiciatur lumen cum objectis luminosis & bonis, tunc vel nictu oculi plus admirabilium, vividarum & delectantium sensationum imaginumque percipiet, quam infinitis annis vel peritissimus pictor mortuo modo potuisset depingere, vel quivis omni activitatis molimine umbratiliter & casse imaginari. Vide ut momento vis Creatoris per naturam agens, totius hemisphærii cœlestis terrestrisque horizontis creaturas innumeras in fundi oculi spatiolo ita exacte & admirabiliter depingat, ut frustra fuerint si vel mille annis immensoque labore idem conarentur imitari; ne dicam modum quo mens inde afficitur, esse omni humanæ activitati & rationi inimitabilem, imo &, nunc quidem, incomprehensibilem: & tamen id passivo modo nictu oculi perficitur in nobis, dummodo oculos tantum aperiamus, eosque luci objiciamus passivos. De infinitis aliis similia detegere possis circa corporea : at circa divina, quanto infinities id verius est? Intelleetus tui (animæ oculi) actívitate fi Deum, fi divinas res, lumina, obiecta, affectus, sensus, vias, opera, & quæ immensa ejusmodi sunt in rebus spiritualibus & internis, ea, inquam, fi velis rationis tuæ actívitate atque ideis repræsentare, tibique ita opem adferre; miserandis & operosis chimæris te ipsum misere circumvenis, etiamsi tibi soli plus quam omnibus simul hominibus suppeteret ingenii supellex amplissima. At si oculo intellectus actívi clauso, passivam Deo obvertas intelligentiam, is vel uno momento omnes aut quascunque volet, & quando volet, divinitatis veritates atque thesauros perfecte tibi & vivide suo lumine detecturus est, quod lumen idcirco in sacris adeo ardenter effagitant Sancti, tanquam omnis boni & perfectionis compendium atque complementum.
units.tr: Similar things can be observed in the accessory perfection, which concerns the external and bodily. For although we had freedom and active faculties to move the body and its members, to open the mouth and eyes, to desire pleasant sensations, to arouse or imagine various ideas of objects in our conception, yet if, apart from these acts, there were no agreeable, luminous and well-ordered objects from elsewhere, and no actions of these upon us which we might receive passively, what else would the whole man with all his acts be but misery, outer darkness and anxieties? Desire for food, without food, would itself torment him with hunger; desire for light and the opening of the eyes, without light, would by no means dispel its darkness; freedom to move actively wherever it wishes would certainly not prevent it from throwing itself over a precipice. But if he should think that the lack of good objects and light could be remedied by acts and ideas of reason, and so should strive by himself to arouse ideas of food and satiety, ideas of light, ideas of roads, cities, regions, bodies, plants, animals, and of the things he needs for governing and preserving himself, who does not see that he would produce mere chimeras, and, if he believed himself helped by them, would rave and perish? For although, with all the industry he could muster, he should strive for a whole century to arouse the idea of a single ray of light, or of some simple little house and the things contained in it, he would nevertheless accomplish nothing right with all his labour, and would procure for himself far less of any profit. But if, with his eyes open and his faculties, light is presented to him by the Creator's generosity, together with luminous and good objects, then in a single blink of an eye he will perceive more wonderful, vivid and delightful sensations and images than the most skilled painter could depict in infinite years when dead, or anyone could vainly and feebly imagine by any effort of activity. See how, in a moment, the power of the Creator, acting through nature, paints the countless creatures of the whole celestial and terrestrial hemisphere on the little space of the bottom of the eye so exactly and admirably that they would be in vain if anyone tried to imitate them even for a thousand years with immense labour; not to mention that the manner in which the mind is affected thereby is inimitable by all human activity and reason, and even, for now, incomprehensible. And yet this is accomplished in us in a passive manner in a blink of an eye, provided we only open our eyes and expose them passively to the light. From countless other things you could discover similar things concerning bodily matters; but concerning divine matters, how much more infinitely true is this! If, by the activity of your understanding (the eye of your soul), you wish to represent God, divine things, lights, objects, affections, senses, ways, works, and the immense things of this kind in spiritual and inward matters, by the activity and ideas of your reason, and so to bring them to yourself, you will miserably surround yourself with wretched and laborious chimeras, even though you alone should have a stock of intelligence more ample than all human beings together. But if, with the eye of the active intellect closed, you turn a passive understanding toward God, He, in a single moment, will reveal to you perfectly and vividly, by His own light, all or whatever truths and treasures of the divinity He wills, and when He wills; and it is this light that the saints in Scripture so ardently seek, as the sum and completion of all good and perfection.

units.la: Ex his clarum est, præcipua & fere omnia hominis bona, tam divina quam naturalia, consistere & perfici in passivis; etsi in libertate ejus activa positum sit (quod nunquam negandum est) ea vel admittere vel rejicere. Atque adeo liquidum est, delirare illos qui nolunt nisi ex excitatis sua actívitate ideis sapere, quique irrident eos qui sapientiam & cognitionem aliunde quam a se exspectant: qua in re profecto imitantur tenebriones, qui in tenebris nil nisi actívitate manuum, palpando & contrectando cognoscentes, rejicerent omnes vias aliis modis objecta percipiendi, & verò irriderent cunctos de rebus per lumen oculósque passivo plane modo cognoscendis loquentes. Sed redeamus ad quæstiones nostras, quarum erit,
units.tr: It is clear from these things that the chief and nearly all of man's goods, both divine and natural, consist in and are perfected by passive faculties, although it lies within his active freedom (which must never be denied) either to admit or to reject them. And so it is plain that those are deluded who will not be wise except from ideas stirred up by their own activity, and who mock those who look for wisdom and knowledge from elsewhere than themselves. In this they truly imitate blind men who, in darkness, know things only by the activity of their hands, by feeling and handling, and who would reject all the ways of perceiving that are opened by other means, and would mock everyone who speaks of things to be known wholly in a passive manner, through light and the eyes. But let us return to our questions, of which the third is:

units.la: 3. Tertia: Unde sciam Deum dedisse hac in vita menti meæ ejusmodi passivam eum cognoscendi facultatem, intellectu activo, sive ratione recta majorem? Unde qui nondum id expertus, idipsum sibi persuadebit, ut de eo sipem sibi faciat, eoque adspiret, & media, si quæ dantur, adhibeat?
units.tr: 3. Third: how do I know that God has given my mind, in this life, such a passive faculty of knowing him, greater than active intellect or right reason? And how can one who has not yet experienced it be persuaded of it, so as to form a hope for himself, aspire to it, and use the means, if any are given?

units.la: Respondeo; qui in altera vita ejusmodi facultates dandas esse solum profiterentur hic autem non; illi & rerum naturæ, & sibi implicite contradicerent. Notandum quippe est, ea quæ sunt homini maxime essentialia & intima, talia esse, quæ semper adsint homini, non autem quæ uno tempore absint, alio adsint, veluti sunt accessoria. Atqui facultates nostras passivas, qualis hæc est de qua quæritur, esse homini maxime essentiales & intimas modo ostendimus in responsione ad tertiam quæstionem de impotentia intellectus activi: & nunc concediturvel supponitur eas aliquando (in altera nempe vita) in homine esse futuras: Ergo jam nunc adsunt. Præterea, si illas possumus in altera vita recipere; ergo habemus capacitatem sive facultatem illas recipiendi: atqui hæc facultas illas recipiendi sunt ipsissimæ illæ jam facultates, quæ quia summæ sunt, non habent opus ut insint in aliis facultatibus, sed insunt ipsi immediate rei naturæ. Contradictio itaque est, dicere, haberi quidem facultatem eas facultates recipiendi, non vero haberi facultates ipsas.
units.tr: I answer: those who profess that such faculties are to be given only in the other life, but not here, would contradict both the nature of things and themselves. For it must be noted that the things most essential and intimate to man are those which are always present to him, not those which are absent at one time and present at another, as accidentals are. But we have just shown, in the answer to the third question concerning the impotence of the active intellect, that our passive faculties, such as the one in question, are most essential and intimate to man; and now it is granted, or supposed, that they will at some time (namely in the other life) be in man. Therefore they are already present now. Moreover, if we can receive them in the other life, then we have a capacity or faculty of receiving them; but this faculty of receiving them is itself those very faculties, which, because they are supreme, do not need to inhere in other faculties, but inhere immediately in the nature of the thing itself. It is therefore a contradiction to say that one has the faculty of receiving those faculties, but does not have the faculties themselves.

units.la: Quod experientia ejus se dicant destitui, querela erit justa, ubi media omnia ad experientiam faciendam, in regulis praecedentibus exposita, adhibuerint, & tamen rem ad cujus experientiam adspirant, videbunt non obtineri. Spem autem rei consequendae, animumque ad media exsecutioni mandanda addere, imo plenam certitudinem generare debent sequentia. Primo quidem, & praecipue, Dei potentia, cum ejus bonitate & sapientia. Quis enim dubitabit, posse Deum per actum suum excitare in intellectu nostro majorem & clariorem sui cognitionem quam nos ipsi per industriam atque activitatem nostram? Si Deus hoc potest in homine efficere; ergo homo habet potentiam idipsum a Dei actu patiendi. Ergo habemus de facto potentiam seu facultatem qua magis cognoscamus Deum passivo modo, quam facultate seu potentia activitatis intellectus, sive rationis nostrae, etiam rectae & incorruptae. Et quemadmodum ex Sapientia & bonitate Creatoris in operibus suis recte sequitur: homo habet facultatem esuriendi, ergo & facultate edendi cibosque admittendi donatus est & esse debet: ita ex desiderio quod unusquisque (juxta leges 2 & 3) in se experiri poterit, adspirandi ad cognitionem excellentissimam, omnibusque tenebris carentem, sequitur dari in eo facultatem istam cognitionem recipiendi, tanquam cibum animae suae desiderantis. Te-
units.tr: If they say that they are destitute of this experience, their complaint will be just when they have used all the means for making the experience, set out in the preceding rules, and yet see that the thing they aspire to is not obtained. But the following considerations ought to add hope of attaining the thing, and a mind to put the means into execution, indeed to generate full certainty. First and chiefly, the power of God, together with his goodness and wisdom. For who will doubt that God, by his act, can stir up in our intellect a greater and clearer knowledge of himself than we ourselves can attain by our own diligence and activity? If God can bring this about in a man, then man has a power to suffer this very thing from God's act. Therefore we in fact have a power or faculty by which we know God more in a passive way than by the faculty or power of intellectual activity, or of our reason, even when it is right and uncorrupted. And just as from the wisdom and goodness of the Creator it rightly follows in his works that man has a faculty of hunger, and therefore is endowed with, and ought to have, the faculty of eating and of receiving food, so from the desire which each person (according to rules 2 and 3) can experience in himself, aspiring to the most excellent knowledge, free from all darkness, it follows that there is in him a faculty of receiving that knowledge, as food for his desiring soul.

units.la: Testimonia etiam probarum mentium id expertarum, nobisque adseverantium dari in interioribus nostris infinitas facultates cognoscendarum & gustandarum rerum spiritualium Dei alteriusque mundi, præ quibus rebus quemadmodum quæcunque hic sunt & nostro modo cognoscuntur, nihil sint; ita & noster cognoscendi hic modus activus & crassus, nihil prorsus sit præ alio interiore & passivo; ea, inquam, testimonia non minus fidem nostram merentur, quam multa alia, quæ etsi non simus experti, aliorum tamen relationibus indubitato credimus, veluti dari Asiam, Africam, Antipodes, Urbes, Nationes aliaque infinita, de quibus quisquis sanus sine propria experientia alienæ credit experientiæ & adseverationi.
units.tr: There are also the testimonies of upright minds who have experienced it, and who assure us that there are in our inner selves infinite faculties of knowing and tasting spiritual things of God and of the other world; and in comparison with these, just as all things here, and all that is known in our own way, are nothing, so also our active and gross way of knowing here is nothing at all in comparison with the other, inner and passive way. These testimonies, I say, deserve our faith no less than many other things which, though we have not experienced them, we nonetheless believe without doubt on the reports of others: such as that there is Asia, Africa, the Antipodes, cities, nations and infinitely many other things, which any sane person believes, without his own experience, on the experience and assertion of others.

units.la: Adde ex natura mille experimentis patere, passivis modis excitari in nobis clariores, vividiores, excellentiores objectorum cognitiones, quam actívo solum intellectu, ut de imaginibus visus modo dictum est: qua via etiam convincimur latere in nobis facultates percipiendi infinita naturalia, quorum hactenus nullas habemus ideas nec experientias: nemo siquidem dubitat se habere facultates gustandi vel in se admittendi infinitos sapores, odores, sensus, sonos, aliaque quæ ipse nec dum expertus est, nec vel novit quidem. Si ergo lateant in nobis innumeræ quoad naturalia ipsa facultates, quæ per præsentiam objectorum nondum sunt actuatæ; quidni quoad Deum divinaque, præ quibus mille mundi naturales punctuli instar sunt.
units.tr: Add that nature shows by a thousand experiments that clearer, livelier and more excellent knowledge of objects is aroused in us in a passive way than by the active intellect alone, as was just said of the images of sight. By this way we are also convinced that there lie hidden in us faculties of perceiving infinite natural things, of which hitherto we have neither ideas nor experience. For no one doubts that he has the faculties of tasting, or of admitting into himself, infinite flavours, odours, sensations and sounds, which he himself has not yet experienced, nor even knows. If, then, there lie hidden in us countless faculties, as regards natural things, which have not yet been actuated by the presence of objects, why should there not be such faculties as regards God and divine things, in comparison with which a thousand natural worlds are like tiny specks?

units.la: Ex naturalibus id etiam patere. sunt, nobis inesse colligendum est multo immensiora vasa, & (si ita loqui licet) capacitates infinitiores? Ignoratur profecto hominis immensa dignitas atque capacitas. Est homo vas Dei, in quo Deus totus cum omnibus suis luminibus & beatitatibus, quantum quidem immensa ejus potentia & bonitas se ipsum communicare potest, inveniatur & hospitetur. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram & similitudinem. Delicia mea, esse cum filiis hominum. Gloria tota filia Regis (animae filiae Dei) est intrinsecus. Estis domus & templum Dei & Spiritus Sancti. Qui mandata mea habet eaque observat, is est qui me amat; qui autem amat me, a Patre meo amabitur, & amabo illum ego, & veniemus ad eum, & apud illum mansionem faciemus. Oculus (intellectus naturalis) non vidit, nec auris audivit; neque in cor hominis adscendit id quod Deus reservavit amantibus se, quaeque per Spiritum suum revelat, & quae infinita alia sunt Dei effata: quae sane nobis, quia de nobis maxima in re agitur, familiarissima esse deceret.
units.tr: Is it not to be gathered from natural things that we have in us far more immense vessels, and (if one may so speak) more infinite capacities? The immense dignity and capacity of man is certainly not known. Man is a vessel of God, in which God, whole with all his lights and beatitudes, is found and lodges, insofar as his immense power and goodness can communicate himself. Let us make man in our image and likeness. My delight is to be with the sons of men. All the glory of the king's daughter (the soul, the daughter of God) is within. You are the house and temple of God and of the Holy Spirit. He who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me; and he who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him. The eye (the natural intellect) has not seen, nor the ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him, and which he reveals through his Spirit; and there are infinitely many other sayings of God, which surely ought to be most familiar to us, since the greatest matter is treated concerning us.

units.la: Atque his constat, in nobis longe alias dari ad divina facultates, quam histrionicum & corruptum illum intellectum activum, qui cum multa sua & chimaerifica activitate tantopere clamat, & de omni homine conclamatum esse contendit, nisi ipse asinus elevetur in supremum mentis thronum, ibi omnia divina ac spiritualia ad stolidum examen suum revocaturus, atque ea omnia quae ipse ad modum suum non percipiet, rejecturus turus tanquam falsa aut nulla, utpote non congrua secum, qui sit sola facultas omnia percipiendi & cognoscendi. O stolidum brutum, infima omnium vacerra dignissimum!
units.tr: From these things it is established that in us there are, far otherwise, faculties for divine things than that histrionic and corrupt active intellect, which with all its activity and chimerical busyness cries out so loudly, and contends that everyone has been shouted down, unless the ass himself is raised to the supreme throne of the mind, there to bring all divine and spiritual things before its stupid tribunal, and to reject all those things which it does not perceive in its own way, as false or null, as not agreeing with itself, being alone the faculty of perceiving and knowing everything. O stupid brute, most worthy of the lowest basket of all!

units.la: 4. Alia quaestio. Siquidem ratione constet atque doceatur, & Deum esse, & eum amandum, qua in re totum hominis officium hac in vita comprehenditur, superfluae videntur esse superiores aliae facultates, quae ad hoc ipsum sint. Annon ergo, hac saltem in vita, ratione ista contentos nos esse decet, & aliarum curam atque exercitia ad futuram vitam differre? Resp. Mira objectio & ratiocinatio! Perinde diceres: Siquidem ratione constat, assumendos esse cibos, qua in re tota hominis vita animalis constiit, superflua videtur facultas edendi quae ad hoc ipsum sit. Imo eo ipso esse necessariam sequitur. Quid enim cum tua ratione & tuis cibis in idea atque demonstratione ratiocinata, illos esse realiter assumendos, conficies, nisi praeter illam facultatem picturariam, alias habeas facultates reales assumendi cibos? Ita ratio (aliquali lumine perfusa) ostendit Deum ejusque amorem esse animae cibum: at ostendit idealiter, picturarie, modo sterili & inefficaci: non ut picturae hujus speculationi inhaereamus otioso rationis oculo: hoc enim neque nostrum est officium, neque vero animam satiaret; sed ut de re ipsa vivide admittenda simus solliciti, atque adeo, ut quaeramus in nobis facultates reali-ores, quibus ipsa res perfici possit. Ergo postquam ratio monuit, & Deum esse, & amandum esse ; opus est facultatibus superioribus, quibus monitum hoc ideale possit vivide & realiter exsecutioni mandari. Hoc inquam ipsa ratio utcunque bene adjuta docet, ostenditque & se & idealem suorum monitorum considerationem esse deferendam, ut aliis quam frigidis suis viribus rem ipsam adorti facultatibus, iis non tenuia, non umbras, non inefficacia lumina picta, ut prius; sed magna, realia, viva, efficacia amplectamur.
units.tr: 4. Another question. If it is established and taught by reason that both God exists and that he is to be loved, in which the whole duty of man in this life is comprised, then other higher faculties, which are for this very purpose, seem superfluous. Ought we not, then, at least in this life, to be content with reason, and to defer the care and exercise of the others to the future life? Answer. A strange objection and reasoning! You might just as well say: since it is established by reason that food must be taken, in which the whole of animal life consists, the faculty of eating, which is for this very purpose, seems superfluous. Indeed it follows that it is necessary for that very reason. For what will you accomplish with your reason and your food, in the idea and reasoned demonstration that they must really be taken, unless besides that pictorial faculty you have other real faculties for taking food? So reason (bathed in some light) shows that God and his love are the food of the soul; but it shows this ideally, pictorially, in a barren and ineffective manner: not so that we should cling to this picture in idle contemplation with the eye of reason, for this is neither our task nor would it satisfy the soul; but so that we should be anxious to admit the thing itself vividly, and therefore to seek in ourselves more real faculties by which the thing itself can be perfected. Therefore, after reason has admonished that both God exists and is to be loved, there is need of higher faculties, by which this ideal admonition can be carried into execution vividly and really. This, I say, reason itself, however well it is aided, teaches; and it shows that its own ideal consideration of its admonitions must also be set aside, so that, approaching the thing itself with faculties other than its cold powers, we may embrace not thin things, not shadows, not ineffective painted lights as before, but great, real, living and efficacious things.

units.la: IV. De actione sive operatione Dei in homine.
units.tr: IV. On the action or operation of God in man.

units.la: 1. An Deus in anima corrupta (qualem supra descripsimus) possit operari, non quidem ex defectu potentiae; sed ob ejus quasi horrorem immensum quo corruptionem aversatur? Respondeo: Deus in anima corrupta agere potest, non tanquam amicus, qui corruptioni se uniat, sed veluti inimicus qui corruptionem in anima invadat, & exterminatam velit: quemadmodum Sol oriens, tenebras noctis aut nebulas invadit, & in eis agit, non ut illis se accommodet; sed ut eas dispellat. Et sane patet adversarios duos non posse inter se pugnare, nisi unus in alium agat, & concurrant, seseque attingant, non unionis, sed destructionis quaerendae gratia. Ergo praesentia corruptionis in anima, non officit praesentiae Dei eam impugnaturi. At si hominis libertas atque consensus malit adhærere corruptioni suæ quam Deo eam impugnanti, tunc actus Dei non potest diu manere in illo. Est enim a Deo decretum, ut non diu nec inhabitanter maneat cum homine, nisi ipso homine consentiente, seque Deo libere adjungente: alioqui Deus se negaret & profititueret ignominiæ, si homini ipsum reiectanti & contemnenti perpetuo vellet se offerre.
units.tr: 1. Can God operate in a corrupt soul (such as we described above), not indeed for lack of power, but because of his immense abhorrence of corruption? I answer: God can act in a corrupt soul not as a friend who joins himself to corruption, but as an enemy who attacks the corruption within the soul and wishes it destroyed. Just as the rising sun attacks the darkness of night or the mists, and acts upon them, not by accommodating itself to them but by dispersing them. And it is plain that two adversaries cannot fight unless one acts upon the other and they meet and touch, seeking not union but destruction. Therefore the presence of corruption in the soul does not hinder the presence of God, who is about to attack it. But if human freedom and consent prefer to cling to their own corruption rather than to God, who attacks it, then God's action cannot remain long in that person. For God has decreed that he will not remain long, nor dwell within a man, unless the man himself consents and freely joins himself to God. Otherwise God would deny himself and expose himself to dishonour, if he were to offer himself perpetually to a man who rejects and despises him.

units.la: 1. An non modo possit sed & velit Deus in anima corrupta agere & operari, atque de facto etiam operetur in interioribus animarum? R. Quod velit, patet (præter revelationis testimonium) ex eo, quod nobis det desiderium sui suæque in nobis actionis ut cuivis sibi sincere attendenti patet: patet etiam ex ipso facto, siquidem reipsa in intimis animarum operetur. Factum autem constat experientia cujusque qui debita media adhibuerit; imo omnes, ne pellimis quidem exceptis, si verum dicere volent, fateri & agnoscere cogentur in se (atque etiam extra se) operationes Dei gratiosas, quibus undique penetramur & circumcinguntur. Quot, quæso, hominibus accidunt inexspectato bonæ cogitationes, internæ admonitiones, motus & impulsus diviniores, reprehensiones & ictus validiores, gaudiorum solidorum sensus, terrores a malis revocantes, similiaque infinita? quæ sane non sunt nostræ operationes, quippe nec a nobis quæsitæ, nec ad libitum præsentes; imo sæpe & invitis nobis præsentes, nobisque adversantes: sed sunt operationes benignitatis Dei, nostris cordibus, medullis, ipsisque conscientiæ radicibus potenter ingestæ atque incussæ, queis Deus nos mille modis abiis, quæ opus suum in nobis perficiendum impedirent, retrahit, & invitat ad se, qui omnia ad consummationem operaturus & perducturus est. Præter quas experientias, ipsa creationis restaurationisque nostræ natura, ratio & scopus postulant necessario, ut Deus in animarum nostrarum intimis operetur.
units.tr: 1. Not only can God act and work in a corrupt soul, but does he also wish to, and in fact does he work in the inmost parts of souls? A. That he wishes it is plain, apart from the testimony of revelation, from the fact that he gives us a desire for himself and for his action in us, as is clear to anyone who sincerely attends to himself. It is plain also from the fact itself, since he really does work in the innermost parts of souls. The fact is established by the experience of everyone who has used the proper means. Indeed, all people, not even the worst excepted, if they wish to speak truly, will be compelled to confess and acknowledge in themselves (and also outside themselves) the gracious operations of God, by which we are penetrated and surrounded on every side. How many people, I ask, unexpectedly experience good thoughts, inner admonitions, more divine motions and impulses, rebukes and stronger blows, sensations of solid joys, terrors recalling them from evils, and countless similar things? These are certainly not our own operations, since they are neither sought by us nor present at our pleasure. Indeed they are often present even against our will and opposed to us. But they are operations of the goodness of God, powerfully poured and struck into our hearts, our marrow, and the very roots of our conscience. By these God draws us back in a thousand ways from the things that would hinder his work in us from being completed, and invites us to himself, he who is going to bring all things to their fulfilment and completion. Besides these experiences, the very nature of our creation and restoration, reason and purpose, necessarily demand that God work in the innermost parts of our souls.

units.la: Causam rerum efficientem dicunt vulgo metaphysici externam esse: id quod excellenter falsum est, nisi ubi de artefactis agitur, non item de systematibus naturalibus, in quibus causa efficiens semper est maximē interna: quanto plus in spiritualibus, quæ ex natura omnia sua intus possident? imo etiam eò magis, quando causa vult sibi domicilium, cui inhabitet, construere? In rebus corporeis, (quæ prout sunt, se nec penetrare, nec in se mutuo immeare aut insinuare possunt, uti res cogitantes) videmus apes v. g. ostreas, aliaque animantia intus esse, quando domunculas suas sibi circumfabricant, neque architectus atque operarii, nisi intus essent, interiora palatii construere unquam possent. In rebus cogitantibus facultates immensi desiderii, intellectus, aliaque factas esse, ut maneant objectis vivis vacuæ, dici non potest; effetque abnegatio Dei, si pro alio quam pro objecto illo summo, ejus lumine & motibus factæ dicerentur. Is autem quomodo eas efficere potuisset, quomodo intima nostra fabricatus esset, eaque ad sui imaginem & capacitatem adaptasset, nisi intus fuisset? & qui ea nosset, nisi intus esset? Si fecit ea intus operans, & circa se (ut Scripturæ verba adhibeam) tabernaculum suum disponens, ergo & continuo delectatus est & usus est inhabitatione ac operatione interna in illis, ne scopi operisque prævaricator esset. Iam veritas est nemini in dubium revocanda, res ubi corruptæ fuerint, si forte sint reficiendæ, eadem via restaurari qua prius sunt factæ: facta autem est anima in bono & primævo statu per Deum intus habitantem & operantem: Ergo & eodem modo restituenda est. Hoc est, absolute necessariæ sunt operationes Dei internæ ad animam a corruptione, a tenebris, ab inordinatione, ab arctitate & angustia in quam se reduxit, vindicandam & liberandam.
units.tr: Metaphysicians commonly say that the efficient cause of things is external. This is excellently false, except where artefacts are concerned, but not in the case of natural systems, in which the efficient cause is always most internal. How much more is this so in spiritual things, which by their nature possess everything within themselves? Indeed, it is even more so when the cause wishes to build for itself a dwelling in which to live. In corporeal things (which, being what they are, cannot penetrate one another or move into or insinuate themselves into each other, as thinking things can), we see that bees, oysters, and other animals are within when they fashion their little houses around themselves; nor could architects and workmen ever build the inner parts of a palace unless they were inside. In thinking things, it cannot be said that the faculties of immense desire, the intellect, and the others were made to remain empty, without living objects. It would be a denial of God if they were said to be made for any object other than that supreme one, by his light and motions. But how could he have produced them, how could he have fashioned our inner parts and adapted them to his image and capacity, unless he had been within? And who could know them unless he were within? If he made them by working within, and "arranging his tabernacle around himself" (to use the words of Scripture), then he has continually delighted in and made use of his inward indwelling and operation in them, lest he should be a transgressor of his purpose and work. Now it is a truth that no one may call into doubt: where things have been corrupted, if they are to be repaired at all, they are restored by the same way by which they were first made. But the soul was made in its good and original state through God dwelling in it and working within it. Therefore it must be restored in the same way. That is, the inward operations of God are absolutely necessary to vindicate and free the soul from corruption, from darkness, from disorder, and from the narrowness and straitness into which it has reduced itself.

units.la: Liceat simili aliquo rem, ad hebetudinem captus nostri juvandam, illustrare. Si quando officinam vitrariam fusilem ingredi tibi accideritt, inspice, si placet, quomodo ex vili cinere in ignem conjecto, nitida & egregia vasa vitrea fiant per immissionem flatus, qui intus movens & operans, dat vasis capacitatem & formam suam: hincque cogita, hominem ita ex cinere nihili desumptum, atque ab igne amoris Dei susceptum, per inspirationem intimam Spiritus Dei formatum fuisse, atque suas capacitates, facultates, nec non omnia, etiam accessoria, per illum inhabitantem & intus operantem Spiritum accepisse.
units.tr: Let me illustrate the matter with some comparison, to help the dullness of our understanding. If ever you happen to enter a glass-blowing workshop, look, if you like, at how, from worthless ash cast into the fire, bright and excellent glass vessels are made by the blowing in of breath. This breath, moving and working within, gives the vessel its capacity and form. From this, think of man, taken thus from the ash of nothing and received by the fire of God's love, as formed through the inward inspiration of the Spirit of God, and as having received his capacities, faculties, and all else, even accessory things, through that indwelling and inwardly working Spirit.

units.la: Et quemadmodum, si accidat vitrum frangi ejusque fragmenta in lutum sordesque abjici, non potest aliter restitui, nisi ut resumtum, contusum & in fornacem immissum, ibique purgatum & igne liquefactum & penetratum, de novo assumatur & inspiretur ut prius interno flatu fabricatoris in centrum ejus immisso: sic homo lapsus, fractus, corruptus; sordibus & tenebris errorum & malorum plenus, restitui non potest, ne quidem quoad externa & rationem, nisi a Deo ex cœno lutosarum suarum occupationum assumptus, contusus, atque in purificationis amorisque divini ignem immissus, ab adorandi Spiritus ejus intimis inspirationibus & arcanis operationibus de novo inspiretur & agatur, unde priores capacitates, facultates, statum decorum, formamque adeo cum hisce etiam externam & congruam accipiat. Quodsi hæc ab irrisoribus rideantur, næ intimâ ipsi commiseratione sunt dignissimi!
units.tr: Just as, if a glass happens to break and its fragments are cast into mud and filth, it cannot be restored except by being taken up again, crushed, put into the furnace, purified there, melted and penetrated by the fire, and then taken up anew and breathed into, as before, by the inward breath of the maker placed at its centre; so fallen, broken, corrupted man, full of the filth and darkness of errors and evils, cannot be restored, not even as to external things and reason, unless he is taken up by God from the mire of his muddy occupations, crushed, and placed in the fire of purification and divine love, and is breathed into anew and moved by the innermost inspirations and secret operations of his adorable Spirit. From this he receives his former capacities, faculties, decorous state and form, and so with these also his external and fitting form. But if these things are laughed at by mockers, they are most worthy of our inward pity!

units.la: 3. Sed quæret aliquis: Quandoquidem Deus est summe luminosus & beatus, persectissimoque modo agens, nonne videtur, si in homine operaretur vere, hominem inde mox fieri debere & luminosum & beatum, neque dein perire posse? Resp. diuncut recte Philosophi, actionem non recipi ad modum agentis, sed ad modum subjecti recipientis, atque pro ejus vel capacitate, vel infirmitate. Quapropter quando Deus in anima explicat operationes suas, tenebris animæ adversantes, easque impugnantes; anima quidem eo momento luminosa fit; sed aliquatenus tantum, & ex parte nonnulla folum: quia Deus non impugnat simul & femel uno actu omnes ejus tenebras, quod si faceret, id nulla posset perferre anima: isthæc enim pugna foret ei terribilior quàm ut vires ejus languidæ eam sustinere possent: haud secus ac videmus subitum & inexspectatum solis lumen ab ægris oculis tolerari non posse. Quapropter Deus ex aliqua duntaxat parte nonnullas mentis aggreditur luminoso actu suo tenebras; tuncque videt quidem mens aliquid veri, at contra se, suum statum, suam corruptionem, opiniones, amorem proprium, superbiam, cæteraque sua vitia pugnantis; id quod non sine ingenti percipit sentitque dolore atque anxietate. Cum autem ista Dei operatio menti fit dolorifica atque angens, & multo magis adhuc cæteræ sequentes; si anima tunc nolit eas perpeti anxietates, velitque impatientius ab iis liberari, atque adeo si a Dei operatione eas causante velit subduci, & vanis sese dare occupationibus, queis divinæ operationis importunus sensus, minus sentiatur, aut prorsus in ea supprimatur; tum Deus, postquam diu satis tentavit illam ad frugem revocare & expertus est illam pleno consilio nolle redire, retrahit operationem suam benignam, & animam sibi relinquit. Atque tunc infelix illa anima ma nullas amplius sentit in se pugnas ; sed plane dedoluit, devenitque in periculosissimum illum perditionis statum, qui est ipfiffima Spinoziana tranquillitas.
units.tr: 3. But someone will ask: since God is supremely luminous and blessed, and acts in the most perfect manner, does it not seem that, if he truly worked in a man, the man ought at once to become luminous and blessed, and be unable to perish afterwards? Answer: The Philosophers rightly distinguish that action is received not according to the mode of the agent but according to the mode of the receiving subject, and according to its capacity or its infirmity. Therefore, when God unfolds his operations in the soul, opposing and assailing its darkness, the soul indeed becomes luminous at that moment, but only to a certain degree and in some part alone. This is because God does not attack all its darkness at once and in a single act. For if he did, the soul could bear none of it, since that struggle would be more terrible than its feeble powers could sustain. Just as we see that a sudden and unexpected sunlight cannot be endured by sick eyes. Therefore God attacks the darkness of the mind only partly, with his luminous act. Then the mind indeed sees something of the truth, but at the same time it sees itself, its state, its corruption, its opinions, its self-love, its pride and its other vices resisting. This it perceives and feels not without great pain and anxiety. But when this operation of God becomes painful and distressing to the mind, and much more so the others that follow, if the soul then does not wish to endure these anxieties, and wants more impatiently to be freed from them, and so if it wishes to withdraw from the operation of God that causes them, and to give itself to vain occupations, by which the troublesome sense of the divine operation is less felt or wholly suppressed in it; then God, after he has tried long enough to bring it back to fruitfulness, and found that it wills with full deliberation not to return, withdraws his kindly operation and leaves the soul to itself. And then that unhappy soul no longer feels any conflicts within itself, but has become wholly insensible, and falls into that most perilous state of perdition, which is the very Spinozist tranquillity.

units.la: Operatio divina utut luminosa & beatificans non tamen est beatitudo animæ actualis, quamdiu in anima invenit tenebras & corruptionem quas impugnet; e contra, tunc ea operatio ex sensu ictuum omnipotentis adversarii in animam corruptioni unitam pugnantis dolorem ingentem potius efficit. At ubi in anima nil adversi superest quod impugnet divinæ operationis redditudo, ea tunc triumphum agit, & beatitudinem seu gaudium immensum pleno effundit sinu : namque tunc amicus cum amico plena pace conjungitur & se se iam mutuis excipiunt amplexibus. Perficies in me misericordias tuas usque ad pacem plenariam quam tecum habebunt interiora & exteriora mea cum absorpta fuerit mors in victoriam. Augustinus.
units.tr: The divine operation, however luminous and beatifying it may be, is not yet the actual beatitude of the soul as long as it finds in the soul darkness and corruption to attack; on the contrary, then that operation produces rather great pain, from the feeling of the blows of the almighty adversary fighting against the corruption united to the soul. But when nothing hostile remains in the soul for the rectitude of the divine operation to attack, then it celebrates its triumph and pours forth beatitude, or immense joy, from a full bosom: for then friend is joined with friend in full peace, and they now welcome each other with mutual embraces. Thou wilt perfect Thy mercies in me, even to that full peace which my inward and outward parts shall have with Thee, when death is swallowed up in victory. Augustine.

units.la: Ergo ad percipiendas & sentiendas in se gratas lætasque & lætificantes Dei operationes, mens corruptione rerumque omnium amore prius purgata ut sit necesse est, sicut nullis amplius rebus adhæreat affectu. Non dico usu, qui necessarius sit, & ad vitæ naturalis conservationem faciat: hic enim non obest divino sensui: nam licet eo tempore cum mens pura creaturarum usui necessario deditur, à sensibus interioribus divinisque interdum distrahatur; non tamen inde contrahit obstaculum aut ineptitudinem ad operationes Dei admittendas & sentiendas; quod fieret si inutilibus aut noxiis pateretur se distrahi & occupari.
units.tr: Therefore, in order to perceive and feel within oneself the pleasing and joyful operations of God, which bring joy, the mind must first be purged of corruption and of love for all things, so that it clings to no things any longer with affection. I do not mean use, which is necessary and serves the preservation of natural life: for this does not hinder the divine sense; for although at the time when the pure mind is necessarily given over to the use of creatures, it is sometimes drawn away from the inner and divine senses, yet it does not thereby contract an obstacle or unfitness for admitting and feeling the operations of God; which would happen if it allowed itself to be distracted and occupied by useless or harmful things.

units.la: V. De Lumine Dei in homine.
units.tr: V. On the Light of God in Man.

units.la: De hoc multa quæri possent: sed ad præsens institutum exercitiumque, sufficient nobis sequentia.
units.tr: Many questions could be raised about this, but for the present purpose and exercise the following will suffice.

units.la: 1. An detur lumen Dei distinctum a lumine Rationis? Annon forte idea Dei in ratione, cæteræque ideæ, sint lumen Dei? aut saltem an Ratio luminis divini possit esse capax? Tiimembris quæstio, cujus prima pars eo redit: An Deus per se lucere possit in anima; &, An Dei actus immediatus & lucidus, sit actus imperfectus ipsius animæ ideas sibi excitare conantis? Quis de hoc unquam quæstionem movebit, nisi simul confundenda esse putet Deum & creaturam, actumque Dei & actum creaturæ? Sed quoniam auctoritatibus humanis non pauci ducuntur, subjiciam hic locum insignem ex Cartesio, unde hæc distinctio pateat.
units.tr: 1. Is there a light of God distinct from the light of Reason? Might the idea of God in reason, and the other ideas, be the light of God? Or at least, can Reason be capable of the divine light? This is a three-part question, the first part of which comes to this: Can God shine in the soul through himself? And: Is the immediate and luminous act of God an imperfect act of the soul itself, striving to excite ideas in itself? Who would ever raise this question unless he thought that God and the creature, and the act of God and the act of the creature, must be confused? But since not a few are led by human authorities, I shall set here a notable passage from Descartes, by which this distinction may become clear.

units.la: * Is est in Epistolarum suarum ultima, ubi etsi agat de cognitione intuitiva post hanc vitam, quia tamen explicat ibi lumen divinum, ejusque modum agendi in anima, illud an in hac an in altera vita fiat, jam ad hanc rem perinde est. Dicit ergo: dari cognitionem, quæ sit (a) illustratio mentis per quam conspicit in lumine Dei res illas quas ipsi placuit ei detegere per IMPRESSIONEM DIRECTAM CLARITATIS DIVINÆ in nostrum intellectum, qui in eo non consideratur tanquam AGENS.
units.tr: This is from the last of his Letters. There, although he is treating of intuitive knowledge after this life, nevertheless, since he explains in that place the divine light and its mode of acting in the soul, it makes no difference to the present matter whether this takes place in this life or in the other. He says, therefore, that there is a knowledge which is (a) an illumination of the mind, through which it perceives in the light of God those things which it has pleased God to disclose to it, by a DIRECT IMPRESSION OF DIVINE CLARITY upon our intellect, which in this case is not regarded as the AGENT,

units.la: (a) Cartes. Epist. Tom. III. Ep. 114. gens : sed saltem veluti recipiens aut patiens radios divinitatis. Deinde postquam ixit quædam de notitiis intellectus nostri, & ctivitate hujus, ratiocinantis ex ideis conlifloribus vel ex auctoritate revelata & obcura, addit : Quicquid acquirimus per vias illas quibus ratio insistit, primo involutum est rum e quibus dutum est principiorum tenoris ; tum etiam incertitudini, quam in omnibus nostris argumentationibus experimur, rum hæc comparaturus pergit : Confer jam luas istas cognitiones, & perpende, utrum in ac perceptione turbida & incerta, quaque nobis multum negotii fecerint, & quâ etiam acquisita non nisi quibusdam momentis utimur, quippiam simile sit lumini puro, constanti, claro, certo, facili et semper præsenti. Postea hæc de altera vita proaturus per experientiam ejusdem & similium quæ in hac vita experimur, sic orationis filum persequitur : Cæterum, an mens nostra tum cum a corpore erit separata, aut cum corpus illud glorificatum ipsi nullum amplius impedimentum creaverit, non possit tales recipere demonstrationes & cognitiones directas, & eo num tu dubitare possis, cum in hoc ipso corpore sensus ipsi ejusmodi cognitiones suppeditent rerum corporalium & sensibilium, cumque anima nostra jam habeat earum quasdam ex beneficentia sui Creatoris, fine quibus ratiocinationis capax non effet ? Fateor esse illas aliquantulum obtenebratas mixtura corporis : attamen subministrant nobis cognitionem quandam primam, gratuitam, certam.
units.tr: (a) Descartes, Letters, Vol. III, Letter 114: but only as receiving or suffering the rays of the divinity. Then, after saying certain things about the notions of our intellect and its activity, reasoning from ideas that are concurrent or from revealed and obscure authority, he adds: Whatever we acquire by those ways along which reason proceeds is at first involved both in the principles from which it is drawn, and in the uncertainty which we experience in all our arguments. Intending to compare these, he goes on: Now compare those knowledges of yours, and consider whether anything in that turbid and uncertain perception, which has given us so much trouble, and of which we use only certain moments even when it has been acquired, is like the pure, constant, clear, certain, easy and always present light. Afterwards, intending to treat of the other life by means of experience of the same and similar things which we experience in this life, he follows the thread of his discourse thus: Moreover, whether our mind, when it is separated from the body, or when that glorified body will no longer create any impediment for it, cannot receive such demonstrations and direct cognitions, and whether you can doubt this, since in this very body the senses themselves supply such cognitions of corporeal and sensible things, and since our soul already has some of them from the kindness of its Creator, without which it would not be capable of reasoning? I confess that these are somewhat obscured by the admixture of the body; nevertheless they supply us with a certain first, gratuitous and certain knowledge.

units.la: {4} tam, quamque mente nostra MULTO MAIORI CONFIDENTIA ATTINGIMUS, quam relationi oculorum nostrorum tribuamus. Infundi autem menti cognitiones quasdam oculorum relatione multo certiores, easque argumentum esse capacitatis animæ ad recipiendas simili modo a lumine Dei cognitiones passivas; adducto exemplo particulari sic illustrat. Nonne mihi largieris, minus te certum esse præsentia objectorum quæ vides, quam veritatis hujus propositionis, Cogito ergo sum. Cæterum cognitio ista non est opus tuæ ratiocinationis, neque præceptum tibi a Magistris tuis traditum, Anima tua eam sentit, videt, contrectat. Et quamvis imaginatio tua, quæ se per summam importunitatem cogitationibus suis intermiscet, claritatem ejus diminuit, dum eas suis figuris replere satagit, est tamen illa cognitio argumentum capacitatis animarum nostrarum ad recipiendam a Deo cognitionem intuitivam. Quo in egregio Cartelii loco nil ad rem nostram desiderari posse videtur, nisi quod exemplum, Cogito ergo sum, nimis frigidum sit, potuissetque ejus vice nonnulla alia, quæ supra (a) protulimus apponere: deinde etiam quod male ad vitam futuram videatur relegasse specialiores ejusmodi per lumen divinum de rebus cognitiones, quæ etsi demum in altera vita plenæ sint ac perfectæ, hic tamen in bene dispositis mentibus initium sumunt, & communicantur interdum quam liberalissime. Sed quia Cartefius extra viam earum quærendarum erat, ideo non potuit de iis rectius dijudicare.
units.tr: {4} Let us take hold of it WITH FAR GREATER CONFIDENCE than we ascribe to the report of our eyes. Moreover, certain knowledges are infused into the mind which are far more certain than by the report of the eyes, and these are a proof of the capacity of the soul to receive in a similar way, from the light of God, passive knowledges. He illustrates this by a particular example: Do you not grant me that you are less certain of the presence of the objects you see than of the truth of this proposition, I think, therefore I am? Then he continues: But that knowledge is not the product of your reasoning, nor a precept handed down to you by your masters; your soul feels it, sees it, handles it. And although your imagination, which mingles itself with your thoughts with the greatest importunity, diminishes its clarity while it labours to fill them with its figures, that knowledge is nevertheless a proof of the capacity of our souls to receive intuitive knowledge from God. In this excellent passage of Descartes nothing seems lacking to our purpose, except that the example, I think, therefore I am, is too cold, and that some other example, such as those we have set forth above (a), might have been put in its place. Further, he seems to have wrongly relegated to the future life the more particular knowledges of things through the divine light; although these are at last full and perfect in the other life, here they nonetheless begin in well-disposed minds, and are sometimes communicated most liberally. But since Descartes was outside the way of seeking them, he could not judge of them more rightly.

units.la: E dictis liquet satis, Ideam Dei, quam intellectus actibus jam nobis repræsentamus, non esse ipsum lumen divinitatis directum, quod est ipsissimus Deus vivide lucens; sed esse cogitationem hominis creatam, cui inest tantum nota & pictum quoddam Dei simulacrum, obscurum, crassum, umbratile & imperfectissimum, quod ad lubitum vel in mente excitari, aut ab ea revocari potest, quodque in ea nullam vim, virtutem, claritatem vividam, nullam tranquillitatem, lætitiam, delicias Deo dignas generare aptum est. Et revera, si ratio nostra excitans in se quando vult ejusmodi de Deo ejusque attributis ideas steriles, mortuas, atque imperfectissimas, eo ipso excitaret in se lumen Dei, Deumque ipsum tangeret, manifeste sequeretur Deum ejusque lumen forem rem sterilem, mortuam, inefficacem; non infinitæ, sed exiguæ aut nullius virtutis, nec non & productionem esse creaturæ: cum tamen evidens per se sit, rem infinitæ virtutis, potentiæ & luminis non posse vere tangi nec effici per actus crassos & steriles ejusmodi in nobis facultatis, quæ adeo superficiaria est, ut ne quidem ipsas creatas res, seu corporales sint seu spirituales, vere attingat, aut eas in se revera deducat. Etenim quando in ratione excito ideam v. g. mentis Salomonis, ejus Sapientiæ, virtutum & gloriæ: ipsa propterea Salomonis mens, sapientia virtusque non sunt in ratione animaque mea: ita & quando corporum, gemmarum, urbium, lucis, sensationum ideas efformat intellectus, non tamen res aut sensationes ipsas habet aut tangit; sed picturas earum duntaxat. Sic quoque se res habet quando actívitate nostra ideam Dei, ejusque luminum & virtutum formamus: non Deum, non lumen divinum, non virtutes ejus reales ideo habemus ac vere tangimus mente; nisi sane putarës. Deum ejusque lumen esse rem & virtutis fere nullius, & mentis tuae producionem. Quod quam sit absurdum, non opus est quaesito argumento evincere.
units.tr: From what has been said it is sufficiently clear that the idea of God, which we now represent to ourselves by acts of the intellect, is not the direct light of divinity itself, which is the very God shining vividly; rather it is a created thought of man, in which there is only a mark and a certain picture, a simulacrum of God, dim, gross, shadowy and most imperfect, which can be excited in the mind or recalled from it at will, and which is not apt to generate in the mind any power, virtue, vivid clarity, any tranquillity, joy or delights worthy of God. And indeed, if our reason, when it wills, excited in itself such sterile, dead and most imperfect ideas of God and his attributes, then by that very act it would excite in itself the light of God and would touch God himself; and it would clearly follow that God and his light would be a sterile, dead and ineffective thing, of no infinite but of slight or no virtue, and also that it would be a product of the creature. Yet it is evident in itself that a thing of infinite virtue, power and light cannot truly be touched or effected by such gross and sterile acts of a faculty in us, which is so superficial that it does not even truly attain the created things themselves, whether corporeal or spiritual, nor truly bring them into itself. For when in my reason I excite the idea, for example, of the mind of Solomon, of his wisdom, virtues and glory, the mind of Solomon itself, his wisdom and virtue, are not thereby in my reason and soul; so too when the intellect forms ideas of bodies, gems, cities, light and sensations, it does not thereby have or touch the things or the sensations themselves, but only their pictures. It is the same when, by our activity, we form the idea of God and of his lights and virtues: we do not thereby have God, the divine light, or his real virtues, nor truly touch them with the mind; unless, indeed, you should think that God and his light are a thing of almost no virtue and a product of your mind. How absurd that is, there is no need to prove by a laboured argument.

units.la: Hinc patet etiam (quod tertium quaestionis membrum respicit) rationis facultatem superficiariam atque desultoriam, intimi atque tranquilli luminis Dei capacem esse non posse; sed tantum nonnullorum ejus essectorum, quae eam sanent, restituant, restitutamque capacem reddant non quidem efficiendi lumen divinum, at picturas tamen rerum ordinatas loco chimaerarum priorum depingendi. Tametsi quando ratio sese passive Deo objicit, nonnullos divini conceptus arbitrarii radios recipere tunc sit apta.
units.tr: Hence it is also clear (which concerns the third member of the question) that the superficial and wandering faculty of reason cannot be capable of the intimate and tranquil light of God; it is capable only of certain effects of it, which heal it, restore it, and, once restored, make it capable not indeed of producing the divine light, but of depicting in place of the former chimaeras orderly pictures of things. Although, when reason presents itself passively to God, it is then apt to receive some rays of the divine conception that are not of its own making.

units.la: 2. De amissione luminis divini praelumine rationis.
units.tr: 2. On the loss of the divine light, which goes before the light of reason.

units.la: 2. An lumen divinum possit amitti ? & cur facilius amittatur quam lumen rationis ? Resp. De priori crediderim neminem posse dubitare, etsi rationes fundamentales non statim quibusvis pateant: sunt autem illae ex ista distinctione desumendae, qua aliquoties dona Dei divisimus in naturalia, quae naturam hominis constituunt; & gratuita, quae sunt instar ornamentorum quibus natura ornatur, perficitur, & gloria amicitur. Illa non possunt amitti, quoniam ipsa natura amitti nitti non potest;cum sit absolutissime a Deo ita: hæc, quæ non sunt pars naturæ, quoniam a creatore perpetuo & continuo in creuram (velati lux Solis in corpora opaca) funduntur ea conditione, ut creatura illis se obvertat, consentiat, & recepta grato animo imper agnoscat; sevenit inde ut quam primum ab his conditionibus deficit, dona Dei mittat, quæ non in ipsa, sed in solo Deo sunt indicata: omnino veluti in luce naturali fit, uæ non in corporibus opacis, sed in Sole radicata, singulis momentis ab eo ad corporea ebet ita emanare, ut si vel per momentum essaret autSol agere, aut corpora versus illum converti, hæc illico lumine carerent. Hoc sensi maxime illustris est & conspicuus concursus Dei simultaneus: non autem ille qui statuitur in eis rebus quæ sic mere sunt naturæ: ut in miseris atque damnatis inveniuntur, uibuscum non opus est ut Deus concurrat d inordinatorum actuum suorum, lumine stitutorum, constitutionem.
units.tr: 2. Can the divine light be lost, and why is it more easily lost than the light of reason? I answer: as to the first, I believe no one can doubt it, although the fundamental reasons are not at once evident to everyone. They are to be drawn from the distinction by which we have several times divided God's gifts into natural gifts, which constitute the nature of man, and gratuitous gifts, which are like ornaments that adorn nature, perfect it, and clothe it in glory. The natural gifts cannot be lost, since nature itself cannot be lost, having been made absolutely so by God. The gratuitous gifts, which are not part of nature, are poured out by the Creator perpetually and continually upon the creature (as the light of the sun falls on opaque bodies), on the condition that the creature turn toward them, consent, and, receiving them with a grateful mind, retain them. It follows that as soon as the creature fails these conditions, God withdraws his gifts, which are rooted not in the creature but in God alone. This is exactly what happens in natural light, which is rooted not in opaque bodies but in the Sun, and which the Sun emanates to bodies from moment to moment. If the Sun were to cease acting even for a moment, or if bodies were turned away from it, they would at once be without light. The most illustrious and conspicuous instance of this is God's simultaneous concurrence. It is not, however, that concurrence which is posited in things that are merely natural, as is found in the wretched and the damned, with whom God need not concur in the constitution of their disordered acts.

units.la: Lumina rationis sunt duorum generum, quibus rerum naturalium origines, vires, effectus, ornatus, & combinationes, tque hinc orientia systemata egregia, & mirabilis rerum universitas deteguntur; & hæc uidem amittuntur cum luminis divini amissione: alia sunt & generaliora & crassiora, uæ concernunt tantum communiora & exeriora naturæ utut lumine & bono statu destitutæ, qualia diximus ea esse quæ numeros, figuras, & similia concernunt: & hæc, quia eorum subiectum non est a natura
units.tr: There are two kinds of light of reason, by which the origins, powers, effects, ornaments and combinations of natural things are discovered, and from which arise the excellent systems and the wonderful order of the universe. These are indeed lost with the loss of divine light. The other kind is more general and cruder, and concerns only the more common and external aspects of nature. It remains even in one destitute of the divine light and of a good state. Such are the things we said concern numbers, figures and the like. These are not lost as the former are, because their subject is not separable from nature.

units.la: e feparabile, idcirco non ita ut priora amittuntur discedente divino lumine.
units.tr: ...inseparable, and therefore they are not lost in the way the former are when the divine light departs.

units.la: 3. Quæri potest tertio, An ad restitutionem luminis rationis, opus fit prius restitui in homine lumen divinum? Respondeo, quatenus lumen rationis respicit externas illas veritates in natura vel maledicta radicatas, non requiri restitutionem luminis divini præcedaneam; at eam requiri pro veritatibus quæ rerum origines, naturas, proprietates, vires, earumque complementa & perfectiones explicant. Hæc enim quia admirabiliter omnia quæ in Deo inque ejus lumine & perfectionibus sunt, repræsentant & depingunt, ejusque etiam luminis & bonitatis effluviis fruuntur, non minus impossibile est ab eo percipi qui divino caret lumine, quam impossibile est; lumine e natura sublato icones quibus corpora luminosa repræsentabantur, cognoscere. Lumen rationis non efficit se ipsum, neque simpliciter efficitur a ratione quâ tenebrosa: non enim potest lumen a tenebris procedere: sed debet prius ratio illuminari ab alio; quo facto, ipsa deinde lumina sua picta, seu ideas claras efformare poterit: Luna nostra, seu ratio, lucere neutiquam potest, nisi prius luceat in facultatum superiorum cœlo Sol divini luminis, de quo reducendo solliciti sint oportet, qui vel lumine lunæ gaudere cupiunt.
units.tr: 3. A third question may be asked: is the divine light first required to be restored in man for the restoration of the light of reason? I answer: insofar as the light of reason regards those external truths rooted in nature, or even in what is cursed, no prior restoration of the divine light is required. But it is required for those truths which explain the origins, natures, properties and powers of things, and their complements and perfections. For these truths admirably represent and depict all that is in God, in his light and in his perfections, and they also enjoy the outflow of his light and goodness. It is therefore no less impossible for one who lacks the divine light to perceive them than it would be, once light is taken from nature, to recognise the images by which luminous bodies were represented. The light of reason does not produce itself, nor is it simply produced by reason while reason is dark, for light cannot proceed from darkness. Reason must first be illuminated by another, and once this is done it can then form its own illuminated pictures, or clear ideas. Our moon, that is, reason, cannot shine at all unless first the Sun of divine light shines in the heaven of the higher faculties. Those who even wish to enjoy the light of the moon must be anxious to bring that Sun back.

units.la: In lumine tuo videbimus lumen.
units.tr: In your light we shall see light.

units.la: 4. Quæri potest quarto: An homo divini luminis magis compos fieri possit, quando illud quærit rationis adhibita activitate, quam iam ea seposita? Huic quæstioni conabor sactius & uberius satisfacere, quia multa in a quali concentrantur, & multis inde lux fulgere potest.
units.tr: 4. A fourth question may be asked: can a man become more possessed of the divine light when he seeks it with reason's activity applied, than when he has set reason aside? I shall try to answer this question more carefully and fully, since many things are concentrated in it, and from it light can shine on many.

units.la: Quod ut efficiam, duo præuotabo, ium definiam, & tandem duo concludenda proponam.
units.tr: To do this, I shall first premise two things, then define one, and finally propose two things to conclude.

units.la: Notandum 1. non requiri hic absolutam tionis rejectionem; sed tantum ejus abractionem, vel separationem a suo exercio, idque loco & tempore debitis: ratio si- uidem sit etiam medium ad Deum ejusque imen; sed medium remotum, non proximum: ita tamen, ut hoc in rerum statu remoto illo medio prius uti necesse sit: quo ifficienter peracto, tunc medium illud re-iotum est relinquendum, ut soli proximo os dedamus. Eadem etiam ratio reddit de Deo ejusque lumine testimonium, quod utique audiendum est: sed quia illa non est Deus omnipotens & omniscius, neque ejus umen immensum, profecto nondum omnia quæ Dei sunt dixit, testata est & fecit; nelum vive & solide dixerit & fecerit omnia; ut illa saltem quæ umbratiliter tantum & trasso delineavit penicillo. Infinita Deo, infinita lumini ejus reliquit vive & infinitis nodis perfectius atque solidius detegenda.
