Ipsa quippe creatura debilis cum sit, illuminatio & instructio illius non potest non infinito intervallo ab ea quæ ab Omnipotente Deo fit, superari.
units.tr: Note first: what is required here is not the absolute rejection of reason, but only its withdrawal or separation from its exercise, and that at the proper place and time. For reason is indeed a means to God and his light, but a remote means, not a proximate one. Yet in the present state of things it is necessary first to use that remote means. When this has been sufficiently accomplished, the remote means must then be left behind, so that we may give ourselves to the one proximate means. Reason likewise gives testimony concerning God and his light, and this must indeed be heard. But because reason is not the omnipotent and omniscient God, nor is its light immense, it has certainly not yet said and done all that belongs to God. Much less has it spoken and done everything fully and solidly, still less those things which it has only sketched dimly and roughly with its brush. Infinite things remain to God, and infinite things to his light, to be disclosed more perfectly and solidly in infinite connections. For since the creature itself is weak, its illumination and instruction cannot but be surpassed by an infinite interval by that which is done by Almighty God.

units.la: Alterum quod notandum est, ne quis se deceptum putet, illud est: Animum, qui reremoto rationis medio prius recte usus, eam debite reliquit, ubi se obtulit traditutque passivum Deo, non tamen illico divino assici lumine eo quem speraverat modo, sive, non sequi in eo actualiter tale lumen quale sibi imaginatus erat. Cujus rationes sunt, 1, quod in ipso adhuc occultentur multae radices malae plurimique habitus peccaminosi, quibus æquum est debita pœnitentia justaque luminis privatione prius purgari. 2, quia cum Deus non det lumen nisi sincere desiderantibus, atque decernentibus se impostterum ei adhaesuros, solet exspectare ut sinceritatis hujus videat documenta & habitum aliquem; 3, quia junctus est animus corpori ipsum valde aggravanti Deique influxus insensibiles reddenti, veluti accidit, dum opressi sumus somno, etsi objecta externa tum sint praesentissima nosque afficiant, nos tamen iis sensibiliter non affici: & 4, quia Deus prospiciens ne anima iterum abutens puris luminibus donisque pretiosis, peccet exitiali & irreparabili modo; ex bonitate admiranda servat illi in recondito lumino sam sui communicationem ad illud tempus, quo illa eis in perniciem abuti amplius nequibit; interimque illi tales primitias, talemque acquiescentiam concedit, ut omnino contenta sit quomodocunque Deus cum illa agat. Et hoc sane sufficit, nec ultra quicquam desiderari potest, estque id ipsum divini luminis, etsi sensibilitati nostrae obscuri, ingens argumentum.
units.tr: Another thing must be noted, lest anyone think himself deceived. A soul which, having first rightly used the remote means of reason, has duly left it behind, and which, when it presents itself and surrenders itself passively to God, is not at once affected by the divine light in the manner it had hoped. Nor does such a light actually follow in it as it had imagined. The reasons for this are: (1) many bad roots and many sinful habits are still hidden in the soul, and these must first be purged by due repentance and by a just privation of light; (2) God does not give light except to those who sincerely desire it and resolve to cling to him henceforth, and he is wont to wait until they show evidence of this sincerity and of some settled habit; (3) the soul is joined to a body which greatly weighs it down and renders God's influx imperceptible, as happens when we are oppressed by sleep: though external objects are then most present and affect us, we are not sensibly affected by them; and (4) because God foresees that the soul, abusing pure lights and precious gifts again, would sin in a deadly and irreparable manner, out of admirable goodness he keeps in hiddenness for it the communication of his light until the time when it can no longer abuse these gifts to its destruction. Meanwhile he grants it such first-fruits and such acquiescence that it is wholly content however God may deal with it. This certainly suffices, nor can anything more be desired. And this very thing is a great argument for the divine light, although it is obscure to our sensibility.

units.la: Jam definiendum est, quid per rectum rationis tionis mis usum intelligendum hic sit, ne quid perfit obscuri. Intelligo igitur per eum, timonium quod ratio (gratiis Dei praeviis buta) dat attendentibus, videlicet, nos in esse a nobis ipsis: Auctorem nostrum & omnium esse omnipotentem, sapientem, optimum, benevolum, veracem, justum: colere nos eum grato animo laudare, amare, ei obsequi, ab eo bona summisse postulare & exspectare, abstinere a superbia, iniquitate, mendacio, & imitari erga omnes ejus benevolentiam, aequitatem & veritatem. Quae omnia testatur ratio, modo ei attentio debita praebeatur. Testatur eadem, se per ideas hasce suas de istis quas nobis dat, non dare hoc ipso vim istaliter assequendi vel imitandi; alioqui dormissimi quique essent & optimi, ipsique ui a scientia vocantur daemones, essent Dei nitatores maximi, a quo tamen absunt uam longissime. Testatur & illud ratio, in eam, quae ipsi deest, (quippe quae pituras tantum efficit & dat, non res ipsas,) retendam esse a fonte omnis boni. Haec postquam a ratione audivimus; & cordi nobis ita sunt sincere (& hucusque quidem proreditur rectus rationis usus,) tunc tempus est, ut juxta ipsiusmet rationis dictamen, illam ipsam cum picturis suis & testimoniis reponamus, (illa enim omnia ex suppositione sufficienter scimus,) nosque totos cum omni capacitate nostra ad Deum convertanus, ejus vim, efficaciam lumenque effla- gantes & implorantes eum in finem, ut quae nobis modo piʒto, mortuo atque ineffīcaci & sterili, similiter imperfectissimoque & superficiali dixit ratio; eorum ille non umbram & pictūram, sed rem ipsam luminosam, vividam & efficacem det & producat in intimis nostris: id quod ipse etiam modis ineffabilibus, & infinities rationis potentiam superantibus efficere potest.
units.tr: Now it must be defined what is meant here by the right use of reason, lest anything remain obscure. By it I understand the testimony which reason gives (with the grace of God going before and assisting) to those who attend to it: namely, that we exist not of ourselves but from another; that our Author, and the Author of all, is omnipotent, wise, best, benevolent, truthful and just; that we should worship him with a grateful mind, praise him, love him, obey him, ask and humbly expect good things from him; that we should abstain from pride, iniquity and lying, and imitate his benevolence, equity and truth toward all. Reason testifies to all these things, provided due attention is given to it. The same reason testifies that by these ideas of its own about the things it sets before us, it does not thereby give the power actually to attain or imitate them. Otherwise the most sleepy would be the best, and the demons, who are called learned by science itself, would be the greatest imitators of God, from whom yet they are as far as possible. Reason also testifies that for what it lacks (since it produces and gives only pictures, not the things themselves) one must be drawn toward the fountain of all good. After we have heard these things from reason, and they are sincerely dear to us (and so far the right use of reason proceeds), then it is time, according to reason's own dictate, to set reason aside with its pictures and testimonies (for we know all these things sufficiently on that supposition). We should turn ourselves wholly, with all our capacity, to God, sighing after his power, efficacy and light, and begging him to that end that what reason has told us now, being dead, ineffective, sterile, and likewise imperfect and superficial, he may give and produce within our inmost being, not as a shadow and a picture, but as the thing itself, luminous, living and effective. He can do this by ineffable means, which surpass the power of reason infinitely.

units.la: Jam illud quod mihi primo sumsi oftendum & concludendum ad postulati solutionem, tale est: Animam majoris esse luminis capacem per Deum quam per rationem; sive per Dei actum, quam per intellectus & ratiocinationis activitatem.
units.tr: Now the first point I took up to show and conclude, for the solution of the question, is this: the soul is capable of a greater light through God than through reason; that is, through the action of God rather than through the activity of the intellect and reasoning.

units.la: Alterum est: Lumen illud divinum & majus, cujus anima per Dei actum capax est, impediri quando illa plus, diutius, instantius, adhaeret rationi quam Deo; juvari autem, quando illa Deo magis adhaeret quam rationi.
units.tr: The second is this: that divine and greater light, for which the soul is capable through the action of God, is hindered when the soul clings to reason more, longer and more eagerly than to God, and is helped when it clings to God more than to reason.

units.la: Quae quidem ita clara sunt, ut solis terminis perceptis mihi videantur demonstrata; & sine ullo argumento, sola hac comparatione contrectari & palpari possint. Videlicet, ex dictis ratio se habet ad nos veluti famulus, qui in densis tenebris subministrata facula nos intus vocaret ad Dominum prope in palatio glorioso lumine omnisque generis bonis affluentem. Certe bonum esset extra attendere servo ejusque lumini: absurdum vero, & contra scopum Domini famulum mittentis foret, huic foris adhaerere continuo ejusque faculae, quam fors, ventus, tempestas saevior, aliudve incommodum difflare possit, simulque nos cum n illa exstinguere: & nullum est dubium, n qui famulum cum facula relinqueret, Dominum pergendi gratia, majori luie felicitateque beandus esset per Domin, quam per famulum allucentem foris; etiam quin eo majoris luminis foret mpos quo magis Domino adhæreret re:o famulo, minoris vero, quo magis ac ultimum primo præferret. Sed missa nparatione, rationibus comprobemus umque propositionem.
units.tr: These things are so clear that, once the terms are grasped, they seem to me proved, and they can be handled and felt without any argument, by this comparison alone. For, from what has been said, reason stands toward us as a servant who, in deep darkness, carries a small torch and calls us inward to the Lord, who dwells in a glorious palace abounding in light and every kind of good. Certainly it would be good to attend to the servant and his light from outside; but it would be absurd, and contrary to the purpose of the Lord who sent the servant, to keep clinging continually to him outside and to his little torch, which chance, wind, a fiercer storm or some other mishap may blow out, and with it extinguish us. And there is no doubt that one who left the servant with the torch and went on to the Lord would be blessed with a greater light and happiness through the Lord than through the servant shining from outside; indeed he would have the more light the more closely he clung to the Lord and the less he clung to the servant; and the less light the more he preferred the servant to the Lord. But, setting the comparison aside, let us prove the proposition by reasons.

units.la: i) Prima. Anima est capax majoris lunis per Deum quam per rationem. 1. ia Deus ipse est lumen infinitum, vivum, inipotens: Ratio autem est lumen finitum, veluti pictum & vere sterile. Ergo parte Dei anima infinities plus luminis, isque vividissimi & efficacissimi potest requere, quam ex parte rationis, quae nil i finitum communicare potest. 2. Ratio n potest animae capacitates ad recipienda nina sua idealia majores reddere quam it, neque potest eas imperfectionibus & pedimentis suis, quae multa sunt, libee. At Deus & animam omnibus impenentis quae lumini obstant, liberare po-:, & ejus capacitates in infinitum amplia-: est ille namque omnipotens; adeoque entia ejus in dilatando animo exhauriri juit. Ergo ex parte Dei anima est infinitiinis divini, actusque ejus eam illustran-, recipiendi capax; cum ex parte ranis fit tantum capax finitorum & impertorum luminum.
units.tr: i) First: the soul is capable of a greater light through God than through reason. (1) For God himself is an infinite, living and powerful light, whereas reason is a finite light, like a painted and truly sterile one. Therefore, on God's side, the soul can receive infinitely more light, and that most living and most effective, than on reason's side, since reason can communicate nothing infinite. (2) Reason cannot make the soul's capacities for receiving its ideal lights greater than it is, nor can it free them from their imperfections and hindrances, which are many. But God can free the soul from all the impediments that stand in the way of light, and enlarge its capacities to infinity; for he is almighty, and so his resources cannot be exhausted in enlarging the mind. Therefore, on God's side, the soul is capable of receiving the infinite light of the divine and his enlightening action, whereas on reason's side it is capable only of finite and imperfect lights.

units.la: (2) Siqui-
units.tr: (2) Since-

units.la: (z) Siquidem igitur anima ex parte Deifit capax lumen infinitum, vividissimum, efficacissimum recipiendi, & ab eo agente patiendi: quia tamen actu non potest eo frui, nisi media proxima ad fruendum illo adhibeat, quæ media proxima sunt oblatio facultatum seu capacitatum superiorum ipsi Deo, vive illuminanti & admittendo; ergo sequitur, omnem animæ actum qui non includit hanc facultatum superiorum oblationem, neque pro objecto admittendo habet Deum vivide illuminantem, non esse medium obtinendi illud lumen. Atqui ipsa ratio ejusque actus, non sunt actus talis oblationis facultatum superiorum, nec eos involvunt in se, neque pro objecto habent ipsum vividum Dei lumen. Ergo ratio ejusque actus, non sunt medium participandi illius luminis. Igitur qui adhæret rationi ejusque actibus, per ista luminis divini particeps fieri non potest; affert enim facultatem ineptam, & aliam quam par est, ad objectum aliud. Sed qui offert facultates superiores Deo vivide illuminanti, is affert vasa debita ad objectum debitum & admittendum. Ergo qui affert facultates suas superiores Deo, sive qui adhæret Deo supra omnem rationem, eo ipso infiniti luminis compos & particeps fieri potest.
units.tr: (z) Since, then, on God's side the soul is capable of receiving the infinite, most living and most effective light, and of being acted upon by that agent: yet because it cannot actually enjoy that light unless it uses the proximate means for enjoying it, and these proximate means are the offering of its higher faculties to God himself, the living illuminator, and the admitting of him; it follows that every act of the soul which does not include this offering of its higher faculties, and which does not have as its object the admitting of God, the vividly illuminating one, is not a means of obtaining that light. But reason and its acts are not acts of such an offering of the higher faculties, nor do they include it, nor do they have the living light of God as their object. Therefore reason and its acts are not the means of partaking of that light. Hence whoever clings to reason and its acts cannot become a partaker of the divine light through them; for he brings an unsuitable faculty, and one other than is fitting, to another object. But whoever offers his higher faculties to God, the vividly illuminating one, brings the proper vessels to the proper object to be admitted. Therefore whoever offers his higher faculties to God, or who clings to God above all reason, can by that very act become master of and a partaker of infinite light.

units.la: Si igitur homo adhærendo rationi non potest luminis divini fieri compos; fiqueadhærendo Deo, sive tradendo se illi per facultates ratione superiores potest lumine infinito perfundi & frui; Ergo comparative verum est, quod homo luminis divini & infiniti minus capax sit quando se tradit rationi magis quam Deo; & quod sit ejusdem luminis divini magis capax, quando minime adhaerebit rationi, Deo vero maxime adhaerebit, eique se tradet totum. Quod erat ostendendum.
units.tr: If, then, by clinging to reason a man cannot become master of the divine light, but by clinging to God, that is, by giving himself to him through faculties higher than reason, he can be flooded with and enjoy the infinite light; therefore it is true in comparative terms that a man is less capable of the divine and infinite light when he gives himself more to reason than to God, and that he is more capable of the same divine light when he least clings to reason and most clings to God, giving himself to him wholly. Which was to be shown.

units.la: §. Quaeri potest, quinto: An luminis divini certitudo in anima possit esse tanta, quanta est certitudo luminis naturalis, v. g. quo videtur Sol, aut corpus lumine illustratum: aut vero luminis rationalis, v. g. veritatum de numeris & figuris? Respondeo, eam esse incomparabiliter, imo infinities majorem. Quod ut pateat vere dici, notandum est nos eo magis de veritatibus persuaderi, quo vividius & penetrantius ab illis afficimur: exempli causa, inveniuntur qui vigilantes dubitent aut dubitare possint vigilentne an secus, item sintne sani an aegri: at nemo dum vehementer dolet, dubitat se dolere; quia nempe magis vivide a dolore quam a vigilia aut a valetudine afficimur. Hac ratione, quando lumen Dei purum, vividum, penetrans afficit animam, haec ita penetranter & immense de eo persuadetur, ut veritatiunculas caeteras ne quidem inspicere dignetur, quae tunc sunt menti velut bullae futiles ac nullae, nomineque veritatis & luminis indignae: quemadmodum homini in extremis posito nihil aut parum admodum est sua illa prior lux & certitudo, omnis trianguli duo latera simul sumta tertio esse majora, & similes quisquiliae. Et
units.tr: §. It may be asked, fifthly: Can the certainty of the divine light in the soul be as great as the certainty of natural light, for instance by which the sun or a body illuminated by light is seen; or indeed of rational light, for instance of truths about numbers and figures? I answer that it is incomparably, nay infinitely, greater. To see that this is rightly said, it should be noted that we are persuaded of truths the more, the more vividly and penetratingly we are affected by them. For example, there are those who, when awake, doubt or can doubt whether they are awake or not, and likewise whether they are well or ill; but no one who is in great pain doubts that he is in pain; because, of course, we are affected more vividly by pain than by being awake or by health. In the same way, when the pure, vivid and penetrating light of God affects the soul, the soul is persuaded of it so penetratingly and immensely that it does not deign even to glance at other little truths, which then are to the mind like futile and empty bubbles, unworthy of the name of truth and light: just as, to a man at the point of death, his former light and certainty, or that every triangle's two sides taken together are greater than the third, and similar trifles, are nothing or very little.

units.la: hæc est ratio, quare qui lumine divino potiuntur, omnia hominum studia veritatesque habeant pro vanis, pro nullis, pro falsis & mendaciis. Filii hominum, quousque diligetis vanitatem & quaeretis mendacium? Profetto in imagine, sive inter ea quæ solum speciem habent, ambulat homo, & tumultuantur omnes in vanum. Tantum vanitas sunt filii hominum, mendacium filii viri; ut si simul in statera ponantur, sint ipsa vanitate leviores. Cogitationes eorum cogitationes inutiles, telas aranearum texuerunt, &c. uti vidimus supra.
units.tr: And this is the reason why those who possess the divine light regard all the studies and truths of men as vain, as nothing, as false and lies. Sons of men, how long will you love vanity and seek lies? Surely man walks in an image, or among things that have only the appearance, and all are in tumult in vain. Only vanity are the sons of men, lies the sons of men; so that if they are placed together in the balance they are lighter than vanity itself. Their thoughts are useless thoughts; they have woven spiders' webs, etc., as we saw above.

units.la: Notandum interim, a certitudine subjectiva luminis divini exceptionem fieri, quando ipse Deus ob rationes ei cognitas vult sic lumine suo operari in homine, ut tamen homo id nescire, neque de eo certus esse debeat.
units.tr: Meanwhile it should be noted that an exception is made to the subjective certainty of the divine light when God himself, for reasons known to him, wills so to work in a man by his light that the man does not know it and ought not to be certain of it.

units.la: Quando vero Deus luminis sui evidentiam impedire non vult, ea tanta est, ut quamvis omnes animæ facultates essent inhabiles, detentæ, ligatæ, sopitæ, mille impedimentis objectisque intricatæ, modo non peccaminosis nec voluntariis, illico tamen omnia sic disjiciat, sic unico radio mentem afficiat divina lux, ut eam reddat habilem, lucidam, tranquillam, laetam, ac veluti ex mortua vivam, & ex infernalibus tenebris & anxietatibus, certissima, præsentissima atque gloriosa luce triumphantem & conspicuam. At miserae rationis lumen, etiam Mathematicum, ejus est impotentiae & debilitatis ad sese menti insinuandum, ut omomnis ejus vis atque certitudo vel somno, vel febricula, vel alia quavis intemperie frangi & plane ex anima deleri possit: namque si homini illud adepto, accidat ejusmodi casus morbosus aut apopleēticus, etiamsi tunc omnium totius mundi rationum lumina ipsi adjumento esse eniterentur, ingeminarentque omnes Mathematici vocibus & ictibus suum illud: duo & tria faciunt quinque, & anguli tres æquantur duobus rectis in quovis triangulo, non tamen id possent ipsi perceptibile nedum certum reddere; aut vero ex facultate oppressa, ubi misella isthæc lumina latere dicuntur, in apertum ea educere.
units.tr: But when God does not wish to hinder the evidence of his light, that evidence is so great that, although all the faculties of the soul were unfit, held back, bound, lulled to sleep, entangled in a thousand hindrances and objects (provided these are not sinful or voluntary), yet the divine light at once scatters all these, so affects the mind with a single ray, that it makes it able, bright, calm and glad, and as if from dead it becomes alive, and triumphs and shines forth from infernal darkness and anxieties in a most certain, most present and glorious light. But the wretched light of reason, even mathematical reason, is so impotent and weak in insinuating itself into the mind that all its force and certainty can be broken, and altogether wiped out of the soul, by sleep, a slight fever, or any other indisposition. For if a man who had acquired it should suffer such a morbid or apoplectic attack, then even if the lights of all the reasons of the whole world strove to help him, and all the mathematicians chanted their "two and three make five" and "the three angles of any triangle equal two right angles" with blows and cries, they could not make these things perceptible to him, let alone certain; nor could they bring those poor little lights out into the open from a faculty that has been oppressed, where they are said to lie hidden.

units.la: 6. Quæstio sexta: Si lumen divinum sit tantæ certitudinis & efficaciæ, unde ergo tot hominum circa illud illusiones & deceptiones ; e quibus apparere videtur, illud lumen non tam certo percipi quam lumen rationis? Aut quænam est via percipiendi illud modo certo & non fallente, quodnamve ejus Criterium ? Respondeo : Lumen divinum quod a Deo mentibus infunditur, non tantum illusionibus carere, sed & certissimum & infallibile esse, si modo mentes ab impedimentis peccati & corruptionis atque superbiæ, nec non ab affectu & adhæsione erga omnia liberati, soli auxilio Dei innitantur. Neque ulla præterea via alia opus est ad illud certo cognoscendum : nec id alio criterio quam sui præsentia & sensu, opus habet : perinde atque videmus lumen Solis vivide perceptum, esse sui criterium omnibus id percipientibus, non item aliis: neque dari aliam illius certò obtinendi viam quam removere obstacula quæ inter illum & oculos nostros interjacent. Sed hic notandum est (quod modo diximus) Deum in homine interdum lumine suo operari eo id nesciente, vel de Dei lumine incerto: quod accidit, vel quia nondum bene ab impedimentis omnibus liber est, vel quia superest causa timendi ne inde in superbiam cadat; aut ad majorem fidei & constantiæ ejus amorisque purioris probationem & augmentum. Quibus in casibus conducit homini lumen Dei ab illo nondum percipi. Deinde notandum est: quemadmodum lux corporea non videtur sicut systema aut objectum aliquod, quod visum terminet; & nihilominus tamen vere possidetur, suo modo eoque certissimo percipitur, ejus ope corpus regitur, præcipitia evitantur, proficua suscipiuntur & peraguntur: ita etiam non putandum esse lucem divinam tanquam objectum aliquod speciale videri; etsi suo modo vividissime percipiatur, ipsaque præsentissima operetur. Cujus efficacis præsentiæ certissimum argumentum est vis & principium internum quo anima respicit, considerat, magnifacit sola æterna, seque & omnia ex illorum visu & respectu regit, cætera autem despicit, & non tantum ea nihili facit; sed sub eorum etiam pondere gemit, optans ab eis liberari, quo omnes ejus curæ, affectus, ipsaque tota, solis dedantur æternis: quæ sanæ mentis afsectio solius divinæ lucis solida operatio est, veraque Dei illuminatio. Et ex ea tantum est ut inde in illusiones incidat, ut potius modo ab illusionibus, nec non ab incerudine periculosa & diffidente reddatur im-inis.
units.tr: 6. Sixth question: If the divine light is of such certainty and efficacy, whence come so many illusions and deceptions among men about it? From these it seems that the divine light is not perceived as surely as the light of reason. Or what is the way of perceiving it with certainty and without error, and what is its criterion? I answer: The divine light, which God pours into minds, not only lacks illusions but is also most certain and infallible, provided that minds, freed from the hindrances of sin, corruption and pride, and also from attachment and adherence to all things, rest solely on the help of God. Nor is any other way needed to know it with certainty, nor does it need any criterion other than its own presence and sense, just as we see the light of the sun, vividly perceived, to be its own criterion for all who perceive it, but not for others. Nor is there any other certain way of obtaining it than to remove the obstacles that lie between it and our eyes. But here it must be noted (as we have just said) that God sometimes works in a man with his light while the man does not know it, or is uncertain about the light of God. This happens either because the man is not yet fully free of all hindrances, or because there remains a cause for fear lest he fall into pride from it, or for a greater proof and increase of his faith and constancy and purer love. In such cases it is good for the man that the light of God not yet be perceived by him. Next, it must be noted that just as bodily light is not seen like some system or object that bounds the sight, and yet is truly possessed, is perceived in its own way and most certainly, and by its help the body is guided, precipices are avoided, and profitable things are undertaken and carried out, so too we must not think that the divine light is seen as some particular object, even though it is perceived in its own way most vividly and works most present in us. The most certain proof of this efficacious presence is the inner power and principle by which the soul looks to, considers, and esteems the eternal things alone, and orders itself and all things by their sight and regard, while it despises the rest, and not only makes nothing of them but groans under their weight, desiring to be freed from them, so that all its cares, affections, and indeed its whole self, are given over to the eternal alone. This disposition of a sound mind is the solid work of the divine light alone and the true illumination of God. And from it alone does it follow that the mind is kept from falling into illusions, and is rather rendered free from illusions, and also from a dangerous and distrustful uncertainty.

units.la: At si qui ad lumen divinum accedere prænant mente corrupta, imaginibus & figntis propriis adhuc inhiante, iisve plena t impedita, si Deum ejusque auxilium non re & unice velint; si ex divino lumine sibi satisfactionem, emolumentum, commentionem, existimationem & applausum orum aut suum, intus apud se quærant; in mirum sane tales mille illusionibus irrei: interponunt enim vel immiscent divino mini (si modo ejus radiolos quosdam haierint, ) chimærarum atque figmentorum nnium fontes & origines, atque adeo, it fabula fert de Ixione) nubem pro June amplexi, monstra turbulenta tantum oducunt.
units.tr: But if any come to the divine light with a corrupt mind, still gaping after their own images and fictions, or full of them and hindered by them; if they do not seriously and solely desire God and his help; if they seek within themselves from the divine light satisfaction, advantage, commendation, esteem and applause, either for themselves or for others; then such people are indeed caught in a thousand illusions, to a remarkable degree. For they interpose or mix into the divine power (if they have caught some rays of it) the sources and origins of a thousand chimeras and fictions, and so, as the fable tells of Ixion, embracing a cloud for Juno, they bring forth only turbulent monsters.

units.la: Et hæc est ratio, quare divini luminis evientia & vis infinita in quam paucissimis sit onspicua, idque multo minus quam lumen itionis vel mathematicum. Scilicet longe iucifsimi sunt qui lumini divino pure adhæant,-aut quidem ad illud adspirent: vixie unus est qui ea puritate ab obstaculis iibusvis liberatum se illi offerat, qua raonem offerimus ideis quibusdam naturaliis aut mathematicis de numeris atque figus: -& hinc non mirum hasce & similes apirere hominibus quibusvis fere evidentiores iam lumen divinum. Sed si omnia ex utraque parte, saltem quoad praeparationem, aequalia forent, tunc appareret tanta divini luminis evidentia prae lumine rationis, ut haecce qualis jam est, cum frigidis suis atque pauperculis veritatiunculis ne quidem adspectu digna censeretur. Nempe quemadmodum ex una parte ponitur anima sine praejudiciis contra numeros v. g. quaeque somno aut distractionibus aliis non impediatur aut avocetur, sed cum serio desiderio illis se totam applicet; ita ex altera parte ponenda esset anima ab obstaculis omnibus libera, sequeque totam cum desiderio & amore divino, omni alio affectu nudam, divino lumini offerens eique soli vacans. Atque tunc, ut dixi, illud ita illustre appareret, ut solum esse aliquid, imo esse omnia videretur, caetera nihil & mendacium. Ita Augustinus: (a) Intravi in intima mea duce te: & potui; quoniam factus es adjutor meus. Intravi, & vidi qualicunque oculo animae meae supra eundem oculum animae meae, supra mentem meam, lucem Dei incommutabilem.... Qui novit veritatem, novit eam; & qui novit eam, novit aeternitatem. Charitas [amor Dei] novit eam. O aeterna veritas, & vera charitas, & chara aeternitas! Tu es Deus meus. Tibi suspiro die ac nocte. [hoc est medium participationis.] Et cum te primum cognovi, tu assumsisti me, ut viderem esse quod viderem, [hoc solum lumen quod tunc videbat, ipsi videbatur esse] & nondum me esse qui viderem: [omnia ei, & ipsemet sibi, nihil esse videbantur] Et reverberasti infirmitatem aspectus mei radians diana dians in me vehementer: & contremui amore & horrore, [tanta est vividitas & realitas divini luminis, ut ferri nequeat] & inveni me longe esse ate in regione dissimilitudinis, [jam non modo nihil, sed oppositi & dissimiles apparemus Deo] tanquam audirem vocem tuam de excelso: Cibus sum grandium: cresce & manducabis me. Nec tu me in te mutabis sicut cibum carnis tuae, [non est quod timeas aliquid indignum mihi eventurum si tu me admittas in te] sed tu mutaberis in me. [O divinam transformationem intellectus & mentis totius a lumine Dei, divinam formam suam animae communicante!] Et cognovi quoniam propter iniquitatem erudisti hominem, & tabescere fecisti sicut aranearum animam meam, [reprehendisti & convicisti me quod fuerim in erroribus propter corruptionem meam, & ostendisti mihi omnia mea studia atque opera extra divinum lumen tuum esse tantum inania, & sicca aranearum opera & studia:] Et dixi, nunquid nihil est veritas quoniam neque per finitum neque per infinita locorum spatia diffusa est? [namque non capiunt divinum lumen naturalia & crassa.] Et clamasti e longinquo, Imo vero, Ego sum qui sum. [Iterum sola ipsi videtur esse divina Veritas, caetera non esse.] Et audivi sicut auditur in corde: & non erat prorsus unde dubitarem. Facilius dubitarem vivere me, quam non esse [ejusmodi] veritatem. Et alibi (a) Vidisplendorem tuum confaucio; & repercussus dixi; Quis ille qui pro- sit? Projectus sum a facie oculorum tuorum. Tuos veritas super omnia praesidens [omnia antecedens.] At ego per avaritiam non amitte-re te volui ; sed volui tecum possidere mendacium ; sicut nemo vult ita falsum dicere, ut nesciat ipse quid verum sit. Itaque amisi te, quia non dignaris cum mendacio possideri. Hoc est, homines qui volunt curiositatem suam pascere per infinitas veritates vanas & nugaces, quae coram divino lumine non veritates, sed mendacia dici merentur; quique etiam ex eadem avara cupiditate omnia scita coacervandi, quid sit divinum lumen scire, idque possidere volunt; eo non possunt non omnimode privari quantacunque sint seculi splendida ingenia. Dedecore afficiunt divinum lumen quando illud ita non ambiunt ut propter id caeteris omnibus velint carere, vel ea ut stercora contemnere, dissimiles divino Paulo inclamanti (a) Omnia damnum reputo, propter excellentiam cognitionis Jesu Christi, Domini mei, propter quem omnium jacturam feci, eaque pro stercoribus habeo ut Christum lucrer. Christum autem esse ipsam lucem divinam, lucem mundi, lucem animae, lucem illuminantem omnem hominem venientem in mundum, juxta Euangelicam veritatem, nemo, opinor, dubitare potest.
units.tr: And this is the reason why the evidence and infinite force of the divine light is so little visible to very few, and much less so than the light of reason or of mathematics. Clearly, those who cling purely to the divine light, or at least aspire to it, are very few indeed: scarcely any one offers himself to it freed from all obstacles of any kind, with the same purity with which we offer our reason to certain natural or mathematical ideas about numbers and figures. Hence it is no wonder that these and similar things appear to almost any men more evident than the divine light. But if everything were equal on both sides, at least as regards preparation, then the great evidence of the divine light would appear in comparison with the light of reason, so that the latter, as it now is, with its cold and paltry little truths, would hardly be thought worthy of a glance. Indeed, just as on one side we place a soul without prejudices against numbers, for example, which is not hindered or diverted by sleep or other distractions, but applies itself wholly to them with serious desire; so on the other side the soul ought to be placed free from all obstacles, offering itself whole with desire and divine love, stripped of every other affection, and given over to the divine light alone and free for it. And then, as I have said, that light would appear so illustrious that it alone would seem to be something, indeed to be everything, and all else nothing and falsehood. So Augustine: I entered into my inmost being, under your guidance, and I was able, since you became my helper. I entered, and I saw with whatever eye of my soul, above that same eye of my soul, above my mind, the unchangeable light of God... He who knows the truth knows it, and he who knows it knows eternity. Love knows it. O eternal truth, and true love, and beloved eternity! You are my God. To you I sigh day and night. [This is the means of participation.] And when I first knew you, you took me up, that I might see that there is what I might see, [this light alone which he then saw seemed to him to be] and that I was not yet the one who saw. [to him all things, and he himself to himself, seemed to be nothing] And you beat back the weakness of my sight, shining strongly upon me, [so great is the vividness and reality of the divine light that it cannot be borne] and I trembled with love and with dread, [and I found that I was far away in a region of unlikeness,] [now we seem not only nothing but opposed and unlike God] as if I heard your voice from on high: I am the food of grown men; grow, and you shall eat me. Nor shall you change me into you, as the food of your flesh, [there is no need to fear that anything unworthy will happen to me if you admit me into you] but you shall be changed into me. [O divine transformation of the intellect and of the whole mind by the light of God, communicating its divine form to the soul!] And I knew that because of iniquity you chastened man, and made my soul to waste away like a spider's web, [you rebuked and convicted me that I had been in errors because of my corruption, and showed me that all my studies and works outside your divine light are merely empty, and dry works and studies like spiders' webs.] And I said, is truth then nothing, since it is spread neither through finite nor through infinite spaces of place? [for natural and gross things do not grasp the divine light.] And you cried to me from afar, Nay indeed, I am who am. [Again, divine Truth alone seems to him to be, and all else not to be.] And I heard as one hears in the heart, and there was not at all anything from which I might doubt. I could more easily doubt that I live than that there is not [such] truth. And elsewhere: I was dazzled by the splendour of your eyes, and being struck back I said: who is that who is there? I have been cast away from the face of your eyes. Your truth presiding over all things [going before all things]. But I, through avarice, did not wish to lose you, but I wished to possess falsehood along with you; just as no one wishes to say falsely in such a way that he himself does not know what is true. And so I lost you, because you do not deign to be possessed together with falsehood. That is, men who wish to feed their curiosity on infinite vain and trifling truths, which in the presence of the divine light deserve to be called not truths but lies; and who, from the same avaricious desire of heaping up all knowledge, wish to know and possess what the divine light is; they cannot but be utterly deprived of it, however brilliant the geniuses of the age may be. They bring dishonour upon the divine light when they do not seek it in such a way as to wish, for its sake, to be without all other things, or to despise those other things as dung, unlike the divine Paul, who cried out: I count all things loss for the excellence of the knowledge of Jesus Christ, my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them but dung that I may gain Christ. That Christ is himself the divine light, the light of the world, the light of the soul, the light that enlightens every man coming into the world, according to the Gospel truth, no one, I think, can doubt.

units.la: VI. De Statu supernaturali Mentis.
units.tr: VI. On the Supernatural State of the Mind.

units.la: Quoniam ex istis pleraque ad statum mentis supernaturalem spectare videntur, quaeri de hoc potest, an uostri sit eo adspirare? forsan
units.tr: Since most of these things seem to bear on the supernatural state of the mind, it may be asked whether we should aspire to it at all? Perhaps

units.la: (a) Phil. 3. 8. forsan melius fuerit, naturaeque convenientius, si intra ea quae naturalia sunt nos contineamus: arrogantiae fuerit majora moliri quam quae possumus: actus nostros ad naturam nostram dicunt esse metiendos, & quae supra nos, ea nihil ad nos spectare.
units.tr: (a) Phil. 3. 8. it would be better, and more in keeping with nature, to keep ourselves within what is natural. It would be arrogance to undertake greater things than we are able to do. They say that our actions must be measured by our nature, and that things above us have nothing to do with us.

units.la: Respondeo: Agnosco vocem Socraticam, at sensu procul dubio non Socratico sed Epicureo prolatam, dum quae de speculativa perversa & culpanda curiositate dicta erant, perperam transferuntur ad ea quae omnium hominum spectant officium. Natura humana si sibi soli adhaerere velit, praeter facultates vacuas, tenebrosas atque anxias, hoc est, praeter statum miserandum, nihil quicquam possidere poterit. At si perfectionem, complementum, ornamentum, scopumque ad quem facta est, ipsa velit & cupiat, (quod sane ejus naturae omnium maxime conveniens est,) tunc omnium maxime necessarium est, ut supra se ad supernaturalia adspiret. Sumus enim revera ad supernaturalia facti, utque vel ipsi Deo evadamus similes. Hinc tantum abest ut legi naturae adversetur, si majora moliamur quam quae possumus; ut econtra, nil magis cum naturae nostrae lege conveniat.
units.tr: I answer: I recognise the Socratic voice, but it is clearly uttered in a sense that is not Socratic but Epicurean, since what was said about speculative, perverse and blameworthy curiosity is wrongly transferred to the duty that belongs to all people. If human nature wished to cling only to itself, it could possess nothing beyond empty, dark and anxious faculties; that is, nothing beyond a wretched state. But if it wills and desires its perfection, its completion, its adornment, and the goal for which it was made (which is surely most fitting to its nature), then it is most necessary that it aspire above itself to the supernatural. For we were indeed made for the supernatural, so that we might even become like God himself. Hence it is so far from being contrary to the law of nature to attempt greater things than we can do, that on the contrary nothing agrees more with the law of our nature.

units.la: Quod vere dici facile apparebit, si potentiam nostram meminerimus recte distingui in activam, qua possumus agere & efficere; & passivam, qua possumus recipere & pati. Illa est finita valde, imperfecta, crassa, corrupta: haec infinita, etsi obstaculis corruptae naturae nostrae nunc veluti clausa. Jam fi moliamur quædam bene & perfecte agere ex activitate corrupta, aut ex eadem quædam vere divina & supernaturalia, capacitatem activitatis nostræ superantia, efficere : id quidem est contra legem naturæ, estque non exiguæ arrogantiæ: siquidem causa producere velit effectum in quo plus sit realitatis quam in ipsa causa est: quod est contra ideas luminis naturalis. At si moliamur majora a Deo recipere quam quæ ipsimet possumus efficere, id & congruum est legi naturali divinæque, qua tenemur bona quæ Deus offert & largiri vult, (offert autem se ipsum) non rejicere, sed admittere; & vero convenientissimum idem est potentiæ passivæ (quam a Deo habemus) infinita & supernaturalia ab ipso recipere. Annon, quæso, naturæ quisque suæ convenientissima molimur, si facultates quidem activas, imperfectas, crassas, steriles, corruptas, ad supernaturalia faciamus quiscere ; facultatibus autem passivis, infinita a Deo recipere aptis, moliamur maxima & infinita a Deo recipere? Nolcat homo, & alta mente reponat, naturam suam non esse finem & scopum sui ipsius, sed Deum, & supernaturalia sola, humanæ naturæ scopum & finem esse: ita ut qui se suaque omnia non dirigunt ad supernaturalia, non tantum infra canes & infra bruta aut inanimata quævis, (quæ scopum suum attingunt.) sese abjicere, sed & naturam ipsam ejurare sint revera dicendi.
units.tr: This will readily appear to be true if we remember that our power is rightly distinguished into the active, by which we can act and produce effects, and the passive, by which we can receive and suffer. The former is very finite, imperfect, gross and corrupt; the latter is infinite, although for now it is, as it were, shut in by the obstacles of our corrupted nature. Now, if we attempt to do certain things well and perfectly from our corrupt activity, or from that same activity to produce things truly divine and supernatural, which exceed the capacity of our activity, this is indeed contrary to the law of nature and is no small arrogance, since a cause would then be producing an effect containing more reality than is in the cause itself, which is contrary to the very ideas of natural light. But if we attempt to receive from God greater things than we ourselves can produce, this agrees both with the natural and with the divine law, by which we are bound not to reject but to admit the good things that God offers and wishes to bestow (and he offers himself). And indeed it is most fitting to our passive power (which we have from God) to receive from him the infinite and the supernatural. Pray, does anyone attempt what is most suited to his own nature when he makes his active faculties, which are imperfect, gross, barren and corrupt, aspire to the supernatural, while with his passive faculties, which are fit to receive infinite things from God, he attempts to receive from God the greatest and infinite things? Let no one, with lofty mind, suppose that his nature is not its own end and goal, but that God is, and that the supernatural alone is the goal and end of human nature. For those who do not direct themselves and all that is theirs toward the supernatural are not merely to be said to cast themselves beneath dogs and beneath brute animals or any inanimate things (which attain their goal), but to be truly said to renounce nature itself.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: VII. De Desiderio ut medio ad obtinenda divina.
units.tr: VII. Concerning desire as a means of obtaining divine things.

units.la: Superest tantum ut petatur, an desiderium fit (ex parte hominis) medium efficax ad obtinendum id quod ad restitutionem facultatum nostrarum necesse est, sive, objectum desideratum? & quomodo id sine revelatione probari possit? Respondeo, Id ex natura probari, quatenus illa consideratur ut opus Dei optimi, sapientis, potentis. Namque primo, anima nostra ex natura sua cupida est, ita ut non possit sibi interdicere quin cupiat, sive desideria habeat. Secundo, si desideria illa (ubi scilicet bene directa sunt ad objecta sibi convenientia) non essent unquam implenda, tunc anima ex natura sua non posset non semper torqueri sine ulla spe remedii: quod est indignum opere illius Entis, quod ex potentia quidem sua desideria illa torquentia implere posset; ex bonitate ad id ipsum invitatur; ex sapientia non potest dare facultates ad objectum sese vehementer serentes, ac interim tamen vel objectum non concedere, vel ejusdem cum facultatibus conjunctionem negare. Quae omnia cum absurda sint, sequitur necessario, desideria bene directa de facultatibus restituendis & implendis, non esse rejectanea, sed efficacia.
units.tr: It remains only to ask whether desire, on man's part, is an effective means of obtaining what is necessary for the restoration of our faculties, or rather the object desired; and how this can be proved without revelation. I answer: it can be proved from nature, insofar as nature is considered as the work of a good, wise and powerful God. For first, our soul by its nature is desirous, so that it cannot forbid itself to desire, that is, to have desires. Secondly, if those desires (when they are rightly directed to objects suited to them) were never to be fulfilled, then the soul by its nature could not help being tormented always, with no hope of relief. This is unworthy of the work of that Being, who by his power could indeed fulfil those tormenting desires, who is invited by his goodness to do so, and who by his wisdom cannot give faculties that strain vehemently toward an object and yet in the meantime either withhold the object or deny that the faculties be united with it. Since all of these are absurd, it follows necessarily that rightly directed desires for the restoration and fulfilment of our faculties are not empty, but effective.

units.la: Haec autem facultatum impletio faciendia est sine medio aut cum medio. Si sine
units.tr: Now this fulfilment of the faculties is to be brought about either without a means or with a means. If without a means,

units.la: medio ; ergo jam statim effent impletæ, quod est contrà experientiam : fi cum medio ; (quia supponimus hic mentem solam ex una parte, & omnia objecta alia quæcunque extrà mentem ex altera parte) medium illud non potest esse ipsa objecta : nam nondum sunt possessa ; & ut possent esse media possessionis suæ, deberent prius possideri quam possideri, quod est absurdum : Ergo medium possessionis debet esse in mente. In mente vero sunt præcipue defiderium , intellectus , acquiescentia. Acquiescentia medium possessionis esse non potest, quia ipsa resultat ex possessione objecti. Intellectus etiam id esse nequit : is est (in spiritualibus) vas, ubi objectum debet locari, non medium ejus efficax : alias omnium hominum intellectus lumine impletus esse deberet. (Non nego tamen in intellectus atque acquiefcentiæ facultate conditiones certas præraequiri ; sed acquiescentia in his adhuc est magis sub forma desiderii, quam sub forma acquiefcentiæ completæ.) Ergo superest pro medio desiderium : illud autem est triplex, vel conjunctionis, vel feparationis (quod aversatio & odium dicitur) vel indifferentiæ: quæ duo ultima non possunt esse media possessionis objecti obtinendæ, siquidem illud potius rejiciunt, aut saltem non intromittunt. Restat igitur solum desiderium conjunctionis, extra quod, nullum aliud aptum in mente esse potest; nam fi aliud effet, effet non desiderium, hoc est, vel aversatio vel indifferentia, quæ modo rejecta.
units.tr: then they would already have been fulfilled at once, which is contrary to experience. If with a means (since we here suppose the mind alone on one side, and all other objects whatsoever outside the mind on the other), that means cannot be the objects themselves, for these are not yet possessed; and in order to be the means of their possession, they would first have to be possessed before they are possessed, which is absurd. Therefore the means of possession must be in the mind. Now in the mind there are chiefly desire, understanding and acquiescence. Acquiescence cannot be the means of possession, because it itself arises from the possession of the object. Nor can the understanding be so: in spiritual matters it is a vessel in which the object must be placed, not its effective means; otherwise the understanding of all men would have to be filled with the light. (I do not deny, however, that certain conditions are required beforehand in the faculty of understanding and of acquiescence; but acquiescence in these matters is still more in the form of desire than in the form of complete acquiescence.) Therefore desire remains as the means. This is threefold: of conjunction, of separation (which is called aversion and hatred), or of indifference. The last two cannot be means of obtaining possession of the object, since they rather reject it, or at least do not admit it. There remains therefore only the desire of conjunction, outside of which no other fitting thing can be in the mind; for if there were something else, it would not be desire, that is, either aversion or indifference, which have just been rejected.

units.la: cultatum reflitu-tionem & imple-tionem recipi-endam. rejecta sunt: cum è contra, desideria sint tanquam translatio vasis versus objectum quo vas impleri debet: quo quidem medio proximius & efficacius ex parte vasis exhiberi non potest.
units.tr: ...the restoration and filling of the faculties to be received. Those have been rejected; whereas, on the contrary, desires are like the carrying of the vessel toward the object by which the vessel must be filled. Indeed, on the part of the vessel, nothing closer or more effective can be shown as a means than this.

units.la: Cum igitur desideria sint naturalia possidendi objecti media, & cum modo probatum sit ex potentia, sapientia & bonitate Dei, desideria bene constituta non posse vacua relinqui, sequitur ea esse efficacia possessionis boni vel luminis, aut restitutionis media. Quod erat probandum.
units.tr: Since, therefore, desires are the natural means of possessing an object, and since it has been shown from the power, wisdom and goodness of God that well-ordered desires cannot be left empty, it follows that they are effective means of possessing the good or the light, or of restoration. This was to be proved.

units.la: Nota 1. efficaciam, quae hic tribuitur desiderio, non esse efficientem sed admissivam objecti sui divini.
units.tr: Note 1: the efficacy attributed here to desire is not efficient but admissive of its divine object.

units.la: Nota 2, quod summopere animadverti velim quanta sit precum (quae ipsissima descriptio fidei sunt) necessitas utilitasque summa ad veritatem solidam obtinendam, quae non tam cerebro frigide contendente acquiritur, quam ardentis instantiae desideriis, corde, votis & postulationibus divinis. Et hae tamen, vel ut nullae, vel ut ad eruditionem non spectantes, negliguntur ab eruditis plerisque, hanc clavem esse ad veritatis possessionem ignorantibus: aliis quidem per nescio quae de quibusvis personalibus rebus certo eventuris anilia decreta; aliis autem per atheisticum Spinozae fatum & effatum, quod volunt fata, non tollunt vota: quod sane origine sua dignum est. Cujusvis hominis libertati permissum hactenus voluit Deus, ut posset non quidem efficere, sed a Deo oblatum admittere aut secus, divi-
units.tr: Note 2: I should very much like it to be noticed how great is the necessity and the supreme usefulness of prayers (which are themselves the very description of faith) for obtaining solid truth, which is acquired not so much by the brain contending coldly as by desires of burning urgency, by the heart, by vows and by divine petitions. Yet these are neglected by most of the learned, either as useless or as not pertaining to learning, since they do not know that this is the key to the possession of truth; some by I know not what foolish decrees about personal matters certain to come about, others by the atheistic fate and saying of Spinoza, what the fates will, prayers do not remove, which is indeed worthy of its origin. God has hitherto willed that the freedom of every man should be permitted so that he could not indeed bring about, but could admit or refuse, what is offered by God: light, good, the healing of the faculties, and their restoration to integrity.

units.la: {f} Precum ad veri-tatis pos-sessionem obtinen-dam necessitas utilitasque summa ad eruditionem ratio. num lumen, bonum, facultatum fanationem, & in integrum restitutionem. Itaque homo bonis istis non defit per desideriorum suorum tepiditatem aut relaxationem. Et ut ad ea magis sese stimulet, consideret, utioftenfum est, impletionem eorum fundari in natura rei, Dei opere ; itemque in sapientia, bonitate & potentia Dei, hoc est, in natura Dei, qui dando menti facultatem desiderandi obiecta decentia, eo ipso voluit mentem apprehendere desideri o obiectum suum. Et quia Deus nil frustra velle potest, igitur non fine effectu & realitate id fieri potest: estque bene attendentibus desiderium (conditionibus debitis conceptum) ex natura sua jam quoddam initium fruitionis obiecti, & veluti promissum Dei de ejus impletione. Nam ideo dedit Deus facultatem defiderandi, quia vult dare rem desideratam: Ergo desiderium ex origine naturæ suæ est testimonium voluntatis Dei de dando obiecto desiderato, sive est promissio Dei naturalis, & ipes certa de postulatis nostris obtinendis, ab Eo nobis facta qui failere nescit.
units.tr: The necessity and supreme usefulness of prayers for obtaining possession of the truth, for learning, the reasoning. Therefore man is not lacking in these goods through any lukewarmness or slackening of his desires. And so that he may be stirred up more to them, let him consider how it has been shown that their fulfilment is founded in the nature of the thing, in the work of God; likewise in the wisdom, goodness and power of God, that is, in the nature of God, who, by giving the mind the faculty of desiring fitting objects, has by that very act willed that the mind should apprehend its desired object. And because God can will nothing in vain, this cannot happen without effect and reality; and to those who consider it well, desire (conceived under due conditions) is by its very nature already a certain beginning of the enjoyment of the object, and as it were a promise of God concerning its fulfilment. For God gave the faculty of desiring for this very reason, that he wills to give the desired thing. Therefore desire, from the origin of its nature, is a testimony of the will of God to give the desired object; or it is a natural promise of God, and a certain assurance from him, who cannot deceive, that our petitions will be obtained.

units.la: Est desiderium non tantum, uti diximus, translatio valis versus obiectum seipsum dandi cupidum, sed est etiam veluti immerfio in illud & tanquam os animæ, quo cibus pro omnibus facultatibus admittitur : (a) Aperi os tuum, & ego implebo illud. Hominis facultates veris suis obiectis debite adhibitis sustentari, & iis in bono statu conservari, notum est. Notum est & illud, hominem, quia finitus est, non posse simul omnes facultates suas, activas atque passivas, cum omnibus objectis suis jungere & exercere. Notum est & hoc tertium; debere id fieri ea cum temporis mensura, eoque cum mentis affectu, ut digniores facultates digniora objecta habentes, saepius & ardentius cum objectis suis uniantur, quam facultates minus dignae cum objectis suis imperfectioribus. Et quia mediante desiderio facultates supremae cum divinis objectis uniuntur, sequitur demonstrative, hominem, qui facultates suas in veritatem & sanitatem vult restitui, restitutasque conservari, debere propterea saepius & ardentius precibus vacare, sive, offerre Deo per desideria frequentia & ardentia facultates suas diviniores & sublimiores, ut suum illae cibum vigorisque nutrimentum ab illius communicatione ac liberalitate recipiant: atque etiam aequum esse, ut eo tempore ab aliarum facultatum inferiorum exercitio, quatenus hic impedimento essent, abstineat. Sin vero homo hisce ultimis se dedat totum neglecta superiorum saluberrima exercitatione, primo quidem peccat in Dei voluntatem & paratam bonitatem; secundo se ipsum beneficiis Dei sammis, ejusque gratia & lumine defraudat; tertio facultates ejus digniores fiunt inde languidae & caecae, tum obscurae, insensibiles, & veluti mortuae, haud secus ac corpus cui alimentum suum denegares; quarto & in facultates activas rationis, caeterasque inferiores, descendunt inde tenebrae, inordinationes, morbi, corruptio: unde is hohomo, jam Deo ipso in facultatibus supremis carens, & in ratione cœca & morbida ideas falsas atque chimæras, quas sæpe pro Deo jactitat, parturiens, coram Deo inter atheos numeratur: eo quod a Deo desciverit per intermissum exercitium libere & cum affectu sese illi passivum offerendi, ad quod tamen facultates idoneas recepit, ipseque adeo ab Auctore suo conditus fuerat.
units.tr: Desire is not only, as we have said, a carrying of the vessel toward the object, eager to give itself; it is also as it were a plunging into that object, and like the mouth of the soul, by which food is admitted for all the faculties: (a) Open your mouth, and I will fill it. It is known that man's faculties, when rightly applied to their true objects, are sustained and kept by them in a good state. It is known also that man, because he is finite, cannot join and exercise all his faculties, active and passive, with all their objects at once. It is known also, thirdly, that this must be done with such a measure of time and such an attitude of mind that the more worthy faculties, having more worthy objects, are united with their objects more often and more ardently than the less worthy faculties are with their more imperfect objects. And since by means of desire the highest faculties are united with divine objects, it follows demonstratively that a man who wishes his faculties to be restored to truth and health, and kept restored, ought therefore to give himself more often and more ardently to prayers; that is, he should offer to God, through frequent and ardent desires, his more divine and sublime faculties, so that they may receive from God's communication and bounty their food and the nourishment of their strength; and that it is also fair that at that time he should abstain from the exercise of the other, lower faculties, insofar as these would be a hindrance here. But if a man gives himself wholly to these last, neglecting the most salutary exercise of the higher faculties, then first, indeed, he sins against the will of God and his ready goodness; secondly, he defrauds himself of the chief benefits of God, and of his grace and light; thirdly, his more worthy faculties thereby become languid and blind, then obscure, insensible and as it were dead, no differently than a body from which one has withheld its food; fourthly, darkness, disorder, diseases and corruption descend upon the active faculties of reason and the other lower ones. Whence such a man, now lacking God himself in his highest faculties, and bringing forth in a blind and diseased reason false ideas and chimeras, which he often vaunts as God, is counted before God among the atheists; because he has fallen away from God through the neglect of freely and affectionately offering himself to him in a passive way, for which exercise nevertheless he received suitable faculties, and for which he had been created by his Author.

units.la: PARS TERTIA.
units.tr: PART THREE.

units.la: Ob neglectum superiorum regularum Cartesium cum suis in multa incidisse errata, quorum aliquot in illius Methodo & Meditationibus, in horum autem opinionibus nonnullis, deteguntur.
units.tr: Because the above rules were neglected, Descartes and his followers fell into many errors, some of which are exposed in his Method and Meditations, and some in the opinions of these men.

units.la: I. ET hactenus quidem de hisce sufficienter: quamvis enim plura adhuc circa hæc moveri possent, crediderim tamen iis facile ab exercitatis satisfieri posse, maxime si ad leges Methodi ad inveniendam veritatem hic propositas, velint se componere: nempe 1. Ordine procedendo; 2. idque mente sincera nec fraudulenta; 3, incipiendo in se & a se; 4. agnoscendo ægritudinem, qua durante, veritas acquiri non potest; 5. quæque adeo prius sit curanda & fananda,6.idque per oblationem constantem sui Deo Optimo, Maximo. Quas regulas qui observabit, multo verius & tutius se ad fosolidæ veritatis fontem, & hinc manantes rivulos, perventurum animadvertet, quam vel opeaut imitatione Methodi Mathematicæ, (quæ est id quod est cæcis aut iis qui in tenebris versantur, methodus corpora per palpationem cognoscendi, ipsis quidem proficua; sed ad cognitionem eorum quæ alio medio lumineque deteguntur, inutilis: ) vel observatione ipsius Cartesianæ methodi, cujus quidem leges quaternæ suis nævis erratisque non deStituuntur.
units.tr: I. So much for these matters, which I think is sufficient. Many further questions could still be raised about them, but I believe that experienced readers can easily answer them, especially if they conform themselves to the rules for finding truth proposed here, namely: (1) proceed in order; (2) do so with a sincere and honest mind; (3) begin in oneself and from oneself; (4) acknowledge the sickness, for as long as it lasts truth cannot be acquired; (5) and therefore the sickness that comes first must be cared for and healed; (6) and this by constant self-offering to God, the best and greatest. Whoever observes these rules will find that he reaches the fountain of solid truth, and the streams that flow from it, much more truly and safely than by either the mere imitation of the mathematical method (which is for the blind, or for those who move in darkness, a method of knowing bodies by touch: useful to them, but useless for knowing those things that are revealed by another medium and light), or by observing the Cartesian method itself, whose four rules are not free from its own blemishes and errors.

units.la: II, Nam in prima statim supponitur salsum, nempe rationis facultatem esse eousque sanam, ut nec alio lumine quam naturali, eoque quod nunc habet, opus sit ei: & vero eam hoc suo lumine clare & distincte videre posse non modo quædam generaliora; sed (quæ Cartesii verba sunt, ) nulla esse tam remota, ad quæ tandem non perveniat: nec tam occulta, quæ non detegat: atque ab eis quæ suo modo non deteget nec videbit, summopere esse cavendum. Quod profecto perinde est, ac si qui in tenebris nonnulla corpora facultate palpandi percipiunt, putarent nil tam remotum ac occultum esse, quod sua palpatione non possint detegere atque cognoscere: & vero pro regula cognoscendi ulterius corpora decernerent, sibi cavendum esse ab omni eo quod palpatione non perciperent, soliqueque contrectationi palpabili & distinctæ in cognitionibus acquirendis innitendum esse.
units.tr: II. For in the very first rule it is assumed, falsely, that the faculty of reason is so sound that it needs no other light than the natural light and the light it now has; and that by this light it can see clearly and distinctly not only some more general things, but (to use Descartes' own words) nothing so remote that it does not finally reach it, nor so hidden that it does not uncover it; and that one must be most careful of those things which in its own way it does not uncover nor see. This is indeed just as if some people, who perceive certain bodies in the dark by the faculty of touch, were to think that nothing is so remote or hidden that it cannot be detected and known by their touching it; and then, as a rule for knowing bodies further, were to decide that they must guard against everything they do not perceive by touch, and must rely only on palpable and distinct handling in acquiring knowledge.

units.la: In altera, ubi de rerum distinctionibus ad earum difficultates solvendas loquitur, omifit semper ubi ad rem ventum est, primas, capitales, necessarias, radicalesque rerum omnium distinctiones, nempe 1, in æternas & temporarias; 2, in sufficientes & arbitrarias; 3, in naturales sive absolutas (quæ amitti non possunt) quæque se solis imperfectæ sunt, & gratuitas, complentes atque perficientes, sed amissibiles; 4, in activas & passivas; 5, in reales, & umbratiles; 6, in superiores (respectu facultatum mentis) sive divinas, & inferiores; 7. in sanas & corruptas: & quæ ejusmodi nonnullæ sunt, veluti necessariæ & accidentariæ; sine quibus ausim dicere, nullas rerum difficultates præcipuas solvi posse, & quarum auxilio (cæteris non exclusis) ea quæ alioqui vel omnium difficillima aut insolubilia habita sunt, dissolvi possunt facillime, quod non uno in loco arbitror me non paucis exemplis manifestum dedisse.
units.tr: In the second rule, where he speaks of the distinctions of things in order to resolve their difficulties, he always omitted, when it came to the point, the first, chief, necessary and radical distinctions of all things, namely: (1) into eternal and temporal; (2) into sufficient and arbitrary; (3) into natural or absolute (which cannot be lost), and those which are imperfect in themselves alone, and gratuitous, completing and perfecting, but capable of being lost; (4) into active and passive; (5) into real and shadowy; (6) into superior (with respect to the faculties of the mind) or divine, and inferior; (7) into sound and corrupt. Some of these are, as it were, necessary and accidental. Without them I dare say that no principal difficulties of things can be resolved, and with their help (not excluding the others) those things which were otherwise held to be the most difficult of all, or insoluble, can be dissolved very easily. I think I have made this plain by many examples in more than one place.

units.la: In tertia Methodi lege, ubi de instituendo ordine, a simplicissimis incipiendo egit, debuisset maxime ad distinctiones modo rensitas respicere; & in aggredienda re, post generale illud cogito, ad earum pleraque attendisse; maxime vero a Divina Sufficientia, veluti a prima atque simplicissima omnium veritate, philosophandi exordium defumsisse: ex qua quippe omnibus rebus concipiendis difficultatibusque capitalibus dispellendis lux accedit sufficiens & necessaria: ut in aliis tractatibus probatum dedimus.
units.tr: In the third rule of the Method, where he treats of arranging an order, beginning from the simplest things, he ought above all to have looked to the distinctions just mentioned; and in undertaking the matter, after that general I think, he should have attended to most of them. Above all, he should have taken the beginning of philosophy from Divine Sufficiency, as from the first and simplest of all truths: for from it there comes, to the conceiving of all things and the dispelling of chief difficulties, a sufficient and necessary light, as we have proved in other treatises.

units.la: In quarta denique, de quæstione mediorum, rum, & difficultatum enumeratione, quoniam in prima lege male supposita est rationis non ægrę potentia; neque juxta secundam ac tertiam rerum divisiones necessariæ rectę factæ sunt, sed multæ omissæ, cæteræ nec omnes ordine apparentes, magni hiatus reliđi, non potuit enumeratio requisita re- ctę fieri, etsi philosophanti visum sit nihil a se omitti. Ita ut ex legis primæ suppositione falsa, ipsa & cæteræ leges cassæ sint, inobservatæ sint, & in veritatis quæsito Systemate non impedierint quin & debita multa abessent vera, & multa indebita falsa admiscerentur.
units.tr: Lastly, in the fourth rule, concerning the question of means, ends and the enumeration of difficulties: since the first rule wrongly supposes that the power of reason is not sick, and since, according to the second and third, the divisions of things were not rightly made as they should be, but many were omitted and the rest not all apparent in order, with great gaps left, the required enumeration could not be rightly made, even though it seemed to the philosopher that nothing had been omitted by him. So, from the false supposition of the first rule, both it and the other rules were rendered void and were not observed, and in the system sought for truth they did not prevent much that was due from being absent and much that was not due from being mixed in as false.

units.la: III. Solis quippe legibus & regulis, quas senario inclusimus numero, potest veritas solida & integra debite quæri & inveniri, & ita quidem, ut nemo eorum, qui ad illarum tenorem se gesserit, maxime non neglectis rerum distinctionibus modo dictis, quæ & in prima nostra regula sunt indicatæ, conquesturus sit sibi deesse, quantum optare potest, veritatem solidam. At sine illis, nulla vis ingenii pertinget unquam ad acqui- sitionem veritatum quibus mens destituitur & indiget, etsi in supplementum indigentiæ ac paupertatis suæ a punctis & lineis emendicatum eat aliquas minusculas propositiunculas, importuna sagacitate extortas, quibus speciem divitiarum veritatisque acquisitæ ridicule mentiens, sibi aliisque absurde imponat; tametsi immensis, solidis, æternisque luminibus, quæque ipsam & verum ejus statum quam maxime & intime spe- { rum ejus statum quam ...} {*}stant, interiora ejus destituuntur, atque immanibus tenebris & erroribus oppositis infacta sunt. Quorum quidem exempla non pauca in medium produci possent, fi beneficii loco reputarent homines errores suos sibi ostendi; sed praestat ab eo abstinere, nisi, quia Cartefiani caeteris fe ingenuiores profitentur, qui scilicet in verba magistri non jurarint, soliusque veritatis, seu adverfa fit seu conformis primis cogitatis, amore duci velint, spes effet fore inter eos qui revera tales sint, quibusque non ingrata sutura sint similium erratorum exempla, quae vel ex Cartefio vel ex ipsismet adduci possent.
units.tr: III. Solid and whole truth can be rightly sought and found only by the rules and precepts which we have included in the number six; and so indeed that no one who has conducted himself according to their tenor, especially without neglecting the distinctions of things just mentioned, which are indicated in our first rule, will complain that solid truth is lacking to him as much as he could wish. But without those rules, no power of mind will ever reach the acquisition of the truths of which the mind is destitute and in need; even if, to supply its want and poverty, it goes begging from points and lines for some tiny little propositions, extorted by importunate cleverness, by which, ridiculously feigning the appearance of riches and of acquired truth, it imposes absurdly on itself and on others. Although immense, solid and eternal lights, which touch its very being and its true state most closely and intimately, are wanting to its inner parts, and it has been made to suffer under monstrous darkness and opposed errors. Not a few examples of these could be brought forward, if men regarded it as a benefit to have their errors shown to them. But it is better to refrain from that, except that, since the Cartesians profess themselves more ingenuous than others, namely in that they have not sworn to the words of their master, and wish only to be led by love of truth, whether it be opposed to or in agreement with their first thoughts, there is hope that among those who are really such, examples of similar errors, which could be drawn either from Descartes or from themselves, would not be unwelcome.

units.la: IV. Id quod ex benevolentia quae mihi animitus insidet erga mentes solidae veritatis cupidas, aliquoties in aliis editis meis jam feci, in iis etiam quae in hoc ipso tradatu modo praecesserunt, nec non & quae fequentur, non omittendum credidi. Nunc autem, ubi quaestio est de observatione vel negleftione sex regularum nostrarum seu Methodi nostrae (fi nostrum licet dicere quod est omnium vel ad omnes spectat & pertinet) nolim quidem in specie ostendere, quomodo in unamquamque illarum ab omnibus fere peccatum fit: hoc uniuscujusque examini discutiendum relinquo: sed tamen errata nonnulla adhuc annotare libet, quae ob eas negleftas admissa sunt in rebus quae ipsis sunt inter praecipuas, quales v. g. fuerint inter multa Cartefii Meditationes.
units.tr: IV. Out of the goodwill that dwells deep within me towards minds eager for solid truth, I have thought it not right to omit this, as I have already done several times in my other published works, both in those which have gone before in this very treatise and in those which follow. Now, however, since the question is about the observance or neglect of our six rules, or of our Method (if it is permitted to call ours what concerns and pertains to all), I would not indeed wish to show in particular how almost everyone sins against each of them: I leave that to be examined by each person. Yet it pleases me to note some errors that, because of those neglected rules, were admitted in matters that are among the chief ones, such as, for example, those found among the many Meditations of Descartes.

units.la: V. In prima propositurus ille morbi descriptionem (ut ipse (a) ait) cujus curandi methodum volebat docere, morbum & morbi causam quæriit & ponit (vel supponit) ubi revera non est. Equidem de sensuum præjudiciis, quatenus judicantur quædam qualitates inesse rebus, formaliter similes eis quibus afficimur, merito dubites, judiciaque ejusmodi habeas de morbo suspecta : at ex iis concludere in genere, dari revera corpora quibus afficimur, & inter ea certum aliquod ad nos pertinere, nosque vigilare, morbus non est, nisi in stultorum quorundam Scepticorum mente, de quibus, quia non sincere agunt, nos neutiquam decet esse sollicitos: neque etiam ullis demonstrationibus ratiocinatis prætenfus hic morbus solide depelli poterit, (ut alibi notavimus,) sed solis sensibus atque sinceritate mentis. Qui autem eo non laborant, illi nec ipsis demonstrationibus (ne potius inde ægri fiant, ut evenit) tentandi sunt ad sanitatem non amissam revocari. Deinde loco illius suppofitionis de Deo per omnipotentiam suam faciente forsitan apparere corpora quæ tamen non sunt, aut de deceptore summe potente & maligno qui semper nos fallat, oportuifset ad radicem morbi tangendam, adducere, tum nos ipsos esse deceptores, qui cum auctorem nostrum & conscientiam nostram officiis debitis & promissis sæpe defraudaverimus, habitum jam deceptionis & fallaciæ nostri contraximus; tum Deum ex justitia erga istiusmodi deceptores æquissime permittere, ut, quando judicia facere volunt, non quidem necessaria de suo corpore exsistente cum aliis; sed curiosa, de natura & essentia rerum spiritualium & corporalium, veritatem non attingant, at fallantur perpetuo. De numeris autem dubitatio, ut insana & impossibilis ne quidem tangenda suisset. De Dei etiam exsistentia dubitantis personam nec sibi nec lectori ullo modo imponere debuisset; sed alicui tertio, cujus scrupulis tollendis nonnihil operæ esset dandum. Atque sic quidem dubitatio intra suæ naturæ suæque caussæ, nec non & animi sinceritatis limites stetisset: cum alioqui non parvas illa ubique fere, nec omnino absque culpa, turbas excitaverit.
units.tr: V. In the first place, Descartes, about to set out (as he himself says) a description of the disease whose method of cure he wished to teach, seeks out and posits (or supposes) the disease and the cause of the disease where in truth there is none. Certainly one may rightly doubt the prejudices of the senses, insofar as they judge that certain qualities formally similar to those by which we are affected are present in things, and one may hold such judgments as suspect as a disease. But to conclude from them in general that there really exist bodies by which we are affected, and that some one of these belongs to us and that we are awake, is not a disease, except in the minds of certain foolish Sceptics, with whom, since they do not act sincerely, we ought in no way to be concerned. Nor can this alleged disease be solidly driven out by any reasoned demonstrations (as we have noted elsewhere), but only by the senses and the sincerity of the mind. Those who are not afflicted with it should not even be attempted, by the demonstrations themselves, to be recalled to a health they have not lost (lest they rather become sick from them, as happens). Next, instead of that supposition that God by His omnipotence might cause bodies to appear which in fact do not exist, or the supposition of a most powerful and malignant deceiver who always deceives us, one ought, to touch the root of the disease, to have brought forward this: that we ourselves are deceivers, who, since we have often defrauded our Author and our conscience of the duties and promises owed to them, have already contracted a habit of deception and falsehood; and that God, out of justice towards such deceivers, most justly permits that when they wish to make judgments, they do not attain the truth, not indeed in necessary matters concerning the existence of their own body with others, but in curious matters concerning the nature and essence of spiritual and corporeal things, and that they are deceived perpetually. As for doubt about numbers, it, being insane and impossible, should not even have been touched.
