Also, concerning the existence of God, he ought not to have imposed on himself or on the reader in any way by the person of one who doubts, but on some third party, whose scruples it would be worth some effort to remove. And so doubt would have stayed within the limits of its own nature and cause, and also of the sincerity of the mind; whereas otherwise it has stirred up, almost everywhere and not altogether without fault, no small disturbances.

units.la: VI. In secunda, potuisset initio ordinis & perspicuitatis gratia, & ut quisque a se ipso & in se, inque intimis suis inciperet, postulari ut supponeretur nulla adhuc dari corpora, spatia, loca, ut natura Mentis & primi cogniti clarius detegi posset. Sed quando inveniebatur illud, Cogito ergo sum, recensebanturque varii modi diverseque facultates cogitandi, hoc maxime (cujus omissio immensum multis Cartesianis nocuit) erat monendum, illud cogito, cum ex usu ordinario activitatem mentis sive subjecti cogitantis maxime significet, non esse hoc sensu præcipuum quod est in nobis; sed esse etiam in nobis cogitationes quas patimur seu passive habemus, non tantum eas quæ a corporibus externis procedere videntur, & sensationes vocantur; sed maxime quasdam alias, quibus sentimus nos ab intimis impelli ad obiecta aeterna, immensa, optima desideranda, admiranda, veneranda, quorum impressione maxime intimis & realibus afficimur attractibus, gaudiis, timore, ictibus, a quibus obiectis etiam infinita alia possumus recipere & pati: & has quidem facultates talia patiendi sive recipiendi, aut percipiendi & cogitandi, in nobis esse vel videri saltem pro obiectorum ejusmodi praestantia & potentia, digniores, praecipuas, numerosiores, item & maxime intimas & essentiales, quamvis nunc, quia in actum non sunt deductae omnes, & si quae deductae sint, non fuerunt nisi imperfectissime exercitae, nos ferme omnes lateant: quibus detegendis, quia sunt praecipua pars nostri, impostérum cura sit danda potissimum. Haec atque similia, quamvis ibi nondum explicanda aut demonstranda, fuissent tamen veluti praeparatio tum materiae postmodum tractandae, tum mentis ad divinas facultates suas passivas, fundumque animae aeternum, deinceps agnoscenda.
units.tr: VI. In the second part, for the sake of order and clarity, and so that each person might begin from himself and from his own inmost self, it could have been asked at the outset that we suppose no bodies, spaces or places yet exist, so that the nature of the mind and the first thing known might be revealed more clearly. But since the statement I think, therefore I am is found there, and the various modes and faculties of thinking are listed, this above all should have been pointed out (the omission of which harmed many Cartesians greatly): the word think, while in ordinary use it chiefly signifies the activity of the mind or of the thinking subject, is not the principal sense in which we have it. There are also in us thoughts which we undergo, or have passively, and not only those which seem to proceed from external bodies and are called sensations. Above all there are certain others, by which we feel ourselves driven from within toward eternal, immense, supremely good objects to be desired, admired and revered. By the impression of these objects we are most deeply affected in our inmost and real attractions, joys, fears and blows, and from these objects we can receive and suffer countless other things. These faculties of suffering or receiving such things, or of perceiving and thinking, are in us, or at least seem to be, in proportion to the excellence and power of such objects, more worthy, more principal, more numerous, and also most inward and essential. Yet, because not all of them have been brought into act, and those that have been brought into act have been exercised only most imperfectly, nearly all of us are for the most part unaware of them. Since they are the principal part of ourselves, care should be given to uncovering them above all in the future. These and similar points, though not yet to be explained or demonstrated there, would nonetheless have served as a kind of preparation, both for the matter to be treated afterward and for the mind to acknowledge in what follows its passive divine faculties and the eternal ground of the soul.

units.la: VII. In tertia Meditatione, existere Deum aggreditur demonstrare. Cartesius, eamque conclusionem, mea quidem sententia, bene efficit atque demonstrat: attamen in ejus praeparationibus & praemissis, non pauca insunt minus ad rem apta minusque vera, quanquam non in eis partibus unde vis demonstrationis dependet.
units.tr: VII. In the third Meditation, Descartes sets out to demonstrate that God exists. In my opinion he brings this conclusion about and proves it well; yet in his preliminaries and premises there are not a few things less apt to the matter and less true, although not in those parts on which the force of the demonstration depends.

units.la: Sed fallitur profecto Cartesius quando illas suas de Dei existentia demonstrationes sic effert & omnibus praefert, ut (a) nullam viam
units.tr: But Descartes certainly errs when he sets forth and prefers above all his demonstrations of God's existence in such a way that (a) he thinks no way

units.la: {a}viam putet ingenio humano patere per quam meliores inveniri unquam possint. Quod ut redam evidens, nonnullas ego jam, si modo quis sincera mente velit sibi ordinate attendere, indigitabo demonstrationes Cartesianas multo meliores, & præ quibus illæ vix postea alicujus momenti videantur. Ad quod non opus erit ut superficiariam aliquam ideararum rationis in classes distinctionem præparationis gratia proponam, aut insistam (uti male Cartesius) incertitudini malesanæ de corporum exsistentia, unde concludi posset, solius frigidæ istius ideæ Dei, quæ est in ratione, hanc esse prærogativam, ut exsistentiam sui objecti necessario inferat: Sed dimissa petitione, qua modo postulaveram supponi nondum existere corpora, relinquam eorum exsistentiæ naturalem & certitudinem indubitatam in suo statu, atque ex eo oltendam certius & solidius demonstrari Dei exsistentiam, quàm ex idea; tum eandem incomparabiliter adhuc excellentius ex facultatibus passivis æque earum actuationibus consequi. Et hoc ipsum jam mihi videor (b) superius oltendisse, (b) quo velim lectorem remitti, ut hic brevior esse possim.
units.tr: way lies open to the human mind by which better ones could ever be found. To make this plain, I shall now point out, if anyone will attend to them in an orderly way with a sincere mind, some Cartesian-style demonstrations far better than his, in comparison with which his own will scarcely seem of any worth afterward. For this there will be no need, for the sake of preliminaries, to propose some superficial division of the ideas of reason into classes, nor to dwell (as Descartes does badly) on the unhealthy uncertainty about the existence of bodies, from which it might be concluded that this cold idea of God, which is in reason, has the sole privilege of necessarily implying the existence of its object. But, setting aside the request I just made, that we suppose bodies do not yet exist, I shall leave the natural existence of bodies and their undoubted certainty in their own state. From that I shall show that the existence of God is demonstrated more certainly and solidly than from the idea; and then that it follows from the passive faculties and their actuations in an incomparably more excellent way still. I seem to myself already to have shown this above, and to it I wish the reader to be referred, so that I may be briefer here.

units.la: VIII. Præmoto primo, mentem meam sic naturaliter constitutam esse, ut eo magis certioretur de causæ alicujus exsistentia, quo magis effectus ejusdem eam afficit, ita ut si afficiatur modo potentissimo, vividissimo, luminosissimo, acquiescentissimo, non pollit, nisi fraudulenta sibi & mendax sit, non certa esse hoc ipso, & sine ope ulterio-ris.
units.tr: VIII. Having first set down that my mind is so naturally constituted that it is the more assured of the existence of some cause as the effect of that cause affects it more strongly, so that if it is affected in a most powerful, most vivid, most luminous and most satisfying way, it cannot be uncertain of that cause (unless it is deceitful and lying to itself), without further help.

units.la: (a) in dedic. ad Sorbon.
units.tr: (a) in the dedication to the Sorbonne.

units.la: Part. I. num. XII. & XIII. VIII. Præno-tata quæ-dam ad exsisten-tiam Dei solidius demon-. is ratiocinationis, de re five causa exsistente, & hæc efficiente.
units.tr: Part I, nos. XII and XIII. VIII. Certain premises concerning the existence of God, demonstrated more solidly by reasoning, concerning the thing or cause that exists, and this as efficient.

units.la: 2. Præno‑to secundo, vim cogitandi vel percipiendi quæ in me est duplicem esse: unam actívam, quæ tenuis, limitatissima obscuraque valdeest, quæque contentione & actívitate sua mihi nihil repræsentat nisi ideas pictur arias, parum efficientes, & veluti mortuas: alteram passivam, qua vel me invito, saltem me nil efficiente, in me recipio perceptiones & impressiones potentissimas, vividissimas, valdeque luminosas & acquiescentiam inferentes; quæque cum objectis quibusdam mihi sic videntur indivulse conjunctæ, ut & nequeam nexum illum solvere, aut eum mea actívitate imitari; neque etiam a me impetrare possim ut acquiescenter considerem illas meas perceptiones ab objectis eos excitantibus esse ita disjunctas, ut sine illis exsistentibus sint aut esse possint. Cæterùm, nil impedire quo minus vis illa mea passiva sit infinita, pro infinitate illorum quæ in ea agere possunt, quemadmodum indies experior nova semper in illa excitari.
units.tr: 2. I set down secondly that the power of thinking or perceiving which is in me is twofold: one active, which is very slight, very limited and obscure, and which by its own striving and activity represents to me nothing but picture-like ideas, having little efficacy and as it were dead; the other passive, by which, even against my will, or at least with me doing nothing, I receive perceptions and impressions which are most powerful, most vivid, very luminous, and bring with them satisfaction. These seem to me so inseparably joined to certain objects that I cannot dissolve that connection or imitate it by my own activity. Nor can I bring it about that I calmly consider those perceptions of mine, which the objects exciting them produce, to be so disjoined from them that they are or can be without those objects existing. Moreover, nothing prevents that passive power of mine from being infinite, in proportion to the infinity of those things that can act upon it, as I daily experience new things always being stirred up in it.

units.la: 3. Noto tertio, in potentia illa mea, sive in facultatibus passivis, in aliis quidem mihi repræsentari potenter, vivide, luminose & acquiescenter, velim nolim, corpus meum, multis constans partibus & diverse motum, & præterea alia etiam corpora existentia præter illud: in aliis vero, me allici modis quibusdam adhuc dignioribus & potentioribus ad ineffabile aliquod reale, potens, luminosum, bonum, quod ubi id passive & quiete cum affectu contemplor, fiens me ab illo allici, id mihi quidem indivulse adesse, meque per se solum afficere videtur; at ubi activitate mea id considerare, deque eo conceptus & ratiocinationes formare satago, tunc ejus praesentes vividissimique ictus, & inimitabiles tactus intimi, cum eo sentiuntur secedere, & in eorum locum succedere perceptiones frigidae, inefficaces, mortuae, impotentes, confusae etiam, neque me tranquillantes, quae respectu priorum se habent ut merae picturae ad rem ipsam vividam.
units.tr: 3. I note thirdly that in that power of mine, or in my passive faculties, there is presented to me, whether I will or not, in some perceptions powerfully, vividly, luminously and satisfyingly, my body, made up of many parts and variously moved, and besides it other bodies existing apart from it. In other perceptions I am drawn, by certain modes still more worthy and more powerful, toward some ineffable real thing, powerful, luminous and good. When I contemplate it passively and quietly, with feeling, and I am drawn by it, it seems to me indeed to be present inseparably and to affect me by itself alone. But when I strive, by my activity, to consider it and to form concepts and reasonings about it, then its present and most vivid blows and inimitable inward touches are felt to withdraw from it, and in their place come cold, ineffective, dead, powerless and even confused perceptions, which do not calm me. In relation to the former they are like mere pictures compared with the living thing itself.

units.la: 4. Unde quarto annoto & illud, argumenta Cartesii, etsi bona in suo genere, non posse tamen non esse multo minus afficientia, atque adeo minus persuadentia quam sibi imaginabatur. Et hoc quidem experientia tristi patet in illis qui ad Atheismum a Cartesianismo sunt delapsi: deinde etiam ex jam dictis: Sunt quippe defuncta ex effectu (ex idea) qui non est effectus immediatus Dei, sed facultatis activae rationis, (tametsi haec vim eam a solo Deo immediate potuit accipere, unde argumenti praecipuum robur.) Interim quia ille effectus & remotus est, & participat de causae suae proximae (activitatis rationis) impotentia, sterilitate, obscuritate & vacuitate, non potest ita vivide & inconcusse in intimis causae remotae & umbratiliter solum atque imperfectissime depictae, exsistentiam evincere, uti quidem effectus proximi, potentes, vividi, luminosi & infinite lætificantes atque afficientes, qui indivulse percipiuntur cum causa potentissima, vividissima, luminosissima, & optima atque felicissima connecti.
units.tr: 4. Hence I note fourthly that the arguments of Descartes, though good in their own kind, cannot but be far less affecting, and therefore less persuasive, than he imagined. This is plain from sad experience in those who have slipped from Cartesianism into atheism. It is also plain from what has already been said: they are derived from an effect (the idea) which is not an immediate effect of God but of the active faculty of reason, although that faculty could have received its power immediately from God alone, which is the chief strength of the argument. Meanwhile, because that effect is remote, and shares in the powerlessness, sterility, obscurity and emptiness of its proximate cause (the activity of reason), it cannot prove the existence of the remote cause so vividly and unshakeably, since that cause is painted only in shadow and most imperfectly. The proximate effects, however, are powerful, vivid, luminous, and infinitely gladdening and affecting; they are perceived inseparably as joined with a most powerful, most vivid, most luminous, best and most blessed cause.

units.la: IX. His præno-tatis; quicunque vult demonstrationum infinite Cartesianas superantium vim potentissimam, vividissimam, luminosissimam atque acquiescentissimam in intimis suis indubitato percipere; quandoquidem isti effectus vividi in passivis facultatibus ab activitate nostra non pendent, sed experimur tantum in nobis libertatem osserendi facultates objectis suis; is ergo inti-ma omnia sua offerat objecto sæpissime prævenienti, animæ bonis impulsibus illabenti, & perceptionum modo dictarum efficienti causæ, quæcunque illa sit aut esse possit; quod quidem si ex animo & sine fraude egerit, tunc vero videbit & contrectabit vividis effectis tantam certitudinem Dei exsistentis, ut ad argumenta ratiocinativa risurus sit ob eorum inutilitatem; haud secus ac risu dignum esset, si quis candelam adferret homini ad Solem exposito ut per eam posset conspicere Solem. Sed si quis nolit requisita ad hanc demonstrationem præstare, is si forte de ejus inevidentia conqueratur, non erit magis audiendus, quam qui neglectis faciendis ad solutionem problematis Mathematici, de eo non invento moveret querelam. At enim, inquiet quispiam, quomodo tradam facultates meas objecto incerto:, quod nondum novi esse? timeo decipi. Inconsiderate! Si nondum nosti ea certitudine quæ adhuc quæritur, nosti tamen satis, ut siquidem, solidissimarum demonstrationum sis cupidus, moveri possit inde, spes & diligentia tua ad jaciendam aleam, & experientiam tentandam, quam sæpe in rebus nauci laboriosissimam & fallacissimam suscipere non recusas, cum hic nullum sit deceptionis aliud periculum, quam te ad cogitabile omne bonum reale, luminosum, potens, fontem vividitatis & felicitatis, a quo capiaris & possidearis, trahi & deduci. O felicem vero deceptionem! Utinam omnes cæteræ veritates contemnerentur, hæc vero sola deceptio ubique obtineret!
units.tr: IX. With these things premised: whoever wishes to perceive undoubtedly within himself the most powerful, most vivid, most luminous and most satisfying force of demonstrations surpassing the Cartesian ones, let him, since these vivid effects in the passive faculties do not depend on our activity, but we only experience in ourselves the freedom to open our faculties to their objects, offer all his inmost self to the object which very often comes first, which flows into the soul with good impulses, and is the efficient cause of the kind of perceptions just described, whatever that cause may be or could be. If he does this from the heart and without deceit, then he will indeed see and feel, through vivid effects, such certainty of the existing God that he will laugh at syllogistic arguments because of their uselessness. It would be no less laughable than if someone brought a candle to a man set out in the sun so that by it he might see the sun. But if anyone is unwilling to perform the requirements for this demonstration, and perhaps complains that it is not evident to him, he is no more to be heard than one who, having neglected the steps needed to solve a mathematical problem, complains that the solution has not been found. But someone will say: how shall I surrender my faculties to an object which is uncertain, which I do not yet know to exist? I fear being deceived. Thoughtless! If you do not yet know it with the certainty that is still being sought, you know enough that, if you are eager for the most solid demonstrations, your hope and diligence can be stirred to cast the die and to try the experiment, which you often undertake, in matters of no worth, very laboriously and with the greatest risk of error. Here there is no other danger of deception than that you are drawn and led toward every good thing that can be thought of, real, luminous, powerful, the source of life and happiness, by which you may be seized and possessed. O happy deception! Would that all other truths were despised, and that this deception alone prevailed everywhere!

units.la: X. Quando ex vividis ejusmodi effectibus in pallivis facultatibus oblatis certitudo de Deo summa in mente nata est, potest hæc inde ad gradum certitudinis altiorem & ineffabiliorem ascendere, si nimirum ea quæ cognovit in priori certitudine esse Deo grata, fideliter & sincere pro viribus exequatur, si gratitudine, laude, amore, obsequio erga Deum agnitum exerceat se totam. Tunc enim supernaturales & omne cogitatum transcendentes actus atque essectus in intimis suis sic excitari sentiet, ut jam ipsa sui non amplius futura sit memor, suaeque activitatis, sed totam sinat vivere in se causam admirandam ejusmodi effectuum, a fonte omnis veri & boni individuorum. Et hæc sunt quidem quam admirabilissima percipientibus aut degustantibus, quin & vere sperantibus, demonstrata; cum quibus nulla alia comparari possunt.
units.tr: X. When a supreme certainty about God has arisen in the mind from such vivid effects in the passive faculties, it can rise from there to a higher and more ineffable degree of certainty, if it faithfully and sincerely carries out, as far as its powers allow, what it has recognised in the earlier certainty to be pleasing to God, and if it exercises itself wholly in gratitude, praise, love and obedience towards the God it has come to know. For then it will feel supernatural acts and effects, transcending all thought, stirred up in its inmost being in such a way that it no longer remembers itself or its own activity, but allows the wonderful cause of such effects, the source of all truth and goodness, to live wholly within it. These are indeed the most admirable things, shown to those who perceive or taste them, and to those who truly hope; no other things can be compared with them.

units.la: XI. Post ista ex effectis & actibus duorum generum in facultatibus passivis argumenta, sequitur aliud ex ipsarum facultatum consideratione desumendum, & Cartesianis adhuc longe praferendum. Illud autem est, quod facultates optandi fruitionem luminis & boni infiniti, immortalis, perfectissimi, felicissimi, quae a nobis ipsis capacitationem sunt factae, & ne quidem a nobis ipsis te ipsa actuari possunt, non possint esse nisi a causa infinite, immortaliter sive aeterne, perfectissime & felicissime luminosa & bona. Nam cum facultates sint capacitates admittendi objecti, omnis causa quae non esset infinita, operans in subjecto aliquo secundum suam mensuram finitae vim, in eo non posset efficere nisi capacitatem finitam, & suae naturae congruam: nisi effectum credas sua causa posse praestare, & realitatis causam esse posse nihil.
units.tr: XI. After these arguments drawn from the effects and acts of the two kinds in the passive faculties, there follows another, to be drawn from the consideration of the faculties themselves, and one still to be preferred far above the Cartesian arguments. It is this: the faculties for desiring the enjoyment of an infinite, immortal, most perfect and most blessed light and good, which have been made capable of it by ourselves, and which cannot even be actuated by ourselves, cannot be except from a cause that is infinite, immortal or eternal, most perfect and most blessedly luminous and good. For since faculties are capacities for admitting an object, any cause that was not infinite, acting in some subject with a finite power according to its measure, could produce in it only a finite capacity, congruent with its own nature; unless you believe that an effect can produce its own cause, and that nothing can be the cause of reality.

units.la: XII. Insuper, argumenta exsistentiae Dei ex corporum exsistentia, effectis & considerationibus desumta; Cartesianis validiora sunt, siquidem ex praenotatis, corpora sint effectus reales & immediati potentis, sapientis & bonae causae, qui effectus nos, facultatefve nostras quasdam passivas, vivide, potenter, luminose & acquiescenter afficiunt; quod non ita facit idea Dei ex facultate rationis. Et quemadmodum quando quis perspicit effectus reales cujusdam causae, magis de causae exsistentia convincitur, quam quando perspicit picturam vel iconem causae: sic de Deo magis convincimur, (& experientia id confirmat) sentiendo vivide efsectus causæ potentis, sapientis, optimæ in mirabili mundi corporei systemate, quam excitando in nobis ideam live pictuTam causæ potentis sapientis & optimæ. Dices, ideam illam Dei ratione, oportere intervenire in argumento ex consideratione mundi existentis defumto: at falleris sane, idque ob usum generaliorem & æquivocum vocis ideæ, quæ diversas, ut hic, species continet. Idea potentiæ, sapientiæ, bonitatis quæ in anima excitatur per contemplationem operum Dei, alius est naturæ, quam idea ejusdem potentiæ, sapientiæ, bonitatisque quæ excitatur actívitate solius rationis. Illa (quoniam operationes nonnullæ Dei immediatæ insunt lumini & bonitati operum naturæ,) & quia cum Dei omnipotentis actu immediate juncta est, excitatque interiora cordis, mentis, iplumque intellectum passivum ; vivida est, valde afficiens, suffultaque effectu præsentissimo, palpabili, reali & mirabili potentis causæ: hæc, languida & iners, innixa & immixta actibus nostris imperfectiffimis & umbratilibus solum. Qui actibus animi cognoscendis utcunque exercitati sunt, illico inter illas duas ideas immensam deprehendent differentiam, eamque haud minorem, quam inter ideam quam quis sibi ratiocinando formaffet de alicujus regis liberalitate, & inter eam quæ nasceretur ex eo quod immensi thesauri a rege ei donati effent. Utra magis convinceret animum de existentia liberalitatis regiæ ?· vel saltem, utra magis essetvivida & afficiens ? Cæterum, quia me hæc omnia argumenta obiter tantum tangere oportet, ne excedam limites, plura de iis profundius meditanda relinquo, cum nonnullis facillime solvendis objectiunculis.
units.tr: XII. Moreover, the arguments for the existence of God drawn from the existence, effects and considerations of bodies are more valid than the Cartesian ones. For, as has been noted before, bodies are real and immediate effects of a powerful, wise and good cause, which effects affect us and certain of our passive faculties vividly, powerfully, luminously and restfully; the idea of God from the faculty of reason does not do this. Just as, when someone perceives the real effects of some cause, he is more convinced of the cause's existence than when he perceives a picture or image of the cause, so we are more convinced of God (and experience confirms this) by vividly feeling the effects of a powerful, wise and best cause in the wonderful system of the corporeal world, than by arousing in ourselves the idea or picture of a powerful, wise and best cause. You will say that this idea of God must necessarily intervene by reason in the argument drawn from the consideration of the existing world; but you are certainly mistaken, and that because of the more general and equivocal use of the word idea, which here covers different kinds. The idea of power, wisdom and goodness that is aroused in the soul through contemplation of the works of God is of a different nature from the idea of the same power, wisdom and goodness that is aroused by the activity of reason alone. The former, since some immediate operations of God are present in the light and goodness of the works of nature, and because it is immediately joined to the act of almighty God and stirs the inner parts of the heart and mind and the passive intellect itself, is vivid, strongly affecting, and supported by the most present, palpable, real and wonderful effect of a powerful cause. The latter is languid and inert, resting only on and mixed with our most imperfect and shadowy acts. Those who are at all practised in knowing the acts of the mind will at once detect an immense difference between these two ideas, no less than between the idea someone had formed for himself by reasoning about a king's generosity and the idea that would arise from the fact that immense treasures had been given to him by the king. Which of these would more convince the mind of the existence of royal generosity, or at least which would be more vivid and affecting? Since I must touch on all these arguments only in passing, lest I exceed my limits, I leave their more profound consideration to be undertaken, together with some objections that are very easily answered.

units.la: XIII. Quintum quoddam exištentiæ Dei argumentum (quatuor enim jam præcessere) idque Cartesianis efficacius, desumendum est ex activitate nostra, quatenus illa in nobilissima illa libertatis dote (quæ cuivis sese sincere insp icienti infinitis documentis & experimentis est intime præsens, ) conspicitur illimitata & infinita. Libertas illimitata & infinita est effectus cujusdam causæ, quæ, ut causa, infinita, illimitata & liberrima, non potest non esse : causa in genere causarum infinita, libera & illimitata, perinde est ac Deus. Hujus argumenti vim sentientes Athei, ipsi malunt stoliditate horribili libertatem suam, quam solo nomine absurde affirmant, re ipsa negare, & se ipsos in brutas machinas transformare, quam eandem concedendo, admittere vim argumenti cogentem, ut agnoscant sui & omnium causam ex libertate potente, intelligente & liberalissima, rebus, ortum, ordinem, naturam & complementum dantem.
units.tr: XIII. A fifth argument for the existence of God (four have already gone before) is to be drawn, and it is more effective than the Cartesian ones, from our activity, insofar as that activity is seen, in the most noble gift of freedom (which is intimately present to anyone who sincerely looks into himself, through infinite proofs and experiences), to be unlimited and infinite. Unlimited and infinite freedom is the effect of some cause which, being infinite, unlimited and most free as a cause, cannot but exist; a cause that is infinite, free and unlimited among causes in general is the same as God. Atheists, feeling the force of this argument, prefer, with horrible stupidity, to deny in fact their freedom, which they absurdly affirm in name only, and to turn themselves into brute machines, rather than concede it and admit the compelling force of the argument, and acknowledge as the cause of themselves and of all things a powerful, intelligent and most generous freedom, which gives things their origin, order, nature and completion.

units.la: XIV. Iam sequuntur argumenta desumenda ex actiua facultate rationis, quae a&ibus suis ideam seu iconem Dei in se excitat. Et illa quidem in suo genere (hoc est in genere probationum a pictura sive ab ecg typo ad archetypon & originale) sunt quoque optima : quare ea dignitati suæ relinquo & laudo in Cartesio, etsi non præfero præcedentibus. Illorum autem (nam plura prorulit) præstantissimum exstat in Meditatione quinta ; quod etsi non exercitatis Sophisma videri posset, est tamen validum & mirabile, eflque una ex illis notis artificis operi suo impressis, quâ voluit artifex, ne rationis facultas (opus suum) eum concipere nisi ut existentem, sive non posset formare ideam ejus, nisi ut existentis.
units.tr: XIV. Now follow the arguments to be drawn from the active faculty of reason, which by its acts excites within itself an idea or image of God. These, in their own kind (that is, in the kind of proof that goes from a picture or type to the archetype and original), are also the best; so I leave them their dignity and praise them in Descartes, although I do not prefer them to the preceding ones. Of these (for he put forward several), the most outstanding is in the Fifth Meditation. Although it might seem a sophism to the unpractised, it is nevertheless sound and admirable, and is one of those marks of the craftsman impressed on his work, by which the craftsman wished that the faculty of reason, his work, could conceive him only as existing, or could not form an idea of him except as existing.

units.la: Cæterum, in argumento tertiæ Meditationis, circa finem, assumit Cartesius aliquid nec ad conclusionem necessarium, & vero in se falsum. Illud est doctrina de confervatione physica creationis instar influente singulis momentis ad creaturæ exiftentiam, eo quod momenta, inquit, a se invicem non pendeant. Ubi equidem a Cartesio, multisque etiam aliis, confunduntur ea quæ natura sunt, cum eis quæ sunt gratiæ. Quæ gratiæ sunt, quia sunt vel lumen amorque Dei, sive Deus ipse, vel immediati effluxus Dei, ab ipso solo immediate promanantes; ea sane non possunt absolute dari creaturæ sic ut sint partes naturæ ejus, ab ea individuæ; & quia Deus ea tantum largiri voluit homini non ut ejus naturam constituerent, sed ut illius effent, homine consentiente, perfectio, beatitudo, complementum; patet hinc, cur in ejusmodi donorum gratuitorum positione, unum eorum momentum in creatura positum & existens, ab alio non pendeat ; sed debeant continuè à Deo promanare singula momenta , secundum, tertium, quartum, & sequentia omnia in infinitum, perinde omnino atque primum momentum, nulla prorsus cum differentia; quemadmodum lux ex sole in corpora opaca continuè sic procedit effluxu & concursu per omnia momenta æquali & continuo ; ita ut si vel per momentum Sol cessaret influere , vel corpora opaca se illi obvertere desinerent, cessaret & ilico in hisce lumen: ita quoque si vel per momentum intermitteret Deus se suaque gratiosa homini offerre ; vel homo se ab illis sponte averteret, cessarent etiam in eo dona ejusmodi gratuita: quæ proinde conservatione & repositione continua opus habent uti perdurent. At de eis quæ meræ naturæ sunt, aliter longe se res habet. Natura , creaturæ subsistantia ejusque facultates et actus, quia absolute a Deo donata sunt creaturæ, ut essentiam ejus naturamque constituerent, cujus sunt essentiales partes , vel potius ipsamet ; sequitur, hæc non ita tolli posse, vel non ita in nihilum aut in evanescentiam tendere, ut singuli momentis habeant opus repositione & quasi creatione continua, uti Cartesius male affirmat: non quod statuendum sit, creaturam si solam ejusve facultates & actus species, unum momentum eorum existentiæ inferre sequentia independenter a Deo; sed quod pendeat a natura sive perfectione Dei dantis aliquid absolute pro natura rei, & tanquam partem essentialem & naturalem creaturæ, ut illud semel datum & positum subsistat vi hujus unius Dei voluntatis & actus absoluti, neque adeo tendat in non ens, nec egeat, qua tale, reproductione continua: quod satis per se evidens est in naturis rerum illarum unde omne donum gratiæ abest, veluti in mentibus dæmonum aut damnatorum hominum, quarum facultates, cogitata, actusque miseros & horrendos quis dicet continuè a Deo reproduci? At in rebus ubi cum meris naturalibus intermiscentur & nonnulla quæ ex gratia vel ex gratiosis donis sunt, eatenus continua Dei positione & influxu singulis momentis opus habent, quatenus de gratia Dei et quæ illam spectant donis, participant. Et quia in idea Dei, maxime quando animus inde afficitur, aliquid è divino lumine refulgens intervenit, hic potest habere locum causa conservans & influens singulis momentis, non autem, ut dictum, respectu naturæ durantis ipsius animæ, quæ ex vi primi Dei actus semper duratura est. Hic Cartesii schola-rumque error ex ignoratione aut negleCtu distinctionis modo dictæ quantorum deinde aliorum absurdorum faufa fuerit, hujus loci non est enumerare: rem ipsam de concursu alibi (a) pluribus explicui.
units.tr: Moreover, in the argument of the Third Meditation, near the end, Descartes assumes something that is neither necessary to the conclusion and is in itself false. It is the doctrine that the physical conservation of creation is like a continual influx into the existence of the creature at every moment, because, he says, the moments do not depend on one another. Here Descartes, and many others too, confuse things that belong to nature with those that belong to grace. Those that belong to grace, since they are either the light and love of God, or God himself, or immediate outflows of God proceeding immediately from him alone, certainly cannot be given absolutely to a creature so as to be parts of its nature, inseparable from it. Since God willed to bestow these gifts on man not to constitute his nature but to be his perfection, blessedness and completion, with man consenting, it is plain why, in the case of such gratuitous gifts, one moment of them, placed and existing in the creature, does not depend on another; rather, each moment, the second, third, fourth and all following to infinity, must continually flow from God, just as the first does, with no difference whatever. So light proceeds continually from the sun into opaque bodies, by outflow and concurrence, equally and continuously through all moments; so that if the sun ceased to flow in for a moment, or opaque bodies ceased to turn towards it, the light would at once cease in them. Likewise, if God were for a moment to cease offering himself and his grace to man, or if man were of his own accord to turn away from them, such gratuitous gifts would cease in him too; they therefore need continual conservation and renewed positing in order to endure. But with things that are purely natural the case is quite different. The subsistence of the creature, and its faculties and acts, since they are given absolutely by God to the creature so as to constitute its essence and nature, of which they are the essential parts, or rather are itself, cannot be removed in this way, nor tend into nothing or vanish, so that at each moment they need renewed positing and, as it were, continual creation, as Descartes wrongly affirms. This is not to say that the creature, if its faculties and acts alone were considered, would bring the following moments into existence independently of God; rather, it depends on the nature or perfection of God, who gives something absolutely as the nature of a thing and as an essential and natural part of the creature, so that once given and placed it subsists by the power of this one will and absolute act of God, and so does not tend towards non-being nor, as such, need continual reproduction. This is sufficiently self-evident in those natures of things from which every gift of grace is absent, such as the minds of demons or of damned men: who would say that their faculties, thoughts, and wretched and horrible acts are continually reproduced by God? But in things where purely natural elements are mingled with some that come from grace or from gracious gifts, these need continual positing and influx from God at every moment, insofar as they share in the grace of God and in the gifts that pertain to it. And since in the idea of God, especially when the mind is moved by it, something shining from the divine light intervenes, here there can be a cause that conserves and flows in at every moment; but not, as has been said, with respect to the nature of the soul that endures, which by the force of God's first act is always to endure. The error of Descartes and of the schoolmen here arose from ignorance or neglect of the distinction just described, and from the false consequences that followed from it, together with other absurdities. It is not the place here to enumerate these; I have explained the matter of concurrence at greater length elsewhere.

units.la: XV. Quid in quarta Meditatione Cartesiana desideretur, (b) superius abunde commemoravimus, & de ingenti monumus hiatu hic a Cartesio suisque relicto, qui non impletus, præcipitii loco currentibus
units.tr: XV. What is lacking in the Cartesian Fourth Meditation we have already noted above at length, and we have warned that Descartes and his followers left a huge gap here, which, not being filled, serves as a precipice for those who run along it.

units.la: (b) Supr. part. I. §. 50. fit. Alibi (a) etiam ejus errorem hic primo (ingratiam opinionis Janseniftarum ni falsò lor) prolatum, de indifferentia ad essentiam libertatis non spectante, confutavimus; nec non & id (b) quod de inutilitate causæ finalis in naturalibus propositi periculosissimè, etsi forte periculi inscius, nec prævidens Atheos atque Libertinos de ejusmodi sententiis admodum sibi congratulaturos.
units.tr: (b) See above, part I, §. 50. Elsewhere (a) we also refuted his error, first put forward here (perhaps to please the Jansenists, if I am not mistaken), concerning indifference, which does not belong to the essence of liberty. We likewise refuted what he said, most dangerously and perhaps without realising the danger or foreseeing it, about the uselessness of final cause in natural matters. Atheists and Libertines will be very pleased with opinions of this kind.

units.la: XVI. In quinta, postquam initio fateri videtur se vacuum aliquem hiatum relinquere, eumque postea implendum, sibi persuadet rerum materialium essentiam ibi a se explicari, depromendo ex corrupta facultatis ratione, methodo quasi cœcorum palpatoria, ideas aliquot Mathematicas & mechanicas de extensione, motu, figuris & similibus, quibus deinde conabitur aliis in locis totum physices Systema eodem modo superstruere ac cæci, qui palpationi suæ omnia inædificarent, rejicerent vero quæ per eam non perciperentur; qua de causa etiam rejecit Cartelius omnem vim motumque in corporibus præter localem, eumque impulsionis. Et revera non mirandum est intellectum nostrum nunc adeo perversum & depravatum, nil (pro statu in quo est) præter istiusmodi crassamenta concipere, palpare & statuere. Incidit (quod absque injuria profiteor dici) comparatio intellectus nostri post lapsum ægri & stupidi, causas tamen rerum concipere volentis, cum asino animali, a quo si quæreretur, quomodo posset aliquis ad agilitatem & diligentiam provocari, respondere id impulsivo motu & fustium impactione fieri : seenim id clare & distincte concipere, & praeterea nihil : nempe illum lateret vis illa ignea & animosa quae intus refider, quaeque ex principio intimo agiliores producit dispositiones. Stupiditatem ergo naturae corruptae folam nimisque confiderat Cartefius, & praeterea ad divinas proprietates non fatis attendit, nec ad illas ut ad exemplaria rerum creatarum respicit, ob quos multosque alios defectus, ubi ad rem ventum erit, deprehendetur immensum a vera & primaeva rerum natura aberraffe, & ex principiis Mathefeos atque mechanices totam vitiaffe physicam, quae dignior est quam ut ex brutis istis principiis oriatur & constet : quae alibi, (a) & in sequentibus (b) ostensa fufius, hic nos diutius non morabuntur. Occurrit tamen hic egregia de Deo existente demonstratio modo dicta ex eo quod in idea Dei five in conceptu ejus, existentia necessaria repraesentative involvatur : Sed fi conceptus noster passivus bene dispositus effet, quoniam tunc ipsemet Deus exsistens necessario illum impleret, & realiter in illo involveretur, quanto, quaeso, praestantius Cartefiano id effet Dei existentis argumentum quod cuivis periculum facere volenti experiri licet.
units.tr: XVI. In the Fifth Meditation, after first seeming to admit that he leaves some empty gap, and that this is to be filled later, he persuades himself that the essence of material things is explained there by him. He draws from a corrupted faculty of reason, by a method like the groping of the blind, a few mathematical and mechanical ideas about extension, motion, figures and the like. On these he then tries to build the whole system of physics in the same way as the blind, who would build everything on their groping and reject whatever is not perceived by it. For this reason Descartes also rejected every force and motion in bodies except local motion, and that only as impulsion. And indeed it is no wonder that our intellect, now so perverted and depraved, can, in the condition it is in, conceive, grope at and establish nothing beyond such coarse matter. (I say this without offence.) There arises a comparison between our intellect after the Fall, sick and stupid yet wishing to grasp the causes of things, and a donkey. If someone asked the donkey how one might be stirred to agility and diligence, it would answer that this is done by a push and by blows of a stick, for it conceives this clearly and distinctly and nothing more. It would be hidden from the donkey that there is that fiery and spirited power within, which from an inner principle produces more active dispositions. Therefore Descartes considered only the stupidity of corrupted nature, and considered it too much, and he does not pay enough attention to the divine perfections, nor does he look to them as the exemplars of created things. Because of these and many other defects, which will be shown when we come to the matter, it will be found that he has strayed immensely from the true and primal nature of things, and has spoiled all of physics by the principles of mathematics and mechanics. Physics is too worthy to arise from and rest upon those brutish principles. These things have been shown more fully elsewhere and in what follows, and here they will not detain us longer. Yet there occurs here the excellent demonstration of the existence of God mentioned just above, from the fact that necessary existence is involved representatively in the idea of God, or in the concept of him. But if our passive concept were well disposed, since then the existing God himself would necessarily fill it, and would really be involved in it, how much, I ask, would that argument for the existence of God be more excellent than the Cartesian one, which anyone who wishes may try out for himself. which anyone who wishes may try out for himself.

Ridiculum est doctos sibi imaginari omnem invictam certitudinem ratione sua activa debere niti: cum vis Dei statuentis ut passivae facultates suis objectis appulsae certitudine summa de existentia objectorum securae effent, mille ratiocinationum plaustris antecellat. Addit deinde ibidem Cartesius nonnullas difficultates circa incertitudinem, obscuritatem & deceptionem sensuum tam externorum, quam internorum, quas ubi fuius & operose admodum conatus est cum bonitate Dei conciliare, ut inde non sequatur Deum, naturae auctorem, esse fallacem, revera tamen non conciliat (ut alicubi (c) Coftendi-) imo concludit, naturam (Dei o pus) ut ex corpore & mente compositam, non posse non aliquando esse fallacem, & §. 5. erroribus obnoxiam & infirmam: quod sane Auctore Deo summe bono & verace indignissimum opus esset. Miror Cartesium se non sensisse hinc veluti impulsum atque coactum ad fatendum, neminem posse recte philosophari, nec occurrentium difficultatum nodos solvere, nisi redeat ad agnitionem tum corruptionis nostrae, naturaeque per nos, tum justitiae castigantis Dei, optime hujusmodi difficilibus phaenomenis satisfacientis. Nec minus miror, quod, ubi in sua tiam provocari, responderet id impulsivo motu & fustium impactione fieri: seenim id clare & distincte concipere, & praeterea nihil: nempe illum lateret vis illa ignea & animosa quae intus resider, quaeque ex principio intimo agiliores producit dispositiones. Stupiditatem ergo naturae corruptae solam nimisque considerat Cartesius, & praeterea ad divinas proprietates non satis attendit, nec ad illas ut ad exemplaria rerum creatarum respicit, ob quos multosque alios defectus, ubi ad rem ventum erit, deprehendetur immensum a vera & primaeva rerum natura aberrasse, & ex principiis Mathesios atque mechanices totam vitiasse physicam, quae dignior est quam ut ex brutis istis principiis oriatur & constet: quae alibi, (a) & in sequentibus (b) ostensa fuisus, hic nos diutius non morabuntur. Occurrit tamen hic egregia de Deo exsistente demonstratio modo dicta ex eo quod in idea Dei sive in conceptu ejus, existentia necessaria repraesentative involvatur: Sed si conceptus nolter passivus bene dispositus esset, quoniam tunc ipsemet Deus exsistens necessario illum impleret , & realiter in illo involveretur, quanto, quæso , præstantius Cartesiano id esset Dei existentii argumentum quod cuivis periculum facere volenti experiri licet.

Obviously he does not perceive that fiery and spirited power which lies within, and which from its inner principle produces more active dispositions. Descartes therefore considers only the stupidity of corrupt nature, and too much so, and he pays too little attention to the divine properties, nor does he look to them as to the exemplars of created things. On account of these and many other defects, which will be detected when we come to the matter, he has strayed immensely from the true and original nature of things, and has vitiated the whole of physics by the principles of mathematics and mechanics. Physics is too worthy to arise and stand on such brute principles. These matters have been shown elsewhere (a) and in what follows (b), and they will not detain us longer here. Yet there occurs here that excellent demonstration of the existence of God, mentioned just above, from the fact that necessary existence is involved representatively in the idea or concept of God. But if our passive concept were well disposed, then the existing God himself would necessarily fulfil it, and would be really involved in it. How much more excellent, I ask, would this be as an argument for the existence of God, than the Cartesian one, which anyone willing may test by experiment.
