Nec minus miror, quod, ubi in sua
units.tr: XVII. In the sixth and final Meditation, where he explains quite well the unextended mind, the nature of imagination, and the use of the senses, he makes a rather useless attempt to prove, from the senses aided by reasoning, that bodies exist, that each person has a body of his own, and that waking must be distinguished from sleep. We have already touched on the fact that the intervention of reasoning here is useless and harmful, and it will be shown at greater length below. It is ridiculous for learned men to imagine that all unshakeable certainty must rest on their own active reasoning, when the power of God, who established that our passive faculties, when struck by their objects, should be secure with the highest certainty about the existence of those objects, surpasses a thousand wagonloads of arguments. Descartes then adds, in the same place, some difficulties about the uncertainty, obscurity and deception of the senses, both external and internal. He tries very laboriously and at length to reconcile these with the goodness of God, so that it does not follow that God, the author of nature, is deceitful. In truth he does not reconcile them (as I have shown elsewhere (c)). Indeed he concludes that nature, as God's work, composed of body and mind, cannot help being sometimes deceptive, and liable to error and weak, which would indeed be a work most unworthy of God, who is supremely good and true. I am surprised that Descartes did not feel himself impelled and compelled by this to admit that no one can philosophize rightly or solve the knots of the difficulties that arise, unless he returns to the recognition both of our corruption and of the corruption of nature through us, and of the justice of a chastising God, which satisfies such difficult phenomena very well. Nor am I any less surprised that, when he was pressed in his

units.la: (c) Conf. Rat. lib. III. cap. 20. §. 3. sua demonstratione de corporum exiſtentia, meminit facultatum quarundam paſſivarum ſentiendi vel ideas recipiendi; nec non & aliarum aſtivarum facultatum ideas producendi vel efficiendi, non subiit ejus mentem cogitatio de distinͤtionis ejus summa utilitate & neceßitate, ſi prius eam ad facultates ſuperiores, quæ Deum reſpiciunt, & ad ration- nem nostram, retulisset & applicuisset.
units.tr: (c) Conf. Rat. lib. III. cap. 20. §. 3. In his demonstration of the existence of bodies, he mentions certain passive faculties of sensing, or of receiving ideas, and also other active faculties of producing or effecting ideas. It did not occur to his mind how very useful and necessary this distinction is, if he had first referred and applied it to the higher faculties, which regard God, and to our reason.

units.la: X. VIII. Ex his omnibus crediderim abunde conflare, quantum vel maxima ingenia a veritate aberrent, quando nonnullis Methodi cujufdam minus præcipuis regulis confisi, a sex illis neceßariis & præcipuis, quæ a nobis commendatæ sunt, aut a quibusdam illarum recedunt. Fuisse enim Cartefium seculi sui maximum ingenium: Meditationes autem ejus, omnium, quæ reliquit, operum, elaboratiffimum, ipsique præ cæteris charißimum, nemo est, opinor, qui ignoret. Sed multo plura tristiorum erratorum exempla ex discipulis ejus nonnullis desumi possent, qui nec eum æquarunt ingenio, nec eadem, qua ipse, fuerunt modestia, ut divino lumini revelationique rationem ejusque claram distinctamque perceptionem postponendam esse agnoscerent; & vero qui errores ejus assumptos eo extremitatis urferunt, ex iisque novos ac tantos eduxerunt, ut nil sacrum jam sit quod non ab aliquo fuerit violatum, & quod impositum tutum sit ab impotentissimæ rationis corruptæ temeraria invasione & nefanda violatione, ubi fræna sibi semel laxaverit.
units.tr: X. VIII. From all of this, I think it is abundantly clear how far even the greatest minds stray from the truth when, trusting in some of the less important rules of a certain method, they depart from some of those six necessary and principal rules that we have recommended. For Descartes was, I suppose, the greatest mind of his age, and no one, I think, is ignorant that his Meditations are the most elaborate of all the works he left and his own favourite above the rest. But many more sad examples of error could be drawn from some of his disciples, who neither matched him in ability nor showed the same modesty, so that they would acknowledge that reason, and its clear and distinct perception, must be placed beneath the divine light and revelation. Indeed, they pushed his assumed errors to such an extreme, and drew from them new and such great ones, that nothing is any longer sacred that has not been violated by someone, and nothing imposed is safe from the rash invasion and wicked violation of a most powerful but corrupt reason, once it has given itself free rein.

units.la: XIX. Hinc alii, ut Spinoza cum suis, ex errore negatæ prius libertatis indifferentiæ, & ex solius rationis corruptæ, expulsi divino lumine, consultatione, in merum tandem Atheismum devenerunt, maluerunt quæ a stolido suo fato pendere, quam a causa intelligente, optima, liberrima, cujus libertatem ipsi conantur extinguere argutiolis vix relatione dignis, qualis est v. g. Ex nihilo nil fieri: & cum Deus dicatur ens necessarium, necessarium autem sit non liberum sive nil libertatis, ex eo nihilo libertatis, libertatem fieri non posse; proinde omnia esse fatalia. Sed ne falsum axioma tangam; negamus Deum (Ens cui nulla deest perfectio, adeoque nec libertas) ita esse necessarium, ut simul non sit liber atque indifferens, non quidem respectu naturæ suæ negandæ aut destruendæ, (quod absurdum esset) sed regendæ, idque tum ergo se, contemplando in se infinitis modis divinarum suarum perfectionum combinationes varias, & inter se veluti lusus & triumphos, in quibus ad lubitum agit & ex indifferentia illas diversimode ordinat, ut fusius & clarius alibi (a) explicui; tum ad illas repræsentandas excitando in conceptu arbitrario ideas rerum, quales voluit; tum denique produ-cendo extra se eﬀectypa earum, nempe creaturas, ad quod etiam erat indifferentissimus; unde poterat ipsas statuere vel mere brutas, quarum omnia determinata & determinate prævisa fuissent; vel liberas, quibus donaret facultatem regendi se singulas ad placitum suum, sic ut ipsemet de earum actibus futuris nil vellet prævidere, quippe cui sola fui ipsius idea & cognitio perfectissima ad omniscientiam suam sufficit, & cui indifferens fuit res ideasque nullas vel alias in se excitare vel non excitare, nosse vel non nosse, producere aut secus, producere non liberas aut liberas: quas ultimi generis postquam creare visum est, illæ jam regiminis sui, eisdonati, compotes, justi & injusti, boni & mali fiunt capaces, prout suum regimen cum divino allimilant, aut ab eo desciscunt. Et sane miror ullum virum honestum hanc libertatem, qua creatura indeterminata ab alia quacunque re a se ipsa solum determinetur, audere negare: namque si libertas non est indifferens relicta, sed aliunde quam a se determinatur, deletur hoc ipso omne jus divinum & humanum, omnis notitia, principiumque justi & injusti, laudis & culpæ, virtutis & criminis, pietatis, honestatis etiam, & bonorum morum; quicquid enim agas, parricida fis, scorteris, mentiaris, rebellem & perfidum te geras, sceleraque omnia & flagitia perpetres, non ipse jam agis, sed pateris a causa summa in mente impressionem, influxum & motum, quibus resistere nulli creaturæ est possibile: quæ quidem horribilia prorsus sunt; & diabolica atque blasphematoria in Deum & naturam Libertinismi principia. Quibus, ad omnia brutalizanda (ut sic loquar) accedit & hæc pestis, præcnobilis illius causæ finalis (adorandæ Sapientiæ Dei) in rerum naturæ constitutione negatio ex Cartesii imprudentia, ab atheis ulnis utrisque excepta, qua adeo stolidi sunt, ut cum Spinosa nugentur, oculos v. g. non esse ideo factos ut homo videret & se regeret, neque dentes ut comederet, neque ulla alia ad aliquem finem; sed cum homines invenirent, se veluti casu aut fato habere oculos, dentes, caeteraque membra, hinc cogitasse eos se posse illis uti ad videndum, ad manducandum, ambulandum, generandum, & similia plus quam incredibiliter omne stultitiae genus exsuperantia, multoque magis quam si quis dicat ac contendat de libro aliquo egregio, eum non esse ex industria & scopo aliquo agentis ita factum; sed fortuito casu & sine intentione typos fuisse conjectos in tabulam, atque inde librum talem emersisse: etenim vel in solo corpore humano plus millies industriae artisque quam in totius mundi excellentissimis & ordinatissimis libris reperire est. Alii qui non eo impietatis labuntur, & vero videri volunt multum Deo tribuere, omnem (quod eo fere redit) creaturarum activitatem negant; tum gesticulationes proprii intellectus activi pro commercio & colloquiis cum Sapientia Dei sumunt, & ipsas etiam rerum extensarum apparentias pro visione substantiae Dei, similiaque inauditae hactenus absurditatis. Alii e contra, Spiritus Dei internam operationem in salutari hominis negotio prorsum eunt inficias. Nonnulli Scripturas & omnia divina ex humanae rationis activitate exponi debere statuunt, aut si quid insuper ad earum exigant interpretationem, id tamen volunt a ratione sua misera totum examinari, dirigi atque disponi.
units.tr: XIX. Hence others, like Spinoza and his followers, from the error of first denying liberty of indifference, and from corrupt reason alone, having driven out the divine light through consultation, at last fell into pure atheism. They preferred to have things depend on a blind fate rather than on an intelligent, most good and most free cause, whose freedom they try to extinguish with little quibbles scarcely worth mentioning, such as: "Nothing comes from nothing." And since God is said to be a necessary being, and what is necessary is not free, or has no freedom, they conclude that from nothing, no freedom can arise; therefore all things are fated. But, to avoid touching a false axiom, we deny that God (a Being lacking no perfection, and so not lacking freedom) is so necessary that he is not at the same time free and indifferent. This holds not indeed with respect to his nature, which cannot be denied or destroyed (that would be absurd), but with respect to its governing. He does this in three ways: first, by contemplating within himself, in infinite ways, the various combinations of his divine perfections, and as it were their play and triumphs among one another, in which he acts at will and, from indifference, arranges them in different ways, as I have explained more fully and clearly elsewhere (a); second, by exciting in his arbitrary conception ideas of things, of what kind he wished, in order to represent them; and finally, by producing outside himself their effects, namely creatures, to which he was also perfectly indifferent. Hence he could establish them either as merely brute beings, all of whose actions would have been determined and determinately foreseen, or as free beings, to whom he would grant the faculty of governing themselves individually at their own pleasure, so that he himself would not wish to foresee their future acts, since for his omniscience his own idea and most perfect knowledge alone is sufficient, and since it was indifferent to him whether he excited in himself this or that thing and these or those ideas or none, to know or not to know, to produce or not, to produce unfree or free beings. When he had decided to create beings of the latter kind, these, having been given a share in his governing, become capable of being just and unjust, good and evil, according as they align their governing with the divine, or depart from it. And indeed I am amazed that any honest man dares to deny this liberty, by which an indeterminate creature is determined by itself alone and by no other thing. For if liberty is not left to indifference, but is determined from elsewhere than by itself, then by this very fact all divine and human right is destroyed, and every notion and principle of just and unjust, of praise and blame, of virtue and crime, of piety, of honesty too, and of good morals. For whatever you do, whether you become a parricide, commit fornication, lie, behave as a rebel and traitor, or perpetrate all kinds of crimes and disgraces, you are not acting yourself, but you suffer an impression, influence and motion in your mind from the supreme cause, which no creature can possibly resist. These are indeed utterly horrible, and diabolical and blasphemous principles of libertinism against God and nature. To these, for brutalizing everything (so to speak), is added this plague, the denial, arising from Descartes' imprudence, of that most noble final cause in the constitution of nature (the adorable Wisdom of God), a denial embraced with both atheist arms. They are so foolish that they babble with Spinoza that, for example, eyes were not made so that a man might see and direct himself, nor teeth so that he might eat, nor any other part for any purpose. Rather, when men found that they had eyes, teeth and other limbs as if by chance or fate, they then thought they could use them for seeing, for chewing, for walking, for generating and the like, surpassing every kind of folly more than incredibly, and far more than if someone were to say and maintain of some excellent book that it was not made deliberately and with some aim by its author, but that by chance and without intention letters were thrown together on a tablet and such a book emerged from them. Indeed, in the human body alone more skill and art can be found a thousand times over than in the most excellent and orderly books of the whole world. Others, who do not fall into such impiety, and indeed wish to seem to ascribe much to God, deny (which comes to nearly the same thing) all activity of creatures. Then they take the gesticulations of their own active intellect for intercourse and conversation with the Wisdom of God, and even take the very appearances of extended things for the vision of the substance of God, and similar absurdities hitherto unheard of. Others, on the contrary, utterly deny the inner operation of the Spirit of God in the work of salvation of man. Some hold that the Scriptures and all divine things must be explained from the activity of human reason, or if they require anything further for their interpretation, they still want all of it to be examined, directed and arranged by their own wretched reason.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: XX. Cujus quidem methodi quinam praeterea fructus in posterum sint exspectandi, patet e specimine decantati ab aliquo tempore libri belgici de fascinato mundo, daemonum inter homines praesentiam atque operationes negantis, cujus fundamentum unicum est Ratio humana; quam dicit a Scriptura supponi, & per eam Scripturas tum inter se conferri, tum adhibitis linguarum & critices adminiculis inde esse interpretandas, methodo sane quam longissime diversa ab ea, quam inculcat ipsa Scriptura; in qua quippe supponitur quidem ratio humana, at ut corruptissima, ut coecissima, ut ad res divinas ineptissima, quaeque idcirco abneganda sit & crucifigenda, cum literali sua sapientia, quo solus invocetur in auxilium Spiritus Dei, qui oculos aperiens detegat sensum Dei, omni sagacitati humanae rationis occultum & inaccessum. Quibus tamen omissis, misera & aegra ratio, libri didi & confarcinatrix, audaci & temeraria sui phalerarumque suarum confidentia plena, tam stupendas & pudendas illic propalavit artis suae absurdae operationes, ut si illustre aliquod exemplum intellectus histrionici cum naturalibus, divinis, humanisque incredibili lascivia ludentis, & histrionicae suae calliditatis atque activitatis ultimos conatus re & stylo exhibentis proferendum effet, nullum posset produci insignius. Et hoc quidem caeteris hominum intellectibus hiftrionicis & activis non poterit quoque non summopere arridere, ob convenientiam inter se mutuam insanae disposition is, quemadmodum videmus comoedias quo magis temeraria, absurda & ridicula continent, eo magis versatili cerebrorum indoli sapere: quod profecto contagium eorum etiam mentibus, qui solidiori veritate & methodo imbuti & exercitati non sunt, posiit non parvum detrimentum inferre, nisi si qui se in regulis verae Methodi inveniendae veritatis solidae aliquandiu exercuerint, & in efflagitando divinae gratiae lumine haud segniter se gesserint: hisce namque ne minimum quidem facessent negotium noxia istiusmodi imaginata. Quae quidem huic uni originis atque basi suum esse suumque robur acceptum ferre debent, quod intellectus histrio activitate sua aegra & caeca capere non posfit Spiritus agere in corpora; proinde nec hoc affirmandum, & vero Scripturae omnia loca eo a corruptae rationis callida inductria & ludificatione esse trahenda & interpretanda, ne hoc affirmare videantur; hominum autem, etiam sanctissimorum & eruditissimorum quorumvis temporum, locorum, conditionum, sensus, experimenta & testimonia, sine pudore sic flocci facienda, ut praenovissimo uno nudius tertius nato intellectulo, cum Spinoza & Hobbesio ternionem hac in sententia constituente omnes pro fascinatis vel a libri titulo proclamari debeant.
units.tr: XX. What further fruit this method may be expected to bear in time to come is clear from a specimen: the Dutch book, much talked of for some time, entitled The Bewitched World, which denies the presence and operations of demons among men. Its only foundation is human reason, which it says is presupposed by Scripture, and by which the Scriptures are then compared with one another and interpreted with the aid of languages and criticism. This method is utterly different from the one Scripture itself urges. Scripture does presuppose human reason, but as most corrupt, most blind, and most unfit for divine things, and therefore to be denied and crucified along with its literal wisdom. Only then is the Spirit of God to be called upon for help, to open the eyes and reveal the sense of God, which is hidden from and inaccessible to all the cleverness of human reason. Yet, leaving these things aside, a wretched and sick reason, a bookish patcher-together, full of bold and reckless confidence in itself and its embellishments, has displayed in that book such astonishing and shameful products of its absurd art that, if one were to bring forward a notable example of a histrionic intellect playing with natural, divine and human things with incredible wantonness, and displaying in matter and style the last efforts of its theatrical cleverness and activity, none more striking could be produced. Such an intellect cannot fail to please other histrionic and busy minds, since they agree with it in their mad arrangement. We see that comedies which contain more that is rash, absurd and ridiculous please the fickle disposition of brains all the more. This contagion can certainly do no small harm even to minds not steeped and trained in the more solid truth and method, unless they have for some time practised the rules of the true method of finding solid truth, and have not been slack in begging for the light of divine grace. For such people these harmful fancies will cause not the least trouble. They owe their existence and strength to this one origin and basis: the sick and blind activity of the histrionic intellect cannot grasp that the Spirit acts upon bodies. Therefore this must not be affirmed, and all the passages of Scripture must not be dragged and interpreted by the crafty industry and mockery of corrupt reason, lest they seem to affirm it. But the senses, experiences and testimonies of men, even the most holy and learned of any time, place or condition, are to be valued so shamelessly cheap that, with the one newly born little intellect of the day before yesterday, which with Spinoza and Hobbes constitutes a triad in this opinion, everyone must be proclaimed bewitched, or be named so by the title of the book.

units.la: XXI. Equidem fi quis juxta regulas Methodi inveniendi verum supra allatas recuset se regere, sibique pertinaciter fraudem facere velit, huic pro morbi sui indole, nil posse consuli, aut consulendum optari, sartis clarum dedimus. At quotquot leges divinas, intellectum passivum illustrante, scripturarum sensa detegente, Sanctorumque confirmante testimonia, adjutæ, facillime veritatum solidiorum principia percipient, per quæ nullis errorum nebulis ullus superfit locus. Agnoscent præprimis, nedum Spiritus in corpora agere nequeant, ipsa corpora nec esse, nec agere in se posse nisi per Spiritus, Spiritus namque est (quippe Deus) qui primùm dedit corporibus & esse, & motum, atque hunc quidem ita, ut conceipi non possit, qui corpus moveat corpus, sive qui motus ex uno corpore in aliud transeat, nili concipiatur vis omnino spiritualis, certâ quadam conatus mensurâ sese veluti in materiam diffundens, inque ejus partes, modo in has, modo in illas successive agens. Et quamvis ex occasione situs corporum diversimode ea determinetur, ipsa tamen quâ agens in corpora & in se spiritualis est, & spirituali prorsus origine oriunda.
units.tr: XXI. Indeed, if anyone refuses to be governed by the rules of the method of finding truth set out above, and wishes to cheat himself stubbornly, we have clearly shown that, given the nature of his disease, nothing can be done for him, or that it is not to be hoped that anything can be done. But all who, aided by the divine laws, which illumine the passive intellect, reveal the senses of the Scriptures and confirm them by the testimony of the saints, will most easily perceive the principles of the more solid truths, through which no room remains for any clouds of error. Above all they will recognise that not only can the Spirit not act upon bodies, but that bodies themselves neither exist nor can act upon themselves except through the Spirit. For the Spirit (being God) is what first gave bodies both their being and their motion. And it is such that one cannot conceive how one body moves another body, or how motion passes from one body into another, unless a wholly spiritual force is conceived, diffusing itself as it were into matter by a certain measure of effort, and acting successively now on these parts, now on those. And although this force is determined in various ways by the occasion of the situation of bodies, nevertheless the very force by which the spiritual agent acts upon bodies and upon itself is spiritual and arises from a wholly spiritual origin.

units.la: Concipient & facile quivis bene dispositi, mentes sive Spiritus esse Dei progeniem, ejusdemque (quicquid obmurmuret cœca ratio) cum Deo naturæ, imaginem Dei vivam proinde gestare, non modo quod eorum intellectus & voluntas lumine, amore & beatitate Dei fuerint ornati ; sed quod eorum desiderium , ad instar desiderii Dei, prototypi & originis suæ , efficax. hoc est, agens & potens fuerit, virtute a Deo (imaginem sui habere volente) semel impressa, nec unquam peritura : ita ut quemadmodum Deus per desiderium suum scit , facit & movet quæ vult ; sic Spiritus creati per desideria sua sciant, agant & moveant quæcunque volunt, puta sciant cogitata sua aliis manifestare , aliorum rescire, corporalia nosse, movere & determinare; hac tamen lege , ut si velint cognitionem suam esse vividam , facilem, certam, beantem, actus item motusque suos ordinatos , decoros, bonos, salutares, non debeant se a Deo separare ; secus si fecerint, scientia sua quam hactenus de præteritis habuerint, sterilis & mortua evasura sit , de futuris incerta & erronea ; actus item & motus sui inordinati , angentes , destructivi : hoc est , nil poterunt illi nisi in tenebris, morte, erroribus , realitatum & perfectionum destructione & privatione ; quæ sane miseranda est scienti & agendi potentia, a potentia Dei longe diversissima.
units.tr: All who are well disposed will also readily conceive that minds, or spirits, are the offspring of God, and that, whatever the blind reason may mutter, they have a nature akin to God and therefore carry a living image of God. This is not only because their intellect and will are adorned with the light, love and blessedness of God, but because their desire, like the desire of God, their prototype and origin, is effective, that is, active and powerful, by a power once impressed by God, who willed to have an image of himself, and never to perish. So just as God by his desire knows, makes and moves what he wills, so created spirits by their desires may know, act and move whatever they will. That is, they may make their thoughts known to others, learn the thoughts of others, know, move and determine bodily things. Yet on this condition: if they wish their knowledge to be lively, easy, certain and blessed, and their actions and motions to be orderly, becoming, good and wholesome, they must not separate themselves from God. If they do otherwise, the knowledge they have so far had of past things will turn out barren and dead, and their knowledge of future things uncertain and erroneous; likewise their actions and motions will be disordered, distressing and destructive. That is, they will be able to do nothing but in darkness, death and error, in the destruction and privation of realities and perfections. Such a power of knowing and acting is surely pitiable, and wholly different from the power of God.

units.la: Animadvertent & hoc atque sequentia: Deo ut repræsentaret in spiritibus vim quam pollet movendi corpora, perinde fuisse, utrum eis daret corpus aliquod speciale & proprium , quo mediante in corpora alia agerent , an vero statuerit eos solis suis desideriis in materiam acturos eamque directuros; nec enim ipsi alterum est altero difficilius ; & utrovis modo fiat, spiritus femper in corpora acturi sunt. Atque id priori modo factum esse cum spiritu humano, cui corpus certum sit adjunctum, patet experientia : adeoque idem eodem vel altero modo cum Angelicis spiritibus fieri, nil ex parte rei prohibet, si quidem mentes humanæ atque angelicæ ejusdem sint essentiæ atque naturæ, proindeque earundem affectionum & operationum capaces. Nec dicas, mentes humanas ad corpora esse factas, non item Angelicas. Absurdum! Mentesne humanæ pro scopo creationis & constitutionis suæ habent corporibus ut uniantur & in ea agant? Nugæ! Uniri & deliciari cum Deo finis est, ad quem Mentes nostræ sunt factæ: cum corporibus uniri & commercium habere, id ipsis demum accessorium est : proinde, dicere mentes factas esse ad corpora, perinde est ac dicere, mentibus pro dono accessorio esse datum ut cum corporibus commercium haberent: quod cum in essentia Spiritus, qua talis, nihil immutet, id non magis Angelico quam humano repugnat spiritui. Hoc autem factum esse mille testimoniis experientiisque divinis literæ sacræ tradunt.
units.tr: They will also notice this and what follows. For God to give spirits the power of moving bodies, it made no difference whether he gave them some special body of their own, through which they might act upon other bodies, or whether he decided that they should act upon matter and direct it by their desires alone. For neither mode is harder for them than the other, and in either way spirits will always act upon bodies. That the first mode has been carried out with the human spirit, to which a definite body is joined, is shown by experience. Hence nothing in the nature of things prevents the same from being done, in the same or the other way, with angelic spirits, provided that human and angelic minds are of the same essence and nature, and therefore capable of the same affections and operations. Nor may you say that human minds were made for bodies, but not angelic ones. Absurd! Do human minds have as the goal of their creation and constitution that they be united to bodies and act in them? Nonsense! To be united with God and to delight in him is the end for which our minds were made. To be united with bodies and to have dealings with them is something incidental to them. So to say that minds were made for bodies is the same as saying that minds were given the incidental gift of having dealings with bodies. This does not change anything in the essence of spirit as such, and it is no more repugnant to an angelic spirit than to a human one. That this has in fact happened, the holy Scriptures hand down through a thousand testimonies and divine experiences.

units.la: Neque obscurum erit candidis rerum scrutatoribus, divinis præsertim oraculis via debita consideratis, si nonnulli spiritus a Deo defecerint, corpoream materiam, cui regendæ præfuerint, non posse non evadere inordinatam, tenebrosam, corruptam; ita ut in posterum Spiritus isti depravati potentiam suam exercere non possunt nisi in elemento corruptionis, tenebrarum & inordinationis ; cum si Deus ejusmodi chaos tenebrosum & confusum in ordinem & statum primævum velit reponere, idque renovatum aliis mentibus, puta, mentibus humanis, certo cuidam corpori unitis, regendum tradere ; priores spiritus lapsos, & tenebris suis alligatos, in mundum hunc novissime e confusione & tenebris liberatum, potentiam suam exercere non posse, neque etiam hominis desideria (quamdiu Deo adhærebunt) suis inordinatis desideriis afficere. At si homo a Deo deficiat, & proinde propriam mentem, propria desideria, mundumque sibi traditum, tenebris, corruptione & inordinatione afficiat ; tunc spiritus lapsos elementum sibi congruum reperientes, potentissime in eo operaturos omnis generis confusiones & inordinationes, eo pejores quo magis speciem aliquam umbratilem bonitatis præ se ferent.
units.tr: Nor will it be obscure to candid investigators of things, especially if they weigh the divine oracles in the proper way, that if some spirits have fallen away from God, the corporeal matter over which they were set to rule cannot but become disordered, dark and corrupt. So in future these depraved spirits cannot exercise their power except in the element of corruption, darkness and disorder. If God should wish to restore such a dark and confused chaos to order and its original state, and to hand it over, renewed, to be ruled by other minds, namely human minds united to a certain body, then the earlier fallen spirits, bound by their own darkness, cannot exercise their power in this world, lately freed from confusion and darkness, nor affect the desires of man (as long as man clings to God) with their disordered desires. But if man falls away from God, and so affects his own mind, his own desires, and the world entrusted to him, with darkness, corruption and disorder, then the fallen spirits, finding an element suited to them, will work most powerfully in it, producing every kind of confusion and disorder, the worse the more they wear some shadowy semblance of goodness.

units.la: Atque in eo consistit malorum spirituum potentia, ejusque extensionis & limitum ratio in hocce mundi systemate. Hominis mens pura si Deo adhæreat, &, quod inde sequitur, si corporea quibus præest debite & ad Dei placitum regat, nullas potest in ejusmodi mente inordinatas cogitationes excitare tentator spiritus ullus, quocunque etiam desiderii conamine id contendat, nullos item in materia homini subjecta motus utut minimos: ita ut hoc respectu sit prorsus impotens. At si anima deficiat a Deo, maleque se regat cum corporibus quibus præest, tunc accessum ad eam habent spiritus maligni, sic ut cogitationes suas tenebrosas & malignas in ea desideriorum suorum telis imprimere possint; in corpore vero ejus, in imaginatione & affectibus, in sanguine, in spiritibus & vitalibus & animalibus, in materia etiam universi, ei subjecta, quousque hæc extra ordinem Dei sunt delapsa, omnis generis inordinationes & confusiones, idque eo magis, quo magis homo suggestionibus & motibus pravis consentit; ita ut si prorsus consensum voluntatis suæ cum mente rebellium spirituum conformet, libertatemque suam cum jure quod in creaturas reliquum habet homo, tradat eis, hi veluti omnipotentes in natura commovenda & turbanda fiant, nisi Deus hominem atque naturam servare volens, opponat eis benedictionum suarum, in quas nil possunt, effluxus continuos, tum & bonos Angelos, qui eorum potentiæ destruendi perpetuæ, suam confervandi & protegendi homines atque omnes creaturas opponant.
units.tr: And in this consists the power of evil spirits, and the extent and limits of that power within the system of this world. If a pure human mind clings to God and, as follows from this, rightly governs the bodies over which it presides according to God's pleasure, then no tempting spirit, however hard he strives by any effort of desire, can stir up disordered thoughts in such a mind, nor any motions, however slight, in the matter subject to man. In this respect he is wholly powerless. But if the soul falls away from God and governs its bodies badly, then evil spirits gain access to it, so that they can imprint their dark and malignant thoughts on it with the darts of their desires. In its body, in imagination and affections, in blood, in vital and animal spirits, and in the matter of the universe subject to it, so far as these have slipped out of God's order, they produce every kind of disorder and confusion, and all the more so as man consents more to wicked suggestions and motions. If he wholly conforms the consent of his will to the mind of the rebel spirits and hands over to them his freedom, together with the right that man still holds over creatures, they become as it were omnipotent in stirring and disturbing nature. Unless God, wishing to preserve man and nature, opposes to them the continual outflow of his blessings, which they cannot touch, and also sends good angels to oppose their perpetual power of destruction by preserving and protecting men and all creatures.

units.la: Nec minus clarum erit quærentibus debite veritatem, non posse aliter fieri, quin quamvis Deus spirituum malignorum potentiam, & operationes in hominibus & naturam multis vicibus atque periodis per benedictionum suarum effusionem reprimat, si tamen homo libere velit a Deo deficere continuo, creaturisque ei subjectis abuti, maligni spiritus iterum accessum ad eum & sua, potentiamque in ea rursus acquirant: ita ut si accidat omnes homines in universum a rerum æternarum amore & studio tandem sic defecisse, ut res caducas in eorum locum inordinate surrogatas totis affectibus prosequantur, tunc Diabolus cum infeernali sua aula totius mundi princeps & Deus tyrannicus futurus sit, totius inferni mirabilia in mundo cum omni iniquitate & abominatione patefacturus, donec verus Deus idemque verus mundi Servator Iesus Christus, omnes impios e terra sic deleat, ut soli qui ad eum toti convertentur, superstint ultimo: unde subjecto diabolicæ potentiæ sublato, voluntate scilicet hominis a Deo aversa, maligni spiritus nec locum hic nec accessum amplius reperientes, sese hinc præcipites proripiant in baratrum suum, ubi totius universi corruptio cum impiis hominibus a Deo segregabitur, illic potentiam regnumque suum tenebrosum, anxium, infelix, omnis generis actibus, motibus, gesticulationibus æternum exercituri.
units.tr: Nor will it be less clear to those who seek the truth rightly that it cannot happen otherwise. Although God, by pouring out his blessings, many times and in cycles restrains the power of evil spirits and their operations in men and in nature, yet if man freely chooses to fall away from God continually and to abuse the creatures subject to him, the evil spirits again acquire access to him and their power over him. So if it happens that all men in general have at last fallen so far from the love and zeal of eternal things that they pursue with their whole affections the perishable things inordinately set up in their place, then the Devil, with his infernal court, will become prince of the whole world and a tyrannical god. He will reveal in the world all the wonders of hell, with every iniquity and abomination, until the true God, who is also the true Saviour of the world, Jesus Christ, destroys all the impious from the earth, so that only those who have wholly turned to him remain at the last. Then, the subjection to diabolical power being removed, namely man's will being turned away from God, the evil spirits, finding neither place nor access here any more, hurl themselves headlong from here into their pit. There the corruption of the whole universe, together with impious men, will be cut off from God, and there they will exercise their dark, anxious and unhappy power and kingdom eternally, in every kind of act, motion and gesture.

units.la: XXII. Patebunt hæc atque similia evidentissime quibusvis sacras Scripturas viis a Deo præscriptis adeuntibus, quibus & detegetur facile & abominationi erit summopere hæc intellectus histrionici Scripturas Hoc de subjecto enervandi methodus, in dicto libro passim obvia. Scilicet quando clarius Sole non modo loca occurrunt in Codice sacro veritatum suis præjudiciis erroribusque adversantium declarativa, sed & palpabilia facti experimenta narrantur, solet ægra & cæca ratio, in illis quidem palpare vocum cortices, si forte æquivocationis aut cavillationis admittendæ capaces in se vel comparatione quadam absurda cum aliis locis fuerint, aut si nomina appellativæ & generalioris significationis, non autem propriæ & individuæ esse possint, unde statim nullo ad totum locum, ad totam scripturam, ad loquentium dispositiones, ad sinceritatem mentis de claro sensu aliter convictæ, habito respectu, pro subjecto proprie designato aliud substituat & arripiat; in his vero quæ narrationes factorum sunt, sollicite animadvertit, utrum inter narrandum non interseratur aliquid utut accessorium, quod rigide ad literam non fit interpretandum, sed vel improprie, aut etiam modo de quo nondum clare constet; unde totam rei narratæ substantiam & existentiam propriam audacter inficietur; quemadmodum si ex eo quod in Symbolo Apostolico verba de descensu Christi ad inferos dicuntur non esse proprie intelligenda, totius symboli sensus proprius negaretur: aut si ex eo quod in Euangelio quædam parabolicæ occurrunt, omnes Evangelii narrationes parabolicas esse contenderes, nullas de eventibus realibus atque propriis. Qua quidem in istis aliisque locis Scripturas audaci interpretandi methodo, nil in eis fuerit quod evirare facile non posset, nulla hæresis adeo perniciosa, quam ex iisdem elicere non detur.
units.tr: XXII. These things and similar ones will be made most evident to anyone who approaches the Holy Scriptures by the ways prescribed by God, by which this method of weakening Scripture, of the histrionic intellect, found everywhere in the said book, is easily exposed and will be utterly abominable. Namely, when there are passages in the sacred Codex, clearer than the sun, that declare the truths opposed by its prejudices and errors, and when palpable accounts of facts are narrated, the sick and blind reason is accustomed to grope at the husks of words in those passages, if perhaps they admit equivocation or quibbling, either in themselves or through some absurd comparison with other passages, or if the terms are general and of wider signification, not proper and individual. Immediately, without regard to the whole passage, the whole Scripture, the dispositions of the speakers, or the sincerity of the mind that has been convinced otherwise of the clear sense, it substitutes and seizes upon something else for the properly designated subject. In those passages that are narratives of events, it carefully observes whether, in the narration, something incidental is not interspersed, which must not be interpreted rigidly according to the letter, but either improperly, or in a manner not yet clearly established. From this it boldly denies the whole substance and proper existence of the thing narrated. It is like someone who, because the words about Christ's descent into hell in the Apostles' Creed are not to be understood properly, denies the proper sense of the whole creed; or who, because some parables occur in the Gospel, contends that all the narratives of the Gospel are parabolic, and that none concerns real and actual events. Indeed, by this bold method of interpreting Scripture in these and other passages, there would be nothing in it that could not easily be emptied of meaning, and no heresy so pernicious that it cannot be drawn out of the same passages.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: XXIII. Jam quid sanioribus mentibus apparebit magis infirmum ac insipidum objectiunculis quae proponuntur contra veritates hactenus agnitas? Spiritus videlicet malignos si ea possent quae ipsis omnium consensu tribuuntur, potentiam Deo aequalem habituros, eos proinde Deum fore, aut Diabolum pro Deo habendum & adorandum esse, similiaque blasphema ejusmodi murmura, quae non nisi e misera admodum ignorantia oppononuntur. Potentia Dei est, producere realitatem, perfectiones, virtutes, in rebus, quae vel nondum erant, & quas facit esse; vel quae jam erant in bono statu quem eis adauget; vel quae in malo erant, unde eas potenter eripit, & in bonum collocat. Potentia Diaboli est, producere & augere malum, defectus, inordinationes, vitia, confusiones, gefliculationes, destructiones in subjectis vel jam prius corruptis, vel sponte seque suaque inordinationi & defectioni a Deo tradentibus; non autem in aliis, neque alia. An ergo hanc ultimam potentiam Diabolo tribuere, idem est ac ei potentiam priorem atque divinam tribuere? Quis non videt diabolica cum divinis ab illo Scriptore puerilter confundi? quemadmodum etiam quando profitetur per potentiam & operationes quae Diaboli esse agnoscuntur, vera Dei, Christi, Sanctorumque miracula, quibus Scripturae & Religionis Christianae probatio innituntur, subverti. Absurda consequentia! Miracula divina sunt extraordinaria quaedam elevatio rerum ad statum reaiiorem, perfectiorem, ordinatiorem, vel etiam justiorem, procedens a motivis Spiritus ritûs Sancti, & indivulsa a motibus quibus animæ ad Dei reverentiam, amorem, sanctitatem, virtutes, selicitatem trahantur: Diabolica sunt extraordinaria quædam confusio, quâ res mentesque ad statum corruptiorem miseriorem, vitiosiorem, a Deo, a perfectione, a felicitate remotiorem deprimuntur; vel si gesticulatione quadam res videantur superficialiter perfici, sub ea apparentia latet verissimum destructionis terminique miserabilis principium. Quis non palpat hæcce toto cœlo distincta esse? Altero probari Divinæ potentiæ, veritatis, voluntatis præsentiam; altero non item, sed Dei potius aversionem, omnemque fallaciæ, seductionis & malitiæ præsentiam: unde hisce quando accident, (quod Scriptura suturum prædicit) fidem abrogare jubemur. Deut. XIII: 1, 2, 3. Matth. XXIV: 23. II. Thess. II: 9, 10. Apoc. XIII: 13.
units.tr: XXIII. Now what will appear to more sensible minds weaker and more foolish than the little objections that are raised against the truths acknowledged so far? They say that if evil spirits could do what is commonly ascribed to them by all, they would have a power equal to God's, and so they would be God, or the Devil would have to be regarded and worshipped as God, and other blasphemous mutterings of this kind, which are raised only out of very miserable ignorance. It belongs to the power of God to produce reality, perfections and virtues in things that either did not yet exist and which he brings into being, or that already existed in a good state which he increases, or that were in an evil state, from which he powerfully rescues them and places them in good. It belongs to the power of the Devil to produce and increase evil, defects, disorders, vices, confusions, grimaces and destructions in subjects that are either already corrupt, or that surrender themselves willingly and their own things to disorder and defection from God; but not in others, nor in any other way. Is it then the same thing to attribute this last power to the Devil as to attribute to him the former, divine power? Who does not see that the diabolical is childishly confused with the divine by that writer? In the same way, when he professes that the true miracles of God, Christ and the saints, on which the proof of Scripture and of the Christian religion rests, are overthrown by a power and operations which are acknowledged to be the Devil's, he does the same. Absurd inference! Divine miracles are a certain extraordinary raising of things to a more real, more perfect, more orderly, or even more just state, proceeding from the motives of the Holy Spirit, and inseparable from the movements by which souls are drawn to the reverence, love, holiness, virtues and happiness of God. Diabolical acts are a certain extraordinary confusion by which things and minds are pressed down to a more corrupt, more wretched, more vicious state, further removed from God, from perfection and from happiness; or if, by a certain show of activity, things seem superficially to be perfected, the most true beginning of destruction and of a miserable end lies hidden under that appearance. Who does not feel that these are wholly distinct? The one proves the presence of divine power, truth and will; the other does not, but rather the aversion of God and the presence of all deceit, seduction and malice. Therefore, when these latter occur (as Scripture foretells they will), we are commanded to withdraw our faith from them. Deut. 13:1, 2, 3. Matt. 24:23. 2 Thess. 2:9, 10. Rev. 13:13.

units.la: Non igitur per potentiam, operationes & miracula, quæ Satanæ malignisque Spiritibus a Scriptura & ab omnibus tribuuntur, aliquid quod Deo competat, iis assignatur: ut vicissim neque Dei potentiæ, operationibus, miraculis tribui possunt ea quæ sunt diabolico genere. Et quamvis Scriptura destructivam potentiam de Deo affirmet, quodque ab eo sint mors, tenebræ, mala & calamitates; nemo non videt hæc positive & proprie non esse interpretanda, quasi mala & privationes a fonte boni & realitatis procederent: sed negative tantum, quatenus Deus hominibus rebellibus creaturisque subjectis subtrahit vel non continuat benedictarum suarum emanationum fontem & rivulos; unde necesse est creaturas a Deo aversas, eoque ipso omni bono privatas, inordinatione & omnis generis miseriis affici, propterea quod vis Divina, facultatesque eis in creatione concessae, objectis eas satiantibus destitutae, in se ipsas sine omni bono sineque lumine tunc agere debeant.
units.tr: Therefore nothing that belongs to God is assigned to Satan and the evil spirits through the power, operations and miracles that Scripture and everyone ascribe to them; and conversely, what is of the diabolical kind cannot be attributed to the power, operations or miracles of God. And although Scripture affirms a destructive power in God, and that death, darkness, evils and calamities come from him, no one fails to see that these are not to be interpreted positively and properly, as if evils and privations proceeded from the source of good and of reality, but only negatively, insofar as God withdraws, or does not continue, the fountain and streams of his blessed emanations from rebellious men and from creatures subject to him. Hence it is necessary that creatures turned away from God, and thereby deprived of all good, are affected with disorder and miseries of every kind, because the divine force and the faculties granted to them in creation, deprived of the objects that satisfy them, must then act in themselves, without any good and without any light.

units.la: XXIV. Quandoquidem circa hanc materiam eousque sum digressus, libet ulterius addere (quia & rogatus id facio) nonnulla quibus pateat sincerius mentibus, quam nulli pretii sint praelicti libri, erroriisque illic propinati, fulcra, praetextus objecti, colores, contradictiones. Praeter ea quae jectorum jam indigitavimus, audias illic passim velut fundamentum inconcussum, Diabolum esse Dei captivum, esse damnatum, regnum ad illum non pertinere, nec proinde eum talipotentia in creaturas pollere uti dicitur, Christo praesertim omnem potentiam in coelo & in terra possidente. At si Scripturas sine infolentibus intellectus histrionici glossis audiamus, discemus ibidem, eum esse (a) Principem seculi hujus (agnoscente hunc sensum divinolgnatio; (b) latuit principem seculi hujus Virginitas Mariae, esse potestatem tenebrarum; esse Deum hujus seculi; esse principem potentiae aeris, spiritum efficaciter operantem in filiis rebellibus; esse cum suis Dominos mundi tenebrosi hujus temporis sive seculi, totamque terram, & omnes habitatores ejus, adoraturos draconem, qui ad certum tempus usque (a) Luc. 2: 53. Joh. 12: 31. Eph. 2: 2. & cap. 6: 12. Apoc. 13: 4, 8. & cap. 20: 3. (b) Ignat. ad Ephes. que omnes nationes sit seduHurus. Idque non obstante quod Christus sit rex omnipotens, cui data est omnis potestas in coelo & in terra. Non enim Christus vult cogere homines ad sibi serviendum : sed ita gaudet populo spontaneo, ut quotquot inimici sui potestati sese sponte per peccatum subjicere volunt, hos sinat ei servire, & hunc dominari eis, etiam omnibus, si id omnes vellent: at omnipotens est ut eripiat ex ejus tyrannide quicunque sponte volent liberari; & qui nolent, eos diu toleratos, tandem ex coelo & terra suo tempore exterminaturus est, omnipotentia sua solus tunc regnaturus. Nec minus Diabolus ut ut regnans, Dei captivus est, hoc est, in tenebrarum & corruptionis elemento sic constringitur, ut nullum amplius habeat accessum ad Deum, neque ad eos qui Deo adhaerent, nisi id speciali permissu Dei fiat, quando scilicet Deus scit hoc certo piis profuturum, adversario autem ignominiae cessurum. Is alioqui, in maledicto suo corruptionis & inordinationis elemento omnino includitur, in cujus sphaera tamen (quod captivus incatenatus potest,) & se & suas agitat catenas, nec non & quicquid id est quod in suae captivitatis sphaeram vult irruere; hoc est, quotquot a Deo deficere volunt, & in statum inordinationis seque suaque conjicere. Ex hac captivitate nunquam liberabitur Satanas, neque ad libertatem gloriosam fruendi Deo omnibusque benedictis in eo creaturis est reditus in aeternum, quod hominibus ejus captivis adhuc dum licet per vim Spiritus Christi, qui (a) captivis liberationem annunciavit. Neque minus idem adversarius, quicquid agat & tumultuetur in confusionis & tenebrarum suarum regno, non minus inquam damnatus est semper: gerit enim in se inferni & damnationis essentialia, Dei, lucis, boni privationem omnimodam & aeternam, tenebrasque & inquietudines atque malignitatem nunquam dispellendas: quod tamen accessoria damnatione olim cumulabitur, quando regni ejus elapso tempore ipse cum omnibus ei morigeris in stagnum ignis projiciendus est, hoc est, in materiam corruptam a toto mundo glorificando seperandam relegandus.
units.tr: XXIV. Since I have digressed so far on this matter, I am pleased to add further (because I do so also at the request of others) some things by which it may be made plainer to minds how worthless are the books mentioned above, and what supports, pretexts, colours and contradictions of the errors poured out there are. Besides those things we have already pointed out, you will hear there everywhere, as an unshakeable foundation, that the Devil is God's captive, is condemned, that the kingdom does not pertain to him, and therefore that he does not have such power over creatures as is said, especially since Christ possesses all power in heaven and on earth. But if we hear the Scriptures without the absurd glosses of a stage-player's intellect, we shall learn there that he is (a) the prince of this world (the divine ignorance acknowledges this sense); (b) the virginity of Mary was hidden from the prince of this world; that he is the power of darkness; that he is the god of this age; that he is the prince of the power of the air, the spirit working effectively in the rebellious sons; that with his followers he is the lord of the dark world of this time or age, and that the whole earth and all its inhabitants will worship the dragon, who will seduce all nations until a certain time. (a) Luke 22:53. John 12:31. Eph. 2:2, and chap. 6:12. Rev. 13:4, 8, and chap. 20:3. (b) Ignatius, to the Ephesians. And this is so although Christ is the almighty king, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given. For Christ does not wish to compel men to serve him; rather he so delights in a willing people that, as many as willingly wish to subject themselves to the power of their enemy through sin, he allows them to serve him, and him to rule over them; even over all, if all were willing. Yet he is almighty to snatch from his tyranny whoever willingly wish to be freed; and those who are unwilling, whom he has tolerated for a long time, he will at length, in his own time, exterminate from heaven and earth, reigning alone then by his omnipotence. Likewise the Devil, though he reigns, is God's captive; that is, he is so bound within the element of darkness and corruption that he has no further access to God, nor to those who cleave to God, unless this takes place by a special permission of God, when God knows with certainty that it will profit the pious and will turn to the shame of the adversary. Otherwise he is wholly enclosed in the element of his curse, which is corruption and disorder; yet within its sphere (as a chained captive can) he both moves himself and his chains, and also stirs up whatever it is that he wishes to rush into the sphere of his captivity; that is, as many as wish to fall away from God and cast themselves and their own into a state of disorder. From this captivity Satan will never be freed, nor is there a return to the glorious liberty of enjoying God and all the blessed creatures in him for ever; but while it is still allowed, men who are his captives are liberated by the power of the Spirit of Christ, who (a) proclaimed liberty to the captives. Nor is that adversary less condemned always, whatever he does and stirs up in the kingdom of his confusion and darkness; for he bears within himself the essentials of hell and damnation: a complete and eternal privation of God and of light and of good, and darkness, restlessness and malignity that will never be dispelled. Yet this will at length be heaped up with an additional damnation, when, the time of his kingdom having run out, he himself, with all who obey him, is to be cast into the lake of fire, that is, relegated into corrupt matter to be separated from the whole glorified world.

units.la: Quod potentiam Diaboli, ejusque operationes ideo inficietur Auctor, quod Diabolum dicat ignarum esse, nec Theologum, nec Physicum, nec linguarum callentem, id admodum ignarum sapit. Diabolus ante lapsum fruebatur luminose Deo, Deique mirabilibus, natura item gloriosa, ex cujus parte ei tradita postmodum chaos sua defectione effecit: harum rerum divinarum naturaliumque ideas, etsi pictas solummodo, non autem vividas & efficaces, retinuit, haud secus ac vir doctus, qui a Deo deficit, ideas tamen speculativas rerum divinarum aliarumque, quas prius habuit, retinet. Et quando ex mundo chaotico Deus iterum excitavit creaturas ad speciem sive similitudinem priorum (quod evidenter sacer textus indigitat,) spiritus maligni per priorum ideas
units.tr: That the author denies the power of the Devil and his operations on the ground that he calls the Devil ignorant, neither a theologian nor a natural philosopher nor skilled in languages, tastes very much of ignorance. Before the fall the Devil enjoyed God luminously, and God's wonders, and likewise a glorious nature, from the part of which, given to him, chaos was afterwards produced by his defection. He retained the ideas of these divine and natural things, though only painted and not living and effective, just as a learned man who falls away from God still retains the speculative ideas of divine and other things that he had before. And when God again raised up creatures out of the chaotic world to the appearance or likeness of the former (which the sacred text clearly indicates), the evil spirits, through the ideas of the former,

units.la: h ideas posteriores utcunque nosse poterant, maxime postquam ipsis per corruptionem naturæ & spontaneam a Deo defectionem aditum ad omnia sibi subjecta aperuit homo peccans, atque insuper ex permultis, quorum in mentibus & cerebris specialissime inhabitant & dominantur, infinita divina, naturalia, humana, cogitata, facta, dicta, res, actiones, locutiones, perspicere, & longissima experientia cognitiones augere, nec non ex ingenii subtilitate plura inde deducere potuerunt. Et quid facilius eis, quam impiorum cogitata, nosse ab effectibus vel signis permultis, v. g. si percipiant conatibus suis in mentes, in imaginationem, in corpora, non resisti; piorum vero, quando sibi suisque impressionibus non dari locum sentiunt, sed multifariam eas repelli; unde facile judicant de statu & cogitationibus mentis varie eis resistentis? Quid possibilius iisdem quam statum, modos, actionesque rerum corporearum percipere ex eo, quod elementum corruptionis suæ, cui præsunt, & quod omnibus modis per omnia insinuare vellent, terminari diversimode & repelli experiantur a subjectis, quorum proinde dispositiones sibi oppositas eo ipso animadvertunt? His, aliisque de causis, non dubitandum est quin Diaboli scientia vel cognitio de præteritis, deque præsentibus, de futuris autem conjiciendi probabilitas, nec non in linguis scientiisque humanis peritia, sint tantæ, ut comparate ad eum multi qui se subtiles admodum Doctores putant, crassi adhuc tyrones, imo meri asini fuerint. Atque si hic objiciant, per istam scientiae Diabolicae de rebus cogitatisque humanis assertionem, labefactari privilegium solius interiora hominum scrutantis Scientiae divinae, (quae tamen est a priori, universalis, infallibilis, & perfectissima,) ii profecto nulla responsione, sed sola admiratione indigent.
units.tr: Yet they could know the later ideas in some way, especially since man, by sinning, had opened to them access to everything subject to them through the corruption of nature and his own voluntary defection from God. Moreover, the demons, who dwell and rule most especially in the minds and brains of many men, could perceive infinite divine, natural, and human thoughts, deeds, sayings, things, actions, and utterances, could increase their knowledge through very long experience, and could deduce much from these through the subtlety of their intellect. What could be easier for them than to know the thoughts of the wicked from many effects or signs? For example, if they perceive that their efforts are not resisted in the minds, imaginations, and bodies of men; but when they feel that no place is given to them or their impressions in the godly, and that these are repelled in many ways, they easily judge from this about the state and thoughts of a mind that resists them in various ways. What could be more possible for them than to perceive the condition, modes, and actions of bodily things from the fact that the element of their corruption, over which they preside, and which they wish to insinuate in every way and through all things, is experienced as being limited in various ways and repelled by the subjects, so that they thereby notice the dispositions opposed to them? For these and other reasons there is no doubt that the knowledge of the Devil about past and present things, and his ability to conjecture probabilities about future things, as well as his skill in human languages and sciences, are so great that, compared with him, many who think themselves very subtle Doctors are still crude novices, indeed mere donkeys. And if they object here that, by this assertion of diabolical knowledge of human things and thoughts, the privilege of divine knowledge alone, which searches the inward parts of men (and which is a priori, universal, infallible, and most perfect), is weakened, such people surely need no answer, only astonishment.

units.la: Praetextus caeteri ex parte Dei, Diaboli, hominum desumti, ob quos veritates receptas rejiciat auctor, suos autem errores commendet, non minus sunt absurdi. Supponit falso, si vera essent quae de daemonibus hominès tentantibus dicuntur, Deum tunc Diabolo vim suam communicaturum, ad ejus fallacias concursurum, aditum ad homines ei patefacturum, & mala quaevis permissurum; quae incommoda divinam ejus potentiam, sanctitatem, veritatem, bonitatem labefactarent. Responsiones: Materiam concursus non intelligit auctor. Deus postquam semel vim & facultates creaturis impressit, eum actum, multoque minus facultatum actus, non reproducit nec reduplicat: creaturarum est vim & facultates semel datas & acceptas, nec unquam annihilandas, regere & exercere: quas si ad Deum dirigant, illae lumine ac bonitate Dei invesiftiuntur & compensantur: si a Deo defle &tant, quod ex libertate possunt, ipsarum culpa est, neque hoc determinavit Deus, nec positive permisit: sivit tantum libertatem esse, & actus suos ad libitum regere, quos concursus Dei bonus & luminosus omnino & juste deserit, & sibi ipsis relinquit. Falsum est Deum (excepto casu ubi scit id piæ menti profuturum certissime) Diabolo ad homines accessum concedere. Econtra, clausit eum potenter & benigne, non semel, sed infinities; maneretque semper aditus occlusus, nisi eum homo sponte sua recluderet, seque in Diaboli elementum, captivitatem, catenas & regnum per peccata sua sæpissime conjiceret, ubi Deus, ipsum inde infinities revocatum, per justitiam tandem relinquere cogitur, quando pervicaciter sese eo conjicere perpetuo volens perseverat.
units.tr: The other pretexts, drawn from the side of God, the Devil, and men, on account of which the author rejects received truths and commends his own errors, are no less absurd. He supposes falsely that, if what is said about demons tempting men were true, then God would impart his power to the Devil, would concur with his deceits, would open access to men for him, and would permit any evils whatever; and these inconveniences would undermine his divine power, holiness, truth, and goodness. Replies: the author does not understand the matter of concurrence. After God has once impressed power and faculties on creatures, he does not reproduce or redouble that act, much less the acts of the faculties. It is for creatures to govern and exercise the powers and faculties once given and received, which are never to be annihilated; if they direct them toward God, these are clothed and compensated by the light and goodness of God; if they fall away from God, which they can do by freedom, this is their own fault, and God neither determined this nor positively permitted it. He has only allowed there to be freedom and to direct their acts at will, and the good and wholly luminous concurrence of God justly withdraws from these acts and leaves them to themselves. It is false that God (except in a case where he certainly knows it will profit a pious mind) grants the Devil access to men. On the contrary, he has shut him out powerfully and kindly, not once but countless times; and access would always remain closed, unless man of his own accord opened it again, and very often by his sins cast himself into the Devil's element, captivity, chains, and kingdom, where God, having recalled him from there countless times, is at last compelled by justice to abandon him when he persists obstinately, wishing to cast himself there forever.

units.la: At timendus est solus Deus, non Diabolus: proinde nil eum posse agnoscendum est. Puerilis æquivocatio. Timendus est Deus, hoc est, ex amore timendum est ne ei displiceamus, neve tantum amittamus bonum. Timendus est Diabolus, hoc est, aversione & fuga prosequendus, quemadmodum & peccatum & quævis mala atque periculosa timenda, cavenda & aversanda sunt. Quis hos timores ἀπωσάμενος esse dicat? Quis nisi hominum saluti iratus, ultimum hunc tollere audeat? Præsumtionem, inquies, aut desperationem gignit ista persuasio de malignorum spirituum homines tentantium potentia. Superbit quisquis tam potenti hosti se resistere posse putat. Desperat si tam potentem hostem continuo adltare, insidiari, fidem precesque etiam, quibus ad Deum recurratur, impedire sibi persuadeat. At hæc ridiridicula. Isne superbiret, qui scit non propria, sed a Deo subministrata vi hostem superari & vinci, vel potius Deum ipsum esse qui Satanam sub pedibus nostris conculcet? Isne desperationis ansam habet cui inculcabitur, falsum esse, preces & recursum fidentem ad Deum ab hoste impediri posse, modo mens sincere & ferio id velit: quo pacto omnipotens auxilium nacta, de hoste procul dubio triumphatura fit. At, objectabis, quilibet peccata sua in Diabolum incitantem rejiciens, hoc modo fui excusationem quaeret, cujus causam proinde tollere expedit. Fateor homines esse proniores ad culpam suam in alios rejiciendam ut excusationem praetendant: at ea excusatio ipsis exercitiendia est non negatione diabolicae tentationis, quemadmodum nec Deus cum primis parentibus sese excusantibus sic egit: sed conscientia convincendi sunt eos esse culpabiles qui tentationi malae sponte consentiunt & morem gerunt, quin eam saepius alliciunt atque provocant; & non raro ulterius in malo, atque impulsi sunt, propria malitia proficiunt. Quicquid fit, quis pro legitimis excusationibus admittat, fi quis dicat, & cum veritate dicat; furatus sum equidem, at a proximo meo incitatus: occidi hominem, incendium excitavi, falsum juravi testimonium, sed requisitus ab alio? Si haecce incitamenta neminem excusent, quia iis resistere oportuit, non consentire, nec fe instrumentum spontaneum eorum exsequendorum praebere; quis causabitur excusationum materiam validam peccatoribus subministrari ex consideratione tentationum diabolicarum, quæ solæ (etiamsi suggestiones & cogitationes perpetuæ horrendissimorum peccatorum essent,) non modo menti non nocent, modo ei displiceant nec eis gestiat consentire; sed & ejus fidelitatis, a Domino magnis postea præmiis compensandæ, probationes & documenta sunt Deo gratissima.
units.tr: But only God is to be feared, not the Devil; therefore it must be acknowledged that the Devil can do nothing. A childish equivocation. God is to be feared, that is, out of love we must fear displeasing him, lest we lose so great a good. The Devil is to be feared, that is, he must be pursued with aversion and flight, just as sin and all evil and dangerous things are to be feared, avoided and shunned. Who would say that these fears are rejecting [ἀπωσάμενος]? Who, except one hostile to the salvation of men, would dare to remove this last one? You will say that this persuasion about the power of evil spirits who tempt men breeds presumption or despair. Whoever thinks he can resist so powerful an enemy is puffed up. He despairs if he is persuaded that so powerful an enemy is constantly assailing, lying in wait for him, and that he can even hinder the faith and prayers by which one has recourse to God. But these things are ridiculous. Would he be puffed up who knows that the enemy is overcome and conquered not by his own strength but by a power supplied by God, or rather that God himself is the one who tramples Satan under our feet? Does he have an occasion for despair to whom it is impressed that it is false that prayers and recourse made in faith to God can be hindered by the enemy, provided the mind sincerely and earnestly wills it? By this means, having obtained omnipotent help, it will undoubtedly triumph over the enemy. But, you will object, anyone who throws the blame for his sins on the Devil who incites him will seek an excuse for himself in this way, so it is expedient to remove its cause. I grant that men are more prone to throw their guilt on others in order to put forward an excuse. But that excuse must be refuted not by denying diabolical temptation (God did not act in that way with our first parents when they excused themselves), but men must be convinced by their conscience that they are guilty, since they freely consent to evil temptation and indulge it, indeed often invite and provoke it; and not rarely, having been impelled, they go further into evil by their own malice. However it may be, who would admit as a legitimate excuse if someone said, and said truthfully: "I did indeed steal, but I was incited by my neighbour; I killed a man, I started a fire, I swore false testimony, but I was asked to by another"? If these incitements excuse no one, because it was necessary to resist them, not to consent, nor to offer oneself as a willing instrument for carrying them out, who will claim that a valid ground for excuses is supplied to sinners by the consideration of diabolical temptations? Even if these were constant suggestions and thoughts of the most horrible sins, they not only do not harm the mind but displease it, and it does not wish to consent to them; indeed they are proofs and evidences of its fidelity, to be rewarded afterwards by the Lord with great prizes, and most pleasing to God.

units.la: Satius est (inquies) hominem in se descendere, & propriam suam corruptionem tanquam omnis generis mali fontem considerare. Ita sane: nam & propria corruptio hominis, causa est & fons introductionis Diaboli; sed is semel intromissus, causa socia & adjuvans fit peccati: quæ ratio est cur interdum hominum, piorum præsertim, nonnulla peccata non ita sint atrocia ac si ex mera sua voluntate essent, quod Dei miserationem non parum commovet, dum peccatoris desperationem consolatione nonnulla impedit, ac præterea efficit, ut is in posterum sibi magis invigilet, ne (ut cum Scriptura loquar) locum det Diabolo, vel incidat in insidias ejus qui tanquam leo circumit quærens quem devoret.' Hæc materia de periculis tentationum diabolicarum, quia est momentosissima, & quoniam inde patere potest quam exitialiter perniciosa sit doctrina quæ Diabolum subtegit & dissimulat, nonnihil hic consideranda est.
units.tr: "It is better," you will say, "for man to descend into himself and consider his own corruption as the fountain of every kind of evil." Certainly so: for man's own corruption is both the cause and the source of the Devil's introduction; but once he has been admitted, he becomes a joint and assisting cause of sin. This is the reason why sometimes some sins of men, especially of the godly, are not so atrocious as if they came from pure will; which does not a little move God's compassion, while it prevents the sinner's despair by some consolation, and moreover brings it about that he watches over himself more carefully in future, lest (to speak with Scripture) he "give place to the Devil," or fall into the snares of him who "as a roaring lion walks about, seeking whom he may devour." This matter of the dangers of diabolical temptations, because it is most important, and because from it may be seen how deadly harmful is the doctrine that hides and dissembles the Devil, must be considered here to some extent.

units.la: XXV. Quando effectus aliquis pendet ab una causa totaliter & proxime, tunc causa ea de effectu suo secura est, eum impedit, producit, revocat, terminat, ubi, quando & quantum vult; & quamvis effectus sit malus, secura mens de ejus ab illa dependentia, parum aut nihil sibi cavendum esse facile persuadet: at quando effectus (quem malum supponimus) pendet & a causa socia & adjuvante, atque a mediis quæ semel adhibita, vel reluctantibus nobis effectum sortiuntur, tunc sane summæ cautelæ locus est, ne quis sociæ causæ se adjungat, mediaque ad effectum in actum deducens, essectum perniciosum amplius impedire non possit.
units.tr: XXV. When some effect depends wholly and immediately on one cause, then that cause is secure about its effect: it can hinder, produce, recall, and end it, where, when, and as far as it wishes; and although the effect is evil, a mind that is secure about its dependence on that cause easily persuades itself that it has little or nothing to guard against. But when the effect (which we are supposing to be evil) depends also on a joint and assisting cause, and on means which, once applied, bring about the effect even though we resist, then surely there is need for the greatest caution, lest anyone join himself to the joint cause, and, by bringing the means into action toward the effect, be no longer able to prevent the harmful effect.

units.la: Exempli gratia, qui vel aquas vel abyssum considerat tanquam quibus appropinquare & a quibus se pro lubitu removere possit, nulla causa (opinione quidem sua) eum præterea propellente, is propius, & ad placitos fines usque, potest securior accedere: at si moneatur latere circumcirca insidiatores, qui approximantes in baratrum propellant, aut venti turbinem oriturum, qui idem efficiat; ille idem, procul dubio, si sapit, ne approximabit quidem: cum e contra, si id ipsi aut dissimuletur, aut negetur, interitus ejus perniciose procurabitur. Ita si quis solus cum igne sic agat, ut a circumstantium rerum concursu nihil ei sit timendum, facile etiam scintillas hinc inde disperget aut cadere permittet, & manum suam vel per flammam celerius trajicere poterit sine timore: at si circumcingatur acer-
units.tr: For example, a man who looks at waters or an abyss as things he can approach and withdraw from at will, with no cause (as he thinks) pushing him, may safely go closer, even up to the boundaries he has chosen. But if he is warned that there are ambushers lying all around who push those who come near into the pit, or that a whirlwind is about to arise that would do the same, then he, without doubt, if he has any sense, will not come near at all. On the other hand, if this is concealed from him or denied, his destruction will be brought about deadly. So too, if someone deals with fire alone, in such a way that he has nothing to fear from the convergence of surrounding things, he may easily scatter sparks here and there or let them fall, and he can pass his hand through the flame more quickly and without fear. But if he were surrounded by a heap of

units.la: Quanta sint pericula tentationum Diabolica, ... (marginal note)
