units.la: vis pulveris pyrii, fique ejusmodi pulveris fomes aut particulae, totos praesentes acervos incendere aptae, ejus manui indivulsé adhaerent, quanta cum cura non cavebit ne forte sua culpa vel scintillula aliqua elabatur, vel manus flammae accedat, quà admissa, ipsi postea vel invito fit pereundum? Quantus autem non esset homicida is, qui hoc periculum ei subticeret aut negaret? Eodem modo tutus incedit, qui vel pedibus graditur propriis, vel equo se vehendum committit cujus motus scit se moderari posse: at si equus ipso inscio fit furiosus, vel li placido equo currum trahenti adjungat furibundum, tunc vel reluctans abripitur quo nollet ad quaevis praecipitia: neque salutarius ullum officium ei ante rem actam exhiberi potest, quam de periculo isto, a causa socia certo imminente, monere, quod reticere, quid aliud efset quam hominem occidere? Atqui res se iisdem prorsus modis habet cum hominibus peccantibus, malignisque spiritibus eis insidiantibus. Mentes corruptae, pravi habitus, elementa, corpora, res omnes quibus corruptio inest & depravatio, nidus sunt, elementum & vehiculum malignorum spirituum, qui inde insidiantur hominibus, qui bus quidem, quanquam tentent, nocere nequeunt quamdiu hi a peccatis & inordinatis actibus sibi cavebunt. At quam primum homo peccatum admittit, ecce, eo ipso solvuntur & excitantur insidiae inimici, peccantem praecipitem agentis, igne infernali eum accendentis, & quo praecipitiorum lubet bet eum abripientis: & tunc qui sibi antea imaginabatur, nullum tale periculum ibi subesse, a se solo effectus malos & pendere & directum iri, serius animadvertit sibi jam sub aliena potestate, cui infeliciter se commisit, pereundum esse; imo nunc illic peribit infscius, vel etiam (quod lamentabilius est) persuasus sibi tunc bene esse, seque ad vitam gradiri æternam, inimico tenebras intellectui ejus activo affundente, eum regente, ficta specie veri decipiente, affectus demulcente, promissis quibusvis illudente, res malas, distractiones, occupationes speciosas, quibus tamen a quærendo Domino impediatur, veluti res aut indifferentes aut etiam bonas objiciente, verbo, omnibus rebus actibusque eum jam, uti muscas filamentis suis solent araneæ, imperceptibiliter retibus suis, donec evadere nequeat & enecetur, innectente. Hoc cum summa paternorum viscerum erga creaturas suas commiseratione videt fidelis animarum amator Deus, atque idcirco hominem cæcum de periculis infinitis & æternis sollicite mille locis, mille modis, mille exemplis admonet & compellat: perniciem generis humani primam hac via accidisse; eădem esse continuatam & continuari; & tandem toti orbi seductionem & interitum hoc modo eventurum: proinde esse orandum, vigilandum, sollicite Deo soli adhærendum; ab omni vel minima inordinatione cavendum, ne inimico locum dantibus, prævaleat nobis & in ejus ungues & captivitatem æternam incidamus. Et niminus tamen reperiuntur miseri coeci, animarum ductores, qui data opera necessarias adeo admonitiones enervent, ipsaque toto animo tantopere venerandas & omni cum simplicitate atque obedientia fidei audiendas Scripturas, adorandumque Dei illic prolatum nomen & verbum, stupenda intellectus gesticulatorii temeritate & astutia, non tantum in vanum sumere, sed & in deceptorium & in contrarium sensum pervertere audeant. O Deus (exclamet quis jure cum Polycarpo) in quae tempora nos reservasti! Et hoc fuerit, scilicet, Diaboli regnum abolere, eique propterea, tanquam devicto vel imbelli erit insultandum, ut qui ejusmodi opus amoliri non potuerit. Certe non erat cur Diabolus a tali opere sibi ulla de causa caveret, quippe quo regnum ejus potentissime propagetur, & quo commodius servitium ei praestari non posset. Nunquam triumphat hostis tutius, quam quando de ejus potentia nil cogitatur, imo ea negatur, & sub callidis tegumentis redditur imperceptibilis; qua arte inexpugnabilia alioqui munimenta expugnari queant facillime. Refert (a) Bodinus, celeberrimus ICtus, inventos fuisse, qui cum voce & scriptis contenderent omnia quae de spiritibus rebusque Diabolicis dicuntur, non esse nisi meras naenias, ipsimet interim & magi & Satanico pacto implicitierant, quos inter nominat Doctorem quendam Theologiae & Concionatorem Pictavienem in Gallia, apud quem suo, aliorum, reique ipsius testimonio de sortilegio magico convictum, inventum fit autographum pacti quod cum Satana inierat, his inter alias scriptis conditionibus, ut scilicet publice concionaretur, ea quae deDiabolis & fortilegiis dicuntur, meras esse fabulas, & impossibilia omnique fide indigna figmenta: ea acta in regestis Parlamenti Pictaviensis adhuc exstare: Diaboli vero regnum istis artibus magna tunc sumsisse incrementa. Sed haec & similia, nec non omnia quaecunque ab omni aevo & ubique locorum ab infinitis sanarum imo & sanctarum mentium hominibus, circa eas, quas experti sunt, angelicas & daemoniacas operationes asseverabuntur, pro nihilo facile ducet nescio quis, praeeuntibus impudentissimis Spinoza & Hobbesio omnia audacter pernegantibus & deridiculo habentibus: quidni enim in gratiam audacis & amati erroris, ut Divinam, sic humanam fidem enervent, tametsi Philosophi pro indubitato habeant axiomate, Ea facta quae sensuum experimentis constant, quando asseverantur a quamplurimis hominibus, variorum temporum, nationum & locorum, qui velut ea experti de iisdem testantur, quique non credi possunt in unum conspirasse ut nos deciperent, tam firmiter credenda esse, ac si ea ipsimet fuissemus experti; qua via etiam maxima pars cognitionum nostrarum nobis accessit.
units.tr: the force of gunpowder, and tinder or particles of such powder, capable of setting fire to whole heaps lying nearby, cling inseparably to his hand. With how much care will he not take heed lest through his own fault some spark slip out, or his hand come near the flame, which once admitted would bring about his own destruction, even against his will? And what a murderer would he be who kept this danger from him or denied it? In the same way, he walks safely who either goes on his own feet, or entrusts himself to a horse whose movements he knows he can control. But if the horse becomes furious without his knowledge, or if a frenzied horse is yoked to a gentle one drawing a chariot, then he is dragged, struggling against his will, to whatever precipices there are. Nor can any more wholesome service be rendered him before the thing is done than to warn him of this danger, which is certainly imminent from a fellow cause; and to keep silent about it would be nothing other than to kill the man. Yet matters stand in exactly the same way with sinning men and the malignant spirits who lie in wait for them. Corrupted minds, evil habits, the elements, bodies, all things in which corruption and depravity inhere, are the nest, the element and the vehicle of malignant spirits, who from there lie in wait for men. These spirits, although they try, cannot harm men as long as these men guard themselves against sins and disordered acts. But as soon as a man admits sin, behold, by that very fact the snares of the enemy are loosed and roused, the enemy who drives the sinner headlong, sets him on fire with infernal fire, and carries him off to whatever precipices he pleases. Then the man who had imagined that there was no such danger there, and that the evil effects depend on himself alone and will be directed by himself, too late perceives that he is already under another's power, to which he has unhappily committed himself, and that he must perish. Indeed, he will now perish there unaware, or even (what is more lamentable) persuaded that all is well with him, and that he is walking towards eternal life, while the enemy pours darkness into his active intellect, governs him, deceives him with a feigned appearance of truth, soothes his passions, mocks him with whatever promises, and presents to him, as if they were either indifferent or even good things, evil affairs, distractions and specious occupations by which he is hindered from seeking the Lord. In a word, he entangles him in all things and acts, as spiders with their threads catch flies, imperceptibly in his nets, until he can no longer escape and is killed. The faithful lover of souls, God, sees this with the greatest compassion of a father's heart towards his creatures, and therefore warns and urges blind man, anxiously, in a thousand places, in a thousand ways, with a thousand examples, about the infinite and eternal dangers: that the destruction of the human race first came about in this way; that the same has continued and continues; and that at last the seduction and ruin of the whole world will happen in this manner. Therefore one must pray, watch, and cling anxiously to God alone; one must beware of every, even the smallest, disorder, lest, by giving the enemy room, he prevails over us and we fall into his claws and into eternal captivity. And yet there are to be found wretched blind guides of souls who, on purpose, weaken these so necessary warnings, and who dare, with astonishing rashness and cunning of a juggling intellect, not only to take in vain, but also to pervert into a deceptive and contrary sense, the Scriptures, which are so venerable with the whole mind and to be heard with all simplicity and obedience of faith, and the adorable name and word of God set forth there. O God (let one rightly exclaim with Polycarp), into what times hast thou reserved us! And this, forsooth, would be to abolish the kingdom of the Devil, and so he is to be mocked as if conquered or powerless, since whoever could not undertake such a work. Certainly there was no reason why the Devil should take any precaution for himself against such a work, since by it his kingdom is most powerfully spread, and no more convenient service could be rendered to him. The enemy never triumphs more safely than when no thought is given to his power, or rather it is denied, and it is rendered imperceptible under clever disguises; by this art fortresses otherwise impregnable can be most easily stormed. (a) Bodin, the most celebrated jurist, reports that there have been men who, with voice and writings, maintained that all that is said about spirits and diabolical things is nothing but idle tales, while they themselves were meanwhile entangled in magic and in a pact with Satan. Among these he names a certain teacher of theology and preacher at Poitiers in France, in whose possession, by his own testimony, that of others and of the matter itself, convicted of magical sorcery, was found an autograph of the pact he had made with Satan, in which, among other conditions, it was written that he should publicly preach that the things said about devils and sorceries are mere fables and impossible, figments unworthy of all faith; that these proceedings still exist in the records of the Parliament of Poitiers; and that the kingdom of the Devil then took great increase by these arts. But these things and the like, and indeed everything that has been asserted in every age and in every place by countless men of sound and even holy minds concerning the angelic and demonic operations which they have experienced, someone easily counts as nothing, the most shameless Spinoza and Hobbes going before, boldly denying everything and making it a laughing-stock. For why should they not, for the sake of a bold and beloved error, weaken human faith as well as divine, although philosophers hold as an indubitable axiom: Those facts which rest on the experiments of the senses, when they are affirmed by very many men of various times, nations and places, who as having experienced them bear witness to the same, and who cannot be believed to have conspired together to deceive us, are to be believed as firmly as if we ourselves had experienced them; by this way also the greatest part of our knowledge has come to us.

units.la: XXVI. Equidem divinam fidem nega- nt hic se tollere, quin potius se, ut ma- nus dent, Scripturarum testimonia clara ope- rtare; atque etiam experimenta propria, fi-
units.tr: XXVI. Indeed, they deny here that they are rejecting divine faith. Rather, so as to give way, they have the clear testimonies of Scripture set aside, and their own experiences too, if indeed a sensation of such an operation must be felt by experience as coming from elsewhere, from a cause acting upon us that is different from us and even hostile to us.

units.la: quidem proprio experimento sentiri debeat tanquam aliunde accedens ejusmodi operatio causæ in nos agentis quæ a nobis diversa nobisque etiam inimica esset, veluti Diabolum dicunt tentationes & cogitationes peccaminosas nobis inspirare. Quibus ego, id demum fore affirmem, si mentes purę, si lucidæ essent, si soli Deo adhærerent & ab omni specie vel apparentia mali abhorrerent: tunc enim illico sentirent & viderent, si quæ a Diabolis suggestiones sibi fierent, eas & aliunde quam a se, & a principio a se diverso procedere: at id debere sic animadverti a mentibus turbulentis, tenebrosis, cæcis, ad spiritualia discernenda ineptis, Deo non adhærentibus, Dæmonis propensioni non obluctantibus, sed ei sic intime unitis, ut una sit mens, unus animus, id perquam absurdum est exigere: nam quis ignorat, ea quæ sic unita sunt intime, non sentiri posse ut a se invicem dissociata, atque diversa? Quod autem Scripturarum testimonia certis terminis ad eorum palatum expressa exigere videantur ut a sententia discedant, timendum est ne merus sit fucus, quo speciose a pertinaciæ insimulatione declinent: namque paratissimi videntur, quæcunque allegari possent, ea iisdem artibus, quibus mille alia loca perverterunt, similiter enervare; & confidenter asseri possit, nullum testimonium locumve adeo conceptis & selectis verbis posse contra ipsorum errorem desiderari aut supponi, quin facile id suo methodo casum fieri vel etiam ad partes suas posset trahi.
units.tr: Such people, they say, are the Devil's doing, since he inspires temptations and sinful thoughts in us. To this I would answer that this would be the case only if minds were pure and clear, cleaved to God alone, and shrank from every appearance or semblance of evil. For then they would at once feel and see that whatever suggestions the Devil made to them came from elsewhere and from a principle other than themselves. But to require that this be noticed in minds that are turbulent, dark, blind, unfit to discern spiritual things, not cleaving to God, not resisting the Devil's inclination but so intimately united with it that there is one mind and one soul, is quite absurd. For who does not know that things so intimately united cannot be felt as separate and distinct from one another? As for the claim that the testimonies of Scripture seem to be forced into fixed terms to suit their taste, so that they must give up their opinion, we must fear that this is mere pretence, a specious way of avoiding the charge of obstinacy. For they seem most ready to weaken, by the same arts with which they have twisted a thousand other passages, whatever texts might be cited. And one may confidently say that no testimony or passage, however carefully framed and chosen in words, could be demanded or assumed against their error that could not easily be made a matter of their own method, or even be drawn over to their side.

units.la: Ratio cur credibile sit eos nullis testimoniis, quanquam desiderata darentur, paratos esse ut cedant, hæc est, quod sibi imaginati sint, impossibile esse & contra naturam ut Spiritus agant in corpora: cui principio revera totum systema (quicquid dissimulent) innitur, & quidem ita palpabiliter, ut malint sibi sæpius contradicere, quam ab eo fundamento discedere. Etenim postquam, ne videantur aperte Scripturam impugnare, pro thesibus posuerunt, Angelos quidem bonos hominibus fidelibus ministrare, eosque protegere; malorum vero (seu Diaboli) ministerio, hominem seductum fuisse; unde sequitur evidenter, bonos quidem Angelos agere in mentes & corpora piorum; malos vero si non directe in hominis mentem, saltem in ejus sensus & corpus; id tamen nolunt agnoscere, maluntque potius quam id agnoscant dicere, se nescire qui id fiat, hoc est, se nolle fateri verbis id quod conscii sunt contra suum præjudicium erroneum esse. Et hinc quando ad Scripturæ loca de his agentia se conferunt, cum deberent illa explicare eo modo qui cum thesibus dictis congrueret, eosque confirmaret, stupendo sibi re & actione ipsa contradicendi & in proprias theses prævaricandi modo, omnia ita explicant, quin potius petulanter detorquent, ut ne unus quidem cum thesibus concordet easve statuminet. Sed parum id esset, nisi etiam sententiæ suæ gratia proferrent ea in medium, unde Christus & Apostoli sibi reapse contradicentes dedeprehenderentur. Nam quando ex una parte docent, Christum, Evangelistas & Apostolos, de Diabolo & Dæmonibus loquentes fuisse sicut homines loquuntur & sentiunt: ex altera vero, eis quæ homines de dæmonibus dicunt & sentiunt, concuti posse Christianismum; quid aliud hoc est quam dicere, Christum & Apostolos, quorum scopus utique erat Christianismum stabilire, ea tamen protulisse unde labefactaretur Christianismus, hoc est, sibi scilicet scopoque suo re ipsa contradixisse?
units.tr: The reason why it is credible that, even if such testimonies were given, they would not be prepared to yield, is this: they have imagined it impossible and contrary to nature for spirits to act upon bodies. Upon this principle, whatever they may pretend, the whole system truly rests, and so palpably that they prefer to contradict themselves often rather than depart from that foundation. For after they have laid down as theses, so as not to appear to attack Scripture openly, that good angels indeed minister to faithful men and protect them, and that man was seduced by the ministry of evil angels (that is, of the Devil), it follows plainly that good angels act upon the minds and bodies of the pious, and evil ones, if not directly upon the mind of man, at least upon his senses and body. Yet they are unwilling to acknowledge this, and would rather say that they do not know how it happens, that is, they are unwilling to confess in words what they are aware of, namely that it is contrary to their erroneous prejudice. And hence, when they come to the passages of Scripture that treat of these matters, though they ought to explain them in a way that agrees with the theses they have stated and confirms them, they, in a marvellous manner of contradicting themselves and prevaricating against their own theses, explain everything otherwise, or rather wantonly twist it, so that not even one passage agrees with their theses or supports them. But this would be a small matter, were they not also to bring forward, for the sake of their opinion, those things from which Christ and the Apostles would in fact be shown to contradict themselves. For when on the one hand they teach that Christ, the Evangelists and the Apostles spoke and thought about the Devil and demons as men do, and on the other hand that Christianity could be shaken by what men say and think about demons, what else is this than to say that Christ and the Apostles, whose aim was surely to establish Christianity, nevertheless put forward things by which Christianity would be undermined, that is, that they thereby contradicted themselves and their own aim in fact?

units.la: Sed hæc de ista quidem materia hactenus sufficiant, quæ currente calamo scribi oportuit, quia urgente prælo aliquantulum serius sunt postulata, eo fine, ut bonæ mentes nullis inimici laqueis se implicari patiantur, aut abiis sese expediant qui sincere veritatem quærent per solidas leges Methodi eam vere inveniendi. His, non autem aliis, hæc paucula sufficere crediderim, in quibus si quædam assumpta principia desiderarent deduci & probari specialius, ea alibi a melius pluribus & ex professo poterunt, si velint, videre exposita. Faxit nunc Deus, ut intellectus nostri corruptissimæ activitati, cujus & causas & exempla tristia hactenus monstravimus, non innitamur diutius: sed ut amemus errores nostros innumeros lumine suo nobis detegi; atque via Methodoque tutiore ad veritatem ostensa, suppeditet vires per eam gradiendi, quo ad ERUDITIONEM SOLIDAM tandem possimus pervenire; non detenti superficiaria, non decepti falsa, nec præpediti superba ac pertinaci non recedendi ab erroribus assuetis præjudiciisque amatis voluntate, qua omne malum concluditur. Ad quæ omnia ut sequentes de Eruditione Libri aliquid conferre possint, concedat ille Optimus Maximus, cujus Nomen sit benedictum in secula!
units.tr: But let these remarks on this matter suffice for now. They had to be written with a running pen, since the press was pressing and they were demanded somewhat later than was convenient. The purpose is that good minds may not allow themselves to be entangled in the snares of an enemy, nor be drawn away by those who sincerely seek the truth through the solid rules of the Method by which it is truly found. To these readers, and not to others, I believe these few words will suffice. If some of the principles assumed here should require to be deduced and proved in more detail, they may, if they wish, see them set out elsewhere, and more fully and expressly. May God now grant that we no longer rely on the most corrupt activity of our intellect, whose causes and sad examples we have hitherto shown, but that we love to have our countless errors revealed to us by his light; and that, once the truth has been shown by a safer way and Method, he may supply us with the strength to proceed along it, so that at last we may attain to SOLID ERUDITION: not detained by the superficial, not deceived by the false, nor hindered by the proud and stubborn will that refuses to depart from its accustomed errors and cherished prejudices, in which all evil is contained. May that Most Good and Most Great One, whose Name be blessed for ever, grant that the following books On Erudition may contribute something to all these ends!

units.tr: Who remembers the wandering errors of the mind? What power of Wisdom will detect them? Therefore cleanse away the stains that devious error has secretly poured out. Let not the dread power of impotent Pride claim the realms of the heart for itself. Thus you will easily release me from the fetters of the greatest evils. Receive, O Lord, God and Redeemer, O Art of our Salvation, appeased, the words the tongue pours forth and what the mind silently turns over within itself!

units.la: {dropcap}RUDITIONE nil magis commendatum esse apud Deum & homines, liquido satis constat, quando ille gratiam suam atque Scripturarum oracula commendat (a) ab eruditione; hi vero, ubi ad altiora adspirant, sibi pro scopo proponunt eruditionem; quæ isthoc pacto Dei hominumque communi suffragio veluti (b) fons vitæ denunciatur. Quanti igitur esset, si de nobilissima utilissimaque materia, ea possent proferri, quæ ei si non emolumento, saltem neque dedecori essent! Et hoc ipsum audeo aggredi, meæ quidem, gratificante Deo, conscius tenuitatis; attamen & Numinis auxilio innixus, & bona erga quosvis prænditus voluntate: qua dum omnibus solida bona peropto, neque ignoro eruditionem dari superficiariam, nec non & falsam, quibus a bonis, quæ sola eruditione solida acquiruntur, fit recessus; de tribus illis quædam in medium proferre inducor, quo, istis cognitis & non confusis, omnes queant cupitis bonis non excidere, sed potius eis tutius potiri. Faveat Deus propositio!
units.tr: Nothing is more commended before God and men than erudition, as is quite plain: when God commends his grace and the oracles of Scripture, he commends them by means of erudition, and when men aim at higher things they set erudition before themselves as their goal. By the common agreement of God and men, erudition is thus proclaimed as the fountain of life. How valuable, then, would it be if, on this most noble and useful subject, things could be brought forward that would be of some benefit to it, or at least no discredit! I venture to undertake this very task, conscious of my own slightness, with God's gracious help, yet relying on the aid of the Deity and driven by a good will toward everyone. While I earnestly wish solid goods for all, I am not unaware that there is a superficial erudition and also a false erudition, by which people fall away from the goods that are acquired by solid erudition alone. I am moved to bring forward some things about those three kinds, so that, once they are known and not confused, everyone may be able to avoid losing the desired goods and rather to possess them more securely. May God favour the undertaking!

units.la: A 2 I. Etsi
units.tr: A 2 I. Although

units.la: I. Etsi, quæ ab etymo vocis communiter desumitur rei explicatio, plerumque vulgarior nec satis solida habeatur; hic tamen loci vocabulum Eruditio tam apte generaliorem ejus ideam, qualem initio de re haberi necesse reor, exprimit, ut nil queat esse convenientius quam ab ejus etymi indicatione ordiri.
units.tr: I. Although the explanation of a thing that is commonly drawn from the etymology of the word is usually considered rather vulgar and not solid enough, here the word erudition expresses so aptly its more general idea, such as I think must be had of the matter at the outset, that nothing could be more fitting than to begin from an indication of its etymology.

units.la: Scilicet omnia ea, quæ operibus nonnullis construendis destinata sunt, puta, lapis ad ædificium, vel marmor ad statuam effigiandam, cum ob inæqualitates, ruditatem, scabriciem, inconcinnam figuram, ad scopum suum adhuc inepta sunt, adeo ut bene cohærere suisque adaptari finibus recusent, dicenda forent proprie eruditi, quando superfluis ramentis suis atque inæqualibus prominentiis per malleum aliaque instrumenta liberantur, sicque complanantur & lævigantur, ut sine ruditate possint postea suis polite & congrue destinatis adaptari locis. At isthæc, quæ in sensu hocce proprio non solet usurpari nomenclatura, eadem metaphorica significatione ad Mentes translata est, quæ erudiri dicuntur, quando ea deponunt, quæ scopo ad quem conditæ sunt & existunt, easdem faciebant ineptas; & cum quasi poliuntur, sive formas aut habitus acquirunt faciles, quibus ad finem suum promte & decenter accommodentur.
units.tr: Clearly, all those things that are destined for the construction of some works, for example a stone for a building or marble for carving a statue, while they are still unfit for their purpose because of unevenness, roughness, scabrousness, or an ungainly shape, so that they refuse to fit well together and be adapted to their ends, are properly called erudite when their superfluous chips and uneven protrusions are removed with a mallet and other tools, and they are so planed and smoothed that, free from roughness, they can afterwards be fitted politely and suitably into the places destined for them. But this term, which is not usually used in its proper sense, has been transferred by a metaphorical meaning to minds, which are said to be instructed when they cast off those things which made them unfit for the purpose for which they were made and exist, and when, as it were, they are polished, or acquire ready forms or habits by which they are promptly and fittingly accommodated to their end.

units.la: Hæc est generalior & verior Eruditionis solidæ idea, per quam concidunt plura monstra ad perniciem mortalium æternam sub nomine Eruditionis temere efficta. Hac refecantur tum Eruditio Superficiaria, quæ molem inordinatam, ineptam & rudem, speciosis coloribus superficie tenus solummodo incrustat; tum Eruditio Falsa, quæ moli ineptæ ineptiorem & contrariam suo scopo figuram conciliat. Quæ omnia specialius sunt commonstranda.
units.tr: This is the more general and truer idea of solid erudition, by which the many monsters rashly fashioned under the name of erudition, to the eternal ruin of mortals, are cut down. By this idea are cut away both superficial erudition, which only encrusts the disordered, unfit and rough mass on the surface with showy colours, and false erudition, which gives to the unfit mass a shape even more unfit and contrary to its purpose. All of these must be shown more particularly.

units.la: II. Cum Mens humana, ad quam Eruditio, prout eam nunc considerare decrevi, proprie spectat, non sit eis absolutum, independens, scopusque sui ipsius; sed ens ab alio, ad aliud, aliumque quam se pro scopo habens: sequitur ejus Eruditionem non consistere in illis, quæ ipsamet sibi ad placitum fingere, statuere, imaginari, amplecti satagit: qualia eruditionis falsæ & chimæricæ propria sunt: sed in his solum, quæ Origo summa, Plastes & Archetypus noster, nobis ipse proponit ad scopum sibi placitum; qui, (quoniam a se ipso Deus in condendis operibus dissentire sive discedere nequit,) alius esse non potest, quam, ut repræsentemus naturam & regimen Dei nostri, prout is erga se, hominem & cæteras creaturas sese gerit & repræsentat. Omnis igitur vera Eruditio in his constituenda est, quæ in mentibus nostris eradunt, dejiciunt, & exterminant quæcunque illas minus Deo similes, minusque cum proximis suis in Deo concordes reddunt; nec non in eis quæ similitudinem cum Deo intimam, concordiamque cum proximis divinæ æmulam, promovere & firmare apta sunt. E quibus satis luculenter patet, Eruditionem veram Amore Dei & proximi absolvi ac perfici, timore vero Dei inchoari; Scripturis -
units.tr: II. Since the human mind, to which erudition, as I have decided to consider it now, properly applies, is not something absolute, independent, and its own goal, but a being dependent on another, and having as its goal something other than itself and beyond itself, it follows that its erudition does not consist in those things which it strives to devise, establish, imagine, or embrace for its own pleasure (such as are proper to false and chimerical erudition), but only in those things which our supreme Origin, Maker and Archetype sets before us as his own chosen goal. Since God cannot differ or depart from himself in creating his works, this goal can be nothing other than that we should represent the nature and government of our God, as he conducts and presents himself toward himself, toward man and toward the other creatures. All true erudition, therefore, consists in this: that it eradicates, casts down and exterminates whatever makes our minds less like God and less in concord with our neighbours in God; and likewise in those things which are apt to promote and strengthen an inner likeness to God and a concord with our neighbours that rivals the divine. From these points it is quite clearly evident that true erudition is completed and perfected by the love of God and of neighbour, but begun by the fear of God; Scripture

units.la: sæpissime inculcantibus, (a) timorem Domini initium esse omnis sapientiæ sive Eruditionis veræ: nam ex timore sincero, quo Mens erga Deum tangitur, timens ne ipsa Deo dissimilis sit, ei displiceat, neve in se habeat aut acquirat multa quæ non congruunt cum simílitudine & mente Dei, fit, ut incipiat & decernat a se removere, repellere, dijicere quicquid rude & Deo dissimile, quicquid ei ingratum, in se suspicari potest; quo ab iisdem abstineat, atque iis solum acquirendis incumbat, quæ divinam illam similitudinem divinumque placitum decent ac referunt. Et hoc ipsum est vere erudiri, & ad veram tendere eruditionem; cujus initium, primumque punctum non potuit ordine magis exacto, severo atque, ut ita dicam, magis mathematico vel philosophico proponi, quam in divinis Scripturis designatum est, dum pro saliente veræ Eruditionis puncto hoc nobis commendat, Timor Domini, initium Sapientiæ.
units.tr: very often inculcating that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of all wisdom, that is, of true erudition. For from the sincere fear by which the mind is touched toward God, fearing lest it be unlike God, displease him, or have in itself or acquire many things which do not agree with the likeness and mind of God, it comes about that it begins and resolves to remove, repel and cast away from itself whatever is rude and unlike God, whatever it can suspect to be unpleasing to him; so that it abstains from these things and applies itself only to acquiring those things which befit and reflect that divine likeness and divine pleasure. This very thing is truly to be instructed and to tend toward true erudition. Its beginning and first point could not have been set forth in a more exact, severe and, so to speak, more mathematical or philosophical order than it is designated in the divine Scriptures, where, as the leading point of true erudition, it commends to us: The fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom.

units.la: III. Hic ostendendum foret, { quantum imbecillitas nostra fert} quid sit Deus, qui
units.tr: III. Here it would be necessary to show, as far as our weakness allows, what God is,

units.la: 3. De Deo Menteque sese gerat, quibus dotibus mentes humanas beaverit, ut illae possint Deum suum imitari, cum illo congruere, & ruditates, si quae illis insint, deponere, sicque per veram Eruditionem Deo, ejus conversationi, deliciis, inhabitationi, ipsae fieri accommodatissimae. Ad hoc autem non est necesse æterni Dei existentiam & naturam, aut animae naturam & immortalitatem, quae alibi ex professo contra Scepticos dubitantes & Spinozianos Atheos demonstravimus, de novo evincere: aut eorum regiminis libertatem & modos mutuos, quae ibidem abunde deduximus, iterum depingere. Operae pretium tamen est nonnulla generaliora tum de Deo, tum de mentis facultatibus, prae oculis praesentia habere, quae alioqui, cum subjectum ipsum, de quo agimus, immediate concernant, plane non possent sine ejus detrimento & consusione praetermitti. Sequentia itaque haud oscitanter sunt expendenda.
units.tr: 3. Concerning God and the mind: how God conducts himself, with what gifts he has endowed human minds, so that they may imitate their God, agree with him, and put off whatever crudeness may be in them, and so by true learning become most fitting for God, for his fellowship, delight and indwelling. For this purpose it is not necessary to prove afresh the existence and nature of the eternal God, or the nature and immortality of the soul, which we have demonstrated elsewhere at length against the doubting Sceptics and the atheistic Spinozists; nor to describe again the freedom of their government and their mutual modes, which we have there set out fully. Yet it is worth keeping before our eyes some more general points both about God and about the faculties of the mind. Since these bear directly on the very subject we are treating, they cannot be passed over without harm and confusion. The following, then, must be weighed carefully.

units.la: IV. Deum nempe infinite perfectam, incomprehensibilem, atque aeternam Mentem esse, hoc est, talem, quae non modo initio & fine existendi caret, sed & quae realitates infinitas unite totas semel actu velut in puncto indistincto simul possidet: Eundem quoque, cum distinctius & veluti aliquo modo extra aeternitatis hujus indistinctae consiberationem punctumque indivisum sese respicit, in adorandum aliquod Trinum discerni, quod Desiderio immenso atque vividissimo erga se suasque perfectiones, Luminosa sui intellectione atque Idea, Acquiescentia denique & Amore seu Laetitia infinita, (sive Patre, Filio, & Spiritu Sancto, Trinitate adorabili,) perficitur. In his autem, ut ita loquar, totam Dei naturam, solidam existentiam, perfectionem, felicitatem, contineri, exclusis quibuslibet aliis quarumcunque rerum ideis, & realitatibus, quae coram illo non modo non res aut ideae accessoriae, sed & purum nihil sunt, quo beatum & perfectum Ens absolute carere ad perfectionem & felicitatem posset.
units.tr: IV. Namely, God is an infinitely perfect, incomprehensible and eternal Mind; that is, one that not only lacks beginning and end of existence, but also possesses all infinite realities together, wholly and at once, as in an undivided point. This same Mind, when it considers itself more distinctly, and as it were apart from this indistinct consideration of eternity and its undivided point, is discerned as a Trinity worthy of adoration. This Trinity is completed by an immense and most lively desire for itself and its perfections, by a luminous self-understanding and Idea, and finally by an infinite acquiescence and love or joy (namely, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the adorable Trinity). In these, so to speak, the whole nature of God is contained: his solid existence, perfection and happiness, excluding any other ideas and realities of whatever things. These are not merely accessory things or ideas in his sight, but pure nothing, which the blessed and perfect Being absolutely could lack, and still be perfect and happy.

units.la: Capacitate sua cultatesque admittendi correspondentes in esse.
units.tr: Having its own capacity, and the power to admit corresponding realities into being.

units.la: Deum
units.tr: Of God

units.la: Deum illum voluisse, (ut se qua talem vivide repraesentaret,) condere Mentes, quae non tantum in sempiternum duraturae sunt; sed & quarum substantialissima atque essentialissima portio, vel dos, vel naturae recondita radix & substantia, sit fundus vel receptus quidam immensus, sive intima nonnulla capacitas, & aptitudo quaedam immensa & infinita, quae ipsam aeternitatem, sive Deum aeternum modo unito, simultaneo & indistincto vivide & plane mirabiliter, sine ulla successionis & pluralitatis distinctione & duratione, admittere, percipere, possidere valet; (quae ardua, alibi a me exposita, videat qui velit.) Hic est ille animae fundus tantopere nonnullis celebratus, quem nulla creatura, nec vero ipsa creata Mens, non modo non replere, sed quidem movere aut attingere potest: locus ideis vacuus, thronus Deo aeterno sacer, ejusque solius aeternas impressiones suscipere aptus.
units.tr: God willed (so that he might vividly represent himself as such) to create minds, which are not only to endure forever, but whose most substantial and essential portion, or dowry, or hidden root and substance of their nature, is a kind of immense ground or receptacle, or an inner capacity and immense and infinite aptitude, which is able to admit, perceive and possess the eternity itself, that is, the eternal God, in a united, simultaneous and undivided mode, vividly and quite wonderfully, without any distinction of succession, plurality or duration. (Whoever wishes may see these difficult matters, which I have set out elsewhere.) This is that ground of the soul so much celebrated by some, which no creature, not even the created mind itself, can not only fill, but even move or touch: a place empty of ideas, a throne sacred to the eternal God, fit to receive his eternal impressions alone.

units.la: Observandum praeterea iisdem mentibus inesse quoque distinctiores facultates sive capacitates ad idem Numen relatas: puta, Desiderium immensum, sive facultatem desiderandi Deum immensum, divinique desiderii infiniti impressiones & actus admittendi: Intellectum immensum, sive capacitatem immensam recipiendi Intellectionem, sive Lucem, sive Verbum Imaginemque Dei luminosam: denique Acquiescentiam, seu facultatem atque capacitatem immensam admittendi & possidendi divinam Acquiescentiam, Dilectionem, Laetitiam, Spiritumque que Dei adorabilem, cumque eo æternum deliciandi. Atque ita Mentes nostras non modo conditas esse ad Imaginem & repræsentationem Immensi & Æterni Dei, adorandique Mysterii Trinitatis, (Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti;) sed & ad Ejusdem admissionem, inhabitationem, immeationem, possessionem, commercium, æternasque & incomprehensibiles omnium in bonis & realitatibus Divinitatis perceptiones & voluptates: quam ob causam, his, quas diximus, substantialissimis & essentialissimis capacitatibus sive facultatibus, sunt a Plaste potentissimo Optimoque donatæ.
units.tr: It should further be observed that the same minds also have more distinct faculties or capacities related to the same Deity: namely, an immense desire, that is, the faculty of desiring God immensely, and of admitting the impressions and acts of infinite divine desire; an immense understanding, that is, an immense capacity for receiving intellection, or light, or the Word and luminous Image of God; and finally an immense acquiescence, or faculty and capacity of admitting and possessing divine acquiescence, love, joy, and the adorable Spirit of God, and of taking eternal delight with him. And so our minds were not only created to be an image and representation of the immense and eternal God and of the adorable mystery of the Trinity (Father, Son and Holy Spirit), but also for his admission, indwelling, entrance, possession, and intercourse, and for eternal and incomprehensible perceptions and pleasures in all the goods and realities of the Godhead. For this reason they were given these most substantial and essential capacities or faculties, which we have described, by the most powerful and best Maker.

units.la: V. Impense optarem hæc jam pro dignitate sua diutius considerari, nec non memoriæ atque cordia alte vivideque imprimi. Hæc enim sola ad mentes proprie spectant, sola earum æternum duraturam perfectionem, felicitatem, solidam atque essentialem sic constituunt, ut cætera omnia, omnesque de rebus aliis quibuscunque creatis ideæ, perceptiones, sensationes, non modo mere externæ & accessoriæ sint; sed &, maxime in quo nunc sunt statu, ad interitum universæ pertineant. Hinc proinde in erudienda Mente filum Ariadneum est desumendum. Nam si aliud quam facultates nostras fundamentales, æternas & (capacitate) immensas, quibus vere homines sumus, Deique imagines vivæ, curaverimus; si his prætermissis superficiarias, deceptorias & instabiles facultates Rationis, Imaginationis, aliasque minusculas parvulis inferioris sortis objectis occupaverimus & coluerimus, ad interitum tantum laboravimus, omnibus quidem olim evanescentibus, mente vero remanente in eo vacuitatis statu, in quo a propria & insanabili facultatum inanium fame immensa, aeternum cruciabitur. Sed redeamus ad propositum, & rerum considerandarum indicemus seriem.
units.tr: V. I would earnestly wish that these things were now considered at length, in keeping with their dignity, and deeply and vividly impressed on memory and heart. For these alone properly concern the minds; these alone constitute their eternally enduring perfection, happiness, and solid and essential being. So all else, all ideas, perceptions and sensations of any other created things, are not only merely external and accessory, but, especially in the state they now are in, tend to destruction. Hence, in the education of the mind, the Ariadne's thread must be taken up. For if we have been concerned with anything other than our fundamental, eternal and (in capacity) immense faculties, by which we are truly human and living images of God; if, neglecting these, we have occupied and cultivated the superficial, deceptive and unstable faculties of Reason and Imagination, and other trifling powers, with the petty objects of an inferior sort, we have laboured only toward destruction. All these things will indeed vanish one day, and the mind will remain in that state of emptiness, where it will be tormented forever by its own and incurable hunger for empty faculties. But let us return to our purpose, and point out the order of the things to be considered.

units.la: VI. Scilicet Deum, qui se solo aeterno & trino sibi sufficiebat, ex mera & indifferenti arbitrii libertate voluisse ad lusum gaudiumque arbitrarium depingi & repraesentari, non solum modo vivido, quam ob rem mentes, quales nunc diximus, effecit; verum etiam modo umbratili, & (comparate ad veram vitam veraque interiora) veluti mortuo & superficiario. Hinc in conceptu ejus natas esse ideas rerum, totiusque universi, quarum unaquaeque repraesentabat suo modo tum praecipuam aliquam Dei perfectionem, tum vero (quia perfectio nulla in Deo a caeteris separatur,) indirecte & dilutius omnes caeteras: hinc nulla res est, nullave idea seu natura, quae non aliarum rerum sive ideatarum rerum aliquid (unde rerum nexus & immeationes mirabiles) secum involvat; quia nempe perfectio divina quaelibet, quam idea rei creabilis cujuscunque repræsentat, aliquid, etsi indirectius, cæterarum divinarum persectionum secum in conceptu involvit; quod rerum ideis & naturis simili modo decuit repræsentari.
units.tr: VI. Namely, God, who was sufficient to himself in his solely eternal and triune being, willed, from pure and indifferent freedom of choice, to be depicted and represented in play and arbitrary joy, not only in a lively mode, for which reason he made minds such as we have now described, but also in a shadowy mode, and (compared with true life and true inner things) as it were dead and superficial. Hence, in his conception, the ideas of things and of the whole universe were born, each of which represented in its own way either some particular perfection of God or, since no perfection in God is separated from the others, all the others indirectly and more faintly. Hence there is no thing or idea or nature which does not involve within itself something of other things or ideas (whence come the wonderful connections and interpenetrations of things); for any divine perfection which the idea of any creatable thing represents, involves within its conception something, though more indirectly, of the other divine perfections. It was fitting that the ideas and natures of things should be represented in this similar way.

units.la: Notari hic velim, Deum, cum ideas rerum, quas excogitavit, contemplatur, duo in illis conspicere; primo, sui suarumque perfectionum, puta potentiae, activitatis, felicitatis, foecunditatis, aliarumque, imaginesque sive ideas nonnullas speculativas, illis, quas ipse a se & in se directe habet, dilutiores; secundo, ipsarum ideas rerum prout ad ipsas res terminantur. Quae consideratio magnae & perniciosae in rebus eruditionis sallaciae evitandae ansam dabit, uti mox monebimus.
units.tr: I would have it noted here that when God contemplates the ideas of things which he has devised, he perceives two things in them. First, the images or ideas of himself and of his perfections, such as power, activity, happiness, fruitfulness and others, which are somewhat fainter than those he has directly from himself and in himself, and some speculative ideas; second, the ideas of the things themselves as they are bounded by the things. This consideration will provide an occasion for avoiding a great and harmful fallacy in matters of learning, as we shall warn shortly.

units.la: Quam vis autem Deus, Mentes ad sui Imaginem condere volens, eis praeter illam vividam Aeternitatis Sanctaeque suae Trinitatis Imaginem nil largiri praeterea potuisset, ipsaeque hac sola dotatae perfectione, & felicitate essentialissima (hoc est, maxime intima, completa, plena & solidissima) praeditae & perfectissime satiatae fuissent; placuit tamen Numini liberalissimo & accessorias, superficiariasque nonnullas capacitates sive facultates Menti donare, quibus illarum Dei de rebus externis idearum, illorum Dei arbitrariorum ludorum, esset aemula & repraesentatrix. Unde orta est in mente facultas accessoria & superficiaria Rationis, quae alias intellectus activus dicitur, estque rerum ideis efformandis & continendis destinata.
units.tr: Although God, wishing to create minds in his own image, could have bestowed on them nothing beyond that vivid image of eternity and of his holy Trinity, and they would have been endowed with this one perfection and most essential happiness alone (that is, most inward, complete, full and solid) and perfectly satisfied; nevertheless, it pleased the most liberal Deity to grant the mind also some accessory and superficial capacities or faculties, by which it would be a rival and representative of God's ideas of external things, that is, of God's arbitrary games. From this arose in the mind the accessory and superficial faculty of Reason, which is otherwise called the active intellect, and is destined for forming and containing the ideas of things.

units.la: VII. Haec autem facultas nullam Aeternitatis divinae, nullam sanctae Trinitatis, divinorumque attributorum ideam vividam (prout facultates superiores) admittit; sed tantum eorundem umbras, ideas dilutas, mortuas, & veluti externas & superficiarias, quales modo diximus & in rebus creabilibus ideas de Deo divinisque posse conspici. Quod diligentissime advertendum est: quoniam inde exitialis quidam error poterit & debet maxime praecaveri. Quicunque enim ideas de Deo rebusque divinis per Rationis suae actus efformatas, confunderet cum lumine Dei vero, Ideisque vividis, quae in intellectu supremo per Lumen Verbumque Dei excitantur, nec non cum inspirationibus luminosisque Spiritus Sancti quibus divina salutariter & solide explicantur, is erraret omnium exitialissimo errore; & pro Deo vivo, solidoque ejus Verbi ac Spiritus lumine & motu, simulacra inania, sterilia, frigida Rationis suae, facultatis superficiariae, ampletereturque; a quibus cum non posset perfici nec beari, vacuitas & miseria aeterna ei, (nisi resipisceret) certo certius superesset. Atque hoc morbo periculosissimo Cartesiani quam plurimi hodie laborant, dum ideas steriles, ne dicam saepe ridiculas, Rationis suae, pro divino lumine, pro Scripturarum sive sensus Dei interpretamentis, pro Spiritus Dei actibus, notionibus, inspirationibusque (quales ad salutarem Scripturarum rerumque divinarum cognitionem requiri confitentur omnes,) nobis obtrudunt. Quae perniciosa confusio inde orta est, quod Cartesius ipse, eorum Antesignanus, in Natura mentis cognoscenda, qualem jam per fundum, capacitates facultatesve ejus pro Deo solido, vel pro ideis ejus rerumque accessoriis factas, explicuimus, plane coecutierit. Sed nec eidem malo minus obnoxii sunt & cæteri non-Cartesiani: quamvis enim divinum lumen divinumque actum, ab actibus Rationis distinctum, verbis profiteantur, nihilominus tamen de facto nil aliud plerique quam propriæ Rationis suæ actus amplectuntur, quos nomine actuum Spiritus S. fideique infigniunt. Utinam omnes ab hoc errore resipiscerent, cujus pericula, & tandem emergentem inde Atheismum, (a) alibi pluribus ostendi!
units.tr: VII. This faculty, however, admits no vivid idea of the eternity of God, of the holy Trinity, or of the divine attributes (as the higher faculties do), but only their shadows, faint, dead ideas, as it were external and superficial, such as we have just described, and such as concerning God and divine things can be seen in creatable things. This must be noted most carefully, since from it a certain deadly error can and must be especially guarded against. For whoever confuses the ideas of God and divine things formed by the acts of his Reason with the true light of God, and with the vivid ideas which are stirred up in the supreme intellect through the Light and Word of God, and also with the inspirations and luminous influences of the Holy Spirit, by which divine things are explained saving and solidly, would fall into the most deadly of all errors. In place of the living God, and of the solid light and motion of his Word and Spirit, he would embrace empty, barren, cold images of his own Reason, a superficial faculty; and since he could not be perfected or blessed by these, emptiness and eternal misery would surely await him, unless he came to his senses. Many Cartesians today suffer from this most dangerous disease, while they thrust on us barren ideas of their own Reason, often ridiculous, not to say so, in place of the divine light, in place of the interpretations of the sense of Scripture and of God, in place of the acts, notions and inspirations of the Spirit of God (which all admit are required for the saving knowledge of the Scriptures and divine things). This pernicious confusion arose because Descartes himself, the leader of these men, in investigating the nature of the mind, which we have just explained through its ground, its capacities and faculties, made for solid God or for his ideas and accessory things, was utterly blind. Yet the other non-Cartesians are no less liable to this same evil. For although they profess in words a divine light and a divine act distinct from the acts of Reason, nevertheless in fact most of them embrace nothing but the acts of their own Reason, which they label with the name of the acts of the Holy Spirit and of faith. Would that all might come to their senses from this error, whose dangers, and the atheism finally arising from it, I have shown at greater length elsewhere!

units.la: VIII. Quia vero & Ratio suo modo, hoc est, dilute & per adumbrationem, Sanctæ Trinitatis gerit Imaginem, (quæ & in omnibus rebus atque ideis, nulla prorsus excepta, diversis modis depingitur) hinc in illa deprehendere est, primo, desiderium aliquod sciendi, sive ideas rerum detegendi, quod jam, post peccati dominium, concupiscentia oculorum Johanni & Augustino dicitur, & curiositas vulgo appellatur: secundo, lumen rationis, ideæ ipsæ, intellectiove superficiaria, & activa suarum, quicquid alii dicant, idearum certis conditionibus effectrix; tertio, acquiescentia quædam in idearum ejusmodi di contemplatione & combinatione; quæ acquiescentia aliàs affirmatio dicitur. Et circa hæc quidem sola eruditionem veram versari vulgo produnt: sed quam prave, quamque periculose id fiat, jam aliquatenus monuimus, monebimusque deinceps distinctius, dum Rationis proprietates, usum, abusumque indicabimus obiter. Discursum yel ratiocinationem ad activam vim rationis ideas sibi excitantis, atque ad acquiescentiam referimus; quando nempe ideæ quædam primo intuitu vel obscuriores, vel complicatiores sunt quam ut mens possit eis acquiescere, adeoque opus habet eas pluribus actibus, modis, respectibus, conjunctione aut sejunctione cum & ab aliis intueri, ut ipsæ ei clariores appareant, quo tandem eis acquiescere possit.
units.tr: VIII. Since Reason also bears, in its own way (that is, faintly and by way of shadow), an image of the Holy Trinity, which is portrayed in all things and ideas without exception and in various ways, we may detect in it, first, a certain desire of knowing, or of uncovering the ideas of things, which after the dominion of sin is called the lust of the eyes by John and Augustine, and is commonly called curiosity; second, the light of reason, the ideas themselves, and the superficial and active intellect, which, whatever others may say, effects its ideas under certain conditions; third, a certain acquiescence in the contemplation and combination of such ideas, which acquiescence is elsewhere called affirmation. And people commonly declare that true learning is concerned with these things alone. But how wrongly and how dangerously this is done we have already pointed out to some extent, and we will warn more distinctly hereafter, while we indicate in passing the properties, use and abuse of Reason. We refer discourse, or reasoning, to the active power of reason which excites ideas in itself, and to acquiescence; namely, when certain ideas, at first sight, are either too obscure or too complicated for the mind to acquiesce in them, and so it needs to view them by several acts, modes and respects, and by joining or separating them, and also by means of others, so that they may appear clearer to it, and at last it may be able to acquiesce in them.

units.la: IX. Quemadmodum autem Deus ille, qui se solo æterno sibi sufficiebat plene, non tantum arbitraria voluntate accessorias rerum creabilium ideas ad sui accidentariam (ut sic loquar) delectationem contemplari voluit; sed & ipsi placuit, ut illæ, hoc est, res ipsæ ideatæ, existerent, quas Deus de facto existentes haberet, possideret, quasque adeo singulari modo veluti præsentes sibi stitit, imaginatus est, disposuit, percepit, deque eis est lætatus; Ita etiam non satis ei fuit considere Mentes, quæ fundi & facultatum divinarum & essentialium donatione, solo Deo sofuum, modi, & passionum, tionis accessu non necessario, ideas rerum ad cumcorpore accidentariam delectationem intuerentur: sed & voluit ut illæ cum rebus ipsis commercium haberent, easque perciperent, possiderent, regerent. Unde & mentibus donavit capacitates sive facultates cum corpore certo, quibus hæc exequerentur, videlicet, Imaginationem, Sensus, facultatem motricem, (quæ loquelam includit) & affectus sive passiones animæ; de quibus omnibus, etsi in Oeconomia fuius egi, tamen in hoc argumento, de quo agimus, ea oculis subduci omnino non debent, siquidem permulti si non totam, maximam tamen eruditionis partem in illis nunc constituunt quae ad imaginationem, sensus, motus & affectus pertinent.
units.tr: IX. Just as that God, who was fully sufficient to himself by his eternal self alone, willed not merely by arbitrary will to contemplate the ideas of created things, which were accessory to him, for his accidental (as I may say) delight, but also it pleased him that those things, that is, the things themselves that had been conceived, should exist, which God would have, possess, and which he thus set before himself in a singular way as if present, imagined, arranged and perceived, and in which he rejoiced; so too it was not enough for him that minds, which by the gift of divine and essential faculties were founded upon God alone, should behold the ideas of things in an accidental delight, without any necessary approach of body, modes and passions. He willed also that these ideas should have intercourse with the things themselves, and that minds should perceive, possess and direct them. Hence he also gave to minds capacities or faculties to carry these out together with a certain body, namely, imagination, the senses, the motive faculty (which includes speech), and the affections or passions of the soul. Although I have treated of all these in the Oeconomy of this work, yet in the present argument, which we are discussing, they must by no means be withdrawn from our eyes, since very many people now place in these, if not the whole, at least the greatest part of learning, namely that which pertains to imagination, senses, motions and affections.

units.la: X. Atque haec sunt omnia, quibus hominem perfici potuisse, cogitari potest: complete nempe perfectione solida & essentiali per divinas intimas & immensas sui fundi, desiderii, intellectus, suaeque acquiescentiae capacitates, Deo aeterno & Triuno repletas; accidentarie vero per umbratiles, superficiales & limitatas facultates Rationis, imaginationis, sensuum, motuum, & passionum, obiectis suis tenuiusculis & limitatis, ideis videlicet, figuris, coloribus & sonis, motibus & similibus affectas, &, non repletas, sed impulsas & tactas, in quibus tamen imagines potentiae, sapientiae, & bonitatis Dei sui, magis quam ipsas sensationes ad se spectantes homo curabat. Hisce omnibus is in creatione a Summo Rerum Auctore instructus antequam ad deteriora laberetur, omnibus erat numeris absolutus, (quod singulatim (a) alibi exposui,) hincque Sapiens, non vero Eruditus erat proprie dicendus: siquidem haec ipsa non acquisiverat per viam erudiendi & poliendi in se quae antea incondita, rudia, aspera & incomposita fuerint; sed per simplicem sui cum divina Sapientia conjunctionem & familiaritatem.
units.tr: X. These are all the things by which man could be thought to have been perfected: complete, that is, with solid and essential perfection, through the divine, inward and immense capacities of his foundation, desire, intellect and acquiescence, filled with the eternal and triune God; and accidentally, through the shadowy, superficial and limited faculties of reason, imagination, senses, motions and passions, endowed with their slight and limited objects, namely ideas, figures, colours and sounds, motions and the like; not filled, but impelled and touched. Yet in these things man attended more to the images of the power, wisdom and goodness of his God than to the sensations themselves as they related to himself. Equipped with all these things by the Supreme Author of all things in creation, before he fell into worse, he was perfect in every respect (which I have set forth singly elsewhere), and therefore he was to be called wise, not properly learned; since he had not acquired these things by the way of teaching and polishing within himself what had previously been crude, rough, harsh and unformed, but by a simple conjunction and familiarity of himself with divine Wisdom.

units.la: XI. Postquam autem homo aeternam (sensu jam dicto) atque immensam fundi sui capacitatem, nec non divinas desiderii infiniti, intel-
units.tr: XI. But after man chose to recall from the eternal (in the sense already stated) and immense capacity of his foundation, and likewise the divine faculties of infinite desire, intel-

units.la: intellectus & acquiescentiæ facultates ab objecto æterno, divino, solo solido, Triuno Deo, revocare, ab ejus adhæsione & contemplatione continua cessare; facultates accidentarias & superficiales præcipue exercere, ad exteriora sese convertere, & ex proprio figmento ad arbitrium sapere & beatus esse voluit; mox omni ex parte, intus & extus, factus est obscurus, confusus, miser & stupidus, in quo omnia, fundus, diviniores facultates, ratio, imaginatio, cæteraque, cæca, rudia & aspera; verbo, ipse totus homo crassus & rudis: qui nisi quoad omnes facultates penetrante lixivio lavetur, forti pumice fricetur, impigra dolabra lævigetur & erudiatur, manebit crassus & rudis asinus in omnem æternitatem.
units.tr: intellect and acquiescence, from the eternal, divine, sole solid object, the triune God; to cease from his continual adherence to him and contemplation of him; to exercise chiefly the accidental and superficial faculties, to turn himself to outward things, and, from his own invention, to be wise and happy at his own pleasure: at once, on every side, within and without, he became dark, confused, wretched and stupid. In him everything was so: the foundation, the more divine faculties, reason, imagination, and the rest, blind, rough and harsh; in a word, the whole man himself was gross and crude. Unless he is washed with a penetrating lye in all his faculties, rubbed with a strong pumice, smoothed and educated with a tireless adze, he will remain a gross and crude ass for all eternity.

units.la: Quod autem inferiores facultates, quales ratio & cæteræ jam nominatæ, integræ non potuerint permanere, postquam superiores & solidæ a Deo defecerunt, patet ex eo, quod earum natura non modo superiorum imitatrix & veluti eẜtypa erat, quodque etiam ex ab illis & regebantur & lumen mutuabantur; sed ex eo quoque & præcipue, quod Deus posthabitus & contemtus non potuit contemtum sui effusa benedictione approbare; quin potius eum decuit neglectores & contemtores sui negligere, & in sensum omnino reprobum tradere, uti Paulus loquitur & ostendit, Rom. 1. Quam inordinationem, ejusque necessariam seriem, cum alibi integro libro tradiderim, illius commemoratione hic supersedeo,
units.tr: That the inferior faculties, such as reason and the others already named, could not remain whole after the higher and solid ones had fallen away from God, is plain from this: their nature was not only an imitator of the higher faculties and, as it were, their copy, and was both governed by them and borrowed light from them; but also, and especially, because God, being set aside and despised, could not approve the one who despised him by pouring out his blessing. Rather, it was fitting for him to disregard those who neglect and despise him, and to give them over to a reprobate mind, as Paul speaks and shows, Rom. 1. Since I have set out this disorder and its necessary sequence in an entire book elsewhere, I forgo here any mention of it.

units.la: XII. Quænam vero in homine erudienda sint, e superiori facultatum suarum enumera- tione satis patescere puto.
units.tr: XII. What in fact is to be taught in man, I think, is sufficiently clear from the earlier enumeration of his faculties.

units.la: Verum ut ratio distinctionis, quam circa Eruditionem sumus adhibituri, dum eam in solidam, superficiariam & falsam dividimus, evidentius inspicere possit, eam per similitudinem sic elucidabo, ut facili negotio possit & comprehendi & retineri. Imaginemur ergo Mentem esse veluti Globum quendam crystallinum infinitæ amplitudinis, qui replendus sit infinito lumine a centro in omnem capacitatem ejus sese diffundente. Talis enim est Mens ejusque fundus, tales ejus facultates seu capacitates respectu Dei, luminis æterni & infiniti: At vero globus iste, qui in relatione ad Deum est capacitatis immensæ, itidem, quatenus cum rebus ideisve, quæ Deus non sunt, commercium habere debet, quadam veluti superficie (qua respectu divini commercii caret) præditus considerari debet. Superficiei huic tria, plurave accidere possunt; primo, ut in illa lineamentis & coloribus quibusdam multa depingantur & delineentur; secundo, ut ipsa superficies figuram suam rebus applicitis accommodet, eamque multifariam immutet; tertio, ut de loco in locum transportetur; quarto, ut fortiter pulsetur ab illis quæ fortiter in eam irruunt: quorum omnium primum, Rationem & imaginationem; secundum, sensus; tertium, facultatem motricem; quartum, affectus sive passiones designat. Quemadmodum autem hæc ante hominis lapsum ordinatissima erant; ita post eundem, lumen e fundo & e capacitatibus immensis evanuit, succedentibus tenebris asperrimis & immanibus: Superficies vero coloribus atris, monstrosis lineamentis atque figmentis, utrDque commaculata & incrustata, ipsamet in monstrosas, turpes asperasque formas effigiata, incompositte tremula ubi quiescere, vel stupide immota ubi moveri deberet, denique quibusvis extraneis impulsibus obnoxia. Si jam supponamus, aliquem fundo & facultatibus intimis depurandis & disponendis, (ad quas & externae inordinationes aliquatenus (sed non funditus) radices egerunt nonnullas,) vacare, id Eruditionis solidae speciem nobis exhibet, (quae, sicuti a bono facultatum internarum statu, status superficiariarum bonus est individuus; ita & haec exteriora quoque complectitur:) si vero externae superficiei detergendae, laevigandae, sedandae, lineamentis, figuris, motibus ordinatis perficiendae praecipue incumbat, id Eruditionem superficialem ob oculos ponit: Eruditio autem falsa depingitur, si neglecto fundo cum facultatibus suis divinioribus, superficies chimaeris, nugis, inutilibus, noxiis, luto, & quibuslibet quisquiliis, incrustetur & contaminetur. Quorum omnium ἀπόδειξις quia facilis est & clara, praetermittimus.
units.tr: To make the principle of the distinction we are about to use concerning Erudition more evident, as we divide it into solid, superficial and false, I will explain it by a comparison, so that it can be easily grasped and retained. Let us imagine the Mind to be a kind of crystal globe of infinite extent, which is to be filled with infinite light spreading from the centre into all its capacity. For such is the Mind and its ground, and such are its faculties or capacities in relation to God, the eternal and infinite light. But this globe, which in relation to God has immense capacity, must also, insofar as it ought to have dealings with things and ideas that are not God, be considered as provided with a kind of surface (which lacks any such relation to divine dealings). Four things can happen to this surface: first, that many things are painted and drawn on it with certain lines and colours; second, that the surface itself adapts its shape to the objects applied to it and changes it in many ways; third, that it is carried from place to place; fourth, that it is struck hard by whatever rushes violently against it. Of these, the first denotes Reason and imagination; the second, the senses; the third, the motive faculty; the fourth, the affections or passions. Now, before the fall of man these were perfectly ordered; but after it, the light vanished from the ground and from the immense capacities, with the darkest and most savage shadows succeeding it. The surface, however, was stained and encrusted on both sides with black colours, monstrous lines and figments, and shaped into monstrous, foul and rough forms; it trembles without composure where it ought to rest, or lies stupidly motionless where it ought to move, and is finally exposed to every foreign impulse. If we now suppose someone to be occupied with cleansing and arranging the ground and the innermost faculties (into which outward disorders have also struck some roots, though not deep ones), this presents us with the appearance of solid Erudition (which, just as a good state of the inner faculties goes together with a good state of the surface, also embraces these outer things). But if someone devotes himself chiefly to cleansing, smoothing and calming the outer surface, and to perfecting it with lines, figures and ordered motions, this sets before our eyes superficial Erudition. False Erudition, however, is depicted when, with the ground and its higher faculties neglected, the surface is encrusted and contaminated with chimeras, trifles, useless and harmful things, mud, and all kinds of rubbish. Since the demonstration of all these points is easy and clear, I pass it over.

units.la: XIII. Eruditionis generalioribus perspectis, nec non ejusdem speciebus commemoratis, e re foret de unaquaque singulatim ostendere quomodo acquiratur, quomodo possideatur, quomodo denique communicetur; sive, quod eodem recidit, quomodo fiant, qui
units.tr: XIII. Having considered Erudition in its more general aspects, and having also mentioned its kinds, it would be fitting to show for each one separately how it is acquired, how it is possessed, and finally how it is communicated; or, what comes to the same thing, how those become

units.la: Tria in unaquaque eruditione perpetuo studiosa modum spectanda. qui affecti sint, & quibus modis doceant sive sese propagent solidi, superficiales & falsi eruditi; aut denique spectanda esset eruditio in acquisitione, possessione, & communicatione sui: quod brevibus subindicare potius quam tractare annitemur.
units.tr: Three things are always to be considered in any studious erudition: the manner in which solid, superficial and false scholars are formed, and how they teach or propagate themselves; or finally, Erudition should be considered in its acquisition, possession and communication of itself. We shall endeavour to point these out briefly rather than to treat them at length.

units.la: XIV. Initio, considerandum est serio, I. hominem respectu durationis suae futurae, creaturam esse aeternam, hujusque aeternae durationis hanc praesentem vitam, quam hoc in statu, haec inter corporea vivimus, non partem, sed vix punctulum & momentum evanidum esse, quo evanescente, omnia quae inseriores & superficiarias facultates, rationem, sensus, caeterasque concernunt, qualia jam sunt, aeternum quoque penitus evanescunt.
units.tr: XIV. First, it must be seriously considered: 1. that man, with respect to his future duration, is an eternal creature; and that this present life, which we live in this state, among bodily things, is not a part of this eternal duration but scarcely a point and a passing moment. When this vanishes, all that concerns the lower and superficial faculties, reason, the senses and the rest, as they now are, will also vanish utterly and for ever.

units.la: 2. Observandum deinde, fugax hocce momentum ea nobis conditione concessum esse, ut a modo quo fuerimus eo usi, idque impenderimus, pendeat tota sequens aeternitas, in plena fundi & facultatum omnium perfectione, illustratione & deliciis; aut in earundem imperfectione, tenebris & anxietatibus perpetuis ducenda, prout diversis modis momentulum hocce fuerit transactum.
units.tr: 2. Next it is to be observed that this fleeting moment is granted to us on the condition that the whole eternity that follows depends on how we have used it and how we have spent it: whether it is passed in full perfection, enlightenment and delights of the ground and of all the faculties, or in their imperfection, in darkness and perpetual anxieties, according to the different ways in which this little moment has been spent.

units.la: 3. Notandum tertio, nobis hac in vita eam esse facultatum infirmitatem, ut pluribus simul vacare non possimus; sed alia dimittenda esse, si aliis fuerit incumbendum.
units.tr: 3. Third, it is to be noted that in this life our faculties are so weak that we cannot attend to several things at once; if we must attend to some, others must be put aside.

units.la: 4. Animadvertendum quarto, eam esse & facultatum, actuum objectorumque suorum naturam, ut sese adjuvent & promoveant, si debito ordine exerceantur; se vero impediant & tollant, si ordine praeposteró & perverso pertractentur. Debitus autem ordo is est, quem superius in enumerandis facultatibus sumus secuti ; nimirum, primo, Fundus sive capacitas mentis immensa ad Deum æternum, nec non facultates diviniores desiderii, intellectus & acquiescentiæ ad eundem Deum Triunum, (sese desiderantem, contemplantem, in se acquiescentem,) ejusque ad attributa & perfectiones divinas conditæ : dein, Ratio, data ad ideas umbratiles tum Dei, ejusque attributorum, (quæ immensum a vividis facultatum superiorum ideis sive lumine differunt,) tum rerum a Deo creatarum : postremo, Imaginatio & reliquæ. A fundo enim superioribusque inferiora omnia veluti catenatim dependent, fluunt, & inde robur, lumen & decus mutuantur, cum sint ejus, quod in centro est, ceu expansio & explicatio atque repræsentatio dilatior. Unde qui rite incipit a centro, huic veluti sine labore alio omnia cætera, saltem necessaria & debita, per se videntur advolare : qui vero interiora omittit ut inferiora curet, hic & divinioribus atque solidis sese æternum privat, & quæ agit, non potest non perverse agere : nam qui recte agat is, quem tenebræ & inordinationes infinitæ interius possident & obruunt.
units.tr: 4. Fourth, it is to be observed that the faculties, their acts and their objects are of such a nature that they help and advance one another when they are exercised in due order, but hinder and destroy one another when they are handled in a preposterous and perverse order. The due order is the one we followed above in enumerating the faculties; namely, first, the Ground or immense capacity of the mind for the eternal God, together with the more divine faculties of desire, understanding and acquiescence in the same triune God (desiring, contemplating and resting in himself), and its being formed for the attributes and perfections of God; then Reason, given for the shadowy ideas both of God and of his attributes (which differ immensely from the living ideas or light of the higher faculties) and of the things created by God; last, Imagination and the rest. For all lower things depend in a chain upon the ground and the higher faculties, flowing from them and receiving from them strength, light and grace, since they belong to what is at the centre, as a wider expansion, explanation and representation of it. Hence, whoever rightly begins from the centre, to him all the rest, at least what is necessary and due, seem to fly to him of themselves and without effort. But whoever leaves the inner things aside in order to attend to the outer, he deprives himself eternally even of the more divine and solid things, and whatever he does he cannot but do perversely; for he who acts rightly is not someone whom infinite darkness and disorder possess and overwhelm inwardly.

units.la: 5. Ex his autem observatis, illud est quinto concludendum, & alta mente, veluti immota veræ eruditionis Regula, recondendum, Mentem se suasque hac in vita facultates diversas eruDiendo, debere eum modum eamque proportionem in his TENERE, QUÆ EST INTER ÆTERNA SOLIDA ET MOMENTANEA PERITURA; vel inter punctulum tenue evanidumque & lineam immensam, vel potius solidum infinitum. Secus qui fecerit, ad interitum atque tenebrarum æternarum augmentum certo cerrius properat, & coram Deo solidaque veritate insanus, stolidus, & {a}quibuscunque præterea prærogativis gaudeat} ineruditus stipes habebitur. Ethæc est ratio, quod Scripturæ sacræ tales mundi præpostere eruditos veluti fatuos, animales, & brutos passim proclament, quos Deus contemnat, rejiciat & abominatione habeat.
units.tr: 5. From these observations, the fifth conclusion to be drawn, and to be stored deep in the mind as the unshakeable rule of true erudition, is this: in cultivating the mind and its various faculties in this life, one must HOLD THAT MEASURE AND PROPORTION WHICH EXISTS BETWEEN ETERNAL SOLID THINGS AND MOMENTARY PERISHING ONES; that is, between a thin point that vanishes and an immense line, or rather a solid infinity. Whoever does otherwise hastens with certainty toward ruin and the increase of eternal darkness, and before God and solid truth he will be held an insane, stupid and uneducated blockhead, whatever other prerogatives he may enjoy. This is why Holy Scripture everywhere proclaims such preposterously learned men as foolish, animal and brutish, whom God despises, rejects and holds in abomination.

units.la: XV. A fundo igitur atque intimis animi recessibus est omnino inchoandum. Hic vero non parva occurrit difficultas. Fundus enim mentis divinioresque facultates cum pro solo Deo æterno & immenso sint facta; homo industria sua nil hic polire & erudire, nilque agere posse videtur, neque eo penetrare. Id quod omnium, dubio omni procul, est verissimum. Nihil enim præter solum Deum ejusque actum, admittunt capacitates illæ, quæ pro Dei æterni admissione & inhabitatione sunt conditæ: neque pro ullo alio potuit Mentis substantia facultatesque ejus substantialiores seu essentialiores creari; siquidem solus Deus tali scopo & loco fit dignus. Igitur solus Deus interiorum animæ centralis est Eruditor & Doctor, testantDe quoque id sæpius Divina Scriptura. Isolus Mentis centrum divinasque facultates aptus est aperire, intrare, tangere, commovere, erudire. Is solus fundi nostri clavem habet; eoque aperiente, claudere nemo; claudente, aperire nullus valet. Nihilominus tamen ut Deus in intimis agat & erudiat, homo, ex quo Deus illum prævenit & compellit, aliquid ad hoc contribuere & potest & debet: & quidem ex parte centri fundiquefui immensi, omnium primo offerat necesse est centralem atque immensam aliquam cordis sinceritatem & ἀλιπεξίνειαν, quæ nullo limite terminetur, nullaque conscia fraudetur exceptione. (a) Abominationi est Domino cor fraudulentum; neque inhabitabit sapientia animam maleuolam: beatus vero in cujus animo non est dolus. Hic primus est ædificii Eruditionis verę lapis, quem ponit Timor Domini: etenim coram Deo illo tremendo, qui renes ac corda scrutatur, quis fucate vel astute apparere non pertimescet ac verebitur? Lapis secundus est, centralis atque profundissima sui abjectio & humiliatio, ex eo orta, quod conscia fit mens se non modo a se nil esse & nil posse; sed & se e centro locoque suo Deum expulsse, ejus lumen atque inspirationes extinxisse, adeoque veluti Deicidam esse abominandam. Qui huc non redit, is Deum, Eruditorem verum, cum habeat adversantem, perpetuo rudis & fatuus fit necesse est: (b) resistit enim Deus superbis, humilibus autem suam largitur gratiam. Et hæ sunt duæ, quas homo ex parte centri seu fundi tenetur offerre, conditiones. Tertia ex omnium facultatum parte est, tam internarum quam externarum: ea vero est, inferiorum, quæ rationem & exteriora spectant, omnimoda ( necessariis exceptis) desertio atque secessus, & sui totius Deum versus collestio atque conversio. Diximus namque modo, id nobis infirmitatisinesse, ut facultates nostræ omnes simul exerceri nequeant, & unam ab alia semper præpediri, videlicet superiores ab inferioribus, ubi his præpostere adhæretur.
