Quapropter ne Mentis intima ab operatione, exercitatione & eruditione Dei impediantur & revocentur, sileant & quiescant inferiora, nexusque cum suis obje&tis non necessarius rumpatur necesse est, ut solius divinæ eruditionis animus sit auditor: ad hoc autem sæpe requiritur, ut, qui serio ejus cupidus est, vim sibi faciat, duriter aspereque se limet tractetque, quò vinculum delectabile, quo cum externis vinciitur, disrumpat: Quod Deus plerumque adversis rebus & calamitatibus acutis promovere solet, eo semper fine, ut impedimentis suis externis valedicat animus, quem cæteroquin tantis circumsonant ea rumoribus, ut ad Eruditoris interni vocem penitus obsurdescat. Quæ ratio est quod Jesus Christus, Deus ille noster atque Eruditor & Doctor unicus, ipsaque Veritas & Lux, asseveret, neminem qui non omnia ejusmodi dimiserit, suum esse posse discipulum.
units.tr: XV. Therefore one must begin entirely from the ground and from the innermost recesses of the soul. Here, however, a considerable difficulty arises. For since the ground of the mind and its more divine faculties were made for the eternal and immense God alone, man seems unable to polish, educate or do anything here by his own diligence, nor to penetrate there. This is, beyond all doubt, most true. For those capacities, which were created for the admission and indwelling of the eternal God, admit nothing except God alone and his action; nor could the substance of the mind and its more substantial or essential faculties be created for any other purpose, since God alone is worthy of such a purpose and place. Therefore God alone is the Teacher and Instructor of the inner centre of the soul, as Divine Scripture testifies again and again. He alone is fit to open, enter, touch, move and instruct the centre of the mind and its divine faculties. He alone holds the key to our ground, and when he opens it no one can shut it; when he shuts it, no one can open it. Nevertheless, in order that God may act and teach within, man, since God forestalls and compels him, both can and must contribute something to this; and indeed, on the side of the centre and of his immense ground, he must first of all offer a central and immense sincerity of heart, [ἀλιπεξίνειαν], which is bounded by no limit and is not corrupted by any exception of conscience. (a) An abomination to the Lord is a deceitful heart; nor will wisdom dwell in a malicious soul; but blessed is he in whose mind there is no guile. This is the first stone of the true building of Erudition, which the Fear of the Lord lays down: for before that awesome God who searches the reins and hearts, who would not be afraid and stand in dread of appearing feigned or crafty? The second stone is a central and most profound self-abasement and humiliation, arising from the mind's awareness that it is not only nothing and can do nothing of itself, but has also expelled God from its centre and its place, extinguished his light and inspirations, and so is to be abhorred as if it were a killer of God. Whoever does not return to this, since he has God, the true Teacher, as an adversary, must necessarily become continually untaught and foolish: (b) for God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble. These are the two conditions which man is bound to offer on the side of the centre or ground. The third, on the side of all faculties, both inner and outer, is the complete desertion and withdrawal (except for what is necessary) from the lower faculties, which concern reason and external things, and the gathering and turning of his whole self toward God. For we have just said that it is the weakness of our nature that all our faculties cannot be exercised at once, and that one is always hindered by another, namely the higher by the lower, when the lower are clung to in a preposterous way. Therefore, so that the innermost parts of the mind are not hindered and called away from the working, exercise and instruction of God, the inferior faculties must be silent and at rest, and the unnecessary bond with their objects must be broken, so that the soul may be a hearer of divine instruction alone. For this, it is often required that the one who earnestly desires it should use force on himself, and harshly and sharply file and handle himself, so that he may break the pleasant bond by which he is bound to external things. God usually promotes this by adversities and severe calamities, always with this end: that the soul, which is otherwise surrounded with such a din of rumours that it is completely deaf to the voice of the inner Teacher, may bid farewell to its external hindrances. This is why Jesus Christ, our God and the one and only Teacher and Instructor, who is Truth and Light itself, declares that no one who has not let go of all such things can be his disciple.

units.la: Ecce igitur tres primos lapides ad Eruditionis earum, quæ nobis maxime intimæ & essentiales sunt, capacitatum solidum ædificium: qui in unum coagmentati & quasi coementati, per sinceraм & humilem Mentis ad Deum æternum conversionem exprimi possunt commode.
units.tr: Here, then, are the three first stones of the solid edifice of that erudition which is most intimate and essential to us. Joined together and, as it were, cemented, they may conveniently be expressed as a sincere and humble conversion of the mind to the eternal God.

units.la: XVI. Pergamus porro ad enumerationem conditionum, quas ex parte facultatum superiorum ab homine exigit Deus, ut divinæ & solidæ ejus eruditionis sit capax. Quarta ordine, sed prima ex parte desiderii, est, desiderii ad Deum conversi ardor, qui si ad cujusvis rei adeptionem (etiam in naturalibus) pernecessarius est, multo magis is in supernaturalibus requiritur: hic enim est punctum saliens, uti & locus, amoris Dei, omnis rei complementi. Altera est ejus ardoris indeterminata generalitas; hoc est, ut Mens non determinate a Deo optet hoc & illo loco, modo, tempore, hæc illave dona, haud inquam naturalia, sed ne quidem spiritualia & quæ gratiam concernunt: ut enim non est ægri ignari & stupidi Medico sapienti præscribere, quid Medicus ei debeat injungere aut propinare; ita nec ineruditi & ægri hominis est a Deo hæc vel illa dona, has illasve in specie vias, lumina, virtutes, operationes, ex se poscitulare. Id equidem mali non est ominis, nec a Deo in peccatum imputatur: est tamen imprudentis, & operationi eruditionique divinæ morâm injicientis; maxime ubi pertinacia quædam tenacior bono ejusmodi desiderio est immixta. Desideranda est igitur indeterminate divina in nobis eruditio atque operatio, ut nempe Deus, quocunque modo velit, ruditates nostras eliminet, & duritIES emolliat: eruditiat & operetur quidem in nobis, sed eo mo-do do eaque mensura prout ipse e re esse sapientissime judicabit, posthabito ad particularia nostra (quæ abnegationis sunt materia) respectu. Tertia conditio erit, Desiderii constantia; ut ut a Deo diu repulsam ferre videatur. Hoc enim Justitiæ Divinæ est, ut, qui sæpe Deum vocantem audire recusavit, & ipse clamans non statim ad lubitum sese audiri sentiat; ne dicam ardorem desiderii sic augeri, ejus sinceritatem infucatam sic probari, hominis abjectionem & humilitatem sic promoveri, gratiam denique Dei, cum tandem obtenta est, eo majoris fieri, quo longiori mora, labore atque ardore acquisita est. Quarta conditio, consistit in eo, ut exspectet & confidat Mens se a Dei benignitate ea suo tempore obtenturum, quæ judicabit Deus ipsi ad solidam & salutarem Eruditionem profuturna. Atque hisce quatuor perficiuntur veræ preces, quas veluti clavem unam ad omnis Sapientiæ & Eruditionis inquisitionem & adeptionem ipse Deus Eruditor nobis diligentissime in Scripturis commendat, dum vult, (a) nos quærere, petere, pulsare, precari assidue, postulare bonum Spiritum suum, qui Spiritus est sapientiæ & eruditionis, quotquot se asserverat daturum petentibus. (b) Si cui deest Sapientia, inquit Apostolus, petat illam a Deo, qui eam omnibus confert... Sed in fide eam petat, non autem in fluctuatione atque dubitatione. Habemus hic præ oculis in exemplum admirabilem illum Davidis psalmum, qui or-dine dine 119 occurrit, quique expresse eo fine nobis a divina providentia relictus est, ut sit desideriorum nostrorum noctu diuque excitamentum, & exercitatio. Hac via experimento probavit & protestatus est David se sapientiorem, se eruditiorem factum esse suis inimicis, magistris, senibus denique atque prudentibus ipsis. Hac via sapientissimus processit Salomon: (a) Ut scivi, inquit, quoniam non possem aliter esse continens (& hoc ipsum vera erudi-tio est, a vanis & malis contineri,) nisi Deus det. . . adii Dominum & deprecatus sum illum, & dixi ex totis præcordiis meis; Deus patrum meorum, & Domine misericordiæ, qui fecisti omnia verbo tuo, & sapientia tua constituisti hominem, ut dominaretur creaturæ, quæ a te factæ est... tecum Sapientia tua, quæ novit opera tua, quæ & affuit tunc cum orbem terrarum faceres, & sciebat quid esset placitum oculis tuis, & quid direktum in præceptis tuis. Mitte illam de cœlis sanctis tuis & a sede magnitudinis tuæ, ut mecum sit & mecum laboret, ut sciam quid acceptum sit apud te: scit enim illa omnia, & intelligit, & deducet me in operibus meis sobrie, & custodiet me in sua patentia. Et erunt accepta opera mea, & disponam populum tuum, (quisque quæ sui sunt officii,) & ero dignus sedium patris mei, (recuperare sedem gloriæ, a qua Adamus defecit, & cum Christo, Fratre nostro, throno ejus insidere; Apoc. 2.) Quis enim hominum poterit scire consilium Dei? aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus? Cogitationes enim mortalium timidæ, & incertæ providentiæ nostræ. Corpus enim quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam; & terrena inhabitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitantem. Et difficile æstimamus quæ in terris sunt; & quæ in prospectu sunt invenimus cum labore: quæ autem in cœlis sunt quis investigabit? Sensum autem tuum quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam & miseris Spiritum sanctum tuum de altissimis, & correctæ (eruditæ) sint semitæ eorum qui sunt in terris, & quæ tibi placent didicerint homines?
units.tr: XVI. Let us go on to the conditions that God requires of the man in respect of his higher faculties, so that he may be capable of his divine and solid erudition. The fourth in order, but the first on the side of desire, is the ardour of desire turned towards God. If this is absolutely necessary for obtaining anything whatever, even in natural things, it is required all the more in supernatural things. For this is the leaping point, and also the place, of the love of God, the completion of everything. The second is the generality of that ardour, undetermined: that is, the mind should not desire determinately from God this or that place, manner, time, or these or those gifts, not natural, I say, but not even spiritual ones that concern grace. For just as it is not for a sick and ignorant patient to prescribe to a wise physician what the physician ought to impose on him or give him to drink, so it is not for an unlearned and sick man to demand from God, on his own account, these or those gifts, or particular ways, lights, virtues or operations. This is indeed no evil omen, nor is it imputed to us by God as sin. Yet it is imprudent, and it places an obstacle in the way of divine operation and erudition, especially where some stubborn obstinacy is mixed with such a desire. Therefore the divine erudition and operation in us should be desired indeterminately, so that God may in whatever way he wills remove our roughness and soften our hardness: he may instruct and work in us, but in that manner and measure which he himself shall judge most wisely to be fitting, setting aside regard for our particular wishes, which are the matter of self-denial. The third condition will be the constancy of desire, even though it seems to be repulsed by God for a long time. For it belongs to the justice of God that one who has often refused to hear God calling, and who cries out himself, should not at once feel himself heard at his pleasure. Not to mention that the ardour of desire is thus increased, its sincerity thus proved without pretence, the abjection and humility of man thus advanced, and finally the grace of God, when at last obtained, becomes all the greater for having been acquired with longer delay, labour and ardour. The fourth condition consists in this: that the mind should wait and trust that it will obtain from the goodness of God, at its proper time, those things which God shall judge will profit it for solid and saving erudition. By these four things true prayers are completed, which God himself, our Teacher, most diligently commends to us in the Scriptures as one key to the inquiry into and attainment of all wisdom and erudition, when he wills (a) that we seek, ask, knock, pray constantly, and ask for his good Spirit, which is the Spirit of wisdom and erudition, since he assures us that he will give it to all who ask. (b) "If anyone lacks wisdom," says the Apostle, "let him ask it of God, who gives it to all..." But let him ask it in faith, and not in wavering and doubt. Here we have before our eyes, as a wonderful example, that psalm of David which occurs in order 119, and which was expressly left to us by divine providence for this end: that it might be a stimulus and exercise of our desires by night and by day. By this way David proved by experience and declared that he had become wiser and more learned than his enemies, his teachers, the elders, and indeed than the prudent themselves. By this way the very wise Solomon also proceeded: (a) "As I knew," he says, "that I could not otherwise be continent (and this itself is true erudition, to be restrained from vain and evil things), unless God gave it... I went to the Lord and besought him, and I said with my whole heart: God of my fathers, and Lord of mercy, who made all things by your word, and by your wisdom established man, that he should have dominion over the creature which was made by you... with you is your Wisdom, which knows your works, which was also present when you made the world, and knew what was pleasing in your eyes, and what was right in your commandments. Send her from your holy heavens, and from the throne of your greatness, that she may be with me and labour with me, that I may know what is acceptable before you: for she knows and understands all things, and will lead me soberly in my works, and will guard me in her glory. And my works will be acceptable, and I shall order your people (each one in what belongs to his office), and I shall be worthy of the seat of my father (to recover the seat of glory from which Adam fell, and with Christ, our Brother, to sit on his throne; Rev. 2). For who among men can know the counsel of God? or who can think what God wills? For the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our providence is uncertain. For the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks many things. And we judge with difficulty the things that are on earth, and we find with labour what is before us; but who will search out the things that are in heaven? Who will know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high, and so the paths of those who are on earth are made straight (taught), and men learn what pleases you?

units.la: Hæc ex parte desiderii.
units.tr: These things concern the side of desire.

units.la: XVII. Ex parte intellectus, duas tantum conditiones requiri autumo: Primam quidem, præteritorum evacuationem; alteram vero, ab activitate præsenti & futura, abstinentiam, sive quietem. Et prima quidem, intellectus, quia variis rerum non modo naturalium & humanarum, sed & spiritualium & divinarum imaginibus sive ideis, vel etiam, ut plurimum, præjudiciis sollicitatur; ea omnia, quatenus particularia sunt, a se removeat, ut purius & verius a fonte luminis lumen recipiat vel exspectet; vel, si non recipiat, vacuitate sua contentus, Deo divinisque rebus gloriam hanc adorabundus tribuat, quod incomprehensibiles sibi sint: quæ quidam agnitio eminentissima quæpiam eruditionis solidioris pars est quam sæpissime. Dixi autem eam rerum, notionumve, etiam divinarum; ab intellectu remotionem ad particulares debere restringi, non vero ad generales extendi: nam Deum esse, æternum, potentem, {17} Ex parte intellectus conditiones duae; dua evacuatio, quies. Ne fallit philosophos. tem, justum, veracem, sapientem, bonum, incomprehensibilem: eum in Scripturis (sicut notæ sint) esse locutum vera, eum adeoque esse incomprehenfibiliter Triiñum, ad noftram salutem incarnatum, passum, & similia quæ facræliteræ tradunt; hominem in rectitudine conditum esse; per peccatum vero cum posteris ita depravatum, ut fine speciali atque intimo Dei auxilio, operatione, lumine, motu, ad statum priorem per purificationem veram redire nequeat; hæc inquam generaliora, talia sunt, ut sincera mens, cujus fundus & desiderium iis, quas jam enumeravimus, dispositionibus, sunt prædita, de iis dubitare non possit, neque fe eis evacuare: secretius enim a Deo operante retinetur hoc ne committat, ad quod etiam, dum sincera, humilis, pia & precibus bene dedita est, ipsa neutiquam est propensa. At vero aliud est hæccè fovere & retinere, aliud scrutari, cogitare, decernere fpecialius, quid fit in Deo, quid ejus æternitas, quæ, quanta, quibus viis procedat ejus potentia, justitia, veracitas, sapientia, bonitas ? in quibus consistat, quæ proprie contineat adorabilis. Trinitas ? qui incarnatio fit facta, quidve determinatius de viis Redemtionis, actionum & passionum Christi, divinis mysteriis sensu Scripturarum determinatiore fit statuendum: quid corruptio hominis & quanta; quid & qualis Dei intima operatio, & infinita ejusmodi; quæ omnia in homine corrupto ista ante divini luminis adventum determinante, fi non fundi-tus tus falsata, ad minimum confusa, obscura, chimæris & monstris quam plurimis intermixta non possunt non esse: Et quamvis ad Scripturas provocet homo corruptus, & falsa literalique eruditione caput infarctum habeat, temere revera nugatur, & hæreses tantum ex iis fabricari aptus est, quamdiu Spiritu Eruditionis divinæ, unde Scripturæ emanarunt, non est prædítus. Ut ut etiam se clare & distincte res concipere sibi prorsus atque aliis persuadeat, fallitur tamen: nam in rebus divinis, quin etiam in naturalibus & humanis, quatenus earum radix & natura penitior & solida, non autem una atque altera ex quibusdam minutiis requiritur, sciri nequit quid clara, quid distincta sit perceptio, quid verum lumen spiritale & naturale, antequam per viam solidæ Eruditionis perque conditiones, quas annotamus, progressus sit factus: alioqui, quivis ignes fatui, quævis vanæ & per spiritus erroris calliditatem lucis specie delibutæ fictiones, veluti claræ & distinctæ perceptiones a nobis habebuntur: quæ observatio totum fere Cartesianismum, ejusque, quam ad divina etiam extendere non verentur, methodum, labefactat. Plura dicam. Ipsi etiam sancti atque illuminati, postquam ea quæ de Deo divinisque luminose percepere, verbis vel scriptis, quam exactissime potuere, expresserunt, profitentur tamen, se, si quæ dixerunt cum rerum ipsarum veritate & excellentia conferantur, potius divina deturpasse, quin blasphemasse & falsa dixisse, quam ipsas res prout sunt, vive prodidisse, nedum conceptibus & verbis adæquasse. Quam importuni igitur, (ut id obiter moneam) imo quam absurdi sunt qui e falsorum eruditorum grege, alios, ipsis in divina eruditione sæpe immensum provectiores, ad formulas suas scholasticas, sæpe ineptas, ne dicam ad conceptus suos obscuros, tenebrosos, sæpissime chimæricos & monstrosos, quibus ipsimet res, sua confessione incomprehensibiles, non vere describi fatentur, adstringere decernunt, eos alioqui veluti hæreticos vel blasphemos traducturi & diffamaturi; quia postquam verbis & formulis, cogitatisve etiam non-nullis Magistrorum istorum abstinuerunt, de mysteriis divinis quædam novo modo novâve nomenclaturâ dixere, quæ ad divinum in homine amorem, pietatem, humilitatem, sanctimoniam, justitiam, veracitatem, bonitatemque provehendam, & ad mala averruncanda conferunt, ipsis mysteriis divinis in adoranda incomprehensibilitate sua interim tectis manentibus, atque, ut quæ vere incomprehensibilia, infinita & ineffabilia sint, ex animo agnitis & declaratis? Hujus iniquitatis a mundo condito infinita exempla hic prætermitto, qui recentioris notæ quam plurima producere possem, si res id postularet.
units.tr: XVII. On the side of the intellect I hold that only two conditions are required. The first is the emptying of past things; the second is abstinence, or rest, from present and future activity. The first is this: since the intellect is troubled by various images or ideas of things, not only natural and human but also spiritual and divine, and very often by prejudices, it should remove all these from itself, insofar as they are particular, so that it may receive, or wait for, light more purely and truly from the fount of light. Or, if it does not receive it, content with its own emptiness, it should in adoration give this glory to God and divine things, that they are incomprehensible to it. This recognition is very often the most eminent part of more solid erudition. I said, however, that this removal of things and notions from the intellect, even divine ones, must be restricted to particular ones and not extended to general ones. For that God exists, is eternal, powerful, just, truthful, wise, good, and incomprehensible; that he has spoken truths in the Scriptures (as they are known); that he is therefore incomprehensibly Triune, incarnate for our salvation, suffered, and similar things which the Holy Letters hand down; that man was created in uprightness, but through sin was so depraved with his posterity that without the special and inward help, operation, light and motion of God he cannot return to his former state by true purification: these, I say, are the more general matters, and such that a sincere mind, whose ground and desire are endowed with those dispositions which we have now enumerated, cannot doubt them, nor empty itself of them. For this is more secretly retained by God working, so that it does not commit this sin, to which it is by no means inclined, provided it is sincere, humble, pious, and devoted to prayers. But it is one thing to cherish and retain these things, and another to examine, think about, and determine more specifically what is in God, what his eternity is, how great it is, by what ways his power, justice, truthfulness, wisdom and goodness proceed, in what the adorable Trinity properly consists, what the incarnation is and how it was made, and what is to be determined more definitely about the ways of redemption, and about the actions and sufferings of Christ, in the more determinate sense of the divine mysteries of the Scriptures; what the corruption of man is and how great, what and of what kind is the inward operation of God, and other such infinite things. In a corrupt man, before the coming of the divine light determines these matters, they cannot but be, if not utterly falsified, at least confused, obscure, and mingled with very many chimeras and monsters. And although the corrupt man appeals to the Scriptures, and has his head stuffed with false and merely literal erudition, he truly trifles rashly, and is apt only to fabricate heresies from them, as long as he is not endowed with the Spirit of divine erudition, from which the Scriptures came forth. Even if he persuades himself and others that he conceives things clearly and distinctly, he is nevertheless deceived. For in divine things, and indeed in natural and human things, insofar as their root and nature are deeper and solid, and not merely one or another of certain trifles, it cannot be known what a clear and what a distinct perception is, or what true spiritual and natural light is, before one has made progress by the way of solid erudition and through the conditions which we have noted. Otherwise, any will-o'-the-wisps, any vain fictions tinged with the cunning of the spirit of error in the appearance of light, will be held by us as clear and distinct perceptions. This observation overthrows nearly all of Cartesianism, and its method, which they do not hesitate to extend even to divine things. I shall say more. The holy and enlightened themselves, after they have expressed in words or writings, as exactly as they could, what they perceived luminously about God and divine things, still declare that if what they said is compared with the truth and excellence of the things themselves, they have disfigured divine things, indeed blasphemed and spoken falsely, rather than revealed the things themselves as they are, living, let alone equalled them in concepts and words. How troublesome, then (to remark this in passing), nay how absurd, are those of the flock of false scholars who decide to bind others, who are often immeasurably more advanced than they themselves in divine erudition, to their scholastic formulas, often inept, not to say to their obscure, murky, very often chimerical and monstrous concepts, by which they themselves confess that the incomprehensible things are not truly described; and they intend otherwise to brand and defame these others as heretics or blasphemers. This is because, after they have abstained from the words and formulas, or even some thoughts, of those masters, they have spoken of divine mysteries in a new way and with new nomenclature, things which contribute to advancing divine love, piety, humility, holiness, justice, truthfulness and goodness in man, and to averting evils, while the divine mysteries themselves remain covered in their adorable incomprehensibility, and as things which are truly incomprehensible, infinite and ineffable are acknowledged and declared from the heart. I omit here the infinite examples of this iniquity since the creation of the world; I could produce very many of more recent date, if the matter required it.

units.la: Ex dictis abunde patescit alterius, quam abstinentiam vel quietem ab activitate dixi, dispositionis necessitas: qua enim ratione præterita, uti diximus, abdicanda sunt, eadem etiam a similibus, quæ & nunc & in posterum offerrentur, quiescendum est eodem modo atque sensu: alioqui abdicata impersectio, obscuritas, tenebrae, falsa & figmenta, iterum assumerentur; quae in proprium scopum praevaricatio est. Nil autem evidentius per se est, quam Deum, divinum lumen, & quae ex eo vivide sequuntur, ab intellectu creato produci non posse: sed si quae ab illo produci putantur, vel conamina sunt inania, quae tenebrosa figmenta & confusa tantum efficiunt; vel ideae sunt superficiariae, umbratiles, steriles, quae a Ratione humana, sive ab intellectu activo, facultate ad res externas, vel potius ad superficiarias picturas data, proficiscuntur, & ad eruditionem superficialem pertinent: ipsum enim intellectum verum & diviniorem, qui ad vera solida, divina, Deumque ipsum factus est, non nisi mere passive se habere ad objectum suum divinum & immensum, eum erudiens, illuminans & replens, omnium clarissima est notio.
units.tr: It is abundantly clear from what has been said that the disposition I called abstinence, or rest from activity, is necessary. Just as past things must be renounced, as we have said, so the like things that are offered now and in future must be rested from in the same way and in the same sense. Otherwise imperfection, obscurity, darkness, and falsehoods and fictions, once renounced, would be taken up again, and that is a betrayal of the proper goal. Nothing is more evident in itself than that God, the divine light, and what vividly follows from him cannot be produced by the created intellect. If anything is thought to be produced by it, it is either empty efforts, which bring about only dark fictions and confusion, or superficial, shadowy, barren ideas, which proceed from human reason, or from the active intellect, the faculty given for external things or rather for superficial pictures, and which belong to superficial learning. It is the clearest notion of all that the true and more divine intellect, which has been made for solid, divine truths and for God himself, is only passively disposed toward its divine and immeasurable object, while God teaches, illumines and fills it.

units.la: XVIII. Supersunt ex parte divinioris facultatis acquiescentiae, quae ad solidam eruditionem praerequiruntur, conditiones itidem duae: una, ut acquiescentia indeterminate & absolute se tradat Deo erudienti & operanti, ob aliud nec laetans, nec gaudens, nec acquiescens, quam quod Deo placeat mentem in suam discipulam suscipere, & in ea erudienda operari eis modis, tempore, & circumstantiis, quae Divinae ejus Majestati placebit ad libitum suum determinare, ita ut mentis acquiescentia in solam Dei voluntatem, quamvis ei absurda, repugnans, & fulta iIulta appareret, resolvatur. Altera requisitio est, ut facultas ea parata fit & dolori, & inopiæ, & ipsi coram mundo infamiæ atque condemnationi acquiescere & subjici,hoc est, vera patientia indui. Namque (ne impios commemorem, qui ex opposita malitiæ indole, probos vexationibus persequi consueverunt,)solet Deus quos erudire vult, veraque donare sapientia, prius variis modis, anxiis, tenebrosis, tristibus, animæ carnique horrendis, ad probationem, firmitatem,fexcentaque alia, ipsis tunc incognita emolumenta admirabilia, castigare & exercere ex omni parte, intus & extus,ut in Jofepho,Davide, aliisque theodidactis videre est : quem procedendi modum egregie describit Syracides ( cap. 4. & 6.) Distorte quidem & in tentatione ambulatura est (Sapientia) primum cum eo, ( erudiendo.) Timorem & metum & probationem adducet super eum, & cruciabit illum in tribulatione doctrinæ suæ, donec tentet eum in cogitationibus suis & credat animæ illius. Sed rursus firmabit illum, & itinere recto adibit illum, eumque lætificabit: & denudabit absconsa sua illi & thefaurijabit super illum scientiam & intelleftum justitiæ.
units.tr: XVIII. There remain, on the side of the more divine faculty of acquiescence, two further conditions required beforehand for solid learning. The first is that acquiescence surrender itself, indeterminately and absolutely, to God teaching and working, rejoicing in nothing else, delighting in nothing else, and resting in nothing else, than that it pleases God to take the mind up as his pupil and to work in it to teach, by those means, at those times, and in those circumstances, which it pleases his Divine Majesty to determine at his own will. The mind's acquiescence must thus be resolved into the will of God alone, even if that will appears absurd, repugnant, or foolish. The second requirement is that this faculty be prepared to acquiesce in and submit to pain, want, and even infamy and condemnation before the world, that is, to be clothed with true patience. For (not to mention the impious, who from their opposite evil disposition are accustomed to harass the upright with vexations) God usually, before he grants true wisdom to those whom he wishes to teach, chastises and exercises them in every way, inwardly and outwardly, by various anxious, dark, sad means, horrible to soul and flesh, for testing and for firmness, and for six hundred other wonderful benefits then unknown to them, as may be seen in Joseph, David, and other God-taught men. Ben Sira describes this manner of proceeding excellently (chs. 4 and 6): Wisdom will walk with him at first by crooked paths and in temptation (wisdom, in teaching him). She will bring fear and dread and trial upon him, and will torment him with the discipline of her instruction, until she tests him in her thoughts and trusts his soul. But again she will strengthen him, and bring him by a straight way, and make him glad, and she will reveal her secrets to him and store up over him the knowledge and understanding of righteousness.

units.la: XIX. Atque istæ sunt fundi & divinarum facultatum, a quibus erudiendis incipiendum esse diximus, dispositiones, quæ ex illarum parte requiruntur, ut earum actor ac Eruditor Deus, eas suscipiat solide erudiendas. Hanc autem Eruditionem quia ad rationem infimasque facultates corporeas non referimus primario & directe,ideo de harum facultatum ad illam requisitis, præterea quæ jam dictis implicita sunt, non hic erimus ultra solliciti. Interim, cum ex nota tertia superiore (artic. 14.) pluribus simul vacare non possimus, & exercitium indebitum unius facultatis alteram impediat, requiritur hic indirecte exparte rationis & aliarum inferiorum, ne ultra quam necesse est, agant: corporex quidem non plusquam necesse sit ad vitæ corporeæ conservationem; ratio vero tum ad hoc ipsum, tum ad promotionem conditionum modo dictarum in facultatibus supremis: alioqui hæ impedirentur.
units.tr: XIX. These are the dispositions of the foundation and of the divine faculties, with which, as we said, teaching must begin, the dispositions required on their side, so that God, the author and teacher of them, may take them up to be solidly taught. Since we do not refer this learning primarily and directly to reason and the lowest corporeal faculties, we shall not here be further concerned with what those faculties require for it, beyond what is already implied in what has been said. Meanwhile, since (from the third note above, art. 14) we cannot be occupied with several things at once, and the undue exercise of one faculty hinders another, it is required here, indirectly, on the part of reason and of the other lower faculties, that they not act beyond what is necessary: the body indeed no more than is necessary for the preservation of bodily life; reason, however, both for that very purpose and for promoting the conditions just described in the highest faculties. Otherwise these would be hindered.

units.la: At vero, inquies, dictas hasce conditiones si offerant facultates supremæ prius quam agat Deus, nonne prius ipsæ eruditæ fuerint an easne etiam posse conditiones hasce sine Deo præcedente dare censendum est? Absit hoc ut statuam. Prævenit omnes mentis dispositiones Eruditor Deus impulsibus suis; sed generalioribus, iisque, qui mentibus vim dant, qua si bene, sicuti diximus, usæ fuerint, (id quod generalior nonnulla eruditio censeri potest) tum demum ad specialissimam & proprie dictam, de qua nobis quæstio est, Eruditionem a Deo suscipiuntur & exercentur; aliter, remotæ si hæ sint conditiones, non suscipientur: quæ causa est cur diutius iis atque operis hujus brevitas postulare videbatur, indicandis instituerimus: sed neque id inique: non enim per dies aliquot, sed & per menses, & per annos, forte & per lustra in his fuerit serio & de facto Mens exercenda, antequam sese in discipulam sentiat assumi: Nonnunquam pulsandum dia & constanter. itanter ut aperiatur : quamvis Deus tamen agere & erudire interim tacite & secretius incipiat.
units.tr: But indeed, you will object, if the highest faculties offer these conditions before God acts, should they not be taught first, or must we think they can give these conditions even without God's prior action? Far be it from me to assert this. The divine Teacher anticipates all dispositions of the mind by his impulses, but general ones, which give the minds a power by which, if they have used it well, as we have said (which may be called a certain general learning), then at last they are taken up by God and exercised in the most special learning, properly so called, which is our question. Otherwise, if these conditions are removed, they will not be taken up. This is why we have decided to indicate these matters at some length, though the brevity of this work seemed to require otherwise. Nor is this unfair. For the mind must be exercised seriously and in fact, not for a few days but for months, years, and perhaps for five-year periods, before it perceives itself to be taken up as a pupil. Sometimes one must knock long and constantly, so that it may be opened, although God meanwhile begins to act and teach quietly and more secretly.

units.la: Cæterum vix credo opus esse ut moneam, id quod lector per se satis animadvertet: me videlicet in acquisitione eruditionis explicanda temporis ordinem non spectare, quasi velem ut ab hominis infantia persequentes ætatis periodos hac serie procederetur. Ordinem rerum, ipsarumque naturæ & dignitatis, hic & in sequentibus propono, hominemque non infantem, sed facultatum suarum superiorum usu vel utendi facilitate præditum; is enim, præviis conditionibus præcedaneis, operationum erudientis Dei capax est.
units.tr: Moreover, I hardly think I need to warn what the reader will notice for himself: namely, that in explaining the acquisition of learning I am not looking at the order of time, as though I wished to proceed in this sequence, following the periods of life from infancy. Here and in what follows I set out the order of things, and of their nature and dignity, and I presuppose a man not in infancy but endowed with the use or ready facility of his higher faculties. For such a man, with the preceding conditions fulfilled, is capable of the operations of God teaching him.

units.la: XX. Atque primo quidem solet æternus Deus, qui pro se solo, proque suis operationibus Mentis fundum facultatesque diviniores, (jam rudes, asperas, & confusas,) creavit, ita erudire mentes, ut quas illæ crassiore minerva dedolatas obtulerint dispositiones, is gradatim & perfectiores & immensiores, & divinas prorsus atque purissimas efficiat, reddendo videlicet perfectas, immensas, purissimasque sinceritatem, humilitatem, rerum caeterarum abjectionem, ad se unum conversionem, cupiditatem sui ardentem, indefinitam, constantem, fidem tem; intuitum intellectus nudatum, quietum, continentem, castum; acquiescentiam illimitatam nec non quorumvis patientissimam: quæ omnia, quia longioris operis essent, non explico: continent enim inter alia ipsissimam, quam Theologi nonnulli nominant, Animæ passivam purificationem, uti quam activam vocant, iis quæ mox præcedunt involvitur.
units.tr: XX. First, then, the eternal God, who created the ground of the mind and the more divine faculties for himself alone and for his own operations, (which are still rough, harsh and confused), usually teaches minds in such a way that he gradually makes the dispositions they have offered, roughly hewn with a cruder tool, both more perfect and more immense, and wholly divine and most pure. He does this by making perfect, immense and most pure sincerity, humility, the rejection of other things, conversion to himself alone, a burning, unbounded, constant desire for himself, faith, an intellectual gaze stripped bare, quiet, restrained and chaste, and a boundless and most patient acquiescence. All these I do not explain, since they would require a longer work. For they include, among other things, that most true purification of the soul which some theologians call passive, and which is involved in those things that immediately precede what they call active purification.

units.la: XXI. Sic autem Deus Mentium nostra-rum dura, crassa, rigida, rudia, incomposita ramenta, asperitates, aliaque mala, quæ peccatum intulerat, erudit & amputat. Nec vero tunc subsistit & cessat: sed deinde, expulsis formis incompositis atque monstrosis, suam Menti divinam atque æternam formam reddere, eam polire, ornare, perficere aggreditur: quæ divinæ, solidæ, & nunquam perituræ Eruditionis pars est præcipua. Id autem exequitur divinus ille Præceptor atque Eruditor, Luminumque Pater, dum capacitatem Mentis æternam, sive fundum immensum, ad æternitatem Dei factum, sic sua afficit æternitate, ut Mens revera elemento æterno immergi videatur, nil nisi æterna sapiens & ambiens, cæteris quibuscunque nauseæ & horrori habitis, nisi quantum æterna referunt & promovent.
units.tr: XXI. So God teaches and cuts away the hard, coarse, rigid, rough and disordered shavings, the roughnesses and other evils, which sin had brought into our minds. Nor does he stop or cease at that point. Then, having expelled the disordered and monstrous forms, he undertakes to restore to the mind his own divine and eternal form, to polish it, adorn it and perfect it. This is the chief part of the divine, solid, and never-perishing learning. That divine Teacher and Educator, the Father of lights, carries this out by affecting the mind's eternal capacity, or its immense ground, made for the eternity of God, with his own eternity, so that the mind seems truly to be immersed in the eternal element, savouring and embracing nothing but the eternal, and finding all other things nauseating and horrible, except insofar as they relate to and promote the eternal.

units.la: Pariter & desiderium, & intellectus, & acquiescentia imbuuntur, penetrantur & quasi condiuntur gloriosis & deliciosis Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus adorandi potentiis atque virtutibus, justitia, luce veritateve, amore, lætitia, bonitate, sapientia, prudentia, aliisque infinitis, quas Anima desiderio iisdem vulnerato & transfixo amplectitur, oculo intellectus supernaturaliter evecto intuetur, acquiescentia divinitata, ut sic loquar, degustat, modis admirandis, unde ipsa redditur divinitus potens, dives atque virtuosa, justa, verax, bona, læta, sapiens, prudens, & verbo, ipsi similis Deo, cujus vitâ vivit & animatur: hæc, inquam, omnia experitur modis, vel, {a}cùm modus vox abjecta sit nimium, ) realitatibus centralissimis & exaltatissimis, admirandis, ineffabilibus, immensis, captum omnem, rationem, imaginationem, virtutem humanam omnem tanto magis superantibus, quanto arenulæ granulum ab immensitate totius universi superatur: Clarius enim est luce, Deum ejusque potentiarum vividos actus, tanto, & adhuc majori, humana superare intervallo. Hinc est quod homines meri, quantumvis industria, eruditione humana (superficiaria & falsa) polleant, ad hæc plane coecutiant, eaque parum abest quin coram irrideant, & pro figmentis plurimi traducant, haud secus ac oculis capti si se solos consulant, quæ de modo cognoscendi per lumen & colores profferrentur, risu exciperent miseri.
units.tr: Likewise the desire, the intellect and the acquiescence are imbued, penetrated, and as it were seasoned, with the glorious and delightful powers and virtues of God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, to be adored: justice, light or truth, love, joy, goodness, wisdom, prudence, and countless others. The soul embraces these, its desire wounded and pierced through with them; the eye of the intellect, supernaturally raised, gazes upon them; acquiescence, so to speak, tastes them divinely, in wonderful ways. Thereby the soul is made divinely powerful, rich, virtuous, just, true, good, joyful, wise, prudent, and in a word, like God himself, by whose life it lives and is animated. I say that it experiences all these things in ways (or, since the word "way" is too degraded, in most central and most exalted realities), which are wonderful, unutterable and immense, and which surpass every grasp, every reason, every imagination, and all human power, as far as a grain of sand is surpassed by the immensity of the whole universe. For God and the living acts of his powers are clearer than light, and surpass human understanding by a distance so great, and even greater. Hence it is that mere men, however strong they may be in industry and human learning (superficial and false), are utterly blind to these things. They are hardly prevented from mocking them openly and dismissing most of them as fictions, just as miserable men born blind, if they consulted only themselves, would laugh at what is said about the way of knowing by light and colours.

units.la: XXII. Hæc vero est Eruditionis veræ atque solidæ subfantialis essentialisque pars, thesaurus & cor. Hæc forma illa divina, immortalis, solida, nunquam peritura, substantiam intimam & facultates mentis æternas, principales, immensas, concernens, implens, perficiens & beans: hæc Eruditio sola homine (creatura æterna) vere digna, ei necessaria, utilis, jucunda, ad quam propriè factus est, & quâ post ejus amissionem, debet iterum de novo muniri & erudiri, cæteris ex animo ei vilescentibus: quia præter hoc quæcunque sunt, nil sunt nisi vanitas vanitatum,
units.tr: XXII. This is the substantial and essential part of true and solid Erudition, its treasure and heart. It is that divine, immortal, solid form, never to perish, which touches, fills, perfects and blesses the inmost substance and the eternal, principal and immense faculties of the mind. This Erudition alone is truly worthy of man, a creature who is eternal; it is necessary, useful and pleasant to him, the purpose for which he was made, and after its loss he must be fortified and instructed anew, all else becoming worthless to him in his heart, because apart from this whatever exists is nothing but vanity of vanities,

units.la: & & omnia vanitas, uti hominum sapientissimus & eruditissimus expressis verbis declarvit.
units.tr: and all is vanity, as the wisest and most learned of men has declared in plain words.

units.la: Hac Eruditione politus & praeparatus divinus ille & immortalis aeterni aedificii lapis, Mens nostra, ad divini palatii, quod Deus inhabitare vult, exstructionem quam maxime consentanee & summo cum decore atque ornatu adaptatur; & non solum cum divino Inhabitatore, sed & cum caeteris totius domicilii lapidibus, nec non ornamentis, quam congruentissime convenit & intercedit. Hoc est, oratione simplici rem ut eloquar, non Dei solum rerumque divinarum respectu mens erudita est, cum illis ut congruat, habeat commercium lucis, usus, dispositionis, fruitionisque aptissimae; sed & ut id ipsum, suo tamen gradu, cum quibusvis aliis creaturis, seu ipsi aequales natura sint, (uti mentes caeterae,) sive inferiores, (ut res corporeae & naturales,) habeat, cum illis optime ex vera luce, sive ex vera illarum cognitione, usu, dispositione & fruitione concordet, hac quidem in vita quantum necesse est; olim vero, plenissime & super omne jucundum. Neque enim committere potest Sapientissimus Deus, ut quae res secum concordar optime, ea a caeterarum suarum creaturarum harmonia, ordine, usu & vinculo necessario atque a Dei statuto, sit discors; cum utrarumque una eademque sit origo, unus omnium conditor & conformator, Deus, qui eo ipso dum mentem divinitus erudit & sibi aptat, seque adimplet, eoipso quoquoque illi principia atque femina solida infundit eruditionis quæ res alias spectat & respicit, idque sine Rationis humanæ laboriosa excussione & investigatione, ac multo magis etiam sine chartarum humanarum a seculi eruditis conscribillatarum & commaculatarum tædiosa evolutione & devoratione. Etenim ab æternis & invisibilibus rebus visibiles & temporariæ processerunt: unde est, ut qui solide illas inspicit, novit, tenet, cumque iisdem apte se gerere novit; has quoque, quæ e typæ sunt ab archetypis illis, noscat, teneat, & cum iisdem sese optime gerat. Et quamvis istarum particulariores ideas & distinctiores in specie nec haberet antequam ageret, imo nec postquam egit; Deus tamen ille, qui Mentem ejus sibi eruditi eamque inhabitat & vivificat, secretiori suo impulsu & regimine sic eum regeret, ut nil non aptissimum & decentissimum inter quæcunque versaretur, committeret.
units.tr: Polished and prepared by this Erudition, our mind, that divine and immortal stone of the eternal building, is fitted in the most fitting way and with the highest grace and ornament to the construction of the divine palace which God wills to inhabit, and it fits and agrees most congruently not only with the divine Indweller but also with the other stones and ornaments of the whole dwelling. To put it simply: the enlightened mind is not only in agreement with God and divine things, so that it has a fellowship of light, use, arrangement and enjoyment most suited to them; it also has, each in its own degree, the same relation to any other creatures, whether they are equal to it in nature (like other minds) or inferior (like bodily and natural things). With these it agrees best, out of the true light, that is, out of the true knowledge of them, in their use, arrangement and enjoyment, in this life as far as is necessary, and hereafter most fully and beyond all delight. For the most wise God cannot allow that which agrees best with itself to be at odds with the harmony, order, use and necessary bond of his other creatures, and with God's own ordinance; since both have one and the same origin, one Creator and Shaper of all, God. By that very act, while he divinely enlightens and fits the mind to himself and fills it, he pours into it at the same time the principles and seeds of solid erudition concerning other things, which it looks upon and regards, and this without the laborious sifting and searching of human reason, and much less without the tedious unrolling and devouring of human papers scribbled over and defiled by the learned of this age. For visible and temporal things have proceeded from eternal and invisible things. Hence it is that one who looks upon the latter solidly knows them, holds them, and knows how to conduct himself aptly toward them; he also knows and holds those things which are copies of those archetypes, and conducts himself best with them. And although he did not have more particular and distinct ideas of these in detail before he acted, nor even after he has acted, yet that God who enlightens his mind for himself and dwells in and quickens it, by his more secret impulse and rule, so guides him that he commits nothing that is not most fitting and proper amid whatever he deals with.

units.la: XXIII. Atque hæc fuit sanctorum universalis Eruditio, divinissima ea, sapientissimaque, quâ, sine ullo idearum penu, de rebus quibusvis, tunc cum tempus & circumstantiæ præcise id postularent, cogitabant & disponebant sapientissime, illarum extra usus necessarii casum, prorsus ignari vel obliti, Illorum immortales & æternæ Mentes, Deo suo, ad quem factæ, quemque culpâ sua amierant, divina jam eruditione inventa, sic gaudent, cæteris contemtis; ut ab illo ad cætera vana sese distrahi neutiquam patiantur. Cum tamen animadvertant se nonnullum Ium cum eis habere nexum, eumque neceffarium, primo quidem suspirant gravati, ut cum (a) Paulo loquar; deinde vero ad Dominum suum animitus sese convertentes, ex rimore ne eum denuo ut olim amittant, eum
units.tr: XXIII. This was the universal Erudition of the saints, most divine and most wise, by which, without any store of ideas, they thought and arranged most wisely about whatever things, whenever time and circumstances precisely demanded it, while they were utterly ignorant of or had forgotten those things outside the occasion of necessary use. Their immortal and eternal minds, now that divine erudition has been found, rejoice in their God, for whom they were made and whom they had lost through their own fault, all else being despised; so that they never allow themselves to be drawn away from him to other vain things. Yet when they notice that they have some connection with those other things, and a necessary one, they first sigh, weighed down, as (a) Paul would put it; then, turning themselves inwardly to their Lord, fearing lest they lose him again as before, they

units.la: “precantur supplices, Qui solus & tibi & “nobis sufficis, Domine, quique conspicis “miseriam nostram, quâ cogimur inviti de “aliis ac de te uno interdum cogitare & oc“cupari, qui nosti, Te quidem (b) homi“nem creasse rectum, ipsum vero distractione “externorum ac inquisitione idearum & ratio“cinationum multarum suarum, a tui possef“sione dejectum esse, eum (c) vanum dis“curs ibus suis esse redditum; ejusque cor, “sapientia vacuum, esse obtenebratum, dein“de in sensus reprobos traditum; itane nos “& eidem periculo expositos patieris? Ec“ce in te omnium quae nos concernunt, cu“ram rejicimus; suscipe tu eam; tu de rebus “internis, externisque, de viis, de ossi“ciis, de actibus, de locis & temporibus, “de statu & labore, de possidendis & relin“quendis, de adhibendis & rejiciendis, de “sciendis & ignorandis, de loquendis & ta“cendis, de sanitate & morbis, de vita & “morte, ubi & uti opus esse scis; mone, age, “dispone, elige & rege ad placitum, ne “earum rerum adhaesione, amore, affectu, “inani gloriatione, voluptate, inimicique “sub eis latentibus tricis & astutiis implici“ti, a te separemur iterum. Quam quidem mentis & viarum oblationem non modo non rejicit Deus; sed & ultra spem omnem atque desiderium adimplet. Hoc Sacri eruditi, hoc quotquot se Deo sic tradiderunt, plenissime sunt experti; hoc David, nectestimonio omni abstineamus, calculo suo approbat: (a) Revela Domino (vel rejice in Dominum) viam tuam, & spera in eo; & ipse faciet: hoc exemplo proprio confirmat: namque postquam sapius constantiusque vias suas Deo commendasset, rogasset eum ut se dirigeret, seque Spiritus ejus bonus in viam rectam duceret, ait postmodum confidentissime & laetissime, (b) Dominus regit me, & nihil mihi deerit. In loco pascuae ibi me collocavit: super aquam refectionis educavit me: animam meam convertit. Deduxit me super semitas justitiae propter nomen suum. Quin & si ambulavero in medio umbrae mortis, non timebo mala, quoniam tu mecum es: virga tua & baculus tuus ipsa me consolata sunt. Parasti in conspectu meo mensam adversus eos qui tribulant me: impinguasti in oleo caput meum, & calix meus inebrians quam praeclarus est! Et misericordia tua subsequetur me omnibus diebus vitae meae, ut inhabitem in domo Domini in longitudinem dierum. Similia exempla millena in omni re, virtute, regimine, notitia, praxi videre est abundantissime in divinis & solide eruditissimis illis solitariis, qui apud Palladium, Ruffinum, Cassianum, Theodoretum, Ecclesiasticosque historicos Sozomenum, Socratem, Euagrium, aliosque occurrunt.
units.tr: "pray humbly: O Lord, who alone suffices both for us and for thee, who beholdest our misery, by which we are compelled, against our will, to think and be occupied sometimes with other things and only sometimes with thee, who knowest that thou didst create man upright, but that by the distraction of external things and the inquiry into many ideas and reasonings he has been cast down from possession of thee, and his mind has been made vain in its discourses, and his heart, empty of wisdom, has been darkened, and then given over to a reprobate mind: wilt thou suffer us, too, to be exposed to the same peril? Behold, we cast upon thee all care of the things that concern us; do thou take it up. Concerning things inward and outward, concerning ways, duties, actions, places and times, concerning condition and labour, concerning what to possess and what to leave, what to employ and what to reject, what to know and what to be ignorant of, what to say and what to keep silent, concerning health and sickness, life and death, where and as thou knowest it to be needful, direct, act, arrange, choose and rule as thou pleasest, so that we are not again separated from thee, entangled in attachment to those things, love, affection, vain glory, pleasure, and the snares and cunning of the enemy lying hidden beneath them." This offering of mind and ways God not only does not reject; he fulfils it beyond all hope and desire. The holy learned men, and all who have so given themselves to God, have fully experienced this. David too approves it with his own judgment, without any reservation: (a) Reveal your way to the Lord (or cast your way upon the Lord), and hope in him, and he will act. He confirms it by his own example: for after he had more often and more steadily committed his ways to God, and asked that he would direct him, and that his good Spirit would lead him into the right way, he afterwards said most confidently and joyfully, (b) The Lord rules me, and nothing will be lacking to me. He has placed me in a place of pasture; he has led me up beside the water of refreshment; he has turned my soul. He has led me along the paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Yes, even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will not fear evil, for you are with me: your rod and your staff have comforted me. You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me; you have anointed my head with oil, and my cup is overflowing. How splendid it is! Surely your goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, so that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days. Thousands of similar examples, in every matter, virtue, government, knowledge and practice, may be seen in abundance among those divine and most solidly learned solitaries who occur in Palladius, Rufinus, Cassian, Theodoret, and the ecclesiastical historians Sozomen, Socrates and Evagrius, and others.

units.la: XXIV. Verum quando Deo placitum est
units.tr: XXIV. But when it has pleased God

units.la: Mentem de rebus quibusvis particularius informationem
units.tr: to form the mind more particularly with information about all kinds of things,

units.la: Secundus formare, deque earum ideis specialibus luminose & distinctissime erudire, hoc admirando juxta & facili modo exequitur. Nam cum ille fundum mentis secretius inhabitet qui rerum omnium causa est & archetypus, qui fundamentum, basis, radix, vis & ratio est universorum, (a) omnia ferens verbo potenti suo; quando omnipotens & immensa illa Majestas, omnia secum portans, e fundo mentis evigilare aut exurgere vult, se talem menti spectandam praebere.
units.tr: the Second accomplishes this in a wonderful yet easy manner: he instructs the mind about the special ideas of these things luminously and most distinctly. For since he who is the cause and archetype of all things dwells more secretly in the ground of the mind, he who is the foundation, base, root, power and reason of the universe, bearing all things by his powerful word (a), when that almighty and immense Majesty, carrying all things within himself, wishes to awaken or rise up from the ground of the mind, he presents himself to the mind to be beheld.

units.la: tunc ecce, (o admirandum spectaculum!) pervidet mens in nictu oculi cum immensa illa Majestate totam universi molem, infernalem, coelestem, atque terrestrem, cum omnibus creatis ad radices usque primas suae realitatis. Videt in Deo potentes, luminosas, deliciosas proprietates numinis, qui eas infinitis modis combinaverit, cumque iis diversimode luserit divina Sapientia: qui ad illarum diversas combinationes & ordinationes repraesentandas, rerum creabilium infinitas ideas effinxerit, quarum quaeque suum divinum lusum divinarumque virtutum complexionem repraesentat; qui ex divinarum virtutum proprietatumve suarum, diversimode complicatarum, per potens desiderium suum impraegnatione, res omnigenae natae sint & emanarint, quae in se habent non periturAS impressiones virtutum originantium atque archetyporum suorum. Videt praeterea mens in eadem Majestatis gloriosa manifestatione, qui illa se gerat cum creaturis suis spiritualibus beatis, qui cum miseris, qui cum hominibus bonis, malis, infirmis. Ex quibus omnibus solida eruditio, & ad ultimos usque recessus penetrata scientia Metaphysica, Physica & Ethica, (ad quas scientiæ cæteræ omnes reduci possunt, uti & ex iisdem pendent) in homine tali exurgit. Ita doctus est Salomon per stupendam illam Majestatis Sapientiæque divinæ possessionem & manifestationem, ex qua omnia ei abundavere: (a) Venerunt mihi omnia bona pariter cum illa, & innumerabilis honestas per manus illius; & lætatus sum in omnibus, quoniam antecedebat me ista Sapientia; & ignorabam, quoniam horum omnium Mater est. ... Infinitus thesaurus est hominibus, quo qui usi sunt, participes facti sunt amicitiæ Dei propter eruditionis dona commendati. Dedit mihi Deus dicere ex sententia & præsumere signa horum quæ mihi dantur; quoniam ipse sapientiæ dux est & sapientium emendator: in manu enim illius & nos & sermones nostri, & omnis sapientia, & operum scientia ac disciplina. Ipse enim dedit mihi horum quæ sunt scientiam veram, ut sciam dispositionem orbis terrarum & virtutes elementorum, initium & consummationem & medietatem temporum, vicissitudinum permutationes, morum mutationes & divisiones temporum, anni cursus & stellarum dispositiones, naturas animalium & iras bestiarum, vim ventorum & cogitationes hominum, differentias virgultorum & virtutes radicum, & quæcunque sunt abscondita & improvisa didici: omnium enim Artifex docuit me Sapientia. Est enim in illa Spiritus intelligentiæ SanSanctus, unicus, multiplex, subtilis, disertus, mobilis, incoinquinatus, certus, suavis, amans bonum, acutus, qui nil vetat bene facere, humanus, benignus, stabilis, certus, securus, omnem habens virtutem, omnia prospiciens, & qui capiat omnes spiritus intelligibiles, mundos, subtiles: Omnibus enim mobilibus mobilior est Sapientia, attingit autem ubique propter suam munditiam: vapor est enim virtutis Dei, & emanatio quaedam claritatis Dei omnipotentis sincera, & ideo nihil inquinatum in eam incurrit: Candor est enim lucis aeternae, & speculum sine macula Majestatis Dei, & imago bonitatis illius. Et cum sit una, omnia potest, & in se permanens omnia innovat, & per nationes in animas sanctas se transfert, amicosque Dei & Prophetas constituit. Attingit a termino ad finem fortiter, & disponit omnia suaviter. Hanc descriptionem, etsi longiorem, praetermittere nolui, quia & admirabilis est, & exemplum divinitus de rebus quibusvis eruditi continet, quod etsi rarius, non tamen & alia exempla desunt: hoc enim modo eruditus fuit olim quidem Josephus, qui deinde & ipsis Aegypti Sapientibus erudiendis praefuit; neque posterioribus etiam saeculis similia exempla defuere hic jam non recensenda.
units.tr: Then, behold (O wonderful sight!), the mind in the twinkling of an eye perceives, together with that immeasurable Majesty, the whole mass of the universe, infernal, celestial and terrestrial, with all created things, down to their first roots of reality. It sees in God the powerful, luminous and delightful properties of the divine nature, which He has combined in infinite ways, and with which divine Wisdom has played in various manners. To represent their various combinations and arrangements, He has formed infinite ideas of creatable things, each of which represents its own divine play and combination of divine powers. From the divine powers and properties of His own, variously intertwined, by the impregnation of His powerful desire, all things of every kind have been born and have issued forth, which carry in themselves the imprints, not destined to perish, of the originating powers and their archetypes. Moreover, the mind sees in the same glorious manifestation of Majesty how He conducts Himself towards His blessed spiritual creatures, how towards the wretched, and how towards good, bad and weak men. From all these things a solid learning and a knowledge penetrated to the furthest recesses arises in such a man: Metaphysics, Physics and Ethics (to which all the other sciences can be reduced, and on which they also depend). Thus Solomon was taught, through that astonishing possession and manifestation of the Majesty and divine Wisdom, from which all good things came to him: (a) All good things came to me together with her, and innumerable honour through her hands; and I rejoiced in all these things, because this Wisdom went before me; and I did not know that she is the mother of all these things. ... She is an infinite treasure to men, and those who use it become partakers of the friendship of God, commended for the gifts of learning. God has granted me to speak according to my judgment and to conceive the signs of those things which are given to me; for He Himself is the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise: for in His hand are both we and our words, and all wisdom, and knowledge and skill in works. For He Himself has given me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I know the arrangement of the world and the powers of the elements, the beginning, end and middle of times, the changes of seasons, the alterations of customs and the divisions of times, the course of the year and the positions of the stars, the natures of animals and the rage of beasts, the force of winds and the thoughts of men, the differences of plants and the virtues of roots; and whatever things are hidden and unforeseen I have learned: for Wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me. For in her is a spirit of understanding, holy Holy, one, manifold, subtle, eloquent, mobile, undefiled, certain, sweet, loving the good, keen, which forbids nothing to do well, humane, kind, steadfast, sure, secure, having all power, overseeing all things, and which penetrates all spirits that are intelligent, pure and subtle. For Wisdom is more mobile than all mobile things, and she reaches everywhere because of her purity: for she is a vapour of the power of God, and a certain pure emanation of the clarity of Almighty God, and therefore nothing defiled falls into her: for she is the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of the Majesty of God, and the image of His goodness. And although she is one, she can do all things, and remaining in herself she renews all things, and passing over into holy souls through the nations she makes them friends of God and prophets. She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly. I did not wish to omit this description, although it is rather long, because it is admirable and contains an example, divinely given, of learning about all things whatever; and although such examples are rarer, they are not lacking. For in this way Josephus was once taught, who afterwards presided over the instruction of the very wise men of Egypt; nor in later centuries have similar examples been lacking, which need not be recounted here.

units.la: XXV. Solet & nonnunquam Deus de rebus externis & necessariis erudire suos tertio quodam modo, a duobus jam recensitis diverso; dum videlicet eis non actuales quaedam pro tempore notitias aut motus; non universalem & in habitu durantem omnium scien-
units.tr: XXV. God is also accustomed, at times, to instruct His people about external and necessary things in a third manner, different from the two already described: namely, when He pours into them not some actual knowledge or movements suited to the moment, nor a universal knowledge of all things lasting as a habit, but a particular knowledge, durable nonetheless, of certain things that are necessary at that time.

units.la: {25} Tertius erit ditioncm habendi modus: cur ejus experimenta pauci capiant. scientiam ; sed particularem quandam, durabilem tamen, certis de rebus quæ eo tempore sunt necessariæ, scientiam infundit. Ita olim Noacho architectonicam, cum arca fabricanda esset, qua ab aquis diluvii servaretur cum omni animantium genere : ita Jacobo eam physicæ partem, quæ multiplicandis ejus gregibus inserviebat: ita Bezsaleeli, quotquot artes Tabernaculo Dei exstruendo, vasis ornandis, & vestibus Sacerdotum conficiendis, conferre poterant, suggefsit Sapientissimus. Hæc autem præstat Deus erga illos qui ad æterna divinamque voluntatem solum anhelantes, de cæteris sese ejus committunt providentiæ, quæ talibus nequit omnino deesse: pertinent enim ista ad illa cætera de quibus promissum Christi, Non autem hæc ultra necessaria debent extendi, eaque necessaria, quæ Deus ad æternitatem salutemque conducere novit. Equidem & in necessariis Deum hic defuturum omnes fere suspicantur; & revera si id experimento tentare vellent, falleret procul dubio plurimos eventus. Verum id non a Dei, sed ab hominum defectu procedit, qui fide, qui resignatione vera, qui conditionibus supra enumeratis omnino destituuntur. Si eis essent præditi, & tamen in erudiendo deesset Deus; tunc ansam & suspicandi & conquerendi haberent: sed quod iis conditionibus privati, imo contrariis, animo malo, elato, a Deo ad creaturas conversò, tepido, im-puro puro, inconstanti, insidenti desiderio; intellectu turbulento & nugis perpleno, propria & impatienti acquisecntia affecti, nil de divina hacce eruditione se experiri conquerantur, id absurdissimum & insanum est querelae genus. Retrahunt nos a Deo non tantum haec, quaejam enumeravimus, mala; sed & improvidae & fallaces providentiae nostrae, studiaque propria, ex Dei diffidentia; ex avaritia, cupiditate oculorum, honorum voluptatumve siti, oriunda, quae nos prorsus divinae curae subtrahunt, ejusque reddunt indignos providentia; cum huic minus sidatur quam miseris mortalibus ab unoquoque fit quotidie: Nemo enim est, qui, etsi sciat sibi necessaria esse cibum & potum, vestes & aedes, vasa & instrumenta, tentet tamen omnes eas artes, quibus ista parantur, ediscere: de his unusquisque in hominum societatem, in qua sibi satis prospectum iri confidit, totus recumbit, unam solummodo, caeteris praetermissis, artem amplectens. Eccur nos, ad Deum & aeterna conditi, arte una Deum & aeterna amplectendi, caeteris dimissis, non occupamur, confisi, Deum de caeteris rerum notitiis atque peritiis, in quantum nobis vere necessariae erunt, prospectum vel per se ipsum, vel per alios a se ad id impulsos vel oblatos? Etiamne hoc respectu necesse est id implere verbum Christi; (a) Filius hominis cum venerit, putatis-ne eum in terris reperturum fidem?
units.tr: {25} The third way of having knowledge: why few grasp its experience. Thus of old He instilled architecture into Noah, when the ark was to be built to preserve him from the waters of the flood together with every kind of living thing; thus He gave to Jacob that part of natural science which served the multiplying of his flocks; thus the Most Wise supplied to Bezaleel, and to all who could contribute to building the Tabernacle of God, adorning the vessels and making the garments of the priests, the arts required. God does this for those who long only for eternal things and the divine will, and who commit themselves to His providence in other matters, which cannot wholly fail such people: for these things belong to those other things of which Christ promised that they would be added. Yet these things ought not to be extended beyond what is necessary, and only those necessary things which God knows to be conducive to eternity and salvation. Indeed, almost everyone suspects that God will fail here even in necessary things; and in truth, if they wished to test this by experience, the outcome would undoubtedly deceive most of them. But this does not proceed from the defect of God, but from the defect of men, who are wholly destitute of faith, of true resignation, and of the conditions listed above. If they possessed these, and yet God were lacking in instructing them, they would then have cause both to suspect and to complain; but since they are deprived of these conditions, or rather have the contrary dispositions, with an evil, proud mind turned from God to creatures, lukewarm, impure, inconstant, with a sitting-still desire, a turbulent intellect full of trifles, affected by their own and impatient acquiescence, and yet complain that they experience nothing of this divine instruction, that kind of complaint is most absurd and insane. It is not only these evils, which we have already enumerated, that draw us away from God, but also our improvident and deceitful providence and our own pursuits, arising from distrust of God, from avarice, lust of the eyes, and thirst for honours and pleasures, which wholly withdraw us from the divine care and make us unworthy of His providence; whereas we trust Him less than wretched mortals do every day. For there is no one who, though he knows that food and drink, clothing and houses, vessels and tools are necessary to him, nevertheless tries to learn all the arts by which these are procured: each one, leaving the rest aside and embracing only one art, relies wholly on human society, in which he trusts that enough provision will be made for him. Why, then, we who were created for God and eternity, and who are not occupied with the one art of embracing God and eternity, leaving the rest aside, do we not trust that God will provide, either by Himself or through others whom He impels or offers to us, for knowledge and skills of other things, insofar as they will truly be necessary to us? Is it necessary even in this respect that the word of Christ be fulfilled: (a) When the Son of Man comes, do you think He will find faith on earth?

units.la: XXVI. Dixi modo Deum de istiusmodi
units.tr: XXVI. I have just said that God provides for instruction of this kind either by himself or also through others.

units.la: eruditione vel per se, vel etiam pet alios provisurum; quod nos quarti cujusdam eruditionem adipiscendi modi facit memores. Vult enim interdum Deus non ita, ut tribus primis, sine mediis, sed aliorum interventu homines erudire, idque & in mere spiritualibus atque divinis, & in iis quae inferiorum sunt facultatum atque rerum. Et quidem quoad ea quae Deum divinioresque mentis facultates Deo divinisque aptandas & replendas respiciunt, quoniam hominum pars maxima ita stupida, incrassata & male dispositi ta est ut Deo, etsi interibus vocanti, conditionibus requisitis correspondere, seque ei aptare non possint, imo vix ejus dictamina intelligant; hinc, procurante Numine, habent qui ipso eo veluti manu, modoque crasso & pabili[?], eorum ruditati congruente, adducant.
units.tr: I have just said that God will provide for such instruction either by himself or also through others, which reminds us of a certain fourth way of acquiring knowledge. For God sometimes wishes to teach people not, as with the first three ways, without intermediaries, but through the intervention of others, and this both in purely spiritual and divine matters and in those that concern the lower faculties and things. As to those things that concern God and the higher faculties of the mind, which are to be fitted and filled with the divine, most people are so dull, coarse and ill-disposed that, although God calls them inwardly, they cannot meet the requisite conditions or adapt themselves to him, and they can scarcely understand his dictates at all. Hence, by God's providence, there are those who lead them, as it were by the hand, and in a crude, nourishing manner suited to their rudeness.

units.la: Hisce vero Ductoribus, ubi certo dignoscuntur, (quod animis desiderantibus & sinceris facile efficit Deus: harmoniam enim eam inter veri eruditoris vocem, discipuli que sinceri sensum internum statuit, ut se inde vere affici sentiat eo modo de cujus veritate in conscientia sua certus est, quemque ab errore discernit, uti Pastoris vocem discernunt, oves a voce latronis, illamque hac rejecta, sequuntur, talibus, inquam, ubi dignoscuntur, sese ob Deum ex animo subjicere, palmarium est, nec sine ingenti utilitate, Deinque benedictione poterit fieri, ita ut interdum etiam emolumentum majus inde eveniat, quam si Deo soli immediate mens vel subjecta fuisset, vel subjici voluisset: set : Nulla enim mens adeo superba est, quin sibi videatur se Deo vel subjectam esse, vel subjici velle, imo & ex animo se coram Deo humilem, & ad sua mandata obeunda paratam existere: quae fallacia & superbia (impedimentum primum eruditionis solidae divinaeque) tolli non potest per subjectionem, quam mens quaeque ipsi Deo immediate offerre parata est: quis enim vel e superbissimis ab ipso Deo immediate dirigi, juberi, eique sic soli subesse recusef, & non potius id gloriae ducat, superbiamque suam inde augeat, quae quo major, eo magis ad Deum solum provocare gestit? At vero propter Deum sese ex animo aliis subjicere, non habito respectu ad ea quae vel natura vel mundus in iis magni vel parvi aestimat, sive nempe nobiles seu ignobiles sint, literati vel illiterati, celebres vel contemti, viri an mulierculae, modo Deum possideant, sintque ab eo eruditi; hoc cordis superbiam frangit & eliminat; neque hic superbo cordi dabitur subsistere. Vel enim sese iis, quos mundus reputat vilissimos, subjiciendo, humiliabitur; vel ejusmodi viarum & humiliationis irrisor, suam prodet ac retinebit superbiam, hac occasione, (eo quod ad lapidem Lydium probata ac detecta fuerit,) eo improbiorem, furiosiorem, atque in probos magis indignabundam & calumniis persecutionibusque grassantem: dum interim sincerae humilesque animae ex utraque proficient parte: Nam superborum mundanorumque convicia, calumnias, irrisiones, necnon perfecutiones tolerando, sic magis magisquè humiliabuntur, nec non a creaturis & ab omnibus quæ respicit mundus, separari difcent: nec minus proficient sese vel vilissimis Dei instrumentis atque organis summittendo, & ad eorum vocem omittendo vel exequendo quæcunque ipsis indicabuntur. Atque hoc tum tutius est, siquidem cor nostrum, cum de faciendis & omittendis, de veris & falsis, de divinis & moralibus illud interrogamus, sæpe nos imbecilles fallat; id quod Mens a Deo erudita, & aliis erudiendis a Deo præfecta, facere non potest: tum etiam id ipsum est perfectius; plus enim est Deo & creaturis, quàm Deo solivelle subjici: quare id quoque benedictione divina fit cumulatius: namque vel uno ejusmodi subjectionis actu, plus, prosperante Deo, proficit sincera mens, quam infinitis aliis quos ex propria voluntate vel ipsi Deo exhiberet: ne dicam eos qui vere a Deo præficiuntur, nil revera aliud inculcare, nil pro scopo aliis commendare, quam ipsamet, quas diximus ad eruditionem solidam requiri ex parte hominis, conditiones, sinceritatem videlicet simplicem, humilitatem, a creaturis defectionem & ad Deum conversionem, desiderium Dei æternorumque ardens, illimitatum, stabile, fidens; intellectus puritatem & tranquillitatem; acquiescentiæ continentiam & patientiam; in quibus nulla prorsus fraus, nullum periculum subesse potest: hæc enim fraudum & periculorum quorumvis sunt ipsissima, omniumque potentissima alexipharmaca ; quæis Deus nec novit potentiora, & vero illis uti, ut sic dicam, cogitur ad hominum, maxime vero improborum literatorum fraudes, superbiam, fastum, edomanda. Ista enim est ratio cur Deus voluerit literatos interdum vel illiteratis idiotis, ut Prophetis & Apostolis, vel simplicissimis mulierculis, veluti Deborae, Huldae, Magdalenae, aliisque sexus sequioris subjici; &, ubi corruptio superbiaque invaluerint, similibus quoque subjicere decreverit; quoniam videlicet virorum maximè doctorum, dolus, astutia, fastus, adhaesio rebus mundi sibique ipsis, desiderium proprium seu propria voluntas, res inanes sciendi cupiditas & curiositas, inconstantia, propria confidentia, propria sapientia, rationis audacia atque activitas, sui quaesitio, impatientia, loquacitas & docendi praesumtio, non aliter coërceri, impugnari & frangi, non aliter domari, supprimi & deleri possunt, quam per ea quae illis sunt maximè opposita, & veteris hominis ambitiosum fermentum reprimentia.
units.tr: When such guides are recognised with certainty (and God easily brings this about for those who are earnest and sincere, for he establishes a harmony between the voice of the true teacher and the inner sense of the sincere disciple, so that the disciple feels himself truly moved in the way whose truth he is certain of in his conscience, and so distinguishes it from error, as sheep distinguish the voice of the shepherd from the voice of a thief, and reject the latter and follow the former), then to submit oneself from the heart to such people for God's sake is an outstanding thing, and it cannot happen without great profit and God's blessing. Indeed, it sometimes brings a greater benefit than if the mind had been subject, or had wished to be subject, to God alone and immediately. For no mind is so proud that it does not think it is, or wishes to be, subject to God, and that it is from the heart humble before God and ready to carry out his commands. That deceit and pride, the first obstacle to solid and divine learning, cannot be removed by the submission that any mind is ready to offer to God immediately.
