For who, even among the most proud, would refuse to be directed, commanded and ruled by God himself immediately and alone, and would not rather count it a glory and increase his pride thereby? The greater his pride, the more eagerly it longs to be called out by God alone. But to submit oneself from the heart to others for God's sake, without regard to what nature or the world values highly or lowly in them, whether they are noble or ignoble, learned or unlearned, famous or despised, men or mere women, provided they possess God and are taught by him, this breaks and expels the pride of the heart, and a proud heart will not be allowed to remain. For either, by submitting to those whom the world reckons most worthless, it will be humbled; or, mocking such ways and such humiliation, it will betray and keep its pride, and on this occasion, since it has been tested and exposed as on a touchstone, it will become all the more wicked, more furious, and more indignant against the upright, raging with slanders and persecutions. Meanwhile, sincere and humble souls profit on both sides. For by enduring the reproaches, slanders, mockery and persecutions of the proud and worldly, they are humbled more and more, and they learn to be separated from creatures and from everything the world regards. They also profit no less by submitting themselves to the most lowly instruments and organs of God, and by omitting or carrying out whatever is pointed out to them at their voice. This is also safer, since our heart, when we question it about what is to be done or left undone, about true and false, divine and moral, often deceives us, whereas a mind taught by God, and set over others by God to teach them, cannot do so. It is also the more perfect course, for it is more to be willing to be subject to God and to creatures than to be willing to be subject to God alone. Therefore this too is increased by the divine blessing. Indeed, by a single act of such submission, a sincere mind, with God prospering it, profits more than by infinite other acts which it might offer to God by its own will. I need not add that those who are truly set over others by God inculcate nothing else and commend nothing else to others as their aim than those very conditions we have said are required on the part of man for solid learning: namely, simple sincerity, humility, withdrawal from creatures and conversion to God, a burning, unlimited, steadfast and trusting desire for God and eternal things, purity and tranquillity of the intellect, and continence and patience in acquiescence. In these there is absolutely no fraud and no danger. For these are the very antidotes to all frauds and dangers, and the most powerful of all; God knows none more powerful, and he is, so to speak, compelled to use them to subdue the frauds, pride and arrogance of men, and especially of wicked learned men. This is the reason why God has sometimes willed the learned to be subject to the unlearned, idiots, like the Prophets and Apostles, or to the simplest women, like Deborah, Huldah and Mary Magdalene, and other members of the weaker sex; and, when corruption and pride have taken hold, he has decided to subject them likewise. For the cunning, craft, arrogance, attachment to worldly things and to themselves, self-will or one's own will, the vain desire and curiosity to know, inconstancy, self-confidence, one's own wisdom, the audacity and activity of reason, self-seeking, impatience, loquacity and presumption in teaching, of even the most learned men, cannot be restrained, opposed and broken, nor tamed, suppressed and destroyed, except by the things most opposed to them, which check the ambitious leaven of the old man.

units.la: Haec autem, quâ Deus utitur, homines erudiendi per alios via, eaque, quae ipsi debetur subjectio, non tantum ad illos, eorumve scripta vel monita, qui dudum mortui sunt, referendae sunt; sed & maximè de his, qui quovis tempore in vivis sunt, debent intelligi: Deus enim, qui se non pristino tantùm, sed & quovis tempore, mentibus puris aptisque communicat, & eas per se erudit, quovis etiam tempore ad caeterarum eruditionem
units.tr: This way, by which God uses other people to instruct men, and the submission due to it, must be referred not only to those who have long been dead, or to their writings and admonitions, but must be understood above all of those who are alive at any time. For God, who communicates himself not only in former times but at every time to pure and fit minds, and instructs them directly, also at every time uses the same means for the instruction of others.

units.la: C eiusdem eisdem utitur. Ipsa praeterea hominum erudiendorum & domandorum superbia & pertinacia, non ita superantur scriptis, & dudum mortuorum praeceptis (queis sine multa repugnantia, imo cum honorifico sui incremento, cedunt,) quam vivorum exemplis atque voce. Accedit quod non-viventium scripta facile possint glossis & interpretamentis adulterinis sine sui reluctantia eludi & corrumpi: non ita viventium voces & opera; quippe qui se ipsos ad quamvis occasionem explicant, a falsis interpretationibus vindicant, sensus suos multifariam inculcant, consiliaque & documenta pro varia auditorum dispositione, variant & diversimode dispensant applicantque, dum interim semper ad interiora, internumque Eruditorem Deum remittunt, se nil nisi ad illum manuductores & monitores, neminem interius illuminantes & erudientes, humiliter professi.
units.tr: Moreover, the pride and obstinacy of men, which are to be instructed and tamed, are overcome less by writings and the precepts of those long dead (to which they yield without much resistance, indeed with an honourable increase of their own standing) than by the examples and voice of the living. Added to this is that the writings of the dead can easily be mocked and corrupted by spurious glosses and interpretations without any resistance from them; but the voices and works of the living are not so. For they explain themselves on every occasion, defend themselves against false interpretations, impress their meanings in many ways, and vary and dispense and apply their counsels and teachings in different ways according to the varied dispositions of their hearers. Meanwhile they always refer people to what is inward and to God as the inner Teacher, humbly professing that they are only guides and reminders to him, and that they enlighten and teach no one inwardly.

units.la: Quod si quis obtenderet, tum difficultatis nodum hic esse, reperire nempe certo tales; tum periculosum quoque esse alieno magis quam suo judicio niti; is vel elementa viarum Dei se nescire sic testaretur: hoc enim, quod ultimo praetendit, aut nullum est, aut evertit, quaecunque Deus olim per Sanctos egit. Nullum majus periculum quam a judicio proprio; nullum vere periculum illi, qui mente sincera, desiderio caeterisque dispositionibus bonis praeditus, infucate quaerit Dominum qui tunc ejus protector est, praeservans eum a lapsu; (a) simplices enim, ut ait Psaltes, custodit Dominus; tum etiam ejus est Ductor, eum ad vera sui instrumenta adducens, atque etiam criterium luminis & acquiescentiæ intimum largiens, quo sciat fetales reperisse, in quibus Deum erudientem magis audire possit eique morem gerere, quam vel spectare creaturam, vel ei obtemperare.
units.tr: But if someone should object that there is a knot of difficulty here, namely, that it is hard to find such people with certainty, and that it is also dangerous to rely on the judgement of another rather than one's own, then he would show that he does not even know the rudiments of God's ways. For what he finally puts forward is either nothing at all, or it overturns whatever God has at any time done through the saints. There is no greater danger than that from one's own judgement. There is truly no danger to the one who, endowed with a sincere mind, a desire and other good dispositions, seeks the Lord without pretence; for then the Lord is his protector, preserving him from falling. (a) The simple, as the Psalmist says, the Lord preserves. Then also he is his guide, bringing him to his true instruments, and bestowing the inner criterion of light and acquiescence, by which he may know that he has found the right people, in whom he can more readily hear God teaching and obey him, than either look to a creature or obey it.

units.la: Hæc vero de iis præcipue quæ diviniora sunt, quæque diviniores facultates quoad æterna ministerio hominum erudiendas primario respiciunt. Solet etiam Deus, ut diximus, quoad exteriora & quæ facultates rationis, sensuum, & si quæ inferiores spectant, humano ministerio & medio uti sapius, idque ubi opus est. Sic, opus est arte nonnulla? opus eruditis qui eam doceant? opus desiderio necessaria discendi? suppeditat peritos, mittit atque convertit eruditos, impellit erudiendos ad ea discenda & exercenda quæ eis necessaria sunt & ad æternitatem proficua, relictis millenis nugis & inutilibus occupationibus, ad quas qui proprio impulsu feruntur & dictamine, præter inutilia onera, & noxia figmenta, nil colligunt. Hic nonnullarum regularum Rationis, quæ tunc exercetur, decet nos esse memores. Eam videlicet non nisi ex motivo sive impulsu divino, nec nisi ad Deum recurrendo, & per intervalla, debere exerceri, servata proportione inter æterna solida atque temporaria & momentanea evanida.
units.tr: These things, however, apply chiefly to those matters which are more divine, and which the higher faculties primarily regard as to eternal things to be taught through the ministry of men. God also, as we have said, is accustomed to use human ministry and means more often in outward matters and in those which concern the faculties of reason and the senses, and the lower faculties, and this where there is need. Thus: is some art needed? Are there learned men needed to teach it? Is the necessary desire to learn needed? He supplies skilled persons, sends and turns learned men, and impels those to be taught to learn and practise those things which are necessary for them and profitable for eternity, setting aside a thousand trifles and useless occupations, to which those who are carried along by their own impulse and judgement gather nothing but useless burdens and harmful fictions. Here we ought to remember some rules of reason, which is then exercised. Namely, it should not be exercised except from a divine motive or impulse, nor except by recourse to God, and at intervals, the proportion being observed between solid eternal things and temporary and fleeting ones.

units.la: LIBRI PRIMI PARS ALTERA, quæ est DE VERÆ ERUDITIONIS POSSESSIONE.
units.tr: THE SECOND PART OF THE FIRST BOOK, which concerns THE POSSESSION OF TRUE ERUDITION.

units.la: ET hactenus quidem de Eruditione Solida respectu acquisitionis consideranda. Consideranda nunc est & in statu possessionis; deinde in statu communicationis: in quibus erimus breviores, quia quæ acquisitionem spectant, quoniam primaria erant, & omnium origo, non debuerunt non copiosius perpendi.
units.tr: So far we have considered Solid Erudition with respect to its acquisition. Now it must be considered in its state of possession, and then in its state of communication. In these we shall be briefer, because what concerns acquisition was primary and is the origin of everything, so it could not but be weighed more fully.

units.la: XXVII. Ejus, qui Eruditionem Solidam est adeptus, quidam sunt, respectu sui, Dei, rerum æternarum & divinarum, rerum temporariarum, proximi denique sui, characteres, quos obiter libet recensere. Et primo quidem, omnes, quas habuit hactenus ad eruditionem veram adipiscendam dispositiones bonas, quasque Deus illi insuper infudit prærogativas, virtutes & dotes, non tolluntur; sed econtra, magis magisque augentur. Hæc quænam sint, quoniam aliquoties supra memoravimus, hic loci non resumam.
units.tr: XXVII. Those who have attained Solid Erudition have certain marks, with respect to themselves, God, eternal and divine things, temporal things, and finally their neighbour, which I may briefly list. First, all the good dispositions they had hitherto for acquiring true erudition, and the further prerogatives, virtues and gifts God has poured into them, are not taken away but on the contrary grow more and more. What these are, since we have mentioned them several times, I shall not repeat here.

units.la: At quoniam inter hasce conditiones nonnullæ vacuitatem veluti quandam denotant, & realitatis sive boni, aut luminis per eruditionem acquirendi absentiam; quæri potest, quomodo eruditione adepta, ejusmodi dispositiones, vacuitatem & absentiam boni per eruditionem acquirendi includentes, augeri dicantur. Hoc vero ex admiranda boni æterni natura, quæ infinita & interminabilis est, nec non ex illimitata fundi & facultatum mentis capacitate fluit, quæ, maxime hoc in mundo, ita objecto æterno, immenso, interminabili, incomprehensibili affici, penetrari, satiari non possunt, quin objectum id habeat sine termino in se nova quædam perpetua vel novas saltem suarum infinitarum proprietatum combinationes, quibus mentem ejusque facultates novis semper modis afficiat: ipsaque Mens præterea cum suis facultatibus nunquam tam penetranter, tantisque modis ab Omnipotente bono affecta est, quin possit ab eodem pluribus, in infinita variatione & complicatione facultatum suarum, nec non in gradibus percipiendi, affici. Terrestria & temporalia, ubi facultatibus nostris inferiores sortis juncta sunt, naufeam parere, ab illisque separanda esse, ni insanire, & perire velimus, nemo est qui nesciat, nemo qui non experiatur: quod apertum est documentum, nos ad ea non esse factos, esseque adeo scopo ejusmodi indignos. Æternorum & divinorum contraria est ratio, contrarius eventus. Non nauseam, non desectum, non subjecti interitum pariunt eorum desiderium, adeptio, fruitio: sed desiderium majus, deliciosius, magis perficiens, magis vivificans, mentemque magis beans sine termino afficiunt; admirandum & nulli alii rei assimilandum infinite perfecti & æterni Dei signum & monimentum. Hoc respexit Syracides cum Divinam Sapientiam ita de se verba facientem introducit: (a) Qui edunt me, adhuc esurient; & qui bibunt me, adhuc sitient: Quod theodidactus Bernhardus mellifluis suis rythmis de JESU CHRISTO, omnis verae Eruditionis authore, objecto, via, thesauro, in quo quippe, Paulo si credamus, (b) omnes scientiarum thesauri sunt absconditi, sic efferebat: Tua, JESU, dilectio Qui te gustant esuriunt, Grata menti refectio; Qui bibunt adhuc sitiunt, Replens sine fastidio, Desiderare nesciunt Dans famem desiderio. Nisi Jesum quem diligunt.
units.tr: But since some of these conditions seem to denote a certain emptiness, and an absence of the reality or good, or of the light to be acquired through erudition, it may be asked how, once erudition is attained, such dispositions, which include an emptiness and an absence of the good to be acquired through erudition, are said to grow. This follows from the wondrous nature of the eternal good, which is infinite and boundless, and from the unlimited capacity of the mind's ground and faculties, which, above all in this world, cannot be affected, penetrated or satisfied by an object so eternal, immense, boundless and incomprehensible, without that object having in itself, without limit, some new and perpetual combinations, or at least new combinations of its infinite properties, by which it affects the mind and its faculties in ever new ways. Moreover, the Mind itself with its faculties is never so deeply and so fully affected by the Almighty good that it cannot be affected by it again in many ways, in the infinite variation and complication of its faculties, and in degrees of perception. That earthly and temporal things, where they are joined to a lower lot than our faculties, produce nausea, and must be separated from us unless we wish to go mad and perish, no one is unaware, no one who has not experienced it. This is clear proof that we were not made for such things, and are therefore unworthy of such an aim. With eternal and divine things the case and the outcome are contrary. Their desire, attainment and enjoyment produce no nausea, no deficiency, no ruin of the subject; rather they stir a greater desire, one more delightful, more perfecting, more quickening, and making the mind more blessed, without end. This is the wonderful sign and monument of the infinitely perfect and eternal God, not to be compared with anything else. The son of Sirach had this in view when he introduced Divine Wisdom speaking of herself: (a) Those who eat me shall still be hungry, and those who drink me shall still be thirsty. Bernard, taught by God, expressed this in his honeyed rhythms about JESUS CHRIST, the author, object, way and treasure of all true Erudition, in whom, if we believe Paul, (b) all the treasures of knowledge are hidden, in these words: Your love, O Jesus, Those who taste you hunger for, A grateful refreshment to the mind; Those who drink you still thirst, Filled without weariness, They do not know how to desire, Giving hunger through desire. Unless Jesus whom they love.

units.la: XXVIII. Inter omnes autem veri Eruditi characteres, primas tenet sui, Dei, omniumque aliarum rerum respectu, Pax & laetitia, sive animæ tranquillitas: per solidam namque eruditionem, ut vidimus, adepræsunt (quantum hac in vita fieri potest,) fundamentales & immensæ mentis ejus capacitates sive facultates, (præcipua & tota sui pars essentialis & solida,) suum, ad quod factæ erant, & cujus capaces erant, objectum, suam æternam formam ruditate & asperitate quavis repugnante eliminata: adeoque habent quo solide ac funditus acquiescant, carentque interno turbationis & repugnantiæ principio. Hinc quicquid ex tali mente ad quæcunque effluit, mera pax est & tran-
units.tr: XXVIII. Among all the marks of the true learned, the first, with respect to himself, God and all other things, is peace and joy, or tranquillity of soul. For through solid erudition, as we have seen, the fundamental and immense capacities or faculties of his mind (the principal and whole essential and solid part of himself) are brought to rest, as far as is possible in this life, in their object, for which they were made and to which they are capable of reaching, their eternal form having been removed of every roughness and harshness that resists. Hence they have something in which they can rest solidly and thoroughly, and they lack any inner principle of disturbance and resistance. Hence whatever flows from such a mind to anything whatever is pure peace and tran-

units.la: Veri eruditi character primus, Pax, in intimis, in externis, & cum proximus. Vera pax, qua. Qui cal- lumnan- tium & adversan- tium im- petus, ejus pacem non turbent. Alii characteres tranquillitas, modo subjecta pacis recipiendæ capacia sese offerant. Hinc Eruditor summus discipulis suis: (a) pacem relinquo vobis; & discipuli sibi ipsis, pacem, & lætitiam, & gratiam, salutandi more offerebant. Eruditi fundus in pace est, quoniam æternitas aliquatenus degustata, & plenius sperata, ipsum tranquillat. Desiderium in pace est: nam ad peritura quidem inconstantia & torquentia non fertur: Deus vero & divina ad quæ fertur, eatenus id afficiunt, ut, etsi sese ei plene nondum communicent, ei tamen plenam sui mox communicandi spem faciant, quæ abunde eum lætificat & tranquillat: indicat enim erudito Divina, cui junctus esset, Sapientia, ei, certis de causis, nondum completa danda vel ostendenda, sed reservanda donec crassamine corporis fit solutus, ea bona ad quæ factus est: cui sapientissimæ dispensationi acquiescit sapiens, nil particularius de Deo, deque æternis, nunc sentire cupiens, nisi ipsa ea singularior cupiditas a Deo illi infundatur: quod fit rarius. Unde patet ejus intellectum in plena tranquillitate esse quoque positum, & quidem ita, ut ipsi scire Deum cum divinis suis rebus incomprehensibilem esse, sufficiat, quando tamen de illis, multoque magis de rebus aliis, nullas specialiores haberet notiones, quas revera, ex propria voluntate atque cupiditate adipisci nollet, quanquam vel nictu oculi eas posset acquirere; satius nimirum ducens, intellectum suum sub Dei lumine & regimine mere passivum esse, quam sub proprio regimine
units.tr: The first mark of the true learned man is peace: within, without, and with his neighbour. True peace, which the assaults of slanderers and adversaries do not disturb. The other marks are tranquillity, provided the subject offers itself capable of receiving peace. Hence the supreme Teacher said to his disciples: (a) I leave you peace; and the disciples, in turn, greeted one another with peace, joy and grace, as was the custom. The ground of the learned man rests in peace, since eternity, partly tasted and more fully hoped for, brings it tranquillity. His desire is in peace: for it is not drawn to perishable things, which are inconstant and torment; but God and the divine things toward which it is drawn so affect it that, although they do not yet fully communicate themselves to him, they hold out to him the sure hope of soon communicating themselves fully, which greatly gladdens and calms him. For divine Wisdom, to which he is joined, indicates to the learned man that, for certain reasons, it is not yet to be given or shown to him in full, but reserved until he is loosed from the coarseness of the body, together with the good things for which he was made. The wise man acquiesces in this most wise dispensation, not desiring to feel anything more particular about God, or the eternal things, now, unless that very special desire is poured into him by God, which happens rarely. Hence it is clear that his intellect is also placed in full tranquillity, and indeed so that it suffices for him to know that God, with his divine things, is incomprehensible, although he would have no more specific notions of those things, or much more of other things, which indeed he would not wish to acquire by his own will and desire, although he could acquire them in the blink of an eye. For he judges it better that his intellect be purely passive under God's light and direction, than to have, under its own direction, an angelic knowledge.

units.la: angelicam habere notitiam. Porro tanta pace ejus acquiescentia perfunditur, ut, quicquid de eo fiat, turbari non possit: est enim veluti lapis divina manu politus, & ad loca sua a Deo adaptatus, qui patitur se ab illa potenti & sapienti manu ibi collocari, in eo loco & statu teneri, ubi architecto sapientissimo placet, ibidem sese quam congruentissime componens, veluti qui ad hoc ipsum, in quo tunc est, positus sit atque formatus.
units.tr: Moreover, he is so suffused with the peace of acquiescence that, whatever happens to him, he cannot be disturbed. For he is like a stone polished by a divine hand and fitted by God to its place. He allows himself to be placed by that powerful and wise hand there, to be held in that place and state where the most wise Architect pleases, fitting himself most congruently there, as one who was positioned and formed for the very place he now occupies.

units.la: De externis autem, sive corpus ea, sive bona, sive elementaria sint, quocunque modo illa ei eveniant, non habet quod tranquillitatis perturbationem extimescat, solidæ pacis fontem æternum in intimis possidens. Si namque cuncta ei arrideant, quando tamen ea ipse intus non admittit, neque in iis pacem constituit, iis non distrahitur præsentibus, iisdemque non fit inquietus absentibus; sed lætior magis & pacatior. Externa siquidem, ex quo peccatum est, miseriarum & tenebrarum sunt vincula, quin & pondera, mentes ab æternis bonis dividentia, removentia, & deprimentia: quapropter, quo magis iis solvitur vinculis, tenebris, miseriis, pondere, eo purius majoris lætitiæ ansa gaudet tranquillior animus, a Deo eruditus, quem Si fractus illabatur orbis, Impavidum ferient ruinæ:
units.tr: As for external things, whether they are of the body, or goods, or elemental things, whatever way they come to him, he has no reason to fear a disturbance of tranquillity, since he possesses within himself the eternal fountain of solid peace. For even if everything smiles on him, yet since he does not admit those things within, nor place his peace in them, he is not drawn away by them when present, nor made restless by their absence, but is rather the more cheerful and more peaceful. For external things, since sin entered, are the chains of miseries and darkness, indeed burdens, dividing, removing and weighing down minds from eternal goods. Therefore, the more the taught soul is loosed from these chains, darkness, miseries and burden, the more purely and tranquilly it rejoices in a greater ground of joy, the soul taught by God, of whom: If the broken world should fall upon him, the ruins will strike him unafraid.

units.la: vel, ut Sanctioris Lyrici verbis utar, eo magis (a) benedicit Domino consulenti ei in noctibus (adversitatibus) in quibus ita a renibus (interioribus facultatibus a Deo asse-ctis) ētis) erudiatur, ut non commoveatur; sed lætetur cor, & exultet in spe, (a) Beatum prædicans quem Dominus sic erudierit, quietem ei præstans in diebus malis, dum fovea paratur impio; ipsi vero, consolationes divinæ, quæ secundum multitudinem dolorum cordis sui, lætificant animam ejus.
units.tr: Or, to use the words of the more holy Lyric poet, he blesses the Lord who counsels him in the nights (adversities), in which his reins (inner faculties touched by God) are taught so that he is not moved; but his heart rejoices, and exults in hope, (a) calling blessed the man whom the Lord thus teaches, granting him rest in evil days, while a pit is dug for the wicked; and the divine consolations, which according to the multitude of the sorrows of his heart, gladden his soul.

units.la: Nec minori gaudet tranquillitate cum proximis suis bonis malisve, quos tolerat in rebus divini cultus, nemini vim inferens, suam cuique libertatem permittens, imo ea omnia probans & promovens, quibus ad Dei memoriam & amorem homines revocari possunt: in politicis autem & civilibus, sese legibus & moribus per se non malis accommodans & subjiciens, omnesque officiis devincire allaborans, gaudet tranquillitate: politus namque a manu Domini ille ædificii divini lapis, aliis ita comiter sese adaptat, ut eos etiam poliat & erupiat, nedum impetat, mordeat, rejiciat: quanquam ubi bruti lapides in eum protervius & petulantius irruunt, a firma ejus consistentiæ soliditate vehementius nonnunquam repellantur; &, veluti tela in adamantinum impulsa scutum, cuspide refracto reflectuntur & disjiciuntur, sine interna interim animi perturbatione, vel potius, cum lætitiæ augmento & blando risu, quando maxime calumniis & conviciis inconditis ab insana nonnullorum idiotarum vel falsorum eruditorum caterva sese videt impeti: tunc enim
units.tr: He rejoices in equal tranquillity with his neighbours, whether good or bad, whom he tolerates in matters of divine worship. He does violence to no one, allows each person his own liberty, and indeed approves and promotes all those things by which men can be called back to the memory and love of God. In political and civil matters, he accommodates and submits himself to laws and customs that are not in themselves evil, and labours to bind everyone to himself by duties; in this too he rejoices in tranquillity. For that stone of the divine building, polished by the hand of the Lord, adapts itself so courteously to others that it even polishes and smooths them, let alone attacks, bites, or rejects them. Yet when brute stones rush against it more insolently and wantonly, they are sometimes driven back more forcefully by the firm solidity of its steadfastness. Like missiles hurled against an adamantine shield, they are reflected and scattered with their points broken, and the mind suffers no inner disturbance, or rather, its joy increases and it smiles gently. This is especially so when it sees itself assailed by slanders and unseemly insults from the mad crowd of some ignorant people or false scholars. For then

units.la: Conscia mentis recti famæ mendacia ridet; & commiseratione potius quam ira erga ejusmodi detractatores malevolos & insulsos commovetur, queis tamen duriora interdum responsa fuerint tanquam salutaria contra morbum ipsorum alexipharmaca, & professe possint: ita namque falsa & mala vividius dedocentur, bona & vera (queis nullum beneficium majus) docentur, si modo inde emolumentum incomparabile deducere non recusent maledicentium mentes ægrae necplane insanabiles, sique inde cautiores in posterum fieri curaverint. At cum probis, vel etiam cum eis qui non mordaces sunt aggressores, vero erudito quid tranquillius & facilius?
units.tr: Conscious of an upright mind, he laughs at the lies of rumour; and he is moved by pity rather than anger towards such malicious and foolish detractors. Yet harsher replies may sometimes be given to them, like wholesome antidotes against their disease, and they may prove beneficial. For false and evil things are unlearned more vividly, and good and true things (than which no benefit is greater) are taught, if only the minds of the slanderers, sick and almost incurable, do not refuse to draw from this an incomparable advantage, and if they take care to become more cautious in future. But with upright people, or even with those who are not biting assailants, what is more tranquil and easy for the true scholar?

units.la: Porro, idem quoque & omnibus bonus est, & erga universos beneficus: siquidem læta pax sit ipsa boni fruitio; bonum autem omne se ex natura sua quovis diffundere conetur: unde is intus quidem omnibus bona peroptat, extus vero factis & verbis, quantum res exigit & fert occasio, ea exhibet, quæ ad æterna bona quosvis impellant. Nec minus omnibus justus, quando bella & contentiones, a quibus tranquilla pax abhorret, soleant emanare ab injustitiæ fonte, quem idcirco amore justitiæ exstinguit: proinde, nil in alios juris, quod in se sumi nollet, usurpat; imo sibi quam aliis durior: in se enim quisque hoc habet juris, ut se ipsum contemnat, condemnet, deprimat; in alios non item: erga omnes denique patiens, injurias & persecutiones pacis amore & animi bonitate tolerans ab improbis, queis vel prodesse cupit cos alloquendo, vel quos etiam prætermiserat tacendo: habet enim & id proprii vera Eruditio, ut libentius retinendæ tranquillitatis ergo, taceat, & solitaria, a turba & tumultibus remota occultetur, quam sese multo cum strepitu foras prodat, & aliorum negotiis, mundique officiis sese intermiscat; etsi, quicquid agat, impiorum dentes evitare sit impossibile, qui neque loquentes neque tacentes, nec publicos nec privatos, nec eos qui aperte degunt, nec qui secedere a mundo & solitarie vivere quærunt, possunt sufferre; quia obliquum pertinescit sui indicem, rectum.
units.tr: Moreover, he is likewise good to all and beneficent towards everyone, since peaceful calm is itself the enjoyment of good. Every good tends by its own nature to spread itself in every direction. Hence he inwardly wishes good things to all, and outwardly, by deeds and words, as the matter demands and the occasion allows, he shows those things that impel everyone towards eternal goods. He is no less just towards all, since wars and quarrels, from which peaceful tranquillity shrinks, usually spring from the fountain of injustice, which he therefore extinguishes by his love of justice. Accordingly, he claims for himself no right over others that he would not wish to be claimed against himself. Indeed he is harsher on himself than on others, for each person has this right over himself, to despise, condemn and humble himself, but not over others. Lastly, he is patient towards all, enduring injuries and persecutions from the wicked with love of peace and goodness of mind. He either wishes to benefit them by speaking to them, or passes them by in silence. For it is also a peculiar trait of true scholarship that, for the sake of preserving tranquillity more willingly, it keeps silent and lies hidden in solitude, remote from crowds and tumults, rather than thrusting itself out with much noise and mixing itself in the affairs of others and the duties of the world. Yet whatever he does, it is impossible to escape the teeth of the impious, who can tolerate neither those who speak nor those who keep silent, neither public nor private persons, neither those who live openly nor those who seek to withdraw from the world and live alone. For a crooked man cannot bear a straight judge of himself.

units.la: XXIX. Paci, tranquillitatique, & huic annexis, quæ Eruditum quoad Deum, homines, resque cæteras, ornant, succenturiatur quæ in eo Deum præcipue respicit, animi gratitudo lausque divini Numinis, quod primum est officium creaturæ intelligentis, haud secus ac inter homines si quis generosioris est indolis, accepitque vel a sui similibus (quanto magis si ab infinite superioribus?) beneficia excellentis præstantiæ, nil antiquius habet quam grato animo benefactorem semper recolere, venerari, præconiis extollere, facta depræticare: sine quo ossicio, turpis oblivio ingratitudoque, justissima fuerint causa cur benefactor sua interrumpat beneficia, ingratumque animum propriæ suæ indigentiæ permittat; cum econtra, beneficiorum datorum grata agnitio ad plura excellentiora recipienda sint gradus medium quoque efficacissimum. Idem inter Deum eosque, de quibus nunc quæstio est, agitur. Illi cum a Deo receperint & fe & facultates suas, Dei luminosi deliciosique nec non & creaturarum percipiendarum capaces, cumque insuper & lumen & fruitionem tranquillam omnium istorum ab eodem illa continue largiente & conservante habeant; de hisce illi homagium (ut sic dicam) si praestent, si ea cum laudibus perpetuis (quo nil aequius est) illi accepta referant, in suae eruditionis sapientiaeque possessione ab eodem omnis boni Auctore, conservantur. Quae causa, est cur qui voluerunt continue sapere, ut Deo grati generosique animi encomia canerent, fuerint solliciti quam maxime, eum solum Sapientem magnificientes, cui uni gloriam, honorem, gratiarumque actiones aeternas reddi optaverint, uti saepe in sacris voluminibus occurrit, in divinis praesertim divinitus eruditi Davidis canticis, ubi animam suam, cunctos homines, omnes creaturas, Deumque etiam ipsum ad divinorum operum magnificentiaeque agnitionem & gaudium in eis provocat & invitat, atque ad laudem liberalissimae admirandaeque Sapientiae Creatoris. Quin & ex Ethnicis ii qui rectam rationem non ejuraverunt sed audierunt, simili gratitudinis charactere suam eruditionem exornarunt. Epistetus: (a) Si sani essemus, quid aliud nobis agendum foret & publice & privatim quam Numen celebrandum & laudandum, & grates ei persolvendae? Nonne & inter fodiendum, & arandum, & edendum hymnus hic cantandus esset Deo: Magnus est Deus, qui nobis instrumenta praebuerit haec. hæc, quibus terrem excolamus ; Magnus est Deus , qui manus dederit , qui deglutiendi vim, qui ventrem ; qui ut latenter crescamus, qui ut dormientes respiremus , effecerit ? Hæc singulis in rebus cantanda erant ; & hymnus maximus & divinissimus resonandus, quod facultatem dederit harum rerum INTELLIGENTEM& UTENDI RATIONE instructam. Quid igitur ? siquidem vulgo excæcati sitis, nonne saltem oportebat esse aliquem qui hoc munere fungeretur, & loco omnium hymnum Deo publicaret ? Ecquid aliud possim ego, senex & claudus, nisi ita celebrare Deum ? Lusciniα si essem, fungerer luscinie officio ; si olor, oloris. Atqui intelligentia præditus sum; mihi igitur Deus imcumbit celebrandus : munus meum ipsum est, ipso defungor, nec stationem hanc deseram quoad licuerit ; quin & vos omnes ad eandem mecum cantilenam exhortor. At qui inter eos facere id recusarunt, eruditionis suæ soliditate, si quam habuerunt, destituti sunt, tenebris immersi, & traditi in sensum reprobum : neque enim decuit Deum administrare impiis lucem quâ legitime & prout æquum erat, nolebant uti. Commemorat id egregie divus Paulus de iis gentium Philosophis, qui, cum cognovissent Deum, nec tamen eum uti Deum gloria affecissent, neque ei egissent gratias, evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis, tenebrisque & stoliditate cordis plexi sunt: & putantes se esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt, & a Deo tradui impiis, tenebrosis, impuris & enormibus suis concupiscentiis, ut qui adhæserint creaturis, deserto Creatore benedicto in sæcula. cula. Ad quæ præcipitia faxit Deus ne proclives ruant ingratæ eruditorum seculi hujus mentes quam plurimæ, quæ eo usque obbrutescere cœperunt, ut nobilissimum Dei donorum, libertatem, omnis boni justique fundamentum, Dei sufficientiam, perfectionesque, quin & exsistentiam cum Spinoza miserisque suis discipulis ex animo jam delere cogitent. Sed redeamus ad bonos.
units.tr: XXIX. To peace, tranquillity, and those things joined to them, which adorn the scholar in his relation to God, to men, and to other things, there is added, as a reinforcement, the gratitude and praise of the mind towards the divine Majesty, which regards God above all. This is the first duty of an intelligent creature. Just as among men, if someone is of a generous disposition and has received from his equals (how much more from one infinitely superior?) benefits of outstanding excellence, he considers nothing more important than always to remember his benefactor with a grateful mind, to venerate him, to extol him with praises, and to proclaim his deeds. Without this duty, shameful forgetfulness and ingratitude would be the most just cause for a benefactor to interrupt his benefits and leave the ungrateful mind to its own need. On the contrary, the grateful acknowledgement of benefits received is also the most effective means of gaining more and greater ones. The same holds between God and those of whom we now speak. Since they have received from God both themselves and their faculties, capable of perceiving God, who is luminous and delightful, and also of perceiving creatures, and since, moreover, they have both light and tranquil enjoyment of all these things from him, who continually grants and preserves them, then if they render to him, as it were, homage for these things, and if they refer them back to him with perpetual praises (nothing is more fitting), they are preserved in the possession of their scholarship and wisdom by him, the Author of every good. This is why those who wished to be wise continually, so as to sing the praises of God with a grateful and generous mind, were most anxious to magnify him alone as the Wise One, to whom alone they wished glory, honour and eternal thanksgivings to be rendered. This recurs often in the sacred volumes, especially in the divinely taught songs of David, where he calls and invites his soul, all men, all creatures, and God himself to the recognition of and joy in his divine works, and to the praise of the most liberal and admirable Wisdom of the Creator. Indeed, among the Gentiles, those who did not renounce right reason but listened to it adorned their learning with a similar character of gratitude. Epictetus says: (a) If we were sound, what else should we do, both publicly and privately, than celebrate and praise the Divinity and give thanks to him? Should not this hymn be sung to God while we dig, while we plough, while we eat: Great is God, who has given us these instruments with which we cultivate the earth; great is God, who has given us hands, the power to swallow, the belly; who has brought it about that we grow without our knowledge, and that we breathe while sleeping? These things should be sung on every occasion, and the greatest and most divine hymn should resound, because he has given us the faculty of INTELLIGENCE and the ability to use these things rightly. What then? Since you are blind like the common people, should there not at least be someone to perform this office and proclaim the hymn to God on behalf of all? What else can I do, an old man and lame, but celebrate God in this way? If I were a nightingale, I would do a nightingale's work; if a swan, a swan's. But I am endowed with intelligence; therefore I am bound to celebrate God. This is my task; I perform it, nor will I desert this post as long as I am allowed. Indeed I exhort you all to join me in the same song. But those who refused to do this were deprived of whatever solidity of scholarship they had, were immersed in darkness, and were given over to a reprobate mind. For it was not fitting that God should give light to the impious, which they were unwilling to use lawfully and as was right. The apostle Paul excellently recalls this about those philosophers of the Gentiles who, though they knew God, did not glorify him as God, nor give him thanks, and so they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and were given up by God to the impure and shameful lusts of their own hearts, since they worshipped the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. for ever. May God grant that the ungrateful minds of many scholars of this age do not fall headlong into such precipices, minds which have begun to grow so brutish that they now think of wiping from their hearts the noblest gifts of God: liberty, the foundation of all good and of justice; God's sufficiency and perfections; and even his existence, together with Spinoza and his wretched disciples. But let us return to the good.

units.la: XXX. Hi agnito celebratoque Deo, sic sua omnia in eum refundunt, ut ab ipso prorsus (character insignis) in posterum velint pendere, constituantque eum sui Directorem ac Ductorem, scientes id jure ad ipsum pertinere, conscïque impotentiæ & fragilitatis suæ, qua non modo sua bona non conservantur, sed & certo certius perdenda sunt, suo fi consilio prudentiæque propriæ confidant. Humilitatem recensui, cum dixi eruditionis acquirendæ quæ fuerant dispositiones hic remanere & augeri: inter quas cum hæc præcipua effet, ea ex statu desiderii (in quo tunc ipsa erat) acquirit hic actualem subsistentiam per lumen quo solide convincitur verus eruditus de sui ex se nihilo & impotentia, unde & minus quid cinere coram Deo, corana cæteris etiam ut omnium indignissimus sibi apparet: errata libenter agnoscit & fatetur, nec futiliter excusare tentat, a quovis etiam puero quæ nondum novit discere paratus: rerum autem externarum, iis si careat, privationem sibi debitam putat: si mediocriter adsint, gratiam Numinis reputans, non negligit eas, sed curat, illisque {a} Alii characterés, Dependentia a Deo, solida humilitas cum ejus effectis ergo se, rei hominesque. Amor Dei & proximi. que utitur in necessariis cum omni temperantia & mediocritate : si vero abundent, timens ne iis a se ipso, ab intimis, a dignioribus revocetur, animoque illis adhaereat & maculetur, fugit, easque quovis luto & stercore viliores reputat, nisi in quantum per eas aliis subvenire poterit, extra quod, sunt profecto contagiosae, quando ad concupiscentias proprias adimplendas stimulant & inserviunt. Proximos quod concernit, eadem humilitate disponitur eruditus ne se praeferat ulli; sed ex animo se quovis inferiorem judicet, certus se in lumina, quibus prae aliis abundare poterit, praevaricando, etiam aliis culpabiliorem esse: neminemque irridet; sed commiseranti oculo aliorum errata, si quidem dissimulari nequeant, intuetur, cane pejus & angue a charactere irrisoris abhorrens. Nam sanum aegris irridere, iisque insultandis assuescere, malignam vecordiam esse nemo non videt. Superbiam & animi malignitatem, ne plura dicam, prodit irrisor, ob ea gaudens quorum causa dolendum ei esset: errantium autem commiserari, hominis est fragilitatis propriae humiliter conscii, amoreque erga proximum, uti debet, praediti, exemplo Dei, in quo capitalis est virtus charitas, errantiumque commiseratio & amplexatio. Quapropter qui Deum, omnis boni virtutisque Archetypum, amat, is eum quoque in amore erga eos, qui in tenebris sunt aegritudineque mentis, imitatur, quod evidentissimum signum est, eum vere, imo a Deo ipso, esse eruditum. tum : Neque enim Deus lumen suum eis denegat qui ejus Charitatem cupiunt exprimere ; & si ejus Apostoli verbis fidem habeamus, (a) qui amat Deum, is eruditus est; sive cognitor factus est ab illo, quod idem est ac si dicat, eum qui amorem Dei, a quo amor proximi est indivulsus, possidet, esse vera divinaque eruditione praeditum.
units.tr: XXX. Having acknowledged and honoured God, such people refer all their concerns to him, so completely that (a distinctive mark) they wish to depend entirely on him from now on. They appoint him their Director and Guide, knowing that this right belongs to him, and, aware of their own powerlessness and frailty, by which their goods are not only not preserved but are certain to be lost, they do not trust their own counsel and prudence. I have already mentioned humility when I said that the dispositions required for acquiring learning remain here and grow. Among these, since this was the chief one, it passes from the state of desire (in which it then was) into actual existence here, through the light by which the true learned person is firmly convinced of his own nothingness and impotence, and so he sees himself as little more than ashes before God and, before others, as the most unworthy of all. He willingly acknowledges and confesses his errors and does not try to excuse them lightly; he is ready to learn what he does not yet know even from any child. As for external things, he considers it his due to lack them, and if he has them in moderate measure, he regards them as the grace of God; he does not neglect them but takes care of them, and uses them in necessary matters with all moderation and restraint. If, however, they abound, he fears that through them he may be drawn away from within, from what is inward and more worthy, and that his mind may cling to them and be stained; so he flees them and considers them baser than any mud or dung, except insofar as through them he can help others. Beyond that they are truly contagious, when they stir up and serve the fulfilment of his own lusts. (Other characters: dependence on God; solid humility with its effects; love of God and neighbour.) As for his neighbours, the learned person is disposed by the same humility not to put himself before anyone, but sincerely to judge himself inferior to all, aware that by sinning against the light in which he can excel others, he would be more guilty than they. He mocks no one; rather, he looks on the errors of others with a pitying eye, if indeed they cannot be overlooked, and he shrinks from the character of the mocker more than from a dog or a snake. For everyone sees that to mock the sick, and to make a habit of insulting them, is a wicked madness. The mocker, to say no more, betrays pride and a malicious spirit, rejoicing in the very things over which he ought to grieve. But to pity those who err belongs to a person who humbly knows his own frailty and is endowed with the love towards his neighbour that he ought to have, after the example of God, in whom the chief virtue is charity, and whose pity and embrace extends to those who err. Therefore, whoever loves God, the Archetype of all goodness and virtue, imitates him also in his love towards those who are in darkness and sickness of mind, which is the clearest sign that he is truly learned, indeed learned by God himself. For God does not deny his light to those who desire to express his charity; and if we give faith to the words of his Apostle, (a) he who loves God is learned; or he is made known by him, which is the same as saying that the one who possesses the love of God, from which the love of neighbour is inseparable, is endowed with true and divine learning.

units.la: XXXI. Et sane si paucis omnes aut praecipui veri eruditi characteres recensendi vel resumendi essent, dicerem eos charitate sive amore Dei & proximi contineri & absolvi, enumeraremque charitatis notas characteristicas, quales ei assignat Paulus, cum dicit, (b) Charitas patiens est, benigna est: Charitas non aemulatur, non agit perperam, non inflatur, non est ambitiosa, non quaerit quae sua sunt, non irritatur, non cogitat malum, non gaudet super iniquitate, congaudet autem veritati. Omnia suffert, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet, nec unquam excidit: quae omnia, cum vere eruditus, ut dictum est, charitate seu amore praeditus sit, ei tribuerem, siquidem patet ea fluere ex amore: namque amor, maxime vero is qui praevenit, nutritur spe; adeoque amans est patiens sive longanimis, ea quae ad perfectionem desiderant ipsi desunt, non inquiete ciroque expostulans, sed cum mora & tranquillitate expectans; eademque ratione, quos desiderat modos in proximi erga se regimine, eorum defectum etiam sufferens. Praeterea cum quaerat amor benefaciendi ansas, dissimuletque illas quibus a benefaciendo revocari posposset, ideo insuper benignus est, defectûs proximi miserans, & quantum fieri potest excusans, illumque verbis & actibus gratis disponens ad boni, quod ei communicare peroptat, receptionem. Porro cum verus amor fit sui circa alium occupatio, adeoque sui ipsius praetermissio, & fere oblivio, sequitur eruditum amore praeditum, non esse aemulum, nec agere perperam, nec inflari, neque esse ambitiosum, nec quae sua sunt quaerere. Non est aemulus atque invidus: si quos videat se praestantiores esse vel haberi, oculosque nec non aestimationem omnium a se ad alios converti; se dimitti, alios recipi: non fert id aegre, neque quicquam facit quo se aliis anteponat; sed gaudet ab aliis superari, contentus forte vel ultima, quam Auctor suus ei assignavit, paratusque vel quae habet dona omnia in alterius gratiam dimittere, si quidem Auctoris sui placito & gloriae melius satisfieri posset iis in alium translatis. Non agit perperam, nec quo sui eminentiam prae aliis tueatur alios verbis factisve deprimit; neque perversos amoris proprii naturaeque corruptae impulsus adimplet. Non inflatur donis quae possidet; non respicit ea tanquam sui naturaeque suae partem debitam, ita ut, se cum considerare vult, ea involvat in idea sui quasi ejus partem constituentia; sicque eis inflatus magnus sibi appareat. Scit se vas natura sua vacuum, tenebris solis anxietateque plenum; quae intus sunt, dona mera Auctoris sui esse, quae ad vasis natunaturam non pertineant, sed ad Datoris magnificentiam manifestandam: veluti lumen ad corporis illuminati naturam non pertinet, sed ejus aliunde donum & ornamentum est, quod singulis momentis continue ab alio dependens, gratis communicari debeat, possitque tolli, remanente postmodum in tenebris corpore prius illuminato. Non est ambitiosus itaque, vel immoderatus, nec, sibi cum nihil sit, vult aut agit aut loquitur ut ab aliis magnifiat, vel aliquid reputetur, aut in amore, existimatione laudandique facultate aliorum, teneat locum soli omnium bonorum fonti debitum. Non quaerit quae sua sunt, detestabilem illum Amoris proprii naturaeque corruptae impulsum, quo se quisque veluti centrum considerat, ad quod omnia spiritualia corporeaque attrahat & referat, non sequitur. Facula est ardens & lucens, ad factoris sui magnalia illustranda hominesque illuminandos cum sui dispendio, nullo ad se respectu habito, sese consumens: canalis est, aquarum fluenta sibi a scaturigine administrata, sibi non retinens; sed quibusvis nullo pretio communicans. Et quia amor solidus non datur nisi fuerit probatus, probatio vero nil aliud est quam ictus & adversae oppositiones Dei & hominum, quibus amans succumbere non debet, paret inde eum non irritari, neque cogitare malum. Non irritatur, quando nempe Dei hominumve tangitur ictibus; non adversus illum murmurat ad querimonias, non adversus hos indignabundus ad acerbam malevolentiam aut benignitatis in illos sufpenfionem commovetur. Nec cogitat malum reddere pro malo, neque ad vindictam factis aut ad verbales responsationes provolat eo animo, opere, verbis, ut ei adversantes veluti aculeis perciti iraque commoti & irritati, fiant inde mali aut pejores quam prius fuerint: quod inter signa eruditionis sive sapientiæ diabolicæ Jacobus annumerat. Præterea cum Deus sit Deus justitiæ & veritatis, non potest ejus amans delectari injustitia, dum veritati ubique favet; adeoque non gaudet super iniquitate sive injustitia: cumque videt ab hominibus, etiam ab inimicis, peccati & inique agi, non lætatur quod inde habeat ansam sua eis iniqua exprobrandi, propalandique eum insultatione, triumpho, ironicisque sarcasmis; sed ecce congaudet veritati, lætaturque cum ea quam falsum malumque sensum torquieri potuissent a malevolis, videt in boni verique partem capi posse, veritati gratulans, quod ea ibi inveniatur unde putabatur abesse: lætatur etiam veritatem a quocunque dici & promoveri: maximum vero gaudium capit, cum ipsemet a veritate arguitur, & erroris næyorumque convincitur, siquidem næyos agnoscere viro probo, se corrigere erudireque volenti, inter maxima bona annumeretur. Tandem quoniam amor imitatur amatum, videlicet Deum, qui sic egit erga homines ut ab illis omnia tolerraverit, rigide omnia non exegerit, bona sibi de ipsis quaevis promiserit, obstacula bonitati suæ inhibendæ ab eis oblata vicerit, nec a charitate erga nos excident; eisdem etiam doribus præditus est qui amore præditus est eruditus : Ergo omnia quoque juffert ab omnibus, etsi illi non se modis dictis erga eum gerant uti is erga illos. Omnia credit ex quibusse proximosque disponi posse videt ut ad Deum æternaque amplectenda ferantur, probioresque fiant, posthabita inani morosaque externarum nullius momenti quisquiliarum crisi. Omnia sperat quæ sincero bonoque animo gesta sunt, a Deo Optimo Maximo complementum bonumque finem adeptura; spesque ejus, dum perituris, quæ nil sunt, non inhiat, solis æternis intenta, omnia hoc ipso complectitur: eaque de causa sustinet magno animo omnia quæ ad speratorum adeptionem tendenti obstacula, pericula probaminaque objiciuntur; nec ab incepta excidit via virtutequ sed perseveranter ad finem in iis permanet usque dum perficiatur.
units.tr: XXXI. Indeed, if all, or the chief, marks of the true learned person were to be listed or summed up briefly, I would say that they are contained and comprised in the charity or love of God and neighbour, and I would recount the characteristic marks of charity, such as Paul assigns to it when he says: (b) Charity is patient, charity is kind; charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, and never fails. All of these I would attribute to the truly learned person, who, as has been said, is endowed with charity or love, since it is clear that they flow from love. For love, especially that which goes before, is nourished by hope; and so the one who loves is patient, or long-suffering: what he desires for perfection is lacking to him, yet he does not complain restlessly and clamorously, but waits with patience and calm. And for the same reason he also bears with the failings of his neighbour in the ways in which he is ruled by him, even though he would wish them otherwise. Moreover, since love seeks opportunities for doing good, and sets aside those things by which it might be called back from doing good, he is therefore also kind, pitying the faults of his neighbour and excusing them as far as possible, and disposing him by words and deeds, freely, to receive the good which he most gladly wishes to share with him. Further, since true love is the occupation of oneself with another, and so the setting aside, and almost the forgetting, of oneself, it follows that the learned person endowed with love is not envious, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, and does not seek his own things. He is not a rival or envious: if he sees others who are, or are thought to be, more eminent than himself, and the eyes and esteem of all are turned from himself to others, and he is set aside while others are received, he does not take it badly, nor does he do anything by which he may put himself before others; rather he rejoices to be surpassed by others, content perhaps even with the lowest place which his Author has assigned him, and ready to give up all the gifts he has for the benefit of another, if indeed the pleasure and glory of his Author could be better served by transferring them to another. He does not act perversely, nor does he, to defend his own eminence above others, depress them by word or deed; nor does he fulfil the perverse impulses of self-love and corrupted nature. He is not puffed up by the gifts he possesses; he does not regard them as a due part of himself and of his own nature, so that when he wishes to consider himself, he includes them in the idea of himself as if they were constituent parts of him; and thus, inflated by them, he appears great to himself. He knows that by nature he is an empty vessel, full only of darkness and anxiety; and that the things within are pure gifts of his Author, which do not pertain to the nature of the vessel but serve to show forth the magnificence of the Giver. Just as light does not belong to the nature of an illuminated body, but is a gift and ornament to it from elsewhere, which, depending continually at every moment on another, ought to be freely communicated, and can be taken away, the body remaining afterwards in darkness as it was before it was illuminated. He therefore is not ambitious, nor immoderate; since he is nothing, he neither wishes, does, nor says anything in order to be magnified by others, or to be counted as something, or to hold, in the love, judgement and praise of others, the place due only to the sole fount of all goods. He does not follow the seeking of his own things, that detestable impulse of self-love and corrupted nature by which each person considers himself as a centre to which he draws and refers all things, spiritual and bodily. He is a torch, burning and shining, consuming himself at his own cost, to illustrate the marvels of his Maker and to enlighten people, with no regard to himself. He is a channel, not keeping for himself the streams of waters supplied to him from the spring, but communicating them to anyone without any price. And since solid love is not given unless it has been tested, and testing is nothing other than the blows and adverse assaults of God and men, to which the one who loves ought not to yield, it follows that he is not provoked, and does not think evil. He is not provoked when he is struck by the blows of God or men; he does not murmur against God with complaints, nor is he moved with indignation against men to bitter malice or to withdrawing his kindness from them. He does not think of rendering evil for evil, nor does he rush to vengeance by deeds or by verbal retorts, with the intent, in work or word, that those who oppose him, stung as it were by goads and stirred and provoked to anger, should become thereby worse than they were before; this James counts among the marks of diabolical wisdom or learning. Moreover, since God is the God of justice and truth, his lover cannot delight in injustice, but always favours the truth; and so he does not rejoice in iniquity or injustice. And when he sees that sin and wrong are done by men, even by enemies, he does not rejoice that he has thereby an occasion to reproach them with their wrongs, and to publish them with insult, triumph and ironic sarcasm; but, on the contrary, he rejoices with the truth, and is glad with it. What the malicious might have twisted into a false and evil sense, he sees can be taken in the part of good and truth, and he gives thanks to the truth that it is found there where it was thought to be absent. He rejoices too that the truth is spoken and promoted by whoever it may be; but he takes the greatest joy when he himself is reproved by the truth and convicted of error and fault, since to a good man who wishes to correct and instruct himself, the recognition of his faults is counted among the greatest goods. Finally, since love imitates the one loved, namely God, who has so dealt with men that he has borne all things from them, has not exacted everything rigidly, has promised them every good, and has overcome the obstacles offered by them to the restraint of his goodness, and does not fall away from charity towards us, the learned person who is endowed with love is also endowed with the same gifts. Therefore he also bears all things from all people, even if they do not behave towards him as he behaves towards them. He believes all things by which he sees that neighbours can be disposed to be carried towards God and to embrace eternal things, and to become better, setting aside the vain and fussy judgement of external trifles of no moment. He hopes all things which are done with a sincere and good heart, expecting that they will be brought to completion and a good end by God, Best and Greatest; and his hope, while it does not gape after perishing things, which are nothing, but is fixed on eternal things alone, embraces all things by this very fact. For this reason he endures with a great spirit all things that are set against the one who strives to attain what he hopes for, obstacles, dangers and trials; nor does he fall away from the way he has begun in virtue, but perseveres steadfastly in it to the end, until it is completed.

units.la: XXXII. Inter veri eruditi characteres, & hic recensendus est, quod de contingenti- bus futuris, maxime vero inutilibus, haud adeo sit sollicitus.
units.tr: XXXII. Among the marks of a true scholar is this: that he is not greatly anxious about future contingent events, and least of all about useless ones.

units.la: Solent plerique de eruditione judicantes, vel ad eam aspirantes, credere solide eruditos melius de futuris prospicere quam caeteros; & ad omnes casus excipiendos, seque recte in illis gerendum, habere continuo in promtu paratas de omnibus demonstrationes, veluti paratissima agmina, quorum singula singulis opponere possint casibus, quando evenient: quin etiam ea penetrasse, solvisse & decidisse, quae ab ingenio humana
units.tr: Most people who judge learning, or who aspire to it, commonly believe that solidly learned men foresee the future better than others. They think that to meet every eventuality and conduct themselves rightly in each, they must always have at hand ready demonstrations on every subject, like fully prepared battle lines, each of which can be set against a particular case when it arises. They even suppose that such men have penetrated, resolved and settled all the questions that human ingenuity could raise.

units.la: { } Eruditum verum non esse sollicite curiosum de futuris; nec habere in promtu repertorium idearum & demonstrationum ad quosvis casus possibiles paratarum. Sed humano possent eis, etsi nunquam eventura mereque speculativa & inania, proponi: adeoque securitatem pacemque Erudi- tæ mentis fundari in possessione actuali & penu idearum, principiorum, conclusionumque, quæ vel ei præsentes sint, vel saltem ei præsentes esse possint ex memoria & habitu quo illis contemplandis & decidendis sese non semel applicuerit: quæ insignis sane est hallucinatio. Exonerat se tædiosis illis næniis libera veri Eruditi mens, ad quem non magis spectat de omnibus casibus objectisve cogitare vel cogitasse, deque illis principia quibusque sua, solutiones demonstrationesque proprias habere, quam ad hominem visu luceque gaudentem, ut vere id sit, pertineat omnia objecta quæ luce oculisque detegi possent, jam detexisse, atque ad unumquodque eorum suum singulare lumen habere. Cui oculus mentis eruditus beneque dispositus est, cuique cum lumine luminumque Auctore bene convenit, is scit se habere fundum cui acquiescat, sufficientemque ex tempore & quovis momento ad ea quæ sese offerunt, & ex necessariis utilibusve sunt, percipienda, & cum fructu debiteque digerenda atque tractanda; modo tamen illum eo quo acquisivit modo, nec non grato erga boni omnis Auctorem Conservatoremque animo ipse, quantum potest, conservare non negligat.
units.tr: The true scholar is not anxiously curious about the future, nor does he keep ready at hand a storehouse of ideas and demonstrations prepared for every possible case. The human mind could put to him any number of such speculative and empty questions, even ones that will never happen. So the security and peace of a learned mind is not founded on actually possessing and having at hand a store of ideas, principles and conclusions, which are either present to him or could be present to him from memory and from the habit he has acquired by applying himself more than once to contemplating and settling them. That is a remarkable delusion. The free mind of the true scholar is relieved of those tiresome trifles. It is no more his concern to have thought, or to have thought in advance, about every case or object, and to hold for each of them its own principles, solutions and demonstrations, than it is for a man who enjoys sight and light to have already uncovered all the objects that could be detected by light and eyes, and to have a separate light for each of them. The learned mind, which is well disposed to the eye of the mind, and which agrees well with the light and with the Author of light, knows that it has a foundation on which it can rest, and that it has enough, at any time and in any moment, to perceive the things that present themselves and are necessary or useful, and to arrange and handle them profitably and properly. Provided, of course, that he does not neglect to preserve that foundation, as far as he can, in the way in which he acquired it, and with a grateful mind towards the Author and Preserver of every good.

units.la: Prolixior hic non ero, postquam modo monui dispositiones omnes bonas, quas in acquirenda eruditione quisque habuit, dotesque quas suo labore Deique dono insuper adeptus est, huc etiam spectare, sive erutionis possessori manere, quin & augeri & perfici, idque ejus inter notas esse. Pergamus ad statum in quo eum eruditionis suae communicatorem consideravimus.
units.tr: I shall not be more lengthy here, since I have just pointed out that all the good dispositions which each person had in acquiring learning, and the gifts which he gained besides by his own labour and the gift of God, also bear on this: that they remain in the possessor of learning, and indeed grow and are perfected, and that this is among the marks of it. Let us proceed to the state in which we have considered him as a communicator of his learning.

units.la: LIBRI PRIMI
units.tr: BOOK ONE

units.la: PARS TERTIA, quae est DE VERAE ERUDITIONIS COMMUNICATIONE
units.tr: PART THREE, which is ON THE COMMUNICATION OF TRUE ERUDITION

units.la: XXXIII. QUandoquidem vere eruditus clare perspicit & se & omnia sua esse a placito meraque liberalitate Dei, solius idcirco requirendi & laudandi; suaeque tenuitatis fragilitatisque conscius est; tum alios sibi ratione cognitionis, maxime vero fidelitatis quâ cognita exsequuntur, praeferre solet; idcirco timens, ne caeteri, si quos doceret, magis ipsi quam Deo adhaerere quaererent, ne laudum Deo debitarum furro ipsius ad fastum sollicitent proclivitatem, neve ejus commoda (amori proprio aut corrupto grata) nimis in suam mollitiem promoveant, vel etiam (quia veritas odium parit) ne iseos, fui persequendi occasione suggestā pejores culpæ magis obnoxios pejores reddat; simulque ne conversione sui ad exteros se ipsum distrahat aut negligat, ea quoque verbis inculcet, quæ ipse in se necdum satis radicata, nec satis sese factis exprimere conscit, aut quæ alii forte jam sciant nec faciant tamen, horum proinde inculcatione reatui majori obnoxii futuri; his, aliisque de causis, libentius sibi soli intendit, nec non apud se manetque tacetque, quam foras prodeat locuturus, haud immemor pretiosi apud Epictetum verbi; Magni periculi est statim evomere quod non concoxeris. Quod si quis dixerit te nihil scire, Tuque commotus non fueris, tum scito rem esse imboatam. Nam & oves non fœnum afferunt opilionibus ac demonstrant quantum comederint: sed pastu intra se concoctlo, extra ferunt lanam & lac. Et tu igitur ne verba celeriter ostendas imperitis; sed opera, quæ verborum cosdionem sequuntur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Since the truly erudite man clearly perceives that both he himself and everything he has are the pure gift of God's pleasure and sheer generosity, he seeks and praises God alone for them. Aware of his own slightness and frailty, he is accustomed to prefer others to himself, both for their knowledge and, above all, for the faithfulness with which they carry out what they know. For this reason he fears that others, if he were to teach them, might seek to cling to him rather than to God, and that the flattery of his own praises, which are owed to God, might stir the proneness to pride in himself. He also fears that he might push his own advantages, which are pleasing to self-love or corrupted by it, too far into his own softness. Or again (since truth breeds hatred) he fears that, by giving occasion to persecute himself, he might make others worse and more liable to blame. At the same time, lest by turning himself toward outsiders he should distract or neglect himself, he refrains from pressing upon them, in words, those things which he knows are not yet rooted firmly enough in himself, nor expressed enough in his deeds, or which others perhaps already know yet do not practise, so that by his urging them he would become more liable to guilt. For these and other reasons he gladly attends to himself alone, and remains and keeps silent within himself, rather than come forth to speak, not forgetting the precious saying of Epictetus: It is a great danger to vomit out at once what you have not digested. If someone says that you know nothing, and you are not disturbed, then know that the matter has been begun. For sheep do not bring fodder to the shepherds to show how much they have eaten; but, having digested the pasture within, they bring forth wool and milk outwardly. So you too should not quickly display your words to the unskilled, but your works, which follow the digestion of words.

units.la: Interim tamen accidit interdum eruditis sua ut cum aliis teneantur communicare: quod oneris Socrates sibi a Deo impositum esse testabatur; quodque in aliis verum legitimumque ut sit, ipsi, sine sui adulatione, in interioribus suis viderint utrum, non dicam a sordida lucri cupiditate; verum annon a superba titillatione pruritueve se suaque coram producendi, famam, rumusculos laudecuplasque hominculonum emendicandi; prodeant, sed a Deo O. M. ad id disponantur & trahantur: cujus erunt certa criteria, si ipsi plus quam prose sufficit veri bonique dotibus abundent: tum si ex luminosa hujusmodi abundantia nec sibi delectationem ullam capiant, nec aliis meliores sibi esse videantur. O rem difficilem & gravem humanis creaturis, quæ annexæ carnis vinculo, unde per dæmonis instinctus incitatur proprius amor, ut vel de gratissimis veluti cibis oblatis aliquantulum sibi degustet, abstinere tamen debent, ni divino furto, dæmonisque lapsu rem velint effici! Non mirum sane si quos Deus ipse ad præfecturam & doctrinam aliorum vocabat, ipsi aliquoties eam refugerint stationem, ubi & tentatio ad sibi ipsi placendum datur periculosa, nec tamen, nisi sub criminis reatu, licet in divitiis cibisque divinis proximo communicandis delectari sibi; sed contra, ubi magis quam prius requiritur, rem suam, famam, commoda, placita odisse, ut purissime res Dei in proximo modis appositis promovenda, infucate & unice quæratur. Alio modo dispositos, Deo probari non posse, per se cuivis patet censcientiam debite inspicienti.
units.tr: Yet it sometimes happens to the erudite that they are bound to share what is theirs with others. Socrates testified that this burden was laid upon him by God. Whether this is true and lawful in others, they themselves must see, in their inner selves and without self-flattery, whether they are drawn forth by God, the Best and Greatest, and disposed to this end. I will not say whether they are driven by sordid greed for gain, but whether they are driven by a proud itch and tickle to display themselves and their own things before others, and to beg for fame, little rumours and the praises of puny men. Clear criteria for this will be these: if they themselves are abundantly endowed with the gifts of truth and goodness beyond what is enough for themselves; then, if out of this shining abundance they take no delight in themselves and do not seem to themselves better than others. O difficult and grave matter for human creatures, who, bound by the chain of the flesh, whence self-love is stirred up by the prompting of the demon, must abstain even from the most pleasant foods set before them, so that they do not even taste a little of them for themselves, unless they wish the thing to be accomplished by divine theft and by the fall of the demon! It is no wonder indeed if those whom God himself called to the leadership and teaching of others have sometimes shrunk from that station, where the temptation to please oneself is dangerous. Yet it is not permitted, except under the guilt of sin, to take delight in sharing the divine riches and food with a neighbour. On the contrary, when more is required than before, let them hate their own affairs, reputation, advantages and pleasures, so that the things of God may be promoted in the neighbour by fitting means, and sought purely and singly, without pretence. That those disposed in another way cannot please God is plain to anyone who carefully examines his conscience.

units.la: XXXIV. Ex ea, qua illi gaudent intus, luminis bonique abundantia, fit ut prius tacentes (quod semper malint esse,) simulque agentes doceant erudiantque, quam loquentes: Exemplis namque plus quam verbis attenditur a plerisque, saltem ab iis qui sapere debite cupiunt; siquidem exempla viva & doctrinam, & doctrinæ implendæ possibilitatem, & fructum ejus (tranquillitatem pacemque agentis,) denique & alacritatem ad imitandum in spectatore exhibeant ingenerenrque: neque enim hi (per- 34. Eos primo facilis docere: quae omnium efficacissimo via. (perverse maligni ni fuerint) continua specimina verae eruditionis, contemtus scilicet & praetermissionis rerum evanidarum, amplexationis solidarum, intimarum, duraturarum; usus moderati externarum & ad tempus necessariarum, regiminis denique debiti erga Deum, se & alios, coram oculis habere queunt, quin inde meliores, regulariores eruditioresque ab ejusmodi instructoribus quamquam vel silentibus discedant.
units.tr: XXXIV. From the abundance of light and good which they enjoy within, it comes about that they teach and instruct by their silence and their action before they speak (which they always prefer). For most people, or at least those who earnestly desire to be wise, attend more to examples than to words. Living examples set before the observer both the doctrine itself, the possibility of practising it, its fruit (the tranquillity and peace of the one who practises it), and finally an eagerness to imitate. For these teachers, unless they are perversely malicious, can keep before people's eyes continual specimens of true erudition: namely, contempt and neglect of fleeting things, embrace of solid, inward and lasting things, moderate use of external things that are necessary for a time, and finally a due ordering of themselves and others toward God. Thus their pupils, even though the teachers are silent, depart from such instructors better, more ordered and more learned.

units.la: XXXV. Factis superaddunt haud raro verba, tum scriptis, tum viva voce, ii queis sua aliis eruditio probato principio communicanda incumbit. Verum siquidem Deo neutiquam gratum esse queat, suae ut opes diviniores coelestesque thesauri proculcandi, dilapidandi, irridendi exponantur; cumque inter eos qui eruditionis acquirendae desiderium prae se ferunt, haud pauci sint qui veram solidamque (quia severior est, corruptis pravisque suis affectibus acerba & adversa) parati sint vel irridere, vel etiam odisse & impugnare, suis ut minutiis, sterilibusque ac frigidis quisquiliis, quibus non arguitur nec dedolatur prava mentis suae dispositio, sed fovetur potius & demulcetur, securius obdormiscant; hinc fit ut quantum fieri potest, quantumque eos cognoscere datur, ab ejusmodi irrisoribus, luminisque purioris hostibus prohibenda sint sapientiae verba, etsi ea se peroptare simularent, aut etiam scriptis provocassent veritatem, de ea imaginarios acturi triumphos si taceatur. Id exigit cula. Ad quæ præcipitia faxit Deus ne proclives ruant ingratæ eruditorum seculi hujus Sed redeamus ad bonos.
units.tr: XXXV. Those to whom it falls to communicate their learning to others, by an approved principle, often add words to their deeds, whether in writing or by the living voice. But since it can by no means be pleasing to God that his more divine riches and heavenly treasures should be trampled, squandered and mocked, and since among those who profess a desire to acquire learning there are not a few who, because true and solid learning is stricter (bitter and adverse to their corrupt and perverse affections), are ready either to mock it or even to hate and assail it, so that they may sleep more securely in their trifles, their barren and cold rubbish, by which their perverse disposition of mind is not reproved or planed away, but rather cherished and soothed; hence it follows that, as far as can be done, and as far as one can know them, the words of wisdom must be kept from such mockers and enemies of purer light, even if they pretend to desire them, or even have challenged the truth in writing, since they would celebrate imaginary triumphs if the truth were kept silent. This calls for caution. May God grant that the ungrateful erudite of this age do not rush headlong into these precipices. But let us return to the good.

units.la: XXX. Hi agnito celebratoque Deo, sic sua omnia in eum refundunt, ut ab ipso prorsus (character insignis) in posterum velint pendere, constituantque eum sui Directorem ac Ductorem, scientes id jure ad ipsum pertinere, conscilque impotentiæ & fragilitatis suæ, qua non modo sua bona non conservantur, sed & certo certius perdenda sunt, suo sifi consilio prudentiæque propriæ confidant. Humilitatem recensui, cum dixi eruditionis acquirendæ quæ fuerant dispositiones hic remanere & augeri: inter quas cum hæc præcipua esset, ea ex statu desiderii (in quo tunc ipsa erat) acquirit hic actualem subsistentiam per lumen quo solide convincitur verus eruditus de sui ex sese nihilo & impotentia, unde & minus quid cinere coram Deo, coram cæteris etiam ut omnium indignissimus sibi appareat: errata libenter agnoscit & fatetur, nec futiliter excusare tentat, a quovis etiam puero quæ nondum novit discere paratus: rerum autem externarum, iis si careat, privationem sibi debitam putat: si mediocriter adsint, gratiam Numinis reputans, non negligit eas, sed curat, illisque utitur in necessariis cum omni temperantia & mediocritate: si vero abundent, timens ne iis a se ipso, ab intimis, a dignioribus revocetur, animoque illis adhaereat & maculetur, fugit, easque quovis luto & stercore viliores reputat, nisi in quantum per eas aliis subvenire potest, extra quod, sunt profecto contagiosae, quando ad concupiscentias proprias adimplendas stimulant & inserviunt. Proximos quod concernit, eadem humilitate disponitur eruditus ne se praeferat ulli; sed ex animo se quovis inferiorem judicet, certus se in lumina, quibus prae aliis abundare potest, praevaricando, etiam aliis culpabiliorem esse: neminemque irrider; sed commiseranti oculo aliorum errata, si quidem dissimulari nequeant, intuetur, cane pejus & angue a charactere irrisoris abhorrens.
