Nam fanum aegris irridere, iisque insultandis assuescere, malignam vecordiam esse nemo non vider. Superbiam & animi malignitatem, ne plura dicam, prodit irrisor, ob ea gaudens quorum causa dolendum ei esset: errantium autem commisereri, hominis est fragilitatis propriae humiliter conscii, amoreque erga proximum, uti debet, praediti, exemplo Dei, in quo capitalis est virtus charitas, errantiumque commiseratio & amplexatio. Quapropter qui Deum, omnis boni virtutisque Archetypum, amat, is eum quoque in amore erga eos, qui in tenebris sunt aegritudineque mentis, imitatur, quod evidentissimum signum est, eum vere, imo a Deo ipso, esse eruditum; tum : Neque enim Deus lumen suum eis denegat qui ejus Charitatem cupiunt exprimere ; & si ejus Apostoli verbis fidem habeamus, (a) qui amat Deum, is eruditus est; sive cognitor factus est ab illo, quod idem est ac si dicat, eum qui amorem Dei, a quo amor proximi est individuus, possidet, esse vera divinaque eruditione praeditum.
units.tr: XXXVI. These, having acknowledged and celebrated God, so refer all their things to him that they wish to depend on him alone from now on (a distinguishing mark), and they set him up as their Director and Guide, knowing that this right belongs to him, and aware of their own powerlessness and frailty, by which their goods are not only not preserved but are certainly bound to perish, they do not trust in their own counsel and their own prudence. I have reviewed humility when I said that those dispositions which were necessary for acquiring learning remain here and are increased. Since this was the chief among them, it passes from the state of desire (in which it then was) to actual existence here, through the light by which the true erudite man is firmly convinced of his own nothingness and impotence from himself; whence he appears to himself, even before God and before others, as the most unworthy of all. He willingly acknowledges and confesses his errors, and does not futilely try to excuse them; he is ready to learn from anyone, even a child, what he does not yet know. As for external things, if he lacks them he thinks the deprivation is his due. If they are present in moderate measure, reckoning them a gift of the divine favour, he does not neglect them but takes care of them, and uses them for necessities with all temperance and moderation. But if they abound, fearing lest through them he be called away from himself, from what is inward and more worthy, and lest his mind cling to them and be stained, he flees them and counts them baser than any mud and dung, except insofar as through them he can help others. Beyond that, they are truly contagious, when they stir up and serve to fulfil one's own desires. As for the neighbour, the erudite man is disposed by the same humility not to put himself before anyone, but from his heart to judge himself inferior to every man, certain that by transgressing against the lights in which he can abound beyond others, he is more guilty than they. He mocks no one, but when the errors of others cannot be overlooked, he looks upon them with a pitying eye, shrinking from the character of a mocker more than from a dog or a snake. For that to mock the sick, and to become accustomed to insulting them, is a malignant madness, as everyone sees. In short, the mocker betrays pride and malice of mind, rejoicing at those things which ought to grieve him. But to take pity on the erring belongs to a man who humbly knows his own frailty, and who has, as he ought, love toward his neighbour, after the example of God, in whom the chief virtue is charity, and the pity and embrace of those who err. Therefore he who loves God, the archetype of all goodness and virtue, imitates him also in love toward those who are in darkness and sickness of mind. This is the most evident sign that he is truly erudite, indeed erudite by God himself. For God does not deny his light to those who desire to express his charity. And if we give credence to the words of his Apostle, (a) he who loves God is erudite, or has been made known by him; which is the same as saying that he who possesses the love of God, from which love of neighbour is inseparable, is endowed with true and divine erudition.

units.la: 31. XXXI. Et sane si paucis omnes aut praecipui veri eruditi characteres recensendi vel resumendi essent, dicerem eos charitate sive amore Dei & proximi contineri & absolvi, enumeraremque charitatis notas characteristicas, quales ei assignat Paulus, cum dicit, (b) Charitas patiens est, benigna est: Charitas non aemulatur, non agit perperam, non inflatur, non est ambitiosa, non quaerit quae sua sunt, non irritatur, non cogitat malum, non gaudet super iniquitate, congaudet autem veritati. Omnia sufferit, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet, nec unquam excidit: quae omnia, cum vere eruditus, ut dictum est, charitate seu amore praeditus sit, ei tribuerem, siquidem patet ea fluere ex amore: namque amor, maxime vero is qui praevenit, nutritur spe; adeoque amans est patiens sive longanimis, ea quae ad perfectionem desiderantur ipsi desunt; non inquiete citoque expostulans, sed cum mora & tranquillitate expectans; eademque ratione, quos desiderat modos in proximi erga se regimine, eorum defectum etiam sufferens. Praeterea cum quaerat amor benefaciendi ansas, dissimulerque illas quibus a benefaciendo revocari possit. posset, ideo insuper benignus est, defectûs proximi miserans, & quantum fieri potest excusans, illumque verbis & actibus gratis disponens ad boni, quod ei communicare peroptat, receptionem. Porro cum verus amor sit sui circa alium occupatio, adeoque sui ipsius prætermissio, & fere oblivio, sequitur eruditum amore præditum, non esse æmulum, nec agere perperam, nec inflari, neque esse ambitiosum, nec quæ sua sunt quærere. Non est æmulus atque invidus: si quos videat se præstantiores esse vel haberi, oculosque nec non æstimationem omnium a se ad alios converti; se dimitti, alios recipi: non fert id ægre, neque quicquam facit quo se aliis anteponat; sed gaudet ab aliis superari, contentus forte vel ultima, quam Auctor suus ei assignavit, paratusque vel quæ habet dona omnia in alterius gratiam dimittere, si quidem Auctoris sui placito & gloriæ melius satisfieri posset iis in alium translatis. Non agit perperam, nec quo sui eminentiam præ aliis tueatur alios verbis factisve deprimit; neque perversos amoris proprii naturæque corruptæ impulsus adimplet. Non inflatur donis quæ possidet; non respicit ea tanquam sui naturæque suæ partem debitam, itaut, se cum considerare vult, ea involvat in idea sui quasi ejus partem constituentia; sicque eis inflatus magnus sibi appareat. Scit se vas natura sua vacuum, tenebrisolis anxietateque plenum; quæ intus sunt, dona mera Auctoris sui esse, quæ ad vasis natu-
units.tr: 31. XXXI. Indeed, if all the marks of a true learned person, or the chief ones, were to be listed or summed up briefly, I would say that they are contained and comprised in charity or love of God and neighbour. I would list the characteristic marks of charity, such as Paul assigns to it when he says: (b) Charity is patient and kind. Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, and never fails. Since the learned person, as has been said, is endowed with charity or love, I would attribute all these qualities to him, since it is clear that they flow from love. For love, and especially the love that anticipates, is nourished by hope; and so the one who loves is patient, or long-suffering. The things that are still lacking for perfection are not demanded restlessly and hastily, but awaited with delay and calm. In the same way, he also endures the failings of his neighbour in the way he is governed by him, even where he desires something different. Moreover, since love seeks opportunities for doing good, and sets aside those things by which it could be called back from doing good, it is therefore further kind, pitying the faults of his neighbour and excusing them as far as possible, and by words and deeds graciously preparing him to receive the good that he eagerly wishes to share with him. Again, since true love is the occupation of oneself with another, and thus the neglect and almost the forgetting of oneself, it follows that the learned person endowed with love is not envious, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, and does not seek his own things. He is not a rival or grudging: if he sees others to be, or to be considered, more outstanding than himself, and the eyes and the esteem of all turn from himself to others, and he is set aside while others are received, he does not take it badly, nor does he do anything by which he might put himself before others. Rather he rejoices to be surpassed by others, content perhaps with the lowest place that his Author has assigned to him, and ready to give up all the gifts he has for the sake of another, if indeed the pleasure and glory of his Author could be better satisfied by those gifts being transferred to another. He does not act wrongly, nor does he, to protect his own prominence over others, disparage them by words or deeds; nor does he indulge the perverse impulses of self-love and of corrupted nature. He is not puffed up by the gifts that he possesses; he does not regard them as a due part of himself and of his own nature, so that when he wishes to consider himself, he includes them in the idea of himself as if they constituted a part of him; and thus, swollen by them, he appears great to himself. He knows that by his nature he is an empty vessel, full of darkness, emptiness and anxiety; and that the things within him are pure gifts of his Author, which do not belong to the nature of the vessel,

units.la: naturam non pertineant, sed ad Datoris magnificentiam manifestandam: veluti lumen ad corporis illuminati naturam non pertinet, sed ejus aliunde donum & ornamentum est, quod singulis momentis continue ab alio dependens, gratis communicari debeat, possitque tolli, remanente postmodum in tenebris corpore prius illuminato. Non est ambitiosus itaque, vel immodestus, nec, sibi cum nihil sit, vult aut agit aut loquitur ut ab aliis magnifiat, vel aliquid reputetur, aut in amore, existimatione laudandique facultate aliorum, teneat locum soli omnium bonorum fonti debitum. Non quaerit quae sua sunt, detestabilem illum Amoris proprii naturaeque corruptae impulsum, quo se quisque veluti centrum considerat, ad quod omnia spiritualia corporeaque attrahat & referat, non sequitur. Facula est ardens & lucens, ad factoris sui magnalia illustranda hominesque illuminandos cum sui dispendio, nullo ad se respectu habito, sese consumens: canalis est, aquarum fluenta sibi a scaturigine administrata, sibi non retinens; sed quibusvis nullo pretio communicans. Et quia amor solidus non datur nisi fuerit probatus, probatio vero nil aliud est quam ictus & adversae oppositiones Dei & hominum, quibus amans succumbere non debet, paret inde eum non irritari, neque cogitare malum. Non irritatur, quando nempe Dei hominumve tangitur ictibus; non adversus illum murmurat ad querimonias, non adversus hos indignabundus ad acerbam malevolentiam aut benignitatis in illos suspensionem commovetur.
units.tr: but serve to make manifest the magnificence of the Giver. Just as light does not belong to the nature of an illuminated body, but is a gift and ornament to it from elsewhere, which, depending continually at every moment on another, ought to be communicated freely, and can be taken away, the body previously illuminated remaining afterwards in darkness. Therefore he is not ambitious, or immodest, nor, since he is nothing, does he wish or act or speak so as to be magnified by others, or to be reckoned as something, or to take in the love, esteem and capacity for praise of others the place due only to the sole fount of all good. He does not seek his own things; he does not follow that detestable impulse of self-love and of corrupted nature, by which each person considers himself as the centre, to which he draws and refers all spiritual and bodily things. He is a torch, burning and shining, to illustrate the marvels of his maker and to enlighten men, consuming himself at his own expense, with no regard for himself. He is a channel, not keeping back for himself the streams of waters supplied to him from the spring, but communicating them to anyone at no price. And since solid love is not given unless it has been tested, and testing is nothing other than the blows and adverse assaults of God and men, to which the lover ought not to yield, it follows that he is not provoked and does not think evil. He is not provoked when he is struck by the blows of God or of men; he does not murmur against God with complaints, nor is he stirred against men, indignant, to bitter malice or to withdrawal of his kindness toward them.

units.la: Nec cogitat malum reddere pro malo, neque ad vindictam factis aut ad verbales responsationes provolat eo animo, opere, verbis, ut ei adversantes veluti aculeis perciti iraque commoti & irritati, fiant inde mali aut pejores quam prius fuerint: quod inter signa eruditionis sive sapientiæ diabolicæ Jacobus annumerat. Præterea cum Deus sit Deus justitiæ & veritatis, non potest ejus amans delectari injustitia, dum veritati ubique favet; adeoque non gaudet super iniquitate sive injustitia: cumque videt ab hominibus, etiam ab inimicis, peccari & inique agi, non lætatur quod inde habeat ansam sua eis iniqua exprobrandi, propalandique eum insultatione, triumpho, ironicisque sarcasmis; sed econtra congaudet veritati, lætaturque cum ea quam falsum malumque sensum torqueri potuissent a malevolis, videt in boni verique partem capi posse, veritati gratulans, quod ea ibi inveniatur unde putabatur abesse: lætatur etiam veritatem a quocunque dici & promoveri: maximum vero gaudium capit, cum ipsemet a veritate arguitur, & erroris nævorumque convincitur, siquidem nævos agnoscere viro probo, se corrigere erudireque volenti, inter maxima bona annumeretur. Tandem quoniam amor imitatur amatum, videlicet Deum, qui sic egit erga homines ut ab illis omnia toleraverit, rigide omnia non exegerit, bona sibi de ipsis quævis promiserit, obstacula bonitati suæ inhibendæ ab eis oblata vicerit, nec a charitate erga nos excident; eisdem etiam donibus præditus est qui amore præditus est eruditus : Ergo omnia quoque iuffert ab omnibus, etsi illi non se modis dictis erga eum gerant uti is erga illos. Omnia credit ex quibus se proximosque disponi posse videt ut ad Deum æternaque amplectenda ferantur, probioresque fiant, posthabita inani morosaque externarum nullius momenti quisquiliarum crisi. Omnia speFrat quæ sincero bonoque animo gesta sunt, a Deo Optimo Maximo complementum bonumque finem adeptura; spesque ejus, dum perituris, quæ nil sunt, non inhiat, solis æternis intenta, omnia hoc ipso complectitur : eaque de causa sustinet magno animo omnia quæ ad speratorum adeptionem tendenti obstacula, pericula probaminaque objiciuntur; nec ab incepta excidit via virtuteque sed perseveranter ad finem in iis permanet usque dum perficiatur.
units.tr: Nor does he think evil, to return evil for evil; nor does he rush to vengeance by deeds, or to verbal retorts, with the intent, in work or words, that those who oppose him, stung and roused and provoked by anger, should become worse for it than they were before. James reckons this among the signs of diabolical "wisdom" or learning. Moreover, since God is the God of justice and truth, his lover cannot take delight in injustice, while he everywhere favours the truth; and so he does not rejoice in iniquity or injustice. And when he sees men, even enemies, sinning and acting unjustly, he does not rejoice that he has thereby an occasion of upbraiding them with their wrongs, and of publishing them with insult, triumph and ironic sarcasm; but on the contrary he rejoices with the truth, and is glad, when something that malicious people could have twisted into a false and evil meaning is seen to be taken in a good and true sense, rejoicing with the truth that it is found there where it was thought to be absent. He also rejoices when the truth is spoken and advanced by anyone whatever; and he feels the greatest joy when he himself is reproved by the truth and convicted of error and faults, since, for a upright man who wishes to correct and instruct himself, to recognise his blemishes is counted among the greatest goods. Finally, since love imitates the one loved, namely God, who has so dealt with men that he has borne all things from them, has not demanded everything rigidly, has promised himself every good from them, has overcome the obstacles offered by them to the hindering of his goodness, and does not fail in charity toward us, the learned person who is endowed with love has the same gifts too. Therefore he also bears all things from all, even if they do not behave toward him in the ways mentioned as he behaves toward them. He believes all things by which he sees that himself and his neighbours can be disposed to be carried toward God and to embrace eternal things, and to become more upright, setting aside the empty and fussy judgement of external trifles of no moment. He hopes all things that are done with a sincere and good mind, since they will obtain their completion and good end from God, the Best and Greatest; and his hope, not gaping after perishable things, which are nothing, but intent only on eternal things, embraces all things by this very fact. And for this reason he endures with a great mind all things that obstacles, dangers and trials put in the way of one who strives to attain what is hoped for; and he does not fail from the way he has begun and from virtue, but perseveres steadfastly in them to the end, until it is brought to completion.

units.la: XXXXII. Inter veri eruditi characteres, & hic recensendus est, quod de contingenti- bus futuris, maxime vero inutilibus, haud adeo sit sollicitus.
units.tr: XXXLII. Among the marks of a true scholar is this one, which must be listed here: he is not much troubled about future contingencies, and least of all about those which are of no use.

units.la: Solent plerique de eruditione judicantes, vel ad eam aspirantes, credere solide eruditos melius de futuris prospicere quam cæteros; & ad omnes casus excipiendos, seque recte in illis gerendum, habere continuo in promtu paratas demonstrationes, veluti paratissima agmina, quorum singula singulis opponere possint casibus, quando evenient: quin etiam ea penetrasse, solvisse & decidisse, quæ ab ingenio humanahumano possent eis, etsi nunquam eventura mereque speculativa & inania, proponi: adeoque securitatem pacemque Eruditæ mentis fundari in possessione actuali & penu idearum, principiorum, conclusionumque, quæ vel ei præsentes sint, vel saltem ei præsentes esse possint ex memoria & habitu quo illis contemplandis & decidendis sese non semel applicuerit: quæ insignis sane est hallucinatio. Exonerat se tædiosis illis næniis libera veri Eruditi mens, ad quem non magis spectat de omnibus casibus objectisve cogitare vel cogitasse, deque illis principia quibusque sua, solutiones demonstrationesque proprias habere, quam ad hominem visu luceque gaudentem, ut vere id fit, pertineat omnia objecta quæ luce oculisque detegi possent, jam detexisse, atque ad unumquodque eorum suum singulare lumen habere. Cui oculus mentis eruditus beneque dispositus est, cuique cum lumine luminumque Auctore bene convenit, is scit se habere fundum cui acquiescat, sufficientemque ex tempore & quovis momento ad ea quæ sese offerunt, & ex necessariis utilibusve sunt, percipienda, & cum fructu debiteque digerenda atque tractanda; modò tamen illum eo quo acquisivit modo, nec non grato erga boni omnis Auctorem Conservatoremque animo ipse, quantum potest, conservare non negligat.
units.tr: Most people who judge about learning, or who aspire to it, are wont to believe that solidly learned men foresee the future better than others, and that they have ready at hand, continually to hand, demonstrations for meeting every case and for conducting themselves rightly in them, like most ready battle-lines, each of which can be set against each case as it arises. Indeed, they suppose that such men have already penetrated, solved and settled everything that human intellect could put before them, even things that will never happen and are purely speculative and empty. And so they think the security and peace of the learned mind rests on the actual possession and store of ideas, principles and conclusions, which are either present to him or at least can be present to him from memory and from the habit he has acquired by applying himself more than once to contemplating and settling them. This is indeed a remarkable delusion. The free mind of a true scholar is relieved of those tedious worries. It is no more his concern to have thought, or to have thought beforehand, about all cases and objects, and to have his own principles, solutions and demonstrations for each, than it is the concern of a man who enjoys sight and light (as he truly does) to have already discovered all the objects that could be detected by light and eyes, and to have for each of them its own particular light. The learned mind's eye, when it is well disposed, and when it agrees well with the light and with the Author of light, knows that it has a ground on which to rest, and sufficient ability at any time and moment to perceive whatever presents itself and is necessary or useful, and to arrange and handle it fruitfully and duly. Provided, that is, that he does not neglect to preserve it, as far as he can, in the way he acquired it, and with a grateful mind toward the Author and Preserver of every good.

units.la: Prolixior hic non ero; postquam modo monui dispositiones omnes bonas, quas in acquirenda eruditione quisque habuit, dotesque quas suo labore Deique dono insuper adeptus est, huc etiam spectare, sive erudition possessori manere, quin & augeri & perfici, idque ejus inter notas esse. Pergamus ad statum in quo eum eruditionis suæ communicatorem considerabimus.
units.tr: I shall not be more lengthy here. Having just pointed out that all the good dispositions which each person has had in acquiring learning, and the gifts he has obtained besides by his own labour and the gift of God, also tend to this: that learning remains with its possessor, and that it is increased and perfected, and that this is among its marks. Let us proceed to the state in which we will consider him as a communicator of his learning.

units.la: DE VERÆ ERUDITIONIS COMMUNICATIONE. XXXIII. QUandoquidem vere eruditus clare perspicit & se & omnia sua esse a placito meraque liberalitate Dei, solius idcirco requirendi & laudandi; suaeque tenuitatis fragilitatis que conscius est; tum alios sibi ratione co- gnitionis, maxime vero fidelitatis quā co- gnita exsequuntur, praeferre solet; idcir- co timens, ne caeteri, si quos doceret, ma- gis ipsi quam Deo adhaerere quaerent, ne laudum Deo debitarum furro ipsius ad fa- stum sollicitent proclivitatem, neve ejus com- moda (amori proprio aut corrupto grata) nimis in suam mollitiem promoveant, vel etiam (quia veritas odium parit) ne is eos, sui persequendi occasione suggestia pejores & cul-
units.tr: On the Communication of True Learning. XXXIII. Since the truly learned man clearly sees that both he himself and all that he has are from the good pleasure and pure generosity of God, and so are to be sought and praised only in God; and since he is conscious of his own littleness and frailty; he is accustomed to prefer others to himself on account of their knowledge, and above all on account of the faithfulness with which they carry out what they know. Therefore he fears that the others, if he were to teach them, would seek to cling more to himself than to God; that by usurping the praises due to God he would stir up in them a tendency toward pride; that they would promote his advantages (pleasing to self-love or corrupted by it) too much into their own softness; or even (since truth breeds hatred) that he, taking the occasion of being persecuted, would make them worse and more liable to fault

units.la: culpæ magis obnoxios pejores reddat; simulque ne conversione sui ad exteros se ipsum distrahat aut negligat, ea quoque verbis inculcet, quæ ipse in se necdum satis radicata, nec satis sese factis exprimere conscit, aut quæ alii forte jam sciant nec faciant tamen, horum proinde inculcatione reatui majori obnoxii futuri; his, aliisque de causis, libentius sibi soli intendit, nec non apud se manetque tacetque, quam foras prodeat locuturus, haud immemor pretiosi apud Epictetum verbi; Magni periculi est statim evomere quod non concoxeris. Quod si quis dixerit te nihil scire, Tuque commotus non fueris, tum scito rem esse imboatam. Nam & oves non fœnum afferunt opilionibus ac demonstrant quantum comederint: sed pastu intra se concocto, extra ferunt lanam & lac. Et tu igitur, ne verba celeriter ostendas imperitis; sed opera, quæ verborum cosiionem sequuntur.
units.tr: more liable to fault; and at the same time, lest by turning to outsiders he should distract or neglect himself, he does not inculcate in words those things which he knows are not yet sufficiently rooted in himself nor sufficiently expressed in his deeds, or which others perhaps already know and yet do not practise; for by inculcating these he would become liable to greater guilt. For these and other reasons he more willingly attends to himself alone, and remains and keeps silent within himself, rather than going forth to speak, not forgetting the precious saying of Epictetus: It is a great danger to vomit out at once what you have not digested. If someone says you know nothing, and you are not moved, then know that the matter has been well begun. For sheep do not bring fodder to the shepherds and show how much they have eaten; but, having digested the pasture within, they bring forth wool and milk. So you too, do not quickly show words to the unlearned, but works, which follow the digestion of words.

units.la: Interim tamen accidit interdum eruditis sua ut cum aliis teneantur communicare: quod oneris Socrates sibi a Deo impositum esse testabatur; quodque in aliis verum legitimumque ut sit, ipsi, sine sui adulatione, in interioribus suis viderint utrum, non dicam a sordida lucri cupiditate; verum annon a superba titillatione pruritúve se suaque coram producendi, famam, rumusculos laudecusque homuncionum emendicandi; prodeant, sed a Deo O. M. ad id disponantur & trahantur: cujus erunt certa criteria, si ipsi plus quam prose sufficit veri bonique dotibus abundent: tum si ex luminosa hujusmodi abundantia nec sibi delectationem ullam capiant, nec aliis meliores sibi esse videantur. O rem difficilem & grávem humanis creaturis, quæ annexæ carnis vinculo, unde per dæmonis instinctus incitatur proprius amor, ut vel de gratissimis veluti cibis oblatis aliquantulum sibi degustet, abstinere tamen debent, ni divino furto, dæmonisque lapsu reæ veliut effici! Non mirum sane si quos Deus ipse ad præfecturam & doctrinam aliorum vocabat, ipsi aliquoties eam refugerint stationem, ubi & tentatio ad sibi ipsi placendum datur periculosa, nec tamen, nisi sub criminis reatu, licet in divitiis cibisque divinis proximo communicandis delectari sibi; sed contra, ubi magis quam prius requiritur, rem suam, famam, commoda, placita odisse, ut purissime res Dei in proximo modis appositis promovenda, infucate & unice quæratur. Alio modo dispositos, Deo probari non posse, per se cuivis patet censcientiam debite inspicienti.
units.tr: Yet it sometimes happens that the learned are bound to communicate their own things to others. Socrates testified that this was a burden laid on him by God. And so that in others it may be true and lawful, they themselves should see, without flattering themselves, in their inmost hearts, whether they come forth (I will not say from sordid greed of gain) but at least not from a proud itch to display themselves and their own, begging for fame, little rumours and the praises of little men. Let them come forth, but let them be disposed and drawn to it by God Most Good. The certain criteria of this will be if they themselves abound in the gifts of truth and goodness more than is enough; and then if from such luminous abundance they take no delight in themselves, nor seem better to others. O difficult and heavy matter for human creatures, who, bound by the chain of flesh, whence self-love is incited by the instigation of the demon, must nevertheless abstain from tasting even a little for themselves of the most pleasant foods set before them, lest by divine theft and the demon's fall they be made guilty! Indeed it is no wonder if those whom God himself called to the office and teaching of others have sometimes fled that station, where temptation to please oneself is dangerously given; nor is it permitted, unless under the guilt of sin, to delight in sharing the riches and divine food with one's neighbour. On the contrary, where more than before is required that one hate one's own affairs, reputation, advantages and pleasures, so that the things of God may be promoted in the neighbour by appropriate means, purely and singly sought, there the thing is clear. That those disposed otherwise cannot please God is plain to anyone who carefully examines his conscience.

units.la: XXXIV. Ex ea, qua illi gaudent intus, luminis bonique abundantia, fit ut prius tacentes (quod semper malint esse,) simulque agentes doceant erudiantque, quam loquentes: Exemplis namque plus quam verbis attenditur a plerisque, saltem ab iis qui sapere debite cupiunt, siquidem exempla viva & doctrinam, & doctrinæ implendæ possibilitatem, & fructum ejus (tranquillitatem pacemque agentis,) denique & alacritatem ad imitandum in spectatore exhibeant ingenerentque: neque enim hi (per
units.tr: XXXIV. From that abundance of light and goodness which they rejoice in within, it comes about that they teach and instruct, first by being silent (which they always prefer to be) and at the same time by acting, before they teach by speaking. For by examples, more than by words, most people pay attention, at least those who desire to be wise in the right way; since living examples present both the doctrine and the possibility of fulfilling it, and its fruit (of one who acts in tranquillity and peace), and finally arouse and produce in the spectator an eagerness to imitate. For these (through

units.la: {34} Eos primo sacris docere: quæ omnium efficacissimo via. (perverse maligni ni fuerint) continua specimina verae eruditionis, contemtus scilicet & praetermissionis rerum evanidarum, amplexationis solidarum, intimarum, duraturarum; usus moderati externarum & ad tempus necessariarum, regiminis denique debiti erga Deum, se & alios, coram oculis habere queunt, quin inde meliores, regulariores eruditioresque ab ejusmodi instructoribus quanquam vel silentibus discedant.
units.tr: {34} They teach them first by example, which is the most effective way of all (unless they are perversely malicious): they can keep continually before their eyes genuine specimens of true learning, namely contempt and neglect of empty things, embrace of solid, inward and lasting things, moderate use of external things that are needed for a time, and finally due order toward God, toward themselves and toward others. Thus those who are taught by such instructors, even though they are silent, depart from them better, more orderly and more learned.

units.la: XXXV. Factis superaddunt haud raro ver- ba, tum scriptis, tum viva voce, ii queis sua aliis eruditio probato principio communi- canda incumbit.
units.tr: XXXV. Those to whom it falls to communicate their learning to others, on an approved principle, often add words to their deeds, both in writing and by spoken voice.

units.la: Verum siquidem D.o neutiquam gratum esse queat, suae ut opes diviniores coelestesque thesauri proculcandi, dilapidandi, irridendi exponantur; cumque inter eos qui eruditionis acquirendae desiderium prae se ferunt, haud pauci sint qui veram solidamque {quia severior est, corrupti pravisque suis affectibus acerba & adversa) parati sint vel irridere, vel etiam odisse & impugnare, suis ut minutiis, sterilibusque ac frigidis quisquiliis, quibus non arguitur nec dedolatur prava mentis suae dispositio, sed fovetur potius & demulcetur, securius obdormiscant; hinc fit ut quantum fieri potest, quantumque eos cognoscere datur, ab ejusmodi irrisoribus, luminisque purioris hostibus prohibenda sint sapientiae verba, etsi ea se peroptare simularent, aut etiam scriptis provocassent veritatem, de ea imaginarios acturi triumphos si taceatur. Id exigit solidæ Veritatis honos, ut ne iis prostituatur qui non reverenter eam ambiunt, sed procaciter illi quidem dedecus, sibi vero ipsis hic majus nequitiæ augmentum, olim autem castigationis Divinæ copiosiorem mensuram conciliare volunt. Coram Judæis instantibus, judiceque inepto, tacuit olim summa veritatis sapientiæque organum, suos; ne canibus sancta, ne suibus margaritas objicerent, instruens. Sed nec etiam invitis, nec præjudicio pertinaciter libenterque constrictis obtrudenda est veritas: his quia frustra erit, illisquia nullius libertas (quam ne Deus quidem velit cogere) violandaest, nauseam siquidem cum odio parit, non amorem, quicquid ingeritur non appetentibus. Quapropter cum disputationes instantes rixosæque vim aliorum cogitationibus inferre videantur, ab illis abstinebit omnino solide eruditus, qui impossibilia non captans, neque sibi arrogabit jus potestatemque aliorum libera judicia flectendi vel immutandi, cassò conamine, temporis jactură, nullo nisi odiorum apud alios fructu, apud se culpâ amissæ tranquillitatis suæ. Quod tamen, si interdum Apologia veritatis veré sit opus, & tempus id postulet, patietur suam excepționem, quando videlicet, illâ per malevolorum calumnias deformatâ maleque expositâ, alii qui inde alioqui adjuvari & proficere possent si eam adirent, aufugiunt ab illa, nil de calumniantium fraudibus suspicantes: quod tamen locum non habet, ubi malignitas, affectus, aut ignorantia adverfantium nimis sunt in propatulo. Ea cæteroquin elt veritatis αὐτόπχεια, ut aliunde ap-plausus non quæret; namque ei (uti ajebat ille) auditores sufficiunt duo, sufficit unus, sufficit nullus : dignior quam ut homuncionum suffragia debeat emendicare ; dignissima quæ ab omnibus quæratur, nec tamen statim & promiscue quibusvis ejus cupidis communicetur.
units.tr: Now, since it can by no means be pleasing to God that his greater riches and heavenly treasures be exposed to be trampled, squandered and mocked; and since among those who profess a desire to acquire learning there are not a few who are ready to mock true and solid learning (because it is severer, and bitter and adverse to their corrupt and perverse affections), or even to hate and attack it, so that they may fall asleep more securely in their trifles, sterile and cold trivia, by which their perverse mental disposition is not reproved or planed away but rather fostered and soothed; hence it comes about that, as far as can be done, and as far as one can know them, the words of wisdom must be withheld from such mockers and enemies of the purer light, even if they pretend to desire them, or even have challenged truth in writing, intending to win imaginary triumphs if it is silent. The honour of solid Truth demands that it not be prostituted to those who do not approach it reverently, but impudently wish to bring disgrace upon it, and for themselves a greater increase of wickedness and, in time, a fuller measure of divine chastisement. Before Jews who pressed upon him, and an inept judge, the greatest organ of truth and wisdom once kept silence, instructing his own not to give holy things to dogs nor pearls to swine. But truth is not to be thrust even on the unwilling, nor on those obstinately and gladly bound by prejudice: for the former it will be in vain, and in the latter the liberty of no one (which God himself would not wish to force) may be violated; for whatever is thrust upon those who do not desire it produces nausea and hatred, not love. Therefore, since contentious and quarrelsome disputations seem to force their way into the thoughts of others, the solidly learned man will altogether abstain from them; not seeking impossibilities, he will not arrogate to himself the right and power of bending or changing the free judgments of others, by a vain effort, with loss of time and no fruit except hatred among others and, in himself, through his own fault, the loss of his tranquillity. However, if at times an apology for truth is truly a task, and the time demands it, he will allow himself this exception: namely when truth has been deformed and badly presented through the calumnies of the malevolent, and others who might otherwise be helped and advanced if they approached it flee from it, suspecting nothing of the frauds of the slanderers. This, however, has no place where the malice, passions or ignorance of the opponents are too obvious. Moreover, such is the autopsy [αὐτοψία] of truth that it seeks applause from nowhere else; for (as that man used to say) two hearers suffice, one suffices, none suffices. It is too worthy to beg votes from little men, and most worthy to be sought by all; yet it is not to be communicated at once and indiscriminately to whoever desires it.

units.la: XXXVI. Sunt namque inter eos qui erudiri cuperent nonnulli interdum animo vi-tiis aut desidia aut inconstantia ita fracto, habitibusque corruptis sic capto, ut verendum sit eos, ubi novissimæ curiositatis primus fervor refrigueri, mox terga versuros, cum veritatis eamque communicantis despectu : quare & ab istiusmodi hominum ge-nere cauté cavetur. Notabile apud Senecam (Epist. 112.) cujusdam exemplum est; de quo is inter alia : Hic de quo scribis & mandas, non habet vires. Indulsit vitiis, simul & emarcuit & induruit. Non potest recipere rationem, non potest nutrire. At cupit ipse. Noli credere. Non dico illum mentiri tibi. Putat se cupere. Stomachum illi fecit luxuria : cito tamen redibit in gratiam. Sed dicit se offendi vita sua. Non negaverim : quis enim non of-fenditur? Homines vitam suam & amant simul & oderunt. Illustrius exemplum præbet Ser-vator in plurimis qui ipsum avide audituri sequebantur ad admirationem usque, deinde vero deserebant continuo. Quapropter de Christo dicit Joannes, quòd etsi multi crediderunt in illum, ipse tamen, quia eos, &
units.tr: XXXVI. For among those who wish to be taught there are sometimes some whose minds are so broken by vices, or idleness, or inconstancy, and so captured by corrupt habits, that one must fear that when the first fervour of their latest curiosity has cooled, they will soon turn their backs, with contempt for truth and for the one who communicates it. Therefore one is cautious of this kind of men. A notable example of such a man is given by Seneca (Epist. 112), who says among other things: This man of whom you write and whom you commend has no strength. He has indulged his vices, and at the same time has grown feeble and hardened. He cannot receive reason, he cannot nourish it. Yet he himself desires it. Do not believe him. I do not say that he lies to you. He thinks he desires it. Luxury has made him sick of it, but he will soon be reconciled. But he says his life offends him. I would not deny it: for who is not offended? Men both love and hate their own lives. A more illustrious example is provided by the Saviour, in the many who followed him eagerly to hear him, even to the point of admiration, but then immediately deserted him. Therefore John says of Christ that although many believed in him, yet Jesus himself did not trust them, because he knew them, and

units.la: Joh. 2:23. quid in homine esset, dignoscebat, non sidebat iis. Ita sane agendum, etsi alioqui nullum aliud sequeretur incommodum, quam quod qui se cum ejusmodi hominibus docendis exercere vellet, proprium tempus vitamque totam inutiliter transigendi, inque lapidosum & sterile solum semina nil profutura dispergendi occasionem posset nancisci amplissimam. At cum inter eos qui eruditioni admittendæ sunt accommodatiores, sic intermixti sint & male dispositi, ut vel non satis discerni, vel non tuto separari possint, quo solis dignis communicetur veritas, accidit ut ea sæpe sit promiscue propalanda omnibus, ne si reticenda esset ob imparatos, & boni, qui intersunt, ea privarentur: quod tamen non habet locum nisi in summe necessariis, ubi veritatis reticentia probis foret damnosa atque exitialis. Quando vero abusus, cujus eruditionis veræ incapaces ex veritate percepta se reos facere possent, insignis esset, hac cautela utuntur Erudientes, ut vel obscurius vel ænigmaticè sua enuncicent, clariori expositione seorsim discipulis fidis reservata; vel communia palam dicant, secretiora pro suis recondentes: quod in sacro volumine legimus a Christo factum esse fidis discipulis, quibus omnia allegorica explicabat, inquiente, (a) Vobis quidem datum est Regni Dei mysteria nosse: cum cæteris vero non nisi per parabolas agitur: quodque Philosophis ipsis ansam dedit ea quæ docerent vel scriptis consignarent, distinguendi in exoterica, omnibus exponenda, & acroamatica, quibus artis præcipua & intima continerentur, solis auditoribus fidis concredenda.
units.tr: Joh. 2:23. He knew what was in man, and did not trust them. This must indeed be the rule, even though no other inconvenience would follow than this: whoever wished to spend himself in teaching such men would waste his own time and his whole life, and would have a very ample opportunity of scattering seeds that would profit nothing on stony and barren ground. But since among those who are more suitable to receive learning, the others are so mixed in and badly arranged that they cannot be sufficiently distinguished or safely separated, so that truth may be communicated only to the worthy, it happens that truth must often be proclaimed publicly to all, lest, if it were withheld because of the unprepared, the good who are present be deprived of it. This, however, applies only to the most necessary matters, where withholding the truth would be harmful and deadly to the upright. But when the abuse, by which those incapable of true learning could make themselves guilty from the truth they had perceived, would be serious, teachers use this caution: they either express their own matters more obscurely or enigmatically, with a clearer exposition reserved apart for faithful disciples, or they declare common things openly and keep the more secret things for themselves. We read in the sacred volume that Christ did this with his faithful disciples, to whom he explained all the allegories, saying, "To you indeed it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, but with the rest it is only by parables." The same gave the philosophers themselves occasion to divide what they taught or committed to writing into exoterica, to be explained to all, and acroamatica, in which the principal and inmost things of the art were contained, to be entrusted only to faithful hearers.

units.la: XXXVII. Soli namque ii qui apti sunt, materia vera sunt, quam docens erudiendam & formandam suscipiat, nisi artifice quovis imprudentior ineptam inducendæ formæ materiam assumens, operam velit ludere.
units.tr: XXXVII. For only those who are fit are the true matter which the teacher takes up to instruct and form; unless he is more unwise than any craftsman and, taking up matter unsuited to the form he wishes to introduce, chooses to play at work.

units.la: A{a}prosappello illos, qui qualitatibus a me sup{b}prà, dum de subjecto eruditionem acquisitu{c}ro agerem, recensitis præditi sunt, quas, quia verbo reperi possunt, repetitione nomino, fundi sinceritatem, humilitatem, se{d}rium a cæteris ad Deum recursum; desiderii ardorem, flexibilitatem, constantiam, spem; intellectûs vacuitatem & quietem; acquie{e}scentiæ traditionem fortitudinemque: quarum prima protinus actu adsit, necesse est; utile cæteræ si adsint quoque actu ipso; alioqui sufficiat initiò, si incerus illarum amor, ad illasque adspiratio cupida reperiatur: infirmis namque bonæ voluntatis non præcludenda ad eruditionem via est; sed potius lexviganda, maxime initiò, ubi docentis animum ad discentis mediocritatem debilitatem que sese accommodare & uti necesse est; non modo quia omnem discipulum principio esse debilem per se patet; sed & quod momenta accidant quibus bonarum etiam quas possidet qualitatum veluti eclipsin patiatur, quod & ipsis eruditioribus, juxta diversium, neminem omnibus horis sapere, contingere poterit. Tunc igitur prudentis est institutoris, vel omnino ad tempus cessare, ne tempore paroxysmi præceptis intem-
units.tr: I call upon those who possess the qualities I listed above, when I was treating of the subject who acquires learning, and which, because they can be named in a word, I repeat by name: a sound and sincere heart, humility, a serious turning to God apart from all others; ardour of desire, flexibility, constancy, hope; an emptiness and quietness of the intellect; a surrender of acquiescence and fortitude. Of these, the first must be present at once in act; the others are useful if they too are present in act. Otherwise it is enough at the start if a sincere love of them and an eager aspiration towards them be found. For the way to learning must not be closed to the weak of good will, but rather kept wide open, especially at the start, where the teacher must accommodate and adapt his mind to the mediocrity and weakness of the learner. This is not only because every pupil is by nature weak at the beginning, which is plain, but also because moments occur in which even the good qualities he possesses suffer, as it were, an eclipse; and this can happen even to the more learned teachers, since no one is wise at all hours. Therefore it is the mark of a prudent instructor either to cease altogether for a time, lest in a time of paroxysm he should provoke with untimely

units.la: {a} Notes in the right margin are shown as marginal notes above. tempestivis irritet morbum alioqui fanabilem, & mora nonnulla diffipabilem, neve reddat vim veritatis frustraneam, callam & odiolam; (unde temporis observatio, ut quis eruditionem dispenset tum cum illa a subjecto disposito recipi eique proficere poreit, inter primarias veri Eruditoris regulas est; ) vel, si discentis status incommodus ferat tamen nonnullam disciplinam, verbis actisque ea illi sunt proponenda, eoque modo, ut cum ejus imbecillitate proportionem servent: alioqui communicationis medium erit nullum, si altero jacente, ad sublimia alter velit evolare. Sermo igitur exemplaque, & quae exhibentur agenda, temperari opus est, omniaque modis proponi pinguioribus, crassis ac materiatis, quin & praejudiciorum discentis falsitati accommodatis; ipsisque interdum praejudiciis quasi fundamentis & veritatibus utendum est ad promotionem scopi praecipui & necessarii; veluti, si, exempli causa, sinceritatis, innocentiae, patientiae, similiumque virtutum incrementa nonnullis maxime necesse sit inculcare; ut fiat efficacius, cum illis (si in hoc sint praejudicio) statui potest & debet, virtutes hasce eisve analogas, in brutis ovibus aut columbis reperiri, inde ut pudere possit eos si a brutis se superari, iisque deteriores se esse patiantur. Ita animi gratitudinem erga Auctorem omnis boni, ejusque obsequium impriment facilius, si canes ipsos id suis dominis praestare inculcetur. Similiter de caeteris. Verorum eruditorum docendi modi (quos superius appositos esse volui) iflis abundant exemplis, quorum idcirco scripta morosiores Critici cùm severius & exactitudinis externæ omnium circumstantiarum ratione habita examinant tractantque, absurde admodum ludunt operam. Non autem solorum præjudiciorum respectu se suis accommodat solide eruditus, verum etiam quoad passiones (ut sic loquar) affectusve, etiam pravos, quibus non utique caret primùm erudiendus, præsertim Amore proprio: qui & præcipuus & omnium, morbus, ita dextre sanandus, & exterminandus est, ut initiò se demulceri & foveri potius sentiat, quam impeti: fugeret alioqui & medicum & sanitatem æger. Caute igitur inceptanda & agenda hujus mali curatio, evitatis potissimum duobus, quibus amor proprius potissimum efferatur, irrisione & dura severitate; quorum utrumque, proximum maximè, exhibet discentibus eam sui Erudientis ideam, in qua amoris exæstimationisque erga se extinctionem videant, id quod ipsi facile diffidentiâ, dispositionis suæ statusque occultatione, odio fugaque compensare possent. Sed nec periculum est ne vere eruditus irrisioni indulgeat, siquidem eâ ad acquirendam & fovendam eruditionem ipse carere debuerit, ut superius observatum est; periculum majus, ne severitatem, qua ipse erga se debuit uti, ad alios intempestive extendat; quorum amor proprius est potius alliciendus: quod tamen ut fiat sine periculo, id est, ne proprius amor inde magis crescat & corroboretur, quam decrescat, sine numine divinaque prudentia, precibus a Deo impetranda, fieri neutiquam potest. Ipse Deus populum olim per ejusmodi συγκαταβάσεις (condescendentias, si liceret, dicerem) innumeras ad veram eruditionem allicuit Israeliticum, quibus cum plurimi prius ad scopum verum pervenissent, postremo tandem ab eo omnes desciscere.
units.tr: precepts a disease otherwise curable and dispellable with some delay, and so render the force of truth vain, harsh and hateful. (Hence observing the time, so that one may impart learning when it can be received by a suitably disposed subject and make progress, is among the primary rules of the true teacher.) Or, if the learner's condition still bears some instruction, things are to be set before him in words and deeds in such a way that they keep proportion to his weakness; otherwise there will be no means of communication at all, if while one lies prostrate the other wishes to fly up to lofty things. Therefore speech and examples, and what is presented to be done, need to be tempered, and everything proposed in the plainer, coarser and more material ways, even adapted to the falsity of the learner's prejudices. Sometimes the prejudices themselves must be used as foundations and truths for the advancement of the chief and necessary aim. For instance, if it is especially necessary to instil in some people the growth of sincerity, innocence, patience and similar virtues, then, so that it may be more effective, one can and should tell those who hold such a prejudice that these virtues, or analogous ones, are found in dumb sheep or doves, so that they may be ashamed if they are surpassed by brute beasts and allow themselves to be worse than them. So too one may more easily impress gratitude of soul towards the Author of every good, and obedience to him, if it is inculcated that dogs themselves render this to their masters. Likewise in other cases. The methods of teaching of true learned men (which I wished to set out above) abound in such examples, so that when more morose critics examine and handle their writings severely, taking account of the external exactness of every circumstance, they play at work most absurdly. Nor does the solidly learned man accommodate himself merely to the prejudices, but also to the passions (so to speak) or affections, even the bad ones, of which the learner at first certainly is not free, especially self-love. This is both the chief and the most universal disease, and it must be healed and rooted out so skilfully that at first the learner feels himself soothed and cherished rather than attacked; otherwise the patient would flee both doctor and health. Therefore the cure of this evil must be begun and carried on cautiously, avoiding above all two things by which self-love is especially inflamed: mockery and harsh severity. Of these, especially the nearer, shows the learners that idea of their teacher in which they see the extinction of love and esteem for him, which they could easily repay with distrust, concealment of their disposition and state, hatred and flight. But there is no danger that the truly learned man will indulge in mockery, since he ought himself to lack it in acquiring and fostering learning, as was observed above. The greater danger is that he extend to others, untimely, the severity which he ought to use towards himself; their self-love is rather to be enticed. Yet that this be done without danger, that is, that self-love not grow and be strengthened by it rather than diminish, cannot by any means be achieved without the divine will and divine prudence, to be obtained by prayer from God. God himself once drew the Israelite people to true learning by such innumerable condescensions [συγκαταβάσεις] (I would call them condescensions, if that were permitted), by which, although very many had earlier reached the true goal, at last all of them in the end fell away from it.

units.la: Tantæ molis erat sapientem condere gentem.
units.tr: So great a labour it was to found a wise nation.

units.la: XXXVIII. Postquam eousque cum eruditis condescendit Eruditor (venia sit verbis,) jam quaerendum est medium communicationis, quo ea quae in mente docentis sunt, in discipulorum mentem ingredi & transfundi queant. Id vulgo verbis absolvi putant. Verborum intercessionem fateor ordinariè necessariam; at eam non sufficere, tot sectarum de divinis humanisque disputantium & altercantium discrimina, quae tamen omnes Praeceptoris unius alicujus verba scriptave pro principio admittunt, satis luperque oltendunt. Naturalium scientiarum scrutatores de sensu verborum Auctoris alicujus fui, quem omnes pariter audiunt, inter se disputant. Christianos iisdem verbis omnes alloquitur divinum Volumen, tametsi alii aliorum cogitata factaque tam majoris quam minoris momenti, quae ex Scripturae verbis pariter utrobique auditis se haurire prositentur, falsitatis arguant. Quid hic agas? Non certe, in verbis, sed in eorum qui verbis utuntur dispositione clavem veram sensuum latere, hinc satis patescit; idque divinis, exempli causa, (quia in illis evidentius negotium capietur, ) libet hic applicare. Constat a Dei actu pendere lumen veri, quo erudiendorum mentes illustrandae sunt. Hujus Dei in mentibus actus, verba docentis non possunt esse causa nisi occasionalis, eaque non necessaria, sed a libera Dei voluntate pendens: hoc est, quando docens loquitur, & discens audit, non ideo tenetur Deus ex verborum auditorum occasione lumen suum in mente auditoris excitare: sed id faciet cum ipsi lubebit: lubebit autem id facere quando docens & discens ipsi Deo sunt grati, sive, quando sincera mente ut divinae voluntati pareant, dant operam: Deus enim eorum qui ipsum amant & reverentur, voluntatem implet atque desideria. Ergo quando docens sincere ardenterque desiderat & precatur ut verbis quae profert jungat Deus gratiosam luminis sui in mente auditorum operationem; quando etiam auditores sinceri sunt, humiles, ad Deum conversi, gratiosum ejus luminis virtutisque actum in se optantes & deprecantes, iisque conditionibus praediti, quas ad acquisitionem veritatis solidae requiri aliquoties diximus; tunc Deus, amator & fautor amatorum suorum, eorum voluntatibus obsecundans ob bonas mentis ipsorum dispositiones, lumen suum in illis excitat, quandoque sine verborum occasione, ordinarie tamen ex occasione eorundem; quae verba alioqui, Dei actu bonaque mentium constitutione absen-
units.tr: XXXVIII. Once the teacher has thus condescended so far with the learned (let the expression be pardoned), we must now seek the means of communication by which what is in the mind of the teacher can enter and be poured into the minds of the pupils. Most people think this is accomplished by words. I admit that words are ordinarily necessary, but that they are not sufficient is sufficiently and abundantly shown by the divisions and quarrels of so many sects disputing and contending about divine and human matters, all of whom nonetheless admit the words or writings of some one teacher as their principle. Investigators of the natural sciences dispute among themselves about the sense of the words of some one author whom they all alike hear. The divine Volume addresses Christians all in the same words, although some charge others with falsity regarding thoughts and deeds of greater or lesser weight, which each side professes to draw from the words of Scripture heard alike by both. What, then, are you to do? That the true key to the senses lies not in the words, but in the disposition of those who use the words, is clear enough from this; and I wish to apply this here to divine matters, for example, because the matter will be grasped more evidently in them. It is established that the light of truth, by which the minds of learners are to be enlightened, depends on the action of God. The action of this God in minds: the words of the teacher cannot be its cause except an occasional one, and that not a necessary one, but dependent on the free will of God. That is, when the teacher speaks and the learner hears, God is not bound by the occasion of the hearers' words to excite his light in the hearer's mind; but he will do so when it pleases him. It will please him to do so when teacher and learner are pleasing to God himself, or when they labour with a sincere mind to obey the divine will, for God fulfils the will and desires of those who love and revere him. Therefore, when the teacher sincerely and ardently desires and prays that God join to the words he utters a gracious operation of his light in the minds of the hearers; when the hearers too are sincere, humble, turned to God, desiring and praying for the gracious action of his light and power in themselves, and endowed with those conditions which we have several times said are required for the acquisition of solid truth; then God, the lover and patron of his lovers, yielding to their wills because of the good dispositions of their minds, kindles his light in them, sometimes without the occasion of words, but ordinarily on the occasion of the same words; which words otherwise, in the absence of God's action and the good constitution of the minds, are dead words, and the letter of death, as Paul calls the Scriptures themselves, while he also distinguishes there the ministers of the letter from the ministers of the Spirit, who are those very persons we have just described. And this is the true sense of Scripture and its divine meaning.

units.la: D 5 ibus tibus, verba sunt mortua, & litera mortis, ut Paulus (a) Scripturas ipsas nominat, dum & ministros literæ ibidem distinguit a ministris Spiritus, qui hi ipsi sunt quos modo descripsimus. Atque hæc vera est Scripturæ, divinique sensus ejus clavis, non autem millena nugamenta de critica, de linguis originalibus, de legibus interpretationum, quibus instructissimi Judæi circa vetus Organum, illum qui promissus & depictus ibi erat, non modo non agnoverunt, sed & eum crucifixerunt; Christiani vero illum charitatis & Dei Spiritum, qui librorum fœderis novi scopus & finis est, non modo nesciunt; sed & in Scripturis spiritum odii & discordiarum atque Antichristianismi videntur deprehendisse cum suis egregiis interpretationum legibus; quarum tamen nonnullæ, ubi prædictis, quæ præcipua sunt, adhæretur, suum, sed eum accessorium & minusculum usum habere queant. De naturalibus similia fere dixeris. Eorum essentiæ proprietatumque solida & radicalis cognitio, temperatus bonusque usus, cùm sine Deo haberi non possint, (uti dictum est ubi de acquisitione,) sine eodem etiam, nec hon sine docentium ac discentium debita habitudine, nequeunt communicari. Atque hæc omnia eo mägis sunt observanda, quo plura sunt in natura & in gratia ad quæ homines cœci sunt, ex quo impuri nascuntur & depravati. Et revera qui hoc ex tenebroso cœcoque statu emerserunt alios docturi, se ad illos in plerisque habent veluti videntes ad caecos, quos de lumine, de coloribus, de objectis visus, deque modo ea per oculos percipiendi alloquuntur; aut veluti si quis ultra quinque sensus naturales nobis communes, alios quinque aut plures insuper haberet, quibus res nobis imperceptibiles & incognitas perciperet, is, si nos de hisce quibus praepolleret vellet alloqui, frustra sane funderet verba, nisi medium sciret aliud quo sensus in nobis desiderari vel sopiti aut emortui, reviviscerent; nisi etiam ad haec media, quibus ex parte sua quicquid posset conferret, eos ablegaret, qui illi primo fidem habentes, eis uterentur, ac demum sensus istos reciperent. Crediderim, hominem, cum integer esset, habuisse ad divina, nec non ad naturalia in origine sua, quae divina est, cognoscenda, vel plus centum percipiendi facultates, quibus nunc destituimur, aut quae in nobis sopitae & veluti emortuae sunt. Et certe hoc testantur Deus & experti, dum ajunt, nos ad ista caecos, surdos, mortuos esse, affirmantque (a) homines naturales non posse percipere ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei: habere ea abipsis pro stultitia & fabulis; donec principia spiritualia, per quae possint ea percipi, receperint: proindeque & nos hortantur, & precibus sua ex parte juvant, ut (eis si primum in caecitate nostra crediderimus) media aliquoties dicta, quae in eruditione acquirenda admiserunt eam adepti, adhibeamus; quibus mediis percipiendi facultates consecuti, eas res ipsimet cognoscamus, quas primum incognitas, ex relatione & sine ideis distinctis credebamus; sicque capiamus deinceps sensa verborum, quibus ista nobis particularius explicare voluerunt aut volent in posterum.
units.tr: When these are absent, the words are dead, and they are "the letter of death," as Paul calls the Scriptures themselves, when in the same passage he distinguishes the ministers of the letter from the ministers of the Spirit, who are exactly those we have just described. This is the true key to Scripture and to its divine sense, not the thousand trifles of criticism, of the original languages, and of the rules of interpretation. The most learned Jews, with all these, did not merely fail to recognize in the old instrument the one who was promised and portrayed there; they crucified him. Christians, for their part, not only do not know that Spirit of charity and of God, which is the aim and purpose of the books of the New Covenant; they seem rather to have detected in the Scriptures, with their excellent rules of interpretation, the spirit of hatred, of discord, and of Antichristianism. Some of these rules, however, can have their own use, though an accessory and minor one, where the principal things mentioned above are adhered to. Of natural things one may say much the same. Solid and radical knowledge of their essences and properties, and their temperate and good use, cannot be had without God (as was said where we spoke of acquisition). Nor can they be communicated without him, nor without the due relation between teacher and learner. All these things must be observed the more carefully, the more there are, in nature and in grace, things to which men are blind, from which they are born impure and depraved. Indeed, those who have emerged from this dark and blind state, and wish to teach others, stand toward them in most respects as the seeing to the blind. They speak to them about light, colours, the objects of sight, and the manner of perceiving these through the eyes. Or it is as if someone had five or more senses beyond the five natural senses common to us, by which he perceived things imperceptible and unknown to us. If he wished to speak to us about what he excels in, he would surely pour out words in vain, unless he knew some other means by which the senses we lack, or which are dozing or dead in us, could come back to life. Unless, too, he sent us away to those means, to which he would contribute on his part whatever he could, so that we, first believing him, might use them and at last receive those senses. I believe that man, when he was whole, had for knowing divine things, and also natural things in their origin, which is divine, more than a hundred faculties of perception, of which we are now deprived, or which are dozing and as if dead in us. And certainly God and those who have experienced it testify to this, when they say that we are blind, deaf, and dead to these things, and affirm that natural men cannot perceive the things of the Spirit of God, but hold them to be folly and fables, until they receive the spiritual principles through which they can be perceived. And so they both exhort us and help us on their part by prayers, that, if we first believe them in our blindness, we should apply the means mentioned several times, which they admitted in acquiring erudition. By these means, having obtained the faculties of perception, we may ourselves know those things which at first we believed unknown, on report and without distinct ideas; and so we may then grasp the meanings of the words by which they wished, or will wish in future, to explain these things to us more particularly.

units.la: Hinc patet nil mirandum esse quòd veri eruditi, de rebus divinis nec non naturalibus solidius loquentes, non capiantur vulgo, neque a falsis superficiariisve eruditis, nec quidem ab incipientibus bona voluntate praeditis. Nec mirum igitur si ab irrisoribus criticis irrideantur, & in ludibrium coram ignaris vertantur ea, quae caeteroquin revera omnium divinissima, solidissima, praestantissimaque sunt. Faciunt id quod coeci, si qui totam alfquam regionem incolerent, qui nunquam corpora nisi tactu palpandique facultate percepissent, quosque accederet oculatus qui eos de corporibus per oculos percipiendis alloqueretur: hunc, sermonesque ejus non intellectos, cachinnis procul dubio exciperent, ipsi miserrimi, risuque & commiseratione dignissimi.
units.tr: Hence it is plain that there is nothing to wonder at in the fact that true erudite men, speaking more solidly of divine and natural things, are not understood by the common people, nor by false and superficial scholars, nor even by beginners who have good will. Nor is it surprising, then, that they are mocked by scoffing critics, and that the things which are in truth the most divine, most solid, and most excellent of all are turned into ridicule before the ignorant. They do what the blind would do if some whole region were inhabited by people who had never perceived bodies except by touch and the power of feeling, and a man with eyes came among them to speak of bodies as perceived through the eyes. Those most wretched people, worthy of both laughter and pity, would no doubt greet him and his words, which they did not understand, with guffaws.

units.la: XXXIX. Hisce praemissis, quam materiae aptae formam superinducendam alla- borat, ea est, qua ipsemet est eruditus:
units.tr: XXXIX. Having premised these things, the form which he labours to impose on the fitting matter is this: the erudite man himself.

units.la: quae quoniam plura complectitur, a maxime necessariis, quae ut plurimum & simplicissima sunt, exordium capit, semotis tantisper omnibus caeteris, iis tamen non repulsis quae necessariorum veluti vehicula sunt & adminicula. Rudis & incomposita mens, cum fit instar lapidis aedificio destinati, sic erudienda est & laeviganda, ut cum ceteris lapidibus, angulari quidem & fundamentali, Deo; collateralibus vero, hominibus reliquis, caeterisque rebus creatis, bene coveniat, aedificiumque unum ornate componat; sic tractanda adaptandaque, ut si contingeret, quod quovis momento contingere poterit, eam quocunque tempore sua mortalitate exui, dispositiones haberet, quae beatae aeternitatis domicilio eam non sisterent ineptam, incapacemque quae ad divinam hanc structuram concurreret. Et quamvis primae hujusmodi operationes, quoniam corrupto & bruto mentium instituendarum statui adversae sunt, eumque destruere annituntur, sint iis quam maxime acerbae; nihilominus postquam satis hactenus praeparandis alliciendisque animis operam navavit docens, discentiumque animi dispositionibus praeviis fortiores viriliorésque facti sunt, tandem frangenda glacies est, & elementis primis diu satis tritis, surrogandi cibi solidiores, iique non tantum in genere veri aut agendorum, sed & in modis quo erudiens erga suos utitur. Hoc est, cum tempus est, veritates suorum praejudiciis, iisque gratissimis maxime oppositas, praecepta amori proprio propensionibusque intimis & perversis quam plurimum adversantia sic eum proponere necesse est, ut si pertinacius inolita consuetudo prava recalcitret, huic oppositae durioribus verbis modisque imperentur, erudiendique de pertinaci
units.tr: Since this form comprises many things, it begins with the most necessary, which for the most part are also the simplest. For the time being all other things are set aside, though not rejected, namely those which serve as vehicles and aids to the necessary things. A rude and unformed mind, since it is like a stone destined for a building, must be so taught and smoothed that it fits well with the other stones: with the corner and foundation stone, which is God; with the stones at the side, which are other men and other created things; and so that it composes one building in good order. It must be handled and adapted in such a way that, if it should happen, as it can at any moment, that it is stripped of its mortality at any time, it has dispositions which do not render it unfit for the abode of blessed eternity, and incapable of joining in this divine structure. And although these first operations, since they are opposed to the corrupt and brutish condition of minds that are to be instructed, and strive to destroy it, are most bitter to them, nevertheless, after the teacher has laboured enough so far in preparing and attracting souls, and the pupils have grown stronger and more manly through their preliminary dispositions, the ice must at last be broken. Once the first elements have been rubbed in long enough, firmer food must be substituted, and not only in the general sense of truth or of duties, but also in the manner in which the teacher deals with his own people. That is, when the time comes, it is necessary to set forth truths, which are most opposed to men's prejudices and to those most pleasing to them, and precepts that greatly oppose self-love and deep and perverse inclinations, in such a way that, if a more stubbornly ingrained evil custom kicks back, it is commanded against with harder words and methods, and the learners are rebuked for their stubborn resistance.

units.la: D resistentia corripiantur : & id quidem rarius, atque appositè ; sed tamen quandoque. Necesse enim est falsa, præjudicia, pravum sui ipsius amorem, sibimet ipsi desideriisque vanis adhærentiam, & cætera quæ solide & æternum subsistere non possunt, semel frangi & deleri, si animus ab ineruditione ruditateque sua fit liberandus, & solido atque æterno ædificio initiandus. Et quamvis ineruditi, & quorum oculi tenebris adhuc obducuntur, ejusmodi duriorem agendi rationem odii signum esse existiment, ex doloris sensu inde enato rem penitantes; ea nihilominus majoris est quam dici possit amoris argumentum: siquidem nil melius sit quam tenebris & malo carere; quod ingens beneficium summæ charitatis est non vereri procurare eo modo, qui & reprehendentem odii alicujus periculo exponat, & ipsummet cum illo quem amat, ingenti afficiat doloris sensu. Namque quo vividiores sunt eruditi docentis facultates præ facultatibus discipulorum adhuc semisopitis, & quo teneriori amore verum bonumque is prosequitur, eo quoque vehementiori dolore afficitur ob ofsensas in bonum verumque pertinaciter ab iis commissas & defensas, idemque etiam magis eorum anxias pœnas persentiscit quam ipsimet; cum is illos magis quam ii semetipsos vero amplexetur amore. Nil autem absurdius sibi promittere possunt ii qui in tenebris, erroribus, præjudiciis, corruptisque ac vanis moribus indolis perversæ nati sunt & educati, quam quod sine sensu anxio & repugnante in viam veritatis virtutisque credant se posse reduci. Facilius omnia corporis alicujus membra luxata, inque luxatione diu indurata, sine adverso sensu in locum reducenda expectares. Inimica est solida veritas dispositionibus in quibus induruimus; & qui non sperat & optat ejus in se oppositos ictus, sanabitur nunquam; sed tanquam rejectaneus lapis, examen & operam non patiens, projicietur foras, iturus, si lubet, eos ad Doctores; qui quoniam nihil nisi propria emolumenta quaerunt, illum in placitis erroribus & naevis quiescere sinent, non nisi quae auribus & propensionibus ejus grata erunt, ipsi praecipientes atque laudantes, donec emendationis tempus praeterierit. Aliis se erudiri optet doctoribus & modis, qui sui emendationem quaerit, dicatque potius cum vate regio: (a) Percutiat me justus, beneficii loco ducam: castiget me, id mihi pro praestantissimo erit unguento: neque solum caput mihi non ledet, verum etiam in ejus incommodis pro eo precabor.
units.tr: And this indeed is done more rarely and fittingly, but still at times. For it is necessary that falsehoods, prejudices, perverse self-love, attachment to oneself and to vain desires, and everything else that cannot stand solidly and eternally, be once broken and destroyed, if the mind is to be freed from its ignorance and roughness and started on a solid and eternal building. And although the unlearned, whose eyes are still covered with darkness, think that such a harsher way of acting is a sign of hatred, and repent of it from the feeling of pain that arises from it, nevertheless it is a proof of love greater than can be said. For nothing is better than to be free from darkness and evil; and it is a great kindness of the highest charity not to fear to bring this about in a way that exposes the one who rebukes to the risk of hatred, and inflicts a great feeling of pain on himself as well as on the one he loves. For the more vivid the teacher's faculties are compared with the pupils' faculties, which are still half-asleep, and the more tender the love with which he pursues the true and good, the more vehemently he is also pained by the offences committed against the good and truth, and stubbornly defended by them. He also feels their anxious punishments more than they themselves do, since he embraces them with a greater love of truth than they have for themselves. Nothing more absurd can be promised to themselves by those who were born and brought up in darkness, errors, prejudices, and corrupt and vain morals of a perverse disposition, than that they can be led back into the way of truth and virtue without an anxious and resisting feeling. You would more readily expect any dislocated limb of the body, long hardened in its dislocation, to be returned to its place without any feeling of resistance. Solid truth is hostile to the dispositions in which we have grown hard; whoever does not hope for and desire its blows opposed to himself will never be healed. Like a rejected stone, which does not endure testing and labour, he will be thrown out, free to go, if he likes, to those teachers who, since they seek nothing but their own advantage, will let him rest in his pleasing errors and blemishes, commanding and praising only what is agreeable to his ears and inclinations, until the time for amendment has passed. Let him who seeks his own amendment wish to be taught by other teachers and by other methods, and let him say rather with the royal poet: (a) Let the righteous strike me; I will count it a kindness. Let him rebuke me; it will be for me the finest ointment. My head shall not refuse it; indeed, in their misfortunes I shall pray for them.

units.la: Tanti momenti hic est articulus, (eo quod ibi latet causa, cur quam plurimi bonae voluntatis animi a via solidae eruditionis inceptá discesserint perierintque; ut non pigeat omnia haec Mentis cujusdam divinius eruditae testimonio, etsi longiuscule, illustrare, quae sic de istiusmodi Eruditionibus, de quibus agimus: Non possunt illi erga suorum discipulorum naevos, siquidem id conducere videant, ulla simulatione aut dissimulatione uti; neque eorum recordari, quin ipsi eos indicent, siquidem dem ipsos virtutibus ditescere peroptent quam vehementissime. Ad hoc nil fere intactum & non tentatum relinquunt, etsi alioquin creatarum rerum fere sint obliti. Nil illi agunt aliud, neque se impenso illo amoris impulsu liberare valent. Et quia erga suos nec adulationes nec dissimulationem adhibent, hi necessario aut emendabuntur, aut dissolvetur mutua amicitia; siquidem hic agendi modus nisi cum emendatione excipiatur, intolerabilis est, bellumque reciprocum & continuum. Equidem caeteros mundanos non curant (ejusmodi solide Erudientes,) nec advertunt an caeteri Deo pareant nec ne, sibi quippe solis invigilantes: at id cum familiaribus erudiendis neutiquam queunt observare, nec ipsos quicquam celare. In eis tam acutum cernunt, ut vel atomi visum eorum non effugiant: quod ipsis sane immensae crucis magnique laboris est carpere; felicitatis autem ingentis omnibus qui isto pacto a talibus amantur: Fortunatam dicant diem qua ad eorum pervenerunt notitiam. Quis det mihi, bone Deus, ut me multi tali amore prosequantur! Id ardentiori desiderio peroptem, o Deus, quam ab omnibus saeculi Regibus & Magnatibus amari: & merito sane; siquidem nil illi molimine omni agunt quam ut toti mundo dominari possimus, omniaque nobis subjiciantur. Itaque si ejusmodi (Ductores) repereritis cum ipsis agite, & laxis eos habenis amate: perrarienim sunt. Nulla via ad Deum tutior quam cum ejus amicis agere. Semper ex hoc profectus manat ingens. Id experientia me docuit; & dicere ausim, me; si perditionem evitavero, id, praemissa Dei commiseratione, ejusmodi hominibus tributum debere. In rebus aliis sequioris momenti nil efficacius esse quam in tempore subjectum meritum cum sale nonnullo corripere, omnium artium disciplinarumque periti atque Magistri unanimi consensu verbo & opere prositentur.
units.tr: This point is of such importance (because it is here that the reason lies why so many well-intentioned people have turned aside from the path of solid learning once begun, and have come to ruin) that it is worth illustrating all this, though at some length, by the testimony of a certain divinely learned mind. Writing of the kind of teachers we are discussing, he says: They cannot use any pretence or dissimulation towards the faults of their disciples, if they see that it will be of benefit; nor can they refrain from pointing them out, since they desire with the greatest possible intensity that the disciples grow rich in virtues. For this purpose they leave almost nothing untouched and untried, although otherwise they have almost forgotten created things. They do nothing else, nor are they able to free themselves from that intense impulse of love. And because they use towards their own people neither flattery nor dissimulation, these must either be amended, or the mutual friendship will be dissolved; for this manner of dealing, unless it is accompanied by amendment, is intolerable, and a reciprocal and continual war. Indeed they do not concern themselves with other worldly people (such solid teachers), nor do they notice whether the others obey God or not, being watchful over themselves alone. But with their familiars they cannot in any way keep to this, nor can they conceal anything from them. They see in them so keen a sight that not even an atom escapes their eyes; for those who are loved in this way by such teachers, the task of being scrutinised is indeed a great cross and a heavy labour, but their happiness is immense, and they say that the day on which they came to know such teachers is a fortunate day. Who will grant me, good God, that many people pursue me with such love!
