I would wish this with a more ardent desire, O God, than to be loved by all the kings of the world and magnates; and rightly so, since all their effort is directed only to our dominating the whole world and having everything subjected to us. Therefore, if you find such guides, act with them and love them, giving them free rein, for they are very rare. There is no safer way to God than to deal with his friends. Great progress always flows from this. Experience has taught me this, and I dare to say that if I have avoided ruin, I owe it, with God's mercy going before, to men of this kind. In matters of lesser importance, it is agreed unanimously by all the skilled and masters of the arts and disciplines, in word and deed, that nothing is more effective than to rebuke a subject's merit with some salt at the right time.

units.la: XL. Dixi modo obiter, erudientem a necessariis in eruditione aliis communicanda exordium capere, caeteris tantisper semotis: qua in re permultum interest, etsi ignari id nesciant, vel etiam naufeabundo animo jactueantur nonnullarum materiarum, quae admodum siccae & steriles istis videntur, inculcationem, eamque semel iterumque, imo multoties repetitam fieri. Multos ex benevolis etiam, sed animo leviore, praecipitantiore, impatientiore praeditis, a summa solidae eruditionis communicatione impediit isthaec eruditionem communicandi ratio. Gestit animus illico videre flores & fructus bene coloratos & odoriferos; palatia aulaque bene ornata atque picta: terram autem invertere, semina illi immittere, primordia radicis curare diu & inspicere; foveam fundamento aedificii locando necessariam repetitis ejectionibus effodere, lapides simpliciores haud ita elegantes nec pigmentatos cum sudore & labore non jucundo ibidem diu defodere, aut saltem haec inspicere; non adeo gratum est mentibus molioris & parum masculae indolis. Sed ob ejusmodi absurdam ignoviam non interver-tet. tet in eruditione communicanda naturæ ori- dinem solide eruditus, qui primum suos præjudiciis falsis malisque rejiciendis, dein principiis fundamentisque locandis, hoc est, terræ lutosæ vertendæ & effodiendæ, seminibus radicibusque siccis & deformibus, lapidibus inelegantibus defodiendis occupabit diu: idque eo magis, quod eruditio menti communicanda sese habeat quam maxime instar lucis a Sole emanantis, ad quam recipiendam omnis præparatio, & tantum non acquisitio, consistit in remotione obstaculorum, quæ illam ab oculis prohibebant. Et quoniam illa obstacula plura sunt, amata sunt, recurrunt sæpissime; ideo non semel, sed iteratis sæpe vicibus eorum rejectio est inculcanda, nec non fundamentalium principiorum positio repetenda, maxime quando res concurrunt quæ quotidie in praxin reduci debent; contra quas corrupta indoles oblivione, distractione, aversione sese opponit, consusione etiam, miscendo & turbando necessaria & principalia cum accessoriis & minus præcipuis: cui perniciosæ permissioni non aliter obviam itur quam variata reiteratione, quæ non patitur summe necessaria ignorari, oblivione obduci, cum accidentariis confundi, quæque etiam animorum fastidiosum gustum, proprium placitum, activiores & indebitos motus supprimit & domat; nec non, si bonus sit mentis fundus, intimius amorem inculcatorum implantat. Ipsa sane natura in operum perfectorum necessariorumque negotio repetitione & revolutione continua agit: sola monstra, quæ morbidam nonnullorum curiositatem titillant, repetitione crebra non profert. Nec pudét doctos quacunque in arte, fundamentaliora sua plus semel inculcare, sicut Mathematici in qualibet propositione præcedentium repetitionem recolunt. Cartesius fundamenta suæ metaphysicæ, quæ alicujus pretii esse putavit, vel decies in operibus suis repositit: Eruditi vero sacri ( quorum gratiâ hæc potissimum profero ) nec minùs sæpe ingerunt ea quæ tanquam capitalia commendant; uti luculenter videre est in divinis Scripturis, preces, abnegationem nostri, amorem atque charitatem sic ingerentibus, ut omnia cætera, etiam divinissima & sublimissima removeant, imo fere interdum videantur tollere & negare (quod nempe ad tempus eorum cognitio & occupatio menti neganda fit,) quo hisce solis detur opera, quamdiu hic vivitur. Nempe inflant cætera: his vero solidius fundatis tutius & magnificentius superædificabuntur suo tempore illa ipsa quæ tantisper seposuerimus, etiamsi tantisper illud totius vitæ spatio mensurandum esset, quod revera præ æternitate volucre momentum est, eo tamen concessum, ut pro ejus circa necessaria occupatione, æterna æternùm distribuenda sint. Prudentissime ergo agunt qui hæc sæpius inculcant, licet & ingrata sint, & rudimenta sint discipulorum; quia summe tuta & proficua: alia vero, licet sublimia & angelica, differunt; quia periculo-sa. fa. Nonne ( inquiebat divinus ille martyr Ignatius Antiochenus ) possim vobis supercœlestia scribere ? Sed timeo ne parvulis vobis ita damnum inferam, neve, (parcite,) istorum incapaces, suffocemini: neque etiam secundum hoc ligatus sum. Verum cum scire possim cœlestia, & dispositiones angelicas, & constitutiones principatuum, visibiliaque & invisibilia ; his prætermissis malim & adhuc esse discipulus : multa enim adhuc nobis desunt ne ipsi desimus Deo.
units.tr: XL. I have just remarked in passing that the teacher begins with the necessary things in communicating learning to others, setting the rest aside for the time being. In this matter it matters greatly, although the ignorant do not know it, or even with a squeamish mind they complain of the repeated inculcation of certain subjects which seem to them very dry and barren, and that this is done once, twice, indeed many times over. This method of communicating learning has hindered many who are well-disposed but of a lighter, more hasty and more impatient temperament from receiving the highest level of solid learning. The mind longs at once to see flowers and fruits well coloured and fragrant, halls and palaces well adorned and painted; but to turn over the earth, sow seed into it, and for a long time attend to and examine the first beginnings of the root; to dig out, by repeated removals, the trench necessary as foundation for a building, and to bury for a long time there, with sweat and unpleasant labour, the simpler stones which are not very elegant nor coloured, or at least to examine these things, is not pleasing to minds of a softer and less manly disposition. But the solidly learned teacher, who in communicating learning will not pervert the order of nature for such absurd squeamishness, will occupy himself for a long time first with rejecting false and harmful prejudices, then with laying principles and foundations, that is, with turning and digging up the muddy earth, and with burying dry and misshapen seeds and roots and inelegant stones. He will do this all the more because the learning to be communicated to the mind is most like light emanating from the sun, and for receiving it all the preparation, and almost all the acquisition, consists in removing the obstacles which kept it from the eyes. And since those obstacles are many, are beloved, and recur very often, their rejection must be inculcated not once but again and again, and the laying of fundamental principles must be repeated, especially when there are matters which must be daily put into practice; against these the corrupt disposition sets itself by forgetfulness, distraction, and aversion, and also by confusion, mixing and disturbing the necessary and principal things with accessory and less important ones. This pernicious tendency is met only by varied repetition, which does not allow the most necessary things to be ignored, to be covered by forgetfulness, or to be confused with incidentals; and which also suppresses and tames the fastidious taste of the minds, their own opinion, and their more active and undue movements; and, if the mind's ground is good, it more deeply implants love for the things inculcated. Indeed nature itself, in the business of perfect and necessary works, acts by continual repetition and revolution; only monsters, which tickle the morbid curiosity of some, do not produce themselves by frequent repetition. Nor are learned men ashamed in any art to inculcate their fundamentals more than once, just as mathematicians recall the preceding propositions by repetition in every proposition. Descartes repeated the foundations of his metaphysics, which he thought to be of some worth, ten times in his works. The learned men of Scripture (for whose sake I especially put these things forward) inculcate no less often those things which they commend as chief; as is clearly seen in the divine Scriptures, which inculcate prayer, self-denial, love and charity so insistently that they seem at times almost to remove, and even to deny, all other things, even the most divine and sublime (namely, because for the time being their knowledge and occupation must be denied to the mind, so that these alone may be the work during the time we live here). Indeed other things puff up; but when these have been solidly founded, those very things which we have set aside for the time will be built upon them safely and magnificently in their own time, even if that for the time were to be measured by the whole span of life, which in truth is a fleeting moment compared with eternity, yet granted to us so that, in relation to its occupation with necessary things, eternal things may be distributed eternally. Those therefore act most wisely who inculcate these things often, even though they are unwelcome and are the rudiments of disciples, because they are most safe and profitable; other things, though lofty and angelic, are deferred, because they are dangerous. Could I not (said that divine martyr Ignatius of Antioch) write to you of things above heaven? But I fear that I would do harm to you who are still little ones, lest (spare us) you, being unable to bear them, should be choked: nor am I bound to this on that account. But although I can know heavenly things, and angelic dispositions, and the constitutions of principalities, visible and invisible things; I would rather, with these set aside, still be a disciple: for many things are still lacking to us, lest we be lacking to God.

units.la: XLI. Illud etiam omittendum non est, ne
units.tr: XLI. This also must not be omitted, lest

units.la: alioqui solidioris eruditionis scriptores ob desectus frivolos praetermittantur aut contemnantur; eos videlicet ut plurimum in verbis eloquentiam, in tractandi ordine methodum rigidiorem negligere: quod multis contingere potest de causis. Namque primò, ex ratione disposition is suae, animus excellentiâ intimâ rerum occupatus, earumque fructu solido sese pascens, non sustinet ad cortices fucandos, aut arboris foliola certo ordine disponenda revocari; neque methodici sunt cordis animique sinceri motus, nisi simul & languidi fuerint & frigidi. Deinde res ipsae ex se tanti sunt pretii vivique luminis, ut malint propria praestantia nativaeque pulchritudinis decore, quam aliunde conquisito fuco commendari. Eorum est, quae nullius per se sunt pretii, ascitiis aliunde phaleris speciosisque pompis ad sui commendationem indigere, quod in se nil commendabile habeant. Tertiò, ipsa verborum artisque conquisitior affectatio ejus est indolis, ut tum audientes sive legentes pervertat, qui lenociniis ejusmodi decepti captique in vero bonoque proficere se putant, dum potius eorum tenebrae, amor corruptus suarum titillationis aurium, vitia augentur; tum docentium ostentationi ambitiosaeque vanitati inserviat: quae sane mala sunt praecavenda quam maxime. Denique ipse Deus ab ejusmodi ambitiosis & exquisitis ornamentis non parum abhorret: nihil enim coram ipso magis invisum quam idea homuncionum veritates divinas, quae ad nostri humiliationem nobis communicatae sunt, sic torquentium & amicire admirentium, ut in aliis sui existimationem excitent: a quo crimine cum Deus sit maxime alienus, non poterit verbis eorum, ut ut de rebus divinissimis, suam adjungere operationem; atque adeo sic evacuatur & effectu caret verbum veritatis, quod Paulus in re Euangelii praedicanda verbis politis, appellabat (a) evacuare re crucem Christi. Inde est quod in spiritualibus solidissimi quique Institutores omnium sint simplicissimi & minime fucati, uti ex Scriptis sacris antiquioribus, nec non ex recentioribus, (inter quos Kempisius unus loco omnium sit,) perspicere datur: tametsi nihilominus nec eloquentia, nec arte, nec similibus seculi scientiis detrectent uti, quando conducit usus. Accidit scilicet non raro, ut illi queis eruditio est communicanda, ea sint mentis imbecillitate, quae nil nisi ad formulas artis compositum, dispositum oblatumque admittere, nec quidem audire velit. His si salutare esse potest ut pro eorum palato præparentur & proponantur solidæ veritates, eos sanaturæ & erudituræ, faciunt id illas communicaturi, siquidem & eloquentiam & artis methodum ipsi sciant: namque eis si destituantur, licet facili opera brevique mora eas possent addiscere, prætermittent tamen, rem veritatis i totam genuinæ suæ sinceritati simpliciitatique commissuri, quod & in modo agendi cum adversantibus humana edoctis observabunt, qui artes callebunt adversariorum strophas sophismataque detegendi, ne per ea simpliciores aut minus cauti a solida veritate absterreantur, agent optime si sua ad hoc utentur peritia; quam, qui ea carebunt; disputandi aut cavillatorum argutias discutiendi gratiā, non curabunt comparare; quandoquidem veritatis lux, ubi solide possidetur, sola præsentia sua quarumvis nebularum tenebras dispellere aptanata sit. Nec dissitebuntur ex discentibus, qui saniore gustu erga solida pollent. (aliis enim id nec persuaderi nec explicari porest) se nuda simplicique veritate magis affici, quam eådem quando multis illecebris {quæ semper aliud quid quam veritatem sapiunt) est implicita.
units.tr: solidly learned writers be passed over or despised on account of trivial faults, namely that they usually neglect eloquence in their words and a stricter method in their arrangement of material. This can happen for many reasons. First, because the mind, occupied with the inner excellence of things and nourished by their solid fruit, does not consent to be called back to painting the bark or arranging the little leaves of a tree in fixed order. The movements of a sincere heart and mind are not methodical unless they are also sluggish and cold. Second, the things themselves are of such worth and living light that they prefer to be commended by their own proper excellence and native beauty rather than by some borrowed paint. It belongs to things that have no worth in themselves to need decorations and showy pomp brought in from elsewhere to recommend them, because they have nothing commendable in themselves. Third, such a overly sought-after affectation of words and art has a nature that corrupts both hearers and readers. Those who are deceived and captivated by such enticements think they are making progress in what is true and good, while in fact their darkness is increased and their corrupt love of tickling the ears grows. Such affectation also serves the showing-off and ambitious vanity of teachers. These evils must be guarded against as much as possible. Finally, God himself greatly abhors such ambitious and exquisite ornaments. Nothing is more hateful before him than when petty men twist and dress up the divine truths, which were communicated to us for our humbling, and admire them in such a way that they stir up esteem for themselves in others. Since God is most remote from this crime, he will not add his own working to their words, however divine the matters may be. And so the word of truth is emptied and lacks effect, which Paul, in preaching the gospel, called "making the cross of Christ void by polished words" [(a) evacuare re crucem Christi]. Hence it is that among spiritual writers the most solid are all the most simple and least gaudy, as can be seen from the older sacred writings and also from more recent ones, among whom Kempis is one above all. Nevertheless they do not reject eloquence, art, or the similar learning of the age when use requires it. It does happen not infrequently that those to whom learning is to be communicated have such feebleness of mind that they will not even listen to anything not composed, arranged, and presented according to the rules of art. For such people, if it can be helpful that solid truths be prepared and set before them to suit their taste, in order to heal and instruct them, those who will communicate them do so, provided they themselves know both eloquence and the method of the art. For if they lacked these, though they could learn them with little effort and short delay, they would nevertheless neglect them, entrusting the whole matter of truth to its own genuine sincerity and simplicity. This they will also observe in how they deal with opponents, having been taught human learning. Those who are skilled in the arts of detecting the wiles and sophisms of adversaries, so that simpler or less cautious people are not frightened away from solid truth by them, will act best if they use their skill for this purpose. Those who lack such skill will not care to acquire it for the sake of disputing or of dismantling the subtleties of sophists, since the light of truth, when it is solidly possessed, is fit to dispel the darkness of any clouds by its presence alone. Nor will those among the learners who have a sounder taste for solid things deny that (for this cannot be persuaded to others nor explained) they are more moved by bare and simple truth than when it is entangled in many allurements, which always taste of something other than truth.

units.la: Cæterum, non solum non pudet vere eruditos fateri suam de istiusmodi verbalibus artibus, quando eas non tenent, ignorantiam, sed & ingenue profitentur de rebus ipsis multa se nescire, quæ vel ab infantulo vel meliercula, ubi opus esset, discere parati sint: imo quod plus est, cum solus Deus sit infallibilis, non modo se falli posse agnoscunt; sed & quando Deus ad humilitatem confervandam eos permisit falli, aut quando eos ex naturæ nostræ imbecillis conditione falli contigit, se lapsos esse aperte & candide declarant, idque (quod Augustinus scripto retractationum exsecutus est) retractare ex animo non verentur.
units.tr: Moreover, true scholars are not only not ashamed to confess their ignorance of such verbal arts when they do not possess them, but they also openly profess that they do not know many things about the matters themselves, which they are ready to learn, when need requires, even from a child or a little woman. Indeed, what is more, although God alone is infallible, they not only acknowledge that they can err, but when God has allowed them to err in order to preserve humility, or when they have fallen into error through the weakness of our nature, they openly and candidly declare that they have slipped, and they do not hesitate to retract it wholeheartedly, as Augustine did in his work of Retractations.

units.la: XLII. Quamvis autem nullis noxia, omnibus bona procurare animo atque opere omni conentur;: non est tamen quod sperent alios ergase eodem desiderio animari. Sunt namque perplures falsa superficiariaque eruditione delibuti, qui artium suarum futilitatem, adeoque & quæ inde captant, famam, lucrum, commoda, in fumum abi-re ex solidæ eruditionis admissione metuentes, omni molimine eos opprimere ma chinantur. Hi cum plebem habeant facilem, itemque fallaciarum suarum multos discipulos, qui omnes a vera propensione ad sapientiam & alieni sunt, & ejus irrisores, vitiisque & moribus indulgent quibus vera eruditio est maxime inimica; facile eos in illos commovent: & cum hanc seditionis suæ veram causam præten dere & profiteri non audent (cederet enim id ipsis quidem in vituperium, adversariis vero in laudem,) fingunt caussas alias, imponunt, mentiuntur, innocue dictis factisve mille sensus sco-posve perversos assignant; clamant omne bonum, verum, honestum periclitari, po-tentiores ad tristiora compellunt, denique nil non tentatum relinquunt contra eos, quo-rum rum fruitione & convictu nec mundus dignus est. Quibus artibus optimi quique olim apud Judæos, Gentiles, Christianos, vel e medio sublati, vel ejecti sunt, vel saltem coloribus atris ita deformati, & omnibus suspecti redditi, ut ab eis eorumve scriptis veluti ab angue abstinuerint & ipsæ simpliciores bonæque mentes, quæ alioqui per hæc servari potuissent. Istis malis subinde apologias opponebant, quandoque vehementiores, interdum leniores; plerumque cum per has nil fieret, furorque magis inde exacerbaretur, silentium, patientiam, ipsamque beneficentiam in inimicos: quorum exempla nonnulla inter Ethnicos visa, apud Christianos veros verum locum invenerunt ex præceptis Divini sui Præceptoris, genuinorumque ejus successorum, quos inter medis in vinculis persecutioneque durante divinus ille Ignatius rem suis sic commendat:
units.tr: XLII. Although they strive with mind and every effort to procure good for all, though harmful to none, there is nevertheless no reason for them to hope that others are moved by the same desire. For there are very many who are steeped in false and superficial learning. Fearing that the futility of their arts, and so also the fame, profit, and advantages they seek from them, will vanish into smoke once solid learning is admitted, they labour by every device to crush such men. Since they have an easily swayed common people, and many disciples of their deceits, who are all alien to a true inclination toward wisdom and mock it, and who indulge in vices and habits to which true learning is most hostile, they easily stir these people up against the solid scholars. And since they do not dare to pretend or profess this as the real cause of their sedition (for that would bring them shame and their adversaries praise), they invent other causes, impose, lie, and, though nothing harmful has been said or done, they assign a thousand perverse meanings and aims. They cry out that every good, truth, and honesty is in danger, they drive the more powerful to harsher measures, and in short they leave nothing untried against those "of whom the world was not worthy." By these arts the best men of old among Jews, Gentiles, and Christians were either removed from the midst, or expelled, or at least so disfigured with black colours and rendered suspect to all that even the simpler and good minds, who might otherwise have been saved through them, abstained from them and from their writings as from a snake. Against these evils they from time to time offered defences, sometimes more vehement, sometimes milder. But mostly, when nothing was achieved by these, and rage was only the more inflamed, they resorted to silence, patience, and even beneficence toward their enemies. Some examples of this were seen among the heathen, and among true Christians they found a true place, from the precepts of their divine Teacher and his genuine successors. Among these, the divine Ignatius, while in chains and under continuing persecution, commends the matter to his people thus:

units.la: Permittite eis (adversantibus) ut sipote ex operibus a vobis erudiantur. Adiras ipsorum este vos mites; ad magniloquia vos humilia sapientes; ad blasphemias eorum vos orantes; ad errores eorum vos in fide firmi; ad eorum feritatem vos manjueti; nec festinetis imitari ipsos, sed agite ea manstuetudine, qua fratres ipsis fiamus; imitatoresque Domini esse contendamus; quis plus patiatur injustum, quis fraudes, quisque contemtum magis perferat: Quid vero vel nunc, vel in posterum, cum similes quæpiam malorum technæ revivisent, eruditis veris sit agendum, verbisne an silentio utendum, ipsi lumine, quo pollent, viderint: ego non determinem, quineque hæc, nec quæ præcesserunt ea animi arrogantia scripsi ut eis præcepta darem; sed tantum ut si qui ex iis, qui eruditione nondum instructi ad illam adspirant, adeo felices sint ut in solidioris eruditionis formatores incidant, non patiantur se ab illis eorumve scriptis abduci propter ea quæ diximus præjudicia, offendicula, maledicta; neque etiam credulitate adeo stolida duci, ut de eorum dogmatibus atque sensu ex relationibus scripturisve adversantium aggressorum criticorumque ut ut cristatorum, dijudicent: qui me modus juvit non mediocriter in eis detegendis atque inveniendis, etiam in sexu sequiori. Optem omnibus, ut nullis obstaculis à consecutione ejus quod semper eos tranquillitate lumine beare potest, discludantur.
units.tr: Allow them (the opponents) to be instructed by your works, if perhaps. Be gentle toward their anger; humble yourselves against their boasting; pray against their blasphemies; be firm in faith against their errors; be meek against their savagery; and do not hasten to imitate them, but let us act with that gentleness by which we may become their brothers and strive to be imitators of the Lord; let us see who suffers injustice more, who bears fraud, who bears contempt more. What the learned true men should do now, or in future, when similar tricks of evil have revived, whether they should use words or keep silence, they themselves will see by the light they possess. I do not determine this, nor did I write these things, nor those that went before, with such arrogance as to give them precepts. I write only so that if any of those who are not yet instructed in learning but aspire to it should be so fortunate as to fall in with the formers of more solid learning, they will not allow themselves to be drawn away from them or their writings on account of the prejudices, stumbling-blocks, and slanders we have mentioned. Nor should they be led by such foolish credulity as to judge their doctrines and meaning from the reports or writings of adversaries, aggressors, and critics, however crested they may be. This method has greatly helped me in detecting and discovering them, even among the weaker sex. I wish for all that they not be shut out from attaining that which can always make them blessed with tranquillity and light.

units.la: De ERUDITIONE SUPERFICIARIA.
units.tr: On Superficial Erudition.

units.la: I. UAecunque hactenus de Erúditione Solida dicta sunt, cùm præcipuam dicendorum, materiæque tractandæ partem contineant, sufficiantque cuivis ingenuæ & sinceræ Menti ad ostendendam viam quâ ad solidiora vera bonaque pervenitur, (quod pro scopo maxime mihi in scribendo assumsi,) non erit cur in sequentibus tam exactè, copiosè, methodicèque occuper circa ea quæ Superficiariam atque Falsam Eruditionem concernunt. Non proponam mihi earum divisiones partesque omnes, ordinem, vias acquirendi, notas & proprietates tum possidentis tum communicantis sic exponere, ut veluti conspectum atque aream regionis istius superficiariæ lutosæque universam in aspectum protraham, quod aliis nil inde utilitatis, mihi vero etiam bonarum horarum jacturam, falsis autem eruditis irritationem pro fructu fore videam. Ea solum de istis hic subjungere animus est, quæ quibusvis ingenua & candida indole præditis cautelæ loco esse possint, cui attenti (si solida peroptent) ab iis quæ solummodo superficiem habent, etsi decoram, at perituraм tamen; aut abiis quæ omnimode etiam corrupta sunt, cavere & abstinere queant. Vanis aut malevolis animis si non satisfecero, neque id mihi pro scopo duxi, qui nolim unquam credi scripsisse nisi proiis, qui ad solida & permanentia mente sincera adspirant. Tales nec ullos alios opto & requiro Lectores. Cæteri abstineant, ni tædeat eos crepundia ac nugamenta sua videre de ponte dejici. Jam ad rem accedamus.
units.tr: I. Whatever has so far been said about solid erudition, since it contains the principal part of what was to be said and the subject to be treated, and since it is enough for any ingenuous and sincere mind to show the way by which one arrives at the more solid truths and goods (which I have taken as my chief aim in writing), there is no reason for me to dwell in what follows so exactly, fully and methodically on matters concerning superficial and false erudition. I do not propose to set out all their divisions and parts, their order, the ways of acquiring them, and the marks and properties both of those who possess them and of those who impart them, so as to lay open before the eyes the whole surface and field of that shallow and muddy region. I see that this would bring others no benefit, would cost me the loss of good hours, and would bring the false scholars only irritation rather than profit. My intention here is only to add those things about them which can serve as a safeguard for anyone of ingenuous and candid disposition, so that those who are attentive (if they desire solid things) may be able to avoid and abstain from what has only a surface, though a handsome one, which will nevertheless perish, or from what is corrupt in every way. If I do not satisfy vain or ill-disposed minds, I have not made that my aim. I would not wish to be thought to have written except for those who aspire with a sincere mind to what is solid and lasting. Such readers, and no others, I wish for and seek. Let the rest keep away, unless they are weary of seeing their baubles and trifles thrown off the bridge. Now let us come to the matter itself.

units.la: II. Principio, ne qui fine ratione offendantur si in sequentibus quam plurima ad Superficiaria revocavero, concipiant velim me de iis sic profiteri, eam nempe cognitionem, vel scientiam, seu virtutem, aut generalius eruditionem, quam superficiariam nominabo, non ideo nullam aut nullius pretii a me dici: habet utique pretium sibi debitum, usum quoque necessarium, interdumque talem, ut ad solida debeat evehi, atque ad solidè Eruditum referri, ut ut in se superficiaria sit; quemadmodum & ad falsa eadem erit referenda ob principia, vel usum, vel scopum minus legitima. Similitudine res clara fiet.
units.tr: II. First, so that no one may take offence without reason if in what follows I often refer things to the superficial, let them understand that in saying this I do not mean that the knowledge, or science, or skill (or, more generally, the erudition) which I shall call superficial is no knowledge at all, or of no worth. It has, of course, the value due to it and a necessary use, and sometimes such a use that it ought to be raised up to the solid and attributed to the solidly learned, although in itself it is superficial. In the same way, it will also have to be counted among the false, on account of principles, use, or aim that are less legitimate. The matter will be made clear by a comparison.

units.la: Homo sanus non internis tantum viscoribus membrisque solidis constat, sed & superficie & cute. Hanc si curet, mundet & ornet; superficiaria cura est, non modo non contemnenda, sed & necessaria. At si quis sic cutis haberet curam, ut ejus bonum statum non ab interna corporis dispositione, sed ab externis tantùm adscisceret; imo corpus solidis falubribusque cibis & exercitiis destitutum relinqueret, ut cuticulæ saltem lotionibus & frictionibus illustrandæ esset intentus; falsa sane & inanis hæc cura ejus esset: uti contrà, ad solidam id ipsum pertineret curam, si corpore bene intus cibis aut medicaminibus munito, lavandæ aut unguendæ incumberet superficiei, quo supposita membra vel roborarct, vel incommodo aliquo levaret. Idem de re Eruditionis quam superficiariam dicemus, est judicandum. Alphabetum, v. g. discere aut docere, ( simile quid in omnibus scientiis reperies, ) superficiarium sane est: & dum quis per totam vitam nil aliud quam hoc intenderet, cæteris internis aliisque posthabitis, id ridendæ fallacissimæque occupationis & eruditionis genus esset. at si quis internis suis cum Deo & æternitate bene curatis, ex amore solido quo erga puerum quempiam ferretur, cujus saluti per lectiones bonas procurandæ vellet prospectum, doceret eum alphabetum & legendi methodum, jam sane, etsi illa cura in se superficiaria esset, inter solida tamen ob principium & scopum mereretur annumerari, virque docens, non superficiarius, sed (ob interna ex quibus hoc fluerct) solide eruditus vere habendus esset. Denominatio enim a potiori, non a minus præcipuo, facienda est. Adeoque non habent quod sibi injuriam fieri putent eruditi, seque credant inter superficiarios eruditos connumerari, ex eo eo quòd scientiæ nonnullæ quas possident, vel etiam quas speciatim profitentur, superficiariæ sint in posterum dicendæ: tunc enim demum ejusmodi denominatio in eos refiliiret, cum hi solidioribus æternisque neglectis, & oblivioni vel despectui traditis, tempus, vires eruditionemque totam in istis solummodo collocarent: quod neminem de se suaque eruditione putem dicturum; neque adeo conquesturum se per hæc nostra eruditionis solidæ titulo spoliari, nisi hoc ipso profiteatur atque agnoscat se solidis æternisque valedixisse, quo evanidis speculationibus suis unice adhæreat, easque dignas reputet quæ totum hominem occupent. Quo in casu, nedum justa sit causa conquerendi velut de injuria, quod ejusmodi eruditio inter superficiarias sit designata, gratuletur potius sibi si in classe falsi non constituatur, ut ut materialia vera in se contineat. Nummus argenteus, qui pro aureo ducato substitueretur & commendaretur, falsus nummus esset dicendus etsi ex bono argento conflatus. Quæ scientiæ supra locum & valorem suum extolluntur, quæque, cum infimæ esse deberent, & velut accessoriæ, paululum temporis atque existimationis apud nos habere, econtra nos totos veluti summæ & præcipuæ occupant, ex falsis procul dubio accenseri merentur.
units.tr: A healthy man consists not only of internal organs and solid limbs, but also of surface and skin. If someone takes care of this, cleans it and adorns it, that is a superficial care, not to be despised but even necessary. But if someone took such care of his skin that he looked for its good condition not from the inner arrangement of the body but only from external things, and indeed left the body without solid and wholesome food and exercise, so that he was intent only on brightening the little skin by washings and rubbings, this care of his would certainly be false and empty. On the other hand, it would be a solid care if, with the body well nourished inside by food or medicines, he applied himself to washing or anointing the surface, by which the limbs underneath were either strengthened or relieved of some discomfort. The same judgment must be made about what we call superficial erudition. Learning or teaching the alphabet, for example (you will find something similar in all sciences), is certainly superficial. And if someone were to intend nothing else all his life, setting aside all other inner and higher concerns, that would be a kind of ridiculous and most deceptive occupation and erudition. But if someone, with his inner life with God and eternity well cared for, out of the solid love he bore toward some boy, whose salvation he wished to secure through good lessons, taught him the alphabet and the method of reading, then indeed, although that care is superficial in itself, it would deserve to be counted among the solid because of its principle and aim, and the man who teaches would be truly held to be solidly learned, not superficially so, on account of the inner things from which this flowed. For a name is to be given from the chief element, not from the lesser one. Therefore the learned have no reason to think they are wronged, or to believe that they are numbered among superficial scholars, because some of the sciences they possess, or even those they specifically profess, are to be called superficial from now on. That designation would rebound upon them only when they neglect the more solid and eternal things, leave them to oblivion or contempt, and devote their time, strength and whole erudition only to those other things. I do not think anyone will say this of himself and his own learning, nor will he complain that by these remarks of ours he is stripped of the title of solid erudition, unless he himself professes and acknowledges that he has bidden farewell to what is solid and eternal, so that he clings solely to his fleeting speculations and thinks them worthy to occupy the whole man. In that case, far from having a just cause to complain of injury because such erudition has been marked among the superficial, he should rather rejoice that he is not placed in the class of the false, even though it contains true material in itself. A silver coin which was put forward and commended in place of a gold ducat would rightly be called a false coin, even if it were struck from good silver. Those sciences which are raised above their proper place and value, and which, though they ought to be lowest and as it were accessory, hold a little time and esteem among us, while on the contrary they occupy us wholly as if they were the highest and chief concerns, deserve without doubt to be counted among the false.

units.la: III. Quemadmodum eruditionis solidæ f- undamentum est Deus in centro & facul- tatibus animæ sinceræ beneque dispo- sitæ operans, prout superius indicatum est; &c.
units.tr: III. Just as the foundation of solid erudition is God, working at the centre and in the faculties of a sincere and well-disposed soul, as was indicated above, etc.

units.la: est ; ita eruditionis superficiariæ fundamentum est ratio humana, sive intellectus actívus, cujus naturam & proprietates, nævosque etsi alibi (a) explicui aliquoties, quoniam tamen res non ita acta est quin adhuc multa de isthoc argumento momentosa dici possint, non modò si ex professo esset tractandum, sed & ex occasione, certarum materiarum particularium, veluti hæc est de eruditione superficiaria ; necesse erit ut hic de eodem subjecto aliquid penitius proponam; idque eo libentius, quod res sit, licet maximæ consequentiæ & considerationis, tamen omnibus fere neglecta & incognita.
units.tr: So the foundation of superficial erudition is human reason, or the active intellect. I have explained its nature, its properties and its faults several times elsewhere. Yet the matter has not been so completely handled that much weighty about this subject cannot still be said, not only if it were to be treated professedly, but also on the occasion of certain particular topics, such as this one on superficial erudition. So it will be necessary to set out here something more thorough on the same subject. I do so the more willingly because the matter, though of the greatest consequence and importance, is nevertheless almost neglected and unknown to everyone.

units.la: IV. Mentem humanam condidit Deus O. M. ut posset omni bono & reali objecto, cujus est capax, eam implere vel munerare. Objectorum genera duo sunt, unum spirituale, intimum, perfectum, immensum, quod nil aliud est quam ipsemet Deus, qui sese mentibus vult tradere & insinuare; alterum corporeum, externum, imperfectum, atque limitatum, qui mundus corporeus est. Ut hisce realitatibus, tum divinis atque intimis, tum externis & corporeis, frui posset anima, dedit illi Deus duo facultatum genera, quæ quasi vasa essent, hisce realitatibus (sic, si placet, loquemur) aut his realibus objectis recipiendis idonea. Nempe pro realitatibus divinis, intimis & immensis, quæ in Deo sunt, Menti dedit facultates divinas, intimas & immensas, desiderii, intellectus passivi, & acquiescentiæ, cum fundo æternitatis degustandæ capaci : pro realitatibus autem, sive pro objectis realibus corporeis, externis, limitatis, dedit cum corpore facultates sensuum qui corporei appellantur. De quibus omnibus notandum est, I. Ista objecta esse & realissima & realissimè a mente possidenda; ipsomet siquidem Deo possit & debeat frui, ipsoque etiam mundo & rebus creatis. 2. Mentem, ut istis fruatur, non posse illa sibi efficere; clarum enim est per se, & experientia evidens, Mentem non posse sibi Deum, divinum lumen, divinas delicias, sive Deum secum deliciantem, efficere; ut neque etiam creare corpora, eorumque, quibus per corpus proprium gaudere debet, vires, virtutes, proprietates, puta lumen, sapores, odores & omnia cætera. 3. Adeoque Mentem respectu realitatum omnium recipiendarum, cum divinarum & internarum, tum corporearum & externarum, se habere mere passive, nisi quod activam habeat libertatem, non quidem quæ efficiat realitates quibus frui velit; sed quæ facultates suas diversimode & proplacito vertat ad objecta realia, hæc illave, ex qua facultatum ad objecta conversione & applicatione libera, ipsa objecta sese menti realissime communicant, afficiuntque eam modis realibus, vivis, efficacibus, per se certis, luminosis, satiantibus, deliciantibus, solidis (unumquodque pro suarum realitatum sive perfectionum dignitate atque proportione) quique modi a mente ipsa non causantur; sed quos aliunde quam a se ipsa passive recipit.
units.tr: IV. God, the best and greatest, created the human mind so that it could fill and enrich itself with every good and real object of which it is capable. There are two kinds of objects. One is spiritual, inward, perfect and immeasurable, and this is nothing other than God himself, who wishes to give and insinuate himself into minds. The other is corporeal, external, imperfect and limited, and this is the bodily world. So that the soul might enjoy both these realities, the divine and inward as well as the external and corporeal, God gave it two kinds of faculties, which are like vessels suited to receiving these realities (or, if you like, these real objects). Thus, for the divine, inward and immeasurable realities that are in God, he gave the mind divine, inward and immeasurable faculties of desire, of passive intellect, and of acquiescence, capable of tasting the depth of eternity. For the realities, or real objects, that are corporeal, external and limited, he gave, together with the body, the faculties called the senses. Concerning all of these it must be noted: first, that these objects are both most real and to be possessed by the mind in the most real way, for it can and must enjoy God himself, and also the world itself and created things. Second, the mind cannot make these things for itself in order to enjoy them. For it is clear in itself, and evident from experience, that the mind cannot produce for itself God, the divine light, divine delights, or God delighting with it; nor can it create bodies, and the powers, virtues and properties of those things with which it ought to rejoice through the body, such as light, tastes, odours and all the rest. Third, therefore the mind, with respect to all the realities to be received, both divine and inward, and bodily and external, stands in a purely passive relation, except that it has an active freedom. This freedom is not to produce the realities it wishes to enjoy, but to turn its faculties in various ways and at its pleasure towards this or that real object. By this free turning and application of its faculties to objects, the objects themselves communicate themselves to the mind in the most real way, and affect it in real, living, effective, self-evidently certain, luminous, satisfying, delightful and solid modes (each according to the dignity and proportion of its reality or perfection). These modes are not caused by the mind itself, but it receives them passively from elsewhere than from itself.

units.la: Si Mens libertate sua in facultatum suarum regimine ita debitè utitur, ut eas applicet realibus suis objectis juxta regulam proportionis quæ inter objecta est, nempe si objectis divinis, quæ primaria sunt, & origo & scopus omnium, & infinita, & æterna, & intima, applicet facultates suas intimas, totas, primariò, intensissime absolutissimeque; si vero objectis corporeis, quæ veluti accessoria sunt, non per se nec ob se sunt, nec infinita, nec (in quo statu jam sunt) permanentia, applicet facultates suas externas sive sensuum secundariò, nec semper, nec terminative, sed quandoque, cùm necesse est, referendo hæc ad scopum divinum & ultimum: sique in hujusmodi usu facultatum superiorum & inferiorum cum suis objectis ita sese sponte & ex libertate exercuerit, ut inde habitum ejusmodi usûs fit adepta, tunc dicenda vere est & virtute & eruditione gaudere solida, de qua superius egimus, & ad quam facultatum inferiorum usum, necessariamque artium praxin reduximus: est enim solidum & reale quid facultates ejusmodi & sensus exercere debitè cum objectis suis realibus ad vitam suam secundum Dei placitum & ad ejus honorem transfigendam. Et sane tales eruditi, etsi artifices, otiosis atque ignavis multis doctoribus, speculatoribusque chimæricis anteponendi sunt.
units.tr: If the mind uses its freedom in governing its faculties so properly that it applies them to their real objects according to the rule of proportion that obtains among the objects, namely, if it applies its inward, whole, chief, most intense and most complete faculties to the divine objects, which are primary and are the origin and goal of all things, and are infinite, eternal and inward; but applies its external faculties, that is, the senses, to the corporeal objects, which are secondary, since they are, as it were, accessory, are not for their own sake or by themselves, are not infinite, and (in the state they are now in) are not permanent, applying them secondarily, not always and not as ends, but sometimes, when necessary, referring these things to the divine and ultimate goal; and if in this use of higher and lower faculties with their objects it has so exercised itself spontaneously and freely that it has acquired a habit of such use, then it is rightly said to enjoy both virtue and solid erudition, of which we spoke above, and to which we have reduced the use of the lower faculties and the necessary practice of the arts. For it is something solid and real to exercise such faculties and senses rightly with their real objects, so as to spend one's life according to God's pleasure and to his honour. Indeed, such learned men, even if they are craftsmen, are to be preferred to many idle and lazy teachers and fanciful speculators.

units.la: V. Verùm (ne alias Rationis humanæ causas, alibi expressas tangam) quandoquidem facultates nostras simul omnes exercere non possumus, neque omnibus simul objectis realibus frui; estque necesse ut modò ex facultatibus unam ad objectum hoc applicemus, modò aliam ad aliud tunc absens, idque ordine & modis debitis; non posset sane pro libertate nostra, neque ordinatim & facile ista facultas & objectorum commutatio sive successio fieri, nisi facultatem quandam novi generis haberet Mens, quae objecta absentia, eaque simul multa, ei depingeret, ut ex illa pictura substitutione, objectorum realium vices agente, memor esset sese ad realia objecta absentia, sed repraesentata, convertendi; & de illis simul repraesentatis in mente, idealiter disponendi, quae postea facultatum realium objectis veris communicatione exsequeretur. Haec facultas depingendi nobis in mente objecta, quando tamen eorum realis praesentia a suis cuique propriis facultatibus abest, ea est quae Ratio humana sive intellectus actibus dicitur, feque extendit ad pingenda quaevis tum spiritualia, tum corporea, Deum videlicet, ejus attributa, resque creatas cæteras, quarum picturæ vel icones ideæ jam vulgo dicuntur, harumque idearum complexus, comparatio, separatio, aliarum idearum ex prioribus deductio, ratiocinia vel ratiocinationes appellantur. Horum primum, Ratio videlicet, cùm sit eruditionis superficiariæ efficiens causa, idea vero ejus materia; ratiocinatio autem ejusdem tum ampliandi tum communicandi instrumentum; eorum proprietates affectionesve non sunt hic silentio praetermittendae, ut ex iis eruditionis superficiariae genium dignoscamus.
units.tr: V. But (not to touch on other causes of human reason, which I have set out elsewhere), since we cannot exercise all our faculties at once, nor enjoy all real objects at once, and since it is necessary that we apply now one faculty to this object, and now another to another object, then absent, and this in due order and manner, the mind could not, by its freedom, carry out this change or succession of faculties and objects in an orderly and easy way, unless it had a certain faculty of a new kind, which paints for it absent objects, and many at once. Then, from that substitute picture, which acts in place of the real objects, it could remember to turn itself towards absent but represented real objects, and to arrange them ideally in the mind, these represented objects being simultaneously before it, which it would afterwards carry out by communicating with the true objects of the real faculties. This faculty of painting objects for us in the mind, when yet their real presence is absent from each one's proper faculties, is what is called human reason, or the intellectus activus. It extends itself to painting whatever things, whether spiritual or corporeal, namely God, his attributes, and the other created things; their pictures or images are now commonly called ideas. The combination, comparison and separation of these ideas, and the deduction of other ideas from earlier ones, are called reasonings or ratiocinations. Of these, reason, of course, is the efficient cause of superficial erudition, the idea is its matter, and ratiocination is the instrument both of enlarging it and of communicating it. Their properties and affections must not be passed over in silence here, so that from them we may recognise the character of superficial erudition.

units.la: VI. Ab ideis ut incipiamus, siquidem patet eas non esse res ipsas, sed in mente subsitui tanquam picturas vel tabulas loco ac vice rerum & objectorum realium, sequitur inde, eas habere & naturam & proprietates ab objectis realibus eorumque affectionibus prorsus diversas; atque adeo quemadmodum objecta affectionesque quas in mente, quae earum particeps est, excitant, sunt realia, viva, efficacia, per se certa, luminosa, satiantia, deliciose afficientia, atque solida; sequitur econtra ideas non esse ejusmodi realia entia neque res mentem afficientes modis realibus, vivis, efficacibus, per se certis, bene luminosis, satiantibus, reficientibus, solidis; sed esse quasdam umbras mortuas, steriles, dubiis plenas, valde obscuras, non reficientes, prurientes potius quam tranquillantes, & evanidas. Quae omnia utinam ab ideistis eruditis bene caperentur, eisque bene cordi essent! non ita cum ideis suis turpius quam infantuli cum pupis luderent, iis sese totos occupantes, easque veluti Deas omnibus, solidis neglectis, praeponentes in exitium proprium. Differentias datas facilius concipiemus ex similitudine.
units.tr: VI. Let us begin with ideas. It is plain that they are not the things themselves, but are put in the mind, like pictures or tablets, in the place and stead of real things and objects. It follows that they have a nature and properties wholly different from the real objects and their affections. Therefore, just as the objects, and the affections they stir up in the mind that shares in them, are real, living, effective, self-evidently certain, luminous, satisfying, delightfully affecting and solid, it follows on the contrary that ideas are not such real beings, nor things that affect the mind in real, living, effective, self-evidently certain, truly luminous, satisfying, refreshing and solid modes. Rather they are certain dead, barren shadows, full of doubts, very obscure, not refreshing, stirring up itches rather than calming, and fading away. Would that all these things were rightly grasped by learned idealists, and taken to heart! They would not play with their ideas more shamefully than little children with dolls, devoting themselves wholly to them, and setting them up, as it were, as goddesses above everything, neglecting all solid things, to their own ruin. We shall understand the differences given more easily by means of a comparison.

units.la: Eamus, si placet, ad Solem, facultatemque quam habemus videndi oculis, ei exponamus. Ecce, eo inspecto percipis rem veram, solem ipsum ejusque in te sensationes & affectiones reales; sic vividas, ut inde vivigor vitæ tuæ accedat ; sic efficaces, ut vim radiorum vel caloris ferre vix possis; sic certas, ut nullo ratiocinio nullaque alia probatione egeas qua persuadearis te frui lumine ; sic luminosas, ut & sua luce ipsum solem videas & cætera alia objecta ; sic satiantes, ut plus luminis non soleas desiderare ; sic lætificantes, ut inde totus cum tota natura reficiaris & reviviscas ; denique sic solidas, ut effectus inde reales, non imaginarios in te & extra te diu permanentes deprehendas. At vero recedamus a Sole in locum obscurum, & ibi excitemus in mente nostra imaginem sive ideam Solis & omnium quas ab illo experti sumus sensationum, quid ibi, quæso, non umbraticum ? an ex ista mortua imagine vividus sensus nobis accedet ? an ex tali efficacem calorem percipiemus ? an inde certum quid de Solis diametro v. g. aut de objectis Soli expositis concludemus ? an imaginariæ istius de luce imaginis ope illustrabimur ad objecta extra nos perspicienda ? an desiderium nostrum videndi inde satiabitur ? an ab isto lumine fi&o vigorem ac lætitiam reportabimus ? Nil minus certe. Ita prorsus res se habet cum ideis nostris, (sive eæ divina sive corporea repræsentent,) earumque in mente effectis, si cum facultatibus objectisque realibus ac solidis, horumque effectis comparentur. 1. Nil illæ reale sunt ejus quod repræsentant. Dæmon & eruditus impius ideas habent Dei rem tamen, Deum, neutiquam possident. 2. Non vivæ sunt, sed mortuæ, cum homo perditæ vitæ virtutum omnium ideas habere possit, dum interim ex iis non imbuitur virtute viva, neque calefit ab istiusmodi sole pisto. 3. Inefficaces sunt; siquidem cum animus molis terrestris tentamine ad inferiora totus allicitur, ex frigidis quas habet omnium rerum divinarum & cœlestium ideis vim haurit nullam qua pravis resistat propensionibus, feque divinis imbuat. 4. Incertæ sunt; siquidem qui vel doctissimi habentur, de eo quod in istis ideis continetur vel ex iis excluditur, imo an dentur nec ne, difputant & dubitant. Facultates passivæ quando objectis suis realibus applicitæ sunt, eas assectiones & impressiones ab illis habent quæ ita certæ sunt, ut omnes de iis fine controverfia in idem consentiant; nemo enim unquam negavit, Solem objecta sua lumine perfundere, illa detegere, calore afficere, & infinita alia, de quibus in nullius fani fyncipitis mentem unquam dubitatio irrepfit: at de ideis humanæ rationis, etiam quæ fimplicifimæ effent dicendæ, dubitatur: v. g. an in idea Dei includatur sufficientia? an libertas? an prævisio & decreta contingentium? an in idea libertatis indifferentia involvatur, nec ne? an detur idea animæ? idea motus per attractum? idea lineæ rectæ æqualis circulari, & infinitæ aliæ, de quibus inter fe sic digladiantur eruditi, ut quot capita, tot sensus sint. Quæ oftendunt nil fere esse ideis incertius: namque omnes omnino in quibuscunque fcientiis controversiæ, quæ tantum non infinitæ.
units.tr: Let us go, if you please, to the sun, and set before it the faculty of sight that we have in our eyes. Look: when you gaze at it, you perceive the true thing, the sun itself, and its real sensations and affections in you. They are so lively that the vigour of life comes into you from them; so effective that you can scarcely bear the force of its rays or heat; so certain that you need no reasoning or other proof to be persuaded that you enjoy its light; so luminous that by its own light you see the sun itself and other objects; so satisfying that you are not wont to desire more light; so gladdening that you are refreshed and revived, with all nature, by it; and finally so solid that you find real effects in you and outside you, lasting for a long time, and not imaginary. But now let us withdraw from the sun into a dark place, and there excite in our mind an image or idea of the sun and of all the sensations we have had from it. What, I ask, is there not shadowy there? Will a vivid sensation come to us from that dead image? Will we perceive an effective heat from it? Will we conclude anything certain from it about the sun's diameter, for example, or about objects exposed to the sun? Will we be enlightened by the aid of that imaginary light of the image, so as to see objects outside us? Will our desire to see be satisfied by it? Will we draw vigour and joy from that feigned light? Certainly not at all. Just so is it with our ideas (whether they represent divine or corporeal things) and their effects in the mind, when they are compared with the faculties and real and solid objects, and their effects. (1) They are in no way real of what they represent. A demon and an impious scholar have ideas of God, yet by no means possess God himself. (2) They are not living but dead, since a man of lost life can have the ideas of all virtues, while meanwhile he is not imbued with living virtue from them, nor warmed by such a painted sun. (3) They are ineffective; since when the soul is wholly drawn downward by the pull of earthly mass, it draws no strength from the cold ideas it has of all divine and heavenly things, by which it might resist its wicked inclinations, and clothe itself with divine things. (4) They are uncertain; since even those who are held most learned dispute and doubt what is contained in these ideas, or excluded from them, indeed whether they exist or not. When passive faculties are applied to their real objects, they have from those objects affections and impressions that are so certain that all agree on them without any controversy; for no one has ever denied that the sun bathes its objects in light, reveals them, warms them, and does countless other things, about which no doubt has ever crept into the mind of any sane person. But about the ideas of human reason, even those that would be called the simplest, there is doubt. For example: whether sufficiency is included in the idea of God? whether liberty? whether foreknowledge and decrees of contingent things? whether indifference is involved in the idea of liberty or not? whether there is an idea of the soul? an idea of motion by attraction? an idea of a straight line equal to a circle? and countless others, over which learned men so quarrel among themselves that there are as many opinions as heads. These things show that there is scarcely anything more uncertain than ideas. For in all sciences there are controversies, almost infinite in number, which must all come back to this: whether the ideas of the things in question have, or can have, the affections or properties that are under discussion.

units.la: nitæ sunt, huc redeant necesse est, an ideæ rerum de quibus quæritur, habeant aut habere possint eas affectiones aut proprietates de quibus agitur. 5. Adeoque patet eas esse etiam parum luminosas, vel multum obscuras, ut ut tanquam simplices jactitentur; lumenque pusillum, si quod habent, nullum fere est comparatum cum lumine quod objecta realia divina atque creata, in facultates sibi destinatas infundunt. 6, 7, 8. Porro animam nec satiant, nec solida ac læta quiete implent; etenim cum picturæ tantum atque umbræ sint, necesse est animam, quæ facultatem cupiendi res solidas applicat ad ideas, se ipsam frustrari, atque famelica inde anxietate, nec non naufeabunda tandem omnium istarum vacuarum ampullarum rejectione torqueri, ita ut plurimi ex iis qui se maxime istis devoverunt, exercuerunt & impleverunt, in Pyrrhonismum, vel etiam in Atheismum sese tandem projiciant, vel, si meliores, circa vitæ finem vocibus lamentabilibus suam deplorent vacuitatem, vanumque cum ideis suis studium, ex quo se nullatenus levamine solido adjuvari, sed potius angi infinito moerore vel desperatione sentiunt. Quae cum ita sint, concludendum est, eruditionem quae ejusmodi idearum coacervatione comparatur non solidam, sed mere superficiariam esse, insuperque, idearum suarum instar, umbratilem, mortuam, sterilem, incertam, obscuram, torquentem, laslantem & evanidam.
units.tr: ...nitæ sunt, must come back to this: whether the ideas of the things under discussion have, or can have, the affections or properties that are being debated. 5. It is therefore clear that these ideas are also only faintly luminous, or very obscure, however much they are boasted of as simple. And the little light they have, if they have any, is almost nothing compared with the light that real objects, divine and created, pour into the faculties destined for them. 6, 7, 8. Moreover, they neither satisfy the soul nor fill it with solid and joyful rest. Since they are only pictures and shadows, the soul, whose faculty of desire is directed to solid things, necessarily cheats itself when it turns to ideas. Driven by a hungry anxiety, and finally sickened by rejecting all these empty bottles, many of those who have most devoted, exercised and filled themselves with such things throw themselves into Pyrrhonism or even Atheism. Or, if they are better men, near the end of their lives they lament their emptiness in mournful words, and their vain pursuit of ideas, by which they feel they have not been helped at all by any solid comfort, but rather tormented by endless grief or despair. Since this is so, we must conclude that the learning which is acquired by such a heaping up of ideas is not solid but merely superficiary, and besides, like its ideas, shadowy, dead, sterile, uncertain, obscure, tormenting, wearying and fading away.

units.la: VII. Quod adhuc magis patebit ex cons- ideratione Rationis, sive intellectus activi, idearum fontis & fabri.
units.tr: VII. What will become still clearer from a consideration of Reason, that is, of the active intellect, the source and craftsman of ideas.

units.la: Namque ea facultas est corruptissima, atque etiam limitatissimæ, & admodum parvæ extensionis; est umbratilis; nec non ita superficiaria accidentariaque Menti creatæ, ut Mens (quicquid in oppositum garriant Philosophi) potuerit æternùm perfecta ac beata esse, ut ut rationis facultatem nunquam habuisset; quod a me (a) alibi est demonstratum & explicatum. Ejus corruptionis & depravationis immensæ argumentum si non haberemus ex eo, quod quotquot Rationi colendæ & exercendæ incubuerunt, in diversas & oppositas quasque partes abierint, unde omnia monstra, chimæras, rixæ, pugnæ, omneque horrendarum tempestatum & tragœdiarum genus promanarunt; id tamen hinc indubitato colligere esset, nempe quod homo, postquam a Deo sic gratis creatus est, quæ etiam Deus illi ex immenso amore obtulerat; ut bonorum omnium esset capax, ingratus nihilominus factus, terga Deo bo-
units.tr: For that faculty is very corrupt, and also very limited and of very small extent. It is shadowy, and so superficial and accidental to the created mind that the mind (whatever the philosophers may babble to the contrary) could have remained perfect and blessed for ever even had it never possessed the faculty of reason. I have demonstrated and explained this elsewhere. If we did not have a proof of this immense corruption and depravity in the fact that all who have devoted themselves to cultivating and exercising Reason have gone off into diverse and opposite directions, whence have sprung all monsters, chimeras, quarrels, battles, and every kind of horrible storm and tragedy, we could still gather from the following beyond doubt: that man, after God had created him so freely, and had offered him out of immense love all the things by which he might be capable of every good, nevertheless became ungrateful and turned his back on the divine goods, (a)

units.la: (a) In Disc. prælim. Cogit. Rat. Edit. II. & Oeconomie de la Creation, chap. 20 & 21. nisque divinis dedit, quo se versus activitatem propriam suæ Rationis verteret, ex illa factsurus Deum suum, scopum, sinem, delectamentum unicum cum idolis idearum suarum: a quo ingrato & insano crimine tantum abest ut ad Deum cum anxio & pœnitenti amore revertatur, ut contra negligat etiam illum magis magisque idoli sui unice colendi gratiâ. Quæ sane cum immensa perversitas atque corruptio sit, quæque placere Deo non possit, (ni Deus sibi ipsi displiceat, suique neglectum approbet) sequitur, Deum jam ab illa (ratione) esse alienissimum, nec illi concedere aut conservare lumen, (potest enim Deus & in ratione agere) quo illa & opus habet a Deo postquam corrupta est; sed quod tamen nunquam recipiet ab eodem, quisquis vult neglecto Deo lumen illud ad se suumque amorem proprium terminare. Ergo hinc & corrupta est ratio, & coeca; adeoque quicquid ab illa proficisci potest, mancum & deficiens esse oportet; nisi statuas, causam effectui dare posse perfectiones quas ipsa non habet, & plus esse in effectu quam in causa: quod nemo opinor admittet. Jam quis exigat ab homine claudo & caeco rectus ut incedat, viamque rectam teneat, quaeque invia sunt permeet ac videat? Idem exigat a Ratione clauda, sive corrupta, & caeca sive lumine destituta, ut in excitando sibi ideas recte procedat utque videat.
units.tr: (a) In the Preliminary Discourse to the second edition of the Cogitationes Rationales, and in Oeconomie de la Création, chapters 20 and 21. and gave himself to the active power of his own reason, so as to make from it his god, his aim, his end, and his only delight, along with the idols of his own ideas. Far from returning to God from this ungrateful and mad crime with anxious and penitent love, he instead neglects God more and more, for the sake of serving his idol alone. Since this is surely an immense perversity and corruption, and one that cannot please God (unless God is displeased with himself and approves the neglect of himself), it follows that God is now most alien to that reason, and does not grant or preserve for it the light (for God can also act in reason) which reason needs from God after it has been corrupted. Yet it will never receive that light from him, whoever wishes, neglecting God, to confine that light to himself and his own self-love. Therefore reason is both corrupt and blind, and so whatever can proceed from it must be defective and deficient, unless you hold that a cause can give to its effect perfections it does not itself have, and that there is more in the effect than in the cause, which I suppose no one will admit. Now who would demand that a lame and blind man walk straight and keep to the right path, and pass through and see what is trackless? Let him demand the same of a lame or corrupt Reason, and of a blind Reason, that is, one deprived of light, that it proceed rightly in stirring up ideas for itself and see rightly.

units.la: Neque est quod dicas, Rationem, cum activa sit facultas, sibi suum lumen ex se, sine alterius ope excitare posse: id namque falsum esset: non enim est Ratio facultas a Deo independens. Vis ejus excitandi sibi luminis nisi sit adjuta, & veluti foecundata a lumine Dei in facultatibus superioribus lucentis, sterilis est, nisi ad monstra & chimaeras vel figmenta nullius momenti parienda. Solius Dei haec est praerogativa, ut quicquid ipsi placet in conceptu suo fingere, verum sit & lucidum, neque cum aliis suis de rebus ideis pugnans: est etenim is fons realitatis, veritatis, ipsaque sapientia: ast anima, nisi eas quas in se excitat ideas, ad similitudinem & imitationem divinarum formet, falsa & absurda figmenta, in quibus nil verum est, praeterquam quod ea in ipsa sint, at opposita veris rerum a Deo statutarum ideis naturisque, quas ipsa nescit. Quapropter quaecunque Mens non habet intellectum passivum divino lumine illustratum, nec Dei amico favore auxilioque gaudet, ejus Mentis intellectus activus, sive Ratio, nihil recti agere potest.
units.tr: Nor can you say that Reason, since it is an active faculty, can of itself and without another's help kindle its own light. For that would be false: Reason is not a faculty independent of God. Its power of kindling light for itself, unless it is aided and as it were fertilised by the light of God shining in the higher faculties, is barren, and can bring forth only monsters, chimeras, or fictions of no worth. It is the sole prerogative of God that whatever pleases him to imagine in his conception should be true and luminous, and not conflict with his other ideas of things. For he is the fount of reality, of truth, and of wisdom itself. But the soul, unless it shapes the ideas it kindles within itself into likeness and imitation of the divine ideas, produces false and absurd fictions, in which nothing is true except that they exist in the soul itself, and are opposed to the true ideas and natures of things established by God, which the soul itself does not know. Therefore, whatever mind does not have a passive intellect illuminated by the divine light, and does not enjoy the friendly favour and help of God, its active intellect, or Reason, can do nothing right.

units.la: VIII. Idque adhuc multo magis verum est de ratiocinatione, quae praeter idearum rationisque defectus communes, proprios, insuper habet, exsurgentes ex conjunctionum, separationum, comparationum, consequentiarumque complicatissimis actibus, qui sic errori sunt obnoxii, ut quamvis ipsa ratio ejusque ideae sanae essent, in ratiocinando tamen vel attentio minor, vel memoriae angustia, vel cujusdam ideae necessariae absentia; vel propensio aliqua in affectibus animi occulta, totum ratiocinandi negotium vitiare possint.
units.tr: VIII. This is far more true of ratiocination, which, besides the common and particular defects of ideas and reason, has in addition those that arise from the very complicated acts of joining, separating, comparing and inferring. These are so liable to error that, even if reason itself and its ideas were sound, a smaller attention, or a narrowness of memory, or the absence of some necessary idea, or some hidden inclination in the affections of the mind, could spoil the whole business of reasoning.

units.la: Jam perpende ex tribus illis putridis atque corruptis fulcris, ideis scilicet, intellectu activo, & ratiocinatione, quantum eruditionis superficiariae, iis subnixae, sit deferendum & confidendum: atque si id ne sic quidem videre possis, inspice an & inter eruditiores aliquid sit incontroversum; & vel duos nobis fitte & commonstra, qui in omnibus sint concordes & unanimes.
units.tr: Now consider from those three rotten and corrupt props, namely ideas, the active intellect, and ratiocination, how much trust and reliance is to be placed in superficial learning supported by them. And if you cannot see this even so, examine whether there is anything uncontroversial even among the more learned, and show us two men who agree and are unanimous in everything.

units.la: IX. Sed, inquies, ifthæc idearum, ratiónis & ratiocinationis extenuatio nil aliud fuerit quam Pyrrhonismi & Scepticismi ipsissima restitutio. Nonne contrà, palam est ex experientia, uti e Mathematicis disciplinis patet, eruditionem ex rationis ideis & ratiocinandi actibus atque exercitio dari, quæ constet veritatibus apud omnes semper & constanter non controversis? Quid quod & apud omnes, & in saeris etiam voluminibus, ipsa commendetur ratio; tuque ipse nunc eâ utaris, nec dici velles, sine ratione vel irrationabiliter te jam quæ agis agere, nisi eo ipso causam tuam destrueres? Tum autem ad quid ratio nobis data esset, nisi illam ut exerceremus, atque in suos actus deduceremus? Ad quæ omnia peræquum est me omnium primo respondere; deinde aliquid specialius de Eruditione Superficiaria subjungere.
units.tr: IX. But, you will say, if this weakening of ideas, reason and reasoning were so, it would be nothing other than a restoration of Pyrrhonism and Scepticism itself. Is it not rather plain from experience, as is evident from the mathematical disciplines, that learning arises from ideas of reason and from acts and exercise of reasoning, which consist of truths never controverted by anyone at any time? Moreover, reason is commended by all, and even in the sacred volumes; and you yourself now use it, and would not wish to be said to do what you do without reason or irrationally, unless you destroyed your own cause by that very fact. Then again, to what end would reason have been given to us, unless that we should exercise it and bring it to its own acts? It is only fair that I should first answer all these points, and then add something more specific concerning Superficiary Learning.

units.la: X. Ad primum igitur dico, me, absit ut velim Scepticismum (qui ipse a rationis exercitio ortus est, ) in medium revocare; econtra, veritatis fundamenta tam inconcussa proponere, ut nullo modo queant concuti in illis qui ea in se volent struere. Annon igitur datur quid ratione ejusque actibus certius & luminosius? Ecce facultates, quas diximus pro objectis realibus factas, divinæ & superiores, corporeæ & sensiles, illæ aliquid omni rationis apparatu certius apprehendunt, quando ex illis aliæ quidem ad Deum sese debitè convertunt, aliæ autem ad objecta jecta sua creata: tunc enim Deum, ejus virtutes, res divinas, æternas, immortales, tam realiter, vivide, luminose certoque percipiunt sine ullo rationis examine, ut nullatenus de iis dubitare possint. Ita etiam qui ad Solem oculos convertit & aperit, is se Solis lumine & calore frui, illiusque ope objecta corporea diversimode disposita perspicere scit utique adeo sufficienter, ut omnis quæ ex facultate rationis peteretur causa ad illum de hac veritate percepta persuadendum, inutilis & nugatoria existat. Est enim lex immutabilis atque efficax, ab omnipotente Dei placito statuta, ut positis objectis & applicatis ad ea facultatibus, sequatur certitudo summa, infallibilis & inconcussa in homine de objectorum præsentia, veritate, relationeque & communicatione cum ipso. Et cum omnis certitudo tranquillans sit a lumine, quo magis objecta lumen diffundentia facultatesque lumen admittentes & percipientes ... realia; eo magis quoque vividum, efficaciusque afficiens eorum est lumen. Quapropter cum divina naturaliaque objecta, nec non facultates ipsis respondentes, multo plus realitatis omnino habeant quam picturaria rationis facultas cum picturis suis idealibus, sequitur eorum lumen omni rationis picto lumine efficacius, vividius & magis reale esse; atque adeo magis certum.
units.tr: X. To the first point, then, I say: far be it from me to wish to bring back Scepticism (which itself arose from the exercise of reason). On the contrary, I propose foundations of truth so unshaken that they cannot in any way be overturned by those who wish to build upon them. Is there then not something more certain and more luminous than reason and its acts? Behold the faculties which we said were made for real objects, divine and higher, bodily and sensible. These apprehend something more certain than any apparatus of reason, when some of them are rightly turned towards God, and others towards their created objects. For then they perceive God, his virtues, divine, eternal and immortal things, so really, vividly, luminously and certainly, without any examination by reason, that they cannot in any way doubt them. So too one who turns and opens his eyes to the Sun knows that he enjoys the light and heat of the Sun, and by its help sees bodily objects variously arranged, so sufficiently that any cause drawn from the faculty of reason to persuade him of this perceived truth is useless and idle. For there is an immutable and effective law, established by the pleasure of almighty God, that when objects are placed and faculties are applied to them, there follows in man the highest, infallible and unshaken certainty of the presence, truth, relation and communication of the objects with himself. And since all tranquillising certainty comes from light, the more the objects that diffuse light, and the faculties that admit and perceive light, are real, the more vivid and effective is the light that affects them. Therefore, since divine and natural objects, and the faculties corresponding to them, have far more reality altogether than the picture-making faculty of reason with its ideal pictures, it follows that their light is more effective, more vivid and more real than any light painted by reason, and therefore more certain.

units.la: XI. Dantur quippe (ut hoc obiter inculcem) trium luminum genera, quorum primum divinum est, facultates mentis superiores, intellectum
units.tr: XI. There are, to mention this in passing, three kinds of light. The first is divine, which the higher faculties of the mind, especially the intellect, receive.

units.la: Lumi-num genera tria, tresque telleƈtum præsertim passivum, feriens modis omnium certissimis, quando nullum impedimentum est interpositum; alterum externum est & naturale, quod etiam ubi ab objectis in facultates diffunditur, omnem dubitationem de rei exsistentia & relatione ad vitam corporalem excludit: tertium est rationis, tenue illud & veluti pictum, atque in quo jam statu sumus, illorum trium incertissimum & obscurum valde, nec, ubi solum consulitur neglectis cæteris, a dubitatione& incerto liberum: quod satis patet ex illis qui e rationalibus demonstrationibus Cartefianismi, etsi veris, prolapsi sunt in Atheismum, Spinosianismum, negationem libertatis animæque immortalitatis; quodque egomet experientia propria edoctus scio: namque etsi de istis nunquam serio dubitaverim, eorumque demonstrationes a ratione desumtas bene perceperim, & in consensum admiserim; non tamen eamomnimodæ certitudinis sensi fiduciam, quam postmodum deprehendi tum quando ab idealibus istis speculationibus desiderium meum intelleƈtumque passivum ad Dominum ex animo aliquantisper converti: tunc enim scrupuli circa Dei exsistentiam & animæ immortalitatem nescio qui animum meum præter rationem & voluntatem importune antea, etsi raro, vellicantes, ex me ita evanuerunt, ut inde in me ea de Deo, divinis, æternis, immortalitate beata vel misera animarum, certitudo nata fit; quæ omnes meas de his demonstrationes priores infinite, & supra quam dici possit superet; ita, ut quamvis omnes quotquot excogitari possunt difficultates & objectiones mihi opponerentur, illæ me haud aliter efficerent, quam ratiocinia cæci alicujus, qui alium Solis lumine utentem argutiis suis persuadere conaretur, non dari lumen, nec objecta vera illius ope percipi. Unde didici falsum esse quod Cartesius asserit, (a) nos, si idea illa Dei pictura{ta}, quæ ex rationis censu est, destituerem{u}r, non posse unquam cognoscere Deum, ne quidem lumine fidei, hoc est, lumine Dei in facultates ratione superiores sese diffundente. Animadverti etiam inde salsissimum esse quod afferunt nonnulli, certitudinem de exsistentia Dei magis desumendam esse a demonstratione ex idea ejus hausta, quam ex eo quod Deus exsistens per se notus sit, hancque certitudinem illi esse posteriorem; cum contra, Deus ut exsistens, sit infinities notior per se, hoc est, per actum lumenque suum in facultatibus animæ superioribus, quam per actum rationis, quæ est facultas divinioribus, ipsoque intellectu passivo, infinities inferior: siquidem intellectus passivus tantus sit, quanta Dei est in ipsum agendi potentia; neque posse in errorem inducere, quippe, passivus cum sit, a Deo in errorem agi non potest. Ignorant hoc isti rationalistæ, qui non nisi ex facultate limitatissima, atque ex corruptione sua erroribus quam maxime obnoxia, omnem suam certitudinem omneque lumen & verum exspectant.
