Nolim equidem probationem exsistentiæ Dei, quæ ex ratione petitur, negare garè aut infirmare; vera siquidem & legitima est: at est certitudinis secundariæ respectu alterius illius, eique longe postponenda; ausimque affirmare eos, qui de Deo exsistentes certi sunt, si bene se examinent, reperturos veram suam de Deo exsistente certitudinem atque confidentiam, non ex vi demonstrationis suæ ratiocinatæ procedere, sed potius ex intimo quodam sensu a rationis suæ actibus non pendente, ad quem mere passive se habent, quique ipsos vel invitos & reluctantes divine afficit, imprimitque eis vividius quam ex idea, Deum potentem, sapientem, bonum, justum, veracemque, sui & omnium Auctorem; eodem prorsus modo atque certitudo de Solis luminisque ejus, nec non corporum exsistentia, discretio item certa vigiliæ a somno, non ex ideis rationis ratiocinandique actibus desumenda est; sed ab ipla sensus sive conscientiæ experientia, immediate & indubitate ex applicatione facultatum ad objecta enascente, juxta legem sive statutum omnipotentis Dei modo dictum.
units.tr: There are three kinds of light. The first, which strikes the passive intellect in the most certain way when no obstacle is interposed, is divine. The second is external and natural: when it spreads from objects into the faculties, it excludes all doubt about the existence of a thing and its relation to bodily life. The third is the light of reason, that thin and, as it were, painted light in which we now stand. It is by far the most uncertain and obscure of the three, and when it is consulted alone, with the others neglected, it is not free from doubt and uncertainty. This is plain enough from those who, by the rational demonstrations of Cartesianism, though these are true, have fallen into atheism, Spinozism, the denial of freedom and the denial of the immortality of the soul. I know this too from my own experience. For although I never seriously doubted these things, and had grasped their demonstrations drawn from reason and had assented to them, I did not feel that confidence of complete certainty which I later found when my desire and my passive intellect were for some time turned from those ideal speculations to the Lord with my whole heart. For then the scruples about the existence of God and the immortality of the soul, which had before troubled my mind, beyond reason and will, though rarely, vanished from me so completely that there arose in me a certainty about God, about divine things, about eternity, and about the blessed or wretched immortality of souls, which infinitely surpasses, and more than can be said, all my earlier demonstrations of these things. So that, even if every difficulty and objection that could be devised were put to me, they would have no more effect on me than the reasonings of some blind man who tried to persuade another, who was using the light of the sun, by his subtleties that there is no light and that true objects are not perceived by its help. Hence I learned that what Descartes asserts is false, namely that if we were deprived of that painted idea of God which belongs to reason, we could never know God, not even by the light of faith, that is, by the light of God spreading into the faculties that are superior to reason. I have also observed that it is most false what some assert: that certainty about the existence of God must be derived more from the demonstration drawn from the idea of him than from the fact that the existing God is known through himself, and that this certainty is posterior to that. On the contrary, God as existing is infinitely better known through himself, that is, through his own act and light in the higher faculties of the soul, than through the act of reason. Reason is a faculty more suited to lower things, and is infinitely inferior to the passive intellect itself, since the passive intellect is as great as the power of God acting upon it; and it cannot lead into error, since, being passive, it cannot be driven into error by God. These rationalists do not know this. They expect all their certainty and all light and truth only from a very limited faculty, and from their corruption, which is most liable to error. Indeed I would not wish to deny or weaken the proof of the existence of God that is sought from reason, for it is true and legitimate. But it is of secondary certainty in comparison with that other, and is far to be placed after it. And I would venture to affirm that those who are certain that God exists, if they examine themselves well, will find that their true certainty and confidence about the existence of God does not proceed from the force of their reasoned demonstration, but rather from a certain inner sense that does not depend on the acts of their reason, to which they stand purely passively, and which, even against their will and resisting, God affects and impresses upon them more vividly than any idea does: God the powerful, wise, good, just and true, the Author of himself and of all things. In exactly the same way, the certainty about the sun and its light, and also about the existence of bodies, and likewise the certain distinction of waking from sleep, is not to be derived from ideas of reason or from acts of reasoning; it arises from the very experience of the sense or consciousness, immediately and indubitably, from the application of the faculties to objects, according to the law or ordinance of almighty God mentioned above.

units.la: XII. Neque credo ullum unquam, qui sincere aget (cæteros non moror) dicturum, sive, cum respicit Solem, ut bene certus sit de eo illuminante, debere certitudinis suæ causam in ideis rationis, hujusque ratiociniis quærere & fundare; nescire alias, an ne forte tunc somniet. Certe Cartesius, qui in Meditatione sexta certitudinem distinctionis vigiliæ & somni perperam vult a ratione arcessere, multo veriorem viam in Epistolis
units.tr: XII. Nor do I believe that anyone who acts sincerely (I do not mention the others) will say that when he looks at the sun, and wants to be well certain of its shining, he must seek and found the cause of his certainty in the ideas of reason and its reasonings, and otherwise not know whether perhaps he is then dreaming. Certainly Descartes, who in the sixth Meditation wrongly wants to derive from reason the certainty of distinguishing waking from sleep, took a far truer path in his Letters.

units.la: {a}stolis suis iniit, ubi {a}postquam distinxerat tria notionum primitivarum genera, nempe notiones spirituum, notiones corporum, & notiones quæ conjunctionem sive commercium mentis cum corpore spectant, de hac tertia notionum specie ait, res quæ pertinent ad conjunctionem mentis & corporis non nisi obscure cognoscuntur solo intellectu; neque recte intellectu etsi per imaginationem adjuto; at OMNIUM CLARISSIME. NOSCUNTUR PER SENSUS.
units.tr: For after he had distinguished three kinds of primitive notions, namely notions of spirits, notions of bodies, and notions that concern the union or commerce of mind with body, he says of this third kind of notion: things that pertain to the union of mind and body are known only obscurely by the intellect alone, nor rightly by the intellect even when aided by imagination; but MOST CLEARLY OF ALL, THEY ARE KNOWN THROUGH THE SENSES.

units.la: Nugæ ergo meræ sunt, velle corporum exsistentiam, nec non distinctionem vigiliæ a somno, ex ideis rationis sibi demonstrari, ac si velles tibi demonstrari Solem esse lucidum ex pictura potius solis quam ex ejusdem vivido sensu. Nam idem sane facit qui vult sibi demonstrari vividam vigiliam per ideas & ratiocinia, hoc est, per picturam vigiliæ potius, quam per ipsam experientiam, quæ per se, sine ratione alia, certa & indubitata est; cum cuivis sincerum fateri volenti constet ex conscientia, certitudinem de exsistentia vigiliæ priorem esse certitudine de exsistentia deque forma ratiocinationis: atque adeo, cum ratiocinationes ideæque nequaquam sint tam vivæ quam ipsa vigilia; quamvis per ideas aliquid conficere tibi videaris, id tamen quia non erit tam vivum nec tam certum quam ipsamet vigilia, si hanc in dubium revocas ut de eadem certus fias per eas minus vivas & minus certas, rem absurdam agis & impossibilem, omnesque tuæ de re vivida probationes pictæ ſtæ & fictæ, nullius pretii sunt & utilitatis: quin contra noxiæ sunt, & ad quandam insaniæ speciem ducunt illos qui eis potius quam sensibus fidere vellent. Nam quisquis ea quæ viva sunt, vivaque experientia juxta Dei ordinationem debent percipi, vult tamen per picturas steriles, mortuas, inanesque percipere præcipue, is tum certa de rebus certitudine sese spoliat, tum mille se incertis & absurdis exponit. Hinc est quod Cartesianus (a) non incelebris, qui huic viæ rationis circa corporum exsistentiam demonstrandam instituit tenacius, eo tandem devenerit, ut negaverit alio modo posse certo sciri corpora dari exsistentia, quam per revelationem divinam; posse ea quæ a nobis percipiuntur nil aliud esse quam apparentias sub quibus nil aliud subsit quam vel cogitatio humana, vel substantia Dei quatenus corporum est repræsentativa, & nescio quot alia absurda, quæ alibi (b) discussa sunt. Nempe postquam male in dubium revocaverat veram certitudinis corporum exsistentium causam; ejus quæ certitudinis istius causa vera non est, ratiocinationis scilicet inutilitatem sentiens & infirmitatem, fateri eam cogebatur, hincque ad minus aptam (sensus enim nolebat admittere) recurrere. Atqui ex dictis credo constare, idque si opus esset diductius probare possem, inter omnes vias quibus quæritur certitudo clara & inconcussa de entibus realibus, sive ea ipsimet simus nostræque facultates, sive ea a nobis sint diversa, uti Deus & omnes creaturæ, viam omnium infimam & minùs certam esse viam rationis humanæ, cui via sensuum {ubi in sphæra sua circa corporum exsistentiam modosque ad usum vitæ relatos manet} longe maximè est anteponenda; eidem autem via facultatum superiorum, ad Deum divinaque sese convertentium infinities præpollet. Et quamvis per illam sibi persuadeant sese adipisci posse certitudinem quam nominant Metaphysicam; atque ad rerum naturæ cognitionem & veritatem detegendam sic per eandem sperent se perventuros, ut alium non dari aditum putent, siquidem hunc Rationis esse finem vel rectum usum opinentur: in utroque tamen mire falluntur.
units.tr: It is therefore mere trifling to want the existence of bodies, and also the distinction of waking from sleep, to be demonstrated to oneself from ideas of reason, as if you wanted the sun's shining to be demonstrated to you from a picture of the sun rather than from its own vivid sensation. For whoever wants a living waking state to be demonstrated to him through ideas and reasonings, that is, through a picture of waking rather than through the experience itself, does exactly the same thing. That experience is certain and indubitable of itself, without any other reason, since anyone who is willing to confess sincerely knows from consciousness that the certainty of the existence of waking is prior to the certainty of the existence and form of reasoning. And so, since reasonings and ideas are by no means as vivid as waking itself, although you seem to achieve something through ideas, you still, because it will not be as vivid or as certain as waking itself, if you call this into doubt in order to become certain of it through ideas that are less vivid and less certain, you do an absurd and impossible thing. All your proofs of a living matter, being painted and fictitious, are of no worth or use. Indeed they are harmful, and they lead those who would rather trust them than the senses into a kind of madness. For whoever, while things that are alive and must be perceived by living experience according to God's ordering, wants above all to perceive them through sterile, dead and empty pictures, deprives himself of certainty about things and exposes himself to a thousand uncertain and absurd things. Hence it is that a not unknown Cartesian, who pursued most tenaciously this way of rational demonstration of the existence of bodies, at last came to deny that the existence of bodies can be known for certain in any other way than through divine revelation. He said that the things perceived by us can be nothing but appearances, beneath which there lies nothing but either human thought or the substance of God insofar as it represents bodies, and I know not how many other absurdities, which have been discussed elsewhere (b). Having wrongly called into doubt the true cause of the certainty of existing bodies, and feeling the uselessness and weakness of reasoning, which is not the true cause of that certainty, he was forced to confess this and to have recourse to something less suitable (for he was unwilling to admit the senses). But I believe it is evident from what has been said, and I could prove it at more length if needed, that among all the ways by which clear and unshaken certainty is sought about real beings, whether we ourselves and our faculties are such beings or whether they are different from us, as God and all creatures are, the lowest and least certain way is the way of human reason. Far above it is to be placed the way of the senses, where it remains within its own sphere concerning the existence of bodies and their modes related to the use of life. But the way of the higher faculties, turning to God and divine things, surpasses it infinitely. And although they persuade themselves through reason that they can attain the certainty they call metaphysical, and that by it they can reach the knowledge and discovery of the truth of nature, so that they think no other access is open, since they suppose this to be the end of reason or its right use, they are in both respects wonderfully mistaken.

units.la: XIII. Certitudo Metaphysica, quæ quidem est, neque enim eam negare velim in eis quæ sunt suæ sphæræ; non tamen ejus finitimatis est, mitatis est, cujus est certitudo facultatum sæpe dictarum, ubi illæ suis objectis debitè applicantur: cùm quarum certitudine si comparetur certitudo Metaphysica rationis, ea (juxta idearum proprietates recensitas) umbratilis, picta, sterilis, mortua, impotens deprehenderetur, uti nimio plus patet ex otiosorum cerebrorum de divinis humanisque speculantium comparatione, cum hominibus qui Deo rebusque etiam ipsis creatis debitas suas facultates internas externasque applicant & exercent. Metaphysica illa & rationalis via, lusus quidam est, aut animi exercitium, cujus omnis utilitas in eo est, ut quis se sic accommodet nonnullis extravagantium Certitudo Metaphysica nec summa est, nec tenuis, nec pauci usus. tium dubitatorum atque Sceptícorum dubitationibus, a rationis nimio exercitio, facultatumque solidarum rejectione insana ortis, si pote eorum stultitia sic fanari, vel reduci ad orbitam utcunque posset: alias qui sinceri sunt, bonaque fide quæ in se sentiunt agnosere volunt, istis cùm non sint dubitationibus obnoxii, neque etiam hac certitudinis specie opus habent; nec iidem multum curabunt ut sponte insanientes nec sincera fide agentes Scepticos voluntario suo delirio liberent. Quis enim sanus sibi id negotii assumat, ut stultos, qui ipsummet insanire judicarent, convincat se quidem stultum non esse, ipsos vero insanire? Tametsi quando morbus sinceriores, at eos simpliciores, infecit; operæ sit pretium semel atque iterum cum illis hanc palæstram ingredi, eis medendi gratiâ.
units.tr: Metaphysical certainty, which does exist (for I would not deny it in those matters that belong to its own sphere), is not akin to the certainty of the faculties I have so often mentioned, where those faculties are rightly applied to their objects. If metaphysical certainty of reason is compared with their certainty, it will be found (according to the properties of the ideas already reviewed) to be shadowy, painted, barren, dead and powerless. This is plain enough from comparing idle brains that speculate about divine and human things with men who apply and exercise their proper inner and outer faculties towards God and even towards created things. That metaphysical and rational way is a kind of game, or an exercise of the mind, whose whole usefulness lies in this: that someone may adjust himself, by it, to the doubts of certain eccentric doubters and Sceptics, doubts that arise from an excessive use of reason and a mad rejection of solid faculties. Metaphysical certainty is neither supreme, nor slight, nor of little use. If their folly could somehow be cured, or brought back to the right track in any way, well and good. Otherwise, those who are sincere and want to acknowledge in good faith what they feel within themselves are not liable to such doubts, and they have no need of this kind of certainty. Nor will the same people much trouble themselves to free from their voluntary delirium Sceptics who go mad of their own accord and act without sincere faith. For what sane person would take on the task of convincing fools, who judge themselves not to be fools, that they are not fools but that they themselves are mad? Yet when the disease has infected even the more sincere, and simpler folk too, it is worth the effort to enter this wrestling ground once and again, for the sake of healing them.

units.la: XIV. Quod ad rerum naturalium cogn- itionem veram, ad quam se itidem per ra- tionis viam, ad hoc, ut credunt, datam, perventuros putant, major adhuc est fallacia.
units.tr: XIV. The greater error lies in the belief that by the way of reason, which they think is given for this purpose, they will arrive at a true knowledge of natural things.

units.la: Equidem facile concedam multarum rerum historiam atque facta per rationem percipi, alia ex aliis deduci posse: verum ipsam penitiorem rerum notitiam, ultimumque fundum, ac primum ortum, per eam detegere aut sibi repræsentare verè, id a vero longe alienum est: Rerum namque fundus & ortus, vividus est, nec non centralissimus, tangens immediate vividos Dei actus, quos præter Deum atque illos quibus Deus sese lumine suo communicat, concipere poffant nulli; repræsentantque intimas & admirandas Dei virtutes, simplices atque complicatas, rerum omnium causas & origines; quas proinde solus Deus, & ii in quibus Deus lumen & actum suum de his diffundit, concipere possunt. Quod fi quis neque hæc generalia quæ profero, concipere fe dicat, hoc ita habeat, me jam de sexto quodam, vel adhuc superiore, naturæ sensu loqui, cujus qui experientiam non habent, neque ejus ideam specialem sibi formare possunt. Rem tamen simili proponam utcunque concipiendam Minerva crassiore.
units.tr: I will readily concede that the history and deeds of many things can be grasped by reason, and that some things can be inferred from others. But to uncover by reason, or to represent to oneself truly, the deeper knowledge of things, their ultimate ground and their first origin, is far removed from the truth. For the ground and origin of things is living and most central, touching immediately the living acts of God. Apart from God, and from those to whom God communicates his light and his act, no one can conceive these acts. They represent the inner and wonderful virtues of God, simple and yet complex, the causes and origins of all things; and therefore only God, and those in whom God pours out his light and his act concerning these matters, can conceive them. But if anyone says that he cannot conceive these general things that I put forward, let it be so: I am now speaking of a certain sixth sense of nature, or one still higher, of which those who have no experience cannot form a specific idea. Nevertheless I will put before them a comparison, to be conceived, as best it may be, by a coarser intellect.

units.la: Consideret quis pictorem, eumque quantumvis artis suæ peritum, nec non penicillis, coloribus & omnibus ad artem requisitis abunde instructum: iscum omnibus instrumentis suis, omnique activa sua industria, nunquam depingere poterit motum, vel respirationem, vel vitam, vel rem lucidam, aut ejus odores, similiaque sexcenta quæ vitalia sunt & vivida, quæ ideis suis picturatis referri non possunt, hæ siquidem sint immobiles, mortuæ, non lucidæ nec odoriferæ: At si tabula, in qua colores penicillo disponendi erant, ejus esset constitutionis, ut instar speculi posset poliri; siquè pictor eam, coloribus suis inde erasis, mundaret sic & perpoliret, ut lævis & nitida fieret ad modum speculi; tunc quæ antea motum, res vivas, lumenque opea-tiva pictoris colorumque suorum repræsentare non poterat, si ei offerantur lumen homihominesque & se moventes & respirantes, ea ipsos eorumque motus cum vivo lumine exacte repræsentabit, quanquam nec omnimode, quippe quæ nec verborum sonos, nec objectorum odores poterit imitari. Idem concipe de ratione nostra, quæ cum activitate industriaque sua pictor quidam peritus est, ideæ autem & ratiocinationes penicilli sunt & colores diversi in tabula mentis diversimode disponendi. Hæc coloribus illis nil sibi vere vivum (quales sunt res naturæ in scaturigine sua) ob oculos ponere potest: rerum siquidem originantes veritates (ut sic dicam) altioris sunt indolis quam ut per ejusmodi artificis miseri actum sistantur: at si ea (rationem dico) idearum suarum colores, penicillique sui labores ex se clueret, seque nudam & nitidam luminoso Creatori suo exponeret, is nullo negotio quotquot ex actibus operationibusque suis vividis vellet, illico in ea, tunc passive se habente, repræsentaret, si id e re sua fore, neque mentem inde superbiorem aut donis suis abutentem futuram, judicaret. Nec tamen ea in facultate, ut ut passive se haberet, omnia repræsentare posset Omnipotens; quoniam voluit eam vas esse angustius quam ut quædam divinissima, facultatibus superioribus solum reservata, caperet. sunt namque in rebus naturalibus quædam quæ ad earum naturam non pertinent, neque illarum sunt naturales modi; sed dona seu ornamenta supernaturalia, & effusiones præternaturales & continuæ Dei: hæcque nullatenus in ratione ne quidem passive se habente (quemadmodum nec odores in speculo) repræsentari possunt; sed vel in sensibus a Deo in primam originem revectis, vel in facultate intellectûs superioris. Equidem scio me hic iterum loqui quæ vel a paucissimis concipientur, & veluti de sexto quodam naturæ sensu; quod irridebunt fortasse ignari nonnulli irrisores; quibus compescendis jam mihi suffecerit magni Augustini verbum: Rideat me ista dicentem, qui non intelligit; & ego doleam ridentem me.
units.tr: Consider a painter, however skilled in his art, and well supplied with brushes, colours and everything needed for the craft. With all his tools and all his active diligence, he can never paint motion, or breathing, or life, or a shining thing, or its odours, or the countless other living and lively qualities that cannot be conveyed by his painted images. For these are immobile, dead, neither shining nor fragrant. But suppose the panel on which the colours were to be laid were of such a nature that it could be polished like a mirror; and suppose the painter, having scraped off his colours, cleaned and polished it so that it became smooth and bright like a mirror. Then, whatever could not be represented by the painter's work and colours, namely motion, living things and active light, would be exactly represented, if men, moving and breathing, were offered to it with living light. It would reproduce them and their movements with living light, though not in every respect, since it could not imitate the sounds of words or the smells of objects. Conceive the same about our reason. It is, with its activity and industry, a sort of skilled painter; but ideas and reasonings are its brushes, and the various colours to be arranged in the panel of the mind in various ways. These colours can place before our eyes nothing truly living (such as the things of nature in their spring), for the originating truths of things, so to speak, are of too high a nature to be set forth by the wretched handiwork of such an artist. But if reason itself, the colours of its ideas and the labours of its brush, shone forth from itself, and exposed itself, bare and bright, to its luminous Creator, then the Creator, without any trouble, would at once represent in it, now passively disposed, as many of his living acts and operations as he wished, provided he judged this to be to its advantage, and that the mind would not thereby become more proud or abuse his gifts. Yet even so, the Almighty could not represent everything in that faculty, though it was passively disposed; for he willed that this vessel should be too narrow to hold certain most divine things, which are reserved for the higher faculties alone. For there are in natural things certain things that do not belong to their nature, nor are they natural modes of them, but supernatural gifts or ornaments, and preternatural and continuous outpourings of God. These can in no way be represented in reason, not even in reason passively disposed (just as odours cannot be in a mirror), but only in the senses, when they have been raised by God to their first origin, or in the faculty of the higher intellect. Indeed I know that I am again speaking of things that will be grasped by very few, and as if of some sixth sense of nature. Some ignorant mockers may perhaps laugh at this. To restrain them, the saying of the great Augustine will now suffice for me: Let him laugh at me who says these things, since he does not understand; and I shall grieve for him who laughs at me.

units.la: XV. Ex omnibus his dictis velim jam judicium ferat cordatus quivis de eo quod mihi primo objiciebatur, me nempe Pyrrhonismo januam pandere: cum econtra, illi eam tutissime obturaverim, ostendendo indubitatæ certitudinis fundamenta, primo quidem in facultatibus supremis a lumine Dei, ad quem se converterunt, illustratis, quoad res divinas, æternas, spirituales, penitioresque naturæ origines certissime percipiendas: deinde in facultatibus sensuum a sensuali lumine, ubi ei sese dibite exponunt; affectorum, quoad objecta naturalia, eorumque quatenus vitam naturalem concernunt, habitudines ad nos, sine hæsitatione percipiendas: tertio in ratione ipsa, ubi activitatem suam aliquantisper seponens, tradit se Auctori suo, qui, quando e re esse judicat, rerum naturalium veras ideas in illa exprimit; nec non & vel illi reluctanti, attamen passive se habenti, imprimit veritates quasdam, sive axiomata, quæ scientiæ tiæ principia deinde vocantur: denique & in eadem active sese gerente, atque ideas & ratiocinia in se excitante, modo supremæ facultates sensualesque in mente bene sint dispositæ, ipsaque conetur Deum debite sequi ac imitari. In quibus omnibus certitudinis tres classes sive species videre est pro triplici classe facultatum, objectorum atque luminum, de quibus dictum est; nempe primo Divinam certitudinem, quæ est facultatum, objectorum, luminisque divinorum & primi ordinis; secundo certitudinem naturalem sive physicam, quæ est facultatum, objectorum, luminisque naturalium & secundi ordinis; tertio certitudinem metaphysicam, quæ tertii cujusdam generis facultates atque ideas umbratiles respicit, in quibus mens sese active habet; quod ultimum addo, quia quando Deus operatur in ratione sese passive habente, id ad primam speciem certitudinis refero. Moralis certitudo hujus loci non est. Prima est infallibilissima: altera neque dubitationem admittit: tertia ubi bene fit, dubitationes ex ratione ortas, ipsas quoque discutit, etsi aliis sit inferior. Quæ cum ita sint, quis igitur jam est qui de certitudinis sublatione possit jure mecum expostulare? At si cujusdam facultates diviniores neglectæ fuerint, & obscuratæ; si contra conscientiam rejiciat ratio sensibilem certitudinem; si ipsa superba Deo subjici & grata esse nolit, neque ei sese curet conformare, sed sui solius juris velit esse, sequeque solam spectare, & a se sola sua exspectare; tunc sane non mirum perditam ejusmodi atque irrationalem rationem, ubi ejus, quibus perniciose utitur, fundamentorum caries & putrefactio ei deteguntur, conqueri se sic Pyrrhonismo exponi. Id suaculpa, quam diu solidiora non bene quaerer, erit quam verissimum.
units.tr: XV. From all that has been said, I would now have any sensible person judge what was first objected to me, namely that I open the door to Pyrrhonism. On the contrary, I have most securely closed it against that very charge, by showing the foundations of indubitable certainty: first, in the supreme faculties, illumined by the light of God to whom they have turned, for most certainly perceiving divine and eternal and spiritual things, and the deeper origins of nature. Second, in the faculties of the senses, illumined by the sensual light where they are rightly exposed to it, for perceiving without hesitation the relations of natural objects to us, insofar as they concern our natural life. Third, in reason itself, where, setting aside its activity for a while, it yields itself to its Author, who, when he judges it fitting, imprints in it true ideas of natural things. He also imprints, even on a reason that resists yet remains passively disposed, certain truths, or axioms, which are afterwards called the principles of science. Finally, the certainty is found in reason when it is actively engaged and stirs up ideas and reasonings within itself, provided that the supreme and sensual faculties in the mind are well ordered, and that reason itself strives to follow and imitate God as it ought. In all of these one may see three classes or species of certainty, corresponding to the threefold class of faculties, objects and lights of which we have spoken. Namely: first, divine certainty, which belongs to the faculties, objects and light that are divine and of the first order; second, natural or physical certainty, which belongs to the faculties, objects and light that are natural and of the second order; third, metaphysical certainty, which regards a third kind of faculties and shadowy ideas, in which the mind is actively engaged. I add this last, because when God works in reason that is passively disposed, I refer that to the first species of certainty. Moral certainty is not in question here. The first is most infallible; the second admits no doubt; the third, where it is rightly done, also dispels the doubts that arise from reason, although it is inferior to the others. Since this is so, who then can justly complain with me about the removal of certainty? But if the higher faculties of someone have been neglected and darkened; if, on the contrary, reason rejects sensible certainty against conscience; if reason, proud, refuses to be subject to God and to be pleasing to him, and does not care to conform itself to him, but wishes to be under its own authority alone, looking only to itself and expecting everything from itself, then it is hardly surprising that such a ruined and irrational reason, when the rot and putrefaction of the foundations it uses so harmfully are revealed to it, complains that it is thus exposed to Pyrrhonism. That will be entirely its own fault, for as long as it does not seek the more solid things well.

units.la: XVI. Fortassis antequam ad alteram e superioribus objectionem properem, pertierit a me aliquis, quid sint tria illa, quae modo nominavi, luminum genera, lumen divinum, lumen sensuale, lumen rationis: haec videri sibi verba sine sensu, quem tamen desideraret aliquem percipere. Certe si quis est qui lumina illa non sit expertus, frustra ei verba dixero; veluti frustra caeco, qui solis lumen viderit nunquam, tentabis id explicare verbis, sic ut te percipiat. Experientia sola id poterit docere, atque conscientia eorum, dum in nobis fiunt: & quia nemo lumen rationis negabit se percepisse, ut ab illo de caeteris generaliora dicendi sumam occasionem; peto dicat mihi quis, quid sit illud rationis suae lumen? quid cogitatio sua sit? quid cogitatio clara? quid evidentia? Certe conscientia & sensu intimo id, ni noscas, illud nequaquam tibi dicet alter: nam quaecunque verba dici possunt, excitant tantum in mente sonos, non autem res ipsas, quas ut capias, suas quibusque facultates debes appositè applicare, & tibi attendere: tuncque percipies certo quid sit id generis lumen cui te applicueris. Est namque lumen quodcunque impressio quaedam ab objectis in facultates eis oblatas fafacta, cum perceptione indubitata objecti, ejusque ad nos habitudinis: quae perceptio ita certa est, ut qui eam vere habet, neutiquam dubitare possit de illa, neque dubitare an fallatur; neque etiam (ubi debite sibi attendit,) errare quando aliquid ejusmodi postea recurrit de quo quaeri potest, anne sit de genere istius luminis, nec ne. Sic qui lumen Dei semel vere & pure senserunt, illi non tantum omni certitudine certiores sunt se ibi non falli; sed & cum postmodum aliquid eis occurrit de quo quaeritur, an ad divinum pertineat lumen, vel divine luminosum sit, tuto, omnique procul errore, si sibi redditi sint, respondere illico possunt. Pari modo res se habet cum illis qui sensibus corporeis lumen aliquod corporeum vere sunt experti: eorum unusquisque de hoc; v. g de lumine Solis, tum certus est apud se, tum inter se sine controversia consentiunt omnes, & praeterea semper decidere possunt, an hoc illudve lumen eis oblatum sit, ejusmodi sit, nec ne; quod caeci nec facere nec capere queunt, uti neque nos jam capere possumus, quid sit lumen aliud corporeum quod non oculis, sed tota superficie corporis (ubi debite temperata est) cernitur, & cujus experimentum memini me legisse apud Digbaeum in tractatu Physico quem de animae immortalitate inscripsit, ubi se inter domesticos habuisse affirmat liberorum suorum praeceptorem quendam, qui ipsis organis oculorum prorsus captus, omnium corporum circum jacentium situationes, figuras, motus, dispositionesque nihilominus percipiebat, per impressiones nimirum a corporibus circumpositis, quamvis dissitis, oriundas, & in superficiem sive cutem corporis sui irradiantes atque impingentes, quali modo mihi persuaserim hominem si non se peccato corrupisset, aut eundem cum restaurabitur in resurrectione, toto corpore haud minus visurum quam nos jam oculis, oculos vero tunc illi fore & admirabilia ornamenta, & totius visionis luminisque summa exaltatio (ut sic loquar) atque centrum. Sed hæc nos jam superant, exiguntque principia Physices a vulgaribus diversa, qualia hujus loci non sunt, & alibi sunt.
units.tr: XVI. Perhaps before I come to the second of the objections above, someone will ask me what those three kinds of light I have just named are: the divine light, the sensory light, and the light of reason. They may seem to him words without meaning, though he would want to grasp some meaning in them. Certainly, if someone has never experienced those lights, I will be speaking to him in vain, just as you would be trying in vain to explain light to a blind man who has never seen the sun, so that he could understand you. Experience alone can teach this, and consciousness of these lights as they arise within us. No one will deny that he has perceived the light of reason, so I will take that as my starting point for speaking more generally about the others. Let someone tell me: what is that light of his reason? What is his thinking? What is clear thinking? What is evidence? Unless you know these by consciousness and inner sense, no one else will ever tell you, for whatever words can be spoken only stir sounds in the mind, not the things themselves. To grasp those things, each person must apply his own faculties appropriately and attend to himself. Then you will surely perceive what kind of light it is to which you have applied yourself. Light is any impression made by objects upon the faculties presented to them, together with an indubitable perception of the object and of its relation to us. This perception is so certain that whoever truly has it cannot doubt it, nor doubt whether he is deceived. Nor, when he attends to it rightly, will he err when something of this kind later recurs, about which one may ask whether it belongs to the kind of that light or not. So those who have truly and purely perceived the light of God are not only more certain than any certainty that they are not deceived there; but when something afterwards comes to them and it is asked whether it belongs to the divine light, or is luminous with the divine, they can answer at once, safely and free of all error, if they have recovered themselves. It is the same with those who have truly experienced some bodily light through their bodily senses. Each of them, for example about the light of the sun, is certain within himself, and all agree among themselves without dispute; moreover they can always decide whether this or that light presented to them is of that kind or not. The blind can neither do this nor grasp it, just as we cannot now grasp what other bodily light it is that is perceived not by the eyes but by the whole surface of the body (when it is suitably tempered), and of which I remember reading an experiment in Digby's physical treatise entitled On the Immortality of the Soul. There he affirms that among his household he had a certain tutor for his children who, although wholly deprived of the organs of sight, nevertheless perceived the positions, shapes, motions and arrangements of all the bodies lying around him, namely through impressions arising from the surrounding bodies, however distant, and striking and shining upon the surface or skin of his body. In the same way I am persuaded that a man, had he not corrupted himself by sin, or when he is restored in the resurrection, would see with his whole body no less than we now see with our eyes, and that the eyes would then be for him an admirable ornament and, so to speak, the summit and centre of all vision and light. But these matters are beyond us now; they require principles of physics other than the common ones, which do not belong to this place but elsewhere.

units.la: (a) propositä. Redeamus ad nostra lumina, quorum ultimum cum sit rationis, idque repictum, & veluti mortuum respectu duorum præcedentium, si tamen illa, Mensque ea utans, in bono esset statu a me aliquoties indicato, idem illi accideret ac aliis duobus luminum generibus, ut nempe & hoc cum certitudine indubitata perciperetur a sua facultate, (ratione,) quæ etiam sine erroris periculo judicaret quid cum illo lumine conveniat aut secus, vel quid ad id pertineat: sed depravatio defectusque Mentis & rationis, alia negligentis, alia pervertentis & extra scopum detorquentis, efficiunt ejus infirmitatem atque incertitudinem, universalem ferme. Ferme inquam, sunt enim in eadem lumina nonnulla (quæ naturalia vulgo dicunt) v. g. impossibi e est idem esse & non esse; non potest esse plus in effectu quam in causa, & similia. milia theoretica, quæ dubium non admittunt; idque ideo, quod sint Dei in ratione, passive tunc se habente, impressi actus; veluti etiam in practicis ea sunt quæ principia moralia vel synthereseos dicuntur: Amandum esse Deum; nemini faciendum quam quod tibi fieri velles; permanentia peituris esse anteponenda; aliaque de bono justoque non tantum scita & dictamina, verum etiam instinctus & impulsus, qui apud omnes (nisi quis studio se in atheisticum monstrum transformaverit) obtinent; quæque quoniam nos ad æterna & solida bona impelluntac disponunt, malim ego ad lumen Divinum præveniens, inque facultatibus superioribus lucens & agens revocare, quam ad facultatem superficiariam rationis. Meminit etiam Scripturæ (a) Verbi Dei, lucis verae illuminantis omnem hominem venientem in mundum: quam hoc ipsum esse, cuivis facile pateret qui hujusmodi impulsibus atque dictaminibus obtemperaret: namque ex illis sese aperientibus, ac veluti expandentibus, divinissima quævis prodirent sequerenturque lumina, quæ sui cum illis unitatem probarent, hominemque tum divinum, tum in omnibus restitutum ac eruditum solidissime redderent. Sed tempus est, ut discussa jam Scepticismi objectati suspicione, ad cætera quæ objiciebantur, aliquid quoque dicamus, idque multo brevius.
units.tr: (a) as proposed. Let us return to our lights. Since the last of them is that of reason, and that is weakened and, as it were, dead in comparison with the two preceding ones, nevertheless if that light, and the mind that uses it, were in the good state I have indicated several times, the same would happen to it as to the other two kinds of light: namely, it too would be perceived by its own faculty (reason) with indubitable certainty, and that faculty would also judge, without danger of error, what agrees with that light or not, or what pertains to it. But the depravity and defect of mind and reason, some neglecting it and others perverting it and turning it away from its aim, bring about its weakness and uncertainty, almost universally. I say "almost", for there are in the same light certain theoretical items, which they call natural, e.g. it is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be; there cannot be more in the effect than in the cause, and similar ones, which admit no doubt. This is because they are acts impressed by God on reason, which is then passive. Likewise, in practical matters there are those which are called moral principles or synderesis: God is to be loved; one should do to no one what you would not wish done to you; things that endure are to be preferred to perishable ones; and other matters concerning the good and the just, not only the rules and dictates but also the instincts and impulses which hold among all people (unless someone has deliberately transformed himself into an atheistic monster). Since these impel us towards eternal and solid goods and dispose us towards them, I would rather trace them back to the divine light that goes before us and shines and acts in our higher faculties, than to the superficial faculty of reason. Scripture also speaks of the Word of God, the true light which enlightens every man coming into the world. That this is so would be easy for anyone to see who obeyed such impulses and dictates. For from these, as they open and as it were expand, there would issue and follow the most divine lights, which would prove their unity with those impulses and render the man at once divine, and most solidly restored and instructed in all things. But it is time, now that the suspicion of Scepticism has been discussed, to say something also about the other objections raised, and that much more briefly.

units.la: XVII. Mathesis secundo adducebatur veluti experimento convincens dari e ratione scientias veritatesque certas, de quibus apud omnes
units.tr: XVII. Secondly, mathematics was put forward as a convincing experiment that certain sciences and certain truths can be derived from reason, about which all agree

units.la: Respon- dtur in- stantia om- nes
units.tr: The objection is answered: all

units.la: omnes constet sine controversia: rationis proinde, & eorum quae ab illa proficiscuntur, imbecillitatem incertitudinemque non tantam esse, quantam diximus. At una hirundo, inquam ego, non facit ver, neque una Mathesis totum rationis objectum complectitur, imo minima pars ejus est: Praeterea ipsa non detegit ullas rerum naturalium originales causas, sed tantum versatur circa craffiora, qualia sunt numeri, figurae, motus, eorumque comparationes, separationes conjunctionesque, quae supponunt res jam factas, atque datas, earum autem naturales non ostendunt origines; quemadmodum fruges, fructus, animaliumque carnes videmus per artem quandam varie praeparari & disponi, non autem per eandem artem harum rerum naturales productiones capi ac detegi. Et quemadmodum coecus potest quodam sensu, partibusque corporis quibusdam, puta tactu manibusque palpantibus, percipere evidenter materiei quam tangit tractatque figuras; sic tamen ut inde non sequatur eum alia objecta per medium subtilius, etsi corporeum, puta per radios luminis, perque partes sui corporis a manibus diversas, puta oculos, perspicere: eodem modo se res habet respectu Matheseos, quae crassius quidam est modus vel ars palpandi veluti manibus rationis ea quae exteriora sunt in rebus, veritatulas quasdam superficiarias valde; unde minime sequitur, rationem ideo posse oculis suis magna, intima & subtilia rerum principia intuispicere. Ita ut mire sibi imponant,
units.tr: all agree without dispute. The weakness and uncertainty of reason, and of what proceeds from it, are therefore not as great as I have said. But one swallow, I reply, does not make a spring, and mathematics alone does not embrace the whole object of reason; indeed it is the smallest part of it. Moreover, it does not disclose any original causes of natural things. It deals only with the grosser matters, such as numbers, figures, motion, and their comparisons, separations and combinations, which presuppose things already made and given, and do not reveal their natural origins. We see that grain, fruit and the flesh of animals are prepared and arranged in various ways by a certain art, but the same art does not grasp or disclose their natural production. A blind man can perceive clearly, by a certain sense and by certain parts of his body, namely touch and feeling hands, the material he touches and the figures he handles; yet it does not follow that he can perceive other objects through a subtler medium, even though it is corporeal, such as rays of light, or through parts of his body other than his hands, such as his eyes. It is the same with mathematics, which is a cruder mode or art of feeling, as it were with the hands of reason, the things that are external in objects, and only certain very superficial truths. It by no means follows that reason can therefore see with its eyes the great, inner and subtle principles of things. So those who, as many as try to persuade themselves and others that they have the ideas and knowledge of spiritual and corporeal things from the faculty of reason, are wonderfully deceived when they appeal to the similar certainty and clarity of mathematics, as if they perceived those other things they discuss in the same way and with the same clarity. In this matter they seem to me to imitate our blind man, who, after hearing much about light and colours, and about the way of recognising by them the figures, motions and positions of bodies, or after imagining much about this mode of perception, believes that he perceives these things himself, and wishes to explain them to other blind men like himself. To win their trust, he uses similar examples drawn from the feeling of bodies, which are certainly known to him and to all the blind. What, I ask, would this help them, except that they deceive themselves all the more securely? For just as one part of the body, such as the hand and its office of feeling, may be sound without it following that another part, such as the eyes and their office, is sound, so, although one function of reason, such as knowing numbers, motions and quantity, is sound enough, it does not follow that other functions of reason, such as knowing the ideas, nature, roots, origins, growth and inner state of spiritual as well as corporeal things, are sound and fit for their office. Indeed, even within mathematics itself, the maximum and minimum principles of every quantity, of motion and its speed and slowness, of circular and straight lines and their proportions, and likewise of surfaces

units.la: Mathesi desumte, frustra eam allegari ad probandam soliditatem cognitionem per rationem quaerendarum. nant, quotquot ut sibi aliisque persuadeant se rerum spiritualium corporearumque ideas & cognitionem ex rationis facultate habere, ad Mathematicæ certitudinis & claritatis similia provocare solent, quasi & eodem modo eademque claritate illa alia, de quibus agunt, perciperent. Qua in re mihi videntur imitari cæcum nostrum, qui postquam plurima de lumine & coloribus deque modo per ea corporum figuras, motus & situs dignoscendi audivisset, aut de hocce percipiendi modo sibi plurima imaginatus esset, seque ista percipere crederet, vellet eadem cæcis aliis sui similibus explicare; & ut fidem apud eos haberet, uteretur similibus ex corporum palpatione (sibi omnibusque cæcis certo nota) desumtis. Quid, quæso, hoc eos juvaret, nisi ut se fe tutius deciperent? Namque quemadmodum corporis una pars, puta manus, ejusque officium palpandi, etsi sana sint, non tamen sequitur aliam corporis partem, puta oculos eorumque officium sana esse: sic quamvis una rationis functio, puta numeros, motus, quantitatem noscendi, sit sana satis; non sequitur tamen inde alias rationis functiones, puta functiones rerum tam spiritualium quam corporalium ideas, naturam, radices, ortus, augmenta, statumque intimum cognoscendi, sanas, & suum ad officium aptas esse. Imo & in ipsis mathematicis, principia maxima & minima omnis quanti, motus, ejusque celeritatis tarditatisque, linearum circularis & rectæ, earumque proportionum; ut & superficierum,
units.tr: Taken from mathematics, it is in vain that this is cited to prove that knowledge sought through reason is solid. For all who try to persuade themselves and others that they have ideas and knowledge of spiritual and bodily things from the faculty of reason are accustomed to appeal to the certainty and clarity of mathematics, as if they perceived those other things they treat of in the same way and with the same clarity. In this they seem to me to imitate our blind man, who, after hearing much about light and colours, and about how bodily shapes, motions and positions are distinguished by them, or after imagining much about this mode of perception, believed that he perceived these things himself, and wished to explain them to other blind men like himself. To win their belief, he would use comparisons drawn from the touching of bodies, which is certainly known to him and to all blind men. What, I ask, would this help them, except to deceive themselves more safely? For just as one part of the body, say the hand, and its function of touching, may be sound, it does not follow that another part, say the eyes and their function, is sound too. So although one function of reason, say that of knowing numbers, motions and quantity, is sound enough, it does not follow that the other functions of reason, namely those for knowing the ideas, nature, roots, origins, growth and inner state of things both spiritual and corporeal, are sound and fit for their task. Indeed, even in the mathematical sciences themselves, the principles of the maximum and minimum of every quantity, motion, and its speed and slowness, of circular and straight lines and their proportions, as also of surfaces and solids, transcend all the power of human reason and have no ideas; or if you wish to form some ideas of these, you could form diverse and contradictory ideas of one and the same thing, each of which you would prove to be true, although the contradiction persists.

units.la: & solidorum, omnem vim rationis humanæ transcendunt, nullasque habent ideas; aut si quasdam de his efformare voles, diversas easque contradictorias unius ejusdemque rei efformare possis, quarum unamquamque demonstrabis veram esse, non obstante contradictione persistente: v. g. lineas duas rectas concipies, quæ versus unam partem continuatæ sese interse cabunt, eædem in eodem situ & dispositione versus eandem partem continuatæ nunquam se interse-cabunt: spatium dari latitudine infinitum, per cujus latitudinis superficiem infinitam non posse tamen trajici linea: dari spatium infinitum quod sit media, vel quarta, vel alia quæcunque pars spatii finiti: & ejusmodi alia infinita ex consideratione divisionis & quanti oriunda. Si igitur in istiusmodi minusculis, ubi rei ad maxima & minima fit devolutio, humana ratio sibi, suis actibus atque ideis valedicere debeat, impotentiamque agnoscere propriam; quanto magis ipsa, omnisque ejus in ideis suis excitandis & compingendis labor, fructranei & ineapaces fuerint qui rerum tam spiritalium quam corporearum naturam solide, ex fundamento & a radice capiant, siquidem rerum principia quævis in se contineant, & maxima & minima: namque ea ex una parte, nihil creaturæ tangunt, ex alia vero, vel primum realitatis punctum, a Deo positum, continet effluxus, actus, repræsentationesque Omnipotentis perfectissimique & infiniti Creatoris; quæ qui sibi repræsentare poterit activus noster, & quod plus est, ægrotus intellectulus? ea siquidem solus Deus, qui se omnipotentem, infinitum agentemque infinite & omnipotenter novit, possit & cognoscere ipse, & vivida eorum vestigia Mentibus, passive sese coram illo habentibus, imprimere ubi placuerit. Ergo vel ex consideratione ipsius Mathesèos, quæ objecta fuerat, quæque rationi in omni objecto, quanto, motuque ea offert, quæ rationem transcendunt, discamus & ejusdem rationis in rebus naturæ solide cognoscendis ineptitudinem vel agnoscere, vel saltem suspicari.
units.tr: For example, you may conceive two straight lines which, when continued towards one side, will meet each other; yet the same lines, in the same position and arrangement, continued towards the same side, will never meet. You may conceive a space infinite in breadth, through whose infinite surface a line nevertheless cannot be drawn; or an infinite space which is a half, or a quarter, or any other part of a finite space; and other such infinities arising from the consideration of division and quantity. If therefore in such trifling matters, where a thing is reduced to maxima and minima, human reason must bid farewell to itself, its acts and its ideas, and acknowledge its own impotence, how much more fruitless and incapable will all its labour be in exciting and framing ideas of those who would grasp the nature of spiritual and corporeal things solidly, from the foundation and from the root! For the principles of things contain in themselves both maxima and minima. On the one hand these touch nothing of the creature; on the other, the first point of reality, placed by God, contains the outflows, acts and representations of the Omnipotent, most perfect and infinite Creator. Who, then, will be able to represent these to himself, our active and, what is more, sick little intellect? Indeed God alone, who knows himself as omnipotent and infinite, and as acting infinitely and omnipotently, can know them himself and impress their living traces on minds that stand passively before him, wherever he pleases. Therefore, either from the consideration of mathematics itself, which was the objection, and which offers reason, in every object of quantity and motion, things that transcend reason, let us learn to acknowledge, or at least to suspect, the ineptitude of that same reason for knowing the nature of things solidly.

units.la: XVIII. Quod tertiò objiciebatur supra, aut ex æquivocatione est; aut eis non opponitur quæ propòsui. Nàm quando vel ab omnibus passim, vel etiam in sacris, & a multis quoque sanctis scriptoribus commendatur ratio; ii per rationem non intelligunt facultatem sive intellectum illum activum, ideas ratiociniaque sibi de rebus excitantem, eumque qualem habemus imperfectissimum; sed intelligunt vel donum intelligentiæ sapientiæ que; vel discretionem ac prudentiam; vel justitiam æquitatemque; vel causam rei cuiusque sufficientem; vel etiam (uti apud Joannem) ipsum Dei verbum quod λόγος, hoc est, ratio appellatur. Primo sensu dicit Paulus (a) cultum nostrum divinum debere esse rationalem, hoc est, non ex humanæ rationis facultate, sed ex spiritu intelligentiæ & sapientiæ proficisci: Altero dicunt sanctiores, eorum qui ad Deum adspirant vitam, non affectibus etiam spiritualibus, sed ratione, hoc est, prudentiâ & discretione, esse moderandam: Tertio ab omnibus dicitur, Deum sine ratione, hoc est, sine justitia & æquitate, nil agere; non autem sine facultate humanæ rationis, quod absurdum esset: ita solemus ab iis quibuscum nobis res est postulare, quam rationem habuerint hoc vel illud agendi? quod non significat, quem intellectum activum habuerint hoc agendi? (absurdum id esset,) sed qua æquitate tale quid patraverint? Quarto sensu passim asseverant, nil, nullum in natura motum, effectum, casum sua ratione carere; omnia suam habere rationem, hoc est, causam; non autem omnia habere rationis facultatem. Denique quando Johannes τὸν λόγον dicit Deum esse, clarius est quam ut credatur hoc ad facultatem rationis humanæ pertinere. Ita ut istiusmodi quintuplex rationis allegatio & commendatio nil pro commendatione universali humanæ rationis faciat, ac proinde nil contra nos de intellectu activo, eoque corrupto, atque adeo de ratione in sexto quodam sensu, eoque communiore, agentes. Quod si nonnullis accideriht facultatem humanæ rationis intelligere dum rationem commendarent; tunc eam ut Deo passive subjectam considerant, ut a Deo illuminatam; Dei auxilio singulari de sua activitate disponentem, tum ad propriæ pigritiæ impugnationem, tum ut aliis aliquatenus possit esse auxilio: qualem statum usumquè rationis tantum abest ut hic impugnem, ut potius, is ut bene restituatur in integrum, ideo rationis morbosas dispodispositiones in medium protulerim, quò ab eis caveatur, nec sidatur ægro quamdiu morbo infectus est. Sed & ægræ rationi, quod plus est, exercitium aliquod tutum, actusque falsi non suspectos tribuerim, quando nempe illa ad hoc laborat ut se ægritudinis & corruptionis atque impotentiæ convincat: nam etsi ea convictio non possit rectè persecteque fieri nisi divino lumine, neque adeo ipsa ratio, nisi imperfectè admodum, id facere possit; quia tamen verum est eam in corruptione esse, sequitur eandem dum sic se exercet, ( præterquam quod a Deo tunc adjuvetur) in elemento veri esse; haud aliter atque mendax & improbus aliquis, qui diceret se esse mendacem, sibique non esse fidendum, hac demum in re fide dignus esset habendus. Atque id genus argumenti, quo quis suo ipsius gladio conficitur, censetur omnium efficacissimum: nam si quis sine ratione aut irrationabiliter, rationem impugnaret, profecto haud putaretur multum curandus: sed quod rationem per rationem impotentiæ convincat, id demum valere censendum est.
units.tr: XVIII. What was objected thirdly above is either an equivocation or is not opposed to what I propose. For when reason is commended everywhere, and even in sacred writings and by many holy writers, they do not mean by reason that active faculty or intellect which excites ideas and reasonings about things for itself, and which we have in its most imperfect form; they mean either the gift of understanding and wisdom, or discretion and prudence, or justice and equity, or the sufficient cause of any thing, or even (as in John) the Word of God itself, which is called the Word [λόγος], that is, reason. In the first sense Paul says that our divine worship ought to be rational, that is, to proceed not from the faculty of human reason but from the spirit of understanding and wisdom. In the second sense the more holy say that the life of those who aspire to God is to be governed not only by spiritual affections but by reason, that is, by prudence and discretion. In the third sense it is said by all that God does nothing without reason, that is, without justice and equity, though not without the faculty of human reason, which would be absurd. Thus we usually ask those with whom we have dealings what reason they had for doing this or that; which does not mean what active intellect they had for doing it (that would be absurd), but with what equity they carried out such a thing. In the fourth sense they assert everywhere that nothing, no motion, effect or chance in nature, lacks its reason; all things have their reason, that is, their cause, not that all things have the faculty of reason. Finally, when John says that God is the Word [τὸν λόγον], it is too clear to be believed that this pertains to the faculty of human reason. Thus this fivefold allegation and commendation of reason does nothing for a universal commendation of human reason, and therefore nothing against us who speak of the active intellect, and that corrupted, and so of reason in a certain sixth sense, a more common one. But if some, while they commended reason, happened to mean the faculty of human reason, then they consider it as passively subject to God, as illuminated by God, and as disposing its own activity by God's singular help, both for combating its own laziness and so that it may in some measure be of help to others. Such a state and use of reason I am so far from attacking here that, on the contrary, so that it may be well restored to its integrity, I have brought forward the morbid dispositions of reason, so that one may be warned against them and not trust the sick man as long as he is infected by the disease. But I would also grant to sick reason some safe exercise, and acts not open to suspicion of falsehood, namely when it labours to convince itself of its sickness, corruption and impotence. For although that conviction cannot be rightly and perfectly made except by divine light, nor can reason itself do this except very imperfectly, yet because it is true that reason is in corruption, it follows that while it so exercises itself (besides being helped by God then) it is in the element of truth. Just as a liar and a wicked man who said that he was a liar and not to be trusted would, in this very matter, be deemed worthy of belief. And this kind of argument, by which someone is overcome with his own sword, is judged the most effective of all. For if someone attacked reason without reason, or irrationally, he would certainly not be thought worth much concern; but that which convicts reason of impotence by reason, that is what is to be judged valid.

units.la: XIX. Et hoc modo isti sophismati, Rationem semper validam esse, quia id non sine ratione ostenditur, in se ipsum est retorquendum: Idea enim quia per rationem ostenditur eam esse in divinis & quibusvis solidis impotentem, ideo, inquam, illi in istis non esse fidendum sequitur. Ne dicam (ut alibi ostendi) hoc sophisma, quod omnium fere mentibus obvium est, æquivocatione vocis ratio modò expositá,
units.tr: XIX. And in this way the sophism Reason is always valid, because this is shown not without reason must be turned back upon itself. For since it is shown through reason that reason is powerless in divine matters and in all solid matters, it follows, I say, that reason is not to be trusted in these matters. Not to say (as I have shown elsewhere) that this sophism, which is almost obvious to everyone's mind, labours under an equivocation in the word "reason", as has now been explained.

units.la: Sophismata vulgaria tum pro rationis validitate, tum pro rationis solvi tur. posita, laborare. Namque quando dicunt, Qui vult rationem impugnare, id facit aut cum ratione, aut sine ratione. Si sine ratione, est absurdus. Si cum ratione, ergo ratio semper obtinet: in argumenti hujus conclusione vox ratio significat intellectus activi facultatem, in omnibus sese miscentem, siquidem conclusionis vis & sensus sic debet esse, Ergo ratio, sive facultas intellectus activi semper obtinet. In praemissis autem eadem vox ratio significat jus, causam sufficientem, fundamentum solidum, ut patet. Qui vult rationem (intellectum activum) impugnare, id facit aut cum ratione, hoc est, jure, cum fundamento & causa sufficiente; aut sine ratione, seu sine causa & fundamento solido. Et sic nihil sequitur. Adde enim assumtum eodem sensu: Si cum ratione, si cum fundamento & jure: Ergo ratio, intellectus activus, obtinet, non sequitur: sequeretur potius contrarium; & sunt quatuor termini si syllogismus ad formam reducatur hoc modo: Cum ratione agere, est facere ut obtineat ratio. Atqui rationem impugnare est cum ratione agere. Ergo, rationem impugnare est facere ut obtineat ratio.
units.tr: The common sophisms, both for the validity of reason and for its refutation, are solved. For when they say, Whoever wishes to attack reason does so either with reason or without reason. If without reason, he is absurd. If with reason, then reason always prevails, in the conclusion of this argument the word "reason" means the faculty of the active intellect, which mingles itself in all things, since the force and sense of the conclusion must be this: Therefore reason, that is, the faculty of the active intellect, always prevails. In the premises, however, the same word "reason" means right, a sufficient cause, a solid foundation, as is plain. Whoever wishes to attack reason (the active intellect) does so either with reason, that is, with right, with a foundation and a sufficient cause; or without reason, that is, without cause and solid foundation. And so nothing follows. For add the assumption in the same sense: If with reason, that is, with a foundation and right: therefore reason, the active intellect, prevails. It does not follow; rather the contrary would follow. And if the syllogism is reduced to form in this way, there are four terms: To act with reason is to bring it about that reason prevails. But to attack reason is to act with reason. Therefore, to attack reason is to bring it about that reason prevails.

units.la: Homonymia sublata, syllogismus per propositiones sic resolvendus est: - Cum ratione, JURE, CAUSSA & FUNDAMENTO SUFFICIENTE agere, est facere ut ratio, MODUS AGENDI CUM JURE & CAUSSA SUFFICIENTE, obtineat. (talis debet esse redditio secundi membri, aliàs. alijs & negaretur propositio, quod scil. cum jure agere idem fit, ac activitatem intellectus in omnibus flatuminare) & nihilominus quatuor essent semper termini.)
units.tr: With the ambiguity removed, the syllogism must be resolved through its propositions as follows: To act with reason, that is, with right, cause and sufficient foundation, is to bring it about that the mode of acting with right and sufficient cause prevails. (The second member must be rendered in this way; otherwise the proposition would be denied in another sense, namely that to act with right is the same as to set the activity of the intellect above all things; and nonetheless there would always be four terms.)

units.la: Atqui rationem, INTELLECTUS ACTIVITATEM impugnare, est cum ratione, INTELLECTUS ACTIVITATE agere.
units.tr: But to attack reason, that is, the activity of the intellect, is to act with reason, that is, with the activity of the intellect.

units.la: Ergo, rationem, intellectus, activitatem, impugnare; est facere ut ratio, activitas intellectus, obtineat.
units.tr: Therefore, to attack reason, that is, the activity of the intellect, is to bring it about that reason, the activity of the intellect, prevails.

units.la: Nemo non videt hic esse quatuor terminos, nempe in majore: 1. cum ratione & jure agere. 2. facere ut ratio & jus obtineat, vel ut facultas seu activitas rationis obtineat in minore: 3 rationem, seu intellectus activitatem impugnare. 4. cum ratione vel intellectus activitate agere: qui si sint evitandi, & vox ratio in duabus praemissis aliter resolvenda ac hic, propositiones statim poterunt negari, & conclusio nil efficiet, ut tentanti patebit.
units.tr: Everyone sees that there are four terms here: in the major premise, (1) to act with reason and right, and (2) to bring it about that reason and right prevail, or that the faculty or activity of reason prevails; in the minor, (3) to attack reason, or the activity of the intellect, and (4) to act with reason or the activity of the intellect. If these are to be avoided, and the word ratio in the two premises is resolved otherwise than here, the propositions can at once be denied, and the conclusion will achieve nothing, as anyone who tries will see.

units.la: Non crediderim necessarium esse ut principia data applicem aliis sophismatibus vendis, veluti cum dicunt nonnulli, Nulla posse capi, ne quidem quae de fide divina sunt, nisi per rationem, eamque humanam; siquidem nec bruta simus irrationalia, nec angeli, aut facultatibus Angelicis gaudentes. Verum est, nulla, neque etiam divina, capi posse nisi ratione eâ quae intelligentia est: verum haec passive sese habentes coram Deo eam illuminante (unde divina dicitur) sine activitate propria infinities plus de divinis & creatis capere potest, quam intelleƨus actiuus industria, labore & actiuitate mera humana & ægra capere possit: quapropter si illeper rationis vocem intelligatur quando instatur, nil nos capere posse nisi per rationem humanam, salsissima hæc est propositio atque plane neganda: siquidem potius per rationem humanam, siue per intellectum actiuum, nil possimus capere solide; sed imperfectissime, superficiarieque tantùm, ut ostensum est. Quæ omnia quia (a) aliis in locis pluribus explicui; pergo ad obiectionem ultimam.
units.tr: I would not think it necessary to apply the principles given here to other sophisms, such as when some say: nothing can be grasped, not even what concerns divine faith, except through reason, and human reason at that, since we are neither brute beasts without reason nor angels, nor endowed with angelic faculties. It is true that nothing, not even divine things, can be grasped except by that reason which is understanding. But these, passively disposed before God illuminating them (whence they are called divine), without their own activity can grasp infinitely more of divine and created things than the active intellect can grasp by its own industry, labour and purely human and feeble activity. Therefore if by the term "reason" is understood, when it is pressed, that we can grasp nothing except through human reason, this proposition is most false and must plainly be denied. For rather, through human reason, or the active intellect, we can grasp nothing solidly, but only most imperfectly and superficially, as has been shown. Since I have explained all these things in several other places, I proceed to the last objection.

units.la: XX. Ea erat; rationis vsum, scopum- que, ad quem dedit illam Deus, nullos posse statui, si quæ diximus ad deprimendam ra- tionem, valere deberent.
units.tr: XX. The objection was this: no use of reason, nor the purpose for which God gave it, could be established, if what we have said to depress reason were to hold good.

units.la: Quasi vero nullus alius Rationis vsus esset scopusve, quam is quem isti Rationalistæ proponunt, dum actiua illa atque desultoria facultate, neglectis superioribus, omnia diuina naturaliaque perreptare, scrutari, detegere, ac iudicio eius subiicere volunt; qui non vsus, sed abusus dignus est. Homo ægrotus membrorum suorum meliorem vsum habere non potest, quam si quiescat, si actiuitati suæ ad tempus renunciet, permittatque se alterius regimini donec sit sanus. Talem sui vsum agnoscat & in praxin deducat ratio, quæ vbi sana erit, tunc videbit quo scopo a Deo sit data, quomodoque semet ipsa vti debeat: imo dum sanari incipiet, incipiet & paulatim detegere verum sui vsum, regulasque ipsi obseruandas ne exorbitet. Harum quasdam diximus superius: alias in aliis operibus ubi de Ratione agebatur. Eas hic repetere non est necesse: sed ut uno verbo omnes complectamur, dicimus: Rationem non debere æterna & facultates superiores, resque agendas, sui exercendi gratia sic negligere, ut proportio inter æternas realitates & evanescentes exercitationes violetur; neque etiam ob aliud nec ad aliud quam ob & ad Deum quicquam incipere & finire. Ostendimus insuper, rationem esse datam ad felicitatem hominis accessoriam, dum ea magnalium Dei picturas ad ejus admirationem & laudem efformat; nec non quoque (quod supra tetigimus,) ut absentium rerum atque objectorum, quibus, (dimissis quæ nos tunc occupant,) applicari debemus, vices per ideas suas teneret, memoriamque eorum nobis imprimeret: Quæ omnia sane non sunt usum rationis tollere, uti objectantes pertimescebant.
units.tr: As if there were no other use or purpose of reason than the one these Rationalists propose, when with that active and restless faculty, neglecting the higher things, they want to range over, search out, uncover and subject to their judgement all divine and natural things. That is not a use but an abuse. A sick man cannot have a better use of his limbs than to lie still, to renounce his activity for a time and to allow himself to be governed by another until he is healthy. Reason should recognise such a use of itself and put it into practice. When it is sound, it will then see for what purpose God gave it and how it ought to use itself. Indeed, as it begins to be healed, it will gradually begin to discover the true use of itself and the rules to be observed so that it does not go astray. We have stated some of these above and others in other works where we treated of reason. There is no need to repeat them here, but to embrace them all in one word, we say: reason ought not to neglect eternal things and higher faculties and the matters to be done, for the sake of exercising itself, in such a way that the proportion between eternal realities and passing activities is violated; nor should it begin and end anything for any other purpose than for God and toward God. We have shown further that reason is given to man as an auxiliary to happiness, while it forms pictures of God's great works for his admiration and praise; and also (as we touched on above) that it holds the place, through its ideas, of absent things and objects, to which we ought to apply ourselves (setting aside what then occupies us), and imprints their memory upon us. None of these things indeed takes away the use of reason, as the objectors feared.

units.la: At quoniam ad acquisitionem eruditionis non superficiariæ modò, verùm etiam illius quæ solida est, ratio debet ordinariò intervenire, inservitque illi communicandæ, hunc usum ejus paucis ut exponam operæ pretium est.
units.tr: But since for the acquisition of erudition, not only superficial but also that which is solid, reason must ordinarily intervene and serve to communicate it, it is worth setting out briefly this use of it.

units.la: XXI. Homines cùm ex infantia emergunt, paulatimque adolescunt; sunt etiam paulatim, quantum ejus sunt capaces, æternitati divinisque; nec non humanis necessariis præparandi: Verùm quia nostri ortus ea est miseria eaque corruptio, ut omnia perversa sint, hinc in erudiendis facultatibus verus naturalisque dignitatis ordo, qui esset inci-
units.tr: XXI. When men emerge from infancy and gradually grow up, they are also gradually to be prepared, as far as they are capable, for eternity and divine things, as well as for the necessary human matters. But because of the misery and corruption of our birth, by which all things have become perverse, the true and natural order of dignity in training the faculties, which would be to begin with the highest faculties and descend to the lowest, is also inverted and cannot be observed,

units.la: (a) Cog. Rat. disc. part. anic. 76. ad 80. Occ. de la Creation. ch. xi. §. 13.
units.tr: (a) Cog. Rat. disc. part. anic. 76. ad 80. Occ. de la Creation. ch. xi. §. 13.

units.la: incipere a facultatibus summis, & descendere ad infimas, etiam inversus est, nec observari potest, siquidem infantes facultatum digniorum usui & regimini sunt impares, aptiores autem ad ea quæ facultates inferiores concernunt, a quibus ad imaginationem, ex hac ad rationem, denique ex ratione ad divinas superioresque facultates cum procedat eorum maturatio, eodem quoque ordine cum illis agendum est: non quòd ubi imaginationis rationisque ipsi capaces fiunt, non sint eorum superiores facultates excitandæ, nec exercendæ; ( possunt enim omnia simul excitari, uti etiam eò tendunt & a Deo disponuntur) ; sed quòd crassiora & inferiora tunc sic prævaleant superioribus, ut ea veluti obtegant, nec detur ad hæc aditus nisi per ista crassamina.
units.tr: since infants are unfit for the use and direction of the more worthy faculties, and are more apt for those things which concern the lower faculties. From these, as their maturing proceeds, they advance to imagination, from imagination to reason, and finally from reason to the divine and higher faculties; and in this same order we must also deal with them. Not that when they become capable of imagination and reason their higher faculties should not be aroused and exercised (for all of them can be aroused at once, as indeed they tend and are disposed by God), but that the cruder and lower faculties then so prevail over the higher that they, as it were, cover them over, and no access to the higher is given except through those coarser things.

units.la: Igitur quemadmodum optimum est, verbis, imaginibus aliisque quæ imaginationis sunt, eos sic allicere, ut eorum desiderium atque acquiescentia ( intellectus enim cum istis imaginatis haud ita convenit, ) excitentur ad bona originaria & permanentia; sic eorum, quantum per ætatem permittitur, ratio paulatim ita colenda, ut in ea ideæ de æternis, divinis, spiritualibus sanctisque rebus excitentur, earumque nexus & sequela, quantum potest, ostendantur, nec non ut officia ad quæ, ex rebus, per ideas istas repræsentatis tenemur, simul proponantur & consideranda exhibeantur.
units.tr: Therefore, just as it is best to attract them by words, images and other things belonging to the imagination, so that their desire and assent are stirred (for the intellect does not agree so well with these imaginings) toward original and abiding goods, so their reason, as far as age permits, is to be cultivated gradually, so that ideas of eternal, divine, spiritual and holy things are aroused in it, and their connection and sequence are shown as far as possible; and the duties to which we are bound by the things represented through those ideas are set forth at the same time and presented for consideration.

units.la: Addenda tamen hic duo perquam necessaria monita. Primum, ista omnia, prout a nobis concipiuntur, non res ipsas esse; sed earum picturas umbratiles, mortuas, steriles, nec ullo modo animam illuminantes, satiantes, ditantes, verosolidoque bono implentes; sed potius, nisi ab illis ad res ipsas, sive ad Deum, omnium luminum bonorumque solidorum fontem & dispensatorem unicum, convertamur, ab illo rerum suarum substantiam petituri & exspectaturi, nos ex ideis nostris ratioque circa illas occupata, evasuros & pejores, ob culpam neglecti officii; & miseriores, ob poenam vacuitatemque animae, a divina justitia bonorum quae non desideravit copia privandae.
units.tr: Two very necessary warnings must be added here. First, all these things, as we conceive them, are not the things themselves. They are shadowy, dead, barren pictures of them, which by no means illuminate, satisfy or enrich the soul or fill it with true and solid good. Rather, unless we turn from them to the things themselves, that is, to God, the sole fount and dispenser of all lights and solid goods, seeking and expecting from him the substance of his creatures, we will come out of our ideas and of the reasoning we have spent on them worse, through the fault of neglected duty, and more wretched, through the punishment and emptiness of the soul, to be deprived by divine justice of the abundance of goods it did not desire.

units.la: Alterum eis inculcandum, illud est: ideas nostras in elemento suo consideratas, hoc est, quatenus cum rebus ipsis non confunduntur, sed ut picturae saltem umbratiles, quales vere sunt, habentur; non tamen picturas tales esse, quae res exacte repraesentent, aut quae persectiones illas habeant quas tanquam picturae & naturae suae congruas possent habere, idque ex depravata nostra origine & nativitate esse, nec emendari utcunque posse nisi auxilio tum divino, precibus implorando; tum humano, eorum in quibus haec magis quam in nobis correcta sunt.
units.tr: The second point to be impressed upon them is this.
