Our ideas, considered in their own element, that is, insofar as they are not confused with the things themselves but are held to be only shadowy pictures, as they truly are, are not pictures that represent things exactly, or that have those perfections which, as pictures and in keeping with their nature, they could have. This comes from our depraved origin and birth, and they can be corrected in no way except by the help of the divine, to be implored in prayer, and of the human, from those in whom these things are more correctly ordered than in ourselves.

units.la: Duarum istarum observationum ope, si ex non negligantur, hoc consequentur adolescentes rationi exercendae vacantes, nempe, ne ex ideis quas acquirunt, actibusque propriis circa illas, fiant tumidi (quasi qui res solidas haberent,) nec pervicaces (quasi eorum pictae ideae, ut ut bellae, defectibus omnibus bus carerent, nec quicquam eis accederé posset, ) nec impii, a Deo evanescentes, & tandem æternùm miseri : quod acciderét fi ideis & rationis exercitio sicco unice inhærerent, non remeando ab umbris illis ad res rerumque Auctorem, scopum unum creationis nostræ & omnium quibus fumus præditi. Ita pro superba, obstinata, frigida, atque impia opinionibus & judiciis propriis adhæfione, ( quæ universalia eruditorum seculi vitia sunt cum iis a pueritia inolita ) acquiret juventus cum cultura & augmento rationis animum docilem, humilem, atque pietate imbutum non fucatâ, quæ quidem ad omnia, teste Paulo, atque adeo ad eruditionem solidam acquirendam, utilis futura est.
units.tr: If these two observations are not neglected, young people devoted to exercising their reason will gain the following: they will not become puffed up by the ideas they acquire and their own acts concerning them, as if they possessed solid things; nor obstinate, as if their painted ideas, however fine, lacked all defects and nothing could be added to them; nor impious, falling away from God and at last eternally wretched. That would happen if they clung only to ideas and to a dry exercise of reason, not returning from those shadows to things and to the Author of things, the one goal of our creation and of everything with which we are endowed. Thus, instead of a proud, obstinate, cold and impious adherence to their own opinions and judgments (which are the universal vices of the learned of this age, ingrained from childhood), the youth will, through the cultivation and growth of reason, acquire a mind that is teachable, humble and imbued with unfeigned piety. This piety, as Paul witnesses, is profitable for all things, and so for acquiring solid erudition.

units.la: Tales qui du&ores ab adolescentia aut a primis annis habent, possunt rationis cultura hac ad omne bonum verumque adjuvari excellentius quam dici possit. Qui vero iis destituuntur, insuperque per eos qui contrariis modis agunt educantur, non videntur rationis animæque perniciem, nisi per quoddam miraculi genus evitare posse; cum infinities difficilius fit, Mentem, quando a pravis præceptoribus obsidetur, ad veram eruditionem per rectum rationis usum, eis ignoratum, disponi, quam si sola esset, atque sibi permissa sibi soli attenderet. Namque etsi corruptione naturæ simus ab ortu propensi ad omne malum, nec non ad omnem errorem pravis nostris propensionibus propitium & faventem; is tamen a quo & ob quem conditi sumus boni verique solidi fons, qui sibi suisque donis animæ nostræ interiora ac facultates diviniores tanquam habitacula condidit, ab intimo mentium centro, ubi cœcis nobis occultissimus adest, pellit radiis & motibus nonnullis (qui naturalia veri, boni, justique principia dicuntur) mentem ad ea, quæ si fideliter obiret, illam, præter cætera solida, etiam docerent rectum in omnibus rationis usum, idque multo melius quam omnes possint externi institutores: quod vel in Ethnico Socrate videre est, cujus præpositis prohibebatur ne eum reprehenderent vel informarent; habere enim eum in se præceptorem omnibus præstantiorem institutoribus: qui certe ubi inepti sunt (quæ maxima turba est) nil aliud agunt suâ curâ, quam ut Dei pulsus in illis quos ipsi instituunt supprimant, & cassos reddant; tum teneras mentes (quod nunquam satis deplorari potest) a divinis illis dictaminibus & attractibus ad evanida sua nugamenta, tanquam ad res serias solidasque, sic alliciunt iisdemque affigunt, ut laudibus maximis, quando nugis istis tenaciter adhærescunt, eos tumefaciant; vituperiis autem vel etiam pœnis, ubi morem non gesserint, inculcent vividius rem maximi momenti esse negledam. Sed de hisce jam agere nolim, quæ falsæ eruditionis potius sunt quam superficiariæ. Si qui autem sint quibus cum istiusmodi quidem pædagogis conflictandum non sit, sed qui tamen nec bonos habeant ductores, cupiantque nihilominus rationis facultatem non relinquere incultam, iis nihil potest esse convenientius, quam ut intima sua Deo offerant eo modo, quem in primo libro tractatus hujusce exposuimus. Is enim postea movebit ducetque mentem ad ea omnia, etiamque ubi opus erit, ad rationem scientiasque concernentia, quæ Menti necessaria & proficua poterunt esse: Alias quisquis ex sui ipsius scopo vano corruptoque rationem suam in his volet dirigere, seseque prout videbitur ideis scientiisque hujus aut istius generis pluribus paucioribusve applicare & exercere; is nec modum nec usum rectum in iis poterit tenere; & ex superficiaria eruditione ( siquidem illam etiam obtinere queat ) ad falsam indubitanter præceps ruiturus est.
units.tr: Those who have such guides from adolescence or from their earliest years can be helped toward every good and true thing by this cultivation of reason more excellently than can be said. But those who lack them, and who are besides brought up by those who act in contrary ways, seem unable to avoid the ruin of their reason and soul except by some kind of miracle. It is infinitely harder for a mind besieged by wicked teachers to be disposed toward true erudition through the right use of reason, which is unknown to them, than if it were alone and left to itself, attending only to itself. For although by the corruption of nature we are born inclined to every evil and to every error that our wicked propensities favour and promote, yet he from whom and for whom we were made, the fount of true and solid good, who established the inner parts and more divine faculties of our soul as his own dwelling places and gifts, drives the mind from the innermost centre of minds, where he is most hidden yet present to our blind eyes, by certain rays and motions (called the natural principles of the true, the good and the just) toward those things which, if it faithfully performed them, would teach it, besides other solid matters, the right use of reason in all things, and far better than all external instructors could. This can be seen even in the pagan Socrates, whose superiors forbade anyone to reprove or instruct him, since he had within himself a teacher better than all instructors. Certainly those instructors, when they are foolish (and this is the greatest crowd), do nothing by their care except suppress the promptings of God in those they teach and render them void. Then they lure tender minds, which can never be lamented enough, away from those divine dictates and attractions to their own vanishing trifles, as if these were serious and solid things, and fasten the minds to them. So when the pupils cling stubbornly to these trifles, the teachers puff them up with the greatest praises, but where they have not complied, they inculcate with blame or even punishment that it is a matter of the greatest moment to be neglected. But I would not now treat of these things, which belong rather to false erudition than to superficial erudition. If, however, there are some who need not struggle with such teachers, yet have no good guides and nonetheless desire not to leave their faculty of reason uncultivated, nothing can be more suitable for them than to offer their inmost selves to God in the way we set out in the first book of this treatise. For he will afterwards move and lead the mind to all those things, including, where needed, those concerning reason and the sciences, which can be necessary and profitable for the mind. Otherwise, whoever wishes, from his own vain and corrupt aim, to direct his reason in these matters, and to apply and exercise himself, as seems good to him, to more or fewer ideas and sciences of this or that kind, will be unable to keep the right measure or use in them, and will undoubtedly rush headlong from superficial erudition (if indeed he can attain even that) into false erudition.

units.la: Fateor id periculi utcunque evitari posse per eorum librorum lectionem, qui solidiora præcipuarum scientiarum fundamenta, principaliores queratione rationis & rerum ideas, veritates, leges, scopos solidos sinemque verum sic proponerent, ut hæc sufficerent rationi ipsorum qui ad potiora adspirant satis exercitandæ & ornandæ; nec diffiteor me in eis quæ hactenus edidi, id mihi pro scopo præscripsisse omnium quæ huc conferre possunt, sufficientem proponere veluti epitomen: At mentis ad Deum recursum istiusmodi medio non excludi, ut hic, sic & ibidem etiam non semel commonimus.
units.tr: I grant that this danger can somehow be avoided by reading those books which set out the more solid foundations of the principal sciences, the chief ideas, truths, laws, and solid goals and true end of reason and things, in such a way that these suffice to exercise and adorn the reason of those who aspire to higher things. Nor do I deny that in what I have hitherto published I set before myself as my aim to offer something sufficient, as an epitome, of all that can contribute to this. But the mind's recourse to God is not excluded by such a means, as we have warned here and elsewhere more than once.

units.la: XXII. Quemadmodum subjectum eruditionis superficiariæ vidimus rationem esse; ideas vero ratiocinioque ejus materiam; eandemque & tribus hisce acquiri: ita nequit etiam facile sine iisdem tribus communicari ab eo qui
units.tr: XXII. As we have seen that the subject of superficial erudition is reason, and its matter the ideas and their reasoning, and that it is acquired by these three, so it cannot easily be communicated without these same three by one who

units.la: 22. Superficiaria, viasque ad solidas, non nisi a solidis, vel ab eis qui soliqui illius aliis communicandæ capax est, sive hic superficiarius sit eruditus, sive solidus : solidi namque, ut in prima parte vidimus, & superficiaria veluti accessoria habent, ratio-nemque vel cæteris saniorem, uti accidit corporibus bene sanis, ut eorum superficies cutisque coloratior vividiorque cæteris sit. Et hi soli (quod vix crederetur) ipsam etiam superficiariam eruditionem recte communicare possent, quanquam abstineant, nisi quando via esse potest adjumentumque ad solida : & tunc quidem ex scopo non dicendi sunt superficiaria docere, sed ad solida per media externa auditores aptos adducere. Superficiarii autem, qui tantum superficiarii (quales sane adhuc valde rari sunt, ) si ipsi suam superficiariam ex solida quam olim habuerint, sed postmodum amiserint, non hauserunt, eidem communicandæ sunt omnimode inepti : nam ab illis facillime quicquid aliunde quam ex propria experientia hauserunt, pervertitur, & admissum falso in falsum degenerat. Putarent multi se affici injuria quam maxima, si eruditionem superficiariam possidere dicerentur. Atqui, nisi jam satis patet, ex mox dicendis animadvertat quivis, an inter quam plurimos vel paucissimi digni sint, qui hoc saltem superficiariæ elogio insigniantur. Procedit namque eruditio superficiaria, ut vera sit in suo genere, a solida, haud secus ac superficies a solido, & cutis bene disposita a bene disposito corpore. Quapropter etiamsi quis solide eruditum docentem audivisset, ejusque sermones sensusque, quantum in ratione humana repræsentari ideis possunt, percepisset, non tamen ideo capax esset eos aliis bene communicandi, nisi præcise iisdem verbis sese adstringeret; alioqui, quam primum ab illis (si alicujus momenti sint) recederet sub quocunque prætextu, veluti explicationis, paraphraseos, amplificationis, consequentiarum deducendarum, statim se exponeret periculo errandi, & alios in errorem ducendi. Namque is, dum resipsas intus (ut supponimus) non habet, sed tantum picturas earum ideales, his & istis verbis in illo excitatas & communicatas, si audeat eas aliis alia quadam facie conspiciendas dare, conjecturæ sunt ad minimum errori obnoxiæ, cum ipsi non liceat rem originemque, qua destituitur, ex omni parte consulere; neque adeo ex ea parte quam ex se ipso exprimere ausus est: unde non minus fallit quam sculptor, qui urbe aliqua a latere visa, planum ejus ex sua opinione & ratiocinatione describere tentaret. Quæ ratio est quare ii, qui sacra volumina ex originali idiomate in aliud interpretantur, nisi res ipsas divinas intus in se habeant, fidelius agunt quando prestius de verbo ad verbum transferunt, etsi id barbarius quoad stylum sonet, quam si dimissis verbis, secundum ideas quas putant verbis originalibus denotari, interpretationem suam accommodent; siquidem non possunt ideas suas cum rebus, si iisdem careant, comparare. Id non minus periculosum esse, cum non verba solum in alia verba transferenda, sed & res ipsas cum suis consequentiis ita tractare præsumunt, loquitur universa & lugubris experientia: hinc scilicet omnis in sacris calamitas, dum unusquisque e sacris literis res eas, quibus ipsus destituitur, alios tamen docere satagit; etsi Deus, quo huic malo iret obviam, videatur ideo sacrum codicem claudere solenni protestatione, qua plagae divinae & expunctio e libro vitae denunciantur illi, qui volumini sacro aliquid addiderit vel demserit: quod non solum ad additionem vel subtractionem verborum, sed & sensus, quando quis eum de suo addit vel tollit, extendendum est. Quin etiam tam exacte verum est, eum a cujus instructione ideae rerum exspectantur, debere res eas possidere, si velit suis uti verbis in earum expositione, ut quamvis aliquis res de quibus agitur divinas, v. g. quae Deum & coelestia respiciunt, possedisset & expertus esset; si tamen earumdem postea passus esset jacturam, non posset de iis debite loqui nisi quousque earum habuisset experientiam, cujus experientiae memoria ideas umbratiles in ratione excitaret eousque, nec ultra, nisi equidem vellet falli. Hinc est, quod Daemon, qui Deo coelestibus pulcritudinibus & bonis fruebatur antequam lapsus esset, non possit nunc illas enarrare, nisi quousque eas expertus, ab experientiae memoria ideas umbratiles, steriles sibi, efformare potest: illa vero, quorum nondum habebat experientiam, quaeque novafemper in aeternum in Deo sunt detegenda; nequaquam ita. Caute igitur non ex parte docentis solum, sed & ex parte discentium, ideasque rerum veras ab aliis accipere volentium, caute, inquam, admodum procedendum est, dispiciendumque omni cura, in errorem ni velimus induci, an qui rerum ideas nobis imprimere earumque naturas, proprietates, effecta explicare conantur, res originesque ipsas in se possideant, necne, aut quousque realitate ipsa imbuti inveniantur, & pro ratione suae hisce in rebus copiae vel inopiae, aures iis vel praebendae sunt vel denegandae.
units.tr: 22. Superficial knowledge, and the ways that lead to solid knowledge, can be communicated only by solid people, or by those who are capable of communicating that solid knowledge to others, whether the superficial person is learned or solid. For solid people, as we saw in the first part, also possess superficial knowledge as an accessory, and a judgement sounder than others', just as healthy bodies have a skin and surface more colourful and lively than others. These alone (which would hardly be believed) could rightly communicate superficial learning itself, though they refrain from it, unless it can serve as a way and an aid towards solid things. Then indeed they should not be said to teach superficial matters for their own sake, but to lead their hearers, by external means, towards solid things fit for them. But superficial people, who are merely superficial (of which kind there are indeed still very few), if they have not drawn their superficial knowledge from solid knowledge which they once had but afterwards lost, are wholly unfit to communicate it. For whatever they have drawn from elsewhere than their own experience is very easily perverted by them, and what they admit as false degenerates into falsehood. Many would think they were greatly wronged if they were said to possess superficial learning. Yet, unless it is already plain enough, anyone may judge from what is said presently whether very few or none among very many are worthy to be distinguished even by this title of superficial learning. For superficial learning proceeds, to be true in its kind, from solid learning, just as a surface comes from a solid body, and well-ordered skin from a well-ordered body. Therefore, even if someone had heard a solidly learned teacher and had grasped his words and meanings, as far as they can be represented to human reason by ideas, he would not for that reason be able to communicate them well to others, unless he bound himself precisely to the same words. Otherwise, as soon as he departed from them (if they are of any weight) under any pretext, such as explanation, paraphrase, amplification, or drawing out consequences, he would at once expose himself to the danger of erring and of leading others into error. For he, since he does not have the things themselves within him (as we suppose), but only their ideal pictures, aroused and communicated in him by these and those words, if he dares to set them before others in some other aspect, his conjectures are at least liable to error, since he is not permitted to consult the thing and its origin, of which he is destitute, on every side, nor indeed on that side which he has ventured to draw from himself. Hence he errs no less than a sculptor who, having seen one side of a city, tries to describe its plan from his own opinion and reasoning. This is why those who translate the sacred volumes from the original language into another act more faithfully, unless they have the divine things themselves within them, when they render word for word, though this sounds more barbarous in style, than if, dismissing the words, they adapt their translation to the ideas which they think the original words denote. For they cannot compare their ideas with the things, if they lack them. That this is no less dangerous, when men presume to handle not only words to be rendered into other words, but the things themselves with their consequences, is attested by universal and lamentable experience. Hence comes every calamity in sacred matters, when each man, from the sacred letters, strives to teach others those very things of which he himself is destitute. God, to meet this evil, seems therefore to close the sacred book with a solemn protestation, by which plagues and erasure from the book of life are denounced against whoever adds anything to the sacred volume or takes anything away. This must be extended not only to the addition or subtraction of words, but also of meaning, when someone adds or removes it from his own mind. Indeed it is so exactly true that the one from whose instruction ideas of things are expected must possess those things, if he wishes to use his own words in expounding them, that although someone had possessed and experienced divine things, for example those which concern God and heavenly things, yet if he afterwards suffered their loss, he could not speak of them properly except so far as he had experience of them. The memory of that experience would stir up in his reason shadowy ideas only so far, and no further, unless he wished indeed to be deceived. Hence the Devil, who enjoyed the heavenly beauties and goods of God before he fell, cannot now recount them, except so far as, having experienced them, he can form for himself from the memory of experience shadowy ideas, which are barren to him. But of those things of which he had no experience, and which are always to be newly discovered in God for ever, he cannot speak at all. Therefore one must proceed with great caution, not only on the part of the teacher, but also on the part of the learners who wish to receive true ideas of things from others. With great caution, I say, and with every care, one must examine, lest we be led into error, whether those who try to impress upon us ideas of things and to explain their natures, properties and effects possess the things and their origins themselves, or not, or how far they are found imbued with the reality itself. According to their store or lack of this in these matters, ears are to be either lent to them or refused.

units.la: XXIII. Ponamus jam, si placet, ad ex- hibendam eruditionis superficiariae ideam ex- actissimam pleniss imamque; ponamus, in-
units.tr: XXIII. Let us now, if you please, set out the most exact and most complete idea of superficial erudition. Let us suppose, I say,

units.la: quam, aliquem ex illuminatissimis de coelo Angelis ad homines descendere, omnia eos quae tenet edocturum, quiquae ea propter vocce aut scriptis quam exactissime ab Angelica industria atque dexteritate fieri potest, omnia iis, quae de Deo, deque rebus divinis & spiritualibus omnibus, de natura spirituali, corporea, humana, deque toto universo sciri & exprimi possunt, describat. Itaque si quis hominum ex desiderio sciendi ista, eis attendat, horum omnium ideas exactissimas verbis Angeli praecise respondentes in ratione sua excitet, atque adeo omnium quae Angelus verbis detexit idealem & cogitaris Angeli conformem habeat notitiam, nec tamen se, etsi bono scopo his vacare inceperit, elevet inde ad Deum, ab eo desideraturus ut is res ipsas, harumve originantes virtutes in facultates suas passivas vivido lumine suo infundat; neque etiam fungatur officiis, quibus ex amplissima exactissimaque sua ideali scientia
units.tr: that one of the most enlightened Angels from heaven comes down to men, to teach them everything he knows, and describes, by word of mouth or in writing, as exactly as Angelic diligence and skill can manage, everything that can be known and expressed about God and all divine and spiritual things, about spiritual, bodily and human nature, and about the whole universe. Suppose that someone among men, from a desire to know these things, attends to him, and arouses in his own mind the most exact ideas of all of them, corresponding precisely to the Angel's words, so that he has an ideal knowledge of everything the Angel disclosed in words, conformed to the Angel's own thought. Suppose further that he does not, although he has begun this with a good purpose, raise himself from it to God, to ask of him that God pour the things themselves, or the powers that originate them, into his passive faculties with his living light. Suppose too that he does not perform the duties which, from his most ample and exact ideal knowledge,

units.la: Exactius offenditur quid sit Eruditio superficiaria, ejus amplitudo, raritas, ejusdemque vanitas. itia videt sese erga Deum, erga proximos, creaturas cæteras seque teneri; sed tantummodo in bellissima illa rerum divinarum, naturaliumque consideratione ideali subsistat: is demum agnoscendus est verus eruditionis superficiariæ possessor, eruditique superficiarii axiomate demum dignus. Ecce, hæc vere est superficiaria eruditio in purissimis suis essentialibus, veróque ac proprio gradu & statu: qui infra sunt, nondum eousque attigerunt, ii, si quid sint non pudeat eos fateri, ignorantes plus minusve, aut etiam errantes ex sincera conscientia, palam sese profiteri debebunt, id quod etiam doctiores fecere, exclamantes, Quantum est quod nescimus! quod idem est ac si dicerent: Vah quanti quanti sumus adhuc reipsa idiotæ & ignorantes. Imo ô mortales! ô eruditorum gens! rationi qui uni formandæ totos vos devovistis quo eruditionis titulo possetis vere celebrari! si sciretis quam onerosam atque impostabilem, quamque ventosam simul & inanem sarcinam humeris vestris imposuistis, non esset sane unde vobis de studiis vestris facile intus applauderetis, & multum in sinu gauderetis: siquidem post immensos rationis labores, vix uni e mille datur ad millesimam eruditionis superficiariæ partem attingere. Et quamvis miraculi instar ad plenitudinem ejus aliquis sic perveniret ut vel Angelus illius rationem ulterius polire atque erudire non possit; tunc demum, si in istis maneat terminis, erit is qui splendidius & via tutiore, clarius & distinctius ad inferos mortalitate pereunte descendat, sui ipsius superba admiratione & complacentiæ fermento turgidus, Deo ejusque amore sive charitate vacuus. Nec ego is sum qui ista effingam & temere in medium proferam. Dei ipsius est isthæc sententia, Paulino calamo ita expressa: (a) Si linguis hominum loquar & Angelorum, charitatem autem (sive Amorem Dei, hoc est, traditionem animæ facultatumque intellectus, cordis, virium, cogitationum, quibus totis vult Deus amari) non habuero, factus sum velut æs sonans, aut cymbalum tinniens (res superficiariæ & soliditate vacuæ :) Et si habuero prophetiam, & noverim mysteria omnia, & OMNEM SCIENTIAM: & si habuero (quod plus est) omnem fidem ita ut montes transferam (scientia quâ inaniter se jactant Cabalistæ) charitatem autem non habuero, NULLUS SUM. Et ratio dictat, illum qui bellissime & Angelica manu haberet depictos cibos, thesauros, vestitus, exteraque totius mundi commoda, hæreretque ita in iconibus illis suis, ut de rebus ipsis acquirendis nil cogitaret, superficiariæ atque etiam stolidæ mentis fore; nec non fame, frigore omnique inedia non posse non perire.
units.tr: he sees himself bound to God, to his neighbours and to the other creatures, but remains only in that fine contemplation of divine and natural things as ideas. Such a man must at last be acknowledged as the true possessor of superficial erudition, and deserves at last the name of a superficial scholar. Behold, this is truly superficial erudition in its purest essentials, and in its true and proper degree and state. Those who are below this have not yet reached so far. If they are anything, they should not be ashamed to confess it: those who are more or less ignorant, or even in error, must in sincere conscience openly profess it. The more learned have done this too, crying out, How much we do not know! which is as much as to say: Alas, how little we still are in fact, however much we are laymen and ignorant! Oh mortals! Oh race of scholars! Who have devoted yourselves wholly to forming reason alone, by what title of erudition could you truly be celebrated! If you knew what a burdensome and unbearable, and at the same time windy and empty, load you have placed on your shoulders, there would surely be no reason for you to applaud your studies inwardly, or to rejoice much in your bosom. For after immense labours of reason, scarcely one in a thousand reaches even the thousandth part of superficial erudition. And although by some miracle someone should attain to its fullness, so that not even an Angel could polish and instruct his reason further, then at last, if he remains within these limits, he will be one who, with a dying mortality, descends to the lower regions more brilliantly and by a safer road, more clearly and distinctly, swollen with the leaven of his own proud admiration and self-satisfaction, and empty of God and of love for him, that is, of charity. I am not the man to invent these things and rashly bring them forward. This judgment is God's own, expressed by the pen of Paul: (a) If I speak with the tongues of men and of Angels, but have not charity (that is, the surrender of the soul and of the faculties of understanding, heart, strength and thoughts, with which God wishes to be loved with all of them), I have become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal (things superficial and empty of solidity). And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries, and ALL KNOWLEDGE: and if I have (what is more) all faith, so that I could remove mountains (the knowledge in which the Cabalists vainly boast), but have not charity, I AM NOTHING. And reason dictates that a man who had most beautifully painted pictures of food, treasures, clothing and the other advantages of the whole world, by an Angelic hand, and who stayed so fixed in those images that he thought nothing of acquiring the things themselves, would be of a superficial and even foolish mind, and would certainly perish of hunger, cold and every want.

units.la: XXIV. Ex dictis patet quanta sit am- plitudo Eruditionis superficiariæ, siquidem ad omnia, quæ ideis rationis repræsentari possunt, divina, naturalia, humana sese ex- tendat.
units.tr: XXIV. From what has been said it is clear how great is the breadth of superficial erudition, since it extends to all things that can be represented by the ideas of reason: divine, natural and human.

units.la: Datur itaque & THEOLOGIA superficiaria, & PHILOSOPHIA cum omnibus suis partibus atque membris, quæ jam non libet accuratius recensere, tametsi generalius
units.tr: There is therefore both a superficial THEOLOGY and a superficial PHILOSOPHY, with all their parts and members, which I do not now wish to review more precisely, though I shall speak of them rather more generally.

units.la: 24. Eruditionis superficiaria in partes notabiliores distributio. lius dixero, omnem Philosophicarum rerum ambitum tribus comprehendi membris, Metaphysica nempe, ad quam rerum affectiones communes spiritualiumque notitiam specialem sive Pneumaticam, referimus; Physica, cujus Medicina & Mathematicæ scientiæ fuerint veluti partes aut appendices; Ethica denique, ad quam juris scientiam, nec non eam historiarum, haud absurde referas. Illarum autem tum acquirendarum tum communicandarum instrumenta fuerint, tum Grammatica, cujusdependentiæ sunt Rhetorica seu eloquentia, & Critica; tum Logica. Nolim jam operose cum aliquo contendere hancce meam de rebus quæ a ratione humana sciri possunt, & in specie de Philosophiæ partibus distributionem, exactam satis esse; atque omnia, quæ quis causari posset illi deesse, tacite sub partibus recensitis includi; veluti sub juris scientia eam quæ politicum & œconomicum jus & officium concernunt, & sic de cæteris. Habeatur, per me licet, manca & deficiens: mihi liceat saltem de istis in cogitatione mea ita disponere, dum illarum systemata proponere & discutere non intendo; verùm tantum obiter designare, quatenus in Eruditione superficiaria suas habent partes. XXV. Vulgo sane qui se his omnibus, quas jam enumeravi, scientiis (voce hac latissime sumta) præditum intueretur, haud dubio se solidissima crederet imbutum eruditione. Verum enimvero, tota ista tam grandis scientiarum supellex aut gaza, earumque unaquæque, tunc demum superficiaria erit dicenda, quando ejus systematis omnes ideæ præ- cipuæ, ideatis suis vere conformes in ratione humana præcise habebuntur aut considerabuntur, vel ex eadem in tractatum aliquem didacticum debite disponentur. At quam rarum est inter homines aliquem eruditi superficiarii titulo vere dignum inveniri! sed & rarius sane vel alicujus e recensitis scientiæ dari scriptis systemata; fateorque me hactenus non ita fuisse felicem, ut vel unum reperirem hac dignum appellatione. An alii viderint quæ talia esse reputent, ipsorum id permitto judicio. Sed profecto si ea quæ ad talia diximus requiri consideraverint diligentius; parciores erunt ac circumspectiores in enumerandis scientiarum opibus, queis mundum jam ita abundare putant, ut seculum nostrum lucis atque eruditionis seculum arbitrentur celebrari posse, cum potius quæri posset, annon confusionis, vertiginis atque ineptiarum seculum dici mereretur, ut ut ingeniis præstantibus, atque ad res penetrantius percipiendas natis exuberet: siquidem & excellentiora ingenia quando se minutiis nugisque homine indignis mala via, pessimaque methodo atque Logica dedunt, nil quod vel superficiarie verum dici mereatur, possunt acquirere.
units.tr: 24. Distribution of superficial erudition into its more notable parts. I say that the whole compass of philosophical matters is comprised under three heads: namely Metaphysics, to which we refer the common affections of things and the special knowledge of spiritual things, or Pneumatics; Physics, of which Medicine and the mathematical sciences are as it were parts or appendices; and finally Ethics, to which one may not unreasonably refer the science of law and that of history. The instruments both for acquiring and for communicating these are, on the one hand, Grammar, on which Rhetoric or eloquence and Criticism depend, and on the other hand Logic. I do not now wish to contend laboriously with anyone that this distribution of mine, of the things that can be known by human reason, and in particular of the parts of philosophy, is exact enough, and that whatever anyone might argue is lacking in it is tacitly included under the parts listed: for example, under the science of law are included what concerns political and domestic law and duty, and so on for the rest. Let it be held, if you like, to be incomplete and defective. It is enough for me to have arranged these things thus in my thinking, since I do not intend to set out and discuss their systems, but only to indicate in passing how far they have their parts in superficial erudition. XXV. Commonly, certainly, anyone who looked upon himself as endowed with all the sciences I have just listed (taking the word very broadly) would doubtless believe himself imbued with the most solid erudition. Truly, however, this whole so great store of sciences, or treasure of them, and each of them, will then first be called superficial when all the chief ideas of its system, truly conformed to their ideals, are precisely held or considered in human reason, or are duly arranged from it into some didactic treatise. But how rare it is to find among men anyone truly worthy of the title of superficial scholar! And even more rarely indeed is there any systematic writing in any of the listed sciences. I confess that hitherto I have not been so fortunate as to find even one worthy of that name. Whether others see fit to count such things as these, I leave to their own judgment. But surely, if they had considered more carefully what is required for such things, they would be more sparing and more circumspect in counting up the riches of the sciences, with which they think the world now so abounds that they believe our age may be celebrated as an age of light and erudition. Rather one might ask whether it does not deserve to be called an age of confusion, giddiness and trifles, although it abounds in outstanding minds, born to perceive things more deeply. For even excellent minds, when they give themselves over to trifles and idle matters unworthy of a man, by a bad road, with the worst method and logic, cannot acquire anything that could deserve to be called even superficially true.

units.la: Non jam specialius recensebo rationes, cur e scientiis enumeratis, prout ea jam obtinent & exstant, nullæ sint quæ ad superfi- ciariam dignitatem mereantur extolli; & si quæ mathefeos sunt, quæque mille inutilibus ambagibus confusis, turgidisque, imo & noxiis quisquiliis scatent, aliquatenus ex aliis superius exceperim. De caeteris, ne quidem spes est unquam eas superficiarium suum statum, qui illis ex natura sua comperere debet, consecuturas: non modo iis de causis quas jamjam in ingeniorum praestantium agendi modis dixi, aut quas terigi dum de rationis & ratiocinationum imperfectionibus agerem; sed & ideo, quòd homines in fundamentis scientiarum ponendis longe nimis a se repellant considerationem Dei, omnium scientiarum fontis; tum quòd sese interius minus inspiciant & consulant; praetereaque plus quam par est adhaerent iis qui eisdem secum defectibus sunt obnoxii, a quorum tamen institutione scientias exspectant, easque, quod malum adauget, diversas a diversis, quorum unusquisque proprios conceptus proponit, aliorum scitis sic oppositos, ut qui ex diversis istisquas hinc inde hausit scientiis aliquod in se eruditionis corpus velit per earum compagem efformare, haud secus facere videatur, acsi quis horologium integrum comparare volens, ad decem vel plures horologiorum fabricatores, quorum quisque diversam horologii disponendi ideam & methodum haberet, sese conferret, ab unoquoque singulas rotulas, aut aliam quamque partem comparaturus, quas deinde omnes in unum simul systema horologicum compingere tentaret. Qua ratione sane nil praeter irregularem, absurdam atque incompositam & secum ipsa pugnantem machinam, adipisceretur.
units.tr: I shall not now review more particularly the reasons why none of the sciences enumerated, as they now stand and exist, deserves to be exalted to the dignity of superficial erudition. Where some of them belong to mathematics, and teem with a thousand useless, confused and bombastic ambages, or even harmful trifles, I have already partly excepted them above from the others. As for the rest, there is no hope that they will ever attain that superficial state which by their nature they ought to reach. This is not only for the reasons I have just given about the ways of acting of outstanding minds, or which I touched upon while treating of the imperfections of reason and of reasonings; but also because men, in laying the foundations of the sciences, keep the consideration of God, the fountain of all sciences, far too much at a distance from themselves. Further, they examine and consult themselves too little within, and moreover cling more than is right to those who are subject to the same defects as themselves, expecting the sciences from their instruction. And, what adds to the evil, these sciences differ from one to another, since each of their authors puts forward his own concepts, opposed to the knowledge of others, so that whoever wishes to form for himself a body of erudition through the joining together of the sciences he has drawn from here and there seems to act no differently from someone who, wishing to obtain a complete clock, went to ten or more clockmakers, each of whom had a different idea and method of arranging a clock, intending to get from each one separate wheels or some other part, which he would then try to fit together into one clock-system. By such a method he would obtain nothing but an irregular, absurd, incoherent machine, at odds with itself.

units.la: XXVI. Sunt & speciales de unaquaque scientia causæ, cur eæ ad debitam statui suo perfectionem non perveniant, eaque in fundamentis male politis latentes. Has explicare, vel saltem enumerare alterius majorisque operis esset quam ferat nostrum institutum: tametsi nil vetat obiter quasdam uno alteroque verbo indicare in una atque altera ex præcipuis Philosophiæ partibus, Metaphysicâ scilicet, Physicâ, Ethicâ, nec non in earum organis, tum Logica, tum Grammatica atque Critica, cæteris aliis prætermissis.
units.tr: XXVI. There are also special causes in each science why it does not reach its due perfection, and these lie hidden in badly laid foundations. To explain them, or even merely to list them, would be the work of another and larger book than our plan allows. Still, nothing prevents me from pointing out in passing some of them, in a word or two, in the principal parts of philosophy, namely Metaphysics, Physics and Ethics, and also in its instruments, Logic, Grammar and Criticism, while passing over the rest.

units.la: XXVII. In Metaphysicæ statim limine non satis consideratur Deus solitarie; nec mens se sufficienter a creaturarum ideis purgat & separat. Cartesiani quidem a rerum corporearum imaginibus, ne illæ se spiritualium ideis immisceant, satis abstinent: sed iidem non satis, uti nec ulli alii, quod sciam, Metaphysici, ab omnibus creaturarum proprietatibus abstrahunt, ut puræ Dei naturæ aliqualem ideam veram in sua ratione excitent. Hinc statim sese insinuant nebulæ & errores, quibus non modo Metaphysices incrementum impeditur; sed & tota hæc scientia inde fit falsa, atque etiam noxia.
units.tr: XXVII. At the very threshold of Metaphysics, God is not sufficiently considered in himself alone, and the mind does not sufficiently purge and separate itself from the ideas of creatures. The Cartesians indeed abstain enough from images of bodily things, lest these mingle with the ideas of spiritual things. But they do not sufficiently abstract, nor, so far as I know, do any other metaphysicians, from all the properties of creatures, so as to excite in their reasoning some true idea of the pure nature of God. Hence clouds and errors at once creep in, by which not only is the growth of Metaphysics hindered, but the whole science is made false and even harmful.

units.la: Falsam transcendentalis, quam vocant, Metaphysicæ partem non removent, sed supponunt.
units.tr: They do not remove the false part of what is called transcendental Metaphysics, but take it for granted.

units.la: Inde non considerant illico Divinæ naturæ purissimam atque ab omni creatura separatissimam proprietatem primam, Sufficientiam sine qua tamen Ens perfectissimum (qualem esse Deum fatentur) non est perfectissimum, sed ab aliorum accessione pendens.
units.tr: Hence they do not at once consider the first property of the divine nature, the purest and most separate from every creature: Sufficiency. Without this, a most perfect Being (such as they confess God to be) is not most perfect, but depends on the addition of others.

units.la: Eam, tametsi verbo profiteantur, re ipsa tamen, uti par est, non meditantur esse talem, ad quam omnia quae creaturarum sunt, non accedant; atque adeo Essentiam divinam, naturae suae necessitate nullis creaturis creaturarumque ideis indigere; sed illis carere, sui solius idea & fruitione perfecte completam atque contentam.
units.tr: Although they profess this in words, in reality they do not, as they ought, think that God is such that nothing belonging to creatures adds to him. Thus the divine Essence, by the necessity of its nature, needs no creatures or ideas of creatures; rather it lacks them, being perfectly complete and content in the idea and enjoyment of itself alone.

units.la: Deum, qua se collecto & veluti in se concentrato fruentem, sic aeternum esse, ut, puncti instar, nulla tunc in eo pluralitas, duratio aut successio sit consideranda; sed unitissima omnium perfectionum in puncto indivisibile possessio.
units.tr: God, enjoying himself as gathered together and, as it were, concentrated in himself, is eternal in such a way that, like a point, no plurality, duration or succession is then to be considered in him; rather he is the most unified possession of all perfections in an indivisible point.

units.la: Verum eundem qua se in se veluti expendit, cumque suarum perfectionum diversitate perfectissima ludit, in eodem esse tum libertatem & arbitrium eas diversimode complicandi, & diversimode ordinatas considerandi & percipiendi; tum eas diversimode depingendi per excitationem arbitrariam in conceptu suo idearum rerum creabilium, in quibus ideis plus minusve realitatis suae repraesentatae includeret; tum etiam res eas extra conceptum suum per creationem efformandi, datis ipsis quas vellet realitatibus, & praescriptis iis, sibique, regulis quibusdam commercii mutui: quae omnia libertas arbitraria & indifferens antecesserit, atque durationis & successionis species quaedam persectissima comitetur. Denique in eis quae spectant Deum secum solo delectantem, consideranda esse praecipue haec tria, Desiderium Dei erga se; Idea seu intellectio Dei de seipso; & Laetitia sive acquiescentia Dei in sui contemplatione & fruitione.
units.tr: Yet the same God, as he weighs himself within himself and plays with the most perfect diversity of his perfections, has in himself freedom and arbitrary power to fold these together in different ways, to consider and perceive them ordered in different ways, and to portray them differently by arbitrarily exciting, in his conception, ideas of creatable things, in which ideas he would include more or less of their represented reality. He also has the power to form those things outside his conception by creation, giving them whatever realities he wishes, and prescribing for them and for himself certain rules of mutual intercourse. All these things are preceded by a free and indifferent arbitrary choice, and accompanied by a certain most perfect kind of duration and succession. Finally, in those matters which concern God delighting in himself alone, three things are chiefly to be considered: God's desire for himself; the idea or understanding that God has of himself; and the joy or acquiescence of God in his contemplation and enjoyment of himself.

units.la: Haec omnia quando non debite considerantur, omnis Metaphysica manca est: ausimque affirmare, haec ipsa jam memorata, Dei videlicet Sufficientiam, Aeternitatem, distinctionem naturalium & arbitrariorum in Deo ejusque regimine; Libertatem, & perfectissimam delectationum arbitrariarum successionem; nec non desiderii, intellectus & acquiescentiae meditationem; clavem esse non Metaphysicae modo, sed & omnium cognitionum quae ratione acquiri possunt. Quapropter enixe dedi operam ut haec accuratius explicarentur, tum in altera Cogitationum Rationalium editione, tum vero praecipue in Gallico tractatu Oeconomiae Divinae, ubi re ipsa ostendi, omnium rerum, tam spiritualium & divinarum quam naturalium & humanarum naturas & regimina istis omnibus inniti.
units.tr: When these things are not duly considered, all Metaphysics is maimed. I dare affirm that these very points just mentioned, namely God's Sufficiency and Eternity, the distinction between natural and arbitrary things in God and in his governance, Freedom and the most perfect succession of arbitrary delights, and likewise the meditation on desire, understanding and acquiescence, are the key not only of Metaphysics but of all knowledge that can be acquired by reason. For this reason I have earnestly taken pains to explain them more accurately, both in the second edition of the Cogitationes Rationales and especially in the French treatise on the Divine Economy, where I have shown in fact that the natures and governance of all things, spiritual and divine as well as natural and human, rest upon all these.

units.la: XXVIII. In Physica, quoniam haec sanam praesupponit Metaphysicam, utpote quae principiorum ideas debeat Physicae subministrare; Metaphysici autem Deum debite non considerant, vix est quod quicquam exspectetur. Etenim considerato, quod Deus sit ens permanens, sit potens atque activus, sit luminosissimus, optimus, sapiens, felix, vividus atque fecundus: quodque quo perfectior est, eo perfectiora (verba Cartesii sunt) debeant esse ejus opera, nec posset quid producere, quod non sit icon atque argumentum & documentum suarum perfectionum: cum debuissent deducere ex his talia naturæ principia, unde sequeretur res naturæ esse ex origine sua permanentes, non autem flaccescentes nec morientes; esse potentes atque activas, luminosas, optimas, concordantissimas, deliciosissimas atque foecundissimas, quales mortalitate depositæ ipse Deus testatus est, se eas in resurrectione æternum reposituras: nil minus quam de his cogitant. Et quamvis hæc ipsa principia brevius ex Deo sese desiderante, intelligente, in se lætante, seque in creaturis ad modum quo in se delectatur depingere volente, derivari itidem possint, sintque hæ verissimæ eæque unicæ naturalium rerum origines simul & archetypi; siquidem omnia naturalia a Deo taliter affecto ad suarum persectionum demonstrationem profluxerunt: altum tamen de his est silentium.
units.tr: XXVIII. In Physics, since this presupposes a sound Metaphysics, which ought to supply Physics with the ideas of its principles, and since metaphysicians do not duly consider God, there is hardly anything to be expected. For if one considers that God is a permanent being, powerful and active, most luminous, best, wise, happy, lively and fruitful; and that the more perfect he is, the more perfect (these are Descartes' words) his works ought to be, and that he could produce nothing which is not an image, argument and proof of his perfections; then they ought to have deduced from these such principles of nature that it would follow that natural things are, by their origin, lasting, not withering or dying; powerful and active, luminous, best, most harmonious, most delightful and most fruitful. Such, once freed from mortality, God himself has testified they will be, and that he will restore them eternally in the resurrection. Yet they think of none of these things. And although these very principles could be derived more briefly from God desiring himself, understanding himself, rejoicing in himself, and willing to represent himself in creatures in the way he delights in himself; and although these are at once the truest and the only origins and archetypes of natural things, since all natural things, flowing from God so disposed, have issued forth to demonstrate his perfections, yet there is a profound silence about them.

units.la: Hinc ignorantes naturam non potuisse aliter quam gloriosam creari, & re vera ita creatam fuisse ab illo qui se ipsum falsa & turpi imagine repræsentare, aut potius deturpare non posset; non concludere, eam in statu in quo nunc est per accidens esse; quod nempe, postquam homini omnia essent a Deo concredita, is vero ingratus & rebellis contra benefactorem factus esset, non decebat Deum, isti impio ea omnia perfectissima conservare, in quibus ille spretis Dei amore atque intimis deliciis, delectari unice volebat. Ne dicam ex inordinato statu hominis non potuisse non sequi confusionem atque conturbationem rerum quibus regendis ipse praficiebatur. Adeo ut natura veluti putridum aliquod cadaver effecta sit, ex cujus particulae unius intuitu haud rectius de toto ejus systemate primo judicare est, quam ex cadaveris membro putri de totius corporis fanissimi atque elegantissimi structura, dotibus ac functionibus cognoscere.
units.tr: Hence, not knowing that nature could not have been created otherwise than glorious, and that in truth it was so created by him who could not represent himself by a false and foul image, or rather disfigure himself, they do not conclude that nature is in its present state by accident. Namely, after everything had been entrusted by God to man, and man had become ungrateful and rebellious against his benefactor, it was not fitting for God to preserve for that impious creature all those most perfect things in which man, having scorned the love of God and his inner delights, wished to take his pleasure alone. Not to mention that from the disordered state of man there could not but follow confusion and disturbance among the things he had been appointed to govern. So far has nature become, as it were, a putrid corpse, that from the sight of one particle of it one can no more rightly judge its whole original system than one could learn the structure, endowments and functions of the most healthy and elegant body from a putrid limb of a corpse.

units.la: Si quis autem sit qui cuperet ista, quae vulgari Physicae desunt, pluribus deduci, nec non veriora principia cum eorum consequentiis specimininibusque nonnullis consideratu dignis tractari, non aegre ferat se ad Oeconomiam meam aliquoties memoratam remitti.
units.tr: If anyone wishes that those things which are lacking in common Physics be deduced more fully, and that truer principles be treated together with their consequences and some specimens worth considering, let him not take it amiss to be referred to my Economy, mentioned several times above.

units.la: XXIX. In Ethica non satis attenduntur, ut decet, ad hoc principium, quod homo non si ens absolutum; sed ad aliud & ob aliud factus, cujus sit representativus oporteret: adeoque quod is summum bonum non in se absolute inque actibus suis, ut in se exsistentibus & ad se terminatis quaerere debeat, sed vero in relatione sui ad aliud, inque actione quam patitur ab alio (Deo) in se, si debite se ei per virtutes paraverit & tradiderit. Hic demonstrationes Metaphysicae de fine hominis quales alicubi tetigi, (a) apprime ad rem faciunt.
units.tr: XXIX. In Ethics, the principle is not sufficiently attended to as it should be: that man is not an absolute being, but was made for another and by another, and ought to be his representative. Therefore he ought to seek his highest good not absolutely in himself and in his actions, as existing in themselves and terminating in themselves, but truly in his relation to another, and in the action which he undergoes in himself from another (God), if he has duly prepared and given himself to him through virtues. Here the metaphysical demonstrations about the end of man, of which I have touched on some elsewhere, (a) are especially to the point.

units.la: Praeterea nec quae sit hominis potentia & impotentia, quid possit & non possit, expendunt; libertatisque ideam veram ex veriore Metaphysica non habentes, aut doctrina quadam de decretis particularibus & infallibilibus ad omnes actus cogitationesque etiam sese extendentibus (qualia somnia ipsemet Cartesius in Ethicam suam introduxit) vim praeceptorum & animorum ad virtutem frangunt; aut vero hominis depravationem atque impotentiam ignorantes, libertatemque ejus ad operationem virtutis, viribus propriis condendae extendentes, exitiali superbia virtutis loco animam adimplent. Sed ad Ethicam falsam incogitans devolvor, cum de vera veritate ideali agere tantum debuissem, saltemque monere, ei condendae ignorationem libertatis, potentiae impotentiaeque hominis officere: libertatis potentiaeque & impotentiae hominis ideam talem debere prius proponi, ut homo sciat bona quidem omnia externa atque interna a Deo effici; homini vero ex potentia libertatis a Deo donatae liberum esse, facultates suas ad bona illa flectere vel ab iisdem deflectere, ea admittere vel non admittere: Et quamvis homo, postquam facultates suas ab illis per vitia removit, dignus evasit cui Deus bona sua non amplius offerret, tum intus motibus luminibusque suis, tum extus; Deum nihilominus ea, intima maxime, de quibus in Ethica agitur, offerre adhuc, sic ut homo ea posset etiamnum ex libertate, non quidem efficere, sed admittere: hoc tamen pacto, ut quoniam ex vitio pravos habitus contraxit, initio sentiat in se a bono utcunque admisso, contentiones, anxietates, labores, oppositiones, quae omnia tolera-re,
units.tr: Moreover, they do not weigh what the power and impotence of man is, what he can and cannot do. Not having a true idea of liberty from a truer Metaphysics, or else holding some doctrine of particular and infallible decrees extending even to all acts and thoughts (such dreams Descartes himself introduced into his Ethics), they break the force of precepts and of souls toward virtue. Or else, ignorant of man's depravity and impotence, and extending his liberty to the practice of virtue by his own powers, they fill the soul with deadly pride in place of virtue. But I am drifting unthinkingly into false Ethics, when I ought only to treat of the true, ideal truth, and at least to warn that ignorance of liberty, and of the power and impotence of man, stands in the way of framing it. The idea of man's liberty, power and impotence ought first to be set out, so that man knows that indeed all good things, external and internal, are effected by God; but that it is up to man, by the power of liberty given him by God, freely to bend his faculties toward those goods or away from them, to admit them or not admit them. And although man, after he has removed his faculties from those goods through vices, has become worthy that God should no longer offer him his goods, both inwardly by his motions and lights and outwardly, nevertheless God still offers those things, most of all the inner ones of which Ethics treats, so that man can still, from freedom, not indeed effect them but admit them. Yet in this way: since through vice he has contracted depraved habits, at first he will feel in himself, from whatever good he has admitted, contentions, anxieties, labours and oppositions, all of which he must bear with patience,

units.la: re, nec non vi boni sese offerentis impugnare & ejicere debeat. Qui labor is est in quo praecipue Ethices praecepta omnia, cunctaque virtutum dogmata & exercitia versari debent.
units.tr: ...and to resist and cast out even by the force of the good that presents itself. This is the labour in which all the precepts of Ethics, and all the doctrines and exercises of the virtues, ought chiefly to be engaged.

units.la: Sed & tertiò, Dei, rerum æternarum atque permanentium nimis sunt immemores in Ethicis: non respiciunt satis hominem ceu creaturam æternùm duraturam, Dei sobolem, quæ conversationi cum Deo cumque Dei filiis per eruditionem morum Deum decentium apta reddenda est, adeo ut Ethices qualis homini convenit, fundamenta & principia non debeant esse veluti pro creatura temporali, hîc cum sui similibus inter crassamenta terrena aliquamdiu convictura, postmodum verò summo suo bono virtutibusque, quæ hac mortali & naturali vita circumscripserit, valedictura. Hanc, ut cum Lactantio dicam, veram virtutem esse nego, quia sit tota terrena; quandoquidem nil efficit nisi quod remaneat in terra. Ex Dei æterni rerumque æternarum, facultatibus nostris summis & æternis complectendarum, amore, equedesiderio proximum nostrum huc quoque promovendi, emanent verae Ethices principia necesse est. At, dices, hæc Theologiæ esse, non Philosophiæ. Quasi vero quemadmodum datur Theologia naturalis theoretica, quæ est Metaphysices, sic & Theologia quoque naturalis practica non daretur, hujusque consideratio idealis non esset Philosophica, ipsissimaque Ethica, de cujus descriptione, prout in facultate rationis per ejus ideas depingi potest, hic agitur.
units.tr: But thirdly, in the Ethics people are far too forgetful of God and of eternal and abiding things. They do not regard man sufficiently as a creature who will endure for ever, a child of God, who must be made fit, through the teaching of morals becoming to God, for converse with God and with the sons of God. Thus the foundations and principles of Ethics, as they befit man, ought not to be laid as though for a temporal creature, who is to live for a while here among earthly dregs with his like, and afterwards bid farewell to his highest good and to the virtues that this mortal and natural life has circumscribed. I deny, to use Lactantius' words, that this is true virtue, because it is wholly earthly, since it achieves nothing except what remains on earth. The true principles of Ethics must necessarily flow from the love of the eternal God and of eternal things, which we are to embrace with our highest and eternal faculties, and from the desire to bring our neighbour thither too. But you will say that these belong to Theology, not to Philosophy. As if, indeed, just as there is a theoretical natural theology, which belongs to Metaphysics, so there could be no practical natural theology, and its ideal consideration would not be philosophical; and as if Ethics itself, whose description, as it can be portrayed by ideas in the faculty of reason, is what is at issue here, were not philosophical. ## XXX.

units.la: XXX.

XXX. At vero, quicquid dicas, inquiat aliquis, & hæc, & quæ mox de hominis impotentia dixisti, quæque & ubi de Metaphysica & ubi de Physica modò agebas assumsisti de Deo, deque naturæ tum glorioso creationis, tum depravato corruptionis sta-tu, & quam plurima alia, quæ Philosophicatantum esse deberent, nimis sunt Theologi-ca. Sumus Philosophi. Rebus naturalibus circumscribimur. Cætera quà Philosophi nescimus. Quæ supra nos nihil ad nos: proinde dimisso Deo, maxime vero prætermissis iis, quæ ex revelatione constant, de naturalibus in se fac agamus solum, deque temporalibus: quid hic æternitatis consideratio? Hæc quoniam totum veritatis Philosophiæ systema ideale spectant, operæ pretium est amoveantur sollicitius.
units.tr: XXX. But whatever you say, someone may object, both these things and what you said just now about human weakness, and what you assumed when treating of metaphysics and of physics, about God, about the glorious state of nature at creation and its corrupted state after the fall, and very many other things, which ought to belong only to philosophy, are far too theological. We are philosophers. We are confined to natural things. The rest, as philosophers, we do not know. What is above us has nothing to do with us. Therefore, let us set God aside, and especially omit those things that rest on revelation, and deal only with natural things in themselves and with temporal ones. What has the consideration of eternity to do here? Since these matters concern the whole ideal system of philosophical truth, it is worth the trouble to remove them more carefully.

units.la: XXXI. Vix credi potest ejusmodi quere-
units.tr: XXXI. It can scarcely be believed that such a complaint

units.la: lam ab alio fieri serio posse quam ab aliquo forte Epicuri de grege animalculo, Atheove Spinozista. Horrendum enim est, atque indignatione, aut potius ingenti commiseratione dignum, hominem usque adeo naturam exuere, & sponte sua veluti in monstrum quoddam transformari, ut tædio ipsi sit, Deum in illis de quibus serio agit, intervenire. Atqui, miser, non tamen ideo, quicquid agas, Deum reapse excludes a te, nec a natura, neque ab eo quod benignè suscepit officio, unde rerum rationes ipsæque res manarunt, sunt, confervantur & perficientur. Tu ipse es creatura Theologica, a πνεῦμα λόγῳ expresse facta eò ut is te inhabitet tuque eum opere & verbis magnifacias; & væ tibi nisi sis Theologus æternus. Omnia una tecum a Deo, in Deo, ad Deum, pro Deo. Deus & idearum, & veritatum, & boni, & rerum causa efficiens, finis, forma beandarum, adjunctum, relatum, omnia: omnium omnino radix & basis, ratioque fundamentalis, sine quo nihil valet, neque est. Is re intus & extus perpetuo se suisque beneficiis afficit & circumcingit, vultque tecum perpetuo delectari, sua omnia, nil excipiens, tecum communicaturus: alioqui de neglectu fui, deque suorum beneficiorum tuarumque facultatum per te abusu ex justitia a te rationem exacturus, in cujus quippe, quicquid sine eo philosophari velis, tremendas manus cras aut perendie incidere debes. Et tamen hujus te memorem fieri, tibi tædiosum est, mallesque cum Ethnicis philosophis scotomate & insipientia percuti, & in reprobum tradi sensum: quippe quod Ethnicis ideo accidit, quia noscentes Deum, illum non affecerant gloria ut Deum decebat, hoc est, eo honore non afficiebant, ut ipsum in omnis boni, veri, rerumque causis intervenientem considerarent, ceu omnium radicem & fontem; archetypum, cujus omnia sunt ectypi; medium, cujus placito & intuitu omnia sunt regenda; finem, ad quem omnia cum amore, laude, veneratione & gratiarum actione remeent. Tales sane, in quos justitiæ divinæ ejusmodi exempla facta sunt, decet divina revelata aspernari, ut veluti lethargici & sopore oppressi, præter ideas & phantasmata, mata, quæ ipsis dormitantibus a somniis & a morbi sui indole suggeruntur, nihil admittant, hominum interim vigilantium discursus & ideas saniores repellentes ex hac ratione, quod lethargici sint, & suo more quà lethargici & dormitabundi cogitare ac philosophari velint; unde eum expergisci nolint, quid ad eos vigilia & vigilantium ideæ? Videamus tamen an ex ratione a morbo sanari & evigilare possint.
units.tr: could be made in earnest by anyone other than some Epicurean herd-animal or Spinozist atheist. For it is dreadful, and deserving of indignation or rather of great pity, that a man should so strip off his nature and of his own accord transform himself, as it were, into some kind of monster, that he finds it tiresome for God to intervene in the matters he treats seriously. Yet, wretch, whatever you do, you do not in fact shut God out from yourself, nor from nature, nor from that office which he kindly undertook, from which the reasons of things and the things themselves flowed, and by which they exist, are preserved and are perfected. You yourself are a theological creature, expressly made by spirit and word [πνεῦμα λόγῳ], so that he may dwell in you and you may magnify him in deed and word; and woe to you unless you are an eternal theologian. All things are with you from God, in God, toward God, for God. God is the efficient cause, the end, and the form of ideas, truths and good things, and of things to be blessed; he is the adjunct, the relation, everything: the root and foundation of all things altogether, and the fundamental reason, without which nothing has worth or exists. He affects and surrounds himself and his benefits, both within and without things, continually, and he wishes to delight in you continually, sharing with you all his things without exception. Otherwise, he will exact from you, by justice, an account of your neglect of him and of your abuse, through yourself, of his benefits and of your faculties; for whatever you wish to philosophize without him, you must fall into his dreadful hands tomorrow or the day after. And yet it is tedious for you to be mindful of him; you would rather be struck with blindness and folly along with the heathen philosophers, and be given over to a reprobate mind. Indeed this happened to the heathen because knowing God, they did not honour him with the glory that befitted God, that is, they did not pay him the honour of considering him as intervening in the causes of all good, truth and things, as the root and source of all, the archetype of which all things are copies, the medium by whose pleasure and regard all things are to be governed, the end to which all things return with love, praise, veneration and thanksgiving. Surely such people, on whom examples of divine justice of this kind have been made, deserve to spurn divine revelations, so that, like the lethargic and oppressed by sleep, they admit nothing beyond ideas and phantasms, which are suggested to them while they sleep by dreams and by the nature of their illness, while rejecting the discourses and saner ideas of waking men, on the grounds that they are lethargic and wish to think and philosophize in their own manner as lethargic and drowsy men; so, since they are unwilling to wake, what do waking and the ideas of the waking matter to them? Let us see, however, whether by reason they can be healed of the disease and wake up.

units.la: XXXII. Quemadmodum dantur tria lumen genera, lumen divinum videlicet, lumen naturæ, & lumen rationis, illaque tria in uno eodemque homine esse possunt; sic etiam unus idemque homo potest & esse & considerari, ut Theologus, ut Naturalis, & ut Philosophus.
units.tr: XXXII. Just as there are three kinds of light, namely divine light, the light of nature, and the light of reason, and these three can be in one and the same man, so also one and the same man can both be and be considered as a theologian, as a natural man, and as a philosopher.

units.la: Ut Theologus (non loquor hic de Theologia consulere, ut ex illis prosiciat rationis suæ ideis) fuperficiaria, de qua adhuc, sed de solida, utitur lumine divino, cui dat facultates supremas.
units.tr: As a theologian (I am not speaking here of consulting theology so that from it he may advance the ideas of his reason), the superficial theologian, of which more shortly, but the solid one, uses divine light, to which he gives his highest faculties.

units.la: Ut Naturalis, utitur rebus naturalibus ad vitæ suæ conservationem, puta elementis, cibis, vestimentis, artibusque hæc & similia parandi, quibus facultates suas inferiores accommodat.
units.tr: As a natural man, he uses natural things for the preservation of his life, such as the elements, foods, clothing, and the arts of procuring these and similar things, to which he adapts his lower faculties.

units.la: Ut Philosophus autem excitat in ratione sua ideas seu icones rationales vel, si mavis, intellectuales earum rerum quas facultatibus suis percepit, sive res illæ sint divinæ, sive naturales. Quod maxime observandum est.
units.tr: As a philosopher, however, he stirs up in his reason ideas, that is, rational or, if you prefer, intellectual images of those things which he has perceived with his faculties, whether they be divine or natural. This is especially to be observed.

units.la: Namque sequitur inde, hominem Philosophum, ubi philosophari vult, majori jure tenere rationem suam occupare ideis sive picturis, ut sic dicam, rerum divinarum, (quæ infinities & majores sunt, & magis ad eum spectant, & ampliores in ipso facultates habent, ) quam quidem ideis rerum naturæ; neque etiam eum posse rejicere testimonium luminis divini; quod potius contrà, desidererare & quærere debet; &, ubi adest, admirtere, suaque cum illo philosophemata conformare, ut ut dicat se non philosophari quà Theologum, sed abstrahendo a Theologia. Namque observemus, quæso, primò, quod quemadmodum iste, si sanus sit, non dicit quando sit philosophaturus: Ego quà philosophus nolo me gerere sicut homo naturalis, seu communis; adeoque nolo facultatibus externis, oculis, auribus, manibus uti. Volo quidem ideas formare rerum corporalium naturaliumque; sed non talium rerum quas homo, quà naturalis, sensibus detegat; adeoque ad res quas sensibus percipio nolo attendere; nolo admittere lumen solis, non corpora quæ per id percipio: non cætera; quemadmodum, inquam, hoc non faciet philosophus sanus: sic nec idem dicet: Ego quà philosophus nolo admittere lumen quod non percipio nisi quà Theologus; adeoque ad res divinas hoc lumine detectas attendere nolo. Namque sicut res naturales re vera ad ipsum pertinent; ita & divinæ. Et prout qua philosophus in mente sua excitat ideas sive icones intellectuales seu rationales rerum quas sensibus percepit quà homo naturalis, easque ideas considerat, non tanquam res ipsas, quibus vesci, vestiri, aut ex quibus sibi de necessariis proprospicere velit; sed tanquam picturas & imagines ad animi relaxationem & delectationem: ita etiam idem quà philosophus debite in mente sua excitat ideas rerum quas quà Theologus solidus percepit, easque ideas non æstimat veluti res ipsas, nou credit eas esse Deum ipsum, ipsum lumen Dei, ipsas res æternas & divinas; sed habet eas pro rerum divinarum picturis & imaginibus, quæ, quà tales, ad philosophum quà talem optime pertinent, non ut eis se pascat solide, iisque servari velit; sed ut in illis delectetur, videns in eis repræsentationes & rerum earum & earundem auctoris.
units.tr: For it follows from this that when a man wishes to philosophise, as a philosopher he has greater right to occupy his reason with ideas, or pictures, so to speak, of divine things (which are infinitely greater, concern him more, and have wider faculties in him) than with ideas of natural things. Nor can he reject the testimony of divine light, which rather he ought to desire and seek, and, where it is present, admit it and conform his philosophical positions to it, even though he says he is not philosophising as a theologian, but abstracting from theology. For let us observe, I beg you, first, that just as a sound philosopher does not say, when he is about to philosophise, "As a philosopher I refuse to behave like a natural or common man; I therefore refuse to use my external faculties, eyes, ears, hands. I do indeed want to form ideas of corporeal and natural things, but not of such things as a man, as a natural man, detects by the senses; so I refuse to attend to the things I perceive by the senses; I refuse to admit the light of the sun, nor the bodies I perceive by it, nor the rest"; so, I say, a sound philosopher will not do this. Nor will he say the same: "As a philosopher I refuse to admit the light that I perceive only as a theologian, and so I refuse to attend to divine things revealed by that light." For just as natural things truly pertain to him, so do divine things. And just as, as a philosopher, he stirs up in his mind ideas or intellectual and rational images of the things he has perceived by his senses as a natural man, and considers those ideas not as the things themselves, with which he wishes to feed, clothe himself, or provide for his necessities, but as pictures and images for the relaxation and delight of his mind; so likewise he who, as a philosopher, duly stirs up in his mind ideas of the things which he has perceived as a solid theologian, does not value those ideas as the things themselves, nor believe that they are God himself, the very light of God, the eternal and divine things themselves; but he holds them as pictures and images of divine things, which, as such, pertain best to the philosopher as such, not so that he may solidly feed on them and wish to be preserved by them, but so that he may delight in them, seeing in them representations both of those things and of their author.

units.la: Porrò quemadmodum Philosophus, nisi ad ideas ratiociniaque de rebus corporeis adhibeat experimenta quæ ope naturalis & sensibilis sive externi luminis detegit, chimæras tantum explodendas in otiosò suo cerebro & museo conderet, nullatenus rebus naturalibus conformes; idemque stultescceret, si re vera lumine illo, rebusque per illud detectis, nullatenus vellet uti, sed totam vitam quà philosophus & meris ratiociniis transigere: ita quoque is ipse, quando vult de rebus divinis, incorporeis & Metaphysicis agere nisi ad suas de illis ideas ratiociniaque adhibeat experimenta quæ ope divini luminis deteguntur, explodendas chimæras de rebus spiritualibus otiosus condit, a rebus ipsis prorsus abludentes; prorsusque stultescit idem si ideis suis inhæreat, ut ad res ipsas divinas, divinumque lumen, suas primi ordinis facultates non admoveat. Philosophi objectum, seu materia, ut sic dicam, prima, debent esse restum cogitantes, Deus, mentes, earumque proprietates; tum corporeæ, quas omnes, lumine unamquamque suo, experiri, sensibusque suarum facultatum percipere debet ante omnem rationis actum, veluti etiam fit in rebus externis: postmodum illis sic experientia in se perceptis, ratio demum activitate sua circa illa ideisare, ut sic loquar, & ratiocinari debet, sic ut repugnantia expertis non proferat: & hoc est vere philosophari.
units.tr: Moreover, just as a philosopher who does not apply experiments, which he discovers by means of natural and sensible or external light, to his ideas and reasoning about bodily things would only frame chimeras to be dismissed in his idle brain and museum, bearing no resemblance to natural things, and would be equally foolish if he refused altogether to use that light and the things disclosed by it, spending his whole life as a philosopher on pure reasoning alone, so too that same man, when he wishes to treat of divine, incorporeal and metaphysical things, if he does not apply experiments, which are disclosed by means of divine light, to his ideas and reasoning about them, idly forms chimeras about spiritual things to be dismissed, wholly unlike the things themselves. He becomes equally foolish if he clings to his ideas and does not apply his faculties of the first order to the divine things themselves and to the divine light. The object, or as I may call it, the primary matter of the philosopher, must be the things that are thinking, God, minds and their properties; and then the bodily things, all of which each person must experience by his own light and perceive by the senses of his faculties before any act of reason, just as is done with external things. Afterwards, once experience has been perceived in this way, reason must at last set its activity to work upon those things, so to speak, shaping them into ideas and reasoning about them, so that it does not produce anything contrary to what has been experienced. This is truly to philosophize.

units.la: XXXIII. Atqui dices, lumen equidem externum & sensibile in promptu habeo, quod quidem cum ejus experimentis ex sensibus & modo agendi omnibus hominibus non philosophis communi, perlibenter ad philosophandum adsumam, quo mea de rebus cogitata idealia rationabiliaque juventur & dirigantur; verum non ita mihi obtinget divinum lumen, cujus experientia divinas res intuitus, adsumere inde possim quae cogitata mea de spiritualibus divinisque possint dirigere & confirmare; quod alias perlibenter facerem: quis enim divinas experientias, omnium certissimas, rejiciat ad ideisandum & ratiocinandum, cum ipsae divinae res sint rerum omnium origines, inque rebus omnibus multifariam depictae repraesententur? Bene est: si quis eò redeat, illius ego difficultati huicce mox satisfaciam, ubi prius dixero, cur voce hac, ideisare maluerim hic uti quam vocabulo philosophari. Nempe observavi, homines, postquam philosophiam a Theologia suo more distinxerunt, veluti pro facinore quodam habere, si quis ab una ad aliam trajiciat; hoc appellant μεταφορὰν εἰς ἀλλο γένος, crimen ut barbarum sic mere scholasticum & pædagogicum. Equidem non sunt confundendæ Theologia & Philosophia: una siquidem res divinas spiritualesque ipsas possideat lumine divino; altera, earum tantum imagines nonnullas, quas activirate rationis depingit. Verum si quis philosophantem ideo reprehendat, quod mentem ad divina theologicaque convertat, idem facit ac si hominem depingentem, seu imagines facientem, qui ad rem ipsam archetypumque suum interdum respiceret, sic alloqueretur: Heus tu, pictor, jam quæstio est de effigie manu coloribusque in tabula pingenda; quid tu nunc rem ipsam archetypumque oculis tuis adspicis? tu quà pictor jam non rei ipsius spectatorem, sed pictorem imaginis gerere te debes. Qua reprehensione sane nihil esset stolidius.
units.tr: XXXIII. But you will say: I certainly have the external and sensible light at hand, and with its experiments, drawn from the senses and from the way of acting common to all non-philosophers, I readily take it up for philosophizing, so that my thoughts about things may be aided and directed by ideas and reason. But the divine light is not so available to me; I cannot take from it an experience that is an intuition of divine things, by which my thoughts about spiritual and divine things might be directed and confirmed. I would gladly do this otherwise. For who would reject divine experiences, the most certain of all, for forming ideas and reasoning, since the divine things themselves are the origins of all things and are represented in many ways as depicted in all things? Very well: if anyone returns to this point, I shall answer this difficulty presently, once I have first said why I preferred to use the word ideisare here rather than the word philosophari. I have observed that men, after they separated philosophy from theology in their own fashion, regard it as a kind of crime if someone passes from one to the other. They call this μεταφορὰν εἰς ἄλλο γένος [transference into another genus], a charge as barbarous as it is purely scholastic and pedagogic. Certainly theology and philosophy are not to be confused: the one possesses the divine and spiritual things themselves by divine light; the other depicts only some images of them, by the activity of reason. But if anyone should reproach the philosopher for turning his mind to divine and theological matters, he does the same as if he were to address a painter, who sometimes looked at his original and archetype while making his images, in this way: "Hey you, painter! The question now concerns the likeness to be painted on the panel with hand and colours; why are you now looking with your eyes at the thing itself and its archetype? As a painter you ought not to act as spectator of the thing itself, but as painter of the image." Such a reproach would indeed be nothing more foolish.
