units.la: Est enim requisitum necessarium omni bono pictori, ut per vices ab actione & usu manûs, penicilli, colorumqueecesset, ipsissimamquerem & archetypum suum respiciat. Sic quoque necessario requiritur ab omni bono philosopho, quem idcirco idearum pictorem, seu ideisantem appello, ut, nisi propriæ imaginationis figmenta cudere velit, philosophationem, sive actum ideas depingendi per intervalla intersecet, ut archetypum suum identidem intueatur: adeoque nil ineptius est querela ista de transitu illo perennecessario actionis philosophandi ad actum theologizandi, si fiat quandoque eo modo eoque fine hucusque dicto.
units.tr: For it is a necessary requirement for every good painter that, by turns, he cease from the action and use of his hand, brush and colours, and look at the very thing and his archetype. Likewise every good philosopher, whom I therefore call a painter of ideas, or one who forms ideas, is necessarily required, unless he wishes to fashion the fictions of his own imagination, to interrupt at intervals his philosophizing, that is, his act of depicting ideas, so that he may look again and again at his archetype. Thus that complaint about the constant and necessary transition from the act of philosophizing to the act of theologizing is utterly pointless, if it is made at times, in that manner and to that end as stated above.

units.la: XXXIV. Jam quid agendum illi, qui se lumine illo divino, quo divinarum rerum experientiæ deteguntur, destitutum profiter- etur? Dico primò, male illum id profiteri.
units.tr: XXXIV. Now what is to be done with those who profess that they are deprived of that divine light by which the experiences of divine things are disclosed? I say first that it is wrong for them to profess this.

units.la: Instinctus, sensus, dictamina, desideria de æternitate, de beatitate, de omnis boni veritate que possessione, cæteraque de justo deque virtutibus, actus sunt immediati divini luminis, sese in infinitum & ad infinita sublimissimaque dilaturi, si hisce principiis homo debite responderet. Secundo, videamus exemplo, quid faciendum esset, si quis, v. g. philosophiam naturalem discere volens, non haberet unde experimenta ad eam requisita faceret ipse; sique agnosceret præterea, uti omnes agnoscere debent, in corporibus tum prope positis tum longe a nobis distantibus multa esse quæ oculis suis nudis detegere non posset. Is, quoad primum, aliorum experimenta, aliorum a viris fide dignis sibi relata, non negaret; sed veluti a se facta & assumeret & crederet. Quoad alterum, non negaret dari posse media seu adminicula quorum ope plura, & rectius, quam nudis oculis videantur: sique adminicula talia, puta microscopia & telescopia, ipsi exhiberentur, ea sane lubens adhiberet, maxime si & modus ea parandi iisque utendi simul ei declararetur. Quibus aliunde assumtis & adhibitis, tunc operam daret ut speculationes ratiociniaque sua phænomenis quæ per media illa novit, non contradicerent; sed ab illis potius corrigerentur & dirigerentur. Eadem quoque ratio habenda in speculationibus philosophicis rerum spiritualium, quarum soliditora experimenta & rarissima sunt, penesque paucissimos; & tamen non deest medium plura detegendi quam nudis rationis oculis detegi possint. Experimenta aliorum, hoc est, quæ probi & sancti de his per lucem experientiamque divinam perceperunt, ea non tantum non neganda, sed in lucrum etiam & fidem reponenda sunt: deinde non negandum, nos posse multa, eaque clariori luce quam nudis oculis videre; sed potius revelationes divinæ, quæ veluti telescopia & ocularia quædam vitra sunt, assumendæ: quibus ut bene utamur, sensumque earum capiamus, quâ mentis dispositione considerandæ sint, ibidem docemur: atque sic ratiocinationes speculationesque nostræ de divinis & dirigendæ erunt & corrigendæ. Neque sane negabit Philosophus, si sapiat, Deo non fallenti, rerum conditori & cognitori atque revelanti, magis esse credendum quam rationi speculanti & ratiocinanti. Hoc Cartesius modeste agnovit, estque demonstratio evidens, perfectissimo & infallibili rerum auctori magis fidendum esse, quam rationi deceptionibus obnoxiæ & tenebris multis obsitæ.
units.tr: Instincts, feelings, judgements and desires concerning eternity, blessedness, the possession of every good and truth, and the other things concerning what is just and concerning the virtues, are immediate acts of the divine light, which will extend themselves to infinity and to the most sublime infinite things, if man responds to these principles as he ought. Secondly, let us see by an example what would have to be done if someone, for instance, wishing to learn natural philosophy, had no means of making for himself the experiments required for it; and if he acknowledged, as all should acknowledge, that in bodies both near at hand and far away from us there are many things which he could not detect with his naked eyes. As to the first point, he would not deny the experiments of others, related to him by trustworthy men, but would accept them as if they had been made by himself and believe them. As to the second point, he would not deny that there may be means or aids by which more things are seen, and more accurately, than with the naked eye; and if such aids, for instance microscopes and telescopes, were offered to him, he would certainly gladly use them, especially if the way of obtaining them and of using them were explained to him at the same time. Having taken and used these from elsewhere, he would then take care that his speculations and reasonings did not contradict the phenomena which he knew through those means, but rather allowed themselves to be corrected and directed by them. The same method must be followed in philosophical speculations about spiritual things, of which the more solid experiments are both rare and in the possession of very few; and yet there is no lack of a means of detecting more than can be detected by the naked eyes of reason. The experiments of others, that is, those things which the upright and holy have perceived about these matters through divine light and experience, are not only not to be denied, but are to be received for profit and with faith. Next, we must not deny that we can see many things, and in a clearer light than with the naked eyes; rather the divine revelations, which are like telescopes and certain magnifying glasses, must be taken up. How we should use them well, and grasp their meaning, and in what disposition of mind they are to be considered, we are taught in the same place; and thus our reasonings and speculations about divine things are both to be directed and corrected. Nor, if he is wise, will the philosopher deny that the God who does not deceive, the Creator, Knower and Revealer of things, is to be believed more than reason which speculates and reasons. Cartesius acknowledged this modestly, and it is an evident demonstration that the most perfect and infallible Author of things is to be trusted more than reason, which is liable to deceptions and beset by many shadows.

units.la: XXXV. Et quamvis Philosophus ipsa Dei revelata dicat se non capere, saltem plene; debet tamen ad minimum cavere ne eis, quousque illa capit, adversentur speculationes suæ: dein agnoscat, omni laude digna
units.tr: XXXV. And although the philosopher may say that he does not grasp the revealed things of God, at least not fully, he must nevertheless take care at least that his speculations do not oppose them, so far as he does grasp them. Then let him acknowledge that it is a work worthy of all praise, if he strives to find philosophical principles, through and from reason, which agree with those things he has perceived from revelation, and, if it can be done, explain them in his own way.

units.la: Philosophi citra revelata officium. gnum esse, si conetur in & ex ratione principia invenire philosophica cum eis quae ex revelatis percepit convenientia, & si fieri potest, ea suo modo explicantia. Atque quando talia invenit, quae, postquam eo a revelatione quasi manu ductus est, videt postmodum, ubi res penitus philosophice intuetur, convenire reapse cum eis quae ratio sana ibidem detegit, tunc revera habet quod rationi Philosophiaeque de revelatione gratuletur.
units.tr: The duty of the philosopher apart from revelation. And when he finds such things, which, after he has been led by revelation as if by the hand, he afterwards sees, when he contemplates the matter thoroughly and philosophically, to agree in fact with those things which sound reason there discovers, then he truly has cause to rejoice with reason and philosophy over revelation.

units.la: XXXVI. Et sane nemo negabit veritates dari quas ratio quidem, in quo nunc est statu, nunquam esset per se sola inventura; quas tamen philosophus, postquam ex ipsi sunt aliunde detectae, non modo veras esse percipit, sed ita etiam in ipsa ratione fundari agnoscit, ut necessario sic esse debeant nec ex sana ratione aliter esse possint. Atque talia sunt quae de veris Philosophiae principiis, physices praestenduntur fertim, suis in locis hic & alibi protulimus. Namque postquam ex divina revelatione audivimus, Deum vidisse omnia quae fecerat esse optima, hominem in gloria fuisse, creaturas tendere ad priorem statum libertatemque, quae sint glorificatio; easdem autem nunc esse steriles, angentes, dolorosas, venenatas, mortales, evanidas, hominemque ipsum vel ipsis brutis similem esse & mortibundum; & horum omnium causam esse hominis in Deum suum rebellionem & vitium: Deum tamen creaturas in priorem statum gloriosum, (quod resurrectio vel restitutio omnium dicitur,) repositurum, ut omnia æternùm sic renovata permaneant; quæ cuncta ex revelatione {a} per Scripturas divinas constant, ) hæc, inquam, postquam e revelatis assumta sunt, facile est non modo cum ratione conciliare; sed & ostendere & demonstrare ista sic cum ratione convenire, sic in ea fundari, ut nullo modo res aliter se habere possit; omniaque phænomena, hactenus inexplicabilia, & cum Dei attributis pugnantia, per hæcce sic explicare, ut eadem per alia declarari non possint. Quod ita esse, videbunt qui quæ de Dei æternitate, potentia, pulcritudine, bonitate, sapientia, felicitate, fertilitateque aliisque, in libris Oeconomiæ Divinæ meditati sumus, & ex quibus vera rerum principia, qualia ex revelatione indigitabantur, sequi necessario demonstravimus; uti & ibidem ostensum est principia peritura corruptionis miseriæque, quibus nos cum mundo hoc ad tempus involvimur, ex hominis malo erga Deum regimine, & vitiis, quorum quisque satis apud se conscius est, ortum ducere, nec non e Dei justitia, quam decere, ut homo iis castigetur quibus in benefactorem suum peccat, ipsa ratio demonstrare apprime apta est.
units.tr: XXXVI. And indeed no one will deny that there are truths which reason, in its present state, would never have discovered by itself alone; yet the philosopher, once they have been revealed to him from elsewhere, not only perceives that they are true, but also recognises that they are so grounded in reason itself that they must necessarily be so and cannot be otherwise according to sound reason. Such are those things which are set forth, chiefly in physics, from the true principles of philosophy, as we have presented in their places here and elsewhere. For after we have heard from divine revelation that God saw all the things he had made to be very good, that man was in glory, that creatures tend towards their former state and freedom, which is glorification; but that they are now barren, distressing, painful, poisonous, mortal, fading away, and that man himself is like the brutes and is dying; and that the cause of all this is man's rebellion and vice against his God; yet that God will restore the creatures to their former glorious state (which is called the resurrection or restoration of all things), so that all things renewed in this way remain for ever: all these things are established by the divine Scriptures from revelation {a}. These things, I say, once they have been taken up from what is revealed, are easily not only reconciled with reason, but also shown and demonstrated to agree with reason in this way, and to be so grounded in it that things cannot in any way be otherwise; and all phenomena, hitherto inexplicable and at odds with the attributes of God, are explained by these in such a way that they cannot be explained by anything else. That this is so will be seen by those who have meditated, in the books of the Divine Economy, on the eternity, power, beauty, goodness, wisdom, happiness and fertility of God, and the rest, from which we have demonstrated that the true principles of things, such as were pointed out by revelation, necessarily follow; and as was shown in the same place, that the principles of decay and misery, in which we are involved with this world for a time, arise from man's evil government towards God and from the vices of which each is sufficiently conscious within himself; and that reason itself is most fitted to demonstrate that God's justice requires that man be punished by those things by which he sins against his benefactor.

units.la: Cum igitur ratio in viam suam rectam vereque rationabilem reduci possit per unum atque alterum monitum Revelationis; quid absurdius, quid ingratum magis, magisque stolidum
units.tr: Since reason can therefore be brought back onto its right and truly rational path through one or another warning from Revelation, what could be more absurd, more ungrateful, or more stupid than not embracing such help with both hands? (This is the help by which Christian philosophers can rejoice over the heathen.)

units.la: {a} Perpende si placet e plurimis loca sequentia. Gen. 1: 31. c. 3: 16, 17. Ps. 8: 6, 7. &c. Ps. 49. (vulgat. 48:) 21. Esa. 11: 6...10. c. 24:23, &c. 65: 17, &c. Ezech. (typus originis primæ hominis) 28: 12... 16. Sap. 1: 13, 14, 15, 16. Act. 3: 20, 21. Rom. 8: 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. Apoc. cc. 21 & 22. lidum est, quam ejusmodi auxilium (quo Philosophi Christiani prae Ethnicis gaudere possunt, ) non ambabus amplecti manibus? Ergone arbitrantur istiusmodi quaeruli Philosophastri se errare non posse? aut vero se, cum erraverint, non posse per alloquium alicujus de errore moneri & in viam reduci? Atqui hujusmodi alloquium & monitum detectio & revelatio est: humana, si ab homine fiat; divina, si a Deo, qui sane quovis alio monitore aptior est, rationem exorbitantem ad orbitam rectam revocare, ingenti rationis emolumento atque beneficio.
units.tr: {a} Please weigh the following passages from among many: Gen. 1: 31. c. 3: 16, 17. Ps. 8: 6, 7. &c. Ps. 49. (Vulgate 48:) 21. Esa. 11: 6...10. c. 24:23, &c. 65: 17, &c. Ezech. (a type of the original state of man) 28: 12...16. Sap. 1: 13, 14, 15, 16. Act. 3: 20, 21. Rom. 8: 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. Apoc. cc. 21 & 22. Do these inquisitive little philosophasters think they cannot err? Or, if they have erred, do they think they cannot be warned of their error by someone's address and brought back to the right path? Yet such an address and warning is a detection and a revelation: human if it comes from a man, divine if it comes from God, who is surely a more fitting monitor than any other for calling an aberrant reason back to its right course, to the great profit and benefit of reason.

units.la: Hisce aliquantulum copiosius institi, quod sciam hinc praejudicium potentissimum, inveteratissimum idemque perniciosissimum omnibus ad unum fere Philosophis & philosophaturis insidere, per quod a veritate ideali detegenda aeternum amovebuntur, quamdiu ejusmodi beneficentissimo atque pernecessario auxilio monitoque uti recusabunt: a cujus privatione vel rejectione, opinionum monstra in Deum blasphema, in naturam absurda, rationem rectam non placantia sed angentia, totam suam Philosophiam deturpantia, oriri, pluribus ostendere possem, nisi id ab hocce meo esset instituto alienum.
units.tr: I have dwelt on these matters at some length, because, as far as I know, from this source there sits upon almost all philosophers, and those who will philosophise, a most powerful, most inveterate, and most pernicious prejudice, through which they will be kept forever from detecting the ideal truth, for as long as they refuse to use this most beneficent and most necessary help and warning. I could show at greater length that from the lack or rejection of it arise monstrous opinions, blasphemous against God, absurd concerning nature, not pleasing to right reason but distressing it, and disfiguring their whole philosophy, were this not foreign to my present purpose.

units.la: XXXVII. Dixeram me de Logica, philosophandi instrumento, aliquid etiam monitum, per quam cum intelligi debeat Methodus rerum ideas veras in mente excitandi, excitatas jungendi & disjungendi, ex his complicationes & consequentias deducendi; omnia mnia denique proponere ordine modisque ad usum verum relatis; aliud quid requirit quam quæ in vulgaribus Logicis ostenduntur, post quorum adeptionem videmus nihilominus homines, ut ut Logicos, longe a veritate unanimi per oppositas sententias abesse, nec non ἀλλήλως valde sese in omnibus gerere, ita ut quo magis Logici, eo absurdiores videantur. Non de illis loquor qui nugaces multas Scholarum Logicas in spem futuræ oblivionis atque inutilitatis, memoriæ mandarunt. Eos intelligo qui indagandi veri præcepta, nugis inutilibus exonerata, magisque præcisa, & ut putant, efficacia, remque magis tangentia, adhibuerunt. Verùm non animadverterunt satis, cum nonnullis rebus sic naturâ comparatum esse, ut, ubi doceri debent, altius repetendæ sint quam videatur postulare præcisus usus ad quem sunt destinatæ. Si, quemadmodum homines omnes quoad verum mente ægri & infirmi sunt; iidem & corpore ægri essent; vellent tamen addiscere exercitium aliquod corporis relaxationi inserviens, puta artem saltandi; non sufficerent sane eis præcepta hujus artis specialiora, sed ab altioribus incipiendum esset, ut primo corpora sana vegete moveri possent. Aut si quem doceri vellemus justitiam & fidelitatem in rebus minoris momenti, ei dandæ essent leges quæ etiam in rebus majoris momenti valerent. Vera Logica, seu via tuta ducendi & regendi rationem, e totius mentis facultatumque illius omnium bona dispositione exsurgat oportet. Evidens enim est, eum, qui efformare vult, quantum a rationis facultate fieri potest, icones rerum quæ in facultatibus supremis atque etiam infimis sunt, vel eas afficiunt, sano facultatum suarum omnium statu ante omnia frui debere, adeoque ad illam sanitatis dispositionem primo ducendum. Qua de causa hinc inde in toto hoc opere, præcepta plura interspersi, quæ tanquam ad Logicam veram necessaria considerari possunt; adeoque me labore ea hic reponendi levant.
units.tr: XXXVII. I have said that I would also give some warning about Logic, the instrument of philosophising. Since it must be understood as the method of rightly exciting ideas of things in the mind, of joining and separating the excited ideas, and from these deducing complications and consequences, and finally of setting out all things in order and in modes related to true use, it requires something more than what is shown in the common Logics. After acquiring these, we nonetheless see that men, however logical, are far from the truth, since they differ in their opposed opinions, and [ἀλλήλως] conduct themselves very badly towards one another in all matters, so that the more logical they are, the more absurd they appear. I am not speaking of those who have committed to memory the many trifling school Logics in hope of future oblivion and uselessness. I mean those who have adopted precepts for inquiring into the truth, freed from useless trifles, more precise, and, as they think, more effective, and touching the matter more closely. But they have not sufficiently noticed that in some things it is so constituted by nature that, when they are to be taught, they must be traced back further than the precise use for which they are destined seems to require. If, as all men are sick and weak in mind as regards the truth, they were also sick in body, and yet wished to learn some exercise of the body serving relaxation, say the art of dancing, the more specific rules of this art would certainly not suffice for them; one would have to begin with more basic matters, so that they might first be able to move their healthy bodies with vigour. Or if we wished to teach someone justice and faithfulness in matters of small importance, we would have to give him laws that also hold in matters of greater importance. A true Logic, or the safe way of directing and governing reason, must arise from the good disposition of the whole mind and all its faculties. For it is evident that one who wishes to form, as far as the faculty of reason can do so, images of things, which lie in the highest faculties and even in the lowest, or affect them, must above all enjoy a sound state of all his faculties, and so must first be led to that soundness of disposition. For this reason I have scattered many precepts here and there throughout this whole work, which may be regarded as necessary to a true Logic; and so I spare myself the labour of setting them down again here.

units.la: XXXVIII. Si quis tamen optaret ut uno verbo atque conspectu quæ sparsa sunt, nonnullaque alia e magis necessariis hoc loco exhiberentur, age, id igitur esto:
units.tr: XXXVIII. If anyone nevertheless wishes that what is scattered, and some other of the more necessary matters, be set forth here in one word and at one glance, then let it be so:

units.la: 1. Philosophaturus pro scopo habeat, ut animum suum in Deo relaxet atque lætificet, perfectiones illius contemplans, tum in ejus idea, tum in ideis creaturarum quæ ejus potentiam, sapientiam, bonitatem aliaque ob oculos ponunt; deinde quoque ut inde aptior fiat ad bonum proximi promovendum.
units.tr: 1. The one who is to philosophise should have as his aim that he relax and gladden his soul in God, contemplating his perfections, both in the idea of him and in the ideas of creatures which set before our eyes his power, wisdom, goodness, and other attributes; and then also that he thereby become the more fit to promote the good of his neighbour.

units.la: 2. Philosophaturus, cum homo sit, constans facultatibus 1. realibus Divinis, intimis & æternis, ad objecta æterna & realissima omniumque maxime necessaria factis: 2. realibus externis & naturalibus ad objecta realia, necessaria, sed transeuntia hujus mundi datis: 3. facultate picturaria rationis, sive intellectus activi ad objectorum picturas umbratiles relaxationis ergo effingendas: (quas facultates primi, secundi & tertii ordinis, similiterque objecta & lumina singularum vocare possis, ) sic de se disponat, ut tempus, curas ardoremque suum inter illas dispenset pro ratione & proportione quae est inter aeterna, temporaria, & pictouratas umbras: sic ut rationem philosophationemque suam non nisi proportione hac cum caeteris servata exerceat; idque eo magis, quod brevissimum saltem hujus vitae spatium ad aeterna comparanda sibi datum esse norit. Secus si agat, omnia in se confundit & turbat, ἀλόγως agit, muscis capiendis impendens pretiosissima momenta, quae immensis thesauris colligendis insumi poterant: a qua iniqua insania absorptus tandem, sic fascinabitur, ut nugacissimis evanidisque nugis totus traditus, putaturus sit se res quam maxime serias agere.
units.tr: 2. The one who is to philosophise, since he is a man, is endowed with faculties: (1) real, divine, inward, and eternal, made for eternal and most real objects and the most necessary of all; (2) real, external, and natural, given for real, necessary, but passing objects of this world; (3) the pictorial faculty of reason, or of the active intellect, for fashioning, for the sake of relaxation, the shadowy pictures of objects (these faculties and objects and lights of the first, second, and third order, and likewise of each, you may call them). Let him so dispose himself that he apportions his time, cares, and zeal among them according to the reason and proportion that exists between the eternal, the temporal, and the painted shadows; so that he exercises his reasoning and philosophising only with this proportion preserved in relation to the others; and all the more so because he knows that only the very brief span of this life has been given him to prepare for eternal things. If he acts otherwise, he confounds and disturbs everything within himself, [ἀλόγως] acting irrationally, spending the most precious moments on catching flies, which could have been spent on gathering immense treasures. Finally, absorbed by this unjust madness, he will be so bewitched that, wholly given over to the most trifling and fleeting trifles, he will think he is doing the most serious things of all.

units.la: 3. Caveat summopere, ne ideas confundat cum rebus ipsis, maxime in spiritualibus, in ideis suis acquiescentiam suam terminando, nec aliud lumen aliaque realia exspectando: memor semper, ideas esse picturas mortuas, steriles, inefficaces, deficientes, non satiantes, nec veris defectibus nostris ferentes supplementum: quod a rebus ipsis, per facultates passivas admittendis, exspectandum est.
units.tr: 3. He must take great care not to confuse ideas with the things themselves, especially in spiritual matters, by ending his contentment in his ideas, and by not expecting other light and other realities: always mindful that ideas are dead, sterile, ineffective, deficient pictures, which do not satisfy and do not bring a supplement to our real defects; this is to be expected from the things themselves, which must be admitted through the passive faculties.

units.la: 4. In ideis suis per activitatem suam depingendis, recurrat saepe ad ipsa rerum originalia, tum corporea, per experientias rerum externarum; tum spiritualia, per intimas facultatum interiorum cum objectis divinis exercitationes, maxime vero cum Originali summo, omnis realitatis, veritatis, bonitatis, rectitudinis sapientiaeque son-te, te, Deo, ad quem iteratis sæpe vicibus respiciendum est, cum oblatione desiderii, intellectûs & acquiescentiæ iis conditionibus prædictorum, quas antea descripsimus. Hoc est punctum saliens sanitatis intellectûs actívi, seu Rationis nostræ. Opinantur multi, sese rationi suæ vim, amplitudinem rectitudinemque acquisituros vel per sæpe repetita exercitia ejus, vel si onerent sese Mathematicis, geometriâ, & maxime quidem operosis atque inutilibus Algebræ crepundiis; tametsi experimentis vidimus nonnullos, qui in inquirenda veritate & ratione bene disponenda, Algebram ferè unam tantùm non ut Deam commendaverunt, hoc auxilio in Metaphysicis absurditates tam[?]monstrosas & noxias peperisse, ut qui pro medio rationis bene disponendæ exercitium commendarent syllogisandi in baralipton & frisesomorum, non ineptius delirarent.
units.tr: 4. In depicting his ideas through his own activity, let him often return to the originals of things themselves: both bodily, through experience of external things; and spiritual, through the inward exercises of the inner faculties with divine objects; but above all with the supreme Original, the fount of all reality, truth, goodness, rectitude, and wisdom, God, to whom we must look again and again, with the offering of desire, understanding, and acquiescence under the conditions described earlier. This is the leading point of the soundness of the active intellect, or of our reason. Many suppose that they will gain for their reason strength, breadth, and rectitude by repeated exercises of it, or by burdening themselves with mathematics, geometry, and especially the very laborious and useless trinkets of Algebra. Yet we have seen by experience some who, in inquiring into truth and rightly ordering reason, have almost praised Algebra alone as a goddess, and by this aid have brought forth in Metaphysics absurdities so monstrous and harmful that those who commended, as a means of rightly ordering reason, the exercise of syllogising in baralipton and frisesomorum could not have raved more foolishly.

units.la: 5. Ex rerum ideis, quibus ratio exerceri potest, eas ad ejus exercitium præferat quæ sunt de rebus dignioribus, profuturis & utilibus.
units.tr: 5. Among the ideas of things by which reason can be exercised, let him prefer for its exercise those that concern more worthy, profitable, and useful things.

units.la: 6. Inter ideas de rebus profuturis seligat eas, quarum originalia maxime ipsi sunt vel erunt necessaria, vel quæ re ipsa ex usu erunt.
units.tr: 6. Among the ideas of profitable things, let him choose those whose originals are most necessary to him, or will be, or which will in fact be of use.

units.la: 7. Mere curiosa, quorumque speculationes probabile est ad praxin, utilemque usum futuras esse nullas, dimittenda sunt; quaiia sunt quam plurima studiorum genera, e quibus nullum exspectant fructum, nisi ut data occasione una vel altera apud vanos quosdam homunculos citatione forte vel sermunculo nonnullo gloriolam pædagogicam πολυμαθίαν acquirant scioli.
units.tr: 7. Merely curious things, whose speculations are unlikely to have any practical or useful application, must be dropped. Many kinds of study are of this sort, and from them the superficial expect no fruit except that, on some occasion, with a quotation perhaps or a little chatter before certain vain little men, they may win the schoolmaster's glory of "polymathy" [πολυμαθίαν].

units.la: 8. Nunquam judicandum est dum affectus indebitus, seu passio aliqua turbida erga objecta aut partes sectasve aliquas, mentem occupat. Dico de affectibus indebitis atque turbidis. Sunt namque affectus quidam debiti, pro quibus mens facta est, quique eam non turbant, sed illuminant atque serenant: veluti desiderium & amor erga Deum, animi humilitas, & ejus generis similes. Hi ubi adsunt, tunc maxime judicia de rebus sana sunt; eadem ubi absunt, frigida, turgida & parvi facienda. Huc respexere divinius solidiusque eruditi, cum dixere, judicia de rebus sanissima atque solidissima tunc fieri quando mens in procinctu est a mortalibus ad immortalia ut transeat, vel cum se, acsi in eo migrationis statu esset, considerat: quod non intellexere, acsi otiose semper de aeternis meditabunda esse deberet; uti patet ex unius illorum responsione, qui rogatus, quo in statu, aut qua in actione eo tempore esse optaret, ajebat: Se optare tunc deprehendi agens quae acturus est. Nempe, quicquid agerent, respiciebant semper de Archetypum summum, cujus imagines cum in omnibus viderent, ad eundem etiam, semper praesentem, omnia referebant judicata.
units.tr: 8. One must never judge while an improper affection, or some disturbing passion towards objects, parties or sects, occupies the mind. I mean improper and disturbing affections. For there are certain proper affections, for which the mind was made, which do not disturb it but illuminate and calm it: such as desire and love for God, humility of spirit, and others of that kind. When these are present, judgments about things are most sound; when they are absent, judgments are cold, swollen and worth little. The more divine and solid scholars had this in view when they said that the soundest and most solid judgments about things are made when the mind is on the point of passing from mortal to immortal things, or when it considers itself as if it were in that state of migration. They did not mean that the mind ought always to be idly meditating on eternal things. This is clear from the answer of one of them, who, when asked in what state or in what action he would wish to be at that time, said that he found himself wishing to be doing then what he was about to do. Indeed, whatever they did, they always looked to the supreme Archetype, whose images they saw in all things, and to that same ever-present One they referred all their judgments.

units.la: 9. De casibus mille, qui vel nunquam accident, vel nos non tangunt, de iis aut nunquam, aut caute, & raro judicandum est: neque tam de penu atque copia judiciorum conclusionumve est laborandum, quam de rcrectitudine mentis per harum & sequentium regularum observationem conservanda.
units.tr: 9. Of the thousand cases that either never happen or do not touch us, one should judge never, or cautiously and rarely. Nor should we labour so much over the store and abundance of judgments and conclusions as over keeping the rectitude of the mind by observing these and the following rules.

units.la: 10. Cavendum est, ne ex apparentibus, aut ex iis quæ arte superficiaria, aut verborum lenocinio, aut critica futilitate incrustata, speciem rerum gravium mentiuntur, judicia fiant, utpote plerunque fallacissima; siquidem hæ artes, quamvis interdum bonis, potissimum tamen, nunc præcipue, aut malis aut nugacibus inserviant, simulque superficiem mentis sic demulceant & occupent, ut sibi tunc videatur rebus quam plurimis momentosis & pretiosis pasci, quando non nisi errores quosdam, insulsos pariter & perniciosos, vel nullius momenti futilitates, absorber aut lambit.
units.tr: 10. Care must be taken that judgments are not formed from appearances, or from things which, encrusted with superficial art, with verbal allurement, or with critical triviality, falsely present the look of weighty matters, since these are for the most part most deceptive. For these arts, although sometimes they serve good ends, now chiefly serve bad or trifling ones, and at the same time so soothe and occupy the surface of the mind that it seems to itself to be feeding on very many weighty and precious matters, when it is only swallowing or licking certain errors, equally silly and harmful, or trifles of no importance.

units.la: 11. Non omnia ratiocinationibus submittantur: siquidem infinita sint, tum in Deo ejusque potentia & rebus divinis, tum etiam in naturæ principiis primis & vividis, item maximis & minimis, quæ ideis intellectus activi seu rationis humanæ repræsentari non possunt, adeoque nec de illis ratiocinationes nec consequentiæ proferri.
units.tr: 11. Not everything should be submitted to reasoning. There are infinite things, both in God and his power and in divine matters, and also in the first and living principles of nature, likewise the greatest and the smallest, which cannot be represented by the ideas of the active intellect or human reason; and so neither reasonings nor consequences can be brought forward about them.

units.la: 12. Rerum quæ facultates vividas realesque primi & secundi ordinis concernunt, solida certitudo non exspectetur nec quæratur e demonstrationibus ratiocinatis: siquidem harum rerum certitudo omni rationis actu atque demonstratione sit superior. Causam speciale m (a) alicubi dixi.
units.tr: 12. Solid certainty about things which concern the living and real faculties of the first and second order is not to be expected or sought from reasoned demonstrations, since the certainty of these things is superior to every act and demonstration of reason. I have spoken of the special cause somewhere (a).

units.la: (a) Oecon. de la Creat. ch. 23. & 24.
units.tr: (a) Oecon. de la Creat., ch. 23 and 24.

units.la: 13. Etsi quod jam dicam, in aliis quoque exercitiis locum habeat, quia tamen ratiocinatio omnium maxime est errori obnoxia, non recusanda sunt auxilia aliunde quam a nobis venientia; quam ad rem maxime hic usui sunt diffidentia nostri, docilitas, neglectus propriae gloriae aut commoditatis, elevatio animi ad Deum, aliorumque consultatio. Nempe contrariis de causis fere fit ut solidissima & momentosissima quaeque vel apud ingeniosissimos non admittantur, aut etiam ne audiantur quidem, quoniam pudet eos de se diffidere, aut de valore famae, eruditionis partae dubitare; multo magis e docentium cathedra ad discentium quasi subsellia descendere; insuperque ea amplecti & profiteri, ob quae ab aliis & nominis fama & lucrosi officii proventu mulctarentur.
units.tr: 13. Although what I am about to say holds in other exercises too, yet because reasoning is most of all liable to error, aids coming from outside us are not to be refused. For this purpose the most useful are: diffidence in ourselves, docility, neglect of our own glory or convenience, the lifting up of the mind to God, and consultation of others. Indeed, from contrary causes it comes about that the most solid and most weighty matters are not admitted, or are not even heard, even by the most gifted. They are ashamed to distrust themselves, or to doubt the value of the reputation and learning they have acquired; much more so are they unwilling to come down from the teacher's chair to what are, as it were, the benches of the pupils. Moreover, they will not embrace and profess those things for which they would be penalised, both in the fame of their name and in the income of their lucrative office.

units.la: 14. Nemo in ratiocinando sibi pro scopo proponat, aliorum cogitata absolute immutare: hoc enim impossibile est: siquidem mens aliorum libera semper sit ad partes contrarias pertinaciter amplectendas, atque ita vindictae speciem quandam sumendam ab illo, qui superbae aliorum mentis cogitationibus per superbiam non minorem imperitare, easque sibi subditas videre vellet. Scopus esto, cogitata propria, ubi aliis utilia esse possunt, simpliciter & sine fuco sinceris mentibus proponere, plenissimam omnibus relinquendo libertatem ea vel amplectendi, vel dimittendi. Qua de causa multo minus cum malignis atque rixosis adversariis contentionis serra est reciprocanda. Haec enim mentem & vitiant & lassant eamque ab utiliori fruge revocant ad asinorum, quibus vesci volunt, carduos, non sine punctis lacerisque manibus tractandos.
units.tr: 14. In reasoning, no one should set for himself the aim of changing the thoughts of others absolutely. This is impossible, since the mind of others is always free to embrace contrary positions stubbornly; and so one would be taking a kind of vengeance on those who, with no less pride, wished to rule over the thoughts of another's proud mind and see them made subject to himself. Let the aim be to set forth one's own thoughts, where they may be useful to others, simply and without paint, to sincere minds, leaving complete freedom to all either to embrace or to reject them. For this reason there is much less need to enter into strife with malicious and quarrelsome opponents. Such contention both corrupts and wearies the mind and calls it back from more useful fruit to the thistles of asses, which they want to eat, and which cannot be handled without pricks and torn hands.

units.la: 15. Omnia vellead tractatus methodicos & ad artis formam reducere, non minus est absurdum atque pædagogicum, quam manducandi, respirandi, gaudendi, ambulandi, spiritus animales in vasa debita derivandi artes habere aut cudere velle. Sunt quæ natura duce vividius & facilius fiunt, quam inutili, operosa, & nauseabunda arte inculcari possint.
units.tr: 15. To wish to reduce everything to methodical treatises and to the form of an art is no less absurd and pedantic than to wish to have, or to devise, arts of eating, breathing, rejoicing, walking, and of directing the animal spirits into their proper vessels. There are things which, with nature as their guide, are done more vividly and easily than they can be instilled by a useless, laborious and nauseating art.

units.la: 16. Rerum scriptis tractandarum optima atque utilissima methodus est, eorum quæ quis apud se sibi attendens est expertus, simplicissima, narratio, eaque e mentis dispositione erga alios benevola, Deinque opera ad illius honorem patefaciendi cupidâ proficiscens.
units.tr: 16. The best and most useful method of treating matters in writing is the simplest narration of those things which one has experienced by attending to oneself. This should come from a disposition of mind benevolent towards others, and be undertaken eagerly, for the sake of making the work known to the honour of God.

units.la: Hæ sunt ex præcipuis regulæ, quibus & minus æquo attenditur, & omnium maxime attendendum esset veluti Logicæ pernecessariæ in philosophando; etsi, ut dixi, ad altiora pleraque non minus valeant quam ad ea quibus nunc eas destinavimus. Primam atque alteram observabis facile philosophandi officium in genere respicere: 3,4,5,6,7, ideas concernere: 8, 9, 10, ad judicia referri: 11, 12, 13, 14, de ratiocinatione esse: 15, 16, ad methodum pertinere: quæ quatuor totidem sunt partes in quas Logicam dividunt, quibus etiam singulis præcepta alia, ab aliis petenda, adjungere cuivis erit liberum.
units.tr: These are among the chief rules, which are paid less attention than they should be, and which most of all ought to be attended to, as very necessary to Logic in philosophising. Yet, as I have said, they are no less valuable for higher matters than for those for which we have now designated them. You will easily observe that the first and second concern the office of philosophising in general; 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 concern ideas; 8, 9, 10 pertain to judgments; 11, 12, 13, 14 concern reasoning; 15, 16 pertain to method. These four are as many parts into which they divide Logic, and anyone will be free to add to each of them other precepts, to be sought elsewhere.

units.la: XII. Jam & de altero notitias acquirendi Organo, GRAMMATICA, verbum proferam eodem modo quo de cæteris. Et quidem primo notabitur, me per Grammaticam, quam veluti rerum noscendarum instrumentum hic, ut dixi, confidero, intellectam velle non eam loquendi artem quæ verbis doceat uti quatenus eorum periodis forumque mensura & numero prurientes auriculæ atque imaginatio demulceri possunt; sed eam cujus adeptione e verbis aliorum, Eruditorum præsertim, eas de rebus ideas in nobis excitare possumus, quas ipsimet habuerunt dum scriberent: quod officium cum CRITICA sibi etiam vendicet, ejus quoque obiter quosdam defectus hic, abusus alibi, notabimus hoc in subjecto, non autem quatenus librorum exemplaria, auctores, tempora, historiam atque circumstantias externas examinat.
units.tr: XII. Now I shall speak, in the same way as about the others, of the second instrument for acquiring knowledge, GRAMMAR. And first it should be noted that by Grammar, which I here regard, as I said, as an instrument for knowing things, I do not wish to be understood that art of speaking which teaches the use of words so that itching ears and the imagination may be soothed by the periods, measure and rhythm of their phrases. I mean rather that art by whose attainment we can, from the words of others, especially learned men, arouse in ourselves those ideas about things which they themselves had when they were writing. Since CRITICISM also claims this office for itself, I shall here note in passing some of its defects, and elsewhere its abuses, in this subject; but not so far as it examines copies of books, authors, dates, history and external circumstances.

units.la: Interpretationis leges nos hic requirere nemo non videt; sed quarum primarias quæ fundamenti vicem gerant apud Grammaticos apudque turgidiores Criticos frustra quæsiveris. In superioribus, præsertim circa finem libri primi, nec non hinc & inde, sine jactantia spondere ausim complures earum repertum esse lectorem qui sensu pollet. Resumam tamen ipsam rem ab ultimo omnium fundamento, a cujus omissione omnes interpretationis defectus, qui ubivis ingentes agnoscuntur, promanasse videntur.
units.tr: No one fails to see that we here require the laws of interpretation. But among the Grammarians, and among the more bombastic Critics, you would seek in vain for the primary laws which should act as foundation. In the earlier parts, especially near the end of the first book, and here and there, I would venture to promise without boasting that several of them have been found by a reader who has good sense. I will, however, take up the matter itself from its ultimate foundation, from whose neglect all the defects of interpretation, which are everywhere recognised as enormous, seem to have sprung.

units.la: 1. Omnis boni interpretis, sive ejus qui libri cujusvis sensum e verbis concipere nititur, officium palmarium & principale est, sese suamve mentem aut intellectum transformare, ut sic dicam, in statum formamve scri-re, ut sic dicam, in statum formamve scriptoris aut loquentis, cujus sensum per verba vult adipisci. Neque hic audiendi sunt ii qui ingerunt, nos in interpretando non de loquentis sive scribentis mente, sed de verbis ejus debere esse sollicitos, ut nimirum eis, quamcumque demum mentem scriptor apud se intus habebat, jungamus eas ideas, quas homines ex usu ordinario, veluti ex generali pacto, ejusmodi verbis jungere solent. Hæc non minus fallunt quam splendent. Obtineant hæc apud rixosos rabulas, aut in foro litigantium, ubi cum iniquis contendentibus res geritur: nos hic de rebus tranquille inter sinceriores cognoscendis agimus. Horum, ubi loquuntur seu scribunt, scopus omnium primus directissimusque est, ut auditoris seu lectoris mentem menti suæ conformem reddant: deinde, secundario, cogitant de verborum ad hunc scopum adminiculo: quod valde imperfectum atque incompletissimum est nisi quis, postquam verba audiit, eademque per communes & vulgares idiomatis leges generalius confususque interpretatus est, animadverso, qui satis inde patet, scriptoris scopo atque mentis statu, omni molimine sese in eum veluti vertere conetur: quo pacto quæ antea superficiaria prorsus & fere nulla erat interpretatio, intima fit & vera. Neque aliter mentem aliorum datur vere assequi: quod per se ita clarum esse puto, uti clarum est dissimilia non esse similia.
units.tr: 1. The chief and principal duty of every good interpreter, that is, of one who strives to grasp the sense of any book from its words, is to transform himself, or his own mind and understanding, as I may say, into the state and form of the writer or speaker whose sense he wishes to gain through the words. Nor should those be listened to who insist that in interpreting we ought to be concerned not with the mind of the speaker or writer but with his words, so that we join to those words, whatever mind the writer had within himself, the ideas which men are wont to join to such words in ordinary usage, by a kind of general agreement. These things deceive no less than they dazzle. They may prevail among quarrelsome wranglers, or in the law courts of litigants, where things are conducted with unfair contenders; but we are here dealing with matters to be known calmly among the more sincere. For those who speak or write, their first and most direct aim is to make the mind of the hearer or reader conformable to their own; secondarily, they think about the aid of words for this end. This aid is very imperfect and most incomplete unless someone, after he has heard the words and interpreted them in a general and confused way by the common and ordinary rules of the language, notices the writer's aim and state of mind, as is sufficiently clear from this, and by every effort tries to turn himself into that state. By this means an interpretation which before was entirely superficial, and almost nothing, becomes inward and true. Nor is it otherwise possible to grasp truly the mind of others; which I think is as clear in itself as it is clear that dissimilar things are not alike.

units.la: Ex fundamentali hac insignique lege, pleraque quæ sequuntur, veluti consectaria fructuosa pendent.
units.tr: From this fundamental and remarkable law, most of what follows hangs as fruitful consequences.

units.la: 2. Omnem Interpretem Scriptori suo, vel ei cujus verba audit, benevolum atque faventem esse debere. Cum enim vera interpretatio non ex solo verborum adminiculo, quo admodum imperfecte interpretis mentem inflectere potest scriptor; sed ex concursu libero atque activo interpretis, mentem suam ad mentem scriptoris omni activitate componere, eique concordem reddere conantis, resultet; si hic istud requisiti ex parte sua afferre recusel, ineptus interpres est. Hinc nullius malevoli aut irrisoris aliena sensa referentis narrationibus fides adhibenda est, nisi quis ex professo decipi voluerit.
units.tr: 2. Every interpreter ought to be well disposed and favourable toward his author, or toward the one whose words he hears. A true interpretation does not result from the words alone, which can only imperfectly bend the interpreter's mind toward the author's. It results from the free and active cooperation of the interpreter, who by his own full effort adjusts his mind to the author's and tries to make it agree with it. If the interpreter refuses to supply this on his own part, he is an unskilled interpreter. Hence no account of the views of others given by a malicious or mocking person deserves belief, unless one wishes to be deceived on purpose.

units.la: 3. Libros omnes & vanos, & rixosos, & impios atque profanos, veluti animorum pestem esse fugiendos. Namque si quis eorum sensa exacte scire volet, is in scribentium horum & vel improborum vel insanientium mentem sese quantum potest transformare necesse habet: quod facere si nolit, eccur ea legat quae conditione negata non capiet? Equidem ii qui prius veritatis lumine atque rectitudine imbuti sunt, improborum sensa per id ipsum detegere ac percipere possunt, siquidem lumen & se & tenebras manifestet, sitque rectum sui & obliqui index: sed & illi, ubi id aggrediuntur sine praevia abundantissimaque in bono & vero confirmatione, neque ex officio injuncto, neque ex scopo ut tenebras dispellant, aliosque vel ab iis deterreant, vel ex iis liberent, periculo non carent: quandoquidem profanorum & vanorum hominum verba vel invitis mentibus semper plus nimis vanæ improbæque formæ affricant. Quæ causa est quare, quo majores quis in eruditione solida fecit progressus, eo magis ineptas futilesque sciolorum vanorum, mundanorumque & omnium falsoaut superficiarie eruditorum chartas lectione indignas censeat. Contrà, nullum certius est vani, falsati atque profani cerebri indicium, quam studium perreptandi, legendi & sciendi omnia quæ a quibusvis ubique fiunt vel scribillantur. Verbo, tuto judicare datur, talem unumquemque in animi fundo esse, quales sunt libri, ad quos evolvendos pronus, quorumque lectioni potissimum deditus est.
units.tr: 3. All books that are empty, quarrelsome, impious, and profane are to be shunned as a plague of souls. For if anyone wishes to know their views exactly, he must transform his mind as far as he can into the mind of these writers, who are either wicked or deranged. If he is unwilling to do this, why should he read what, without that condition, he will not understand? Indeed, those who have first been steeped in the light and uprightness of truth can detect and perceive the views of the wicked through that very light, since light reveals both itself and the darkness, and is the standard of what is straight and what is crooked. Yet even they, when they undertake such reading without a prior and thorough confirmation in the good and the true, and without a duty laid upon them, or a purpose of dispelling darkness and either deterring others from it or freeing them from it, are not free from danger. The words of profane and empty men always cling, even to unwilling minds, with too much of their vain and wicked form. This is why the further anyone has advanced in solid learning, the more he judges the papers of shallow, vain, worldly, and all superficially learned or falsely learned men unworthy of reading, as useless and foolish. On the other hand, there is no surer sign of a vain, corrupted, and profane mind than the eagerness to rush through, read, and know everything that is done or scribbled by anyone anywhere. In short, one may safely judge that each person is in the depths of his mind such as the books are that he is inclined to unroll and to which he is chiefly devoted.

units.la: 4. Libros Spiritus Sancti motu & lumine scriptos per grammaticam & criticam interpretari & intelligere velle, impossibile est. Per se namque patet Grammaticam Criticamque non posse legentis mentem in mentem scribentis, hoc est, Spiritus Sancti transformare, eive lumen motusque divinos imprimere. Non negem, grammatices & critices ope dari posse librorum divinorum interpretationem quoad dictionem & literas, qualis est cum ex uno idiomate in aliud vertuntur: sed interpretatio ejusmodi dictionaria ad vivam, spiritualem solidamque mentem Spiritus Sancti comparata, eadem plane est cum interpretatione cœci, qui ex grammatices, critices, pluriumque idiomatum peritiâ suæ linguæ ignaris, puta Græcis, Hebræis, Gallis, voces lumen, album, coloter, videre & similes, singulis per totidem voces alias cuique vernaculas, interpretaretur, dum ipse interim, si cum homine has ipsas res oculis & sensu percipiente compararetur, quantumcunque de iis garriret, nesciret tamen revera quid isthaec verba vere & vivide significarent.
units.tr: 4. It is impossible to wish to interpret and understand books written by the motion and light of the Holy Spirit through grammar and criticism. It is plain in itself that grammar and criticism cannot transform the mind of the reader into the mind of the writer, that is, into the Holy Spirit, nor impress upon it the divine light and motions. I do not deny that the interpretation of divine books can be given with the aid of grammar and criticism, as far as wording and letters go, as when they are rendered from one language into another. But an interpretation of this sort, drawn from dictionaries, when set against the living, spiritual, and solid mind of the Holy Spirit, is exactly the same as the interpretation of a blind man. Suppose he, with his skill in grammar, criticism, and many languages, but ignorant of his own tongue, rendered the words light, white, colour, to see, and similar words, in Greek, Hebrew, French, or any other language, each by as many words of the vernacular. Meanwhile, if he were set beside a man who perceives these very things with his eyes and senses, however much he chattered about them, he would still not know what these words truly and vividly mean.

units.la: 5. Nullus liber divinus ab improbis aut irrisoribus, quacunque supellectile instructis, vere intelligi potest: status enim & dispositio mentis eorum directe repugnat statui mentis divine scribentis; cum tamen ad interpretationem bene faciendam, huic conformem esse, sit necessarium.
units.tr: 5. No divine book can be truly understood by the wicked or by mockers, however well equipped they may be. Their state and disposition of mind directly opposes the state of mind of the divine writer, whereas good interpretation requires that the interpreter be conformed to that state.

units.la: 6. Igitur, Scripturarum sanctarum interpretes veri non sunt grammatici & critici dictionaristae; sed soli sancti, iive qui humiliter, sincere, & ardenter Spiritui Sancto sese transformandos offerunt. quippe qui solus omnipotens, id, quod omni creaturae possibile non est, quodque omnem hominum capacitatem, activitatem artesque superat, mentes puta divinas divinisque sensibus conformes efformare, aptus est efficere. Hoc notatu dignum est, si forte miserum quoddam criticorum genus vel sanctissimis, quando aut peritia primarii idiomatis Scripturae, aut trita ejus literae lectione, aut critices lubricitate grammaticesve paedagogica tumiditate destituuntur, proterve insultare vellent, tanquam Scripturae interpretibus pessimis aut nullis, dum ipsimet interim syllabicis suis crepundiis referti, ipsas Spiritus Sancti operationes intimas rejicere atque irridere haud verererentur. Mirabantur olim grammatici Scribae, ecqui Discipuli Christi Scripturarum substantiam tenerent sine grammatico criticoque suo apparatu atque studio. Sed Paulus vice omnium dicebat: (a) Quae Dei sunt nemo novit nisi Spiritus Dei: Nos autem non spiritum huius mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quae a Deo donata sunt nobis; quae & loquimur, non in doctis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in doctrina Spiritus, spiritualibus spiritualia comparantes: animalis autem homo non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei, &c. Transformamur a claritate in claritatem a Domini Spiritu.
units.tr: 6. Therefore the true interpreters of the holy Scriptures are not the grammarians and critics, the mere dictionary-men, but only the holy, that is, those who humbly, sincerely, and ardently offer themselves to be transformed by the Holy Spirit. For he alone is almighty, and he alone is able to form minds, namely divine minds conformed to divine feelings, which is beyond the power of any creature and beyond all human capacity, activity, and skill. It is worth noting that if some wretched kind of critics should wish to insult proudly the most holy men, when they are lacking either in skill in the original language of Scripture, or in the well-worn reading of its letters, or in the slipperiness of criticism or the pedantic pomp of grammar, they would be treating them as the worst or no interpreters of Scripture. Meanwhile these critics, stuffed with their syllabic trinkets, would not hesitate to reject and mock the very inner operations of the Holy Spirit. Of old the grammarian scribes wondered whether the disciples of Christ grasped the substance of the Scriptures without the apparatus and study of grammar and criticism. But Paul, speaking for them all, said: (a) No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we may know the things that have been freely given us by God; which things also we speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, etc. We are transformed from glory to glory by the Spirit of the Lord.

units.la: 7. Omnium scriptorum scopus verus praecipue est attendendus; atque ad eum & secundum eum omnis interpretatio facienda est.
units.tr: 7. The true aim of every writer is above all to be attended to, and every interpretation is to be made toward it and according to it.

units.la: 8. Scriptores simplices atque solidi (divini praesertim) cum exactitudinem externam circa argumentorum, rerum, historiarumve, quas ad scopum moralem praecipuum statuminandum afferunt, circumstantias, de nominibus, locis, temporibus, non curaverint, nec praecise observaverint, ad leges morosae critices minime sunt examinandi. Itaque
units.tr: 8. Simple and solid writers, especially divine ones, when they have not taken care over, nor precisely observed, the outward exactness of the circumstances of the matters, facts, or histories they bring forward to establish their chief moral aim, namely the names, places, and times, are by no means to be examined by the laws of a fastidious criticism. And so

units.la: 9. Neutiquam errare judicandus est Scriptor, quamvis externa nonnulla minus exacte vera, ad scopum bonum; ad virtutes & officia debita hominibus commendanda, assumat; siquidem ad commendanda ea quae per se laudabilia, vel etiam necessaria esse patet, sed ad quae capessenda ignavia & torpor hominum animos relaxavit, illa etiam inter alia optime adhiberi possint, quae vel scriscriptori vera videantur, vel auditorum cogitatis aut præjudiciis sint conformia. Ipsimet sacri scriptores hoc aliquoties in usu habent. Divinus ille Clemens in divinissima sua ad Corinthios epistola ex narratione de Phœnice considerationem resurrectionis laudat: alii alia. Haud recte igitur incedit Critica, quando eo fine ab ea sanctorum Patrum similiumque scripta diceres inspici, ut istiusmodi prætextibus eos Scriptores in ludibrium verteret. Non advertit istiusmodi critica cœca sanctissimas hasce animas, pro scopo nil aliud lectoribus suis auditoribusque inculcare, quam Dei æstimationem, admirationem, amorem, venerationem, imitationem; hominis vero humilitatem, charitatem virtutesque omnes & officia omnia erga Deum, se proximosque. At vero limis detegitur, maleferiatæ hujusmodi critices opera, inter argumenta quibus divina ista commendant Sancti, minuscula quædam esse, quæ grammatice & critice non ita se habeant: & hinc quidem omnia, & sanctos piosque ipsos scriptores, coram profana plebe aut falsis superficiariisve eruditis, & rejiciunt & deridendos exponunt. quod quam absurdum & profanum sit, judicium penes mentes cordatas fuerit.
units.tr: 9. A writer is by no means to be judged to err if he takes up some outward matters that are less than exactly true, in order to commend a good purpose, namely the virtues and duties owed by people. For it is plain that to commend things that are praiseworthy in themselves, or even necessary, but which the sloth and torpor of people have relaxed their minds from pursuing, other means may also be used to good effect, including those which seem true to the writer himself or which conform to the thoughts or prejudices of his hearers. The holy writers themselves often employ this method. That divine Clement, in his most divine letter to the Corinthians, praises the consideration of the resurrection from the story about the Phoenix, and others do other things. It is therefore not right for criticism to proceed as it does when, for that purpose, one says the writings of the holy Fathers and similar authors are inspected, so that under such pretexts it may make those writers a laughing-stock. Such blind criticism does not notice that these most holy souls, in their purpose, impress on their readers and hearers nothing but the esteem, admiration, love, reverence, and imitation of God, and the humility, charity, and all virtues and duties of man toward God and his neighbours. But indeed it is only too plain, from the work of such ill-directed criticism, that among the arguments by which the holy men commend these divine things there are some trifling ones that do not stand up to grammar and criticism. From this, it both rejects everything, including the holy and pious writers themselves, and exposes them to be mocked before the profane crowd or the false and superficially learned. How absurd and profane this is, let the judgement rest with sensible minds.

units.la: 10. Si quis Auctorem aliquem ita interpretetur, ut in interpretatione fallatur quidem quoad literam, dictionem, grammaticam, & criticam: ejus tamen interpretatio ad scopum auctoris redeat, eumque promoveat; is non pro inepto, sed pro vero interprete non quidem dictionis & literæ, sed rei medullæ essentiæque habendus est. Atque ita explodendæ sunt irrisiones ineptæ illius Critices, quæ Augustinum v g. sanctioresque Patres, haud verita est risui profanorum exponere, & pro pessimis Scripturarum interpretibus traducere, etsi hi verissime ad unum Scripturarum scopum, amorem Dei proximique cum horrore peccati & sanctimoniæ adeptione, omnes suas interpretationes vivide referant, at per vias in quibus nonnulla reperire est ad grammaticam & criticam dolabram minus lævigata: dum interim istiusmodi Critices de Scripturis interpretationes, Pharisaicam speciem æmulantes, externe quidem exactæ sunt, tornatæ, dealbatæ, revisæ, ne quid in litera indecens oculos carnales & criticos offendat, ornatæ etiam phylacteriis & dictis Ovidii, Virgilii, Martialis & nescio quot impiorum Ethnicorum, egregie scilicet Scripturas illustrantium: intus vero, sepulcrorum instar, spiritu vitaque destituuntur, siccis ossibus, omnique putredine, iniquitate, errore, hæresi, venenoque exitiali perplenæ.
units.tr: 10. If someone interprets an author in such a way that, though he errs in the letter, the wording, the grammar, or the criticism, his interpretation nevertheless leads back to the author's purpose and advances it, he is to be regarded not as an unskilled but as a true interpreter, not of the wording and letter, but of the marrow and essence of the matter. And so the ridicule of that foolish criticism must be cast out, which has not been ashamed to expose Augustine, for example, and the holier Fathers to the laughter of the profane and to represent them as the worst interpreters of Scripture. Yet these men most truly and vividly present, in all their interpretations, the one purpose of Scripture: love of God and neighbour, together with abhorrence of sin and the attainment of holiness. They do so by ways in which some things are less smoothed by the grammatical and critical adze. Meanwhile the interpretations of Scripture by such criticism, imitating the Pharisaic show, are outwardly exact, turned, whitewashed, and revised, so that nothing indecent in the letter offends carnal and critical eyes. They are also adorned with phylacteries and with sayings of Ovid, Virgil, Martial, and I know not how many impious heathens, who are of course splendid illustrations of the Scriptures. But inwardly, like sepulchres, they lack spirit and life, full of dry bones and of all putrefaction, iniquity, error, heresy, and deadly poison.

units.la: II. Critica non venditanda est ut necessaria interpreti ad scopum scriptoris assequendum, nisi quando scriptor ipse ex professo criticus est: id nisi fit, interpretationis instrumentum a scopo discordat; atque adeo omnis interpretatio seu vitilitigatio critica, falsa est, & temeraria, imo & exitiosa si tunc ejus ex regulis de divinioribus judicandum esset. Quod utinam exemplis non esset infeliciter confirmatum nostro hoc seculo, quando eousque profana Critica extensa est, ut per eam quam plurima divinæ Scripturæ, Jobi, Psalmorum, Proverbiorum, Ecclesiastæ, & Cantici Salomonis, multaque alia e Ϭεοπνεύστοις Dei verbis rejicere haud vereantur: quod ipsum pari ratione vel ad omnem Scripturam, etiam Novi Testamenti, extendi posset, si frena laxarentur impiæ Criticæ, quæ solidiora quæque & maxime fructuosa antiquioris & sanctioris Christianismi, nec non saniorum Ethnicorum monumenta, e manibus & existimatione omnium excutere conatur.
units.tr: II. Criticism should not be recommended as necessary for the interpreter to reach the author's purpose, unless the author himself is a critic by profession. If he is not, the instrument of criticism disagrees with the purpose, and so every interpretation or wrangling over words by criticism is false and rash, and even deadly if its judgments were to be made by its rules about the more divine matters. Would that this had not been unhappily confirmed by examples in our own age, when profane criticism has been extended so far that, through it, very many parts of divine Scripture (of Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Solomon, and many other things in the God-breathed [θεοπνεύστοις] words of God) are not ashamed to reject. The same reasoning could be extended to all Scripture, including the New Testament, if the reins were loosened for impious criticism, which tries to strip from the hands and esteem of all people the more solid and especially fruitful monuments of the older and holier Christianity, and of the saner heathens too.

units.la: 12. Critica per se omnium artium maxime est superficiaria, sterilis, periculosa, &, quando extra sphæram evagatur, ridicula. Est maxime superficiaria: quod si enim rerum in rationis facultate depictas ideas ostendimus esse superficiarias, quanto magis superficiaria dicenda est Critica, quæ non rerum ideas, sed cortices, verba, aliaque externa; nec hæc quidem, sed eorum minutias complectitur? Pari ratione cum idearum sterilitatem vidimus, ipsis steriliorem esse criticam evincere datur. Periculosissima quoque est, quandoquidem iis, qui plusculum ei applicantur, dispositiones ingenerare apta est, unde superficiarii fiant, vani, superbi, irrisores, impii, frigidi, morosi, irritabiles, calumniatores, non nisi ineptias scholasticas pædagogica vanitate crepantes & meditantes. Animus superficialibus nimis impense deditus iisdem conformis fit, ac interiora negligens, solidитate vacuus redditur & vanus; dum interim occupatus minutis cocogita- gitatiunculis inter homines rarius occurrentibus (quia haud multi hocce morbi genere laborant) omnibus sese mortalibus præcellere superbe somniat, cæterosque qui alibi quam inter imaginarios vitreosque istiusmodi thesauros divitias veras requirunt, irridet: & quoniam speculationes ejus steriles mortuæ sunt & frigidæ, hinc igneos (si quos habuit) pietatis motus desuescit, sitque paulatim impius in Deum & in omnia divina; deinde & in homines, charitate rejecta, morosus, atque irritabilis & calumniator, si contradicant; si vero audiant, imperiosus, pædagogica vanitate insolescens, & syllabicas nugas frivolasque ineptias veluti maximi momenti res magna cum gravitate inculcans, quales Galli vocabulo omnibus jam satis noto des pedants, suo idiomate appellant. Non affero tales esse omnes Criticæ rei studiosos vel peritos: absit! sed demum eos, qui tum immodice ei deduntur, tum vero qui propensionibus, quas immodica hæc applicatio imprimit, non restiterunt: quibus certe resistere se debuisse, adeoque rem periculo maximo non caruisse, fatebuntur quotquot candidi inter eos ab istis nævis hoc in negotio sunt præservati: ut non item minus sinceri, & critico cucullo toti infruniti. Hi vero, ubi ita exorbitant ut defumtam ex Scripturarum exterioribus verbis literam, eamque critico pulvere delibutam, proponant, demum veluti solidum Scripturarum sensum, animarumque cibum, adeo ridiculi sunt, ut comparari debeant cum coriariis, qui detracta animalibus pelle, eaque corticibus bus arborum pulveratis macerata, artem suam veluti artem parandi, ex animalibus cibos, coriaque sua ut delicias altiles commendarent: aut cum nonnullo, qui in amoeno & fructifero horto constitutus, neglectis fructibus & floribus paleas, spinas, festucas, & aranearum telas veluti thesaurum sacrum colligeret: vel denique cum milite, qui in coloribus armaturæ, gladiorum vaginis, caudæ equinæ pilis singulis recensendis totus versaretur, idque pro militaris officii functione, victoriæque laudandæ materia reputaret. Sumus namque hic veluti milites, quibus cum ignorantia, cum errore, cum vitiis pugnandum est: ad hoc autem tanquam medium e tenebris adjunctisque earum eluctandi, affertur nobis a quibusdam frigida & macra Critica. Quæ insulsitas! De talibus crediderim Græcos olim adagio dixisse: Exceptis Medicastris, nil Grammaticis esse stultius. Nec minus absurde agit vel subtilissima quæque sua opinione Critica, quando inductria suâ de lumine Dei aut inspirationibus divinis, (quæ resimmensius omnem criticam excedunt quam bovem aquila volatu) tractare præsumit, atque judicare, qui libri vel auctores sacri sese inspirationis vel luminis Dei respectu habeant. Tutius quemvis cœcum de coloribus & luce consules & sequeris, quam de istis quidem divinis rebus literales criticos, quorum extra sphæram suam extravagantes conatus atque discursus ita inepti sunt, ut non possint non movere risum aut commiserationem iis, qui vel aliquantisper solidiora & diviniora delibarunt. Ab exemplis abstinebo, ne se lædi conqueratur ullus.
units.tr: 12. Criticism in itself is, of all the arts, the most superficial, barren, dangerous and, when it wanders outside its own sphere, ridiculous. It is most superficial: for if we show that the ideas of things formed in the faculty of reason are superficial, how much more superficial must criticism be called, which embraces not the ideas of things but the husks, the words and other externals, and not even these as a whole but their trivia? By the same reasoning, since we have seen the barrenness of ideas, it can be shown that criticism is more barren than they are. It is also most dangerous, since it is apt to engender in those who apply themselves to it a little too much the dispositions by which they become superficial, vain, proud, mockers, impious, cold, peevish, irritable, calumniators, chattering only about scholastic trifles with schoolmasterly vanity and brooding over them. A mind too intensely given over to superficial things becomes conformed to them, neglecting what is within, and is emptied of solidity and made vain. Meanwhile, busy with petty little thoughts that rarely occur among men (since not many suffer from this kind of disease), it dreams that it proudly surpasses all mortals, and mocks the others who seek true riches anywhere other than among such imaginary and glassy treasures. And since its speculations are barren, dead and cold, it grows out of the habit of the fiery motions of piety (if it ever had any), and gradually becomes impious toward God and toward all things divine, and then toward men as well, with charity cast aside: peevish, irritable and a calumniator if they contradict it; if they listen, imperious, growing insolent with schoolmasterly vanity, and inculcating syllabic trifles and frivolous silliness with great seriousness, as if they were matters of the greatest importance. The French call such people, in a word now known to all, des pedants, in their own idiom. I do not claim that all who study or are skilled in criticism are like this: far from it! I mean only those who both give themselves to it immoderately and have not resisted the inclinations this immoderate application imprints. Those who are candid among them, and have been preserved from these blemishes in this business, will admit that they ought to have resisted them, and so had not been free of the greatest danger; the equally sincere, who are wholly unhampered by the critical hood, will say the same. But these men, when they go so far astray as to put forward the letter, taken from the outward words of Scripture and smeared with critical dust, as the solid sense of Scripture and food for souls, are so ridiculous that they ought to be compared with tanners who, after stripping the hide from animals and steeping it in pulverized tree bark, commend their craft as one of providing food from animals, and their hides as fattening delicacies; or with someone standing in a pleasant and fruitful garden who, neglecting the fruits and flowers, gathers chaff, thorns, straws and spiders' webs as if they were a sacred treasure; or finally with a soldier who occupied himself in counting the colours of his armour, the sheaths of his swords and each hair of a horse's tail, and reckoned this the performance of his military duty and matter for praising his victory. For we are here like soldiers who must fight against ignorance, error and vices; and to this end, as a means of struggling out of the darkness and its accompaniments, some offer us a cold and meagre criticism. What folly! Of such people I would believe the Greeks once said in their proverb: "Except for quacks, nothing is more foolish than grammarians." No less absurdly do even the most subtle critics act, in their own opinion, when they presume by their industry to treat of the light of God or of divine inspirations (which far exceed all criticism, as an eagle's flight exceeds an ox's), and to judge which books or sacred authors stand in relation to inspiration or the light of God. You would do better to consult and follow any blind man about colours and light than literal critics about these divine matters. Their efforts and digressions outside their own sphere are so silly that they cannot but move laughter or pity in those who have tasted even somewhat of the more solid and more divine things. I will refrain from examples, lest anyone complain of being hurt.

units.la: 13. Criticæ verus usus atque fructus, non ab ipsa sola, sed a concursu & efficacia scopi pendet. Accidere potest, ut Critices ope in Scripturæ v. g. historiis, circumstantiis, verbis, novus sensus detegatur: hic sensus per se non magis nos juvat, nec meliores reddit, quam qui priùs obtinebat; atscopo, hoc est, amori Dei intimo & spirituali adjunctus, egregiorum motuum atque fructuum in anima occasio esse potest. Atque hic est verus & legitimus sobriæ & sanæ critices usus, ut videlicet externa quædam detegat & illustret, ex quorum occasione ad intima Deo amato tradenda, virtutibus ornenda, & a peccatis & vanitate vindicanda fiat regressus. Critica sobria amori divino, vitæque spiritualis studio ut marito copulata, bonos quandoque fructus ad Dei honorem eniti potest: ast ab eo separata, nil aliud facit quam meretricari, spurias cogitationes edere, animamque tandem pessimæ tabis morbo misere interficere.
units.tr: 13. The true use and fruit of criticism depend not on criticism alone, but on the concurrence and efficacy of the purpose. It may happen that by means of criticism a new sense is discovered in, for example, the histories, circumstances or words of Scripture. This sense in itself helps us no more, nor makes us better, than the one we had before; but joined with the purpose, that is, with intimate and spiritual love of God, it can be the occasion of excellent movements and fruits in the soul. This is the true and lawful use of sober and sound criticism: that it uncovers and illustrates certain outward things, from whose occasion a return may be made to what is inward, to be handed over to the beloved God, adorned with virtues, and rescued from sins and vanity. Sober criticism, joined as a husband to love of God and the pursuit of the spiritual life, can sometimes bring forth good fruits to the honour of God; but separated from these, it does nothing but play the harlot, produce spurious thoughts, and at last miserably kill the soul with the disease of the worst corruption.

units.la: 14. Ubi de auctoris cujuscunque sensu citra Criticam non constat, caute de eo decidendum est. Vix quod in nobis ipsis est, rectè noscimus: cor nostrum fallax, tenebræ intus magnæ. Quanta ergo temeritas de aliis, præsertim ubi judicia sunt de rebus alicujus momenti, judicare velle? Præstat aliunde lucem omnia suo tempore manifestaturam expectare.
units.tr: 14. Where the sense of any author's meaning is not established apart from criticism, one must decide about it cautiously. We scarcely know rightly what is in ourselves: the heart is deceitful, and the darkness within is great. What rashness, then, to wish to judge about others, especially where the judgments concern matters of some weight? It is better to await the light that will make everything manifest in its own time, from elsewhere.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt præcipua quæ citra rem grammatices & critices essent observanda, ea ut saniores & utiliores essent, quae tamen apud harum artium professores vel negliguntur, vel prorsus ignorantur. Caetera, de textu aliquoties attente legendo, de idiomatis notitia, de circumstantiarum loci, temporis, occasionum scribendi observatione, de exemplarium collatione, aliorum aptorum interpretum consultatione, analoga sensuum auctoris cum principiis suis conformitate, & similia, abundantius quam modo dicta apud eosdem reperies. Quanquam autem ex iis, quae attuli, axiomatis, plura ad omnis generis libros atque auctores interpretandos referri possint, observabis tamen me plurimam partem ad scripta divina sanctaque dixisse & retulisse, quoniam scripta caetera non ita censentur digna quae exactius & laboriosius considerentur, saltem apud saniores. Cum de scriptis loquor, hoc & de verbis viva voce prolatis dictum velim, quantum id subjectum non recusat. Caeterum aliquantulum hoc in articulo si fui prolixior, id necessitati, qua abusus maximos praecaveri aequum est, praesertim vero ubi & ad sacra & ad aeterna extendi possunt, ab aequis rerum aestimatoribus imputabitur.
units.tr: And these are the chief things that should be observed apart from the business of grammar and criticism, so that these arts might be saner and more useful, though they are either neglected or entirely ignored by their professors. As to the rest (reading the text attentively several times, knowledge of idioms, observing the circumstances of place, time and occasion of writing, collating copies, consulting other suitable interpreters, the conformity of the author's analogous senses with his principles, and similar things), you will find these in the same authors more abundantly than I have set them out.
