Although many of the axioms I have stated could be referred to the interpretation of all kinds of books and authors, you will observe that I have spoken and referred for the most part to divine and holy writings, since other writings are not considered worthy of being examined so exactly and laboriously, at least by the saner sort. When I speak of writings, I wish this to be taken also of words spoken aloud, so far as that subject allows. Moreover, if I have been somewhat lengthy in this article, let it be imputed by fair judges of things to the necessity of guarding against the greatest abuses, especially where these may extend to sacred and eternal things.

units.la: XL. Super est ut, quia superius Theologiae superficiariae mentio facta est, paucis quid ea sit indigitem. Atque ut ostendam, quinam a falsa nec non a vera distincta sit, de hujus natura & communicatione paucis dicendum est. Theologia vera primitus in hoc consistebat, ut homo loqueretur cum Deo per oblationem facultatum suarum realium & intimarum, desiderii, intellectus & acquiescentiæ; Deus verò cum homine per communicationem suæ virtutis, lucis, & pacis intimæ. Hoc in statu, & ad perpetuam ejus continuationem, hoc est, ut æternus esset Theologus, conditus est homo; cui ad liberalitatis suæ magnificentiam testandam superaddidit Deus facultates tum externas, reales, quibus homo operibus Dei frui posset; tum superficiarias & picturarias intellectus activi sive rationis, ut homo imaginibus operum Dei efformandis & considerandis accessoria uteretur delectatione: Atque his omnibus facultatibus libertas præficiebatur, ut, quia virtutes seu perfectiones, lumina gaudiaque Dei, pariter & opera Dei externa infinita sunt, adeoque etiam infinitæ sunt iconcs, quæ de persectionibus divinis, deque externis Dei operibus fieri possint, mens ad placitum & jucundissime sese delectaret modo in his, modo in illis, sic uta nullis prohiberetur; omniaque ipsi ad lubitum paterent. Verum hac libertate abusus homo, intimarum divinarumque suarum facultatum exercitium cum Deo, primo quidem intermisit; deinde vero facultates externas rerum corporearum voluptatibus afficiendas tradidit; superficiarias autem rationis, picturis rerum istarum externarum effigiandis, parandis, disponendis dedidit, quibus etiam, omisso Deo, delectaretur. Huic hominis lapsui, (quo omnis boni scaturigine & effectis miser æternum destitutus fuisset, nisi inde relevaretur) opem ut ferret Deus, primo quidem eum ad intimas suas facultates Deo suo, ut prius, tradendas revocavit, nempe ut amorem denuo redderet Deo cum corde, animo, intellectu cogitationibusque totis, quod magnum æternumque mandatum est omnia complectens, fonsque unus vitæ; deinde ut eum quoque ab externorum voluptate rationisque superficiariæ iconolatria revocaret, id executus est mandatis aliis nonnullis, quæ quidem simul & carni molesta mentem a voluptatibus externarum facultatum continerent, & rationi obscura, curiositatem ejus frangerent; ut in lege Mosaica maxime pater, ubi vel mille mandatis ceremoniariis obediendum erat, ratiocinatione omni propulsa. Et hæc causa est cur Deus mandatis illis rationes suas non adjecit, nec explicationes addidit, ut nempe mens disceret simpliciter sineque activa sui ipsius consultatione ac ratiocinatione obedire, idque honoris Creatori exhiberet, quo subditi Reges suos, vel milites præfectos suos prosequuntur, quorum legibus & jussis illico morem gerunt, non postulata imo nec desiderata mandati ratione: quo sane simplicis obedientiæ honore illi & superioribus suis gratiores sunt, & minus errandi periculo expositi, quam secus: id quod etiam hominibus cum Deo accidisset. Verum enimvero, hi priorem errorem maluerunt continue errare, facultates Deo debitas ab illo cessare; alias externas, voluptatibus demulcere; rationem vero ideis atque ratiociniis de Deo, de attributis, decretis & mandatis ejus, deque explicationibus atque rationibus divi-
units.tr: XL. It remains for me to say briefly what superficial theology is, since I mentioned it above. To show how it differs from both false and true theology, I must say a few words about its nature and how it is communicated. True theology at first consisted in this: man spoke with God by offering his real and inward faculties of desire, understanding and acquiescence, and God spoke with man by communicating his power, his inward light and peace. Man was created in this state, and for its perpetual continuance, that is, so that he might be an eternal theologian. To attest the magnificence of his liberality, God also gave him external, real faculties by which man could enjoy God's works, and superficial, pictorial faculties of the active intellect or reason, so that man might take added pleasure in forming and contemplating images of God's works. Over all these faculties liberty was set, so that, since God's virtues or perfections, his lights and joys, and his external works are infinite, and therefore the images that can be made of the divine perfections and of God's external works are also infinite, the mind might delight itself at will and most pleasantly, now in these, now in those, being barred from none, and with everything open to it at its pleasure. But man abused this liberty. First he ceased the exercise of his inward and divine faculties with God. Then he gave over his external faculties to be stirred by the pleasures of bodily things, and he devoted his superficial faculties of reason to forming, arranging and ordering pictures of these external things, taking delight in them even with God left out. To help man in this fall, by which he would have been miserably and eternally cut off from every spring and effect of good unless he were relieved, God first called him back to surrender his inward faculties to his God as before, namely to render love to God again with heart, soul, mind and all his thoughts. This is the great and eternal commandment, which embraces all things and is the one fountain of life. Then, to call him back also from the enjoyment of externals and from the image-worship of superficial reason, God carried this out by several other commandments, which at once troubled the flesh and restrained the mind from the pleasures of the external faculties, and which, obscure to reason, broke its curiosity. This is seen most clearly in the Mosaic law, where obedience had to be given to a thousand ceremonial commandments with all reasoning driven away. And this is why God did not add his reasons to those commandments or supply explanations, so that the mind might learn to obey simply and without active self-consultation or reasoning, and so render to the Creator the honour that subjects render their kings, or soldiers their commanding officers, whose laws and orders they obey at once, neither asking nor even desiring the reason for the command. By this honour of simple obedience they are indeed more pleasing both to themselves and to their superiors, and less exposed to the danger of error, than they would otherwise be. This would also have happened to men with God. But these men preferred to go on erring in the former way: to withhold from God the faculties owed to him, to soothe the others with external pleasures, and to daub reason with ideas and reasonings about God, his attributes, decrees and commandments, and with explanations and grounds of the divine commandments.

units.la: norum mandatorum perpingere : quas ideas non tantùm chimæris suis erroribusque perniciosis miscuerunt; sed etiam putarunt eas obsequii cultusque divini vices supplere. Atque ista omnia , etsi aliquoties monita, sic in consuetudinem abierant, ut ipse Deus humanitate indutus accedere debuerit, mandata ista sua, de tradendis Deo amatorie facultatibus intimis, de externis, deque superficiariis, sive ratione & sensibus reprimendis , homines non modò vivo exemplo docturus, sed & de omnibus, queis ipsis opus erat, iisdem provisurus. Quapropter & vita & morte totus intimus Deo fuit Christus; totus extimus abstinentia voluptatum, poenisque omnis generis; denique totus in simplicitate, sine ullis ratiociniis, sineque sui ipsius consultatione Deo obediens; ut homines eodem per ejus imitationem redirent. Ac nec hi vel crederent vel profiterentur ejusmodi vias, carni ingratas, perditionis esse vias, effectusque irati in se Dei, se præterea infirmos esse nimis quam ut per eas transfire possint, ipsus per eas transiit qui Deo semper dilectus ad gloriosam vitam inde emersit, quique in iis Dei benevolentiam veniamque peccatorum pro hominibus deprecatus, eam & meritus est & obtinuit pro sui sequacibus, quibus etiam seipsum suaque omnia donare velit meritatum & omnipotentem impetravit & promisit Spiritum, quo induerentur, & cujus auxilio omnia possent, caeteraque si quæ necessaria, scirent ac agerent quotquot confidenter facultates spirituales Deo, corporeas mortificationi abstinentiæque, superuperficiarias seu rationem cum suis phaleris simplici obsequio committere vellent. Atque hoc ipsum cum fecissent Ecclesiæ primitivi homines, Spiritum promissum adepti, qui & vim sancte agendi & supernum lumen de divinis rebus mysteriisque antea sine ratiocinationibus creditis, & obscurius vel nullatenus perceptis suppeditabat, iterum veri Theologi, qualis primum conditus fuerat homo, evadebant, qui a Spiritu Christi acti & docti, vitam quidem quoad facultates supernas vivebant (a) in cœlestibus, abscondita cum Deo in Christo; quoad externas & superficiarias, (b) spiritu carnis opera mortificabant, & sapientiam carnalem, inimicam Deo reputabant; dabant autem operam ut ad Theologiam eandem solidam; sive theologicum statum primævum, quotquot ex hominibus possent, adducerentur, eo modo iisque viis, quibus ipsi ad ejus adeptionem pervenerant: hoc est, hortabantur homines uti facultates intimas suas ad Dei amorem elevarent, externas crucifigerent, superficiariaque ratiocinia contemnerent, quo spiritus Christi ipsis fieret sapientia. Atque hæc est summa Theologiæ, omniumque eorum, quæ sola Paulus animis hominum imprimere allaborabat, (c) puta Charitatem sive amorem Dei, sine quo cætera nulla sunt; (d) Christum crucifixum, cum vetus noster homo crucifigeretur, corpusque peccati aboleretur; tum & (e) cogitationum ratiocinationumque destructionem atque intellectus captivitatem sub obsequio Christi. Cum autem præter eos qui isthæc experti erant, quique præditi erant Spiritu Christi eos regente, illuminante, docente quid in Deo miserante, quid in hominibus ægris, quomodo cum unoquoque agendum ut obstacula in eis occulta viisque Dei opposita removeantur, nemo esset qui solidam hanc Theologiam propagare atque communicare posset vel audereteam: cumque initio solidi hi Theologi auditores reperirent bene dispositos, hoc est, desiderio, sinceritate & simplicitate insignes, paratosque qui se totos in Deum, in crucem, inque regimen ejus candide projicerent, tantos faciebant in illa propagarda progressus, ut ob nonnulla unius Petri verba, mox (a) ter, mox quinquies mille homines ad eorum sodalitatem accederent.
units.tr: These ideas they not only mixed with their chimeras and pernicious errors, but also thought they could take the place of obedience and divine worship. All these things, although warned against several times, had become so customary that God himself had to come clothed in humanity, to teach men by living example, and to provide for everything they needed, through those commandments of his: to surrender to God lovingly the inward faculties, to restrain the external and the superficial, that is, reason and the senses. So Christ, in life and in death, was wholly inward toward God; wholly outward in abstaining from pleasures and enduring every kind of suffering; and finally wholly simple, obeying God without any reasonings and without self-consultation, so that men might return by imitating him. Nor would they believe or confess that such ways, ungrateful to the flesh, are the ways of perdition and the effects of God's wrath against themselves, or that they are too weak to pass through them. He passed through them, he who was always beloved of God and emerged from them into a glorious life, and who in them begged God's goodwill and the forgiveness of sins for men. He both deserved and obtained these for his followers, to whom he also wishes to give himself and all that is his. He obtained and promised the Spirit, with whom they would be clothed, and by whose help they could do all things, and know and do whatever else was necessary, all who were willing to entrust their spiritual faculties to God, their bodies to mortification and abstinence, and their superficial reason with its ornaments to simple obedience. When the men of the primitive Church had done exactly this, and had received the promised Spirit, who supplied both the power to act holily and the heavenly light about divine things and mysteries, which before had been believed without reasonings and perceived more dimly or not at all, they again became true theologians, such as man had first been made. Moved and taught by the Spirit of Christ, they lived in their supreme faculties (a) "in heavenly places, hidden with God in Christ"; in their external and superficial faculties, (b) "they put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit, and they counted carnal wisdom hostile to God." They took pains to bring as many men as they could to that solid theology, or to the primeval theological state, by the same way and the same means by which they themselves had attained it. That is, they urged men to use their inward faculties to raise themselves to the love of God, to crucify the external, and to despise superficial reasonings, so that the Spirit of Christ might become their wisdom. This is the sum of theology, and of all that Paul alone laboured to impress on men's minds: (c) namely charity, or the love of God, without which nothing else counts; (d) Christ crucified, when our old man was crucified and the body of sin was destroyed; and also (e) the destruction of thoughts and reasonings, and the captivity of the intellect to the obedience of Christ. But apart from those who had experienced these things, and who were endowed with the Spirit of Christ governing, illuminating and teaching them what in God is merciful, what in sick men, and how each person must be dealt with so that the hidden obstacles within them, and those opposed to the ways of God, might be removed, there was no one who could or would dare to propagate and communicate this solid theology. At first these solid theologians found hearers well disposed, notable for desire, sincerity and simplicity, and ready to cast themselves wholly and candidly upon God, upon the cross, and upon his governance. They made such progress in spreading it that, on account of some words of Peter alone, soon three thousand and soon five thousand men joined their fellowship.

units.la: Non exigebat pia eorum simplicitas rationcinationes ullasve argumentatiunculas, non rhetorices lenocinia, non futilis criticces praecisas morositates. Sola (b) lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas, testimonium unum Domini fidele, sapientiam praestans parvulis, praeceptum Domini lucidum illuminans oculos, praeceptum magnum, Amoris hominis interni ad Deum, crucifixionis & abnegationis hominis externi & ratiocinantis, simplicissimis verbis propositum, illos, desideriis ad Spiritum Dei directis, sic convertebat ut Spiritu, sapientia, lumine Dei supremæ facultates implerentur, infimæ & activæ a voluptatibus & erroribus præservarentur, nec non sic custodirentur, ut ad finem usque possent perfecte conservari.
units.tr: Their pious simplicity required no reasonings or little arguments, no rhetorical enticements, no sharp and pointless fussiness of criticism. The law of the Lord alone, "undefiled, converting souls," the one "faithful testimony of the Lord," "making wise the simple," "the commandment of the Lord, enlightening the eyes," the great commandment of love of the inward man for God, and of the crucifixion and renunciation of the outward and reasoning man, set out in the plainest words, so converted those men, with their desires directed to the Spirit of God, that their supreme faculties were filled with the Spirit, wisdom and light of God, while their lowest and active faculties were guarded from pleasures and errors, and were so kept that they could be perfectly preserved to the end.

units.la: XLI. Verum enimvero docentium & di-
units.tr: XLI. But indeed, through the fault of teachers and learners

units.la: discentium culpâ, mox degeneravit solida ista Theologia in superficiariam, atque etiam in falsam. Namque cum satanas per Ethnicos Christianis insultaret, tanquam hominibus idiotis & plebejis, omnis literaturæ politioris atque Philosophiæ ignaris, (quò vafer genius simplicitatem Christi in ipsis corrumperet,) primo quidem aures dedêre tentatori, sic ut humanæ literaturæ sapientiæque oratoriæ darent operam, bono quidem animo, ut Ethnicos scilicet vel vincerent, vel ad silentium reducerent; at pessimo eventu, non attendentes ad exemplum Pauli has artes fugientis, quoniam eis(a) evacuaretur crux Christi, hoc est, doctrina de crucifigenda ratiocinatione & voluptate hominis externi, quæ sane etiam in titillatione aurium per artes Rhetoricas excitata hospitantur. Postmodum etiam eodem tentationis genere, oratoriis artibus Philosophicas scientias addiderunt, neglecto iterum Pauli consilio: (b) Videte, ne quis vos seducat per philosophiam & vanam fallaciam, prout homines sibi ista tradunt; & per elementa mundana, quæ non sunt secundum Christum, in quo vere reperitur perfecta plenitudo divina, in quo etiam plenitudinem habetis. Tandem duo hæcce mala tertiâ clade cumularunt, critica videlicet inani de litera, de corticibus, circumstantiis atque quæstionibus Scripturarum frivolis, ad amorem Dei proximique, nec non ad externi hominis crucifixionem non modo nil facientibus, sed & illum quidem extinguentibus, hunc vero foventibus: qua in re itidem Pauli monito non obtem- (a) 1 Cor. 1: 17. (b) Col. 2: 8.
units.tr: Through the fault of both teachers and learners, this solid theology soon degenerated into a superficial one, and even into a false one. When Satan assailed Christians through the Gentiles, as men who were simple and common folk, ignorant of all polished literature and philosophy (so that the crafty spirit might corrupt the simplicity of Christ in them), they first lent their ears to the tempter and devoted themselves to human literature and rhetorical learning. They did so with good intentions, namely to conquer the Gentiles or to silence them, but the outcome was disastrous. They did not heed the example of Paul, who fled these arts lest the cross of Christ be made void (a), that is, the doctrine of crucifying the reason and the pleasures of the outward man, which indeed take up residence in the tickling of the ears that rhetorical arts excite. Afterwards, by the same kind of temptation, they added philosophical sciences to the rhetorical arts, again neglecting the counsel of Paul: (b) See to it that no one lead you astray through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the traditions of men, and according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, in whom truly dwells all the fullness of the Godhead, and in whom you also have fullness. At last they heaped these two evils together with a third calamity, namely a vain criticism of the letter, of the husks, of the circumstances, and of the frivolous questions of Scripture, which not only do nothing for the love of God and neighbour or for the crucifixion of the outward man, but actually extinguish the former and foster the latter. In this matter too they did not obey the admonition of Paul (a) 1 Cor. 1:17. (b) Col. 2:8.

units.la: obtemperarunt:(a) Annuncia ne attendant fabulis (sic istas nominat quisquilias,) & (exemplo rem indigitans,) genealogiis interminatis, quae quaestiones magis exhibent quam aedificationem divinam in fide. Siquidem finis mandati sit amor e corde puro, conscientia bona, fideque sincera: a quo scopo nonnulli declinantes conversi sunt ad vaniloquia: & cum velint legis doctores esse, non tamen intelligunt quae dicunt, (substantiam ipsam rei) nec de quibus maxime asseverant. Cumque horum trium ex sint proprietates, Philosophiae quidem, ut ideas picturatas mortuasque de rebus excitet atque disponat; Critices, ut etiam quisquilias ridenda operosaque exactitudine referat; Rhetorices vero, ut haec apte ornateque coloret: hinc nata est Theologia superficiaria, quae in summo perfectionis suae gradu, notitia est idealis rerum divinarum, Scripturarum, earumque circumstantiarum, una cum peritia omnia ista ordinate & ornate referendi. Quisquis sine falso admixto ideas claras habet atque distinctas, quantum fieri potest, omnium quae sunt in Dei natura, quae sunt a Deo facta, quae sunt in Scripturis descripta, quae a ratione ex illis deduci possunt, quae illis ornatius proponendis inserviunt, is demum eatenus titulum Theologi superficiarii meritus est, neque is, si tria quae diximus mandata, de facultatibus internis Deo, de externis & superficiariis mortis dandis, neglexerit, alius revera est: in cujus ore verbum Dei definit esse verbum Dei, sitque verbum hominis vani, nil de verbo Dei praeter cortices mortuos habentis, invito vel improbante Deo, nec pro rato habente quicquid ejusmodi superficiarius effutiat: haud secus atque Rex aliquis, si legato suo regium verbum concredidisset, deinde hic deferto Rege ad propria se conferret, regium verbum nec haberet amplius, nec posset ad alios deferre, etsi materialia Regis verba atque syllabas recitare posset; quod sane casfsum per se foret, nec a Rege ratihabitum. Ita quoque non agnoscit pro verbo suo Deus voces ac sonos superficiariorum, etsi materialiter eadem sint quae dixit Deus: verum approbatione, forma, scopo atque efficacia Spiritus ejus destituta, divina dici non possunt; atque adeo nulla sunt cum superficiariis declamatoribus suis.
units.tr: they did not obey: (a) Charge them not to give heed to fables (so he calls these trifles), and (pointing at the thing by example) to endless genealogies, which minister questions rather than godly edifying which is in faith. For the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned: from which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling; desiring to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm. Since these three have their own properties (philosophy, to call up and arrange dead, painted ideas of things; criticism, to report even trifles with laughable and laborious exactitude; rhetoric, to colour these things aptly and elegantly), superficial theology was born from them. At its highest degree of perfection it is an ideal knowledge of divine things, of the Scriptures and their circumstances, together with the skill to present all these things in good order and ornate style. Whoever has clear and distinct ideas, as far as possible and without any admixture of falsehood, of all that is in the nature of God, all that has been made by God, all that is described in the Scriptures, and all that can be deduced from these by reason, and of what serves to present these things more elegantly, he at last deserves the title of superficial theologian. Nor is he truly anything other than this if he has neglected the three commandments we have mentioned: to give internal faculties to God, and external and superficial ones to death. In his mouth the Word of God ceases to be the Word of God, and becomes the word of a vain man who has nothing of the Word of God but dead husks, without God's will or approval, and God does not acknowledge as his own whatever such a superficial man utters. It is just as if some king had entrusted his royal word to an envoy, and this man, having deserted the king, went to his own affairs; he would then no longer have the royal word, nor could he convey it to others, even though he could recite the king's words and syllables materially. That would certainly be a mistake in itself, and not ratified by the king. So too God does not acknowledge as his word the voices and sounds of superficial men, even though they are materially the same as what God said. But being destitute of his approval, form, purpose and efficacy of his Spirit, they cannot be called divine; and therefore they have nothing in common with their superficial declaimers.

units.la: XLII. Atque hi quidem in degenere Christianismo mox se satis prodidere verbo ad bonum sterili, dum ex Ethnicis infidelibusque nullos ad verum Christi statum convertebant; eos vero qui se Christianos dicebant atque ejusmodi frigidis delectabantur pictoribus, nequaquam Spiritu Christi vivido imbuebant; sed picturis suis frigidis atque sterilibus de Deo, Christo, spiritualibusque ideis, nec non prout ex historia Ecclesiastica videre est, fertilibus contentionibus ac divisionibus beabant: ex quibus tamen merito excipias sanctiores aliquot verioresque Theologos, quorum plerique, his relictis, deserta petebant, ibi solidiorem Theologiam in animis sincerioribus propagaturi per Animae sanctimoniam, perque verba, quae in simplicitate e virtute Spiritus Sancti luminéque divino proferebant, quemadmodum demonstrant egregiæ Sanctorum Patrum Vitæ, atque vel unius ex illis Macarii Ægyptiaci admirabiles & divina prorsus sapientia abundantes Homiliæ. Cumque superficiarii viderent acquisitarum suarum ratiocinatarum artium inutilitatem, atque interim adhuc bonæ voluntatis essent, ad alios hosce, solida discendi gratiâ, sese conferre cogebantur, eosdemque & e solitudinibus suis evocare, si quis nodus vindice dignus incideret, aut si cui pertinaci adversario obviam ire necessarium esset, quod etiam hi opere magis quam verbo perficiebant, veluti is ipse faciebat Macarius, qui argutiolis philosophastri cujusdam thæretici resurrectionem negantis respondere verbis quasi impar, re fidem veritati præstabat, mortuum e monumento palam surgere jubens: Ita quoque narrat {a} Sozomenus, tempore Concilii Niceni philosophos nonnullos, unum præcipue loquendi & disputandi dexteritate præ cæteris insignem, Christianis veritatibus per argutias suas insultare voluisse: id quod cum non ferret senex quidam idiota, Christum inter persecutores antea profession, congredi cum ipso, irridentibus licet Theologis superficiariis, cæteris autem trepidantibus, non recusavit: tumque in nomine & virtute Christi Philosopho intrepide injunxit, uti quæ simplicissime exponebat de Deo Creatore, Verbo ejus per quod omnia creavit, Spirituque Sancto omnia conservante, deque Verbi incarnatione ad homines in viam reducen-
units.tr: XLII. And these men, in a degenerate Christianity, soon showed themselves to be words barren of good: while they converted no Gentiles or unbelievers to the true state of Christ, and those who called themselves Christians and delighted in such cold pictures they by no means imbued with the living Spirit of Christ. Instead they fed them with their cold and sterile pictures of God, Christ and spiritual ideas, and with fruitful contentions and divisions, as can be seen from ecclesiastical history. Among these, however, one should rightly except some holier and truer theologians, most of whom, leaving these things, sought out the desert, there to propagate a more solid theology in sincere souls through the holiness of the soul, and through words which they spoke in simplicity, by the power of the Holy Spirit and divine light. The outstanding lives of the holy Fathers show this, and so does the admirable homilies of Macarius of Egypt alone, which abound in truly divine wisdom. And when the superficial theologians saw the uselessness of their acquired and reasoned arts, while still of good will, they were compelled to betake themselves to those others, for the sake of learning solid things, and even to summon them from their solitudes if some knot worthy of a champion arose, or if it was necessary to meet some stubborn adversary. These men accomplished this more by deed than by word, as Macarius himself did. When a certain heretical little philosopher who denied the resurrection pressed his subtleties, Macarius, being no match in words, upheld the truth by the deed, bidding a dead man rise openly from the tomb. So too Sozomen relates that at the time of the Council of Nicaea some philosophers wished to insult Christian truths with their subtleties, one of them being especially distinguished above the rest in skill of speaking and disputing. When a certain old uneducated man, who had previously professed Christ among the persecutors, saw this, he did not refuse to meet the philosopher, although the superficial theologians laughed at him and the others trembled. In the name and power of Christ he boldly commanded the philosopher to listen, as one should, to what he set forth most simply about God the Creator, about his Word through whom he created all things, about the Holy Spirit who preserves all things, about the incarnation of the Word to lead men back into the way,

units.la: {a} (a) Hist. Eccl. Lib. i. c. 18. ducendos, & de ultimo judicio, debite tantum audiret, neve de eis disputare præsumeret; quippe quæ non ratione humana, sed divina fide (hoc est, traditione facultatum, intellectus passivi præsertim, Deo illuminanti) percipiantur: at crederet modo. Id quod Philosophus, divina vi perculsus, protinus & fecit, & interiora sua a Domini virtute tacta professus, suos sodales se ut imitarentur, adhortabatur. Subjungit auctor, idem & Alexandro cuidam Episcopo, minus subtili, nec disputatori admodum, accidisse, cum Philosophi omnes per unum ex suis subtilissimum Christianos ad certamen provocassent: siquidem is oblatum certamen acceptans, hisce verbis solum erga adversarium usus: Philosophe, in nomine Jesu Christi tibi injungo utitaceas, eum cum sociis suis ita ad mutum adstrinxit silentium, ut omnes vim Dei in ore loquentis, simplicis, at solidi Theologi, cernerent & admirarentur. Plura similia allegari possent, nunc temporis forte inutilia, vel etiam ab irrisoribus ridenda, tum ob defectum ejusmodi solide Theodidactorum, tum quia desunt qui audeant cum fide, hoc est, committendo desiderium, intellectum acquiescentiamque Deo, confidentia freti illum potenti luminosaque vi sua in ipsis infinities melius operaturum, quam possit vel omnium creaturarum ratiocinans & rhetorica activitas omnis, quæ ne superficiariam quidem Theologiam acquirere aut communicare valet.
units.tr: {a} (a) Hist. Eccl. Lib. i. c. 18. and about the last judgment, and not to presume to dispute about these things. For these are perceived not by human reason but by divine faith (that is, by the handing down of faculties, especially of the passive intellect, God enlightening it), but one must simply believe. The philosopher, struck by divine power, at once did so, and, professing that his inner self had been touched by the power of the Lord, he urged his companions to imitate him. The author adds that the same thing happened to a certain Bishop Alexander, who was less subtle and not much of a disputant, when all the philosophers challenged the Christians to a contest through their most subtle man. For he, accepting the challenge offered, used only these words towards his opponent: Philosopher, in the name of Jesus Christ I command you to be silent, and so he bound him and his companions to a dumb silence, so that all beheld and admired the power of God speaking through the mouth of a simple but solid theologian. Many similar examples could be cited, which perhaps are now useless, or even ridiculed by mockers, both because of the lack of such solid teachers of divine things, and because there are none who dare, with faith, that is by committing their desire, intellect and assent to God, trusting in his powerful and luminous strength, which will work in them infinitely better than all the reasoning and rhetorical activity of all creatures, which can neither acquire nor communicate even superficial theology.

units.la: XLIII. Namque etsi Theologia superficia- ria
units.tr: XLIII. For although superficial theology

units.la: ria in rationis humanæ facultate idearia refideat, non tamen in ea adesse posset nisi ex origine altiori, & alio quam proprio auxilio eam haberet ratio: quod similiter de omnibus, vel de præcipuis quæ in ratione sunt aut esse possunt, verum esse, antea oltensum est. Ilta vero adminicula, non in solis Scripturis, aut in alicujus, etsi Solide eruditi, viva voce consistere possunt; sed requiritur aliquid divinius, nimirum vel Deus solidaque Theologia quæ præcesserit, vel idem Deus cum & in bona voluntate discentis operans. Non quod Dei vel Theologiæ solidæ operatio in superficiariam illam terminetur; sed quod qui solidam per operantem Deum perque suam illi traditionem habuit, is si facultates supremas a Dei lumine & amore declinet, soliditate & realitate tunc privetur, remanente tamen pictura vel idea umbratili earum quas possidebat vel experiebatur rerum divinarum: veletiam inde, quod cum superficiariæ addiscendæ activitate rationis incumberet discipulus, idque bono scopo, bonisque desideriis ageret, Deus precum & bonæ voluntatis fautor, luminibus gratiisque nonnullis solidis eum affecerit, a quibus postmodum ille desciscens, imagines tantum superficiarias inde retineat. Alioqui hisce sine adminiculis bonis, quamvis vel Angelus Theologiam superficiariam, idealiter veram, aliis vellet instillare, non magis tamen id sine aliquo in discentibus divino lumine benevoloque animo efficere posset, quam vel excitare, non dico ideas colorum vivas in senfibus, sed ideas colorum in sola imaginatione eorum qui nunquam viderunt; vel non magis quam alteri vultum alicujus, quem nunquam viderit, ita verbis exprimere, ut inde ejus ideam sibi in imaginatione æque bene repræsentare possit ac si oculis suis eum vidisset. Quod nemo non impossibile esse agnoscet: idque etiam demonstrat experientia in illis qui Scripturis divinis humana activitate incumbunt, quorum fere unusquisque in diversas ab aliis partes tandem secedit. Et quemadmodum, si quis cæcus, v. gr. audivisset aut etiam memoriæ impressisset omnia quæ Physicus aliquis, vel Cartesius in Physica & Dioptrica de lumine coloribusque explicuit, posset quidem illa recitare, forte etiam unum atque alterum de his ratiocinium satis rectum ex suo addere, id aliis docere, sibique forsitan aliquid in imaginatione depingere, & tamen revera nescires quid diceret, ejusque imaginata certo essent falsa: ita qui nunquam bene dispositio animo (quo aperitur mentis oculus) Deum in intimis operantem (cujus operatio lumen est) respexit, is etsi omnia quæ sanctissimi quique de divinis rebus dixere aut scripsere, memoria teneat, sibi de his activitate intellectus ideas efformet, ratiocinetur, recitet, doceat; nescit tamen revera quid dicat, falsa imaginatur, meroque casu accidit, ut quædam haud absurda ratiocinio exprimat, etsi sibi aliisque magnus solidusque habeatur Theologus, qui tamen certe ne quidem superficiarius adhuc est, quamvis hoc si esset, nullus esset, teste Paulo; stultus esset, teste Christo comparante eum qui verba sua audiverit seu perceperit, nec tamen in praxin reduxerit, cum homine insano, qui in superficie arenosa domum, ingenti ruina dilapsuram construxisset.
units.tr: Superficial theology resides as ideas in the faculty of human reason, but reason could not have it there unless it had it from a higher origin and by a help other than its own. This, as was shown earlier, holds similarly for all, or the principal, things that are or can be in reason. Yet these aids do not consist only in the Scriptures, or in the living voice of any teacher, however learned in solid theology. Something more divine is required: either God and the solid theology that has gone before, or God himself working together with the good will of the learner. This is not because the work of God or of solid theology is confined to that superficial kind. Rather, one who has received solid theology through God working in him and through his own handing-over of himself to it, if he turns his highest faculties away from the light and love of God, is then deprived of solidity and reality, though the picture or shadowy idea of the divine things he once possessed or experienced remains. Or again, it may be that while the pupil applies himself to the active work of reason in learning superficial matters, and does so for a good purpose and with good desires, God, the favourer of prayers and good will, bestows on him some solid lights and graces; but he then falls away from these and keeps only superficial images. Otherwise, without these good aids, even if an angel wished to instil into others a superficial theology that is true in idea, he could no more bring this about without some divine light and kindly disposition in the learners than he could stir up (I do not say living ideas of colours in the senses, but) ideas of colours in the imagination alone of men who have never seen them; or than he could describe to another, in words, the face of someone the other has never seen, so that the hearer could represent its idea in his imagination as well as if he had seen it with his own eyes. Everyone will acknowledge that this is impossible, and experience also shows it in those who apply themselves to the divine Scriptures by human activity alone: almost every one of them at last goes off into a different path from the others. And just as, if some blind man had heard, or even fixed in his memory, everything that some natural philosopher, or Descartes, has explained about light and colours in physics and optics, he could indeed recite those things, and perhaps add one or two fairly sound reasonings of his own about them, teach them to others, and perhaps paint something in his imagination; yet he would really not know what he was saying, and his imaginings would certainly be false; so too one who has never looked, with a well-disposed mind (by which the eye of the mind is opened), upon God working inwardly (whose working is light), even if he holds in memory all that the most holy men have said or written about divine things, and forms ideas of them by the activity of his intellect, reasons about them, recites them, and teaches them, does not really know what he is saying, imagines falsehoods, and only by pure chance does he express some reasoning that is not absurd. He may be held by himself and others to be a great and solid theologian; yet he is certainly not even a superficial theologian yet. And although, if he were, there would be none such, as Paul testifies, he is foolish, as Christ testifies when he compares to a madman the man who has heard or grasped his words but has not put them into practice: a man who built his house on sandy ground, which would collapse with great ruin.

units.la: XLIV. Cæterum ne quis justam querendi ansam, etsi præcisam, pertinacius captet, ex præcedentibus constare arbitror, qui ea in superficiariis hisce cum philosophicis tum theologicis disciplinis continentur, possint veluti postliminio vel accommodative pro hominum infirmitate ad usum bonum transferri: quamvis pro eo qui via omnium rectissima ad solida tendere velit, his dimissis, eo modo qui in priori libro descriptus est, progredi tutius fuerit.
units.tr: XLIV. Moreover, lest anyone seek a just occasion for complaint, though a narrow one, more stubbornly, I think it is clear from what has gone before that the things contained in these superficial disciplines, both philosophical and theological, may, as it were by right of postliminy, or by way of accommodation to the weakness of men, be turned to good use. Nevertheless, for one who wishes to make his way to solid things by the most direct route of all, it will be safer to set these aside and proceed in the manner described in the earlier book.

units.la: XLV. Hactenus ad Eruditionis superficiariæ naturam, dignitatem, proprietatesque exponendas, de ratione, ideis, ratiociniis, scientiisque in genere ea diximus, quæ ad illud quod suscepi propositum, sufficere videntur. Et quamvis ea methodi severitate, qua cum de Eruditione solida principio agerem, uti conatus sum, rem totam hic non exegi; crediderim tamen, substantiam eorum quæ eruditionis superficiariæ acquisitionem, possessionem & communicationem concernunt, me hinc inde ex occasionibus natis sic proposuisse, ut nihil quod præcipuum sit, intactum esse arbitrer, etsi non in partes suas expansum: esset enim res invidiæ plena, eorum quæ maximi fere apud omnes æstimantur, tenuitatem ac fere nullitatem pluribus exponere. Namque etsi superficiarii, si qui sint, eruditi , in possessione eruditionis suæ sint quietiores, modestiores, virtutibus ornatiores, magis cæteris hominibus sese accommodantes, censuræque patientiores, quam solent esse falsi; neque etiam admodum curent vi aut artibus pravis sua communicare, aut etiam tueri: quoniam tamen sic se plerumque gerebant, quando cum Sophistis certamen erat, vel cum a nugacibus arbitrabantur se impeti, quid iidem essent facturi cum a veritate solida sese crederent impugnari, (rectius sanari dicendum foret;) haud adeo tutum esset experiri: quandoquidem amor proprius, qui gaudet & lætatur cum ab iis impugnatur qui ineptis telis contra eum pugnantes victoriæ ansam subministrant, si videret de sua turpitudine deque suo occasu serio agi, non posset non furore percelli, etsi occultius. Sunt namque virtutes superficiariorum, quies, pax, modestia, æquitas, lenitas, prorsus, ut eruditio eorundem, superficiariæ, quæ oblatione veritatis solidæ concuti facile possunt; eorumque affectus subtiliores cum sint, sunt etiam, cum excitantur, perniciosiores, rationis, virtutis veritatisque speciem mentientes, dum odio tacito & veluti ridendo, veritates solidas ludunt, contemnunt, dedignantur, atque abiis, tanquam a rebus nullis, moderatiori modo avocant, quotquot timent ne se relictis ad solidiora adspirent. Sunt namque ex amore proprio, (cujus motibus non adversantur,) & discipulorum suis conceptibus mancipandorum cupidi, & ex tumiditate, qua se inflari sinunt, quibusvis aliis veritati rati solidæ magis inimici, minusque falsis eruditis apti, qui ad eam ex animo convertantur. Sed quid brevitati meæ excusationem quæram in ratissimo superficiariæ eruditionis crimine, cujus si fe reos per me declarari timerent multi, rogo, ex initio sequentis libri credere id dedisцant; simulque habeant rationem cur paucis de eruditionis superficiariæ possessione & communicatione hic egi, eam esse quam illic pronunciaturus propero, subjecturus quæ de Eruditione falsa suscepi dicenda.
units.tr: XLV. Thus far we have set out the nature, dignity and properties of superficial erudition, and have spoken generally of reason, ideas, reasonings, and sciences, which seem sufficient for the purpose I have undertaken. And although I have not carried the whole matter through here with the strict method I tried to use when I first treated of solid erudition in principle, I believe that I have set out, here and there as occasions arose, the substance of what concerns the acquisition, possession and communication of superficial erudition, so that nothing principal, I think, has been left untouched, even if it has not been expanded into its parts. For it would be an invidious business to expound at length the thinness and almost nullity of things that are held in greatest esteem by almost everyone. For although superficial scholars, if there are any, are calmer in the possession of their learning, more modest, more adorned with virtues, more accommodating to other men, and more patient of criticism than false scholars usually are, and although they do not much care to communicate or even defend their learning by violent or wicked arts, still, since they usually behaved in this way when they were in contest with the Sophists, or when they thought they were being attacked by trifling persons, it would not be very safe to test what they would do if they believed themselves to be assailed by solid truth (it should rather be said, healed). For self-love, which rejoices and delights when it is attacked by those who, fighting against it with feeble weapons, provide it with an occasion for victory, could not help being struck with fury, though more covertly, if it saw that its own baseness and its own downfall were being seriously dealt with. For the virtues of superficial scholars, their quiet, peace, modesty, fairness and gentleness, are wholly like their erudition, which is superficial and can easily be shaken by the presentation of solid truth. And their more subtle affections, when they are stirred up, are also the more pernicious, wearing the appearance of reason, virtue and truth, while with a hidden hatred, and as if mocking, they play with, scorn and disdain solid truths, and with a sort of moderate manner they turn away from them, as from nothing, all those who fear that, leaving superficial things behind, others may aspire to more solid ones. For they are, through self-love (to whose impulses they do not object), eager to have disciples enslaved to their own conceptions, and, through the puffed-up vanity by which they let themselves be swollen, they are more hostile to solid truth than any other kind of people, and less apt to be converted to it from the heart than false scholars are. But why should I seek an excuse for my brevity in the most evident crime of superficial erudition? If many men fear to be declared guilty of it through me, I ask them to believe it from the beginning of the following book, and at the same time to bear in mind why I have treated here briefly of the possession and communication of superficial erudition: because I am hastening to state, there, what it is, and to add what I have undertaken to say about false erudition.

units.la: Eccles. VIII. 17.
units.tr: Eccles. VIII. 17.

units.la: Intellexi, quod omnium operum Dei nullam possit homo (propria industria) invenire rationem eorum quæ fiunt sub sole: & quanto plus laboraverit ad quærendum, tanto minus inveniet: Etiamsi dixerit sapiens (sive Philosophus) se nosse, non poterit (tamen) reperire.
units.tr: I perceived that man (by his own industry) cannot discover the reason of all the works of God that are done under the sun; and however much he labours to seek, the less he will find: even if the wise man (or philosopher) says that he knows, he will not be able (nevertheless) to find it.

units.la: LIBER TERTIUS, qui est DE ERUDITIONE FALSA
units.tr: BOOK THREE, which is on FALSE ERUDITION

units.la: I. Nter res humanas nonnullæ ita sunt comparatæ, ut quando acquisitæ sunt, statum fixum non habeant; sed illico mutationem patiantur, eamque vel in melius, vel etiam in deterius. Hujusmodi Eruditionem Superficiariam esse agnoscimus: quippe quæ acquisita, non patitur se in statu suo mere superficiario possideri; (quæ causa est cur de possessionis ejus statu multa non dixerimus;) sed ab eo vel in falsam transit, vel ad veram enititur & pervenit. Etenim, vel mens in superficiaria illa eruditione non subsistet, sed ex idealibus notitiis ad Originale Summum elevabitur, ab illo & ejus & creaturarum suarum nobis necessariarum solidam communicationem peritura illis modis viisque, de quibus in libro primo egimus; atque sic ad veram solidamque Eruditionem itura est: aut vero in eadem Superficiaria terminabitur, omittetque id ipsum quod jam faciendum dixi. Et hoc in casu primum tenebris, dein erroribus, tandemque insania percellitur tur ita mens, ut ejus omnis eruditio præcedanea prorsus falsetur : etsi quam deinceps acquirit, eam falsam esse omnino necesse est : destituitur siquidem solido fundamento, omniumque rerum radice & nutriente succo, Deo nempe, ejusque vitalibus effluviis. Quapropter omnino emarcescat oportet. Quemadmodum namque si quis iconibus pingendis ita totus dederetur, ut rebus omnibus renunciaret, is eo pacto vitæ, calori, luci etiam sic valediceret, ut quamvis penicillum pictorium pertinacius aliquamdiu motitaret adhuc, inconcinnæ tamen & absurdæ ejus motitationes essent, queis non elegantes imagines, sed chimæræ, aut incompositi convulsique ductus repræsentarentur : ita etiam quæ rerum ideis in se excitandis incumberet mens ab origine omnis realitatis rivulisque ejus abstinens, ea non posset non (cibo quippe solido vitalique calore & lumine destituta) sic languida & impotens fieri, ut omnia ejus excitandi sibi ideas conamina nil aliud essent quam inconcinnorum figmentorum molimina, tametsi casu inter hæc etiam nonnihil realitatis cujusdam parvulæ repræsentativum occurrere posset.
units.tr: I. Among human things, some are so constituted that, once acquired, they do not keep a fixed state but immediately undergo change, and that change may be for the better or also for the worse. We acknowledge that superficial erudition is of this kind. Once acquired, it does not allow itself to be possessed in its merely superficial state. (This is why we have not said much about the condition of that possession.) Instead it passes from there either into falsehood or strives on and reaches the true. For either the mind will not stay in that superficial erudition, but will be raised from the ideal notions to the Supreme Original, and, once there, will obtain a solid fellowship with it and with its creatures, which we need, by the means and ways we discussed in the first book, and so it will proceed to true and solid erudition. Or else it will stop at that superficial erudition and omit the very thing I said must be done. In this case the mind is first struck with darkness, then with errors, and at last with madness, so that all its previous erudition is utterly falsified. Even whatever it acquires afterward must necessarily be wholly false, since it lacks a solid foundation, the root of all things and their nourishing sap, namely God and his vital emanations. Therefore it must wither away. For just as if someone were so wholly given over to painting pictures that he renounced all other things, he would in this way bid farewell to life, warmth, and even light. Although he might for some time still wave his painter's brush more stubbornly, his clumsy and absurd strokes would be such that they would represent not elegant images but chimeras, or disordered and convulsive lines. Likewise, a mind that sets itself to stir up ideas of things, while keeping away from the origin of all reality and its streams, cannot help becoming so languid and powerless (being deprived of solid food, vital warmth, and light) that all its efforts to stir up ideas are nothing but the labours of misshapen fictions, even though by chance some small representation of a certain reality might occur to it among these.

units.la: II. Quemadmodum obliquitatis & mendacii plura sunt genera, pluraque ad ea media, quam rectitudinis & veritatis; sic etiam Eruditionis falsæ plures sunt species pluresque viæ quam Eruditionis solidæ. Has etsi singulatim omnes recensere & explicare nec facile sit, neque etiam utile, de eis ta-men men quædam rangemus, ubi prius aliquid de nostro argumento dixerimus generalius.
units.tr: II. Just as there are more kinds of crookedness and falsehood, and more ways to them, than of rectitude and truth, so too there are more species and more ways of false erudition than of solid erudition. Although it is neither easy nor useful to list and explain all of these one by one, we will nonetheless touch on some of them, after first saying something more general about our subject.

units.la: Eruditio omnis cum fit præparatio subjecti rudis ad scopum suum, ea quæ falsa est, si nomen saltem eruditionis aliquatenus mereatur, scopum habeat oportet ad quem subjectum suum disponat vel disponere tentet. Quando autem re ipsa falsa est, ergo aut scopum non ferit, aut scopus ipse falsus est, vel alia quædam solida & ei necessaria desiderantur: de his ultimis in posterum disquiremus: nunc de scopo.
units.tr: Every erudition, since it is a rough preparation of the subject for its goal, if false erudition deserves at least the name of erudition in any way, must have a goal toward which it disposes, or tries to dispose, its subject. But when it is really false, then either it does not hit the goal, or the goal itself is false, or other solid things that are necessary to it are lacking. We will inquire into these last points later. For now, let us speak of the goal.

units.la: Scopus hominis, a Deo ei constitutus & assignatus, est beata æternitas, sive ipsemet Deus æternus, summus ac felix, aut æterna & felix cum Deo communicatio, cui per traditionem rudium nostrarum facultatum, rerumque pro divino placito usum, hocce vitæ brevis tempore præparanda mens est: id quod per Eruditionem solidam fieri, libro primo potuimus cernere. Sed & dantur (quod dolendum est) alii plures hominis scopi, non a Deo quidem propositi, sed ab ipso homine, qui factori perfectorique suo terga obvertens, sibi ex ingenii libidine scopos viasque proprias efformat queis totam impendat vitam. Tales Dei desertores propriorumque scoporum fabricatores, ubi Deum tanquam scopum ex anima ejecerunt eique facultates negarunt supremas, patet non posse non destitui divino lumine, atque ignorantia tenebrisque erga Deum ergaque ea quæ ab illo sunt percelli. Patet & eosdem, ubi se ipsos tan-
units.tr: The goal of man, assigned and appointed to him by God, is blessed eternity, that is, God himself, eternal, supreme and happy, or an eternal and happy communion with God. For this, the mind is to be prepared during the brief time of this life, by the surrender of its own faculties and the use of things according to the divine pleasure. We were able to see in the first book that this is accomplished through solid erudition. But (to our regret) there are also several other goals of man, not indeed proposed by God, but by man himself, who, turning his back on his Maker and Perfecter, fashions for himself, from the lust of his own mind, goals and ways of his own, to which he devotes his whole life. Such deserters of God and makers of their own goals, when they have cast God out of their soul as a goal and denied him his supreme faculties, it is plain that they cannot but be deprived of the divine light and be struck with ignorance and darkness regarding God and the things that are from him. It is plain also that these same people, when they have put themselves in God's place as their own goals,

units.la: 1 tanquam sui scopos in Dei locum surrogarunt, non posse quoque non propriis fictisque luminibus, hoc est, figmentis chimærisque variis, aliquam lucis speciem varie mentientibus, abundare: quod quidem pro multiplici animorum dispositione diversi diversis exequuntur modis.
units.tr: 1 as goals of themselves, cannot but abound in their own fictitious lights, that is, in various figments and chimeras, which variously counterfeit some appearance of light. They carry this out in various ways, each according to the manifold disposition of their minds.

units.la: III. Etenim nonnulli sic se ipsos pro scopo habent, ut delectationem & voluptatem suam quærant in admiratione & contemplatione actīvitatis & industriæ proprii ingenii sui suarumque inventionum, (quod coram Deo inter omnia crimina caput est, & abominatio maxima;) & isti huic scopo media convenientia adhibentes, atque ut plurimum sibi solis agentes, inventionibus propriis (eis sæpe spretis quæaliorum, etiam erudite solidorum sunt, ) tori deduntur. Alii dum pro scopo animi voluptatem suique admirationem habent, eam conquirunt quæ ipsis accedat ab hominibus, idque vel a plebecula & multitudine, quales animi ut plurimum sacris Theologicisque studiis, linguis etiam peregrinis addiscendis & polymathiæ inutili sese applicant: in quibus dent operam oportet ne a vulgaris plebisque usu trito gratis recedant; sed ut recepta placita, & suæ quisque sectæ proprias opiniones mordicus teneant atque propugent; si vero a Magnatibus etiam æstimationem famamque exspectant, tunc scopi hujus gratia fit, ut edificant mores, historias, jura aut artes quibus magnatum commodis vel deliciis inserviendo, eorum favorem demereantur, & quibus vel pompa posa ædificia, vel spectacula jucundaque exercitia, vel rara acquisita, ve exitiosa belligerandi media, & cætera ejusmodi, perficiantur. Nonnulli ut commoda opesque sibi ipsis, (dum etiam suus sibimet ipsis scopus sunt,) accumulent; quibus acquisitis vel solo divitiarum spectaculo (quæ avarorum est insania) se delectent, vel earum opera, si non omnia, saltem plurima quæ ad voluptates terrestriores & animales faciunt, comparent; vel etiam potentiam (opibus enim omnia cedunt) auctoritatemque in alios exerceant, eisve habeantur commendabiles, sese quoque vel omnibus eisdem, quæ jam diximus, studiis atque artibus sacrorum & jurium, morum & mathematum; vel etiam aliis philosophantium medicorum puta, literatorum, & si quæ hujusmodi plura, addicunt præcipue.
units.tr: III. For some men so make themselves their own goal that they seek their delight and pleasure in admiring and contemplating the activity and industry of their own wit and their own inventions (which before God is the head of all sins and the greatest abomination). Such men, employing fitting means for this goal, and for the most part acting for themselves alone, are carried away by their own inventions, often scorning those of others, even those that are solidly learned. Others, who have as their goal the pleasure of their mind and admiration of themselves, seek that which comes to them from men, whether from the common crowd and the multitude. Minds of this kind for the most part apply themselves to sacred and theological studies, to learning foreign languages too, and to useless polymathy. In these pursuits they must take care not to depart freely from the worn-out usage of the common people, but to hold fast and defend stubbornly the accepted tenets and the opinions peculiar to each one's sect. If, however, they also look for esteem and fame from the magnates, then for the sake of this goal they undertake to build customs, histories, laws or arts, by serving the conveniences or pleasures of the magnates, so as to win their favour, and to produce by these means either splendid buildings, or spectacles and pleasant exercises, or rare acquisitions, or deadly means of waging war, and other things of this sort. Some men, in order to accumulate for themselves conveniences and wealth (since they too are their own goal), then either delight in the mere spectacle of their riches (which is the madness of misers), or by their means procure most, if not all, of the things that serve earthlier and animal pleasures; or else they exercise power and authority over others (for all things yield to wealth), and wish to be commended by them. Such men also devote themselves especially to all the same studies and arts that we have just mentioned: sacred and legal studies, morals and mathematics, or else the studies of philosophers, physicians, literary men, and whatever other things of this kind there are.

units.la: IV. Hic, ne calumniæ locus relinquatur, ea quæ initio partis proxime præcedentis declaravi, iterum ingeminare cogor; a me videlicet nequaquam hic intelligi eos qui exbono scopo bonisque viis ejusmodi studiis navant operam: adeo ut nullus, qui bene actorum sibi conscius est, credere se debeat a me hic tangi. Sed sic rem se habere velim credant omnes; me in thesi exponere quid omnibus omnino, nullo excepto, accideret, si scopo vero oblivioni tradito, sese studiis quibusvis applicarent; aut etiam quid de facto eis acciderit quos in genere, nullius persona designata, agnoscunt omnes omni tempore, hocce etiam nostro, repertos esse plus
units.tr: IV. Here, lest room be left for slander, I am again compelled to repeat what I declared at the beginning of the preceding part. Namely, I by no means mean here those who labour in such studies for a good goal and by good ways. So much so that no one who is conscious of having acted well should believe that he is touched upon by me here. Rather, I would have all believe that I am setting out in theory what would happen to everyone, without exception, if, with the true goal forgotten, they applied themselves to whatever studies; or also what in fact has happened to those whom all acknowledge, in general and without any particular person being named, to have been found in every age, and in this our own too, to be more than

units.la: {4*} Monitum ad cautionem: vellatio- nem, nec non & deceptionum cautionem. plus nimis, qui quavis in arte & scientia indebite sese erudire conati sunt, non ex Dei proximorum ve justa dilectione: sed ex voluptatum, famæ, opum potentiæque proprio amore. Quo posito, omnes quibus se imbuere potuerunt, scientias & artes, sacras atque profanas, necessum est falsas fieri. Non quod per eas ad scopos illos suos adduci non possint: ad hoc enim valent plurimum, tametsi interdum & hic fallant, nec attingantur scopi. Sed quod istiusmodi scopi (atque ideo etiam eorum media viaeque) non sint resistabiles & solidæ, verum evanidæ atque fallaces, a quibus sæpe in vita, in morte semper deciditur.
units.tr: {4*} Warning for caution: against vellication, and also against deception. too many, who in any art or science have tried to educate themselves improperly, not out of a just love of God and neighbour, but out of a proper love of pleasures, fame, wealth and power. Given this, all the sciences and arts they were able to imbibe, sacred and profane, must necessarily become false. Not that they cannot be led by these to their own goals, for these serve very well for that purpose, although sometimes they deceive even here, and the goals are not reached. Rather, it is because such goals (and therefore also their means and ways) are not solid and lasting, but fleeting and deceptive, and from them one falls away often in life and always in death.

units.la: V. Et tunc quidem deprehendendum erit ejusmodi erudito, quàm falsus sit ipse, & quàm sit falsa ejus eruditio, quando videbit sibi, cum Dei desertoribus, qui fonte vivificantis aquæ relicto venenatis e lacubus aquas haurire maluerunt, pereundum esse: tametsi nec semper eousque fit exspectandum ut falsæ eruditionis documenta appareant, quæ & dum vivitur satis sese produnt; siquidem ea mens tota sit & tenebris & erroribus horumque annexis penetrata, eorum quæ solida sunt prorsus ignara, interimque cognitiunculis quarundam festucarum atque vanarum minutiarum cum incredibilis arrogantiæ gibbo tumida: aut si de solidioribus divinisve utcunque sit sollicita, in eis pertinaci errore placita ampletatur figmenta amori proprio demulcendo apta, eaque cum furore & vitiosis affectibus, nec non cum odio & persecutione solide eruditorum, propriique animi fui anxietate & conturbatione propugnet.
units.tr: V. Then the learned man will indeed discover how false he himself is, and how false his learning is, when he sees that he must perish along with the deserters of God, who, having abandoned the fountain of living water, preferred to draw water from poisoned pools. Yet one need not wait until the proofs of false learning appear, for they betray themselves while a man is still alive. His mind is wholly steeped in darkness and error and their attendants, utterly ignorant of what is solid, and puffed up with a hump of incredible arrogance over some trifling knowledge of straws and empty trifles. Or, if he is concerned with more solid or divine matters in any way, he embraces with stubborn error the inventions that pleased him, inventions suited to soothing self-love. He defends them with fury and vicious passions, with hatred and persecution of those who are truly learned, and with anxiety and disturbance of his own mind.

units.la: VI. Hisce omnibus, quæ ex neglectione veri scopi falsique substitutione, eruditioni falsæ generandæ atque corroborandæ inferviunt, accedunt & alia, ad eandem formandam & ftatuminandam non minus facientia: qualia sunt, 1. ipse modus animos tenetos ab ineunte ætate erudiendi: 2. materiarum seu documentorum quibus imbuuntur falsitas: 3. Magistrorum conditiones: 4. instrumenti denique fui, five rationis, corruptio. Quæ, ut eruditionis falsæ aliqualem ideam habeamus, resumemus paucis singula, ab ultimis retrogradatim incipientes.
units.tr: VI. To all these things, which serve to generate and strengthen false learning through the neglect of the true goal and the substitution of a false one, there are added others no less conducive to forming and establishing it. Such are: (1) the very method by which minds are trained from early youth; (2) the falsity of the materials and teachings with which they are imbued; (3) the conditions of the teachers; and (4) finally, the corruption of their instrument, that is, of reason. To give us some rough idea of false learning, we shall briefly take up each of these, beginning with the last and working backwards.

units.la: VII. Ratio humana, eruditionis, de qua agimus, acquirendæ instrumentum, quia & corruptissima est & cœciffima, milleque catenis præjudiciorum tum a fe ipsa, tum ab aliorum auctoritate venientium capta, mille etiam affectuum jugis veluti servitute quadam oppressa, non potest non parere falsam eruditionem. Tametsi enim eruditi nonnulli rationem suam ab affectuum & ab auctoritatis alienæ vinculis, nec non a propriorum præjudiciorum jugo in libertatem afferere enitantur; id tamen frustra erit & in cassum ibit, quamdiu a Deo & ab ejus per facultates supremas amplexatione recefluri sunt. Solus erga Deum amatorius affectus nos a pravis affectibus liberare potest: solo Dei lumine constare potest, cui auctoritati (incipientibus enim auctoritas quædam necessaria est,) nuncius sit mittendus : neque etiam tirones praejudicia sua ex se possunt deponere, quin eo ipso tum nova, atque depositis pejora, assumant; tum e veteribus praejudiciis quam plurima, ipsis occulta, latenter & perniciose retineant, ut ut Cartesius cum quibusdam ex suis opinetur, errorem, quem detegere humanae inductriae impossibile fuerit, nocere non posse, eo nempe quod non percipiatur: tametsi revera eo erit nocentior, quo occultior, & quo minus ab ullo, praeterquam a solo Dei lumine, detegendus.
units.tr: VII. Human reason, the instrument of acquiring the learning we are discussing, is most corrupt and blind, held captive by a thousand chains of prejudices arising both from itself and from the authority of others, and oppressed by a kind of constant slavery to a thousand passions. It cannot but produce false learning. Some learned men do strive to free their reason from the bonds of passions and of foreign authority, and from the yoke of their own prejudices. Yet this will be in vain and come to nothing, as long as they stand aloof from God and from embracing him through the highest faculties. Only a love directed toward God can free us from wicked passions. Only the light of God can establish what authority ought to be followed, for beginners indeed need some authority. Nor can novices lay down their prejudices of their own accord without at the same time taking up new ones, and worse than those they put down. Moreover, they secretly and harmfully retain very many old prejudices that remain hidden from them. Descartes and some of his followers hold that an error which cannot be detected by human industry cannot do harm, since it is not perceived. Yet in truth it will be the more harmful the more hidden it is, and the less it can be detected by anyone except by the light of God alone.

units.la: VIII. Ejusmodi autem praejudicia latentia , quae vel a maximis dubitatoribus, retinentur, & a sola Dei luce clare ut erronea deteguntur, haec sunt & similia. Rationis aestimatio vitatem depravatam non esse: posse eam sibi ipsi suppetias ferre: posse labore suo detegere veritatem, & se ipsa bene uti: judicare item bene de lumine, de claritate, de bonitate aliisque rerum affectionibus: excitare sibi ideas rerum, easque cum consequentiis bene disponere: Ideas non esse (quod revera sunt) steriles, mortuas, inefficaces, obscuras, & quae ejusmodi in ideis itemque in rationinis superiori libro notavimus: Lumen rationis non ex Deo in superioribus facultatibus lucente, ad rationem reflecti & accedere debere: eum (siquidem ejus auxilio opus se habere cogitent,) non debere tamen negare adjutorium hominibus tum curiosulis, qui ex mera libidine se ipsos admirandi, amandi, voluptatibus suis prospiciendi, rationem peccaminosam mille phaleris honorare-vel onerare contendunt ; tum Dei amandi, serviendi, laudandi obliviosis, adeoque ingratis & impœnitentibus: non debere itaque Deum eos qui tales sunt tenebris & insania potius percutere, quam aliquali lumine perfundere. Hæc & similia perniciosissima præjudicia in animis eruditorum primitus & medullitus latere, etsi prius non animadversa, quis est ex omnibus sibi attendentibus qui non fateatur? Aliter si foret, siquè abessent a nobis hæ præjudiciorum exitialium pestes, philosophari certe inciperemus a poenitentia & revocatione intima nostrarum ingratitudinum in Auctorem nostrum benefactoremque perpetuum a deprecatione pœnarum ac tenebrarum juste nobis debitarum & adhærentium, a laudibus immensis amoreque obsequioso & tenerrimo Majestatis ut Maximæ ira Optimæ, quæ rebellibus aditum ad bona sua gratiosum hactenus non interclusit; tum quoque a contemtu ægræ potentiæ & activitatis rationis nostræ, & a submissis petitionibus ut Deus seperiora quidem nostra potissimum reformaret, sibique tota vendicaret; rationi autem cæterisque externis facultatibus tantum auxilii interim præstaret, quantum sapientiæ suæ notum est id conducturum ad disponenda atque debite usurpanda externa & evanida pro intimorum & æternùm duraturorum adeptione & promotione. At vero inter eos qui eruditionem quærunt, quotusquisque est qui hac via solide ostendat se dicta præjudicia vere deposuisse ? quis, cum se per dubitationem de omni-
units.tr: VIII. Such latent prejudices, which are retained even by the greatest doubters and are clearly exposed as erroneous only by the light of God, are these and similar: that the judgment of reason is not depraved as to truth; that reason can help itself; that by its own labour it can uncover truth and make good use of itself; likewise that it judges well about light, clarity, goodness and the other affections of things; that it stirs up ideas of things for itself and arranges them well together with their consequences; that ideas are not (which in fact they are) sterile, dead, ineffective and obscure, as we noted in the earlier book about ideas and reasoning; that the light of reason, shining from God in the higher faculties, ought to be reflected back to reason and approach it; that God, if indeed they think they need his help, should nevertheless not deny help to men, on the one hand to the curious, who out of mere lust to admire themselves, to love themselves and to provide for their own pleasures, strive to honour, or rather burden, sinful reason with a thousand trappings, and on the other hand to those who forget to love, serve and praise God, and are therefore ungrateful and unrepentant; so God ought not to strike such people with darkness and madness rather than to suffuse them with some light. That these and similar most pernicious prejudices lie hidden at first and deep in the minds of the learned, though not noticed before, who among all who attend to themselves does not admit? Otherwise, if these deadly plagues of prejudice were absent from us, we would surely begin to philosophize from repentance and an inward turning back from our ingratitude toward our Author and perpetual benefactor; from the deprecation of the punishments and darkness justly owed to us and clinging to us; from immense praise and obsequious, most tender love of the Majesty as most great and best in its anger, which has not hitherto closed to rebels the gracious way to its goods; then also from contempt for the feeble power and activity of our reason, and from submissive petitions that God would chiefly reform our higher faculties and claim them wholly for himself, while meanwhile giving to reason and our other external faculties as much help as his wisdom knows will serve to arrange and rightly use external and fading things for the attainment and promotion of the inward and eternally enduring. But indeed, among those who seek learning, how few are there who by this way solidly show that they have truly laid aside the said prejudices? Who, in preparing himself by doubting all things,

units.la: K omnibus præpararet, in censum dixerit adduxisse etiam dubitationem de rationis suæ rectitudine, sufficientia, potentia, quæ sane satis dubiæ esse debent ex debitis Dei judiciis in peccatores curiosos, impotentes, ingratos, confusos, qui non incipiunt ab illo a quo omnia sunt: necesse suaque omnia ad illum referunt atque terminant, ad quem tamen omnia spectant & remeare debent?
units.tr: has taken into account also doubt about the rectitude, sufficiency and power of his reason? Surely this ought to be quite doubtful, in view of God's due judgments upon sinners who are curious, impotent, ungrateful and confused, who do not begin from him from whom all things are, and who do not refer and bring all their own things back to him, toward whom all things tend and to whom they ought to return.

units.la: Rara avis in terris nigroque simillima cygno.
units.tr: A rare bird on earth, and very like a black swan.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, non aliter fieri potest quin eruditio tantorum & tam culpandorum præjudiciorum affectuumque servituti superexstructa, sit omnino falsa, quin etiam in dies evadat salsior & portentosior quo magis temeraria ratio scopum summum realemque deferens, activitate limitata, debili, ægra, luxata, ideisque umbratilibus, imperfectissimis & fere nullis innixa, ædificium suum elevare conabitur: quod non tantum, ut ut splendidum appareat, confusum & Babylonicum fiet; sed & tandem eò pro operis coronide deducet illos qui ipsi miseræ toti innituntur, ut ex alto opinione sua ædificio, in atheismi barathrum ferantur præcipites. Cum enim ea mentis & facultatum nostrarum sit indoles, ut sola objecta agnoscant cum quibus sese exercent, cætera vero pro nullis habeant & ignorent; hinc est quod mens, si facultates supremas non exerceat cum rebus ipsis divinis ipsoque Deo; sed solam rationem (quæ ex inferioribus est) cum umbris tantum idealibus Dei divinorumque excolat; necessario sane eo lapsura est, ut & Deum ipsum sit nescitura, & ideæ Dei umbratili obscuræque multa ex corruptione & tenebris suis admiscens, ejusmodi portentum ideale inde cudat, unde negatura sit exsistere posse aliquid ei simile; quod hac aliisque de causis, diversimode pluribus accidisse, ostendi ex professo ubi atheismi genera novem, in quæ multifariam eruditi aliique incidunt, e rationis nimio exercitio vel amplexu prodire demonstravi, & Rationis excusatiunculas palliativas, quibus lethalem suum morbum dissimulare, coloremque validæ sanitatis sibi superinungere fatagit, ibidem dissipatas exhibui; quapropter hic de argumento isthoc plura addere superfluum foret.
units.tr: Since these things are so, it cannot but be that a learning built upon the servitude of so many blameworthy prejudices and affections is altogether false; indeed it grows ever more insipid and monstrous the more rashly reason, bearing its highest aim and true goal, with its activity limited, weak, sick and dislocated, and resting on shadowy, very imperfect and almost nonexistent ideas, tries to raise its edifice. This edifice, however splendid it may appear, will become confused and Babylonian; and at last, as the crown of the work, it will carry down those who wholly rest their trust in it, so that, lifted high by the opinion of their building, they are borne headlong into the abyss of atheism. For since it is the nature of our mind and faculties to recognise only the objects with which they occupy themselves, and to regard and ignore the rest as nothing, it follows that if the mind does not exercise its supreme faculties upon the divine things themselves and upon God himself, but cultivates only reason (which belongs to the lower things) together with the merely ideal shadows of God and divine things, it will necessarily come to this: that it will not know God himself, and, mixing into its idea of God many things from its own corruption and darkness, it forges from that a monstrous ideal, from which it will deny that anything like him can exist. That this has happened in many diverse ways, for this and other causes, I have shown professedly, where I demonstrated that the nine kinds of atheism into which learned men and others fall in many ways arise from an excessive exercise or embrace of reason; and there I also set out and dissipated the little palliative excuses of reason, by which it strives to dissemble its deadly disease and to paint over itself the colour of robust health. Therefore it would be superfluous to add more on this subject here.

units.la: IX. Accedo ad Magistros, quatenus insti- tutione sua falsæ eruditionis causa vel promo- tores esse possunt.
units.tr: IX. I come now to the teachers, insofar as by their instruction they may be promoters of false erudition.

units.la: Hi cum vel viva voce docent, (qui e viventium numero sunt,) vel libris ac scriptis mutis, (quæ & post mortem auctorum superstunt;) de utrisque nonnihil dicendum est specialius. Sed ne omnis malæ eruditionis culpa in eos solos refundatur, agnoscendum utique est, (id quod verius,) ante omnes alios hic primò in cura liberorum peccari ab ipsorum parentibus: non modo quando ex nullo scopo divino agunt, neque ut creaturas generent, quæ Deum æterno amore, honore, obsequio, laudeque prosequantur, meræ potius libidini carnis propriæque voluptatis prurigini inhiantes; sed etiam quando, ubi jam nati sunt, animæ eorum curam seriam plane deserunt, non magis de prole sua solliciti, quam de fœtu agrestiori stupidioresferæ. Ipsi quippe prædis conquirendis, rapiendis nummis, vel aliis voluptatibus toti intenti & dediti, liberorum interima animos formandos quo securius negligant, totam eam curam in alios devolvunt, Ethnicos, qui nulla difficultate & sine scrupulo natorum corpora exponebant, eo magis astorgia vincentes, quo animæ infinitis parasangis corpora antecellunt. At negotiis scilicet gravioribus & majoris momenti vacare tenentur parentes.quasi vero negotia momentosiora dari possint, quam natos proprios æternitati beatæ vel miseræ præparare! Huic supinæ negligentiæ cum providentia divina utique favere non possit, hinc fit ut infelices istiusmodi erudiendorum liberorum animulæ in pædagogos incidant vel impios, vel ineptos, qui malis parentum exemplis domesticis, exempla propria pejora, pessimaque præcepta superaddentes, perniciosæ eruditionis fundamentis, nunquam postea delendis, recentes discipulos sibi commissos imbuunt. Neque aliter fieri potest, ubi pædagogi isti rum pietate & sapientia vera destituti, rum frigidis ac inanibus variarum notionum farraginibus referti sunt, cumque præterea ex rei suæ vel angustia vel amore nil aliud in instituendo præter lucelli mercedem aucupantur, & simul parentum juventutis sibi commissæ, ad commoda item sua promovenda, favorem: quem quidem mirifice sibi demereri videntur, siquidem lepidarum suarum mentium formam deformem in discipulorum mentibus, veluti in speculo expresserint, cum omnibus futilibus & periturís notiunculis nugisque, quibus interdum liberaliter satis exuberant. Atque id parum esset nisi etiam eo tenderet infelix quorumdam opera, ut a Dei internis motibus, aut ab eorum animadversione & obsequio, praepediantur tenerae mentes, quo solis rebus externis & evanidis reddantur sensibiles.
units.tr: Since they teach either by the living voice (they belong to the number of the living) or by mute books and writings (which survive the deaths of their authors), something more particular must be said about both.
