But so that the whole blame for bad erudition is not poured onto them alone, it must be acknowledged (and this is the truer view) that before all others the first fault lies here with the parents themselves in the care of their children. This happens not only when they act with no divine purpose, neither to beget creatures who will pursue God with eternal love, honour, obedience and praise, but rather greedily pursue mere lust of the flesh and the itch of their own pleasure. It happens also when, once the children are born, they utterly abandon the serious care of their souls, being no more concerned for their offspring than for the young of a wild and stupider beast. Indeed, wholly intent and devoted to hunting prey, snatching up money, or other pleasures, they hand the whole care over to others, so that they may neglect the forming of the children's minds the more securely. They copy those heathens who exposed their children's bodies without difficulty or scruple, and they surpass them in cruelty to the same degree that souls surpass bodies by infinite parasangs. Yet parents are supposed to be busy with weightier affairs and matters of greater moment. As if any more important business could be found than preparing their own children for blessed or wretched eternity! Since divine providence cannot possibly favour this supine negligence, it comes about that the unhappy little souls of such children fall into tutors who are either impious or incompetent. These tutors, adding worse examples and worse precepts of their own to the bad domestic examples of the parents, imbue the fresh pupils committed to them with the foundations of a pernicious erudition that can never afterwards be erased. Nor can it be otherwise when such tutors, destitute of true piety and wisdom, are stuffed with cold and empty heaps of various notions, and when, moreover, out of either the narrowness or the love of their own affairs, they seek nothing in teaching but the reward of a little profit, and at the same time seek the favour of the parents in order to advance their own interests. They seem to win this favour wonderfully, inasmuch as they show the deformed image of their own wretched minds in the minds of their pupils, as in a mirror, together with all the trifling and perishable little notions and nonsense with which they are sometimes lavishly enough supplied. This would be a small matter if the labour of certain unhappy people did not also aim to keep tender minds from God's inward movements, or from attending to them and obeying them, so that they become sensitive only to external and fading things.

units.la: Quoniam vero istiusmodi magistrorum mentes, etsi suis bullis superabundent, plerunque tamen adeo steriles sunt, ut ne quidem illas ex se ipsis habeant, (nedum splendida & fertilis de omnibus veritas ex eorum cordibus scaturiat,) sed potius si quae habent, ea ex aliorum scriptis hinc inde excerpta & compilata sint: ideo ad librorum acervos non secus ac claudi ad grallas & ipsi confugere & compellere alios consueverunt.
units.tr: But since the minds of such teachers, although they overflow with their bubbles, are for the most part so sterile that they do not even have these notions from themselves (much less does splendid and fruitful truth about all things well up from their hearts), but whatever they have has been excerpted and compiled here and there from the writings of others, therefore they, like the lame with their crutches, are accustomed to flee to heaps of books, and to drive others there too.

units.la: X. Sed antequam de his nonnulla hic subjiciamus, duo adhuc monenda restant. Alterum quidem: haec non tantum in aetate tenera, sed & in provectiori saepe sic se habere. Nempe quotusquisque est inter adultos virosque, qui sui ipsius recte erudiendi curam vere & serio gerat, quique propria conscientia proprioque lumine in mentis recessu de rerum soliditate doceri, & experientia sua convinci cupiat ac studeat? Aliorum scilicet is labor esto. Ipsi quidem argenti comparandi curam non abdicabunt aut in alios rejicient, neque nummos aliena fide sic recipient, ut eos in arcam recondant antequam bene examinaverint sintne adulterini, necne: at vero in Mente sua tenebris, præjudiciis vitiisque eluenda veraeque eruditionis candore & decore illustranda, ut ipsimet tantum laboris suscipiant, quid adeo opus sit? Sufficerit, si animas suas eodem loco habeant, eademque cura dignentur, qua quisque induvia sua prosequitur, videlicet illas lotricibus aut lotoribus quibusdam spiritualibus certo pretio lavandas uti tradant, lotas vero atque lævigatas qualicunque modo recipiant, donec eas iterum ab externarum rerum pulvere purgandas existiment, sicque ad lotores suos per intervalla recurrant, cum quibus per circulum continuum ad finem usque vitæ tale exercitium fiat. Et horum quidem lotorum officium & cura esto, de animis eluendis & poliendisque deque diversis methodis & instrumentis quibus res suas peragant, sollicitos esse, ac inter se disputare: ipsis autem sufficerit discipulis, Mentium formas, speciem candidas, politas & aliquali ruditate exutas ab eis porrecto nummo & aliena fide recipere. Hæc nisi ita se habere videas, lector, haud sane multum te perspicacem esse merito crediderim. E vulgo quidem vix ullus, cui vel tantillum sinceritatis superest, negaverit, omnes laborem Eruditioni solidæ adipiscendæ necessarium defugere, nec animi sensus anxios & perduros, quos in illa acquirenda sustinendos esse suis locis vidimus, subire aut perferre velle: sed potius ante tempus lætari, securos esse, & genio suo dulciter indulgere. Quapropter eos etiam Magistros conquirentes qui id ossicirçis præstent, eosdem divina permittente justitia, & procurante naturæ calliditate, abunde satis consequuntur, qui scilicet, ut sacræ prophetiæ verbis utar, aures prurien- tes eis titillent, qui eos, dum mancipia corruptionis sunt, liberos pronuncient, a quibus denique veluti mulierculæ discant semper, nunquam autem perveniant ad agnitionem veritatis, solidæque eruditionis: cujus inter veræ eruditionis notas cum hæc sit præcipua, eis videlicet quæ in intimis animi penetralibus sunt gerunturque, ita contentum esse, ut quamvis Magistri cæteri omnes, omnesque libri & totus mundus cum iis perirent, nil tamen Eruditioni huic ea propter fit decessurum, consequens omnino est, eam non posse non ingratam esse illis Magistris qui semper omnibus pernecessarii esse cuperrent.
units.tr: X. But before we add some remarks on these, two further things remain to be warned of. The first is that these things are often so not only in tender age but also in more advanced years. For how few are there among adults and grown men who genuinely and seriously take care to educate themselves rightly, and who desire and strive to be taught, by their own conscience and their own light in the recesses of the mind, about the solidity of things, and to be convinced by their own experience? That labour, of course, is for others. They themselves will not renounce the care of acquiring silver, nor throw it onto others, nor accept coins on another's trust and store them in the chest before they have carefully examined whether they are counterfeit or not. But in their mind, which must be cleansed of darkness, prejudices and vices and illuminated with the candour and grace of true erudition, why should they undertake so much labour themselves? It will suffice if they hold their souls in the same regard and give them the same care with which each person looks after his clothes: that is, to hand them over to certain spiritual launderers to be washed for a fixed price, and then to receive them back washed and smoothed in whatever way, until they think them again in need of cleansing from the dust of external things, and so return to their launderers at intervals, with whom this exercise goes on in a continuous circle until the end of life. Let it be the office and care of these launderers to be anxious about washing and polishing souls, and to dispute among themselves about the different methods and instruments by which they carry out their work. For the pupils it will suffice to receive, for a coin offered and on another's trust, minds that look white and polished and are freed of some roughness. If you do not see these things to be so, reader, I should justly think you not very perspicacious. Hardly anyone from the crowd who has even a little sincerity left would deny that all men shun the labour needed to attain solid erudition, and are unwilling to undergo or endure the anxious and lasting feelings of mind which, as we have seen in their places, must be borne in acquiring it. Rather, they rejoice in advance, are carefree, and sweetly indulge their own genius. Therefore those who seek out teachers to perform these services for them obtain, with divine justice permitting and nature's cunning procuring, exactly what they want. These are the teachers who, in the words of sacred prophecy, tickle itching ears, who promise them liberty while they themselves are slaves of corruption, and from whom they are always learning and never come to the knowledge of the truth. Since one of the principal marks of true erudition is to be content with those things which are in the innermost recesses of the soul and are done there, so that even if all other teachers, all books and the whole world perished, nothing would be lost to this erudition on that account, it necessarily follows that such erudition cannot but be unwelcome to those teachers who would always wish to be thought indispensable to all.

units.la: XI. Alterum, quod dixi observandum, illud est: Magistrorum operam nequaquam tamen subabrogatam optari quando unumquemque suæ stitutionem & suorum eruditioni operam dare debere hic monetur.
units.tr: XI. The second point I said should be observed is this: the labour of teachers is nevertheless not to be wished away altogether, even though it is admonished here that each person should attend to his own instruction and to the erudition of his own.

units.la: Neglectum saltem sui & suorum castigatum volui, quem plerunque comitatur succenturiatio pædagogorum ineptorum: & hos quidem notari cupiam ac improbari, nequaquam autem bonos, qui sane bonis parentibus, in se suisque erudiendis ut impigris, ita nec undiquaque huic officio sufficientibus, a singulari divinæ Providentiæ gratia administrantur, veluti beneficium ingens bonorumque desideriorum & precum pretiosa compensatio, unde & æterna animarum salus pendeat quam sæpissime. Hæc hujus loci non esse videri possent, nisi calumniæ prævertendæ causa interponerentur: quæ libris etiam eadem ratione applicari debent: de quibus nunc dicemus.
units.tr: I wished at least to rebuke the neglect of oneself and one's own, which is usually accompanied by the substitution of incompetent tutors. I want these men noted and condemned, but by no means the good ones. Indeed, good parents are given good teachers by the singular grace of divine providence, teachers who are diligent in their own instruction and are not altogether sufficient for this duty in the case of their children. They are a great benefit and a precious recompense for good desires and prayers, and the eternal salvation of souls very often depends on them. These matters might seem not to belong to this place, were they not inserted to forestall calumny. The same caution must be applied to books, and of these we shall now speak.

units.la: XII. Omnem Eruditionem vel in libris continery vel a libris pendere, quam plurimis persuasum est: sed contrarium potius est verum. Ipsi libri pendent ab eruditione. Hæc libros prior produxit, non ita illam libri: neque hi sane intellectum dant, sed intellectus hos, ut lepide Divus Antonius in Iteratos quosdam sophistas, ipsi de ineruditione sua literali tacite insultantes, retorquebat. Ilthæc ergo sententia Criticorum ineptioribus est relinquenda, quorum omnis eruditio periret, quinque cornicula Æsopica nudiores redderentur, omnes libri si tollerentur e medio. Omnis Eruditionis veræ fons primarius, atque sedes & habitatio, in Mente est, quæ si nunquam ab origine sua recessisset, omnigenam sine libris habere potuisset Eruditionem, non tantum quoad res divinas, sed etiam quoad corporeas: siquidem & post lapsum sine hisce adminiculis eam de facto adepti sint ante & citra omnes libros primarii quotquot Eruditi, uti ex historiis sacris profanisque patescit.
units.tr: XII. Very many are persuaded that all erudition is contained in books or depends on books; but the contrary is rather true. The books themselves depend on erudition. Erudition produced books, not the other way round, and books do not give understanding; rather, understanding gives books meaning. St Antony made this point wittily when he retorted against certain repeaters of other men's words, who were silently insulting each other's literal ignorance. So this opinion of the critics is to be left to the more inept, for whom all erudition would perish, and who would be left as naked as Aesop's jackdaw, if all books were removed from the midst. The primary source of all true erudition, and its seat and dwelling, is the mind. Had the mind never departed from its origin, it could have possessed every kind of erudition without books, not only in divine things but also in bodily ones. Even after the fall, all the learned men there have been obtained it without these aids, before and apart from all books, as is clear from sacred and profane histories.

units.la: XIII. At vero cum ejusmodi animæ soliditate eruditæ in aliis mentibus, nec sibi ipsis nec interno veritatis germini satis attendentibus, perqué alligationem ad res corporeas distractionibus, non possent dispositiones suis similes excitare sine signo eis dato in rebus externis, quibus adhærebatur; hinc primò voces, deinde & scripta adhibuerunt, illas auribus, hæc visui corporeo objicientes, quo animæ primò crassius inde commotæ, subtilius postea in se redirent, & ad interna attenderent lumina, a quibus proprie eruditiores evaderent. Atque hæc est vera librorum & solidorum & primariorum origo, nempe, prodire eos ab hominibus intus lumine & eruditione gaudentibus, qui, ut aliæ animæ itidem ad intima sua sibi attendendo retrocederent, eis ad exemplum & imitationem narrabant seu scribebant quæcunque ipsimet apud se experiebantur.
units.tr: XIII. But since minds that were not sufficiently attentive to their own inner seed of truth, and were distracted by their attachment to bodily things, could not stir up dispositions like their own in other minds without a sign given to them in external things, to which they clung, they first used voices and then writings, presenting the former to the ears and the latter to the bodily sight. By this means souls were first stirred more coarsely, and afterwards turned back into themselves more subtly and attended to the inner lights, from which they would properly become more learned. This is the true origin of books, both solid and primary: they came forth from men who rejoiced within in light and learning, and who, so that other souls might likewise attend to their own inner depths and turn back, related or wrote for them, as an example and model, whatever they had themselves experienced within.

units.la: At quando cæteri legendis librisistis (audiendis etiam Magistris) sic incumbebant, ut sibi ipsis intus non satis attendentes, parum aut nihil luminis in se haberent, & nihilominus vel ex gloriolæ desiderio ad commendationem sui, vel ex commodorum aliorum cupiditate, ipsi magistrorum instar scriptitare vellent: hinc primum omnis generis libri absurdi, vani, falsique enati sunt: & systemata quidem, cum auctorum vel librorum primariorum veros sensus, eorumque cohærentiam se percipere, idque aliis commodius referre posse putaverunt; vel quando ipsimet propriorum figmentorum compaginem & structuram imaginati fuut: Variorum vero & particulariorum argumentorum volumina, quando varia sua quæ hinc indesinenexu habuerunt cogitata, vel deliramenta voluerunt exprimere: commentarios autem, cum aliena sensa & scripta explicare præsumserunt: diariorum, actorum & relationum, quando eorum quæ legerunt bona malaque, farragines, epitomas aut veluti indices conscribere volebant: confutationum tandem & disputationum tunc cum aliena, sæpe verissima, sæpiusque nullo modo a se intellecta, destruere nitebantur, quo sua in locum eorum surrogarent. Hi autem primi repertorii vel indebite scripti libri, novis lectoribus etiam lecti, qui eos adhuc ineptius capiebant quam proprii auctores, quique novas hallucinationes & ineptias antiquis adderbant, pepererunt iterum atque iterum novos voluminum omnis generis acervos, immanesque interpolationum sarcinas, quæ in dies veluti morbus quidam sacer aut ignis surens incrementum nullo obstaculo remorante capientes, totum orbem quasi diluvio quodam sic inundarunt, ut præter chartas erroribus aut quisquiliis deturpatas, vix solidi quicquam appareat, omnibus primariæ veræque eruditionis libris ad unum fere suppressis, oblivionque aut contemtui traditis, ut ut hi satis per se numero sint rari, atque paucissimi semper fuerint.
units.tr: But when the others applied themselves to reading books (and also to hearing teachers) in such a way that, not sufficiently attending to themselves within, they had little or no light in themselves, and nevertheless wished, either from a desire for a little glory and self-commendation, or from a greed for other advantages, to scribble like the teachers themselves, then first of all books of every kind, absurd, empty and false, were brought forth. Thus systems were produced, when people thought they could perceive the true senses of authors or primary books and their coherence, and could report these to others more conveniently; or when they themselves imagined the framework and structure of their own fictions. Volumes of miscellaneous and particular arguments were produced when they wished to express the various thoughts, or nonsense, that they had linked together without end. Commentaries were produced when they presumed to explain the opinions and writings of others. Diaries, acts and reports were produced when they wished to draw up medleys, epitomes or, as it were, indexes of the good and bad things they had read. Finally, refutations and disputations were produced when they strove to destroy the views of others, often most true, and very often not understood by themselves at all, so that they might put their own in their place. These first finds, or improperly written books, were then read even by new readers, who understood them even more foolishly than their own authors, and who added new delusions and absurdities to the old ones. They gave birth again and again to new heaps of volumes of every kind and enormous burdens of interpolations, which, seizing hold day by day like some sacred disease or raging fire and increasing without any obstacle to check them, have so inundated the whole world, as if by a kind of flood, that apart from pages defiled by errors or trifles, scarcely anything solid appears; nearly all the books of primary and true learning have been suppressed, handed over to oblivion or contempt, although such books are in themselves rare enough in number and have always been very few.

units.la: XIV. Quantulum enim ejusmodi librorum reperire est, qui ex intimo & luminoso proprii cordis fundo ab Auctoribus conscripti sint, eoscqpo, ut provocentur iis lectores ad admirationem & amorem Creatoris & Auctoris omnis boni, enarratis ejus mirabilibus virtutibus operationibusque tum in animorum intimis, tum in universitate rerum externa? qui libri sane soli aliquid solide fructuosi & ad eruditionem veram sine fraude facientis continere possunt, merenturque soli inter primarios annumerari. At vero vix numerum faciunt, dum praeter alios veteranos prodeunt in dies copiae interpolatorum auctorculorum,nomina sua chartis publicatis illini gestientium, tanto numero, ut, quod dixit nonnemo, in cavea si forent conclusi omnes, itidem ut pulli gallinacei, tamen haud possint, opinor, uno anno circumiri.
units.tr: XIV. For how few books of this kind can one find, written by authors out of the innermost and luminous depths of their own heart, and so written that readers are stirred thereby to admiration and love of the Creator and Author of all good, the wonders and powerful works of God being set forth both in the inmost parts of souls and in the external universe of things? Such books alone can truly contain anything solidly fruitful and something that makes for true learning without deceit, and they alone deserve to be counted among the primary books. Yet they hardly make up a number, since, in addition to the old ones, there daily come forth such swarms of interpolating little authors, eager to have their names printed on paper, that, as someone has said, if they were all shut up in a coop, like chickens, still I suppose they could not be gone round in a year.

units.la: Ita fit ut mali quique libri affatim superabundent, iisque potissimum charactere triplici. Quidam enim (quæ maxima turba est) praeter trivialia nemini non nota, & nauseabunda saltem interpolatione, nullo lumine nullaque arte incrustata, nihil aliud continent. Alii materiam similem, vel etiam figmenta sua, aut minutias forte quasdam observatiunculasque, at sine solidis fundamentis, tametsi non sine arte aliqua & ingenio, exponunt. Caeteri (Ethnico animo Gentilium impuorum imitatores,) vel vana, vel obscoena nugamenta terso stylo politissimisque modis describunt. Quibus omnibus cum sublevandus & expurgandus esset Christianus orbis eo modo, quem apud divinius eruditos olim in usu fuisse (a) Acta tradunt Apostolorum: ii tamen & ubique non modo tolerantur; sed & tales lactucas nunc potissimum labra hominum petunt veluti verae eruditionis cibos, & diversas pro suo quisque palato, diverso que item praetextu.
units.tr: So it comes about that bad books abound in plenty, and these bear especially a threefold character. For some (which is by far the largest crowd), apart from trivialities known to everyone and at best nauseating patchwork, contain nothing else, encrusted with no light and no art. Others set forth similar matter, or their own fictions, or perhaps some trifles and little observations, but without solid foundations, although not without some art and ingenuity. The rest (imitators of the impure Gentiles with a heathen spirit) describe vain or obscene trifles in polished style and in the most elegant manner. Although the Christian world ought to be relieved and cleansed of all these, in the way which, as the Acts of the Apostles tell us, was once in use among the more divinely learned, nevertheless these books are not only tolerated everywhere, but such lettuces now chiefly seek the lips of men as the food of true learning, each according to his own palate and for various pretexts.

units.la: XV. Sunt enim qui ideo eos requirunt,
units.tr: XV. For there are those who seek them out for this reason:

units.la: quod primariorum originariorumque librorum nonnulli dicantur explicatores. Sed quamvis hoc præ se ferant, (eos non tango quilumine divino intus gaudent.) tamen in solidiorum librorum expositione textûs sensum glossis atque interpretamentis suis ita pervertunt, ut & lucem extinctum eant, & quod contrarium est textui scopoque ejus, id prorsum verbis & factis inde eliciant atque commendent: unde ipse textus omnino fit cassus, haud secus atque in compositione Musica, ubi circumstrepentium vocalurum organiculorumve interludentes ac luxuriantes soni, & veluti glossæ tonum textumque præcipuum. sic intersecant, absorbent atque suffocant, ut is jam non possit amplius animadverti. Et hoc quidem in rebus minoris momenti levius efset quam ut querelæ justæ locum dare deberet. Ad maximas atque omnium omnino ponderosissimas idem agendi modus perreptavit, quem profecto palam produnt ferme omnes inter diversas Christianismi sectas quotquot sunt Divini Codicis explicatores, commentatores & ex uno eodemque textu oppositorum Systematum atque Institutionum conditores; ita ut nullus jam lector, quisquis is sit & quocunque apparatu instructus, possit certum quendam ex iis interpretem aut abbreviatorem consulere & assumere, quin eo ipso ab omnibus aliarum Sectarum explicatoribus ei contradicatur, sensusque, quem ex auctore suo discet, ut falsus scripturisque oppositus condemnetur quam sententiam auctores ipsi contra sese reciproce pronunciant, dum singuli unum quidem scripturæ sensum separatim, omnes vero conjunctim diversos & oppositos amplectuntur. Quod indicium certum est, ut in his, sic in aliis, primariorum librorum dilucidationem a secundariis ejusmodi libris nequicquam debere exspectari ad acquirendam eruditionem, quam frustra quoque nonnulli quærunt apud eos, quorum intentio minime fuit e fundamento erudire, sed veluti indices aut relationes breviores memoriæ gratia factitare, quæ etsi suum habeant usum bonum ubi bona fide quæ utilia eduntur, indicant; tamen inter scriptores illos si nonnulli reperiantur vel minus periti, qui ex omnibus promiscue bonis malisque sua sine delectu sineque recensitis librorum fundamentis coacervent; vel minus sincerè, qui præjudiciis aut sectæ suæ plusculum devoti, Punica fide ea referant & deturpent quæ sibi judicant adversari; atque ita solidissima quæque, sed ipsis minus sapientia, vel contemtui vel etiam odio perversis relationibus exponant, non possunt inde nisi fraudes lectoribus fieri. Et ab his quidem, a quibus saltem historiæ vel indicis fides exspectabatur, solidæ eruditionis media seu instrumenta, ab eis falso interversa aut adulterata, contemnere discunt lectores: ab illis vero de quibuslibet, mente confusa, per rhapsodiarum inconcinnarum numerosas farragines superficiarie garrire. Verbo, non video, quinam apud omnes qui ex alio principio scoscopoque quam ex quo bonos libros prodiifse diximus, aliena interpolarunt aut retulerunt, vel propria etiam prodiderunt, eruditionem aliam nisi falsam, conquirere pofsint ea mentes, quæ auctores eos ut audiant & capiant, similem cum illis sibi formam intus ut superinducant, allaborare tenentur.
units.tr: because some are said to be explainers of the primary and original books. But although they make this profession (I do not touch on those who rejoice in divine light within), yet in the exposition of more solid books they so pervert the sense of the text by their glosses and interpretations that they extinguish its light, and they draw out and commend from it, by words and deeds, the very opposite of the text and its purpose; whence the text itself is wholly made void, just as in a musical composition, where the interweaving and luxuriant sounds of the accompanying voices or little instruments, like glosses, cut across and absorb and smother the tone and principal text, so that it can no longer be noticed. Now in matters of lesser importance this would be more tolerable and would not deserve to give cause for just complaint. But the same way of acting has crept into the greatest and most weighty matters of all: almost all who are expositors, commentators and framers of opposing systems and institutions out of one and the same text of the Divine Code, among the various sects of Christianity, openly betray it. So that no reader now, whoever he is and however equipped with learning, can consult and adopt one of these interpreters or abridgers without being at once contradicted by the expositors of all the other sects, and the sense that he learns from his author is condemned as false and opposed to Scripture. The authors themselves pronounce the same opinion against one another reciprocally, while each embraces one sense of Scripture separately, but all of them together embrace diverse and opposed senses. This is a certain sign that, in these matters as in others, one must in vain expect from secondary books of this kind an elucidation of the primary books for the acquiring of learning, which some also seek in vain from those whose intention was by no means to teach from the foundations, but rather to produce, as it were, indexes or shorter reports for the sake of memory. These, although they have their good use where useful things are published in good faith, still indicate—if among those writers there are some less skilled, who heap together without discrimination all good and bad things from all books, without selection and without the foundations of the books having been examined; or some less sincere, who, too devoted to their prejudices or their sect, report and distort with Punic faith whatever they judge to be hostile to them, and so expose the most solid matters, though they themselves understand them less, to contempt or even hatred by perverse reports—they cannot produce anything but deceptions for the readers. From those, at least, from whom the reliability of a history or an index was expected, readers learn to despise the means or instruments of solid learning, falsely perverted or adulterated by them; and from the others they learn to chatter superficially about whatever it may be, with confused minds, through the numerous farragoes of ill-matched rhapsodies. In short, I see no way that minds which are bound to labour to take up and understand those authors, and to superinduce within themselves a form similar to theirs, could acquire any learning other than false learning, from those who, starting from a different principle and aim from that from which we said the good books came forth, have interpolated or reported the views of others, or even put forth their own.

units.la: XVI. At eruditionis veræ fundamenta sifuerint æternorum & durabilium prætermissio, internæ tenebræ, superficiariorum, periturorum, vanorum, falsorum, obscœnorum & impiorum commendatio, ea sane partim apud similes, partim vero (quoad ultima recensita) apud Archetypos suos, impuros istos Ethnicos, animorum juventutis corruptores & constupratores non frustra quæsiveris. Propudiosum est hujusmodi canes a puerorum institutoribus Christianis (scilicet!) qui non ignorant quanta denunciaverit Christus mala eis qui pueris offendicula præbent, præstare molarem lapidem collo sibi alligari, cumque eo in mare demergi; nefandum est, inquam, & horrendum ab iis inquinatissimos & impios gentium canes ætati teneræ omnisque formæ suscipiendæ capaci, tradi, prælegi & laudari, unde prima fides (ut Tertulliani verba adhibeam) Diabolo ædificatur ad initium eruditionis. Quamvis enim (quod a paucissimis fit, & rarissime) ab horrendis suis sordibus castrarentur, remanet tamen regnatque in illis spiritus prosani Ethnicismi, amoris proprii, ambitionis atque gloriæ, vindictæ, voluptatum, gulæ atque luxuriae, irrisionis, impietatis, vanitatis, nugacitas, atque adeo omnis generis malorum femina in unum quasi acervum collecta, quae legentium mentibus non possunt non pedetentim insinuari, maxime vero aetati tenerae, quae cum eos legendo cogitationes suas hisce formis diabolicis induendas debeat tradere ac confidere, vere ad initium ejus eruditionis fidem sive confidentiam Diabolo in eis aedisicari dictum est. Ego sane, quod me attinet, vere fateor, me nunquam in illis animi gratia vel unicam legisse pagellam, quin inde postea me senserim in bono debilitatum; qua boni jactura, me ab illis curiosius legendis deterruit divina dignatio. De illis autem Ethnicis non loquor, quorum lectione sanctius ad meliora ducimur, veluti sunt libri nonnullorum Pythagoreorum, Epicteti & similium, quos Christiano spiritu praeditos jure merito agnoscebat cum multis aliis Justinus Martyr, uti ex Apologiis ejus patet. Et dolendum est, hos non ita manibus hominum versari, atque illos, in quibus vel omnes vel plerique ex recenstitis pessimae notae characteribus visuntur, quique a literatis veluti media ad eruditionem veram ita extolluntur, ut qui ex hujus Babylonicae meretricis poculo exuberantius biberint, (a) pectora divina, caelestia ingenia, inexhaustaque doctrinae fontes atque thesauri, proclamentur, non sine risu, aut commiseratione potius eorum qui solidiora aliquantulum norunt, quibus magis
units.tr: XVI. But the foundations of true learning are, if you look for them, the neglect of eternal and lasting things, inner darkness, and the commendation of superficial, perishing, vain, false, obscene and impious things. You will not have searched in vain for these among their like, and partly, as to the last-listed items, among their own archetypes, those impure heathen, corrupters and violators of young minds. It is shameful that such dogs should be handed over, read and praised to tender children by Christian teachers (forsooth!), who do not know what evils Christ declared against those who put stumbling blocks before little ones: that it would be better for a millstone to be hung about their neck and for them to be drowned in the sea. It is, I say, abominable and horrible that these most polluted and impious dogs of the Gentiles should be given over to tender age, which is capable of receiving any form, to be taught, read aloud and praised, whence (to use Tertullian's words) the first faith is built up for the Devil at the beginning of learning. For although (which is done by very few and very rarely) they are cleansed of their horrible filth, there still remains and reigns in them the spirit of profane heathenism: self-love, ambition and the lust for glory, revenge, pleasures, gluttony and luxury, mockery, impiety, vanity and triviality, and indeed every kind of evil, gathered together as in one heap, which cannot but gradually insinuate itself into the minds of readers, and especially of tender age, which, since by reading them it must hand over its own thoughts to be clothed in these diabolical forms, is rightly said to be the place where faith or trust in the Devil is built up in them at the very beginning of that learning. For my own part I truly confess that I have never read in those books, for the sake of their charm, even a single page without afterwards feeling myself weakened in goodness; and by the loss of that goodness the divine condescension deterred me from reading them too curiously. I am not speaking, however, of those heathen writers by whose reading we are led more holily to better things, such as some books of the Pythagoreans, of Epictetus and the like, which Justin Martyr, along with many others, rightly acknowledged to be endowed with a Christian spirit, as is clear from his Apologies. And it is to be lamented that these are not so handled by men, while those books in which all or most of the aforementioned marks of the worst repute are found, and which are thus extolled by the literati as the middle way to true learning, are read so eagerly. Those who have drunk more deeply from the cup of this Babylonian harlot are proclaimed to have divine breasts, heavenly genius, and inexhaustible fountains and treasuries of learning, not without laughter, or rather pity, from those who know somewhat more solid things, to whom it would be more pleasing

units.la: (a) Vide (ut minorum gentium lite-ratos prae-teream) magis volupe esset cum Augustino exclamare : (a) O flum tartareum, jactantur in te filii hominum cum mercedibus ut hac discant; & magna res agitur, cum hoc agitur.
units.tr: (a) See (to pass over the literati of the lesser nations) it would be more pleasing to cry out with Augustine: (a) O Tartarean river, into you the sons of men are cast with their fees, that they may learn these things; and a great matter is at stake when this is the matter.

units.la: in fene&ute sic deliraret, ut totus Terentianis nugis sese traderet, dicitur pr&sus divinum, quod futili illa loquione expleri non poterat. Ita in Praefat. Annalium Grotii, similes, atque hic, titu-li ei tribuuntur, quod stylum & artes Ethnicorum vaniffimo-rum in suis historiis esset imitatus. (a) Confess. Lib. I. cap. 16.
units.tr: ...in old age he was so deranged that he gave himself wholly to Terentian trifles, is said to have been utterly divine, which could not be filled by that frivolous speech. Thus in the Preface to the Annals of Grotius similar titles are ascribed to him, because he imitated the style and arts of the most vain Gentiles in his histories. (a) Confessions, Book I, chapter 16.

units.la: XVII. At vero non desunt studiorum
units.tr: XVII. But indeed there are no lack of

units.la: humanitatis, (uti vocantur,) patronis caussae, cur vanos atque locutulejos istos graculos ita commendent. Quae vero? scilicet abundant egregiis sententiis. Eorum cum historiae tum scribendi modus ad sacra intelligenda faciunt. Latinus inde sermo Graecusque discendus est. Didicisse fideliter artes Emollit mores nec finit esse feros. Vide a renatis literis quanta politura, quanta lumina, quae omnium rerum reformata facies orbi accesserint! quam antea non obscura tantum secula, sed & barbara & Cimmeriis tenebris plane immersa!
units.tr: defenders of the so-called studies of humanity, who recommend these empty and babbling jackdaws. What are their reasons? Surely that they abound in excellent maxims; that their manner of narrating history and of writing is useful for understanding the sacred books; that one must therefore learn Latin and Greek. To have learned the arts faithfully softens the morals and does not allow them to be savage. See what great polish, what light, what reformed face of all things has come to the world since the revival of letters! Whereas before there were not merely obscure ages, but barbarous ones, plunged in Cimmerian darkness!

units.la: XVIII. Ego vero ejusmodi crasse hallucinantes sic miserpr, ut nisi bono animo ita coecutirent, istiusmodi mendaciis, quae omnia confutabo, nil reponendum ducerem. Non dicam, paucula bona, quae iis passim intermixta esse possent, operae pretium non esse in tantis sterquiliniorum acervis, tanta cum temporis jactura, necessarium, riisque aliis posthabitis, quaerere; sententiafque, si quas utiles profani protulerunt, sic aliorum opera collectas jam esse & seorsim exstare, ut necesse non sit ex impuris & venenatis fontibus (e qualibus sane non purius bibuntur aquæ) eas adhucdum haurire: sed crediderim salutis humanæ inimici instinctu eos auctores suis impuris bona interspersisse eo consilio, ac veneficis suis venenis bonos intermiscent cibos, ut scilicet cum bonis exitiosa sese ingerant hominesque conficiant. Quis vero ejusmodi cibis vellet vesci quia & iis bona interpositasunt? Quasi vero in sanctis coelestium animarum scriptis non haberemus affatim divinas sententias, easque sine ulla mali suspicione purissimas & saluberrimas. Ex pluribus divinæ Scripturæ, vide vel unum Proverbiorum Salomonis aut Syracidæ librum: aut e sanctioribus, Christianorum quidem, Joannis Climaci Scalam, vel Nili Admonitiones, aut Kempisii libellum: Ethnicorum vero, Sextii Pythagorei sententias, ne plures non ignotos commemorem.
units.tr: XVIII. Indeed I pity such grossly deluded people, and if they were not going astray with good intentions, I would think nothing should be opposed to such falsehoods, all of which I will refute. I will not say that the few good things which might be scattered among them here and there are not worth seeking, in such heaps of dung and at such great loss of time, and that, other things being set aside, it is unnecessary; and that if the profane writers have offered any useful sayings, these have already been so collected by the labour of others and exist apart, so that it is not necessary to draw them still from impure and poisonous sources (from which certainly no water is drawn more purely). But I would believe that the enemies of human salvation, at the prompting of the Devil, have interspersed good things among their impure writings with the same purpose as poisoners mix good food with their poisons: namely, that along with the good they may thrust in destruction and destroy men. Who, indeed, would wish to eat such food just because good things are placed in it? As if we did not have in the holy writings of the heavenly souls enough divine sayings, and these most pure and most wholesome, free from any suspicion of evil. Out of the many, look at the one book of the Proverbs of Solomon or of Sirach; or among the more sacred Christian writings, John Climacus's Ladder, or the Admonitions of Nilus, or the little book of Kempis; or among the heathen, the sayings of Sextius the Pythagorean, that I may not mention many others not unknown.

units.la: XIX. Falsum est ex Ethnicorum historiis & stylis, Scripturas solide & secundum Dei mentem posse intelligi: at forte aliquatenus & superficiarie atque secundum mentem Diaboli, hoc est, eo modo quem bolus ipse eruere, habere & communicare potest, literali scilicet externo, tenebris & erroribus mixto, ipsumque non beante, sed miseriorem & pejorem reddente, id fieri posse non nego. Historiarum Scripturæ soliditas typica est, & plerumque adhuc tota futura. esse: tu, uti unius forte ex illis judicio Augustani ævi graculus habearis, ætatem in sutilibus iis inaniter consumes. Age si tanti facis istiusmodi inanias, fac ut vel solam Romani soni pronunciationem genuinam tota vita expisceris, & eris mihi magnus Apollo. Non dedignatus est Deus, ubi per organa sua locutus est, crassiore & simpliciore stylo semper uti, imo dedignatus est stylum exquisitum, ob causas libro primo expressas: & nos puderet in his Deum sequi, & eo loqui more qui animos sinceriores, candidos, rerum magis quam verborum tenaces, deceat! Falsorum eruditorum isthæc esto occupatio, itaque simplicioris idiomatis, in sanctissimis atque solidissimis quibusque confpicui, redargutio. Ego equidem crediderim, sic coram Deo rem se habere, in scholis eos, qui in infimis cathedris communia litterarum, lectionis & scriptionis elementa docent, etsi tanquam imæ professionis atque vilissimæ habeantur a mundi magistris, a Deo pro primis & præcipuis haberi: tum proximos ab his, qui linguarum peregrinarum rudimenta tradunt; ut qui uno gradu superiores ab hominibus reputantur, jam uno gradu coram Deo inferiores sint: atque ita gradatim, prout inter homines adscendere creduntur ad digniora, potiora & eruditiora, coram Deo econtra ordine inverso eos descendere semper ad viliora, inaniora & sutiliora; donec tandem qui omnium primas sedes attigisse & exquisitiora profiteri putantur, in deliramenta desinere ac evanescere coram Deo judicentur. Nec dubito, quin omnes,dummodo ex eorum quæ docentur necessitate ac usu & fructibus provenientibus rem pensare volent, idem judicium facile sint facturi.
units.tr: XIX. It is false that Scripture can be understood solidly and according to the mind of God from the histories and styles of the Gentiles; but I do not deny that it can perhaps be done in some measure, and superficially, and according to the mind of the Devil, that is, in the way which the Devil himself can discern, possess and communicate: namely, by the external letter mixed with darkness and errors, which does not make a man blessed but more wretched and worse. The solidity of the histories of Scripture is typical, and for the most part still wholly future: you, perhaps because you are regarded as one of the jackdaws of the Augustan age by the judgement of some of them, will waste your time in these trifles to no purpose. Come, if you value such emptiness so much, make it so that you spend your whole life searching out only the genuine pronunciation of Roman sound, and you will be a great Apollo to me. God has not disdained, when he has spoken through his instruments, always to use a cruder and simpler style; indeed he has disdained the exquisite style, for the reasons expressed in the first book. And we should be ashamed to follow God in these things and to speak in that manner which befits sincere, candid minds, more attached to things than to words! Let this be the occupation of the false learned: the refutation of the simpler idiom, conspicuous in the most holy and most solid writings. I for my part would believe that, as regards God, the matter stands thus: in the schools, those who teach the common elements of letters, reading and writing, in the lowest chairs, though they are regarded by the world's teachers as of the lowest and most worthless profession, are regarded by God as first and chief; then next to them those who hand down the rudiments of foreign languages; for those who are considered one step higher by men are already one step lower before God. And so gradually, as they are believed to rise among men to higher, weightier and more learned things, so before God, on the contrary, in inverted order, they always descend to viler, emptier and more trifling things; until at last those who are thought to have reached the first seats of all and to profess the more exquisite things are judged before God to end in delusions and to vanish away. Nor do I doubt that all, provided they are willing to weigh the matter by the necessity and use of what is taught and by the fruits that come from it, will easily make the same judgement.

units.la: XXI. At, at, a literis humanioribus re- novatis, omnia renovata & polita audivimus.
units.tr: XXI. But, but, we have heard that with the revival of the humane letters everything has been renewed and polished.

units.la: Scilicet! Diabolus nimirum, qui antea feritate aperta, ac crassa turpitudine tumultuose sese prodebat; unde boni quique haud falsi, in quiete ac sine rumore solide Deo sibique agebant, ab inimico aperto facile caventes; is animarum hostis, jam Angeli lucis speciem vestemque ab eruditione mundana nactus, sinceriores elegantiusatque tutius seducit, dum pulso æternarum rerum ardore, divinoque lumine intus prorsum extincto, pro crassis terrestribusque vitiis, spiritualia, proque externarum quarundam rerum, plerumque inanium ignorantia,tenebras de;rebus internis & divinioribus horribiles,ideas cassas, obscuras, chimfiricas & futiles, errorum & hæreseos fontes, restituit; quæ omnia, ipsamque cum vitiis quibusvis injustitiam, & doctius proponere & subtilius defendere didicit, vel adhibitis Scripturis ipsis per literaturam suam versipellem ad quævis adaptatis: sic uterrores perniciosissimi jam appareant veluti veritates divinæ; vitia vero exitiosissima, qualia amor sui, amor gloriæ, delectationum, pecuniæ, rerum seculi, jactura temporis Deo subducti, rixæ, odia interna, contemtus aliorum, simpliciorum irrisiones, rerum æternarum oblivio, imo & divinarum illusio, jam in virtutum & sagacioris prudentiæ speciem figuratæ & politæ sint jucundis atque artificiosis istiusmodi eruditionis saeculi artibus; quarum genio & debemus feralia illa schismata, a bono quovis lugenda, queis nullas nisi hujusmodi falsatas virtutes atque veritates debet orbis Christianus; id quod vel pueri luce clarius detegere possunt, si animad vertant, Christianismum, qui Christo teste e charitate mutua & propriæ voluntatis oblivione ut æterni Patris voluntas sola suscipiatur, agnosci debebat, jam inde non amore & æternarum rerum amplexatione, sed odiis & terrestrium rerum curis ubique concrevisse. Unde sequitur, judice Deo, tenebras, animarumque coram illo barbariem & brutalitatem, ne dicam Diabolicam malignitatem, incrementa inde cepisse, atque in dies, dum seculum magis magisque lucidum falsa ista eruditione fieri putatur, augescere. Sed quid pluribus id argumenti persequar, quod nemo bonus ex se non perspiciat, nemo vero ex iis qui minus sinceri sunt, quique se non divino æterno que ædificio; sed mundano & perituro veluti lapides polliendos, & erudiendos devoverunt, non rejiciat atque improbet, ut ut rationibus æterno pondere validis urgeri se sentiant? His, ne iræ eorum acuantur, concedamus, eruditionem suam ad suos scopos esse & validam, & utilem, neque falli: sed ad solidum permanentemque statum id neutiquam fuerit. Atque hoc nobis satis esto.
units.tr: Indeed! Surely the devil, who formerly showed himself openly in savage tumult and gross vileness, so that all good people who were not deceived lived quietly and without noise, solidly for God and for themselves, and easily guarded against an open enemy, now has this enemy of souls, having taken on the appearance and garb of an angel of light from worldly learning, seduce them more sincerely, elegantly and safely. For, with the ardour for eternal things driven out and the divine light within utterly extinguished, he restores spiritual vices in place of crude earthly ones, and in place of ignorance of certain external things, mostly empty, he restores horrible darkness about inner and more divine things, empty, obscure, chimerical and futile ideas, the sources of errors and heresies. He has learned to propose all of these, and injustice itself with all vices, more learnedly and to defend them more subtly, either by applying the Scriptures themselves, through his versatile literature, to whatever he likes. So the most pernicious terrors now appear as divine truths, while the most destructive vices, such as self-love, love of glory, of pleasures, of money and of worldly things, the loss of time withdrawn from God, quarrels, inner hatreds, contempt of others, mockery of simpler people, forgetfulness of eternal things, and even the mockery of divine things, are now shaped and polished into the appearance of virtues and of a shrewder prudence, by the pleasant and artful arts of this worldly learning. To its spirit we owe those deadly schisms, to be lamented by every good person, and the Christian world owes it no virtues or truths other than such falsified ones. Even boys could see this more clearly than daylight, if they considered that Christianity, which by Christ's testimony ought to be recognized by mutual love and by forgetting one's own will, so that the will of the eternal Father alone is accepted, has since then grown everywhere not from love and the embrace of eternal things, but from hatreds and cares for earthly things. Whence it follows, with God as judge, that darkness, and barbarism and brutality of souls before him, not to say diabolical malignity, have taken increase from this and grow daily, while the age is thought to become ever more enlightened by this false learning. But why should I pursue this argument at greater length, when no good person fails to see it for himself, and no one among those who are less sincere, who have devoted themselves not to the divine and eternal building but to the worldly and perishable, as stones to be polished and educated, rejects and condemns it, even though they feel themselves pressed by reasons of eternal weight? Lest their anger be sharpened, let us concede to them that their learning is strong and useful for its own aims, and not mistaken; but it will by no means lead to a solid and lasting state. Let this be enough for us.

units.la: XXII. Enumeravimus inter quatuor supe- riora
units.tr: XXII. We have counted among the four superior means of acquiring false learning

units.la: riofa eruditionis falsæ acquirendæ media, ipsam eruditionis,quæ proponitur, materiam, hoc est, scientias ipsas, quando eæ ne quidem superficiariæ sunt; sed falsæ, erroneæ-que, e principiis falsis falsas conclusiones deducentes & proponentes; quales fere ubique gentium vulgo obtinent. Hoc ita esse, non est cur multum allaboremus ostendere. Ipsimet qui scientias tradunt, hoc ipsum aperte declarant, dum se mutuo refutant ac conficiunt; at eo tamen modo, qui refutatis non succenturiat meliora. Sola quippe veritas lumine suo & errorem confutat, & vero adstruit quod ad plenam mentis acquiescentiam quærebatur. Etsi autem hoc officio conatus sim in eis quæ edidi, quantum pro viribus licuit defungi; notabo tamen hic obiter nonnulla quæ errorum sunt origines in scientiis illis præcipuis, de quibus in libro præcedente quædam monueram.
units.tr: the matter of learning itself that is proposed, that is, the sciences themselves, since these are not even superficial, but false and erroneous, drawing and proposing false conclusions from false principles, such as commonly prevail almost everywhere among the nations. There is no need for us to labour long to show that this is so. Those who teach the sciences openly declare it themselves, while they refute and overthrow one another; yet they do so in a way that does not supply better things in place of those refuted. For truth alone refutes error by its own light, and confirms by the true what was sought for the full assent of the mind. Although I have tried in what I have published to discharge this task as far as my powers allowed, I will nevertheless note briefly here some of the origins of errors in those principal sciences, of which I gave some warnings in the preceding book.

units.la: XXIII. Omnia illa omissa, quæ in libro proxime præcedente ostendi in causis esse cur scientiæ ad perfectionem superficiariam & idealem non attingant, eadem quoque efficiunt ut in errores deveniant. Namque si quis destitutus quibusdam ad operandum necessariis operari tamen velit, eum perverse operari necesse est: prout si quis destitutus viribus necessariis, lumine viaque plana ad ambulandum, ambulare tamen vellet, is certe non posset non cadere atque errare. Verum, inquiet quispiam, ejusmodi in scientiis lapsus atque errores non sunt tanti, ut idcirco tota eruditio dicenda sit falsa, siquidem ejusmodi defectus ideas rationis tantum concernunt, quibus licet nutantibus, eruditionem veram remanere posse ex eo sequitur, quod hæc consistat in facultatum quas reales diximus atque in superiores & inferiores distinximus, bono cum objectis suis necessariis statu. Ad quæ respondeo, me nequaquam afferere eos, quorum cæteroqui facultates reales eruditione solida politæ sunt, ideo vera eruditione sua destitui falsaque imbui, quod in nonnullis, quæ ideales scientias speciant, ipsi fallantur. Minime hic de talibus agitur: sed de illis tantum qui solide reliquæ eruditione repulsa, pro eruditione tota acquirenda nil sibi proponunt præter ideas ejusmodi quæ in scientiis venditantur, quæ sane si falsæ fuerint, jam tota eorum eruditio falsa sit necesse est. Neque tantum hoc, sed & potentissimum ad eruditionem aspirandi & perveniendi impedimentum fuerint illi circa ideas meras errores. Namque ex quo humanum genus veluti brutum nascitur, neque ad superiora & solida nisi per externa, per sensus crassos, per imaginationem, per rationem denique & ejus ideas assurgit, fit inde ut ii, quibus externa & sensus & imaginatio & ideæ supprimerentur aut falsarentur; veluti si aut nulla verba aut falsa auribus perciperent, falsasque imaginatione versarent imagines, non possent certe ea ratione ad vera, divina, sublimia pertingere; sed potius per corrupta illa media ab iis amoverentur. Eodem modo, si ratio erroneis falsisque ideis, dum scientias discit, repleatur, impeditur mens, (quamdiu ratioHi tioni vult insistere) à superioribus & divinioribus inveniendis, imo & quærendis: per falsas enim ideas dum originalia ipsa divina deturpantur, obscurantur, imo odiosa & velut inania repræsentantur, sequitur eadem contemni ac fugi, vel etiam derideri à misera, & rationis ideis seducta Mente, contrariis ut sese dedat. Unde patet errores circa ideas in scientiis propositos, ut ut Mentibus quæ quoad facultates supremas solida gaudent eruditione, nullius momenti essent, perniciosissimos tamen illis esse quæ eruditione vera nondum sunt præditæ: atque adeo sollicite cavendum, iis ne tales propinentur: ut si quando spes sit illas solida quærere posse, eis a ratione, per falsas ideas seducta, non occludatur janua; sed potius per ideas, vera quantum fieri potest repræsentantes, adjuventur. Hisce quo magis prodesse possit falsitatum scientias vitiantium detectio, paucula etiam de quibusdam dicemus.
units.tr: XXIII. Leave aside all those points that I showed in the immediately preceding book to be the causes why the sciences do not attain superficial and ideal perfection; these same things also bring it about that they fall into errors. For if someone lacking certain things necessary for working nonetheless wishes to work, he must necessarily work amiss, just as someone lacking the necessary strength, light and a plain road for walking, who wished to walk, would certainly be unable to avoid falling and going astray. But, someone will say, such slips and errors in the sciences are not so great that the whole of learning should therefore be called false, since such defects concern only the ideas of reason; and it follows from this that true learning can remain even though these ideas waver, since it consists in the faculties which we called real, and which we distinguished into superior and inferior, being in good condition with their necessary objects. To this I reply that I by no means assert that those whose real faculties are otherwise adorned with solid learning are therefore deprived of their true learning and imbued with falsehood, merely because they are deceived in some matters that concern the ideal sciences. That is not what is at issue here, but only those who, having solidly rejected the rest of learning, propose to themselves, for acquiring learning as a whole, nothing but such ideas as are hawked in the sciences. If these are false, then their whole learning must necessarily be false. And not only this: errors about mere ideas are also the most powerful impediment to aspiring to and attaining learning. For from the time the human race is born like a brute, and rises to higher and solid things only through external things, through the gross senses, through imagination and finally through reason and its ideas, it follows that those whose external things, senses, imagination and ideas were suppressed or falsified (as if they perceived no words or false ones by their ears, and turned over false images in their imagination) could certainly not reach true, divine and sublime things by that route, but would rather be drawn away from them by those corrupt means. In the same way, if reason, while learning the sciences, is filled with erroneous and false ideas, the mind is impeded, for as long as it wishes to dwell on reason, from finding, indeed even from seeking, higher and more divine things. For while the divine originals themselves are defaced and obscured by false ideas, and represented as hateful and as it were empty, it follows that they are despised and shunned, or even mocked, by the wretched mind led astray by the ideas of reason, so that it gives itself to the contrary. Hence it is plain that errors about the ideas proposed in the sciences, though they would be of no moment to minds that enjoy solid learning in their supreme faculties, are nonetheless most pernicious to those not yet endowed with true learning. Therefore one must take careful heed that such things are not handed to them, so that if ever there is hope that they can seek solid things, the door is not closed to them by reason seduced through false ideas, but rather they are helped by ideas representing the truth as far as possible. So that the detection of falsehoods vitiating the sciences may be more useful to this end, we will say a little about some of them.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Quæ superius de iis quibus impeditur, ne Metaphysica, Physica, Ethica, Logica etiam atque Critica, ipsaque denique Theologia, fiant superficialiter perfectæ, retulimus; ea hic possunt recenseri tanquam fontes errorum, qui in istas disciplinas & scientias derivantur apud omnes eos, qui omissis veritatibus vel dispositionibus quas ibi recensuimus, tentant eas scientias acquirere. Possunt igitur ea suis è locis repeti, & veluti huc pertinentia considerari. Quibus nunc adjungimus sequentia.
units.tr: The causes that were mentioned above as preventing Metaphysics, Physics, Ethics, Logic and Criticism, and finally Theology itself, from being made thoroughly perfect can be listed here as sources of errors. These errors flow into those disciplines and sciences for everyone who, neglecting the truths or dispositions we set out there, tries to acquire those sciences. These causes can therefore be recalled from their places and considered here as belonging to this discussion. To them we now add the following.

units.la: L
units.tr: L

units.la: In Metaphysicis (praeter alios errores in Dissertatione initio operis hujus praefixa annotatos, falsaque praejudicia mox ante recensita, nec ab ipsis quidem Cartesianis deposita, ex quibus tamen omnia sua falsantur,) falsa statim est doctrina de transcendentalibus, de idearum aeternitate, deque veritatibus idearum aeternis & immutabilibus, de earum necessitate ad Dei Omnisciensiam constituendam, ex quibus stultum dogma de fato, vel de necessitate rerum fatali, de libertatis vel negatione vel in dubium revocatione, deque feris & absurdis quibusdam omnium rerum & recularum decretis, nec decretis modo, sed & ad quaevis concursibus praeviis simultaneisque,& nescio quot monstris, quibus Deus & natura, opera item naturae & gratiae, activitasque creaturarum & actus Dei confunduntur, obtenebrantur, negantur. Substantiae quoque & accidentium, imo dicere ausim, omnium pene rerum, ideas nullas, ne quidem generales & dilutas, nisi absurdas & chimaericas habent. Quae non dicta modo, sed & probata a me videre potuerunt, qui Cogitationes & Oeconomiam inspexerunt.
units.tr: In Metaphysics (besides the other errors noted in the Dissertation prefixed to the beginning of this work, and the false prejudices just listed, which the Cartesians themselves have not abandoned, and by which all their other doctrines are falsified), the doctrine of the transcendentals is false from the start, as is the doctrine of the eternity of ideas, and of truths about ideas that are eternal and immutable, and of their necessity for constituting the omniscience of God. From these comes the foolish dogma of fate, or of a fatal necessity of things, the denial or calling into doubt of freedom, and certain savage and absurd decrees about all things and events, not only decrees but also concurrences going before and accompanying everything, and I know not how many monsters by which God and nature, the works of nature and of grace, and the activity of creatures and the acts of God are confused, obscured and denied. They also have no ideas of substances and accidents, indeed of almost all things, not even general and vague ideas, except absurd and chimerical ones. I dare say this not only as something said but as something proved by me, which those who have looked into their Cogitationes and Oeconomia could see for themselves.

units.la: XXV. Sed ne hic sola errorum indica- tione aut ad scripta alia remittione agam, de- monstrationibus brevioribus praecipua evin- cere animus est.
units.tr: XXV. But I do not wish to rest here with a mere indication of the errors, or to refer the reader to other writings. I intend to prove the main points by shorter demonstrations.

units.la: 1. Deus (omnium consensu) est ens perfectissimum: Ergo est sibi se solo sufficientissimus: nam si sibi non sufficeret ex se solo, certe in se & ex se deficeret; quod est contra tra definitionem agnitam. Si sibi se solo sufficit, igitur nullius rei idea, praeter ideam sui ipsius, est ei necessaria ad sui persectionem. Ergo idearum, veritatumque de illis necessitas, aeternitas & immutabilitas ab-solutae, falsae sunt, suntque ideae non nisi ex arbitrio & statuto Dei, a quo arbitrio abstinere potuisset, vel aliter de eo ideisque difponere, is qui se solo contentus est ac persectissimus.
units.tr: 1. God is (by universal agreement) the most perfect being. Therefore he is wholly sufficient in himself alone. For if he were not sufficient to himself from himself alone, he would certainly be lacking in himself and from himself, which is contrary to the accepted definition. If he is sufficient to himself alone, then the idea of no thing, apart from the idea of himself, is necessary to him for his own perfection. Therefore the necessity, eternity and absolute immutability of ideas and of the truths about them are false, and the ideas are only by the free choice and decree of God, from which choice he could have abstained, or he could have arranged things otherwise, since he is content with himself alone and most perfect.

units.la: 2. Igitur ad perfectionem Omniscientiae
units.tr: 2. Therefore for the perfection of God's omniscience

units.la: Dei non requiritur nisi sola cognitio sui ipsius, qui omne perfectissimum est: non autem cognitio aliarum rerum aut idearum, quae absolute nil sunt, arbitrarie aliquid sunt, & imperfectae sunt: quaeque non cognitionis absolutae & perfectissimae; sed cognitionis arbitrariae Dei obiecta sunt, picturas suas, plures, pauciores, videre aut effigiare gestientis, & cum illis ludere volentis: quae obiecta, ut ut se habeant, plurave sint an pauciora, cognitionem arbitrariam; quia arbitraria est, imperfectionis arguere non possunt. Haec Dei cognitio arbitraria si nulla volet cognoscere, non ideo imperfectionis Deum arguit: contra, perfectionis: nam nec Deum ipsum concernit seu pro obiecto habet; & vero potius sic patet Deum caeteris non egere, eisque carere posse: quod si plura velit, cognoscet & plura, & quaecunque volet; indeque sequetur Deum sibi sufficientem sic esse, ut eis quae volet esse vel cognosci, sufficiat eo modo ponendis uti volet.
units.tr: only the knowledge of himself, who is all most perfect, is required, and not the knowledge of other things or ideas, which are absolutely nothing, are arbitrarily something, and are imperfect. These are not objects of absolute and most perfect knowledge, but of God's arbitrary knowledge, which, desiring to see or to fashion its pictures, more or fewer, and wishing to play with them, takes them as its objects. However these objects stand, and whether they are more or fewer, they cannot prove imperfection in arbitrary knowledge, because it is arbitrary. If this arbitrary knowledge wishes to know nothing, that does not prove God imperfect; on the contrary, it proves him perfect. For it does not concern God himself nor have him as its object; and indeed it rather shows plainly that God has no need of other things and can do without them. If he wishes to know more, he will know more, and whatever he wishes. And from this it follows that God is so sufficient to himself that, for whatever he wishes to be or to be known, it suffices that he uses the positings in whatever way he wills.

units.la: ꝛ L 2 3. Si magis volupe effet cum Augustino exclamare : (a) O flumen tartareum, jactantur in te filii hominum cum mercedibus ut hæc discant; & magna res agitur, cum hoc agitur.
units.tr: 3. If it were more pleasant to exclaim with Augustine: (a) O tartarean river, into you the sons of men are cast with their fees, so that they may learn these things; and a great matter is at stake when this is at stake.

units.la: in senedute sic deliraret, ut totus Terentianis nugis sese traderet, dicitur pretius divinum, quod futili illa lectione expleri non poterat. Ita in Præfat. Annalium Grotii, similes, atque hic, tituli ei tribuuntur, quod stylum & artes Ethnicorum vaniffimorum in suis historiis esseт imitatus. (a) Confess. Lib. I. cap. 16.
units.tr: In his old age he so raved that he gave himself wholly to Terentian trifles; it is said that a divine price, which could not be made up by that frivolous reading. So in the Preface to the Annals of Grotius, similar titles, like this one, are given to him, because in his histories he imitated the style and arts of the most vain Gentiles. (a) Confessions, Book I, ch. 16.

units.la: XVII. At vero non desunt studiorum humanitatis, (uti vocantur,) patronis causæ, cur vanos atque locutulejos istos graculos ita commendent.
units.tr: XVII. Yet there are no lack of patrons of the so-called humane studies who commend these vain and chattering jackdaws in this way.

units.la: Quæ vero? scilicet abundant egregiis sententiis. Eorum cum historiæ tum scribendi modus ad sacra intelligenda faciunt. Latinus inde sermo Græcusque discendus est. Didicisse fideliter artes Emollit mores nec finit esse feros. Vide à renatis literis quanta politura, quanta lumina, quæ omnium rerum reformata facies orbi accesserint! quam antea non obscura tantum secula, sed & barbara & Cimmeriis tenebris plane immersa!
units.tr: But what are they? Surely they abound in excellent maxims. Their manner of writing history and of writing in general helps one understand sacred things, so one must learn Latin and Greek from them. To have learned the arts faithfully softens the character and does not let it remain savage. See how much polish and how much light, what a reformed face of all things has come to the world since the revival of letters! Before that, the ages were not merely obscure but barbarous, and sunk in Cimmerian darkness.

units.la: XVIII. Ego vero ejusmodi crasse halluci-nantes sic miseror, ut nisi bono animo ita coecutirent, istiusmodi mendaciis, quæ omnia confutabo, nil reponendum ducerem. Non dicam, paucula bona, quæ iis passim intermixta esse possent, operæ pretium non esse in tantis sterquiliniorum acervis, tanta cum temporis jactura, necessarium aliis posthabitis, quærere; sententiasque,
units.tr: XVIII. I pity these men, who hallucinate so crudely, and if they were not blundering with good intentions, I would think nothing needed to be answered to such falsehoods, all of which I will refute. I will not say that the few good things scattered here and there among them are not worth seeking out in such great heaps of dung, at such great cost of time, when other things must be set aside as necessary; and the sentences,

units.la: {18} Confutantur omnes quædam mnemonica ta bona, egregiaque in lis occurrant sententiæ. tiasque, si quas utiles profani protulerunt, sic aliorum opera collectas jam esse & seorsim exstare, ut necesse non sit ex impuris & venenatis fontibus (equalibus sane non purius bibuntur aquæ) eas adhucdum haurire: sed crediderim salutis humanæ inimici instinctu eos auctores suis impuris bona interspersisse eo consilio, ac veneficis suis venenis bonos intermiscent cibos, ut scilicet cum bonis exitiosa sese ingerant hominesque conficiant. Quis vero ejusmodi cibis vellet vesci quia & iis bona interposita sunt? Quasi vero in sanctis cœlestium animarum scriptis non haberemus affatim divinas sententias, easque sine ulla mali suspicione purissimas & salubberrimas. Ex pluribus divinæ Scripturæ, vide vel unum Proverbiorum Salomonis aut Syracidæ librum: aut e sanctioribus, Chrisianorum quidem, Joannis Climaci Scalam, vel Nili Admonitiones, aut Kempifii libellum: Ethnicorum vero, Sextii Pythagorei sententias, ne plures non ignotos commemorem.
units.tr: {18} All these are refuted. Even if some useful sayings of the profane writers have been brought forward, they have already been collected by the work of others and exist separately, so that it is not necessary to drink them still from impure and poisonous sources (though surely no water is drunk more purely from equal sources). But I would believe that those authors, at the instigation of the enemy of human salvation, mixed good things into their impure writings with the same purpose by which poisoners mix good food with their poisons: namely, so that, along with the good, they may thrust in the deadly and destroy people. Who would wish to feed on such food, merely because good things have been put into it as well? As if we did not have in the holy writings of the heavenly spirits an abundance of divine sentences, and these most pure and most wholesome, without any suspicion of evil. Of the many, look at the one book of the Proverbs of Solomon or of Jesus the son of Sirach; or among the more holy Christian writers, John Climacus's Ladder, or the Admonitions of Nilus, or the little book of Kempis; and among the heathen, the sayings of Sextius the Pythagorean, to say nothing of the many other well-known ones.

units.la: XIX. Falsum est ex Ethnicorum historiis & stylis, Scripturas solide & secundum Dei mentem posse intelligi: at forte aliquatenus & superficiarie atque secundum mentem Diaboli, hoc est, eo modo quem bolus ipse eruere, habere & communicare potest, literali scilicet externo, tenebris & erroribus mixto, ipsumque non beante, sed miseriorem & pejorem reddente, id fieri posse non nego. Historiarum Scripturæ soliditas typica est, & plerumque adhuc tota futura. Eam explicat Deus lumine suo puris mentibus quæ suæ sunt, ubi id eorum saluti conducere judicat, extra quem casum ista nec optanda, nec curiose ruspanda sunt: perindeque externos etiam eventus historiæ præteritos cum præsentibus ostendit Deus suis quando e re est: dum impii aut frigidi literati (qui hæc forte irridebunt) ex lecturis librisque suis non modo nil recte scient, sed & pro interpretamentis prophetiarum Scripturæ historiarumve, (quæ omnes sunt etiam typicæ & propheticæ, nil nisi fabulas dabunt, quales Grotii de Antichristo deque cæteris propheticis, quæ apparatu omni suo Ethnico &Critico voluit explicare: nec vero eventus, in quibus ipsimet vivunt, videbunt in Scripturis descriptos, neque cognoscent tempus visitationis suæ (uti ait Scriptura, ) donec ipsi excisi sint.
units.tr: XIX. It is false that, from the histories and styles of the heathen, the Scriptures can be understood solidly and according to the mind of God. But I do not deny that they may perhaps be understood in some measure, superficially, and according to the mind of the Devil; that is, in the way that the Devil himself can bring forth, hold and communicate them: namely, in a literal and external sense mixed with darkness and errors, which does not make a person happy but makes him more wretched and worse. The solidity of the Scripture histories is typical, and for the most part still wholly future. God explains it with his light to pure minds that are his own, when he judges that this is conducive to their salvation; outside that case such things are neither to be desired nor to be pried into with curiosity. In the same way God shows his own people the external events of past history together with the present, when it is fitting. Meanwhile the impious or cold scholars (who will perhaps laugh at these things), from their readings and their books, not only will know nothing rightly, but, as interpretations of the prophecies of Scripture and its histories (which are all typical and prophetic too), they will give only fables, such as Grotius's about the Antichrist and about the other prophetic matters, which he wished to explain with all his heathen and critical apparatus. Nor will they see in the Scriptures described the events in which they themselves live, nor will they recognise the time of their visitation (as Scripture says) until they themselves are cut off.

units.la: XX. De Latino sermone ab Ethnicis dissendo, ajo cum Augustino: (a) Ita vero non cognosceremus verba hæc, imbrem aureum, & gremium, & fucum, & templa cœli, & alia verba, nisi Terentius induceret nequam adolescentem proponentem sibi Jovem ad exemplum stupri, dum speciat tabulam quandam in pictura, ubi inerat pictura hæc: Jovem quo pacto fieri ajunt in gremium quondam imbrem aureum, fucum factum mulieri, &c.... non omnino per hanc turpitudinem verba ista commodius discuntur, sed per hæc verba turpitudo ista confidentius perpetratur. Non accuso verba, quasi vasa electa & pretiosa: sed vinum erroris quod in eis nobis propinatur ab ebriis doctoribus. Quasi vero (a) Conf. lib. I. vero nobis deesset in Cyprianis, Lactantiis, Sulpiciis, Minuriis, Hieronymis, Salvianis, aliisque quam plurimis piis Cæsares, Cicerones, Sallustii, & omnis generis sufficientissimi, ut sic dicam, Latinistæ Christiani, soluta æque ac ligata oratione optima ac sanctissima quæque animis nostris cum puritate sermonis instillantes, ne in Græcis eloquentissimos Patrum similiter commemorem. Neque nobis defuerunt ultimis hisce seculis, qui sermone Latino præstantissima & laudabilissima quæque tradere allaboraverunt. Sebastianus Castalio, vir ut pietate sic eruditione vera excellens, omnes Latinæ linguæ opes in Bibliis, aliisque divinis libris, Kempisio nempe, Theologia Germanica, & ejusmodi vertendis congessit: ipseque libros tersi styli & bonæ materiæ ad adultorum in divinis, & puerorum in ipsa latinitate instructionem, compositi: nec minus fecit magnus Erasmus: præcipue quando per egregias ejus in Novum Testamentum Paraphrases conatus est consequi, ut pro vano Ethnicismi spiritu, qui e fucatis Gentilium scriptis hauriebatur, e Christi doctrina clarius & ornatius ad hominum palatum ægrum exhibita, hauriretur veri Christianismi spiritus. Ast, inquies, ex illis non discetur puritas Romani sermonis qualis erat tempore Augusti Cæsaris. Quæ nugæ! Dantur forte in toto terrarum orbe duo tresve pædagogi, in pulvere scholæ obscure latitantes, qui sibi imaginantur istiusmodi stylorum inania nugamenta se callere, atque idcirco solos se viros esse: tu, uti unius forte ex illis judicio Augustani ævi graculus habearis, ætatem in sutilibus illis inaniter consumes. Age si tanti facis istiusmodi inanias, fac ut vel solam Romani soni pronunciationem genuinam tota vita expisceris, & eris mihi magnus Apollo. Non dedignatus est Deus, ubi per organa sua locutus est, crassiore & simpliciore stylo semper uti, imo dedignatus est stylum exquisitum, ob causas libro primo expressas: & nos puderet in his Deum sequi, & eo loqui more qui animos sinceriores, candidos, rerum magis quam verborum tenaces, deceat! Falsorum eruditorum isthæc esto occupatio, istaque simplicioris idiomatis, in sanctissimis atque solidissimis quibusque conspicui, redargutio. Ego equidem credederim, sic coram Deo rem se habere, in scholis eos, qui in infimis cathedris communia litterarum, lectionis & scriptionis elementa docent,etsi tanquam imæ professionis atque vilißimæ habeantur a mundi magistris, a Deo pro primis & præcipuis haberi: tum proximos ab his, qui linguarum peregrinarum rudimenta tradunt; ut qui uno gradu superiores ab hominibus reputantur, jam uno gradu coram Deo inferiores sint: atque ita gradatim, prout inter homines ascendere creduntur ad digniora, potiora & eruditiora, coram Deo econtra ordine inverso eos descendere semper ad vilíora, inaniora & sutiliora; donec tandem qui omnium primas sedes attigisse & exquisitiora profiteri putantur, in deliramenta desinere ac evanescere coram Deo judicentur. Nec dubito, quin omnes, dummodo ex eorum quæ docentur necessitate ac usu & fructibus provenientibus rem pensare volent, idem judicium facile sint facturi.
units.tr: XX. On the Latin language, which must be shunned for the sake of the heathen: I say with Augustine: (a) Thus we would not know these words, "golden rain," and "lap," and "disguise," and "the temples of heaven," and other such words, unless Terence introduced a worthless young man who sets Jupiter before himself as an example of debauchery, while he gazes at a certain painting in which this picture appeared: how they say Jupiter once turned into golden rain into a lap, made into a disguise for a woman, and so on.... These words are not learned more conveniently through this indecency, but through these words the indecency is carried out more boldly. I do not accuse the words, as if they were chosen and precious vessels, but the wine of error that is poured out to us in them by drunken teachers. As if, indeed, we lacked, in Cyprian, Lactantius, Sulpicius, Minucius, Jerome, Salvian, and very many other pious men, Caesars, Ciceros, Sallusts, and Christian Latinists of every kind, most capable, so to speak, who, in both prose and verse, instilled into our minds, with purity of style, all that is best and most holy; not to mention the most eloquent of the Greek Fathers in the same way. Nor in these latest ages have we lacked men who labored to hand down all that is most outstanding and praiseworthy in the Latin tongue.
