Sebastian Castalio, a man as excellent in learning as he was in piety, gathered together all the resources of the Latin language in translating the Bible and other divine books, namely Kempis, the German Theology, and such like; and he himself composed books of polished style and good matter, for the instruction of adults in divine things and of boys in Latinity itself. Great Erasmus did no less, especially when through his excellent Paraphrases on the New Testament he strove to achieve that, in place of the empty spirit of heathenism that was drawn from the painted writings of the Gentiles, the spirit of true Christianity should be drawn from the doctrine of Christ, presented more clearly and elegantly to the sick human palate. But, you will say, one does not learn from those men the purity of the Roman speech such as it was in the time of Augustus Caesar. What trifles! Perhaps there are in the whole world two or three schoolmasters, hidden obscurely in the dust of their schools, who imagine that they are skilled in these empty trifles of style and therefore think themselves alone to be men; you, perhaps, may be counted a jackdaw in the judgment of one of them from the Augustan age, and waste your life in vain on those trifles. Come, if you value such emptiness so highly, spend your whole life sifting out the genuine pronunciation of the Roman sound alone, and you will be a great Apollo to me. God did not disdain, when he spoke through his instruments, always to use a cruder and simpler style; indeed he disdained an exquisite style, for the reasons expressed in the first book. And should we be ashamed to follow God in this, and to speak in that manner which befits sincere and candid minds, more attached to things than to words! Let this be the occupation of false scholars, and let them make a show of refuting the simpler idiom in the most holy and most solid works. I would indeed believe that this is how the matter stands before God: that in the schools, those who teach the common elements of letters, reading and writing, in the lowest chairs, although they are regarded by the masters of the world as belonging to the lowest and most worthless profession, are held by God to be first and foremost; then next after them those who teach the rudiments of foreign languages; so that those who are reckoned by men to be one step higher are already one step lower before God; and so gradually, as men believe they rise to more worthy, more powerful and more learned things, so before God, conversely, in the inverse order, they always descend to baser, emptier and more trifling things; until at last those who are thought to have reached the first seats of all and to profess the more exquisite subjects are judged before God to end in delirium and to vanish away. Nor do I doubt that all, provided they are willing to weigh the matter by the necessity, use and resulting fruits of what is taught, will easily make the same judgment.

units.la: XXI. At, at, a literis humanioribus renovatis, omnia renovata & polita audivimus. Scilicet! Diabolus nimirum, qui antea feritate aperta, ac crassa turpitudine tumultuose sese prodebat; unde boni quique haud falsi, in quiete ac sine rumore solide Deo sibique agebant, ab inimico aperto facile cavent es; is animarum hostis, jam Angeli lucis speciem vestemque ab eruditione mundana nactus, sinceriores elegantiusque tutius seducit, dum pulso æternarum rerum ardore, divinoque lumine intus prorsum extincto, pro crassis terrestribusque vitiis, spiritualia, proque externarum quarundam rerum, plerumque inanium ignorantia, tenebras de rebus internis & divinioribus horribiles, ideas cassas, obscuras, chimiricas & futiles, errorum & hæresels fontes, restituit; quæ omnia, ipsamque cum vitiis quibusvis injustitiam, & doctius proponere & subtilius defendere didicit, vel adhibitis Scripturis ipsis per literaturam suam versipellem ad quævis adaptatis: sic ut errores perniciosissimi jam appareant veluti veritates divinæ; vitia vero exitiosissima, qualia amor sui, amor gloriæ, delectationum, pecuniæ, rerum seculi, jactura temporis Deo subducti, rixæ, odia interna, contemtus aliorum, simpliciorum irrisiones, rerum æternarum oblivio, imo & divinarum illusio, jam in virtutum & sagacioris prudentiæ speciem figuratæ & politæ sint jucundisque atque artificiosis istiusmodi eruditionis seculi artibus; quarum genio & debemus feralia illa schismata, a bono quovis lugenda, queis nullas nisi hujusmodi falsatas virtutes atque veritates debet orbis Christianus; id quod vel pueri luce clarius detegere possunt, si animadvertant, Christianismum, qui Christo teste e charitate mutua & propriæ voluntatis oblivione ut æterni Patris voluntas sola suscipiatur, agnosci debebat, jam inde non amore & æternarum rerum amplexatione, sed odiis & terrestrium rerum curis ubique concrevisse. Unde sequitur, judice Deo, tenebras, animarumque coram illo barbariem & brutalitatem, ne dicam Diabolicam malignitatem, incrementa inde cepisse, atque in dies, dum seculum magis magisque lucidum falsa ista eruditione fieri putatur, augescere. Sed quid pluribus id argumenti persequar, quod nemo bonus ex se non perspiciat, nemo vero ex iis qui minus sinceri sunt, quinque se non divino æternoque ædificio; sed mundano & peritauro veluti lapides polliendos, & eruditos devoverunt, non rejiciat atque improbet, ut ut rationibus æterno pondere validis urgeri se sentiant? His, ne iræ eorum acuantur, concedamus, eruditionem suam ad suos scopos esse & validam, & utilem, neque falli: sed ad solidum permanentemque statum id neutiquam fuerit. Atque hoc nobis satis esto.
units.tr: XXI. But, but, we have heard that from the renewed humane letters all things have been renewed and polished. Indeed! Clearly the devil, who formerly used to reveal himself tumultuously in open savagery and gross filthiness, so that good people, not deceived, could attend solidly to God and to themselves in quiet and without noise, easily guarded against the open enemy; this enemy of souls, having now obtained from worldly learning the appearance and garb of an angel of light, more safely seduces the more sincere and refined. For, with the ardor for eternal things driven out and the divine light extinguished within, in place of gross earthly vices he restores spiritual ones, and in place of ignorance of certain external things, mostly empty, he restores horrible darkness concerning inner and more divine matters, empty, obscure, chimerical and trifling ideas, the sources of errors and heresies. All these things, and injustice together with every vice, he has learned both to present more learnedly and to defend more subtly, even by adapting Scripture itself to whatever purposes through his shifty literature; so that the most pernicious errors now appear as divine truths, and the most deadly vices, such as self-love, love of glory, of pleasures, of money, of worldly things, the waste of time withdrawn from God, quarrels, inner hatreds, contempt for others, mockery of simpler folk, forgetfulness of eternal things, and indeed the mockery of divine things, are now shaped and polished into the semblance of virtues and of a keener prudence, by the pleasing and artful arts of this worldly learning. To the spirit of these arts we owe also those deadly schisms, to be lamented by every good person, for which the Christian world owes no virtues or truths except such falsified ones. Even boys can detect this more clearly than the light, if they notice that Christianity, which, Christ being witness, ought to be recognized by mutual charity and by forgetting one's own will, so that the will of the eternal Father alone is accepted, has since then grown everywhere not by love and the embracing of eternal things, but by hatreds and cares for earthly things. Whence it follows, God being judge, that darkness, and barbarism and brutality before him, not to say diabolical malignity, have taken their increase from this, and grow day by day, while the age is thought to become ever more enlightened through that false learning. But why should I pursue this argument at greater length, which no good man fails to see for himself, and which no one among those less sincere, who have devoted themselves not as stones to be hewn for the divine and eternal building but as stones to be polished for the worldly and perishing one, and as learned men, would not reject and condemn, unless they feel themselves pressed by arguments strong with eternal weight? To these, lest their anger be sharpened, let us concede that their learning is valid and useful for its own ends, and not deceptive; but it will by no means lead to a solid and lasting state. And let this be enough for us.

units.la: XXII. Enumeravimus inter quatuor supe- riora
units.tr: XXII. We have listed among the four preceding

units.la: {22} Defect. riofa eruditionis falsæ acquirendæ media, ipsam eruditionis,quæ proponitur, materiam, hoc est, scientias ipsas, quando eæ ne quidem superficiariæ sunt; sed falsæ, erroneæque, e principiis falsis falsas conclusiones deducentes & proponentes; quales fere ubique gentium vulgo obtinent. Hoc ita esse, non est cur multum allaboremus ostendere. Ipsimet qui scientias tradunt, hoc ipsum aperte declarant, dum sese mutuo refutant ac conficiunt; at eo tamen modo, qui refutatis non succenturiat meliora. Sola quippe veritas lumine suo & errorem confutat, & vero adstruit quod ad plenam mentis acquiescentiam quærebatur. Etsi autem hoc officio conatus sim in eis quæ edidi, quantum pro viribus licuit defungi; notabo tamen hic obiter nonnulla quæ errorum sunt origines in scientiis illis præcipuis, de quibus in libro præcedente quædam monueram.
units.tr: {22} Defect. The means of acquiring false erudition that we listed are four, and the fourth is the matter of the erudition offered, that is, the sciences themselves, since these are not even superficial. They are false and erroneous, drawing and proposing false conclusions from false principles, as nearly all the sciences that generally prevail among the peoples of the world do. There is no need for us to labour long to show that this is so. The very men who teach the sciences declare it openly, while they refute and overthrow one another; yet they do so in a way that does not supply better things in place of what they refute. Truth alone, by its own light, refutes error, and it establishes in place of error what the mind sought for its full assent. Although in the books I have published I have tried to discharge this task as far as my powers allowed, I shall nevertheless briefly note here some of the origins of error in those principal sciences about which I made some remarks in the preceding book.

units.la: XXIII. Omnia illa omissa, quæ in libro proxime præcedente ostendi in causis esse cur scientiæ ad perfectionem superficiariam & idealem non attingant, eadem quoque efficiunt ut in errores deveniant. Namque si quis destitutus quibusdam ad operandum necessariis operari tamen velit, eum perverse operari necesse est: prout si quis destitutus viribus necessariis, lumine viaque plana ad ambulandum, ambulare tamen vellet, is certe non posset non cadere atque errare. Verum, inquiet quispiam, ejusmodi in scientiis lapsus atque errores non sunt tanti, ut idcirco tota eruditio dicenda sit falsa, siquidem ejusmodi defectûs ideas rationis tantum concernunt, quibus licet nutantibus, eruditionem veram remanere posse ex eo sequitur, quod hæc consistat in facultatum quas reales diximus atque in superiores & inferiores distinximus, bono cum objectis suis necessariis statu. Ad quæ respondeo, me nequaquam afferere eos, quorum cæteroqui facultates reales eruditione solida politæ sunt, ideo vera eruditione sua destitui falsaque imbui, quod in nonnullis, quæ ideales scientias spectant, ipsi fallantur. Minime hîc de talibus agitur: sed de illis tantum qui solide reliquæ eruditione repulsa, pro eruditione tota acquirenda nil sibi proponunt præter ideas ejusmodi quæ in scientiis venditantur, quæ sane si falsæ fuerint, jam tota eorum eruditio falsa sit necesse est. Neque tantum hoc, sed & potentissimum ad eruditionem aspirandi & perveniendi impedimentum fuerint illi circa ideas meras errores. Namque ex quo humanum genus veluti brutum nascitur, neque ad superiora & solida nisi per externa, per sensus crassos, per imaginationem, per rationem denique & ejus ideas assurgit, fit inde ut ii, quibus externa & sensus & imaginatio & ideæ supprimerentur aut falsarentur; veluti si aut nulla verba aut falsa auribus perciperent, falsasque imaginatione versarent imagines, non possent certe ea ratione ad vera, divina, sublimia pertingere; sed potius per corrupta illa media ab iis amoverentur. Eodem modo, si ratio erroneis falsisque ideis, dum scientias discit, repleatur, impeditur mens, (quamdiu rationem tioni vult insistere) à superioribus & divinioribus inveniendis, imo & quærendis: per falsas enim ideas dum originalia ipsa divina detorpantur, obscurantur, imo odiosa & velut inania repræsentantur, sequitur eadem contemni ac fugi, vel etiam deriderí à misera, & rationis ideis seducta Mente, contrariis ut sese dedat. Unde patet errores circa ideas in scientiis propositos, ut ut Mentibus quæ quoad facultates supremas solida gaudent eruditione, nullius momenti essent, perniciosissimos tamen illis esse quæ eruditione vera nondum sunt præditæ: atque adeo sollicite cavendum, iis ne tales propinentur: ut si quando spes sit illas solida quærere posse, eis a ratione, per falsas ideas seducta, non occludatur janua; sed potius per ideas, vera quantum fieri potest repræsentantes, adjuventur. Hisce quo magis prodesse possit falsitatum scientias vitiantium detectio, paucula etiam de quibusdam dicemus.
units.tr: XXIII. Set aside all those things which I showed in the immediately preceding book to be the causes why the sciences do not attain superficial and ideal perfection; these same things also bring it about that they fall into error. For if someone, lacking certain things necessary for working, nevertheless wishes to work, he must necessarily work amiss; just as, if someone lacking the necessary strength, and lacking light and a plain way for walking, nevertheless wished to walk, he could not help but fall and go astray. But someone will say: errors and lapses of this kind in the sciences are not so great that for that reason all erudition should be called false, since defects of this kind concern only the ideas of reason; and from this it follows that, even though these ideas waver, true erudition can remain, because it consists in the real faculties, which we have called such, and which we have distinguished into higher and lower, being in a good state with their necessary objects. To this I reply that I by no means assert that those whose real faculties are otherwise adorned with solid erudition are on that account deprived of their true erudition and imbued with falsehood, merely because they are deceived in some matters that concern the ideal sciences. This is not what is at issue here at all. Rather, I speak only of those who, having solidly rejected the rest of erudition, propose to themselves, for the acquiring of all erudition, nothing but such ideas as are peddled in the sciences; if these are false, then their whole erudition must necessarily be false. And not only this, but those errors about mere ideas are also the most powerful impediment to aspiring to and attaining erudition. For since the human race is born, as it were, like a brute, and rises to higher and solid things only through external things, through the coarse senses, through imagination, and finally through reason and its ideas, it follows that those whose external perceptions, senses, imagination and ideas were suppressed or falsified (for example, if they perceived no words, or false words, with their ears, and entertained false images in their imagination) could certainly not reach the true, the divine and the sublime by that route; rather, they would be drawn away from them through those corrupted means. In the same way, if reason, while it learns the sciences, is filled with erroneous and false ideas, the mind is impeded (so long as it wishes to keep to reason) from discovering, indeed even from seeking, the higher and more divine things. For while through false ideas the original divine things themselves are distorted and obscured, or even represented as hateful and as it were empty, it follows that they are despised and shunned, or even mocked, by a wretched mind that has been led astray by the ideas of reason, so that it gives itself over to their opposites. Whence it is plain that errors about ideas proposed in the sciences, although they would be of no importance to minds that enjoy solid erudition in their highest faculties, are nevertheless most pernicious to those not yet endowed with true erudition. Hence one must take careful heed that such errors are not administered to them, so that, if there is ever hope that they can seek the solid things, the door is not shut against them by reason, led astray through false ideas, but rather that they are helped by ideas representing the truth as far as possible. That the detection of the falsehoods that vitiate the sciences may be the more useful for these purposes, we shall also say a few things about some of them.

units.la: XXIV. Quæ superius de iis quibus impeditur, ne Metaphysica, Physica, Ethica, Logica etiam atque Critica, ipsaque denique Theologia, fiant superficialiter perfectæ, retulimus; ea hic possunt recenseri tanquam fontes errorum, qui in istas disciplinas & scientias derivantur apud omnes eos, qui omissis veritatibus vel dispositionibus quas ibi recensuimus, tentant eas scientias acquirere. Possunt igitur ea suis è locis repeti, & veluti huc pertinentia considerari. Quibus nunc adjungimus sequentia:
units.tr: XXIV. What I said above about the things that hinder Metaphysics, Physics, Ethics, Logic and Criticism, and finally Theology itself, from becoming superficially perfect, may be listed here as sources of the errors that flow into these disciplines and sciences among all who, neglecting the truths or dispositions that we enumerated there, try to acquire those sciences. These may therefore be repeated from their proper places and considered as belonging here. To these we now add the following.

units.la: Defalsitate praecipuarum scientiarum vulgo obtinentium. Et primo quidem de generalibus erroribus in mentalibus Metaphysicis, Physicis.
units.tr: On the falsity of the principal sciences commonly current. And first, indeed, on the general errors in the mental, metaphysical and physical sciences.

units.la: In Metaphysicis (præter alios errores in Dissertatione initio operis hujus præfixa annotatos, falsaque præjudicia mox ante recensita, nec ab ipsis quidem Cartesianis depositia; ex quibus tamen omnia sua falsantur, ) falsa statim est doctrina de transcendentalibus, de idearum æternitate, deque veritatibus idearum æternis & immutabilibus, de earum necessitate ad Dei Omniscientiam constituendam, ex quibus stultum dogma de fato, vel de necessitate rerum fatali, de libertatis vel negatione vel in dubium revocatione, deque feris & absurdis quibusdam omnium rerum & recularum decretis, nec decretis modo, sed & ad quævis concursibus præviis simultaneisque, & nescio quot monstris, quibus Deus & natura, opera item naturæ & gratiæ, activitasque creaturarum & actus Dei confunduntur, obtenebrantur, negantur. Substantiæ quoque & accidentium, imo dicere ausim, omnium pene rerum, ideas nullas, ne quidem generales & dilutas, nisi absurdas & chimæricas habent. Quæ non dicta modo, sed & probata à me videre potuerunt, qui Cogitationes & Oeconomiam inspexerunt.
units.tr: In Metaphysics (besides the other errors noted in the Dissertation prefixed at the beginning of this work, and the false prejudices recently listed, which are not even abandoned by the Cartesians themselves; by which, nevertheless, all their own doctrines are falsified), the doctrine of the transcendentals is at once false, as is the doctrine of the eternity of ideas, and of the eternal and immutable truths of ideas, and of their necessity for constituting the omniscience of God. From these comes the foolish dogma of fate, or of the fatal necessity of things, and the denial or calling into doubt of liberty, and certain savage and absurd decrees concerning all things and events, not only decrees but also prior and simultaneous concursuses for whatever occurs, and I know not how many monsters by which God and nature, the works of nature and of grace alike, and the activity of creatures and the acts of God, are confounded, darkened and denied. Substances and accidents, indeed, I would venture to say, almost all things, have no ideas at all, not even general and diluted ones, except absurd and chimerical ones. These things could be seen not only to be said but also proved by me, by those who have looked into my Cogitationes and Oeconomia.

units.la: XXV. Sed ne hic sola errorum indica- tione aut ad scripta alia remissione agam, de- monstrationibus brevioribus præcipua evin- cere animus est.
units.tr: XXV. But lest I proceed here by merely pointing out errors or referring to other writings, I intend to establish the main points by shorter demonstrations.

units.la: 1. Deus (omnium consensu) est ens perfectissimum: Ergo est sibi se solo sufficientissimus: nam si sibi non sufficeret ex se solo, certè in se & ex se deficeret; quod est contra tra definitionem agnitam. Si sibi se solo sufficit, igitur nullius rei idea, praeter ideam sui ipsius, est ei necessaria ad sui persectionem. Ergo idearum, veritatumque de illis necessitas, aeternitas & immutabilitas absolutae, falsae sunt, suntque ideae non nisi ex arbitrio & statuto Dei, a quo arbitrio abstinere potuisset, vel aliter de eo ideisque disponere, is qui se solo contentus est ac perfectissimus.
units.tr: 1. God (by common consent) is the most perfect being. Therefore he is wholly sufficient to himself, for if he were not sufficient from himself alone, he would certainly be deficient in himself and from himself, which is contrary to the accepted definition. If he suffices to himself alone, then no idea of any thing other than the idea of himself is necessary to him for his perfection. Therefore the necessity, eternity and absolute immutability of ideas and of the truths concerning them are false, and ideas exist only by the arbitrary decree of God, from which arbitrary decree he could have abstained, or could have disposed otherwise concerning himself and ideas, since he is content with himself alone and most perfect.

units.la: 2. Igitur ad perfectionem Omniscientiae Dei non requiritur nisi sola cognitio sui ipsius, qui omne perfectissimum est: non autem cognitio aliarum rerum aut idearum, quae absolute nil sunt, arbitrarie aliquid sunt, & imperfectae sunt: quaeque non cognitionis absolutae & perfectissimae; sed cognitionis arbitrariae Dei objecta sunt, picturas suas, plures, pauciores, videre aut effigiare gestientis, & cum illis ludere volentis: quae objecta, ut ut se habeant, plurave sint an pauciora, cognitionem arbitrariam; quia arbitraria est, imperfectionis arguere non possunt. Haec Dei cognitio arbitraria si nulla volet cognoscere, non ideo imperfectionis Deum arguit: contra, perfectionis: nam nec Deum ipsum concernit seu pro objecto habet; & vero potius sic patet Deum caeteris non egere, eisque carere posse: quod si plura velit, cognoscet & plura, & quaecunque volet; indeque sequetur Deum sibi sufficientem sic esse, ut eis quae volet esse vel cognosci, sufficiat eo modo ponendis uti volet.
units.tr: 2. Therefore the perfection of God's omniscience requires only the knowledge of himself, who is all perfection; it does not require the knowledge of other things or ideas, which are absolutely nothing, are arbitrarily something, and are imperfect. These are not objects of absolute and most perfect knowledge but of God's arbitrary knowledge, since he is eager to see or fashion his pictures, more or fewer, and wishes to play with them. Whatever these objects are, and whether they are more or fewer, this arbitrary knowledge cannot argue imperfection, because it is arbitrary. If God wishes to know none of them, this does not show imperfection in God; on the contrary, it shows perfection, for such objects do not concern God himself nor are they his object. Indeed, it rather shows that God has no need of the others and can do without them. But if he wishes to know more, he will know more, and whatever he wishes; and it follows that God is so sufficient to himself that he can use these things, which he wishes to be or to be known, in whatever way he pleases to place them.

units.la: 3. Si autem placeat ei nolle creaturam liberam, cui donet facultatem se ipsam ex proprio (ipsique donato) arbitrio regendi, tunc sequitur evidenter contradictorium esse, si statuatur ejusmodi creaturæ omnes actus regimenque totum præsciri, decerni, agi, præcurri, & influi physice a Deo, uti loquuntur. Unde omnia ista barbara fata atque fictitia de omnibus decreta in fumum abeunt: aut vero ostendendum est, impossibile esse Deo se ipsum per creaturæ constitutionem non posse repræsentare quą ens liberum & activum: quod non facient qui nec ejus omnipotentiam negare, nec omne jus & fas (in libertate fundatum) delere tentabunt.
units.tr: 3. But if it pleases him not to will a free creature, to whom he gives the faculty of governing itself by its own will (given to it), then it evidently follows that it is contradictory to hold that all the acts of such a creature and its whole governance are foreknown, decreed, performed, forestalled and physically influenced by God, as they say. Hence all those barbarous and fictitious fates and decrees concerning everything vanish into smoke. Or else it must be shown that it is impossible for God not to be able to represent himself through the constitution of a creature as a free and active being. Those who will neither deny his omnipotence nor attempt to abolish all right and justice (founded on liberty) will not do this.

units.la: 4. Porro si solus Deus est absolutum ens, falsa ergo est doctrina de ente transcendentali, sive de notione entis Deo & creaturis univoce competente: absolutum enim & arbitrarium, sive absolutum & non absolutum, univoca nou sunt.
units.tr: 4. Further, if God alone is absolute being, then the doctrine of transcendental being, or of the notion of being applying univocally to God and creatures, is false. For the absolute and the arbitrary, or the absolute and the non-absolute, are not univocal.

units.la: 5. Jam posito, Deum ex arbitrio decrevisse se ipsum depingere, atque adeo entia idealia excogitasse, deinde illa produxisse, falsum iterum est eorum entium naturæ omnî competere ex se hæc attributa, unum, verum, bonum: multo minus univoce cum Deo ea participare. Quando Deus vult ponere entium naturas, tunc nil ex naturarum necessitate seu necessaria constitutione ponit tanquam ad naturam illorum pertinens, nisi fundum intimum atque facultates; non autem facultatum objecta, vel ex objectis resultantes perfectiones. hoc ultimum est ex superveniente gratia, non ex naturarum necessitate aut facultatibus. Jam autem in entibus veritas & bonitas non ex naturæ suæ constitutione aut facultatibus, sed ex resultatione actuum alius cujuspiam objecti interni (Dei) enascuntur. Ens omne positum in natura sua hoc includit, ut sit unum, sive fixum & manens, indivisumque. Sed veritas entis, hoc est, ejus luminosus status, resultatio lucida & vera suarum perfectionum ad se, quæ etiam pulcritudo entis est; deinde ejus bonitas, hoc est, communicatio proprietatum suarum decentium jucunda, tum sibi inter se-se, tum aliis extra se, quæ est gloriosa quædam entium in se & inter se concordia & felicitas; hæ duæ, inquam, in nullis entibus sunt, nisi Deo in illa sese insinuante, eaque continuo luminositate & jucunditate sua afficiente, ordinante & ornante: quæ operationes gratiæ sunt, Verbique Dei & Spiritūs S. propriæ; quibus operationibus quæ destituuntur entia, entia quidem una sunt, sed nec vera, nec bona; at falsa & confusa, anxia & mala. Alia entium veritas & bonitas non datur: proinde ea Metaphysicorum chimærica est, qui essentialem realitatem cum pulcra veritate & jucunda bonitate, naturamque cum gratia confuderunt. Quod reale solum debuit dici, id male & verum & bonum dixerunt, etsi obscurum, confusum & pessimum esset; quales sunt tenebrosæ, fraudulentæ, anxiæ æternumque miseræ impiorum seu dæmonum mentes.
units.tr: 5. Now, granted that God by his will decided to portray himself, and so devised ideal beings and then brought them forth, it is again false that these attributes belong to the nature of those beings from themselves: one, true and good; much less do they share these univocally with God. When God wills to establish the natures of beings, he posits nothing of the necessity of natures, or of their necessary constitution, as pertaining to their nature, except the innermost ground and faculties; not the objects of the faculties, nor the perfections resulting from objects. The latter comes from the grace that supervenes, not from the necessity of natures or from their faculties. Now, in beings, truth and goodness arise not from the constitution of their nature or from their faculties, but from the resulting of the acts of some other internal object (God). Every being posited in its nature includes this, that it is one, that is, fixed, abiding and undivided. But the truth of a being, that is, its luminous state, the bright and true reflection of its perfections upon itself, which is also the beauty of the being, and then its goodness, that is, the pleasing communication of its fitting properties both to itself among themselves and to others outside itself, which is a certain glorious harmony and happiness of beings within themselves and among one another: these two, I say, are found in no beings except when God insinuates himself into them, affecting, ordering and adorning them with his continual luminosity and joy. These are the operations of grace, proper to the Word of God and the Holy Spirit. Beings lacking these operations are indeed one, but neither true nor good; rather they are false and confused, anxious and evil. No other truth and goodness of beings is given. Therefore that notion is a fiction of the Metaphysicians, who have confused essential reality with beautiful truth and pleasant goodness, and nature with grace. What ought to have been called only real, they have wrongly called true and good, even though it is obscure, confused and most wretched; such are the dark, fraudulent, anxious and eternally miserable minds of the wicked or of demons.

units.la: 6. At dicent, id ipsum quod confusum & pessimum nominas, id in genere entis & substantiæ verum & bonum est. Error! Ens, qua ens, nullum verum & bonum est nisi solus Deus. De cæteris non in idea & natura entis continetur natura veritatis & bonitatis; sed ea ex Dei supervenientis liberali insinuatione & gratiosa operatione superaccedit naturæ. Hæc alibi () conatus sum pluribus variisque modis explicare, quando ostendi, in rebus esse quædam a Deo sic posita & data ut naturæ rei partes essent; at alia a Deo esse donata non acsi partes naturales essent rerum sive entium, sed veluti eorum statum perficientia, quibus res privari possent; non autem primis, quæ proprie naturalia & realia dicuntur; altera vero ex gratuita donatione (ut dixi) superadduntur naturæ tum corporalium, tum spiritualium rerum. Et hujus generis sunt entium veritas & pulcritudo, bonitas & jucunda concordia, atque similia, quæ an Metaphysicorum tenebris assueti illico capient aut admittent, non ausim asseverare. Bonitas namque & veritas sua absoluta, & transcendentalis & substantialis difficulter, ob diuturnam amicitiam, eorum imaginationem deserent, ut & alia cogitata & voces admittant alias. Et sane distinctio ususque alius in vocibus, quæs hactenus obscuros, confusos falsosque conceptus junxerunt, essent introducenda; neque amplius realitas, natura, unitas, veritas, bonitas, perfectio, & quæ hujus generis, sic confundendæ essent, ut chaos potius omnia promiscue referrent, quam conceptus distinctos & luminosos formarent.
units.tr: 6. But they will say that what you call confused and most wretched is in the genus of being and substance true and good. Error! Being, as being, is no true and good thing except God alone. Concerning other things, the nature of truth and goodness is not contained in the idea and nature of being; rather it is added to the nature of a thing from the liberal insinuation and gracious operation of God supervening upon it. I have tried to explain this elsewhere (), in several varied ways, when I showed that there are some things so posited and given by God that they are parts of the nature of a thing; while others are given by God not as natural parts of things or beings, but as, so to speak, perfecting their state, of which things could be deprived. These are not the primary things, which are properly called natural and real; rather they are added, as I said, by a gratuitous gift to the nature both of corporeal and of spiritual things. Of this kind are the truth and beauty of beings, their goodness and pleasant harmony, and similar things. I dare not assert whether those accustomed to the darkness of the Metaphysicians will immediately grasp or admit them. For their absolute and transcendental and substantial truth and goodness will with difficulty be abandoned by their imagination, owing to long-standing friendship, and they will hardly admit other thoughts and other words. Indeed, a different distinction and use of words would have to be introduced, words which have hitherto joined obscure, confused and false concepts. And realness, nature, unity, truth, goodness, perfection and such things would no longer have to be so confused that they refer everything indiscriminately as a chaos, rather than form distinct and luminous concepts.

units.la: 7. Quæ de substantia & accidente dixerunt, non minori itidem obscuritati & captioni obnoxia sunt. Ex pessima Ethnicorum, maximè verò Aristotelis Metaphysica tenebrosa, pessime ista ad rerum fundamenta & explicationem assumserunt. Alio lumine, quam Aristotelico, in rerum perquirendis fundis opus fuisset. Melius consideranda proponerentur in rebus omnibus primo earum fundus, sive natura & entitas; deinde facultates (quæ cum fundo unitæ, nec unquam ab eo separandæ, unitatem constituere dici possint;) postea objecta facultatum; hinc actus facultatum & modi eorum in objecta; & tandem resultatio novique actus objectorum & facultatum postquam in se unite egerunt. Atque ista sola quicquid in rebus est præcipuum exhaurire posse, exercitatis non erit dubium. At per vias substantiæ & accidentis, generumque accidentium novem, nil nisi nugas & affanias proferri experientia docet plus satis. Ipsi quid sua sit substantia suaque accidentia, sane nesciunt; mihi vero nunc opportunum non est ista pluribus persequi, quæ ne sic quidem tetigissem, nisi inde tenebras & errores exitiosos in omnibus divinis atque naturalibus, imo & ipsum Atheismum nonnulli arcessivilent.
units.tr: 7. What they have said about substance and accident is likewise liable to no less obscurity and deception. From the very poor metaphysics of the Gentiles, and above all from the obscure Metaphysics of Aristotle, they have very badly taken these things as the foundations and explanation of things. Another light than the Aristotelian would have been needed in seeking out the foundations of things. The following would be better considered in all things: first their ground, or nature and entity; then their faculties (which, united with the ground and never to be separated from it, can be said to constitute unity); then the objects of the faculties; then the acts of the faculties and their modes toward the objects; and finally the resulting and new acts of the objects and faculties after they have acted together in themselves. For the experienced it will not be doubtful that these alone can exhaust whatever is principal in things. But through the ways of substance and accident, and the nine genera of accidents, experience teaches more than enough that nothing but trifles and babble are produced. They themselves certainly do not know what their substance is or what their accidents are. But it is not opportune for me now to pursue these matters at length; I would not even have touched on them thus, had not some people brought from them dark and destructive errors into all divine and natural matters, and even atheism itself.

units.la: XXVI. De Physicis quotquod scripse- runt, aut aliquid se scire putant, nil aliud similiter agunt quam quòd se ipsos mutuo ignorantiæ & errorum convincant. Sincerio- res
units.tr: XXVI. Of all who have written on physics, or who think they know anything about it, they do nothing else, in the same way, than convict one another of ignorance and error.

units.la: res autem fateri tenentur omnia ad minimum dubia esse & incerta, quando de causis naturalibus atque earundem effectis ratiocinari volunt. Cartesiani quidem se prae cae-teris hic sapere sibi persuadent; at non difficulter falsitatis convinci possunt circa physicam, fere totam, tum (1) ex propriis suis Metaphysicis principiis, quae ipsi male secuti sunt; tum (2) ex veritatibus aliunde indubitatis, quibus physica sua principia & quae ex iis deducuntur, repugnant aperte; tum denique (3) ex aliis quam plurimis hallucinationibus in quas inciderunt dum propria principia minus recte secuti, eadem quadam vi detorserunt ad conclusiones minime exiis sequentes, sed quibus opus habebant ut rerum phaenomenis essent conformes.
units.tr: More candid writers are bound to admit that everything they say about natural causes and their effects is at least doubtful and uncertain. The Cartesians in particular persuade themselves that they are wiser than the rest in this matter. Yet they can easily be convicted of falsehood almost throughout their physics: (1) from their own metaphysical principles, which they followed badly; (2) from truths otherwise indubitable, with which their physical principles, and what is deduced from them, plainly conflict; and finally (3) from very many other hallucinations into which they fell, when, following their own principles less correctly, they twisted them by a certain force to conclusions that do not follow at all, but which they needed in order that they might agree with the phenomena of things.

units.la: XXVII. Ex Metaphysicis principiis physica sic desumsit. CARTESIUS, ut quamvis agnoscat Deum esse perfectissimum, & ab eo non nisi perfectissima opera prodire posse, eundemque & simplicem esse & constantem non modo, sed & potentem sive activum, & bonum seu realitatum communicativum atque fertilem, & pulcherrimum, aliaque: tamen principia sua physica sic constituat in aliquibus ex iis attributis, ut ad cetera non attendat, nec etiam ea quae ex uno principio sequuntur, vere vel ex toto affirmat: quod fallaciae divisionis & inconsequentiae genus quoddam est. Verbi gratia, Ex simplicitate Dei una deducit unam motus secundum lineam rectam tendentis proprietatem, & nil praeterea: ex constantia deducit & rerum & motus continuationem in statu suo suaque quantitate: Ex Dei infinita potentia & bonitate, opera Dei non nimis ampla & pulcra & absoluta posse cogitari, cavendumque ne in eorum perfectionibus quosdam limites nobis non cognitos, praefigamus: Ex imperscrutabilitate Sapientiæ ejus, omnes rerum physicarum fines nobis esse absconditos.
units.tr: XXVII. Descartes derives his physics from his metaphysical principles in this way. Although he acknowledges that God is most perfect, that only most perfect works can come forth from him, and that he is simple and constant, and not only that but also powerful, or active, and good, that is, communicative and fruitful of reality, and most beautiful, and other things besides, nevertheless he so constitutes his physical principles on some of these attributes that he does not attend to the rest, nor does he truly or fully affirm even those things which follow from a single principle. This is a kind of fallacy of division and inconsistency. For example, from the simplicity of God he deduces the single property of motion tending along a straight line, and nothing besides. From constancy he deduces the continuation both of things and of motion in their state and quantity. From God's infinite power and goodness he concludes that God's works cannot be thought too ample, beautiful, and perfect, and that we must take care not to set down for their perfections certain limits unknown to us. From the inscrutability of his Wisdom he concludes that all the ends of physical things are hidden from us.

units.la: At vero, quid lineæ rectæ commune cum Simplicitate Divina, vel cum repræsentatione ejus perfectionis, quæ collectim omnes Dei perfectiones in unum complectitur? An motus secundum lineam rectam ex eo sequitur, vel probatur, vel illustratur, quod Dei omnes perfectiones sint simul unitæ? Cur ex hac simplicitate non conclusit potius, Deum non sic unum attributum solum repræsentare in operibus suis, vel in uno aliquo opere, ut repræsentatio aliorum attributorum inde separetur? atque adeo & Dei sufficientiam seu non indigentiam, liberalitatem, felicitatem, sui secum concordiam seu pacem, luminositatem, gloriam, amorem, justitiam, unitatem, activitatem, & similia, debere non excludi quando Dei opera eorumve leges & rationes considerantur in relatione ad causam suam, Deum sicut analoga inter illa & hunc, velut inter typum & Archetypum deprehendatur conformitas? Hæc sane ex Simplicitate Dei, hoc est, ex omnium ejus perfectionum indissolubili connexione, magis sequuntur, quam ex eadem motus secundum lineam rectam.
units.tr: But what has a straight line in common with the divine simplicity, or with the representation of that perfection which gathers all of God's perfections together into one? Does motion along a straight line follow from it, or get proved or illustrated by it, because all the perfections of God are united together? Why did he not rather conclude from this simplicity that God does not represent only one attribute in his works, or in some one work, so that the representation of other attributes is thereby separated off? And so, when the works of God, or their laws and reasons, are considered in relation to their cause, ought not God's sufficiency, or non-indigence, his liberality, his blessedness, his concord and peace with himself, his luminosity, glory, love, justice, unity, activity, and the like, to be excluded? Ought not a conformity between those things and him to be discerned, as between type and archetype? These things indeed follow more from the simplicity of God, that is, from the indissoluble connection of all his perfections, than from the same simplicity does motion along a straight line.

units.la: Cur etiam ex Dei Constantia non conclusit, rerum systemata non debere interitui & destructioni esse obnoxia ?
units.tr: Why also did he not conclude from God's constancy that systems of things ought not to be subject to decay and destruction?

units.la: Cur ex ejus potentia & actiVitate & fertilitate, ut sic dicam, non deduxit, motûs quantitatem datam non manere, sed augeri in rerum natura, constituisseque Deum principia non sterilia & veluti mortua, aut mere passiva; sed activa, fertilia, & quæ ex paucis datis infinita producant ?
units.tr: Why did he not deduce from his power, activity, and, so to speak, fruitfulness, that the quantity of motion given does not remain fixed but increases in the nature of things, and that God has established principles that are not sterile and, as it were, dead, or merely passive, but active, fruitful, and which from a few given things produce infinite results?

units.la: Cur ex Dei pulcritudine, concordia, luminositate non deduxit principia, e quibus sequeretur, in operibus Dei nulla esse deformia sive monstrosa, nulla sibi adversantia seque destruentia, nullasque tenebras; sed meram lucem, concordiam, pulcritudinem ?
units.tr: Why did he not deduce from God's beauty, concord, and luminosity principles from which it would follow that there are no deformed or monstrous things in the works of God, nothing opposed to itself or self-destructive, and no darkness, but pure light, concord, and beauty?

units.la: Quare ex simplicitate Dei & Unitate, atque perfeƈtissima infinitorum attributorum Multiplicitate, nec non ex Amore,quo Deus omnia sua simul in se velut in centro unit, singulaque etiam (ut sic dicam) seorsim in se velut in propriis centris compleƈtitur, ( amore enim divino quævis attributa sibi ipsis adhærent, se probant, in se feruntur; dein id agunt omnia simul in unum simplicitatis & unitatis centrum tendentia: ) cur inquam inde deduci potius non possit, Deum ad se qua talem repræsentandum, impressisse materiæ motum quidem totius generalem quo feratur ea ad commune centrum, quibusque vero partibus speciales motus ad centra sua propria, qui & attraƈtionis, & rerum nexûs, & aliorum effeƈtuum causæ fuerint.
units.tr: Why, from the simplicity and unity of God, and from the most perfect multiplicity of his infinite attributes, and also from the love by which God unites all his things together in himself as in a centre, and each of them is also (so to speak) complete separately in himself, as in its own proper centres (for by divine love each attribute clings to itself, proves itself, and is carried into itself; then all of them together act, tending into one centre of simplicity and unity), why, I say, could it not rather be deduced from this that God, in order to represent himself as such, impressed upon matter a general motion of the whole by which it is carried to a common centre, and upon its particular parts special motions towards their own proper centres, which are the causes of attraction, of the connection of things, and of other effects?

units.la: Quare ex eo quòd Deus, dum Amore & Desiderio sua omnia in unum, præterea- que singula etiam in se quæque attrahit & concentrat, non tamen ita se suaque sibi occultat; sed se omniaque veluti ex centro sibi in prospectum & contemplationem expandens, luminose intuetur; non concludas inde eundem, ut se perfecte repræsentaret, postquam universam materiæ molem fecit ad unum centrum commune, singulas autem partes ad sua quasque centra tendere, non sinat eas ita in molem compactam tenebrosamque condensari; sed impressa resultatione tum totius ex centro communi ad circumferentiam, tum uniuscujusque ex centro proprio extrorsum versus, totam omnesque partes reddat ita lucidas, ut ex universæ materiæ centro summa lux, ex cujusque vero etiam particulæ centro lux quoque sua eniteat; atque sic nil occultum; nil tenebrosum; sed omnia & lucida & diaphana sint?
units.tr: Why, from the fact that God, through love and desire, draws and concentrates all his things into one and each of them also into himself, yet does not so hide himself and his own things, but shines with light, spreading himself and all things out from his centre for view and contemplation, do you not conclude from this that, in order to represent himself perfectly, after he made the whole mass of matter tend to one common centre and its individual parts to their own several centres, he would not allow them to be condensed into a compact and dark mass; but, by impressing a resultant motion both of the whole outward from the common centre to the circumference and of each part outward from its proper centre, would make the whole and all its parts so bright that from the centre of all matter a supreme light shines, and from the centre of each particle its own light also gleams forth; and thus nothing is hidden, nothing dark, but all things are both luminous and transparent?

units.la: Quamobrem ex imperscrutabilitate Sapientiæ Dei pronunciavit Cartesius veluti oraculum, omnes rerum physicarum fines nobis in ea esse occultos; non autem, eos quidem nulli creaturæ esse perveltigabiles propria industria, siquè Deus non effet sui communicabilis; at vero quoniam sit liberalis, adeoque omnis luminis communicativus, eos præ cæteris omnium cognitioni primitus exposuisse? Aut cur ex dicta imperscrutabilitate Dei concludit potius fines rerum occultos esse, quam principia, regulas, leges, modos, secundum quæ Deus res effecit? Dei sane agendi modus videtur occultius quid esse, difficilisque est eum scire vel divinare; quam quidem finem cur agat Deus, agnoscere.
units.tr: Therefore, from the inscrutability of the Wisdom of God, Descartes pronounced, as if it were an oracle, that all the ends of physical things are hidden from us in it. But should he not rather have said that, although they cannot be investigated by any creature through its own diligence, nevertheless, since God is not incommunicable of himself, but is liberal and so communicative of all light, he has laid these ends open first of all to the knowledge of all things beyond others? Or why, from the said inscrutability of God, does he conclude that the ends of things are hidden rather than the principles, rules, laws, and modes according to which God has effected things? Surely the manner of God's acting seems to be something more hidden, and it is more difficult to know it or divine it than to recognise for what end God acts.

units.la: XXVIII. Namque ex Sufficientia Dei demonstrari potest, Deum non agere propter fui indigentiam; sed eum ex placito bono liberalique velle extra se communicare seque, suisque effectus. Se autem cum communicare non possit subjectis eum recipere aptis, ex hoc fine fecisse res cogitantes, desiderii, intellectus, & acquiescentiae facultatibus immensis praeditas.
units.tr: XXVIII. For from the sufficiency of God it can be demonstrated that God does not act on account of any need of his own, but that from a good and liberal purpose he wills to communicate himself and his effects outside himself. Since, however, he cannot communicate himself to subjects not fitted to receive him, for this end he made thinking things, endowed with immense faculties of desire, understanding, and acquiescence.

units.la: Ex eo autem quod ipse (uti ens perfectissimum & dignissimum) sit scopus sui & omnium, nec se possit negare, effectus suos, hoc est, res universi, non posse non esse Dei ejusque perfectionum repraesentativas, sive, rationes cur sint, & cur tales vel tales sint, desumendas esse ex eo, quod Deus eas hoc fine hacque intentione sit fecit, ut illae ejus perfectiones perfectionumque infinitas combinationes infinitis systematibus, proprietatibus, effectisque suis repraesentarent. Et quoniam Deus est Omnipotens, sequitur, finem & intentionem quam habet in rebus producendis non esse inefficacem & effecto destitutum, sed efficacissimam, hoc est, sequitur causam finalem esse eam quae res efficit, atque causam efficientem ad causam finalem esse referendam, rerumque adeo ipsarum non habere causas solidas & sufficientes donec ad finalem. (quae efficientiam complectitur, estque ejus motrix & exemplar) deventum sit. Atqui hic possem ingenuas mentes omnes, quae sibi debite attendunt, testes conscii sui sensus vocare, num possint solide in alicujus rei cognitione veluti completa acquiescere, quando tamen nesciunt qua mente & intentione, quo scopo & ad quid res ea facta sit, etsi alioqui scirent (quod difficilius & occultius revera est) quibus modis & mediis eadem esset facta? Quis pateretur sibi satisfieri, si quaerenti, v.g cur exercitus hostilis urbem aliquam cingat obsidione? responderetur, quoniam spiritus animales ex cerebris hostium in eorum musculos eo modo fluxerunt, qui necessarius erat ad movenda eorum corpora tum versus arma, tum versus eum locum. Aut si postulanti causam ob quam suas scripserit Meditationes Cartesius? itidem dicatur, id ex eo esse, quod ejus glandula pinealis impulerit spiritus in tubos admovendas manui ad pennam & pennae ad atramentarium aptos, similiterque postea ad digitos calamo munitos eis modis motitandos e quibus fierent in papyro litterae & vocabula, unde ejus Meditationes constant. Quis, inquam, ita contentus esset si praeter haec nulla in responsione mentio fieret de mente qua vel hostis sua direxit, vel Cartesius vocabula ejusmodi adhibuit, idque ideo scilicet, quod illa in animis hostium vel Philosophi occulta sit, nemo autem eorum intentionem ac scopum sine temeritate positi scrutari, perinde uti Cartesius de finibus Dei idem dixit. Cujus rei causa fuit haec, quod non posset in Meditatione sua IV enodare difficultatem haud (a) adeo insolubilem; quare nempe, posito finem Dei esse facere semper id quod est optimum, sequetur
units.tr: Moreover, since he himself (as the most perfect and most worthy being) is the goal of himself and of all things, and cannot deny himself, it follows that his effects, that is, the things of the universe, cannot but be representations of God and of his perfections, or that the reasons why they exist, and why they are such and such, must be derived from the fact that God made them for this end and with this intention: that those perfections, and the infinite combinations of perfections, might be represented by infinite systems, properties, and effects of his. And since God is omnipotent, it follows that the end and intention he has in producing things is not ineffective and destitute of effect, but most efficacious; that is, it follows that the final cause is that which produces things, and that the efficient cause must be referred to the final cause, so that things themselves do not have solid and sufficient causes until one arrives at the final cause, which includes efficiency and is its moving force and pattern. But here I might call upon all honest minds, who pay due attention to themselves, to bear witness from their own consciousness whether they can rest solidly, as if in a complete knowledge of some thing, when they do not know with what mind and intention, to what end, and for what purpose that thing was made, even if otherwise they knew (which is in truth more difficult and more hidden) by what modes and means it was made. Who would allow himself to be satisfied if, when he asked, for example, why a hostile army surrounds some city with a siege, he were answered: because animal spirits flowed from the brains of the enemy into their muscles in the manner necessary for moving their bodies both towards their weapons and towards that place? Or if, when someone asked the reason why Descartes wrote his Meditations, it were likewise said that this was because his pineal gland had driven the spirits into tubes suited to move the hand to the pen, and the pen to the inkstand, and similarly afterwards to move the fingers armed with the quill in such ways as to form on the paper the letters and words of which his Meditations consist? Who, I say, would be so content if, apart from these things, no mention were made in the answer of the mind by which the enemy directed his army, or by which Descartes used such words, and that simply because those things are hidden in the minds of enemies or of philosophers, and no one may, without rashness, scrutinise their intention and purpose, just as Descartes said the same about the ends of God? The reason for this was that in his Fourth Meditation he could not unfold the difficulty, not very insoluble, namely why, granting that the end of God is always to make what is best, it nevertheless follows that man is subject to error (which is an imperfection). Hence, since he could not answer otherwise than by saying that the ends of God in this matter are not sufficiently clear to him, he concluded from this...

units.la: (a) Hujus & similium locum solutionem vid. Oeconomiae pehé cap. 1. retur tamen hominem esse errori (qui imperfectio est) obnoxium. hinc cum non posset aliter respondere quam dicendo, fines Dei hac in re non satis sibi perspectos esse, conclusit ab omnium finium consideratione pariter esse abstinendum: haud aliter ac si quis concluderet, nullos amplius hostium scopos, nullam in causa Cartesianorum scriptorum mentem ideo quaeri debere, quod hac in quaestione difficultas, & forte hallucinatio una atque altera interdum occurrat; quodque hostium finis in consilio eorum occulto lateat, uti & mens Cartesii apud ipsum nobis jam sit inaccessibilis; ac proinde in causis physicis motuum deducendis subsistendum esse.
units.tr: (a) For the solution of this and similar passages, see his Oeconomiae pehé, chap. 1. Yet man is nonetheless subject to error, which is a form of imperfection. Hence, since he could not answer otherwise than by saying that the ends of God in this matter are not sufficiently clear to him, he concluded that one must likewise abstain from considering all ends. This is no different from concluding that there are no longer any aims of enemies, and that no mind of the Cartesian writers in their cause should be sought, because in this question difficulty and perhaps one or another error sometimes occurs; and because the end of enemies lies hidden in their secret counsel, and the mind of Descartes is now inaccessible to us. Accordingly, one must rest content with deducing motions from physical causes.

units.la: Quae quidem si ridicula sunt, uti revera sunt, non minus profecto ridiculae dicendae sunt in admirandis & perfectissimâ intelligentiâ factis operibus Dei, tum causae finalis rejectio, tum vero deductio illa fabulosa de fabricatione omnium rerum ex musicis quibusdam de motu legibus brutis. Quid quod Cartesius ipse leges suas & principia ex finibus revera desumsit, etsi verbis id dissimulavit.
units.tr: If these things are ridiculous, as indeed they are, then no less ridiculous must be called both the rejection of final cause and that fabulous deduction of the fabrication of all things from certain blind laws of motion set to music, in works of God that are to be admired and that display the most perfect intelligence. What is more, Descartes himself drew his laws and principles from ends in fact, although he concealed this in words. ## XXIX.

units.la: XXIX. Namque quando dicit motum v. g. quem Deus materiae impressit, fieri secundum lineam rectam, idque esse ex Simplicitate Dei: idem prorsus est ac si diceret; quia scopus ac finis Dei fuit, repraesentare in operibus suis simplicitatem suam, ideo taliter de motu statuit. Simili modo, quando durationem statûs rerum & permanentem momotûs quantitatem ex Dei immutabilitate atque constantia deducit; idem est ac si dicat, Deum in dispositione ac regimine rerum eum finem sibi propositum habuisse, ut immutabilitatem ac constantiam suam repraesentaret, & inde has in isthac rerum ordinatione depinxisse. Similiter se res habet in omnibus aliis ubi ad perfectiones vel attributa Dei provocat. Vera finalis causae allegatio ista est, quae quomodo etiam sit rerum efficiens simili illustrabo.
units.tr: For when he says that the motion which God imparted to matter, for example, takes place along a straight line, and that this follows from the simplicity of God, it is exactly the same as if he said: because it was the aim and purpose of God to represent his simplicity in his works, therefore he determined motion in this way. Similarly, when he deduces the duration of the state of things and the permanent quantity of motion from the immutability and constancy of God, it amounts to saying that God, in the disposition and governance of things, proposed to himself the end of representing his immutability and constancy, and so depicted these in that ordering of things. The case is the same in all other instances where he appeals to the perfections or attributes of God. That is the true allegation of a final cause, and I shall illustrate by a similar example how it is also the efficient cause of things.

units.la: XXX. Quemadmodum quando aliquid agere volumus, ad quod certa corporis northi positio certusque situs requiruntur, sequitur ex vi intentionis optatae spiritus animales in musculos eo influere modo, corpusque totum ita disponi, uti par erat ad hunc situm atque effectum: ita, quando Deus ex fine repraesentandi se, suas perfectiones, infinitasque multiplicitates combinationis earum inter se, excogitavit in conceptu suo tum Universi Systema unum atque in eo capitalia aliquot generaliora, tum vero infinita particulariora corporum systemata, in quibus combinationes generaliorum proprietatum inessent, & quae infinitis modis agerent; is Dei scopus, ea intentio non inefficax, sed potens, sic disposuit universi materiam mollesque ejus diversas, uti tales evaderent; nec non etiam eis immediate impressit principia motusque varios quibus in talia systemata formarentur, taliaque effecta ex eis sequi possent. Quin, quod plus est, ex constantia Dei impressiones illas divinas motusque principia, in unoqueunoquoque systemate a divino scopo omnipotente pro cujusque systematis natura & constitutione posita, semper ibidem manere; nec unquam ex se divinaque ordinatione evanescere, evidenter datur concludere. Alia jam non addo; sed, quaeso, nonne isthaec omnia bene inter se cohaerent, idque magis certe quam linea recta & simplicitas Dei apud Cartesium? Annon major est conformitas inter Deum Omnipotentem & sufficientissimum, volentem se suaque perfectiones & earum combinationes infinitas repraesentare, & hanc effectorum, uti jam diximus, positionem; quam inter Deum volentem repraesentare Simplicitatem suam, & lineam rectam pro regula morus?
units.tr: XXX. Just as, when we wish to do something for which a certain posture and a fixed position of the body are required, it follows from the force of the desired intention that the animal spirits flow into the muscles in such a way that the whole body is arranged as was fitting for this position and effect: so, when God, from the purpose of representing himself, his perfections, and the infinite manifoldness of their combinations among themselves, devised in his conception both one System of the Universe, with some chief and more general elements in it, and also infinitely more particular systems of bodies, in which the combinations of more general properties would inhere and which would act in infinitely many ways, that aim of God, that intention which is not ineffective but powerful, so disposed the matter of the universe and its various smaller parts that they would become such; and he also immediately impressed upon them the principles and various motions by which such systems would be formed, and such effects could follow from them. Indeed, and what is more, it can clearly be concluded that from the constancy of God those divine impressions and principles of motion, posited in each and every system by the omnipotent divine purpose according to the nature and constitution of each system, always remain there, and never vanish of themselves or from the divine ordering. I add nothing further; but, I ask, do not all these things cohere well with one another, and certainly more than the straight line and the simplicity of God in Descartes? Is there not a greater conformity between an Omnipotent and most sufficient God, willing to represent himself and his perfections and their infinite combinations, and this positing of effects, as we have already said, than between a God willing to represent his simplicity and a straight line as the rule of motion?

units.la: Jam si qui essent quibus Deus se suaque sic communicaret, ut deregeret eis in se (Deo) primo quidem, (quod facilius videtur esse,) divinas suas perfectiones earumque inter se lusus & combinationes quatenus sunt exemplaria rerum; deinde vero (quod appareret reconditum magis) vim intentionis divinae, & qua ratione illa res efficiat & moveat; ii causas rerum noscerent a priori vere & solide: & nemo alius. Etenim jam a peccato rerum causas (quod male Cartesius de sola finali) in Sapientiae divinae abysso reconditae sunt, atque illic per mentem Dei cupidam, ejusque amicitiam & communicationem precibus rite effla gitantem, quaerendae sunt, quantumvis isthaec scioli, irrisores aut impii ignare rideant aut falsis seu insulsis potius cachinnis excipiant, quando ipsi
units.tr: Now, if there were some to whom God so communicated himself and his own, that he disclosed to them, first indeed (which seems easier) his divine perfections in himself and their play and combinations among themselves, insofar as they are the exemplars of things; and then (which would appear more hidden) the force of the divine intention, and by what means it produces and moves things, those men would know the causes of things truly and solidly a priori, and no one else would. For indeed the causes of things are hidden in the abyss of divine wisdom, and from the time of sin (which Descartes wrongly did in regard to final cause alone) they are to be sought there, through the mind of God, eagerly and duly asking by prayer for its friendship and communication; however much scoffers, the half-learned, or the impious, in their ignorance, laugh at these things or greet them with false or rather insipid guffaws, when they themselves

units.la: potius sua ridere debererent ( cum Socrate
units.tr: ought rather to laugh at their own (with Socrates

units.la: (a) apud Platonem ) dum principia bruta & mechanica ad rerum præstantissima mente factarum rationes reddendas allegant, quibus deinde fabellas suas superexstruunt secundum ejusmodi leges e quibus ostendi possit eos æque potuisse esse truncos quam homines, si cui luberet cum istis principiis ingenium ludendo exercere.
units.tr: (a) in Plato), while they put forward brute and mechanical principles to render the reasons of the most excellent things made by mind, and then build their fables upon them, following such laws, from which it could be shown that they might just as well have been stumps as men, if anyone pleased to exercise his wit in playing with those principles.

units.la: XXXI. Et hoc satis subolfecit Cartesius,
units.tr: XXXI. Descartes had a sufficient inkling of this,

units.la: inquiens, (b) principia sua esse tam vasta & tam fœcunda, ut multo plura ex iis sequantur, quam in hoc mundo aspectabili contineri videamus; ac etiam multo plura quam mens nostra cogitando perlustrare unquam possit: hoc est, principia sua esse vaga & insufficientia ad hoc ut sint causæ determinatæ & propriæ effectuum qui revera exsistunt. Neque idem alienus videtur fuisse apud se a sententia nostra de rerum ortu ad perfectiones Dei repræsentandas, quem modo expositmus: ait enim (c) nec se credere res ita productas esse uti ipse describit; tum vero subjungit, attendando ad immensam Dei POTENTIAM, non posse exi-stimari illum unquam quicquam fecisse quod non omnibus suis numeris fuerit absolutum ; idque rationem naturalem plane persuadere. Cui si addas, tum ex Constantia Dei, impressiones quaque, quas rebus quibusvis indidit eas producendo, durare nec evanescere debere; tum ex eius bonitate atque fertilitate, easdem impressiones esse sui productivas, designabis generalius causas atque effectus & proprietates rerum quales modo recensuimus, ut mirandum fit Cartesium hæc ipsa e datis principiis non conclusisse.
units.tr: saying that his principles are so vast and so fruitful that far more follows from them than we see contained in this visible world, and even far more than our mind can ever survey by thinking. That is, his principles are vague and insufficient to be determinate and proper causes of the effects that really exist. Nor does he seem to have been out of step with our opinion about the origin of things, which we have just set out as representing the perfections of God. For he says that he does not believe things to have been produced as he describes them. Then he adds: attending to the immense POWER of God, it cannot be thought that he ever made anything that was not absolute in all its respects, and natural reason plainly persuades this. To this you may add that from God's constancy the impressions he put into things by producing them must last and not vanish, and that from his goodness and fertility those same impressions are productive of themselves. You will then designate more generally the causes, effects and properties of things such as we have just listed. It is remarkable that Descartes did not draw these very conclusions from the principles he had given.

units.la: Et hic quidem est defectus ille primus, e quo diximus Cartesianos multorum in physicis falsorum argui posse.
units.tr: This is indeed the first defect, from which we said the Cartesians can be charged with many errors in physics.

units.la: Ast, inquiet aliquis, si Cartesius ex principiis recensitis talia deduxisset, non tantum suæ Physicæ, sed omnibus phænomenis naturæ rerum, prout jam ea est, contradixisset. Hæc namque nec realitatum & motuum productrix est, nec corruptioni non obnoxia, nec luminosa, concors, gloriosa, nec, uno verbo, talis, qualem ex principiis a Dei proprietatibus supra deductis, eam diximus esse debere: sed potius tota, in multis saltem, mechanicia est & veluti mortua, tenebrisque & corruptione, pugnis & deformitatibus deturpata: quod & cum principiis Cartesii concordat, & eorum veritatem experimentali probatione confirmat. Insuper, si rerum finales causæ consulendæ essent, cur eas Deus a nobis occultasseт?
units.tr: But someone will say: if Descartes had deduced such things from the principles listed, he would have contradicted not only his Physics but all the phenomena of nature as it now is. For nature is neither productive of realities and motions, nor free from corruption, nor luminous, harmonious, glorious; nor, in one word, is it such as we said it ought to be from the properties of God deduced above. Rather, the whole of it, at least in many respects, is mechanical and as it were dead, and disfigured by darkness and corruption, conflicts and deformities. This agrees with the principles of Descartes and confirms their truth by experimental proof. Moreover, if the final causes of things were to be consulted, why would God have hidden them from us?

units.la: XXXII. Hisce dum respondebo, ostendam simul (quod alterum est modo (a) a me notatum) qui Cartesii principia multaque ex iis deducta veritatibus quibusdam aliunde indubitatis adversentur. Cartesii mens & verba sunt: (b) Auctoritatem Divinam nostræ perceptioni esse præferendam. Memoriæ nostræ pro summa regula esse infigendum, ea quæ nobis a Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda: & quamvis forte lumen rationis quam maxime clarum & evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videtur,
units.tr: XXXII. While I answer these objections, I will at the same time show (which is the second point I noted above) that the principles of Descartes, and many things deduced from them, oppose certain truths otherwise indubitable. The mind and words of Descartes are these: (b) The divine authority is to be preferred to our perception. Our memory must be impressed with the supreme rule that those things which have been revealed to us by God are to be believed as the most certain of all; and although perhaps the light of reason, very clear and evident, seems to suggest something else to us,

units.la: (a) supra XXVI. (b) Princ. P. I. art. 78. retur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ potius, quam proprio nostro judicio fidem esse adhibendam. Atqui e divina revelatione {a} constat, naturam rerum conditam fuisse in statu in quo omnia erant optima, sic ut & terra ex se omnis generis bona, sine ullo labore, etiam sine spinis & carduis produxisser; homines vero & anxietates & dolores nescivissent; tum mors & mortis causa consequenter, rerum videlicet pugnæ intemperiesque elementorum, putrefactiones, tenebræ, excessus, atque vanus & inglorius creaturarum status, quæ Paulus per peccatum introducta. esse asseve-rat, ignorata fuissent. Eadem divina revelatio praeterea affirmat, omnia in statum ejusmodi gloriosum, luminosum, potentem atque concordem reponenda esse, id quod restaurationem, relevationem, repositionem rerum in primaevam libertatem appellat, & hunc naturae felicem gloriosumque statum aeternum fore declarat, excepta portione impiis debita, quam Deus lumine sic destitutam relinquet, ut in ea & miseri manent perpetim & mori non possint. His igitur quae de statu solido, vero, primaevo naturae, a quo quidem ipsa per peccatum dejecta est, sed in quem tamen est reponenda, revelat cognitor naturae, idemque ejus fabricator perfectissimus Deus, aequum fuisset a Cartesio (omnibusque caeteris) assensum praeberi; idque eo magis, quod eadem ex Divinis attributis sequi recta evincat ratio, uti modo ostendum est: atque ea deo rerum principia quae quaerebat ut essent vera, cum hisce debebant concordare & accommodari : quibus cum repugnent, certissime sequitur eadem esse falsa. Quod autem videantur interdum vera esse & cum rerum naturæ experimentis conformia, id sic se habet.
units.tr: (a) see above XXVI. (b) Princ. P. I. art. 78. returns, but rather that faith is to be given to the divine authority alone than to our own judgment. Yet it is established from divine revelation {a} that the nature of things was created in a state in which all things were best, so that the earth too would have produced of itself all kinds of good things, without any labour, even without thorns and thistles; men would have known nothing of anxieties and pains; and consequently death and the cause of death would have been unknown, namely the conflicts of things, the intemperance of the elements, putrefactions, darkness, excesses, and the vain and inglorious state of creatures, which Paul asserts were introduced through sin. The same divine revelation moreover affirms that all things are to be restored to such a glorious, luminous, powerful and harmonious state, which it calls the restoration, relief and repositioning of things into original freedom, and it declares that this happy and glorious state of nature will be eternal, except for the portion owed to the impious, whom God will leave deprived of light in such a way that they remain in misery forever and cannot die. It would therefore have been fair for Descartes (and all others) to give assent to what the knower of nature, and its most perfect maker God, reveals about the solid, true, primeval state of nature. From this state nature was indeed cast down by sin, but into it nature is nevertheless to be restored. All the more so, because right reason demonstrates that these same things follow from the divine attributes, as has just been shown. The principles of things which he sought to be true ought to agree with these and be accommodated to them. Since they conflict with them, it most certainly follows that they are false. But that they sometimes seem to be true and in conformity with the experiments of nature, is the case as follows.

units.la: XXXIII. Homo pessime sese erga Deum Creatorem suum gessit, ejusque creaturis est abusus. Ergo, ex justitia, Deus ea, quæ modo diximus in entis natura non esse essentialia, sed ex Dei gratiosa liberalitate accedere, maximam partem suppressit, invitque ex hominis inordinatione omnia fieri languida, tenebrosa, confusa, æruginosa, rigida, cadaverosa: ita ut ad veram & primævam naturam comparata non aliter se habeant, quam cadaver ad vegetum hominis corpus. Quemadmodum autem circa cadavera, eorum motum, conservationem, putrefactionem, aliaque possunt multa observari certa, unde leges certæ & experimentis conformes fiant, sed quas tamen absurdum esset pro principiis naturæ corporum viventium venditare, cum non sint nisi observationes de statu accessorio, corrupto, mortuo & non mansuro cadaverum; ita, de principiis Physices Cartesianæ deque dogmatibus & experientiis ejus idem plane dicendum est. Sunt observationes nonnullæ superficiariæ de ærugine accessoria nec duratura, sive de cadavere naturæ; sed quæ a principiis veris naturæ vegetæ & primævæ, vel ejusdem a morbo suo restitutæ magis absunt ac cœlum a terra, aut tantundem atque principia Aristotelica a rerum veritate. Et sane id experientia splendide confirmat.
units.tr: XXXIII. Man behaved most wickedly toward God his Creator, and abused his creatures. Therefore, from justice, God suppressed for the most part those things which we have just said are not essential to the nature of being, but come from God's gracious liberality. By man's disorder he has brought it about that all things become languid, dark, confused, rusty, rigid and cadaverous, so that compared with the true and primeval nature they are no different from a corpse compared with a living human body. But just as with corpses, many certain things can be observed about their motion, preservation, putrefaction and so on, whence certain laws arise that conform to experiments; yet it would be absurd to peddle these as principles of the nature of living bodies, since they are nothing but observations about the accessory, corrupt, dead and non-enduring state of corpses. So the same must plainly be said of the principles of Cartesian physics and of its doctrines and experiments. There are some superficial observations about accessory and non-lasting rust, or about the corpse of nature. But these are as far from the true principles of living and primeval nature, or of that same nature restored from its disease, as heaven is from earth, or just as far as Aristotelian principles are from the truth of things. And indeed experience splendidly confirms this.

units.la: Namque si Philosophi Cartesiani prae caeteris vera naturae principia nacti essent, fieri non posset quin eorum ope vita humana & longius produceretur, & a morbis facillime liberaretur, aut ab iis immunis conservaretur: cum tamen non videamus Cartesianos caeteris hominibus diutius vivere, aut etiam minus morbis esse obnoxios.
units.tr: For if the Cartesian philosophers had obtained the true principles of nature before others, it could not be that by their means human life would not be prolonged, and that they would not be most easily freed from diseases, or kept immune from them. Yet we do not see the Cartesians living longer than other men, or even being less subject to diseases.

units.la: Ea vero justitia qua Deus liberalitatis suae gratiosa fluenta ab ingratis inhibuit, eadem & particulares rerum singularum causas sinales, quae & efficientes sunt, iis cognoscendas offerre noluit, nisi admodum paucis, quibus nunquam licitum fuit cum profanis aut de ea minus dispositis eas communicare. Generaliter tamen satis prostant attendentibus, quod alibi me (a) ostendisse puto.
units.tr: But that same justice by which God withheld the gracious streams of his liberality from the ungrateful, he was also unwilling to offer them the knowledge of the particular final causes of individual things, which are also efficient causes, except to a very few. To these few it was never permitted to communicate them to the profane, or to those less well disposed. Generally, however, they are sufficiently evident to those who attend, which I think I have shown elsewhere.

units.la: XXXIV. Longior forem, si singulatim ostendendum esset, (qui tertius supraditus errorum fons est) quomodo & ex propriis principiis brutis mancisque multa aliter derivaverint Cartesiani atque par erat; aut potius quomodo detorserint & ad rerum phaenomena accommodaverint conclusiones suas, quae sane aliae ex datis confici debuissent, sint. Sufficiat sola unius atque alterius indicatione, non autem deductione justa (quae & cuivis attendenti facilis erit & hic esset proliciōr) nunc palam id facere.
units.tr: XXXIV. I would be longer if it were to be shown individually (which is the third source of error mentioned above) how the Cartesians, from their own principles, crude and maimed as they are, have derived many things otherwise than was fitting. Or rather, how they have twisted their conclusions and adapted them to the phenomena of things, when in fact other conclusions ought to have been drawn from the given principles.
