It is enough to make this plain now by indicating one or two instances, not by a full deduction (which will be easy for anyone who attends, and which would here be too lengthy).

units.la: XXXV. Viderint & judicent sinceriores, annon ex legibus brutis de mutu, negato interventu causae agentis quae ex intelligentia & vi intentionis suae omnia disponat, debeat Cartesianos vortices, hoc est, in ex mera vi sequi,
units.tr: XXXV. Let the more sincere see and judge whether the Cartesian vortices ought not to follow from the brute laws of motion, once the intervention of an acting cause that arranges all things by intelligence and by the power of its purpose is denied; that is, whether they follow from mere force.

units.la: gentes materiæ fluidissimæ moles, quarum partes singulæ omni tendunt conamine ut a suo vortice in omnes alios recedant, non posse, non dico per annum, sed ne per mensem quidem aut diem unum subsistere, quin simul in unum chaos confundantur. Mirus est Cartesius in repagulis & æquilibriis condendis quæ vorticibus suis apponat, quasi inter muros æneos, aliquibus tantum particulis pervios, unusquisque versaretur.
units.tr: masses of most fluid matter, each part of which strives with all its effort to recede from its own vortex into all the others. These cannot remain standing, I do not say for a year, but not even for a month or a single day, without being at once confounded together into one chaos. Descartes is remarkable in establishing the barriers and balances that he places among his vortices, as if each were turning between brazen walls, pierced by only a few particles.

units.la: XXXVI. Sed nec in elementorum suorum generatione figuraque & situ constituendis minus mireagit. Postquam gratis suppositu materiam suam in partes æquales per motum divisam esse & quasque partes sua circa centra rotare, concludit primo eas fieri debere globulorum instar rotundas. At vero debent potius ellipticæ fieri: nam quia rotantur singulæ circa suum axem, atque adeo singulæ circa suum polum lentius moventur minusque deteruntur quam circa eclipticam, ubi longius spatium æquali tempore conficiendo, celerius utique moventur, magisque idcirco & vehementius in corpora circumfusa impingunt: (quod, nì fallor, in tornandis vitris a Cartesio non prævisum, ejus omnes machinas reddidit ineptas) patet inde, particulis figuram ovalem sive ellipticam hinc accedere debere, non vero sphæricam: nisi forte ad evitandum hoc incommodum, supponere velit Cartesius globulos ita esse dispositos (quod de vorticibus dixit, ) ut prope unius globuli polos sint ecliptica alterius; vel eos non circa fixum axem certum, sed ita gyrare, ut puncta singula totius superficiei suæ sphæricæ fiant successive puncta axis. Verum tantæ varietatis causam, ubi opus erat, ageretque de primordio impressi motus, non modo nullam assignat Cartesius; sed & id regulis motus adversaretur. Etenim, dum infiniti illi globuli, qui totum vorticem Solarem constituunt, & diversa in eo efficiunt plana, quæ circa diversas axis vorticis solaris partes tanquam circa sua (quorumque planorum) centra gyrantur; globuli inquam illi omnes & singuli suos axes particulares ita accommodare debent ad axem communem vorticis, ut ei fere paralleli ferantur.
units.tr: XXXVI. But he acts with no less wonder in determining the generation, shape and position of his elements. After he gratuitously supposes that his matter has been divided by motion into equal parts, and that each part rotates about its own centre, he concludes first that they must become round, like little globes. In truth, however, they ought rather to become elliptical. Since each rotates about its own axis, each moves more slowly and is worn down less near its pole than near the ecliptic, where in the same time it covers a longer distance and so moves more swiftly, and therefore strikes the surrounding bodies more forcefully and violently. (Unless I am mistaken, Cartesius did not foresee this in the turning of glass, and it has rendered all his machines useless.) It is clear from this that the particles must acquire an oval or elliptical figure, not a spherical one. Unless perhaps, to avoid this inconvenience, Cartesius wishes to suppose that the globules are so arranged (as he said of the vortices) that near the poles of one globule lies the ecliptic of another; or that they do not turn about a fixed and certain axis, but spin in such a way that each single point of their whole spherical surface becomes in turn a point of the axis. But Cartesius not only assigns no cause for such great variety, though where it was needed, and where he ought to have treated the origin of the impressed motion; this variety even conflicts with the rules of motion. For while those infinite globules which make up the whole solar vortex, and produce in it various planes, which revolve about different parts of the axis of the solar vortex as about their own centres (and the centres of those planes), all those globules, I say, each and every one, must adjust their particular axes to the common axis of the vortex, so that they are carried nearly parallel to it.

units.la: Ratio hujus parallelismi inter axes globorum & axem Vorticis solaris hæc est, quod cum in unoquoque globulo toto eadem sit undique soliditas, debeant omnes globorum partes & facies recedere æqualiter, quantum fieri potest, ab axe vorticis solaris circa quem gyrantur: id quod non fieret si unus globuli cujusque polus respiceret introrsum magis versus axem vorticis solaris, alter vero globuli polus ei axi obversus esset: tunc enim gyrando circa axem Vorticis, pars seu facies globuli introversa, minorem circulum, obversa ambitum majorem circa axem vorticis efficeret. Vide hanc ad rem quid de Luna dicat Cartesius, Princ. III. §. 152. atque ita axis uniuscujusque globuli ab ecliptica plani sui in quo versatur, secari sic debet, ut pars ejus infra, pars vero supra eclipticam sit, qualis præter propter situs est terræ circa solem gyrantis: quod & instantiam allaallatam subvertit, & ellipticam figuram globulis assignat. Insuper, si puncta singula superficiei globulorum confuse & succesiive fiant modò puncta axis, modò circuli nunc majores nunc minores: perit tota colorum atque adeo Iridis Cartesiana explicatio, in qua quippe supponit globulorum axes veluti fixos esse, eundemque ab illis situm durabiliter servare, ut circularis eorum motus cum progressivo vel directo comparatus, colores diversos & fixos repræsentet. Atque hæc de secundo, quod sic appellat Cartesius, elemento.
units.tr: The reason for this parallelism between the axes of the globules and the axis of the solar vortex is this: since in each globule the solidity is everywhere the same, all the parts and faces of the globules must recede equally, as far as possible, from the axis of the solar vortex about which they turn. This would not happen if one pole of each globule faced inward, more towards the axis of the solar vortex, while the other pole faced that axis directly. For then, turning about the axis of the vortex, the inward-facing part or face of the globule would describe a smaller circle, and the outward-facing part a larger circumference. See what Cartesius says about this in the case of the Moon, Princ. III. §. 152. And so the axis of each globule must be cut by the ecliptic of the plane in which it lies, in such a way that part of it lies below and part above the ecliptic, roughly the position of the earth as it turns about the sun. This both overturns the instance he brings forward and assigns an elliptical figure to the globules. Moreover, if the individual points of the surface of the globules become, in a confused and successive way, now points of the axis, now circles, now larger, now smaller, then the whole Cartesian explanation of colours, and hence of the rainbow, perishes. For there he supposes that the axes of the globules are, as it were, fixed, and that they keep the same position for a lasting time, so that their circular motion, compared with a progressive or direct one, represents colours that are diverse and fixed. And so much for the second element, as Cartesius calls it.

units.la: XXXVII. Primum autem elementum est materia subtilissima, ex angulis globulorum abrasa, quæ dum formatur & augetur, quod plus ejus est quam ut interstitia globulorum repleat, nec per ecliticam elabi totum potest, ad centrum vorticis repelli dicitur.
units.tr: XXXVII. The first element, however, is the most subtle matter, rubbed off from the angles of the globules. As it is formed and increases, and since there is more of it than is needed to fill the interstices of the globules, and it cannot wholly escape through the ecliptic, it is said to be driven back to the centre of the vortex.

units.la: At cur non potius ex ecliptica, per quam ulterius erumpebat in vortices innumeros contiguos, siquidem motûs infinite celeris erat capax, nec deerant poli vel spatia inter globulos vorticum circumstantium eam recipere apta? Sed bene: eat ad sui vorticis centrum. At vero cum totus vortex circa axem gyrans constet diversis planis circularibus quæ, plana singula circa diversas axis partes tanquam circa propria centra volvuntur; cur ad centrum sphæræ, sive plani maximi, omnis illa materia confluet, non autem singulæ particulæ in singulis planis ad suorum centra planorum potius repellentur? atque ita, cur non ad axem formabitur in columnæ speciem? Nisi potius is locus tertio elemento de jure debebatur: nam cum hoc ineptum fit ad motum, debuit omnino, ex legibus motus, ad centra omnium circulorum, quos totius vorticis diversa plana circa diversas axis partes describunt, repelli: hoc est, debuit tertium elementum totum axem vorticis occupare. Nec dicas, id inde expelli debuisse a materia primi elementi per polos vorticis ex vicinis vorticibus affluente: nam cum tertium elementum supponatur formari ex primo & in primo, imo & in ipsis vorticum centris, procul dubio (quod Cartesius de crusta terrae interiore & aliis adjacentibus dicit) materia primi elementi in massis illis columnaribus tertii elementi, meatus & poros sibi ad transitum illum suppositum sufficientissimos servare, ne dicam excavare potuit. Atque sic tum Solis loco, tum in vorticibus aliis omnibus, ubi tertii elementi quantitas aliqua reperitur, haberemus columnas compactas, easdemque obscuras & totum vorticis sui axem a polo ad polum occupantes: quod mirum sane & alterius mundi foret spectaculum.
units.tr: But why not rather out through the ecliptic, through which it could burst further into countless neighbouring vortices, since it was capable of infinitely swift motion, and there were not lacking poles, or spaces between the globules of the surrounding vortices, fit to receive it? But grant it: let it go to the centre of its own vortex. Yet since the whole vortex, turning about an axis, consists of various circular planes, which, each plane, revolve about different parts of the axis as about their own centres, why should all that matter flow together to the centre of the sphere, or of the greatest plane, and not rather single particles in single planes be driven back to the centres of their own planes? And so why would it not be formed along the axis in the shape of a column? Unless perhaps that place was due by right to the third element. For since this is unsuited to motion, it ought altogether, by the laws of motion, to be driven back to the centres of all the circles which the different planes of the whole vortex describe about different parts of the axis; that is, the third element ought to occupy the whole axis of the vortex. Nor should you say that it ought to have been expelled from there by the matter of the first element flowing in through the poles of the vortex from neighbouring vortices. For since the third element is supposed to be formed from the first and in the first, indeed even in the very centres of the vortices, no doubt (as Cartesius says of the inner crust of the earth and other adjacent bodies) the matter of the first element could keep, or rather hollow out, passages and pores quite sufficient for that supposed transit within those columnar masses of the third element. And so, both in the place of the Sun and in all the other vortices where some quantity of the third element is found, we would have compact columns, dark ones, occupying the whole axis of their vortex from pole to pole. This would indeed be a strange spectacle, one of another world.

units.la: XXXVIII. Jam de luce: si ea efficeretur a globulis vorticum quatenus a vorticis centro recedere conantur, quoniam non tantum adest conatus recedendi a centro totius sphaerae seu Ecliptica, sed & a centris omnibus circulorum quos plana diversa globulorum non modo circa ecliptica centrum, sed & circa totam axis longitudinem a polo ad polum describunt, sequeretur inde manifestissime solem teretem esse debere instar columnae, pariterque
units.tr: XXXVIII. Now concerning light: if it were produced by the globules of the vortices, insofar as they strive to recede from the centre of the vortex, then since there is not only a striving to recede from the centre of the whole sphere or ecliptic, but also from the centres of all the circles which the different planes of the globules describe, not only about the centre of the ecliptic but also about the whole length of the axis from pole to pole, it would follow most manifestly that the sun must be round, like a column, and likewise

units.la: M riterque & stellas omnes. Insuper quia maxima recessio seu maximus recedendi conatus qui per hanc gyrationem efficitur, non fit nisi secundum tangentes circulorum, quos describunt globuli inter superficiem Solis & circumferentiam vorticis sui gyrantes, sequereturque tum in Sole illo columnari nil nobis videri præter solam occidentalem partem eam, a qua tangentes ad nos veniunt; tum & a singulis globulorum circulis qui solem inter & terram circumfluunt, venientes lineas tangentes, hoc est, radios ibidem interjectos videri debere, atque ita Solis pars occidentalis tanquam caudata, cometæ instar, conspicienda esset, cauda semper crescente a mane, ad vesperam usque, dein post occasum sola cauda ad mediam fere noctem usque decrescens appareret: quod e sola figuræ Rinspectione patet, in qua S sit sol gyrans juxta ordinem literarum a b c d cum globulis sui vorticis, inter quos versetur tellus T, circa axim proprium gyrans secundum viam 1, 2, 3, 4. Si globuli omnes conentur recedere a centro secundum tangentes circulorum, quos circa Solem describunt, evidens est, globulos solos solaris lateris a, quod latus e terra prospicientibus est pars Solis occidentalior, tendere versus T vi hujus gyrationis: globulos autem qui sunt in parte b non tendere ad T, sed versus l: multo minus eos qui ad c partem Solis orientalem ) tendere ad T, siquidem omnium longissime inde recedant, puta versus m. Proinde habitantibus in T versus 3, tola pars Solis a videri posset: at illis qui habitant versus 4, videri debérent radii omnes globulorum, qui sunt in circulis quorum tangentes ex occidentali parte vorticis ad 4 terminantur, v. g. in circulis e,f,g,h,i, tuncque cauda solis ibi apparitura esset ejus fere longitudinis cujus est semidiameter circuli quem tellus annuo motu circa solem describit: habitantibus vero ad 1, ubi insuper recipiuntur radii ex spatio interi & k, eadem cauda adhuc longior conspiceretur: at inde progrediendo ab 1 ad 2, sola cauda trabis instar paulatim diminuens tandemque disparens versus x aut o iis qui in 2 & ultra versantur. Atque notandum est, caudam illam occidentalem meridionali & orientali Solis parte eo splendidiorem apparere debere, quo magis patet globulos e locis & circulis efghikx ad T, vi gyrationis suæ vehementius ruere, quam eos qui sunt in parte solis b & c. Imo & cauda hæc vividior splendidiorque apparere deberet, quo magis a sole absunt circuli unde tangentes ad terram veniunt; atque ita fulgida magis videnda esset in x vel o, quam in p: & magis in p, quam in q, vel i, & sic deinceps: tum quia globuli a sole remotiores celerius & majori vi moventur quam propiores; tum etiam quod in remotioribus circulis puncta a quibus tangentes, seu radii, procedunt versus T, minus distent a T quam in circulis Soli propioribus, ut patet in punctis seu radiis x, k, i, b, g, &c. Et sane si spatium T vacuum fieret, non illuc properarent ad id replendum globuli contenti in spatio coni{a}co a T c: sed potius illi qui sunt in spatio a e f g h i k x T a, & quidem qui circa x k i omnium vehementissime, caeteri paulo minus vehementer.
units.tr: and likewise all the stars. Moreover, since the greatest recession, or the greatest striving to recede, which is produced by this rotation, arises only along the tangents of the circles which the globules describe, turning between the surface of the Sun and the circumference of its vortex, it would follow that in that columnar Sun we would see nothing but that western part from which the tangents come to us. Also, from the individual circles of the globules which flow around between the sun and the earth, the tangent lines coming to us, that is, the rays lying in between, ought to be seen there. So the western part of the Sun would be seen as if tailed, like a comet, the tail always growing from morning until evening, and then, after sunset, only the tail would appear, decreasing until about midnight. This is clear from the mere inspection of the figure, in which S is the sun turning, following the order of the letters a, b, c, d, with the globules of its vortex, among which the earth T is situated, turning about its own axis along the path 1, 2, 3, 4. If all the globules strive to recede from the centre along the tangents of the circles they describe about the Sun, it is evident that the globules of the side a alone, which side is the more western part of the Sun for those looking from the earth, tend towards T by the force of this rotation. But the globules in the part b do not tend to T but towards l; much less do those at c, the eastern part of the Sun, tend to T, since they recede from it furthest of all, say towards m. Accordingly, to those dwelling at T towards 3 the whole part a of the Sun could be seen; but to those dwelling towards 4 all the rays of the globules ought to be seen, which lie in circles whose tangents from the western part of the vortex end at 4, e.g. in the circles e, f, g, h, i. Then the tail of the Sun would appear there, of about the length that the semidiameter of the circle which the earth describes in its annual motion about the Sun has. But to those dwelling at 1, where moreover rays are received from the interior space at i and k, the same tail would be seen even longer. But proceeding from 1 to 2, the tail alone, diminishing gradually like a beam, and at last vanishing towards x or o for those who are at 2 and beyond. And it must be noted that this western tail ought to appear the more brilliant than the southern and eastern parts of the Sun, the more the globules from the places and circles e, f, g, h, i, k, x rush towards T with greater violence by their rotation than those which are in the parts b and c of the Sun. Indeed this tail ought also to appear more vivid and brilliant the further from the Sun are the circles from which the tangents come to the earth; so that it would be seen more brightly at x or o than at p, and more at p than at q, or i, and so on. This is partly because globules more remote from the Sun move more swiftly and with greater force than nearer ones; and partly because in the more remote circles the points from which the tangents, or rays, proceed towards T are less distant from T than in the circles nearer the Sun, as is clear in the points or rays x, k, i, b, g, etc. And indeed, if the space T were made empty, the globules contained in the space of the cone a T c would not hasten there to fill it; rather, those which are in the space a e f g h i k x T a would do so, and especially those about x, k, i, most violently of all, the rest somewhat less violently.

units.la: XXXIX. Scio non deesse Cartesio unam atque alteram ratiunculam, vel potius comparatiunculam, ab ipso (ut putat) motu globulorum desumtam, quibus ostendere conetur eos qui in b & c sunt, ad T quoque tendere debere; sed haec revera si tantillum examinentur, mancae sunt ac nullae: & si quae essent, tendentia tenuis globulorum in b & c versus T, prae vehementia illorum qui in x, k, i, b, g, f, e, a, ita evanesceret, ut, veluti in stellis meridiano tempore, plane sentiri non deberet. Quare Cartesius non diu his insistit; sed ad materiam subtilem in sole S, qua negotium peragatur, se recipit.
units.tr: XXXIX. I know Descartes has one or two little arguments, or rather comparisons, which he takes (as he thinks) from the very motion of the globules, by which he tries to show that those at b and c must also tend towards T. But if these are examined even a little, they are lame and worth nothing. And even if they had some force, the tendency of the thin globules at b and c towards T would vanish, because of the great violence of those at x, k, i, b, g, f, e, a, so that, as with the stars at midday, it should not be felt at all. So Descartes does not dwell on this long, but retreats to the subtle matter in the sun S, by which the business is carried out.

units.la: Verum & haec materia primi elementi (ut ei dicitur) frustra fingitur in Sole omnes ejus particulas, eisque circumjacentes globulos, quaquaversum impellere, atque ita solem totum visibilem reddere; tum quia ipsa etiam circulariter moveri censetur perinde ut globuli, atque adeo motum eorum, si quem imprimit, auget tantum versus earn partem qua illi jam prius tendebant; tum quia, etsi ille causetur eam materiam, quando novafemper per polos solis tanquam per tubum ingreditur, eadem vi, perinde ut aer in fabricatione ampullae, quaquaversum ad totam superficiem internam globulorum circumjacentium repelli, id tamen novas potius difficultates parit, quam priorem solvit; quam
units.tr: But this matter of the first element (as they call it) is also feigned in vain: that in the sun it drives all its particles, and the globules lying around them, every way, and so makes the whole sun visible. It is so because it is itself thought to move circularly, just like the globules, and so whatever motion it imparts only increases their motion in that direction in which they were already tending. It is so also because, although he alleges that this matter, since it always enters new through the poles of the sun as through a tube, is driven back with the same force, just as air is in the making of a glass bulb, every way against the whole inner surface of the surrounding globules, this creates new difficulties rather than solving the former one, which

units.la: Fig. B. quam etiamsi solveret, tamen pars solis occidentalior millecuplo clarior apparere deberet quam altera, adjuta quippe propria globulorum suorum gyrantium tendentia ad nos, quò cæteræ solis partes globulos circumpositos non ita determinant.
units.tr: Fig. B. which, even if it solved it, the western part of the sun would still have to appear a thousand times brighter than the other, since the tendency of its own whirling globules towards us would be added to it, whereas the other parts of the sun do not so determine the globules around them.

units.la: XL. At vero nihil infelicius est isto de materia per Solis polos ingrediente invento. Namque, si materia illa primi elementi per Solis polos corpus ejus ingressa, ibique quaquaversum mota, minorem habeat conatum recedendi a centro Solis, quam globuli circumjacentes, sequitur ex legibus motus, hos non posse per illam pelli, neque adeo per eandem lumen nobis communicare: sin majorem habeat, sequitur itidem necessario, eam debere inde elabi, globulis ei cedentibus & versus centrum Solis ab ea repulsis, adeoque per illos non lucem sed tenebras potius nobis communicari. Nisi forte Cartesius intra concavam superficiem Solis circum materiam ingredientem primi elementi muros quosdam atque parietes fabrefaciat, perinde uti vitriarii, qui dum ventum per tubulos intra materiam eis adhærentem immittunt, eadem inflatione ampullas sive parietes vitreos conficiunt, quibus parietibus impeditur ne intrusus elabatur aër, fitque ut hicce quaquaversum uniformi modo diffundatur. At tunc solares isti parietes dubio procul verterentur in maculas, quæ Solem potius obscurarent vel extinguerent. Et vero qui fiet ut materia illa dum versus globulos impellitur non elabatur, siquidem inter ternos quosque globulos reperiat spatia triangularia infinita, ejus totius recipiendæ & transmittendæ eo capaciora, quo plura semper & majora accurrunt, prout a Sole longius recedit.
units.tr: XL. But nothing is more unhappy than this invention of matter entering through the poles of the sun. For if that matter of the first element, having entered the body of the sun through its poles and moved there every way, has a smaller tendency to recede from the centre of the sun than the surrounding globules, it follows from the laws of motion that these cannot be driven by it, and so cannot communicate light to us through it. But if it has a greater tendency, it follows just as necessarily that it must slip out from there, the globules giving way to it and being repelled by it towards the centre of the sun, and so darkness rather than light would be communicated to us through them. Unless perhaps Descartes builds certain walls and partitions within the concave surface of the sun, around the matter of the first element entering it, just as glassmakers, who blow air through tubes into the material clinging to them, make glass bulbs or walls by the same blowing, and by these walls the entering air is prevented from escaping, so that it spreads evenly every way. But then those solar walls would undoubtedly turn into spots, which would rather darken or extinguish the sun. And indeed, how will it come about that this matter, while it is driven against the globules, does not escape, since between every three globules it finds infinite triangular spaces, the more capacious for receiving and transmitting all of it the more numerous and larger they are that come rushing in as it recedes further from the sun?

units.la: XLI. Imo novum incommodum: materia ex polo vorticis solaris A (fig. Q.) secundum axem ejus ad Solem per hujus polum unum a impetuose accurrens, non deberet ibi reflecti in circulum a b c d, sed per polum Solis alterum b pergere ad finem usque vorticalis poli alterius B, a quo etiam reciproce materia alia eodem modo ad Solem per b decurrens inde ultra ad polum oppositum A fluere deberet; atque adeo vel nullum Solem, vel Solem teretem instar cylindri seu columnæ A C B d A, vel ellipseos, uti in figura T, aut coni duplicis per bases juncti sive rhombi, uti ad V haberemus: idque propterea, quod globuli rotantes circa totam axis vorticalis longitudinem, conentur linguli recedere a centris circulorum, quos ab uno polo vorticis ad alium circa diversas longitudinis axis partes describunt; atque adeo enitantur totum vorticis axem relinquere vacuum, quem non potest non occupare materia subtilis, versus polos eadem via qua appellitur progrediendo, cum facillime ei cedant globuli axis vorticalis jam aliunde ad aufugiendum parati, nedum eam repellere apti sint.
units.tr: XLI. Moreover, there is a new inconvenience: the matter from the pole of the solar vortex A (fig. Q.), rushing violently along its axis towards the sun through one of its poles a, should not be turned back there into the circle a b c d, but should pass through the other pole of the sun b as far as the end of the other vortical pole B; and from there, in turn, other matter running down to the sun through b in the same way should flow on from there to the opposite pole A. And so we would have either no sun, or a sun shaped like a cylinder or column A C B d A, or an ellipse, as in figure T, or a double cone joined at the bases, or a rhombus, as at V. This is because the globules revolving around the whole length of the vortical axis strive to recede, each one, from the centres of the circles which they describe from one pole of the vortex to the other around the different parts of the length of the axis; and so they strive to leave the whole axis of the vortex empty, which the subtle matter cannot but occupy, moving towards the poles along the same path by which it is driven, since the globules of the vortical axis, already prepared to flee from elsewhere, give way to it very easily, let alone being fit to repel it.

units.la: XLII. Neque solum haec incommoda aut falsa, quibus cuncta coelorum phaenomena destruuntur, ex Cartesii principiis vorticibusque sequuntur necessario; sed & alia generalissimis opposita quae terram concernunt. {a}nunt, quæque circa terram observamus, qualia sunt, v. g. figura terræ, gravitas ac magnetismus. Et primum quidem, quia terra juxta Cartesium antequam a Sole abforberetur, erat ipsa parvus quidam Sol; igitur quæ de figura Solis modo diximus, id terræ competere deberet, cujus figura vel cylindracea esset, vel elliptica, vel rhombiformis.
units.tr: XLII. Nor do these inconveniences or falsehoods, by which all the phenomena of the heavens are destroyed, follow necessarily from Descartes' principles and vortices alone; there are also other things, most opposed to the most general principles, which concern the earth. These are the phenomena we observe about the earth, such as the figure of the earth, gravity and magnetism. And first, because according to Descartes the earth, before it was absorbed by the sun, was itself a small sun, therefore what we have just said about the figure of the sun ought to apply to the earth as well, whose figure would be either cylindrical, or elliptical, or rhombus-shaped.

units.la: Gravitatem autem ita obscure explicat Cartesius, ut nescias an velit dicere eam effici a materia subtili sive globulis cœlestibus, quatenus a centro vorticis solaris recedere tendentes offendunt in via circa terram materiam quam gravem dicunt, quæ recessum illum a centro impediat; an vero procedat abiisdem globulis, quatenus circa Solem in orbita sive circulo annuo terræ gyrantes, impingunt in terrestrem materiam circulari suo cursui circa Solem obstantem; an denique a globulis vorticis terræ propriis, quæ gyrum proprium circa terram faciunt & a telluris centro recedere conantur. In primo casu, statuendum esset, corpora gravia repelli devere versus Solem ea via, quæ radii solaris nos veniunt; hoc est, versus occidentalem Solis partem a, (Fig. R) item versus spatium efghikx, pro diversa terræ, ubi corpora gravia jaciuntur, ad ea loca positione: in secundo deberent corpora gravia repelli cœlum versus, ad eam partem orbitæ quam progressu suo circa Solem quotidie relinquit terra: in tertio vero deberent gravia ad terram juxta lineam horizonti propemodum parallelam a parte orientali versus occidentalem ferri, aut ad minimum non versus terræ centrum, sed versus axem ejus propelli. Quorum omnium causa est, quod materia gravis protrudi debeat versus eum locum quem cœlestes globuli proxime & potissimum paratissimi sunt deserere: quem locum pro modo, quem diximus, variare nemo per se non perspicit. Hæc enim tantum indicamus.
units.tr: Now Descartes explains gravity so obscurely that you cannot tell whether he means it to be produced by the subtle matter or celestial globules, insofar as they, tending to recede from the centre of the solar vortex, strike on their way around the earth the matter which they call heavy, which hinders that recession from the centre; or whether it proceeds from the same globules, insofar as they, revolving around the sun in the annual orbit or circle of the earth, strike the terrestrial matter that opposes their circular course around the sun; or finally, from the earth's own vortical globules, which make their own revolution around the earth and strike to recede from the centre of the earth. In the first case, it would have to be granted that heavy bodies ought to be repelled towards the sun by the path along which the rays of the sun come to us, that is, towards the western part of the sun a (Fig. R), and likewise towards the space efghikx, according to the different positions of the places on the earth where heavy bodies are thrown. In the second case, heavy bodies ought to be repelled towards the heavens, towards that part of the orbit which the earth leaves behind every day in its progress around the sun. In the third case, heavy bodies ought to be carried on the earth, along a line nearly parallel to the horizon, from the eastern side towards the western, or at least they ought to be pushed not towards the centre of the earth but towards its axis. The cause of all these is that heavy matter must be pushed towards that place which the celestial globules are closest to and most ready to abandon; and that this place varies according to the manner we have described, no one fails to see of himself. For these things we only indicate.

units.la: XLIII. De Magnetis explicatione.
units.tr: XLIII. On the explanation of the magnet.

units.la: XLIII. Magnetis autem, quam ex principiis suis proponit, explicationem, ea prorsus est inconsequens & deficiens. Fundatur enim tota (a) in striatis suis particulis, quatenus contorta sunt, & contorta quidem modis oppositis. Sed neque ista contorlio, neque etiam ulla talis materia oblonga & striata ex ejus principiis sequitur, nisi increbibilia quædam & aperte ficta ad eas striandas & contornandas in medium adducat, quod vix sine figura bene explicari aut capi posset.
units.tr: XLIII. The explanation of the magnet which he proposes from his principles is altogether inconsequent and deficient. For the whole of it rests on (a) its striated particles, insofar as they are twisted, and twisted in opposite ways. But neither this twisting nor any such oblong and striated matter follows from his principles, unless he brings in certain incredible and openly invented things to stripe and twist them, which could hardly be explained or grasped well without a figure.

units.la: Sit EFGH (fig. X.) pars vorticis alicujus superior circa polum, globulis constans gyrantibus secundum ordinem literarum E, F, G, H, per diversos circulos b, c, d, e, &c. circa centrum A. Supponamus jam materiam e vorice superne incumbente in hunc polum affundi, & prænotemus in illa hæcce tria: 1. eam nondum formatam esse in strias contortas; (neque enim formationem hanc refert Cartefius ad elapsionem ejus ex vortice per eclipticam & globulos modo minores, modo majores, seosque inæqualiter gyrantes, inter quos dum huc illuc inæqualissime movetur, non posset non frangi; sed ingressum in polos, & quidem diverse intortos.) Eam antea nondum rotasse circa centrum, (tunc enim in globulos formata fuisset; ) sed motam fuisse irregularissime, potissimum vero antrorsum. Eandem materiam non posse statim in primis globulorum occursibus plene & solide striatam formari, nisi eadem facilitate ad quemvis oppositorum corporum occursum figuram suam mutet, & ad quodcunque spatium sese accommodet. Itaque videamus nunc qui materia ejusmodi informis, confuse antrorsum mota, facile impressiones & assumens & immutans, formari debeat intra globulos novi vorticis quem circa polum ingreditur.
units.tr: Let EFGH (fig. X) be a part of some vortex, its upper part about the pole, consisting of globules revolving in the order of the letters E, F, G, H, through various circles b, c, d, e, etc., about the centre A. Let us now suppose matter from the vortex lying above to pour into this pole, and let us premise three things: 1. that it has not yet been formed into twisted streaks (for Descartes does not refer this formation to its escape from the vortex through the ecliptic and globules now smaller, now larger, and turning unequally, among which, while it moves this way and that most unequally, it could not fail to be broken; but to its entry into the poles, and indeed twisted in different ways). That it had not yet rotated about the centre (for then it would have been formed into globules), but had been moved very irregularly, and chiefly forward. That the same matter cannot be formed at once, at the first encounters of the globules, fully and solidly striated, unless with the same ease it changes its shape at the encounter of any opposing bodies and adapts itself to any space. Let us see now how matter of this kind, formless, moved confusedly forward, easily receiving and changing impressions, ought to be formed within the globules of the new vortex which it enters about the pole.

units.la: XLIV. Et primo quidem patet eam quae intra ternos globulos contiguos cadet, fieri debere triangularem, angulis acutis & lateribus cavis constantem. At quoniam sub his globulis subesse aliud folium seu aliud planum globulorum itidem sic mororum, hisque rursus planum aliud subjacet & sic continuo, fieri non potest quin fere semper tribus quibusque globulis aut eorum interstitio subsit, directeque opponatur in plano subjacente alius & quartus globus, (est enim hic situs naturalissimus) qui transeunti materiae directo occurrat, eamque statim retundat. Haec materia obtusa omnino retrorsum repelleretur (non enim pollet pellere globulos) nisi nova superveniens, illamque vi protrudens, cogeret eam ulterius pergere, non quidem per lineam rectam, cui obsistit globulus suppositus, sed ad latus per unum ex tribus spatiis triangularibus,
units.tr: XLIV. And first of all it is clear that the matter which falls within three contiguous globules must become triangular, consisting of acute angles and hollow sides. But since beneath these globules there lies another layer or plane of globules likewise arranged, and beneath that again another plane, and so continually, it cannot but happen that almost always, beneath each triad of globules or their interstice, there is directly opposite in the plane below another, a fourth globule (for this position is most natural), which meets the passing matter head-on and at once blunts it. This blunted matter would be wholly driven back (for globules have no power to push), unless a new matter coming on and forcing it with violence compelled it to proceed further, not indeed along a straight line, which the globule lying beneath opposes, but to the side through one of the three triangular spaces

units.la: {y} Lauded in the margin: "triangularem" — see the italic side glosses at right. laribus, quæ globus globulis tribus suppositus ad latera relinquit: quò cum pergit, iterum ut plurimum novo occurrit globulo obstanti ut priùs, eamque retundenti relictis itidem tribus spatiis ad latera, quorum unicuique rursus objicitur alius globulus, & sic in infinitum, ita ut materia transiens non possit moveri per lineam rectam, & verò debeat semper flecti & frangi, dum ex ternione globulorum unius plani transit ad alium in plano sequenti. Unde patet (secundo) particulas hasce fieri non posse instar columnarum rectarum striatarum, sed veluti pyramides aut triangula solida, quorum angulus anterior, in globulos ternioni directè oppositos semper impingens indeque reflexus, obtusus fit & veluti rotundatus.
units.tr: which the globule lying beneath three globules leaves at the sides: whither, as it goes, again for the most part it meets a new globule standing in its way, as before, and blunts it, leaving likewise three spaces at the sides, to each of which in turn another globule is opposed, and so on to infinity; so that the passing matter cannot move along a straight line, but must always be bent and broken as it passes from one triad of globules of one plane to another in the following plane. Whence it is clear (secondly) that these particles cannot be like straight striated columns, but rather like pyramids or solid triangles, whose front angle, always striking against the globules directly opposed to the triad and thence reflected, becomes blunt and as it were rounded.

units.la: Tertiò patet, etiamsi, (quod impossibile est naturaliter,) ponamus globulis ternis in centro A gyrantibus juxtà numeros 1, 2, 3, subesse alios ternos, hisque rursus alios, ita ut semper interstitia interstitiis respondeant, materiaeque influenti transitum rectum & liberum relinquant, non posse tamen particulas materiae striatae quoad striias suas intorqueri, nisi duo supponantur: alterum, particulas illas longiores esse diametro unius globuli; alterum vero, globulos ternos, ternis semper in plano subjacente immediate respondentes, ita simul cum superiori ternione circa centrum moveri; ut tamen celerius paulo aut lentius circulum absolvant. Neque enim particula striata intorqueri potest, nisi dum una ejus extremitas haeret, v.g. inter globulos A, A, A (vid. fig. Z.) in spatio f, i, i, i s altera
units.tr: Thirdly, it is clear that even if (which is naturally impossible) we suppose that beneath the triads of globules turning about the centre A, according to numbers 1, 2, 3, there lie other triads, and beneath these again others, so that interstices always answer to interstices and leave a straight and free passage to the incoming matter, still the particles of striated matter cannot be twisted as regards their streaks unless two things are supposed: first, that those particles are longer than the diameter of one globule; second, that the triads of globules, always lying immediately beneath the upper triad in the plane below, move together with the upper triad about the centre, yet so as to complete their circle a little faster or slower. For a striated particle cannot be twisted unless one of its ends sticks, e.g. between globules A, A, A (see fig. Z) in the space f, i, i, i, while the other

units.la: Fig. Z. altera pars sit inter globulos subjacentes BBB, in spatio f, 222 a priori paululum deflectente; tertia vero (si adsit) inter globulos CCC in spatio f,333, adhuc magis inflexo. Ad quod requiritur, tum, ut particula quævis longior sit diametro unius globuli, quò ita duæ ejus extremitates eodem tempore duo ad minimum spatia triangularia inter duo planaglobulorum occupent; alioqui enim ab uno ternione circulante abriperetur sine reluctantia, nullaque fieret infortio: tum ut globuli terni primis ternis subjacentes, parum lentius vel celerius moveantur, ita ut dum primi, v. g. circulum suum circa centrum f absolvunt, alteri BBB, qui subsunt, ita cum illis pergant ut tamen plusculum moti angulos sive cuspides spatii sui triangularis 2,2,2, parum promoverint & deflexerint a cuspidibus primi i i i; idemque de tertiis CCC, deque eorum motu celeriore aut lentiore, cuspidumque 333 situatione dicendum. Ita demum in terniouibus (& sic in omnibus ab uno polo ad alium) dum anguli cuspidum 1,2,3 paulatim inflectuntur, materia oblonga per interstitia globulorum transiens, similiter contorquebitur: quod fieri non posset, si terniones uniformiter seu æque celeriter moverentur, siquę ita omnes spatii triangularis f cuspides 1, 2, 3 in omnibus planis globulorum similiter motæ, in eadem linea recta sibi responderent: tunc enim materia ingressa recta pergeret sine intorsione.
units.tr: Fig. Z. other part lies between the underlying globules BBB, in the space f,222, bending a little more than the former; and a third part, if there is one, lies between globules CCC in the space f,333, bent still more. For this is required: first, that any particle be longer than the diameter of one globule, so that its two ends at the same time occupy at least two triangular spaces between two planes of globules; otherwise it would be torn away without resistance from one circulating triad and no twisting would occur. Second, that the triads of globules lying beneath the first triads move a little slower or faster, so that while the first ones, e.g., complete their circle about the centre f, the BBB below them go on with them, yet having moved a little more, they have advanced and deflected the angles or cusps of their triangular space 2,2,2 a little from the cusps i, i, i of the first. And the same is to be said of the third CCC, and of their faster or slower motion and the position of the cusps 333. Thus at last in the triads (and so in all from one pole to the other), while the angles of the cusps 1, 2, 3 are gradually bent, oblong matter passing through the interstices of the globules will be similarly twisted; which could not happen if the triads moved uniformly or equally fast, and if thus all the cusps 1, 2, 3 of the triangular space f in all the planes of globules, moved alike, corresponded to one another in the same straight line: for then the matter entering would pass straight on without twisting.

units.la: Et hæc quidem de iis tantum globulorum termonibus qui sunt in ipso axe, circa quem totus vortex gyratur: de iis autem qui sunt ad latera axis & circa axem decurrunt (fig. X.) in circulis B, C, D, E, longe aliter se res habet. namque de his clarissime patere puto, nullam materiam subtilem posse inter eos in strias contortas formari vi rotationis eorum circa axem vortices: siquidem ternio quivis globulorum, v. g. qui in E unam tantum intorsionem facere potest, tota eo tempore quo circulum totum E F G H circa poli axem absolvit, ut in figura patet: angulus enim l, qui dum ternio globulorum est in E, supremus est spatii triangularis inter globulos, quarta parte circuli peracta in F fit lateralis: medio cursu absoluto in G infimum locum occupat: post tres quartas est lateralis dexter in H, donec toto circulo peracto in E ad priorem locum supremum redeat, atque ita unam intorsionem acquirat. Ut ergo una pars intorquendae materiae vel unam contorsionem acquireret dum per globulos hos transit, deberet ea particula ab ingressu suo in ternionem ad exitum ibi permanere tantum temporis donec totus vorticis circulus sit absolutus; vel dimidiam, quartam, octavam partem temporis ejus, ut dimidia vel quotacunque pars circuli absoluta imprimat dimidiam vel quotamcunque unius contorsionis partem materiae inter globulos permanenti: cum tamen vix possint globuli locum mutare quin particulae plures intermeantes jam fuerint elapsae; quippe quae celerius multo moventur quam globuli: globulorum autem circulus, (maxime eorum qui parum remoti sunt ab axe , ) hora, die, mense interdum vix fiat.
units.tr: And these things indeed concern only those triads of globules which are on the axis itself, about which the whole vortex turns; but as to those which lie at the sides of the axis and run round the axis in circles B, C, D, E (fig. X), the case is quite different. For I think it is most clearly evident that no subtle matter can be formed into twisted streaks among them by the force of their rotation about the axis of the vortex; since any triad of globules, e.g. one which at E can make only a single twist, during the whole time in which it completes the whole circle E F G H about the axis of the pole, as the figure shows: for the angle l, which when the triad of globules is at E is the uppermost of the triangular space between the globules, after a quarter of the circle is completed at F becomes lateral; after the middle of the course is completed it occupies the lowest place at G; after three quarters it is the right lateral at H, until, the whole circle being completed, it returns to E to its former uppermost place, and so acquires one twist. So for one part of matter to acquire one twist while passing through these globules, that particle would have to remain there from its entry into the triad to its exit for just as long as the whole circle of the vortex takes to be completed; or for half, a quarter, an eighth part of that time, so that when half or whatever fraction of the circle is completed it imprints half or whatever fraction of one twist on the matter remaining between the globules. Yet the globules can hardly change place without several intervening particles having already passed out, since these move much faster than the globules; and the circle of the globules (especially of those that are not far from the axis) is sometimes hardly completed in an hour, a day, or a month.

units.la: Quod si dicas, globulos plani subjecti moveri circa axem poli,& quidem paulo celerius, idque intorquendæ materiæ sufficere ; ajo contrarium esse verum: non enim moventur uti illi in signra Z, circa centrum sui termionis; sed circa axem vorticis sui rotantes, subducuntur iis qui immediate in folio superposito illis incumbunt, eo modo qui videri potest ad C, in globulis 10, 11, 12; & alii in eodem circulo proxime adstantes, eos in linea fere recta protrudunt: quod sane materiam striatam rumpere & perdere, non autem tornare valet.
units.tr: But if you say that the globules of the flat underlying layer move around the axis of the pole, and somewhat faster, and that this is enough to twist the striated matter, I say the contrary is true. They do not move as those in figure Z do, around the centre of their own ternion. Rather, rotating around the axis of their own vortex, they are pushed out from beneath by those that lie directly on them in the superposed sheet, as can be seen at C, in globules 10, 11 and 12. And others in the same circle standing close by push them out in an almost straight line. This can indeed break up and destroy the striated matter, but it cannot twist it.

units.la: XLV. Verum ut materia striata illis in locis intorqueretur, supponenda essent hæc præterea: primo, globulos præter motum circa axem poli, moveri etiam ternos quosque circa centrum spatii sui interni, puta globulos in circulo B per 4, 5, 6, 4: ternionem C, juxta 7, 8, 9: tertionem E secundum l, m, l, n: sicque cæteros omnes in omnibus circulis circa axem & in toto polo. Nec hoc tantum, sed & secundò, globulos subjecti plani moveri etiam circa se ternos; similiterque globulos tertii & sequentium planorum ad polum oppositum usque, idque (tertiò) eadem inter superiores & inferiores celeritatis & lentitatis proportione semper servata, quæ ad figuram Z explicita est. Atque ita haberemus infinitas veluti columnas ab uno polo ad alium excurrentes constantesque infinitis ternorum globulorum tabulatis, quorum singula circa se diversimode & veluti harmonice gyrando, contorquentur, ad formationem materiæ striatæ contortæ, qua Cartesius indiget ad explicationem magnetis. Quibus suppositionibus unam deesse adhuc video, nimirum, singulos globulos esse veluti totidem glandulas pineales, quæ singulæ genio suo, totius lusus conscio, & omnia sic methodice dirigente, sint præditæ. Ecquis enim non videt, materiam istam striatam & diverse intortam præter puram putam chimæram nihil esse? quod non per insultationem dictum velim, sed ut videant ingenui, quibus figmentis mentes suas captivent, Auctori uni, ut ut ingeniloso, nimia cum veneratione adhærentes, dum revera ea ejus inventa, quæ vel maxime inter omnia tanquam veritatis principiorum insignia specimina passim jactantur, non nisi fictiones absurdæ sunt: quod de pluribus insuper ad hunc scopum ut ingenuorum mentes libertati restituantur, ostendi posset, si vel locus vel necessitas id postularet.
units.tr: XLV. But for the striated matter to be twisted in those places, the following would also have to be supposed. First, that the globules, besides moving around the axis of the pole, also move in threes around the centre of their own inner space: for example, the globules in circle B through 4, 5, 6, 4; the ternion C according to 7, 8, 9; the ternion E according to l, m, l, n; and so on for all the others in all the circles, around the axis and throughout the whole pole. Secondly, not only this, but that the globules of the underlying flat layer also move in threes around themselves, and similarly the globules of the third and following layers up to the opposite pole. Thirdly, that this happens with the same proportion of speed and slowness between upper and lower globules always preserved, which is set out in figure Z. And so we would have, as it were, infinite columns running from one pole to the other, made up of infinite storeys of triads of globules. Each of these, turning about itself in various ways and as it were harmonically, is twisted, to form the twisted striated matter that Descartes needs for the explanation of the magnet. To these suppositions I see that one more is still lacking, namely that each globule be, as it were, a pineal gland, each endowed with its own genius, aware of the whole play and directing everything so methodically. For who does not see that this striated and variously twisted matter is nothing but pure chimera? I do not say this in mockery, but so that honest minds may see by what fictions they hold their minds captive, clinging with excessive veneration to one author, however ingenious. In truth, those of his discoveries which are most often boasted of everywhere as marks of the principles of truth are nothing but absurd fictions. This could be shown of many others as well, for the purpose of restoring the minds of honest men to freedom, if either place or necessity demanded it.

units.la: XLVI. Monebo tantum verbo, in eis
units.tr: XLVI. I will give only a brief warning about those

units.la: quæ explicanda suscepit Cartesius, quæque sæpe inter specimina ejus præcipua annumerantur, si propius inspicias, errorem inde plurimum (ut in jam recensitis) proficisci, quod contra primam methodi suæ regulam multa assumat ut evidentia quæ talia tamen non sunt: tum & contra regulam alteram, subjectum & difficultates in omnes suas partes non dividat; quod multa in Metaphysicis, v.g. quæ ad rem necessaria essent prætermittat: in PhyPhysicis vero, ea quæ corpora solida sunt, consideret ut plana, quemadmodum figuris exhibentur; non vero ut solida, qualia revera sunt. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: matters which Descartes undertook to explain, and which are often counted among his chief specimens. If you look closer, the error arises very largely (as in the ones just reviewed) from this: against the first rule of his method, he assumes many things as evident which are not really so. Also, against the second rule, he does not divide the subject and the difficulties into all their parts. Thus in Metaphysics he omits many things that would be necessary to the matter; and in Physics he considers solid bodies as flat, as they are represented in figures, and not as solid, as they really are. But enough on these.

units.la: XLVII. ETHICA, de cujus falsitate etiam nonnulla annotanda sunt, considerari potest, vel qualis ex Ethnicorum vulgarium scriptis hauritur sive hauriri potest; vel qualis ex hominum actionum observationibus acquiritur; vel qualis a Philosophis, iisque præcipuis, passim traditur & commendatur. De illa quæ in Gentilium scriptis apparet &inde eruì potest, Cartesii sententiam nunc faciam meam. Sic autem ille: (a) Veterum Ethnicorum moralia scripta, palatiis superbis ad modum, & magnificis, sed arenæ tantum aut cœno inædificatis esse comparanda. Virtutes summis laudibus in cœlum ab iis tolli; quas cæteris omnibus rebus longe anteponendas esse, rē​ste contendant: sed non satis explicare, quidnam pro virtute sit habendum; & sæpe quod tam illustri nomine dignantur, immanitatem potius & duritiem, vel superbiam, vel desperationem, vel parricidium dici debere. Ita ex copiosis verbosi Ciceronis scriptis, nil præter vanam animi ambitionem atque ostentationem virtutis loco elici posse ab iis qui in ejus lectione morum institutionem quærunt, verissimum effatum est. Neque hoc ipse Seneca, multique inter Stoicos destituuntur vitio. Si quis autem ex observatione eorum, quæ agunt illi qui prudentiores in seculo habentur, Ethicam vitæque leges sibi velit præscribere, Superbiam & Amorem proprium pro principiis (a) Disc. de Methodo thodo. piis suis sibi assumat necesse est. Ex his enim fontibus proficisci, & ad hæc tanquam ad scopum suum collimare quæcunque a mundi probissimis geruntur, quæque inter virtutes numerantur, elegantius & nervosius, quam ab alio describi possit, illustris Auctor quidam (a) vel palpandum exhibuit.
units.tr: XLVII. Ethics, whose falsity also needs some remarks, can be considered either as it is drawn, or can be drawn, from the writings of the common Gentiles; or as it is acquired from observations of human actions; or as it is generally taught and commended by philosophers, and especially the chief among them. As for that which appears in the writings of the Gentiles and can be drawn from them, I will now make Descartes's opinion my own. He speaks thus: (a) The moral writings of the ancient Gentiles are to be compared to proud and magnificent palaces, but built only on sand or mud. They extol virtues to heaven with the highest praises, and strongly maintain that these are to be placed far above all other things; but they do not explain sufficiently what is to be regarded as virtue. And often what they honour with so illustrious a name ought rather to be called savagery and hardness, or pride, or despair, or parricide. Thus it is most true that from the copious and verbose writings of Cicero, nothing can be drawn, in place of virtue, but vain ambition of the mind and display, by those who seek moral instruction in his reading. Nor are Seneca himself and many among the Stoics free of this fault. If anyone, however, wishes to prescribe to himself ethics and laws of life from observing what those considered more prudent in the world do, he must necessarily take pride and self-love as his principles. (a) Discourse on Method. For from these sources all the actions of the most upright in the world proceed, and toward these as their aim they are all directed, including those counted among the virtues. A certain illustrious author has exhibited this more elegantly and forcefully than anyone else could describe it, so that it can almost be touched: (a)

units.la: XLVIII. Jam si quam Philosophorum recentiorum Sectam in virtutis via præmon- stranda ducem seligere tibi fit animus, quam ex omnibus commendem, video sane nul- lam.
units.tr: XLVIII. Now if you want to choose some sect of recent philosophers as your guide to show the way of virtue, I see indeed that I could commend none of them above the rest.

units.la: Vel in primo quæstionis momento a scopo aberrant simul omnes, dum pro fine quærunt Summum bonum, quatenus in hac vita naturaliter acquiri & possideri potest: quæ quidem quæstio est perabsurda. Si potularent, quodnam ex multis imperfectis, ad quæ hic accessus dari potest, optimum sit, quod cum universali Dei gratia sic possit obtineri, ut pereunte hac vita, maneat tamen instar fundamenti nos ad Summi Boni fruitionem aptos reddentis, tunc equidem non inepte quærerent. At si non omnes, multi saltem, tale quærunt hic Summum bonum, quo, respectu nostri, non datur majus; deinde & quod in hac vita datur; & postremo, quod natura corruptæ viribus acquiri possit. Illud dico abiurde sic quæri. Namque cum hæc inter mortales vita, ad veram & æternam nostri, quæ post hanc vitam futura est, durationem, ne eam quidem rationem habeat quæ est capillorum ad corpus, vel momenti ad seculum; cumque in illa versemur, ( ex rei veritate & sincerioris sensus dictamine) non ut principis filii in paterno palatio, principale bonum ibi poslessuri; sed ut fontes in carcere, in quo humiliter & patienter rebellionis poenas sustinere debent, quaerere illic Summum bonum perinde est ac si quaereretur, quomodo reus per occupationem circa capillos in carcere possit primariam dignitatem obtinere & possidere? Deinde quaerere Summum bonum quod non sit supernaturale, sed naturale, idem est, ac quaerere summam lucem quae non sit lucida sed tenebrosa. Praeterea, quaerere Summum bonum, quatenus naturae viribus, non autem gratiae auxilio & operatione interna acquiri potest, perinde est ac quaerere lucem vel illuminationem, quatenus per coecitatem acquiri potest; aut quaerere rectum atque agilem incessum, quatenus per luxatas & claudicantes tibias acquiri potest. Non Physici tantum, sed & Ethici Philosophi currunt post chimaeras in spatiis imaginariis volitantes. Obliviscuntur (quod supra notavi) Dei, sui, aeternitatis, rerumque supernaturalium, ad quas & ob quas nos esse factos negabit nemo, nisi dicat Deum rem supernaturalem non esse, aut nisi credat eundem sese negare tanquam finem & scopum hominis dariquealiquid Deo dignius, ob quod homo sit & vivat. Sed necessatis memores sunt iidem vanitatis atque brevitatis hujusce vitae, quae cum considerari non possit ut scopus fixus, sed solummodo (uti revera est) tanquam medium labile & momentaneum, non permittit ut in ea quaera-turtur summi boni possessio, sed usus saltem rectus medii; & medii quidem non fruitivi, sed poenalis, quale reus in carcere quaerere vel exspectare debet: quod alia in re consistere nequit quam in humilitate & patientia, quas etiam adorandus noster Philosophus Ethicus Jesus Christus, benedictus in secula, tanquam omne hac in vita punctum ferentes, discipulis suis discendas tradidit: (a) Discite a me quod sim mitis & humilis corde: & Si quis vult me sequi, (hoc est, ad summum bonum per hujus vitae rectum usum ceu per medium tendere) is abneget se & tollat crucem suam.
units.tr: Indeed, at the very first step of the question, all of them go astray from the goal, while they seek as their end the Highest Good, so far as it can naturally be acquired and possessed in this life. This question is utterly absurd. If they were asking which of the many imperfect things that can be approached here is best, namely the one that can be obtained through the universal grace of God in such a way that, when this life perishes, it nevertheless remains as a foundation making us fit for the enjoyment of the Highest Good, then indeed they would not be asking foolishly. But if not all, at least many seek here such a Highest Good as, with respect to us, none greater exists; and which is given in this life; and lastly, which corrupt nature can acquire by its own powers. I say that to seek it in this way is absurd. For since this life among mortals, compared with our true and eternal duration which is to come after this life, does not even bear the proportion that a hair bears to the body, or a moment to an age; and since we dwell in it (by the truth of the matter and the verdict of a more sincere sense) not as a prince's son in his father's palace, about to possess a principal good there, but as prisoners in a jail, where they must humbly and patiently bear the penalties of rebellion, then to seek the Highest Good there is just the same as to ask how a convict in jail, by busying himself with his hair, could obtain and possess the first place of dignity. Further, to seek a Highest Good that is not supernatural but natural is the same as seeking a highest light that is not luminous but dark. Moreover, to seek the Highest Good so far as it can be acquired by natural powers, and not by the help of grace and inward operation, is like seeking light or illumination so far as it can be acquired through blindness; or seeking a straight and nimble gait so far as it can be acquired through dislocated and limping shins. Not only physicists but also ethical philosophers run after chimeras flitting about in imaginary spaces. They forget (as I noted above) God, themselves, eternity, and supernatural things, for which and to which we were made; no one will deny this unless he says that God is not a supernatural thing, or believes that God denies himself as the end and goal of man, or that there is something more worthy than God for which man exists and lives. But these same men are mindful of the vanity and brevity of this life, which, since it cannot be regarded as a fixed goal, but only (as it truly is) as a slippery and momentary means, does not allow the possession of the highest good to be sought in it, but only the right use of the means; and indeed of a means not for enjoyment but for penalty, such as a convict in jail ought to seek or wait for. This can consist in nothing other than humility and patience, which our adorable Ethical Philosopher, Jesus Christ, blessed forever, handed down to his disciples to be learned, as bearing every point of this life: "Learn from me, that I am meek and humble in heart;" and "If anyone wishes to follow me" (that is, to strive toward the highest good through the right use of this life as through a means) "let him deny himself and take up his cross."

units.la: XLIX. Non negavero, Summum Bonum utique hac in vita quaeri debere: verum non ut tale hic possidendum; sed olim: neque inficior, Deum etiam interdum quibusdam id hic communicare; at nec fruitive, nec (quia nullum hominis studium activum est medium proximum possidendi summi boni) id ipsum ex se quaerentibus; ne dicam & eos qui id praegustant, vitae mundique hujus metas quadam veluti mortis imagine, (ipsa corporea morte hominem magis immutante) prius esse praetergressos: de qua morte Paulus, (b) Mortui, inquit, estis; & vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Verum divinam hanc Viatorum Ethicam a Christianismi nostri Philosophis nec proponi nec quaeri, non tantum patet ex absurda quaestione summi boni hac vita circumscripti, naturaque (corrupta ut est) viribus adipiscendi; sed & ex documentis expressis contra
units.tr: XLIX. I would not deny that the Highest Good ought indeed to be sought in this life, but not as something to be possessed here; rather it is to be sought hereafter. Nor do I deny that God sometimes grants it to some people here; but not in enjoyment, and not to those who seek it of themselves (since no active effort of man is the proximate means of possessing the highest good). Not to mention that those who taste it beforehand have already passed beyond the limits of this life and world by a kind of image of death (death itself changing a man more). Of this death Paul says: <hi>"You are dead,"</hi> he says, <hi>"and your life is hidden with Christ in God."</hi> (b) But that this divine ethics of wayfarers is neither proposed nor sought by the philosophers of our Christianity is clear not only from the absurd question of a highest good circumscribed by this life and sought by nature's powers (corrupt as nature is), but also from explicit teachings against the cardinal virtues of humility and patience.

units.la: haud quae-rere Chri-stianam E-thicam. (b) Co-loss. 3: 3. tra cardinales humilitatis & patientiæ virtutes. Novi Scholam, ubi docebatur humilitatem esse abjecti vitium animi; & patientiam non merereri nomen inter virtutes, quod pati ignavum sit: hocque thesi publica totidem verbis sustinebatur, quanquam Superbus & Impatiens Dn. Præses pudore suffundi debuit, prolato Divi Jacobi loco: (a) Exemplum capite, fratres mei, tolerantiæ & patientiæ de prophetis, qui Domini nomine locuti sunt. Equidem Beatos judicamus eos qui patiuntur. Jobi patientiam audivistis, & quem eis finem dederit Dominus misericors & clemens, vidistis. Sed hæc forte Aristotelicismo debebantur: Cartesianismus fuerit forsitan purior. Viderint quorum interest. Ego, qui illum olim utcunque feci meum, de eo, uti a me olim suscepto, sensus meos exponam breviter.
units.tr: I know of a school where it was taught that humility is a vice of a base mind, and that patience does not deserve the name of a virtue, since to suffer is cowardly. This thesis was defended in public in just these words, although the proud and impatient Mr. President ought to have blushed when the passage of St. James was brought forward: <hi>"Take, my brothers, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord as an example of suffering and patience. Indeed we count those blessed who endure. You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end that the Lord gave him, for the Lord is merciful and compassionate."</hi> But perhaps these views were owed to Aristotelianism; Cartesianism may be purer. Let those whom it concerns see to that. As for me, who once made it mine to some extent, I will briefly set out my opinions about it, as I once took it up.

units.la: L. Cum Cartesii Epistolas, quæ in Tomo primo ab initio exstant, primum legerem, eas veluti de cœlo labentes suspiciebam & toto pectore amplectebar, ob egregia atque pia & fundamentalia Ethices cogitata hinc inde ibi exstantia. At postquam deinde omnia simul conspicere & diligentius perpendere cœpi, video de ejusmodi Ethica idem judicium fieri posse, quod ipsum de Ethicorum moralibus scriptis fecisse supra retulimus: Superbha esse palatia arenæ impositæ, nec quid pro virtute & pro summo bono habendum sit explicantia. Arena est vel cœnum dogma illud quod pacificandis animis nostræ propensiones omnes non prævidente modo, sed & eas nobis infundeŭte : quod & statum Spinozianum redolet, tum vero animum ad virtutem obtundit, atque vitiis quibuscunque defendendis, pœnitentiæque excutiendæ potius inservit quam ut virtutem promoveat. Id {a}( quia perniciosum puto ) a radice resecui (a) aliis locis: Sed quid de Summo bono deque virtute minus vere docuerit, cum nullibi ostenderim, jam libet in lucem protrahere.
units.tr: L. When I first read the letters of Descartes, which stand at the beginning of the first volume, I looked upon them as if falling from heaven, and embraced them with my whole heart, on account of the excellent, pious, and fundamental ethical thoughts found there here and there. But after I began to survey all of them together and to weigh them more carefully, I see that the same judgment can be made of this kind of ethics as I reported above that I had made of the moral writings of the ethicists: <hi>"Proud palaces built on sand, which do not explain what is to be counted as virtue and the highest good."</hi> That dogma, which by pacifying minds foresees all our propensities and not only foresees them but pours them into us, is sand or mud. It also smells of Spinozism, and it dulls the mind toward virtue, serving rather to defend any vices and to shake off repentance than to promote virtue. Because I think this is harmful, I have cut it out by the root in other places. But what it has taught less truly about the highest good and about virtue, since I have shown this nowhere, I now am pleased to bring into the light.

units.la: Summum bonum, nisi res definita vocis dignitati respondeat, superbus titulus : qualis sæpe prostat multis in libris, qui ( ne Spinoza quidem cum suis excepto ) nobis Summum illud bonum, pantosophias, medicamina animarum, aliaque ejusmodi in fronte promittunt quidem; at ubi ad rem ventum est, nugas meras in recessu habent de logica, de motìbus, deque figuris, numeris & rebus mathematicis, quæ non magis ad summam felicitatem quam ad summam miseriam conferunt. Neque aliter se res habet: si quis considerans miserias humanas, mentiumque ægritudines, quæ beatitudini solidæ opponuntur omnes, ab errore proficisci, in exordio libri promittat quidem se de errore pellendo per Inquisitionem Veritatis asturum; verum tamen toto opere nil agat quam de erroribus inani scientiæ & curiosæ oppositis, deque veritate ideali & philosophica, nullius miseriam depellere apta; unde ipsemet tandem "concludat in fine operis: Itta quæ de veri"tate exposuit, cum laboriosa esse admo"dum, tum vero ut plurimum ad eas tantum "quæstiones proficua, quæ nullius fere sunt "usus: {u}usus: nisi quod superbiæ nostræ adulentur magis, quam mentem vere perficiant: proinde melius esse ea ignorare cum prosbis ac piis, qui postea per aliam viam æternoluimine subito illustrabuntur, quam per istam laboriosam nonnulla imperfectissime scire, deinde vero post tantillum temporis æternis tenebris esse plectendum. Quæ conclusio sane spem exordio operis factam plane tollit. Idem & Summo bono Cartesii commune erit, si quod abillo affertur tale fuerit, ut & post ejus adeptionem, ni accedat aliud, summa tandem miseria suum maneat possessorem.
units.tr: <hi>"The highest good"</hi>, unless the defined reality answers to the dignity of the word, is a proud title, such as often appears on the title-pages of many books. These promise us (Spinoza and his followers not excepted) that highest good, pansophies, medicines for souls, and other such things on their fronts; but when it comes to the matter, they keep in reserve mere trifles about logic, motions, figures, numbers, and mathematical things, which contribute no more to supreme happiness than to supreme misery. Nor is the case otherwise: if someone, considering human miseries and the sicknesses of minds, all of which are opposed to solid blessedness, and recognizing that they arise from error, promises at the beginning of his book that he will drive out error through <hi>"An Inquiry into Truth"</hi>, yet throughout the whole work does nothing but deal with errors opposed to empty and curious learning, and with an ideal and philosophical truth fit to drive away no one's misery; then he himself at last concludes at the end of the work: <hi>"What he has set out about truth, although very laborious, and for the most part useful only for those questions which are of almost no use, except that they flatter our pride more than they truly perfect the mind; therefore it is better to be ignorant of these things with the simple and pious, who will afterwards be suddenly illumined by the eternal light by another way, than by that laborious way to know a few things very imperfectly, and then after a little time to be punished in eternal darkness."</hi> This conclusion certainly wholly takes away the hope raised at the beginning of the work. The same will be true of the highest good of Descartes, if what is brought forward from it is such that, unless something else is added, after its attainment it will remain at last the highest misery for its possessor.

units.la: LI. Summum bonum Cartesius distinxit in illud quod absolute in se est tale, de quo non dubitatur id esse ens perfectissimum: & in illud quod tale est quoad nos, sive quod nostrum quodammodo est, vel ad nos spectat: hoc autem unicuique nil aliud esse ait, quam libertatem arbitrii, aut potius illius bonum usum. Qui sane paralogismus est non minor, quam si quærenti qua in re consistat illumination, responderetur, non in Sole ejusve actu, sed in recto usu, seu in apertione libera oculorum, quippe quæ sola hac in re ad nos spectat. Est quidem hæc apertio, fateor, necessaria ad illuminationem conditio: at illuminatio ipsa vere est actio Solis in oculos ei sponte apertos. Ita quoque fatendum est, libertatis interpositionem necessario quidem requiri ad Summum bonum; quippe quod bonum sit actio luminosa & amatoria Dei in anima se suaque facultates ad eum libere convertente: at ille sane libertatis usus sive admissivus actus, Summum bonum nec est nec constituit: admittit tantum: perinde ut porrectio spontanea manus in mendico non est thesaurus, etsi thesauri admissio esse possit. Et superbo amoris proprii fundo ergo est, quod in libertate propria potius quam in divina operatione summum quaeratur & collocetur bonum: idque sub callido illo praetextu, bonum illud aliter non fore nostrum, quandoquidem praeter libertatis usum nil nostrum proprie sit. Atqui palam est posse aliqua duobus modis nostra fieri: alia quidem ita ut nobis sint naturalia, sive pars naturae & dos, prout sunt ipsa animae natura facultatesque, e quibus nullum majus donum fieri nobis potuit a Deo, quam quidem est libertatis ejusque usus donatio: Alia vero sic nostra esse possunt, ut ad naturae nostrae constitutionem non pertineant, sed ad ejus ornamentum & beatitatem; & haec dona sunt a liberalitate Creatoris nostri oblata ut fiant nostra per libertatis ea sponte admittentis cooperationem & consensum. Atque sic Deus ejusque actus, qui summum bonum in se sunt absolute, fient etiam nostrum summum bonum, si eis sponte facultates libertatemque ipsam tradimus. Sic Deus, fiet Deus noster; vita ejus, vita nostra; bonum & felicitas ejus, bonum nostrum. Nec facile concedendum arbitrer, appellationem illam summi boni a Deo ad libertatis usum transferri, nisi quis occasionem amet sibi periculosissime adhaerendi, postmodum tamen per lamentabilem & & forte irreparabilem lapsum, qui superbos manet, serius dedocendus.
units.tr: LI. Descartes distinguished the highest good into that which is such absolutely in itself, about which there is no doubt that it is the most perfect being, and that which is such with respect to us, or which is in some way ours or pertains to us. He says that for each person this is nothing other than freedom of the will, or rather its good use. Certainly this is a paralogism no less than if someone asked in what illumination consists and were answered: not in the sun or its action, but in the right use, that is, in the free opening of the eyes, since this alone pertains to us in the matter. This opening is indeed, I admit, a necessary condition for illumination; but illumination itself is truly the action of the sun on eyes that have spontaneously opened to it. So too it must be admitted that the interposition of freedom is indeed required for the highest good, since the good is the luminous and loving action of God on the soul, and on its faculties, which freely turn to him. But that exercise of freedom, that act of admitting, neither is nor constitutes the highest good; it only admits it. Just as a beggar's spontaneous stretching out of his hand is not a treasure, though it may be the admission of a treasure. And it springs from the proud foundation of self-love that the highest good is sought and placed in our own freedom rather than in the divine operation, under the crafty pretext that the good would otherwise not be ours, since nothing is properly ours except the use of freedom. But it is plain that some things can become ours in two ways. Some are ours so that they are natural to us, a part of our nature and our endowment, such as the very nature and faculties of the soul; of these no greater gift could be given us by God than the gift of freedom and its use. Others can be ours without belonging to the constitution of our nature, but to its adornment and blessedness; these are gifts offered by the generosity of our Creator, to become ours through the cooperation and consent of freedom, which admits them spontaneously. And so God and his acts, which are the highest good absolutely in themselves, will also become our highest good, if we freely surrender to them our faculties and freedom itself. Thus God will become our God; his life our life; his good and blessedness our good. Nor do I think it should readily be conceded that the name of the highest good is transferred from God to the use of freedom, unless someone loves the occasion of clinging to it most dangerously, only to be later unlearned through a lamentable and perhaps irreparable fall, which awaits the proud.

units.la: Neque est quod quis causetur, liberi arbitrii bonum usum ideo pro summo bono relativo haberi, quod virtus in eo usu libertatis consistat: virtutem autem ab augusta hac denominatione Summi Boni excludi non posse. At Virtutes ex sublimiori Theologia diffcat in increatas & creatas distingui. Illæ, quoniam ipsius Dei actus sint, animæ præsentis, eamque agentis & regentis; vel etiam sint ipsemet Deus agens, Summum quidem bonum dici possunt: hæ, quæ sunt libertatis divino auxilio adjutæ actus, non item Summum bonum; sed viæ tantum ad illud consequendum. At eæ virtutes quæ sunt actus libertatis sese bene agere præsumentis, tantum abest ut sint Summum bonum, aut media ad illud; ut ad summum potius malum superba media & infelices viæ sint agnoscendæ.
units.tr: Nor can anyone plead that the good use of free will is therefore held to be a relative highest good, because virtue consists in that use of freedom, and virtue cannot be excluded from this august title of the Highest Good. But higher theology distinguishes virtues into uncreated and created. The former, since they are the acts of God himself, present to the soul and acting and ruling it, or even God himself acting, may indeed be called the highest good. The latter, which are acts of freedom aided by divine help, are not the highest good, but only the ways to attain it.
