But those virtues which are acts of freedom presuming to act well by itself are so far from being the highest good, or means to it, that proud means and unhappy ways are rather to be recognised as leading to the highest evil.

units.la: Hic consideremus obiter Cartesianæ Virtutis naturam sive definitionem. Is illam in hoc constituit, ut quis faciat ea quæ meliora esse judicat. Media autem ad eam esse ait, nil negligere ad inquisitionem veri, tum cognitionem ipsam veri & boni, judiciaque de illis, itemque decreta firma vitam secundum judicia illa regendi. Verum enimvero, quando inter media inquirendi veri non numerantur ea quæ præcipua esse aliquoties diximus; recurrere ad fontem luminis, Deum, ex animo de ingratitudine sua & vitiis dolente, æternorum autem luminisque divini cupido, cumque præter ideales notitias vi & actívitate rationis corruptæ in anima sui ipsius amante acquisitas, judiciaque in præsumtione se vero lumine assici fundata, nil intelligitur vel optatur; patet cuivis veritatem solidam sine adulatione adire volenti, ejusmodi virtutes non esse nisi coecam atque superbam pertinaciam, &, si quicquam aliud, has vere dici posse palatia admodum superba arenæ aut cæno corruptæ naturæ superædificata.
units.tr: Here let us consider in passing the nature or definition of Cartesian virtue. He places it in this: that a person does what he judges to be better. The means to it, he says, is to neglect nothing in the search for truth, both knowledge of truth and good itself and judgments about these, and likewise firm resolutions to govern life according to those judgments. Truly, however, when among the means of seeking truth are not counted those things which we have several times said are chief (to have recourse to the fountain of light, God, from a heart grieved over its ingratitude and vices, and a longing for eternal things and divine light), and when, apart from ideal notions and judgments acquired by the force and activity of corrupted reason in a soul that loves itself, and judgments founded on the presumption of being influenced by the true light, nothing is understood or desired, it is plain to anyone who wishes to approach solid truth without flattery that such virtues are nothing but blind and proud obstinacy. And if they are anything else, they may truly be called palaces very proud, built on sand or mud by corrupted nature.

units.la: LIV. E Cartesii autem discipulis nonnulli,
units.tr: LIV. Some of the disciples of Descartes, however,

units.la: prout de adipiscenda veri & boni cognitione magis vel præsumserunt vel desperarunt, in diversas & sibi oppositas abiere partes. Qui veri & boni cognitione sese certo præditos crediderunt, quia id conscientiâ suâ certo sibi intus constare putabant, sic virtutem in conscientiæ dictamine sequendo constituerunt, ut pro principio illis sit, conscientiam errare non posse. At vero qui aliquantum sincerius & perspicacius luminum rationisque suæ desectus scrutati sunt, videntes vix se quicquam indubitato certum suis viis possidere, & præterea animo gratificandi illis qui, cum non sint Philosophi, neque adeo circa veri & boni cognitionem commode occupari queant, non sunt tamen a virtute & felicitate arcendi; eò in contrarium abierunt, ut dicerent, veri atque boni cognitiones ad virtutem & felicitatem non adeo necessarias esse; sufficere ut quis bona fide putet sive judicet quaedam esse vera & bona, alia autem mala & falsa, dirigatque actiones suas secundum judicia
units.tr: according as they presumed more or despaired more of attaining knowledge of the true and the good, went off in different and opposing directions. Those who believed they were endowed with certain knowledge of the true and the good, because they thought this was certainly evident to them inwardly in their own conscience, made virtue consist in following the dictate of conscience, so that their principle was that conscience cannot err. But those who examined the defects of their own light and reason somewhat more sincerely and perceptively, seeing that they hardly possessed anything with indubitable certainty by their own methods, and wishing also to oblige those who, not being philosophers and so unable to occupy themselves conveniently with knowledge of the true and the good, nevertheless should not be shut out from virtue and happiness, went to the opposite extreme and said that knowledge of the true and the good is not so necessary for virtue and happiness; it is enough that someone in good faith thinks or judges some things to be true and good, and others bad and false, and directs his actions according to the judgments

units.la: {y} Circa Conscientiam Cartesianorum quorundam sententia oppositas atque erroneas. dicia quæ sibi conscius est esse optima, etsi res ipsæ in se aliter se haberent, judiciaque cum ipsis rebus & absoluta veritate collata, essent toto cœlo ab his aliena: id felicitati exspectatæ non obfuturum : e contra, teneri quemque conscientiam suam etiam errantem semper sequi; atque ita æque bene rem virtutis salutisque geri, ac si erratum non esset. Quæ quidem longius adhuc quam priora a veritate & virtute aberrant.
units.tr: Concerning the opposed and erroneous opinions of certain Cartesians on conscience: the judgments which a person is aware are the best, even if the things themselves are otherwise in themselves, and even if those judgments, compared with the things themselves and absolute truth, are worlds apart from them, will not stand in the way of the happiness hoped for. On the contrary, each person is bound always to follow his conscience even when it errs, and so the matter of virtue and salvation is handled just as well as if there were no error. These views stray from truth and virtue even further than the earlier ones.

units.la: LV. Qui conscientiam errare non posse putant, aut quid conscientiafit ignorare videntur, aut vero nova utuntur nomenclatura communi usui contraria. Res in homine sic se habet. Homines (utinam Philosophi exciperentur!) Dei, æternorum, iniquitatis propriæ pœnitentiæque oblivi, amore vero proprio capti, optantes suismet oculis apparere tanquam veritatis & virtutis possessores, hoc agunt, ut sua quisque via & rationis activitate ægra, veritates picturatas & ideales de rerum & actionum bonitate vel pravitate excitare sibi diversis modis annitatur. Id faciendo, diversi ad diversa & quandoque oppositaprolabuntur. Tum pro suo quoque modo judicant, & hujus apud se conscii sunt. Dein judicia sua de bono & malo, vero & falso, per reflexionem intuentes sistunt eadem sibi, veluti coram novo Tribunali dijudicanda. Hic judex autem est Amor proprius, sive desiderium quo homo optat a se ipso veritate & justitia præditus haberi. Ab eo postulatur, ut quod semel judicatum est, revideat, & ex revisis rationibus pronunciet. Is igitur desideratis annuit; N atque ita eadem quæ prius (quæ sua omnia sunt) rata certe (pro sua indole) pronunciat, aut etiam pejora prioribus addita confirmat. Atque hoc ipsum est quod homines appellant conscientiam. De hac jam quæritur, an ea errare non possit? Mira quæstio! An Amor proprius & superbus, qui, sibi ipsi ut satisfaceret, semel judicavit directe de rerum bonitate ex iis quæ ipsi apparuere, non possit errare, quando ipsemet deinde reflexive judicia priora ad judicium reflexum & iteratum appellat? taceo sæpe illum ne quidem tam exacte se gerere; ita ut præter meram pertinaciam nil sit interdum ea ad quam multi provocant conscientia ejusque luminis prætextus.
units.tr: LV. Those who think that conscience cannot err either seem not to know what conscience is, or else they use a new terminology contrary to common usage. The matter stands thus in man. Men (would that philosophers were excepted!), forgetful of God, of eternal things, of their own iniquity and of repentance, and captivated by self-love, wishing to appear to themselves as possessors of truth and virtue, act in such a way that each, by his own method and by the activity of his sick reason, strives in various ways to stir up for himself painted and imaginary notions about the goodness or wickedness of things and actions. In doing so they slip into different and sometimes opposite positions. Then each judges in his own way and is aware of this judgment within himself. Next, looking at their judgments about good and evil, true and false, by reflection, they set these same judgments before themselves, as though to be decided before a new tribunal. But the judge here is self-love, or the desire by which a man wishes to be regarded by himself as endowed with truth and justice. It is demanded of this judge that he review what has once been decided and pronounce from the reviewed reasons. He therefore nods assent to what is wished for, and so pronounces the same things as before (which are all his own), and, as far as his nature allows, certainly approves them, or even confirms worse things added to the earlier ones. And this very thing is what men call conscience. Now the question is raised about it: can it not err? A strange question! Can self-love, which is proud, and which, in order to satisfy itself, once judged directly about the goodness of things from what appeared to it, not err, when it then reflexively appeals its earlier judgments to a second and repeated reflexive judgment? I say nothing of how often it does not even conduct itself so exactly; so that sometimes, apart from mere obstinacy, there is nothing in that to which many appeal as conscience and as a pretext of its light.

units.la: LVI. At enim, inquient, quid tu hic nobis de conscientia, quæ sit Amor proprius, disputas? Quasi vero Paulus non testaretur, inscriptam esse hominum etiam Ethnicorum cordibus legem divinâ vi eos de bono & malo arguentem & instruentem. Hanc divinam esse legem negabit nemo. Eandem nos Conscientiam cum Paulo dicimus. Et quia lex Dei errare non potest: Ergo conscientia errare non potest. Quod adhuc fortius stringit, quam quando probatur illam errare non posse ex eo quod illa idem sit ac clara & distincta perceptio Cartesiana; cum utique majus quid sit, eam esse vividam perceptionem divinam.
units.tr: LVI. But, they will say, why do you here dispute with us about conscience, which is self-love? As if Paul did not testify that a law is written in the hearts of men, even of the Gentiles, by divine power accusing and instructing them about good and evil. No one will deny that this law is divine. We call this same thing conscience, with Paul. And because the law of God cannot err, therefore conscience cannot err. This binds even more tightly than when it is proved that conscience cannot err because it is the same as the clear and distinct perception of Descartes; since it is surely something greater, namely a divine living perception.

units.la: LVII. Sic illi. Videamus nunc quænam iis respondenda sint, & quidem non abludendo a mente Pauli.
units.tr: LVII. Thus they. Let us now see what must be answered to them, and indeed not departing from the mind of Paul.

units.la: Doctrina Pauli est, hominem a peccato ita penitus immersum esse corruptioni, ut merae in eo sint tenebrae & vanitas ac stultitia Mentis, donec Deus ei illucescat per operationis suae intimae nonnullos radios, prout & fecit, ipsis etiam gentilibus; ostendens eis suam potentiam, bonitatem, liberalitatem, simulque eos convincens, quod debeant ei gratias agendo & obtemperando, honoremque & gloriam ejus quaerendo, viam suam transfigere, abjectis stultis & vanis suis ratiociniis, atque insano illo desiderio, quo sibi aliisque sapientes videri volebant. Haec illi si audivissent, judicassent & fecissent; tunc vero habuissent unde de sana & non errante conscientia gloriari potuissent Illi autem quid egerunt? Nimirum, neglectis Dei impulsibus, ejusque honoris, gloriae, laudumque zelo, attenderunt tantum ad gloriam quisque propriam, nec non ad impulsus tenebrarum, vanitatum, sultitiarumque mentis suae, (ab humanae salutis inimico ad hoc adjuti,) quaerentes scilicet, quomodo sibi aliisque possent viri magni & sapientes haberi, ratiocinando de mundo & elementis, de coelo & terra, de numeris & motibus, figuris & angulis rectis ac curvis, de nive & pluvia, de aliorum factis & scriptis, deque ratiocinationum formis & artificiis, milleque aliis nugis vanissimis & in aere volitantibus chimaeris. Quo factum est non tantum ut impulsus Dei minus in se sentirent, sed & ut Deus, videndo eos frustra intus ase moveri, quem negligere decreverant; atque adeo culpabiliores & poenis severioribus magis obnoxios fieri; eas ne demererentur, impulsus suos retineret: At illi inde motibus tenebrosæ vanæque mentis suæ sese tradentes sine repagulo, ea sibi tanquam ad sapientiam aut felicitatem adipiscendam convenientia quæsiverunt & fecerunt quæ prorsus absurda, & nullatenus creaturas ad imaginem Dei & pro Deo factas decentia. Jam quæso, quid in talibus conscientia, aut provocatio ad conscientiam suam aliud esse posset, quam provocatio ad insanum & tenebrosum corruptionis suæ amorem, qui in eis est omnia? Quotusquisque autem nunc est, qui secundum Dei impulsus totam vitam, uti dictum, disposuerit, aut potius qui iis neglectis, se suaque figmenta consulere & sequi non amet? Quam rara ergo, imo quam nulla in omnibus fere est ea conscientia quæ non errare sit censenda: cum econtra, quam jactat maxima pars hominum conscientiam, ipsissimus sit errorum & malorum fons. Nullus quippe recta gaudet conscientia, nisi qui impulsibus vanæ atque corruptæ mentis naturæque suæ, tanquam exitiosis operandi principiis depositis, & (ut verbo sacro utar) cruci cum Christo confixis (quod Apostolo est purificare conscientiam ab operibus mortuis per sanguinem Christi) ab impulsu & vita Spiritus Dei novam vitam, novos impulsus, novum lumen, novum regimen, omniaque nova (uti in Christo e morte suscitato) suscepserit. Quicunque talis est, is demum, non alius, con-
units.tr: The doctrine of Paul is that man is so thoroughly plunged into corruption by sin that in him there is nothing but darkness, vanity and foolishness of mind, until God shines upon him through some rays of his inward operation, as he has done even for the Gentiles themselves, showing them his power, goodness and generosity, and at the same time convincing them that they ought to give him thanks and obey him, seeking his honour and glory, and to turn their way, casting off their foolish and vain reasonings and that mad desire by which they wished to seem wise both to themselves and to others. If they had heeded these things, judged and acted accordingly, then they would have had cause to boast of a sound and unerring conscience. But what did they do? Clearly, neglecting the impulses of God and the zeal for his honour, glory and praise, they attended only to each one's own glory, and to the impulses of the darkness, vanities and foolishness of their own minds (aided to this by the enemy of human salvation), seeking, namely, how they might be held great and wise by themselves and others, reasoning about the world and the elements, about heaven and earth, about numbers and motions, figures and right and curved angles, about snow and rain, about the deeds and writings of others, and about the forms and artifices of reasoning, and a thousand other trifles, most vain chimeras flitting in the air. The result was that they not only felt the impulses of God less within themselves, but also that God, seeing them stirring in vain within, whom they had decided to neglect, made them more guilty and more liable to severer punishments; lest they should deserve these, he would hold back their impulses. But they, surrendering themselves without restraint to the movements of their dark and vain minds, sought and did for themselves, as though to attain wisdom or happiness, things that were utterly absurd and by no means fitting for creatures made in the image of God and for God. Now I ask, what could conscience, or appeal to one's own conscience, in such people be, other than an appeal to the mad and dark love of their corruption, which is everything in them? And how few now are there who have ordered their whole life, as has been said, according to the impulses of God, or rather who, neglecting these, do not love to consult and follow themselves and their own inventions? How rare, then, indeed how almost none, among almost all people is that conscience which is not to be judged erroneous; whereas, on the contrary, that conscience which the greatest part of men boast of is the very source of errors and evils. For no one rejoices in a right conscience except one who has laid down the impulses of his vain and corrupt mind and nature as deadly principles of action, and (to use the sacred word) has crucified them with Christ (which for the Apostle is to purify the conscience from dead works through the blood of Christ), and who has taken up from the impulse and life of the Spirit of God a new life, new impulses, new light, a new rule, and all things new (as in Christ raised from the dead). Whoever is such, and no other, rejoices at last in a conscience that is not erroneous, judges rightly about things in the light of God, and knows that he has judged and judges rightly both directly and reflexively; and so then the appeal or attestation of his conscience has infinite weight, both among all those who...

units.la: { } conscientia gaudet non erronea, bene judicat de rebus in lumine Dei, & scit directe ac etiam reflexive se bene judicasse & judicare: atque adeo tunc provocatio seu attestatio conscientiæ suæ infinitum habet pondus, tum apud omnes qui eum talem norunt, nec minus apud se, ut tranquillus sit; tum quoque apud Deum, cujus divinum judicium is homo scit a suo non dissentire, imo scit, ut cum Davide (a) dicam, judicium suum (quod is homo judicat) a facie sive a præsentia Dei procedere. Cæteri vero cum conscientiam suam sibi aut aliis allegant, ad eamque provocant, non minus ridendi sunt aut miserandi, quam si apertis verbis amorem proprium restarentur: namque, ut cum Paulo loquar, (b) eorum mens & conscientia polluta sunt, &c. perinde ut ipsi ad omne bonum opus reprobabiles.
units.tr: The conscience that is not mistaken rejoices, judges rightly of things in the light of God, and knows both directly and by reflection that it has judged well and that it does judge well. Its appeal or attestation therefore carries infinite weight, both with all who know the person to be such, and no less with himself, so that he is at peace; and also with God, whose divine judgment this man knows does not differ from his own. Indeed, to use David's words (a), he knows that his judgment (which this man makes) proceeds from the face or presence of God. But others, when they plead their conscience to themselves or to others and appeal to it, deserve to be laughed at or pitied no less than if they were openly defending self-love. For, to speak with Paul, (b) their mind and conscience are defiled, etc., so that they are reprobate for every good work.

units.la: LVIII. Nolim negare multos intercedere status medios eorum, in quibus & Deus impulsibus dictaminibusque suis interiora movet, & tenebræ mentisque ac potestatis inimicæ corruptela suos etiam motus inspirant.
units.tr: LVIII. I would not deny that there are many intermediate states, in which God also stirs the inner person by his impulses and dictates, while the darkness and corruption of the hostile power and mind also inspire their own motions.

units.la: At hi, quamdiu corruptionem naturæ & amoris proprii non vicerunt nec ejecerunt, conscientiæ suæ fidere non debent. Ut ut enim radioli motusque divini insint: si tamen corruptio tenebræque cum amore proprio ibidem adhuc vivunt, suos illæ motus cum divinis miscent, turbant, confundunt: sic ut pura Dei lumina & motus impermixti discerni bene non possint ab impulsibus corrupti tenebrosique amoris: unde commixtione facta
units.tr: But such people, as long as they have not conquered and cast out the corruption of nature and self-love, must not trust their conscience. For although the rays and motions of the divine are present, if corruption and darkness together with self-love still live there, they mix, disturb and confuse their own motions with the divine ones. So the pure lights of God and his unmixed motions cannot well be distinguished from the impulses of corrupt and dark love. From this mixing

units.la: Conscientia dubia & media. facta divinorum motuum cum pravis chaos quoddam fit indigestum, ubi quicquid divini prius inerat extinguitur, & unde praeter actus absurdos, saepeque exitiosos & lamentabiles, nil oritur apud eos, qui fervore Zeli indomito se conscientiae suae motus exsequi debere clamitant; quemadmodum infeliciter visum est in multis qui vel enthusiasmum prae se tulerunt, vel sectas novas condere, vel jam conditas, aut etiam veritatem ipsam, sed sibi haud bene perspectam, defendere allaborarunt.
units.tr: Doubtful and intermediate conscience. the mixture of divine motions with wicked ones becomes a kind of undigested chaos, in which whatever was divine within is extinguished, and from which, apart from absurd and often destructive and lamentable acts, nothing arises among those who cry out that with untamed zeal they must carry out the movements of their conscience. This has unhappily been seen in many who either displayed enthusiasm, or strove to found new sects, or to defend those already founded, or even the truth itself, but which they themselves had not properly understood.

units.la: LIX. Quanto minus igitur staruendum est, conscientiam etiam mere erroneam sequendam esse, &c, quod pejus est, hominem eam sequendo, non ad vitia & perditionem, sed ad virtutem felicitatemque duci, idque ideo quoniam ille sic & non aliter, rem esse conjicit.
units.tr: LIX. Therefore it is all the less to be maintained that one must follow even a merely erroneous conscience, etc.; and what is worse, that a man who follows it is led not to vices and perdition but to virtue and happiness, simply because he conjectures that the matter is so and not otherwise.

units.la: Perinde dicas, eum, qui falsum lumen, aut falsum iter, aut ducem fallacem sequitur, quae ipse interim pro rectis verisque habeat, non tamen a scopo aberrare, neque in praecipitium ruere, aut in latronum manus incidere: idque propterea, quod judicet sese vero lumine, recta via, sincero ductore duci: aut eum, qui venenatis cibis vescitur, propterea veneno non infici, quod cibos eos salubres esse putet. Certe quemadmodum inter edulia corporea nonnulla sunt cibi salubres, qui vere nutriunt; alia vero sunt venena, quae inde comedentes occidunt: ita & de veritate & de virtute res se habet: hae sunt veri cibi animae, independenter ab opinionibus hominum: errores vero & vitia
units.tr: You might as well say that someone who follows a false light, a false road or a deceitful guide, which he meanwhile holds to be right and true, does not stray from his goal, nor rush over a precipice, nor fall into the hands of robbers, because he judges that he is led by the true light, the straight way, a sincere guide. Or you might say that someone who feeds on poisonous food is not infected by the poison because he thinks the food wholesome. Certainly, just as among bodily foods some are wholesome and truly nourish, while others are poisons that kill those who eat them, so it is with truth and virtue. These are the true food of the soul, independent of men's opinions; errors and vices

units.la: 59. Conscientia erronea nec sequenda est, nec ducit ad bonum. vitia, venena sunt animarum, easque juxta naturam suam venenatam perdunt & interimunt si assumantur, quicquid etiam de his animæ judicent opinione sua. An enim quoniam anima quæpiam judicabit, errores ecse lumen divinum, ideo ab errore illuminabitur ? Absurdum ! Et quando judicabit vitium aliquod sibi salubre esse, an idcirco vitium hoc eam sanam & beatam efficere poterit ?
units.tr: 59. An erroneous conscience is neither to be followed nor leads to good. are poisons of souls, and they destroy and kill them according to their poisonous nature if they are taken in, whatever the souls may think of them. For will a soul be enlightened from error because it judges that error is the divine light? Absurd! And when it judges some vice to be wholesome for itself, can that vice make it sound and blessed?

units.la: LX. Sed inquies, an ergo idem quoque dicendum si conscientiæ error sit invincibilis aut in ignorantia invincibili fundatus ? Respondeo, in rebus quæ virtutem & vitium felicitatem & miseriam æternam, sive summum bonum & maximum malum concernunt, nihil esse invincibile dicendum respectu hominis libertatis usu gaudentis, modo Dei beneficiis suoque officio deesse non velit. Si homo quivis instinctibus divinis attendere vellet, si sese illis daret, si quæ impotentiæ & malitiæ propriæ, vanitatis rerum seculi, soliditatis æternarum, officiique erga Deum, erga se & cætera omnia, eum faciunt conscium observaret ut ut initio minima, tunc utique, gradatim tamen, Deo illi lumen, pro mensura & ratione progressus sui magis magisque affundente, ad eam veri bonique cognitionem perventurus esset, quæ tandem luminosæ circa omnia conscientiæ adipiscendæ sufficeret. At vero quando conscii sunt homines se omnia bona ab Auctore optimo & accepisse & exspectare debere, neque tamen ei laudando & amando vivere volunt ; sique propriæ impotentiæ & pravitatis suæ convicti, seipsos tamen æstiment, & ab aliis magni fieri cupiant; si rerum vanitatem conspicientes, iltis tamen nugis ampleftendisse dedere insistant; si rationis suæ imbecillitatem quotidie experti, ad ea tamen medicamentosum lumen ex nugacissimis sæpe circa vana & puerilia obiecta cogitatis sibi quærant & exspectent: quo quæso jure verum lumen communicaret illis Deus? quove jure ipsi de ignorantia conquerentur invincibili, quæ revera culpabilissima est, non autem invincibilis nisi novo sensu, quando nempe homo non vult debito modo apud omnis boni Auctorem relictis nugis quærere animo humili quæ solide bona sunt; quando, etsi sese tenebrosum & impotentem rudemque asinum esse intus conficiat, se tamen omittere non vult, sed propias semper vias sequi amat? Tunc si quidem non velit a se desistere, ignorantia ejus illustrari & vinci non potest: sed maxima culpa non caret ejusmodi stupiditas.
units.tr: LX. But you will object: is the same to be said if the error of conscience is invincible, or founded on invincible ignorance? I answer: in matters that concern virtue and vice, happiness and eternal misery, or the highest good and the greatest evil, nothing can be called invincible with respect to a man who enjoys the use of liberty, provided he is not willing to fail in God's benefits and his own duty. If a man were willing to attend to the divine impulses, if he gave himself up to them, if he observed what makes him aware of his own impotence and malice, of the vanity of worldly things and the solidity of eternal ones, and of his duty towards God, towards himself and all the rest, then, however small at first, God would gradually pour light upon him, more and more, in proportion to the measure and manner of his progress, until he came to that knowledge of the true and good which would at last suffice to obtain a luminous conscience about all things. But when men are conscious that they ought to have received, and ought to expect, all good things from the best Author, yet are unwilling to live by praising and loving him; when, convicted of their own impotence and wickedness, they nevertheless esteem themselves and desire to be great in the eyes of others; when, seeing the vanity of things, they persist in embracing those trifles; when, daily experiencing the weakness of their reason, they nevertheless seek and expect from the most trifling thoughts, often about vain and childish objects, a healing light for themselves: by what right, I ask, would God communicate the true light to them? And by what right would they complain of invincible ignorance, which is in truth most culpable, and is invincible only in a new sense, namely when a man does not wish, in the proper way, to seek with a humble mind from the Author of every good what is solidly good, leaving aside trifles; when, although he inwardly recognises himself to be dark, impotent and a dull ass, he nevertheless does not wish to give up, but always loves to follow his own ways? Then, if he does not wish to desist from himself, his ignorance cannot be enlightened and overcome; but such stupidity is not free from the greatest guilt.

units.la: LXI. At vero inquies, ponamus aliquem qui benevolo animo & debitis viis veritatem atque virtutem quærat; Is sane non illico eas adipiscitur: sed tempore, eoque interdum longo, gradatim procedenti, opus esse nemo negabit: interea vero in vita agenda mille obveniunt occasiones ubi sine proeraftinatione non judicia solum circa res ferenda, sed etiam agendum est, antequam veritatis cognitio certa habeatur? Quid hic agat animus? Nonne tunc de rebus judicia efformet, & secundum ea actiones dirigat, quam optime se posse conscius est? Quo concesso, quia de veritate nondum certus est, nonne eo ipso regulam hanc supponis, conscientiam etiam erroneam sequendam esse: id recte fieri; adeoque nec virtuti nec felicitati adversari? Aut vero an contra conscientiam, etsi errantem, agendum esse dices? Antequam respondeam, omnino statuendum est, eum, de quo haec quaeruntur, animo vere sincero viis modo dictis veritatem solidam quaerere: id vero ni fit, consuli ei non posse, quicquid agat aut omittat, juxta aut contra conscientiam errantem: pariter enim ad interitum properat. Qui autem bene quaerit, necdum tamen invenit, sed ignorat; is non quidem agat & judicet contra conscientiam errantem. Nam etsi interdum quae falsa aut mala perperam judicantur, ipsissima sint bonitas & veritas, mentis adhuc tenebrosae & aegrae dispositionibus malis adversantes: quia tamen Deus non vult ullius libertati in admittendo vero bonoque vim fieri, ideo non probat ut quis ea agat quae non sponte, sed reluctante animo esset facturus. Sed tamen non infertur inde, eum debere errantem conscientiam sequi. Si res officii sui non sint, neque necessariae, aut maximopere urgentes, abstinere ab illis atque quiescere optimum est; sin vero urgeant nec differri queant, tunc sine gravi periculo ex conscientia, quamvis errante, fieri demum poterunt quando homo eas sic aggredietur, ut ex animo sibi quidem diffidente, ad Deum vero cum timore recurrente, vere coram cordium scrutatore attestari possit. “fit: Equidem nofti, Deus, quam vel-” lem hoc in casu ea scire & facere quæ coram te optima sunt, meque ideo non rejectis mediis animo humili a te quantum potui lumen & gratiam postulasse: verum quia ob rationes justas, tibique notas, indigno mihi ea pro voto nondum suppetunt, & tamen in eo sim statu ut actio differri non possit, ecce, agam quod apparet rux voluntati non adversari & verò mihi aliisque ad salutem conducere. Id tu prospera: & si quid me insciô subsit mali, tu paterne condona non malevole erranti, lapsum verò erige, meque inde humiliorem mihique abjectiorem effice; atque largire, in poslerum eam luminis & regiminis tui copiam, qua quæ tibi grata sunt judicem & faciam semper. Talem aut errare graviter non permittet Deus; aut vero si gravis erroris materia subsit, ab actione suscipienda eum adinirandis providentiæ suæ curis revocabit. Est namque ille eorum Deus, qui ipsum sincere & humiliter requirunt, atque adeo non magis auxilio suo eis qui tales sunt deesse potest, quam desinere esse Deus. Cæterum non est quod quis & tempus fallat pretiosum, & se ipsum aliosve inutiliter vexet, casus conscientiæ proponendo imaginarios aut chimæricos, qui vel nunquam accident, aut vero qui supponunt Deum prope non adesse invocantibus eum in veritate, neque illum eis de consilio & ope tunc eam necesse erit, provisurum. Scholarum ardelionibus, qui de omnibus quæ sunt & quæ non sunt decídendi gloriam aucupantur, ista sunt relinquenda.
units.tr: LXI. But you will object: let us suppose someone who seeks truth and virtue with a benevolent mind and by the proper ways. He certainly does not attain them at once; no one will deny that time, and sometimes a long time, is needed as he advances gradually. Meanwhile, in the conduct of life, a thousand occasions arise where judgments must be formed about things, and action taken, without delay, before certain knowledge of the truth is had. What is the mind to do here? Should it not then form judgments about things and direct its actions accordingly, as well as it is conscious it can? Granting this, since it is not yet certain of the truth, do you not by that very fact assume this rule: that even an erroneous conscience is to be followed, that this is rightly done, and so is not opposed to virtue or happiness? Or will you say that one must act against conscience, even an erring one? Before I answer, it must be settled that the man about whom these questions are asked seeks solid truth by the ways just mentioned with a truly sincere mind. If this is not so, he cannot be helped, whatever he does or omits, whether according to or against an erring conscience, for either way he hastens to ruin. But one who seeks well, yet has not yet found and is still ignorant, should indeed not act and judge against an erring conscience. For although sometimes what is wrongly judged false or evil may be truly goodness and truth, opposed by the evil dispositions of a mind still dark and sick, nevertheless, since God does not want violence done to anyone's liberty in admitting what is true and good, he does not approve that someone do those things which he would do not willingly but with a reluctant mind. Yet it does not follow from this that he ought to follow an erring conscience. If the matters are not his duty, nor necessary, nor most pressing, it is best to abstain from them and be at rest. But if they press and cannot be deferred, then they can in the end be done without grave danger from a conscience, however erring, when a man approaches them in such a way that, distrusting himself and turning to God with fear, he can truly attest before the searcher of hearts: "Yes, you know, God, how much I would wish in this case to know and do what is best in your sight, and that therefore, not rejecting the means, I have asked you with a humble mind for light and grace as much as I could; but because, for reasons just and known to you, what I desire is not yet granted to me, unworthy as I am, and yet I am in such a state that the action cannot be deferred, behold, I will do what appears not to oppose your will and to be conducive to salvation for me and for others. Prosper this; and if any evil lies hidden in it unknown to me, mercifully pardon me in my error, not with ill will, but raise up what has fallen, and make me the more humble and the more abject in my own eyes; and grant me hereafter that abundance of your light and guidance by which I may judge and always do what is pleasing to you." God will not allow such a one to err grievously; or, if a grave matter of error lies within, he will recall him from the undertaking by the marvellous cares of his providence. For he is the God of those who seek him sincerely and humbly, and so he cannot be wanting to such people in his help any more than he can cease to be God. Moreover, there is no reason for anyone to waste precious time, and uselessly to trouble himself and others, by proposing imaginary or chimerical cases of conscience, which either never happen, or which suppose that God is not near to those who call upon him in truth, and that he will not then provide them with counsel and help as need requires. Such matters should be left to the scholastic triflers, who seek the glory of deciding on all things that are and are not.

units.la: LXII. De falsis quæ in Ethices fundamentis apud celebriores occurrunt, solito copiosius dixi, quoniam inter scientias omnes ea momenti est maximi, magna secum trahens aut commoda aut incommoda. In cæteris agam contracius, & de arte quidem Logica, ut quo cœptum est ordine pergatur, nil supera-dam iis, quæ ad eam rem, dum de superficiaria eruditione agebam, attuli. Ex iis facile videre est, quantum deest veri, quantum insit falsi Dialecticæ communi sive Logicis vulgaribus, quæ tantum abest ut adolescentum animos ad eruditionem veram (quod Logices officium esset) disponant aut adjuvent, ut eos potius garrulos, rixosos, arrogantes & pertinaces, indociles atque ad veritatem solidam admittendam ineptos efficiant; sic ut non immerito gratulandum sit eis, qui vel ejusmodi Circæo poculo infecti non sunt; vel oblivionis beneficio, se ab illo expurgarunt. Abunde observant ad virilem ætatem provecti, postquam e scholis egressi, ad res serias convertuntur se nil adeo emolumenti ex illis nugis elicuisse, ut aperte sese ludibrio omnium exponerent si ex earum indole negotia, aut etiam scientias, tractare vellent. Sed quoniam plures de isto argumento egerunt, relinquam illud, postquam monuero, ut attendam veritatis cupidi qui fieri possit ut eruditio falsa evitetur, quando quæ rotius eruditionis clavis & instrumentum dicitur, Logica, ipsa falsa & perniciosa propinatur. Logica. LXIII. GRAMMATICÆ, sive arti quæ sermonem tum formare tum intelligere docet, nil falsi inesse dicerem, modo ii qui se vel alios ea imbuere volunt, verum ejus usum scopumque considerarent, operamque suam ad eum potissimum accommodarent. Ante omnia disp iciendum esset, quonam in genere quove in commercio rerum necessariarum & utilium cuique juxta rationem vitæ amplectendæ opus foret tum conceptus suos aliis ore aut scripto exprimere, tum aliorum concipere.
units.tr: LXII. I have spoken of the falsehoods found in the foundations of Ethics among the more celebrated writers more fully than usual, since of all the sciences this one is of the greatest importance, bringing with it either great advantages or great disadvantages. In the other fields I shall be briefer. To keep to the order I have begun, I shall add nothing on Logic to what I brought forward on that subject while treating superficial erudition. From these points it is easy to see how much truth is lacking and how much falsehood is present in common Dialectic, or in the popular Logicians. Far from disposing or helping young minds toward true erudition, which ought to be the office of Logic, it makes them talkative, quarrelsome, arrogant and obstinate, unteachable, and unfit to accept solid truth. So those deserve congratulation who have not been infected by this Circean cup, or who have purged themselves of it by the kindness of forgetfulness. Those who have grown to manhood, left the schools, and turned to serious affairs commonly observe that they gained so little profit from those trifles that they would openly expose themselves to the ridicule of everyone if they tried to handle business, or even the sciences, according to their nature. But since many have written on this subject, I shall leave it, after advising those who love the truth to consider how false erudition can be avoided when Logic, which is called the key and instrument of all erudition, is itself served up as false and pernicious. Logic. LXIII. I would say there is nothing false in GRAMMAR, the art that teaches how to form and understand speech, provided that those who wish to imbue themselves or others with it consider its true use and aim, and direct their labour chiefly to that. Above all, it should be made clear in what kind of dealing with necessary and useful things, according to the rule of life each person embraces, he needs both to express his concepts to others by word or writing and to grasp those of others.

units.la: Atque ita deinde rem sine ambagibus aggredi oporteret, ea edisc endo simpliciter, quibus & se aliis in re proposita intelligibiles, & alios sibi, redderent. At quando solidis & neceffariis posthabitis, vanarum', imo & exitialium cogitationum rerumque commercium sibi proponunt, nec non id agunt, ut nugas subtiles, vel turpitudines impuras, aut adulationes insanas, & quæ supra noravimus, veterum quorundam aretalogorum sermonem, psittacorum instar imitantes, fritinniant; tunc sane fallax & damnosum eruditionis falsæ atque exitiosæ instrumentum fit atque adminiculum Grammatica.
units.tr: The subject should then be approached without circumlocution, learning simply those things by which they may make themselves intelligible to others on the matter at hand, and make others intelligible to themselves. But when, neglecting solid and necessary things, they propose to themselves commerce with vain and even deadly thoughts and things, and aim to chatter like parrots about subtle trifles, impure filthiness, insane flattery, and the speech of those old aretalogi mentioned above, then Grammar indeed becomes a deceitful and harmful instrument and aid of false and pernicious erudition.

units.la: De filiola ejus, Diva CRITICA, quæ & matre argutior, & verò delicatulæ atque admodum sagaciter tornatæ habitudinis meretricula gestit videri, idem sentiendum est quando bona (in regulis ubi de hoc subjecto egimus, ostensa) negligit, mala autem (ibidem indicata) & amplectitur, & novis præterea cumulat: quando se solam librorum, etiam sacrorum, clavem venditat; & tamen, scopo eorum ac mente omissis, sic literalibus, chronologicis, historicis minutiis frigide adhaeret, ut ob circumstantiolas quasdam alicubi forte non observatas, res ipsas fructuosissimas non negeat modo; aut substantiam solidissimarum, quae captum suum superant, judicet & condemnet: sed etiam blasphemet & irrideat. Et nihilominus magnos sibi interim progressus facere ingeniaque lucra comparare videtur, eo quod parvulis observatiunculis, iisque rarius occurrentibus, ( quia nugamenta ejusmodi a solidioribus ingeniis, tanquam objecta suis studiis indigna, praetermittuntur) totae afficiantur & repleantur angustiores animae; omnino quemadmodum pueruli, qui dum ossiculis ob cassam nucem ludunt, ex ludicro ejusmodi lucello magis afficiuntur, quam ex totius hereditatis paternae solidioribus bonis. Faciunt sane id Critici quando divinis operibus tum naturalibus, tum supernaturalibus atque internis suisque deque habitis & neglectis, cassa vanaque hominum scripturientium opera, cortice tenus adradenda, praeponunt: in quibus ubi progressus illos suos pluisculum extendisse videntur, tum vero rem maximi momenti sese praestitisse sibi persuadent, atque in imaginariis suis thesauris triumphant; praesertim postquam ramentis suis paedagogicis superaddiderint historicas notitias variarum cogitationum, etiam maxime anomalarum, quas alii quibusvis de rebus habuerunt; nec non factorum quae ubivis in mundi theatro vani mortales exhibuere, immanem farraginem coacerva instrumenta sane nec non incrementa atque coronidem accepisse; adeoque hisce horridis fere monstris tantum, non autem Deo per omnes istas artes, litari. Quæ cum elegantiorem præ cæteris eruditionis ac veritatis larvam præ se ferant; hominum autem exitium, vitiorumque augmentum, atque adeo miseriam non minus quam cæteras promoveant, non minus etiam quam cæteras inter fallacissimas his de causis sunt annumerandæ. Quamvis enim earum materia in se non sit falsa, qualis est præcedentium, est tamen & vana & multo plus damni quam commodi afferens: utilitas autem si qua interdum inde esse possit, non tamen tanta est atque fingitur: & verò quæ revera talis est, ea quomodo tutò haberi possit, ostendimus ubi de eruditione solida acquirenda actum est. Neque æstimandum est, eos, qui prorsus Deo Optimo Sapientissimoque traditi sorent, ab eo sic neglectum iri, ut ipsis, sicubi re aut luce aliqua opus haberent, non provideretur ab illo, & quidem ita ut ad sola utilia & necessaria manu ducerentur, prætermissis multis noxiis & inutilibus, quæ cum ab aliis, tum præcipue ab istis artibus disciplinisque Mathematicis, copiosissime procedunt.
units.tr: Concerning her younger daughter, the goddess CRITICISM, who wishes to seem more clever than her mother, and to appear a dainty little harlot of very finely turned bearing, the same must be said when she neglects the good things (shown in the rules where we treated this subject) but embraces the bad (pointed out there) and moreover piles new ones upon them. It applies when she peddles herself as the sole key to books, even sacred ones, and yet, with their aim and mind set aside, clings so coldly to literal, chronological and historical trifles that, because of some little circumstances perhaps not noticed somewhere, she not only denies the most fruitful matters but judges and condemns the substance of the most solid things, which exceed her grasp, and even blasphemes and mocks them. Nevertheless, she seems to herself to be making great progress and gaining profit for her talent, because narrower souls are wholly taken up and filled with tiny observations, and rare ones at that (since such trifles are passed over by the more solid minds as unworthy of their studies). This is like little boys who play with knucklebones for a worthless nut, and are more delighted by such a trifling childish gain than by the solid goods of a whole paternal inheritance. Critics certainly do this when they put the vain and empty labours of scribbling men, to be scraped only on the surface, before divine works, both natural and supernatural, inner and their own, and before the things they have and neglect. When their progress seems to have extended a little, they persuade themselves that they have achieved something of the greatest moment, and they triumph in their imaginary treasures. This is especially so after they have added to their pedagogical scraps historical notices of various opinions, even the most anomalous, which others have held about all sorts of things, and of the deeds which vain mortals have displayed anywhere on the stage of the world. Having heaped up this immense hodgepodge, they think they have received instruments, increases and a crown, and so with these horrid, almost monstrous things, and not with God, they seek to propitiate through all these arts. Since these bear a more elegant mask of erudition and truth than the rest, yet promote the ruin of men, the increase of vices, and misery no less than the others, they must be counted among the most deceptive, no less than the others, for these reasons. For although their matter in itself is not false, as that of the preceding arts is, it is nonetheless vain and brings much more harm than benefit. Any usefulness it may sometimes have is not nearly as great as it is pretended, and how what is truly useful can be safely held we have shown where we treated of acquiring solid erudition. Nor should we think that those who have been wholly given over to the Most Good and Most Wise God will be so neglected by him that, wherever they need some matter or light, it would not be provided by him, and indeed they would be led by the hand only to useful and necessary things, with the many harmful and useless ones, which proceed most copiously not only from other arts and disciplines but especially from the Mathematical ones, passed over.

units.la: LXV. Neque hoc tantum, sed periculosis- simis, ni caveatur, dispositionibus imbuere solet animas intemperantius occupatas genius Mathematicus.
units.tr: LXV. Not only this, but the Mathematical genius is wont to imbue souls that are too intemperately occupied with it with most dangerous dispositions, unless they are guarded against.

units.la: Inficit enim eas fatalismo, stupiditate sive insensibilitate spirituali, brutalismo, incredulitate & præsumtione ferme insanabili. Nam quando in pertractandis standis numeris, figuris & machinis suis, omnia vident ex se invicem sequi veluti fataliter, non autem ex libertate; inde principiis & nexibus rerum quasi necessariis & fatalibus considerandis sic afflusiunt, ut e rerum, etiam spiritualium, natura & regimine libertatem prorsus eliminent, fatalemque in omnibus necessitatem adstruant, etiam in se ipsis, repugnante conscientia & interno sensu, (adeo insensibiles sibi facti!) imo & in ipso Deo, cosuque in notionem ejus Suffıcientiæ sine sensu impingentes. Et quoniam in operationibus Mathematicis vident supposita data manere, neque verò minui vel augeri, unde tuto conclusiones ex proportionibus datorum deducunt: idem etiam in physicis voluerunt inter principia supponere, naturæ videlicet materiam positam, positamque motus quantitatem manere, nec augeri: quod & sine causa statuunt, & verò tum contra fœcunditatem & activitatem Dei, tum contra experientiam in nobiliori parte naturæ, in mentibus dico, quæ numerosiore substantia augentur in dies, & in quibus, positâ unâ cogitatione, ejusque uno motu sive impulsu & affectu, plures in infinitum sequuntur; quæ in natura corporea, spiritualis naturæ velut umbrâ, suam proculdubio habent analogiam. Cum autem ex crassis suis quantis, numeratis, figuratis & motis, effectus vident sequi vi materiata & figurata, non autem ex intentione aliqua mentali; inde disponuntur ad negationem nobilis istius causæ finalis quæ nil aliud est in rerum universitate quam.
units.tr: They infect them with fatalism, spiritual stupidity or insensibility, brutishness, unbelief, and a presumption that is almost incurable. When they handle fixed numbers, figures and their machines, they see everything following from one another as if by fate and not by freedom. So in considering the principles and connections of things as necessary and fated, they are so carried along that they completely eliminate freedom from the nature and government of things, including spiritual things, and they assert a fated necessity in all things, even in themselves, though conscience and inner sense resist (so insensible have they become!). Indeed they even bring it into God himself, and so they stumble upon the notion of his sufficiency without any feeling. And since in mathematical operations they see that the given assumptions remain fixed and are neither diminished nor increased, from which they safely draw conclusions from the proportions of the given quantities, they have wanted to assume the same among the principles of physics: namely, that the matter of nature is fixed, and that the quantity of motion once set remains and is not increased. They lay this down without cause, and indeed it is contrary both to the fruitfulness and activity of God, and to experience in the nobler part of nature, I mean minds, which grow in number daily, and in which, once a single thought, and its single motion or impulse and affection, is posited, many more follow without limit. In corporeal nature these have, no doubt, their analogy, as a kind of shadow of spiritual nature. But since, from their gross quantities, counted, shaped and moved, they see effects following from material and figured force, and not from some mental intention, they are disposed to deny that noble final cause, which in the whole universe of things is nothing other than the adorable Wisdom of God, who so destines all things for its uses that by the power of his will such things come to be and exist, and not by a fated and mathematical governing of extended things, without purpose and according to certain blind rules of motion and figure.

units.la: ¹ Text ends at the foot of the page; no further notes printed. quam adoranda Dei Sapientia, omnia ad usus suos sic destinans, ut vi voluntatis suæ ideo talia fiant & exsistant; non autem ex fatali & mathematico rerum extensarum sine scopo & juxta regulas quasdam brutas motarum & figuratarum regimine. Et quoniam de minusculis suis objectis quantitatis nil admittere solent, nisi demonstrationes habeant palpabiles; idem genus agendi ad divinora, ( quorum tamen intelligendorum mentes hominum corruptæ adhuc sunt incapaciores, quam cœcus recipiendi luminis) volunt extendere; atque adeo valde proclives fiunt ut nihil de illis (siquidem ea capere non possint) fide admittant: quod perinde est, ac si cœcus nollet credere corporum figuras lumine percipi, eo quod lumen non palpet: aut ac si filius patrem, paternasque voluntates & res nollet agnoscere, amplecti, reverereri, nisi prius ipsi mathematice demonstretur hunc suum esse patrem, quæque sit paternarum rerum voluntatisque natura. Et sane miror eos ad practicum in omnibus Pyrrhonismum non item deduci, quandoquidem in rebus agendis demonstrationes Mathematicæ haberi non possint: sintque respectu nostri res divinæ, (hoc est, intellectus, facultatumque omnium Deo & placito ejus subjectio) non minus practicæ quam res quæ civiles & œconomicæ vocantur. Denique ex eodem fonte non parva quoque tentantur præsumtione, seu indocili arrogantia, si quando, cogitantes se de objectis scientiæ suæ demonstrationes & certitudines scientisicas habere, sibi quoque persuadeant se similiter quam plurima alia in scientiis, rebus artibusve aliis scire: tunc enim cætera illa quasi inter demonstrata ejusdem cum prioribus evidentiæ connumerantes, quæcunque aliunde tantisper hisce opposita sibi proponi possent, non minori cum indignatione vel fastidio rejiciunt, ac si audirent sibi persuaderi velle bis bina non esse quatuor, aut trigoni angulos duobus rectis non æquipollere. Quæ quidem animi dispositiones omnes quantum sint præcavendæ, &, ni caveantur, quantum detrimenti solidæ eruditioni, virtuti & felicitati afferant, falsam autem eruditionem quam promoveant; omnibus, quorum interest, perpendendum relinquo.
units.tr: ¹ Text ends at the foot of the page; no further notes printed. And since they are wont to admit nothing about their small objects of quantity unless they have palpable demonstrations, they want to extend the same kind of procedure to divine things (though the minds of men, corrupted as they are, are less capable of understanding these than a blind man is of receiving light). And so they become very prone to admit nothing of those things on faith (since they cannot grasp them). This is just as if a blind man were unwilling to believe that the shapes of bodies are perceived by light, because he cannot touch the light; or as if a son were unwilling to acknowledge, embrace and revere his father and his paternal wishes and affairs, unless it were first demonstrated to him mathematically that this is his father, and what the nature of paternal affairs and will is. And indeed I am surprised that they are not likewise led to practical Pyrrhonism in everything, since demonstrations of mathematical kind cannot be had in matters of action, and divine things, (that is, the understanding and the subjection of all our faculties to God and his good pleasure), with respect to us, are no less practical than the things called civil and economic. Finally, from the same source, no small presumption, or unteachable arrogance, is also attempted, when, thinking that they have demonstrations and scientific certainties about the objects of their own science, they also persuade themselves that they similarly know very many other things in the sciences, matters, or other arts. For then, counting those other things among the things demonstrated with equal evidence to their earlier conclusions, they reject with no less indignation or disdain whatever might be put before them from elsewhere as opposed to these, as if they heard someone wanting to persuade them that twice two is not four, or that the angles of a triangle are not equal to two right angles. How much all these dispositions of mind are to be guarded against, and, unless they are guarded against, how much harm they do to solid learning, to virtue and to happiness, and what false learning they promote, I leave for all those concerned to consider.

units.la: LXVI. Verum objiciet forte nonnullus
units.tr: LXVI. But perhaps someone will object

units.la: ea, vel iis similia, quæ in præfatione Novorum Geometriæ Elementorum a Janseniistis jam aliquot abhinc annis editorum, leguntur: per Geometriæ videlicet (abstractæ præsertim) studium sive peritiam, haud parum juvari posse mentes ad pietatem, concupiscentiarum diminutionem, animi æquitatem, ad puræ spiritualisque veritatis amorem, ad veritatis solidioris agnitionem & criterium, ad firmandum, itemque extendendum intellectum rationemque, ad agnoscendam magnitudinem, immaterialitatem, immortalitatemque animæ: quæ omnia suis fulcire volunt rationibus, speciem quidem coram humana corruptaque ratione habentibus; sed quæ ad lumen verum divinumque admotæ mera sunt sophismata.
units.tr: these things, or things similar to them, which are read in the preface to the New Elements of Geometry published some years ago by the Jansenists: that through the study or skill of Geometry (especially abstract geometry) minds can be greatly helped toward piety, toward diminishing concupiscence, toward equanimity of soul, toward love of pure and spiritual truth, toward knowledge and the criterion of more solid truth, toward firming up and also extending the understanding and reason, and toward recognising the greatness, immateriality and immortality of the soul. All of these they wish to support with arguments which have an appearance before corrupt human reason, but which, when brought before the true and divine light, are mere sophisms.

units.la: Nam qui ad pietatem conferre censenda est ea scientia, quae est scientia distractionis a Deo, totam animam occupans frigidis quibusdam speculationibus de sterilissimis inutilitatibus & naeniis, quales sunt quae pro subtilissimis maximeque arduis a peritioribus hujus artis quaeruntur & comprobantur? Qui concupiscentias diminuere juvabit id, quod vice concupiscentiae carnis & suscipitur a concupiscentia oculorum, sive curiositate vana, & verotum hanc, tum perniciosissimas concupiscentias laudum, passiones complacentiae in se, voluptates subtiliores rationis, vitia superbiae excitat vicissim, fovetque & corroborat? Idne etiam ad solidam animi aequitatem disponet, quod allicit mentes ad capitale hoc iniquitatis genus, ut tempus, vita, studia, quae Deo, saluti propriae & proximorum, rebusque necessariis debentur, iis subripiantur furto, tradanturque indignis nullius commodi speculationibus, quae ideo quod nullius commodi sint, speculatoribus suis vocabuntur pure veritates; amorque earum, amor veritatis merae & spiritualis, utpote ubi nullus, inquiunt, respectus ad ullum emolumentum haberi potest, hoc est, opinor, quae sint instar filorum aranearum? Bone Deus, quid audio! Notiunculae & speculationes futiles de crassioris substantiae lineis & superficiebus, & massis, & agitationibus, dicendae fuerint veritates purae & spirituales, mediumque ad amorem & acquisitionem veritatum divinorum & coelestium. Atqui ex eo quod anima assuescit se, amorem & affectus suos tradere inutilibus & pulverulentis minutiis, putarem ego in ea suffocari affectus erga veritates vere puras & spirituales, hoc est, coelestes & divinas & solidas: quod & ratione & experientia tristi plus nimis confirmatur; uti & hoc, nullos esse ad veritates solidas & momentosas percipiendas agnoscendasque minus aptos, quam qui ex armamentario exercitii Mathematici insignia quaedam adminicula ad criterium veritatis dignoscendum exspectant. Sunt namque veritatiuncularum pulverulentarum, veritatumque divinarum & solidarum diversa prorsus (ut vidimus) criteria, diversaque lumina: ita ut ex tractatione & cognitione crassa ac palpatoria (ut sic dicam) materiarum Mathematicarum ad conspicandas res atque rerum solidas veritates, cum criteriis suis non magis praeparari possit animus, quam caecus, qui res corporeas palpationis criterio novit, hinc ad percipiendum dignoscendumque lumen, colores, & cetera quae luminis oculorumque ope noscuntur, disponi queat. Neque minus a vero abest, intellectum iisdem atque rationem firmari & extendi: extenditur quidem & dilatatur ad res abjectas, viles, minutas indignasque mentis divinioris occupatione; at hoc ipsum est intellectus vires & alas ad divina frangere capacitatemque ejus coartare, quando tam saepe se contrahit ut pulvisculos complectatur, tamque frequenter se redigit ad reculas tantillas, quarum e contra depositione, contemtu & oblivione intellectus ad diviniora & solidiora vividius, penetrantius & abundantius capienda fit ideoneus, testibus quotquot rem sunt experti. Kempifius : (a) Quanto aliquis magis sibi unitus & interius simplificatus fuerit, tanto plura & altiora sine labore intelligit, quia desuper lumen intelligentiæ accipit: quæ egregie Gallicus Paraphraftes versibus sic expressit : Plus l'esprit se fait simple, & plus il se rameine Dans un interieur degagé des objets ; Plus lors sa connoissance est diffuse & certaine, Et s'elève sans peine Jusqu'aux plus hauts sujets.
units.tr: For how is that science to be counted as conducive to piety, which is a science of distraction from God, occupying the whole soul with certain cold speculations about most barren trifles and trivia, such as those that the more skilled practitioners of this art seek out and prove as most subtle and most difficult? Will it help to diminish concupiscence, when it stirs up and in turn fosters and strengthens that which takes the place of the concupiscence of the flesh and is taken up by the concupiscence of the eyes, namely vain curiosity; and, at the same time, the most pernicious concupiscences of praise, the passions of self-complacency, the subtler pleasures of reason, and the vices of pride? Will that which draws minds to this capital kind of injustice also dispose them to a solid equanimity of soul, namely that time, life, studies, which are owed to God, to one's own salvation and to one's neighbours, and to necessary things, are stolen away from them and handed over to speculations of no use to anyone, which, because they are of no use, are called by their practitioners pure truths; and the love of these, the love of pure and spiritual truth, since, they say, no regard to any advantage can be had there, that is, I suppose, they are like threads of spiders? Good God, what do I hear! Little notions and idle speculations about lines, surfaces, masses and motions of grosser substance are to be called pure and spiritual truths, and a means to the love and acquisition of divine and heavenly truths! Yet from the fact that the soul accustoms itself to surrender its love and affections to useless and dusty trifles, I would think that its affections toward truths that are truly pure and spiritual, that is, heavenly, divine and solid, are suffocated in it; and this is confirmed too much by reason and by sad experience. So too is this: that there are none less fit to perceive and recognise solid and weighty truths than those who expect from the armoury of mathematical exercise certain distinguished aids for discerning the criterion of truth. For there are indeed quite different criteria and different lights for dusty little truths and for divine and solid truths (as we have seen). So just as a blind man, who knows corporeal things by the criterion of touch, cannot thence be prepared to perceive and discern light, colours, and the other things that are known by the help of light and the eyes, so the mind cannot be prepared, by the crude and tactile (so to speak) handling and knowledge of mathematical matters, to behold things and their solid truths with their own criteria. Nor is it less far from the truth that the understanding and reason are firmed up and extended by the same means. It is indeed extended and enlarged towards abject, vile, minute things unworthy of the occupation of a more divine mind; but this very thing breaks the powers and wings of the understanding for divine things, and confines its capacity, when it so often contracts to embrace dust-motes, and so frequently reduces itself to tiny trifles. On the contrary, by setting these aside, despising them and forgetting them, the understanding becomes fit to grasp diviner and more solid things more vividly, penetratingly and abundantly, as all who have experienced it bear witness. Kempis: (a) The more one is united to oneself and inwardly simplified, the more and higher things one understands without labour, because one receives the light of understanding from above. The French paraphrast has expressed this excellently in verse: The more the spirit makes itself simple, and the more it withdraws into an interior freed from objects, the more its knowledge becomes diffuse and certain, and rises without effort to the highest subjects.

units.la: Oui, Dieu prodigue alors ses graces plus entieres, Et portant n'btre idée au dessus de nos sens, Il nous donne d'entraut d'autant plus de lumieres, Qui percent les matieres Par des traits plus puissants.
units.tr: Yes, then God pours out his graces more fully, and lifting our thought above our senses, he gives us within, more and more, lights that pierce through matters with more powerful strokes.

units.la: Aliam viam & oppositam quidem commendare, est ignorare, quando intellectus ad divina & momentosa disponatur. Mentis autem magnitudinem inde perspici, hoc est, inde patere mentem esse magnam & ampliffimam gesticulatricem in rebus nauci, exilem autem & abjectissimam, quæ se tantulis pulvisculis pariatur detineri & ligari, fateor melius per ista agnosci quam ejusdem inde immortalitatem probari: Nam quæ hæc est consequentia? Anima immaterialis cogitat de iis quæ concernunt quantitatem. Ergo non desinet cogitare in æternum, sive, est immortalis? Nexum capiat qui potest.
units.tr: To recommend another and opposite way is to be ignorant, when the intellect is disposed toward divine and weighty matters. But that the greatness of the mind is seen from this, that is, that the mind is great and very ample in gesturing about trifles, and slight and most abject when it allows itself to be held and bound by such tiny dusts, I admit is recognised better through these things than its immortality is proved thereby. For what kind of consequence is this? The immaterial soul thinks about things that concern quantity. Therefore it will not cease thinking for eternity, or, it is immortal? Let him who can grasp the connection.

units.la: LXVII. Ex quibus omnibus constat ma-gis
units.tr: LXVII. From all these things it is established more and more

units.la: gis magisque nulla numerosiora & nocentiora animæ impendere a scientiis pericula, quam ab iis de quibus quæstio est. Monui autem alicubi, (ut causa cavillandi præcidatur) ista non sic esse extendenda ad communia principia operationesque vulgares, quatenus ad vitæ usum sunt necessariæ: & præterea ex ipsis speculationibus vel vanissimis in cœcitate mentis dudum acquisitis, posse ab iis qui ad divina postmodum convertuntur, postliminio nonnulla bona deduci, veluti si ipsi qui has disciplinas callent, ubi se per eas insinuaverint in amicitiam & confidentiam eorum qui illis delectantur, eorundem deinde animos, jam eis addictos & confidentes, facilius convertant ad Deum unum; nec non & quasvis revocent animas, ad divina & æterna natas, a quæsitione & desiderio iltarum vanitatum, quæ cum ipsis perspectæ sint; de earum etiam inanitate quando testantur, merentur magis fidem, & plus etiam eis ab inexpertis creditur. Atque hic est verus ille horum retrogradus usus, non autem ut eas operosas nugas commendent imperitis & veritatem quærentibus, tanquam media quibus animæ ad divina & salutaria magis idoneæ reddantur; cum revera, etiamsi unum atque alterum inde posset emolumentum animæ rarius provenire, infinita sint & perniciosa, & ob nativam corruptionem certa nimis pericula in quæ concidunt ad unum fere omnes quotquot hac via procedunt.
units.tr: that from the sciences no more numerous or harmful dangers hang over the soul than from those things under discussion. I have warned somewhere (so that the occasion for quibbling is cut off) that these things are not to be extended so far as to common principles and ordinary operations, insofar as they are necessary for the use of life. Besides, from the very speculations, even the most vain ones acquired long ago in blindness of mind, some good things may be drawn back by those who afterwards turn to divine things. For example, if those who know these disciplines, having insinuated themselves through them into the friendship and confidence of those who delight in them, then more easily convert the minds of these, now attached and trusting to them, to the one God; and also if they recall souls born for divine and eternal things from the seeking and desire of those vanities, which they themselves have seen through, and when they bear witness to their emptiness, they deserve more trust, and more is believed of them by the inexperienced. This is the true retrograde use of these things, and not that they commend those laborious trifles to the unskilled and to those seeking truth, as means by which souls are made more fit for divine and saving things. For in fact, even if one or another advantage might rarely arise for the soul from them, they are infinite and pernicious, and on account of native corruption the dangers into which almost all who proceed this way fall are too certain.

units.la: Ita ut incassum prætextus utilitatum, nunquam hinc de facto emergentium, obtendantur
units.tr: So that, in vain, pretexts of usefulness, which never in fact emerge from these things, are put forward.

units.la: LXIII. GRAMMATICÆ, sive arti quæ sermonem tum formare tum intelligere docet, nil falsi inesse dicerem, modo ii qui se vel alios ea imbuere volunt, verum ejus usum scopumque considerarent, operamque suam ad eum potissimum accommodarent. Ante omnia dispiciendum esset, quoniam in genere quoveis commercio rerum necessariarum & utilium cuique juxta rationem vitæ amplectendæ opus foret tum conceptus suos aliis ore aut scripto exprimere, tum aliorum concipere.
units.tr: LXIII. Grammar, or the art that teaches us both to form speech and to understand it, I would say contains nothing false, provided that those who wish to imbue themselves or others with it consider its true use and aim, and direct their effort chiefly to that. Above all, it should be considered that, in general, for every commerce of necessary and useful things, which each person needs according to the rule of the life he is to embrace, it is required both to express his concepts to others by word or writing and to understand theirs.

units.la: Atque ita deinde rem fine ambagibus aggredi oporteret, ea ediscendo simpliciter, quibus & se aliis in re propositā intelligibiles, & alios sibi, redderent. At quando solidis & necessariis posthabitis, vanarum, imo & exitialium cogitationum rerumque commercium sibi proponunt, nec non id agunt, ut nugas subtiles, vel turpitudines impuras, aut adulationes insanas, & quæ supra notavimus, veterum quorundam aretalogorum sermonem, psittacorum instar imitantes, fritinniant; tunc sane fallax & damnosum eruditionis falsæ atque exitiosæ instrumentum fit atque adminiculum Grammatica.
units.tr: And then the matter should be approached without circumlocution, learning simply those things by which people make themselves intelligible to others in the matter proposed, and others intelligible to themselves. But when, with solid and necessary things set aside, they propose to themselves a commerce of vain, nay even destructive thoughts and things, and take care to chatter subtle trifles, or impure foulnesses, or insane flatteries, and those things we noted above, imitating the speech of certain old aretalogists like parrots, then indeed grammar becomes a deceitful and harmful instrument and aid of false and pernicious erudition.

units.la: De filiola ejus, Diva CRITICA, quæ & matre argutior, & vero delicatulæ atque admodum sagaciter tornatæ habitudinis meretriucula gestit videri, idem sentiendum est quando bona (in regulis ubi de hoc subjecto egimus, ostensa) negligit, mala autem (ibidem indicata) & amplectitur, & novis præterea cumulat: quando se solam librorum, etiam sacrorum, clavem venditat; & tamen, scopo eorum ac mente omissis, sic literalibus, chronologicis, historicis minutiis frigide adhaeret, ut ob circumstantiolas quasdam alicubi forte non observatas, res ipsas fructuosissimas non neget modo; aut substantiam solidissimarum, quae capcum suum superant, judicet & condemnet: sed etiam blasphemet & irrideat. Et nihilominus magnos sibi interim progressus facere ingentiaque lucra comparare videtur, eo quod parvulis observatiunculis, iisque rarius occurrentibus, (quia nugamenta ejusmodi a solidioribus ingeniis, tanquam objecta suis studiis indigna, praetermittuntur) totae afficiantur & repleantur angustiores animae; omnino quemadmodum pueruli, qui dum officiculis ob cassam nucem ludunt, ex ludicro ejusmodi lucello magis afficiuntur, quam ex totius hereditatis paternae solidioribus bonis. Faciunt sane id Critici quando divinis operibus tum naturalibus, tum supernaturalibus atque internis suisque deque habitis & neglectis, cassa vanaque hominum scripturientium opera, cortice tenus adradenda, praeponunt: in quibus ubi progressus illos suos pluisculum extendisse videntur, rum vero rem maximi momenti sese praestitisse sibi persuadent, atque in imaginariis suis thesauris triumphant; praesertim postquam ramentis suis paedagogicis superaddiderint historicas notitias variarum cogitationum, etiam maxime anomalarum, quas alii quibusvis de rebus habuerunt; nec non factorum quae ubivis in mundi theatro vani mortales exhibuere, immanem farraginem coacervaverint; non eo scopo, ut quid in illis veri aut falsi, boni aut mali, fugiendi vel admittendi sit, inquirant; sed tantum ut ex stolida quadam & morbosa curiositate sciant ipsi, & ex prædagogica superbia nonnullis vel publico prodant se scire quid aliorum cogitationibus & motibus acciderit. Qua in re ad eum modum insanire videntur ac si cæci quidam, de lumine aut visu recipiendo nil curantes, id unicum sibi agendum credèrent, ut sollicite inquirerent de gestis ac factis pictorum, deque suarum picturarum statu & proprietatibus, nec non de luce, & quinam de ea, & de coloribus, deque visu scripserint? quo tempore? quâ lingua? quot inde versiones? an bene factæ? an variantes dentur lectiones? qui codices optimi? quomodo implendæ lacunæ? & similia. Quod si cum frivolo hoc inaniarum & omnis generis ramentorum hinc inde congestorum magis magisque inflati, apparatu suo sese præ aliis sapere, eruditionem solidam a se solis possideri, cæteros qui sui similes non sint ab ea excludi, somnient; nonne tunc tibi videre videaris mendicos mente & oculis captos, qui ex proprio fundo nil possidentes, per civitatem vagabundi denariolos oftiatim emendicant atque veteramenta, cineres, lapillos, vitrea fragmenta vel e sterquiliniis & fimetis hinc inde collecta, tanquam gemmas pretiosas thesaurosque insignes ampleCtuntur; fervantque in sinu: & tum se ditissimos sic esse delirantes, postquam de iltis perbelle garrire assuefacti sunt, iis insultant quibus verÆ
units.tr: Concerning her little daughter, the goddess Criticism, who wishes to seem both more shrewd than her mother and a delicate little harlot of very cleverly turned habit, the same must be felt when she neglects the good things (shown in the rules where we treated this subject) but embraces the bad (indicated there) and moreover piles on new ones; when she sells herself as the sole key to books, even sacred ones; and yet, with their aim and mind omitted, she so coldly clings to literal, chronological and historical minutiae that, on account of some little circumstances perhaps not observed somewhere, she not only denies the most fruitful things themselves, but judges and condemns the substance of the most solid things, which surpass her capacity, and even blasphemes and mocks them. Nevertheless, she seems meanwhile to be making great progress and acquiring huge gains, because narrow souls are wholly affected and filled by tiny observations, and those rarely occurring (since such trifles are passed over by more solid minds as unworthy of their studies). They are like little boys who play at small chores for a worthless nut, and are more affected by such a playful little gain than by the more solid goods of their whole paternal inheritance. Critics certainly do this when they put the vain and empty labours of scribbling men, to be scraped only on the surface, before divine works, both natural and supernatural, and internal ones, and their own, both those held and those neglected. In these matters, when they seem to have extended their progress a little, they persuade themselves that they have accomplished something of the greatest moment, and they triumph in their imaginary treasures. This is especially so after they have heaped onto their pedagogical scraps an enormous mass of historical notices of various thoughts, even the most anomalous, which others have held about all sorts of things, and of deeds which vain mortals have displayed anywhere on the world's stage. They do this not with the aim of inquiring what in those things is true or false, good or bad, to be shunned or admitted, but only so that, out of a foolish and morbid curiosity, they themselves may know, and out of pedagogical pride may publicly reveal to some that they know what has happened to the thoughts and motions of others. In this they seem to rave like certain blind men, caring nothing for receiving light or sight, who believed that the only thing to do was to inquire carefully into the deeds and acts of painters, and the state and properties of their pictures, and also who wrote about light, and about colours and sight: at what time, in what language, how many translations thence, were they well made, are there variant readings, which manuscripts are best, how are the lacunae to be filled, and similar things. But if, puffed up more and more with this frivolous apparatus of vanities and scraps of every sort gathered here and there, they dream that they are wiser than others by their display, that solid learning is possessed by themselves alone, and that others who are not like them are excluded from it, then does it not seem to you that you see beggars, blind in mind and eyes, who, possessing nothing from their own estate, wander through the city begging pennies from door to door, and adorn themselves with old rags, ashes, pebbles, glass fragments, or things gathered here and there even from dunghills and dung heaps, as precious gems and remarkable treasures, and keep them in their bosom? Then, raving that they are so very rich, and having become accustomed to chatter prettily about those things, they insult those to whom true

units.la: — (no further text) veræ e propriis fundis emergunt possidenturque divitiæ, quibusque se miseri, tanquam qui soli solide divites sint, ridicule anteponunt? Tales profecto, si quem inter eruditos locum & titulos quærant, iis digni sunt, quos habere decet cœca eruditorum mendicabula.
units.tr: true riches emerge from and are possessed from their own estates, and which wretched men ridiculously prefer to themselves, as though they alone were solidly rich? Such men, if they seek a place and titles among the learned, are indeed worthy of those which befit the blind beggary of scholars.

units.la: LXIV. Dixi cum de superficiariis agerem, cur de cæteris artibus scientiisque nil speciatius moverem, quod nempe plerasque si non omnes, fundarentur præcipue in illis quarum defectus & falsa vidimus.
