Et quamvis nonnullæ non ita videantur speculationibus meris & inutilibus absolvi; sed ad praxin effectusque reales terminari, maxime ex quæ vel ex Mathesi oriuntur, vel eidem quasi implicantur, uti numerorum scientia, musica, astronomia, architectonica civilis, navalis, militaris, atque aliæ quæ magnatibus, mercatoribus, totique civili societati adeo prodesse videntur: tamen si quæ sine fructu sunt, ex iis ejiciserentur; si reliqua, quæ ad usum faciunt, ad bilancem rerum solidarum, æternitatis, amoris Dei & proximi, vitæque hic inter humilitatem & abstinentiam ad beatioris adeptionem transfigendæ, exigantur; si etiam experientia consulta, quinam revera inde fructus inter mortales redundaverint, inspiciamus; fateri cogemur, hominum avaritiam, lasciviam, superbiam, pompas, curiositatem, prodigalitatem, crudelitatem proximi oppressionem, turbulentam atque inordinatissimam vitam, homine, Dei opere, & Christi discipulo & membro indignam, hinc si non exordium, instru-
units.tr: LXIV. I said, when I was dealing with the superficial kinds, why I did not move more specifically against the other arts and sciences: namely, because most if not all of them are founded chiefly on those whose defects and falsehoods we have seen. And although some of them do not seem to be made up of pure and useless speculations, but are directed to practice and real effects, especially those that arise from mathematics or are, as it were, entangled with it, such as the science of numbers, music, astronomy, civil, naval and military architecture, and others which seem so useful to nobles, merchants and all civil society; yet if whatever is without fruit were cast out of them; if the rest, which serve use, were weighed in the balance of solid things, of eternity, of the love of God and neighbour, and of a life passed here between humility and abstinence in order to attain the more blessed; if also, experience consulted, we inspect what fruits have in fact flowed among mortals from them, we shall be compelled to confess that human avarice, lasciviousness, pride, pomp, curiosity, prodigality, cruelty, oppression of neighbour, and a turbulent and most disordered life, unworthy of a man, God's work, and a disciple and member of Christ, have received from these arts, if not their beginning, at least their instruments, increase and crown. Thus sacrifice is made through all these arts to these horrid monsters, and not to God.

units.la: 64. De cate- rarum scientia- rum, & specialium de Mathematicarum disciplinarum fallacia. instrumenta sane nec non incrementa atque coronidem accepisse; adeoque hisce horridis fere monstris tantum, non autem Deo per omnes istas artes, litari. Quæ cum elegantiorem præ cæteris eruditionis ac veritatis larvam præ se ferant; hominum autem exitium, vitiorumque augmentum, atque adeo miseriam non minus quam cæteræ promoveant, non minus etiam quam cæteræ inter fallacissimas his de causis sunt annumerandæ. Quamvis enim earum materia in se non sit falsa, qualis est præcedentium, est tamen & vana & multo plus damni quam commodi afferens: utilitas autem si qua interdum inde esse possit, non tamen tanta est atque fingitur: & verò quæ revera talis est, eaquomodo tutò haberi possit, ostendimus ubi de eruditione solida acquirenda actum est. Neque æstimandum est, eos, qui prorsus Deo Optimo Sapientissimoque traditi forent, ab eo sic neglectum iri, ut ipsis, sicubi re aut luce aliqua opus haberent, non provideretur ab illo, & quidem ita ut ad sola utilia & necessaria manu ducerentur, prætermissis multis noxiis & inutilibus, quæ cum ab aliis, tum præcipue ab istis artibus disciplinaisque Mathematicis, copiosissime procedunt.
units.tr: 64. Of the other sciences, and of the particular deceptions of the mathematical disciplines. They have indeed received their tools, and also their growth and crowning, and so it is only to these almost horrid monsters, and not to God, that sacrifice is made through all these arts. Although these arts wear a more elegant mask of learning and truth than the rest, they promote the ruin of men and the increase of vices, and misery no less than the others, and for these reasons they are to be counted among the most deceptive, no less than the others. For although their subject matter in itself is not false, as that of the preceding sciences is, it is nevertheless both vain and bringing far more harm than good. Any usefulness that may sometimes come from them is not as great as it is imagined; and as for what is truly useful, how it may be safely had, we have shown where we treated of acquiring solid learning. Nor is it to be supposed that those who have been wholly committed to the most good and wise God will be so neglected by him that, wherever they need some matter or light, it is not provided by him; indeed they are led by the hand only to what is useful and necessary, the many harmful and useless things being passed over, which come forth most abundantly both from other arts and especially from these mathematical arts and disciplines.

units.la: LXV. Neque hoc tantum, sed periculosissimis, ni caveatur, dispositionibus imbuere solet animas intemperantius occupatas genius Mathematicus. Inficit enim eas fatalismo, stupiditate sive insensibilitate spirituali, brutalismo, incredulitate & præsumtione ferme insanabili. Nam quando in pertrahandis €tandis numeris, figuris & machinis suis, omnia vident ex se invicem sequi veluti fataliter, non autem ex libertate; inde principiis & nexibus rerum quasi necessariis & fatalibus considerandis sic afluefiunt, ut e rerum, etiam spiritualium, natura & regimine libertatem prorsus eliminent, fatalemque in omnibus necessitatem adstruant, etiam in se ipsis, repugnante conscientia & interno sensu, (adeo insensibiles sibi facti!) imo & in ipso Deo, cousque in notionem ejus Sufficientiæ sine sensu impingentes. Et quoniam in operationibus Mathematicis vident suppositadata manere, neque verò minui vel augeri, unde turo conclusiones ex proportionibus datorum deducunt: idem etiam in physicis voluerunt inter principia supponere, naturæ videlicet materiam positam, positamque motus quantitatem manere, necaugeri: quod & sine causa statuunt, & verò tum contra foecunditatem & activitatem Dei, tum contra experientiam in nobiliori parte naturæ, in mentibus dico, quæ numerosiore subsistantia augentur in dies, & in quibus, posità unâ cogitatione, ejusque uno motu sive impulsu & affectu, plures in infinitum sequuntur; quæ in natura corporea, spiritualis naturæ velut umbrâ, suam proculdubio habent analogiam. Cum autem ex crassis suis quantis, numeratis, figuratis & motis, effectus vident sequi vi materiata & figurata, non autem ex intentione aliqua mentali; inde disponuntur ad negationem nobilis istius causæ finalis quæ nil aliud est in rerum universitate
units.tr: LXV. Nor is this all: the mathematical genius is wont to imbue with most dangerous dispositions, unless guarded against, souls that are too intemperately occupied with it. For it infects them with fatalism, spiritual stupidity or insensibility, brutishness, unbelief, and an almost incurable presumption. For when, in drawing out and measuring their numbers, figures and machines, they see all things following from one another as if by fate and not from freedom, they become so accustomed to considering the principles and connections of things as necessary and fated that they utterly eliminate freedom from the nature and governance of things, even spiritual ones, and assert a fated necessity in all things, even in themselves, their conscience and inner sense resisting (so insensible have they become to themselves!), and even in God himself, striking without perception against the notion of his sufficiency. And since in mathematical operations they see that the supposed data remain, and are neither diminished nor increased, and from these they deduce their conclusions from the proportions of the given data, they have wished to assume the same among the principles of physics: namely, that the quantity of matter is fixed, and the quantity of motion once set remains and is not increased. They lay this down without cause, and indeed both against the fecundity and activity of God, and against experience in the nobler part of nature, I mean in minds, which grow day by day in number of substances, and in which, once a single thought is posited, and with its single motion or impulse and affection, several follow to infinity. These things undoubtedly have their analogy in corporeal nature, as a shadow of the spiritual nature. But since, from their gross quantities, numbered, figured and moved, they see effects follow by material and figured force and not from any mental intention, they are thereby disposed to deny that noble final cause which is nothing else in the whole universe

units.la: quam adoranda Dei Sapientia, omnia ad usus suos sic destinans, ut vi voluntatis suæ ideo talia fiant & exsistant; non autem ex fatali & mathematico rerum extensarum sine scopo & juxta regulas quasdam brutas motarum & figuratarum regimine. Et quoniam de minusculis suis objectis quantitatis nil admittere solent, nisi demonstrationes habeant palpabiles; idem genus agendi ad diviniora, ( quorum tamen intelligendorum mentes hominum corruptæ adhuc sunt incapaciores, quam cæcus recipiendi luminis) volunt extendere; atque adeo valde proclives fiunt ut nihil de illis (siquidem ea capere non possint) fide admittant: quod perinde est, ac si cæcus nollet credere corporum figuras lumine percipi, eo quod lumen non palpet: aut ac si filius patrem, paternasque voluntates & res nollet agnoscere, ampledi, revereri, nisi prius ipsi mathematice demonstretur hunc suum esse patrem, quæque sit paternarum rerum voluntatisque natura. Et sane miror eos ad practicum in omnibus Pyrrhonismum non item deduci, quandoquidem in rebus agendis demonstrationes Mathematicæ haberi non possint: sintque respectu nostri res divinæ, ( hoc est, intellectus, facultatumque omnium Deo & placito cjus subjectio) non minus practicæ quam res quæ civiles & œconomicæ vocantur. Denique ex eodem fonte non parva quoque tentantur præsumtione, seu indocili arrogantia, si quando, cogitantes se de objectis scientiæ suæ demonstrationes & certitudines scienti-sicas sicas habere, sibi quoque persuadeant fe similiter quam plurima alia in scientiis, rebus artibusve aliis scire: tunc enim cætera illa quasi inter demonstrata ejusdem cum prioribus evidentiæ connumerantes, quæcunque aliunde tantisper hisce oppositta sibi proponi possent, non minori cum indignatione vel taedio rejiciunt, ac si audirent sibi persuaderi velle bis bina non esse quatuor, aut trigoni angulos duobus rectis non æquipollere. Quæ quidem animi dispositiones omnes quantum sint præcavendæ, &, ni caveantur, quantum detrimenti solidæ eruditioni, virtuti & felicitati afferant, falsam autem eruditionem quam promoveant; omnibus, quorum interest, perpendendum relinquo.
units.tr: than the adorable Wisdom of God, who so destines all things for his uses that by the power of his will such things come to be and exist, and not by a fated and mathematical governance of extended things without purpose and moved and shaped according to certain brute rules. And since they are wont to admit nothing about their trifling objects of quantity unless they have palpable demonstrations, they wish to extend the same way of acting to higher things (whose minds, corrupted as they are, are still less capable of understanding them than a blind man is of receiving light). And so they become very prone to believe nothing of those things on faith, since they cannot grasp them. This is just as if a blind man were unwilling to believe that the shapes of bodies are perceived by light, because he cannot touch the light; or as if a son were unwilling to acknowledge, esteem and revere his father and his paternal wishes and affairs, unless it were first demonstrated to him mathematically that this is his father, and what the nature of paternal affairs and will is. And indeed I marvel that they are not likewise led in practice into Pyrrhonism in everything, since mathematical demonstrations cannot be had in matters of action; and divine things are, with respect to us (that is, the intellect and the subjection of all faculties to God and his pleasure), no less practical than the things called civil and economic. Finally, from the same source no small presumption, or unteachable arrogance, is also displayed, when, thinking that they have demonstrations and scientific certainties about the objects of their science, they also persuade themselves that they similarly know very many other things in sciences, arts or other fields. For then, counting those other things among the things demonstrated with the same evidence as the former, they reject with no less indignation or weariness whatever might be put to them from elsewhere in opposition, as if they heard it urged that twice two are not four, or that the angles of a triangle are not equal to two right angles. How far such dispositions of mind must be guarded against, and, unless they are guarded against, how much harm they do to solid learning, virtue and happiness, and what false learning they promote, I leave for all whom it concerns to weigh.

units.la: LXVI. Verum objiciet forte nonnullus ea, vel iis similia, quæ in præfatione Norvorum Geometriæ Elementorum a Janseniistis jam aliquot abhinc annis editorum, leguntur: per Geometriæ videlicet (abstractæ præsertim) studium sive peritiam, haud parum juvari posse mentes ad pietatem, concupiscentiarum diminutionem, animi æquitatem, ad puræ spiritualisque veritatis amorem, ad veritatis solidioris agnitionem & criterium, ad firmandum, itemque extendendum intellectum rationemque, ad agnoscendam magnitudinem, immaterialitatem, immortalitatemque animæ: quæ omnia suis fulcire volunt rationibus, speciem quidem coram humana corruptaque ratione habentibus; sed quæ ad lumen verum divinumque admotæ mera sunt sophismata.
units.tr: LXVI. But perhaps someone will object these things, or things like them, which are read in the preface to the New Elements of Geometry published some years ago by the Jansenists: that through the study or skill of geometry (especially abstract geometry) minds can be greatly helped towards piety, the diminishing of desires, equity of mind, love of pure and spiritual truth, knowledge and criterion of more solid truth, the strengthening and also the extending of the intellect and reason, and the recognition of the greatness, immateriality and immortality of the soul. All of these they wish to support with their arguments, which indeed have the appearance of truth to human and corrupt reason; but when brought to the true and divine light, they are mere sophisms.

units.la: Nam qui ad pietatem conferre censenda est ea scientia, quæ est sciëntia distractionis a Deo, totam animam occupans frigidis quibusdam speculationibus de sterilissimis inutilitatibus & næniis, quales sunt quæ pro subtilissimis maximeque arduis a peritioribus hujus artis quæruntur & comprobantur? Qui concupiscentias diminuere juvabit id, quod vice concupiscentiæ carnis & suscipitur a concupiscentia oculorum, sive curiositate vana, & verotum hanc, tum perniciosissimas concupiscentias laudum, passiones complacentiæ in se, voluptates subtiliores rationis, vitia superbiæ excitat vicissim, fovetque & corroborat? Idne etiam ad solidam animi æquitatem disponet, quod allicit mentes ad capitale hoc iniquitatis genus, ut tempus, vita, studia, quæ Deo, saluti propriæ & proximorum, rebusque necessariis debentur, iis subripiantur furto, tradanturque indignis nullius commodi speculationibus, quæ ideo quod nullius commodi sint, speculatoribus suis vocabuntur puræ veritates; amorque earum, amor veritatis meræ & spiritualis, utpote ubi nullus, inquiunt, respectus ad ullum emolumentum haberi potest, hoc est, opinor, quæ sint instar filorum aranearum? Bone Deus, quid audio! Notiunculæ & speculationes futiles de crassioris substantiæ lineis & superficiebus, & massis, & agitationibus, dicendæ fuerint veritates puræ & spirituales, mediumque ad amorem & acquisitionem veritatum diviniorum & cœlestium. Atqui ex eo quod anima assuescit se, amorem & affectus suos tradere inutilibus & pulverulentis minutiis, purarem ego in ea suffocari affectus erga veritates vere puras & spirituales, hoc est, coelestes & divinas & solidas: quod & ratione & experientia tristi plus nimis confirmatur; uti & hoc, nullos esse ad veritates solidas & momentosas percipiendas agnoscendasque minus aptos, quam qui ex armamentario exercitii Mathematici insignia quaedam adminicula ad criterium veritatis digno scendum exspectant. Sunt namque veritatiuncularum pulverulentarum, veritatumque divinarum & solidarum diversa prorsus (ut vidimus) criteria, diversaque lumina: ita ut ex tractatione & cognitione crassa ac palpatoria (ut sic dicam) materiarum Mathematicarum ad conspicandas res atque rerum solidas veritates, cum criteriis suis non magis praeparari possit animus, quam caecus, qui res corporeas palpationis criterio novit, hinc ad percipiendum dignoscendumque lumen, colores, & caetera quae luminis oculorumque ope noscuntur, disponi queat. Neque minus a vero abest, intellectum iisdem atque rationem firmari & extendi: extenditur quidem & dilatatur ad res abjectas, viles, minutas indignasque mentis divinioris occupatione; at hoc ipsum est intellectus vires & alas ad divina frangere capacitatemque ejus coartare, quando tam saepe se contrahit ut pulviseulos complectatur, tamque frequenter se redigit ad reculas tantillas, quarum e contra depositione, contemtu & oblivione intellectus ad diviniora & solidiora vividius, penetrantius & abundantius capienda fit ideoneus, téstibus quot-quot rem sunt experti. Kempisius: (a) Quanto aliquis magis sibi unitus & interius simplificatus fuerit, tanto plura & altiora sine labore intelligit, quia desuper lumen intelligentiæ accipit: quæ egregie Gallicus Paraphrastes versibus sic expressit:
units.tr: For what science is to be thought to contribute to piety, when it is a science of distraction from God, occupying the whole soul with certain cold speculations about most barren trifles, such as those which the more skilled practitioners of this art seek out and prove as most subtle and most difficult? Will it help to diminish desires that which, in place of the lust of the flesh, is taken up by the lust of the eyes, that is, by vain curiosity, and which in turn arouses, fosters and strengthens the most pernicious desires for praise, the passions of self-complacency, the subtler pleasures of reason, and the vices of pride? Will that also dispose to solid equity of mind, which entices minds to this capital kind of injustice, so that time, life and studies, which are owed to God, to one's own salvation, to neighbours and to necessary things, are stolen away and handed over to speculations of no value, which, because they are of no benefit, their devotees call pure truths; and the love of them, love of pure and spiritual truth, since, they say, no regard to any advantage can be had there? That is, I suppose, what is like spiders' threads. Good God, what do I hear! Trifling notions and futile speculations about lines and surfaces and masses and motions of grosser substance are to be called pure and spiritual truths, and a means to the love and acquisition of more divine and heavenly truths! Yet from the fact that the soul accustoms itself to surrender its love and affections to useless and dusty trifles, I would rather conclude that in it the affections towards truly pure and spiritual truths, that is, heavenly, divine and solid ones, are suffocated. This is confirmed all too much by reason and by sad experience; as also is this, that there are none less fit to perceive and recognise solid and weighty truths than those who expect from the armoury of mathematical exercise certain distinguished aids for judging the criterion of truth. For there are, as we have seen, entirely different criteria and different lights for trifling, dusty truths and for divine and solid truths. So the mind cannot be prepared, by the handling and knowledge of gross and, as I may say, tactile mathematical matters, with their criteria, for beholding things and solid truths, any more than a blind man, who knows corporeal things by the criterion of touch, can thereby be disposed to perceive and discern light, colours and the other things known by the aid of light and the eyes. Nor is it less far from the truth that the intellect and reason are thereby strengthened and extended. It is indeed extended and broadened to abject, vile and petty things, unworthy of the occupation of a more divine mind; but this very thing breaks the powers and wings of the intellect towards divine things and narrows its capacity, when it so often contracts itself to embrace trifles, and so frequently reduces itself to tiny little things. Whereas, by laying these aside, despising and forgetting them, the intellect becomes fit to grasp higher and more solid things more vividly, penetratingly and abundantly, as all who have experienced the matter bear witness. Kempis: (a) The more someone is united to himself and inwardly simplified, the more and higher things he understands without labour, because he receives the light of understanding from above: which the French paraphrast has excellently expressed in verse thus:

units.la: Plus l'esprit se fait simple, & plus il se rameneDans un interieur degagé des objets; Plus lors sa connoissance est diffuse & certaine,Et s'élève sans peineJusqu'aux plus hauts sujets.Oui, Dieu prodigue alors ses graces plus entieres, Et portant nôtre idée au dessus de nos sens,Il nous donne d'entraut d'autant plus de lumieres, Qui percent les matieresPar des traits plus puissants.
units.tr: The more the mind becomes simple, the more it withdraws into an inner self freed from objects; then its knowledge becomes wide-ranging and certain, and rises without effort to the highest subjects. Yes, God then bestows his graces more fully, and lifting our thought above our senses, he gives us inner lights all the more, which pierce through matters with more powerful strokes.

units.la: Aliam viam & oppositam quidem commendare, est ignorare, quando intellectus ad divina & momentosa disponatur. Mentis autem magnitudinem inde perspici, hoc est, inde patere mentem esse magnam & amplissimam gesticulatricem in rebus nauci, exilem autem & abiectissimam, quæ se tantulis pulviisculis patiatur detineri & ligari, fateor melius per illa agnosci quam ejusdem inde immortalitatem probari: Nam quæ hæc est consequentia? Anima immaterialis cogitat de iis quæ concernunt quantitatem. Ergo non desinet cogitare in æternum, sive, est immortalis? Nexum capiat qui poterit.
units.tr: To commend another and opposite way is to be ignorant, since the intellect is disposed toward divine and weighty things. That the greatness of the mind is perceived from this, that is, that it is thereby made plain that the mind is great and very ample in gesturing about trifles, but slight and most abject, allowing itself to be detained and bound by such tiny specks of dust, I confess is better recognised through these things than its immortality is proved from them. For what kind of consequence is this? An immaterial soul thinks about things that concern quantity. Therefore it will never cease to think, that is, it is immortal? Let him who can grasp the connection grasp it.

units.la: LXVII. Ex quibus omnibus constat ma-gis
units.tr: LXVII. From all these things it is established more and more

units.la: gis magisque nulla numerosiora & nocentiora animæ impendere a scientiis pericula, quam ab iis de quibus quæstio est. Monui autem alicubi, ( ut causa cavillandi præcidatur ) ista non sic esse extendenda ad communia principia operationesque vulgares, quatenus ad vitæ usum sunt necessariæ : & præterea ex ipsis speculationibus vel vanissimis in cœcitate mentis dudum acquisitis, posse ab iis qui ad divina postmodum convertuntur, postliminio nonnulla bona deduci, veluti si ipsi qui has disciplinas callent, ubi se per eas insinuaverint in amicitiam & confidentiam eorum qui illis delectantur, eorundem deinde animos, jam eis addictos & confidentes, facilius convertant ad Deum unum; nec non & quasvis revocent animas, ad divina & æterna natas, a quæsitione & desiderio iltarum vanitatum, quæ cum ipsis perspectæ sint, de earum etiam inanitate quando testantur, merentur magis fidem, & plus etiam eis ab inexpertis creditur. Atque hic est verusille horum retrogradus usus, non autem ut eas operosas nugas commendent imperitis & veritatem quærentibus, tanquam media quibus animæ ad divina & salutaria magis idoneæ reddantur; cum revera, etiamsi unum atque alterum inde posset emolumentum animæ rarius provenire, infinita sint & perniciosa, & ob nativam corruptionem certa nimis pericula in quæ concidunt ad unum fere omnes quotquot hac via procedunt.
units.tr: that no more numerous or more harmful dangers hang over the soul from any sciences than from those of which the question is treated. I have indeed remarked elsewhere (so that the occasion for quibbling may be cut off) that these things are not to be extended in this way to common principles and ordinary operations, insofar as they are necessary for the use of life; and moreover, that from the very speculations, even the most vain ones, long ago acquired in blindness of mind, some good things can be drawn back, by those who afterwards turn to divine matters. For example, if those who are skilled in these disciplines, once they have insinuated themselves into the friendship and confidence of those who delight in them, then more easily turn the minds of these people, now attached and trusting to them, toward the one God; and likewise if they call back any souls, born for divine and eternal things, from the seeking and longing after those vanities, and when they bear witness to their emptiness, having themselves examined them, they deserve more belief, and are believed all the more by the inexperienced. And this is the true retrograde use of these things, not that they commend those laborious trifles to the unskilled and to those seeking the truth, as means by which souls are rendered more fit for divine and saving things. For in truth, even if one or another advantage could rarely come to the soul from them, they are endless and destructive, and because of our innate corruption the dangers into which almost all who proceed by this way fall are too certain.

units.la: Ita ut incassum prætextus utilitatum, nunquam hinc de facto emergentium, obtendantur illius viæ causa, quæ via mille exitialibus periculis objicit objecitque innumeros, inde postmodum per defectionem a Deo sui perditionem passos. Duobus quippe modis deficitur a Deo: primo quidem sese elevando per animi inflationem & superbiam; altero autem, per distractionem ab illo summo omnis boni fonte, deprimendo se ad res vanas. Priori modo periere Angeli, posteriori homines: ad utrumque autem casum jam iterandum, efficacissimum medium est ipsa Mathesis, subtilior præsertim: maxime vero decantatissima & a summi subsellii Doctoribus supra omnes cœlos elata Algebra, cui in Symbolum vere illud assignaveris: INFLAT ET DISTRAHIT, quæque quo magis inutilissima nugamenta & incredibiliter futiles inanias magno cum sudore perreptat, eo censetur sublimior & divinior; cum tamen nullibi minus quam hic de bonis animæ ad divina dispositionibus inde eliciendis cogitent operantes. Imo tutò deierari possit, nullum ex illis æquationum varanarum & intricatissimarum quæsitoribus, unquam ex suo hoc exercitio occasionem desumisse cogitandi, quinam vitæ actuumque suorum æquatio cum justitia Dei vitaque Christi quærenda & perficienda esset, tametsi absque hujus æquationis inventione & constructione omnes omni demonstratione Algebraica certius æternum sint perituri, & miserrimam status sui cum statu Dæmonum & damnatorum æquationem pro conclusione tandem reperturi, postquam, ubi diu multumque de affectionibus numerorum indeque oriundis argutulis quæstiunculis, deque lineis curvis, parabolicis, ellipticis, hyperbolicis, earumque asymptotis fuerunt solliciti, non tamen curarunt præcipue ut affectiones animi ad numerum ordinemque divinæ voluntatis proportione debita componerent, ne vita sua moresque lineæ essent curvæ, parabolicæ & assimilatæ vanitati, ellipticæ sive deficientes, hyperbolicæ sive modum excedentes, & asymptotæ, sive non concurrentes unquam cum linea divinæ rectitudinis semper ad curvitatem nostram approximantes. Sed sistendus calamus ne forte non pauci ex iis, qui sese his applicant scientiis, ad spiritualia ista & solide proficua cachinnentur; tanta scilicet eis cura est ad divina ex suis scientiis emergendi! Hæc tamen quæ dixi, unde eorum potius occupationes præcipuæ cachinnis dignæ apparent, & pro merito deprimi possunt, supprimere nolui ideo, quod ejusmodi vana tantum non adorentur abiis qui plus cæteris sapere desiderant, & inter eruditorum vulgus caput extollere gestiunt.
units.tr: So the pretext of advantages, which never in fact emerge from them, is put forward in vain as a reason for that way, which way exposes countless people to a thousand deadly dangers, and has afterwards brought them to ruin through defection from God. For there are two ways of defecting from God: first, by raising oneself up through inflation of spirit and pride; second, by being distracted from that supreme fountain of all good and lowering oneself to empty things. By the first way the angels perished, by the second men; and for repeating either fall, the most effective means is mathematics itself, especially the subtler parts, and above all the much-vaunted algebra, which is raised above all the heavens by the teachers of the highest bench, and to which you could truly assign that motto: IT PUFFS UP AND DISTRACTS. The more useless trifles and incredibly silly vanities it crawls through with great sweat, the more sublime and divine it is judged to be; yet nowhere less than here do those who work at it think of drawing from it dispositions of the soul toward divine things. Indeed, it can be safely sworn that none of those seekers of the intricate and hard equations has ever taken from this exercise an occasion for thinking what equation of their life and actions was to be sought and worked out with the justice of God and the life of Christ, although without the discovery and construction of this equation they will perish eternally, more certainly than by any algebraic demonstration, and will at last find, as their conclusion, the most wretched equation of their state with the state of demons and the damned. For after they have long and much been anxious about the affections of numbers and what arises from them, with subtle little questions, and about curved lines, parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic and their asymptotes, they have not cared chiefly to bring the affections of the mind into due proportion with the number and order of the divine will, lest their life and morals become curved, parabolic lines and likened to vanity; elliptic, that is, deficient; hyperbolic, that is, exceeding the measure; and asymptotic, that is, never meeting the line of divine rectitude, but always approaching our curvature. But my pen must be stopped, lest perhaps not a few of those who apply themselves to these sciences laugh at these spiritual and truly profitable things; so great, forsooth, is their concern for rising from their sciences to divine things! Yet I did not wish to suppress what I have said, by which their chief occupations appear worthy of laughter and can rightly be brought low, because such vanities are not admired by those who want to know more than the rest, and who eagerly raise their heads among the crowd of the learned.

units.la: LXVIII. Si quis jam ægre ferens in suas, quas amplectitur, scientias, vel artes fuisse hactenus animadversum, non item in alias quasdam, verbi causa, in Juris aut Medicinæ scientias, quæ forte non minus cæteris corruptæ sunt; is præter causas a me suo loco dictas, sciat & rationem alteram, cur hanc rem nolui meam facere, eam esse, quod id dudum a celeberrimis JCtorum & Medicorum fit factum. Et quidem de theoria Juris a magno JCto Francisco Hotomanno O in libro quem Anti-Tribonianus appellavit; de praxi verò ab illustri Antonio Fabro, aliquot voluminibus in folio, quibus titulum de Erroribus pragmaticorum præfixit. Et quisquis generalius effecti (collecti juris legumque statutarum) naturam e cognitione causæ volet utcunque conjicere; adeat historiam arcanam Procopii, illic quis Justinianus, quis Tribonianus fuerint, multo diductius quam apud Suidam non sine horribili stupore visurus: quæ ibi & qualia sint, dici hic non potest: sunt enim talia quæ de illis narrantur, ut nisi propriis legantur oculis, fides citanti haberi possit nulla. Quoad Medicinam, quam falsa sit & quantum fallat vulgaris atque hodierna, hocipsimet sciunt Medici, & ostenderunt passim & copiose in suis operibus summi hac in arte Heroes, Paracelsus, & Helmontius Pater, quos consulat, cui lubuerit.
units.tr: LXVIII. If anyone, bearing it with resentment that the sciences or arts he embraces have so far been criticised, but not certain others, for example the sciences of Law or Medicine, which perhaps are no less corrupt than the rest, let him know, besides the causes I stated in their place, also another reason why I did not wish to make this matter my own: that it has long since been done by the most celebrated jurists and physicians. Indeed, concerning the theory of Law, the great jurist Francis Hotman did it in the book he called Anti-Tribonianus; and concerning practice, the illustrious Antoine Favre did it in several folio volumes, to which he prefixed the title On the Errors of the Practitioners. And whoever wishes to conjecture in some general way the nature of the compiled law and of the statutes from knowledge of the cause, let him consult the Secret History of Procopius; there he will see, with much more detail than in Suidas and not without horrible astonishment, who Justinian and who Tribonian were: what those things are and of what kind, cannot be said here, for the things related about them are such that, unless they are read with one's own eyes, no faith can be placed in the one citing them. As for Medicine, how false and how much the common and modern kind deceives, the physicians themselves know, and the highest heroes in this art, Paracelsus and the elder Helmont, have shown it everywhere and abundantly in their works; let whoever pleases consult them.

units.la: LXIX. De Theologia falsa si nunc
units.tr: LXIX. Concerning False Theology

units.la: quædam dixero, opinor neminem inde offendi debere, quando Christianismus in plures uti & sectas divisus, quarum unaquæque cæterarum Theologiam pro falsa ducit, hoc pacto unicuique libertatem relinquit, ea, quæ de Theologia falsa in medium afferentur, non suæ, si velit, sed aliarum Sectarum Theologiæ applicandi.
units.tr: If I now say some things about false theology, I think no one ought to be offended, since Christianity is divided into many sects, each of which regards the theology of the others as false. In this way each reader is free to apply what is brought forward about false theology, if he wishes, not to his own sect's theology but to the theology of other sects.

units.la: Quemadmodum quando de aliqua re pingenda agitur, originale verum est unicum, vera & genuina ejus per picturam repræsentatio itidem uniformis; at repræsentationes falsæ numerosiores sunt: ita Theologia solida una est: Theologia superficiaria, quæ est solidæ repræsentatio vera, etsi picta tantum & mortua, similiter una: at Theologiæ falsæ, soliđam ne quidem umbratiliter, sed monstrose & falsò tantum æmulantis, plures sunt species. Et harum quidem etsi unaquæque nonnihil in partibus quibusdam contineat veri, quia tamen id non sincerum est, sed aliarum partium erroribus infectum, hinc & toti Systematî titulum veri id neutiquam jure conciliat, haud secus atque cibus aliquis non est salubris appellandus quando bonæ substantiæ commiscetur venenum interimens. Falsa autem Theologia, ut exposita origine modoque ejus insinuandæ facilius possit evitari, interdum vel inde nascitur, quod post superficiariam acquisitam pausa facta fit, nec ulterius ab imagine ad originale ejus remque ipsam fuerit progressum: unde dum in vacua imagine requiescit mens, aut ne quidem ibi gratæ quietis locum reperiens ad terrenas crassasque delectationes retrocedit, plestitur tenebris: quas non possunt non sequi omnis generis falsa & errores. Sæpius etiam hinc oritur, quod qui nullâ prius erant imbuti, veram dum acquirere volunt, viis non veris procedant: sed rerum terrenarum abnegatione, ratiocinationis corruptæ suppressione, sinceraque & ardenti ad Spiritum Christi (Sapientiam unam veram) conversione omissis, diversas quisque indolis suæ propensiones atque obiecta non divina consulant & sequantur. Unde pro obiectorum atque propensionum suarum diversitate, di-
units.tr: When some object is to be painted, the original is one and unique, and its true and genuine representation by painting is likewise uniform, but false representations are more numerous. So solid theology is one. Superficial theology, which is the true representation of solid theology, though only painted and lifeless, is likewise one. But of false theology, which imitates solid theology not even as a shadow but monstrously and falsely, there are many kinds. Although each of these contains something true in certain parts, that truth is not pure but is infected by the errors of other parts, and so by no right does it win for the whole system the title of true. It is as with a food that is not to be called wholesome when a poison that destroys its good substance has been mixed into it. False theology, however, so that its origin and the manner of its insinuation may be explained and it may more easily be avoided, sometimes arises from this: after superficial theology has been acquired, a pause is made and there is no further progress from the image to its original and the thing itself. Hence, while the mind rests in an empty image, or does not even find a place of pleasant rest there, it falls back to earthly and gross delights and is filled with darkness, which cannot fail to be followed by every kind of falsehood and error. Even more often it arises from this: those who were not previously imbued with anything, wishing to acquire the true, proceed by untrue ways. With the renunciation of earthly things, the suppression of corrupt reasoning, and the sincere and ardent conversion to the Spirit of Christ (the one true Wisdom) omitted, each person consults and follows the various inclinations of his own disposition and objects that are not divine. Whence, according to the diversity of their objects and inclinations, different

units.la: versæ species Theologiæ falsæ sunt enatæ, quas compendii gratia ad quatuor possis referre, omnes cæteras complectentes. Namque vel proceditur per viam rationis corruptæ, quatenus illa sibi præcipue adhæret; & hinc procedit Theologia opiniosa: Vel per eandem, quatenus aliorum consensu magis fulcitur & juvatur; unde est Theologia Sectaria: Vel per viam utilitatis propriæ ab aliis consequendæ; quod Theologiam adulatoriam facit seu culinarem: Vel denique per viam literæ, spiritu destitutæ; unde Theologia literalis & Critica emergit. Hypocriticam Theologiam pro quinta specie non numero, quoniam vel ipsissima est Theologia adulatoria, vel etiam superficiaria, quæ, quatenus ad divini originalis possessionem intus non tendit, speciem & superficiem tantum habet, errores illi implicatos ex opiniosa aliisque interim trahens: id quod cæteris similiter est solemne: sua enim sibi invicem, ubi in aliquo sunt subjecto, sæpe communicant. Nam quamvis singulæ conditiones habeant præ cæteris primarias, harum tamen fluenta in socias derivant: tum communi etiam fulcro simul nituntur omnes, amore proprio videlicet, cui consulendo diceres in unum omnes conspirasse, ira data videtur opera ut is salvus undique fieri possit, non sane per viam interitûsui, moriendo quoad omnia sua cum acerbis debitisque anxietatibus in cruce Christi, ut hujus adorandus Spiritus, vita, virtutes, mores, impulsus & regimen postea inhabitant in homine locum amoris proprii teneant : sed potius ita , ut dum bellissime naturæ motus sequitur, sibique quam optime consulit, quæ interim sibi dura sunt in alium quidem sarcinæ suæ portatorem rejiciat; sibi vero, per externa quædam gestamina vel gesticulatoria, aut opiniones nescio quas de justitia per absolutum assensum vel adstipulationem imaginariam imputative acquirenda , lepide persuadeat, se æternam vitam petendi jure potiri, quando tamen jus tantum habet petendi infernum.
units.tr: kinds of false theology have sprung up, which, for the sake of brevity, you may reduce to four, embracing all the others. For it proceeds either by way of corrupt reason, insofar as that clings especially to it, and from this comes opinionative theology; or by the same way, insofar as it is supported and aided by the agreement of others, whence comes sectarian theology; or by way of one's own advantage to be obtained from others, which makes a flattering or culinary theology; or finally by way of the letter, destitute of spirit, whence literal and critical theology emerges. I do not count hypocritical theology as a fifth kind, since it is either that very flattering theology or else superficial theology, which, insofar as it does not strive inwardly toward possession of the divine original, has only the appearance and surface, meanwhile drawing in the errors entangled in opinionative and other theologies. This is similarly customary for all the others, for they often share their own [errors] with one another where they inhere in the same subject. For although each condition has primary features beyond the others, they nonetheless pour streams of these into their companions. Then all rest together on a common support, namely self-love. One would say that all have conspired together to consult it, and it seems to have been done on purpose so that self-love may be kept safe on every side. This is not, indeed, by way of its own destruction, dying in all its things with bitter and due anxieties on the cross of Christ, so that his adorable Spirit, life, virtues, manners, impulses and rule afterwards dwell in man and take the place of self-love. Rather, it is so that, while most agreeably following the movements of nature and consulting itself as well as possible, it casts what is hard for itself onto another as the bearer of its burden. And for itself, by certain external trappings or gestures, or by I know not what opinions about justification to be acquired by absolute assent or imaginary imputative acquiescence, it charmingly persuades itself that it holds the right to seek eternal life, when in fact it has only the right to seek hell.

units.la: LXX. Sunt autem uniuscujusque , & primo quidem Theologiæ opiniosæ , conditiones ex primariis præcipuæ , sequentes. Hæc quoniam rationem propriam consulit, rationalis Theologia amat dici: non quod Scripturas simul non audiat; sed quod soleat ratiociniis, quibus utitur, Scripturas sacras accommodare , non autem se Scripturæ sensui. Atque hinc est, quod Theologi rationalistæ , quamvis se una Scriptura niti dicant, atque in una etiam eademque versentur sesta, tamen pro rationis idearumque variabili genio dissentiant inter se omnes, etsi modestius, ut & in hoc aliquid rationalis regiminis appareat. Porro quorum ratio , ratiocinatio atque ideæ sunt imperfectissimæ & corruptissimæ , uti antea (a) vidimus, non potest non Theologia hæc habere easdem , quas illæ , conditiones, atque adeo non potest non inter alia esse frigida , sterilis, fluctuans, tenebrosa, & quæ similia. Deinde quia reginam se ratio inter facultates & res omnes numerat,hinc & Theologia hæc rationis superba est, suique admiratrix, tametsi simul ita monstrifera, ut nulla res adeo sacra sit, quam ideis & ratiociniis absurdis, milleque modis oppositis non deturpaverit: quod infiniti esset operis vel solum indigitare: ne dicam plerosque qui proprias ex facultate Theologiæ hujus opiniosæ fabricantur, eas ut ut deosculentur, tamen sibi plerumque occultas servare, quasi suæ absurditatis ridendæ conscii. Et tamen illi ipsi sunt, qui admirabilissima Sanctorum dona atque opera unà cum divina humilitate, simplicitate, innocentia atque infantia Christiana habeant deridiculo.
units.tr: LXX. The conditions of each kind are, first of opinionative theology, the chief ones among the primary conditions, as follows. Since this consults its own reason, it is fond of being called rational theology. This is not because it does not listen to Scripture at the same time, but because it is accustomed to fit the sacred Scriptures to the reasonings it uses, and not to submit itself to the sense of Scripture. Hence it is that the rationalist theologians, although they say they rest on the one Scripture and are occupied in one and the same sphere, nonetheless all disagree among themselves according to the changeable genius of their reason and ideas, though more modestly, so that something of rational control appears even in this. Further, since the reason, reasonings and ideas of these men are most imperfect and most corrupt, as we saw before (a), this theology cannot but have the same conditions as those, and so cannot but be, among other things, cold, sterile, wavering, dark, and the like. Then, since reason counts itself queen among the faculties and all things, this theology of reason is proud and admires itself, though at the same time so monstrous that there is no thing so sacred that it has not disfigured it with absurd ideas and reasonings and a thousand opposing notions. To point this out would be an endless task. Not to mention that most of those who fabricate their own doctrines from the faculty of this opinionative theology, although they kiss them, usually keep them hidden from themselves, as though conscious of their absurdity and ridiculousness. And yet they are the very ones who hold in derision the admirable gifts and works of the saints, together with divine humility, simplicity, innocence and Christian childlikeness.

units.la: LXXI. Theologia Sectaria, opinione qui- dem sua Scripturæ innititur, re ipsa autem rationi corruptæ, eique non tam authorita- te divina quam magno suffragiorum numero circumcinctæ.
units.tr: LXXI. Sectarian theology, which in its own opinion rests on Scripture but in fact rests on corrupted reason, and is surrounded not so much by divine authority as by a great number of votes.

units.la: Hæc, ut fundamentum cui innititur, hoc est, numerositatem & multitudinem propagare & extendere possit, fit illico fervida, dum proselytas convertendos (si non pervertendos) placitorum suorum importuna expositione & commendatione quæritat non sine zelo, disputatrix fit, quando placitis alienis sufflâminata, eadem impugnat; calumniatrix, cùm ea ipsa, ut plurimum non intellecta neque solide ab illa confutanda, mutilat, pervertit & quam pessima potest repræsentat, quo facilius ea dejiciantur ex loco quem ipsa tenere desiderat: fit denique persecutrix, quando nec sic quidem sibi propagationis locum dari videns, vim, coactionem atque pœnas in auxilium appellat. Et tunc quidem aperte & plene demonstrat se ex officina Diaboli prodiisse, qui mendax est & homicida, atque hominum ofor & hostis: Christus vero inimicos nec calumniis, nec poenis, nec vi ulla voluit excipi; sed commiseratione, precibus, beneficiis, propriaque pro illis vitae profusione: in quibus & charaćterem unum eorum qui sui sunt constituit: neminem adeo cogens, ut vel Apostolis suis januam abeundi, si ipsi velint, pandat quam liberalissime, Vultis&Vos abire? quando e contra Sectarum capita cum membris, eos qui ex assectlarum numero discedunt, aut discessus causae sunt, animo persequuntur adeo infesto, ut si vel auderent vel possent, non sine publicis votis divinam in eos vindictam atque damnationem aeternam implorarent, nec a sanguine fundendo essent temperaturi, si modo haberent obsequentes eos qui rebus gerendis praesunt. Et quidem haec omnia sub velo gloriae Dei fideique verae defendendae. Sed quam perverse vel inde patet, quod gloria Dei solius voluntatis ejus executione promoveatur: haec autem contineatur charitate ab ipsis violata. Ecquis vero adeo stolidus sit ut sibi persuaderi patiatur, Zelotas istos veritatis amore animari, quando oculis nostris videmus, eos non ex veritatis agnitae divina vi, sed terrestri nascendi forte sectae suae adhaerere; ita ut maximus quisque partium suarum Zelator, si modo inter adversarios natus fuisset aut educatus, quas jam propugnat, eadem ipsemet inversa mente impugnaturus esset? Neque vero divina fides opinionibus vel ideis, quaecunque illae sint, constare potest, (quod (a) alibi fusius probatum dedi,) sed Dei in anima ma humili, precante, obsequente lucentis operatione, de qua non magis disputatur inter ejus possessores, quam de luce inter videntes. Et hac servantur in diversis Sectis simpliciores quaecunque animae, quando omissis feralibus controversiis, neminequae propterea condemnato, ipsae manifestis Dei mandatis dantes operam, virtutem lumenque ab eo postulant, quibus attingant, quantum Deo gratum est, ad cognitionem & adeptionem eorum, ad quae ex propria ratione & industria non datur accedere. Quod si ista Sectarum disputatoribus, iis maxime quorum ea ex arte fervet olla, non arrideant, cogitent iidem, suum partis zelum, contentiones, rixas & odia, multo minus Deo placere; neque ea divinae Sapientiae, sive Theologiae verae, sed diabolicae ejusque signis, annumerari ab Apostolo: (a) Si zelum, inquit, amarum habetis, & contentiones juntin cordibus vestris, nolite gloriari & mendaces esse adversus veritatem: non est enim ista sapientia de sursum descendens; sed terrena, (quando ex ventris principio culinario quis agit) animalis, (cum ex animae affectibus rationis suae ideis mordicus adhaeret) & diabolica, (cum ad gloriam propriam ejurata pace sensa sua aliorum placitis odiose traductis praeferre contendit.) Ubi enim zelus & contentio, ibi inconstantia (perturbatio animi) & omne opus pravum. Quae autem de sursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, (non se impudenter ingerens eis quae ipsi non patent,) deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, (vel docilis) boni consentiens, plena misericordia, (seu commiseratione erga alios, imo) & fructibus boni; non judicans (ex principiis partium, & multo minus calumnians) & sine simulatione, hoc est, sincera & sine adulatione. Adulatio namque si adesset, jam omnis pacis & mansuetudinis atque moderationis species ei adjuncta, non ideo tamen Sapientiam veram designaret; sed Theologiae falsae speciem, quam tertiam numeravimus, diximusque adulatoriam.
units.tr: Once this theology has, as its foundation, the numbers and multitude on which it depends to spread and extend itself, it at once becomes fervent. As it seeks to win converts (if not to pervert them) by an importunate exposition and commendation of its opinions, it becomes zealous. When its own opinions are hindered by alien ones, it becomes contentious and attacks them. It becomes a slanderer when it mutilates, distorts and presents in the worst possible light those views which it has often not understood, and which it has not properly refuted, so that they may be more easily thrown out of the place it wishes to hold. Finally it becomes a persecutor, when, seeing no room granted to it for spreading itself even in this way, it calls in force, compulsion and punishments to its aid. Then indeed it openly and fully shows that it has come forth from the workshop of the Devil, who is a liar and a murderer, and a hater and enemy of mankind. Christ, however, wished that his enemies should be overcome neither by slander, nor by punishments, nor by any violence, but by compassion, prayers, kindnesses, and the laying down of his own life for them. In this he also set the one mark of those who are his own: compelling no one, he opened the door most freely even to his Apostles, to leave if they wished: Do you also want to go away? On the contrary, the leaders of the sects, together with their members, pursue with such hostility those who leave the number of their followers, or who are the cause of their departure, that if they dared or were able, they would call down divine vengeance and eternal damnation upon them with public prayers, and they would not refrain from shedding blood, provided they had officials who obeyed them in carrying out such measures. And indeed all these things are done under the pretext of defending the glory of God and the true faith. But how perverse this is may be seen from the fact that the glory of God is promoted only by the execution of his will, and that his will is contained in charity, which they themselves violate. Who then is so foolish as to allow himself to be persuaded that these zealots are inspired by love of the truth, when we see with our own eyes that they cling to their sect not from the divine power of the truth they have come to know, but from the accident of where they were born? So that every greatest zealot of their party, had he been born or brought up among adversaries, would himself now be attacking with a reversed mind the very things he now defends. Nor can divine faith rest upon opinions or ideas, whatever they may be (as I have shown more fully elsewhere (a)), but upon the operation of God shining in a humble, praying and obedient soul, about which there is no more dispute among its possessors than there is about light among those who see. And in this way simpler souls within the various sects, setting aside deadly controversies, condemning no one for this reason, and devoting themselves to the plain commands of God, ask him for the virtue and light by which they may attain, as far as is pleasing to God, the knowledge and possession of those things which cannot be reached by their own reason and effort. But if these things do not please the disputants of the sects, especially those whose pot boils with this art, let them consider that their zeal for their party, their contentions, quarrels and hatreds are much less pleasing to God; and the Apostle counts them not among the divine Wisdom, or the true Theology, but among the diabolical and its marks: If you have bitter zeal, says he, and contentions in your hearts, do not glory and be liars against the truth. For this wisdom is not that which comes down from above; but earthly (when someone acts from the principle of the kitchen belly), animal (when he clings stubbornly to his own ideas, from the affections of the soul), and diabolical (when, with peace renounced, he strives to prefer his own feelings to the opinions of others, which are hatefully disparaged, for the sake of his own glory). For where zeal and contention are, there is inconstancy (disturbance of mind) and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first of all pure (not thrusting itself shamelessly into things that are not open to it), then peaceable, gentle, easy to be persuaded (or teachable), agreeing with what is good, full of mercy (that is, compassion towards others, indeed), and of good fruits; without judgement (from the principles of parties, and much less slandering), and without dissimulation, that is, sincere and without flattery. For if flattery were present, even though every appearance of peace, gentleness and moderation were joined to it, it would still not indicate true Wisdom, but the appearance of that false Theology which we have numbered as the third, and called flattering.

units.la: LXXII.Ipsa est, quae teste Scriptura, maxime animis Concionatorum insidiatur, eos ut possideat, gloriae humanae vel rei procurandae desiderio prius seductos, unde vel aulicos vel culinarios Theologos efficiat, quibus deinde efficacissime utatur ad aliorum seductionem: quando nempe adulatores isti aut culinarii Theologi, animalibus mundanisve auditoribus grati ut fiant, & commoda ab illis acquirant, latam, secundum suam cuique propensionis indolem, viam patefaciunt. Ex hoc principio ea multi docent, quae nec credunt ipsi, ut auditorum, a quibus commoda respectant, voluntati se accommodent. Alii quibusvis casibus vincula conscientiarum a mandatis Dei sic dissolverunt, ut quaelibet inordinata sine crimine sineque salutis periculo possint perpetrari. Qui vero se strictius & tutius incedere putant, ii tamen sic agunt cum auditoribus suis, ut quamvis & se, & mundum, & quae in mundo sunt, diligant, neque idcirco (si Johanni fides habenda) in illis sit amor Patris, & multo minus odium atque crucifixio sui cum Christi imitatione, sine quibus utique nemo vivet unquam, eorum tamen nullus fit, qui se ideo cogitet in via mortis esse, sed omnes ad vitam se gradiri cum pace non dubitent, donec fero nimis dedoceantur subito interitu: quem interim si ab illis (depulsis adulatorum cantilenis) avertere quis ex vera charitate conetur, ecce, qui ex adulatoria indole apparebant prius velut agniculi, jam sub agnina pelle animos fovisse lupinos & leoninos ipso opere testatum dabunt, haud minori ira commoti, quam famelici helluones, quorum è culina pulpamentum spe avida jam dudum devoratum irremeabiliter subduceres.
units.tr: LXXII. It is this which, as Scripture bears witness, especially lies in wait for the minds of preachers, to possess them. First it seduces them with the desire to seek human glory or worldly advantage, and from this it makes them courtly or kitchen theologians. Then it uses them most effectively to seduce others. For these flatterers, or kitchen theologians, wishing to be pleasing to animal or worldly hearers and to gain advantages from them, open a broad way, adapted to the character and inclination of each. On this principle many teach things they do not themselves believe, so that they may conform to the wishes of the hearers from whom they hope for advantages. Others have so loosened the bonds of conscience from the commands of God in every kind of case that any disorderly action may be committed without guilt and without danger to salvation. Those who think they walk more strictly and safely, nevertheless deal with their hearers in such a way that, although they love themselves, the world, and the things that are in the world, and therefore (if John is to be believed) the love of the Father is not in them, and much less is there hatred and crucifixion of self, with the imitation of Christ, without which indeed no one will ever live, none of them thinks himself to be on the way of death. Rather, all confidently believe they are walking in peace to life, until they are most cruelly undeceived by sudden destruction. If anyone, out of true charity, tries to turn them from this way (the flatterers' songs having been driven away), behold, those who previously appeared like little lambs from their flattering disposition will show by their actions that under a lamb's skin they had nourished the minds of wolves and lions. They will be moved with no less anger than hungry gluttons, when you snatch away from their kitchen the dainty dish which they had long since greedily devoured in hope.

units.la: LXXIII. Theologia falsa literalis ut omnium est coecissima, sic & arrogantissima est, simulque fallacissima, exitiosissima & vera Christianismo inimicissima, dum tamen nil aliud plenis crepat buccis quam Scripturas & Dei Verbum.
units.tr: LXXIII. False literal theology, as it is the most blind of all, so also it is the most arrogant, and at once the most deceptive, most destructive, and most hostile to true Christianity, while yet it does nothing but bawl with full mouths about Scriptures and the Word of God.

units.la: Verum clamatoribus istis idem dici posset, quod Christus olim Judæis Scripturas scrutantibus & hoc pacto vitam se consecuturos autumantibus: Patris vocem nunquam audivistis, nec ejus similitudinem vidistis: neque habetis verbum ejus in vobis manens, hoc est, nunquam vel unum Dei vivum verumque verbulum vere intellexistis, nec in mente vestra adhuc ullos habuistis vivos conceptus, qui similes sint conceptibus Dei ejusque mentem referant; neque in vobis habetis principium, unde sensus verbis Dei dignos poslitis derivare. Quod olim Augustinus communi praxi & sensu firmatum, dixit: (a) Homo fide, spe & charitate subnixus, eaque inconcusse retinens, non indiget Scripturis, nisi ad alios instruendos: itaque multi per hæc tria, etiam in solitudine, sine codicibus vivunt: quodque olim Abbas quidam, veluti cladium a discipulo spiritu vacuo, literæ buccinatore, suscitandarum, præscius vovebat: Utinam veroperiissent omnes libri, chartas autem inventa esset! Hæc illis blasphema habebuntur, tametsi nullos habeat offensiores hostes Scripturæ spiritus, quam vacuos illos literæ adoratores, qui hic se gerunt ac si Rege quodam subditis suis literas mittente quibus eos ad se, donaturum dona regia literis non satis exprimenda, nonnullisque Regem idcirco adire volentibus, hi nostri literales contemnerent quotquot ad Regem auditis vel semel literis ejus accurrerent: ipsi vero literis istis affixi interim manerent, grammatice eas & critice resolvendo: & vero non modo ad Regem ipsum non properarent; sed & dona sanctissime promissa in dubium revocarent negarentque, & tandem ad negationem hanc statuminandam falsaté scripta regia detorquerent. Quid his prodessent, quæso, scriptæ literæ stultissimo more deamatæ, quando sensum & mentem & rem nec haberent, nec quærerent, nec faterentur? nonne potius ad condemnationem suam literas eas tractarent? Atqui non minus absurde agunt qui simili modo eousque exorbitant, ut, quamvis Scriptura dona Dei spiritualia promittens concep- tis verbis afferat, (b) Literam occidere, Spiritum vero vivificare? parum tamen absit, quin & Hebraea isti & Græca idiomata tanquam ad salutem necessaria exclament; dum interim, si non ut rem noxiam, certe ut inutilem eliminare multis modis contendunt animam Christianismi, sive SPIRITUM SANCTUM, & dona ejus, (a) quæ in Scripturis jubemur postulare cum spe ea adipiscendi: qui Spiritus veritatis ibidem omnibus promittitur credentibus; sine quo nemo dicitur ad Christum pertinere; sine quo nullum ea quæ Dei sunt cognoscere posse docemur, quique ut origo una omnium virtutum, bonorum, luminumque commendatur. Et ecce, infinitis ejusmodi de SPIRITU DEI testimoniis non obstantibus, audent e Criticis, literæ idololatris, pars spem & desiderium Spiritus ut Enthusiasmum blasphemare; pars tollere Spiritum conversionis, negando ejus ad eam operationis internæ necessitatem, & causando, per Spiritum Evangelii nil aliud intelligi debere quam mentis dispositiones Evangelicæ doctrinæ conformes; quasi scilicet dispositiones ejusmodi per humanas vires & actiones, sine actibus Spiritus ipsius Sancti, eas intus operantis, haberi ab hominibus possent! Nec finis: tollunt & eorundem alii Spiritum contritionis & precum, causando, petitione remissionis peccatorum, ut quæ jam dudum facta sit olim in morte Christi, nil amplius opus esse; pars Spiritum sanctificationis, volentes Christi imitationem internamque gratiam jam ita necessario requiri; nonnulli Spiritum illuminationis, volentes sine ejus luminosa irradiatione assequi Scripturarum sensum omni litera superioperiorem, cujus loco alium consequuntur coecitate tali dignissimum, mortuum, materialem, literalem, mere externum, quique in Scripturis nil aliud detegat, quam id quod vacca dum intuetur hominem, corporea & externa mera, spiritu menteque Dei seclusis. Unde fit ut si illiusmodi brutis Scripturarum palpatoribus de earum cum spirituali & interno, tum allegorico & persecto sensu fiat mentio (de quorum sensuum soliditate tot argumentorum fontes sunt, quot foederis novi scriptores & libri, in quibus singulis saepissime externa Veteris Testamenti quaecunque ad interiora & perfectiora tanquam ad veros sensus & scopos trahuntur,) audacter tamen ista soleant irridere. Et quemadmodum sues, si rem sibi contemtam verbis designare possent & vellent, rosas sine dubio & margaritas dicerent; ita hi ex concepto horrore de spirituali & allegorico Scripturarum sensu, quem & mysticum aliquando appellari audierunt, efficere conati sunt, ut quicquid eis risu dignum videretur, id istis vocibus (quae tamen ipsi Paulo, & sanctissimis primitivae Ecclesiae luminibus sacratissimae sunt) exprimeretur, & contemtim diceretur allegoricum, vel mysticum, hoc est, asininis falso eruditi animalis auribus ridiculum.
units.tr: But to these loud critics the same could be said that Christ once said to the Jews who searched the Scriptures and thought that by this means they would obtain life: "You have never heard the Father's voice, nor seen his likeness, nor do you have his word abiding in you." That is, you have never truly understood even one living and true word of God, nor have you yet had in your minds any living concepts that resemble God's concepts and reflect his mind; nor do you have in yourselves the principle from which you could derive meanings worthy of God's words. Augustine once affirmed this from common practice and common sense, saying: (a) A man supported by faith, hope and love, and holding these firmly, has no need of Scripture except to teach others; so many people live by these three, even in solitude, without books. And a certain abbot, foreseeing the ruin that would be caused by a disciple empty of spirit and a trumpeter of the letter, once wished: Would that all books had perished, and paper had been invented! These sayings will be counted blasphemous by those people, although the enemies of Scripture's spirit have no more offensive foes than those empty worshippers of the letter. They behave like this: suppose a king sends letters to his subjects, summoning them to himself, promising royal gifts that cannot be fully expressed in writing, and some want to go to the king. These literalists would despise all who hurried to the king after hearing or reading his letter once. They themselves, meanwhile, remain fixed to the letters, analysing them grammatically and critically. Not only do they not hasten to the king himself, but they call into doubt the gifts most solemnly promised, deny them, and finally twist the royal writing with falsehood to support this denial. What good, I ask, do written letters do when they are loved in the most foolish way, since those who handle them neither possess nor seek the sense, mind and substance, nor acknowledge them? Would they not rather handle those letters to their own condemnation? Yet those act no less absurdly who, in a similar way, go so far astray that, although Scripture sets forth the spiritual gifts of God in plain words, (b) "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life"? Yet it is hardly out of the question that these men also cry out that Hebrew and Greek idioms are necessary for salvation, while meanwhile they strive in many ways to remove, if not as a harmful thing then at least as a useless one, the soul of Christianity, namely the Holy Spirit and his gifts, which we are commanded in Scripture to ask for with the hope of receiving them. This is the Spirit of truth, promised there to all believers, without whom no one is said to belong to Christ, without whom we are taught that no one can know the things of God, and who is commended as the one source of all virtues, goods and lights. And behold, despite countless such testimonies about the Spirit of God, some of these critics, idolaters of the letter, dare to blaspheme the hope and desire for the Spirit as enthusiasm; some remove the Spirit of conversion, denying the necessity of his inner working for it and claiming that the Spirit of the Gospel should be understood as nothing more than dispositions of mind conformed to Gospel teaching, as if such dispositions could be had by men through human powers and actions, without the actions of the Holy Spirit himself working them within! Nor is that the end: others of the same party remove the Spirit of contrition and of prayer, arguing that for the petition of forgiveness of sins nothing more is needed than what was done long ago in the death of Christ; some remove the Spirit of sanctification, wanting Christ's imitation and inward grace to be required now as necessary; some remove the Spirit of illumination, wanting to attain the sense of Scripture, which is above every letter, without his luminous irradiation. In its place they acquire another sense, most worthy of such blindness: dead, material, literal, purely external, which reveals in Scripture nothing more than what a cow sees when it looks at a man, namely bodily and external things alone, with the Spirit and mind of God shut out. Hence it happens that when mention is made to such brutish gropers of Scripture of its spiritual and inward sense, and also of its allegorical and perfect sense (for the solidity of these senses has as many sources of argument as there are writers and books of the New Covenant, in which, in each, the outward things of the Old Testament are very often drawn to the inward and more perfect things as to the true senses and aims), they nonetheless habitually mock these things boldly. And just as pigs, if they could and wanted to name in words what they despise, would doubtless call them roses and pearls, so these men, from the horror they have conceived of the spiritual and allegorical sense of Scripture, which they have heard sometimes called mystical, have tried to bring it about that whatever seems to them worthy of laughter is expressed by these words (which nonetheless are most sacred to Paul himself and to the most holy lights of the primitive Church), and is contemptuously called allegorical or mystical, that is, ridiculous to the asinine ears of a falsely learned animal.

units.la: LXXIV. Sed quid magis ridiculum, quam nova illa, quae haud dudum Critica ista Theologia, Spiritus hostis, parere enixa est, monstra duo; unum quidem uti scripturae literae &c. adhaereatur, ut de sacris nil sit fima duo dicen- monstra. dicendum, audiendum, admittendum, nisi expressis literæ vocibus prolatum. Quasi vero vel ipsi Scriptores sacri, quando unus ex alio quid citat, aut quando plures Euangelistæ, v. g. ipsos Christi sermones referunt, sæpe quoad voces non secuti essent aliam regulam, referendo per diversissima verba id quod Christus uno saltem modo protulerat: & quasi piaculum esset omnia alia verba quæ in Scripturis non sunt, ad amorem, ad laudem, ad gloriam Dei impendere, nec deberet omnis lingua confiteri & laudare Dominum! Alterum autem eorum monstrum illud est, omne illud quod Scripturæ verbis exprimi poterit, id si non ut fide dignum, saltem ut receptione non indignum judicandum esse: quomodo etiam omne Pelagianismi & Socinianismi venenum introducere tentatum est. Et vero ipsum Anti-Christianismum & Diabolicismum hac methodo introducere posit Spiritus (ut verbo Scripturæ dicam) æquitiarum in rebus cœlestibus, cui Scripturæ literam, non autem Scripturæ spiritum atque mentem ad sua trahere, & angelica forma superindui, a multis retro seculis familiare fuit, eritque olim, præmonente Apostolo, eum in templo Dei seduturum, & se tanquam sit Deus, ostensurum. Quibus verbis cum omne sacrum ab eo ad suæ infernalis malitiæ & fraudis palliationem adhibendum esse significetur, ad Scripturæ literam sacram id si applices, nil aliud denotare poterit, quam ipsam etiam a Satana esse assumendam, sub qua tenebras, fraudes, sensusque suos mortificos proponat tantanquam divinos: eaque dignos fide, qua verba Dei decet recipere: quod sane non potest non in illis fieri & impleri, qui Spiritûs Dei arcanis operationibus illudentes, criticisquifquiliis confisi, id omne & solum facrum haberi volunt quod Scripturæ verbis incrustari potest: Satis enim (hoc ut per illos fiat) fe ipsos rejectione Dei Spiritûs in sensus tradiderunt reprobos: ne dicam exemplo sectarum oppositarum eâdem Scripturæ litera sensus contrarios atque adeo salfos vestientium, hoc ipsum evidenter patere.
units.tr: LXXIV. But what is more ridiculous than those new monsters, two in number, which this critical theology, enemy of the Spirit, has lately brought forth? One is that one must cling to the letter of Scripture, so that nothing about sacred matters is to be said, heard or admitted unless it is expressed in the explicit words of the letter. Two monsters. As if the sacred writers themselves, when one quotes another, or when several Evangelists report, for example, the very sermons of Christ, had not often, as to the words, followed a different rule, reporting in very different words what Christ had uttered in only one way! As if it were a sin to devote all other words not found in Scripture to the love, praise and glory of God, and as if every tongue ought not to confess and praise the Lord! The other of their monsters is this: that everything that can be expressed in the words of Scripture, if it is not to be judged worthy of belief, is at least to be judged worthy of acceptance. In this way an attempt has also been made to introduce every poison of Pelagianism and Socinianism. Indeed, the Spirit of error (to use the words of Scripture) could introduce Antichristianism and diabolism itself by this method, for it has been customary for many centuries to draw the letter of Scripture, not its spirit and mind, to its own purposes and to clothe itself in an angelic form; and, as the Apostle forewarned, it will one day sit in the temple of God and show itself as if it were God. Since these words signify that every holy thing is to be used by him to cloak his infernal malice and fraud, if you apply this to the sacred letter of Scripture it can denote nothing other than that Satan himself is to take up even that letter, under which he may set forth darkness, frauds and his own deadly senses as divine, and worthy of that faith with which the words of God ought to be received. This certainly cannot fail to happen and be fulfilled in those who, mocking the hidden workings of the Spirit of God and trusting in critical trifles, want everything and only what can be encrusted with the words of Scripture to be considered sacred. For by rejecting the Spirit of God they have already, in order that this may happen through them, delivered themselves over to a reprobate mind. I need not say that the clear evidence of this lies in the example of opposing sects which, with the same letter of Scripture, clothe contrary and therefore false senses.

units.la: LXXV. Et hinc est quod provida Dei bonitas, errores verbis Scripturarum propinatos, uti redderet cassos, quandoque Sanctiores coacta est impellere mentes, ad salutares veritates iis vocibus proponendas quæ inScripturis nondum adhibitæ effent, neque etiam idcirco à falsis hominum ideis, sensibus, glossematis, quibus Scripturas enervarunt, pravo usu infectæ: imo potius quæ eorum falsis interpretamentis & cogitatis oppositæ, veritatem nullis fallaciis obscurandam, sisterent sincerioribus animis, ex ea fructum sentire ac percipere idoneis. At hocce ultimum ingensque Dei beneficium ipsi maleferiati donorum Spiritus Sancti contemtores non improbant tantum, sed & vitio ac crimini vertunt fanctiffimis divini Spiritus organis, proprias uti tenebras ipsi protegant, postquam eas criticis vel ethnicis fraudibus, aut longo usu, sub Scripturæ vocum cortice & larva abscondere potuerunt, ejecta è vocibus sacris medullâ; reliquæ {75} Quare liceat & salutare fit, interdum adhibere verba vocesque in Scripturis non extantes. reique ipsius veritate atque substantia. Cui infelicissimæ functioni, Scripturarum dico enervationi, diceres nonnullos omni ferme industria & molimine incubuisse: nec circa dogmatica tantum, unde quæ immediate pascant animas, sunt desumenda; sed & in iis, quæ utut sint accessoria, animas tamen ad officium excitant per judiciorum Dei in immorigeros tremendorum eventus, prophetica las-que denuntiationes; quas literalistæ miseri etsi sibi non intellectas neque ex cœcitate dum præ foribus sunt perspectas, jam à multis seculis impletas esse dictitant, vel etiam meras esse hyperbolas grammaticesque suæ figuras & loquendi modos. Atque sic mens scopusque Dei in commovendis hominum animis ad pœnitentiam, per media eos maxime afficere apta, deplorandum in modum evacuantur.
units.tr: LXXV. And hence it is that the provident goodness of God, in order to render the errors poured out in the words of Scripture ineffective, has sometimes been compelled to move holier minds to set forth saving truths in words not yet used in Scripture, and not for that reason tainted by the false ideas, senses and glosses of men, with which they have weakened Scripture, nor by their wicked use; rather, the truth, opposed to their false interpretations and thoughts, which could not be obscured by any deceits, is presented to sincere minds fit to feel and perceive its fruit. But the wicked despisers of the gifts of the Holy Spirit not only disapprove of this last and immense benefit of God, but also charge with vice and crime the most holy instruments of the divine Spirit, as if they were protecting their own darkness, after they had been able to hide it under the bark and mask of the words of Scripture, by critical or heathen tricks or by long practice, with the marrow of the sacred words removed. Wherefore it is lawful, and it is good, sometimes to use words and expressions not found in Scripture, while the remaining substance and truth of the matter is kept. To this most unhappy task, I mean the weakening of Scripture, you would say that some have devoted almost all their diligence and effort; and this concerns not only doctrinal matters, from which souls are to be fed directly, but also those things which, however accessory, nonetheless stir souls to duty through the dreadful outcomes of God's judgments upon the disobedient, and through prophetic threats. Wretched literalists, though these are not understood by them, and though they do not perceive them clearly because they are at the door, keep insisting that they have already been fulfilled for many centuries, or that they are mere hyperboles and figures and forms of speech of their grammar. And thus the mind and aim of God, in moving the hearts of men to repentance, by means most suited to affecting them, are lamentably emptied out.

units.la: Sed quid de iis solis querelæ fiant, qui per sacra verba fumos venditant & fallacias; cum id omnis, suo quaque modo, faciat eruditiofalsa, sive se sacram dicat sive profanam? quippe quæ, ut vidimus, terminos, nomina & speciem veritatis scientiarumque omnium sua faciat, sub his erronea uti propinet omnibus. Et hoc respectu crediderim dictum esse (quisquis est qui dixerit) Humanam Sapientiam quatuor facultatibus constare; quæ in hominibus mira efficiant ad eos perficiendos: nempe, Theologia, qua pereunt animæ; Jurisprudentia, quæ bona & tranquillitatem diripit; Medicina, cujus opera corpora enecantur; & Philosophia, quæ rationem dementat generis humani. Hoc ut de vera Sapientia falsum esset, ita ad salsam eruditionem ejusque partes relatum, verius est quam ut nova nunc probatione indigeat. Quapropter a falsæ eruditionis materia, de qua hactenus multa, ad alium ejus formandæ modum licet ulterius progredi.
units.tr: But why should complaints be confined to those who peddle smoke and deceit through sacred words, when every kind of false learning does the same in its own way, whether it calls itself sacred or profane? For, as we have seen, it makes its own terms, names and semblance of truth, and of all the sciences, and under these it offers its errors to everyone to drink.
