In this respect I believe it was rightly said (by whoever said it) that human wisdom consists of four faculties, which work wonders in men for their ruin: namely, theology, by which souls perish; jurisprudence, which tears apart goods and tranquillity; medicine, by whose work bodies are killed; and philosophy, which drives the reason of the human race mad. If this were false of true wisdom, it applies to false learning and its parts more truly than it needs any new proof. Therefore, having said much so far about the matter of false learning, we may now proceed to the other way of forming it.

units.la: LXXVI. Is modus est animos ab ineunte ætate erudiendi, quod superius (*) unum primumque ex adminiculis quatuor quibus eruditio falsa formabatur & statuminabatur recensuimus: quo non tantum quæ hactenus falsata & corrupta diximus, eis statim atque aliqualis rationis circa hæc sunt capaces, imo etiam ante instillantur; sed & omnia consusa, mutilata, inversa eis proponuntur. Negliguntur in eis instituendis verioris Logicæ insigniores leges (a) superius recensitæ; neque agitur cum illis tanquam creaturis æternum duraturis, & æternitati beatæ præparandis: imo necattenditur quidem tunc, ut quæ eis inculcantur, e numero sint rerum eis olim ad usum futurarum. Diceres de tempore terendo solummodo quæstionem esse: aut vero si de occupandis eis utcumque serio cogitetur, tunc omissis quorum per vices forent capaces, (*) supr. §. VI. (a) Lib.II, §.38.
units.tr: LXXVI. This method is to educate minds from earliest childhood, which we listed earlier (*) as the first and chief of the four supports by which false learning is formed and established. By it, not only the things we have so far described as falsified and corrupted are instilled into them, as soon as they are capable of some reason about these matters, indeed even before; but everything is also set before them jumbled, mutilated and upside down. In their instruction the more important laws of truer Logic (a), recalled above, are neglected; nor are they treated as creatures who will endure forever and who are to be prepared for blessed eternity. Indeed, at that stage no thought is given to whether what is inculcated in them belongs to the things that will one day be of use to them. You would say that the question concerns only how to pass the time; or, if some serious thought is given to occupying them in any way, then, leaving aside the things they would in turn be capable of, (*) see above §. VI. (a) Book II, §. 38.

units.la: laboribus externis, (qui rebus agendis nec non mentibus humiliandis aut ad auxilium proximorum præparandis multum conferunt) jam fere languidis & plerunque speculativis aut vanis tantum occupationculis exercentur, quibus aut memoriola, aut intellectulus, aut loquacitas, vel gesticulandi facultas quæpiam superbiusculè sese prodere gestiant. Quid sit facultates immortales & fundamentales bene colere,
units.tr: they are exercised with external labours (which contribute much to doing things, to humbling minds, or to preparing them for helping their neighbours), now nearly sluggish and mostly with merely speculative or idle trifles, by which either a little memory, or a little intellect, or talkativeness, or some facility in gesturing, eagerly displays itself with a rather proud air. What it is to cultivate the immortal and fundamental faculties well,

units.la: (a) In tráct. Ga lico : Les vrais principes de l'Educa tion Chrétien ne des en fans dans la II Part de la Theolo gie du cœur.
units.tr: (a) In the French treatise: The True Principles of the Christian Education of Children, in the second part of The Theology of the Heart.

units.la: 77. Eorum qui Eruditionem falsam pro fidem, aut propagare volunt characterem aliquot. Impietas Superbia Hypocrisis Adulatio Odium probos. Perfectio Irrisio. Calumnia Absurditas Item Voluptuosi tas. Avaritia colere, idque ordine aliquo, a desiderio exordium faciendo, obiecta indebita, propensionesque & impressiones pravas ab eis removendo; tum vero eas debitis obiectis, sanis principiis, sanctis propensionum seminibus, proficuis exercitamentis beando; id vero si non nesciri dicatur, saltem quoad praxin ita traditur oblivioni, ut ejus tanquam rei prorsus ignoratæ memoriam aliquam revocari justissime exoptes. Quod sane hic utcunque deducere non abs re foret, nisi id ex professo alibi (a) à me factum esset: unde hoc labore supersedens ad finem operis properabo, postquam de præcipuis eorum qui eruditionem falsam vel tenent, vel communicare volunt, dispositionibus breve verbum protulero.
units.tr: 77. A few marks of those who wish to propagate false learning as faith. Impiety, Pride, Hypocrisy, Flattery, Hatred of the upright. Perfection, Mockery. Calumny, Absurdity; likewise Voluptuousness. Avarice to cultivate, and to do so in some order, beginning with desire, removing undue objects and depraved inclinations and impressions from them; and then to bless them with proper objects, sound principles, holy seeds of inclinations, and profitable exercises. If this is not said to be unknown, at least in practice it is so consigned to oblivion that you would most justly wish some recollection of it, as of a thing utterly unknown. This would indeed be no amiss to deduce here in some measure, were it not that I have done so expressly elsewhere (a). Therefore, sparing myself this labour, I shall hasten to the end of the work, after I have offered a brief word on the chief dispositions of those who either hold false learning or wish to communicate it.

units.la: LXXVII. Qui eruditione falsa imbuti sunt, illi (eam nisi contemnant & rejiciant) quia non fundantur in facultatum suarum fundamentalium ad Deum conversione, pro calamitate prima, ad oblivionem Dei, pietatis neglectum, tandemque ad impietatis amplexationem, quæ semper in exitium, quandoque & in Atheismum terminatur, sunt pronissimi.
units.tr: LXXVII. Those who are steeped in false learning, unless they despise and reject it, are most prone to the first calamity: forgetting God, neglect of piety, and finally embracing impiety. Since they are not grounded in the turning of their fundamental faculties to God, this always ends in ruin, and sometimes in atheism.

units.la: Sane haud absurde de quam plurimis doctorum simile quid quaereres ac Julium Cæsarem de quodam Græciæ populo quæsiisse narrat in vita Periclis, ni sallor, Plutarchus. Is videlicet ubi viros conspicaretur cum simiis sese ultra modum delectantes, interrogabat, num in illa regione mulieres deessent: his siquidem alioqui affectus ejusmodi deberi, non simiis. Itaque inspiciatur, quomodo doctí omisso Deo, sinos suos affectus studiaque exerceant circa vanas absurdasque objectorum variorum ideas, quibus toti & occupentur & delectentur, haud inique possit nunc quæri; Num igitur jam Deo careamus, quippe cui soli similia sint ut debita sic solvenda.
units.tr: Indeed, one might not unreasonably ask of very many learned men something similar to what Julius Caesar, as Plutarch, unless I am mistaken, tells in the Life of Pericles, asked of a certain people of Greece. Namely, when he saw men taking excessive delight in apes, he asked whether women were lacking in that region, since such affections were otherwise owed to women, not to apes. So it may now fairly be asked how the learned, leaving God aside, exercise their affections and pursuits on various vain and absurd objects, in which they are wholly occupied and delighted. Do we therefore now lack God, to whom alone such things are owed, and must be paid, in the same way as debts?

units.la: Porro quia Deum pro scopo non habent, sed se ipsos, ideo etiam sunt superbi: atque ex superbia animi, ne ab aliis ut impii contemnantur impietatem dissimulantes, si non pietatem, saltem virtutis & honestatis speciem præ se ferunt, caventque studiosissime ne quempiam, a quo æstimari cupiant, verbis, actis, opinionumque suarum iis ingratarum detectione offendant; ita ut dum honestioribus quibusque placere allaborant, tantum non Stoicos (mirus lusus!) te videre asseveres. Ex hoc principio eos, a quibus vel laudantur, vel se laudandos sperant, ipsi vicissim collaudant; sic ut sæpe mulus mulum scabat. A quibus autem laudes & existimationem non exspectant, (& hi solidiores perspicaciorésque eruditi sunt; præditique lumine solidæ discretionis ficti a vero) eos odio prosequuntur immutabili, sed incluso & occulto; quod tamen, ubi occasio gravissime eis nocendi datur, sese prodit quidem, at non nisi sub specie æquitatis & moderati in eos judicii, quandoque & falsæ irrisionis, plus apud plerosque ponderis habentis, quam maxima ratiocinationum argumenta. Quod si fe ab aliis læsos putant, odii acerbitate impelluntur impatientius ad quamvis occasionem nocendi arripiendam, adhibitis totius artis suæ fraudibus, ut omnia suae veritatis & justitiae coloribus incrustata, non appareant non laudanda : nisi si forte ingenio carentes, affectibus, etiam non provocati, immoderate propalatis, dum æstimationem sui firmare ardentius fiunt, contra spem se deridendos aliis propinant. At quia omnes, qui relicto Deo se ipsos pro scopo habent, non tamen sese considerant veluti præcipue alienis laudibus assiciendos; sed & dantur qui se magis voluptatibus, aut mediis ad voluptates & laudes comparandas, pecuniis, affici malint: hi pro dicta diversitate vel nitidi Epicuri de grege porci vel delicatuli, aut avari & tenaces & quae hinc sequuntur, evadunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, because they do not have God as their goal but themselves, they are also proud; and from pride of mind, lest they be despised by others as impious, they display, while concealing their impiety, if not piety, at least the appearance of virtue and honesty, and most carefully avoid offending anyone by whom they wish to be esteemed, by words, deeds, or the disclosure of opinions unwelcome to such people. So that, while they labour to please the more respectable men, you would declare them, with a strange jest, to be little less than Stoics. From this principle, they in turn praise those from whom they hope for praise or by whom they hope to be praised; so that, as they say, "one mule scratches another." But those from whom they do not expect praise and esteem (and these are the more solid and sharp-sighted learned men, endowed with the light of solid judgement, who are alien to the false) they pursue with unchanging hatred, though hidden and concealed. Yet when occasion of seriously harming them is given, this hatred does break out, but only under the appearance of fairness and of a moderate judgement on them, and sometimes under false mockery, which carries more weight with most people than the strongest arguments. But if they think they have been wronged by others, they are driven by the bitterness of hatred more impatiently to seize any opportunity of harming them, using all the frauds of their art, so that everything is coated with the colours of their own truth and justice, and does not appear unworthy of praise. Unless perhaps, lacking talent, they, even when not provoked, immoderately disclose their passions, and while they more ardently strive to strengthen their own esteem, they offer themselves, against their hope, to be mocked by others. But since all who, having abandoned God, make themselves their goal, do not consider themselves as chiefly to be honoured by the praises of others; and since there are also those who prefer to be governed rather by pleasures, or by the means of acquiring pleasures and praises, namely money: these, according to the said difference, turn out either sleek swine of Epicurus' herd, or dainty and delicate, or greedy and tenacious, and whatever follows from these.

units.la: LXXVIII. Præterea, quoniam circa ideas inanes, entia rationis; aut si circa res, non ut agendas, sed ut speculandas sese otiose occuparunt, & in hoc gloriam quæsiverunt & constituerunt, hinc superbiæ hic stimulos addente pigritia, maximi sunt contemptores ignavique inimici rerum externarum curandarum, maxime vero operum manibus conficiendorum, ut ut innocuorum, utilium & necessariorum, veluti quæ ad cibandum & tegendum corpus conferunt, quæ etiam expresse permisit & injunxit Deus, ut anima inde humilis fieret, sibi & aliis ex amore legitimo prospiceret, & laboriosa occupatione, inobedientiæ præteritæ justas daret pœnas. At hos omni bono omnique Dei consilio diceres oppositos. LXXIX. Porro quoniam ex vanarum notionum vel chimærarum farragines, quibus pro materia eruditionis cerebella repleverunt, nil sunt solidi, quod animam ad æterna & immensa factam replere & tranquillare queat: hinc dum novorum semper curiosi sunt, omnia scibilia, facta, linguas, scripta, opinata, minuta, vana, nugacia perreptantes, & insatiabili desiderio scire & devorare volentes, in hoc magnum eruditionis profectum constituunt; tum inquieti, pace interna & tranquillitate solida nequaquum gaudentes intus, (quicquid externa ostendant specie) tristiores sunt & morosiores, nisi vel objectorum mutatione continua insitæ mœstæque sollicitudinis sensum temperent aut supprimant; aut (quod Spinozæ accideract) inimicæ potestatis maleficio per deploratam ac pertinacem suam a Deo aversionem adjuto, prorsus dedoluerint, donec ex illhoc lethargo in æternæ tristitiæ & angoris immensi abyssio cum morte tandem evigilent.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Moreover, since they have occupied themselves idly with empty ideas, beings of reason; or, if with things, not as things to be done but as things to be contemplated, and since they have sought and established glory in this, idleness adding its spur to pride here, they are the greatest despisers and lazy enemies of external things that ought to be cared for, and most of all of the works to be done by hand, even harmless, useful and necessary ones, such as those that serve to feed and clothe the body. God himself expressly permitted and enjoined these, so that the soul might thereby become humble, provide for itself and others out of lawful love, and by laborious occupation pay the just penalty for past disobedience. But you would say that these men are opposed to every good and to every counsel of God. LXXIX. Furthermore, since the heaps of vain notions or chimeras with which they have stuffed their little brains as the matter of learning are nothing solid, able to fill and calm a soul made for eternal and immense things, therefore, being always curious about novelties, they run through all knowable things, deeds, languages, writings, opinions, trifles, vanities and nonsense, and, wishing to know and devour with insatiable desire, they count this as great progress in learning. Then, restless, not at all rejoicing within in inner peace and solid tranquillity (whatever outward show they make), they become sadder and more morose, unless they temper or suppress the sense of their inborn and sorrowful anxiety by constant change of objects; or else (as happened to Spinoza), helped by the malice of a hostile power through their deplorable and stubborn aversion from God, they utterly grow numb, until at last they awake from this lethargy, together with death, in the abyss of eternal sorrow and immense anguish.

units.la: LXXX. Insuper ista, qua tument aliosque omnes antecedere ardent superbia, illaque ægræ mentis omnia vorandi aviditas, nunquam, ob inanitatem eorum quibus pascuntur, satianda, reddere eos solent invidos veluti canes, ut sine ingenti livore videre non possint ab aliis boni quippiam aut laudabilis, quod ipsimet non habeant, possideri aut proficisci. Nec vero tantum in illos qui solida & egregia habent, pudenda isthæc eruditorum falsorum invidia furit, eoque impotentius, quo præstantiora ab illis possidentur; sed & ne quidem facile patitur canes sui similes vel putrida etiam ossa corrodere, re, inquieta semper, donec & ista sibi ut propria vendicare incipiat, aliique ea aliis præripiant, ac sese invicem idcirco ad rabiem usque demordeant: quod eo frequentius & ferventius contingit, quo ineptiora, minutiora & futiliora sunt obiecta quibus occupantur: id quod superiori hocque seculo, grammatici, critici, & similes pædagogi, orbi literario notum fecêre abundantius.
units.tr: LXXX. Moreover, that swelling pride which burns to outdo all others, and that sickly mind's appetite for devouring everything, which can never be satisfied because of the emptiness of what it feeds on, usually make such people envious like dogs. They cannot bear to see anything good or praiseworthy, which they do not themselves have, possessed or achieved by others without great spite. Nor does this shameful envy of false scholars rage only against those who hold solid and outstanding things; it rages all the more wildly the more excellent the things others possess. Nor can it easily bear that dogs like itself should gnaw even rotten bones. It is always restless, until it begins to claim even these as its own, while others snatch them from it, and so they bite each other to the point of madness. This happens all the more often and fiercely the more trivial, petty and worthless the objects are with which they occupy themselves. The grammarians, critics and similar schoolmasters have made this widely known to the literary world in the previous and in this century.

units.la: LXXXI. Animi interna illa inquietudo, cum laudis suæ, quandoque & nummorum desiderio, admixta, impellit eos extra se uti proruant, suas propalaturi & communicaturi mentis agitationes. Et quoniam, uti proverbio ajunt, mali corvi malum ovum, &, ut quisquis est, ita agit & loquitur: inde fit ut quæ factis proferunt, ad omnia turbanda vel commovenda, quantum fert activitatis sphæra, videantur nata: quæ vero verbis vel scriptis produnt, si materialium quarundam veritatiuncularum habeant speciem, tamen paucissimi periturique sunt usus, nec tranquillant animos, sed occupant & a solidis distrahunt, internique fundamentum mœroris ad momenta tantum interrumpunt, aut etiam omnigenis hominum vitiis augendis inserviunt. At si ne quidem materialis veritatis formam habeant, tunc præter cogitata chimærica, absurda, inordinata, tædiosa, sterilia nil propagant, nisi ea ad omne malum, ad rixas præcipue, fertilissima dicas. Et sane, quid aliud exspectes ab eruditione Deo ejusque divino Spiritu, imo & ejus desiderio vacua, falsis autem repleta scientiis, falsa Metaphyphysica de rationis corruptæ & coecæ ideis obscuris & falsis; falsa Physica, de materiæ corruptæ & cadaverosæ externa scabie, falsâ Ethicâ, de amore sui corrupto & superbo; falsâ Critica, de errabunda corruptæ mentis activitate & garrulitate, aliisque artibus, externa quævis, corrupta, absurda, & falsa delicias suas facientibus? Quid aliud inde quam mentium scripturientium dispositiones eas, ex quibus ejusmodi librorum nascantur auctores quales superius descripsimus? Inquietudo extus pellit. Superbia excæcat. Ingenium, si quod adest, vanas, noxias, monstrosas novitates parit. Si pro fertili ingenio adsit cum sterilitate sola memoria, inde tædiosos omnium jam olim sæpe dictorum repetitores, inordinatos coacervatores, nullius judicii compilatores, multarum lectionum aut forte indicum vanos citatores videmus, qui de numerosa verbositate & ratiunculârum aliunde surreptarum pluralitate solliciti, ostendant se totam eruditionem suam in numerato habere; seque adeo felices esse cordatos, ut melioribus vel prorsus postpositis velobiter tactis, ad tenuiora, inutiliora & ineptiora in componendis libris toti applicentur, iis tenacius adhæreant, & in eis desinant.
units.tr: LXXXI. That inner restlessness of the mind, mixed with a desire for praise and sometimes for money, drives men out of themselves to rush forth and make public their mental agitations. And since, as the proverb says, bad crows lay bad eggs, and each man acts and speaks according to what he is, it follows that what they bring forth in deeds seems born to disturb and stir up everything as far as the sphere of activity extends. What they reveal in words or writings, even if it has the appearance of some material truths, is of very little and passing use. It does not calm minds but occupies them and draws them away from solid things, and it only interrupts for a moment the inner foundation of grief, or else it serves to increase every kind of human vice. But if it does not even have the form of material truth, then it produces nothing except chimerical, absurd, disordered, tedious and barren thoughts, and you would call these most fruitful of all for every evil, especially for quarrels. And indeed, what else can you expect from learning that is empty of God, of his divine Spirit, and even of the desire for them, but full of false sciences: a false metaphysics, of the obscure and false ideas of a corrupt and blind reason; a false physics, of the external scab of a corrupt and cadaverous matter; a false ethics, of a corrupt and proud self-love; a false criticism, of the wandering activity and garrulity of a corrupt mind; and other arts, in which anything external, corrupt, absurd and false is made their delight? What else follows from this but the dispositions of minds eager to write, from which are born authors of books of the kind we described above? Restlessness drives from outside. Pride blinds. Whatever talent there is produces vain, harmful and monstrous novelties. If there is a fertile talent, but with a memory alone and no fertility of mind, then we see tedious repeaters of things long since said many times over, disordered heaps of material, compilers without any judgment, and vain citers of many readings or perhaps of indexes. Anxious about a bulky wordiness and a plurality of little arguments snatched from elsewhere, they show that they hold all their learning in ready money. They are so pleased with themselves that, with the better things either entirely set aside or touched on in passing, they devote themselves wholly in composing books to the slighter, more useless and more foolish matters, cling to them more stubbornly, and end there.

units.la: LXXXII. Quoniam vero istiusmodi Auctores maximam partem non tantum ab eruditis verioribus, sed & a falsis, sui similibus, ejusdem pulpamentis ad nauseam usque dudum pastis, contemnuntur, aut non magni fiunt quando tantum ea proponunt quæ pro proprii fundi
units.tr: LXXXII. Since such authors, for the most part, are despised not only by the more genuine learned men but also by false scholars like themselves, who have long been fed to nausea on the same dishes, or they are not thought much of whenever they put forward only what they can pass off as the produce of their own estate,

units.la: {1} Deserti buntur Eruditi falsi verita tum solida- ram aggressores & impugnatores. fundi fructibus volunt haberi, quæque de suo in alios propagare, ædificare & firmare conantur: hinc fit, ut inquietudine & laudatiuncularum fame obstetricantibus, novum parturiant facinus. Id autem est, aliorum labores, scripta, personas invadere; atque sic se aliorum impugnatione & clade illustres reddere. Et quidem quando sibi similes & armorum viribus pares aggrediuntur, tunc, quoniam eorum interest, ut bellandi duret materia (quid enim sine rixis agerent?) ita inter se pugnant, ut etsi obliquis & indecoris artibus alii in alios utantur, tamen (nisi plane sint agrestes) se mutuo utcunque tolerent & æstiment. At quando accidit eos ex solidioribus nonnullos aggredi, unde mox belli finem cum sui occasu & dedecore pertimescant, tunc alia longe machinamenta moliuntur. Mirum equidem, & solo risu vindice dignum, audere asinos ad cantandi certamen provocare luscinias, nisi temerariis istis animalibus tantum non interessent & milvi rapaces, qui aviculas innocuas, Creatoris sui laudes jucunde decantantes, hominesque ad amandum, adorandum & laudandum Deum ex mirabilium ejus operum inspectione provocantes, ferre non possunt; sed crudeliter gestiunt eas unguibus suis nefariis dilaniare & e medio tollere: quos quidem eo impellit vel ferocior eruditionis falsæ inquietudo, vel malus pravi cujusdam genii instinctus; aut quandoque stolidior vel etiam imprudentior mentis intemperies, eaque omnia cum timore, ne sua nugamenta pereant, conjuncta.
units.tr: {1} False scholars, assailants and opponents of solid truths. they want to be taken for having the fruits of their own estate, and they try to propagate, build up and confirm from their own resources whatever they bring to others. Hence it happens that, with restlessness and a hunger for little praises acting as midwives, they give birth to a new crime. This is to attack the labours, writings and persons of others, and so to make themselves famous by the assault on and ruin of others. And indeed, when they attack men like themselves who are equal in the strength of their weapons, then, since it is in their interest that the matter of the fight should last (for what would they do without quarrels?), they fight among themselves in such a way that, even though some use oblique and dishonourable arts against others, they nonetheless put up with and esteem one another in some fashion, unless they are plain boors. But when it happens that they attack some of the more solid men, and they fear that the war will soon end with their own fall and disgrace, then they devise quite different machinations. It is indeed a marvel, and worthy of laughter alone as punishment, that donkeys should dare to challenge nightingales to a singing contest, were it not that rash creatures of this kind are joined by rapacious kites, who cannot bear harmless little birds that sweetly sing the praises of their Creator and by the sight of his wonderful works urge men to love, adore and praise God. Instead, they eagerly wish to tear these birds apart with their wicked talons and remove them from the world. What drives them to this is either the fiercer restlessness of false learning, or the evil instinct of some wicked genius, or sometimes a more stupid or even more imprudent disorder of mind, and all of this is joined with fear that their little trifles may perish.

units.la: Et hinc quos e divinioribus aggredi tentant, eos non considerant ut communes adversarios, qui & tolerandi sint, & quibus jura honestatis & æquitatis sint servanda; sed ab omnibus diceres fuisse in unum conspiratum ut nullum non ergá illos jus sacrumque violaretur, modo eosdem prorsus de medio tollant & absorbeant. Equidem quorum jam vita, persecutionibus, dum hic essent, vexata, dudum desiit; & quorum scripta a multis retro seculis post multas procellas ut divina habentur, quales sunt Prophetæ, Apostoli, sanctiorésque prioris Ecclesiæ Patres, eos non adoriuntur (saltem aperte & communiter) falsi, de quibus agimus, eruditi: quippe qui ab illis, postquam per glossas omnia enervarunt & ad placita sua accommodarunt, nil sinistri exspectent: & vero timeant potius, ne si eos essent aggressi, tanquam impii ejiciantur ipsimet. At non sic si quos bonorum offendant qui necdum satis noti, multo minus longa & universali approbatione approbati, ea proponant quæ solidæ eruditionis, realitatis, veritatis, virtutis, felicitatis fundamentis innixa duraturis, disjicere apta sint nænias & sophisματa, nugasque & fumos atque ineptias, quibus isti falsæ eruditionis candidati & propagatores sunt turgidi. Tunc enim in eos, (maxime in simpliciores, nec humana edoctos,) verbis, calamo, factis illico insurgunt diversi. Agrestiores & imprudentiores vivis non parcunt; vecordiores & magis timidi mortuos aggrediuntur: omnes in hoc conveniunt, ut ne quidem statum quæstionis vere proponant; sed in hoc dissentiunt. tiunt, quod statûs quæstionis loco, diversi diversa per imposturam substituant: unus odiosas falsitates has, alius contrarias; hic crimina & impias res, ille absurda & ludicra: quibus impositis, tum isthæc commenta sua invadunt pro sua quisque indole, irrisionibus, irâ, convitiis, maledictis, argumentatiunculis, allegatis etiam Scripturarum &|doctorum testimoniis, &c, quod plus est, ipsis adversarii verbis; sed vel mutilatis, vel, si quæ obscuriora sunt, in sensum prorsus diversum detortis, &c, quod solemne ipsis est, suppressis quantum fieri potest libris, vel saltem clarissimis, solidissimis, saluberrimisque principiis, scopo & veritatibus essentialibus scriptoris, eo ejusque operibus per externa quædam accessoria extenuatis, nec non per comparationes & narrationes odiosas tradućtis: quibus artibus, aliisque ejusmodi; excitent in discipulorum, plebis, potentiorum animis non lumen, non charitatem, non patientiam, non beneficentiam etiam in inimicos; sed turbas, indignationem, odia, iras, rei vel sećtæ suæ commiserationem, vindićtam, timorem, & quoscunque ad tristiora compellere aptos affećtus, unde quidem sæpius quam par esset, ob vulgi ignorantiam, nec non indebitum favorem potentiorum, qui calumniatores istos pro non improbis, sed zelo bono fervidis probisque habent, effećtus cupitos sortiantur, hoc est, opprimuntur boni, ignoratur veritas, arcentur (quod deplorandum) ab ea bonæ mentes, quæ inde proficerent, dum ipsi improbi & falsi eruditi manent in statione, honore, auctoritate & commodis suis, utpote quorum portio in hac sit vita. Nec adhuc tuti tamen: namque timentes ne calumniis suis responsa fiant debita, quibus ipsi oppido confundantur; vellent admodum eos confici qui veritatem possent vindicare; aut vero, si quae ejusmodi responsa prodeant, ea illico tentant supprimere atque destruere: cumque id nequeunt, aucto vehementer furore, Fimbriae illius apud Valerium Maximum instar, alta rabie agitantur quod ictus suus fuerit declinatus: atque cum ipsi se aggressores gratis constituerint non provocati, jam persona mutata, defensores se dicent, qui se catervatim invadi exclamabunt, quando tantum a suis, quas intentaverant, accusationibus sunt simpliciter depulsi. Tum si quid iterata aggressione defensionis nomine incoeptant, jam ad lepidum hunc scopum colliment oportet ut cornicum oculos configant, nempe omnibus persuadeant, se eorum, quos sunt aggressi, cogitata, sensa, facta melius scire quam sciant ipsimet, ut ut vel jurati se profiterentur aliter atque impuratum est, cogitare, sentire & fecisse. Sed hoc quidem nemini sano persuaserint aggressores. Nec desunt qui occulte albis ridentibus dentibus turpiter fractos ridiculorum conatus: tamen ut aliqua sibi & multitudini pulpa fiat, neve succumbere videantur, scriptitent oportet & effutiant similia vel pejora quam prius; quibus ne furori ad tristiora propenso infundatur oleum, prudenter responsurus sit nemo: hoc vero illi pro triumpho
units.tr: And so, those whom they try to attack among the more divine things, they do not consider as common adversaries, who ought to be endured and to whom the rights of honour and fairness are to be observed. You would say that all of them had conspired together so that no right, sacred or otherwise, would not be violated against them, provided only that they remove and swallow up those very men. Indeed, the lives of those whom persecutions vexed while they were here have long since ended, and their writings, which after many storms have been held for many centuries as divine, such as the Prophets, the Apostles and the holier Fathers of the early Church, these the false scholars we are discussing do not assail (at least openly and commonly), since they expect nothing harmful from them, having by glosses weakened everything and adapted it to their own purposes. Indeed, they fear rather that if they attacked them they themselves would be cast out as impious. But it is not so if they attack any of the good men who are not yet well known, much less approved by long and universal approval, when these men put forward things that are grounded on the foundations of solid learning, reality, truth, virtue and happiness, and that are fit to overturn the trifles, sophisms, nonsense, smoke and foolishness with which those candidates and propagators of false learning are puffed up. For then various men at once rise up against them, with words, pens and deeds, especially against the simpler men who have not been taught by human learning. The cruder and more imprudent ones spare no living man, while the more reckless and more timid attack the dead. All agree in this, that they do not truly set out the state of the question at all, but they differ in this, that in place of the state of the question each one substitutes different things by deceit: one hateful falsehoods of this sort, another contrary ones; one crimes and impious things, another absurd and ridiculous ones. Having laid these down, they then attack these inventions of their own, each according to his nature, with mockery, anger, insults, curses, little arguments, even with citations of Scripture and the testimonies of learned men, and what is more, with the very words of their opponent. But these are either mutilated, or, if anything in them is more obscure, twisted into a wholly different sense, and, as is their custom, the books are suppressed as far as possible, or at least the clearest, most solid and most wholesome principles, the aim and essential truths of the writer, are reduced by certain external and incidental matters, and presented through hateful comparisons and stories. By these arts and others like them, they stir up in the minds of their pupils, the common people and the powerful not light, not charity, not patience, not beneficence even toward enemies, but tumults, indignation, hatreds, anger, pity for their own party or sect, vengeance, fear, and whatever affections are apt to drive men to sadder things. Thence, more often than is fitting, on account of the ignorance of the crowd and the undue favour of the powerful, who regard these slanderers not as wicked men but as fervent and upright men of good zeal, they obtain the effects they wanted. That is, good men are oppressed, truth is ignored, and good minds, which would profit from it, are kept (a lamentable thing) away from it, while the wicked and false scholars themselves remain in their position, honour, authority and advantages, since their portion is in this life. Yet they are still not safe. For, fearing that proper replies will be made to their slanders, by which they themselves would be thoroughly confounded, they would very much like those who could defend the truth to be destroyed. Or, if any such replies come out, they immediately try to suppress and destroy them. And when they cannot do this, their rage increases greatly, and like Fimbria in Valerius Maximus, they are driven by deep fury that their blow has been turned aside. Then, although they set themselves up as aggressors for no reason and without provocation, they change their role and call themselves defenders, crying out that they are being attacked in crowds, when they have merely been simply repulsed from the accusations they had brought. Then, if they begin anything by a renewed attack in the name of defence, they must aim at this charming goal of fixing the eyes of crows: that is, they persuade everyone that they know the thoughts, feelings and deeds of those whom they have attacked better than those men know them themselves, even though those men were to declare under oath that they think, feel and have done otherwise than these men say. But the aggressors will persuade no sane man of this. Nor are there lacking those who, secretly laughing with white teeth at the ridiculous attempts of others that have been shamefully broken, nonetheless must write and babble similar or worse things than before, so that some food may be provided for themselves and the crowd, and so that they may not seem to give way. No one will prudently reply to these things, lest oil be poured on a fury that is already inclined to sadder things. And they regard this as a triumph, leading it before their fellows and the inexperienced, who think that the last man to talk and the chatterer is the victor. And so they remain, both for themselves and for others, the same men as before, namely enemies of solid learning and propagators of false learning by all the means and methods reviewed in this third book.

units.la: ducans ducant coram fui similibus & imperitis, qui ultimum quemque & multiloquum garrulum, victorem existimant; atque ita & sibi & aliis iidem maneant, qui prius, solidæ riempe eruditionis infensi hostes, falsæque omnibus mediis modisque in hoc tertio libro recensitis propagatores indefessi, sibi suisque bona quævis & perennitatem fallaciter promittentes.
units.tr: They count it a triumph before their own kind and the untutored, who think that whoever has the last word and talks the most is the winner. And so they remain, both to themselves and to others, what they were before: hostile enemies of solid erudition and tireless spreaders of false erudition by every means and method reviewed in this third book, falsely promising themselves and their followers all kinds of goods and permanence.

units.la: LXXXIII. Sed id frustra. Solius veræ Eruditionis hæc est prærogativa: quoniam ea ejus est indoles, ut sua omnia secum intus portet, cui etiam nec bibliothecarum, nec corpusculi, nec totius mundi interitus quicquam detrahat; cum e contra vel una ex his clades, mors præcipue, demonstret omnes falsos eruditos cum omni sua eruditione, coram luminosa & solida veritate nil aliud esse, quam utres vento turgidos, & ut Galli dicunt, voce non apte Latine vertenda, de francs pedants, suamque eruditionem, rien que pure pedanterie. Quod animi vitium in hoc consistit, ut quis res non ex valore & pretio suo & quales revera sunt æstimet, nec consimili proportione cum iis se gerat; sed ut quæ mere accessoria sunt, vel tenuia, aut futilia & nugacia, ampleƈtatur & æstimet ut res essentiales, solidas, momentosas, eisque se totum vel præcipuum serio occupet, atque alios itidem iis occupatos esse velit; dum interim res duraturas, solidas, essentiales, præcipuasve, quasi nil essent, negligit, contemnit & prætermittit. Id quod ab omnibus falsis eruditis fieri & factum esse, omnium optime ipsissimet in morte patet, ubi omnia sua, quibus toros sese dederunt, tanquam fumum vanissimum vident evanescere: ea vero, quae neglexerunt, divina & aeterna, jam equidem vividius patent, sed illis nequaquam degustanda, nisi dum adhuc vivitur, stolido pedantismo suo (liceat hac uti voce) se liberaverint, hoc est, nisi cessaverint minuscula, accidentaria, vana, quisquilias, studio praecipuo & seria aestimationis, affectuum, temporis mentisque applicatione prosequi: inceperint vero & perseverent divina, aeterna, interna, realia (de quibus primo libro egimus) sic totis facultatibus realissimis amplecti, ut cetera omnia non nisi extremo tangant digito, idque solum, quando ex usu necessario ea esse possunt. Haec qui non fecerint, ipsi se falsos, stolidos & fatuos deprehendent, ut ut nunc cum sibi tum aliis impense sapere videantur, veraeque eruditionis titulo cohonestentur; & vero multa methodice, ornate, teque ac facete dicendi facultate pollentes, se a pedantismo, seu a falsorum eruditorum classe, imaginentur remotissimos, ignari horum esse duo genera: alios quidem spinosos, morosos, affectuum intemperatis motibus magis quam intellectus absurda actione pedaneos; alios vero speciosos, floridos, comicos: utrosque pariter aestimatione vanorum & contemtu sive neglectu permanentium bonorum, conspicuos & absurdos, pariterque a divina veritate fatuorum atque insanorum titulis insignitos.
units.tr: LXXXIII. But this is in vain. This privilege belongs to true Erudition alone, since its nature is to carry all its possessions within itself. Neither the loss of libraries, nor the destruction of one's little body, nor the ruin of the whole world takes anything from it. On the contrary, any one of these calamities, especially death, shows that all false scholars, with all their learning, are nothing before the luminous and solid truth but bags puffed up with wind, and, as the French say (a phrase not aptly rendered in Latin), de francs pedants, and their erudition is rien que pure pedanterie. This defect of mind consists in this: a man does not estimate things according to their true worth and price, nor behave toward them in proportion to what they really are. Instead, he embraces and esteems as essential, solid and weighty what is merely accessory, slight, frivolous or trifling, and seriously devotes himself wholly, or chiefly, to these things, wanting others to be occupied with them as well. Meanwhile he neglects, despises and passes over the lasting, solid, essential and chief things, as if they were nothing. That all false scholars do this, and have done it, is most clearly seen in death itself, where they see all their pursuits, to which they gave themselves entirely, vanish like the emptiest smoke. The divine and eternal things they neglected now lie open more vividly, yet they can by no means taste them unless, while still alive, they free themselves from their stupid pedantry (let me use this word), that is, unless they stop pursuing trifles, incidentals, vanities and small matters with their chief zeal, their serious estimation, and their application of emotions, time and mind. Once they begin, and persevere, to embrace the divine, eternal, inward and real things (of which we treated in the first book) with all their most real faculties, and to touch all other things only with the very tip of a finger, and that only when they are necessary in use, then they will be free of pedantry. Those who do not do this will find themselves to be false, stupid and foolish, however wise they now seem to themselves and to others, and however they adorn themselves with the title of true erudition. Indeed, though they are powerful in method, ornament, polish and the skill of speaking wittily and elegantly, and imagine themselves far removed from pedantry, or from the class of false scholars, they do not know that there are two kinds of these: some are thorny and morose, pedantic more through the intemperate movements of their passions than through an absurd activity of the intellect; others are showy, flowery and comic. Both alike are conspicuous and absurd for their esteem of empty things and their contempt or neglect of the enduring goods, and both alike are marked with the titles of fools and madmen before divine truth.

units.la: EPILOGUS.
units.tr: EPILOGUE.

units.la: LXXXIV. Ex omnibus hucusque dictis clare jam & abundanter patere credo, quamobrem Deus in Scripturis sacris eruditionem, quæ ab ipso est & discitur, nobis commendatam velit esse, omnem aliam haberi contemtui, quam & ipse abominetur; & pro insania habeat, & verò sit destructurus; quamque etiam quisquis vere velit erudiri, debeat prius deponere, & ejus respectu veluti idiota, infantulus & quasi stultus fieri; alioqui cum improbis irrisoribus nunquam vere erudiendus. Jam constat, cur Deus scientiarum Dominus ac Deus appelletur: cur vere eruditus David exclamet, (b) Dominus novit cogitationes hominum, quod vanæ sint. Beatus homo, quem tu erudieris Domine! (c) Præ inimicis meis sapientem effecisti me per præcepta tua, quia testimonia tua sunt meditatio mea. Senes intelligentia supero, quod mandata tua observo. Cur passim audias, (d) Dominus dat sapientiam, ex ejus ore scientia est atque prudentia. (e) Habe fiduciam in Domino ex toto corde tuo, & ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ. In omnibus viis tuis cogita illum; & ipse diriget gressus tuos. Ne sis sapiens apud temetipsum; time Dominum & recede a malo. (f) Abominatio Domini est omnis illusor; & cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus. Ipse deludet illusores & mansue-tis dabit gratiam. (g) Sapiens cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum, qui fecit illum, & in conspectu Altissimi deprecabitur. Aperiet os suum in oratione, & pro delictis suis depredeprecabitur. Si enim Dominus Magnus voluerit, spiritu intelligentiæ replebit illum, & ipse tanquam imbres mittet eloquia sapientiæ suæ, & in oratione confitebitur Domino, & ipse diriget consilium ejus. (a) Ad tempus ultimum... credent scientia... nec intelligent ulli impii. (b) Nisi conversi fueritis & efficiamini sicut parvuli, non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum. (c) Amen dico vobis, quisquis non receperit regnum Dei velut parvulus, non intrabit in illud. (d) Amen, Amen, dico tibi; nisi quis RENATUS fuerit ἄνωθεν, EX ALTO, non potest videre regnum Dei, sive cognoscere res sublimes & divinas. (e) Perdam sapientiam sapientum, & prudentiam prudentum abolebo. Ubi sapiens? ubi literatus? ubi conquisitor hujus seculi? Nonne stultam fecit Deus sapientiam hujus mundi? Quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes: & infirma mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia: & ignobilia mundi & contemtibilia elegit Deus, & ea quæ nil sunt, ut ea quæ sunt destrueret: ut non glorietur omnis caro in conspectu ejus, ex quo vos estis in CHRISTO JESU, qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo. (f) Nemo se ipsum fallat. Si quis inter vos sibi sapiens (sive eruditus) videatur in hoc seculo, fiat stultus ut fiat sapiens: Sapientia enim hujus mundi stultitia est apud Deum: scriptum enim est, Comprehendam sapientes in astutia eorum & cogitationum subtilitate: & iterum, Dominus novit cogitationes sapientum, quoniam vanæ sunt. (g) Quæ mihi lucra fuerant, ea propter CHRISTUM arbitratus sum detrimenta. Quin imo omnia damnum esse puto propter eminentem scientiam JESU CHRISTI Domini
units.tr: LXXXIV. I believe that from everything said so far it is now clear and abundantly evident why God in the holy Scriptures wishes the learning that comes from him and is learned from him to be commended to us, and why he counts every other learning as contemptible, abominates it, regards it as madness, and will indeed destroy it. Whoever truly wishes to be taught must first lay aside that other learning and become, in its regard, like an unlearned man, a little child, and something of a fool; otherwise he will never be truly taught among the wicked mockers. It is now plain why God is called the Lord and God of knowledge, and why David, truly learned, cries out: (b) "The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain. Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord!" (c) "You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandments, for your testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the aged, because I keep your precepts." Why you hear everywhere: (d) "The Lord gives wisdom; out of his mouth come knowledge and understanding." (e) "Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will direct your steps. Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord and turn away from evil." (f) "The abomination of the Lord is every scoffer, but his talk is with the upright. He will mock the scoffers and give grace to the meek." (g) "The wise man will set his heart to rise early to the Lord who made him, and will pray before the Most High. He will open his mouth in prayer and make supplication for his sins. If the great Lord wills, he will fill him with the spirit of understanding, and he will pour forth words of wisdom like rain, and in prayer he will confess to the Lord, and he will direct his counsel." (a) "At the time of the end... many shall have knowledge... and none of the wicked shall understand." (b) "Unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." (c) "Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will not enter it." (d) "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born [ἄνωθεν] again, from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God, or know lofty and divine things." (e) "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the base things of the world and the despised things, and things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no flesh may glory in his sight; for of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God." (f) "Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise; for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: I will catch the wise in their craftiness; and again: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." (g) "Whatever were gains to me, these I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them as rubbish, that I may gain Christ and be found in him"

units.la: (a) Dan. 12:4, 10. (b) Matt. 19:3. (c) Marc. 10:15. (d) 1 Cor. 1:19. (e) 1 Cor. 1:19. (f) ib. c. 3:17. (g) Phil 3:7. mini mei, propter quem omnium jacturam feci, eaque prosperoribus habeo, ut CHRISTUM lucri faciam, & inveniar in illo (a) in quo reconditi sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ, & plura hinc inde alia, quæ cum primo aspectu vel obscura, vel mira videri potuerint, ipsa luce clariora nunc apparere debent: quemadmodum & ea quæ de eruditione vera, vanaque & falsa diximus, jam non inter odiosa, aut inter ea quæ novitatis titulo contemnuntur, sunt reputanda, sed illis quæ cum antiqua divinaque veritate sunt maxime conformia, & grandibus exemplis confirmantur, annumeranda.
units.tr: (a) Dan. 12:4, 10. (b) Matt. 19:3. (c) Marc. 10:15. (d) 1 Cor. 1:19. (e) 1 Cor. 1:19. (f) ib. c. 3:17. (g) Phil 3:7. in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; and many other things besides, which, though at first sight they may have seemed obscure or strange, ought now to appear clearer than the light itself. Just as what we have said about true, vain and false learning should not now be reckoned among hateful things, or among those things that are despised under the name of novelty, but rather be counted among those things that agree most closely with ancient and divine truth and are confirmed by great examples.

units.la: LXXXV. Habent equidem & illi, qui mundanas scientias rationis suæ activitate venantur, exemplum non minus grande ex Scripturis divinis, quod pro se perpetuo fere advocant. Is Moses est, de quo Stephanus: (b) Eruditus est Moses omni sapientia Ægyptiorum. At nec certum est, an hæc in eo laudet, an narret tantum Stephanus, siquidem non a piis parentibus, sed a profanis & extraneis sic educatus erat Moses: neque procul dubio ea sapientia ita falsata atque inanis erat uti nunc vulgaris est: tum potuit Moses, ad Deum deinde conversus, ex ea etsi falsata, postliminio, rejectis malis, bona seligere, & Deo impendere: quod etiam de eruditione superficiaria falsaque fieri debere diximus. Imo non potuit Moses prius veriorem a Deo eruditionem suscipere, quam hac deserta, primum rusticus & veluti idiota fieret, perque annos quadraginta exerceret corpus quidem humillimis pecuariæ laboribus, mentem vero precibus continuis. Tum & postea, acquisita eruditione divina, humanam sapientiam priorem, ratiocinationesque proprias, tantum abest ut magnifecerit, consuluerit, secutus sit; ut potius quovis de negotio, de passu, de verbo habendo, ad Dominum in interiora Tabernaculi confugere soleret, ab ejus uno nutu & lumine totus pendens. Sunt enim operationes Dei tales, tam in nostri regimine, quam in mundi œconomia, ut a nulla rationis humanæ sagacitate possint detegi, agnosci, beneque complicari, sive ad usum salutarem adhiberi. Et quemadmodum, si sapientissimus dexterrimusque aliquis artisex machinam tanta arte vellet condere eo proposito, ut qui eam extus adspicerent, nunquam ejus dispositionis rationem, nisi ipse eis revelaret, possent conjicere; non dubium esset quin omnes necessario fallerentur qui sine illo de ea quantacumque vellent ratiocinarentur: sic plane res se habet cum Deo, admirandisque ejus operibus, nec non cum illis qui sua ratione ea ruspantur & expiscari conantur. Quo magis de iis solliciti erunt, ratiocinabuntur, hariolabuntur, vel, ut putabunt, docte, acute, penetranter, σοφῶς & σαφῶς cogitabunt, scribent, different; eo magis aberrabunt a janua & delirabunt.
units.tr: LXXXV. Indeed, those who hunt after worldly sciences by the activity of their own reason also have an example from the divine Scriptures no less great, which they almost always bring forward in their own favour. This is Moses, of whom Stephen says: (b) Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Yet it is not certain whether Stephen praises this in him or merely narrates it, since Moses was brought up in this way not by pious parents but by profane and foreign ones. Nor was that wisdom without doubt so corrupted and empty as it is now commonly held to be. Moses, afterwards turned to God, could from that wisdom, though corrupted, choose by way of recovery what was good, rejecting what was bad, and devote it to God; which we also said ought to happen with superficial and false learning. Indeed, Moses could not receive a truer learning from God before he had forsaken the former, and first became a rustic and, as it were, an unlearned man, and for forty years exercised his body in the humblest labours of shepherding and his mind in continual prayer. Afterwards too, when he had acquired divine learning, he was so far from magnifying, consulting or following his former human wisdom and his own reasonings, that on any matter, about a journey, about what to say, he would rather flee to the Lord in the innermost part of the Tabernacle, wholly dependent on his single nod and light. For the works of God are such, both in the governing of ourselves and in the economy of the world, that they cannot be detected, recognised, rightly put together, or applied to a salutary use by any shrewdness of human reason. And just as, if some most wise and most skilful craftsman were to construct a machine with such art that those who looked at it from outside could never guess the plan of its arrangement unless he himself revealed it to them, there would be no doubt that all who reasoned about it without him, however much they wished, would necessarily be deceived: so the matter stands plainly with God, his admirable works, and those who try to search them out and fathom them by their own reason. The more anxious they are about these things, the more they reason, guess, and think, or, as they suppose, write and argue learnedly, keenly, penetratingly, [σοφῶς] and [σαφῶς], the further they wander from the gate and the more they rave.

units.la: LXXXVI. Quæ non ad præteritorum contemtum, sed ad futurorum cautelam dici sincere profiteor, qui nullius dedecus, sed ad omnium honorem, a gloriosæ radiis veri- tatis
units.tr: LXXXVI. I sincerely profess that what I say is not meant to disparage things past but to guard against things to come. I seek the dishonour of no one but the honour of all, from the rays of the glorious light of truth.

units.la: LXXXVI. Quæ scripta sunt, ad omnium tatis emanantem, promoveri peroptem erroris autem & vanitatis depositione, decoris æterni causam deponi sciam, quamvis aliter iis videatur qui sunt in errore. Hi enim, etsi, nemine designato, generalissimis terminis demonstretur error eo animo ut hoc morbi genere nullus in posterum inficiatur & pereat, tamen magnam sibi ea in re injuriam fieri semper reputabunt.
units.tr: LXXXVI. What has been written is for the benefit of all, and I wish to advance the light of truth. I know that the cause of eternal honour is advanced by laying aside error and vanity, although it may seem otherwise to those who are in error. For these, though no one is named and the error is exposed in the most general terms so that in future no one may be infected with this kind of sickness and perish, will always consider that a great injury is done to them in this matter.

units.la: Quæ causa est etiam, quare istam materiam, etsi ante aliquot annos a me incoeptatam & promissam, ita abruperim, ut vel coactus eam nec resumsissem, nec in manus hominum venire voluissem, non modo ob exiguam omnibus procurandæ utilitatis spem, sed & ne acerbiora inde concipiant plurium animi erroribus hic ostensis impliciti. Verum quoniam in illis & bonos, nec eos numero paucos, superesse confido, vicit cætera hæc consideratio: illis enim non possint non placere quæ candido & bono animo scripta sunt, quæ Scripturis consentientia, quibus in interno conscientiæ sincere coram Deo se examinantis recessu sua constat veritas; quæque (mala hic indicata si respicias,) quotidie factis plus quam satis se produnt. Argumentis istis si morositati suæ satisfieri nolint iniquiores, quid aliud agam præterea nisi eos ad Ethnicos remisero, & quidem ad eos qui suo Eruditorumque omnium calculo, probatissimi sunt, quorum e numero egregius ille Thebanus Cebes rem Eruditionis veræ falsæque præguante ænigmate complexus est: quod etsi totum commendem legendum, ex illo tamen men unum atque alterum, quod eruditionis falsæ hospites concernit, hic annorare non pigebit.
units.tr: This is also why I broke off this subject, which I had begun and promised some years ago. I would not have resumed it, nor wished it to come into people's hands, even if I had been compelled to. This was not only because of my slight hope of promoting the benefit of all, but also so that the minds of many, entangled in the errors shown here, would not conceive bitterer feelings. Yet since I am confident that good people remain among them, and not few in number, this other consideration has prevailed. Those who write with an honest and good mind will certainly please such readers, since their writings agree with the Scriptures, by which truth is confirmed in the inner recess of a conscience that sincerely examines itself before God. And if you look at the evils indicated here, these writings reveal them every day, more than enough, in deeds. If the more unreasonable, out of their own peevishness, are unwilling to be satisfied with these arguments, what else can I do but refer them to the pagans? I mean to those whom everyone of learning and judgment holds in the highest esteem. Among them the excellent Theban Cebes embraced the matter of true and false learning in a riddle, and though I commend the whole work for reading, I will not hesitate to note here one or two points that concern the guests of false learning.

units.la: LXXXVII. Is postquam intra septum aliquod sub mulieris persona ostendit eam, quam vani homines Eruditionem vocant; eandem non nisi falsam Eruditionem esse asseverat, ad quam tamen illos qui servandi sunt, falsa, non & ad veram Eruditionem postea perventuri, primum divertere dicit, etsi alia ad veram eruditionem breviorque sit via. Tum interrogatus de hominibus qui intra septum illud obambulant, quinam illi essent? respondet, falsæ Eruditionis eos amatores esse; at deceptos, se veræ Eruditionis familiaritatem sibi opinantes. Porro rogitatus, quibus nominibus isti appellentur? sic inquit: Alii quidem Poetæ, alii vero Rhetorici, alii Dialectici, alii Musici, alii Arithmetici, alii Geometræ, alii Astrologi, alii Voluptuarii (seu Epicurei) alii Peripatetici, alii Critici, & cæteri omnes bis vicini, quibus veluti socias haud insolitas annectit mulierculas, Incontinentiam, Luxuriam, Avaritiam, Adulationem, Pœnam, Mœstitiam, Infelicitatem & similes: tum & Ignorantiæ & Imposturæ venena, ipsamque etiam clara voce AMENTIAM. Dein subjungit: Neque vero ab iis (falsis Eruditis) vel Opiniones, vel cætera mala recedent, donec repudiata Eruditione falsa veram ingressi viam, Purgatricem illarum rerum Vim biberint, & mala omnia, quibus replentur, Opiniones, Ignorantiam, omnemque reliquam vitiositatem ejecerint: tum demum enim ferbabuntur. Dum vero hic manserint apud Falsam Eruditionem, nunquam liberabuntur; neque ullum malum, si larum quidem disciplinarum subsidio, profligabunt. Postea viam ad Eruditionem veram ostendit, & eam quidem cum a perpaucis tritam, tum præcipitem & asperam; sed ad quam perficiendam hortatione & auxilio conferant Continentia & Tolerantia; (hoc est, verbis Euangelicis, Abnegatio sui, & Patientia sive crucis amplexatio: ) quæ ubi Viatorem ad Eruditionis solidæ præsentiam adduxerunt, hæc, omnium primò, poculum purgante potione, plenum ei ebibendum porrigit, quo quæcunque prius imbiberat, secumque intus inhærentia attulerat, expurget omnia & dejiciat: tum demum Sanitatis, Veritatis, Virtutum & Felicitatis capacem fore; non vero ante, neque aliter. Quæ sane in homine Ethnico admirabilia de Eruditione sunt documenta.
units.tr: LXXXVII. After he has shown, within a certain enclosure, under the figure of a woman, what vain men call learning, he asserts that it is nothing but false learning. Yet he says that those who are to be saved must first turn aside to it, false, not yet to true learning, which they will reach afterwards, although there is another, shorter way to true learning. Then, when asked about the people who walk about inside that enclosure, who they are, he answers that they are lovers of false learning; but they are deceived, imagining themselves to be familiar with true learning. Asked further by what names these are called, he says: Some are poets, some rhetoricians, some dialecticians, some musicians, some arithmeticians, some geometers, some astrologers, some devotees of pleasure (or Epicureans), some Peripatetics, some critics, and all the others who are close neighbours to these; and to these he joins, like companions not unusual, little women: Incontinence, Luxury, Avarice, Flattery, Punishment, Sadness, Unhappiness and such like; then also the poisons of Ignorance and Imposture, and, in a clear voice, MADNESS itself. Then he adds: Nor will the opinions or the other evils withdraw from these (false learned) men until, having rejected false learning and entered the true way, they have drunk the purging power of those things and have expelled all the evils with which they are filled, opinions, ignorance, and all the rest of their vice: for then at last they will be saved. But while they remain with false learning they will never be freed, nor will they overcome any evil by the help of those disciplines alone. After this he shows the way to true learning, which is trodden by very few, steep and rough; but to accomplish it, self-restraint and endurance give help and encouragement (that is, in the words of the Gospel, self-denial and patience, or embracing the cross). When these have brought the traveller into the presence of solid learning, they first offer him a cup to drink in full, a purging draught, so that it may cleanse and cast out whatever he had previously drunk in and had brought with him, clinging within him. Only then will he be capable of health, truth, virtues and happiness; not before, nor otherwise. These are indeed admirable teachings about learning from a pagan.

units.la: In quibus & id notandum, quod dicat eos, qui sunt servandi, & ad veram eruditionem perventuri, primùm ad falsam divertere; &, paulo post, ab ea quædam accipere, quæ postmodum utilia esse possint, etsi non necessaria: hæc dicit esse literas & disciplinas cæteras, quæ, Platonis judicio, sint veluti fræna adolescentibus, ne aliis rebus pejoribus distrahantur: eas autem, etsi commodæ sint, nec inutiles, veluti linguæ cognitio ad hoc ut sine interprete alicujus dicta cognoscamus; non esse tamen necessarias, nec conducere ut viri meliores evadamus. Nonne ergo, quaerit, meliore conditione sunt caeteris scientiae istas non doctis, • Mathematici, sive disciplinis iltis imbuti; nec facilius possunt fieri meliores? Imo, respondet, quare praestant caeteris, cum eos de rebus bonis & malis non minus erronee sentire quam caeteros sit evidens, sintque ipsimet adhuc omnis generis nequitiae constricti? Nil enim verat nosse literas & tenere disciplinas omnes; simul tamen esse ebriosum, intemperantem, avarum, injustum, proditorem, denique amentem: (imo, aeque vel etiam magis superbum, indocilem, ferum, ignavum, bonorum osorem, contemtorem, irrisorem, calumniatorem, persecutorem, impium, atheum.) Multos certe quidem tales videre licet. Quae ergo istorum quasi praerogativa est ob istas disciplinas, ut in viros evadant meliores? Nulla.... Quod si videatur verae Eruditioni vicinores quam idiotae, quem inde capiunt fructum? cum saepe videre liceat aliquos e primo (ineruditorum) septo ab incontinentia caeterisque vitiis in tertium ad veram Eruditionem pervenire, qui istos disciplinarum sectatores praeteretunt? (Quae Augustinum sibi ideo indignabundum in haec verba adegerant: (a) Quid patimur? Quid est hoc? Quid audisti? Surgunt indocti, & caelum rapiunt: & nos cum doctrinis nostris sine corde, ecce, ubi volutamur in carne & sanguine! ) Pergit Cebes: Quis ergo jam dicat istos (doctos) praestare caeteris? Quin potius ignaviores sunt, aut minus dociles..... Namque, ut nil aliud dicam, illud certe peccant, quod ea se scire profiteantur quae nesciunt, quia opinione dum imbuti sunt, ignaviores eos esse necesse est ad veram Eruditionem expetendam. Quare opinionibus solum pleni, nihilo cæteris meliores sunt, nisi cum Pœnitentia seillis adjunxerit, persuasumque habuerint se vera Eruditione carere, falsa potiri, a qua seducti, eo in statu quamdiu sunt nequeunt esse salvi. Hactenus ille.
units.tr: In these words we should also note that he says that those who are to be saved and to reach true learning first turn aside to false learning; and shortly after, they receive from it certain things which may later be useful, though not necessary. He says these are letters and the other disciplines, which, in Plato's judgment, are like reins for young people, so that they are not drawn off into worse things. Yet although these are convenient and not useless (for example, a knowledge of languages, so that we may understand what is said without an interpreter), they are not necessary, nor do they help us become better men. Are not those who are not learned in those sciences, the mathematicians or those steeped in those disciplines, in a better condition than the others? Could they not more easily become better? Indeed, he answers, why should they excel the others, since it is plain that they judge good and evil no less erroneously than others, and they themselves are still bound by every kind of wickedness? For nothing prevents someone from knowing letters and holding all the disciplines, and yet being a drunkard, intemperate, greedy, unjust, a traitor, in short mad (indeed just as proud, unteachable, savage, lazy, a hater of the good, a despiser, a mocker, a slanderer, a persecutor, impious, atheistic). Many such men can certainly be seen. What then is their supposed privilege on account of these disciplines, that they become better men? None.... But if they seem nearer to true learning than the unlearned, what fruit do they gain from it? Since we often see some who, from the first enclosure of the ignorant, pass from incontinence and other vices into the third, true learning, who would overtake those devotees of the disciplines? (These things had moved Augustine to indignation, so that he cried out in these words: "What are we suffering? What is this? What have you heard? The unlearned rise up and seize heaven, and we, with our learning, without heart, behold where we wallow in flesh and blood!") Cebes goes on: Who then will say that these learned men excel the others? Rather they are more lazy, or less teachable..... For, to say nothing else, they certainly err in this, that they profess to know what they do not know; because, steeped in opinion, they must be more lazy in seeking true learning. Therefore, full only of opinions, they are no better than the others, unless they add repentance to these and are persuaded that they lack true learning and possess false learning, by which they have been led astray, and so long as they are in that state they cannot be saved. So far he.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Causa cur omnes ad Eruditionem falsam primo accedant, est, tum quod ipsa ubique fere proflet, tum quod recens animus veritatis avidus, quicquid ut veritatem & eruditionem audit proclamari, velit protinus acquirere: unde eum in quam plurima falsa incidere necesse est. Quod autem inde alii postea elabantur, cæteri non; id ex habitudinum animorumque conditionibus procedit. Namque eos qui quam diutissime in Eruditione falsa consenuerunt, nunquam sperandum est elabi posse, nisi admodum sint indolis sincerae, submississimae, minimeque pertinacis: at si diuturnæ consuetudini accedat cordis malignitas, commodorum atque gloriolæ ex Eruditione falsa manantium amor, tunc ilicet, actum est. Non ita ubi falsa in animis radices profundiores agere non permiserit minus longa mora: quod adolescentibus maxime & juvenibus evenire potest sæpius, quando præsertim nobilioris & liberioris sunt indolis, neque ex turpi scopo commoda sua aut laudeculas aucupandi, sed ex solidæ & æternæ Veritatis amore, cum pietate erga Deum, Eruditionem quærere sibi proposuerunt. Namque postquam omnibus vel præcipuis quæ vulgo tradi solent, se
units.tr: LXXXVIII. The reason why everyone first approaches false learning is that it is almost everywhere widespread, and that the mind, fresh and eager for truth, wishes at once to acquire whatever it hears proclaimed as truth and learning; hence it must necessarily fall into very many falsehoods. That some afterwards slip out of these, and others do not, arises from differences in habits and dispositions of mind. For those who have grown old for the longest time in false learning can never be expected to escape, unless they are of a truly sincere, very submissive and least obstinate nature. But if a malignity of heart is added to long-standing habit, and a love of the advantages and little glories that flow from false learning, then indeed it is all over. It is not so where a shorter delay has not allowed falsehoods to take deeper root in the mind. This can happen most often to adolescents and young people, especially when they are of a nobler and freer disposition, and when they have set themselves to seek learning not for the sake of gaining their own advantages or the applause of others from a base aim, but from love of solid and eternal truth, with piety toward God. For after they have been steeped in all, or at least the chief things that are commonly taught, or have tasted enough of them to be able to judge what they themselves are, behold, they perceive in their hearts, from the longing for solid truth by which they are held, that they are not satisfied by all that they have acquired, nor are they in full possession of their hope; but they are left in greater darkness, ignorance and...

units.la: imbuerunt, sufficienterve de illis degustarunt, quo quænam sint ipsi possint judicare; ecce, percipiunt tamen in cordibus suis, veritatis solidæ desiderio, quo tenentur, non satisfieri per omnia illa sua acquisita, neque se spe sua esse compotes; sed majoribus tenebris, ignorantiis & inquietudinibus se magis obnoxios vident quam ante: unde (Deo secretius animam ad solida vera disponente) fastidio & contemtu illorum paulatim magis magisque tanguntur: tum vero ubi vel lucis clarior scintillula aliunde apparet, sentiunt se interius veluti a potente quodam motore percelli & propelli ita vivide, ut sibi id dissimulare nequeant, nec possint non ad solidorum bonorum, (contemta eruditione vana,) desiderium ardentius incitari. Et tunc quidem jacienda est alea, jacetque hoc in puncto principium æternitatis felicis aut miseræ, luminosæ aut tenebrosæ, prout pretiosissimo hoc momento quis bene aut secus usus fuerit. Si enim se vi quadam ab eo divertat, perque mille vanas & priores occupationes quærat (reluctante conscientia) diviniorem eum sensum supprimere, eo quod illum sequendo, timeat se in tales vias deventurum, ubi vel commodis, vel favore, vel existimatione vanorum hominionum sit decisurus; ecce, tunc pergit inde ad tristem animæ interitum. At si iis spretis sese Veritatis & Eruditionis veræ fonti, Æterno Deo, velit animitus committere illuminandum & regendum, illico fiet in dies fortior, atque tandem totus voti compos, si quidem perseveranter eam viam tenuerit quam libro primo exposuimus: quæ eo redit, ut quis a vanitatibus, ignorantiis & pravitatibus suis corde toto convertatur ad Dominum, tum bene agendo nec non nocte dieque orando insistens, lumen ejus & sapientiam ab eo ardentibus precibus gemitibusque perseveraret efflagitet, exspectetque patienter ejus auxilium. Tunc Dominus, ubi perspexerit perseverantiam ejus non esse fucatam, sed sincerissimam, primo quidem luminis sui radio homini tenebras suas malignitatemque prius occultam sic deteget, ut is horridus sibi appareat: atque hoc ideo ut in vera humilitate fundetur: dein postea amabile præbebit illi vultus sui lumen, intellectum ejus in formas divinas protinus immutans; ubi vividas icones de se ipso, de Deo, deque ejus operibus internis vel externis videbit expressas, quantum e re judicabit Deus. In qua quidem operatione Eruditionis veræ fundamenta fructusque cum gaudio & tranquillitate degustabit & possidebit homo eruditus, hac tamen lege; ut tanquam de thesauro sibi, ex se inopi, concredito, non glorietur, neque sit in se securus, nec se ideo meliorem cæteris existimet, ne forte Domino quod suum est ab eo resumente, in tenebras prioribus multo densiores ruat præceps; sed converseturpotius, quam diu hic vivitur, in continuo timore atque animi humilitate, omnis veri & boni gloriam soli Deo tribuens.
units.tr: They have been steeped in all the chief doctrines that are commonly taught, or have tasted them well enough to judge what they are. Yet they perceive in their hearts, from the longing for solid truth that holds them, that this longing is not satisfied by all their acquired learning, and that they do not possess the hope they had. Instead they see themselves more exposed to darkness, ignorance and restlessness than before. Hence, as God more secretly disposes the soul toward solid truths, they are gradually moved more and more by distaste and contempt for those things. Then, when a brighter little spark of light appears from some other quarter, they feel themselves struck and driven inwardly, as if by some powerful mover, so vividly that they cannot hide it from themselves, and cannot help being spurred more ardently toward solid goods, with vain learning despised. At that point the die is cast, and the beginning of an eternity, happy or wretched, luminous or dark, hangs on that moment, depending on whether a person uses this most precious moment well or badly. If he turns aside from it by some force, and seeks through a thousand vain and earlier occupations to suppress that diviner sense (his conscience resisting), because he fears that by following it he will come to such ways where he will decide for the sake of advantages, favour, or the esteem of vain men, then he proceeds from there to the sad ruin of his soul. But if, having spurned these things, he is willing to entrust himself inwardly to the fount of truth and true learning, to the eternal God, to be enlightened and ruled, he will at once grow stronger day by day, and at last will have all his desire, provided he persevere in the way we set out in the first book. That way comes to this: a person turns from his vanities, ignorances and wickednesses with his whole heart to the Lord, persists in doing good and in praying night and day, and earnestly and perseveringly asks for his light and wisdom with fervent prayers and groanings, and waits patiently for his help. Then the Lord, when he sees that the perseverance is not feigned but most sincere, will first reveal with a ray of his light the darkness and malice that were hidden in the man, so that he appears horrible to himself, and this is so that he may be founded in true humility. Afterwards he will show him the amiable light of his face, at once changing his understanding into divine forms, where he will see lively images of himself, of God, and of his internal and external works expressed, as far as God judges fitting. In this operation the learned man will taste and possess the foundations and fruits of true learning with joy and tranquillity, yet on this condition: that, as with a treasure entrusted to him, poor in himself, he does not boast, nor feel secure in himself, nor think himself better than others, lest, if the Lord takes back what is his, he fall headlong into darkness far denser than before. Rather, for as long as we live here, he should live in continual fear and humility of mind, ascribing the glory of all truth and goodness to God alone.

units.la: LXXXIX. Quæ sane omnia ofcitanter non sunt pertractanda. Sola hæc namque so- lida
units.tr: LXXXIX. All these things certainly must not be treated carelessly, for these alone are solid.

units.la: Ab eru ditione sal-fa ad ve-ram, inci-tamenta. hida sunt, sola nobis digna, sola ob quæ sumus conditi. Hic de bono æterno & de malo immenso agitur; deque corona duraturæ felicitatis, & de doloribus tum ignominiosis, & vero nunquam finituris. Et nunc quidem hæc dum vita est, optionis tempus est inter illa. Datur nunc ætatem impendere vel in colligendis margaritis & thesauris æternis ipsoque omnis boni fonte nunquam desituro comparando; vel in coacervandis pusillis, vanis, nugacissimis & Satanicis nugamentis, cum infinita pœnitudine mox evanescentibus, & post momentaneam titillationem curiositatis, animam æterna solidi boni & veri vacuitate torquendam relicturis. Eja ingenuæ & pretiosæ literatorum animæ! Eccur diutius laudatam partis bonæ differretis electionem, exspectantes ad mortem usque, opinione semper proximiorem, quando in lectulo ferali frustra lugebitis tempora in vestris vanissimis vanitatibus misere nec reparabiliter deperdita; dum tamen nunc solidæ & inenarrabilis lætitiæ pro illa fatali hora materiam nunquam perituram acquirere datur, si modo falsa Eruditione generose extrusa, animitus nos reddamus formandos immensæ Potentiæ & Bonitati omnium primævæ Formatricis, Sapientiæ æternæ, unius veræ Matris & informatricis nostræ, quæ nos & omnia ad hoc produxit, ut & omnium & sui ipsius, æterni hæredes essemus? Sumus namque filii Dei, ejusque progenies, quibus proinde omnes divitiarum, luminum, felicitatum, operum, Sapientiæque thesauros gratis largiri decrevit, nullo alio labore nostro, nisi ut rebellare in eum definentes, è pretioso animæ nostræ vase sordes & ineptias rejiciamus; tum ad eum, Sapientiæ veræ aquas desideranter postulantes, accurramus. Is & nunc se offert intus pulsans, & extus dudum unicuique clamavit: (a) Heus, quisquis sitit, venite ad aquas: quibus nulla est pecunia, comparate & comedite: venite, inquam, comparate absque pecunia & absque pretio vinum & lac, (eruditionem vivificantem pro magnis & parvis.) Cur expenditis pecuniam pro nullo cibo; & laborem vestrum pro re minime satiatura? Audite me sine mora, & bonis vscemini, seque obleƈtabit pinguedine anima vestra. Præbete aures & venite ad me: audite & vivet anima vestra, pangamque vobiscum æternum fœdus, benignitates fideliter Davidi præstitas servaturus. (b) Petite, & dabitur vobis: quærite, & invenietis: pulsate, & aperietur vobis. Si vos, qui estis improbi, scitis bona dona liberis vestris dare; quanto magis Pater cœlestis bona dona & Spiritum sanƈtum dabit petentibus à se. Petentibus dicit & oranti bus, non ratiocinantibus & intellectus sui activitate ideas & notiones omnigenas sibi ad eruditionem excitare conantibus, de quibus quippe istud est Dei decretum, à Christo lætante propalatum: (c) Collaudo te, Pater, cœli terræque Domine, quod hæc eruditos peritosque celaveris, & patefeceris parvulis: ita fiat, ô Pater! siquidem ita tibi placitum est. Omnia mihi tradidit Pater: neque Filium
units.tr: From false erudition to the true; incitements. These alone are solid, alone worthy of us, alone the reason we were made.
