Here the matter concerns eternal good and immense evil, and the crown of lasting happiness, and sorrows both shameful and never to end. Now, while life lasts, there is a time to choose between these. We may spend our age either in gathering the pearls and treasures of eternity and in acquiring the very fount of all good that will never fail; or in heaping up small, vain, trifling and Satanic baubles, which soon vanish with endless regret, and which, after a momentary tickling of curiosity, will leave the soul to be tormented by the eternal emptiness of solid good and truth. Come, noble and precious souls of the learned! Why do you put off the long-praised choice of the better part, waiting until death, which always seems nearer than you think, when on your deathbed you will mourn in vain the time you wasted, miserably and irretrievably, on your most vain vanities? Yet now it is given to acquire, for that fatal hour, a solid and inexpressible joy that will never perish, if only we cast out false erudition with nobility, and give ourselves inwardly to be formed by the immense Power and Goodness, the first of all Formers, eternal Wisdom, the one true Mother and Informer of us, who brought us and all things into being so that we might be heirs of all things and of herself, eternally. For we are the sons of God, and his offspring, to whom he has decided to give freely all the treasures of riches, lights, happiness, works and wisdom, requiring no other labour from us except that we cease to rebel against him, and cast out the filth and follies from the precious vessel of our soul; then we should hasten to him, eagerly asking for the waters of true Wisdom. He both now offers himself, knocking within, and long ago cried out to everyone outwardly: (a) "Ho, whoever thirsts, come to the waters; you who have no money, buy and eat; come, I say, buy wine and milk without money and without price" (the life-giving learning for great and small). "Why do you spend money on what is no food, and your labour on what does not satisfy? Listen to me without delay, and eat what is good, and let your soul delight itself in richness. Incline your ears and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live, and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, faithfully keeping the kindnesses shown to David." (b) "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good gifts and the Holy Spirit to those who ask him." He speaks to those who ask and pray, not to those who reason and try by the activity of their own intellect to stir up for themselves ideas and notions of every kind for learning, concerning which indeed this is God's decree, declared by Christ with joy: (c) "I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the learned and wise, and revealed them to babes. So it is, O Father, since such has been your good pleasure. All things have been delivered to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him."

units.la: (Deum operaque redemtionis) quisquam non vit nisi ille; neque Patrem (Deum operaque creationis) quisquam nisi Filius, atque is, cui voluerit Filius patefacere. Venite ad me omnes laborantes & onusti; ego recreabo vos. Subite jugum meum (abnegationem & crucem, sive, abstinentiam & tolerantiam) & discite a me, mitem me esse & corde humilem; & invenietis animis vestris requiem. ( a ) Qui in me credit (mihi confidit intellectum facultatesque suas implendas & regendas,) ejus e visceribus viventis aquae flumina profluent: quod de Spiritu, quem recepturi erant, fidem ei habentes, proferebat: qui Spiritus sane Spiritus veritatis est & luminis, atque verae, si ulla est, cognitionis & scientiae. At, inquiet aliquis, hoc Spiritu, hocque modo, acquiram forsitan ego donaquidem pietatis & devotionis, aliaque communia quae vel quis e plebe possit adipisci, & quibus ego bonus, simplex & pius idiota evasero, caeterum forte indoctus nec rerum naturas & proprietates supra vulgus apprime callens. Miser & inconsiderate, qui a Dei tui potente & sapiente cura ac regimine vis aufugere & subtrahi, ut ab imbecilla rationis tuae activitate sola pendeas, & omnia exspectes! Itane nescis quid sit illa tui regiminis, tuae activitatis, tuae rationis imbellis & evanida potentia, quam quotidie somnus, intemperies, morbillus insanam, deliram, stolidam, cassam possint reddere? quam interclusus narium tuarum halitus vitaeque labilis vapor evanescens momento possint sic efficere impotentem & nullam, ut ipsemet hinctibi omnino nullus sis futurus ; quando tamen ex istis angultiis ( in quas certo eertius incides) unum Dei regimen omnipotens, te, si ei fueris commissus, totum possit in integrum ,imo in aeternum & perfectissimum statum restituere ; maluerisne proprio ductu evanidas ineptias venari , quam tantisper exspectare, donec omnis boni & veri, increati atque creati fontem tuto accipias?
units.tr: (God and the work of redemption) no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father (God and the work of creation) except the Son, and whomever the Son chooses to reveal him to. Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you (denial of self and the cross, or abstinence and endurance), and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. (a) "He who believes in me (trusts me to have his understanding and faculties filled and governed), out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water," which he said, believing in the Spirit they were about to receive. This Spirit is indeed the Spirit of truth and light, and of true knowledge and science, if there is any. But someone will say: by this Spirit, and in this way, perhaps I shall acquire the gifts of piety and devotion, and other common things which even a man of the common people can obtain, and by which I shall become a good, simple and pious layman, but perhaps unlearned and not especially skilled in the natures and properties of things above the common people. Wretched and thoughtless man, who wish to flee from and withdraw from the powerful and wise care and rule of your God, so that you may depend only on the feeble activity of your own reason, and expect everything from it! Do you not know what that power of your own rule, your own activity, your own reason is, a weak and fading power, which sleep, intemperance, or a little illness can make insane, deranged, stupid and empty every day? How a blocked breath in your nostrils, or the fading vapour of your fragile life, can in a moment make you so powerless and nothing that you will be altogether nothing to yourself? Since, out of these anguishes (into which you will certainly fall more surely than you think), the one omnipotent rule of God could, if you are committed to him, restore you wholly, indeed to an eternal and most perfect state, would you rather hunt after fading follies by your own leading, than wait a little while until you receive safely the fount of all good and truth, both uncreated and created?

units.la: Differ, habent parva commoda magna mora. Etiam hic interdum Deus momento ea-, & plura, largitur, quae propria activitate non ita inventa fuissent. Nec vero rationem & dona naturalia is destruit: sed postquam eurationis pusillo tempore deficere visa sunt, perficit ea demum & ornat quam abundantissime & nitidissime; nisi quando sapientur videt ornamentis suis nos in superbiam & perniciem esse abusuros: quod superbiae periculum fere semper subest, clauditque liberales manus provido salutis animarum curatori & amatori. Ecce enim, quando nugamenta futilissima vix possidemus vanamque eruditionis umbram, illico tamen sic superbimus, ut plebeji simpliciores que animae nobis jam sordeant, & veluti ab alto despiciantur, nec non omnium quae humilia sunt, nos pudeat! Quid ergo ageremus si vera bona nobis essent concredita? Scortaremur sane spiritualiter cum illis, nobiscum & cum spiritibus nequitiae rebusque creatis omnibus, daremusque ideis illarum, rationis agilis exercitio, nec non propriae excellentiae confiderationi, affectus omnes, facultatesque nostras, & delicias totas, relicto Deo, animarum inhabitatore, domino, socio & sponso, qui præcise creavit animas nostras ut illæ cum eo deliciarentur & occuparentur; non autem cum creaturis & chimæris vanis relicto Creatore benedicto, qui sane dudum conqueri posset nos hactenus nil aliud fecisse, quam animas nostras omnis generis vanitatibus eruditionis falsæ Satanæque dominatoris hujus constuprandas prostituere, deserto Ipsomet earum Sponso, qui & adulterii hujus sæpe omnes sub Israelitarum typo admonet, & verò ad pœnitentiam facti animam propitiabili animo sic revocat: (a) Vulgo dicitur, si dimiserit vir uxorem suam, & illa recedens ab eo duxerit virum alterum, nunquid revertetur ad eam ultra? nunquid non polluta & contaminata erit mulier illa? Tu autem fornicata es cum amatoribus multis: tamen revertere ad me, dicit Dominus; & ego suscipiam te. Leva oculos tuos in directum, & vide ubi non prostrata sis, [quibus objectis tete, deserto Deo, non tradideris,] in viis [in diversis modis & methodis falsæ eruditionis] sedebas exspectans eos [observans omnis generis objecta, nova, curiosa, rara, vulgaria etiam] quasi latro in solitudine, [ut ea a scopo suo ad tuam voluptatem avide raperes, & in cerebro tuo, mente, museo sola apud te pertractares] & polluisti terram in fornicationibus tuis, & in malitiis tuis, [ad propriam gloriam, & potentiam & voluntatis tuæ obsequium iis abutens.] Quamobrem prohibitæ sunt stillæ pluviarum, [non amplius descendunt cœlitus super te dona Dei gratiosa.] &
units.tr: Put it off: small advantages carry great delays. Even here God sometimes bestows, in a moment, many things that would not have been found by our own activity. Nor indeed does he destroy reason and natural gifts. Rather, when these seem to fail for a short time through lack of cultivation, he at last completes and adorns them most abundantly and brilliantly, unless he sees that we would abuse his ornaments for pride and our own ruin. That danger of pride almost always lies close at hand, and it shuts the generous hands of the provident caretaker and lover of our salvation. For look: when we scarcely possess the most trivial trifles and a vain shadow of learning, we at once become so proud that simpler, plainer souls already seem contemptible to us, and we look down on them as from a height, and are ashamed of everything humble! What then would we do if true goods had been entrusted to us? We would surely play the harlot spiritually with them, with the spirits of wickedness and with all created things, and we would give over all our affections, faculties and whole delight, to the ideas of those things, to the nimble exercise of reason, and to the contemplation of our own excellence, having abandoned God, the indweller, Lord, companion and bridegroom of our souls, who created our souls precisely so that they might delight in him and be occupied with him. Instead we would turn to creatures and empty chimeras, having abandoned the blessed Creator. He could justly complain that until now we have done nothing but prostitute our souls to be defiled by every kind of vanity of false learning and of Satan, the ruler of this world, having deserted their own Bridegroom. He also warns all of this adultery under the type of the Israelites, and with a merciful spirit calls the soul back to repentance: (a) Commonly it is said, if a man put away his wife, and she going from him become another man's, shall he return unto her again? Shall not that land be greatly polluted? But thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, saith the Lord, and I will receive thee. Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lain with. [By what objects you have not been given over to, having deserted God,] In the ways [in the various modes and methods of false learning] you sat waiting for them [watching every kind of object, new, curious, rare, even common,] as a robber in the wilderness, [so that you might greedily snatch them from their aim for your own pleasure, and handle them alone in your brain, mind and study] and you have polluted the land with your whoredoms and with your wickedness, [abusing them for your own glory, your power and the service of your will.] Therefore the showers have been withholding, [the gracious gifts of God no longer descend from heaven upon you;] and

units.la: (a) Deut. 24. 1–4 (ad vocem Vulgo dicitur, 3: 1). & serotinus imber non fuit, [ repressæ sunt gratiarum divinarum plenitudines, ultimis seculis vesperæque temporum promissæ. ] Frons mulieris meretricis facta est tibi [gloriaris impudenter de ista tua defectione a Deo ad eruditionis falsæ meretricia :- ] & noluisti erubescere [ quod velis scortari continuo cum nube salsæ sapientiæ. ] Ergo saltem a modo voca me, Pater mi, dux virginitatis meæ tu es, [juventutisque verus & unus moderator ! ]
units.tr: (a) Deut. 24:1–4 (at the words Commonly it is said, Jer. 3:1). and there hath been no latter rain [the fullness of the divine graces is withheld, which were promised for the last ages and the evening of time.] Thou hadst a whore's forehead [you boast shamelessly of this your defection from God to the harlotries of false learning;] and thou refusedst to be ashamed [since you wish to play the harlot continually with the cloud of false wisdom.] Wilt thou not from this time cry unto me, My father, thou art the guide of my virginity, [and the true and only governor of my youth!]

units.la: Nunquid vero tu, Domine, irasceris in perpetuum, nec amplius adorandi vultus tui lumine nobis in horrendis nostris cæcitatibus & tenebris, inque vanarum, absurdissimarum & Satanicarum ineptiarum fluctibus hactenus ob ingratitudines nostras in te immanes, obque tui oblivionem demersis & jactatis, illucescesne? Itane patieris animas nostras, thronum gloriæ tuæ, ab inimica tenebrarum potestate profanari in perpetuum, & creaturæ incassum filios hominum! Tune diutius Omnia certo fine gubernans, Hominum solos respuis actus Merito Rector cohibere modo? O jam miseras respice terras, Quisquis rerum fœdera nectis. Operis tanti pars non vilis Homines, quatimur fortunæ salo. Rapidos, Rector, comprime fluctus. Disjice terrenæ nebulas & pondera molis, Atque tuo splendore mica,
units.tr: Will you indeed, Lord, be angry for ever, and will you not again shine upon us with the light of your adorable face, in our dreadful blindness and darkness, and in the waves of vain, absurd and satanic follies, into which we have hitherto been plunged and tossed because of our monstrous ingratitude towards you and our forgetfulness of you? Will you suffer our souls, the throne of your glory, to be profaned for ever by the hostile power of darkness, and the creature to have made the sons of men in vain? Will you still refuse to restrain the deeds of men, you who govern all things by a certain end, and rightly rule them? O, look now upon our wretched lands, you who bind the covenants of things. We men, no small part of so great a work, are tossed on the sea of fortune. Rector, restrain the rapid waves. Scatter the clouds of earth and the weight of its mass, and shine with your splendour.

units.la: Et eripe nos a Spiritu nunc efficaciter operante in filiis tibi rebellibus: saltem eos respice qui non spontanea nec cognita sibi electione; sed veluti misera infelicis nativitatis, educationis, associationis forte hos in casses inciderunt. Ecce enim, a pueritia inscii erudimur in omni re vana; & quod ultimo vel nunquam docemur, viæ sunt Christi tui! Quis vero sic, Domine, præservare possit animam suam ab omnibus istis falsarum disciplinarum tricis & periculis hactenus recensitis? Quomodo misera adolescentis anima, vias tuas nondum experta, atque studiorum periculosum pelagus eruditionis gratia ingressa, naufragium evasura est æternum; nisi tu, Domine, animarum Pater, lux & rector, prehensa manu, & vibrato lucis tuæ in interiora nostra fulgore, eruas nos a blanditiis mulieris illius meretricis, Eruditionis falsæ, cujus parabolica descriptione a sapientissimo Regum proposita clausurus sum hoc quicquid scripsi hic operis ad Sapientiæ tuæ æternæ gloriam, quam in nobis & per nos, Deus, promove ea charitate & potentia, quibus nos & creasti, & ad creationem novam revocasti, paratus illam exsequi, ubi sponte ab eruditione falsa volemus recedere, divinæ vero attendere, ad quam nos ita benigne Sapientis ore allicis:
units.tr: And snatch us from the Spirit now working effectually in your rebellious sons. At least look upon those who did not enter upon this by a choice that was spontaneous or known to themselves, but who, as it were, have fallen by chance into these snares through the unhappy circumstances of their wretched birth, upbringing and companionship. For look: from boyhood we are taught in ignorance every vain thing, and what we are taught last, or never, are the ways of your Christ! Who, Lord, can thus preserve his soul from all these snares and dangers of false disciplines recounted so far? How will a young man's wretched soul, not yet acquainted with your ways, and having entered for the sake of learning upon the perilous sea of study, escape eternal shipwreck, unless you, Lord, Father, light and ruler of souls, take it by the hand and, flashing the lightning of your light into our inmost parts, rescue us from the allurements of that harlot, false learning, whose parabolic description, set forth by the wisest of kings, I shall use to close whatever I have written in this work, to the eternal glory of your Wisdom, which, God, promote in us and through us, with the same charity and power by which you created us and called us back to a new creation, ready to carry it out, when we are willing to withdraw of our own accord from false learning, and to attend to the divine, to which you so kindly invite us with the mouth of Wisdom:

units.la: Proverb. Cap. VII.
units.tr: Proverbs, Chapter VII.

units.la: Fili mi, [dilecta hominum progenies, quæ ut a me Deo tuo nata; sic a me es erudienda] custodi sermones meos, [quibus te conformes] & præcepta mea reconde tibi, [ne per mentis ad ad inania distractionem a te prætermittan- tur. ]
units.tr: My son, [beloved offspring of men, who, as born of me your God, so must be taught by me:] keep my words, [by which you are to be shaped] and store up my precepts for yourself, [lest they be drawn away from you by a distraction of the mind toward vanities.]

units.la: Fili, serva mandata mea, & vives, [non idealibus vanitatibus titillatus, sed vita vera & solide beata inde ditatus : ] & legem meam quasi pupillam oculi tui: [ inde enim animæ visus lumenque pendet. ]
units.tr: My son, keep my commandments, and you shall live, [not tickled by idle vanities, but enriched thereby with true life and solid blessedness:] and my law as the apple of your eye: [for the sight and light of the soul depend on it.]

units.la: Alliga eam digitis tuis, [praxi & exercitiis] scribe illam in tabulis cordis, [ in facultatibus constantis & ardentis desiderii & amoris. ]
units.tr: Bind it upon your fingers, [by practice and exercise] write it upon the tablets of your heart, [in the faculties of a steadfast and ardent desire and love.]

units.la: Dic Sapientiæ, [Eruditioni veræ] Soror mea es: [macte animo, & oratione continua familiaritatem Sapientiæ Dei, Patris communis, quære, pete, spera ] & prudentiam [quæ omnia justo pretio æstimat & tractat] voca amicam tuam [ tuos affectus ei conservando. ]
units.tr: Say to Wisdom, [to true learning] You are my sister: [be of good courage, and by continual prayer seek, ask, and hope for the familiarity of the Wisdom of God, the common Father;] and call prudence [which values and handles all things at their just price] your friend, [by keeping your affections fixed upon her.]

units.la: Ut custodeat te a muliere extranea [ab Eruditione falsa, externas res solum & transeuntes respiciente ] & ab aliena ] quæ nec a Deo est, & vero cor ab eo alienat ] quæ verba sua facit dulcia [ verba eloquenter fucans, & splendidis promissis auriculas demulcens. ]
units.tr: That she may keep you from the strange woman [from false learning, which looks only at outward and passing things] and from the stranger [who is not of God, and estranges the heart from him] who flatters with her words [who dresses up words eloquently and soothes the ears with splendid promises.]

units.la: De fenestra enim domus mea per cancellos prospexi: [ab intimis ad externa meditationem meam traduxi. ]
units.tr: For at the window of my house I looked through the lattice: [I turned my meditation from inward things to outward ones.]

units.la: Et vidi o parvulos [ video adolescentes inexpertos & ad quemvis ductum paratos :] considero vecordem juvenem [cui animus non est resistere vanitati, neque desiderare Creatorem suum in diebus juventutis suæ. ]
units.tr: And I saw among the simple ones, [I see inexperienced young men, ready for whatever leading they receive:] I beheld a young man void of understanding, [who has no mind to resist vanity, nor to desire his Creator in the days of his youth.]

units.la: Qui transit per plateam, juxta angulum, [qui & per mundum locaque mundanis illustriora, ] & prope viam illius [prope loca Eruditioni falsæ propagandæ destinata, ]graditur in obscuro, [ in tenebris mentis suæ, ] advesperascente die, [ quando lucis pii igniculi, quos a prima infantia sentiebat, jam in eo languescere & deficere incipiunt, ] in noctis tenebris & caligine, [ toto mundo tenebris universalibus etiam immerso. ]
units.tr: Passing through the street near the corner, [who passes through the world and the places more conspicuous for worldly things,] and near the way to her house [near the places appointed for spreading false learning,] he goes in the dark, [in the darkness of his own mind,] in the twilight of the day, [when the small pious lights that he felt from earliest infancy begin to grow faint and fail in him,] in the blackness and darkness of the night, [the whole world being plunged in universal darkness.]

units.la: Et ecce occurrit illi mulier ornatu meretricio, [Eruditio falsa, cor adulterans, & ornata titulis graduum magnificis, omnisque generis disciplinarum phaleris, ] parata ad capiendas animas, [ omnia sic disponens, ut animabus persuadere possit sibi magis quam Deo adhærere, ] garrula & vaga, [ rixosa, disputatrix, loquacula, & tumultuans vage in chimæris & in superficie rerum ] quietis impatiens [nec intus quiete fruens, nec alios quiescere permittens ] nec valens in domo consistere pedibus suis; [ impotens spiritualibus & intimis animæ dare considerationes & assectus suos: ] nunc foris, nunc in plateis, nunc juxta angulos insidians, [ quærens allicere animas modo per quævis proposita externa, modo per celebritatem nominis inter eruditos objectam, modo per tritas mundanarum scientiarum vias. ]
units.tr: And behold, there meets him a woman with the attire of a harlot, [false learning, which corrupts the heart, adorned with the magnificent titles of degrees and with the trappings of every kind of discipline,] ready to catch souls, [arranging everything so that she can persuade souls to cleave to herself rather than to God,] loud and wandering, [quarrelsome, contentious, chattering, and roaming about among chimeras and the surface of things,] not able to rest, [neither enjoying inner quiet nor allowing others to rest,] nor able to abide in her house with her feet; [unable to give spiritual and inward considerations and affections to the soul:] now abroad, now in the streets, now lying in wait at the corners, [seeking to entice souls now by any outward displays, now by the fame of a name held before the learned, now by the well-worn paths of worldly sciences.]

units.la: Apprehensumque deosculatur juvenem, [ ea parte, qua amori proprio satis fieri poterit, inexpertum aggreditur, pacemque & omnia fausta ei statim denuntiat, ] & procaci vultu blanditur, [ impudenti adulatione verbisque compositis affectus ejus allicit, ] dicens:
units.tr: So she catches him and kisses the young man, [she approaches the inexperienced one on the side where self-love can be fully indulged, and at once announces peace and every blessing to him,] and with an impudent face she flatters him, [with shameless adulation and polished words she entices his affections,] saying:

units.la: Vltimas pro salute vobis; [ hactenus plus satis & sufficienter de rebus salutis sumus solliciti: exi in tuto sunt. Ecce, Christi mortem obtulimus Patri, victimam salutis; ] hodie reddidi vota mea. [ Sacra etiam quotidie fere frequentamus, & Deum sufficienter colimus. ]
units.tr: I had peacofferings to make; [hitherto we have been anxious enough and sufficiently about the things of salvation: be at ease. Behold, we have offered the death of Christ to the Father, the sacrifice of salvation;] today I have paid my vows. [We also attend sacred rites almost daily, and worship God sufficiently.]

units.la: Idcirco egressa sum in occursum tuum, [ quae cum ita sint, & hac ex parte omnia sint in tuto, superest ut quoad caetera te dones speculationibus & exercitiis, ob quae me tibi offero, ] desiderans te videre; [ inter discipulos eruditionis ] & te reperi ] opportune ad hoc dispositum. ]
units.tr: Therefore I came out to meet you, [since these things are so, and in this respect all things are safe, it remains that, as to the rest, you give yourself to speculations and exercises, for which I offer myself to you,] earnestly seeking to see you; [among the disciples of learning] and I have found you [fittingly disposed to this.]

units.la: Intexui funibus lectulum meum, stravi tapetibus pictis ex Ægypto: [ exercitiorum nostrorum palaestram, ubi deliciabimur, omni philosophica & syllogistica cohaerentia, & dialectica subtilitate rhetoricesque mundanae pigmentis exornavi, ] aspersi cubile meum myrrha, & cinnamomo, [ & quicquid animi sensibus propensionibusque tuis naturalibus gratum est, id apud me paratum est. ]
units.tr: I have spread my couch with cords, and covered it with coloured carpets of Egypt: [the wrestling-ground of our exercises, where we shall take our delight, I have adorned with every philosophical and syllogistic coherence, with dialectical subtlety, and with the paints of worldly rhetoric;] I have perfumed my bed with myrrh and cinnamon, [and whatever is pleasing to your senses and natural inclinations is ready with me.]

units.la: Veni, inebriemur uberibus, & fruamur cupitis amplexibus, [ doctrinae meae succum & lac imbibe, caetera nil curans; ac per me naturae tuae propensiones, queis faveo, fequere, ] donec illucescat dies, [ donec tandem lucidam veritatem apud me sic assequi possis. ]
units.tr: Come, let us take our fill of love, and enjoy ourselves with amorous embraces, [drink in the juice and milk of my teaching, caring for nothing else; and through me follow the inclinations of your nature which I favour,] until the day dawns, [until at last you may thus be able to attain clear truth with me.]

units.la: Non est enim vir in domo sua: [ JESUS CHRISTUS, caput Sapientiae verae, animarumque sponsus & habitator, non amplius habitat nunc in domo animarum, neque est cur ulterius eum intus exspectes. ] abiit via lonlongissima; [ recessit in coelum, procul a nobis. ]
units.tr: For the man is not at home: [JESUS CHRIST, the head of true Wisdom and the bridegroom and dweller of souls, no longer dwells in the house of souls, nor is there any reason to wait for him within any longer.] He has gone a very long journey; [he has withdrawn into heaven, far from us.]

units.la: Sacculum argenti secum tulit: [ dona sua spiritualia, infusione gratuita animam ditare apta, resumfit, ac secum abstulit: ] in die plenae lunae reversurus est in domum suam; [ in die extrema, quando res sublunares mutabilitatis suae cursum impleverint, tunc ad nos redibit, nec ante: cur ergo jam de illo te sollicite maceres? ]
units.tr: He has taken a bag of silver with him: [he has taken back his spiritual gifts, fitted to enrich the soul by free infusion, and has carried them away with him:] he will return to his house on the day of the full moon; [on the last day, when the things under the moon have completed the course of their mutability, then he will come back to us, and not before. Why, then, do you already torment yourself with anxiety about him?]

units.la: Irretivit eum multis sermonibus, [ multis ratiocinationibus & argumentationibus, quas miser & caecus ne discernere quidem, multo minus eis respondere valens, pro meris veritatibus admisit: ] & blanditiis labiorum [ orationibus, panegyricis, encomiis de scientiarum suarum suorumque eruditorum praestantia & laudibus] protraxit illum.
units.tr: He has entangled him with many words, [with many reasonings and arguments, which the wretched and blind man, not even able to discern them, much less to answer them, has admitted as mere truths:] and with the flattering of her lips [with orations, panegyrics, and eulogies on the excellence of her sciences and of her learned men, and with their praises] she has drawn him away.

units.la: Statim eam sequitur quasi bos ad victimam, [ruunt enim ad mortem quotquot ejusmodi vanis futilitatibus applicantur deserto CHRISTO, atque veluti pecora stolide sequuntur quocunque ducantur: ] & quasi agnus lasciviens [ in juvenili, improvida, & petulanti licentia vitam interim ducens, ] & ignorans quod ad vincula, [ tenebrarum, errorum, vitiorum & tandem mortis, ] stultus trahatur.
units.tr: Straightway he follows her as an ox goes to the slaughter, [for all who are given over to such empty trifles, Christ being forsaken, rush to death, and like cattle foolishly follow wherever they are led:] and as a playful lamb, [living meanwhile in youthful, heedless, and petulant licence,] not knowing that he is led [to chains of darkness, of errors, of vices, and at last of death,] as a fool to the stocks.

units.la: Donec transfigat sagitta jecur ejus, [ donec ejus cupiditas infecta sit prorsus telis inimici animarum, bonaque aeternitatis desideria in eo sint omnino mortua: ] veluti si avis festinet ad laqueum; & nescit quod de periculo [ aeterno ] animae illius agitur.
units.tr: Until an arrow strike through his liver, [until his desire is utterly infected with the weapons of the enemy of souls, and the good desires of eternity are wholly dead in him:] as a bird hastens into a snare; and he does not know that his soul is in danger [of eternal ruin].

units.la: Nunc ergo, fili mi, [Creatura mea dilecta, quam potente & bona Sapientia meacreavi, ut omnium meorum sis heres,] audi me [Deum tuum & Patrem tuum, tibidum adhuc tempus est consulentem,] & attende verbis oris [Christi] mei.
units.tr: Now therefore, my son, [my beloved creature, whom I created by my powerful and good Wisdom, that you might be heir of all my things,] hear me [your God and your Father, counselling you while there is still time,] and attend to the words of my mouth [of Christ].

units.la: Ne abstrahatur in viis illius [falsæ & meretricíæ eruditionis] mens tua, neque decipiarissemitis ejus [speciosis.]
units.tr: Let not your heart decline to her ways, [of false and harlot learning,] nor be deceived by her paths [specious ones].

units.la: Multos enim vulneratos dejecit; & fortissimiquique [les Esprits forts, præstantia quæque ingenia Deo non adhærentia] interfectisunt ab ea. [Quid ergo tibi adhuc dum tenero & debili ab ea non timendum?]
units.tr: For she has cast down many wounded; yea, all the strong men [the strong spirits, all the outstanding talents not cleaving to God] have been slain by her. [What, then, is there for you, still tender and weak, not to fear from her?]

units.la: Viæ Inferi, domus ejus, [qui in ea habitant & positi sunt ad diabolum vias decurruntlatas,] penetrantes interiora mortis, [quarumterminus est, penetrantius & profundiusdamnari, quam omnes cæteri qui aliis viisdamnantur.] Et qui timet Dominum ab ealiberabitur. AMEN. Ps. 119:176.
units.tr: Her house is the way to hell, [those who dwell in her and are set to run the broad roads to the devil,] going down to the chambers of death, [whose end is to be damned more deeply and more profoundly than all the others who are damned by other ways.] And he who fears the Lord shall be delivered from her. AMEN. Ps. 119:176.

units.la: ERRAVI SICUT OVIS PERDITA. QUÆRE- SERVUM TUUM MANDATORUM TUORUM- NECDUM OBLITUM.
units.tr: I HAVE GONE ASTRAY LIKE A LOST SHEEP. SEEK THY SERVANT, FOR I HAVE NOT FORGOTTEN THY COMMANDMENTS.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: APOLOGETICA.
units.tr: APOLOGY.

units.la: ETsi in publicandis iis quae a mea tenuitate proficisci possunt, hunc mihi scopum proposuerim, talia expromere, quae hactenus aut praetermissa, aut minus bene explicata, ipseque optassem prius mihi ab aliis ostendi, ut eorum ope liberarer difficultatibus queis circa haec antea premebar, & quarum solutionem postea invenisse mihi visus sum: non dubitavi tamen quin meum illud, quod sane illaudabile esse non poterit, proficiendi aliis studium a plurimis sinistro oculo inspiciendum esset, maxime vero ab illis qui contraria tenebant, aut vero ea ediderant vel defenderant quae ego minus vera esse ostendebam. At quamvis oppositiones aliquot exspectarem, non tamen credideram, ullos eo ignaviae delapsiros, ut me impugnaturi, opiniones, eis quas clarissime meas declaravi contrarias, meas esse dicerent, deinde eas vel refutarent, vel irriderent, ut coram aliis de illorum sinceritate non dubitantibus triumpharent de me, & ita a veritatibus momentosioribus, quae in scriptis meis occurrunt, quaeque illis sunt tam invisae quam silentio dissimulatae, legendis, revocarent quotquot inde si non eruditiores, saltem meliores fieri potuissent. Cui malo
units.tr: Although in publishing those things which can come forth from my slender ability I have proposed to myself this aim, to set out such things as until now have either been passed over or less well explained, and which I myself would have wished to have been shown to me earlier by others, so that with their help I might be freed from the difficulties by which I was previously burdened in these matters, and whose solution I seemed afterwards to have found; nevertheless I did not doubt that my zeal for benefiting others, which certainly cannot be unpraised, would have to be viewed with a jaundiced eye by very many, and above all by those who held the contrary opinions, or who had published or defended things which I showed to be less true. But although I expected some objections, I had not believed that anyone would sink so low in idleness as to attack me by declaring that opinions which I had most clearly stated to be my opposites were my own, and then either to refute or to ridicule them, so that they might triumph over me before others who would not doubt their sincerity, and thus turn away from reading the more weighty truths which occur in my writings, and which are as hateful to them as they are carefully passed over in silence, all those who, if not more learned, could at least have become better men.

units.la: non video me obviam ire posse, praeterquam si semel aperte declaravero, ea quae ab adversantibus mihi ut mea imputantur, nequaquam pro meis a me agnosci; rogaveroque omnes qui de meis judicare falso nolint, uti dignentur quae ipse sentio, in meis libris, non autem in aliorum relationibus, ore, scriptis, inspicere. Et ut appareat me non sine causa id postulare & contestari, exemplis nonnullis nunc probatum dabo, me jam simile quid iniqui a non uno nonnullius nominis aliquoties esse expertum.
units.tr: I see no way of meeting this evil, except by declaring once openly that those things which are imputed to me by my opponents as mine are by no means acknowledged by me as my own; and I ask all who do not wish to judge my views falsely to deign to examine what I myself think in my books, and not in other people's reports, whether spoken or written. And so that it may appear that I make this request and protest not without cause, I shall now give some examples as proof, showing that I have already more than once experienced similar unfairness from more than one man of some standing.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Pauci non norunt, nil emolumenti (ut moderate loquar) per Cogitationum Rationalium mearum de Deo, Anima & Malo editionem decesisse rei Cartesianae in quantum veritati innititur, hoc est, in quantum docet, animam & inextensam esse, & ex natura cogitare, & vero existere Deum, admirabilibus, ilque perfectissimis praeditum attributis, unde ipsa scientiarum fundamenta debeant desumi isque inniti, quas veritates momentosa a Cartesio per rationem demonstratas ut agnovi & falsus sum; sic & iisdem de rebus multo plura quam ipse Cartesius demonstrare sum aggressus, & ea quae ipse demonstratu impossibilia putabar, veluti animam non esse (sepositio revelationis argumento) a Deo annihilandam, praestiti; idque non tantum sterili & mere speculativo differendi modo; sed eo, quo conabar lectorum animos urgentibus demonstrationibus permovere uti meliores, & Dei virtutisque amantiores fierent. Quæ quidem res, quod sciam, nullis e Cartesianorum numero cordatioribus displicuit; etsi in eo libro haud minus decies a Cartesio dissenserim, eumque toties vel pluries erroris in multis redarguerim. Verum sciunt omnes axioma Cartesii esse, ipsi minime credi debere, nisi quantum is rationem & veritatem secutus est: ita ut non dubitem generosioris indolis Cartesianos nequaquam ægre laturos ab eo in omnibus dissentiri, modo ostendatur eum a ratione recta in omnibus declinasse. In hoc ipso enim legem ejus omnium æquissimam observarent, atque ita ab optima parte maxime Cartesiani essent.
units.tr: Few do not know that the edition of my Rational Thoughts on God, the Soul and Evil has brought no small benefit (to speak moderately) to the Cartesian cause, in so far as it rests on truth, that is, in so far as it teaches that the soul is unextended and by its nature thinks, and that God truly exists, endowed with admirable and most perfect attributes, and that from these the foundations of the sciences must be derived and rest on them. These are weighty truths which Descartes demonstrated by reason, and in which, as I recognised, he was mistaken and deceived. Thus I also set about demonstrating far more on the same matters than Descartes himself did, and I accomplished what he thought impossible to demonstrate, for instance that the soul is not to be annihilated by God (setting aside the argument from revelation). And I did this not merely in a barren and purely speculative manner of argument, but in such a way that I tried by pressing demonstrations to move the minds of readers, so that they might become better and more lovers of God and virtue. This indeed, as far as I know, displeased none of the more judicious men among the Cartesians; although in that book I dissented from Descartes no less than ten times, and refuted his errors in many places, more than once or twice. But everyone knows that a maxim of Descartes is not to be believed by anyone, except insofar as he followed reason and truth. So I do not doubt that Cartesians of a more generous disposition would by no means take it badly that I dissent from him in all things, provided it is shown that he has departed from right reason in all points. For in this they would observe his own law, the most just of all, and so they would be, by the best part of themselves, truly Cartesians.

units.la: Postquam autem per tempus & otium plura melius scrutari & videre potui, edidique altera vice Cogitationes easdem, sed prioribus multo auctiores, miratus sum Cartesianos nonnullos, qui Editionem priorem non mediocriter approbaverant, huic esse infensiores, & pro causa dixisse, priorem veluti ab hac destrui, quippe quæ multa opposita & diversa contineret; proinde discipulis suis legendam dissuadebant, quorum nonnulli serviliter admodum obtemperabant dictitantibus. Non putassem sane inter eos, qui liberioris philosophandi methodi se dicunt sectatores, facile reperiendos, qui contra Methodi suæ legem, quicquam aliis sine prævio examine rejicendum injungerent; neque credidissem inter Cartesianismi discipulos tam bruta inventum iri pecora, ut quicquida Magistris suis sibi, nulla allegata ratione,injungeretur improbandum, id ipsi mancipiorum modo sine lectione & examine ejus, protinus improbarent. Si ex prima methodi suæ lege, de magistrorum suorum effato dubitantes, rem ipsam examinare voluissent, illico deprehendissent, id quod Editioni isti imputatur, salsissimum esse; quippe quæ tantum abest ut priori opponatur, ut potius præter ejus textum eundem, notis & augmentis easdem veritates mille in locis & profundius & diductius illustret, multaque de Metaphysicis & Moralibus penitius detegat, quam factum sit antea. Equidem de novo in nonnullis dissensum meum a Cartefio indicavi, nec non in notis sententiam unam atque alteram a priori Editione diversam, veluti de rationis humanæ terminis & imbecillitate,, de Prædestinatione rigida, de animæ propagatione, de motu per attractionem, fovere, non dissimulavi: at quandoquidem & in Editione prima vel plus decies in multis a Cartefio dissenseram, & quædam mea in Appendice correxeram, hæc non possit esse causa, cur Editionem eam improbent totam, quæ, si a potiori denominari debet, dicenda potius est priorem confirmare, uti revera eam vel millies corroborat, ubi solum ter quaterve ab ea dissentit, eoque modo, qui nemini potest esse fraudi: siquidem invariato primæ Editionis textu, rationes dissentiendi sic ad calcem apponuntur, ut liberum cuique sit, examinatis utrinque rationibus, quam judicaverit meliorem sententiam amplecti, atque adeo & priorem retinere si solvere possit rationes dubitandi appositas: quarum appositione gratiam Cartesianorum demereri potius quam improbationem crediderim, quando earum vi prioris sententiae firmitas non labefactata, illustrior & stabilior apparebit.
units.tr: But after I had been able, with time and leisure, to examine and see more things better, and had published a second edition of the same Thoughts, but much enlarged over the earlier ones, I was surprised that some Cartesians, who had not mildly approved the first edition, were more hostile to this one, and argued in their cause that the first was in effect destroyed by this, since it contained many contrary and different things; so they dissuaded their pupils from reading it, and some of these obeyed them very slavishly, as they kept saying. I would certainly not have supposed that among those who call themselves followers of a freer method of philosophising, it would be easy to find men who, against the law of their own method, would enjoin that anything be rejected by others without prior examination; nor would I have believed that among the disciples of Cartesianism there would be found such brutish cattle that, whatever was enjoined on them by their masters to be condemned, without any reason being given, they would at once condemn it, like slaves, without reading or examining it. If, following the first law of their method, doubting the dictum of their masters, they had wished to examine the matter itself, they would at once have discovered that what is charged against this edition is utterly false; for it is so far from being opposed to the first, that rather, apart from the same text, through notes and additions it illustrates the same truths in a thousand places more deeply and at greater length, and reveals much about metaphysics and morals more thoroughly than had been done before. Indeed I have not concealed that I have indicated my new dissent from Descartes in some points, and that in the notes I have fostered one or another opinion different from the earlier edition, such as on the limits and weakness of human reason, on rigid predestination, on the propagation of the soul, and on motion by attraction. But since in the first edition too I had dissented from Descartes more than ten times in many points, and had corrected some of my own views in an Appendix, this cannot be the reason why they condemn that edition as a whole. If it ought to be named from its principal part, it should rather be said to confirm the former, as indeed it strengthens it a thousand times, where it differs from it only three or four times, and in a way which can be no deception to anyone. For with the text of the first edition left unchanged, the reasons for dissent are appended at the end in such a way that each reader is free, after weighing the arguments on both sides, to embrace whichever opinion he judges better, and so also to keep the former if he can resolve the arguments of doubt set out. I would think that by setting out these arguments I earn the favour of the Cartesians rather than their condemnation, since by their force the firmness of the former opinion will not be shaken, but will appear clearer and more stable.

units.la: At revera aliud quid subesse reor ob quod suis dissuaserint novum opus. Vident in illo nonnulla, praesertim de rigida Praedestinatione, errores quos fovent nec deserere audent, irreparabiliter evertentia; sententiam vero suae oppositam (quae & Anglorum & Brandeburgicorum Reformatorum est) firmissime stabilientia. Haec si nobilioris indolis studiosi viderint, ea in disputando illis opponent quibus nec poterunt respondere, & vero erroneae doctrinae ita convincentur. Quod cum jure timeant, revocandi sunt discipuli ab ejus Operis lectione, quo possent Magistros suos vincere: id quod dissimulata hac causa, per generalem libri calumniam, indicata nulla ratione, totius fieri posse judicarunt. Nisi forte quidam minus cauti id faciant ex Spinoziistarum quorundam impulsione, qui videntes omnem Spinozae Atheismum detegi & refutari in Notis, nec non in opusculo adjecto fundamenta exitiosae ejus Ethices eâ methodo Geometrica prorsus subverti qua is illa statuminare conabatur, putaverint non melius posse labenti Atheismo suo consuli, quam si per improvidos minimeque Atheismi suspectos traduci curarent ea, in quibus portentosa impietas & veritate invišta & propriis suis-telis conficitur. Non ausim sane in causam hujus fui agendi modi adferre eam, quam de Virgine quadam divinitus erudita feci in Appendice libri mentionem: ea namque & in Editione prima, nullis non grata, exstabat; & eruditarum foeminarum elogia cum omnium approbatione jam dudum plurimi evulgarunt eruditi quique viri; etsi non nemo, (qui Mentis suæ morbum & tenebras novissime satis prodidit, quando portentosis quibusdam de Angelis & diabolis opinionibus ipse fascinatus iisdemque mundum fascinare gestiens, totas enervavit Scripturas, ) testatus sit non fine calumniis in ea quam Belgice conscripsit, historia Ecclesiastica, id sibi vehementer displicuisse. Sed quid mirum si homini ita afsecto displicere id possit quod rectum est & verissimum? Quicquid sit, nulla de causa ulli credam licere, uti aliis persuadeat, alia in scriptis meis contineri quam revera continentur, maxime vero in isto, cujus augmenta, nedum sint nullius pretii aut momenti, ea sunt, ut quicquid boni in Editione prima continetur vix comparandum veniat vel cum sola præliminari Dissertatione alteri addita, non meo tantum, sed & solidissimorum ac ingeniosissimorum quorumcunque judicio; qui indignabantur, se ab ea tantisper abductos fuisse ignavo linguarum perverse judicantium artificio. Quam culpam tamen iis non ignosco tantum, sed &, si perseverent, possem beneficio compensare, eis penitius & amplius quam adhuc feci, Cartesianismi errores imbecillitatem detegendo, non quemadmodum ab Aristotelicis nonnullisque aliis ad hoc non satis aptis factum est; sed eo modo, cujus nescio an quisquam alius sit me fortitan capacior, qui vel ipsismet forte profundius suorum placitorum validitatem & debilitatem a radice novi. Sed ab ingrato quiescam officio, ipsi a maledicendo abstinere si poterunt.
units.tr: But in truth I suspect that something else lies beneath their reason for dissuading their pupils from the new work. They see in it some things, especially on rigid predestination, which overthrow beyond repair the errors they cherish and dare not abandon, and which firmly establish the opposite opinion (which is also that of the English and Brandenburg Reformed). If studious men of a nobler disposition were to see these things, they would oppose them in debate with arguments to which the Cartesians could not reply, and so they would be convinced of the erroneous doctrine. Since they fear this with good reason, the pupils must be called back from reading that work, by which they might defeat their masters. This they judged could be done by hiding this cause and condemning the whole book in a general calumny, without stating any reason. Unless perhaps some less cautious men do this at the urging of certain Spinozists, who, seeing that all the atheism of Spinoza is uncovered and refuted in the Notes, and that the foundations of his pernicious Ethics have been utterly overthrown in the appended little work by that geometrical method with which he tried to support them, thought they could not better look after their tottering atheism than by arranging that those things be carried to unwary and by no means atheism-suspected readers, in which monstrous impiety is by an unconquered truth and by its own weapons undone. I would certainly not venture to assign as the cause of this way of acting the mention I made in the Appendix of a certain divinely taught virgin: for that was in the first edition too, pleasing to all, and many learned men have long since published, with the approval of everyone, the praises of learned women; although someone (who lately displayed quite clearly the sickness and darkness of his mind, when, himself bewitched by certain monstrous opinions about angels and devils, and eager to bewitch the world with them, he has entirely enervated the Scriptures) has testified, in the Church history he wrote in Dutch, not without calumnies, that this greatly displeased him. But what wonder if what is right and most true can displease a man so affected? Whatever the case, I shall never believe that anyone has any right, for any reason, to persuade others that my writings contain things other than what they really contain; and this is especially so in this edition, whose additions are not only of no worth or importance, but are such that whatever good is contained in the first edition can scarcely be compared even with the preliminary Dissertation added to the second alone, by the judgement not only of me but of all the most solid and ingenious men, who were indignant that they had been led away from it, for a time, by the idle trick of those who judge the languages perversely. Yet I not only pardon them this fault, but, if they persist, I could repay them with a kindness, by uncovering the weakness of the errors of Cartesianism more deeply and more fully than I have done so far, not as some Aristotelians and certain others have done, who are not well fitted for this, but in a manner of which I do not know whether anyone else is perhaps more capable than I am, since I have perhaps come to know the strength and weakness of their own tenets more deeply, from the root. But I shall desist from this ungrateful task, if they can refrain from slandering me.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Lipsienses Actorum Eruditorum conditores simile quid de earundem Cogitationum editione altera commiserunt, quando lectoribus persuadere voluerunt eas & prioribus esse obscuriores, & Theologiae Mysticae, quam passim depraedicent, immersas. Fateor me eam Theologiam semel aut bis nominasse cum elogio: at a veritate alienum est ejus depraedicationem passim ibi occurrere, & salsius illi librum immergi. Confudit articuli hujus Auctor, profundiores Metaphysices meditationes cum Theologia Mystica, quia, utraque quid sint bonus ille vir pariter ignorare videtur: unde quae aptis mentibus philosophemata ex se sunt clarissima, illi mysteria obscura fuerint, velut erant olim Cartesianae Meditationes iis, qui sese egregie eruditos credebant. Iterum, si non de industria, saltem minus caute ea de me ibidem refert, quae falsum lectoribus inculcant sensum, quando ait, me perhibere eos qui verba in Scripturis sacris revelata assumunt atque consulunt, humanam rationem sequi, neglecto fidei immediate a Deo venientis lumine. Atqui mea mens non est, unum & idem esse, vel necessario simul connecti, τὸ assumere & consulere verba Scripturarum, & τὸ humanam rationem sequi neglecto fidei lumine, ita ut qui faciant prius, eo ipso alterum committant; quem admodum ex verbis illorum lector illico colligere posset: sed improbavi & deploravi ibi, dari plurimos, qui verba in Scripturis S. revelata sic assumunt atque consulunt, ut quando de sensu eorum agitur, recurrant magis ad intellectus sui activitatem & ideas corruptas, quam ad Deum, committendo ipsi fideliter & ardenter intellectum suum, ut is in illo lumen gratiosum exciret: quod ultimum fidei dico esse, primum ad rationem spectare: quae si suis Theologis jam dicant non placere, egregia sane laude eos sic mactabunt. Miratus vero sum quid Lipsienses istos, qui Lutherani sunt, commoverit uti sensa mea sic odiose detorquerent & exhiberent, quippe qui gratiam non parvam ab iis commeruisse debui quando iis, praedestinationi rigidae adversantibus, in meo libro de ea, deque libertate, non pauca proposui, e quibus sententiam suam & melius quam factum sit digerant, & firmius statuminent.
units.tr: The Leipzig founders of the Acta Eruditorum made a similar mistake about the second edition of these same Thoughts. They wanted to persuade their readers that the book is more obscure than the earlier one, and sunk in Mystical Theology, which they praise everywhere. I admit that I named that theology once or twice with approval, but it is far from the truth that they meet its praise everywhere in the book, or that the book is steeped in it. This reviewer confused the deeper meditations of metaphysics with Mystical Theology, because that good man seems equally ignorant of what each of them is. So the philosophical points that are in themselves perfectly clear to suitable minds were obscure mysteries to him, just as Cartesian Meditations once were to those who believed themselves thoroughly learned. Again, if not deliberately, at least carelessly, he reports things about me there that give readers a false impression, when he says that I maintain that those who take up and consult the words revealed in holy Scripture follow human reason, neglecting the light of faith that comes immediately from God. But I do not hold that taking up and consulting the words of Scripture and following human reason while neglecting the light of faith are one and the same thing, or necessarily joined together, so that whoever does the first thereby commits the second; a reader could gather as much immediately from his words. What I did say, and deplored, is that there are very many who take up and consult the words revealed in holy Scripture in such a way that, when their meaning is in question, they have recourse more to the activity of their own understanding and to corrupt ideas than to God, committing their understanding to him faithfully and earnestly, so that he may kindle in it a gracious light. This last I call the act of faith; the first pertains to reason. If they now tell their Theologians that these do not please them, they will certainly honour them with signal praise. I do wonder, however, what moved those Leipzig men, who are Lutherans, to twist and present my views so odiously. I ought to have earned no small favour from them, since in my book on predestination and liberty I set out not a few points against rigid predestination, by which they could both arrange their own opinion better than they have done and establish it more firmly.

units.la: Sed desii mirari cum in sequenti Actorum mense illorum unum eo esse animo vidi, ut pro relatione candida Satyram scommatibus & falsitatibus refertam scriptitarit in defunctam D. Antoniam Bourignoniam, admirandae eruditionis divinae Virginem sanctissimam, inque ejus Opera (quorum eo tempore non nisi duodecim octerniones legebat) nec non in ejus Operum Vitæque Apologetem: Quam animosi affectus intemperiem magis adhuc prodidit, quando ab illaudata manes aggrediendi methodo per Monitum necessarium ad Acta sua depulsus, jam non Satyram & scommata; sed ignes & flammas, omnisque generis sordes, & (quæ vel subulco indigna, nec sine lectoris venia referenda) continuo in ore habet) oleta, (honos sit auribus) stercora, vomitus, sputorum linctus, cacationes, luctus, excrementa, fimeta, maledictaque & epitheta omnis generis diabolica & immania; etiam ab ipso titulo expectoravit in libro alio quem Defensionem Relationis Lipsiensis inscripsit: idque ideo quod sibi imaginatus sit, & se invadi, quando tamen ipse invasor erat, prorsum antea incognitus; & vero ratus sit durius se repelli quam pro merito aut dignitate sua debuerit. Atqui si vel Princeps aliquis larva vilibusque colonum vestibus personatus simpliciores & plebejos incognitus lacessitum iret, eorumque operas improbe vexans, inde bonum sustuarium ab illis reportaret, nemo non judicaret sane id uni suæ imprudentiæ culpæque attribuendum fore; nedum sic periculo facto, rem deberet evulgare, aut ridicule conclamare sibi injuriam factam esse; mulierosaque convicia in lacessitos effundere voce lamentabili; imo nil convenientius ab eo fieri posse quam si taceat potius, ne se aliis noscendum præbeat & deridendum. Tale factum vexatori nostro, quantuscunque sit, per sa-tyrityricam tamen chlamydem larvamque ignoto, si accidérit, ejus erat sane, id vel e Politica prudentia tacite apud se solum digerere potius, quam tragice palam exclamare se jam ternis jam senis velitum jaculis (quæ propria tela erant in ipsum revertentia) invadi, atque impotentia convicia muliebriter jactitare, calumniasque nulli credendas; maxime postquam Hamburgenses Ephemeridum Eruditorum Auctores, nescio an ipso conscio vel postulante, declarāverant, me eum esse quem clamoribus suis obtundere voluerit. Namque nemo est qui Cogitationibus meis, Oeconomiaque Divina editis & lectis, non numeret inter calumnias, quæ is passim mihi amicisque meis imputat (a) Vaninismum sive Atheismum, Bodinismum, Naturalismum, Socinianismum, Pelagianismum, & doctrinam Judaismo atque Mahometismo deteriorem; nemo qui inde non judicet ejusmodi auctori ut in his, ita in cæteris quoque minus momentosis, ob nubila per turbidos affectus menti obducta, fidem non esse adhibendam: sic ut mihi non sit opus ostendere, (quod facillime possum) in singulis ejus scripti pagellis, & fere lineis & vocibus, veritatem, æquitatem, modum; charitatem, humilitatem desiderari; namque adeo crassis affectuum motibus istas virtutes conculcavit, ut omnium quæ de Eruditorum falsorum in eos qui solida protulerunt agendi modis superius dixi, ideam & memoriam ista non possint non revocare; & si cui liber ejus imponat seu persuadeat lectori, hunc ego lectorem quovis stipite stupidiorem. rem, in demonstrato habeo. Quia vero iste aggressor veritatis a me audiendæ & recipiendæ adeo incapax est, ut mihi in nugacissimas nugas (a)annumeret quod docuerim ea quæ Christus fecit & passus est, a nobis de facto & inhærenter intus veluti medicamina assumenda esse, si quidem sanari velimus; cum ut non imputative, sed inhærenter sanet Deus, rogo. Cæteros conteστor, ut ne sensa nostra unquam ex adversariorum libris, quippe qui contineant contraria, cognoscere velint; sed cum ex Cogitationibus, Oeconomiaque, nec non ex Irenico Universali cum illa Gallice edito; tum ex incomparabilibus eruditissimæ cœlitus Virginis Antoniæ Bourignoniæ scriptis, omnis Eruditionis solidæ clavem viamque veram vividissimo palpabilissimoque modo subm; ministrantibus: in quibus omnibus passim, maxime vero ex professo in Præfatione Apologetica ejus Vitæ præfixa, videbunt eas cavillationes & calumnias, jam dudum centies a maleferiatis quibusvis calumniatoribus, eadem chorda semper oberrantibus, objectas, & toties repulsas, clarissime dissolvi, & omnibus dubiis sufficientissima luminosæ veritatis detectione satisfieri. Si qui autem adhuc etiam postea calumniis nos obruere velint, & Fimbriæ instar, furere, publicisque accusationibus nos denuo invadere, eo quod toto corpore ictus suos non admiserimus, sed ab eis ita declinaverimus, ut aërem ferierint; sique inveniant, qui sibi in iniquis suis agendi modis & credant & adjumento sint contra nos.
units.tr: But I stopped wondering when, in the following month's Acta, I saw that one of them had set out, instead of a candid report, a satire stuffed with jokes and falsehoods against the late Antonia Bourignon, a most holy virgin of admirable divine learning, and against her Works (of which at that time he had read only twelve octavo volumes), and also against the Apologist of her Works and Life. He betrayed the excess of his heated passion even more when, having been driven off by the unpraised method of attack through a Necessary Warning to the Acta of his own, he now has constantly on his lips not satire and jokes, but fires and flames and filth of every kind, and (what is unworthy even of a swineherd and cannot be reported without the reader's pardon) oleta (let my ears be spared), dung, vomit, dribble of spittle, defecations, wailings, excrements, dunghills, and curses and epithets of every kind, devilish and monstrous. He spat these out even from the title of another book he entitled Defence of the Leipzig Relation, and he did so because he imagined that he was being attacked, when in fact he was the attacker, previously quite unknown; and indeed he thought he had been repulsed more harshly than his merit or dignity deserved. Yet if some prince, masked and dressed in the vile clothes of a farmer, were to go unknown against simple common folk, harassing their labours wickedly, and got a sound thrashing from them, no one would fail to judge that this must be attributed solely to his own imprudence and fault. Much less should he, having made such a trial, publish the matter or loudly proclaim that an injury had been done to him, pouring out womanish insults in a whining voice against those who provoked him. Indeed nothing could be more fitting for him than to keep quiet rather than let himself be known and mocked by others. If such a thing happened to our harasser, however great it was, and he was unknown under a satirical cloak and mask, it was surely for him to digest it quietly to himself on the grounds of political prudence, rather than to cry out tragically in public that he was now being assailed with skirmishing darts, three or six at a time (which were weapons turning back upon himself), and to bawl impotent insults like a woman, and to make accusations no one should believe. This is especially so since the Hamburg authors of the Ephemerides had declared, perhaps with his own knowledge or at his own request, that I am the man he wished to deafen with his clamour. For there is no one who, having read my Thoughts and Divine Economy, does not count among the calumnies that he everywhere imputes to me and my friends: (a) Vaninism or atheism, Bodinism, Naturalism, Socinianism, Pelagianism, and a doctrine worse than Judaism and Mahometanism. Nor is there anyone who does not judge that, for such an author, owing to clouds drawn over his mind by turbid passions, no faith should be given to him on these charges or on the rest, which are of less weight. So I need not show (though I could very easily) that on individual pages of his writing, and almost in every line and word, truth, fairness, moderation, charity and humility are lacking. He has trampled these virtues with such coarse movements of the passions that the things I said above about the ways of false scholars toward those who put forward solid teaching cannot fail to call them to mind. And if his book deceives or persuades any reader, I hold that reader to be more stupid than any block of wood; this I regard as already proved. But since this assailant is so incapable of hearing and receiving the truth from me that he counts among the most trifling trifles (a) my teaching that we must take up, in deed and inwardly, as medicines the things that Christ did and suffered, if we wish to be healed (since God heals not imputatively but inwardly, I ask), I call the rest to witness that they should never wish to learn our views from the books of our opponents, since those books contain the opposite. Instead they should learn them from the Thoughts, the Divine Economy, and also from the Universal Irenicum in its French edition, and from the incomparable writings of the most learned virgin, Antonia Bourignon, which supply the key and true way to all solid learning in the most lively and tangible manner. In all these works, and especially in the Apologetic Preface prefixed to her Life, they will see that those quibbles and calumnies, long since brought a hundred times by wicked calumniators of every kind, always wandering on the same string, and so often repulsed, are most clearly dissolved, and that every doubt is fully satisfied by the complete disclosure of luminous truth. But if any still wish to overwhelm us with calumnies even afterwards, and to rage like Fimbria and attack us again with public accusations, because we did not let their blows land on our whole body but dodged them so that they struck only the air, and if they find people who both believe in their unjust ways of acting and lend them help against us,

units.la: (a) p.115. nos, quamvis contraria eis quæ nobis imputantur (sunt vero cogitata) attestantes: tunc innocentissimæ Susannæ a vetulis veteratoribus falso accusatæ, & a credulis nimium judicibus damnatæ, imitabimur exemplum; atque ab hominibus ad Deum conversi cum eadem dicemus: O Deus immortalis, quiocculta nosti, qui omnia ante eorum ortum prospiciebas (cum hos falsum testatos esse adversum nos, nosque damnari cum nihil fecerimus (nec senserimus) eorum quæ contra nos isti per malitiam commenti sunt. Equidem decuisset Lipsienses Aggressoris nostri Socios ejusmodi conquerendi ansam nobis præripuisse, impediendo ne adversarii istius nostri criminationes Actis suis affuerentur; aut vero, postquam per imprudentiam eis immixtæ semel fuerant, eadem prima occasione data improbando. At vide, quæso, quo usque vincula mundi, vana gloria, eruditionisque falsæ venenum eruditorum corda penetraverint & corruperint! Ipsimet quando Acta sua omnis generis Eruditionis falsæ materiis replere debent, nec non vanissimis nugamentis, v. g. (a) de modis quibus ranæ coëunt, & quomodo se habeant marium & fœmellarum podices ante & post coitum, similibusque mustaceis, ea sunt conscientiæ teneritate, ut ejusmodi futilissimas nugas non audeant referre nisi juratos emissarios testesque oculatos de istis ineptiis prius sancte confestantes audiverint. At quando agitur de proximis suis (quos lege omnium sanctissima, sub vitæ æternæ damno, tanquam se ipsos amare debent) in
units.tr: (a) p. 115. us, although they attest things contrary to what is imputed to us (yet these are only thoughts). Then we shall imitate the example of innocent Susanna, falsely accused by old and crafty men and condemned by judges too credulous, and turning from men to God we shall say the same thing: O immortal God, who knowest secret things, who foresawest all things before they came into being, since these men have borne false witness against us and we are condemned, though we have done nothing (nor even thought) of the things which they have devised against us through malice. Indeed the Leipzig associates of our Assailant ought to have snatched from us this occasion for complaint, by preventing his accusations against us from being brought into their Acta; or, once they had been slipped in through carelessness, they ought at the first opportunity to have disapproved of them. But see, I pray, how far the chains of the world, vainglory, and the poison of false learning have penetrated and corrupted the hearts of these scholars! When they have to fill their Acta with materials of every kind of false learning, and with the most empty trifles, for example (a) on the manner in which frogs couple, and how the posteriors of males and females stand before and after intercourse, and similar cakes and trifles, they have such a tender conscience that they do not dare to report such utterly frivolous trifles unless they have first heard them from sworn agents and eyewitnesses who have solemnly confessed these absurdities. But when it is a matter of their neighbours (whom they must love as themselves, under the penalty of eternal life, by the most holy law of all), in

units.la: (a) Act. Lipf. an. 1687. pag. 248. infamandis, deque rebus divinis, suum & omnium hominum naturalium captuin superantibus, & quod plus est, ea lingua scriptis, quam ipsi ne intelligunt quidem, nedum ea kegerint: tunc conscientia in longum & latum dilatata illis permittit, non modo semel adoptare odiosa ea quae ex illis unus irrisorio & palam inimico, adeoque non credendo stylo retulit; sed etiam, quanquam moniti, cum oblata in monito illo sese excusandi ratione, malunt tamen in perverso isthoc agendi modo pergere, & in Actis suis (a) obfirmato animo de aequitate sua, deque nulla nobis illata a se injuria testari, veluti iniqua illa mulier apud Salomonem, (b) quae postquam comedit [peccatum,] tergit os suum, & ait, non commisi iniquitatem; quam veritati dare manus. Verum, ut cum Augustino (c) loquar, ea putatur gloria vanitatis, nullis cedere viribus veritatis, in perniciem utique ejus cui vitium tam immane dominatur. Ast omnia tandem in veritatis oppressae emolumentum cessura sunt. (d) Omne telum contra te cusum erit infortunatum; & omnem linguam quae consurgit ad disceptandum surrexerit, condemnabis. Haec est Domini servorum hereditas & justitia auctore me, inquit Dominus apud prophetam. (e) Ecquomodo apparebit veritas (Macarii testimonio) nisi habeat adversarios qui sint mendaces, & qui in illam irruant? His auctoribus Lectorum curiositas ita provocabitur, ut partium utrinque dicta videre gestiant: eis vero lectis, postquam visuri sunt se adversariorum quidem scriptis ad nullum bonum nullamque virtutem propelli, sed animas suas per ea omnis generis odiosis & acerbis moribus percelli; per nostra vero se potentissime & sine fuco ad Deum omneque solidum bonum impelli, atque cum inimitabili veritatis, corda penetrantis, irradiatione & efficacia, ab omni malo, vano & falso revocari; non poterunt (quod multis jam accidit) quin indignentur portentosis adversantium calumniis: & vero nostrae innocentiae favebunt, nobisque etsi ejusdem cum adversariis Sectae essent, non recusabunt testimonium, quale olim Christianis dabat Judaeus ille Tryphon apud S. Justinum:(a) Quae a multis in vos jactantur, indigna sunt fide.... Vestra sane praecepta tam magna & admiranda esse novimus, ut suspicio nostra sit a nemine illa ferri posse: incessit enim ea cata mihi ut ea legerem. Nec hic stabitur, sed (ut ait Psaltes) (b) postquam justitia ad judicium reverterit, sive postquam juste judicatum fuerit, omnes qui recto sunt corde convertentur ad justitiam, & ex ore infantium & lactentium perficientur laudes Domini, ut destruatur inimicus & (ut legebatur tempore Sulpitii) DEFENSOR. III. Inter exempla eorum qui parum fidas de nobis relationes divulgarunt, haud jam recensem Auctorem Epistolarum Gallicarum quas Pastorales vocat, si is postquam ei respondi, verioraque ostendi, ea, quae nobis perperam in relatione ejus affricta erant, ex Editionibus postmodum iteratis, nec non e Belgica versione curavisset eliminari: Quod cum non fecerit, stentque, imo & reponantur ejus adversum nos testimonia, cogor hic monere, in eis omnia & dogmata & facta nobis imputari quae nostris sunt omnino contraria. Equidem post responsum(a) meum silentii paritres tenuit, id quod pro agnitione injuriae nobis ab ipso factae interpretor: ac ne aegre ferat illud hic a me dici, id ipsum etiam mihi argumentum est, eum non tam e proprio fundo suo, quam ex improba aliorum relatione & credulitate ea prius scripsisse, quae si certius & exactius cognovisset, per animi honestatem(quae eum, ut opinor, retinet ne similia denuo nobis attribuat) illa haud propalasset: qua in re ex obfirmatorum aliorum calumniatorum familia se neutiquam esse palam facit. Et, ne soli illius culpae insistam, mea dissimulata, fateor & doleo, ab amicis propriaque conscientia dudum monitus, me eo tempore magis cessisse tentationi, qua ex consideratione injuriarum nobis stylo acerbo & minante factarum, aliisque de causis tunc impellebar ad acerbitatem acerbitate pensandam; quam respexisse ad lenitudinem Christi, jubentis benedicere iis qui nobis maledicunt. Dabo operam, cum gratia Divina, in posterum in me id ut emendem, utque per me non stet quin ille & ego postmodum re ipsa de verbis Paulinis implendis inter nos decertemus: (b) Induite ut Dei electi, amatique, affectum misericordiae, benignitatem, humilitatem, mansuetudinem, patientiam, alius alium ferentes , & invicem condonantes si quis habet quod de alio expostulat : quemadmodum Christus vobis condonavit, sic vos quoque facite : Sed super hæc omnia, charitatem, quæ perfectionis vinculum est ; vigeatque divina pax in vestris animis ad quam estis ad unum corpus vocati.
units.tr: (a) Acta Lipsiensia, 1687, p. 248. to defame them, and to say things about divine matters beyond the grasp of all natural men, and what is more, to write in a language that they do not even understand, let alone practise. Then their conscience, stretched wide and long, allows them not only once to adopt the hateful things that one of them, in a mocking and openly hostile, and so unbelieving, style, has reported. Even when they have been warned, and offered a way to excuse themselves in that warning, they would rather persist in this perverse manner of acting, and in their Acts (a) bear witness with a hardened mind to their own fairness and to the injury they have done us, like that wicked woman in Solomon (b) who, after she has eaten [sin,] wipes her mouth and says, I have done no wickedness; and they will not give their hands to the truth. But, to speak with Augustine (c), it is counted a glory of vanity to yield to no strength of truth, to the destruction, surely, of the one whom so monstrous a fault dominates. But in the end all things will turn to the advantage of the oppressed truth. (d) "Every weapon forged against you will be unsuccessful, and every tongue that rises up to contend against you you shall condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness is from me, says the Lord," speaking through the prophet. (e) "How else will the truth appear (by the testimony of Macarius) unless it has adversaries who are liars and who rush upon it?" With these authors the curiosity of the readers will be so provoked that they will be eager to see what both parties have said; and when they have read them, after they see that the writings of our adversaries drive their souls to no good and no virtue, but rather infect them with all kinds of hateful and bitter habits, while through our writings they are most powerfully and without pretence driven to God and to every solid good, and are called back from every evil, vain and false thing by the unmatched radiance and efficacy of the truth that penetrates the heart, they will not be able (as has already happened to many) but to be indignant at the monstrous calumnies of our opponents; and they will favour our innocence, and even if they belonged to the same sect as our adversaries, they will not refuse us testimony such as that which the Jew Tryphon once gave to the Christians, in Justin Martyr: (a) "The things that are thrown at you by many are unworthy of belief.... Indeed we know your precepts to be so great and admirable that our suspicion is that no one could bring them forward; for I have been seized with a desire to read them." Nor will the matter stop there, but (as the Psalmist says) (b) "When righteousness has returned to judgement, or once judgement has been justly given, all who are upright in heart will turn to righteousness, and out of the mouths of infants and sucklings the praises of the Lord will be perfected, so that the enemy may be destroyed and (as was read in the time of Sulpicius) the DEFENDER." III. Among the examples of those who have spread unreliable reports about us, I will not now mention the author of the French letters which he calls Pastorales, if after I answered him and showed the truer facts, he had taken care to remove from the later reprinted editions, and from the Belgian translation, the things that had been wrongly attached to us in his report. Since he has not done so, and his testimonies against us stand, and indeed are reissued, I am forced to warn here that in them all the doctrines and deeds are imputed to us which are wholly contrary to our own. Indeed, after my reply he kept a rather silent peace, which I interpret as an acknowledgement of the injury done to us by him; and lest he take it badly that I say this here, this itself is for me an argument that he wrote those things earlier not so much from his own ground as from the wicked report and credulity of others, and that if he had known them more certainly and exactly, through the honesty of his mind (which, as I think, keeps him from attributing similar things to us again) he would not have published them; in this matter he plainly shows that he is by no means of the family of those obstinate calumniators. And, not to dwell on his fault alone, I confess and grieve that, as my friends and my own conscience have long warned me, I then gave in too much to the temptation, which, from considering the injuries done to us in a bitter and threatening style, and for other reasons, then drove me to answer bitterness with bitterness; instead of looking to the gentleness of Christ, who bids us bless those who curse us. I will take care, with the grace of God, to amend this in me in future, and so that it does not rest with me that he and I afterwards contend between ourselves in actually fulfilling the words of Paul: (b) "Put on, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; just as Christ forgave you, so you also must do. But above all these put on love, which is the bond of perfection; and let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which you were called in one body."
