units.tr: IV.

units.la: Haud ita pridem alius quidam nescio qualis, nomine fictitio Jani Philadelphi assumto, conscriptaque de Optima Christianorum Secta Consultatione Desultoria , e numero eorum esse voluit, qui gratis de me, amicis, librisque meis falsa disseminant. Ispostquam inter alios celeberrimam Virginem aliquoties dictam, amicosque annumerasset iis qui Religionem Christianam magis moribus & ingenio quam verbis contentiosis exprimere volunt, sententiamque suam de illis veluti de hypocritis pronunciasset ipse, antiquo scilicet Jano ( quiante & retro videbat, iste vero &in intimis) oculatior : subjungit , ( * ) Antoniæ Bourignoniæ fœminæ pridem nutanti , magna nunc iterum accessit per Poiremum auctoritas, ut qui magna contentione & ipsam Θεοπνευστον, & veram fuisse Vatem ubertimis OECONOMIÆ DIVINÆ libris ostendisse se putat, opportune ob hoc ipsum multatus. Quis non crederet e verbis hujus Jani Philadelphi, materiam seu argumenta librorum Oeconomiæ hanc esse quæstionem, quam is recenseт ? Atqui in illis, ne hac quidem quæstione semel mo-
units.tr: Not long ago another person, I know not who, assuming the fictitious name Janus Philadelphus and writing a Desultory Consultation on the Best Sect of Christians, chose to be counted among those who freely spread falsehoods about me, my friends and my books. After he had listed among others the most celebrated Virgin, often mentioned, and her friends, those who wish to express the Christian religion more by morals and disposition than by contentious words, and had pronounced his own judgement on them as though they were hypocrites, he adds, forsooth, that Janus of old (who saw things behind and before him, but this man sees even into the inner depths more sharply): * Antonia Bourignon, a woman who was once wavering, has now again gained great authority through Poiret, so that she was opportunely punished for this very reason, since he thinks he has shown, with great labour, that she was both divinely inspired and a true prophetess, in the most copious books of the DIVINE ECONOMY. Who would not believe, from the words of this Janus Philadelphus, that the subject or arguments of the books of the Economy is the question which he goes on to review? And yet in those books this very question was not once raised

units.la: (*) Consult. defult. pag. 82. mota, Dei opera & regimen erga homines tam in creatione, quam in lapsu, in redemtione & restitutione; in internis pariter & externis, sic proponere conatus sum, ut rerum omnium tam naturæ quam gratiæ ortus, causæ & effectus, cum omnium capitalium difficultatum, etiam earum, quàs Athei, Philosophi, Theologi insolubiles putabant, solutionibus ibi apparerent quam clarissime, per demonstrationes & rationes intimas & rebus essentiales, Mathematicam certitudinem æquantes vel superantes, & Scripturarum testimoniis fulcitas. Quæstionum autem omnium momentosissimarum, ibi acquiescentissimo modo solutarum numerus pene infinitus facit, ut ubertas librorum, quam is videtur objectare, in multitudine materiarum, quarum nulla fere est cujus rationes fundamentales ibi non exposuerim, consistere dicenda fit, non in prolixitate sermonis de unaquaque quæstione: qua in re multo sane prefior fui quam Janus noster in consultatione sua desultoria; quippe qui ibi octo octernionum folia huic uni quæstioni de Optima Christianorum Secta, impendere non dubitavit ut inde hanc conclusionem eliceret, suam Sectam esse optimam omnium. Ego autem multis quæstionum millibus ne centum & quadraginta quidem duodernionum folia in toto opere dedi, quæ millena Jani Philadelphi methodo dari debuissent. Quoniam autem celeberrimæ Virginis Bourignoniæ sensus (vel opiniones si vis) cognoscere fi quis alius, dicor, multorumque curiositas eo vergit, ut quid illa senserit, discursus vel historiæ gratia scire peroptent, iis ut satis facerem, interdum in eo opere indicavi (idque aliquoties cum elogii verbo,) quibus in locis materias de quibus agebam illa tractaverit; quod miror Jano nostro adeo inidoneum videri, ut propterea librum meum veluti infamaturus, temerarie dicat, me ob id ipsum opportune esse multatum. De multa vel minima, per Dei gratiam, nil hactenus quicquam scio vel expertus sum, qui scripserim & vivam in Provinciis liberis, ubi pro æquitate Magistratuum, cæteros omnes toto terrarum orbe hac virtute superantium, pia animi sensa palam facere, sine Inquisitionis Ecclesiasticæ timore licet, & facio permultis gratissimus, qui non hic tantum, sed & quocunque loco degunt. Namque nobilissimorum, probissimorum, & in omni scientia, virtute, Secta, etiam in illa quæ est Jani, præstantissimorum Virorum benevolentiam & amicitiam loco multæ conciliavit mihi opus illud Oeconomiæ Divinæ, quod verbis & literis suis non pauci tanti facere voluerunt, ut nec modestia propria, nec invidia aliorum id me proferre patiatur. Quid enim dicerent invidi, si quis propalaret suum quoddam opus ex cordatissimis & excellentissimi ingenii viris nonnullos ut incomparabile extulisse; alios, ut donum cœli; alios, ut cui post Scripturas sacras nil invenerint simile; alios, cui par inter omnia quæ unquam viderunt excusa non legerint; alios, quod dolendum omnium manibus non teri; alios, cujus lestione dubiis omnibus perfecte soluti sint; & multo plura? quæ, nisi quis absurdissimus sit, non licet ei de suo cogitare, nec sine pudore ex aliis indirecte referre, nisi interdum in ruborem dandus esset mendax livor e manibus proborum proficua scripta excutere tentans, supposito falsæ aut ridiculæ materiæ titulo & infami libri successu? quod calumniandi genus ut ex efficacissimis apud simpliciores, ita ex indignissimis est. Quid diceret Janus Philadelphus, si quis calumniator publicaret, eum ob dissertationem suam opportune multatum aut virgis cæsum fuisse? nonne ægre ferret ejusmodi indignâ calumniâ librum suum efficacius horrori vulgi exponi quam si quis ex professo eum refutasset modo aperte calumniatorio? Ergo si vere Philadelphus est, seu fratrum amator, primum, non dicam fraternitatis, sed humanitatis præceptum, quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris, ostendat sibi esse cordi: nec in posterum contemnat eos qui Deo accepti, multa ab ejus divina liberalitate non contemnenda dona receperunt, ut incomparabilis illa Virgo Antonia, quam per contemtum Antoniam fœminam aliquoties vocitat, & cui nuntanti me auctoritatem aitconciliasse, ac pro Vate eam a me haberi & commendari. Ego sane sic habeo, Antoniam fœminam, & Janum Philadelphum masculum, & omnem pariter hominem, in se & sine Deo non nutare tantum, sed etiam omnino nihil esse: At Antoniam fœminam, invito licet Jano masculo, nec nutasse nec nutaturam ununquam, quatenus solidæ veritati Euangelicæ & Spiritui Christi innixa: qua in re neque accessu auctoritatis per Poiretum, aut per ullum alium opus habebit: Verum cum non pauci quibus veritates divinæ per viros aut fœminas prolatæ usui esse possent, cum inde abstrerreantur per falsas aut ridiculas relationes, quapropter opus habere videntur testimoniis vel auctoritate quorundam quibus inducantur ad examinandos proprias utilitatis causa eos libros, quos nonnulli invidi aut saluti hominum irati, eis velut contemnendos aut abjiciendos mala sua auctoritate vellent haberi; si talibus Poireti vel testimonium vel auctoritas circa saluberrima Antoniæ scripta tale quid proficere posset; ea ille lubentissime accommodabit, quo usque hoc vivæ Euangelii veritati & virtuti promovendæ inservire poterit; nec ultra. Neque id tantum circa scripta illa; sed & quorumvis aliorum, seu virorum, seu fœminarum, dum veritates divinas efficaciter continent, & faciam & feci jam aliquoties, quando v. gr. partim verti, partim edidi Gallice libros incomparabiles (quorum substantia mea fides est) Kempisii communis, Theologiæ Germanicæ, Theologiæ Cordis & Theologiæ Amoris, quæ duo ultima collectanea sunt, in quibus inter virorum scripta occurrunt quatuor trium fœminarum, opera virorum longe vincentia. His ego in meis scriptis do interdum testimonia, sic tamen, ut non sequatur mea scripta nil aliud quam tales aliorum commendationes aut Apologias continere; quemadmodum hic auctor videtur persuadere velle. Caeterum omni absurditate est absurdius, virtutem & eruditionem, seu divina haec sit sive humana, in aliquo contemnere ob sexum, quando cordatiores ex eruditis eam in foeminis magis quam in viris laudare soleant. Haud ita diu celebris Hanc vero de qua agitur, sic parum contemnunt doctissimi quique, ut inter ea quae in libris meis gratissima ipsis fuere, numerent occasionem eis a me subministratam divina ejus scripta legitandi & cognoscendi, quando de eis tale protuli in Oeconomia testimonium, cujus nedum me pudeat aut poeniteat, tenorem hic, Jano licet haud arridente, apponere non dubito.
units.tr: (*) Consult. defult. pag. 82. touched upon. Rather, I have tried to set out in them the works and government of God towards men, both in creation and in the fall, in redemption and restoration, inwardly as well as outwardly, in such a way that the origins, causes and effects of all things, both of nature and of grace, together with the solutions of all the chief difficulties, including those which atheists, philosophers and theologians thought insoluble, would appear there as clearly as possible, through demonstrations and intimate reasons essential to the things themselves, equalling or surpassing mathematical certainty, and supported by the testimonies of Scripture. The number of the most weighty questions, solved there in a most satisfying manner, is almost infinite. So the copiousness of the books, which he seems to object to, lies in the multitude of subjects, of which there is hardly one whose fundamental reasons I have not set out there. It is not to be called a matter of wordiness about each question, a respect in which I was certainly much more sparing than our Janus in his Desultory Consultation, since there he did not hesitate to devote eight octernions of pages to this single question about the Best Sect of Christians, in order to draw from it the conclusion that his own sect is the best of all. I, on the other hand, have given not even a hundred and forty duodernions of pages in the whole work to many thousands of questions, which by the method of Janus Philadelphus ought to have taken a thousand. Since I am said to be one who knows, in some way, the views (or opinions, if you like) of the most celebrated Virgin Bourignon, and since the curiosity of many tends to wish to know what she thought, for the sake of discussion or history, I have at times, in that work, indicated (and sometimes with a word of praise) in which places she treated the matters I was discussing. That our Janus should find this so unsuitable that, as if about to defame my book, he rashly says I was for this very reason opportunely punished, I marvel. Concerning her, or anything at all, by God's grace, I have hitherto known or experienced nothing, I who write and live in free provinces, where, through the fairness of the magistrates, which surpasses all others in the whole world, one may openly express pious feelings without fear of ecclesiastical Inquisition, and I do so, and am most welcome to very many who dwell not only here but in whatever place. For that work of the Divine Economy has won me, in place of a fine, the goodwill and friendship of very noble, upright men, most eminent in every science, virtue and sect, even in that of Janus; and not a few of them have valued it by their words and letters so highly that neither my own modesty nor the envy of others permits me to bring them forward. For what would the envious say, if someone were to publish that some of the most judicious and most excellent men had praised one of his works as incomparable; others as a gift of heaven; others as having found nothing like it after the holy Scriptures; others as having never read anything equal to it among all they had seen; others that it is a pity it is not worn by the hands of all; others that by reading it they were perfectly resolved of all doubts; and much more? Such things, unless one were utterly absurd, one may not think of one's own work, nor report them indirectly from others without shame, unless perhaps the envious liar, trying to shake useful writings out of the hands of the upright, were to be put to shame, by pretending the title of a false or ridiculous subject and an infamous success for the book. This kind of slander is as effective among the simpler sort as it is unworthy. What would Janus Philadelphus say if some slanderer were to publish that he had been opportunely punished, or flogged, on account of his dissertation? Would he not be vexed that such an unworthy slander exposed his book to the horror of the crowd more effectively than if someone had refuted it expressly, but in an openly slanderous manner? Therefore, if he truly is Philadelphus, that is, a lover of the brethren, let him show that the first precept, I will not say of brotherhood but of humanity, what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to another, is dear to his heart. Let him not in future despise those who are acceptable to God and have received from his divine liberality gifts not to be despised, like that incomparable Virgin Antonia, whom he repeatedly calls, with contempt, "the woman Antonia", and to whom, he says, I have obtained authority by announcing her, and who is held and commended by me as a prophetess. I for my part hold indeed that the woman Antonia, and Janus Philadelphus the man, and every man likewise, not only wavers in himself and without God but is altogether nothing. But the woman Antonia, though Janus the man object, has neither wavered nor will ever waver, since she rests upon solid evangelical truth and the Spirit of Christ; and in this matter she will have no need of any accession of authority through Poiret or any other. Yet since there are not a few to whom divine truths, uttered by men or women, could be of use, and who are being frightened away from them by false or ridiculous reports, they seem to need the testimony or authority of certain persons to induce them to examine for their own benefit those books which some envious men, or men angry at the salvation of others, would wish, by their evil authority, to have them despise or reject. If Poiret's testimony or authority could bring any such help to Antonia's most wholesome writings, he will most gladly lend it, as long as it can serve to promote the living truth and virtue of the Gospel, and no further. Nor is this only true of those writings, but of those of any others, whether men or women, so long as they effectively contain divine truths. I both do and have often done so, as when, for instance, I have partly translated and partly published in French the incomparable books (whose substance is my faith): Kempis's Common, the German Theology, the Theology of the Heart and the Theology of Love, which last two are collections, in which among the writings of men there occur those of three women, works far surpassing those of men. In my writings I sometimes give testimonies to these, yet in such a way that my writings do not consist of nothing but such commendations or apologies of others; as this author seems willing to persuade. Moreover, it is more absurd than any absurdity to despise virtue and learning, whether divine or human, in anyone on account of sex, when the more judicious among the learned are wont to praise it more in women than in men. Yet the celebrated woman of whom we speak is so little despised by all the most learned that among the things most welcome to them in my books they count the occasion I gave them of reading and knowing her divine writings, when I put forward of her in the Economy a testimony, of which I am not only not ashamed or sorry, but whose tenor I do not hesitate to set down here, even though it does not please Janus.

units.la: "Scilicet, si quid in Theologicis vel naturalibus rectius novi, id ex Virginis admirandae principiis, ejus ore aut libris a me perceptum vel deductum esse, meque inde mentis lumina & aptitudinem, quorum ad omnia usus extendatur, hausisse; sine quibus adhuc implicarer tenebris exitialibus, corde caecus, ratione corruptae adeo mancipatus; ut me non nasci satius fuisset. Sinceras mentes, quae ad divina haec scripta accedent humiles, deprehensuras, quam vivide ea rectam Dei ejusque potentiae, sapientiae, bonitatis, justitiae, libertatis, mysteriorumque Redemptionis nostrae adorandorum cognitionem imprimant mentibus; quam profunde corruptionis humanae immensitatem detegant";
units.tr: "Certainly, if I have learned anything more correct in theology or in natural matters, I have perceived or deduced it from the principles of the admirable Virgin, from her mouth or from her books, and from them I have drawn the lights of the mind and an aptitude that extends to every use. Without these I would still be entangled in deadly darkness, blind in heart, and enslaved by a corrupted reason to such a degree that it would have been better for me not to have been born. Sincere minds who come humbly to these divine writings will discover how vividly they impress upon the mind the right knowledge of God and of his power, wisdom, goodness, justice and liberty, and of the mysteries of our Redemption that are to be adored; how profoundly they uncover the immensity of human corruption;

units.la: quam tranquillum & tutum reddant animum circa ea quæ in Religionibus quibusvis disputantur; quam universaliter controversiis finem imponant; hæresibus omnibus interitum procurent; & verò excitent, percutiant, penetrent nec quiescere sinant cor nostrum donec dedatur Deo, ejusque divinæ uni voluntati tradatur ab omnibus rebus evanidis disjunctum, soli necessario adhærens, partibus nullis vitiose addictum, pacificum, humile, contentum; atque, ut verbo dicam, deprehendent probi lectores sibi per ea satisfieri de omnibus quæ quidem circa theoriam & praexim, externam & internam vitæ institutionem erga Deum, erga se, erga alios, probos juxta atque improbos, moveri & desiderari posse: idque fieri non obscuris quibusdam modis; sed cum incredibili quadam accommodatione & facilitate nulli comparanda, quam etiam vel infantuli bonæ voluntatis capiant in rebus alioqui arduis & sublimibus; cumque tanta evidentia atque claritate indubia, nec non ea scopi, solum amorem Dei spirantis, solam peccati destructionem intendentis puritate; ut non capiam sane qui fieri queat, aliquos coram Deo & in sinu non esse improbos, & simul tamen opera adeo divina damnare aut contemnere posse, si modo ea legerint, aut eorum saltem præcipua, veluti Lucem Mundi, v.g. aut Lucem in tenebris, aut Anti-Christum detectum, aut tractatum de Solida Virtute, aut Renovationem Spiritus Evangelici, aut Lapidem Ly-dium, dium, (qui tres ultimi Latine exstant, caeteri Gallice, Germanice & Belgicè.) Nec ego solus haec sentio. Sunt & fuerunt plures, iique non contemnendi judicii, qui in eadem mecum mente concordant. Nec ignorat, credo, Janus Philadelphus Medicus, Doctorem Swammerdammium, Medicum celeberrimum, in Anatomicis inventis nemini secundum, divinae Antoniae eruditionis admiratione & aestimatione eousque captum fuisse, ut ejus commendandae gratia integros libros, veluti Ephemeri vitam publicaverit, proprioque Antoniae quosdam (librum videlicet de Solida Virtute, quem celebris alius Latino sermone publicavit) Belgice ediderit. Is Dn. Swammerdammius postquam Virginem per aliquot menses visitasset & examinasset, dicere solebat, se duo haec apud illam didicisse: primum quidem eam a Spiritu Dei doceri & regi; alterum vero se, prae illa & scientia & virtute destitutam esse. Fuisse autem sagacissimum scrutatorem eorum quae ipse inquirebat, sciunt quotquot ex conversatione vel operibus illum norunt: neque destitit ad mortem usque Virginis scripta quovis auro habere cariora. Quae omnia refero ut Jani contemtum saltem ad aequilibrium redigam, per testimonia suo non minus ponderosa: quibus alia quam plurima superaddere possem Virorum undiquaque praestantissimorum, quos non tantum non pudet dona Dei in Virgine agnoscere & venerari; sed qui & ipsa publicare sponte sua gestiunt. Celeberrimus Menagius, in omni genere literaturae versatissimus, Antoniam Burignoniam Theologam inter illustres eruditione fœminas atque Principissas honorifice nominat & locat in libro quodam Italico quem una cum historia mulierum Philosopharum haud ita diu Lugduni evulgavit. Id quod inter alia apparet ex illustris Jurisconsulti D. Mackenzei, apud Scotos Advocati Regii, dum hæc scriberem satis functi, & monumentis literariis clari, libello de humana ratiocinationis imbecillitate, ab extremis Europæ terris, Scotia, nuper huc transmisso, & ab humanissimo celeberrimoque D. Græyio Ultrajecti publicæ luci dato: in quo libro clarissimus Auctor, postquam de rationis næyis & imbecillitate disseruisset, ostendisset que multis, verum ejus usum veramque efficaciam in hoc esse, ut ad superna & æterna, cæteris contemtis nos remittat; pro conclusione omnium veluti vim in uno Virginis Antoniæ, etiam adhuc infantis, exemplo comprehensurus, hac peroratione claudit: Tanta est ratiocinationis hujus efficacia, ut etiam in ætatis diluculo infantes illustrare, adultisque ad subtilia ineptis persuadere valeat. Cujus exemplum paucis abhinc annis nobis tulit Flandria, in virgunculà infante, septimum ætatis annum nondum egressa, (Antoniam indigitat) quæ cum vitam hanc spatio brevem, & curriculo miseram satis cerneret, mortales tantopere eâ capi obstupuit. Et cum Jesum Christum vitam immortalem suis acquisivisse audivisset, enixe & continuo parentes rogavit ut se in Christianorum regiones ducerent. Cum autem ipsi Christum in Flandria coli responderent, hoc incredibile exclamavit: Christum enim paupertatem laudasse, illis autem nummos numen esse; illum dignitates spreuisse, istos autem has ambite, flendo arguebat. Et
units.tr: how calm and secure they make the mind concerning the things that are disputed in any religions; how universally they put an end to controversies; how they bring ruin upon all heresies; and how they really arouse, strike and penetrate, and do not allow our heart to rest until it is given over to God and surrendered to his divine will alone, separated from all fleeting things, adhering only to what is necessary, not vitiously devoted to any parts, peaceable, humble and content. In a word, upright readers will find that through these writings they are satisfied concerning all the things that can be stirred up and desired regarding the theory and practice, the outward and inward ordering of life towards God, towards themselves, and towards others, the upright and the wicked alike. And this is done not by some obscure methods, but with an incredible kind of adaptation and ease, which can be compared to nothing, and which even a little child of good will can grasp in matters otherwise difficult and lofty; and with such evident and clear certainty, and with that purity of aim which breathes only the love of God and aims only at the destruction of sin, that I cannot indeed understand how it can happen that some people are not wicked before God and in their own bosom, and yet at the same time can condemn or despise such divine works, if only they have read them, or at least their chief parts, such as Lucem Mundi, for example, or Lucem in tenebris, or Anti-Christum detectum, or the tractatum de Solida Virtute, or Renovationem Spiritus Evangelici, or Lapidem Lydium, dium. (The last three of these exist in Latin, the others in French, German and Dutch.) Nor do I alone think these things. There are and have been many others, of no contemptible judgment, who agree with me in the same mind. Nor, I believe, does Janus Philadelphus, the physician, fail to know that Dr. Swammerdam, a most celebrated physician, second to none in anatomical discoveries, was so captivated by admiration and esteem for the divine Antonia's learning that, in order to commend her, he published whole books, such as Ephemeri vitam, and published certain of her works in Dutch (namely the book on Solida Virtute, which another famous man published in Latin). After Dr. Swammerdam had visited and examined the Virgin for some months, he used to say that he had learned these two things from her: first, that she is taught and ruled by the Spirit of God; and second, that he himself was destitute of both her knowledge and her virtue. That he was a most acute investigator of the things he inquired into, all who knew him through conversation or his works are aware; nor did he cease, until death, to hold the writings of the Virgin dearer than any gold. I relate all these things so that I may at least bring Janus's contempt back to balance, by testimonies no less weighty than his. To these I could add very many others of the most eminent men from every quarter, who are not only not ashamed to acknowledge and venerate the gifts of God in the Virgin, but who even of their own accord are eager to publish them. The most famous Ménage, most skilled in every kind of literature, honourably names Antonia Bourignon, the theologian, among the learned women and princesses, and ranks her with them in an Italian book which he recently published at Lyon, together with a history of women philosophers. This appears, among other things, from the illustrious jurist Mr. Mackenzie, Royal Advocate among the Scots, a man of distinguished career now deceased and famous for his literary monuments, from his little book de humana ratiocinationis imbecillitate, lately sent here from the farthest lands of Europe, Scotland, and published by the most courteous and most famous Mr. Greyio at Utrecht. In that book the most distinguished author, after he had discussed the defects and weakness of reason, and had shown by many arguments that its true use and true efficacy lies in this, that it sends us to things above and eternal, all others being despised, wishing to grasp, as it were, the force of all these in the single example of the Virgin Antonia, still a child, concludes with this peroration: Such is the efficacy of this reasoning, that it is able to enlighten even infants in the dawn of their age, and to persuade adults who are unfit for subtle things. Of this example Flanders has given us a few years ago, in a little virgin, a child who had not yet passed her seventh year (he points to Antonia), who, when she saw this life to be short in its span and miserable in its course, was amazed that mortals were so much captivated by it. And when she had heard that Jesus Christ had obtained immortal life for his own, she earnestly and constantly begged her parents to lead her into the regions of Christians. But when they answered that Christ was worshipped in Flanders, she cried out in disbelief, for Christ, she protested with tears, had praised poverty, while those people regarded money as a god; he had despised dignities, while these people were ambitious for them. And

units.la: quis talia fando Temperet a lachrymis?
units.tr: Who could hear such things and refrain from tears?

units.la: Sit ergo in votis meis primum, ratione recte uti. Sit ratio haec a coelo, unde est profecta, irradiata, nec a coeca turba ducta. Terminetur mea superbia contemtu mundi, & mea seueritas in me solum se exerceat. Nullus sit mihi nisi in coelo thesaurus; nec cupiat animus ea quae sunt a sana ratione aliena. Haec si Desultoria Consultationis Auctor imitatus fuisset, tunc se & verum Ianum, qui posteriora seu temporalia, & anteriora sive aeterna recto videat oculo, & verum Philadelphum, qui ex charitate malum non cogitet & gaudeat de veritate, comprobasset: & vero discerret, divina non desultorio, sed sedatissimo deinceps animo tractare; quod ipsi animitus opto in illo, quem magis a se edendum promittere, quam ab alio dudum editum indicare videtur, tractatu de Religione Medici.
units.tr: My first wish, then, is to use reason rightly. May this reason be illumined from heaven, whence it came, and not led by a blind crowd. May my pride be bounded by contempt for the world, and may my severity be exercised on myself alone. Let me have no treasure but in heaven; and may my mind not desire the things that are alien to sound reason. If the author of the Desultoria Consultatio had imitated these things, he would have shown himself, and the true Janus, who sees with a right eye both the later or temporal things and the earlier or eternal things, and the true Philadelphus, who from charity thinks no evil and rejoices in the truth; and he would have learned to handle divine matters not in a desultory manner but with a most calm mind henceforth. This I sincerely wish for him, in that treatise On the Religion of the Physician, which he seems more to promise to publish himself than to point out as already published by another.

units.la: Quamvis ex omnium partium cordatioribus nemo hactenus scripta mea susceperit modis legitimis impugnanda, non defuere tamen, ut jam visum, e praecipuis Sectis, etiam inter Philosophos, animosiores fumosoque zelo partibus suis pertinacius dediti, qui ea sinistris oculis inspexerint, nec non eadem cupiverint aggredi: quod aperte non ausi, indirecte tamen narratiunculas, historica fide & veritate ne quidem praeditas, eis satis fuit pro-
units.tr: Although none of the more judicious men of any party has so far taken up my writings to attack them by lawful means, there were not lacking, as is now evident, some more spirited men among the principal sects, even among the philosophers, who were devoted too stubbornly to their own factions with a smoky zeal. They looked on my writings with jaundiced eyes and wished to attack them. Not daring to do so openly, they were nonetheless content to publish indirectly some little narratives, endowed with neither historical faithfulness nor truth,

units.la: promulgasse, & vel ridicula, vel calumniosa pro meis haberi voluisse, inter quæ Pelagianismum cum Socinianismo posuerant in Relatione sua Lipsienses. Verum ut simul constaret, & me ab ejusmodi criminatione esse, si quis alius, innocentissimum, & ne ex famosioribus Sectis deesset aliquis iniquior cui scriptorum meorum solidæ veritates displicerent; oportuit & hujus Sectæ vel membrum vel fautorem aliquem exsistere, cui scripta mea essent ideo invisa quod principiis Socinianismi & Pelagianismi maxime opponerentur, quique hac de causa, methodo adversariis meis usitata, hoc est, relationibus falsis & ridiculis ea persequeretur. Is autem cui visum fuit eas partes suscipere, Bibliothecæ Universalis, Gallici libri, viginti vel nescio quot voluminibus constantis, Auctor est, hoc & aliis scriptis eo nomine notissimus, quod non tantum universaliter in quosvis virgulam stringat censoriam; sed & maxime quod in libris suis Pelagianismum & Socinianismum omni arte defendere & propugnare allaboret, nec non & ex sanctioribus purioris Christianismi Patribus, quotquot principiis quibus favet, adversantur, omnium ludibrio & derisioni per artes quasdam suas exponere audeat. Ersi autem istiusmodi hominum stylo ea de causa cum maximis & sanctissimis quibusque impeti, sit argumentum laudis: quoniam tamen illi hanc causam coram aliis dissimulant; alias salsas atque ineptas fingunt; monitis non desuerunt; & præterea latentes indirecte, inspectato & ubi lubet quos volunt, sic adoriuntur, ut quivis malit aperto marte impugnari, quam artibus ita dolosis & tectis invadi, quippe quae sincerioribus sub specie quadam pacis, moderationis, sinceritatis, veritatisque, falsa & mala persuadent in veritatis solidae detrimentum: satius videtur eorum inimica artificia vel saltem semel in apertum protrahi. Quod ego jam opportune de isto omnium universali meoque Censore crediderim esse mihi faciendum, atque ita quidem, ut ab illo discernam & separem eos quibuscum nulla mihi intercedit contentio, ejus nempe in libro componendo tum Socium olim, qui ad hunc articulum (de quo agetur) nil conferre voluit; tum Continuatorem qui non potuit, quippe a vigesimo demum tomo continuationem aggressus, quique praeterea sit animi ad talia sincerioris. Cum autem orbi sit notissimum, quinam ex libris Anonymis nostro tanquam Auctori aut editori tribuantur, frustra de reticendis quae nemini non nota sunt, essemus hic solliciti. Caeterum Epistolam, ne longior aut confusior visa taedio sit lectori, distinxi in Sectiones novem, in quarum singulis haec praecipua spectari poterant.
units.tr: and to have them regarded as either ridiculous or slanderous as my own work. Among these the Leipzig men, in their Report, placed Pelagianism together with Socinianism. But so that it might be clear that I am innocent of such an accusation, and so that among the more notorious sects there might not be lacking some rather unfair person whom the solid truths of my writings displeased, it was necessary that some member or supporter of this sect should also appear, one for whom my writings were hated for the reason that they stood most sharply against the principles of Socinianism and Pelagianism, and who for this reason would pursue them with false and ridiculous reports, the method customary for my opponents. The one who chose to take up that role is the author of the Bibliotheca Universalis, a French work of twenty or I know not how many volumes. He is most notorious, both for this and for other writings, not only because he wields the censor's rod universally against whomever he pleases, but especially because in his books he labours with every art to defend and champion Pelagianism and Socinianism, and dares to expose to the mockery and derision of all, by certain tricks of his own, the holier Fathers of purer Christianity, as many as are opposed to the principles he favours. Now, if such men attack with their pen all the greatest and most holy writers for this reason, that could be a matter for praise. But since they conceal this cause from others, invent salty and silly charges, are not short of warnings, and moreover, lurking indirectly, assail whom they wish, when and where they please, in such a way that anyone would rather be attacked in open combat than invaded by such deceitful and hidden arts (for these persuade the sincere, under a certain appearance of peace, moderation, sincerity and truth, of false and evil things to the detriment of solid truth), it seems better that their hostile devices be at least once dragged into the open. I think it is now right for me to do this against that universal critic of all, and my own censor, and to do so in such a way that I may distinguish and separate from him those with whom I have no quarrel: namely, his former companion in composing the book, who wished to contribute nothing to this article (the one to be discussed), and his continuator, who could not, since he began the continuation only from the twentieth volume, and who moreover is of a more sincere disposition in such matters. But since it is most well known to the world which of the anonymous books are attributed to our man as author or editor, it would be pointless for us to be anxious here about omitting what is known to everyone. Moreover, so that the Letter might not seem too long or too confused and burden the reader, I have divided it into nine Sections, in each of which these main points may be considered.

units.la: In prima, causae & materia Epistolae in genere.
units.tr: In the first, the cause and matter of the Letter in general.

units.la: In secunda, Dominum Clericum non ideo ullis aut mihi postponi, quod nonnulli ejus recensendi sint defectus, & incipiant recenseri.
units.tr: In the second, that Mr. Le Clerc is not to be preferred to me or to anyone else merely because some of his defects are to be listed, and these begin to be listed.

units.la: In tertia, generaliora quaedam, in scriptis D. Cl. consideranda, interserto insigni aliquo errato.
units.tr: In the third, certain more general matters to be considered in the writings of Mr. Le Clerc, with a notable error inserted.

units.la: In quarta, Generaliora sphalmata Domini Cl. in relatione sua de Oeconomia mea Divina.
units.tr: In the fourth, the more general errors of Mr. Le Clerc in his Report on my Divine Economy.

units.la: In quinta, Specialiora sphalmata ejusdem in eadem de Oeconomia Divina relatione.
units.tr: In the fifth, the more specific errors of the same man in the same Report on the Divine Economy.

units.la: In sexta, de articulo quodam Præfationis Tomi V. Bibliothecæ Universalis, & de convicio quodam in Tomo sequenti.
units.tr: In the sixth, concerning a certain article in the Preface to Volume V of the Bibliotheca Universalis, and concerning a certain insult in the following volume.

units.la: In septima, quantum fidei Domini Cl. relationibus de aliorum libris sit habendum, aliquot exemplis ostenditur.
units.tr: In the seventh, how much credit is to be given to the reports of Mr. Le Clerc about the books of others is shown by several examples.

units.la: In octava, de ejus in sanctiores Ecclesiæ Patres, præsertim in S. Augustinum invectivarum perpetuarum causis, fide & æquitate, nec non de ejusdem irrisorio genio agitur.
units.tr: In the eighth, it is treated of his perpetual causes of invective against the holier Fathers of the Church, especially against St. Augustine, as to their grounds, fairness and equity, and also of his mocking temper.

units.la: In nona denique, plura esse in ejus scriptis & propositis irridenda & carpenda, quam quæ in aliis ipse irrisit & carpsit; sed optandum alia & Christianis magis digna methodo dedoceri errores.
units.tr: In the ninth and last, there are more things in his writings and proposals to be ridiculed and censured than those he himself has ridiculed and censured in others; but it is to be wished that errors be unlearned by another method, more worthy of Christians.

units.la: AUCTORI BIBLIOTHECÆ UNIVERSALIS Critico Singulari PETRUS POIRET S. D.
units.tr: To the author of the Universal Library, the singular critic: Petrus Poiret, greetings.

units.la: (De causis & materia hujus Epistolæ.)
units.tr: (On the causes and matter of this letter.)

units.la: DOMINE,
units.tr: SIR,

units.la: Ntempestiva dubio procul videbitur tibi hæcce mea ad te epistola de negotio ob quod vel nunquam, vel alioqui jamdudum interpellandus eras. Discesbinc primo, me ea, quæ contra me verbis aut scriptis passim expromere haud veritus es, & neglexisse hactenus, & neglecturum quoque posthac fuisse, nisi forte nunc quicquam præterea commisisset similimi argumenti cum eis, quæ mihi tecum intercesserant; quando tu quidem in Bibliotheca tuæ Universalis Tomo V. de Oeconomiæ meæ Divinæ tractatibus relationem instituisti; ego vero ei relationi, revera in non paucis fallaci, opposui relationem aliam in Novellis Reip. literariæ anni 1687 mensibus Junio & Julio publicatam. Illius namque occasione argumenti, quod modo præcessit, circa sensus quosdam a meis alienos mihi a pluribus perperam attributos rediit in memoriam, veluti exemplum eorum de quibus tractabam, tua mecum agendi ratio: quam cum non tantum in libri tui editione prima publicam feceris; sed eandem, etsi relatione mea aliter summa cum moderatione monitus, & deinceps renovas verbis simulac de me loquendi tibi nascitur occasio; imo in libro tuo aliquoties denuo repetere ausus es, tum aliis in locis, tum ubi accidit tua sine emendatione eorum quae me concernunt, de novo recudi: propterea non aegre feres si, ad impediendum ne in posterum alii per te credant cogitata & scripta mea esse alia quam revera sunt, ea tibi hic coram propositurio, quae ad hoc efficiendum idonea mihi videntur. Et certe alii, sine exceptione, omnes, (quia hic non quaeretur an meae opiniones tuis veriores sint nec ne, sed tantum quaenam ex sint,) facilius credent, mea cogitata, meorumque verborum sensa mihi magis quam tibi perspecta esse: Tu vero, si exactioris Critici officio fungi cupis, quandoquidem de meis referre & judicare tibi visum fuit, gratulaberis tibi de modis tua circa haec judicia emendandi: tametsi vereor ne ob materiae, quae in tuis & meis scriptis occurrit, oppositionem fere omnimodam, mea tuo sic adversa sint animo, ut quamvis eorum conscius, ipsa nihilominus aliis perpetuo dissimulaturus sis, absurdaque eorum loco cum sarcasmis consuetis illusorie mihi imputaturus. Hoc ipsum sane jam fecisti, & licet monitus, tamen iterare non dubitasti: an ex animi malitia, vel ex timore, ne, scripta mea te sincerius indicante, legentes a sensis tuis, quorum fundamenta ibi convelluntur & contraria commonstrantur, recederent; an vero ex ignorantia, eaque pertinaciori quam ut iis quæ tuæ relationi reposueram, vinci potuerit, id judicandum Deo, tibi, aliisque committo. Attamen quoniam meliora de te tuique animi statu opto, hoc ultimum potius credam; ad quod proinde removendum efficacius quam prius a me factum est, referenda hic erunt nonnulla, prius a me præterita, tibi forte futura minus grata, necessaria tamen ut veritati sua constet apud quosvis incolumitas. Ea veras animi tui in me insensi causas internas externasque complectentur. Quæ quidem omnia parum interesset publicum recire, si personas tantum respicerent: verum ex quo in sinceritate cordis ea scriptis consignavi, quæ si faceremus, omnes, inde & eruditiores & meliores, & Deo beatitudinique propinquiores, nec non in tempore & æternitate perfectiores nos futuros, nemini fit dubitandum; jam non mea, sed gloriæ Dei, utilitatisque communis & veritatis fructuosæ causa exigit, ut & veritati satisfaciam, restituendo eam qualis est; & justitiæ, monendo alios, ne si falli nolint, distortis illusoriisque tuis testimoniis habeant fidem; & charitati, pro emendatione tua argumenta sufficientia proferendo. Quæ omnia quidem ita proponere conabor, ut quoniam non quæ ad me solum, sed quæ & ad alios & ad ipsamet Christianismi fundamenta pertinent, sæpius elenchis tuis & dogmatibus oppositis soles concutere; ex dicendis possit iis iri obviam quæ & objicis plurimis & male differhinare tentas. Hoc ut tibi æque ac aliis omnibus profícuum sit, Deum ex animo comprecor.
units.tr: This letter of mine to you about a matter for which you ought to have been called to account, or at least called to account long ago, will doubtless seem untimely to you. You will learn from this first that I had hitherto neglected, and would have continued to neglect hereafter, the things you have freely put forward against me in word and in writing, unless you had now committed something further of the same kind as what had already passed between us. For you, in Volume V of your Universal Library, gave an account of the treatises on my Divine Economy; and I, in reply to that account, which is in many places false, set against it another account, published in the Novellae Reipublicae Literariae in the months of June and July 1687. For on the occasion of the matter just mentioned, the way you dealt with me came back to my mind, as an example of the things I was discussing: the way in which certain meanings that were not mine were wrongly attributed to me by many people. You made this method public not only in the first edition of your book; and although I warned you in my account, in a very moderate manner, you renew it again and again, whenever you have an occasion to speak of me. Indeed, you have dared to repeat it several times in your book, and where it happened, it was reprinted again without correction, in other places as well, in the passages that concern me. Therefore you will not be vexed if I set before you here, to prevent others from believing through you that my thoughts and writings are other than they really are, the means that seem to me suitable for achieving this. And certainly all others, without exception (since here the question is not whether my opinions are truer than yours, but only what they are), will more readily believe that my thoughts and the meanings of my words are better known to me than to you. If you wish to perform the office of a more exact critic, since you have thought fit to report on and judge my works, you will rejoice in the ways of correcting your judgements on these matters. I fear, however, that because of the almost complete opposition in the subject matter found in your writings and mine, my views are so hostile to your mind that, although you are aware of them, you will go on concealing them from others and will falsely impute to me absurdities in their place, with your usual sarcasms. Indeed, you have already done this, and although you were warned, you did not hesitate to repeat it. Whether this comes from malice of mind, or from fear that readers, if you indicated my writings more sincerely, would turn away from your opinions, whose foundations are overthrown there and whose contraries are shown, or from ignorance, and that of a more stubborn kind than could be overcome by what I opposed to your account, I leave to God, to you, and to others to judge. Nevertheless, since I wish better things for you and for the state of your mind, I shall rather believe the latter. To remove this more effectively than I did before, I must here recall some matters which I have previously passed over, which may perhaps be less welcome to you, but which are necessary so that the truth may stand unharmed before everyone. These will embrace the true internal and external causes of your ill-will towards me. If they concerned only persons, it would matter little to make them public. But since I have set down in writing, in sincerity of heart, things which, if we did them, would make us all more learned and better, nearer to God and blessedness, and more perfect in time and eternity, no one should doubt; now it is required, not for my own sake but for the glory of God, the common good and the fruitful cause of truth, that I satisfy truth by restoring it as it is; justice, by warning others not to put faith in your distorted and deceptive testimonies, if they do not wish to be deceived; and charity, by offering sufficient arguments for your correction. I shall try to set all this forth in such a way that, since you often assail with your refutations and opposing doctrines not only matters that concern me alone, but also matters that concern others and the very foundations of Christianity, what follows may meet those things which you both object to in many places and try to twist badly. I earnestly pray God that this may profit you as much as all others.

units.la: Christi Servatoris verbum est, eos qui opera mala patrant, lucem odisse, neque ad eam accedere, ne opera sua mala patefiant: quod etiam de iis dicendum, qui errores malos fovent & communicant; eos nempe veritatem odisse, neque ad eam accedere, quin & alios ab eadem arcere velle, ne errata sua mala manifestentur. Quibus docemur, eos qui veritatem relationibus falsis, calumniis, aut externis quibusdam modis impugnant, non ex causis quas ipsi prætexunt, sed ex odio ejus occulto id facere; odium autem illud provenire ex tenebrarum & errorum amore: qui quidem non uni, sed omnibus hominibus ex nativitate corrupta inest; si quidem omnis homo naturaliter se ipsum & amet impense & magni æstimet; tenebræ autem & error faveant superbiæ isti & amori proprio, quibus veritas (homines nihili & turpitudinis suæ convincens) est infensa & exitium accelerat. Unde sequitur primò, omnem hominem ex origine sua corrupta & ad amorem tenebrarum errorumque, & ad veritatis odium esse propensum: hinc ejus elogium in Scriptura, Omnis homo mendax: secundò, eum non posse inde liberari, nisi ab alio principio quam a se corrupto impellatur intus a tenebris ad lucem, & verò ipse naturales gratasque propensiones, quas ad errorem & tenebras habet, sponte impugnet, ut amarae veritati, eum prius humilianti & conterenti, sese, ut ut repugnante sensu, animitus tradat: tertiò, non posse eundem per externa ab erroris mala via revocari, nisi ad erroris & tenebrarum internum fontem considerandum revocetur, quem ut melius noscat, nec sibi dissimulet, ejus rivuli externi, quibus vel falsa dissemina-ta sunt vel vera impugnata, ei poterunt oste-ndi. Hac tertia via erga te nunc agam, quando postea quibus ad errorum fontes poteris revocari, rivulos tangam, tum eos quibus errores disseminasti; tum alios, quibus veritates, & obiter quoque aliorum scripta impugnasti: ubi & exempla ex aliis & ex me desumam atque eorundem genium explorare annitar, nec non quædam de odio tuo Mystico, amore Critico, methodoque irrisoria vel interseram vel in conclusionem reservabo. Alteram autem quam modo enarravi, viam, Deo, & tibi (libertate tua ad placitum usuro,) relinquam.
units.tr: The word of Christ the Saviour is: those who do evil deeds hate the light, and do not come to it, lest their evil deeds be made manifest. This must also be said of those who foster and spread evil errors: that they hate the truth and do not come to it; indeed, they wish to keep others away from it too, lest their wicked errors be revealed. From these words we are taught that those who attack the truth with false accounts, calumnies, or certain external methods do so not for the reasons they pretend, but secretly from hatred of it; and that this hatred arises from a love of darkness and error, which is present not in one man only but in all men, from their corrupt birth. For every man naturally loves himself intensely and esteems himself highly; and darkness and error favour this pride and self-love, to which the truth (convicting men of their worthlessness and baseness) is hostile, and it hastens their ruin. Hence it follows, first, that every man, from his corrupt origin, is inclined both to love darkness and error and to hate the truth: hence the Scripture's saying about him, every man is a liar. Second, he cannot be freed from this unless he is driven within from some principle other than himself, which is corrupt, from darkness to light; and he himself must willingly resist the natural and pleasing inclinations he has towards error and darkness, so that he surrenders himself inwardly to the bitter truth, which first humbles and crushes him, even though his feeling resists. Third, he cannot be recalled from the evil path of error by external means unless he is brought back to consider the inner fountain of error and darkness; and so that he may know it better and not dissemble with himself, its external streams, by which either falsehoods have been spread or truths attacked, can be shown to him. By this third way I shall now deal with you: afterwards, to lead you back to the fountains of error, I shall touch upon the streams, both those by which you have spread errors and those by which you have attacked truths, and incidentally the writings of others as well. There I shall draw examples from others and from myself, and strive to explore their genius; and I shall either insert or reserve for the conclusion certain remarks about your mystical hatred, your critical love, and your method of mockery. The other way, which I have just described, I shall leave to God and to you, who will use your freedom as you please.

units.la: §. 2. Dn. Clericum non ideo nllis nec mihi post- poni, quod ejus defectus nonnulli recen- sendi sint & incipiant recenseri.
units.tr: §. 2. That Le Clerc is not on that account to be placed below anyone, nor below me, because some of his defects are to be enumerated and have begun to be enumerated.

units.la: Sed ne tibi asperior videatur meus procedendi modus, adhibebo & priorem viam, qua non tu solus,sed & omnes iisdem internis malis ex ortu pariter implicit apparemus: unde cognosces te nec ulli per me postponi,
units.tr: But so that my method of proceeding may not seem too harsh to you, I shall also adopt the former way, in which not you alone but all of us appear equally entangled from birth in the same inner evils. From this you will learn that I place you below no one.

units.la: K 7 & & multo minus odio cujuscunque exponi; cum omnes ex nobis aeque perditi fimus; & ille omnium fit perditissimus, qui vel omnium ultimo(quem putaret talem)vellet aut faceret male, vel eidem insultaret, ipse fe interim stare credens, qui non nisi per gratiam Dei erigi potuit,& vero a Deo,ob malevolentiam in proximum, vel ad momentum desertus, inferiora petet inferni, dum interim Deus illum qui haetenus in malo & tenebris jacuit, inde eripere potest, & luce donatum in egregium mirabilis suae gloriae instrumentum convertere. Quod tibi ut eveniat, animitus, Deo teste, optavi fapius & opto, ut quas ingenii dotes accepisti naturales nec paucas, ex in manu & regimine Dei opus ejus divinum perficere possint. Nec dubito quin, ut te in naturalibus donis mihi praepollere autumo, sic in eis quae gratiae sunt &divinioris veritatis me infinitis parasangis fuisses cautior, melior & fidelior, si eas gratiae & veritatis adipiscendae occasiones nactus esses, quas indigno mihi & in Deum fere perpetuo rebelli, obtulit prae multis, nescio quare, immensa Dei benignitas. Quapropter non prius ea dicam quibus errorum tuorum fontes & rivos aliquo modo agnoscas, quam in me eas malorum origines, tuis non minores, agnovero.
units.tr: Nor are you to be exposed to hatred of any kind by me, since we are all equally lost. He is the most lost of all who, thinking himself to be standing (though he can be raised only by the grace of God), either wishes or does evil to the last of all, whom he thinks to be such, or insults him. Deserted by God for a moment on account of his malice toward his neighbour, he seeks the lowest depths of hell. Yet God can rescue him who has hitherto lain in evil and darkness, and, having given him light, turn him into an outstanding instrument of his wondrous glory. I have often wished, and from my heart, with God as my witness, that this may happen to you, and I still wish it: that the natural gifts of mind you have received, and they are not few, may, in the hand and under the governance of God, be able to accomplish his divine work. Nor do I doubt that, just as I think you surpass me in natural gifts, so in the things that belong to grace and to a more divine truth, I would have been infinitely more cautious, better and more faithful, had I been given the opportunities of gaining grace and truth which the immense goodness of God, I know not why, has offered to me, unworthy and almost constantly rebellious against God, rather than to many others. Therefore I will not first tell you the things by which you may in some way recognise the sources and streams of your errors, before I have acknowledged in myself the origins of evils, which are no less than yours.

units.la: Namque & ego, perinde atque tu & caeteri omnes, in fundo amoris proprii & superbiae natus sum & crevi. Et cum acciderit ut eruditioni operam deberem navare, ego & qui mecum eruditionis aut promotores aut condiscipuli, loco doctrinæ sanctæ, qua nobis viles & odibiles, tanquam creaturæ quæ ex se nihil, impotentes, rebelles ingrataque in Creatorem essent, nobis appareremus, ut inde ad Sapientiam corruptissimi operis reformatricem discereemus recurrere; horum, inquam, loco, operam vanissimis quisquiliis sic dabamus, ut inde superbia & amor proprius ingenitus crescerent & nutrirentur: etenim propter hæc laudabamur ab iis quos tanquam valoris rerum arbitros æquissimos habebamus; qui cum idcirco gratum nobis animum testarentur, videremque me propterea etiam aliis gratum esse, quæcunque idealiter studiis acquirebam, ea tanquam ornamenta vestesque decoras superbi amoris mei proprii, imo tanquam vitam intuebar; unde iis eo ardore, eaque pertinacia adhærebam, ut non modo ea ab aliis impugnari nollem, sed & quæcunque vel iis opposita, vel ab iisdem diversa erant, ipse voluissem delere funditus; & cum non possem, saltem irrisionibus efficere, ut aliis eadem contemnentibus, ipsa per se caderent. Atque ut superbia mea de solido fundamento sibi congratulari posset, exactiora literarum humaniorum, linguarum & critices studia, quæ cortices, bullas & spumam esse jam videbam, non ob rei veritatem, sed ob animi fastum aspernabar, ut solidiora, Dei videlicet opera, tum corporea & physica, tum spiritualia & metaphysica, ipsa etiam supernaturalia & Theologica, ampleciterer: ex quorum acquisita cognitione
units.tr: For I too, just like you and all the others, was born and grew up at the root of self-love and pride. When it came about that I had to devote myself to learning, I and those who were with me, both as promoters of learning and as fellow students, instead of holy doctrine, by which we would appear to ourselves worthless and hateful, as creatures who of themselves are nothing, powerless, rebellious and ungrateful toward the Creator, and so from it might learn to return to Wisdom, the reformer of corrupted work, instead of that, I say, we gave our labour to the emptiest trifles, so that pride and innate self-love grew and were nourished by them. For on account of these things we were praised by those whom we held to be the most impartial judges of the worth of things. Since they bore witness to their grateful feeling toward us, and I saw that I was thereby pleasing to others too, I looked upon whatever I acquired in my studies as ornaments and fine clothing of my proud self-love, indeed as life itself. Whence I clung to them with such ardour and such obstinacy that I not only did not want them attacked by others, but I would myself have wished to destroy utterly whatever was opposed to them or differed from them. And since I could not, I tried at least by mockery to bring it about that, with others despising them too, they would fall of their own accord. And so that my pride might congratulate itself on a solid foundation, I scorned the more exact studies of humane letters, of languages and of criticism, which I now saw to be bark, bubbles and foam, not for the sake of the truth of the matter but out of the arrogance of my mind. I embraced instead the more solid things, namely God's works, both bodily and physical, and spiritual and metaphysical, and even the supernatural and theological ones. From the knowledge I had acquired of these things,

units.la: {...} gnitione judicarem, meum & aliorum de eruditione mea testimonium, casso non inniti fundamento. Sed quia Deus resistit superbis, hinc multas chimæras ideis meis sterilibus, concupiscentiasque meas infirmare non valentibus, admiscebam & coacervabam, rationisque corruptæ idolo tantum non ut Deo adhærebam; unde in omnem & vanitatem & hærefin potuissem labi, nisi obstitisset cura benigna Optimi Maximi, qui vult omnes homines salvos fieri & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Hic tollebat mihi occasiones & physicorum experimentorum mihi alias exoptatissimorum, & lectionis multæ, quæ jam mihi in perniciso quodam Curcellæi libro legendo circa corruptionis nativæ negationem incipiebat esse damnosa, & verò sanctiora Kempisii, Theologiæ Germanicæ, Taulerique scripta subministrabat; tum a primis annis divini timoris aliquantulum intus instillaverat, servabatque, quo tangebar ante & citra omnem ratiocinationis actum, ita ut corruptæ rationis meæ impetus eo refrænaretur, & sincere optarem omnia quæ haberem divinæ gloriæ inservire posse: quod bonæ voluntatis defideriolum (gratiæ ejus donum) sequebatur nonnulla, sed rudissima cognitio corruptionis, in qua mundus atque Christianismus hodiernus jacent sepulti. Observabam, haud debite commendari animæ purificationem in Theologia, neque eam inniti satis fundamento amoris Dei & proximi. Inde displicere incipiebant Sectarum schismata & rixæ: cumque omnia in concordiam redire optarem, quæcunque in diversis Sectis dissona erant ab illis in quibus fueram educatus, conabar in optimam partem interpretari, & in unum, quoad fieri poterat, concordiæ gratia reducere, ne excepta quidem Socinianorum secta, quam ad veritatem & unitatem facile revocari posse putabam unius atque alterius principii ope, veluti est, 1. Deum, & quæ in Deo sunt, esse humanæ menti incomprehensibilia; quæque de eo capiuntur, sic imperfecte comprehendi, ut infinitiies plura adhuc in Deo supersint. 2. In Deo esse primo quidem ejus naturam directe cogitantem, deinde cogitationis ejus luminosam ideam atque repræsentationem sive formam; & tertiò acquiescentiam lœtam Dei in ea. 3. Trinitatem in Deo toties laudatam hæc tria esse; & præterea in eadem superesse infinita captum nostrum exsuperantia. 4. In Christo esse humanitatem quidem mente & corpore constantem, quæ Deus certe non est; sed & eidem Divinitatem modo strictiore quàm ulli unquam creaturæ adesse, quam unionem omni alia cogitabili arctiorem, ne re concessa de nomine contendatur, personalem nominare non recusaverint, ob quam humanitas, & Divinitas in Christo una persona dicantur, in qua persona supersint (ex principio primo) etiam infinita, quæ humanam mentem superant, agnoscenda, Hæc bene deducta sufficere putabam Socinianis per Christianum amorem redigendis in fidei unitatem: sed mali origo, Pelagianismus, ꝛtebat me. Hic enim unus est omnium Socinianismi errorum maxime capitalis & exitiosus, Pelagianismus, sive propriae, intimae universaeque corruptionis suae negatio; nec non necessariae gratiae divinae, omnia intus & extus purificantis, illuminantis & restaurantis, sublatio: sine quo errore si ipsi ad Deum, humili animo opem lumenque sibi omnino ad intima usque corruptis implorantes, recurrerent, eorum caeteri de SS. Trinitate Christique persona errores facile paulatim dissiparentur divina luce atque opera. At vero qui se nec corruptos uti sunt, agnoscere volunt, nec opitulatione Dei interna pro omnibus facultatibus suis egere, quin potius rationi viribusque suis in divinis rebus perscrutandis confidunt, eos etsi prius orthodoxi in caeteris fuissent, necesse est in omnis generis exitiales haereses ruere, & quandoque tandem in Atheismum dari praecipites, adeoque perniciosa est una haec inter omnes haeresis capitalis, qua sine omnes caeterae collabuntur; qua vero posita universae inde profluunt. Et fateor me ideo quod corruptae rationi nimis adhaerarem, ab eo veneni sonte non fuisse valde remotum, etsi id nescirem dilucidius. Quicquid sit, modis hactenus dictis instructus videbar mihi multis non deterior, ne dicam iis melior, veritati magis amicus, a superbia & amore proprio defaecatior, etsi nunquam carebam stimulo tacite me dejiciente & obscurius condemnante, quando per medium tibi multisque aliis ludibrio habendum, (Virgunculâ ipsa erat, quam in tua relatione non honoris sed irrisionis gratia characteribus majusculis indigitasti) Deo visum est mihi primò quidem generalius meam omniumque universalem corruptionem, tenebras, errores, vanitates, plurimis luminosis veritatibus ostendere, quæ quidem approbante judicio non poteram non ampleƈti: deinde vero specialius superbiam meam amoremque proprium meum, (quæ in me valde minuta ex cœcitate putabam,) vividissime ad intima usque sauciare. Et ecce tunc in fundo meo exurgere advertebam repugnantiam adversus divinam veritatem me carpentem, ut & fugiditatem, indifferentiam, fugam, odiisque adversus eam, nec non contemtus, & forte irrisionis etiam principia & motus. Tum verò obstupui & horrui; meque ipso (qui talium affectuum ac motuum adversus id quod veritatem divinam sciebam esse, prius incapacem existimaveram) aliquantum sollicitius inspecto, expandi in magno angore animam meam coram Domino, exponens & confitens ei miserias meas, atque diabolicas fundi mei, hactenus mihi ea in re incogniti, dispositiones & malitias, eumque deprecans ut vel eas in me occideret; vel, si mala mea essent insanabilia, ipse me potius morti traderet quam ut pateretur infernales istiusmodi radices fructus suos adversus veritatem in gratiam meæ superbiæ & amoris proprii proferre: satius enim esse me tunc unum perire, & solum damnari, quam superesse & instrumentum fieri hostile diminutionis gloriosæ ejus veritatis, nec non forte damnationis plurium aliorum. Atque ab eo tempore affulsit spes, Dominum in bonam partem exaudivifse vocem deprecationum mearum : namque inde Veritatem superbiæ meæ amorique proprio, nec non ornamentis & fulcris imaginariæ vanæque eruditionis, judiciorum & idearum coacervationi, ac dispositionibus propensionibusque aliis adversantem coepi purius noscere & diligere; tum optare & precari ut ictibus suis potentius interiora mea percuteret, donec inde omnis planta quam non plantavit Pater cœlestis tandem eradicaretur; simul tum decrevi veritatem eandem aliis pro virili commendare quocunque calumniarum, oppofitionum, irrifionumque genere superbus meus amor proprius (in suam utique qua opus habet diminutionem meumque adeo bonum) ab hominibus impetatur, modo tantum non defit mihi sperata Dei gratia; siquidem ex eventu modò dicto, didici de me deque mea erga veritatem fidelitate non amplius spondere: favere intime veritati, donum esse gratiæ Dei: in interioribus nostris latere principia inimicitiæ adversus Deum, & odii contra veritatem & præterea eos qui contra veritatem odio feruntur, non omnes id facere scientes, præmeditantes, ex malitia animi præparata; sed interdum ex fundo illo nativo superbiæ & amoris proprii, cœcitati nostræ occulto, in quem totum genus humanum est collapsum: proinde Christiana commiseratione potius quam odio excipiendum. Quæ omnia aliquanto prolixius tibi, Domine, in lenimentum futuræ redargutionis & in auxi-liium lium emendationis profero, ex quibus forte plusquam è multis contentionum aut consutationum chartis proficere possit quisquis irriforio Ismaelis spiritu excluso, in se ipsum descendere volet simili methodo sese excusurus.
units.tr: ...knowledge, I would judge my own testimony and that of others about my learning to be resting on no firm foundation. But because God resists the proud, I mixed and heaped up many chimeras into my barren ideas, which could not weaken my desires, and I clung to the idol of corrupted reason almost as if it were God. From this I could have slipped into every kind of vanity and heresy, had not the kind care of the Best and Greatest, who wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, stood in the way. This care took from me the opportunities for physical experiments, which I had long desired, and for much reading, which had already begun to harm me while I was reading a certain pernicious book of Curcellaeus concerning the denial of native corruption. It supplied instead the more holy writings of Kempis, the German Theology, and Tauler. Moreover, from my early years it had instilled and kept in me a certain measure of the fear of God, by which I was moved before and apart from any act of reasoning, so that the impulse of my corrupt reason was restrained by it, and I sincerely wished that all I had might be able to serve the glory of God. This small desire of a good will, a gift of his grace, was followed by some, though very crude, knowledge of the corruption in which the world and present-day Christianity lie buried. I observed that the purification of the soul was not sufficiently commended in theology, nor did it rest enough on the foundation of the love of God and neighbour. Hence the schisms and quarrels of the sects began to displease me. And since I wished that all things might return to concord, I tried to interpret favourably whatever was discordant in the various sects from those in which I had been brought up, and to bring it, as far as could be done, back into one harmony for the sake of concord. I did this without excepting even the sect of the Socinians, which I thought could easily be recalled to truth and unity by the aid of one or two principles, namely: (1) God, and the things that are in God, are incomprehensible to the human mind; and whatever is grasped of him is grasped so imperfectly that infinitely more still remains in God. (2) In God there is first his nature thinking directly, then his luminous idea and representation or form of that thinking, and thirdly the joyful acquiescence of God in it. (3) The Trinity, so often praised in God, consists of these three; and besides, in the same there remain infinite things that exceed our grasp. (4) In Christ there is humanity, constant in mind and body, which God certainly is not; but there is also in him Divinity, present in a stricter manner than in any creature ever, a union closer than any other conceivable. They would not refuse to call this union personal, lest they dispute about a name when the thing is granted; on account of this, humanity and Divinity in Christ are said to be one person, and in that person (from the first principle) there must be acknowledged also infinite things that surpass the human mind. I thought that these points, well drawn out, would suffice to bring the Socinians into unity of faith by Christian love. But the origin of evil, Pelagianism, pressed upon me. For this is the most chief and deadly of all the errors of Socinianism, Pelagianism, that is, the denial of one's own inward and universal corruption; and also the removal of the necessary grace of God, which purifies, enlightens and restores everything within and without. If they, without this error, were to turn to God with humble minds, imploring help and light for their inmost parts which are wholly corrupted, their other errors concerning the Holy Trinity and the person of Christ would gradually be easily dispelled by the divine light and work. But those who are unwilling to acknowledge themselves corrupt as they are, and who do not need the inward help of God for all their faculties, but rather trust in their reason and their own powers to search out divine things, these men, even if they were orthodox in other matters before, must necessarily fall into deadly heresies of every kind, and at length be cast headlong into atheism. So pernicious is this one chief heresy among all, by which all the others collapse when it is present, and when it is removed, all of them flow from it. And I confess that because I clung too closely to corrupt reason, I was not very far from that fountain of poison, though I did not know this more clearly. Be that as it may, equipped by the means mentioned so far, I seemed to myself not worse than many, not to say better than them, more a friend of truth, and more purged of pride and self-love. Yet I was never without a quiet goad that cast me down and condemned me more obscurely, when, through the means of you and many others to be mocked (it was a little maiden herself, whom in your account you marked out in capitals, not as an honour but as a mockery), it pleased God first, in a more general way, to show my own and everyone's universal corruption, darkness, errors and vanities, with many luminous truths, which, with my approving judgment, I could not but embrace. Then, more specifically, he pierced most vividly to the innermost parts my pride and my self-love, which I had thought to be very small through blindness. And behold, I then noticed rising in my depths a repugnance against the divine truth that was censuring me, as well as a principle and motion of aversion, indifference, flight and hatred against it, and also of contempt, and perhaps even of mockery. Then indeed I was astonished and shuddered; and, looking more anxiously at myself (I who had previously thought myself incapable of such affections and motions against what I knew to be divine truth), I poured out my soul in great anguish before the Lord, laying open to him my miseries and the diabolical dispositions and malice of my bottom, hitherto unknown to me in this matter, and I begged him either to kill these in me, or, if my evils were incurable, to hand me over to death rather than to allow these infernal roots to put forth their fruits against the truth for the sake of my pride and self-love. For it was better for me then to perish alone and be damned alone, than to survive and become a hostile instrument for diminishing that glorious truth, and perhaps for the damnation of many others. And from that time hope shone forth that the Lord had heard favourably the voice of my prayers. For from then on I began to know more purely, and to love, the truth that opposes my pride and self-love, as well as the adornments and props of an imaginary and vain learning, the heaping up of judgments and ideas, and my other dispositions and propensities. Then I began to wish and pray that it might strike my inmost parts more powerfully with its blows, until every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted was at last uprooted. At the same time I resolved to commend this same truth to others, as far as I could, by whatever kind of calumny, opposition or mockery my proud self-love (for its diminution, which it needs, and thus for my own good) might be attacked by men, provided only that the grace of God I hoped for did not fail me. For from the event just described I learned not to promise any more about myself and about my own fidelity towards the truth: that to favour the truth inwardly is a gift of God's grace; that in our inner parts lie the principles of enmity against God and of hatred against the truth; and furthermore that those who are carried by hatred against the truth do not all do so knowingly, deliberately, from a prepared malice of mind; but sometimes from that native ground of pride and self-love, hidden from our blindness, into which the whole human race has fallen; and therefore they should be received with Christian compassion rather than with hatred. I set out all these things at some length for you, Lord, as a solace against the future rebuke and as an aid to amendment, from which perhaps more may profit than from many pages of contentions or refutations, to anyone who, with the spirit of Ishmael the mocker shut out, wishes to descend into himself, to be excused by a similar method.

units.la: Quod ipsum si tentare lubeat, tuum erit Domine, in te inspicere, annon, quamvis in superbiæ & amoris proprii elemento natum te ex communi corruptionis nativæ cæcitate (Pelagianismi erroribus ascitis obfirmata) haud bene agnoscas, annon tamen huic morbo originario testimonia dent primi tui, quantum memor es, anni? Annon ex tui existimatione & amore proprio omnia primitus feceris & judicaveris? Annon his stimulis in eruditione tui fueris educatus, iisque sæpius gratissime affectus? Annon ut commendabilior tibi appareres, tuisque seu parentibus seu institutoribus gratior, ea quæ ipsi æstimavere magni, (qualia ex editis à te, video esse humanarum literarum, linguarum, criticesque minutias,) studiose tibi comparaveris, iisque ex more sæculi, vulgaria philosophemata, Theologiamque qualis in tuis libris apparet, addideris, quibus veluti ornamentis indutus, jam te tibi aliisque gratiorem esse vehementer sis gavisus? Ista quando recte animadverteris, tunc scias hæc esse in te (uti in cæteris) fontem & originem omnium tenebrarum errorumque, & principia unde impellitur animus tum ad falsa & vana propalanda, tum ad contemtum veritatum vanis idoli nostri ornamentis adversantium, tum etiam ad calumniam & irrisionem. nem eorum, qui veritatem proferentes, falsa & vana quibus superbus amor proprius sibi aliisque commendabilis videtur, nihil esse demonstrant. Atque tuum erit inde perpendere, annon nisi tunc Deum exores, ut potenter vividis gratiæ suæ ictibus amorem superbum cum suis phaleris percutiat, nisique eos ictus, etsi amaros hominemque in ruborem dantes, cum tui abnegatione & crucifixione sensus tibi grati, & æstimationis propriæ, humillimè excipere fis paratus; non modo non fis sanandus in æternum, sed ne quidem unquam veritatem pure fis amaturus, ne dicam possessurus: tunc enim amabis tantum eam non ob se ipsam, sed quatenus amorem proprium & superbum ornare videbitur; unde sequetur non eam, sed te, a te diligi; neque veritatem, sed vanum & falsum ejus simulacrum tantum haberi; siquidem veritas non possit subsistere cum vanitate, falsitate, fumo & mendacio, quibus omnis superbia absolvitur. Et in genere non tantum non potest veritas, sed nec ulla virtus vere possideri, antequam quis per amaram contra se pugnam & sui displicentiam, amorem proprium & animi superbiam, (quæ & in ipsis virtutibus tectum sibi nidum condere vellent,) debellaverit, & tandem devicerit; quæ utinam omnibus & cordi esset, & in Ethices suæ principiis de acquirenda virtute, fundamenti instar substernerentur!
units.tr: If you are willing to attempt this, Sir, it will be for you to look into yourself and ask whether, although you were born in the element of pride and self-love, and from the common blindness of native corruption (hardened by the errors of Pelagianism you have taken on), you do not recognise this well. Do your early years, as far as you remember them, not bear witness to this original disease? Did you not do and judge everything at first according to your own esteem and self-love? Were you not brought up in your learning by these spurs, and often most gratefully moved by them? So that you might appear more commendable to yourself and more pleasing to your parents or teachers, did you not diligently acquire those things they valued highly (such as, as I see from the works you have published, the minutiae of humane letters, languages and criticism), and add to them, in the fashion of the age, common philosophical notions and the theology that appears in your books; and clothed in these ornaments, did you not greatly rejoice that you were now more pleasing to yourself and to others? When you have considered these things rightly, then know that they are in you (as in others) the fountain and origin of all darkness and error, and the principles that drive the mind both to proclaim false and vain things, and to despise truths that oppose the vain ornaments of our idol, and even to calumny and mockery of those who, proclaiming the truth, show that the false and vain things by which proud self-love seems commendable to itself and to others are nothing. And it will be for you to weigh from this whether you do not pray to God that he may strike proud self-love with its trappings by the living blows of his grace; and whether, unless you are ready most humbly to receive those blows, bitter as they are and bringing you to blush, together with self-denial and the crucifying of your sense of what is pleasing and of your own esteem, you will not only never be healed for ever, but will never truly love truth, let alone possess it. For then you will love it not for its own sake but only insofar as it seems to adorn proud self-love; whence it will follow that it is you, not truth, who is loved by you, and that not truth but its vain and false image is held; since truth cannot subsist with vanity, falsehood, smoke and lies, of which all pride is made up. And in general not only truth but no virtue can truly be possessed until someone, through bitter struggle against himself and his own displeasure, has fought down and at last overcome self-love and the pride of the mind (which would fain build their hidden nest even in the virtues themselves). Would that this were close to everyone's heart, and that it were laid down as a foundation in the principles of their Ethics on acquiring virtue!

units.la: Porro nolim dubitare quin Benignissimus Deus omnes homines salvos & veritate imbutos volens, ex adversa parte tibi bonos motus non paucos etiam inspiraverit, quibus & & amoris & gloriæ ejus,& proximorum dilectionis atque concordiæ desideria in te excitaveiit,quorum in scriptis tuis comparent vestigia, quando omnia inter Christianos moderatiora & concordantiora peroptas, &, ut huc redeant, in meliorem partem trahis ea in quibus dissentiunt. Equidem ex amore proprio solent sese gloriæ Dei, concordiæ pacisque prætextu velare qui invisos publicant errores. At nolim te ex ejusmodi mera corruptione existimare agentem, tametsi illa è pravo fundo,modo indicato, non semel appareat immissa erratis non paucis, quæ tum in dogmaticis tum in elenchticis tuis interseruntur.
