units.tr: Moreover, I would not doubt that the most kind God, wishing all men to be saved and imbued with truth, has also inspired in you not a few good impulses, by which desires for the love and glory of God, for love of neighbour and for concord have been stirred up in you; traces of these appear in your writings, when you wish all things among Christians to be more moderate and harmonious, and, to bring them back to this, you put the best construction on those points on which they disagree. Indeed, those who publish errors they hate are accustomed to veil their self-love under the pretext of God's glory, concord and peace. But I would not want you thought to act from mere corruption of this kind, although from that corrupt ground, as indicated, it has more than once appeared that not a few errors have been introduced, and these are woven into both your dogmatic and your elenctic writings.

units.la: §. 3. De Generalioribus in scriptis Dn. Cl. conside- randis, & sophismate quodam periculoso.
units.tr: §. 3. On the more general matters to be considered in the writings of Mr. Clericus, and on a certain dangerous sophism.

units.la: Quacunque argumentorum, hic non dicendorum, certitudine apud me persuasus sim, te plurium, de quibus mentio fiet, librorum auctorem esse; non idcirco eos nominabo tuos; sed vel ideo quod à te palam agnoscantur, uti Bibliotheca universalis, nec non Sentimens sur l'histoire Critique du Pere Simon, qui liber in P. Simonis responsione tibi nominato centies sic tribuitur, ut ejus Defensionis (Defense des sentimens) auctor id sibi dictum agnoscat, seque ut qui is sit, defendat: vel etiam tuos dicam, quia publicâ voce (quam mendacii arguere nolim) tui dicuntur, veluti Entretiens sur diverses matieres de Theologie, quoad partem alteram; item & Liberii de S. Amore Epistolæ Theologicæ, quorum principia principiis aliorum tuorum scriptorum non modo sunt conformia, in iisque interdum laudata vel defensa, veluti Entretiens in Biblioth.Tom. V ; sed & quod publicè tibi attributi cum essent (uti Epistola Liberii à P. Simone) nil (a) ausus es hic inficiari: nisi ipse illos forte impofterum cum opinionibus contentis revoces & rejicias: quod ut cum gaudio visuri essemus, nec tibi amplius eos asserturi; sic quia id adhuc infectum est, atque ut tibi hinc purgandi occasio nasci possit, tam publicè tibi assertos, quàm quos ipse agnoscis, pariter tuos hactenus sinemus esse. Qui ergo tuos libros modo dictos legerunt, annotare poterunt, te stylì quidem puritati summam dare operam, ne vocis vel periodi asperitate delicatulus lector offensus, amori proprio laudeculam elegantis recusat scriptoris; At utinam pura & solida materia æque tibi curæ fuisset! In dogmaticis namque tuis, sic desunt veritates solidæ & substantiales, ut non insint nisi vel vanæ de critica minutiæ & de corticibus rerum observatiunculæ, vel errores summè, ut puto, noxii, dum (in Liberio præcipuè) Socinianissimi principia, (quædam & pejora) cum suis argumentis, exceptionibus, Scripturarum depravationibus, nec non & Methodo has explicandi ex grammatica & critica profanisque auctoribus, negata ad hoc & ad virtutes acquirendas Spiritus S. interna operatione sic proponuntur, ut hinc videatur ad salutem perinde esse, an quis sit Socinianus vel secus. In elenchticis verò tuis quivis observare poterit, te impugnare gratiam operationemque Dei internam eo usque, ut & videaris (a) eam chimæris accensere, & vero affirmare audeas, (b) nullum esse in tota Scriptura locum, ubi gratia Dei operationem Spiritûs S. internam in anima immediatamque significet: quum tamen etsi nomenclatura a Scripturis abesset, ipsa res seu operatio Dei in animis interna, in nullo fere capite afferta non occurrat: imo etiam res multis vocibus sæpius eo sensu (cum ipso quoque expresso nomine, ἡ δύναμις ἡ ἐνεργημένη ἐν ὑμῖν,) vel in tribus (c) Epistolæ ad Ephesios capitibus primis reperiatur. Porro observabit & unufquifque te rejicere sensum spiritualem Scripturarum, & cum labe originali quæcunque Pelagianifmo & Socinianifmo in his aliisque quibufdam opponuntur. Præterea te ubi quam plurima (d) de inspirationibus Sanctorum magis absurda & temeraria quam cœci cujufvis de luce & coloribus judicia velut ex alio protulisti, multa etiam ex libris Scripturæ, Jobi, Psalmorum, Proverbiorum, totum quoque Ecclefiaften, totumque Canticum Salomonis veluti Spiritu S. indigna traducere: in personis vero impugnandis te eos affumere ut plurimum adversarios qui opinionibus tuis erroneis, maxime vero Pelagianifmo & Socinianifmo, oblectantur; nec magis parcere recentioribus orthodoxis, quam sanctioribus purioris Ecclesiæ Patribus, in primis S. Auguftino, cui præ cæteris es infenfior. In modo autem quo dogmata personasque impugnare soles, sequentes videris tibi præscripsisse S leges.:
units.tr: Whatever certainty of arguments, not to be stated here, I may be persuaded of, that you are the author of several of the books to be mentioned, I shall not on that account call them yours; but I shall do so either because they are openly acknowledged by you, such as the Bibliotheca universalis, and also the Sentimens sur l'histoire Critique du Pere Simon, which book is attributed to you a hundred times in Father Simon's reply, so that the author of that Defence (Defense des sentimens) acknowledges that the work was addressed to himself and defends himself as being its author; or I shall call them yours because they are publicly said to be yours (a claim I would not care to call a lie), such as the Entretiens sur diverses matieres de Theologie as to the second part; likewise the Liberii de S. Amore Epistolae Theologicae, whose principles are not only in accord with the principles of your other writings, and in them are sometimes praised or defended, as the Entretiens in the Bibliotheca, Tom. V; but also because, since they were publicly attributed to you (as the Epistola Liberii was by Father Simon), you have not dared to deny it here, unless perhaps you later recall them and reject them along with the opinions they contain. We would rejoice to see this done, and would no longer claim them for you; but since this has not yet been done, and so that an occasion of clearing yourself may arise, we shall for now allow them to remain yours, as publicly asserted as those you yourself acknowledge. Therefore those who have read the books just named will be able to note that you indeed take great pains over the purity of your style, lest a fastidious reader be offended by the harshness of a word or period, and vain self-love refuses the small praise of an elegant writer. But would that pure and solid matter had been equally a concern to you! For in your dogmatic works solid and substantial truths are so lacking that there is nothing in them but vain trifles of criticism and little observations on the outward shells of things, or else errors, in my view most harmful, while (chiefly in the Liberius) the most Socinian principles (some even worse), with their arguments, objections, corruptions of Scripture, and the method of explaining these from grammar, criticism and profane authors, are set forth in such a way, the inward operation of the Holy Spirit being denied for these matters and for acquiring the virtues, that it would seem to make no difference to salvation whether a man is a Socinian or not. In your elenctic writings, anyone may observe that you attack the internal operation and grace of God to such an extent that you seem to rank it among chimeras, and you dare to assert (b) that there is no place in the whole of Scripture where the grace of God signifies the internal operation of the Holy Spirit in the soul and immediately upon it; although, even if the name were absent from the Scriptures, the thing itself, namely God's inward operation in souls, occurs in almost every chapter cited; indeed the thing is found, often in many words, in that sense, even with the very name expressed, ἡ δύναμις ἡ ἐνεργημένη ἐν ὑμῖν, and in the first three chapters of the Epistle to the Ephesians. Further, everyone will observe that you reject the spiritual sense of the Scriptures, and that whatever is opposed to these and other matters is set against original sin by Pelagianism and Socinianism. Besides, where you have brought forward very many judgments about the inspirations of the saints, more absurd and rash than the judgments of any blind man about light and colours, as if from another world; and where you have also pulled down many things from the books of Scripture, such as Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, and even the whole of Ecclesiastes and the whole Song of Solomon, as if unworthy of the Holy Spirit; in attacking persons you usually take as your adversaries those who delight in your erroneous opinions, above all in Pelagianism and Socinianism; and you spare the more recent orthodox no more than the holier Fathers of the purer Church, above all Saint Augustine, whom you are more hostile to than all the rest. But in the manner in which you are accustomed to attack doctrines and persons, you seem to have prescribed for yourself the following laws:

units.la: (d) Sentimenslett. 11, & 12. leges: 1. Adversarios tuos (si vivunt) pungere, irritare, & ad iram sic concitare, ut inde turbati, affectuumque nebulis involuti, & lumine & charitate magis destituantur; & vero tunc aliquid dicant aut agant inordinatius, unde tibi aliisque deinde ludibrio esse possint, tuque eorum adversus te veritatibus veluti per homines ob affectuum turbinem veri non capaces prolatis, coram omnibus fidem derogare speciose tentes. 2. Eosdem, mortuos etiam, veluti ridiculos omnium ludibrio exponere, ut tuarum chartarum lectores, ipsos, & quae ab iis sunt, non dilectione, sed contemtu & odio prosequantur. Quae duo efficere soles aculeatis quibusdam irrisionibus & ironicis sannis, non tam in verbis seorsim singulis, quam in modo dicendi consistentibus, eoque magis animum adversarii irritantibus, lectorumque risum concitantibus, quo mente frigidiore & veluti sedata, quasi aliud agendo, eas proferre videris. Atque his (quibus scripta tua in omni, etiam sanctissima materia, abundant) tantopere delectaris, ut hoc elementum tuum esse videatur, tamque dexter & peritus in eis es magister, ut vel ipse Momus quaeta esse tuus discipulus. Quoniam autem possibile non est adversarios omnes tuos, ipsos etiam inter Sanctos venerabiliores, ludibriis istis iustam praebuisse materiam, tu eam sequentibus, quae regularum tuarum numerum producunt, sic comparas. 3. Imponis eis falsa, absurda, contradictoria, verbis tamen vel iisdem vel similibus illis quibus usi sunt; sed compositione, applicatione & sensu diffimillimis, ut artificio altero efficias ne fides tua suspecta videatur; altero vero, ut deridentur tanquam fatui, quos ita traducis. 4. Involvis silentio bona, solida, praecipua quae habent tibi saepius non intellecta, interdum nec lecta; & minutias superficiarias de stylo, de critica deque futilitatibus quibusdam minus observatis, tanquam capitalia mimicodente arrodis. 5. In ipsis bonis, quae a te carpi nequeunt, ut tamen critica tua mordax aliquid reprehendendum habeat, sic agis, ut, si adversarii de subiecto, quod tractant, quaedam notiora non tangant, eos arguis quod praecipua quaedam & notabilia omiserint: si vero eadem recenseant, dices haec superflua esse, & nemini antea non nota. Si ea dicant, quae cum receptis quadrent sententiis, aiseadem ab aliis multoties esse jam dicta, esseque vulgaria: si vero quaedam non ita obvia proponant, jam culpas eos quasi videri vellent aliter atque caeteri homines cogitare, novaque sibi solus e coelo lumina suppeti: ita ut nihil omnino quocunque modo vel dici vel taceri queat, quo, hac methodo, Critices tuae livorem non pascas, quodque ita simpliciorum contemtui non exponas. 6. Ea bona, quae vel non intelligis, vel aliquatenus tantum capis, quaeque vel videri non vis directo impugnare, vel nullis rationibus potes aggredi aut refutare, quando praecipue ea solidissime opiniones tuas noxias distruunt; ea inquam ut tamen conficias, incrustare soles nominibus & titulis ridiculis rerum, quibus in lectorum animis vel jindifferentia, vel nau-
units.tr: (d) Sentiments, letters 11 and 12. The rules are these: (1) Stab, provoke and stir up your opponents (if they are still alive) so that, disturbed and wrapped in clouds of passion, they lose both light and charity; then they will say or do something more disorderly, which can become a laughing-stock for you and others, while you try to discredit their truths, put forward through people who, swept along by passion, cannot grasp the truth, in front of everyone. (2) Expose the same men, even when dead, to the mockery of all as ridiculous, so that the readers of your pages pursue them and their followers not with love but with contempt and hatred. You achieve these two things with barbed jeers and ironic sneers, which lie less in individual words than in the manner of speaking, and which provoke the opponent's temper all the more, and stir the readers' laughter, the cooler and more composed your own mind seems, as if you were doing something else while uttering them. You take such delight in these devices (with which your writings abound, even in the most sacred matters) that they seem to be your native element, and you are so skilful and expert a master in them that Momus himself might seem your pupil. Since it is impossible that all your opponents, even the more venerable among the saints, have not given just cause for such mockery, you arrange the material to suit the following rules, which make up the number of your rules. (3) You attribute to them false, absurd and self-contradictory views, in words either identical or similar to those they used, but in composition, application and sense very different, so that by one trick you make your own faith seem unsuspect, and by another they are mocked as fools, the way you portray them. (4) You pass over in silence the good, solid and principal points they make, which you have often not understood and sometimes not even read, and you nibble at trivial details of style, criticism and certain unimportant points as if they were chief matters. (5) As for the good points which cannot be carped at, so that your biting criticism may still find something to censure, you act so that, if your opponents do not touch on certain matters well known in the subject they treat, you accuse them of omitting certain principal and noteworthy points; but if they recount the same things, you say these are superfluous and known to no one before. If they say things that agree with accepted opinions, you claim the same things have been said many times already by others and are commonplace; but if they put forward some points that are not so obvious, you then blame them as if they wished to appear to "think differently from other men, and to have new lights supplied to them alone from heaven." Thus, by this method, nothing whatever can be said or left unsaid that you do not feed on the spite of your Criticism, and so expose it to the contempt of simpler people. (6) Those good points which you either do not understand, or grasp only partly, and which you either do not want to appear to attack directly, or cannot approach or refute by any arguments, especially when they destroy your harmful opinions most solidly; these, I say, you cover over, in order to finish them off, with ridiculous names and titles, by which indifference, disgust, contempt or laughter is aroused in the minds of readers.

units.la: S 2
units.tr: S 2

units.la: sea, vel contemtus, vel risus excitetur. Ita passim in libris tuis orthodoxia, gratia Dei vera, aliaeque sanae doctrinae audiunt Scholasticorum errores ( abstractiones, chimaeras, ideas Platonicas, ( o quantum Pelagianis ideis anteponendas ! ) Metaphysica subtilitates, mysteria mystica, & quae similia; ipsi etiam orthodoxi mox Scholastici, mox Metaphysici, jam Platonici, nunc Mystici: qua arte postquam Lectores adversariorum tuorum derisores, iisque minus faventes reddere annisus es, eosdem tibi, veluti nugarum & chimaerarum debellatori magno, fautores conaris efficere. Recenserem adhuc & alias tuas artes, nisi solam Criticam tuam Elenchticam, quam in me & in alios multos exercuisti, non autem dogmaticam & positivam, exponere esset animus. Etsi autem quaecunque modo dixi, vel ad primam fere quamlibet scriptorum tuorum aperturam hinc inde pateant, praecipua tamen nonnullis exemplis comprobabo, postquam id quod supra dixi, intermisceri in libris quorum auctor haberis, nonnulla Socinianis etiam pejora prius ostendero, atque specialiores causas, cur in me infensus iniqua de me meisque publico dederis judicia, palam fecero.
units.tr: sea, or contempt, or laughter. Thus everywhere in your books orthodoxy, the true grace of God and other sound doctrines are called the errors of the Scholastics (abstractions, chimeras, Platonic ideas (oh, how much these are to be preferred to Pelagian ideas!), metaphysical subtleties, mystical mysteries, and things of that kind); the orthodox themselves are now called Scholastics, now Metaphysicians, now Platonists, now Mystics. By this art, after you have tried to make the readers of your opponents mockers of them and less favourable to them, you seek to make the same readers, as if you were a great conqueror of trifles and chimeras, your supporters. I would go on to recount your other arts as well, did I not intend to set out only your Elenchtic Criticism, which you have practised against me and many others, and not your dogmatic and positive work. Although whatever I have just said can be seen here and there in nearly any opening of your writings, I will nevertheless prove the chief points with a few examples, after first showing that the things I have mentioned are mixed into books of which you are considered the author, some even worse than the Socinians', and after making plain the more particular reasons why you have been so hostile to me and have given such unfair judgments about me and mine in public.

units.la: In Liberii de S. Amore Epist. I. docetur (a) Divinitatem & humanitatem in Christo non ita stricte inter se uniri atque duae creaturae inter se uniri possunt. Idque ut probetur, demonstraturum te promittis Duas creaturas arctius inter se unitri posse, quam creaturam cum Deo, hoc est, Deum & creaturam minus inter se uniri posse quam creaturas inter se. Quo quidem allerto non tantum id, unde Christo dignitas & gloria sua vera emanat,e medio tollitur; sed & in homine desiderium & amor ejus erga Deum deprimuntur; tum vero amor atque desiderium affectusque ejusdem erga creaturas, (quibus quippe magis quam Creatore frui datur) vehementer extolluntur, praeferentur & incenduntur. Id enim amabilius est cum quo unio & fruitio major & strictior fieri potest. Atqui non credo ullos Socinianos in extenuanda unione, quae in Christo est, hypostatica, eo extremitatis unquam esse prolapsos, aut haeresin suam ex principio in amorem Dei creaturarumque abnegationem (Religionis Christianae fundamenta) tam injurio & pernicioso stabilire voluisse. At vero Liberius haec non modo confidenter asseverat; sed & id demonstrat scilicet, idque hoc modo:
units.tr: In the first letter of Liberius on the Holy Love it is taught (a) that the divinity and humanity in Christ are not united as strictly as two creatures can be united with each other. To prove this he promises to demonstrate that two creatures can be united more closely with each other than a creature with God, that is, that God and a creature can be united less closely than creatures with each other. By this assertion not only is that from which Christ's true dignity and glory flow removed from the midst; but in man his desire and love towards God are also depressed; and then his love and desire, and his affections towards creatures (since indeed it is granted to enjoy these more than the Creator), are vehemently exalted, preferred and kindled. For that is the more lovable with which union and enjoyment can be greater and closer. Yet I do not believe that any Socinians, in weakening the hypostatic union that exists in Christ, have ever fallen to such an extreme, or wished to establish their heresy, from a principle of love of God and of creatures' denial (the foundations of the Christian religion), so unjustly and perniciously. But Liberius not only asserts these things confidently, but also proves them, namely in this way:

units.la: Eo artius res uniri possunt, quo major inter eas est convenientia.
units.tr: Things can be united the more closely the greater the agreement between them.

units.la: Sed major est convenientia inter duos spiritus finitos, (duasve creaturas) quam inter spiritum finitum & Deum, [sive inter creaturam & Deum.]
units.tr: But the agreement between two finite spirits (or two creatures) is greater than that between a finite spirit and God [or between a creature and God].

units.la: Ergo duae creaturae artius possunt inter se uniri, quam Deus & creatura.
units.tr: Therefore two creatures can be united more closely than God and a creature.

units.la: Egregia demonstratio! Patere, quaeso, me insigne hoc sophisma, etsi praeter institutum, hic obiter dissolvere, siquidem perniciosis non nimis obviam iri possit. Res dicuntur inter se convenire duobus modis: 1. ratione suae materiae aut formae similis, deinde ratione sui finis & scopi, quando nempe res una est facta propter aliam & ad aliam. Dabo exempla palpabiliora. Ratione prima inter se conveniunt pes & pes, calceus & calceus, urbs & urbs, homo & homo, ignis & ignis, lignum & lignum, mas & mas, foemina & foemina, creatura & creatura: ratione altera inter se conveniunt pes & calceus, urbs & homo, ignis & lignum, mas & foemina, eademque etiam Deus & creatura. Quo animadverso, patet clarissime Liberiani axiomatis fallacia, aut conclusionis inconsequentia. Si enim axioma illud de priori convenientia intelligas, absurdum est & salsum, ea quae in materia aut forma conveniunt, magis uniri posse, quam ea, quae eo modo disconvenientia, conveniunt tamen respectu finis aut scopi; & ratio disparitatis haec est, quod quae materialiter aut formaliter conveniunt, eatenus tantum similia sunt, non autem ideo praecise unionis capacia: at quae ratione finis conveniunt, horum hoc ipso unius natura, facultates, proprietates, constitutio, effectae sunt & dispositae ad alterum, sive ut alterum exciperent, eique strictissime uniri possent. Atque hoc in exemplis allatis patet: nam etsi calceus & calceus magis inter se conveniant ratione materiae & formae, quam pes & calceus, non tamen magis inter se uniri possunt, quam calceus & pes, qui ratione finis conveniunt: simile de exemplis caeteris aliisque infinitis dicere est. Si vero axioma Liberianum ratione finis (uti fieri debet) interpreteris, tunc falsum est af-fumasumtum : posito namque ea magis inter se uniri posse quae magis inter se ratione finis conveniunt; falso assumitur, creaturam & creaturam magis inter se convenire, quam Deum & creaturam: namque creatura, humana praesertim, de qua hic agitur, non est finis & scopus creaturae alius; sed Deus est finis & scopus creaturae, quae etiam expresse ideo facta & constituta est ut Deo uniretur. Ergo Deus & creatura magis possunt inter se uniri quam creatura & creatura: unde cadit praetensa illa & vere haeretica demonstratio, quam etiam olim alibi (a) ex alia consideratione everteram, cum multis aliis quae in scriptis tuis reperiebam impense, meo quidem judicio, exitiosa. Et hic quidem latet causa specialior, cur scriptis meis in relationibus tuis infensus adeo fueris.
units.tr: An outstanding demonstration! Allow me, I beg, to dissolve here in passing this notable sophism, though it is off my subject, since it may well meet with those who are not too wary of dangerous things. Things are said to agree with one another in two ways: (1) by reason of their similar matter or form, and (2) by reason of their end and purpose, when one thing is made for the sake of another and towards another. I shall give more tangible examples. In the first way, foot and foot, shoe and shoe, city and city, man and man, fire and fire, wood and wood, male and male, female and female, creature and creature agree with one another; in the second way, foot and shoe, city and man, fire and wood, male and female, and likewise God and creature agree with one another. Once this is noted, the fallacy of the Liberian axiom, or the inconsequence of the conclusion, is quite clear. For if you understand that axiom of the former kind of agreement, it is absurd and false that things which agree in matter or form can be united more than those which, though disagreeing in that way, agree with respect to end or purpose. The reason for the disparity is this: things which agree materially or formally are similar only to that extent, and are not for that very reason precisely capable of union; but things which agree by reason of an end, by this very fact have their nature, faculties, properties and constitution made and disposed towards the other, so as either to receive it or to be united to it most strictly. This is plain in the examples given: for although shoe and shoe agree more with each other by reason of matter and form than foot and shoe do, they cannot be united any more closely than shoe and foot, which agree by reason of their end; and the same is to be said of the other examples and of countless others. But if you interpret the Liberian axiom by reason of end (as it must be), then the assumption is false: for, granting that things which agree more closely with each other in end can be united more closely, it is falsely assumed that creature and creature agree more closely than God and creature. For the end and purpose of a creature is not another creature, especially a human creature, which is what is here at issue; rather God is the end and purpose of the creature, which indeed was expressly made and established so that it might be united to God. Therefore God and creature can be united more than creature and creature: and so that alleged and truly heretical demonstration falls, which I also once overturned elsewhere from another consideration, along with many other things I found in your writings, to my judgment truly pernicious. And here lies the more particular cause why you have been so hostile to my writings in your reviews.

units.la: Namque quamvis primo nec te nec ullum adoriri in animo habuerim, cum tamen mihi proponerem ea scribere ex quibus Dei gloria, ejus sanctitas, salutaris veritas ejusque amabilitas, hominis vero solidum bonum, virtutes, solida eruditio, nec non vitiorum superbiae, vanitatis, aliorumque abnegatio promoverentur; ea propter si quando forte in manus meas incidebant libri ubi ista concuterentur, tum principia mea non modo iis libris magis in oppositum stabiliebam, sed & saepe argumenta adversa in iisdem occurrentia vel evertebam prorsus, vel tuto praeveniebam, maxime quando speciem aliquam praefe ferebant, erantque in libris anonymis, quorum cum nullus auctor diceretur aut
units.tr: For although at first I had no intention of attacking you or anyone else, yet when I proposed to write those things by which God's glory, his holiness, his saving truth and his lovableness, and the true good of man, his virtues and solid learning, as well as the renunciation of vices such as pride and vanity, might be advanced, then, whenever books happened to fall into my hands in which these things were shaken, I not only strengthened my own principles all the more against those books, but often also either utterly overthrew the adverse arguments occurring in them or safely forestalled them, especially when they bore some appearance of importance and were anonymous books, since no author was named or identified, and so no one could think himself attacked.

units.la: (a) Cogit Rat. Edit. II. pag. 238. aut nominaretur, nullus etiam idcirco fe pro impugnato habere debuerit. Atque hoc modo cum tui libri anonymi (quorum nonnullos nescivi nisi post annos aliquot tuos esse foetus) in manus meas incidissent, & praeterea cum scirem ea quae prius edideram, & quae sentiebam a te coram aliis contemni, iisque contradici, ut ab eis omnes possent avocari; tunc non modo veritatum a me propositarum principia firmius stabilivi contra anonymorum scriptorum tuorum errores, quos noxios & capitales credidi; sed & ab exceptionibus tuis vera vindicavi, & argumenta tuorum dogmatum everti in omni fere materia. Quod maxime in Oeconomia Divina sum exsecutus, ubi vel a praefatione praejudicia anonymi (a) cujusdam libri tui contra rerum intellectuam cognitionem discutiuntur, dein in reliquo opere apparent hinc inde expressa tui Pelagianismi cum suis rationibus dissipatio principiorum Socinianismi, quae defendenda vel palliandia videris suscepisse, everso; Criticos tuae de Scriptura per eam sine lumine & operatione Spiritus S. interpretanda, deque quorundam librorum canonicorum rejectione destructio; tuae de potentia & statu hominis doctrinae, deque peccati originalis negatione cum omnibus argumentis & exceptionibus quae in eodem libro anonymo a te edito prostant, exterminatio, & plura alia: ita ut qui mea legerit, eum ejusmodi capitales periculofique errores nec movere possint, nec laedere amplius. His ita se habentibus, Oeconomia illa mea, errores illos evertens, tibi vifa est,
units.tr: (a) Cogit Rat. Edit. II. pag. 238. In this way, when your anonymous books (some of which I did not know to be your offspring until several years later) fell into my hands, and when, moreover, I knew that you were scorning in the presence of others what I had earlier published and what I held, and were contradicting it, so that by these means all might be diverted from it, then I not only established the principles of the truths I had proposed more firmly against the errors of your anonymous writings, which I believed to be harmful and deadly, but also vindicated the truths from your objections and overthrew the arguments of your doctrines in almost every subject. I carried this out most fully in the Oeconomia Divina, where, from its preface onward, the prejudices of a certain anonymous book of yours against the intellectual knowledge of things are dismantled; then, in the rest of the work, there appear here and there the expressed refutation of your Pelagianism with its arguments, and the overthrow of the principles of Socinianism, which you seem to have undertaken to defend or palliate; the destruction of your criticism of Scripture as to be interpreted without the light and operation of the Holy Spirit, and of the rejection of certain canonical books; the demolition of your doctrine of the power and state of man, and of your denial of original sin, together with all the arguments and objections which stand forth in the same anonymous book published by you; and many other things. So that whoever reads my work will neither be moved nor further harmed by such deadly and dangerous errors. Things being thus, my Oeconomia of that kind, overturning those errors, seemed to you

units.la: (a) Ea rerum sunt diversae materiae de Theol. fa est, cujus relationem vel Epitomen in Bibliotheca tua dare suscipiebas quidem; sed an sine indignatione & odio id exsequi poteris, judicabunt illi, qui dispicient quid huic præcedaneæ quæstioni respondendum; An probabile sit hominem, cujus principia & studia in eo versantur ut naturæ suæ corruptionem agnoscere nolit, sed eam tegat & excuset, quique præter generales fontes odii contra veritatem, superius dictos, specialiores etiam habet per impugnationem eorum quæ ipsi sunt intima & charissima; an, inquam, probabile sit talem hominem bona fide relaturum esse vim operis & argumentorum quibus charissima sua idola disjiciuntur? Necesse namque est ut nunc publice moneam (quod huc usque tibi parcendi causa tacui) te hic non judicem aut relatorem, sed adversantem partem esse, qui in Opere toto impugnationem tuorum principiorum reperias; ne deinceps judicia tua de meis credantur a Lectoribus e veritatis cognitione potius quam e vindictæ cupiditate & affectu, uti revera sunt, elicita.
units.tr: (a) These are matters of a different kind, from the theology [of the work] which you undertook to give in your Bibliotheca as a report or epitome; but whether you can carry this out without indignation and hatred, those will judge who weigh what must be answered to this preliminary question: whether it is probable that a man whose principles and pursuits are directed toward refusing to acknowledge the corruption of his own nature, but rather covering and excusing it, and who, beyond the general sources of hatred against the truth mentioned above, also has more specific ones through the attack on what is most intimate and dear to him, will, I say, be likely to report in good faith the force of a work and of arguments by which his most cherished idols are cast down. For it is necessary that I now publicly warn (which until now I have kept silent about, out of a wish to spare you) that here I am not judging you or acting as your reporter, but am a party opposed to you, since in the whole work you will find an attack on your principles; lest your judgments of my books be henceforth believed by readers as drawn from a knowledge of the truth rather than, as in fact they are, from a desire for revenge and from passion.

units.la: Equidem non pauca extant in tua relatione, de quibus non debeo conqueri. Et sane si omnia aperte falsa essent, nemo hominum tibi fidem habere potuisset. Quando vero plura recte refers quidem; at non modo præcipua omittis, sed & multa absurda interferere audes; nemo non videt, hæc eo credibiliora aliis fore, quo plura vera iis intermiscebuntur: nisi qui solidioris sunt judicii inde potius contra te concludant, eum qui, te referente, tales aliquot conspicuas momentosas veritates protulit, ejusmodi ab surdorum quæ ei deinde tribuis, capacem non videri; unde tuæ relationis fides hoc ipso eis fiat suspecta.
units.tr: Indeed, there are not a few things in your report with which I ought not to complain. And truly, if everything were plainly false, no one could have given you credence. But since you report many things rightly, yet not only omit the chief points but also dare to insert many absurdities, no one fails to see that these will be the more believable to others the more true things are mixed among them. Only those of sounder judgment will conclude against you, rather, that a man who, according to your report, has put forward several such striking and weighty truths does not seem capable of the absurdities you then attribute to him; and thus the credibility of your report is made suspect by this very fact.

units.la: Generaliora sphalmata D. Cl. in relatione sua de Oeconomia mea Divina.
units.tr: General blunders of the distinguished man in his report on my Oeconomia Divina.

units.la: Tam falsa autem, tam absurda, tamque contradictoria mihi impegisti, eaque modis ironicis atque sarcasmis ita sedate mordacibus & inexspectatis propositi, ut qui verum te narrare putabunt, non possint non me veluti fatuum, meaque tanquam absurda & lectione indigna cum ludibrio & sannis contemnere & deridere: quod me referre non pudet, siquidem & veterum & recentiorum sanctissimos atque doctissimos, nec non divinissima quæque, hac eadem etiam methodo tua irrisoria excipis qua & mea tractasti, quæ quidem cum de diviniore maximeque seria materia agerent, videbantur lectore in meo exigere mentem non profana irrisione, sed Dei timore, rerumque divinarum veneratione percitam. Sed de his & similibus postea. Interim generalia (ut ab his exordiar) quæ in relationis tuæ fide desidero, duo sunt. Primum, quod etsi in præfatione speciali Oeconomiæ Creationis monuerim & rogaverim lectores, ne de opere toto judicent ex libro primo, quia is & abstracta quædam contineret, & omnia fere opinionibus vulgaribus bus vel adversa, vel etiam superiora & sublimiora: tu tamen caeteris quinque libris omissis, & titulo tenus non sine ludificatione indicatis, primi tantum libri contenta recens{a}es; etsi in praefatione monueram, eos qui Metaphysicis non sunt assueti (quales plerumque ii quibus relationes tuas popitlari scribis sermone) lectionem suam ordiri debere a libris sequentibus, qui idcirco eis a sincero relatore potius proponendi erant: atque libri quidem primi contenta (quae non semel mihi aliisque fallus es te non intelligere) sic recenses, ut ne quidem interdum ad ea, nullatenus vero ad sequentium contenta videaris respexisse: censes enim in primo desiderari (a) conciliationem sufficientem praedictionum divinarum de contingentibus cum libertate humana: quam tamen in ultimo libro non tantum tractavi, sed & expressetum in praefatione primi, tum ibidem in fine cap. 12. p. 330. monueram, rem, etsi ejus principia insigniora praecipua in libro primo exstarent, in ultimum tamen rejici, ibique esse quaerendam. Adeo juxta Critices tuae regulas ea legis in quibus crisin tuam vis exercere. Scilicet magni Critici atque Historici non opus habent ut ea legant & inspiciant de quibus referunt & judicant.
units.tr: Yet you have charged me with things so false, so absurd, and so contradictory, and you have put them forward in such ironic and sarcastic forms, so calmly biting and unexpected, that those who think you are telling the truth cannot help despising and mocking me as a fool, and my views as absurd and unworthy of reading, with ridicule and sneers. This I am not ashamed to report, since you treat the most holy and most learned men of old and of recent times, and all the most divine things, with this same mocking method with which you handled my work; though these works dealt with a more divine and very serious subject, and seemed to require of the reader a mind stirred not by profane derision but by the fear of God and reverence for divine things. But of these and similar matters later. Meanwhile, the general things I miss in the good faith of your report (to begin with these) are two. First, that although in the special preface to the Oeconomia Creationis I warned and asked readers not to judge the whole work from the first book, because that book contains certain abstract matters and nearly everything in it is opposed to common opinions, or even higher and more sublime; yet you, leaving aside the other five books and indicating them only by title, and not without mockery, have reviewed the contents of the first book alone. Although in the preface I had warned that those who are not accustomed to metaphysics (such as those for whom you write your reports, for the most part, in popular language) ought to begin their reading with the following books, which for that reason ought to have been put before them by a sincere reporter. And you so review the contents of the first book (which you have more than once, to me and to others, falsely claimed you did not understand) that you seem to have looked at them only occasionally, and by no means at the contents of the following books. For you judge that there is lacking in the first book a sufficient reconciliation of God's predictions about contingent things with human liberty; yet I not only treated this in the last book, but also expressly stated in the preface to the first, and again in the same place at the end of chapter 12, p. 330, that the matter, although its more striking and principal principles stand out in the first book, is nevertheless deferred to the last, and is to be sought there. So closely, by the rules of your Criticism, do you handle those things on which you wish to exercise your judgment. Clearly great critics and historians have no need to read and examine the things about which they report and pass judgment.

units.la: Alterum, ubi in genere aequitatem tuam desidero, illud est: quod inculces materiam aliam in libris meis contineri, quam revera continetur: quod facis asseverando multis modis me mysticum mystica mysticè tractare. Hoc vel in ipso indice omnibus meis cogitatis applicas:
units.tr: Second, where I miss your fairness in general, it is this: you insist that another subject is contained in my books than is in fact contained in them; which you do by asserting in many ways that I treat mystical matters in a mystical way. You apply this to all my thoughts even in the very index:

units.la: (a) Bibl. p. 431. applicas : quin eo usque hac in re ridiculus es, ut non modo librum Irenicum meum, de controversiis hodiernis agentem, mysticum nomines, sed & in uno ex sequentibus Bibliothecæ tuæ tomis, ubi de operibus Molinosii agitur, annum 1687 contendas debere a me & ab illo denominari mysticum: ab illo, qui librum unum; a me, qui libros mysticos ædo edide-rim : & quia isto modo risum & naufeam erga operA mea non dubitas re in lectoribus excitaturum, hoc adeo tibi arridet, tamque sollicite inculcas, ut id mendacii non bis aut ter, sed vel omnino decies in libro tuo repetas, nec non hodieque, quoties de me meisque loquendi ansa tibi datur, eadem continuo oberres chorda. Et mystica quidem ipsa non modo non contemno; sed & ea, quia nil aliud sunt quam totius divinitatis thesauri communicati, tanti facio, ut si bonorum totius mundi jactura, miseriarumque omnium afflictionibus ea redimere possem, hilari animo cum divino Ignatio dicerem: Ignis & crux, bestiarumque congregationes, dispersiones ossium, concisio membrorum, molitiones totius corporis, malæ punitiones diaboli in me veniant, solum ut Jesu Christo fruar, arcanisque & mysticisejus amplexibus. Sed qui infinite ab illis absum, neque de his ex professo scribere haftenus præsumsi, aliorum tamen opera quædam mystica egregie exquisita in lucem edidi, & præfationibus illustravi, nec non ea in meis scriptis aliquoties laudavi, principia quædam generaliora allegavi, phrases aliquas explicui, nonnulla quæ remoram facere possent sustuli, & lectores ad ea legenda prægustu quodam disposui & hortatus sum, ut, quantum in me est, non omittam indicare & commendare media, scriptis meis toto genere & infinito intervallo superiora, quibus bonæ animæ ad amorem Dei puriorem, atque ad felicitatem æternam provocari possint. Sed meos libros inde esse mysticos, aut mystica ibi esse omnia, non magis sequitur, quam Cogitationum mearum editionem primam mysticam esse, id quod nemo unquam somniavit, etsi in illa mysticos auctores aliquoties (a) laudaverim: aut non magis quam verum sit, tuos libros, libros esse poëticos, Horatianos & Ovidianos, eo quod hos auctores, sæpius quam ego mysticos, laudes & proferas, Ovidianasque Metamorphoses & Horatianas cantiunculas pro egregio Scripturas interpretandi adminiculo interaliacommendes. Fatere, quæso, id quod res est. Si Theologia mystica Pelagianis & Socinianis faveret, non adeo ab ea abhorreres, ut libros tibi odiosos ab eadem contemtus ergo nunquam cuparet mysticos. Qu'n videmus Liberium tuum, quando conjiciebat per mystica rem Socinianam sustulciri posse; ad Theologiam allegoricam (quæ tibi mystica est) de facto recurrere, etsi nomen mystices proferre refugiat, ne ipse scilicet in irrisionum tuarum Mysticarum flagellum incurras proprium. Et hinc est quod loca Scripturæ, ubi creatio propria Christo tanquam ejus opus attribuitur, Liberius ut in gratiam Socinianæ opinionis illa explicet, de creatione allegorica, deque operationibus & creaturis Mysticis, ( quas sic nominare non audet, sed novas pro mysticis dicit ) intelligend a esse suggerit. Atque ita haec loca : In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod est factum, &c. & Mundus per ipsum factus est. item: Omnia per ipsum & in ipso creata sunt. Ipse est ante omnia, &c. quae (a) Johannes & (b) Paulus ad Christum referunt, si ex Socinianorum & Liberii expositia mente aliis verbis & terminis propriis explicentur, debebunt rejecto prorsus literali sensu, hoc modo exponi: In principio " mystico erat verbum, & verbum erat mystice apud Deum, & Deus erat mystice verbum. Omnia mystica per ipsum mystice facta sunt; & sine ipso nihil mystici factum est, quod mystice est factum. Item: Mundus mysticus per ipsum mystice factus est. Iterum: Omnia mystica per ipsum & in ipso creata sunt mystice; & ipse est mystice ante omnia mystica; & sic consequenter. In quibus nescio quis risum tenere possit, dum videbit eos qui alioqui sunt mysticae Theologiae irrisores, errorum gratia vel invitos cogi, ut ad eam adeo ridicule tententes recipere. Sic ergo etiam Dominus Johannes Clericus (Liberio ni renunciet) inter Mysticos! At ut non ex animo, ita nec diu: nescit enim adhuc quid sit Theologia Mystica, quod prius ipse ex aliquo auctore (v. g. ex Theologiae Cordis praefatione & ejusdem partis alterius ultimo libro) discere deberet. Subolfecit tantum generalius eam principiis suis erroneis, nec non vanis minutiarum studiis parum favere; novitque eam displicere tum mundanis plurimis, tum eruditis superficiariis falsisve permultis; item & carnali vulgo, forte & simplicioribus quibusdam, aliorum de ea calumniis circumventis: atque hoc factis ei fuit, quo conceptum erga scripta mea suis principiis adversantia odium & contemtum aliis communicaret, ea ut sibi odioso mysticorum titulo falso insigniret, & omnia in eis perridicule ad mystica referret. Indignari quaeso noli, Domine, monenti ut Mysticorum respectu intra grammatices sphaeram te contineas, neve Theologiae mysticae te intermisceas, tyrunculi ne a tergo rideant ad mystica referentem, uti(a) facis, ratiocinationes & probationes quibus usus sum ad libertatem demonstrandam, argumenta peccatum originale animarumque propagationem evincentia, ultimos rerum eventus externos a me recensitos, analysin meam Epistolae ad Romanos, & plura alia quae incapacia per se sunt ut inter obiecta & materiam Theologiae mysticae recipiantur.
units.tr: (a) Bibl. p. 431. you apply it. Indeed you are so ridiculous in this matter that you not only call my Irenicum, which deals with present-day controversies, mystical, but in one of the later volumes of your Bibliotheca, where you discuss the works of Molinos, you insist that the year 1687 must be called mystical by me and by him: by him, who wrote one book; by me, who have published mystical books. Because you do not hesitate to stir up laughter and disgust in readers toward my works in this way, you are so pleased with the idea and press it so eagerly that you repeat this falsehood not two or three times but at least ten times in your book, and even today, whenever an occasion to speak of me and my writings is given you, you keep harping on the same string. Yet I do not merely disdain mystical matters themselves; because they are nothing other than the treasures of the whole divinity communicated to us, I value them so highly that, if I could redeem them with the loss of all the world's goods and with every kind of misery, I would say cheerfully with the divine Ignatius: Let fire and the cross, gatherings of wild beasts, scattering of bones, dismemberment of limbs, torments of the whole body, and the evil punishments of the devil come upon me, provided only that I enjoy Jesus Christ and his secret and mystical embraces. But since I am infinitely far from those things, and hitherto have not presumed to write about them professedly, I have nevertheless brought to light certain excellent mystical works of other authors, illustrated them with prefaces, cited them several times in my own writings, referred to some more general principles, explained some phrases, removed some things that could cause hindrance, and disposed and urged readers to read them, giving them a kind of foretaste; and, so far as lies in me, I will not fail to point out and commend means, far superior to my writings in every respect and by an infinite distance, by which good souls may be stirred to a purer love of God and to eternal happiness. But it does not follow that my books are therefore mystical, or that everything in them is mystical, any more than the first edition of my Cogitationes is mystical, which no one has ever dreamed, although in it I have cited mystical authors several times (a). Nor is it any more true that your books are poetical, Horatian and Ovidian, because you cite and bring forward these authors more often than I cite mystical ones, and recommend the Ovidian Metamorphoses and Horatian little songs as an excellent aid for interpreting Scripture, among other things. Confess, I beg you, what is the case. If mystical theology favoured the Pelagians and Socinians, you would not so abhor it, nor would you ever desire to despise it on account of the mystics, or call my books mystical as an insult. Do we not see your Liberius, when he conjectured that the Socinian thing could be removed by mystical means, have recourse in fact to allegorical theology (which for you is mystical), although he shrinks from uttering the name of mystics, lest, of course, you yourself fall into the very whip of your own mockery of mystics? And hence it is that Liberius suggests that the passages of Scripture where creation proper is attributed to Christ as his work should be explained, in favour of the Socinian opinion, as an allegorical creation and as mystical operations and creatures (which he does not dare to call by that name, but says new instead of mystical). So, for example, these passages: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made by him, and without him was made nothing that was made, etc. And the world was made by him. Likewise: All things were created by him and in him. He is before all things, etc. These words John and Paul refer to Christ; if, according to the mind of the Socinians and of Liberius, they are explained in other words and with other terms, then, with the literal sense entirely rejected, they will have to be expounded in this way: In the beginning was the mystical word, and the word was mystically with God, and God was mystically the word. All mystical things were mystically made through him; and nothing mystical was made without him, which was mystically made. Likewise: The mystical world was mystically made through him. Again: All mystical things were created mystically through him and in him; and he is mystically before all mystical things; and so on consistently. In these things I do not know who could keep from laughing, while he sees those who are otherwise mockers of mystical theology being compelled, whether willing or unwilling, for the sake of their errors, to accept it, attempting it so ridiculously. So then Mr. John Clericus too (unless Liberius disowns him) is among the mystics! But as he is not so from the heart, so not for long either: for he still does not know what mystical theology is, which he ought first to learn from some author (for example, from the preface to the Theology of the Heart and from the last book of its second part). He has only sensed in a general way that it is unfavourable to his erroneous principles and to his vain pursuit of trifles; and he knows that it is displeasing to very many worldly people, to many superficial and false scholars, likewise to the carnal crowd and perhaps to some simpler folk, who have been taken in by the slanders of others against it. This has been enough to make him pass on to others the hatred and contempt he has conceived toward my writings, which oppose his principles, so that he might falsely mark them with the hateful title of mystics, and refer everything in them most absurdly to mystical matters. Please, sir, do not be indignant if I advise you to confine yourself within the sphere of grammar with respect to the mystics, and not to mix yourself up with mystical theology, lest the young apprentices laugh behind your back at you referring to mystical matters, as you do, the reasonings and proofs I have used to demonstrate liberty, the arguments establishing original sin and the propagation of souls, the external final events of things which I have reviewed, my analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, and many other things which are by their nature incapable of being counted among the objects and matter of mystical theology.

units.la: Aegre ferrem tibi dici posse ab imprudentiore forsan tyrone verbum Syracidis, De mendacio intruditionis tuae confundere; vel illud Apellis, Ne sutor ultra crepidam: aut forte aliquid simile, Ne Criticus ultra cortices.
units.tr: I would be annoyed that you might be told, perhaps by some rather imprudent beginner, the saying of Sirach: to confound with lies your intrusion; or that saying of Apelles, let the shoemaker not go beyond the sandal; or perhaps something similar: let the critic not go beyond the bark.

units.la: Hic dices, patescere tuam de meo in Criticos infenso animo querelam esse legitimam, quando refers me CLAMARE in opere meo contra Criticos. Si cum Pareo, celebri Theologo, absolute dixissem, Criticės auctorem omnino esse Diabolum, possem censuram tuam iltam forte aliquo modo meruisse. At ego Criticos sobrios, qui sub litera spiritus quaerunt & venerantur atque commendant, non modo non tango, sed & eos magnifacio & veneror, & vero commendatos maxime volo; qualis inter alios erat nuper Illustris Uslerius, qui S. Barnabæ Epistolam, totam allegoricis & mysticis sensibus plenam, primus edidit & maximi fecit: superiore autem seculo magnus Erasmus, nulli facile post se comparandus. Hic ut ut humanioris literaturæ & Criticæ erudितionis inexhaustæ vir, opera tamen sua, suas præsertim in Novum Testamentum egregias paraphrases, rebus allegoricis & mysticis sæpissime veluti gemmis non dubitavit condecorare: Arnobii junioris commentarios in Psalmos, mysticis quoque sensibus abundantes primus & in lucem produxit & impense laudavit. Denique, quod instar omnium est, in Enchiridii Militis Christiani capite altero, hanc statuit regulam: Ex interpretibus divinæ Scripturæ eos potissimum deligequi A LITERA QUAM MAXIME RECEDUNT. Cujusmodi sunt in primis post Paulum Origenes, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus. Addit: Video enim neotericos Theologos literæ nimium libenter inhærere, & capitiosis quibusdam argutiis magis quam ERUENDIS MYSTERIIS operam dare: quasi vero non vere dixerit Paulus Legem nostram SPIRITUALEM esse. Audivi ego nonnullos qui sibi usque adeo humanis illis commentar
units.tr: Here you will say that your complaint about my hostile attitude toward critics is shown to be legitimate, since you report that I CRY OUT in my work against critics. If I had said absolutely, with Pareus, the celebrated theologian, that the author of criticism is wholly the Devil, I might perhaps have deserved your censure in some way. But I do not touch sober critics, who seek, revere and commend the letter of the spirit; rather, I not only value them highly and revere them, but I want them especially to be commended. Among others of this kind was lately the illustrious Ussher, who first published the Epistle of Barnabas, wholly full of allegorical and mystical senses, and esteemed it greatly; and in the previous century the great Erasmus, to whom hardly anyone is easily comparable after him. Although he was a man of humane literature and of inexhaustible critical learning, he did not hesitate in his works, especially in his excellent paraphrases on the New Testament, to adorn them very often with allegorical and mystical things, as with gems. He was also the first to bring to light the commentaries of the younger Arnobius on the Psalms, which abound in mystical senses, and he praised them greatly. Finally, which is the chief example of all, in the second chapter of the Enchiridion Militis Christiani he laid down this rule: Among the interpreters of divine Scripture, choose especially those who depart as far as possible from the LETTER. Such are chiefly, after Paul, Origen, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine. He adds: For I see that modern theologians cling far too willingly to the letter, and devote their efforts more to subtle quibbles than to UNFOLDING THE MYSTERIES, as if Paul had not truly said that our law is SPIRITUAL. I have heard some who were so pleased with those human little commentaries

units.la: Note: the lines of the last sentence continue at the foot of the page. mentationculis placebant, (inspice fis contra quos hic clamet,) ut veterum interpretamenta pene pro somnis contemnerent. ..... Consenesciunt in litera, neque ad spiritualem scripturarum cognitionem elaborant. Neque audiunt Christum in Euangelio clamantem, Caro non prodest quicquam; Spiritus est qui vivificat: Et, Scimus quoniam lex spiritualis est, non carnalis: & SPIRITUALIBUS SPIRITUALIA COMPARANDA, Olim in monte, nunc in Spiritu vult adorari Pater Spiritum. ....Te ergo, subjungit, qui ingenio tam felici praeditus es, omnino nolim in sterili litera lentum esse; sed ad RECONDITIORA MYSTERIA festinare, & improbum contatum induistriae crebris PRECIBUS adjuvare, donec aperiat tibi librum Is qui habet CLAVEM David, qui claudit & nemo aperit ARCANA PATRIS, quae nemo novit nisi Filius & cui voluerit Filius revelare. Tales ergo mihi nunc Criticos, & eos ego quovis auro cariores aestimabo, commendabo, venerabor. At siqui Critici causam, vim essentiam & centrum omnium realitatum, adorandum Spiritum Dei, ejusque internas operationes atque sensus arcanos rejiciant & irrideant, fiantque idcirco mystico-maltiges: si earundem realitatum ipsis ideis sint infensi, & has, praetexendo Metaphysicum odium, & ideas Platonicas, eliminare cupiant: ipsi ne quidem umbram harum rerum, quibus crassiore modo designetur essentialis realitas, tolerare velint, atque adeo allegoricae Theologiae iludant: sintque insuper infensi omnibus illis, ut ut seculorum antiquitate & sanctitate confpicuis', qui ista commendarunt, ut nil tandem remaneat pro suis deliciis criticis quam cortex corticaliter explicitus, five litera fine spiritu, fine ejus ideis intellectualibus,fineque umbris ejus solum literaliter, perideas grammatisticas & criticas, Pelagianas & ethnicas, Homericas & Virgilianas, Horatianas & Ovidianas, ideis Platonicorum immensum variores, exposita, idque ea temeritate, ut quicquid eis non placet pro captu critico, ex ipsarum etiam Scripturarum codice eliminent, sibique incognita mysteria damnent, & suas praeterea interpretationes grammaticas haberi velint pro Sacris observationibus, quaestionibus, annotationibus, & fi quid eis fimile, quoniam scilicet materia externa aut cortices & verba ex Scriptura sacra desumta sunt; hos ego non clamore, sed demonstrationibus, ut (a) feci, convincam de suae ejusmodi critices inanitate & absurditate stolida: atque fi demonstrationes capere necdum queant, per similitudines magis palpabiles ostendam eos non minus vane atque ridicule agere, quam fi quis olim ex Israelitis, ut sacrificii oblati particeps esset & alios participes redderet, victimae quidem internam substantiam relinquere, ejus vero cutem, pilos, aut excrementa solas suscipere voluisset, quibus postquam ora, vultum sequae totum egregie superillinere absolvisset, curreret per castra clamans, Sacrificium sacrum! Unctio sacra! Edulium sacrum! Scilicet haec e sacra victima defumferat ille eodem modo, quo Critici nostri e Scripturis sacris sacra sua obseruata desumere consueuerunt, iisque se & alios nutrire; sane veluti furfuribus nutriuntur sues, frugis farinâ & substantiâ interna, acsi inanis pulviculus esset, contemtim aliis relicta.
units.tr: ...the little commentaries pleased them (see against whom he cries out here), so that they despised the interpretations of the ancients almost as dreams. ..... They grow old in the letter and do not labour after the spiritual knowledge of the Scriptures. Nor do they hear Christ crying out in the Gospel, The flesh profits nothing; it is the Spirit that gives life; and, We know that the law is spiritual, not carnal: and SPIRITUAL THINGS ARE TO BE OBTAINED BY SPIRITUAL MEANS. Once on the mountain, but now in the Spirit, the Father wishes to be worshipped. ....Now you, he adds, who are endowed with so happy a gift, I would by no means have you be sluggish in the barren letter; but hasten on to the MORE HIDDEN MYSTERIES and, with unwearied industry, help yourself by frequent PRAYERS, until he who has the KEY OF DAVID, who shuts and no one opens, opens the book to you, the SECRETS OF THE FATHER, which no one knows except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal them. Such critics, then, I will now value, commend and revere, dearer to me than any gold. But if any critics reject and mock the cause, power, essence and centre of all realities, the adorable Spirit of God, and his inner operations and hidden senses, and so become haters of mysticism; if they are hostile to the ideas of these realities themselves, and, under the pretext of a hatred of metaphysics and Platonic ideas, wish to eliminate them; if they will not tolerate even the shadow of those things by which the essential reality is indicated in a grosser way, and so mock allegorical theology; and if, moreover, they are hostile to all those men, however conspicuous for the antiquity and holiness of their centuries, who commended these things, so that in the end nothing remains for their critical pleasures but a bark barkishly unfolded, that is, the letter without the spirit, without its intellectual ideas, without even its shadows, explained only literally, through grammatical and critical ideas, Pelagian and heathen, Homeric and Virgilian, Horatian and Ovidian, far more varied than the ideas of the Platonists; and if they do this with such recklessness that whatever does not please them, according to their critical capacity, they eliminate even from the very text of the Scriptures, and condemn mysteries unknown to them, and besides wish their own grammatical interpretations to be taken for Sacred observations, questions, annotations, and whatever is like them, since, of course, the external matter, or the husks and words, are taken from Holy Scripture: these men I will convict, not with noise but with demonstrations, as I have done, of the emptiness and stupid absurdity of such criticism. And if they are not yet able to grasp demonstrations, I will show by more tangible comparisons that they act no less vainly and ridiculously than if one of the Israelites, wishing to share in a sacrifice offered and to make others sharers, were to leave the inner substance of the victim and take up only its skin, hair or dung, and, after he had finished smearing his mouth, face and whole person with these, were to run through the camp shouting, Holy sacrifice! Holy anointing! Holy food! Clearly he would have drawn these things from the holy victim in the same way as our critics are accustomed to draw their own sacred observations from the holy Scriptures, and to nourish themselves and others with them; just as pigs are nourished on bran, while the flour and inner substance of the grain are left contemptuously to others, as if it were empty dust.

units.la: §. 5. Specialiora sphalmata D. Cler. in relatio- ne sua de Oeconomia Divina.
units.tr: §. 5. More specific errors of Le Clerc in his account of the Divine Economy.

units.la: Jam specialiora sunt quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: Now the more specific points follow.

units.la: 1. In Bibliothecæ tuæ Universalis (a) relatione, ubi me introducis promittentem in Oeconomia demonstrationes Geometricis niti cedentes de rebus Theologicis & Philosophicis, Metaphysicis, Physicis & Ethicis, nec non de Politices fundamentis, addis, me non sperare vim earum demonstrationum captum iri a lectoribus, qui solam illic adhibebunt rationem humanam: oportere absolute eos & aliquid Fidei afferte, sine qua affirmem eos nil ibi intellecturos. Et, me credere, illiteratos ipsos omnia, exceptis quibusdam primi & secundi libri, intellecturos, modo & attentionem adferant, & vero RECIPIANT CUM FIDE veritates quas promitto me eos doctururn. E quibus quicunque nec memorunt, nec te audebunt suspicari de eorum irrisorum numero esse, qui impostura pro irrisionum suarum sale de industria excogitant, non poterunt a cachinnis deme temperare, audientes, veritatum demonstrationes a me promiti, modo cum fide recipiantur. Ast, qui
units.tr: 1. In your (a) account in the Universal Library, where you introduce me promising, in the Oeconomia, demonstrations resting on geometrical method concerning theological and philosophical matters, metaphysical, physical and ethical, and also concerning the foundations of politics, you add that I do not hope the force of those demonstrations will be grasped by readers who apply only human reason there; that they must absolutely bring with them some faith, without which, you affirm, they will understand nothing there. And, you believe, the unlettered themselves will understand everything, except certain things in the first and second books, provided they bring attention and truly receive with faith the truths which I promise to teach them. Those who do not remember these words, nor will dare to suspect you of being among the number of those mockers who deliberately devise imposture as the salt of their derision, will not be able to refrain from laughter, hearing that demonstrations of truths are promised by me, provided they are received with faith. But whoever

units.la: (a) pag. 414, 416. quicunque me pro mortalium ignorantissimo non habebunt, quin potius exi-stimabunt, mihi non minus ac tibi, & forte cuilibet alii, notum esse ecquid sit Demonstratio, quique animadvertent me eas promittentem supponere a prima operis pagina, lectorem esse vel scepticum incredulissimum; non dubitabunt sane quin hic malæ fidei subsit cavillatio. Et quando conspicient in serie operis, me nil explicite deducere in conclusionibus meis nisi id quod in principiis implicite & ex natura sua continebatur (quod demonstrare est) principiaque ipsa quando per se nota non erant, iisdem modis ex alio, hocque ex alio, & tandem ex primo incontroverso deducta esse, (quod multi testantur se animadverti-sse) mirabuntur & exiguitatem prudentiæ tuæ & in cavillando intemperantiam, qua ne te gaudiolo privares lepidum hunc aculeum, demonstrationes promittere modo cum fide recipiantur, sarcastice semel & bis proferendi, aliosque eo ad risum concitandi, non potuisti irrisorium stylum continere, quamvis non potuerit non inde fidei malæ dedecus inte redundare. At scilicet fidem nominavi & commendavi ad rerum intellectualium perceptionem! Rem paucis explicabo. Dantur interdum demonstrationes, quarum multi, etsi non parum ingeniosi, vim non capiunt, v. g. Cartesius demonstravit certe animæ immaterialitatem & Dei exsistentiam: quarum tamen demonstrationum, etsi attente sæpiusque lectarum, doctissimi Geometræ vim assequi se non potuisse, (a) testati sunt. Hodie dantur Cartesiani qui non assequuntur demonstrationes de Dei libertate indifferente, aut de Dei sufficientia, etsi immediate sequantur ex eo quod Deus sit ens perfectissimum, adeoque aliis praeter se non indignes, ergo se solo sibi sufficiens; quique adeo, si aliorum habeat ideas aliaque fecerit, ex indifferentia ea cogitavit & fecit, indifferens ergo ipse primus : & tamen haec non capiunt. Quis non capit haec principia, Deum se ipsum suasque proprietates negare non posse, neque conscientia intima, neque dicto aut opere externo? At quotus quisque est, qui capiat sequi necessario & demonstrative, opera Dei non tendere ad annihilationem, non esse inactiva, tenebrosa, sibi adversantia, sese destruentia & angentia; atque adeo esse permanentia, activissima, luminosissima, concordantissima, felicia & gloriosa, ac proinde res non fuisse conditas in statu malo, in quo jam sunt; sed hoc ab auctore inordinationis peccante proficisci? Ecce has multi non capiunt demonstrationes, quemadmodum concipiunt a Deo non posse esse mendacium. Atque id ipsum eo saepius accidere potest, quo magis demonstrationes sunt de veritatibus a primis principiis paulo remotioribus, nec non praejudicia inveterata concutientibus. Quid jam erit remedii ut adjuvetur ratio ad vim ejusmodi demonstrationum sentiendam. Requirunt alii attentionem: ego etiam. At illi, de quibus nunc, dicunt se attentissimos esse & fuisse, nec tamen demonstrationum vim adhuc sentire. Quid ergo praeterea? Alii alia: Ego vero hoc. Requiro ut non attendat solum lectOR ad rationem, sed etiam ut eam sequatur, hoc est, ut praexi efficiat ea quae ratio demonstrativè praescribit esse faciendaantequam ulterius ad plures alias demonstrandas intelligendas sese accingat. Exempli causa, si demonstratio quaedam mathematica, eaque complicatior & operosior esset intelligenda, oporteret etiam, ratione id dictante, ut prout legit, sic quoque actu & praxi describeret circino vel norma aut cyphris ea quae attenta lectione pre currit: alias dissiparetur & confunderetur sola ejus attentio, medio practico alioqui confirmanda. Ita de intellectualibus. Postquam aliquis per rationem seu quocunque alio modo convictus est Deum exsistere, eumque esse & omnis boni & omnis luminis auctorem omnipotentem & benevolum, primum quod ratio dictat esse faciendum antequam ad alia bene se accingat, est, quod debeat laudare Deum, ei gratias agere, deinde ab eo exspectare & optare animo confidente operationes suas bonas & luminosas. Aut mens me destituit, aut hoc omnino ita est. Ratio me impellit necessario ut optem bonum & lumen, idque a Deo & in anima mea, quia is est auctor luminis & boni, ego vero ejus sum opus, & anima mea subjectum luminis: & hoc quoque anima confidente, quia Deus est benevolus & omnipotens. Atque haec animae dispositio, qua offert se Deo confidenter optans lumen & bonum ejus, sive is recursus mentis gratæ & confidenter optantis Deum boni fontem, ea res est quam FIDEM appellavi: quæ Fides, sive, qui recursus mentis Deo se committentis & confidentis, non quidem immediate demonstrationes de intellectualibus ingerit, sed per illum facultates animæ ipsaque ratio fiunt magis magisque a Deo vividæ, sanæ, perspicuæ, habiles atque aptæ, quæ postea facillime rerum intellectualium ideas veras efformént, concipiant, penetrent, videantque quid in illis sit, & quid ex illis necessario sequatur; hoc est, capaces fiant consequenter percipiendi & sentiendi vim demonstrationum de rebus intellectualibus. Istane etiam necdum capis Domine Critice? Hæccine suntpromittere demonstrationes modo cum fide quis eas recipiat, & parum fidei ad eas adferat? Aut vero an ego locutus sum obscurius quam ut possim capi?
units.tr: (a) pp. 414, 416. does not regard me as the most ignorant of mortals, but rather will think that it is known to me no less than to you, and perhaps to anyone else, what Demonstration is; and who will notice that I, promising these, presuppose from the first page of the work that the reader is at least the most incredulous sceptic, will not doubt that some bad faith lies behind this quibbling. And when they see in the course of the work that I deduce nothing explicitly in my conclusions except what was implicitly and by its own nature contained in the principles (which is what to demonstrate means), and that the principles themselves, when they were not self-evident, were deduced in the same way from one thing and another, and at last from the first uncontroverted point (as many attest they have observed), they will wonder both at the slightness of your prudence and at the intemperance in your quibbling, by which, so as not to deprive yourself of the pleasure of this witty barb, you could not restrain your mocking style, sarcastically bringing out once and twice the phrase demonstrations promised, provided they are received with faith, and so stirring others to laughter, although it could not fail to bring some disgrace of bad faith upon you. But of course I named and commended faith for the perception of intellectual things! I will explain the matter briefly. Sometimes there are demonstrations which many, though not without ingenuity, do not grasp; for example, Descartes certainly demonstrated the immateriality of the soul and the existence of God, yet the most learned geometers have testified that they could not attain the force of those demonstrations, even when they read them attentively and often. Today there are Cartesians who do not grasp the demonstrations concerning God's indifferent freedom, or concerning God's sufficiency, although these follow immediately from the fact that God is the most perfect being, and so is not unworthy of anything beside himself, and therefore is sufficient to himself alone; and who, if he has the ideas of others and has made other things, thought and made them from indifference, and so himself is the first indifferent one: and yet they do not grasp these things. Who does not grasp these principles, that God cannot deny himself or his own properties, neither by inner consciousness nor by outward word or deed? But how few are there who grasp that it follows necessarily and demonstrably that the works of God do not tend to annihilation, are not inactive, dark, self-opposed, self-destroying and self-constricting, and therefore are lasting, most active, most luminous, most harmonious, happy and glorious; and consequently that things were not created in the evil state in which they now are, but that this proceeds from the author of disorder who sins? Many do not grasp these demonstrations, just as they do not conceive that God cannot be a liar. And this can happen all the more often, the more the demonstrations concern truths a little more remote from first principles, and shake inveterate prejudices. What then will be the remedy, so that reason may be helped to feel the force of such demonstrations? Others require attention: so do I. But those of whom we now speak say they are, and have been, most attentive, and yet still do not feel the force of the demonstrations. What then remains? Others say other things; I say this. I require that the reader not only attend to reason, but also follow it, that is, that he first do what reason demonstratively prescribes should be done, before he sets himself to understand further demonstrations. For example, if some mathematical demonstration, rather complicated and laborious, were to be understood, reason would also dictate that, as he reads, he should in practice actually describe with compass, rule or counters what he runs through in attentive reading; otherwise his attention alone would be dispersed and confused, though it ought to be confirmed by a practical means. So it is with intellectual things. After someone has been convinced by reason, or by whatever other way, that God exists, and that he is the omnipotent and benevolent author of all good and all light, the first thing reason dictates should be done before he properly sets himself to other things is that he ought to praise God and give him thanks, and then to expect from him, and to desire with a confident mind, his good and luminous operations. Either my mind fails me, or this is entirely so. Reason necessarily impels me to desire good and light, and that from God and in my soul, because he is the author of light and good, while I am his work and my soul the subject of light; and this also with a confident soul, because God is benevolent and omnipotent. And this disposition of the soul, by which it confidently offers itself to God, desiring his light and good, that is, this recourse of a mind grateful to God and confidently desiring him as the fount of good, is the thing I have called FAITH. This faith, or this recourse of a mind committing and trusting itself to God, does not indeed immediately thrust demonstrations about intellectual things upon us, but through it the faculties of the soul, and reason itself, are made more and more, by God, lively, sound, clear, able and apt, so that afterwards they most easily form, conceive and penetrate the true ideas of intellectual things, and see what is in them and what follows from them necessarily; that is, they become capable of perceiving and feeling the force of demonstrations about intellectual things. Do you not yet grasp this, Sir Critic? Is this what it is to promise demonstrations provided one receives them with faith, and to bring little faith to them? Or indeed have I spoken more obscurely than can be understood?

units.la: Quasi non expresse dixerim (a) nos spiritu fidei approximari Deo, unde dum conformes ei in interioribus efficimur, mens ratioque nostra nec omnes facultates habiles fiant pro suo quaque modo AD EXPRIMENDUM (seu in nobis excitandum idealiter) characteres & magnalia Dei & eorum quæ in ipso atque in conceptu divino sunt; ita ut ACTIVITAS RATIONIS acquirat imperceptibiliter HABILITATEM AD REPRÆSENTANDUM modum quo Deus omnia concipit & fecit. Esse in nobis FACULTATEM REPRÆSENTANDI CLARISSIME & FACILLIME IDEAS & OPERA DEI eorumque RATIONES & pulchritudines VIDENDI; quæ facultas quanda approximatur Deo, recipit per lumen fidei, sive per lumen quod Deus animæ mæ fidenti communicat, DISPOSITONEM AD PERCIPIENDAS Veritates & opera ejus, & quæ plura ejusmodi. Vide hinc, quomodo fides seu approximatio fida ad Deum in anima lucentem, disponat actīvitatem rationis ad habilitatem excitandi in se ideas ideis Dei & rebus ipsis conformes, & ad capiendas rerum veritates & rationes. Verùm hoc est antipelagianum, adeoque tibi invisum, uti etiam illud quod ibidem expresse monui, Pelagianos, Criticos literales, eosque qui operationes Dei in anima negant, idcirco esse ineptos ad res intellectuales percipiendas, eo quod ægra sit, crassa & corruptissima eorum ratio. An ergo, quoniam hæc forte tibi dicta putabas, oportebat a te sensum meum clarum, sanum, præstantissimaque & saluberrima præcepta continentem vindictæ ergo in falsum & ridiculum ita perverti? Nonne Paulus ante me annotavit causam cur Philosophi tenebris sint involuti & evanuerint in stultas rationes, hanc esse, quod agnitum Deum non glorificaverint ut Deum, ut auctorem luminis & boni, ad quem recurrendum esset; quodque ingrati fuerint, atque vane confisi sint & inmixi propriis ratiocinationibus deserto Creatore benedicto? Utinam vero omnibus Philosophis inesset divina hæc fides, quo sanaretur eorum ratio, nec minus omnibus relatoribus humana fides, quo candide aliorum facta aut dicta referrent?
units.tr: As if I had not expressly said that we are brought near to God by the Spirit of faith, so that, as we are made conformed to him in our inward parts, our mind and reason become fit, each in its own way, to express (that is, to arouse in ourselves in an ideal manner) the characters and marvels of God, and of those things which are in him and in the divine conception; so that the ACTIVITY OF REASON gradually acquires the ABILITY TO REPRESENT the manner in which God conceives and made all things. There is in us a FACULTY OF REPRESENTING MOST CLEARLY AND MOST EASILY THE IDEAS AND WORKS OF GOD, and their reasons and beauties, for seeing; this faculty, in a certain way drawn near to God, receives through the light of faith, or through the light which God communicates to my believing soul, a DISPOSITION TO PERCEIVE the truths and works of him, and many more things of this kind. See from this how faith, or a faithful approach to God shining in the soul, disposes the activity of reason to the ability to arouse in itself ideas conformed to the ideas of God and to the things themselves, and to grasp the truths and reasons of things. But this is anti-Pelagian, and therefore hateful to you, just as is that which I expressly warned in the same place: that Pelagians, literal critics, and those who deny the operations of God in the soul are for this reason unfit to perceive intellectual things, because their reasoning is sick, gross and most corrupt. Was it therefore necessary, since you perhaps thought these things had been said by you, that my clear and sound sense, containing most excellent and most salutary precepts, should be so perverted into falsehood and absurdity for the sake of revenge?
