Did not Paul, before me, note the cause why the philosophers were darkened and became vain in their foolish reasonings, namely that they did not glorify God as God, as the author of light and of good, to whom one ought to have recourse; and because they were ungrateful, and vainly trusted, and mixed in their own reasonings, having forsaken the blessed Creator? Would that all philosophers had this divine faith, by which their reasoning might be healed, and that all reporters had human faith, so that they might relate the deeds and words of others honestly!

units.la: 2. Pari fidelitate joculariter & contemtim refers Metaphysicam meam non posse multis in locis perfecte intelligi, nisi quis in tenebras ncbras
units.tr: 2. With equal lack of fidelity you report, jokingly and with contempt, that my Metaphysics cannot be perfectly understood in many places unless one is admitted into the divine darkness

units.la: (a) Bibl. p. 418. nebras divinas inque contemplationem principii Dei sit admissus. Debuisses dicere, Metaphysicam meam explicare quaedam de divinis, quae quidem idealiter bene concipi possint, at quae nullus potest vivide experiri in se nisi Deus, principium nostrum, se detegat ipsi eo modo qui jam nobis est tenebrosus, id quod obiter monui appellari a Mysticis, admitti in tenebras divinas & in contemplationem principii sui (non principii Dei, ut male capis.) Atque similia nullus non dixit Metaphysicus. Nam quando v. g. demonstrant, in contemplatione Dei summam felicitatem consistere; hoc quidem quisque capere potest; sed id ipsum neminem experiri sensu sine supernaturali operatione Dei nobis nunc obscura & tenebrosa, fatebuntur. Ita ego in Cogitationibus Rationalibus totum caput circa Æternitatem divinam, nostramque participatam, occupavi, quarum demonstrationum vis facile idealiter percipi potest, at rei ipsius experimentum vivum non potest, ut ibi monui, nisi Optima Menti, quae nos sustinet, placeat se ipsam nobis secundum nostra Cogitationis plenitudinem jungere, & quae sequuntur dicto capite: quae etsi obscura nunc experientiae nostrae, a magnis tamen ingeniosissimisque viris tanti aestimata sunt, ut id unum caput caeteris omnibus totius libri praetulerint, quidam etiam memoriter verbotenus didicerint. Verum ii erant ex eorum numero, qui res Divinas serio & reverenter tractandas, minime vero irridendas esse credebant.
units.tr: (a) Bibl. p. 418. and into the contemplation of one's principle. You ought to have said that my Metaphysics explains certain things concerning the divine which can indeed be well conceived in an ideal way, but which no one can vividly experience in himself, unless God, our principle, reveals himself to him in that manner which is now dark to us. This is what I noted in passing, which the Mystics call being admitted into the divine darkness and into the contemplation of one's principle (not the principle of God, as you wrongly understand it). And no metaphysician has failed to say similar things. For when they demonstrate, for example, that supreme happiness consists in the contemplation of God, anyone can grasp this; but they will confess that no one can experience this itself by sense without a supernatural operation of God, which is obscure and dark to us now. So in my Rational Thoughts I occupied a whole chapter with the divine Eternity, and our participation in it. The force of these demonstrations can easily be perceived ideally, but the living experience of the thing itself cannot, as I noted there, unless the Best Mind, which sustains us, is pleased to join itself to us according to the fullness of our thought, and the things that follow in that chapter. Although these things are now obscure to our experience, great and most ingenious men have esteemed them so highly that they preferred that one chapter to all the others of the whole book, and some even learned it by heart, word for word. But these were among those who believed that divine matters ought to be treated seriously and reverently, and by no means to be mocked.

units.la: §. Facultatum duas dedi definitiones: unam rei (a), quam dixi explicatione indigere, utpote naturam rei indigitantem; alteram nominis, ut quivis sciret quid per nomen facultatis indigitarem, dixitque (b)nomen facultatis perinde mihi esse ac potentiam faciendi sive agendi, & latius (c) capacitatem agendi & recipiendi seu patiendi. Tu vero, (d) quando lectori spem fecisti me ostensurum quid facultas, & quo sensu HOC VOCABULUM sit recipiendum, omittis nominalem definitionem ad captum omnium claram; & realem solam, explicatione destitutam, adeoque obscuram, adfers, ut lectoribus, quibus spes claritatis facta est, inexspectatam pro ea reperientibus obscuritatem, risum moveas, eadem scilicet arte tua vel simili qua gesticulatores quaedam praesentia faciunt dextera agilitate disparere & inexspectata apparere, ut spectatores histrionico hoc agendi modo ad risum concitentur. Et quemadmodum histriones, quando credunt ejusmodi spectacula spectatoribus esse arrisura, ea saepius repetunt; sic tu objecta Mystica hinc inde ex scena tua etiam producis; sed toties, ut ista tua histrionica tandem fiat prosecto nauseabunda.
units.tr: §. I gave two definitions of faculties: one of the thing, which I said needed explanation, as indicating the nature of the thing; the other of the name, so that everyone might know what I meant by the word faculty. I said (b) that the name faculty means to me the same as power of doing or acting, and more broadly (c) capacity of acting and of receiving or suffering. But you, (d) when you gave the reader hope that I would show what a faculty is and in what sense THIS WORD is to be taken, omit the nominal definition, which is clear to all, and bring forward only the real definition, lacking explanation and therefore obscure, so that you may move your readers to laughter, since they find, instead of the clarity they were promised, an unexpected obscurity; by the same art, or a similar one, as jugglers who by the agility of their right hand make certain things vanish in front of you and appear unexpectedly, so that the spectators are stirred to laughter by this theatrical way of acting. And just as actors, when they believe such shows will make the spectators laugh, repeat them often, so you bring forward mystical objects from your stage here and there; but so often that your theatrical tricks at last become truly nauseating.

units.la: 4. Eadem arte ludicra, postquam lectores ad serium & sublime quid a me audiendum de divinitate animae praeparasti, subito introducis me quasi me ipsum nomine proprio & titulo Domini interrogantem; deinde mox, me omisso, caeteris velut ex coelo delapsis, nec interrogantibus, respondentem; omnia modis perriculis, quos in meo opere nemo reperiet, sed tantum difficultatem a lectoribus sibi ipsis proposipositam : quam ut absurdam esse ostendam, removeo eodem omnino responso quo Philosophus Claubergius eam ipsam velut responsione alia indignam rejectabat; Mirum homines doctos scurrandi studio adeo excaecari, ut non videant se, dum omnia mimicis vestibus induere gestiunt, cum Histrionum sartoribus de artificio certare.
units.tr: 4. By the same playful art, after you have prepared the readers to hear from me something serious and lofty concerning the divinity of the soul, you suddenly introduce me as if I were questioning myself by my own name and title of Lord; then soon after, leaving me out, and the others as if fallen from heaven, who do not ask, you answer; all with ways and perils that no one will find in my work, but only with a difficulty that you have proposed to your readers yourself. To show that this is absurd, I dismiss it with the very same answer by which the philosopher Clauberg rejected that same difficulty as unworthy of another answer. It is strange how learned men, in their eagerness for buffoonery, become so blinded that they do not see that, while they strive to put on all the costumes of mimes, they are competing with the tailors of actors on the art of costume.

units.la: §. Sed interim non pauca feria & bene satis relata quandoque interponis, unde etiam Lectorum mentes iis seriis aliquamdiu detentae, eo sapidius deinde affici possint lepidis tuis jocis mysticis hinc inde recurrentibus, quorum uno praemisso pergis postea 1. Esse in Divinitate aeterne Trinitatem adorandam, quae vocibus Patris, Filii sive Verbi, & Spiritus S. in Scripturis designatur. 2. Eam esse quidem, non minus quam omnia quae in Deo sunt, incomprehensibilem finito intellectui nostro; attamen id quod de ea pro modulo nostro concipimus inadaequatissime; hoc esse, quod Pater sit sui fruendi desiderium Divinitati essentiale; Filius imago viva & lux Divinitatis; Spiritus vero sanctus, Amor ejus, fruitionisque laetitia & acquiescentia essentialis. Haec si renuant Socviniani admittere, eo ipso ostendent, se ab eo quod ego de SS. Trinitate sentio & explicui (quæ hæc ipsa sunt) dissentire. Si vero hæc admittant, tibi & illis gratulabor: neque tamen ii omnino erunt innocentes aut excusandi, quod SS. Trinitatem prius ideo negaverint, quod illa eis clare satis non fuerit explicita; quam si vidissent uti nunc proponitur expositam, non utique negare voluissent. Etenim aliquando Deus de operibus suis aut de se ipso quædam obscurius revelat hominibus, tum ut hi id ei honoris deferant quod veracibus solemus, eis credendo de non visis; tum etiam ut tenuitatis intellectus conscii, nobisque diffidentes, humiliemur continuo, petamusque ab ejus ope & lumine dilucidationem necessariam obscurorum. Jam si nonnulli ex superba cæcitate, primo nolint ad Dei operationem lucemque petendam recurrere; sed eas irridentes, suoque intellectui veluti sibi sufficienti audacter confisi, nolint, secundo, admittere res revelatas, eo quod misero intellectui suo, ipsas suis viribus comprehendere nitenti, videantur repugnantes; sique, tertio, intellectus sui corrupti opera, pro Creatore creaturas substituere haud verentur (veluti Socinani, qui ita tria committunt, & pro Spiritu S. creaturas aut dona Dei creata supponunt;) illine extra culpam fuerint, si, quando diceret illis Deus, Ecce, quæ ex superbia non vultis a gratia mea postulare; quæ de me rejicitis, quia ea superbus vester intellectus sibique confisus non capit; & in quorum locum creaturas substituistis: illa ipsa sunt quæ si aliis terminis modisque vobis explicantur, ita de eorum veritate
units.tr: §. Meanwhile, however, you sometimes interpose not a few playful and fairly well-told passages, so that the minds of the readers, held for a while by those serious matters, may then be the more agreeably affected by your witty mystical jokes, which recur here and there. Having premised one of these, you go on: 1. That the Trinity is to be adored in the Divinity eternally, which is designated in Scripture by the names of the Father, the Son or Word, and the Holy Spirit. 2. That this Trinity is indeed, no less than all the things that are in God, incomprehensible to our finite intellect; yet what we conceive of it according to our measure is most inadequate: that the Father is the desire of enjoying himself, essential to the Divinity; the Son is the living image and light of the Divinity; and the Holy Spirit is his love, and the essential joy and acquiescence of enjoyment. If the Socinians refuse to admit these things, they will by that very fact show that they dissent from what I think and have explained concerning the Holy Trinity (which are these very things). But if they admit them, I shall congratulate you and them; yet they will by no means be wholly innocent or excusable, for having previously denied the Holy Trinity on the ground that it was not explained clearly enough to them; for if they had seen it set forth as it is now proposed, they would certainly not have wished to deny it. For at times God reveals certain things more obscurely to men, about his works or about himself: partly so that they may give him the honour we customarily give to truthful persons, by believing him about things not seen; and partly so that, being conscious of the smallness of their understanding and distrustful of themselves, they may be continually humbled, and may seek from his help and light the necessary clarification of obscure things. Now if some, from proud blindness, first will not have recourse to seeking God's operation and light, but mocking these, and boldly trusting in their own intellect as if sufficient to itself, will not, second, admit the revealed things because they seem contradictory to their wretched intellect, which strives to comprehend them by its own powers; and if, third, they do not hesitate, by the work of their corrupted intellect, to substitute creatures for the Creator (as the Socinians do, who commit these three faults together, and put in place of the Holy Spirit creatures or created gifts of God), they will be outside of fault if, when God says to them, "Behold, you do not wish to ask from my grace what you reject out of pride concerning me, because your proud intellect, trusting in itself, does not grasp it; and you have substituted creatures in its place: these are the very things which, if they are explained to you in other terms and ways, you will judge by their truth so convinced of them with everyone else that you cannot reject them." I say, if they have at last believed these latter things, have they therefore been without fault of pride, unbelief, and either idolatry, or injury to God or to the divine things for which they substituted created things?

units.la: / tate vos cum omnibus sentietis convictos, ut ea rejicere non possitis. Illi, inquam, fi jam demum haec ultima crediderint, fuerintne idcirco prius sine culpa superbiae, incredulitatis, & seu idololatriae, seu injuriae in Deum aut divina, pro quibus creata substituerunt? Hoc ipsemet jam judica, & Socinianis applica, quorum primarium praecipuumque malum non tam est in eo quod multa mysteria negent, quam in hoc, quod corruptione sua dissimulata, viribusque rationis corruptae confisi, ab ea, non ab operatione Dei gratiosa, sua exspectant lumina.
units.tr: ...truth, you will with everyone feel convinced of them, so that you cannot reject them. Those, I say, if they have at last believed these final things, have they therefore been free beforehand from the fault of pride, of unbelief, and of either idolatry or injury against God, for the sake of which they put created things in place of these? Judge this yourself, and apply it to the Socinians, whose chief and foremost evil is not so much that they deny many mysteries, as that, dissembling their corruption and trusting in the powers of corrupted reason, they look for their light from that source, and not from the gracious operation of God.

units.la: 6. Non movebor iis quae a me de libertate dicta, pro tua arte perhibes (a) partim mystica esse (hoc est, tibi incognita & antipelagiana, ) partim ab aliis dudum prolata. Cartesio aliquando objectum est, nil adeo novi esse, quod diceret se cogitare: hoc omnes dudum etiam scivisse & dixisse. Is respondebat ita quidem rem esse: at ante eum negabat fuisse observatum, hoc ipsum esse philosophandi principium, ex eo omnia deduci posse, idque se praestitisse. Qui opus meum attente legent, videbunt ex iis quae explicui de libertate, sequi, explicari, solvi omnia, quae gratiam, praedestinationem, justitiam Dei, modosque omnes ejus cum hominibus agendi, concernunt: quae ab aliis hactenus dicta, ea generaliora, obscuriora, minus evoluta, adeoque ad effectus dictos fere inutilia fuisse; non sic ea quae penitius proposui, & ad nodos proinsolubilibus habitos, primus, quod sciam, cum successu application plicui: nec vereor dicere, libertatem si explicuissent ea, qua ego, ratione (praesertim à pag. 510 ad 520, ) nullum Pelagianismum, nullam de gratia haerefin, unquam ausam fuisse caput extollere. Haec me tua censura coactum oportet profiteri simulque monere, ut, quoniam saepius pronunciare gestis quaedam dicta mea jam prius ab aliis esse dicta, tua, si placet, inspicias, videasque an, si quae ex aliis, saepe illaudatis, surripuisti, abessent; Æsopicae corniculae non renovaretur magna ex parte fabula.
units.tr: 6. I will not be moved by what you call, with your usual skill, things said by me about liberty, which are partly mystical (that is, unknown to you and anti-Pelagian) and partly put forward long ago by others. It was once objected to Descartes that there was nothing so new in his saying "I think"; that everyone had long known and said this. He replied that it was indeed so, but that before him no one had observed that this very thing is the principle of philosophy, from which everything can be deduced, and that he had accomplished this. Those who read my work attentively will see from what I have explained about liberty that everything which concerns grace, predestination, the justice of God and all his ways of dealing with men follows, is explained and is solved. Others have hitherto said these things in more general, obscure and less developed terms, and so they were almost useless for the effects mentioned. It is not so with those points which I have set out more deeply, and which were held to be knots not to be untied; these, as far as I know, I was the first to unfold successfully by application. Nor do I fear to say that if they had explained liberty by the reasoning I used (especially from page 510 to 520), no Pelagianism and no heresy about grace would ever have dared to raise its head. Your censure compels me to declare this, and at the same time to advise you: since you often announce that certain of my sayings were already said by others, you should, if you please, look into your own work, and see whether, if the things you have taken from others, often without praise, were removed, the fable of the Aesopian jackdaw would not largely be renewed.

units.la: 7. Nescio, unde asseveres, hominem rectum (a) potuisse, mea sententia, formare vi imaginationis suae corpus aliud, corpori suo simile: quando tantum mea mens est, imaginationem ad ejusmodi formationem non concurrere nisi ut causam sociam & incompletam. Dubito etiam an excitandi risus gratia (quia alioqui materiam de familiaritate cum Deo ludibrio habes) (b) retuleris me scripsisse, inutiliter laborari in detectione naturae quamdiu quis familiaritatem cum Deo non recuperavit: cognosci ideo oportere Divinitatis interiora. Certe Divinitatis interiora, cogitata, ideæ, sunt rerum causæ & efficientes & exemplares; adeoque ut res effectæ per causas cognoscantur, debent per notitias eorum, quæ in Deo sunt, cognosci: hæc autem, Deo ipsa non communicante, assequi neminem posse clarius est, quam ut pluribus verbis egeat.
units.tr: 7. I do not know from where you get the assertion that a righteous man could, in my opinion, by the power of his imagination form another body like his own; for my view is that the imagination contributes to such a formation only as a partial and incomplete cause. I also doubt whether you have reported, for the sake of raising laughter (since otherwise you make a mockery of the matter of familiarity with God), that I wrote that labour in discovering nature is wasted as long as someone has not recovered familiarity with God, and that therefore the inner things of the Divinity must be known. Certainly the inner things of the Divinity, that is, his thoughts and ideas, are the causes of things, both efficient and exemplary; so, for things made to be known through their causes, they must be known through the knowledge of those things which are in God. And that no one can attain this knowledge unless God himself imparts it is clearer than that it needs many words.

units.la: 8. Quando refers(c) me ex vita & visione aliqua S. Teresiæ describere rerum lucem cem primævam, ut ejusmodi allegatio & philosophis & Protestantibus apparear ridicula, omittis indicare, hoc (antea ex attributis Dei deductum) à me ibi confirmari per octo aut decem Scripturæ sacræ testimonia, quibus illustrationis gratia verba S. Teresiæ adjunxi, credens satius esse, res divinas simili sanctæ mentis testimonio illustrare, quam velle Scripturam sacram e Virgilio, Horatio, Martiali & Ovidio similibusque Criticorum Oraculis dilucidare.
units.tr: 8. When you report that I describe from the life and a certain vision of St Teresa the primal light of things, so that such an allegation may seem ridiculous both to philosophers and to Protestants, you omit to mention that this point (previously deduced from the attributes of God) was confirmed by me there by eight or ten testimonies of holy Scripture, to which I added the words of St Teresa by way of illustration. I believed it better to illustrate divine things by the similar testimony of a holy mind than to wish to explain holy Scripture from Virgil, Horace, Martial and Ovid and the like oracles of the critics.

units.la: De Articulo quodam præfationis Tomi V Bibliothecæ Universalis, & de eo quod in Tomo seq. me dicit Enthusiasten.
units.tr: On a certain article in the preface to Volume V of the Bibliotheca Universalis, and on what you call me an Enthusiast in the following volume.

units.la: Cætera ne longior fiam prætereo, illustraturus monitum quod Bibliothecæ tuæ Tomo V præfixisti, ubi conscius te justam conquerendi causam dedisse, tum pervertendo sensum, tum omittendo multa necessaria in relatione tua, utrumque conaris excusationibus frivolis prævenire. Et primum quidem, inculcando te forte non bene satis intelligere potuisse nonnullos auctores, quibus propterea affricas confusas ideas, quando meæ aliis, te intelligentioribus, sunt clarissimæ; enunciationes incommodas, quæ aliis & tibi ipsi alicubi sunt valde emphaticæ; inutilitatem parenthesium, quæ tamen utilissimæ sunt, ne respectus quispiam ad ea quæ tractantur necessarius, oblivioni tradatur; ratiocinationes inordinatas, cum tamen Opus totum fit ratiocinationum concatenatio ordine continuo procedens; æquivocam vocum usurpationem, quando e contextus infpeciione indubitatus vocum sensus patet; linguæ propriæ semi-ignorantiam, cum non minus atque tu subtilantiam ejus intelligant, quanquam grammaticas, criticas & syllabicas minutias, ipsis forte non ignotas, etsi non usu tritas, observare non curent, veluti tu, qui ad ista magis attendis quam ad solidiora, & ad ea quæ de aliquo Augustinus: (a) Faustus, magnus laqueus Diaboli, & multi implicabantur in eo per illecebram suaviloquentiæ: quam ego jam tametsi laudabam, discernebam tamen a veritate rerum, quantum dijcendatum avidus eram. Nec quali vasculo sermonis, sed quid mihi scientiæ comedendum apponeret, intuebar. Verus linguæ usus est magnalia & laudabilia Dei & salutaria proximis simpliciter ex bono corde proferre; non autem operam dare, ut omissis parenthesibus, servato vocularum severiore ordine, loco, sono, fucis minutiisque nugacibus, aures delicatulorum prurientes demulceri possint modis amori proprio gratis, & qui idolo superbiæ nostræ eloquentium virorum vanam gloriolam acquirant. Ita ut ex prætensis horum in observationibus, & pedaneis grammaticaliorum futilitatibus nec possis prætexere obscuritatem, nec causam necessariam obscura per verso sensu referendi: siquidem in eloquentissimos & nitidissimæ elocutionis Auctores, iisdem artibus agas, ut videbimus: & Ill. Episcopi Meldunensis de SS. Trinitate quædam egregia eo styli nitore, ea perfpicuitate, ut nil supra, enunciantis, Orationem nomines (a) semel atque iterum du galimathias, confusam barbaramque vocum congeriem; rem autem ipsam, chimæras. Veriores cur bis modis agas causas, cum generaliores tum fpecialiores, superius commonstravi; ut & causas obscuritatis materiæ, quando dixi illos, qui ægritudine dissimulata, viribusque propriis confifi ad Deum non recurrunt, nec opem ejus internam deprecantur, esse rebus spiritualibus percipiendis omnino ineptos. Quid vero causæ erat, cur cum in istis vel re fatente nil intelligeres (prout longe est certiffimum) in Socium tuum, onus articuli istius componendi non devolveres? An fufpicandum est te timuisse ne ille pro voto tuo non irrideret, sed commendaret quæ tibi erant adeo invisa? Aut vero cur in Opere meo legendo non sequebaris Præfationem monentem, ut, quibus hæc difficilia viderentur, ab ultimis tomis ordine retrogrado lectionem instituerent? Etsi nunc experientia edoctus, video & commendarum optem minus intelligentibus, ut a tertio vel quarto tomo incipientes pergant ad finem Operis; & tunc demum ad præteremiffos tres fi fe accingant, tuas de obscuritate querelas suis non comprobabunt.
units.tr: I pass over the rest, so as not to run on too long, and will address the notice you prefixed to Volume V of your Bibliotheca. There, aware that you have given a just cause for complaint, by both perverting the sense and omitting much that was necessary in your report, you try to forestall both charges with frivolous excuses. First, by insisting that you perhaps did not understand some authors well enough, you charge them with confused ideas, though to others who understand better than you my ideas are most clear; with awkward statements, which are, to others and even at times to yourself, very emphatic; with the uselessness of parentheses, which are nonetheless most useful, lest some reference necessary to the matters treated be consigned to oblivion; with disordered reasoning, though the whole work is a chain of arguments proceeding in continuous order; with ambiguous use of words, when the undoubted sense of the words is plain from the context; with half-ignorance of their own language, when they understand its subtleties no less than you do, although they may not care to observe grammatical, critical and syllabic trifles, which are perhaps not unknown to them though not commonly used, as you do, who attend to these more than to weightier matters. Augustine says of a certain man: (a) Faustus, a great snare of the devil, and many were entangled in him through the enticement of his smooth speech. This I, though I already praised it, nevertheless distinguished from the truth of things, so eager was I to learn. Nor did I look at what vessel of speech it was, but at what knowledge he set before me to feed on. The true use of language is simply to utter from a good heart the great and praiseworthy works of God and what is salutary to one's neighbours; it is not to labour, by leaving out parentheses, keeping a strict order of little words, and by polish, colour and idle trifles, to soothe the itching ears of the fastidious in ways pleasing to self-love, and to win for the idol of our pride a vain little glory as eloquent men. So from the pretended observations of these men and their pedantic grammatical futilities you can neither pretend obscurity nor refer a necessary cause of obscurity to a perverted sense. For you will treat in the same way the most eloquent and most elegant writers, as we shall see; and of the most illustrious Bishop of Meaux's excellent passages on the Holy Trinity, written with such brilliance of style and such clarity that nothing beyond it could be said of the speaker's oration, you once and again call it du galimathias, a confused and barbarous heap of words, and the thing itself chimeras. I have already shown above why you use these two kinds of cause, both general and more specific; and also the causes of obscurity in the matter itself, when I said that those who, dissembling their sickness and trusting in their own strength, do not return to God or seek his inward aid, are wholly unfit to perceive spiritual things. But what reason was there, when you did not understand these things (as is most certainly the case, even by your own admission), for not handing over the burden of composing that article to your associate? Are we to suspect that you feared he would not mock what you found so hateful, but would commend it? Or again, why, in reading my work, did you not follow the preface, which advises that those to whom these things seem difficult should begin reading from the last volumes and go backwards? Now, however, taught by experience, I see that I may advise those less learned to begin from the third or fourth volume and proceed to the end of the Work, and only then to take up the three previously passed over; and then they will not confirm your complaints of obscurity.

units.la: Nec minus invalide tuas suppressiones excusas, tum paucitate pagellarum fcriptioni tuæ destinatarum; quod, fi aliquid, certe ridiculum est: (ne dicam pauciroribus paginis & plura & integriora tractari potuisse. ceu experimento in Novellis Reip. literariæ fidem feci }-tum numerando eos qui de te conqueri possent, inter eruditos inhabiles, literis, lectura, notitia rerum mundi destitutos, aliter opinione sua ac cæteri cogitantes, & imaginata sua veluti lumina sibi solis COELITUS infusa habentes. Quæ omnia, etiamsi vera essent, nil tamen ad rem faciunt: non minus enim talium scripta fideliter & sine truncatione sunt referenda, quam scripta Doctissimorum Criticorum, qui omnia legerunt, exceptis iis quæ legere oportuisset; & qui omnia sciunt, exceptis iis quæ scire oporteret, quique ipsi errores suos sibi proprios valdeque exitiales appellant(a) lumina sibi a Deo data,& admirabilia media quibus providentia Dei utitur ad alios ab erroribus revocandos. Quod me inter minus eruditos subinnuas, non modo non displicet; sed & vere & sincere profiteor, me Solidæ Eruditionis necdum verum adhuc esse discipulum: solum ut a miserationibus & gratia Dei ad illius verum discipulatum disponat & assumar, precibus enixe contendere animus est. Eruditionem autem tuam, omnibus exceptionibus tuis, sententia quidem tua majorem, tibi non invideo. Equidem quid de ea sentiam, jam nil opus est me hic edicere; at precor tantum Deum, utrab illa me & quosvis bonos præserver in æternum. Quid mihi sit legendum aut ex rebus mundi cognoscendum, non quæram ex iis Criticis, qui nesciunt satius esse paucos libros originarios & solidos legere, & paucos unioneslapidesque pretiosos servare, aut etiam sæpius secum intus in intimis animæ recessibus sine omni apparatu externo vera & solida quærere & intueri, quam extus infinitas interpolationes & quisquilias coacervare atque immensos siliquarum acervos infatiabiliter devorare.
units.tr: Your omissions are excused no less feebly, both by the small number of pages destined for your writing, which, if anything, is certainly ridiculous (not to say that more and fuller matters could have been treated in fewer pages, as I proved by experiment in the Novellae Reipublicae Literariae), and by your counting among those who might complain of you learned men unskilled in letters, reading, and knowledge of the world's affairs, thinking otherwise in their opinion than the rest, and having their own imagined lights as if they alone had them poured in from HEAVEN. All these things, even if true, have nothing to do with the matter: the writings of such people must be cited faithfully and without truncation, no less than those of the most learned critics, who have read everything except what they ought to have read, and who know everything except what they ought to know, and who themselves call their own very destructive errors (a) lights given to them by God, and admirable means by which the providence of God uses to call others back from errors. That you hint I am among the less learned not only does not displease me, but I truly and sincerely profess that I am not yet a true disciple of solid learning; I earnestly strive in prayer only that God, through his mercies and grace, may dispose and receive me as his true disciple. Your learning, with all your exceptions, which is indeed greater in your own opinion, I do not begrudge you. As to what I think of it, there is no need for me to declare it here; I only pray God that he preserve me and all good men from it for ever. What I ought to read, or what I should learn of the world's affairs, I shall not ask of those critics who do not know that it is better to read a few original and solid books, and to keep a few pearls and precious stones, or even often to seek and behold the true and solid within the inner recesses of the soul, without any external apparatus, than to heap up infinite outward interpolations and trifles and to devour insatiably immense heaps of husks.

units.la: Quam legem si observasses, omnibus tuis magnis Episcopiis & Curcellæis, illustribus Hammondis, incomparabilibus Grotiis, Polonorum fratrum Bibliothecis immanibus innumerisque ejusmodi prætulisses vel unius vestratis Hermanni Herberti aurea opuscula, tibi, tanto Lectori, ne quidem, quantum conjicere possum, adhuc vel visa; etsi ab eo viro omne, quicquid primi Remonstrantes boni habuerunt, ita desumserint, ut sine eo suissetis nulli : quanquam nunc admirabilis hujus viri, primariæque originis vestræ, non modo quasi nescii & immemores, sed & ejus vere divinorum scriptorum & principiorum defensores & adversarii plerique videmini. Hunc solum si tu, Domine, qui de curiosa eorum cognitione quæ in toto orbe & gesta & chartis illita sunt, etsi ad vos nequaquam pertinentia, videris gloriari, dum proxima tamen, dum interna, dum maxime domestica atque necessaria respuere videris; hunc solum, inquam, si cæteris prætermissis vertisses in succum & sanguinem, nec te sane pœniteret olim, & verò nunc videre potis esses, vel una unius solida lectione plus profici quam infinitorum sutilium continua absorptione. Quemadmodum enim terra quotidie multifariis seminibus consita nil solidi producere potest, sic
units.tr: If you had observed this rule, you would have preferred, to all your great Episcopii and Curcellaeus, the illustrious Hammond, the incomparable Grotius, the huge and innumerable libraries of the Polish Brethren, and suchlike, the golden little works of one of your own, Hermann Herbert, which, as far as I can conjecture, you have not even seen, a man from whom the early Remonstrants took everything good they had, so that without him they would have been nothing. Yet now you and most of you seem not only as if ignorant and forgetful of this admirable man, the primary source of your own movement, but even opponents of him and of his truly divine writings and principles. If you, Sir, who seem to boast of the curious knowledge of those things done and written across the whole world, though they in no way concern you, yet seem to reject what is near, what is inward, what is especially domestic and necessary, had, with everything else set aside, turned this one man into juice and blood, you would not, I think, have regretted it at any time, and you could now see that one solid reading of his alone profits more than the continual swallowing of infinite trifles. For just as the earth, sown every day with many kinds of seed, can produce nothing solid, so

units.la: anima mille recularum farraginibus quoridie conspersa nil eruditionis solidæ productura est unquam: hæc enim paucissima lectione, copiosiore meditatione, amplissima vero atque continua oratione & praxi, nec non in secessu & separatione a vanis ideis & rebus mundi acquirenda est. Sufficit ejus discipulo de mundo ut sciat, id omne quicquid in eo est, esse (a) concupiscentiam oculorum, concupiscentiam carnis, & superbiam vitæ, & hæc perire cum illis qui ea magni faciunt & concupiscunt, dum qui bene studuit ut solum Deum & se cognosceret in Christo, permanebit in æternum, etsi ad tempus ludibrio habitus ab inflatis mundanæ sapientiæ tympanis, quorum mentes vano ære chimæarum, nugarum atque quisquiliarum periturarum repleri gestiunt; ut ut plenæ fieri possint Spiritu Christi æterno, id Judos suos faciant, & pro Enthusiasmo irridçnt, quem mihi a nonnullo disputatore fuisse impactum, ipse in Bibliotheca tuæ Tomo post quintum nescio jam quo, lætus, in medium adducis, nec non & in operis indiculo sollicite annotas Poiretum Philosophum Enthusiastem juxta τὸν ἕνα. At pro tua in excerpendis fide omittis addere istius a me hic non nominandi antagonistam, cujus etiam libri responsorii contenta refers, illi respondisse, Poiretum unum in Philosophicis, de quibus erat quæstio, vel quindecim similibus illius ∑ ἕνα esse præferendum: quod tuum illum Philosophicum Enthusiasmum, quo mihi insultare coram gaudebas, nec non tua ejus publicatione curare, utab omnibus talis habeier (in quo te'jam Hamburgenses quosdam giaculos efle imitatos audio} deflruxiflet. Ego sane fi pulcherrimos titulos qui tibi a quam plurimis tributi sunt, colligere vellem, quot quaeso paginas iflis encomiis non replerem? Sed viles animas esse exiflimo, quae sordes ab aliis didtas resumere & recoquere satagunt. Atque ut scias quam parum tuae ifli recoctioni veritatis subsit, confidenter te provoco ut mihi designes vel unum, qui quam exactius & firmius, atque ego, Enthusiasmum omnem profligaverit a Philosophia, necnon Enthufiafmum fanaticum a Theologia. Haud ignoras Philosophos quosdam, praecipue modernos, omnem actum naturalem voluisse pro Dei actu immediato habere; rationem humanam, ejusque ideas, imo extensionem & figuras oculis perceptas, efle ipsum Deum, ejus lumen essentiale, ejusque substantiam; & per illa nos cum Deo ipso commercium habere, & vero fuaviflima colloquia miscere, quae integris libris meditationum prodiderunt, & plura similia, quae verus Philofophicus Enthusiasmus merentur dici, quaeque ego a fundamentis in Oeconomiae libro primo, a te lecto, nec non in Differtatione praeliminari Cogitationum de Deo, Editionis fecundae, sic everti, ut demonstraverim rationem sensusque nunquam eo pervenire posse, ut cum Deo ipso commercium habeant; sed tantum cum ejus pictouris & imaginibus, quae sunt ex genere rerum creatarum. In Oeconomiae vero Coo-
units.tr: the soul, sprinkled every day with a thousand mixed heaps of novels, will never produce any solid learning. For this is to be acquired by very little reading, by fuller meditation, by ample and continual prayer and practice, and also in withdrawal and separation from vain ideas and the things of the world. It is enough for his disciple to know of the world that all that is in it is the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and the pride of life [1 John 2:16], and that these perish together with those who esteem and desire them; while he who has striven well to know God alone and himself in Christ will remain for ever, even though for a time he is mocked by the puffed-up drums of worldly wisdom, whose minds are eager to be filled with the empty wind of chimeras, idle things and trifles that will perish. However full they may become of the eternal Spirit of Christ, they make it their sport and mock it as Enthusiasm, which, as you now bring forward, with glee, in the midst of your Bibliotheca after the fifth volume (I know not where), was thrown at me by some disputant; and in the index of the work you carefully note that Poiret the Philosopher is an Enthusiast according to [τὸν ἕνα]. But with your usual faithfulness in excerpting, you omit to add the name of the antagonist of mine, whom I shall not name here, whose response you also report, saying that Poiret, in the philosophical matters under dispute, is to be preferred to fifteen like [ὁ ἕνα]. You did this so that your philosophical Enthusiasm, with which you rejoiced to insult me in public, and by your publication of it, might be taken by everyone as such, and would have destroyed me (in which, as I hear, some Hamburg men have already imitated your darts). If I wished to collect the most splendid titles that have been bestowed on you by very many people, pray, how many pages would I not fill with those eulogies? But I think those are base souls who labour to take up again and reheat the filth cast out by others. And so that you may know how little truth there is in this reheating of yours, I confidently challenge you to point out to me even one who has more exactly and firmly than I refuted all Enthusiasm from Philosophy, and fanatical Enthusiasm from Theology. You are not unaware that some philosophers, especially modern ones, have wished to regard every natural act as an immediate act of God; to hold that human reason and its ideas, indeed extension and figures perceived by the eyes, are God himself, his essential light and his substance; and that through these we have fellowship with God himself and mingle the sweetest conversations with him, which they have set out in whole books of meditations, and many similar things that truly deserve to be called Philosophical Enthusiasm. I have overturned these from the foundations, in the first book of the Oeconomia, which you have read, and in the preliminary dissertation of the second edition of the Cogitationes de Deo, so as to show that reason and the senses can never come to have fellowship with God himself, but only with his picture and images, which belong to the kind of created things. In chapter IX of the second part of the Oeconomia I have vindicated theology and Christianity from fanatical Enthusiasm in such a way that I have shown that those who are not perfectly dead to themselves and to the propensities and motions of corrupt nature ought neither to glory in the indwelling and ruling Spirit of Christ, nor are yet capable of him.

units.la: T perationis Cap. IX. Theologiam & Christianismum a fanatico Enthusiasmo sic vindicavi, ut ollenderim eos, qui perfecte sibi corruptæque naturæ propensionibus & motibus mortui non sunt, de inhabitante & regente Spiritu Christi nec debere gloriari, nec ejus adhuc esse capaces. At vero per purificationem non debere eo a nobis adspirari, nec posse Christianos veios debite & vere fieri Spiritus Christi compotes, neceos esse templum, tabernaculum, domum Dei, Christi, Spiritus Sancti, qui in eis inhabitet, maneat, vivat, regat, doceat, sic ut tandem abundent & pleni sint omni plenitudine Dei, hoc, quod hodierni Pelagiani negant, nisi sim impius & profanus irrisor Dei ejusque promissionum & Scripturæ, cujus hæc sunt verba expressa & promissa, non negavero unquam. Atque si hoc ipsum sit quod per ludibrium appellent Enthusiasmum, idque per hoc verbum mihi exprobrent, ego Christum cum ludibrioso titulo opprobrio crucis expositum, non minus propterea cum titulo illo derisorio, Regem & intimum animarum Rectorem & Dominatorem agnoscam & amplectar, nec pudebit palam profiteri me Spiritus ejus donationem, præsentiam, regimen in me efflagitare & vivide sperare. Etiam, Domine, in te speravi: non confundar in æternum. Veniat super me misericordia tua, Domine; salutare tuum secundum eloquium tuum. Et respondebo exprobrantibus mihi verbum; quia speravi in sermonibus tuis. Da mihi lætitiam in salute tua, & spiritu tuo principali fulci me modo: Tunc
units.tr: In chapter IX of the Oeconomia Cooperationis I defended theology and Christianity against fanatical enthusiasm, showing that those who are not yet dead to themselves, to the propensities and motions of corrupt nature, ought neither to boast of the Spirit of Christ dwelling and ruling within them nor are yet capable of him. But that through purification we ought to aspire to him, that Christians can truly and rightly become possessed of the Spirit of Christ, and that they are to be the temple, tabernacle, and house of God, of Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, who dwells in them, remains, lives, rules, and teaches them, so that at last they are filled with all the fullness of God: this, which the present-day Pelagians deny, I would never deny, unless I were an impious and profane mocker of God, of his promises, and of Scripture, whose express words and promises these are. And if the very thing they mockingly call enthusiasm is what they reproach me with by that word, then I will acknowledge and embrace Christ, who was set forth with a mocking title and the reproach of the cross, as King and inmost Ruler and Lord of souls, no less for that derisive title; nor will I be ashamed to profess openly that I long for and earnestly hope for the gift, the presence, and the rule of his Spirit within me. Yes, Lord, in you I have hoped: let me never be confounded. Let your mercy come upon me, O Lord, your salvation according to your word. And I will answer those who reproach me, for I have trusted in your words. Give me joy in your salvation, and strengthen me with your princely Spirit. Thus far.

units.la: non curabo si Enthusiastis accensear, veluti nec moror an mea haecce verba ab irrisorum gente Deifuga pro Enthusiasmi motibus habeantur. O utinam ejusmodi Enthusiastarum, quorum plenum est coelum, etiam terra esset plena, ut sic fieret voluntas Dei ut in coelo sic & in terra, descenderetque de coelo ad nos a Deo nova Jerusalem parata donis Spiritus Christi, sicut sponsa ornata viro suo, essetque tunc cum hominibus tabernaculum Dei habitantis cum eis, ita ut ipsi populus ejus essent, & ipse Deus, Deus eorum cum illis & omnia in omnibus! qualem tibi statum inter eos, exbenevolo apprecor animo, pro eo, quod me absurdum ab aliis haberi haud benevole velis, perperam ita meos erga te agendi modos non hic modo, sed & alibi compensans, quando (vera loquor nec ficta) apud nonnullos probos, quibus ob quaedam opinione sua irreverentius de rebus divinis & spiritualibus dicta & scripta multum male audiebas, effeci ut meliora de te crederent. Consequentiis enim extremis non esse gravandos quotquot principiis quibusdam errorum foecundis sunt impliciti: atque adeo, exempli causa, si qui Dei gratiam Spiritusque ejus internam operationem & inhabitationem non agnoscant, eos, quamvis Deum veluti inefficacem fingant, Spiritumque Christi sanctum habeant veluti pro mortuo & inerti trunco, qui vel non inhabitet membra corporis Christi, (hoc est, Christianos veros) vel eis non communicet vitam & motum, nilque in eis operationum suarum pro-duducat; non ideo exsistentiam Dei negare nec Spiritus ejus, etsi eam in se negent & a se arceant: quod non illis solis peculiare est, sed commune eis omnibus, qui, quamvis ista ore & judicio confiteantur & approbent, de facto tamen concupiscentiarum impulsibus obsequentes, rejiciunt a se gratiæ atque sancti Spiritus Dei operationes & præsentiam: qui practicus Pelagianismus est & Atheismus, isque generalior, quam ut multi se ab eo excipiant. Qua de causa nos oportet erga errantes agere multo quam soleant clementius; siquidem quæ illi idealiter & per theoriam, ea nos re ipsa & per praxin impugnamus omnes in nobis ipsis, ea propter coram tribunali Dei, juste judicantis, errantibus eo damnabiliores, quo plura quam ipsi theoretica cognovimus. Quæ hic obiter dicere non piget, ne erratorum recensione promoveatur potius errantium contemtus vel odium, quam erga eos dilectionis commiserantis motus, nec non ipsorum propria emendatio: qua quantum inter alios opus habeas, in tuis illis præsertim relationibus quæ sunt de materia cum tuis opinionibus non concordante, aut eas concutiente, postquam id meo exemplo hactenus ostendi, tempus est ut & similia in aliis tum recentioribus tum antiquioribus, dem specimina nonnulla; unde condiscant lectores quam parum tuis testimoniis modisque ab aliorum Scriptis & veritatibus salutaribus pati debeant se abduci.
units.tr: I do not care whether I am counted an enthusiast, nor do I trouble myself over whether these words of mine are taken by the race of mockers, who flee from God, for the motions of enthusiasm. O that the earth too were full of such enthusiasts, of whom heaven is full, so that the will of God would be done on earth as it is in heaven, and the new Jerusalem prepared by God would come down from heaven to us, adorned with the gifts of the Spirit of Christ, as a bride adorned for her husband, and the tabernacle of God would then be with men, dwelling with them, so that they would be his people, and God himself would be with them, their God, and all in all! Such a state among them I pray for from a kindly heart, and in return, since you do not wish me to be taken kindly as absurd by others, I here, and elsewhere too, compensate for my own ways of dealing with you, which were wrongly done. For (I speak the truth, not fiction) I have brought it about, among some upright people by whom you were badly spoken of for certain opinions, which you had expressed rather irreverently about divine and spiritual things, that they came to believe better things of you. For those who are entangled in some fruitful principles of error should not be burdened with the extreme consequences: thus, for example, if some do not acknowledge the grace of God, his inward operation, and his indwelling, and regard the Holy Spirit of Christ as a dead and inert trunk, which either does not dwell in the members of Christ's body (that is, true Christians) or does not impart life and motion to them, and produces no operations of his in them, they do not on that account deny the existence of God, nor of his Spirit, even though they deny them in themselves and shut them out. This is not peculiar to those alone, but common to all who, although they confess and approve these things with their mouth and judgment, yet in fact, yielding to the impulses of their desires, reject from themselves the operations and presence of the grace and Holy Spirit of God. This is practical Pelagianism and atheism, and it is so widespread that many do not exempt themselves from it. For this reason we ought to deal with those who err far more gently than they usually do; since we, in our own selves, by practice and in deed, assail everything that they assail in theory and in speculation, we are therefore the more condemnable before the tribunal of God, who judges justly, the more we have known than they in theory. I do not grudge saying these things in passing here, lest through the recounting of errors contempt or hatred of the erring be promoted rather than the motion of loving and pitying concern for them, and their own correction. How much you need such correction among others, especially in those your accounts which concern a matter not agreeing with your opinions, or shaking them, I have so far shown by my own example; now it is time to give some specimens, both of more recent and of older writers, of the same kind, from which readers may learn how little they ought to allow themselves to be drawn away from the saving truths of others' writings by your testimonies and methods.

units.la: Ostenditur aliquot exemplis, quantum fidei sit habendum Dni (Clerici relationibus.
units.tr: Showing by several examples how much faith is to be placed in the reports of Le Clerc.

units.la: Revera ad aperturam libri apud Bibliopolam forte inspecti, & aliud agenti, occurrerunt exempla, quæ proponam, tria vel quatuor: nec alia volui præterea studio quærere; neque enim credo pluribus ad hoc quod suscepi confirmandum opus esse. a recentioribus lubet facere initium.
units.tr: Indeed, the examples I shall set out, three or four in number, came to hand by chance when I opened a book at the bookseller's while I was busy with something else. I have not wished to seek others beyond these, for I do not think more are needed to confirm what I have undertaken. I will begin with recent writers.

units.la: 1. Scripsit Clarissimus Vir quidam de Religionis Christianæ veritate, ea dictionis nitiditate & perspicuitate, ut si a te male referatur, obscuritatem aut æquivocationem elocutionis, ut supra, præterexere nequeas; ea etiam moderatione, & argumentorum præstantia, ut cum omnes habeat applaudentes, te solum' iniquum nisi ob morofitatem tuam, aut ob sensuum a tuis discordantiam, habere non debuerit. Interim tamen eum (ut soles fere omnes) semel atque iterum adortus es: & prima quidem vice (a) in tali materia ob quam quosvis alios potius quam illum tangere potuisses. Secunda autem, ut ei, Spinozæ objectiones contra (b) Pentateuchi Scriptorem Mosen dispellenti, contradiceres, ut (b) fecisti, sed non impune. Is enim respondit tibi eo modo in libri sui (c) editione altera, ut, quamvis moderatissime agat, non possit tamen non inde eluscere critices tuæ supra modum non solum II. lum incogitantia, absurditas & remeritas; sed, quod hic ad rem facit, mala etiam fides, dum & is (a) conqueritur, te sibi imponere ea quæ sua negat esse, quin etiam te (b) Scripturam sacram, omissis & truncatis inde quæ tibi contraria sunt, allegare, palam ostendit.
units.tr: 1. A certain most distinguished man wrote on the truth of the Christian religion with such brilliance and clarity of style that, even if you report it badly, you cannot hide the obscurity or ambiguity of his expression, as above. He also writes with such moderation and excellence of argument that, though he has all men applauding him, you should have held him unjust only if you were moved by your own peevishness or by disagreement between your opinions and his. Nevertheless you have attacked him, as you do almost everyone, once and again. The first time (a) it was on a subject where you could have touched any other writer rather than him. The second time, you contradicted Spinoza's objections against Moses, the writer of the Pentateuch, as you did, but not with impunity. For he replied to you in the second edition of his book in such a way that, although he behaves most moderately, it cannot but appear that your criticism is excessively full not only of thoughtlessness, absurdity and rashness but, what matters here, of bad faith. He complains (a) that you impute to him things he denies are his, and he plainly shows that you quote Holy Scripture (b) while omitting and cutting away those parts which are contrary to you.

units.la: Sed tu inde infensior factus, non cautior, quando tractatibus prioribus tertium de DIVINITATE JESU CHRISTI publice addidit Clarissimus Auctor, tuque egregii hujus libri Epitomen (c) Bibliothecæ tuæ Universali inserere voluisti; id laudatis artibus tuis sic execu-tus es, ut omnino stupendum sit, te non metuisse ne a lectoribus crederetur scopum tuum esse, hoc unum ipsis dispiciendum relinquere, palmamne præripiat tuis in relationibus faciendis falsitas an malignitas. Non quæram hic, quare tam sæpe infensum te ostendas iis, qui Socinianos errores solide refutant; vel cur illis quibus es infensus te opponas ea ex parte qua Socinianis adversantur: quod admodum imprudenter factum ab homine qui Socinianismi suspectus, nollet eam de se suspicionem confirmare. Neque meum faciam vindicare libri, de quo agitur, contenta a tuæ relationis corruptela. Sed ea tantum obiter annotabo, quæ ad scopum meum, de fide tuis relationibus & artibus habenda, conducunt. Constat illa tua relatio partibus quatuor, in quarum prima invidiam pro gratiis & laudibus auctori debitis suscitare conaris: in altera falsam libro ejus materiam assignas: tertia orthodoxorum sententiam irrisorio & ludibrioso modo proponit: quarta quibusque libri partibus imponit & falsa. Et prima quidem nititur sola comparatiuncula, qua vis eos qui sanam doctrinam proponunt, nec non eos qui falsa & noxia docent dogmata, comparari debere cum duabus pugnantium partibus, quibus & campus & favor utrinque æqualiter patere debeant, alioqui indecorum esse generoso militi cum eo decertare cui non æque ac ipsi favetur, nec defensio æque patet: quando tamen econtra, ex tota Scriptura patet, doctores mendacii, non militibus quibus ita favendum fit; sed seductoribus qui sunt evitandi neque audiendi, aut etiam malarum herbarum seminatoribus, quibus invigilandum ne dum dormitur seminet inimicus, esse potius comparandos. In altera parte, quamvis Auctor expressissime (a) monuerit se de sola Divinitate JESU CHRISTI tractaturum, non autem de ejus incarnatione, (sive unione Divinitatis cum humanitate) neque de SS. Trinitate, quandoquidem de istis soorsim & distincte agi possit; tu tamen (b) illum introducis tanquam alicui Sinensi Philosopho, ut supponis, librum suum offerendo, statum quæstionis (c) explicantem de tribus personis Divinitatis deque unione hypostatica secundæ personæ cum humanitate ‡.Christi: ubi evidentissime omnibus notum facis, te libris, de quibus recenses, materiam & subjecta ad lubitum solere imponere: sed nempe sine hoc jocis qui coram Philosopho Sinæ de Orthodoxorum sententia a te exhiberi debebant, locus non fuisseт. Hoc tertia relationis pars continet, ubi hominem ethnicum (egregium arbitrum rerum spiritualium, quæ, juxta Paulum, homini animali, Spiritum Dei non habenti, stultitia sunt) in Judicem constituis sententiarum orthodoxarum, ad sequentes quæstiones a te reductarum. 1. An in Deo sint tres distinctiones, quarum tamen nulla habetur idea; & inter quas certæ sint relationes, quarum etiam nulla habetur idea? 2. An fecunda ex his distinctionibus incognitis unita fuerit humanitati J. Christi modo pariter incognito? Ubi præter repetitionem materiæ falso suppositæ, nemo non videt, mysteria divina iis modis a te exprimi, qui risum non ethnicis aut profanis solum, sed etiam omnibus aliis moveant. Atqui ut sincere ex Auctoris mente status quæstionis recte fuisset expositus, sic "dicendum erat: An illi qui agnoscunt Deum "esse omnipotentem, incomprehensibilem "& veracem, se vero tenuissimi captus & "ne pili quidem naturam capientis, vermiculos, quique præterea agnoscunt aliquem "librum, puta Scripturarum codicem, esse "a Deo prolatum: non debeant, quando "liber ille testatur Deum ipsum ad nos venisse, eumque esse qui locutus est nobis, "nos docuit, vixitque inter nos cum certo "corpore certaque anima, &c. id ipsum credere, etsi id quomodo factum sit non capiant; an vero id rejicere ea de causa, quod "id non comprehendant? Item de SS. Trinitate, (si de ea fuisset agendi locus) An illi "iidem, inter quos de Dei incomprehensi“bilitate, fui ipsorum captûs tenuitate, Scri-“ pturarumque Divinitate constat, non de“beant, Scripturis testantibus Ternarium “quoddam Sanctum in Deo dari, id ipsum, “etsi non perceptum, credere; aut vero id “negare, & Scripturarum verbis vim inferre, “ideo quod id non comprehendant? Atque hinc certum est vel Sinenses ipsos sententiam dicturos contra omnes quotquot hæc negabunt, postquam de principiis dictis convenerint, maxime vero quando hi negantes fatebuntur se Spiritu Dei præditos non esse, neque se ejus gratia, illuminatione & operatione interna opus habere, dum tamen ille liber, quo nituntur, dicit sine Spiritu Dei ea quæ sunt in Deo concipi non posse, nec non ea sine eodem videri debere non falsa solum, sed & stulta & absurda: quæ ipsissima ratio est, cur isti gratiæ internæ negatores dicant se divina illa mysteria nolle admittere. Sed de hoc articulo satis. In quarta parte relationis, cætera quæ huc nil faciunt ne tangam, ubi Sectionum libri materiam refers speciali is, ter vel quater imponendo inculcas, ad argumentorum vel conclusionum Auctoris agnitionem vel admissionem, debere scilicet pemi veras esse interpretationes Scripturæ ab eo allatas: qua in re eodem prorsus agis modo ac superius, cum dixisti, me promisisse demonstrationes modo supponantur lectores eas cum fide recepturi: aut velut si cui demonstrationes mathematicas offerenti, opponeretur a cavillatore aliquo, agnoscendum utique eas esse veras, modo supponantur bene ex principiis deducta. Atqui hoc non supponitur; sed in ipsis demonstrationibus id continetur & probatur, veluti in argumentis Auctoris Clarissimi non supponitur, sed probatur Scripturarum sensum talem esse atque ab ipso proponitur: quod de substantia totius Operis a me lecti testari possum ita esse.
units.tr: But you, made more hostile by this rather than more cautious, when the most distinguished author publicly added a third treatise on the Divinity of Jesus Christ to his earlier tracts, wished to insert an epitome of this excellent book into your Bibliotheca Universalis. You carried it out with your much-praised skill in such a way that it is truly astonishing you did not fear readers would believe your aim was to leave it to them to discern this one thing: whether falsehood or malice wins the palm in your making of reports. I shall not ask here why you so often show yourself hostile to those who solidly refute Socinian errors, or why you oppose, in that respect, those whom you dislike, insofar as they oppose the Socinians. This was done very imprudently by a man suspected of Socinianism, who would not wish to confirm that suspicion about himself. Nor shall I undertake to vindicate the book in question from the corruption of your report. I shall only note in passing those things which bear on my aim, namely that your reports and tricks deserve belief. Your report has four parts. In the first you try to stir up envy against the author for the praises and thanks owed to him. In the second you assign a false subject-matter to his book. The third presents the orthodox view in a derisive and mocking manner. The fourth imposes falsities on each part of the book. The first rests solely on a small comparison, by which you wish that those who propose sound doctrine, and likewise those who teach false and harmful dogmas, be compared to two fighting sides, to which both the field and favour should be equally open. Otherwise, you say, it would be unbecoming for a noble soldier to fight with one to whom he is not equally favourable and whose defence is not equally open. Yet on the contrary, it is clear from all of Scripture that teachers of lies should be compared not to soldiers, who are to be shown such favour, but to seducers who are to be avoided and not heard, or to sowers of bad seed, against whom one must keep watch lest the enemy sow while men sleep. In the second part, although the author most expressly warned that he would treat only the Divinity of Jesus Christ, and not his incarnation (that is, the union of the Divinity with the humanity), nor the Most Holy Trinity, since these can be dealt with separately and distinctly, you nevertheless (b) introduce him as offering his book to some Chinese philosopher, as you suppose, (c) explaining the state of the question concerning the three persons of the Divinity and the hypostatic union of the second person with the humanity of Christ. There you make it most evident to all that you are accustomed to impose at will the matter and subjects of the books you review. But without this, of course, there would have been no room for the jokes which were to be presented before the Chinese philosopher about the view of the orthodox. This is what the third part of the report contains, where you make a heathen man (an excellent judge of spiritual things, which, according to Paul, are foolishness to the natural man who does not have the Spirit of God) the judge of orthodox opinions on the following questions, which you have reduced to these: 1. Are there in God three distinctions, of which no idea is had, and between which there are certain relations, of which also no idea is had? 2. Was the second of these unknown distinctions united to the humanity of Jesus Christ in a likewise unknown manner? Here, apart from the repetition of a falsely supposed matter, no one fails to see that you express divine mysteries in ways that provoke laughter not only among heathens and the profane but among all others. Yet if the state of the question had been set out rightly according to the author's mind, it should have been put thus: Ought not those who acknowledge that God is omnipotent, incomprehensible and true, and that they themselves are worms of the slenderest capacity, not even able to grasp the nature of a hair, and who further acknowledge that some book, namely the codex of the Scriptures, has been published by God, to believe this very thing? That is, that the book testifies that God himself came to us, and is the one who spoke to us, taught us, and lived among us with a certain body and a certain soul, and so on, even if they do not grasp how this was done. Or ought they rather to reject it for the reason that they do not comprehend it? Likewise concerning the Most Holy Trinity, if there had been occasion to treat it: Ought not those same people, among whom it is agreed that God is incomprehensible, that their capacity is slender, and that the Scriptures are divine, to believe, since the Scriptures testify that a certain holy Triad is given in God, this very thing, even if it is not perceived? Or ought they rather to deny it and do violence to the words of Scripture because they do not comprehend it? Hence it is certain that even the Chinese themselves would give judgment against all who deny these things, once they had agreed on the principles stated, most of all when these deniers confess that they are not endowed with the Spirit of God, nor have need of his grace, illumination and inward working. Yet that book on which they rely says that those things which are in God cannot be conceived without the Spirit of God, and that without the same Spirit they must be seen not only as false but as foolish and absurd. This is precisely the reason why these deniers of inward grace say that they do not wish to admit those divine mysteries. But enough on this article. In the fourth part of the report I shall not touch the other things, which have nothing to do with this. There, as you state the subject-matter of the sections of the book, you insist, repeating it three or four times, on the acknowledgement or admission of the author's arguments or conclusions, namely that the interpretations of Scripture which he brings forward must be granted to be true. In this matter you act in exactly the same way as before, when you said that I had promised demonstrations, provided readers would receive them with faith. Or it is as if, when someone offers mathematical demonstrations, some caviller were to object that they must of course be acknowledged as true, provided they are well deduced from principles. But this is not supposed; rather it is contained and proved within the demonstrations themselves. Just so, in the arguments of the most distinguished author, it is not supposed but proved that the sense of the Scriptures is as he proposes. I can testify that this is so from the substance of the whole work I have read.

units.la: 2. In libro, Entretiens fur diverses matieres de Theologie, cujus partem primam, etsi non a te compositam, ut tamen a te editam & tuis principiis conformem in praefatione approbas, citatur aliquoties (a) Voffius, veluti peccati Originalis probationibus juxta mentem vestram adversans; aut objectionibus quibus id concutiatur, favens: imo exstat (b) Objectio sequens, quam dicitis ab ipso relatam, nec tamen solutam. Adamus suum posteritati peccatum transmittere nequivit nisi tanquam causa aut moralis, aut physica & efficiens: non enim datur medium. Atqui id non potuit, &c. deinde eam excusare conamini (c) a mala fide, quod ita causam suam prodiderit. Quis non credat vobis loca libri citantibus, ubi haec ita reperienda sint? Ego sane ita id esse credideram. Sed mihi aliquando nescio quo casu Voffii librum pervolventi, incidit memoria hujus loci, quem quaesivi, & ecce, reperi non sine admiratione Voffio indigne a vobis imponi. Namque Voffius in loco a vobis citato, tantum abest ut causam suam nil respondendo prodat, ut eam confirmet solide. Insuper specialissime dictum argumentum duobus modis benefovit, expresse dicens: (d) Adam id transmissionem
units.tr: 2. In the book Conversations on Various Matters of Theology, the first part of which you approve in your preface, though you did not write it yourself, and which you say agrees with your principles, Vossius is cited several times as opposing your view of original sin by his proofs, or as favouring objections that shake it. There is even the following objection, which you say is reported by the author himself, yet not answered: Adam could not transmit his sin to posterity except as either a moral or a physical and efficient cause, for no middle course is possible. But he could not do this, etc. Then you try to excuse the author, saying that he betrayed his own cause through bad faith. Who would not believe you when you cite passages of the book where these things are to be found? I certainly believed so. But when I was going through Vossius's book some time ago, by some chance I remembered this passage. I looked for it and found, to my surprise, that Vossius is unjustly misrepresented by you. For in the place you cite, Vossius is so far from betraying his cause by giving no answer that he defends it solidly. Moreover, he supports this very argument in two ways, expressly saying: Adam worked morally toward the transmission of his sin to his posterity, inasmuch as by a moral and free act he merited for himself and his posterity the privation of original righteousness. Although Adam is the cause of original sin directly not physically but only morally, nevertheless he can also be called its physical cause indirectly, inasmuch as he is the real cause of that cause to which the privation of righteousness follows. See how clearly he states in two ways the opposite of what you attributed to him!
