units.la: (d) Voff. Hist. Pelag. lib. II. part. 3. Thef. 1. pag. 221. edit. fec. fionem peccati fui ad posteros) moraliter operari: quatenus nempe per actum moralem ac liberum sibi ac posteris meritus est privationem justitiæ originalis. Quanquam autem Adam directe non physica, sed solum moralis sit originalis peccati causa; tamen indirecte etiam physica ejus causa dici potest, quatenus nempe est realis causa illius causæ ad quam privatio justitiæ consequitur. Ecce, quam aperte duobus modis declaret contrarium ejus quod ipsi attribuebatis!
units.tr: (d) Vossius, Historia Pelagiana, book II, part 3, thesis 1, p. 221, edition of Fecs. ...the transmission of his sin to posterity: moral operation... Adam worked morally, that is, by a moral and free act he merited for himself and his posterity the privation of original righteousness. Although Adam is the cause of original sin directly not physically but only morally, nevertheless he can also be called its physical cause indirectly, inasmuch as he is the real cause of that cause to which the privation of righteousness follows. See how plainly he declares the contrary of what you ascribed to him!

units.la: 3. In dicto tuo libro, nec non passim in aliis, sæpissime tribuitis Ecclesiæ primitivæ, e-jusque Doctoribus, corruptionis nativæ omnium qui nascuntur ignorationem; cujus corruptionis asseverationem Augustino soli (quia forte primus termino peccati originalis usus est, primusque rem ex professo & veluti systematice tractavit) ita adjudicatis, (a) ac si is rem ipsam, incognitam prius, excogitavitset primus: qua in re tam Ecclesiæ primitivæ quam Augustino falsum professo impingitur. Et ne quis de hoc dubitet, legatur, si placet, Vossius in historia Pelagiana, vobis aliquoties citata, (b) ubi is viginti tres paginas testimoniis Veterum Augustino priorum hac de materia replevit ad occasionem & probationem hujus suæ thesæos. Probat hoc dogma Augustinus e scriptis priorum Patrum, quorum luculenta adeo testimonia depromit, (nec minus illustria sunt quæ prætariit) ut plane sit mirandum vel olim fuisse, vel hodie inveniri qui hanc doctrinam Augustini esse commentum putent, atque id porro aliis persuasum velint. Dein postquam huic exprobrationi a Pelagianis Augustino factæ, eum originale peccatum confiteri, Augustinum sic respondentem citasset: Non ego finxi originale peccatum, quod Catholica fides credidit antiquitus; sed tu, qui hoc negas, sine dubio es novus hæreticus; pergit Vossius, & allegat in dicti sidem e Græcis Ignatium, Justinum, Tatianum, Irenæum, Originem, Methodium, Macarios duos, Athanasium, Cyrillum, Basilium, Gregorium Nazianzenum, Isychium, Chrysostomum, nec non ex Augustini coævis aut qui eum secuti sunt aliquot alios: e Latinis autem producit Tertullianum, Cyprianum, Arnobium, Reticium, Olympium, Hilarium, Ambrosium, Optatum Millevitanum, Prudentium, Hilarium diaconum, Hieronymum; quæ agmina hac quæstione Vincentii Lerinensis claudit: Quis unquam ante profanum illum Pelagium tantam virtutem liberi præsumsit arbitrii, ut ad hoc in bonis rebus per actus singulos adjuvandum necessariam Dei gratiam non putaret? Quis ante prodigiosum discipulum ejus Cœlestium reatu prævaricationis Adæ omne genus humanum negavit adstrictum? Interim tamen hæc visa & lecta non impediunt quo minus per te & socios omnibus persuadeatur, (a) nil magis distare a fide totius Ecclesiæ Augustinum præcedentis, quam credere, uti ille, omnes generaliter & æqualiter esse corruptos per peccatum Adæ: eumque esse primum qui hanc doctrinam e Schola Manichæorum in medium produxerit.
units.tr: 3. In your book cited above, and in many other places too, you very often attribute to the primitive Church and its teachers an ignorance of the native corruption of all who are born. You give the assertion of this corruption to Augustine alone (perhaps because he was the first to use the term original sin, and the first to treat the matter expressly and as a system), as though (a) he had himself devised the thing, previously unknown, and was its first inventor. In this you charge both the primitive Church and Augustine with a falsehood. And lest anyone doubt this, let him read, if he likes, Vossius's Pelagian History, which you cite several times, (b) where on the occasion of and in proof of his thesis he fills twenty-three pages with testimonies of the ancients who came before Augustine on this subject. Augustine proves this doctrine from the writings of earlier Fathers, whose clear testimonies he brings forward (and those he passes over are no less illustrious), so that it is truly astonishing that there were once, or are now found, people who think this doctrine of Augustine is an invention and want others to be persuaded of it. Then, after Augustine was reproached by the Pelagians for confessing original sin, Vossius cites his answer: I did not invent original sin, which the Catholic faith has believed from antiquity; but you, who deny it, are without doubt a new heretic. Vossius goes on and, in support of this, cites from the Greeks Ignatius, Justin, Tatian, Irenaeus, Origen, Methodius, the two Macarii, Athanasius, Cyril, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, Hesychius, and Chrysostom, together with several others from Augustine's contemporaries or those who followed him. From the Latins he produces Tertullian, Cyprian, Arnobius, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Ambrose, Optatus of Milevis, Prudentius, Hilary the deacon, and Jerome. He closes this array with the words of Vincent of Lérins on this question: Who before that profane Pelagius ever presumed so much virtue in free will that he did not think the grace of God necessary to help us in each single good act? Who before his prodigious disciple Caelestius denied that the whole human race was bound by the guilt of Adam's transgression? Yet these things, seen and read as they are, do not prevent you and your companions from persuading everyone that (a) nothing is further from the faith of the whole Church than to believe, as Augustine did, that all men are generally and equally corrupted through the sin of Adam; and that Augustine was the first to bring this doctrine into the open from the school of the Manichaeans.

units.la: 4. Similia de gratia Dei necessaria & intus operante (b) tribuis tum Ecclesiæ, quasi hæc eam ante Augustinum ignorasset; tum Augustino veluti qui ejus primus auctor esset: quod quam falso utrisque impositum sit, demonstrat Vossius (a) enarratis in eodem libro quam plurimis Latinorum & Graecorum Patrum testimoniis.
units.tr: 4. You likewise attribute to the Church, as though it had been ignorant of it before Augustine, and to Augustine as though he were its first author, the grace of God that is necessary and works inwardly (b). How falsely this has been charged against both is shown by Vossius, (a) who in the same book sets out a great many testimonies of the Latin and Greek Fathers.

units.la: §. 8. De D. (l. in Sanctiores Patres, Augusti- num praesertim, invectivarum conti- nuarum causis, fide & aequitate; deque genio ejus irrisorio.
units.tr: §. 8. Concerning D. (that he tends to attack the holier Fathers, Augustine above all, with continual invectives, without faith or fairness; and concerning his mocking genius.

units.la: Non jam necesse crediderim plura ut adducam exempla, quibus pateat quantum tibi posthac de aliorum mente aut scriptis referenti credendum sit: ea enim ob copiam taediosa nimis essent; ob superfluitatem vero etiam inutilia. Sed patere, quaeso, ut illustre magni Augustini exemplum, nec taedio nec dispendio futurum adducam, in quo & similia & multo plura peccare gestis quam in aliis quibuscunque, idque modis, ut mihi quidem videtur, omnino inhumanis, quibus sanctissimum Ecclesiae Praesulem, eo quod per ejus doctrinam amor tuus nolterque propriusque superbiaque cordis propria, vulnerentur & impugnentur, atrociter insectaris & exagitas hinc inde in scriptis tuis, atque ludibrio omnium sic exponere satagis, ut passim audiat Manichaeus convertus, a Manichaeismo male fanatus, pessimus Scripturarum interpres, declamator quicquid in buccam venit effluens, jomniator perpetuus, & alia ejusmodi dicteria eoufque insolentiæ grassantia, ut etiam carmina Italica(a)in ejus dedecus dictites: qua quidem occasione tum artes illa tuæ, multis hactenus documentis ostensæ & laudatæ, porro magis magisque apparebunt; tum ego aliquid insuper de irrisoria tua methodo specialius postmodum concionabor. Ita enim moralia & practica, quæ quandoque scriptis meis intersero, interdum soles, ut nosti, irrisorie coram aliis appellare.
units.tr: I do not think it necessary now to bring forward more examples, by which it would be clear how little you may be trusted hereafter when you report the opinions or writings of others. Such examples would be tiresome because of their number, and useless because of their superfluity. But, I beg you, allow me to bring forward the notable example of the great Augustine, which will be neither tedious nor costly. In it you sin in the same way, and far more, than in any other case, and by methods that seem to me wholly inhuman. You fiercely attack and harass the most holy Bishop of the Church, in your writings here and there, because his teaching wounds and assails your love of yourself, your pride, and the pride of your heart. You labour to expose him to the ridicule of all, so that everywhere people hear him called a Manichaean convert, badly infected with Manichaeism, the worst interpreter of Scripture, a ranter who spouts whatever comes into his mouth, a perpetual dreamer, and other such insults rage to this extent. You even publish Italian verses to his shame. On this occasion, those arts of yours, already shown and praised by many proofs, will appear more and more clearly. And I shall later preach somewhat more particularly against your mocking method. For you are accustomed, as you know, to mock aloud before others the moral and practical matters that I sometimes insert into my writings.

units.la: Tria sunt in Augustino quæ palato tuo haud penitus arridēnt: 1. doctrina de corruptione nostra originaria, 2. doctrina de gratiæ divinæ intus operantis necessitate, 3. de hujus gratiæ paucis impertiendæ, aliis vero non dandæ particularitate, ejusque irresistibilitate, sive de prædéstinatione absoluta & particulari: quæ singula nil opus est hic exactius referre. Et quidem horum primum atque alterum amori proprio superboque non posse non esse invisa, nil opusest ut moneam: at quotquot se ipsos odisse & deprimere amaverunt, de hisce non modo semper consenserunt, sed & ea pro fundamentis fidei & spei suæ non dubitaverunt assumere. Nam quis Deo fidat nisi sibi ipsi diffidat? & quis sibi diffidat, nisi fundi & principii sui impotentiam & corruptionem agnoscat? Porro quis se suasque animæ facultates, desiderium, intellectum & cæteras confidendas tradat Deo, nisi eum intimorum animo opitulatorem solum, adeoque necessarium, internarum sanationum effectorem agnoscat? Tertium autem assumserunt quidam alioqui Orthodoxi, eo inducti, quod libertatis idea vera carentes, timuerunt ne si in libertate hominis constituerent gratia potiri vel non, salvari vel non, sequeretur inde hominem salutis suæ causam esse, & divinæ gratiæ dominatorem: quod ut amoverent, ceu primæ atque secundæ veritati modo dictæ adversum, nec non amori proprio superbiæque hominis favens, docere maluerunt gratiam qua salvamur sic a Deo pendere, ut, cum contingat ea non omnes salvari, Deus eandem quoque neque dederit, neque voluerit dare omnibus; sed nonnullis tantum, quibus infallibiliter salvarentur: atque hoc e principio amoris Dei, (quo solam ejus gloriam intendebant,) ex odio autem amoris proprii atque superbiæ, (quo omnem gloriandi ansam homini præripere volebant,) defenderunt. Cæteri autem Orthodoxi in hanc non iverunt sententiam; sed quæ aliis difficultatem movebant, cum ipsi solvere sibi viderentur, ac præterea putarent Dei amorem magis promoveri, & homines inde potentius ad eum impelli, si docerentur gratiam divinam omnibus quidem offerri, at liberum esse cuivis eam admittere, aut secus; hanc doctrinam quoque amplexi sunt, non solum ante, sed & post Augustinum, uti videre est e testimoniis Patrum apud Vossium, & hodie in Ecclesiæ Romanæ maxima parte apparet. Ast qui superbiæ & amoris proprii causam agunt, non modo ex his principiis veritatum harum primam & alteram, Augustino cum primæva Ecclesia communes, impugnarunt; sed & in tertia voluerunt voluntque videri sensui quidem Augu-
units.tr: There are three things in Augustine that do not wholly please your palate: (1) the doctrine of our original corruption; (2) the doctrine of the necessity of divine grace working within; (3) the particularity of this grace, which is given to a few and not to others, and its irresistibility, or absolute and particular predestination. There is no need to report each of these more exactly here. That the first and second of these cannot but be hateful to self-love and pride, there is no need for me to point out. But all who have loved to hate and abase themselves have not only always agreed about these, but have not hesitated to take them as the foundations of their faith and hope. For who trusts in God unless he distrusts himself? And who distrusts himself unless he recognises the powerlessness and corruption of his own foundation and beginning? Further, who would commit himself and the faculties of his soul, his desire, his understanding and the rest, to God to be relied upon, unless he acknowledged God alone as the helper of his inmost soul, and therefore as the necessary author of inward healing? The third doctrine was adopted by some who were otherwise orthodox. They were led to it because, lacking a true idea of liberty, they feared that if they placed in man's freedom whether he obtained grace or not, and whether he was saved or not, it would follow that man was the cause of his own salvation and the master of divine grace. To avoid this, as being opposed to the first and second truths just mentioned, and also favouring the love of self and the pride of man, they preferred to teach that the grace by which we are saved depends on God in such a way that, since it happens that not all are saved, God has neither given nor willed to give it to all, but only to some, by whom they would be infallibly saved. They defended this from the principle of the love of God (by which they aimed at his glory alone), but from hatred of self-love and pride (by which they wished to snatch from man every occasion of boasting). The other orthodox did not go into this opinion. Rather, since they seemed to themselves to resolve the difficulties that troubled others, and also thought that the love of God would be advanced more and that men would be driven to it more powerfully if they were taught that divine grace is indeed offered to all, but that it is free for anyone to admit it or not, they embraced this doctrine too, not only before but also after Augustine, as can be seen from the testimonies of the Fathers collected by Vossius, and as appears today in the greater part of the Church of Rome. But those who make pride and self-love their cause have not only attacked, from these principles, the first and second of these truths, which are common to Augustine and the primitive Church; they have also wished, and still wish, to seem, in the third, to agree with the sense of Augustine, though opposed to him, and with the other orthodox. (a)

units.la: (a) Hist. Pelag. Lib. VII. part. 1. & 2. Augustini adversi, cum aliis vero orthodoxis consentientes: quod fallax solummodo larva est. Nam quid ad eos particularitas aut universalitas, resistibilitas aut irresistibilitas gratiæ Dei internæ, qua interiora nostra fanantur, vivificantur & regnantur; quando ipsi aliam gratiam superficiariam & fucatam cordibus superbis & corruptis, (universaliter & resistibiliter, an secus ipsi viderint,) incrustandam, substituunt & intelligunt? Sic itaque sententiam de Gratia Universali non sensu orthodoxo nec ex principiis orthodoxis defendunt. Nempe, non ex humilitate intima & ex solo studio divinæ gloriæ dicunt aut docent, Dei gratiam salutarem omnibus offerri, ut si velint eam non quidem causentur, sed sinant in se intrare, quo illa operationibus suis intimis eos illuminet, sanet, perficiat: verum ex superbia, quæ non vult reprobari, sed amari; & ex amore proprio, qui non vult damnari, sed salvari, docent, Deum omnes homines amare, eosque externis mediis salvare velle, quæ ipsi superbi suique ipsorum intimi amatores, sine sui odio, abnegatione, miseriæ agnitione, Dei intimo auxilio, optime adhibere possint, & ita de salute superbo amori suo danda sibi gratulari. Quæ sane gratiæ Pelagianæ Universalitas Augustiniana prædestinatione & gratia particulari multo est deterior: hæc enim cum fundamentis fidei ac spei adhuc stare potest, imo & in anima sancta inesse, quod alicubi (a) de Augustino ostendi: illa vero & fundamenta fidei modo dicta diruit; & Deus porro, si superbos
units.tr: (a) Hist. Pelag. Lib. VII. part. 1. & 2. This is merely a deceitful mask. For what does it matter to them whether the internal grace of God, by which our inward parts are healed, quickened and ruled, is particular or universal, resistible or irresistible, when they themselves substitute and understand another, superficial and painted grace, to be plastered over proud and corrupted hearts, whether universally and resistibly or otherwise, as they themselves see it? Thus they defend the doctrine of universal grace neither in an orthodox sense nor from orthodox principles. Certainly they do not say or teach, from inward humility and from the sole zeal for God's glory, that God's saving grace is offered to all, so that if they are willing, they may not indeed complain, but allow it to enter into them, that it may enlighten, heal and perfect them by its inward operations. Rather, they teach, out of pride, which does not want to be rejected but loved, and out of self-love, which does not want to be condemned but saved, that God loves all men and wishes to save them by external means, which proud men and inward lovers of themselves, without hatred of themselves, without self-denial, without the recognition of their misery and without the inward help of God, can very well use, and so rejoice that salvation is given to their proud self-love. Surely the Pelagian universality of grace is far worse than the Augustinian doctrine of predestination and particular grace. For the latter can still stand with the foundations of faith and hope, and can even exist in a holy soul, as I have shown elsewhere concerning Augustine. But the former destroys the foundations of faith just mentioned. And God, if he saved the proud and those held captive by self-love, would become (far be the blasphemy) a companion of the devils. That is worse than the Manichaeism which modern Pelagians object to Augustine. For the Manichaeans set up two opposed principles, good and evil, never to be reconciled; but these could be reconciled.

units.la: (a) Occon. VI. ch. 7. n. 15, 16. & Tom. VII. p. 277. perbos & philautia captos salvaret, Diabolorum (absit blasphemia) fieret socius, quod jam plus est quam, quem Augustino moderni objiciunt Pelagiani, Manichæismus: siquidem Manichæi principia opposita duo,boni & mali, nunquam concilianda statuebant; hic vero reconciliari possent. Quoniam autem Augustinus, cum Ecclesia Catholica in fundamentis de corruptione & gratia consentiens, dissentiebat tamen in tertio illo quodam minus præcipuo, Pelagiani autem, qui duo prima fundamenta concutiunt, in tertio cum prioribus plerisque aliis orthodoxis de universalitate gratiæ & libertate ad eamquoad speciem & denominationem solum consentiunt, non autem quoad rem, quæ in utrisque est diversissima; hi propter hanc speciem solam, fallacem & semiverbalem, fallacissime se cum Catholicis primis in omnibus componunt, & postea se Augustino opponentes in omnibus, Ecclesiam primitivam, cum qua se fallaciter composuerant, adducunt velut a suis partibus stantem contra Augustinum, quem, quia is se per doctrinam de corruptione hominis & gratia Dei, oppositum superbiæ Pelagianæ & amori proprio, horribiliter propterea insectantur & traducunt, quo deeo aperte, deque omni puriore ante eum Christianismo implicite vindictam sumant in persona Augustini, eum idcirco confuse & omnis generis artibus invisum omnibus reddere allaborantes. Atque nisi post generale & nativum corruptæ naturæ contra veritatem odium, de quo supra, hasce ejusdem odii tui in Augustinum speciales causas in te agnoscas., orandus est Deus interiora tua tibi ut aperiat; in libellis enim tuis, iis praesertim quos in Simonium (a) scripsisti, quae modo dixi omnia se plus satis talia produnt: quae non ex charitate veritatis, sed ex affectibus & odio irrisorio testentur se emanare.
units.tr: (a) Oecon. VI. ch. 7. n. 15, 16. & Tom. VII. p. 277. Since Augustine, agreeing with the Catholic Church on the foundations concerning corruption and grace, nevertheless dissented in that third, less principal point, while the Pelagians, who shake the first two foundations, agree with most other orthodox writers on the third, namely the universality of grace and freedom towards it, but only in appearance and name, and not in substance, which is utterly different in each: these men, because of this appearance alone, which is deceptive and half verbal, most deceitfully unite themselves with the early Catholics in everything. Afterwards, opposing Augustine in everything, they bring forward the primitive Church, with which they had deceitfully allied themselves, as if it stood on their side against Augustine. Him, because by his doctrine of the corruption of man and the grace of God he stands opposed to Pelagian pride and self-love, they therefore assail and slander with horrible hatred. In this way they openly take vengeance, and implicitly against all purer Christianity before him, upon the person of Augustine, labouring to make him confusedly hateful to everyone by every kind of trick. Unless you recognise in yourself these special causes of your hatred of Augustine, in addition to the general and innate hatred of corrupt nature against the truth, of which I spoke above, God must be prayed to open your inner self to you. For in your little books, especially those you wrote against Simonius, all the things I have just mentioned reveal themselves more than enough, and they bear witness that they flow not from the charity of truth but from passions and mocking hatred.

units.la: Quod si enim ex charitate cum eo ageres, immensae quae in anima Praesulis sanctì erant, vel hostibus non renuentibus, virtutes, praesertim quae omne ferunt punctum, Dei proximique amor cum profundissima humilitate, tibi millies plus erant ubique laudandae, quam exprobrandus unus aut alter naevus nec voluntarius & ei incognitus: errata enim si quae sua cognoscebat, nedum retineret, aut excusaret vel defenderet, deplorare tolebat, & publico etiam stylo coram Deo & hominibus ea mentis sinceritate iisque modis confiteri, ut sentire possint qui audiunt, in sanctissima anima non fuisse dolum. Tu tamen ad haec non attendis, neque ad infinitas & salutares veritates a sancto Doctore ad promotionem Amoris Dei & virtutum Christi prolatas: sed aranearum mos videtur magis arrisisse, vel ex floribus venena legentium. Locos aliquot conjectas communes, ut pieratem Veterum in suspicionem adducas quasi aliter scripserint, aliter vixerint: sed quae cum S. Augustino, cujus vitae bona & mala omnia ab amicis & inimicis, imo & a se ipso (omnium sibi maxime inimico) diffusa & publicata sunt, prorsus non quadrant: dein ubi aliquod sphalma tibi in eo deprehendisse videris, nedum eo moderamine agas quo in Grotio aut Hammondo tuo, similia interdum annotas, ut ne quidem, velut propriæ infirmitatis conscius, modum illius hypocritæ in Euangelio, monentis fratrem modeste de festuca cum trabs ei oculum premeret, in tuis castigationibus obserues : sed veluti oblitus mandati Dei, quo parentes, hoc est, & Seniores etiam, & canos capillos, & qui in Ecclesia Dei cæteris in Christo instituendis præfuerunt, atque jam in pace cum Deo requiescunt, honorare tenemur, æmulusque facinoris Chami, qui venerandi patris nuditatem cæteris irridendam enunciabat, {unde ipse cum posteris maledictus est,} soles modo sanctorum Patrum nuditatem (si quæ forte est) toti mundo cum sarcasmis annunciare & publicare; sed & eam sæpe quæ non est, effingere, & quoisvis ad eam videndam provocare, ad quam cum ventum est, eam (si fieri possit) tegendi gratia, nulla appareat, sed potius contrarium.
units.tr: If you had dealt with him in charity, the immense virtues that were in the soul of that holy Prelate, which even his enemies did not deny, especially the love of God and neighbour, which carry every point, together with the deepest humility, were everywhere to be praised a thousand times over, far more than the one or two blemishes you reproach him with, which were neither voluntary nor known to him. For if he knew of any errors of his own, he not only did not retain them, excuse them or defend them, but was accustomed to lament them, and to confess them publicly, before God and men, with such sincerity of mind, and in such ways, that those who heard him could perceive there was no deceit in that most holy soul. Yet you pay no heed to these things, nor to the endless and salutary truths that the holy Doctor set forth to promote the love of God and the virtues of Christ. Instead you seem to have preferred the habit of spiders, drawing poison from flowers. You pick out a few commonplaces so as to bring the piety of the Ancients into suspicion, as if they wrote one way and lived another. But these do not in the least fit Saint Augustine, whose good and bad deeds alike have been spread abroad and published by friends and enemies, and indeed by himself, who was the greatest enemy of himself. Then, when you think you have detected some slip in him, you do not act with the moderation you show towards your Grotius or Hammond, where you note similar things now and then. Nor do you, conscious of your own weakness, observe in your rebukes the restraint of that hypocrite in the Gospel who, when a beam was in his own eye, gently warned his brother about a speck in his. Rather, as if you had forgotten the command of God, by which we are bound to honour parents, that is, also elders, grey hairs, and those who presided in the Church of God over others being instructed in Christ and who now rest in peace with God, you, a rival in the crime of Ham, who announced to others for their mockery the nakedness of a venerable father, {for which he himself and his posterity were cursed,} are wont to proclaim and publish with sarcasm to the whole world the nakedness of the holy Fathers (if there is any), and often to fabricate one that does not exist, and to summon everyone to see it. When they come to look, there is none to be seen (or, if one could manage it, it is covered over), but rather the opposite.

units.la: Exempli gratia, nemo est eorum qui legerit quæ de Augustino scripsisti in libro ad marginem (a) designato, a pag. 366 ad 371, qui non putet S. Augustinum ea fuisse mentis crudelitate & inhumanitate, ut crediderit & docuerit licitum esse orthodoxis hæreticos aut errantes cogere ad ea quæ sunt contra lumen conscientiæ (uæ circa OPINIONES quas fovent; idque per vim, & quidem eos vel morte assiciendos dum creduntur esse in statu damnationis, ut quemadmodum videtur, horribilis quædam voluptas ex damnatione iis procurata, capiatur. Nisi hanc Augustini ideam ex textu tuo, qui lon-
units.tr: For example, no one who has read what you wrote about Augustine in the book marked in the margin (a), from page 366 to 371, fails to think that Saint Augustine was of such cruelty and inhumanity of mind that he believed and taught it lawful for the orthodox to compel heretics or those in error to do what is against the light of their conscience regarding the opinions they hold, and to do so by force, indeed to put them to death while they are believed to be in a state of damnation, so that, as it seems, a certain horrible pleasure is derived from the damnation procured for them. Unless any reader, whoever he may be, forms this idea of Augustine from your text, which is lon-

units.la: (a) Defen- des len- timens des Theol. de Holl.
units.tr: (a) Defence of the sentiments of the Dutch theologians.

units.la: p. 369. 370. longiųr est & artificiosior, lectores quicunque efforment,eorum cuivis in me judicio subscribam. Ipsemet conceptis verbis ais, ejus doctrina sequi, potentiorem quemque jus habere persequendi alios, & prout quisque de suis OPINIONIBUS persuasus est, creditque alios errare; ita in conscientia tenebitur eos persequi. Appellas item ejus doctrinam (a) abominandam. Ais, Subtilissimum omnium Patrum tranquilla mente promulgasse omnium doctrinarum, de quibus unquam inter homines auditum quidem fit, inhumanissimam; & talem (in fine epist. tuae) agendi morem ei tribuis, ut tibi ipse quasi succenseas, quod de eo non-minori cum reverentia fis locutus. Eousque igitur tua in illum procedit malevolentia, ut per te non stet, quin tanquam immanem, sanguinariam & Diabolica malitia repletam animam totus mundus Augustinum horrescat & abominetur.
units.tr: pp. 369, 370. ger and more elaborate, I will subscribe to whatever judgment of me any of them may make. You yourself say in plain words that his doctrine implies that each man, the more powerful he is, has the right to persecute others, and that, as each is persuaded of his own opinions and believes others to be in error, so in conscience he will be bound to persecute them. You also call his doctrine (a) abominable. You say that the most subtle of all the Fathers, with a calm mind, promulgated a doctrine of all the doctrines of which men have ever heard, the most inhuman; and at the end of your letter you attribute to him such a manner of acting that you seem almost angry with him, because I have spoken of him with no less reverence. So far, then, does your malevolence towards him go, that it is only by you that the whole world does not shudder at and abhor Augustine as a savage, bloodthirsty soul, full of diabolical malice.

units.la: Atqui haec nec in mente nec in scriptis Sanctissimi viri exstare, neque ex eis consequi, sed meras esse in illum invectivas, calumnias & impostauras, advertere potest quisquis eas, quas ex Epistola quadam ejus ad Vincentium allegasti, lacinias legens, observabit lecta tota ejus Epistola, aliisque ejusdem argumenti, omnia quae ille de certis quibusdam subjectis & materiis dixit, te ad diversa prorsus subjecta detorquere, quae (arte tua) substituis illis de quibus apud Augustinum erat quaestio. Nam apud illum cum Donatistis agentem, neutiquam agebatur de rebus (b) fidei sive de articulis qui concernerent
units.tr: Yet anyone who reads the passages you have picked out from a certain letter of his to Vincent, and who reads the whole of that letter and his other writings on the same subject, can see that these things are neither in the mind nor in the writings of that most holy man, nor do they follow from them. They are mere invectives, calumnies and impostures. He will observe that everything Augustine said about certain subjects and matters you have, by your art, twisted to quite different subjects, substituting these for those of which Augustine was treating. For in dealing there with the Donatists, he was in no way dealing with matters of (b) faith, or with articles that concern

units.la: (c) B. 367 ... pellas item ejus doctrinam.
units.tr: (c) p. 367 ... you call his doctrine also.

units.la: (b) Vide quae cita. rent credenda ad salutem, neque igitur, ut quis adeaullo modo, multo minus mortis supplicio, cogeretur credenda. Sedibi quæstio est de præstanda externa obedientia Superioribus in rebus disciplinæ, deque conservanda pace, circa rem facti & personalem a judicibus legitimis, quos ipsæ partes (Donatistæ) petierant, imo & a summa potestate decisam & iussam. Ad quam obedientiam a Potestatibus refractarios potuisse cogi, idque etiam pœnis, si pertinacem rebellionem sceleribus & homicidiis & furiosis cædibus & sævitia defendant, nemo, nisi sceleris propugnator, negare audebit. Atqui sic res se habebat cum Donatistis, de quibus Augustinus. Non erat Secta de rebus fidei disceptans, & a Catholicis circa has dissentiens; sed erat turba nefarie rebellantium in suos Præfectos, quibus quoad externa subjici recusabant. Episcopo, Superiori suo legitime electo, debitam in externa disciplina obedientiam negant, eum rejiciunt, alium seditiose constituunt, postulant judicesque quorum se subjiciant sententiæ; renuunt sententiæ subjici: alios bis & ter postulant quorum fietur decisioni: decisionem Judicum toties rejiciunt: Cæsarem appellant, ejusque sententiæ quæ ad pacem tantum & obedientiam externam erat, non autem ut creditos ullos articulos immutarent, nuntium mittunt: insurgunt odio in omnes totius orbis cœtus, & inobedientiæ superaddunt tumultus, seditiones, furores quoslibet, persecutiones, homicidia & cædes, etiam Episcoporum & Presbyterorum, incendia aliaque tragica & horrenda
units.tr: (b) See the passages cited. things to be believed for salvation, and so he did not hold, in any way, much less with the punishment of death, that anyone should be compelled to believe. Rather, the question there concerns the rendering of external obedience to superiors in matters of discipline, and the keeping of peace, in a matter of fact and a personal one, decided and ordered by lawful judges, whom the parties themselves (the Donatists) had asked for, and indeed by the supreme power. That refractory persons could be compelled by the authorities to this obedience, and even by penalties, if they defend a stubborn rebellion by crimes, murders, frenzied slaughter and savagery, no one will dare to deny except a champion of crime. Yet such was the situation with the Donatists, of whom Augustine writes. This was not a sect disputing about matters of faith and dissenting from the Catholics on these; it was a mob of wickedly rebellious men against their own rulers, to whom they refused to submit in external matters. They deny the due obedience in external discipline to their bishop, their lawful superior, reject him, and seditiously set up another; they demand judges to whose sentence they will submit, then refuse to submit to the sentence; they ask for others twice and three times, to whose decision they will defer; again and again they reject the decision of the judges; they appeal to Caesar and send a messenger to him, whose sentence concerned only peace and external obedience and not the altering of any articles of belief. They rise up in hatred against all the assemblies of the whole world, and to their disobedience they add tumults, seditions, frenzies of every kind, persecutions, murders and slaughters, even of bishops and elders, arson, and other tragic and horrible deeds.

units.la: renda. A quibus ſ qui eorum resipiscere & ad obedientiam redire volebant, ipsi & domus eorum funditus a sociis suis evertebantur: adeo sese ad pacem & frugem nolebant redigi, & vero tum se ipsos, tum Ecclesiam totam suis furoribus & persecutionibus perturbabant. Hic tandem inter Catholicos Episcopos quæsitum est, Num adversus immanes istos perturbatores imploranda essent Imperialia Edicta ut ad ordinem ipsi compellerentur? Augustinus, qua erat indolis mansuetudine, negabat aliis hic mediis utendum quam monitis & patientia adversus illos: cæteri Episcopi censebant Christianorum Imperatorum leges atque auctoritatem esse interpellandas: & hoc factum est. Interveniunt ergo, imo præveniunt, quæ immanem inobedientiam & rebellionem coërceant Imperiales leges, non de capite; sed quæ bona solum aut quorundam exilium respiciunt: non quæ cogant immutare fidem, sed quæ jubeant, rebellioni valedicerent, & in concordiam cum illis redirent, quibuscum jam antea una fides. Hæ leges effectum optatum, redactionem in concordiam, in omnibus fere sortiuntur. Id ex eventu probat Augustinus, & mutat priorem suam sententiam, qua antea opinabatur, refractarios istos non nisi verbis Pastorum, non autem jussis & pœnis Potestatum ad ordinem & obedientiam externam compelli posse. Quid hic Augustino possit vitio verti? Quid huic sententiæ cum illa immani, quam ei imponis, intercedit, nisi forte quædam voces, s dum quandoque schismaticos & refractarios dicit hæreticos, & obedientiam æquitatemque, veritatem vel forte fidem, unde res fidei cum rebus disciplinæ ab incautis forte confundi possent, ) cum subjecta & cautæ nec non & efsecta sint diversissima ? Et revera nullum ex omnibus Patribus eligere posses, cui minus illa de immanitate crudelitateque mentis & doctrinæ impingi posset accusatio: præcæteris enim omnibus relucet in eo scriptisque ejus singularis omnino Spiritus Christi mansuetudo & cordis humilitas incomparabilis. Quin eousque Sanctus Vir abhorruit ab infligendis pœnis atque a sanguine fundendo, ut etsi Donatistæ ob cædes commissas ejusmodi pœnis se obnoxios reddiderant, eum tamen Intercessorem potentissimum habuerint, nedum videndus sit gravissus morte aut damnatione pereuntium, juxta inanem suspicionem tuam. Ecce quæ ad Proconsulem Africæ Donatum scribit: (a) Permescimus..... ne tu pro immanitate facinorum, at non potius pro lenitatis Christianæ consideratione, censeas [malum a Donatistis Ecclesiæ illatum] coercendum: quod te per JESUM CHRISTUM ne facias, obsecramus. Neque enim vindictam de inimicis hac in terra requirimus, aut vero ad eas angustias animi nos debent coarctare quæ patimur, ut oblivisca mur quid nobis præceperit pro cujus veritate ac nomine patimur, qui diligimus inimicos nostros, & oramus pro eis. Unde ex occasione terribilium Judicum ac legum, ne in æterni judicii pœnas incidant, corrigi eos cupimus, non necari; nec disciplinam circa eos neglegi volumus, nec supplicis quibus digni sunt exerceri. Sic igiigitur eorum peccata compesce, ut sint quos pœnitet peccasse. Quæsumus igitur ut cum Ecclesiæ causam audis, quamlibet nefariis injuriis appetitam vel affectam esse cognoveris, potestatem occidendi te habere oblivisceris, & petitionem nostram non obliviscaris. Non tibi vile sit neque contemptibile, fili honorabiliter dilectissime, quod vos rogamus ne occidantur pro quibus rogamus Dominum ut corrigantur, excepto etiam quod a perpetuo proposito recedere non debemus, vincendi in bono malum. Illud quoque Prudentia tua cogitet, quod caulas Ecclesiasticas insinuare vobis nemo, præter Ecclesiasticos curat. Proinde si occidendos in his sceleribus homines putaveritis, deterrebitis nos, ne per operam nostram ad vestrum judicium aliquid tale perveniat: quo comperto illi in nostram perniciem licentiore audacia grassabuntur, necessitate nobis impacta & indicta, ut etiam occidi ab eis eligamus, quam eos occidendos vestris judiciis ingeramus. Hanc admonitionem, petitionem, obsecrationem meam, ne, quæso, aspernanter accipias. Adde & locum de iisdem (Grotio (a) laudatum) ad Marcellinum Tribunum: (b) Mihi sollicitudo maxima incussa est ne forte sublimitas tua censeat eos tanta legum severitate plectendos, ut qualia fecerunt, talia patiantur. Idque hïs literis obtestor fidem tuam, quam habes in Christo, per ipsius Domini Christi misericordiam, ut hoc ne facias, nec fieri omnino permittas, &c. Tota legenda est ardentissima intercessionis Epistola: uti & illa ad Apringium Judicem tota, quæ sic concludit: Contende ergo bonitate cum multis. Illi scelere immani membra de vivo corpore avulserunt; (exoculaverant truculenter Catholicos nonnullos Donatistæ) tu opere misericordi effice ut illa quæ nefandis operibus exercebant, alicui utili operi eorum membra deservant. Illi non pepercerunt correctionem sibi prædicantibus Dei servis; tu parce comprehensis, parce duclis, parce convictis. Illi impio ferro fuderunt sanguinem Christianum; tu ab eorum sanguine etiam juridicum gladium prohibe propter Christum. Illi ministro Ecclesiæ occiso, extorserunt spatium vivendi; tu inimicis Ecclesiæ viventibus relaxa spatium pœnitendi. Talem te oportet esse in causa Ecclesiæ Judicem Christianum, petentibus, monentibus, intercedentibus nobis, &c. Infinita ejusmodi allegari possent, nisi hæc sufficerent ad animam mitissimam gloriosamque famam Sanctissimi Viri a crudeli calumnia ci impositu vindicandam. Cui magis obnoxius esset Erasmus (nulli tamen unquam de crudelitate suspectus) quando illas in Donatistas leges exsequendas, mitiores censuit esse ac per erat; habuerque secum consentientem, cujus indulgentior animus ad ipsas quoque Sagas pessima clementia extenditur, (a) Wierum. Sed inquis, Lactantius david Augustinus leges capitales in sacrificia Paganorum. Iterum status quæstionis immutatur. An laudavit Augustinus leges quasdam jubentes ut Pagani occiderentur propter opiniones suas, etiam eas de sacrificiis, nisi sensa sua vellent immutare aliaque & amplecti & testari contra lumen conscientiæ? Nequaquam: sed laudatas fuisse ab omnibus ait leges vetantes sub pœna capitali externa exercitia sacrificiorum paganorum, in Erasmi. in quibus quippe infinita inerant, quæ contra jus dictamenque ipsum naturæ, bonos mores civilemque etiam societatem pugnabant, ut mirum sit, nisi Satanas hominum oculos occæcasset, hæc ab ullis potuisse unquam tolerari. Litabatur Diis, in quibus omnium spurcitiei vitiorumque moribus honestis adversantium exempla prostabant & laudabantur. litabatur fœdis & horrendis cæremoniis, & humano quoque sanguine, nec lortilegia maleficiaque aberant omnis generis: quæ cum ab ipsis etiam ethnicis capitali lege prohiberi debuissent, cur non a Christiana Poreftate, quando rerum potiebatur, & lux veritatis omnia detexerat, potuissent EXTERNÆ ILLÆ & morum corruptrices ACTIONES prohibeii ad deterrendos ab ejusmodi tetris factis animos? non enim ad exsecutionem, sed ad terrorem revocationemque a malo promulgatæ fuerant (ut sæpe solent) dictæ leges, quæ (quicquid de tuo in contrarium dicas) ab Augustino ejusque coævis non nisi eatenus (juxta principia sua modo visa) probabantur. Quod si & illud tibi displiceat, non mirum. Displicent enim & sacræ Literæ, quando aliquid declarant captui tuo adversans: & tunc tribuis corruptis affectibus effata eorum, qui divina ipsa exarunt, velut illud Ps. 37 : 9. ubi mirandum te, cum hoc reprehenderes, non magis idcirco tragice in Psalmem esse invectum quam in Augustinum: quem ubi serio odiosum uno in loco effigiare conatus es, alibi in ridiculum conaris convertere artibus illis tuis veritati & charitati contrariis: nempe, multa ei imponendo, ut jam aliquoties visum. 2. Iriii.onibus perpetuis; de quibus mox. 3. de minutiis altercando, cum praecipua & solida praeter mittuntur. 4. mox ipsi, mox ejus scriptus & sententiis, quin & Systematì ejus Religionis Christianæ, mox Platonicismi titulum asfluendo, mox muslicum, sive qui communio nub saberret, proclamando, aut allegoricum, cujus allegorias, quia rerum ipsi itualium amor carstratos ad divina animos non afficit, ideo frigidas dicis. Deinde miraris Pelagianos anteceffores aribus istis non Veriffe illum in ridiculum: nempe, non erant magni Criitici, tu vero magnus Criticus pro illis jam rem conficies: élt enim ars illa mimica admirabile talentum tuum, quo hactenus omnes & soles excipere, & exhibere deridendos consuevisti.
units.tr: ...horrendous deeds. Those among them who wished to come to their senses and return to obedience were themselves and their households utterly overthrown by their own companions. So much did they refuse to be brought back to peace and sobriety, and indeed they disturbed both themselves and the whole Church with their frenzies and persecutions. Here at last the Catholic bishops asked whether the imperial edicts should be invoked against these savage disturbers, so that they might be compelled to order. Augustine, by the gentleness of his disposition, maintained that no means other than admonition and patience should be used against them. The other bishops thought that the laws and authority of the Christian emperors ought to be called upon, and this was done. So imperial laws intervened, or rather went before, to restrain their monstrous disobedience and rebellion. These laws did not concern the head but only goods, or the exile of certain persons. They did not compel a change of faith; they ordered men to renounce rebellion and return to concord with those with whom they already shared one faith. These laws achieved the desired effect, the restoration of concord, in almost all cases. Augustine proves this from the outcome, and he changes his earlier opinion, by which he had thought that these refractory men could be brought to outward obedience only by the words of ministers, not by the commands and penalties of the magistrates. What can be found fault with in Augustine here? What does this view have in common with the monstrous one you impute to him, except perhaps certain expressions: when at times he calls schismatics and refractory persons heretics, and calls obedience and fairness truth or perhaps faith, so that matters of faith might perhaps be confused with matters of discipline by the unwary, although their subject matter and their effects are most unlike? And indeed you could choose from all the Fathers none against whom the accusation of savagery and cruelty of mind and doctrine could less be brought. For above all others there shines forth in him and in his writings the wholly singular gentleness of Christ's Spirit and his incomparable humility of heart. Indeed the holy man so shrank from inflicting penalties and shedding blood that, although the Donatists had made themselves liable to such penalties on account of the murders they had committed, they nonetheless had him as their most powerful intercessor. He is not to be seen as one who would have them perish by death or damnation, as your empty suspicion would have it. See what he writes to Donatus, proconsul of Africa: (a) We beseech... that you, not out of regard for the enormity of their crimes but rather out of regard for Christian gentleness, do not judge [the evil inflicted by the Donatists on the Church] to be restrained; this we beg you, by Jesus Christ, not to do. For we do not seek vengeance against our enemies in this land, nor should the straits of mind in which we suffer drive us to forget what he commanded us for whose truth and name we suffer: that we love our enemies and pray for them. Hence, on the occasion of terrible judges and laws, we wish them to be corrected, not killed; nor do we wish discipline toward them to be neglected, nor the punishments they deserve to be withheld. So restrain their sins that they may be those who repent of having sinned. We therefore ask that, when you hear the cause of the Church, however wickedly it may have been assailed or harmed, you forget that you have the power to kill, and do not forget our petition. Let it not be cheap or contemptible to you, most honourably beloved son, that we ask you not to kill those for whom we ask the Lord to make them amend; and besides, we must not abandon our settled purpose of overcoming evil with good. Let your prudence also consider that no one except the Church's own ministers concerns himself with the causes of the Church. Therefore, if you judge men guilty of such crimes to be put to death, you will deter us from bringing anything of the kind before your judgment through our efforts. Once they learned of this, they would rage against us with greater boldness to our ruin, and necessity would be laid upon us and imposed, so that we should choose to be killed by them rather than bring them to be put to death by your judgments. Do not, I beg you, receive this admonition, petition and entreaty of mine with scorn. Add also the passage on the same matter, praised by Grotius, addressed to the tribune Marcellinus: (b) I am struck with the greatest anxiety lest your loftiness should judge them to be punished with such severity of laws that they should suffer as they have done. And I entreat your faith, which you have in Christ, by the mercy of the Lord Christ himself, that you do not do this, nor allow it to be done at all, etc. The whole of that most ardent letter of intercession should be read; likewise the whole letter to the judge Apringius, which concludes thus: Contend therefore with many in goodness. Those men tore limbs from the living body with unspeakable cruelty (the Donatists had savagely gouged out the eyes of several Catholics). You, by a merciful work, bring it about that the limbs of those who practised unspeakable works serve some useful work. They did not spare the servants of God who preached correction to them; you spare those who are seized, spare those who are led away, spare those who are convicted. They poured out Christian blood with impious steel; you, for Christ's sake, keep the judicial sword also from their blood. When they killed a minister of the Church, they wrested from him the space of his life; to the enemies of the Church who are still living, grant space for repentance. Such a Christian judge ought you to be in the cause of the Church, we petitioning, admonishing and interceding, etc. Countless passages of this kind could be cited, were these not enough to vindicate the most gentle soul and glorious reputation of that most holy man from the cruel calumny imposed upon him. Erasmus would be more liable to it (though he was never suspected of cruelty) when he judged that the laws against the Donatists should be carried out more mildly than they were; and he had with him a man whose more indulgent spirit extended to the witches themselves a most wicked clemency, (a) Wierus. But you say that Lactantius, David and Augustine praised capital laws against the sacrifices of the pagans. Again the state of the question is changed. Did Augustine praise certain laws ordering that pagans be put to death for their opinions, even those concerning sacrifices, unless they wished to change their own convictions and embrace and profess others against the light of conscience? By no means. He says rather that all approved laws forbidding pagan sacrificial rites under capital penalty, which are in Erasmus's laws, in which indeed there were countless things that fought against law, the dictate of nature itself, good morals and even civil society, so that it would be a wonder, unless Satan had blinded men's eyes, that these could ever have been tolerated by anyone. They sacrificed to gods in whose morals the examples of every filthiness and of vices opposed to honest conduct stood forth and were praised. They sacrificed with foul and horrible ceremonies, and with human blood too, and there were no lots, sorceries or evil arts of every kind. Since these should have been prohibited by capital law even by the pagans themselves, why could not those external and corrupting ACTIONS be prohibited by the Christian power, when it held the reins of affairs and the light of truth had laid everything bare, in order to deter minds from such foul deeds? For the laws were promulgated, as is often the custom, not for execution but for terror and for calling men back from evil. And these laws (whatever you say to the contrary) were approved by Augustine and his contemporaries only so far as, according to their principles, they seemed fitting. But if that also displeases you, it is no wonder. For the sacred Scriptures too displease you when they declare something opposed to your understanding; and then you ascribe their sayings, which were written under divine inspiration, to the corrupt affections of those who wrote them, as in that verse of Psalm 37:9. Here you should wonder that, when you rebuke this, you have attacked the Psalm no less tragically than Augustine. Where you have tried to make him seem seriously hateful in one place, elsewhere you try to turn him into a figure of ridicule, by those arts of yours which are contrary to truth and charity: namely, by attributing many things to him, as has already been seen several times, 2. with perpetual inversions, of which more shortly; 3. by wrangling over trifles, while passing over the principal and solid matters; 4. by now calling him a Platonist, now mystical, now a proclaimer of the 'communion of ...', or allegorical, and because the love of spiritual things does not stir the minds of the carnal toward divine things, you call his allegories cold. Then you wonder that the Pelagian predecessors did not deride him with these tricks; namely, they were not great critics, but you, a great critic, will now bring the matter to completion on their behalf, for that mimic art is your admirable talent, by which you have hitherto been accustomed to receive all and sundry, and to exhibit them to be mocked.

units.la: Et Augustinum quidem nullo negotio ita tractaveris, si praeterieris silentio scriptorum ejus scopum & substantiam nil aliud spirare quam honorem Christi, pietatem, timorem Domini, poenitentiam, Dei amorem, humilitatem, sanctitatem, divinioresque omnes virtutes; colligas autem hinc inde minuscula quaedam accidentaria, de quibus is, te (a) citante, fatetur, in illa [salva fide qua Christiani sumus, aut ignorari quod verum fit, & sententiam definiitiam suspendi; aut aliter quam est, humana & infirma suspicione comici: quod multum abest ab arrogantia, qua dicis eum ista veluti oracula proferre. Interim propter illas minutulas erratiunculas, e quibus nihilominus bonos reverentiæ & pietatis erga Deum hominesque motus excitare cogitat, quia ta-men
units.tr: And you could treat Augustine in this way with no trouble at all, if you passed over in silence that the aim and substance of his writings breathe nothing but the honour of Christ, piety, the fear of the Lord, repentance, love of God, humility, holiness, and all the more divine virtues; instead you gather here and there certain small incidental points, about which he confesses, as you cite him, (a) in that matter [while keeping the faith by which we are Christians, either the truth is to be regarded as unknown and the final judgment suspended; or else one conjectures otherwise than it is, with a human and weak suspicion]. This is far from the arrogance with which you say he delivers these things as oracles. Meanwhile, on account of those tiny little errors, from which he nevertheless thinks to stir up good movements of reverence and piety towards God and men, because yet

units.la: (a) Sen-timens ... p. 44. men illæ cum morosæ critices tuæ vana atque futili de corticibus exactitudine non concordabunt, ideo illum ludibrio eorum, quos ad virtutes divinas movet, gesties exponere, simili omnino pietate, acsi in familia numerosa ex præcipuis liberis nonnullus aliis præsectus, relictum a Patre ad stabiliendam firmandamque obedientiam & reverentiam in Patrem, fraternamque inter sese concordiam, librum fratribus prælegeret ea mente, & eis modis, ut inde Patris amantes, reverentes, morigeri, unanimes fierent; surgeret vero ex illis protervus quidam irrisor, qui susque deque habita sincera & laudabili illius mente, discursuumque substantia & scopo, eum ludibrio fratrum, quantum in se esset, exponeret, ob dicta quædam exilia, critice minus exacta; eumque, quam visilla ipsa nullius periculi erratula ad voluntatis paternæ amorem & exsecutionem reduceret, pro pessimo tamen Paternæ voluntatis librique interprete traduceret: quod de Augustino eadem revera mentis æquitate fecisti. Ingens vero malum, ex occasione omnium rerum, etiam critice minus exactarum, occasionem sumere bonas cogitationes & pios motus excitandi, homine sque ad frugem virtutesque reducendi! Quem non pudeat istius insultorie carpendi rationis? Sit aliquid in discursus materia minus quoad circumstantias exactum & convenientes, quid tum postea? Animi sinceritas, scopique sanctitas, & bona loquentis voluntas, omnia in aurum amoris Dei & proximi convertunt: possemque ostendere quosvis sanctifsanctissimos, etiam e sacris Auctoribus, etiam Deum ipsum, ejusmodi materialiter minus accurata admisisse, & eis usos esse ad homines in sanctum ordinem reducendos. Si cujus esset scopus, laudeculas in exactitudine critica venari ex recensione multarum vanissimarum quisquiliarum (qualibus Bibliotheca tua superbit) quibus lectorum prurientem curiositatem perfricare vellet, & tamen ibi hallucinationes deprehenderentur; aut si etiam istiusmodi nugae orbi veluti observationes, aut quaestiones sacrae plenis libris ad vanum hunc scopum proponerentur, tunc forte ibi, maxime ob vanitatem gloriolae sic quaesitae, ridendi posset quaeri materia. At longe notissimum est Augustini scopum non esse ex curiosis quaestiunculis c. ptaie laudes, a quibus humillimus ejus animus plane abhorrebat: neque excitare aut titillare hominum inanem cupiditatem critica accuratione; sed unius Dei gloriam tantum & amorem eum intendisse, excitando in animis hominum ex quavis occasione motus sanctos, quibus ad Deum laudandum, venerandum, amandum elevarentur, & ad se ipsos humiliandos deprimerentur.
units.tr: (a) Sentiments ... p. 44. But since those trifling errors do not agree with the vain and frivolous exactness of your fussy criticism about the husks, you are eager to expose them to the ridicule of those whom he moves toward divine virtues. You do this with exactly the same kind of piety as if, in a large family, one of the older sons, placed in charge of the others, were reading to his brothers a book left by the father to establish and confirm obedience and reverence toward the father and harmony among the brothers, with the intent that through it they would become loving, reverent, obedient, and united toward the father. Suppose some insolent mocker stood up among them who, disregarding the sincere and praiseworthy intention of the author and the substance and purpose of his discourses, exposed him to the derision of the brothers as far as he could, on account of certain slight expressions that were less exact in their critical form; and suppose he then condemned him as the worst interpreter of the father's will and of the book, though those same trifling slips would bring the reader back to love and carrying out the father's will. You have done exactly the same with Augustine, with the same lack of fairness. What a great evil it is, to take the occasion from any matter, even one less exact in critical terms, to refuse to stir up good thoughts and pious feelings, and to lead people back to uprightness and virtue! Who is not ashamed of this insulting manner of finding fault? Suppose there is something in the matter of a discourse less exact and suitable as to its circumstances: so what? The sincerity of the mind, the holiness of the purpose, and the good will of the speaker turn everything into the gold of love for God and neighbour. I could show that the most holy men, even from among the sacred authors, even God himself, have admitted such things that were materially less accurate, and have used them to lead people back into holy order. If someone's aim were to hunt for praise for critical exactness, by reviewing a great many most empty trifles (of which your library is proud), with which he wished to satisfy the itching curiosity of readers, and yet mistakes were found there; or if such trifles were offered to the world as observations or sacred questions in full volumes for this empty aim, then perhaps there might be matter for laughter, chiefly because of the vanity of the little glory so sought. But it is very well known that Augustine's aim was not to catch praise by curious little questions, from which his most humble spirit plainly shrank, nor to excite or tickle people's empty desire for critical accuracy; rather, he aimed only at the glory and love of the one God, stirring up in the minds of men, on any occasion, holy emotions by which they might be raised to praise, revere, and love God, and be brought low to humble themselves.

units.la: Atque adeo in scribendo, vel ad populum verba faciendo, constat ejus scopum non suisse auditoribus lectoribusve suis explicare Scripturas critice, dictionario modo; neque etiam simpliciter historico & externo, ut eos inde redderet criticos aut historicos; sed potius eo, qui est Scripturarum principium, scopus & materia, qui est amor Dei & proximi, qui veros Christianos efficiat & confervet. Quod exsequitur Vir sanctus poffeffione principii, scopi, materiæ, Spirituque Scripturarum bono instructus, hoc est, Spiritu (quo pollebat) precum, amoris divini, pœnitentiæ magnæ, charitatis ardentis, humilitatisque incomparabilis, quæ clavis atque dispositiones sunt quibus Pater suis aperit Scripturarum sensa & arcana: Tu tamen non veneris eum ut ridiculum, ut ineptum, ut peffimum Scripturarum interpretem traducere, quique nullis ad interpretandum mediis requifitis instructus fit, idque ais ad operum ejus aperturam fere quamvis constare. Ego vero quovis pignore certavero, etsi forte interpretationibus illius quibusdam aliquid critice & accessorie minus accuratum infit, non deesse tamen vel uni e millibus substantialem Scripturarum sensum & scopum; inter tuas vero ne quidem unicam esse in qua mens Dei sensusque Scripturarum salutaris inveniatur; quin potius iisdem (etsi aliquid cortici & accidenti Scripturarum externe conveniens potueris grammatice proferre) mentem Dei penitus deleri atque impugnari. Quod qua ratione fiat, facile judicabit quisquis ea quæ de interpretationis & criticesmateria in libris superioribus, nec non in ... Quam legitime judicandi viam fi semel inierint co dati lectores, condiscantque hoc modo solidam veritatem a fucata dignoscere salfitate, tunc de iniriforia Critica actum est, nec poterit non recidere irrisio in irridentium capita, præsertim quando animadvertetur (quod a pluribus jam factum est) nil indecentius atque turpius a recentioribus quibusdam vixdum barbatis & aliunde satis male suspectis fieri posse quam si nulla pudoris conscientia publice vel coram juvenili lascivia propudiose exagitent & ludibrio exponant senio, meritis, sanctitate, gratiæ donis, auctoritateque non contemnenda conspicuos; qui dum viverent, perspicacissimis quibusque & sanctissimis, eos prax & usu noscentibus, fuerant commendabiles; rum & universæ posteritati a multis retro seculis quam maxime venerabiles; quique humili mente, sanctum Dei amorem sincere spirante & intendente, divinas sic tractabant Scripturas, ut inde Dei Opt. Max. laus & gloria hominumque sanctimonia crescerent & promoverentur. Tales quippe nec objectum sunt neque materia irrisionis, quæ non tantum erga ejusmodi venerandas animas detestanda est, sed & quæ per se sola, maxime ubi in consuetudinem abiit, pessimi animi nota & character esse solet. Procedit namque habitualis irrisio ab impietate, superbia, invidia, odio, vindicta, crudelitate, malitia & hypocrisi, quæ animæ dispositiones coram Deo sunt omnium maxime abominabiles. Impietas patet, quando irrisor ob nullius utilitatis nugas non dubitat in ludibrium vertere eos & ea quæ infucato corde ad laudum amorisque Dei, nec non ad pietatis motus excitandos dicta sunt & faciunt. Superbia irrisionis mater est, quando animus philautia captus, & eorum quæ possidet admirator, cætera aliorum omnia contemtim despicatui habet; & vero invidiose timens aut videns suis præferri aliena, id eorum irrisione impedire conatur, parum considerans, ridiculæ esse apud omnes superbiæ & invidiæ, sese ob caeas nullius utilitatis solidæ futilitates grammaticas, criticas, historicas, præ aliis quibus solida sæpe & sancta intunt, magni facere & admirari, eosque propter hæc propudiofo insultationis modo infra se dejicere: quo ipso ostendit quoque irrisor animam suam non dignam proximis debita, sed odio erga eos animari, de quibus ut vindicta sumat, non tantum curat ut falsis suis dicteriis, tanquam aculeatis sagittis, corda eorum quos impetit amare vulnerentur, ipsique sentiant se ab irrisore contemni & pro stultis reputari, sed & ut crudelius, & majore cum lasorum dolore id efficiat, eos modos adhibet, quibus læsi videant amorem erga se & exiltimationem in aliis quoque extingui, non tantum sine commiseratione, (quam aliqui omnibus jactuam facientibus non denegatulus; sed & cum gaudio lætisque cachinnis. Quis autem est qui non malit a declarato hoste aperto campo impugnari, quam tecto hoc modo proditoriæ pacis & tranquillitatis specie pungi & consodi? priori enim modo, se non plane pro nihilo contemni videt, & æqua datur omnibus consentientibus sese defendendi causa: posteriori vero sentit duntaxat sui contemtum, & fere absurdus aliis apparet si inde commotus de injuria facta conqueratur, aut de defensione cogitet. Quod lædendi genus, telum esse inter omnia amarissimum, sciunt ipsi qui eo utuntur. Unde eorum malitia non parva ea in re se prodit, quando praesertim irrisor absurda, quorum ipse artifex est, de suo commminiscens, dexteritate sua effectum iri considerat ut non ipse, sed alii quibus ea affricat, quique eo nomine false irridebantur, eorum auctores habeantur; idque artificium suum in se cum maligno gaudio intuetur & miratur: Ubi interim anima ejus justiti r,moderationis & honestatis hypocriticam larvam & titulum coram hominibus servat & obtinet, quando non crassis affectuum motibus, non incompositis verborum modis; sed delicata & circumspecta sermonis aculeati dexteritate, speciem encomii interdum, vel apologiae pro inimico, aut saltem historicae narrationis aemulante, nec non mente frigida, venenata sua dicteria dispensat. Et sic tunc quidem, ut Pharisaei olim, gaudet ab hominibus pro honesto, modesto, passionumque justo moderatore haberi; spernitque & irridet eos qui zelo vel affectu conciti, iratos motus aut convicia apertiora (quorum ipsemet causa est) proferunt: ut coram Deo vitiis impietatis, superbiae, odii, vindictae, crudelitatis, malitiae & hypocriseos scatens, quibusvis apertis & crassis peccatoribus abominabilior & inferior habetur & postponitur. Quae omnia, Domine, si necdum in te sint dudum radicata, aut ea non videas, rogo Deum ut tibi ita vivide horrida, uti sunt, agnoscenda impium imat, ut inde vel revoceris vel praepediaris a eo praecipitio, in quod te caeteroquin procliviorem esse testantur omnia fe-re re scripta tua, præsertim quæ iu alios exarafti, aut in quibus de iis loqueris qui tecum non sentiunt. Sunt enim cuncta illa tua scripta tectis irrisionibus sic referta, ut, dum qui inter lectores tuos minus emunctæ sunt naris nil subesse putant, cæteri sagaciores inde sentiant in se excitari, quæ in nobis omnibus a corruptione naturæ intus latent malignitatis illius irrisoriæ adversus quosvis principia,ita ut & vix possint abstinere quin naso suspendant adunco tum & ipsos irrisos, tum & lectores omnes qui maligna ista spicula pro simplicitate sua non animadvertunt. Equidem interdum falsibus & jocis innocuis uti in eis quæ vel parvi vel nullius sunt momenti, aut etiam quæ vana vel mala non magna sunt, nil prohibet, quando id charitatem in cordibus proximorum non lædit nec diminuit, aut cum male agentes, aliquo pudore incusso, a malis suis sic revocari possunt: quin læta veritas lætioribus interdum temperamentis ad hoc non invita utitur. Etiam proborum hac in re lapsus unus aut alter ex infirmitate excusari potest. At id in rebus & de rebus divinis, id erga sinceras mentes ut a cæteris infamentur, id habitualiter exercere, tametsi torvus irrisori & pallidus renidet in fronte Saturnus, Christiani nullius neque viri probi character esse debet. Honesti clarissimique viri (a) qui Criticos tuæ præxtenfam accusationem veramque de divinis temeritatem, gustum subtilem criticum, rationes criticas, risui & commiserationi exposuerunt, quique (uti nuperrime celeberrimus
units.tr: Indeed, in writing or in preaching to the people, it is plain that his aim was not to explain the Scriptures to his hearers or readers critically, in the manner of a dictionary, nor simply in a historical and external way, so as to make them critics or historians. His aim was rather that which is the principle, aim and substance of the Scriptures, namely the love of God and of neighbour, which makes and preserves true Christians. The holy man carried this out, being endowed with the possession of the principle, aim, substance and good spirit of the Scriptures, that is, with the Spirit (in which he excelled), of prayer, of divine love, of great repentance, of burning charity and of incomparable humility. These are the keys and dispositions by which the Father opens the meanings and secrets of the Scriptures to his own. Yet you should not bring him forward as a ridiculous, foolish, and most wretched interpreter of Scripture, one who is equipped with no required means for interpreting, and who, you say, is nearly unfit to open his works. For my part I would contend with any pledge that, although some of his interpretations may perhaps be less accurate critically and incidentally, the substantial sense and aim of the Scriptures is not lacking in even one of thousands, whereas in yours there is not even a single one in which the mind of God and the saving sense of Scripture is found. Rather, in them (though you may have set out grammatically some matter fitting the bark and accidents of Scripture externally) the mind of God is utterly blotted out and assailed. Whoever reads what has been said about the matter of interpretation and criticism in the earlier books, will easily judge by what reason this comes about. If once such readers have entered upon this lawful way of judging, and have learned in this manner to distinguish solid truth from counterfeit falsehood, then criticism will be finished, and mockery will necessarily recoil upon the heads of the mockers ... especially when it is observed (as has already been done by many) that nothing more indecent and disgraceful can be done by certain recent men, scarcely bearded and otherwise rather badly suspected, than when, with no sense of shame, they publicly, or in the presence of youthful wantonness, shamelessly harass and expose to ridicule those in old age, of merit, holiness, gifts of grace and not contemptible authority, who while they lived were commended by the most penetrating and most holy men, who knew them by experience and practice, and who have been most highly venerated by all posterity for many centuries past; men who, with humble mind, sincerely breathing and intending the holy love of God, so handled the divine Scriptures that from them the praise and glory of God, the best and greatest, and the holiness of men grew and were advanced. Such men are indeed neither the object nor the matter of mockery, which is not only to be detested towards such venerable souls, but which, even by itself alone, is especially, when it has become a habit, wont to be a mark and character of a most wicked mind. For habitual mockery proceeds from impiety, pride, envy, hatred, revenge, cruelty, malice and hypocrisy, which dispositions of the soul are most of all abominable before God. Impiety is plain when the mocker does not hesitate, for trifles of no use, to turn into derision those things which were said and done with an unfeigned heart to stir up praise and love of God, and also the motions of piety. Pride is the mother of mockery, when a mind, seized by self-love and admiring what it possesses, holds all other things of others in contempt; and when, envying and fearing that others are preferred to itself, it tries to hinder this by ridicule, little considering that to everyone pride and envy are ridiculous, and that to make much of and admire one's own grammatical, critical and historical futilities, which are of no solid use, above others in which solid and holy matters are often contained, and to cast those others down beneath oneself by a shameless manner of insult, is itself to show that the mocker does not have a soul worthy of the duties owed to neighbours. Rather, his soul is animated by hatred towards those whom he mocks. In order to take revenge on them, he is not only careful that the hearts of those he attacks should be wounded with love by his false gibes, as with barbed arrows, and that they themselves should feel that they are despised by the mocker and reckoned as fools; but also, so that he may do this more cruelly, and with greater pain to those he has injured, he uses those means by which the injured see love towards themselves and their reputation among others also being extinguished, not only without pity (which some do not deny to all who suffer loss), but even with joy and cheerful laughter. Who indeed would not prefer to be attacked openly by a declared enemy on a clear field, rather than be stung and pierced in this covert manner, under the pretext of a betrayal of peace and tranquillity? For in the former way one sees that one is not altogether held for nothing, and the same opportunity of defending oneself is given to all who consent; but in the latter one feels only one's own contempt, and one appears almost absurd to others if, moved by it, one complains of the injury done, or thinks of defence. This kind of harm, the most bitter of all weapons, is known to those who use it. Hence their malice reveals itself in no small measure in this matter, especially when the mocker, inventing absurdities of his own, considers that by his cleverness the effect will be that not he himself but others to whom he attaches them will be held as their authors, and who were falsely ridiculed on that account; and he looks upon and admires his own artifice with malignant joy. Meanwhile his soul keeps and maintains the hypocritical mask and title of justice, moderation and honesty before men, when he dispenses his poisonous gibes not with coarse movements of the passions or with disordered forms of speech, but with the delicate and cautious skill of a biting discourse, with a semblance sometimes of praise, or of an apology for an enemy, or at least imitating a historical narration, and with a cold mind. And so, like the Pharisees of old, he then rejoices to be held by men as honest, modest, and a just moderator of the passions; and he scorns and mocks those who, stirred up by zeal or feeling, utter angry complaints or more open reproaches (of which he himself is the cause). Thus, teeming before God with the vices of impiety, pride, hatred, revenge, cruelty, malice and hypocrisy, he is held more abominable and inferior, and is put behind, even the most open and gross sinners. All these things, Sir, if they are not yet deeply rooted in you, or if you do not see them, I pray God that he may make you recognise them as frightfully as they are, so that you may either be called back from, or be hindered from, that precipice into which, as nearly all your writings testify, you are otherwise rather inclined to fall; especially those which you have written against others, or in which you speak of those who do not agree with you. For all those writings of yours are so filled with veiled mockery that, while those among your readers whose nostrils are less refined think there is nothing underneath, others who are keener perceive from them that there are stirred up in themselves those things which lie hidden within us all from the corruption of nature, that malignant spirit of mockery against any principles whatever. So much so that they can hardly refrain from turning up their hooked noses both at those who are mocked and at all readers who, because of their simplicity, do not notice those malignant darts. Indeed, I do not forbid, at times, the use of jests and harmless witticisms on matters of little or no importance, or on things that are vain or of small evil, when this does not wound or diminish charity in the hearts of neighbours, or when evildoers, by some shame being struck into them, can thus be called back from their evils; and joyful truth sometimes makes use of more cheerful tempers for this purpose, not unwillingly. Even a slip of one or another of the upright in this matter may be excused on account of weakness. But to do this in matters and about matters of God, to do it to sincere minds so that they may be defamed by others, to practise it habitually, even though the grim Saturn smiles pale on the forehead of the mocker, ought not to be the character of any Christian, nor of any upright man. The honourable and most distinguished men (a) who have exposed to laughter and pity your far-reaching accusation of the Critics and your true rashness concerning divine things, your subtle taste for criticism and your critical reasons, and who (as very recently that most famous man ...
