units.la: {a}(a) Theologus Ultrajectinus, ) dum & Criticam tuam & scripta opinionibus, (b) Arriani-smo, Pelagianismo, Libertinismoque faventibus passim contaminata declarabant, ob interspe-ras absurditates riserunt aliquoties,obiter tantum id, plerique etiam prius a te provocati, fecerunt. Unus P. Simon perpetuos quos de eo prior fecisti publice ludos, eadem mensura redditurus, te arte illa, sed apertius & vehementius, sic exercuit, ut campum ei deinceps debueris relinquere. An multos habituros sit imitatores nescio. De irrisione res se habet veluti de homicidio aut de alia injuria: eam in aliquem inceptare nemini licet; licita tamen videtur ejus in auctorem retorsio, modo nimia vindicta, caeteraque recensita vitia, non subrepant cum illa, quod in hac naturae nostrae corruptione evitare difficillimum est, ne dicam, impossibile.
units.tr: {a}(a) The Utrecht theologian, while declaring both your Critica and the writings everywhere tainted with favour toward Arianism, Pelagianism and Libertinism, laughed at them a few times on account of certain scattered absurdities, though only in passing, and most of them did so after being provoked by you first. Only P. Simon, in return for the perpetual public jests you made earlier about him, paid you back in the same measure, and handled you with that same art, but more openly and more vehemently, so that you ought henceforth to have left him the field. I do not know how many imitators he will have. Ridicule stands in the same case as murder or any other injury: no one may begin it against another; yet it seems lawful to turn it back upon its author, provided that excessive revenge and the other vices already listed do not creep in with it, which in this corruption of our nature is very hard to avoid, if not impossible.

units.la: §. 9. Plura esse in ejus scriptis & propositis irri- denda & carpenda, quam qua in aliis carpsit & irrisit: sed cptan- dum alia methodo, & Christia- nis digna errores dedoceri.
units.tr: §. 9. There are more things in his writings and propositions to be ridiculed and criticised than those he criticised and ridiculed in others; but it must be attacked by another method, and errors must be unlearned in a way worthy of Christians.

units.la: Quapropter si qui eorum quos his modis pupugilti, vel quibus displicet Sanctos a te deridiculo publice exponi, in te etiam calamum dirigant, sive ut tela tua retorqueant,
units.tr: Therefore, if any of those whom you have pricked in these ways, or whom it displeases that the Saints are publicly held up to ridicule by you, should turn their pens against you as well, either to hurl your own weapons back at you,

units.la: sive ut propria tua tibi ostendant absurda, non crediderim eorum quenquam artis istius illaudatæ methodum electurum, etsi non desit forte in tuis scriptis magna carpendi & irridendi materia: non soluth quia multis aliunde imitatis infinitis minutiis, rebusque vanis & indifferentibus, in quibus joci innocentius exerceri possunt, superabundant; sed etiam quod non desit in illis inter multas hallucinationes ridiculum illud errati genus quod contradictionem appellant. Ego sane, plurimane in particularium materiarum numerofitate tangam, cum semel oculo currente proposita tua quædam intuerer, tria aut quatuor præcipua esse animadverti quibus inest contradictio. Primum, cui alia subordinantur, est Pelagianismum & Socinianismum cum Christianismo conciliare. Alterum, Metaphysicam limitare & restræuare. Tertium, Augustinum cum Patribus in ridiculum vertere. Quartum, Criticam & humaniora studia velut nobis valde digna, & ad res fascras tantum non necessaria, commendaie. Per primum vis indifferens esse Christiano ad salutem, utrum habeat obiectum aliquod, puta Filium Dei & Spiritum sanctum, primo summo fidei, spei, & salutis suæ fundamento, dilectionisque & adorationis summæ objecto; an vero id obiectum habeat pro creatura, fidei, spei salutisque non-fundamento, nec dilectionis adorationisque summæ objecto. Præterea indifferens esse Christiano, aut vero vivoque corporis Christi membro, utrum de Spiritu capitis & corporis, ejusque vita. motibus, operationibusque internis in se partici{a}pet, an vero eo Spiritu ejusque internis operationibus in se (quod hodierni Pelagiani volunt) careat, nec eis opus habeat? Hoc est, indifferens esse membro vivo, a capite & Spiritu corporis animari, aut eis carere? Indifferens esse vivo principia vitæ habere vel non habere, atque adeo vivere vel mortuum esse. Quæ manifeste contradictoria sunt. In altero, quo vis Metaphysicam non tollere sed reformare, inter multa & obscura & perturbata, ubi revera sine lumine huc illuc a te oberratur, nec non cognitiones fidei, Metaphysices, sensuumque inter se confunduntur, ais : (a) Metaphysices dodrantem tolli posse..... si cognitiones Metaphysicæ limitentur ad ea quibus ad sperat am felicitatem perduci possumus. item (b) Deum mensuram cognitionum nostrarum, metaphysicarum mensurasse prout illis opus habemus ad salutem sive ad finem propter quem nos creavit. Atqui omnes consentiunt, nec tu diffiteberis, cognitiones Metaphysicas, qua Metaphysicæ sunt, non esse ad salutem necessarias: Quid enim de vulgo tunc fieret? Ais paulo post (c) quicquid necessarium est, id ita clarum esse, ut omnes homines id sciant: atque adeo metaphysicos quando nos hac de re voluerunt aliquid docere, nil novi nos docuisse, aut saltem quod sit essentiale. Ubi per priora vis concedere Metaphysicam, per hæc ultima vero eam tollis totam. Quæ iterum sibi contradicunt. In tertio non minus etiam tibi contradicis. Agnoscis aliquibi (d) Scriptores sacros 15 & 16. styli adeo incuriosos fuisse, ut quovis momento inveniantur in eorum scriptis obscuritates quæ omnibus grammaticis regulis nequeant dissolvi..... grammaticam, criticamque nil facere nisi propositum sciatur Auctoris. Doces (a) & sine eis simpliciores, bona fide intelleƈtu utentes, omne id quod ad salutem necessarium est, quodque fide in Deum, & obedientia erga ejus mandata absolvitur, e Scripturis percipere posse. Augustinus autem procul dubio erit tibi saltem vel e simplicioribus qui etiam hoc essentiale & necessarium ex Scriptura possint recte capere. Scis vero ejus scopum esse populo instruendo, cui præficiebatur, nec non iis quibus scribebat, interpretari Scripturas quatenus illi inde in essentialibus & necessariis, in fide erga Deum, mandatorumque ejus observantia recte formandi, aut fovendi & nutriendi erant; non vero ut docti critici fierent: & tamen contra eum, Sanctosque Patres similes, sæpissime clamas, quasi pro suscepti muneris sui ratione, pessimi ineptissimiqueessent Scripturarum interpretes, ob imperitiam scilicet rei grammaticæ & criticæ, quarum minutiarum inobservantiam, ipsis tamen Scriptoribus sacris, te teste, tritissimam, Augustino aliisque Patribus rationis loco exprobras; tametsi illi insuper Spiritus divini illuminationem, qua Scriptoris sacri propositum & mens sciri possunt, necessariam esse, & sibi interdum contigisse præ te, agnoscant. Quæ nemo non videt contradiƈtionibus abundare: haud secus ac quando, quarto, commendas nescio cio quot humanas & profanas artes & literas & lectiones & crises & historias, vanaque alia studia sexcenta, quibus & serio & totus occupetur animus, tametsi id contradicat tum naturae illi nostrae, qua ad aeterna, non autem ad evanida iştiusmodi nugamenta facti sumus; tum experientiae, qua videmus eos qui bullis istis tument & tenuiculo Criticae supelleclilis apparatu abundè sunt instructi, a veritatis solidae sanctitatisque verae fonte uno, Spiritu Dei Sancto, ejusque possessione vel spe & desiderio, caeteris esse remotiores; contradicatque semel, & recte, istis naeniis ipse Liberius deSanctoAmore inEpistolis suis Theologicis, inquiens (a) Imperfectio est ea scire quae inutilia sunt; & tempus ponere in iis scientiis discendis quae nos nec sanctiores nec beatiores reddunt. O quam multi hac lege pro scopo habent, ut studeant fieri quotidie imperfectiores, idque aliis etiam miserè commendent! Non jam pluribus ostendam quam contradictorie cum Scripturis agatur quando hae ex ejusmodi artibus censentur exponendae: dicam tamen, tuto asseverari posse, Bibliorum Sacrorum interpretatio aut explicatio siqua exspectanda esset ab homine critico simili apparatu atque methodo tecum instructo, nos pro Scripturis divinis ejusmodi cadaver literale habituros, quod non tantum careret Spiritu, sed & ei adversaretur, & eum in nobis impugnaret, nosque letali afficeret contagio & indolentia. Indolentia quidem, si (quod sanguineis lacrymis deplorandum esset) quaecunque immensa Dei
units.tr: or else they show you your own absurdities. I do not think any of them would choose the method of this disreputable art, although your writings perhaps do not lack great material for carping and mocking. That is not only because they abound in countless trivialities borrowed from many others, and in empty and indifferent matters in which jokes can be played more harmlessly; it is also because, among many hallucinations, there is not lacking that ridiculous kind of error which they call contradiction. Indeed, although I could touch on very many particular points, when I glanced quickly over some of your writings I noticed three or four chief places where contradiction is found. The first, to which the others are subordinate, is reconciling Pelagianism and Socinianism with Christianity. The second is limiting and restricting Metaphysics. The third is turning Augustine and the Fathers into ridicule. The fourth is commending criticism and the humane studies as very worthy of us and almost not necessary for sacred things. By the first you want it to be a matter of indifference to the Christian for salvation whether he has an object, say the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, as the first and highest foundation of his faith, hope and salvation and the highest object of love and adoration; or whether he should have that object as a creature, which is not the foundation of faith, hope and salvation, nor the highest object of love and adoration. Furthermore, you want it to be a matter of indifference to the Christian, as a living member of the living body of Christ, whether he shares in the Spirit of the head and body and in the motions, operations and inner works of that life, or whether he lacks that Spirit and its inner operations (as the present-day Pelagians want) and has no need of them. That is, you want it to be a matter of indifference whether a living member is animated by the head and the Spirit of the body or lacks them. You want it to be a matter of indifference whether a living thing has or does not have the principles of life, and so whether it lives or is dead. These things are plainly contradictory. In the second, where you wish not to abolish Metaphysics but to reform it, you wander here and there without light amid many obscure and confused matters, and the knowledge of faith, of Metaphysics and of the senses are confused with one another. You say: (a) Metaphysics can be reduced by three quarters... if metaphysical knowledge is limited to those things by which we can be brought to a hoped-for happiness. Likewise: (b) God has measured the measure of our knowledge, metaphysical knowledge included, in accordance with what we need for salvation, or for the end for which he created us. Yet all agree, and you will not deny, that metaphysical knowledge, insofar as it is metaphysical, is not necessary for salvation. For what would then become of the common people? Shortly afterwards you say: (c) whatever is necessary is so clear that all men know it; and therefore, when the metaphysicians wished to teach us something on this matter, they taught us nothing new, or at least nothing that is essential. Here, by the former statements you grant Metaphysics, but by these last you take it away entirely. These contradict each other. In the third, you contradict yourself no less. You acknowledge somewhere that (d) the sacred writers (15 & 16) had a style so careless that at any moment obscurities are found in their writings which cannot be resolved by any rules of grammar... grammar and criticism accomplish nothing unless the author's purpose is known. You teach that even without them the simpler folk, using good faith in understanding, can perceive from the Scriptures everything that is necessary for salvation, and that is accomplished by faith in God and obedience to his commandments. But Augustine, without doubt, will be to you at least one of the simpler folk who could rightly grasp from Scripture even this essential and necessary matter. And you know that his aim was to instruct the people over whom he was set, and those to whom he wrote, in interpreting the Scriptures insofar as they had to be rightly formed, or nourished and fostered, from them in essentials and necessities, in faith toward God and observance of his commandments; not that they should become learned critics. And yet you cry out against him and the holy Fathers, very often, as if, according to the nature of their office, they were the worst and most unskilled interpreters of Scripture, on account of their ignorance of grammar and criticism. You reproach them, instead of an argument, for not observing these minutiae, which you yourself say is a very common fault even in the sacred writers; although they acknowledge, besides, that the illumination of the divine Spirit is necessary to know the purpose and mind of the sacred writer, and that this has sometimes happened to them, which you do not. Who does not see that these are full of contradictions? Just as when, in the fourth place, you commend I know not how many human and profane arts and letters, readings, critiques, histories and six hundred other vain studies, by which the mind is occupied seriously and wholly, although this contradicts both that nature of ours, for which we were made for eternal things and not for such fleeting trifles, and experience, by which we see that those who swell with these bubbles and are richly equipped with the thin apparatus of criticism are further removed than others from the one source of solid truth and true holiness, the Holy Spirit of God, and from possessing him, or from hope and desire for him. And Liberius de Sancto Amore, in his theological letters, contradicts these trifles once, and rightly, saying: (a) It is imperfection to know things which are useless; and to spend time in learning those sciences which make us neither holier nor happier. O how many, by this rule, make it their aim to become more imperfect every day, and commend this even to others with wretched results! I will not now show at length how contradictorily one deals with the Scriptures when these are judged to be explained by such arts. I will say, however, that it can safely be asserted that if any interpretation or explanation of the Holy Bible were to be expected from a critic equipped with the same apparatus and method as you, we would have in place of the divine Scriptures a literal corpse, which not only lacks the Spirit but is opposed to him, attacks him in us, and afflicts us with deadly contagion and indifference. Indifference indeed, if (which would have to be lamented with bloody tears) whatever immense charity of God has devised, to stir up men of these last, and so of our own, times from deadly lethargy, through the predictions which exist everywhere in the prophetic writings concerning the dreadful judgments of God, the plagues, defeats, scourges and the universal and horrible destruction of men, and which alone remain as a motive by which minds, now utterly dead, might be roused to desire eternity, were to be abolished by unhappy criticism together with the admirable promises of the divine gifts, which it teaches are all equally past and now therefore nothing, so that minds may not awaken to amendment and repentance by the movements of fear and hope.

units.la: (a) Lib. P. 125 charitas excogitavit ad homines ultimorum, nostrorumque adeo, temporum a mortali veterno excitandos, per prædictiones quæ de tremendis Dei judiciis, de plagis, cladibus, flagellis excidioque hominum universali & horrendo passim in Scriptis propheticis exstant, quæque unica supersunt motivo quibus mentes ad æternitatis desideria nunc prorsus mortuæ excitari possint, infelix Critica aboleat juxta cum admirabilibus divinorum donorum promissis, quæ omnia jam dudum pariter præterita, nuncque adeo nulla esse, inculcet, ne timoris speique motibus mentes ad frugem & resipiscentiam evigilent: Contagione vero, cum quæcunque in Scripturis consideranda essent ut typi rerum potiorum, atque adeo ultra cortices ad Spiritualem animarum statum internasque Dei in illis operationes trahenda, modis ita brute, ita carnaliter, ita pulverulenter literalibus & criticis solum venirent interpretanda, ut omnis divinus verusque inde rejiciendus esset scopus & sensus: Sic ut Scripturis veroque eorum Interpretis officio non possit contradici periculosius, quam iliusmodi earum translationibus aut commentariis, quorum errores effectusque malos ut in omnium mentibus velit reddere irritos, imo & eos affusis gratiæ suæ divinæ donis præverte-re Deus Opt. Max. serio rogandus est.
units.tr: (a) Lib. P. 125 Contagion indeed, since all things to be considered in the Scriptures as types of greater things, and so to be drawn beyond the bark to the spiritual state of souls and to God's inner operations in them, would come to be interpreted only in such a brutish, carnal, dusty, literal and critical way that every divine and true aim and sense would have to be rejected from them. So the Scriptures and the office of their interpreter cannot be contradicted more dangerously than by such translations or commentaries of them; and God Most Good and Most Great must seriously be asked that he would prevent the errors and evil effects of these from being rendered void in the minds of all, and even anticipate them by pouring out the gifts of his grace.

units.la: Hæc & similia sphalmata, nec non & quæcunque alia unusquisque committere potest, melius amica & placida mente oftenduntur & dedocentur, quam illusoria & inimica. Optimè autem omnium, omnia errata atque mala quivis apud se ipsum dediscere poterit, si modo vel aliorum monitis, vel propriæ conscientiæ instinctu, ad interiora sua se recipiat, illicque imploret animarum, intelligentiæ, lucisque veræ forem unum, benedictum Dei adorandi Spiritum, cujus lumina, dona, gratiarum effusio, operationes millies sanctis Dei verbis promissæ sunt, pro illis maxime temporibus, quibus abundabunt aliunde tenebræ, iniquitates, errores, impietas, quæ tempora & ultima, & nostra esse, vel saltem tam propinqua ut nil propinquius, dubitari non potest. Cavendum solum ne ex numero eorum simus, vel ab eis seducì nos patiamur, quos Apostolus cautelæ gratia præsignificavit, quando dixit, (a) Venient in novissimis diebus in deceptione illusores, juxta proprias concupiscentias ambulantes, & dicentes ubi est promissio aut adventus ejus? Juxta proprias concupiscentias ambulant, quotquot nolunt unquam de divinis mysteriis rebusque ad- dittere, credere, sperare, nisi id quod ... um intellectui, palato corrupto, captu ... ne naturali arridet & sapit: illusores sunt promissionum Domini, qui Spiritus ejus Sancti præsentiam, gratiam, operationes vitales & intimas, donaque illuminationum & virtutum omnigena, ex incredulitate irridentur exspectanda, etsi sanctissimè ore omnipotentis & falsi nescii Dei promissa sint; illusores sunt adventus Domini, qui non exspectant venturum eum qui do-ceat. ceat, renovet, regatque omnia per effusinem Spiritus sui in omnem carnem effundedi; cœlosque novos & novam terram, quibus habitet justitia, formaturi: quanc tunc cum rerum omnium corruptione veteres derisores ipsos vindice igne exterminatur est. Et tunc (a) memento nostri, Domine, in bene placito populi tui: visita nos in salutari tuo ad videndum bona electorum tuorum, ad lætandum in lætitia gentis tuæ, & laudandi cum hereditate tua. Vivificet Dominus animas nostras in spe gratiæ & salutis suæ, deque ut divini luminis sui auxilio interiora nostra excutiamus serio, (b) ne forte fit in aliquo nostrum cor malum incredulitatis, discedendi a Deo vivo, & ut non obduretur quis nobis fallacia peccati, simulque ex illis qui increduli fuerunt, & non potuerunt introire requiem illius propter incredulitatem. Hoc nobis omnibus tibique speciatim, Domine, indulgeat Deus, ex sincero animi fundo Eum adoro, nec non ut efficiat, ut quæcumque hactenus dixi, tibi non alió dicta videantur quam ad solidum bonum tuum; non aliud in te efficiant, quam ut obstacula moveantur; quibus impeditur inter omnes divinæ veritatis, gratiæ, gloriæque communicatio & permeatio, quo illis remoti (c) & (c) depositá omni malitia, & omni dolo, que simulatione, cum livore & rixis, sutibusque omnibus nostris studiis & partim humanis, sicut infantes modo geniti desiderate lac illud sapientiæ divinæ intelle-ctu & humanis mixturis non fraudatum, ut in-cref. crescamus, gustantes, quam benignus & liberalis sit Dominus, ad quem accedentes tanquam ad lapidem vivum & fundamentum Sapientiae & Eruditionis nostrae verae, Deo, etsi ab hominibus rejectum, electum tamen & pretiosum, Ei ut lapides vivi divina politi atque eruditi manu, superaedificemur ut domus spiritualis, in qua habitet aeternum adorandus Patris Christique Spiritus. Hoc ubi tibi mecum pluribusque aliis acciderit, agemus gratias Omnipotenti animarum Eruditori & Reparatori, cujus in amdein laetabimur perpetuo: neque porro amplius de divinis actis loquentur, spero, testimonia laturus es, quam quae cum veritate, aequitate & charitate concordaverint. Sin minus (quod absit) istis te conformare recusaveris, & simili, qua prius, procedere malis methodo; faxim & ego ut secundum Methodi meae procedam regulas, quarum una est, ut mihi proponam aliorum, maxime eorum qui secum & cum coeteris faciliter, dolose & minus sincere agunt, non immutare animum; sed potius eos neque curare, & sibi ipsis totos permittere. Manebunt ergo illi per me agentque & loquentur aut scribent, quantum quidem voluerint in dolosso suo & illusorio elemento, cujus si vel in Bibliothecae continuatione vel alio quovis modo nova specimina contra me iterum edident, sufficiet pro omni responsione memoria loci annexi, juxta cujus tenorem cogitabit, quisquis lector nolet decipi, eorum verbis fidem non facile adhibendam esse quamdiu
units.tr: These and similar slips, and whatever other errors anyone may commit, are better pointed out and unlearned in a friendly and calm spirit than in a mocking and hostile one. Best of all, anyone can unlearn all errors and evils for himself, provided that, whether prompted by the admonitions of others or by the impulse of his own conscience, he withdraws into his inner self and there implores the Spirit of God, to be adored and blessed, who is the one door of souls, of understanding and of the true light. His lights, gifts, the outpouring of his graces and his workings have been promised a thousand times in the holy words of God, especially for those times when darkness, iniquities, errors and impiety will abound on every side. There can be no doubt that these are the last times, and ours, or at least so near that nothing could be nearer. We must only take care that we are not among those, or allow ourselves to be seduced by those, whom the Apostle foretold as a warning when he said: (a) "In the last days there will come scoffers in mockery, walking according to their own lusts, and saying, Where is the promise or the coming of him?" Those walk according to their own lusts who are unwilling ever to believe, hope for or accept divine mysteries and the things pertaining to them, except what pleases and tastes good to their natural understanding, their corrupt palate and their limited capacity. They are scoffers of the promises of the Lord, who from unbelief mock the expected presence of his Holy Spirit, his grace, his living and inward workings, and the gifts of illumination and of every kind of virtue, although these promises were made most holy by the mouth of the almighty and true God. They are scoffers of the coming of the Lord, who do not look for him who is to teach, renew and rule all things by pouring out his Spirit upon all flesh, and who is to form new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness will dwell; when the old scoffers themselves, together with the corruption of all things, will then be destroyed by avenging fire. And then (a) "Remember us, O Lord, in the favour you have toward your people; visit us with your salvation, that we may see the good of your chosen, that we may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, and glory with your inheritance." May the Lord quicken our souls in the hope of his grace and salvation, and grant that, with the help of his divine light, we seriously search our inner selves, (b) "lest perhaps there be in any of us an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God; and lest anyone be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin; and lest, like those who were unbelieving and could not enter into his rest because of unbelief." May God grant this to all of us, and to you in particular, Lord; I adore him from the sincere depth of my soul; and may he bring it about that whatever I have said so far may seem to you to have been said for no other purpose than your solid good; may it accomplish nothing in you but the removal of the obstacles which hinder the communication and permeation among all of us of divine truth, grace and glory; so that, set free from them, (c) "putting away all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisy, and envy, and all evil speaking, as newborn babes desire the sincere milk of the word, that you may grow thereby, if you have tasted that the Lord is gracious; to whom coming, as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen and precious with God, you also, as living stones, are built up a spiritual house," in which the Father and Christ's Spirit, to be adored for ever, may dwell. When this happens to you and to many others with me, we will give thanks to the Almighty, the Instructor and Restorer of souls, in whom we shall rejoice forever. Nor, I hope, will you bring forward any further testimonies concerning divine matters that do not agree with truth, fairness and charity. But if you refuse to conform yourself to these, and prefer to proceed by the same method as before, then I too, for my part, will proceed according to the rules of my own method. One of these is that I resolve not to change my mind about those who act deceitfully, easily and insincerely toward themselves and others; rather, I do not care about them and leave them entirely to themselves. So they will remain as they are, and will act, speak or write as much as they wish within their own deceitful and illusory element. If they publish new specimens against me again, whether in a continuation of the Bibliotheca or in any other way, the memory of the place annexed will suffice as the whole reply, and by its tenor any reader who does not wish to be deceived will consider that their words are not to be readily trusted, for as long as they proceed from a mind not changed for the better. Farewell.

units.la: EN verité c'est une chose tres fâcheuse, qu'il faille si fort se defier des traducteurs, & des citations, & qu'il se trouve si peu de foy dans la Republique des lettres, qu'il faille traiter les Auteurs comme on fait ceux que l'on a convaincu une fois de parjure, à moins qu'on ne veuille s'exposer à être trompé à tous momens. Il les faut examiner rigoureusement, & conferer incessamment les originaux avec leurs traductions & leurs Extraits, si l'on ne veut tomber dans l'erreur sur la foy de ces Messieurs. Vous avez oüi parler sans doute d'un fameux Chicaneur, nommé Oüir-dire, qui tenoit Ecole de Temoignerie, d'où sont sortis un si grand nombre de faux temoins. Mais, Monsieur, ces gens-là n'y entendoient rien en comparaison d'une infinité d'Autheurs qui disent à tous momens, qu'un tel, ou qu'un tel a dit des choses à quoi il n'a jamais pensé, en faisant des protestations solemnelles qu'ils ne disent que la verité toute pure.
units.tr: In truth it is a very vexing thing that one must distrust translators and citations so greatly, and that there is so little good faith in the Republic of Letters that authors must be treated like those once convicted of perjury, unless one wishes to expose oneself to being deceived at every moment. One must examine them rigorously and constantly compare the originals with their translations and extracts, if one does not want to fall into error on the word of these gentlemen. You have no doubt heard of a famous pettifogger named Oüir-dire, who kept a school of witness-making, from which came so great a number of false witnesses. But, Sir, those people understood nothing of it compared with an infinity of authors who say at every moment that such and such a man has said things he never thought of, while making solemn protestations that they tell nothing but the pure truth.
